## Volume Front Matter

### Series Title Page

**THE COMPLETE COURSE OF PATROLOGY, OR UNIVERSAL LIBRARY**, entire, uniform, convenient, economical, of all the Holy Fathers, Doctors, and ecclesiastical Writers who flourished from the apostolic age to the times of Innocent III; a chronological reissue of all the monuments of Catholic tradition which have existed throughout the first twelve centuries of the Church, according to the most accurate editions, compared with one another and with certain manuscript codices, and corrected with the utmost diligence; continually elucidated with dissertations, commentaries, and variant readings; enlarged by the inclusion of all works discovered after the most extensive editions completed during the last three centuries; furnished with particular analytical indexes following individual volumes or authors of some importance; arranged with chapters properly set out within the text itself, and likewise with headings distinguishing the upper margin of each page and indicating the subject treated; expanded with works both doubtful and apocryphal, yet possessing some authority in relation to ecclesiastical tradition; enriched with two general indexes: one, namely, of subjects, by consulting which whatever each of the Fathers has written on any topic may be seen at a glance; the other, of Holy Scripture, from which the reader may readily ascertain which Fathers, and in what places in their works, have commented upon the several texts of the several books of Scripture. A most accurate edition, readily to be preferred to all others if the following be weighed: the clearness of the type, the quality of the paper, the integrity of the text, the thoroughness of the correction, both the variety and number of works reprinted, the very convenient format of the volumes and its consistently uniform character throughout the whole course of the work, the low price, and especially this single, methodical, chronological collection of six hundred fragments and small works hitherto scattered here and there, but now for the first time in our library brought together from works belonging to every age, place, language, and form.

**SECOND SERIES**, in which appear the Fathers, Doctors, and Writers of the Latin Church from Gregory the Great to Innocent III. Edited by J.-P. Migne, publisher of the Universal Clerical Library, or Complete Courses in the individual branches of ecclesiastical learning. The Patrology has been printed in two editions: one Latin, the other Greek-Latin.—The twelve hundred volumes of the Latin edition are sold for one thousand francs; the thirteen hundred Greek-Latin volumes for one thousand eight hundred.—The purely Latin edition embraces all authors, both Western and Eastern; the latter, however, are supplied in it only in Latin translation.

# [Complete Works of St. Bruno of Asti]

[Col. 0009]

## To His Royal Highness Charles Emmanuel, Prince of Piedmont, etc., etc.

### Bruno Bruni of the Piarist Fathers

[Col. 0009]

When, Your Royal Highness, I had completed, by the command, great authority, and beneficence of Pope Pius VI, a new edition of the works of St. Maximus, bishop of Turin, and had delivered it at Turin, by command of the same Supreme Pontiff, to the august King Victor Amadeus, your excellent father, adorned with his name, it was also my good fortune to obtain what I had long greatly desired: namely, to pay my respects to you in person and, by the command of that same Pontiff, most humbly to offer you the same works of St. Maximus. Then indeed, face to face, I admired those qualities which I had heard celebrated and extolled in the highest praise concerning you while absent: namely, your excellent disposition, keenness of intellect, singular graciousness, and nobility of spirit, by which you give assured hope that you will prove no unequal match for your forefathers, dukes and kings.

But still more did your wisdom draw me into obedience and admiration. For, having scarcely glanced through several homilies of St. Maximus, you immediately showed, as a most expert judge, how soundly and splendidly you judged of the elegance of his Latin style, the abundance of his learning, and the strength of his discourse. This admiration kindled in me the desire to prepare, according to my slender powers, something not unworthy of Your Royal Highness and bearing witness to my reverence for you. Nor did I need long to consider what I should choose, since I knew how highly your royal father had valued the pontifical gift—namely, the edition of the sermons and treatises of St. Maximus—by which the renown of his name, the glory of the Church of Turin, and the honour of the royal family had been strengthened and illustrated.

For a long time I had borne with regret that another light of the Church, born and formed in the region of Piedmont and commended by writers of the highest authority, should lie in a kind of oblivion and obscurity, because his writings had not been sought out with sufficient diligence and, having been committed to print with virtually no care, had fallen almost into contempt. This is St. Bruno of Asti, of the most noble family of Soleri, born in the middle of the eleventh century, bishop of Segni in Campania, and abbot of the distinguished monastery of Monte Cassino.

Bruno wrote most learned commentaries on several books of both Testaments, very many sermons upon the Gospels, and not a few treatises of ecclesiastical learning. Having thereby displayed splendid proofs of learning and wisdom, he was held in very high esteem by the Roman Pontiffs St. Gregory VII, Victor III, Urban II, and Paschal II, who entrusted to him most weighty duties. Having therefore compared the published works of St. Bruno with the best manuscripts of the same or a slightly later age, I realized that those works, undeservedly neglected until now, could be purged of scribal errors and corruptions, supplied where omissions occurred, and restored throughout to their original reading.

I discovered also that the greater part of the homilies, of which the holy bishop himself is most manifestly established as author, had, not without deceit, been attributed to a spurious Greek writer; and that several other books written by St. Bruno had been made public under another name. I therefore considered it worthwhile to expose such injurious thefts from the reputation of this holy bishop, vindicate his writings from usurpation, set against the old corrupt edition one more accurate and complete, and refute and repel the censures fabricated against him.

I plead the cause of a most learned and holy man. I shall think that I have truly proclaimed his merits toward the Christian commonwealth and the ornaments of his extensive learning when I declare that Bruno should with the fullest justice be compared to the most illustrious bishops of Piedmont. For these were men who, in sorrowful times, were the firmest safeguard of the suffering Church; who performed great and arduous deeds for God’s glory; who contended with unconquered spirit for Catholic doctrine. When I name Eusebius of Vercelli, who does not know that he is called the most powerful defender of the Nicene faith and the hammer of the Arians? If I add Valerian, bishop of Cimiez or Nice, the illustrious author of homilies in the middle of the fifth century; Maximus of Turin, a most eloquent preacher from the sacred pulpit; and likewise Turibius, bishop of Astorga, celebrated throughout Spain alike for holiness and learning, commended in letters by St. Leo the Great himself—I shall recall men most renowned in the ecclesiastical annals.

Later men emulated their glory and their services to the Church: Atto of Vercelli, second to none in commentaries on Holy Scripture, theological treatises, and addresses to the people; and Anselm, archbishop of Canterbury, the most unconquered defender of ecclesiastical rights in human memory and a most learned theologian. Come now: does not St. Bruno of Asti, bishop of the Signians, hold a most illustrious place among these, as the acts of his Life and his writings most clearly testify?

For he was sent as a labourer into the Lord’s vineyard in an age when the Berengarian heresy, the schism of Guibert of Ravenna, simony, corruption of the clergy, and usurpation of ecclesiastical rights were laying all sacred things waste. Therefore Bruno, while others shrank back and feared the audacity of that most cunning man, did not hesitate to contend with Berengar in a Roman council and to undertake a long and most vehement disputation concerning the most holy sacrament of the Eucharist. Its final result was that the man, previously most audacious and most stubborn in his error, suddenly changed his mind and condemned his errors.

[Col. 0011]

The most holy man crowned this very great victory with victory after victory. By his sermons and his writings, being bishop of Segni and divinely endowed with pastoral power, he assailed heretics, schismatics, and simoniacs, and suffered them nowhere to stand until they fled to the bosom of the Catholic Church, where they might learn the integrity of sacred doctrines, devote themselves to the love of peace and concord, and observe the laws.

When I recall these things, most excellent Prince, I seem to see your spirit exulting. Formed for every kind of religion and piety, you surely rejoice to hear that the Church has always been defended by the most holy and learned bishops born within your dominion; that errors have been banished; that the holy doctrines of Jesus Christ have been delivered to your peoples and propagated also into other regions. You rejoice, I say, because nothing more fortunate or more delightful can befall kings and princes than that Christian religion should flourish in their kingdom, that the deposit of faith should be preserved uninjured by depraved opinions, and that perfect concord between priesthood and kingship should remain firmly established.

Since I have learned, not without the greatest pleasure, that you hold these convictions and these wishes, and since your deeds appear directed wholly toward this one end, I have not hesitated to pour forth earnest entreaties to you: that you may graciously receive the works of St. Bruno collected by me, enlarged with unpublished writings, furnished with notes, and restored to their integrity, and permit them to be adorned with your name.

Yet I fear that my small capacity will not sufficiently answer to your dignity and wisdom. But it will belong to your magnanimity graciously to grant me the pardon for which I ask and to receive favourably this whatever-it-may-be testimony of my dutiful spirit. Meanwhile I pray and beseech Almighty God to preserve in safety for the longest time your royal father, yourself, and the whole royal family, for the glory of the Christian name, the happiness of your peoples, the protection of the Catholic Church, and the advancement of learning and the fine arts.

Given at Rome, from the Nazarene College of the Piarist Fathers, on the Kalends of August, in the year of the Lord 1789.

[Col. 0011]

# Prolegomena to the Works of St. Bruno of Asti

## First Prolegomenon

### Preface

[Col. 0011A]

Having completed, under the auspices, great authority, and beneficence of Pope Pius VI, the edition of the works of St. Maximus, bishop of Turin—a work applauded by all men of letters, who rendered abundant thanks to that most wise Pontiff for ordering the Church to be adorned with the learned monuments of so illustrious a bishop—the desire to comply with his excellent will and love for the honour of my native country impelled me to bring the published writings of another Piedmontese bishop into a more splendid light.

I knew indeed that St. Bruno of Asti, bishop of Segni in Campania, was the author of commentaries upon both Testaments and of very many treatises. But I deeply regretted that both his interpretations of Holy Scripture

[Col. 0011B]

and his other studies, having been published unsuccessfully, had until now remained obscure and neglected. I therefore thought it worthwhile to compare them with better manuscript codices and to add whatever I found new or of a more complete reading, so that, restored to their integrity and native excellence, they might revive and receive a fuller appreciation.

Accordingly, I eagerly undertook this task, most arduous and difficult though it was, hoping that I should perform a work most welcome to those who delight in sacred studies and who desire to draw the holy doctrines of our religion and ecclesiastical traditions from the Holy Fathers as from the purest springs, if I should offer them St. Bruno,

[Col. 0012A]

purged, elucidated, and enlarged with unpublished writings, to read.

## Chapter I. On the Writings of St. Bruno of Asti Published by Maurus Marchesius, Monk of Monte Cassino, and on the Testimonies of Writers

Marchesius divided the works of St. Bruno into two volumes and published them at Venice, with the Brentani, in 1651. The first contains commentaries on the five books of Moses, the Psalter, the Song of Songs, Job, and the Apocalypse. Before these the editor places his historical dissertation on St. Bruno and his writings. This is followed by the investigation of Philip Malabayla, a Cistercian monk and visitor of the Congregation of St. Bernard,

[Col. 0012B]

on the birth of St. Bruno, his canonry, and his departure from the Cassinese community. Third is read the Life of the same saint, written by Peter the Deacon, librarian of Monte Cassino, in Book IV, chapter 34, of his chronicle of that same monastery. Fourth place is occupied by another Life of the holy bishop, by an anonymous author, said to have been a canon of Segni, divided into five readings. These are the documents by which the aforesaid editor instructs his readers concerning the deeds and writings of St. Bruno.

The second volume contains 145 homilies, or sacred sermons, upon the Gospels of the whole year; six books of *Sentences*, which are sermons on various subjects; further, the treatises *On the Incarnation of the Lord*, *On the Sacrifice of Unleavened Bread*, *On the Sacraments and Ecclesiastical Rites*, and the Life

[Col. 0013A]

of St. Pope Leo IX, to which is added an answer to the question: “Why is the condition of the Church corrupt?” Moreover, in the same volume are found an abridgment of the Life of St. Peter, bishop of Anagni, and two letters: one to Peter, bishop of Porto, the other to Pope Paschal II.

But it is clear from the catalogue of ecclesiastical writers, whose testimonies we shall present in their proper place, that Bruno wrote many other works. Peter the Deacon, just mentioned, was the first to write of him, in Book XXXIV, *On the Illustrious Men of Monte Cassino*, and called him a most distinguished and splendid defender and doctor of the Church. After him, the following treated of the same holy bishop of Segni: Sixtus of Siena; Caesar Cardinal Baronius; Robert Cardinal Bellarmine; Natalis Alexander; Ferdinando Ughelli; Aubertus Miraeus; Johann Albert Fabricius; Antonio Possevino; Theophilus Raynaud; Philippe Labbe; Jacques le Long; William Cave; Casimir Oudin; Jean Mabillon; François Combefis; Louis Ellies Dupin; Augustin Calmet; Remy Ceillier; Domenico Maria Mansi, in the notes to Fabricius’s *Library of Medieval and Modern Latin*; Giovanni Mario, in his notes on Peter the Deacon’s *On Illustrious Men*; Count Giovanni M. Mazzuchelli; and, finally, all the Cassinese writers, whom it would take too long to enumerate.

## Chapter II. On the Disagreement of Writers in Recording Bruno’s Works

[Col. 0013C]

The aforesaid authors disagree among themselves in describing the same catalogue of St. Bruno’s works, since some attribute more and others fewer to him. Some mention certain unpublished works; some take works away from him; and others falsely assign works to him. The writings accorded to Bruno of Asti by the unanimous judgment of all are expositions on the Pentateuch, the Psalms, Job, the Song of Songs, and the Apocalypse. He is likewise held to be the author of very many homilies on the Gospels and sermons, as well as of certain treatises, since Peter the Deacon expressly mentions these and records his sacred sermons under their own titles.

Yet Peter the Deacon did not record each of Bruno’s works with sufficient care.

[Col. 0013D]

For he omits the commentary on Isaiah, which Bruno himself mentions in the preface to the Apocalypse; likewise, he passes over in silence the expositions on Joshua, Judith, and Kings attributed to the same commentator by others. He also leaves unmentioned the excellent exposition on the four Gospels, as well as Solomon’s parable *On the Strong Woman*, interpreted by Bruno.

Jacques le Long indeed recorded almost all such commentaries in his list of the works of St. Bruno, and confirmed Bruno’s exposition on the four Gospels by the testimony of two codices. One is in the Library of St. Victor at Paris; the other in the Royal Athenaeum Library at Turin, as Count Mazzuchelli also observes. Remy Ceillier, monk of the Congregation of St. Maur, was even more diligent in his catalogue of the writings of St. Bruno,

[Col. 0014A]

since he mentions several works entirely omitted by others.

## Chapter III. On the Manuscript Codices by Which a New Edition of the Works of St. Bruno Is Restored

I should not have ventured to undertake a correction of the Venetian edition of St. Bruno unless examination and collation of the best codices had convinced me that it could be purged, supplied, and perfected. Thus, during the autumn vacation of 1785, when I went to Florence for this purpose, I devoted my first efforts to comparing the reading of the five books of Moses used by Bruno with the distinguished biblical codex formerly belonging to the Cistercian monastery of St. Saviour on Monte Amiata, in the territory of Siena, transferred only in the preceding year to the Medicean-Laurentian Library.

[Col. 0014B]

The most illustrious Canon Angelo Maria Bandini, prefect of the Royal Library, immediately published in the Florentine journal a most learned description of this codex and discussed at length its excellence and antiquity. I shall briefly summarize these matters, so that the high value to be attached to that venerable monument of Holy Scripture may become ever more widely known.

This volume is a parchment folio of very great size, most beautifully written in square Roman characters and excellently preserved. Its antiquity is traced back to the sixth century of the Lord, since an inscription indicates that it was copied by one of the disciples of St. Gregory the Great. It contains all the books of both Testaments, whose variant readings we shall note. It differs, however, in its division of chapters, a practice which, as the most learned Giuseppe Maria Bianchini observes, and the most illustrious Pietro Lazzari in the preface to Bruno’s commentary on the Gospels, we find to have been customary among ancient bibliographers.

[Col. 0014C]

No one until now has doubted that St. Bruno, bishop of Segni, composed an exposition on the Pentateuch, since he himself acknowledges in his introduction that he prepared that work at the request of Peter, bishop of Anagni. Many manuscript codices also bear witness to it, whether of the eleventh century, in which St. Bruno flourished, or of the following, thirteenth century.

The first codex which I myself compared with the Venetian edition was supplied to me by the aforesaid Canon Angelo Maria Bandini. It is a parchment small folio, formerly of the Library of Santa Croce Minor and transferred to the Medicean-Laurentian Library; it is found in Pluteus IX, part S.

[Col. 0014D]

Its inscription reads: “Here begins the exposition of the venerable Bruno, bishop of Segni.” This codex displays complete integrity, and from it I extracted many readings highly useful for correcting and supplying Marchesius’s edition.

Likewise, two Cassinese codices were of great use to me: one marked no. 195, formerly 366, of the twelfth century; the other marked no. 619, of the thirteenth century. Both are parchment folios written in Roman characters. From these the most cultivated Dom Thomas Capomatius, the present superior of that distinguished monastery, obligingly gathered for me an abundant harvest for restoring and completing in new form Bruno’s exposition on the Pentateuch. I judge especially worthy of high regard another [reading], which almost surpasses in learning

[Col. 0015A]

and clarity the commentary published by Marchesius. To confirm these, I shall mention three codices of the Royal Library at Paris, marked nos. 2505, 2506, and 2507, which bear the name of Bishop Bruno on their frontispieces.

No less carefully did I seek codices to confirm and elucidate the exposition of A. N. on the book of Job. But although I visited several libraries in order to compare this work with ancient manuscript books, the Ghisian Library alone made my effort not useless, because there I found an outstanding codex furnished with such marks of distinction that it may suffice for many.

For this codex had been examined by the most learned Jacques Sirmond against another codex of the Royal Library at Paris, as he noted in his own hand on its front page,

[Col. 0015B]

and he sent it as a gift in 1638 to the Most Eminent Cardinal Fabio Chigi, afterwards elected Roman Pontiff under the name Alexander VII. This parchment codex, of the fourteenth century, most beautifully written in small folio, is adorned with the name of St. Bruno, bishop of Segni; from it I introduced certain readings into my own copy.

I have said little for the present concerning the commentary on Job, since I shall say more in the preliminary notice. Marchesius’s published exposition on the Psalms, incomplete and suffering from many defects, required that I omit nothing conducive to its correction and completeness. Yet, contrary to expectation, no codices containing this sort of commentary were found either in the Vatican or in the Cassinese Library. Their place was filled, however, by two codices of very great value: one Vallicellian, the other Ghisian.

[Col. 0015C]

From the first I obtained the exposition missing in Marchesius from Psalm LIX to Psalm LXIV, likewise from Psalm LXXVII to Psalm LXXXII, and the middle part of the exposition on Psalm LXX. The same lacunae occur in the Ghisian codex; nevertheless, it was very useful to me because it is most carefully corrected and in certain places superior to the Vallicellian codex. I obtained further additions from both codices, both for the correction of the text of the Psalms and for their proper interpretation; from these it will be evident that Marchesius used corrupt and interpolated manuscripts.

The Vallicellian and Ghisian codices, both parchment folios of the thirteenth century, are confirmed by three codices of the Royal Library at Paris, marked nos. 2508, 2509, and 2902,

[Col. 0015D]

as likewise by two others in the Roman Library of Santa Croce in Gerusalemme, admittedly imperfect but bearing the name of St. Bruno, bishop of Segni. Nor shall I omit to mention a codex of the Medicean-Laurentian Library, which I scarcely sampled because of the short time allowed me to remain in Florence and because I wished to consult other codices, as I shall say below; nevertheless, I received from it certain readings to be added to the other notes.

I must linger longer over establishing the exposition on the Song of Songs, which, all controversy removed, ought to be ascribed to our Bruno. Since Marchesius published among the works of the bishop of Segni that exposition on the Song of Songs, a great dispute arose between Benedictine writers

[Col. 0016A]

and Dominicans. Learned men had received the long-established opinion that St. Thomas Aquinas, while he lay ill in the Cistercian monastery of Fossanova, had expounded the Song of Songs at the request of those monks. This commentary was inserted among the works of the same holy Doctor published at Rome by order of St. Pius V in 1570, and reprinted in the second Venetian edition by Galterius in 1745, vol. XII.

When these matters had been made public and Marchesius’s false attribution became evident—that is, he had ascribed to Bruno of Asti what was asserted to be a genuine work of St. Thomas Aquinas—Angelo de Nuce, a Benedictine writer, adopted Marchesius’s side in his notes on the Cassinese Chronicle, Book IV, chapter 31. He relies especially upon the authority of two Cassinese codices. One he calls very ancient

[Col. 0016B]

and furnished with the heading, “Bruno on the Song of Songs”; the other he admits to be later, namely of the fourteenth century, and on its front is noted: “Contains the Exposition of St. Bruno on the Song of Songs.”

Erasmus Gattola, well known in the Republic of Letters, likewise became a defender of the opinion of Marchesius and de Nuce in his *History of Monte Cassino*, century VII, p. 383 ff., and maintained that St. Bruno, bishop of Segni, must be acknowledged as the author of that commentary.

While this controversy was still pending, there appeared from the press of Giovanni Battista Pasquali at Venice in 1750 the dissertations of the most illustrious Giovanni Francesco de Rubeis, O.P., *On the Deeds, Writings, and Doctrine of St. Thomas Aquinas*. In these he weighs the arguments of the Benedictine writers, who consider their opinion sufficiently secure, and proves conclusively that neither Bruno of Asti nor St. Thomas devoted labour to that exposition.

[Col. 0016C]

For he observes a very great diversity among the manuscript codices: some, such as the most ancient codex of Fabriano, attribute the credit for this work to Haimo of Halberstadt; others to Remigius of Auxerre; still others to Cassiodorus. Amid such great disagreement of manuscript codices, he declares that nothing certain can be established.

Earlier, in 1679 at Rouen, through the efforts of the most learned Jean Garet of the Congregation of St. Maur, there had appeared a revised edition of the works of Cassiodorus, in which, following the opinion of many, he ascribes to Cassiodorus the commentary on the Song of Songs published under Cassiodorus’s name. But in the preface he proves by many weighty reasons that this work ought not to be attributed to Cassiodorus.

[Col. 0016D]

The first of these is that St. Gregory the Great, especially his exposition on the Gospels, is cited in various places. Gregory did not compose that exposition until after he became Supreme Pontiff, which occurred in 590; by then at least seventeen years had elapsed since Cassiodorus’s death, for he was no longer alive in 575. Second, this commentary on the sacred epithalamium differs greatly from Cassiodorus’s style and manner of writing. Third, Cassiodorus himself says not a word of this treatise in the preface to his book *On Orthography*, where he lists all books composed by himself. Fourth, its reading of Holy Scripture is not according to the Vulgate translation, which the aforesaid commentator appears always to have used in his other writings.

Finally, Garet considers

[Col. 0017A]

this commentary an abridgment and epitome of a fuller treatise on the same book of the Song of Songs, commonly circulated under the name of St. Isidore of Seville.

Amid so great a diversity of opinions, our Bruno would have been deprived of the credit for the exposition on the sacred epithalamium, although he himself openly acknowledges that he composed it. “For the canons of Siena,” he says in the preface to his commentary on the Apocalypse, “among whom I myself lived as a humble canon, I expounded the Song of Songs as best I could”; were it not for the fact that the most illustrious Giovanni Lami, in his catalogue of the manuscript codices of the Riccardian Library, had described a volume in which such an exposition of Bruno occurs and had also supplied a specimen of it.

The most learned Domenico Maria Mansi, in his notes to Fabricius’s *Library*, and Remy Ceillier, vol. XXI, p. 101 of the *History of Sacred Writers*, mention this codex.

[Col. 0017B]

At the time when, as I have said, I was staying at Florence, the most courteous Francesco Fontani, prefect of the Riccardian Library, entrusted this excellent codex to me, not merely for consultation but for me to make a copy from it. I shall state the following concerning it.

First, it is a parchment small folio, marked no. VI, Pluteus K, order III; and at the front it is written that the most illustrious Benedetto Varchi, Florentine historian, possessed this codex. It is seen to be very beautifully written and must be assigned to the thirteenth century. Second, it contains a collection of several commentaries on the same book, described as follows:

1. A translation by St. Jerome of Origen’s treatise on the epithalamium.
2. An exposition on the Song of Songs, by Origen, translated by Rufinus the presbyter.
3. An exposition of the blessed Bishop Ambrose on the Song of Songs, collected from his books.
4. An exposition on the Song of Songs, by Pope St. Gregory.
5. An exposition on the Strong Woman, by Lord Bruno, bishop of Segni.
6. An exposition on the Song of Songs, by the same author.
7. Four letters by the same author.

[Col. 0017C]

Since, therefore, it is evident that the compiler’s purpose was to include in one volume the principal commentators on the divine epithalamium, there can be no doubt that he knew our St. Bruno as the true author of that exposition. Bruno’s own style of writing, and poems of different kinds in accordance with the taste of that age, in which the author treated the more beautiful dialogues of the divine bridegroom and bride, likewise provide certain proof that Bruno wrote this commentary.

[Col. 0017D]

These, therefore, are the works of St. Bruno of Asti contained in this first volume: namely, Expositions on the Pentateuch, the Book of Job, the Psalms, and the Song of Songs, before which is placed an exposition of the parable *On the Strong Woman*; both are unpublished. We reserve the remaining works of the same writer for the second volume, which, if God grants life, we hope to publish as soon as possible. There we shall give readers sufficient notice of whatever requires preliminary explanation.

## Chapter IV. On the Lost Writings of St. Bruno

[Col. 0018A]

Among the writings of the holy bishop of Segni which we regret to have lost, the one especially to be mentioned is his Explanation of the Prophet Isaiah. He bears witness to this work in the following words in the preface to his Exposition of the Apocalypse: “Before this I treated, at the request of the venerable Abbot Damian, rather briefly and clearly, the most illustrious of the prophets, Isaiah.” I shall relate what I did in order to obtain that commentary. I had read in Jacques le Long that this manuscript was in the possession of the Carthusians of St Bartholomew at Anagni. Yet that Carthusian monastery is not at Anagni, but at Trisulti, not far from Alatri. Therefore, aflame with the desire of acquiring that precious monument, [Col. 0018B] I asked my colleague Clement Porro, professor of rhetoric at the college of Alatri, to go to the monastery of Trisulti and inspect the manuscripts in its library. That excellent man complied, but his journey was entirely fruitless. For on 17 May 1786 he wrote to me that no manuscript whatever remained in that library, and that an elderly monk had told him that, long ago, a certain Neapolitan president had transferred all the manuscript volumes to Naples, to the Charterhouse of St Martin.

When I spoke of this matter with the most distinguished prelate Domenico Coppola, secretary of the Sacred Congregation of Rites, he, with his singular courtesy and his devotion to every kind of ecclesiastical learning, promised me his patronage so that that Exposition on Isaiah of St Bruno might be sought among the manuscripts of the library of St Martin. [Col. 0018C] He entrusted this task to Signor Advocate Xavier Matteo, well known in the republic of letters. Matteo employed a Carthusian monk who was his friend and omitted nothing in attempting to draw that writing of the bishop of Segni from its hiding places. But the learned monk spent his time and labour in vain, as he himself admitted in a letter printed at Naples in the following year and dedicated to the same Signor Xavier Matteo; this letter will be discussed elsewhere.

Meanwhile, I sent letters to several friends living at Brescia, Novara, Vercelli, Modena, Milan, and Cassino, asking them to discover that exposition on Isaiah in the libraries and archives of those cities. The reply of every one of them affirmed that it had not been found and was regarded as lost. [Col. 0018D] Philip Amadeus Millo, canon of the metropolitan church of Turin and deeply versed in sacred studies, had revived some hope in me. On 30 May of the same year, 1786, he replied that St Bruno’s commentary on Isaiah might perhaps be found at Catania, since Arnold Wion, a monk of Douai, notes in Book I, chapter 8 of his work entitled *Lignum vitae* (*The Tree of Life*) that he had possessed manuscript works of St Bruno, among which he mentions the above-praised commentary; but, Wion says, he had given those manuscripts as a gift of friendship to Constantine, a Benedictine monk of Catania.

Letters were sent to Catania, and inquiry was made whether that exposition of Bruno on Isaiah still existed. But Signor Philip M. Hernandez, a monk, replied to the abbot of Cassino, Thomas Capomatius, on 13 December 1786 that the library of that monastery, richly supplied with manuscripts, had wholly perished in the very violent earthquake of 1693. [Col. 0019A] At last I was scarcely able to gain access to the Vatican Library, superior to all others in the number and rarity of its manuscripts. I was led by the firm hope that I should find there writings of Bruno of Segni, who had been so celebrated in his own day and had held eminent offices in the Roman Church. Yet although I was permitted to see certain works—for example, the commentary on the Apocalypse, the little work *On the Mysteries*, and so forth, and the six books of *Sentences*—I was told that nothing else of St Bruno’s works survived.

Among his lost writings I shall likewise list his first elucidation of the Psalter, of which he himself speaks in the preliminary notice before his second Interpretation of the Psalms; [Col. 0019B] likewise, the commentary on the books of Joshua and Judith, which Peter the Deacon and other writers attribute to him.

## CHAPTER V. ON THE DOUBTFUL WRITINGS OF ST BRUNO

In Vallicellian manuscript C. XII, from which we copied Bruno’s Exposition on the Psalms, we found on page 125 a little work marked with his name, whose title is: *Questions on the Books of Kings*. But since both the title and those questions were printed in precisely the same words [Col. 0020A] among the works of the Venerable Bede, Basel edition published by Johann Hervagius in 1563, volume VII, column 357, I do not venture to call the bishop of Segni their author, although some evidence supports him.

Great weight with some may be given to the authority of the anonymous author of the Life of St Bruno of Segni, who listed among his works a certain Exposition on the Books of Kings in these words: “He not only expounded spiritually the five books of Moses, but also the Psalter, the Prophet Isaiah, the Books of Kings, Job likewise, and so forth.” Nor can the testimony of the most learned Cardinal Sirleto be considered of slight importance. For since, by command of Gregory XIII, the proper lessons for St Bruno, to be recited at the second nocturn on his feast day, were approved in 1584, and since those lessons mention his commentary [Col. 0020B] on the Books of Kings, no one can doubt that Sirleto affirmed this only after mature consideration of the matter.

To these are added the opinions of Jacques le Long, Augustin Calmet, and others, which render this conclusion highly probable. But unless more compelling arguments appear, everyone will always be free to doubt whether that little work should be ascribed to Bruno or to Bede. Likewise doubtful are several sacred sermons attributed to the same holy bishop.

## SECOND PROLEGOMENON

[Col. 0019]

## CHAPTER I. ON THE TRANSLATION OF HOLY SCRIPTURE USED BY ST BRUNO

[Col. 0019B]

[Col. 0019C] We have already said that the text of the five books of Moses, as it appears in the Exposition published by Marchesi, differs in certain words from the text of a most ancient manuscript formerly belonging to the Cistercian monks of Monte Amiata, which follows the version of the Old Latin, translated from the interpretation of the Seventy. The remaining books of Holy Scripture interpreted by Bruno conform to this version.

The case is otherwise with the Psalter, upon two translations of which he himself testifies that he composed commentaries. “While I was still a young man,” he says in the preface to the Psalter, “I expounded the Psalter according to another translation; and that translation differs in so many places from this translation, which the Roman Church uses, that this translation cannot in any way be understood according to the exposition of that one.”

Since Peter the Deacon of Cassino wrote that Bruno’s first commentary had been composed upon the version received for use in the Gallican Church, some have supposed this to be the commentary published under the name of Bruno of Würzburg through the efforts of Johann Cochlaeus, and inserted by the Lyons printers in volume XVIII, page 65, of the *Library of the Fathers*. The defenders of this view appear to have been influenced, first, because the translation said to have been explained by Bruno of Würzburg is indeed according to the text of the Gallican Church. Walafrid Strabo, *On Ecclesiastical Matters*, chapter 25, asserts that St Gregory of Tours introduced this text into the churches of Gaul—although Jean Mabillon disagrees, maintaining in his work on liturgy [Col. 0020B] that this occurred later.

Secondly, they are moved by the age of the two Brunos, namely, the end of the eleventh and beginning of the twelfth century, although Bruno of Würzburg died several years before Bruno of Segni. Thirdly, and most strongly, they are persuaded by Bruno of Würzburg’s birth and education. Since he was born and educated as a prince—for he was a cousin of Emperor Conrad II—it is scarcely credible that he possessed such and so great a knowledge of the divine books as to be able to interpret them.

John Trithemius, however, disagrees with them. While highly praising Bruno of Würzburg, he says: “From the writings of the ancient Fathers he produced a fine exposition upon the entire Psalter.” This testimony is confirmed by a most cogent argument. For although that commentary is brief and resembles an epitome, its interpretations nevertheless appear so full of the substance and solid doctrine of the holy Fathers that they present not the specimen of a diligent young man, but the fruit of long labour and consummate wisdom. [Col. 0020D] This view is further strengthened by Johann Cochlaeus, who reports in his preface to that Psalter that, in the library of the church of Würzburg, there was still preserved in his own time a book of this commentary, written in distinguished and costly script and dedicated to St Kilian, the principal patron of the Church of Würzburg.

The commentary on the Psalms of St Bruno, bishop of Würzburg, was published at Nuremberg in the Year of the Lord 1480, and this edition is very rare. Since these considerations are so weighty and so clear, we think that no one will assign this commentary to Bruno of Segni, [Col. 0021A] but rather to Bruno of Würzburg. Having established these points concerning our Bruno’s first exposition of the Psalms—which we acknowledge has not yet been brought forth from its hiding place—we shall turn our observations to the other exposition, published by Marchesi. First, indeed, we must deal with the translation, since we have it from Bruno himself that he composed that commentary according to the translation used by the Roman Church.

We say, then, that the Roman Psalter, which is still sung in the Basilica of St Peter, is part of the most ancient version of the Bible transmitted to the Latins from the translation made by the Seventy Interpreters from the Hebrew text into Greek. This version was called the Old Latin, the Common Version, and also the Vulgate. [Note: [Col. 0021D] See Antonio Martinetti’s dissertation *On the Roman Psalter*, published at Rome in 1745; also the work of the most learned prelate, now Cardinal of the Holy Roman Church, Stefano Borgia, *On the Vatican Cross*, chapter 7, page 69.]

But because many scribal errors had crept into that [Col. 0021B] translation, St Damasus, Roman pontiff, gave it to St Jerome for correction. Learned men think this occurred in 382, and Jerome himself speaks of it in the preface to the Psalter: “While I was formerly in Rome, I had corrected the Psalter; and in accordance with the Seventy Interpreters, though rapidly, I had nevertheless revised it in large part.”

After returning to Bethlehem, Jerome issued a second revision of the Psalter at the urging of the Roman ladies Paula and Eustochium, because, as he himself says, the preceding text was again being read in a form corrupted through the fault of scribes, and “the old error had more force than the new correction.” This work of Jerome is assigned to the year 390. Jerome rendered a third great service in correcting the Psalms, when, comparing the Hebrew books with the Greek text and consulting the more learned men of that nation, [Col. 0021C] he supplied a more perfect text of the Psalter and of the other divine books. These facts must be held certain and firmly established on Jerome’s authority.

But it is not equally certain whether the Roman Psalter of which we are speaking was taken from the first revision made under Damasus or from the second, carried out more carefully during his retreat at Bethlehem. Yet two considerations seem to permit the inference that the Roman Church retained the Psalms according to the earlier revision. First, all authors acknowledge that it is part of the most ancient Old Latin version. Secondly, our Bruno says that this translation differs in many places from the other translation which he explained while still a young man, so that this translation cannot in any way be understood according to that exposition. This difference is indeed established if Peter the Deacon’s view, indicated above, is accepted: namely, that Bruno’s first exposition of the Psalms follows the text of the Gallican Church.

What that text is may be learned from the Psalter explained by Bruno of Würzburg, where variant readings from the Hebrew text and from Theodotion’s version are marked with asterisks and obeli; this had been done by St Jerome. To this is added the authority of the Venerable Bede, who affirms in the preface to his commentary on the Psalms that the translation used in Gaul was drawn chiefly from the Hebrew text. [Col. 0022A] The Italians, however, recited the Psalms translated into Latin according to the Seventy Interpreters and according to Jerome’s second revision, except for the Roman and Milanese Churches, which retained the ancient Psalter. From that more careful revision came the Psalms read in the Vulgate Bible, and these differ in many words, names, and punctuation from the Psalms of the older translation.

Although St Pius V had ordered all churches to recite the Psalms according to the more thoroughly revised text, he nevertheless permitted the Roman Basilica of St Peter and the Church of Milan to use the ancient Psalter. Nor was anything altered by the popes Sixtus V and Clement VIII, through whose highly commendable efforts, after a further completed revision of the divine books, the Bible was issued with this title on its front page: “The Holy Bible of the Vulgate Edition, revised by command of Sixtus V, Supreme Pontiff, and published by authority of Clement VIII.”

Since our Bruno, as he himself testifies, did not know whether anyone else had applied himself to an exposition of the Psalms of such antiquity, while, on the contrary, many had distinguished themselves in treating the later text, he adorned this exposition with selected authorities from other divine writings. He knew very well the commentaries on the Psalms by Hilary, Ambrose, Augustine, and Cassiodorus, and he showed that he held their learning in the highest esteem. Yet he said that he hoped those who compared the two expositions would not judge this second one superfluous. [Col. 0022C] “At the request,” he says in the preface already mentioned, “of my friends, and especially of the venerable Abbot Peregrinus, I took pains that this also, like the other, might have its own exposition. Whoever reads the whole of it carefully in order, I know, will not judge it superfluous and will readily be able to understand how great is the difference between the first and this second interpretation.”

## CHAPTER II. ON THE INTERPRETATION OF THE PSALMS

Having thus far established the text of the Psalter which Bruno elucidated in his commentaries, we must now discuss the method of his interpretation. The holy bishop, being as deeply versed as he was in the knowledge of Holy Scripture, did not fail to know which matters were to be understood according to the letter and which figuratively according to the spirit. [Col. 0022D] For God prescribed many things to the Israelite people that can be understood in no other way—that is, wholly according to the letter. Yet many things were also done and written which, as St Augustine says in Sermon 101 *On Time*, were “a type and image of things to come.”

Accordingly Bruno says, in his exposition of chapter 22 of Job, page 262, column 1, that allegory must not be sought in matters which clearly express their meaning in the very words; and, conversely, that it is a fault to wish to take literally matters presented under metaphors and allegories: “For it is no less a fault,” he says, “to seek allegory in matters which must be understood according to the letter than [Col. 0023A] to wish to interpret only literally those things which must be understood allegorically.”

The holy bishop more clearly discloses his mind and declares the rules by which he wishes to be guided in his commentary on chapter 7 of the Book of Numbers, page 177, column 2. There, he says, allegory must necessarily be sought where the literal sense commands something either useless or wholly devoid of reason. Therefore, whenever Holy Scripture commands things which indicate no usefulness on the literal level, or whenever no reason is apparent for the delivery of such commands, they must be understood as metaphors and allegories, lest the divine word be considered written in vain or idle; beneath them certain mysteries and truths are contained.

For example, many things are commanded by God in Leviticus and Numbers which, if someone applied them in their literal sense, he would judge to convey nothing conducive to spiritual profit; nor is there any evident reason why they were so ordained. What does it contribute to divine worship that some species of animals are commanded to be slaughtered when sacrifices are offered to God, while the slaughter of others is forbidden? Unless it is because God wished not the things themselves but their significations to be understood, so that the Jews, to whom they had been given as signs and symbols, might draw spiritual knowledge from the analogies set before them. What is the purpose of the highly precise description of the garments of the high priest? What of the tabernacle’s ornaments, so diverse and so precious? What of the many rites and ceremonies in the sacrifice of the Passover lamb, in libations, and in offerings? [Col. 0023C] Certainly no other explanation can be given except that all these things set forth figures and likenesses of matters to be revealed in the new covenant, when divine worship and true religion, with the shadow removed, had shone forth.

Therefore those things, to speak with Augustine in the passage cited, “were prefigured among the Jews and, by the gift of God’s grace, fulfilled in us.” I shall offer one of Bruno’s commentaries as an example of all the rest, on the words of Leviticus 2, page 128, column 2: “When a soul offers a sacrificial offering to the Lord, his offering shall be of fine flour; and he shall pour oil upon it,” and so forth.

“This fine flour,” he says, “was made from that grain of which our Saviour says in John 12:24: ‘Unless a grain of wheat falls into the earth and dies, it remains alone.’ Ground by the millstones of the Jews—of whom it is said, ‘The Lord will break the millstones of lions’—it fittingly signifies Christ’s Passion. This offering is made by the soul, that is, by some good and spiritual person, one who follows the inclinations of the soul more than those of the body, because with a contrite heart and an afflicted spirit he remembers Christ’s Passion. He pours oil upon it, admiring Christ’s loving-kindness and mercy, who, while being crucified by the Jews, nevertheless poured out the oil of loving-kindness and mercy and did not cease from mercy.” [Col. 0023D]

From these matters, the method by which Bruno pursued his interpretations is evident; they also open for us the way to refute the censures chiefly directed against his commentary on the Psalms.

## CHAPTER III. ON THE CENSURES AGAINST ST BRUNO’S INTERPRETATION OF THE PSALMS

At this point, readers, we wish you immediately to keep before your eyes [Col. 0024A] what St Hilary of Poitiers most wisely wrote at the beginning of his exposition of Psalm 125:

“Unless there were in the Psalms certain prophecies of such a kind that they did not fit the circumstances and persons of those times, many would certainly dare to suppose that nothing in the Psalms had been spoken spiritually. They would think that we seek fabricated and fictitious interpretations, by which we might seem to have understood something, I know not what, more elevated and more profound; as though, by relying on our own judgment, we attained in what is written a meaning through careful and anxious understanding.”

The same holy doctor had said earlier, on Psalm 141: “We acknowledge nothing in the Psalms except what is prophetic.” St Hilary therefore teaches that the Psalms must not be understood according to the letter, but that the higher things spoken in them prophetically and figuratively must be apprehended and signified, once the covering of the words has been removed and the hidden mysteries brought forth.

Having thus established from Hilary the appropriateness and usefulness of allegorical interpretations, we must answer those who call Bruno’s interpretations singular and forced. Allegory, which rhetoricians call a sustained metaphor, is a likeness and comparison of one thing with another by reason of some relation to it. When one thing is compared with another, it is usually not compared in all its properties, but in some, or perhaps in one alone. “In metaphorical expressions,” says St Thomas, “a likeness need not be considered in every respect; for otherwise it would not be a likeness, but the reality of the thing” (*Summa*, III, question 8, article 1, reply to objection 4). [Col. 0024C]

For the correctness of a comparison, it is surely enough that the thing taken as one of the terms of comparison possesses the property which we observe in the other term and to which we refer the likeness and allegory. Now, although the one property taken in comparing two terms is not in itself clear or evident to everyone, if it exists, it may rightly be transferred to the other term of comparison. Hence arises the judgment whether allegories are properly or improperly drawn: namely, whether the relation of the terms from which the allegory is deduced appears to the reader’s mind easily, with excessive difficulty, or not at all.

But if sacred interpreters’ allegories had to be rejected for these reasons, who does not see that the interpretations of Christ our Teacher himself would also have to be disapproved? For in the parable in which he set thorns to signify riches, he interpreted thorns as riches. Now riches delight, but thorns prick and produce pain. What could seem more incongruous—indeed, even contradictory—if we wished the relation of likeness to lie only in those properties of thorns and riches which first strike everyone’s eyes at a glance? Nonetheless, Christ called riches “thorns” because of another, more hidden reason, which St Gregory the Great gives in Homily 15 on the Gospels, Luke chapter 6, read on Sexagesima Sunday: “For riches rend the mind with the prickings of its thoughts; and, when they draw it on even to sin, they make it bleed as though by an inflicted wound.” [Col. 0025A]

Therefore, if Christ the Lord used these metaphors, which I would call more difficult because of the more hidden relation between figure and thing figured, it follows that this kind of metaphor is not alien to the character of Holy Scripture. Consequently, those interpretations which appear not readily obvious and enveloped in some obscurity are not foreign to the right method of interpreting Scripture.

Moreover, since the same St Gregory teaches that Christ our Lord himself deigned to explain what he taught in parables, yet did not wish to explain everything in person, he says that Christ did so in order that we too might apply ourselves to the interpretation of these figures and show that the sacred writings contain the teachings of eternal life beneath metaphors and allegories.

What we have said so far concerning the interpretation of all Scripture and its conformity to the rules of allegory has a special application to the Psalms, from which we shall give several examples. First, the words of Psalm 6 cannot in any way be understood according to the letter: “Heal me, O Lord, because my bones are troubled.” For it is not proper to bones to be troubled, since they lack all sensation. But allegorically, according to Bruno’s interpretation, page 309, column 1, “bones” signify the principal virtues—faith, hope, and charity—by which the Christian soul is governed and sustained.

Likewise, Psalm 7 says of God: “He has bent his bow and made it ready; and in it he has prepared instruments of death.” In these allegorical words too a spiritual meaning must be sought, because God uses neither bow nor arrows. Therefore our interpreter thinks, page 312, column 2, that the two Testaments are signified, since they promise life to the good but death to the wicked. Likewise, in Psalm 9, where the Prophet says, “You who raise me up from the gates of death,” Bruno teaches, page 315, column 2, that heretics and sinners represent the gates of death, from which the righteous are mercifully delivered by God.

Nor can that exposition of Psalm 17 seem discordant: “Before the brightness in his sight, the clouds passed.” The same commentator says that the Apostles are signified here, whose pure and holy teaching was spread throughout the whole world. He had also said concerning the words of Job 37, “And the clouds scatter their light,” that by the light of the clouds we should understand the teaching hidden in the Holy Scriptures, page 285, column 1. [Col. 0025D] Six hundred other examples could be drawn from the Psalms which have been interpreted aptly and not forcibly; but I shall set a limit to this discussion, so that I may also say something about the excessive frequency of allegorical interpretations, the second charge against our commentator.

In order that these critics might not appear to assert this gratuitously, they would have to show that Bruno exceeded the principle in which he said: “It is no less a fault to seek allegory in matters which must be understood according to the letter than to wish to interpret literally those things which must be understood allegorically.” How will they explain literally these words of Psalm 71: “Let the mountains receive peace for the people, and the hills righteousness”? Unless, as St Bruno explains, page 450, column 1, the mountains and hills signify the Apostles and doctors, who stand higher than all others and are worthier to receive peace—that is, the Son of God, author of peace—and his righteousness. [Col. 0026A]

Likewise, in the same Psalm, verse 16: “And there shall be a firmament on the earth.” How can the firmament, that is, heaven, which is above the earth, be on the earth? The holy bishop says, page 452, column 1: “The Lord is called the firmament because in him are the sun, the moon, and the beauty of all the stars. And indeed he is the firmament on the earth, because the Church has been made firm and founded upon the earth.”

The same holy doctor also explained certain things both literally and allegorically. For example, Psalm 75: “There he broke the horn, the bow, the shield, the sword, and the battle.” Literally, he says that this is to be understood as the destruction of the Assyrian army, slain by the angel of the Lord in one night; spiritually, however, it signifies all the weapons of the devil and all his devices against the Church, broken and destroyed by Christ, page 461, column 1. [Col. 0026B] From these examples, further instances may be gathered which it is superfluous to enumerate, since his remaining commentaries are composed with the same clarity and usefulness. In them, with the veil of figures removed, the holy bishop conveyed and disclosed the mysteries of divinity and holier instruction.

For who does not recall the warning Christ gave to the Apostles, saying to them in Luke chapter 8: “To you it is given to know the mystery of the kingdom of God; but to the rest, in parables, so that seeing they may not see and hearing they may not understand”? Hence the author teaches that divine wisdom is to be admired, since it denied the knowledge of divine mysteries to the pagans and to the Jews hardened in cruelty, and spoke to them only in parables, figures, and riddles; for the people were stiff-necked and especially devoted to the traditions of Abraham, in which they boasted.

To the Apostles, therefore, and to their successors—the bishops and doctors—has been given the knowledge of the mysteries of the kingdom of God. Thus the teachings of interpretation must be received from them, not from the wise men of this age, of whom the Prophet says in Psalm 69: “But God said to the sinner: Why do you declare my righteous judgments and take my covenant in your mouth?” From those, I say, whom, as the Apostle says in 1 Corinthians 12, God placed in the Church as teachers, and to whom he gave knowledge and understanding both to penetrate the heavenly mysteries [Col. 0026D] and to reveal all the mysteries of eternal life. And those claim for themselves the greater authority whose mission in the Church and sanctity of life were most highly commended and shone forth in many signs. Whether Bruno ought to be reckoned among these is not open to doubt: his election to the episcopate was confirmed by miracles, and the many miracles wrought by him both during his life and after his death do not permit it.

They also object that Bruno did not interpret the meaning of Hebrew words with sufficient exactness. But this is easily refuted from the agreement of Bruno’s interpretations with Augustine, Cassiodorus, and Bede; it would be foolish to affirm that all of them erred. For they must be believed to have consulted Jerome, who wrote a special treatise on interpreting these words. Therefore, if our author followed in their footsteps, he did not depart far from sound interpretation. [Col. 0027A]

For those to whom Bruno’s exposition of the Psalms has seemed insufficiently useful, Augustine’s answer in *On the Trinity*, book I, chapter 3, to someone criticizing him for publishing matters already treated and exhausted by others, is sufficient. Augustine said that not all books reach everyone’s hands, and that, although they may be scattered throughout the whole world, truth gains greater splendour and firmness the more it is affirmed by many writers, especially learned and holy ones. Nor can a multiplicity of interpretations of Holy Scripture be held useless, because, as more rays shine upon Scriptures full of mysteries and sublime matters, we attain their understanding more easily.

One matter remains: namely, that we should answer those who seek to diminish Bruno’s standing because of the age in which the holy Bruno lived. [Col. 0028A] I am indeed astonished that what ought to be celebrated for his singular glory is turned to the detriment of so great a man’s honour. For what is more praiseworthy than to establish that, by his own talent and diligence, he overcame the misfortune of his age—that is, the almost complete loss of the best disciplines and liberal arts—and raised himself so high that outstanding writers on Holy Scripture and theological doctrines confess that he rendered them excellent service?

Were not Peter Damian, Anselm of Canterbury, Ivo of Chartres, and Bruno the Carthusian contemporaries of, or only a little earlier than, our Bruno? If, then, their works are held in esteem and the Church has received from them the continued tradition of sacred doctrine, why should Bruno of Segni not be placed in their number—he who elucidated the sacred writings with so great an abundance of knowledge and such choice learning? [Col. 0028B]

## THIRD PROLEGOMENON

[Col. 0027]

## CHAPTER I. GENERAL OUTLINE OF THE EXPOSITION ON THE PENTATEUCH, JOB, THE PSALMS, AND THE SONG OF SONGS

[Col. 0027B]

Saint Bruno knew that, both to refute the Jews and to strengthen Christians, it was necessary to show them that from the beginning of the world there had been one and the same religion: namely, the worship of the true God, Creator of heaven and earth; and that the old law had bestowed upon human beings nothing other than knowledge of the supreme Ruler, [Col. 0027C] so that later, when through Jesus Christ the Restorer the fullness of grace had come, on hearing higher truths they might give assent and fulfill holier precepts. Accordingly, in order to accomplish this, he says that Genesis first presents God as the maker of all things from nothing by a single word, and as the creator from clay of the first man, Adam, from whom the whole human race descended.

Then, since Moses describes Adam’s fall from innocence and integrity of nature into guilt and condemnation, our author maintains and sets forth that Adam fell into a most miserable condition, together with his descendants, and became incapable of restoring his own salvation. But because the goodness of the divine Craftsman was not going to leave mankind—betrayed through the devil’s envy—in perdition, it was necessary that someone should have pity on him and rescue him from destruction, and that the promise made to Adam should bring salvation to all who believed. Hence the mystery of our restoration began to be established, and knowledge of it was handed down from fathers to sons, so that Abel, Enosh, Enoch, and Noah are celebrated by the sacred writings as the first believers and righteous men.

But when human wickedness was great upon the earth and every thought of the heart was continually bent upon evil (Gen. 6:5), and God repented that He had made man, Noah built an ark at the Lord’s command; and when his family and individuals of every species of animal had been placed in it, all living creatures were destroyed in the floodwaters. That ark, as Bruno observes, signified the future Church: those who enter it are saved, while those outside it attain salvation in no way.

After the world had been restored to inhabitants, [Col. 0028B] God chose from among them the righteous Abraham, so that from him might arise a people which, separated from the other transgressing and idolatrous nations, would obey Him and offer holy worship to Him alone. This people, however, signified the acquisition of another people, whose leader and prince, foretold in Jacob’s prophecy, aroused hope for the heavenly possession to be obtained through Christ.

After Genesis follows the exposition of Exodus, [Col. 0028C] which contains the history of the Israelite people led by Moses out of Egypt: namely, when and by what miracles it was delivered from the yoke of Pharaoh’s bondage. This deliverance represented the redemption of humankind from the devil’s tyranny which Christ was to accomplish. Our commentator omits none of these matters; but, consistently faithful to his own method, he teaches that this people foreshadowed the Church, which was to be established by Christ and endowed with far greater benefits and powers.

And because the law written in their hearts did not restrain human beings from evil, God gave Moses a law inscribed on tablets of stone, so that He might preserve the Israelites in obedience and faithfulness to Himself. They were to keep it always as a reminder, and by it understand what they themselves owed to God and to their neighbor. These, indeed, are also the precepts of the new Christian law: namely, love of God and of neighbor. And just as all the commandments of the Old Testament are referred to these two, so in the new covenant all perfection and the fulfillment of the law are accomplished through obedience to these precepts.

Yet it was not enough for the divine Lawgiver to provide for the inward righteousness of His people; He also wished to direct them toward outward acts of religion, that He might make them His worshippers and that they might acknowledge Him as the supreme Lord. Therefore He commanded Moses to erect the tabernacle and to place within it the ark, a symbol of the divine presence and majesty; and He commanded sacrifices to be offered to Himself, in which the mystery of humanity’s restoration would be signified by the immolation of the true Lamb. Hence Saint Bruno, in his exposition of Exodus, chapter 8, p. 58, col. 1, said:

> “Christ’s Passion, signified in the Old Testament through figures and riddles, was at last fulfilled in the New. There Christ is shown; here He is sacrificed. There it is signified; here it is fulfilled. There, finally, the sacrifice of the lamb is recounted; here the true Passion of Christ is proclaimed.” [Col. 0029A]

And in order that religious worship might take deeper and deeper root in the minds of the Hebrews and be fittingly celebrated, He did not permit all to be ministers of sacred things; rather, out of all the tribes He chose Levi alone, whose men should exercise the priesthood and perform sacrifices according to ceremonies and rites established by God Himself. This second legislation, concerning outward religion, is contained in the book of Leviticus. There the various offices of ministers and the different things to be offered to God are prescribed, so that holiness may shine forth in all things and the greatest obedience may be rendered to the supreme Lord.

Since in this ordering of ministers and this establishment of offices and rites there seems to be delineated the pattern of ecclesiastical hierarchy, Saint Bruno admonishes bishops to make themselves examples of holier life; he impresses upon clerics purity of conduct and zeal for piety, and kindles them toward perfect service of God.

Leviticus is followed by the book of Numbers, so called because it recounts the numbering of the Israelite people, which God commanded Moses to undertake, so that the men fit for arms might be enrolled and march forth to wage the Lord’s battles. Since a land overflowing with every good thing had been promised to the Israelites, it could be obtained only after many enemies had been conquered; it was to be possessed as the reward of enduring labor and courage. Under Bruno’s exhortation, we must fight [Col. 0029C] not for an earthly but for a heavenly kingdom, against visible and invisible enemies; and we must draw up the battle-lines of virtues, by whose strength and firmness the world, the flesh, and the devil may be overcome and trampled down. The crown is given only to conquerors, and only those who, despising earthly goods, have wholly devoted themselves to God will enter the heavenly inheritance. The promises of temporal prosperity made to the carnal and stiff-necked Hebrew people set before us an image of enduring heavenly blessedness and inflame our hearts faithfully to perform this spiritual warfare.

Finally, Saint Bruno, bishop of Segni, interpreted the fifth book written by Moses, Deuteronomy, which he says contains the second law: inasmuch as the precepts promulgated in the earlier books are renewed [Col. 0029D] and confirmed in this one, so that the will of the supreme Lawgiver may become all the more known and the whole and perfect obedience of humankind may answer it. Here I shall briefly note that, just as the sacred writer, divinely inspired, cannot be charged with excessive repetition—not only in this final book but also in the preceding ones—so Saint Bruno should not be accused if he employs the same or similar interpretations whenever the same passages occur.

In this collection the Pentateuch is followed by a commentary on the book of Job, which, since antiquity, has been received throughout the Church as a divine book and therefore called protocanonical. Singular clarity and brevity shine in this exposition: the figures and prophecies [Col. 0030A] concerning Christ are explained admirably, and the moral teachings offered throughout show the writer to be divinely inspired.

The Psalter is added to the book of Job. We have said more above concerning its exposition; therefore it will suffice to note a few points here. First, it should be observed that the Psalmist states some things about Christ in explicit words and represents others in figures and allegories. Keeping this before his eyes, our commentator clearly and lucidly shows those things already fulfilled; while those yet to be fulfilled he proves, by sound arguments, ought to be believed.

Moreover, no order can be established in the Psalms. For the prophets committed to writing not their own thoughts, but what had been inspired in them by the Holy Spirit; and since that heavenly teacher of truth breathes where and how He wills, He must be heard as He reveals Himself. From this it is evident that no one ought to approach the expounding of these mysteries without first imploring heavenly light, knowing that Christ the Lord gave thanks to God the Father because He had chosen to hide from the wise of this age what He revealed to little ones—that is, His disciples.

Bruno strove to acquire this divine wisdom not so much by constant prayers to God as by prolonged reading and meditation upon the Holy Fathers. It is therefore unsurprising that in his commentary we hear now Ambrose, now Augustine, Cassiodorus, or Bede expounding. For Solomon said, *Ecclesiasticus* 39: “The wise man will seek out the wisdom of the saints, and will devote himself to the prophets.” No one should trust in a private spirit, but should consult learned and holy men whose teaching and authority are known to have been approved by the Church. [Col. 0030C]

Certain preliminary remarks must also be made concerning the Song of Songs, a book which, as we have already said, Bruno likewise expounded. First, it cannot be doubted, according to the common judgment of the Holy Fathers, that King Solomon, inspired by God, was the author of this book, despite the vain opposition of certain modern heterodox writers; and the Church has always admitted it among the divine and canonical books.

Second, one must remember what this book contains. It is a sacred epithalamium—that is, a nuptial song—not intended to embellish earthly weddings, but to raise the perceptions of the human mind so that the faithful soul may worthily reflect upon the love of God, aspire to Him, and delight in His most sweet joys as between bridegroom and bride. Saint Bernard says the same in Sermon 1 on the Song of Songs: “Solomon, divinely inspired, sang the praises of Christ and the Church, the grace of sacred love, and the mysteries of the eternal marriage; and at the same time he expressed the longing of the holy soul, and, exulting in the Spirit, composed a nuptial song in delightful, though figurative, language,” etc.

Third, it should be noted that, since while we are wayfarers a conversation between spirit and spirit can be expressed only through bodily things and ideas, the allegorical words used by Solomon must not be understood according to their literal sound, but according to their signification. Nothing whatever impure or unholy, therefore, is to be understood anywhere [Col. 0031A] in the Song; for the bridegroom is holy and the bride is holy, and thus all that is profane and earthly must be far removed.

Fourth, I shall say that this bride, assumed in order to possess the love of God, represents the Church, which Christ the Lord acquired for Himself by His own blood and into which He poured, as it were, all the treasures of His love. But we shall attain the truth of the signification much more sublimely if we recognize in this bridegroom the Son of God, who, pitying the human condition after Adam’s sin, joined our flesh to Himself as a bride—flesh whose sacrifice was to become the price of our salvation—and celebrated that indissoluble spiritual marriage which had been foretold to the first parent Adam and was the expectation of all ages.

And because He who was from eternity the Son of God was to be born in time as Son of Man—not by ordinary generation, but by a generation that was the work of heavenly omnipotence—He chose for Himself upon earth a virgin as mother. He so delighted in the fullness of her purity and holiness that no other creature was dearer to Him, nor did He enrich any with more abundant gifts. Thus, whether in this sacred epithalamium we behold God as the lover of every faithful soul; understand the Church as the bride; recognize the charity of the Son of God in assuming our flesh; or finally refer the mystical senses to the Mother of God: all Catholic interpreters agree that these things are contained and represented in the Song of Songs. [Col. 0031B]

Perfectly understanding mysteries of this kind in the figures and figurative expressions used by the sacred writer, Saint Bruno introduces now God conversing with the soul, at other times the Church with Christ, now the friends of the bridegroom, at other times the friends of the bride; and he wonderfully preserves and describes the proper traits or characters of each person from beginning to end. Yet what is more remarkable, although in his commentary he sought brevity, nothing is omitted: every point is brought to its proper meaning. I shall not hesitate to acknowledge that in many matters Bruno agrees with the interpretation formerly attributed to Cassiodorus, which clearly demonstrates that he used it; yet he does not omit the other Holy Fathers who illustrated the Song of Songs, as we shall note in the proper places. [Col. 0031C]

Before this commentary is placed an elucidation by the same author of Solomon’s parable “On the Valiant Woman,” in which he as it were prepares readers for the mystery of greater elevation which he had proposed to explain in the Song of Songs.

## CHAPTER II. ON THE THEOLOGICAL DOCTRINES

### § I. On the Divine Attributes

Having set forth the order and purpose toward which Saint Bruno directed his interpretations of the divine books, a very broad field now opens to me for discussing the theological doctrines in which he was so deeply versed, as will be evident from what I shall bring forward. And indeed, although God’s attributes are beyond narration, since God inhabits inaccessible light and His nature is immense and incomprehensible, nevertheless Bruno provides such conceptions of His essence, omnipotence, eternity, immutability, and goodness that we must confess they can belong to none other than the supreme Being, the first cause—that is, God.

Accordingly, understanding God’s essence to be indicated by those words of Exodus, chapter 3, “He who is has sent me to you,” he says, p. 49, col. 2:

> “Let Him, therefore, speak who always is; who is always the same; who never began to be; who never ceases to be; who receives being from no one; who gives being to all; who does not change in Himself from being to not-being. He who is thus named has sent me to you; for this name belongs to no other; this is the name of God alone.” [Col. 0032B]

Saint Bruno says similarly of God in his commentary on Job, chapter 14, p. 248, col. 1:

> “Because God always is, He is the same, immutable, and always present to all things and all times. Therefore He alone is, because no other thing is in this manner.”

This image of the divine nature represents God so properly that it belongs to Him alone. For who can claim being as so peculiarly his own that he has always existed from himself, has received being from no one, but has given being, whenever it pleased him, to all things; whom no other cause preceded; who is infinite—that is, who contains within Himself every excellence and property of virtue and cannot be circumscribed by any bounds?

> [Note: [Col. 0031D] “God must be conceived as infinite, because He had no beginning of His existence and will have no end; He is the efficient cause of all creatures, visible as well as invisible; He is everywhere through His essence, presence, and power; He rules and governs all things and fulfills His will in all things.” See St Thomas, *Summa Theologiae*, I, q. 7, arts. [Col. 0032D] 1, 2, and 3.]

He who is infinite must be omnipotent; therefore omnipotence is an attribute of God. Concerning it, Bruno writes on Genesis, chapter 1, p. 1, col. 12:

> “In the beginning of all creatures God created heaven and earth, and namely those things contained therein—that is, the angels and heavenly powers—and the earth, already as it were pregnant and in travail, the matter and mother of all things that arise from it.”

Moreover, on p. 3, col. 1, he adds concerning omnipotence:

> “A twofold firmament is said to have been made by God: that, namely, which revolves without interruption, in which the sun, moon, and stars appear. But there is another heaven above this, of far worthier and more excellent nature, to which the ancient enemy, desiring to ascend, said: ‘I will ascend into heaven,’” etc. [Col. 0032D]

God is immutable; for although He created the world in time, He cannot be said to have changed. “There is no change in God”—these are Bruno’s words in the same place, p. 5, col. 2—“to whom nothing new happens, to whom both past and future are present, and who, before making the world, already held it made in the disposition of His mind.”

> [Note: [Col. 0032D] “In God no will following upon another changed or removed a preceding will; but by one and the same eternal and immutable will He caused the things which He created—first not to be, while they were not, and later to be, when they began to exist.” St Augustine, *City of God*, XII.17.]

> “Nor, when He creates anything, is He moved in any respect, because so far as concerns Himself He does nothing new. Rather, because before times He ordained how and in what place or time things were to be arranged, He commands them to be made in the way and at the place or time in which they were ordained. Therefore the world existed before it was made, because it never had any beginning in God.” [Col. 0033A]

God is eternal. Saint Bruno continues, p. 5, col. 1:
