> “For all things which are made in time lived in Him before times. Hence it is well said: ‘He who lives for ever made all things together.’ For He created all things together, because He disposed together when and in what manner all things should be made.”

Since, therefore, no beginning can be conceived in God—indeed, He Himself is the beginning of all things and the efficient cause of every creature—and since He remains what He has always been, it necessarily follows that throughout eternity [Col. 0033B] He will remain the same.

> [Note: [Col. 0033D] “The notion of eternity follows upon immutability, just as the notion of time follows upon motion, as is clear from what has been said, etc. Hence, since God is supremely immutable, eternity belongs to Him. Nor is He merely eternal: He is His own eternity, whereas no other thing is its own duration. But God is His own uniform being. Therefore, just as He is His own essence, so He is His own eternity.” St Thomas, *Summa Theologiae*, I, q. 10, art. 2.]

The conception which the holy bishop gives of God’s goodness is excellently expressed in these words:

> “God is good of Himself and substantially good; other things neither are nor are good of themselves, but from God they are whatever they are. Let us therefore praise the Lord, for He is good, substantially good, and can never be anything but good.” P. 526, col. 2.

### § II. On the Trinity

He who discussed the divine attributes so excellently gave no less lucid an account of how the august mystery of the Trinity is to be understood. For, expounding the words of Genesis, chapter 1, p. 6, col. 1, “Let us make man,” he says:

> “It is God, therefore, who speaks. Does He speak to the angels? Far be it. For man was not created by angels; otherwise there would be not one Creator but many, whereas God alone is Creator of all. Thus it is written, 2 Maccabees 1:24: ‘Creator of all, terrible and mighty’; and likewise Psalm 103:24: ‘You have made all things in wisdom.’ If, therefore, it is true, as cannot be denied, that God alone created all things, whom was He inviting to create man when He said, ‘Let us make man’? Let us then hear what is said at the beginning of this book: ‘In the beginning God created heaven and earth.’ You have, therefore, God—that is, the Father; and you have also the beginning—that is, the Son. For He Himself says, John 8:25: ‘I am the beginning, who also speak to you.’ But what follows? ‘And the Spirit of God moved over the waters. [Col. 0033C]’ You therefore have the Holy Spirit also.”

> [Note: [Col. 0033D] In his commentary on this passage of the Psalm, Saint Bruno, p. 359, col. 1: “Briefly, in this verse the mystery of the Trinity is declared. For what are [Col. 0034D] the Lord, His Word, and His Spirit, except the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit? One is the God by whose will the heavens were created.”]

> “And that not the Father alone created heaven, but that the Son and the Holy Spirit also created it together with Him, let the Psalmist say, Psalm 32:6: ‘By the Word of the Lord the heavens were established, and by the Spirit of His mouth all their host.’ The whole Trinity—that is, God and His Word and His Spirit—is one God. And this God says, ‘Let us make man,’ not seeking help outside Himself, but disposing all things within Himself together with His Son and the Holy Spirit.” [Col. 0034A]

Nor does our author less forcefully establish the truth of the mystery of the Most Holy Trinity from another testimony of Genesis itself, chapter 18, where it is said: Abraham saw three and worshipped one. On this Saint Bruno speaks as follows, p. 18, col. 2:

> “Abraham always grows in faith; he always deserved to know greater things concerning God. Behold, what was then unknown to all, he sees God in Trinity and worships God in unity—not because he saw the Trinity itself, but because through what he saw he deserved to know God in Trinity and unity. Thus, though he saw only three, he nevertheless worships only one and calls only one ‘Lord.’”

But passing over the remaining testimonies to this mystery drawn from other passages of Scripture, Saint Bruno treats the Trinity most expressly in chapters 1, 2, and 3 of book IV of the *Sentences*, where he clearly, appropriately, and learnedly sets forth the whole theological doctrine. In the first chapter, after citing Deuteronomy 6:3, “Hear, Israel: the Lord thy God is one God,” and Psalm 80:5, “If Israel will hear Me, there shall be no new god in thee, neither shalt thou worship a strange god; for I am the Lord thy God,” he proceeds most wisely:

> “Reading these words and not understanding them, the Jews mock Christians, as though they worshipped not one God but three gods. To them the Lord rightly says in the Gospel, Matthew 22:29: ‘You err, knowing neither the Scriptures nor the power of God.’ For we worship not three gods, but one God in three persons; and we worship the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. God is one, the Son is God, and the Holy Spirit is God; yet not three Gods, but one God. For these three persons are one essence, one deity, one power, one majesty, one wisdom, one strength, one omnipotence, one light, one beginning, one brightness; and whatever else is said of one person, apart from personal property, is said equally of all. And as the Father is God, so also are the Son and the Holy Spirit God, omnipotent, strong, great, and wise, and whatever else may similarly be said. Yet they are not three gods or three omnipotent beings, but one God, one omnipotent, one strong, great, and wise God.” [Col. 0034D]

> [Note: [Col. 0034D] “Whatever devout hearts can conceive concerning the eternal and unchangeable glory of the Father, let them understand this likewise of the Son and the Holy Spirit, inseparably and without distinction. For we confess this blessed Trinity to be one God because in these three persons there is no diversity of substance, power, will, or operation.” St Leo the Great, Sermon 73, On Pentecost 1, ch. 3.]

> “But this is personal property: the Father is believed and understood to be begetter; the Son, begotten; and the Holy Spirit, neither begetter nor begotten, but proceeding from both.”

In the course of this chapter our author expounds the creed commonly called Athanasian and draws from it teachings confirming the Catholic dogma of the Trinity. Especially in the distinction of persons, he establishes identity of nature, as he had already done in his commentary on Psalm 60, p. 434, col. 1, on “He shall dwell in him unto the end”:

> “The Father dwells in the Son, being the same in the same. For although the Father is one and the Son another, the Father is not one thing and the Son another thing. The Father, therefore, will dwell in the Son unto the end; and since neither Father nor Son will have an end, the Father is always in the Son, the Son always in the Father, and the Holy Spirit in both.”

He had likewise said in his commentary on Psalm 70, p. 450, col. 1, that the Son does not differ from the Father in righteousness because He does not differ in substance.

In the second chapter Saint Bruno first discusses the indivisibility of the divine essence, although it is found in three distinct persons:

> “This unity is divided indivisibly; for although the persons are three, God is nevertheless one—not divided into parts, but whole in each. Since one substance of God is in the individual persons, it appears in a certain manner to be divided; but because it is whole in each, it is shown to be undivided. For the whole essence of divinity is in the Father, whole in the Son, whole in the Holy Spirit; because the Father is God, the Son is God, the Holy Spirit is God, and these three are one God.” [Col. 0035B]

Our author teaches the same in chapter 5, book IV of the *Sentences*, “On the Circumcision of the Lord,” expounding the words of John in the First Epistle, chapter 5: “There are three who bear witness on earth: the Father, the Word, and the Spirit; and these three are one.”

After this he establishes the distinction between temporal substance, mutable and capable of contraries, and divine substance, eternal, immutable, and subject to no contrarieties. He says that the latter is always simple and one, the same numerically, though always existing in more than one person. Having laid this down, he proceeds to refute the error of the Arians. He first employs the same exposition of the divine essence that he had given in commenting on Exodus, chapter 3, and draws his conclusion through these arguments:

> “For God is always wholly wisdom, always wholly power, truth, light, beginning, and the like. Nor is being and being omnipotent different in Him; all these things in Him are one.” [Col. 0035C]

> [Note: [Col. 0035D] “This Trinity is one and of the same nature and substance, not less in each person than in all, nor greater in all than in each; but as great in the Father and Son together as in the Holy Spirit alone, and as great in the Holy Spirit alone as in the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit together.” St Augustine, Letter 170, otherwise 66, no. 5.]

> “The Father is all these things, the Son all these things, and the Holy Spirit all these things. How then can the Father be greater than, [Col. 0035D] or older than, the Son, since the Son is eternal and there is nothing before the eternal? If something could exist before the eternal, then the Father could exist before the Son existed. But nothing could exist before the eternal; therefore the Father is not before the Son, especially since the Son of God is the Word of God, the Power of God, the Wisdom of God. For the Father could not exist before the Word, before Power, before Wisdom. What, indeed, would He be if He were not strong and wise? For He cannot be strong without power, nor wise without wisdom. Wisdom is one in the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, and apart from it there is no wisdom. It is that of which it is said: ‘You have made all things in wisdom,’ Psalm 103:24. And this same wisdom is the Word of God, through whom it is written: ‘All things were made through Him, and without Him nothing was made’ (John 1:3). Therefore, if this alone and no other wisdom is in God, either the Father was at some time without wisdom—which it is impious to say or think—or He never existed before this wisdom. It is therefore impossible for the Father to be before the Son.”

To Arius, however, objecting that the begetter naturally precedes the begotten, because one who is begotten presupposes him from whom he is generated, he replies that divine generation is not like the generations of creatures, but is called singular and wonderful in the Scriptures. Yet even among created things there are examples showing that what is begotten need not be later than its begetter: heat and brightness do not appear after fire, but immediately with fire. Therefore the Son of God is called by the Apostle “the brightness” of the Father (Heb. 1:3). Further, the word proceeds from understanding, yet understanding is not prior to the word. Saint Bruno shows this by proving that intelligence, memory, and use in us are one and cannot exist without one another, and that none is prior or subsequent to the others. [Col. 0036B]

In the third chapter our author teaches that the secrets of divinity are unsearchable and that no human wayfarer has been granted comprehension of them. For although Moses and Abraham are said in Scripture to have spoken with God face to face, and although the apostles conversed familiarly with Christ the Lord and heard from heaven the Father’s voice calling Him His beloved Son, they nevertheless did not attain knowledge of what God is in nature or essence. Bruno therefore concludes:

> “If Moses and the apostles, who were full of the Spirit of God, in whom and through whom God spoke, could not see, hear, or understand Him as He is, it seems rash for us to inquire into His essence—especially since He Himself says, Exodus, chapter 33:13: ‘Man shall not see Me and live.’” [Col. 0036C]

Earlier Saint Bruno had established, in chapter 2, book III of the *Sentences*, Christ’s complete equality with the Father as Son of God, explaining Psalm 23:6: “His going forth is from the highest heaven, and His course extends unto its height”:

> “This is what He Himself says, John 16:28: ‘I came forth from the Father and came into the world; again I leave the world and go to the Father.’ Finally, His course is from summit to summit, because in divinity He is equal to the Father in all things. Of Him Daniel also says, chapter 7:13: ‘I saw in the vision of the night, and behold, the Son of Man came in the clouds of heaven; and dominion, honor, and power were given to Him, and He came even to the Ancient of Days.’ The Lord will come even to the Ancient of Days when He appears like the Father and equal to Him in all things. For if there were anything in His divinity in which He differed from Him, He would certainly not attain to Him. Therefore He attains even to Him, because in nothing does He differ from Him.” [Col. 0037A]

A clearer passage in which Saint Bruno asserts the equality of Christ, as Son of God, with the Father is supplied by the commentator on Psalm 109, p. 538, col. 2: “The Lord said unto my Lord, Sit thou at my right hand.” There he recounts the question Christ put to the Jews, Matthew 22:45, what they thought concerning Christ. When they replied that they believed Him to be David’s son, Christ pressed them with these words: “How then does David in spirit call Him Lord, saying: ‘The Lord said unto my Lord, Sit thou at my right hand’? How, when he calls Him Lord, is He his son?” And they could not answer Him a word.

After setting this forth, the holy bishop speaks as follows:

> “This question remains insoluble among the Jews; for no one can understand it except one who believes Christ to be both God and man. For us, therefore, this question is very easy, since we do not doubt that our Savior is David’s Lord according to divinity and David’s son according to humanity. And this is what He says: ‘The Lord, the Father, says to my Lord, His Son: Sit at my right hand.’ To sit with God upon one throne and to sit at the right hand signifies equality. But the Jews believe neither that He is equal to God, nor that He ascended into heaven, nor that He sits together upon the same throne at His right hand. Nor will they depart from this unbelief until they are made the footstool of His feet. This will be at the judgment, when, seeing Him in His majesty, they will most certainly know Him to be both God [Col. 0037C] and man. Therefore the Prophet proves, from the authority of the Father Himself, that the Son is equal to the Father, and that He sits and will sit at the Father’s right hand until His enemies are made His footstool.”

Moreover, in expounding in the same Psalm the words, “From the womb, before the morning star, I begot You,” Saint Bruno teaches most clearly the coeternity of Christ as Son of God:

> “Likewise, the Prophet says that the Lord says to my Lord: ‘I begot You.’ Whence? ‘From the womb.’ When? ‘Before the morning star.’ No time is indicated when ‘before the morning star’ is said, because one ascends into infinity. But what is ‘before the morning star,’ except before it can be spoken, understood, or thought? [lacuna] But what does He mean when He says, ‘From the womb’? For God has neither heart nor womb, nor is there any division of parts in Him. Therefore, when He says, ‘From the womb, before the morning star, I begot You,’ it is as though He said: ‘From Myself, before every creature, and before it can be spoken or conceived, I begot You.’ Thus far the Father to the Son.”

[The supplied source ends here, with this sentence incomplete.]

But St. Bruno also wrote most learnedly on the Holy Spirit and his procession from the Father and the Son in his treatise *On the Sacraments and Mysteries*, where he treats of confirmation, and particularly of John 20:22: that, when Christ was about to give the apostles the Holy Spirit, he breathed upon them. “Our Saviour,” he says, “could have given the Holy Spirit without any breathing; but he gave him by breathing, in order that we might understand that he proceeds from himself also, as from his Father. For although we do not know how the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son [Note: [Col. 0037D] “Let no one, however, suppose that in those things which were seen by bodily eyes his divine substance—that is, the substance of the Holy Spirit—appeared. For the invisible nature, common to the Father and the Son, displayed the character of its gift and work by whatever sign it willed. But it retained the property of its essence within its Godhead; for just as human sight cannot reach the Father or the Son, so neither can it reach the Holy Spirit.” St. Leo the Great, Sermon 73, *On Pentecost* 1, ch. 3.]—for this is revealed to no one in this life, in which we see only through a mirror and in an enigma [1 Cor. 13:12] [Note: [Col. 0038D] “To distinguish between that generation and this procession—I do not know how; I am unable; I am insufficient.” St. Augustine, book II, or III in other editions, *Against Maximinus*, ch. 14, no. 1.]—yet we know with complete certainty and do not in the least doubt that he proceeds from the Father and the Son, that is, from the substance of the Father and the Son. For this belongs properly to him: the Holy Spirit proceeds from no other substance, is sent by no one else, and is given by no one else. He is indeed given through the ministry of priests, but not by priests. Thus the power of Christ is present through the breathing performed by priests, in honour of the signification of the Holy Spirit, through the words spoken in his name.”

A. N. likewise asserted this procession of the Holy Spirit in his commentary on Exodus, p. 89, col. 2; and also his manifestation to the apostles on the day of Pentecost, of which we shall speak below.

That we may assist our own weakness, the holy bishop urges us to consult what the holy Fathers have handed down concerning the ineffable mystery of the Trinity. “Let the faith,” he says, “of the saints suffice us. For we are not better than our Fathers; nor should we seek beyond what has been divinely revealed to them. And since we cannot understand even ourselves and those things which are within us, let us not labour to stretch ourselves out toward things above us.”

## § III. On the Incarnation of the Lord

By his most exalted counsel God had created man in his own likeness and filled him with the spirit of wisdom and understanding, in order to bring him to the knowledge and love of himself. For he made him a participant in such great dignity and light for no other reason than to grant him the capacity and abundance of his own knowledge. Would that he had not fallen from that excellent and blessed state through fault! Would that he had remained in the innocence and integrity of his original condition [Note: [Col. 0038D] “Man was created such that by his own will he was able both to sin and not to sin; and therefore the fall of his voluntary transgression was justly punished in him, because no natural necessity of flesh or soul compelled him to sin.” St. Fulgentius, *On Predestination and Grace*, ch. 2 [Col. 0039D].]! That light, by which he might have looked most closely upon the face of God, would not have been darkened in him [Col. 0038D], nor would he have lost the privileges of his original condition. “Man,” says St. Bruno, Sermon 1 *On the Trinity*, “was created by God as it were in the morning, because, retaining God’s likeness, he seemed truly close to the light. For he was able to behold God at close hand—namely, in himself and through himself, with no external thing intervening. [Col. 0039A] But he lost both nearness and likeness when he subjected himself to the evil of disobedience.”

From this utter calamity it pleased God, in his infinite mercy, to rescue man through his only-begotten Son clothed in human flesh; and he who had not spared the transgressing angels deigned to provide for humankind’s salvation. [Note: [Col. 0039D] “When the fullness of the human race had collapsed in its first parents, the merciful God willed through his only-begotten Son Jesus Christ to assist the creature made in his image, so that the restoration of nature might not be outside nature, and the second creation might advance beyond the dignity of its own origin. Happy would he have been had he not fallen from what God made! Happier if he had remained in what he received!” St. Leo, Sermon 70, *On the Resurrection* 2, ch. 2 [Col. 0040D].]

Many figures of this great mystery and sacrament went before it in the earliest patriarchs, so that the true coming of the promised Restorer—foretold and prefigured so many ages beforehand—might sustain faith and hope of redemption among humankind. First, Bruno said, in his commentary on Genesis, p. 14, col. 1, that Abel, slain by his brother Cain, signifies Christ crucified by his brothers, namely the Jews. Second, Jacob represented Christ. [Col. 0039B] “Jacob came,” he says, p. 32, col. 2; “Christ came. But how? Do you wish to hear how? Wrapped in goatskins—that is, in the likeness of sinful flesh. For he emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, etc. This was the first garment of man, when the first man was expelled from Paradise. Thus Christ came clothed in such a garment, bringing with him two excellent goats: one for sin, the other for a whole burnt offering—namely, his flesh and blood; for by these original sin is remitted and God is appeased from indignation.”

Third, A. N. understood as a symbol of Christ the stone upon which Jacob himself slept. “That stone,” he says, “upon which Jacob slept, is Christ, who in many places is called a stone. John the Evangelist also, reclining upon [Col. 0039C] his breast, deserved to see things no less great than Jacob did,” p. 32, col. 1. And again, p. 34, col. 1, he says of the same stone: “For that stone signified Christ’s flesh, in which all the fullness of divinity dwelt bodily; of whom it is written: ‘Wisdom has built herself a house’ [Prov. 9:1]—that is, the flesh which he assumed, because the Word was made flesh.”

Fourth, he also asserts, p. 39, col. 1, that Joseph prefigured Christ. “For Joseph,” he says, “whose name is interpreted ‘increasing,’ signifies Christ, whose kingdom and dominion grew so greatly that it filled the whole world.”

Fifth, St. Bruno said in two places that Moses bore the type of Christ. In his commentary on Exodus, ch. 2, p. 48, col. 2, he says: “In those days [Col. 0039D] Moses went out to his brothers and saw their affliction. He also saw an Egyptian striking a Hebrew; Moses killed the Egyptian and hid him in the sand. Likewise Christ our Lord, coming into this world, killed many Egyptians—that is, evil spirits—deprived them of their power, and cast them out of possessed bodies.” On Exodus 24, p. 84, col. 1, he writes: “Moses, the lawgiver and mediator of God’s people, [Col. 0040A] signified Jesus Christ, the mediator between God and men, the giver of both Testaments.”

A. N. asks whether a human being or an angel could have been fit to render satisfaction to God, and teaches in his treatise *On the Incarnation of the Lord* that neither could have merited so great a benefit for humankind. No human being, he says, could offer this saving sacrifice, worthy of God, because all were bound by original and actual sin, and consequently were excluded from this sacrifice as hateful and unworthy. Nor could an angel have accomplished it in his own nature; for, being incorporeal and therefore invisible, he could not offer himself as a sacrifice of suffering. Perhaps, if an angel had assumed human nature and suffered in it, he might have brought salvation to all human beings? But such love cannot be supposed in angels; for, according to the Apostle, Romans 5:7, scarcely would anyone die for a righteous person, much less be condemned for an unrighteous one. There was also this consideration: before Christ’s coming, human beings were hated by angels because of sin; and the occasion had to be removed lest, if the same human being were redeemed by an angel, he should venerate that angel as God—he who already worshipped stones, wood, and bronze as God.

Therefore, since an angelic victim was excluded by these and many other reasons, the Creator alone remained: he who, out of mercy and his accustomed compassion for humankind, might free oft-mentioned man and rescue him entangled from the devil’s jaws. And this was not to occur in his own nature: rather, since he had come to redeem man alone, God and man was to be offered in sacrifice. These foregoing statements presuppose St. Augustine’s teaching in book XIII *On the Trinity*, ch. 10: that divine omnipotence was not without other ways of saving humankind, but that the way he chose was the most fitting of all. For God could graciously have forgiven sin, or the injury of sin, and accepted the satisfaction of a human being, even though unequal and imperfect. But on the hypothesis that God was unwilling to free and absolve man except by demanding satisfaction that was commensurate and equal—so that, once it had been made, God would be bound by justice to forgive human guilt—it was necessary that this satisfaction be rendered by God incarnate, since no mere human being, however adorned with grace, could render an equal satisfaction [Col. 0040D].

“Since, however, the Catholic Church believes that there is a distinction of persons in the Godhead—namely, Father, Son, and Holy Spirit—it is not without reason,” says A. N. in the same treatise *On the Incarnation*, “to consider to whom this assumption belonged [Note: [Col. 0040D] St. Fulgentius demonstrates excellently and solidly that the Incarnation did not belong to the Father or the Holy Spirit in his treatise *On the Faith to Peter*, ch. 2.]. If the Father were to assume a human being within the virginal womb and to be born from that human being, Father and Son would be identical: the Father according to divinity, the Son according to [Col. 0041A] humanity—which it is wicked even to believe or say. Another and greater impiety would likewise follow, because there would be two sons in the Godhead: namely, the Father as son according to humanity, and the Son of God as son according to divinity. Thus, this great error being avoided, the aforesaid assumption did not belong to the Father.

“It remains to ask whether the Holy Spirit would be fitting to offer himself in sacrifice. But if that same Spirit were to assume a human being and will to be sacrificed for him, the aforesaid error would fall upon the Godhead; for truly two sons would be believed and held to exist in it: the Son of God according to divinity, as we have said, and the son of the Holy Spirit according to humanity. Therefore the aforementioned assumption was not fitting for either the Father or the Holy Spirit, because neither of them could be admitted in such a matter [Col. 0041B]. The Son alone, then, was suitably present to accomplish this: to him belonged by justice the saving of the human being created by himself, opposition to the devil who claimed his power, deceiving the one who had deceived man, and—after taking away his dominion over the whole world—binding him forever in hell [Note: [Col. 0041] The same truth was established by St. Thomas, *Summa Theologiae*, III, q. 3, art. 8, but by other arguments, which need not be reported here.].”

The holy bishop had already explained this same mystery in his exposition of Psalm 67:20, p. 439, col. 1: “Our saving God, our God, God of salvation, shall make the journey prosperous for us; and to the Lord belong the issues of death. ‘Our saving God,’ he says, ‘shall make the journey prosperous for us’: by whom we may understand especially the Son of God, who saved us by his death. He is also our God, because although he is God of all, he is properly the God of Christians. He is likewise the God of salvation, because he came for this purpose: to redeem and save the world [Col. 0041C]. And he is the God to whom belong the Lord’s issues of death.’ By this is understood that he is God even of himself; for, because he is both God and man, according to his humanity he is a servant and a creature, and is a servant. Yet this servant is Lord. And he himself is the issue of death; for just as all died in Adam, so all have been made alive in Christ [1 Cor. 15:22]. He is the entrance into life; he is the issue of death, because through him death departed and through him life arrived.”

He also said in his commentary on Psalm 115: “Human nature, corrupted and ruined through sin from the first man, and passing in the same condition to all human beings, could be healed and freed only by Christ’s blood.” And below, on the words of Psalm 116, “You have broken, O Lord, my bonds,” etc.: [Col. 0041D] “I was bound,” he says; “the hard chain of the devil constrained and dragged me. But you broke my bonds; you loosed original sin, which could not be loosed except by your blood.”

## § IV. On the Announcement of the Divine Motherhood to the Virgin Mary

For a work of such magnitude and dignity the angel Gabriel was sent by God to the Virgin Mary, betrothed to Joseph and dwelling in the city of Nazareth. Mary is greeted by the angel as full of grace; heavenly blessing is announced to her; the Holy Spirit’s coming upon her and the power of the Most High are promised; [Col. 0042A] and the secret of divine motherhood is revealed.

David had long before prophesied this in Psalm 44: “Hear, daughter, and see, and incline your ear; forget your people and your father’s house, for the King has desired your beauty.” Bruno explains these words in his commentary, p. 389, col. 2: “Hear,” he says, “my daughter, of my stock, of my offspring, the nobility and glory of my race; hear what the angel says, what the heavenly messenger promises you. Be chaste; be watchful; listen attentively, for the things announced to you are very great. Therefore see and understand. Incline your ear, and receive the Word in your heart and womb: a virgin you shall conceive, and a virgin you shall bear. Incline your ear, because through the ear he who shall be born from you will enter into you. For he is the Word, and the ear is the path of the word. [Col. 0042B] The blessed Mary conceived in no other way than by hearing and believing. Had she not heard, she would not have believed; she heard and believed, and by believing conceived.”

Bruno also eloquently adorned the pre-eminent figure of Mary’s integrity in the bush which appeared to Moses burning yet unconsumed, in his commentary on Exodus 3, p. 49, col. 1: “But what does the bush signify, if not the blessed Virgin Mary, who arose from the thorny and sinful race of the Jews as the lovely fragrant rose grows from the roughness of the bramble? She was seen burning, yet did not burn, because, overshadowed by the Holy Spirit, she conceived without the desire of the flesh or the heat of lust. For this is what the angel says: ‘The Holy Spirit shall come upon you, and the power of the Most High shall overshadow you.’ Therefore there was fire in the bush, splendour in [Col. 0042C] the Virgin, light in Mary—that light which says, ‘I am the light of the world’ [John 8:12], the true light which enlightens every person coming into this world [John 1:9],” etc.

He also asserts Mary’s virginity in the clearest terms while explaining the words of Leviticus 12: “If a woman, having received seed, bears a male,” etc. “The fact,” he says, p. 145, col. 2, “that he did not simply say, ‘If a woman bears a male,’ but added quite carefully, ‘if, having received seed, she bears a male,’ was undoubtedly said to distinguish the Blessed Virgin Mary, who bore the Saviour without a man’s seed.”

He further explains at length how the power of the Most High overshadowed the Virgin Mary in the homily on the Gospel *Missus est*, etc., Luke 2. “For this power,” he says, “is common to the whole Trinity. For the whole Trinity is one God, and that same God is the Most High [Col. 0042D]. Therefore Christ was born of the Holy Spirit, from the Virgin Mary—that is, from the power of the Holy Spirit, which is one and common to Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. But the Son is the Son of the Father alone, and the Father is the Father of the Son alone. This power, then, coming upon her, overshadowed Mary and brought about Christ the Lord from two natures. For as rational soul and flesh are one human being, so God and man are one Christ. In respect of his humanity, he was not only made and created by the Father and the Holy Spirit, but also by himself. But in respect of his divinity [Col. 0043A], he was neither made nor created, but begotten by the Father alone.”

## § V. On Christ’s Birth, Circumcision, and Manifestation

“Therefore the most blessed Virgin gave birth,” St. Bruno continues in the same commentary on Luke 2:7, “a virgin conceiving, a virgin giving birth, and a virgin remaining for ever. Closed before childbirth, closed in childbirth, and closed after childbirth [Note: [Col. 0043D] St. Leo the Great agrees, Sermon 2, *On the Nativity of the Lord*, ch. 2: “For it was fitting that the incorruptibility of the one being born should preserve the original integrity of his Mother, and that the unconquered power of the divine Spirit should keep inviolate the enclosure pleasing to itself—of modesty and the dwelling-place of holiness.” [Col. 0044D].] She bore,” he says, “her first-born son, wrapped him in swaddling cloths, and laid him in a manger, because there was no place for them in the lodging. O immeasurable mercy! O ineffable humility! O inexpressible sacrament! God becomes man; the eternal becomes temporal; the immense becomes confined to a place; the immortal becomes capable of suffering; he who, because of his greatness, is not contained by the circuit of heaven [Col. 0043B] is wrapped in little swaddling cloths.”

To shepherds keeping watch over their flock in that same region, the angel immediately announced Christ as born, laid in a manger, and wrapped in swaddling cloths, with Mary his mother and Joseph. Admonished by this vision, the shepherds compared among themselves what they had heard and seen, saying, “These things are wonderful.” Explaining the same passage of Luke, Bruno says: “Wonderful are the things we heard; astonishing are the things we saw. Glory is promised to heaven, peace to earth. A Saviour has today been born to us; a new king has today been given to us, who is Christ in the city of David. Let us go and see this Word, and let us believe, because in the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God [John 1:1]. ‘Which was made’: in respect of itself, it was neither made nor created [Col. 0043C]. It was made only in this sense, that the Word was made flesh—which the Lord has shown us. Let us see bodily what we have conceived in mind and hold by faith; it remains for us to hold it with our eyes. And they came in haste and found Mary and Joseph and the child lying in the manger [Luke 2:6].”

Because Christ the Lord had come to fulfil all righteousness and to show himself a true human being, not shadowy or phantasmal, he chose to submit himself to the law of circumcision at the prescribed time. St. Bruno discusses the circumcision of Christ the Lord in two places. The first is on Luke 2:15: “The Lord is circumcised for us, not for himself. For just as he was born, baptized, and suffered for us, so he was circumcised for us, concerning whom the Apostle says, Romans 4:11: ‘Because he received the sign of circumcision, a seal of the righteousness of faith’ [Col. 0043D].”

Circumcision, then, was given not to take away sins but to signify something and to set the Jewish people apart from other nations by a certain distinction. Therefore, although anyone in former times who was not circumcised because of transgression of the command was condemned, he was not justified through circumcision. For this circumcision was fulfilled in Christ, in whom the other ceremonies of the Law were also brought to completion.

The other passage occurs in Sermon 5, *On the Circumcision of the Lord*, book IV of the *Sentences*: “Since our Saviour received this circumcision in his flesh, there was a very reasonable cause: he did not come to abolish the Law, but to fulfil it. For, as the Apostle says, Romans 10:4, ‘Christ is the end of the Law unto righteousness for everyone who believes.’ In him the Law has been fulfilled; those who are circumcised after him gain nothing.” The meaning of circumcision is explained by St. Thomas, *Summa Theologiae*, III, q. 37, art. 3, where he says: “Just as the Son of God became man and was circumcised in the flesh not for himself but in order to make us gods by grace and that we might be spiritually circumcised, so he is presented to the Lord for our sake, that we may learn to present ourselves to God.”

While Jesus remained in the manger at Bethlehem, [Col. 0044B] the Magi came from the east, guided by a star shining with new brightness, to worship him, and offered him the gifts they had prepared. A. N. contemplates many mysteries in the Gospel passage and explains them in his commentary on Matthew 2; only some of these will be given, lest we become too lengthy. “But why,” he says, “does the star go before them, except to show them the way and lead them to the child? They follow it, therefore, and come to Bethlehem. It stands over that house in which the Virgin Mary was; star stands over star, for Mary is interpreted ‘star of the sea.’ Thus the Son is a star, and the mother also a star; a star rises from a star, but the one which rises is greater than the one from which it rises. Therefore it rightly appears to stand above it. It did not say, ‘above the child’; but what did it say? ‘Above where the child was’ [Col. 0044C]. For where was the child, except in his mother’s bosom? The star therefore stood and cried out—for it has its own language [lacuna]. But what did it signify? What did it say? Do you wish to hear what? ‘This is the child; this is the child’s mother; seek him here; here you will find him; here he lies hidden in a little body; here he is everywhere and fills all things.’ For this is what it says: ‘When they saw the star, they rejoiced with exceedingly great joy.’ What does ‘seeing the star’ mean, except seeing and understanding what was signified and said to them through the star? For it is no great joy to see stars. We often see the sun and moon, and do not greatly rejoice at seeing them. They rejoiced, therefore, not because of the star, but because of what the star signified. And entering the house they found the child with Mary his mother, and, falling down, they worshipped [Col. 0044D] him; and, opening their treasures, they offered him gifts: gold, frankincense, and myrrh. How great your exultation must have been, O most blessed Virgin—who can conceive it? For him whom you had lately borne, you now saw worshipped as though Lord. But why did they offer three gifts, except to reveal the mystery of the Trinity? For we offer the first gift by believing in the Father, the second in the Son, the third in the Holy Spirit. What do we think gold signifies, except royal power, greater than the rest and shining more widely? Thus we offer gold to Christ, whom we believe to be king of all [Col. 0045A]. We also offer frankincense because we confess that he is God; and we offer him myrrh because we believe him to be God in such a way that we do not doubt he is also human and mortal.”

Since these matters have been explained more than sufficiently, they need not be further confirmed by similar statements in Sermon 6, *On the Epiphany of the Lord*, in the same book of the *Sentences*.

That same Christ the Lord, in order to establish the truth of his coming in accordance with the prophets’ oracles, chose to be presented in the Temple and, as first-born, redeemed by the legal offering. St. Bruno is no less copious in expounding the divine matters related by the Evangelist Luke, 2:28, concerning this presentation of Christ. I shall cite only some remarks from his commentary on St. Simeon, who received Christ into his arms. “For the Evangelist briefly shows what kind of man and how great this Simeon was when he says that he was righteous, feared the Lord, waited and longed for the consolation of the people, and that the Holy Spirit, who was in him, had revealed and promised to him the coming of the Son of God [Col. 0045B]. And this is what he says: ‘He had received an answer from the Holy Spirit that he should not see death before he had first seen the Lord’s Christ.’ With what longing to see the Lord did this most blessed old man burn! Age already compelled him to depart this world, but God’s answer held him back. Desiring to die, he could not die, because he had not yet seen the Lord’s Christ, concerning whom he had heard the answer given him: ‘He shall not see death before he has first seen the Lord’s Christ.’ This, then, he desired; this he pondered in his mind; this he always thought upon [Col. 0045C]. Thus Christ revealed himself to Simeon and fulfilled the prophecy of Malachi, who had foretold that he would come into his Temple, 3:1: ‘And immediately the Lord whom you seek shall come into his temple, and the angel of the covenant whom you desire.’”

Jesus fled into Egypt, escaping Herod’s persecution; when Herod had been taken from life, he returned to Galilee and lived with his parents in the city of Nazareth. Now the parents of Jesus went every year to Jerusalem on the solemn day of Passover. And when he had become twelve years old, as they went up to Jerusalem according to the custom of the feast day, and when the days were completed and they returned, the child Jesus remained in Jerusalem, and his parents did not know it, Luke 2:41. The same holy commentator explains what is to be understood in this place of the Gospel: “The devout parents,” he says, “went to Jerusalem each year to hear the Law, participate in the sacrifices, attend the solemn observances, and served the shadow of him whose truth they already possessed. For the whole festival signified Christ’s passion, resurrection, and the other things written concerning him. Jesus, who was the cause of the whole solemnity, was therefore there in the feast together with the others. Mingled among the crowds, he was seen by all, praised by all, proclaimed in the Law and Prophets, signified in the sacrifices, and recognized by no one, because he was covered by a double veil: on one side, the veil of the letter; on the other, the wall of the flesh [Col. 0045D].”

[Col. 0046A] At last the time came when Christ had to give a more splendid testimony of his manifestation and fulfil his mission into the world. Therefore, as we have from Matthew 3:13: “Then Jesus came from Galilee to the Jordan to John, to be baptized by him.” Here the holy bishop includes many teachings in his commentary: on the institution and necessity of Christ’s baptism, the end of circumcision, the revelation of the Holy Trinity, and the truth of the new faith; and at the same time he arouses great wonder at Christ’s and John’s humility.

“For ‘then,’” he says, “is to be understood as the time when John preached such things and baptized, not when he began to preach; for both had already entered their thirtieth year when the Lord came for baptism [Col. 0046B]. Jesus is baptized not for himself, but for us. He washes the waters and sanctifies them by his touch; he is not himself washed by the waters. There the old circumcision perished; there the renewal of the new faith began. There John first learned to baptize, where he came to know, hear, and see the mysteries of the whole Trinity. John was then terrified and trembled to approach the Lord, forbidding him and saying: ‘I ought to be baptized by you, and do you come to me?’ But Jesus answered and said: ‘Allow it now, for thus it is fitting for us to fulfil all righteousness.’ ‘You,’ he says, ‘are greater; you are Lord; I am lesser and a servant. I must decrease, but you must increase. Why, then, do you come to me? I ought rather to go to you. You are clean and cleanse all things; it is not you by me, but I by you, who ought to be cleansed and baptized.’ But he says: ‘Allow it now: what I do is a mystery. While I am baptized, you also are baptized in me, because you are a member of him who is baptized. Thus it is fitting for us to fulfil all righteousness, setting an end and limit to the old things, but giving an example and rule to the new [Col. 0046C].’

“After Jesus had been baptized, he immediately came up from the water; and behold, the heavens were opened, and he saw the Spirit of God descending like a dove and coming upon him; and behold, a voice from heaven saying: ‘This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased.’ What, St. Bruno asks, does it mean that the heavens are opened when the Lord is baptized? And he replies: It is a great mystery and prefigures great joy for those who are baptized. It was previously shut; no one entered it before baptism; but now it is open. He saw the Spirit of God descending like a dove, not because the Holy Spirit was incarnate in a dove—for the Son alone was incarnate—but because the Spirit of God chose to show himself in a dove. And whose was that voice heard from heaven, if not the Father’s? For who else could say, ‘This is my beloved Son’? God the Father is well pleased in his beloved Son because he begot such a Son ineffably and without beginning before time. The Trinity is most openly shown in this passage, in which it is perceived wholly in its persons: the Son is declared in the man, the Holy Spirit in the dove, and the Father in the testimony of his voice [Col. 0046D].”

Up to this point Christ’s manifestation had been made only [Col. 0047A] to certain persons, as though the first fruits of his acquisition—namely, the shepherds, the Magi, Simeon, and John the Baptist. But when the time had come for fulfilment of his mission, and he had drawn some people into following him, he also deigned to confirm them in faith and imitation of him by certain signs. Therefore Jesus, invited to a wedding at Cana of Galilee, went there, attended the marriage feast with his disciples, and there performed the first of his miracles.

But because Christ seemed to have replied somewhat sharply to his mother when she requested that water be turned into wine, because the wine had failed the wedding guests [Note: [Col. 0047C] Petavius, book XIV, *On the Incarnation*, ch. 1, §6. See the note on St. Maximus of Turin, p. 68.], as though she had wrongly asked for something when the time had not yet come for him to do what she desired, our Bruno elegantly explains the mystery concealed in the Evangelist John’s words, chapter 2: “When the wine failed, [Col. 0047B] the mother of Jesus said to him, ‘They have no wine.’ For the Virgin Mary, full of the Holy Spirit, already foresaw the miracle that her Son would perform. What Jesus was thinking of doing, she prompted him to do. And Jesus says to her: ‘What is there between me and you, woman?’ ‘What is common between me and you,’ he says, ‘except this mortal flesh and this humanity which I bear, which knows how to suffer hunger, thirst, and death, but does not know how to perform miracles? For water’s conversion into wine belongs not to humanity but to divinity. My hour has not yet come: the hour of my passion has not yet come, in which what is common between me and you will become known to all. Then you will see the flesh which I received from you not performing mighty works and miracles, but hanging and dying on the cross.’

“His mother said to the servants: [Col. 0047C] ‘Whatever he tells you, do.’ Mother and Son spoke with one another. They understood one another; they knew their own secrets; they knew what ought then to be done and what would happen. But the others did not know what they were saying.”

All marvelled at the water turned into wine by Christ; and through that miracle Jesus, as the Evangelist testifies, manifested his glory, and his disciples believed in him.

But because Christ the Lord had not come to seek his own glory but the glory of his Father, who had sent him to save humankind, he was led by his Spirit into the desert to begin so great a work with prayer and a fast of forty days and forty nights, and to provide his followers with an example of how they might obtain heavenly aid. When the fast was completed and he had three times overcome the devil who came to tempt him, he chose twelve apostles. Among them were first Peter and his brother Andrew, then the sons of Zebedee, James and John, all fishermen, and the rest described by St. Matthew, chapter 4, who were to be the columns and foundations of the Church. He said to them: “Come after me, and I will make you become fishers of human beings” [Mark 1:17]. “But what does ‘Come after me’ mean?” says St. [Col. 0048A] Bruno. “To follow Christ in deed is to follow his footsteps, imitate his works, and maintain his patience and humility. For it is not enough for us merely to walk after Jesus with our feet, unless we follow him also in mind and love.”

Having taken these first followers with him, Christ began his preaching. As St. Matthew testifies, chapter 5:13: “Jesus went throughout all Galilee, teaching in their synagogues, preaching the Gospel of the kingdom of God, and healing every sickness and infirmity among the people. And his fame went throughout all Syria, and they brought him all who were ill and afflicted with diverse diseases,” etc. There St. Bruno adds in his commentary on the same passage, 4:23: “See how suddenly Christ is manifested; see how suddenly the report and fame of his power fill the land [Col. 0048B]. From every side all who are sick and ill are brought to him, and he, as the true physician, heals every infirmity, inward and outward.” He also discusses the same matters more fully in his commentary on Psalm 15, p. 324, col. 1.

## § VI. On Original Sin
What was the cause of the great evils that inundated the world and brought the human race into such calamities? Certainly none other than the fault of Adam, the first parent, in which all his descendants shared. It is certain that all sinned in Adam; and therefore, just as sin passed into all human beings, so death, with all evils, passed into them.

> [Note: Col. 0047C] “For the first man transmitted to all human beings the deserts of his sin, whose flesh is conceived under the law of sin. For this reason, in infants, although there is no sin arising from their own will, there is nevertheless in children born carnally as children of wrath the parental stain, which indeed does not disturb the well-ordered arrangement of divine creation, but by the blemish of the paternal transgression inflicts upon those born a grim deformity.” St Fulgentius, *On Predestination and Grace*, book I, ch. 3.

We have this truth from the Apostle, Romans 5:12: “Therefore, as through one man sin entered into this world, and death through sin, so death passed into all human beings, in whom all sinned.” What and how great was the sin of the first man Adam, which infected and condemned all his offspring, cannot be understood unless the state of perfection, excellence, and dignity in which he had been created is recognized. Bruno describes this outstandingly in his *Commentary on Genesis*, ch. I, p. 6, col. 2, expounding the words, “Let us make man in our image and likeness”:

> “Although ‘image’ and ‘likeness’ are distinct, in this passage both image and likeness signify the same thing. Thus man was made in God’s likeness: he was made wise, righteous, and good, immortal and incorruptible. But since it is said,” says the same St Bruno, “‘God created man in his image,’ and then it is added, ‘in the image of God he created him,’ this may also be understood to mean that God gave man bodily as well such an image as he had ordained before the ages that the Son—who is undoubtedly God—would one day assume. Thus not only our inward but also our outward man might in some manner be like him.”

> [Note: Col. 0048C] St Augustine aptly warns what should be thought concerning this image in man, *On the Trinity*, book XV, ch. 26: “Yet he should not so compare this image, made by that same Trinity and altered for the worse by its own fault, to the Trinity itself as to suppose it similar in every respect; rather, in whatever resemblance he sees, he should also discern a great dissimilarity. I have given this warning as far as seemed sufficient.” [Col. 0049D–0050D]

Bruno derived this teaching from Tertullian. For in *On the Resurrection of the Flesh*, ch. 6, where he treats of the first man formed from clay, Tertullian speaks thus:

> [Col. 0049A] “Consider that God was wholly occupied and engaged upon him—with hand, feeling, counsel, wisdom, providence, and above all with that affection which traced his features. For whatever was being expressed in the clay, Christ, the man to come, was being contemplated: he too was clay and flesh, and the Word likewise, who was then earth. For thus runs the Father’s address to the Son: ‘Let us make man in our image and likeness.’ And God made man—that is, what he had fashioned—and made him in the image of God, namely, of Christ. For the Word too is God, who, existing in the form of God, did not consider equality with God to be robbery. Thus that clay, already bearing the image of Christ to come in the flesh, was not merely God’s work but also a pledge.”

But after Adam sinned, transgressing God’s command not to eat the fruit of the tree of the knowledge of good and evil, he became unlike that image of God in which God had created him. For he lost righteousness, wisdom, immortality, and goodness—gifts of God, not properties of his own nature—and became mortal, unrighteous, a slave of sin, subject to concupiscence, and darkened in understanding. Therefore A. N., speaking of paradise, said, p. 9, col. 1:

> “He also placed the tree of the knowledge of good and evil; after the first human beings had eaten from it, they learned what goods they had lost and what evils they had become subject to.”

They also experienced the corruption of nature and the rebellion of the flesh, which had previously been subject and obedient to the spirit; and this evil was propagated to all their offspring.

> [Col. 0049C] “Human nature,” says the same St Bruno on Psalm 115, p. 547, col. 1, “having been vitiated by sin in the first man, is found corrupted in all human beings and can be healed and liberated only by Christ’s blood.”

He also treated excellently of the state of innocence in which Adam was created, at the same place, p. 9, col. 1:

> “How greatly the Lord loved man can also readily be understood from this: that he had prepared for him such a dwelling-place that, if he had not sinned and had begotten children in a most chaste marriage without any concupiscence, then, when the number of the elect had been completed, he would ascend to the heavenly Jerusalem without tasting any bitterness of death; differing from the angels neither in merit nor in number, he would enjoy eternal blessedness.” [Col. 0049D]

The author of so great a calamity for our first parents was the devil. Cast out of heaven with his followers through pride and hurled into the abyss of fire, he envied the condition of man and sought, through the enticement and persuasion of the woman, to cast him down from the happiness he enjoyed.

> [Note: Col. 0050D] See Augustine, *City of God*, book XIV, ch. 2; and Fulgentius, *On the Faith addressed to Peter*, ch. 3, no. 33, Roman edition, 1740.

Hence A. N. found occasion to ask how, after all things which God intended to create had been completed on the sixth day, it could be said, “God saw all the things that he had made, and they were very good,” if evil—or the devil himself, prince of evil—were there. He answers, p. 7, col. 2:

> [Col. 0050A] “Had he not yet fallen, though John 8:44 says, ‘He did not stand in the truth, and from the beginning he was a liar’? Or perhaps on the very day on which man was made, envying his glory and therefore giving deadly counsel, he lost his own dominion together with his goodness. For the condemnation of man and demon is read as occurring at the same time, not one earlier than the other. Since the woman said, ‘The serpent deceived me, and I ate,’ the Lord immediately cursed the serpent, saying: ‘You shall be cursed among all living creatures and beasts of the earth.’ He also said to the woman: ‘I will multiply your afflictions.’ But to Adam: ‘Cursed is the earth in your work.’ I have found nothing certain concerning these matters in the books of the apostles and prophets, and I have learned that the doctors of the Church held differing views. Yet I say that, even if he had fallen earlier, it could nevertheless have been said that God saw all the things he had made, [Col. 0050B] and they were very good, because even in the devil himself there still remains good which God had made.”

Nor can any evil be conceived in the fruit which Adam and Eve ate; for, as St Augustine teaches in the same book of the *City of God*, ch. 12, in a paradise of such happiness there was nothing that was not good. But eating that fruit was evil because it was forbidden. The transgression of the command, however, involved grave guilt, since, as the same holy doctor continues:

> “The virtue of obedience is, in a rational creature, in some manner the mother and guardian of all virtues, since that creature was so made that subjection is beneficial to it, while it is harmful for it to do its own will rather than that of him by whom it was created. Thus, this command concerning not eating one kind of food—when such an abundance of others lay at hand—so slight to observe and so [Col. 0050C] brief to retain in memory, especially when desire did not yet resist the will, as afterwards resulted from the penalty of transgression, was violated with so much the greater injustice because it could have been kept by an easier observance.”

Yet let no one, with the heretics, conclude from this that concupiscence, or the inclination toward evil, which arose in man as the penalty of sin, took away freedom of choice—that is, the power to do good. That desire indeed wounded and weakened free choice, so that man experiences resistance in choosing good; but it did not extinguish it. He still retains the capacity of active indifference and can turn himself in whichever direction he wishes. I shall adduce our Bruno as an upholder of this orthodox doctrine. Expounding Psalm 69, p. 446, col. 1, “O God, attend to my help; O Lord, make haste to help me,” he teaches:

> [Col. 0050D] “This prayer suffices for us in all that we ask, especially if we are afflicted by enemies and adversaries. Everywhere and in all things God’s help is to be sought, because everywhere and in all things it is necessary, since without his help we can do nothing. If we wish to do good, we pray well and profitably; and if we wish to do evil—which we ought not to wish—we likewise pray well and profitably: it is indeed a great help from God if he resists evil desires and does not permit them to be fulfilled. Therefore let one who desires to do some evil first say, ‘O God, attend to my help,’ and he will not be able to do what he desires. Let the Lord therefore hasten to help the good, that they may do what they wish; and let him hasten also to help the wicked, that they may not do what they wish.” [Col. 0051A]

> [Note: Col. 0051D] What Bruno teaches here—that the good should implore the Lord’s help in order to do the good they wish, and that the wicked should use the same prayer in order to be turned away from the evil they desire—rests on Augustine. In book I, ch. 3, *Against Two Letters of the Pelagians*, Augustine states that the freedom to act well is given to human beings by God himself, in accordance with John 8:36: “If the Son shall make you free, you shall be truly free.” Having established this truth, he adds: “Therefore power is given for them to become children of God, who believe in him, when that very thing is given them—namely, to believe in him. Unless this power is given by God, it cannot arise from free choice; for that which the Liberator has not made free will not be free for good, though the will is free for evil when either a hidden or open deceiver implants in it the delight of wickedness, or when it has persuaded itself.” [Col. 0052D]

But such freedom of choice seems scarcely preservable in hardened persons, who are left in such great wickedness that, suffering in it, they do not repent—as happened to Pharaoh, concerning whom God said to Moses, Exodus 4:20: “I will harden his heart.” A. N. proposed this difficulty to himself in his commentary on this passage of Exodus, p. 53, col. 1, and resolved it as follows, affirming that freedom of choice remains [Col. 0051B] untouched:

> “I will harden his heart. What is this, Lord? Will you harden his heart? For, as the Apostle says, ‘You have mercy on whom you will, and whom you will you harden.’ But if you harden him, and no one can resist you, what fault is Pharaoh’s? Why is he punished for not dismissing the people when he cannot dismiss them? He cannot because he is hardened. By whom? By you. For you say: ‘I will harden his heart.’ It must be understood otherwise. Therefore the statement, ‘I will harden his heart,’ is as though he said: ‘I will permit his heart to be hardened; I will use no force and will leave him wholly to himself. Let him do what he wishes, so that, if he acts well or ill, it may all be imputed to himself and not to me.’”

Therefore, just as Pharaoh’s hardening, according to Bruno, came wholly from himself—for he would have overcome it had he wished—so also all sinners, if they wish, can overcome their inclination toward evil. Yet that someone may be left in an evil will because of long resistance to grace was the view of Bruno and other holy Fathers. For in the same *Commentary on Exodus*, ch. X, p. 57, col. 1, where he treats of the darkness which had occupied all Egypt, Bruno says:

> [Col. 0051C] “Behold those who follow the king of darkness: though so often warned and scourged, though seeing so many signs and miracles, they still persist in wickedness with hardened heart; wrapped in darkness, they see nothing and remain immovable like stones.”

Once these matters concerning original sin have been ascertained—“which,” as St Augustine says in book VI *Against Julian*, ch. 12, “is proper and voluntary for each individual: voluntary indeed by the will of origin, but proper by the property of nature and person”—we can understand what A. N. said in many places concerning the effects of original sin. For in Genesis, ch. II, p. 9, col. 2, upon the words spoken by God to Adam, “On whatever day you eat from it, you shall die the death,” he says:

> “Adam indeed died as soon as he ate—not because he immediately departed from this life, but because, when he should depart from it, he took death [Col. 0052A] into himself.”

He confirmed the same point on Deuteronomy, ch. XXI, p. 205, col. 1: “When a man has sinned in a matter punishable by death and has been condemned to death”:

> “Perhaps this is because the first man then hung on a tree when he took the forbidden fruit from the tree, and the human race was condemned to death. Therefore everyone who hangs on a tree and is still held by original sin is accursed.”

Further, in Exodus, ch. XII, p. 60, col. 2, where the destruction of all the Egyptian firstborn is recounted, he says:

> “All the firstborn in the land of Egypt died, because original sin perished throughout the whole world in all those who believed and were baptized, so that the sin which began through the tree of concupiscence might be destroyed through the tree of the cross. For as many human beings as there are, so many original sins there are; for every one of them is born with that sin, which could not be erased except by Christ’s blood and the water of baptism.” [Col. 0052B]

Finally, omitting other testimonies, I shall add this one from the *Commentary on Exodus*, ch. XXXIV, p. 123, col. 1: “Who take away iniquity, crimes, and sins, and with you no one is innocent by himself.”

> “No one,” says St Bruno, “is innocent before you, because not even an infant one day old is without sin. Hence the Psalmist, Psalm 50: ‘For I was conceived in iniquities, and in sins my mother bore me.’ Therefore one who is not innocent by himself becomes innocent through you, because you alone can make clean one conceived from unclean seed” (Job 14:4).

## § VII. On the Grace of God the Saviour

Therefore, once man had been deprived of original righteousness and rendered unable to recover it by his own powers—since, as Scripture says in Genesis 8, the sense and thought of his heart had become inclined to evil—there follows the necessity of divine assistance: namely, grace, which supplies fallen man with powers by which he may perform the good ordered toward eternal life. It is called grace because it is given freely; it is illumination in the intellect and devout affection in the will. St Bruno taught this grace and its necessity in many places, following St Leo, who said: “What fell in the first Adam is raised in the future one.” Expounding the Genesis passage mentioned above, p. 19, col. 2, Bruno says:

> “Human nature, frail and miserable in itself, easily falls into sin unless it is protected by God’s help; therefore it appears worthy of mercy.”

In the same spirit he speaks on Psalm 139:8, “Lord, Lord, strength of my salvation,” saying: “Without his help and strength I cannot be saved.” Likewise, on Psalm 144:20, “The Lord directs the righteous,” he says: “For it is by his grace that they do not depart from the straight path.”

> [Note: Col. 0052D] Augustine, *Against Two Letters of the Pelagians*, book I, ch. 3, no. 7: after stating that no one believes in Christ unless it has been given to him, he continues: “Therefore no one can have a righteous will unless, with no preceding merits, he has received from above true—that is, gratuitous—grace.” [Col. 0053D]

Again, on Psalm 62:7, “Thus I remembered you upon my bed; in the mornings I shall meditate [Col. 0053A] on you, because you have been my helper,” he says the same:

> “Ungodly people and sinners are in night and darkness. But the saints are in the mornings, since they see the light of truth and draw near to the Sun of righteousness. ‘Because you became my helper’: therefore I have always remembered you, and will remember you, because in every place and in all my needs you have always become my helper.”

Moreover, on Psalm 83:6, “Blessed is the man whose help is from you,” he says:

> “Blessed is that man whom you so assist in this life that by your help he may be able to ascend to that home. For no one comes unless you draw him.”

And on Psalm 59:14, “In God we shall act valiantly, and he will bring to nothing those who afflict us”:

> “In God we shall act valiantly, and he will go forth in our acts of strength, [Col. 0053B] because, as he said, without him we can do nothing.”

But since the Semi-Pelagians admitted the necessity of grace for the completion of a good work, though not for the beginning of a good work, he opposed to them Catholic doctrine, expounding Psalm 118:117, “Help me, and I shall be saved”:

> “God is the one who works in us both willing and being able, and without his help we can do nothing.”

> [Note: Col. 0053D] See St Fulgentius, *On the Faith addressed to Peter*, book I, ch. 3, no. 34; and ch. 16 of *On Predestination and Grace*, where he teaches: “Just as no one can have the beginning of a good will unless he has been enlightened by the prevenient mercy of God, because ‘the will is prepared by the Lord’ [Proverbs 8:35], and again it is written in Psalm 58:11, ‘My God, his mercy will go before me’; so too no one can preserve that same good will until the end unless he is continually kept by that same ensuing mercy.”

When St Augustine was asked whose a good will is—God’s or man’s—he answered in *On the Merits and Remission of Sins*, book II, ch. 18, no. 30:

> “For if we have from God a certain free will which can still be either good or evil, while a good will is from ourselves, then what is from us is better than what is from him. But if this is said most absurdly, they must admit that we too are divinely taught to have even a good will.” [Col. 0053C]

Therefore, if a good will is from God, the beginning of a good work will also be from God, and not from ourselves, “because,” as the same holy doctor says in *On Grace and Free Will*, ch. 17, “he works in us that we may will, by beginning; and, in those who will, he cooperates by bringing to completion.”

> [Note: Col. 0053D] The same St Augustine had said in *On the Grace of Christ*, ch. 14: “For if, as Truth declares, everyone who has learned comes, then whoever does not come has certainly not learned. Who, moreover, does not see that whether one comes or does not come depends on the choice of the will? But that choice can stand alone if one does not come; it cannot stand alone, however, if one wishes to come, unless it is helped—and so helped that one not only knows what ought to be done, but also does what one knows.” [Col. 0054D]

A. N. teaches that this power of doing good, or grace, which is called sufficient grace, is given to all; but not so effective grace, which is an impulse of the will, or a heavenly desire carrying man toward the fulfilment of God’s commands. Therefore, illustrating Psalm 118:40, “Behold, I have desired your commandments,” he says:

> “I have not merely performed your commandments, but have desired [Col. 0053D] to perform them. For anyone can perform them, but to perform them with desire belongs to heavenly grace.”

St Bruno set forth the same doctrine more clearly in his commentary on Psalm 102:2–4, p. 517, col. 2:

> [Col. 0054A] “Forget not all his recompenses: who will be gracious to all your iniquities; who heals all your infirmities; who redeems your life from destruction; who satisfies your desire with goodness; who crowns you in pity and mercies.”

> “These recompenses,” says the holy bishop, “are great, and so great that we should never forget them. The Lord became gracious to all our iniquities, because by his blood he wiped away not only original sin but, together with it, all other sins. And this is what he says: ‘Who heals all our infirmities’; all, indeed, because he leaves none to be healed. He speaks of the soul and calls its sufferings infirmities. He redeems [Col. 0054B] its life from destruction, which could not happen unless he had first forgiven its sins. He also satisfies its desire with good things, because he has bestowed upon it the most steadfast hope of eternal blessedness. Hence the Apostle says, Romans 9:24: ‘For we were saved in hope.’ He crowns in pity and mercy because he who gives the crown is himself the one who gave the victory; nor could it have conquered unless his help had been present.”

A. N. maintains that the benefit of this help is given with no preceding merits, but proceeds solely from the good will of God. Explaining Psalm 29:8, p. 353, col. 2, “Lord, in your good will you bestowed strength upon my beauty,” he says:

> “You added beauty, and beyond beauty you added this strength which I possess. But this was [Col. 0054C] with no preceding merits, but from your good will. Hence the Apostle says, Romans 9:16: ‘It is not of him who wills, nor of him who runs, but of God who shows mercy.’ ‘What do you have that you did not receive?’ (1 Corinthians 4:7.) Therefore all the virtue, constancy, and strength of the saints belongs not to themselves but to God.”

> [Note: Col. 0054D] Whatever good the saints do, according to St Augustine, *On Grace and Free Will*, ch. 16, must be referred back to God: “Therefore, that we may will, he works without us; but when we will, and so will that we act, he cooperates with us.” In agreement is the author of *On the Calling of the Gentiles*, book II, ch. 8: “Grace is therefore given without merit, so that it may advance toward merit; and it is given before any labour from which anyone may receive recompense according to his labour.”

I shall add another most beautiful passage of the same holy bishop, p. 388, col. 2, on Psalm 44:8: “Therefore God, your God, has anointed you with the oil of gladness above your companions.” After saying that all the fullness of divinity dwelt in Christ, he teaches that, besides the apostles, all others too become participants in it, “who have been chosen, not by their own merits, but by his adoption, to share in the inheritance.” [Col. 0054D] The grace by which they are raised to this adoption he calls the oil of gladness because of the joy which rightly acting souls feel so long as they do not lose such an anointing. These are his words:

> [Col. 0055A] “This oil is rightly called the oil of gladness because it grants joy and gladness to all who are anointed, provided that they do not lose the anointing.”

Although Christ died for all and, as the Apostle says in 1 Timothy 2, wills “all human beings to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth,” to which all are called, nevertheless not all are chosen. When A. N. reflected on this mystery, he referred it wholly to the most profound divine will. What he thought of it appears in his commentary on Psalm 91:6, “Your thoughts are exceedingly deep”:

> “Why one vessel is made for honour and another for dishonour; why Jacob is chosen and Esau rejected before they are born—let him who can [Col. 0055B] resolve it.”

He had said similar things on Job 41:2, p. 295, col. 1, “And who has first given to me, that I should repay him? All things under heaven are mine”:

> “It is as though he said: Those whom I defend are defended by mercy; those whom I do not defend are dealt with by justice. For although all things are mine, they do not all serve me as mine; and even if they did serve, they would serve not from their own but from what is mine. Those who have given me nothing beforehand ought not to demand anything from me as if it were owed. Concerning this most profound question the Apostle says, Romans 11:33: ‘O the depth of the riches of the wisdom and knowledge of God! How incomprehensible are his judgments and unsearchable his ways!’”

Since it is established that God freely chooses some and deprives others of this election, I shall put forward our Bruno as an upholder of this truth. In his exposition of Psalm 58:6, p. 417, col. 2, “And you, Lord God of hosts, God of Israel, attend to visit all nations,” he says:

> [Col. 0055C] “He is the God of hosts, in whose hand and power are all powers; he bestows them on whom he wills, dispenses them as he wills, and rejects from himself whom he wills. ‘It is not of him who wills, nor of him who runs, but of God who shows mercy’” (Romans 9:16).

The same author teaches still more clearly the election of the righteous before foreseen merits in his commentary on Exodus 33:19, p. 122, col. 1. Having recounted Moses’ prayer beseeching God for the people who had transgressed by worshipping the golden calf, he says:

> “What follows, ‘I will have mercy on whom I will, and I will be gracious to whom it pleases me,’ is as though he said: ‘You pray for your people; you intercede for those whose hearts and thoughts you do not know. I know whom I have chosen; I will have mercy on whom I will, for I will nothing but good.’” [Col. 0055D]

> [Note: Col. 0055D] The doctrine expounded is wholly from St Augustine. For in *On the Merits and Remission of Sins*, book II, ch. 17, he teaches: “Why he wills to convert some, while punishing others for turning away—although in bestowing a benefit no one can justly blame one who is merciful, and in exacting vengeance no one can justly blame one who is true, just as among those Gospel labourers no one could justly blame him for giving some their agreed wage and reproving others for not accepting the agreed wage—belongs to the counsel of a more hidden justice in himself. Let us be wise and understand, as far as is granted us and as far as we can, that the Lord God, who is good, sometimes does not grant even his saints either certain knowledge of some good work or victorious delight, so that they may know that the light by which their darkness is illumined and the sweetness by which their land yields its fruit come to them not from themselves but from him.” [Col. 0056D]

The exposition of Psalm 133:4 says the same:

> [Col. 0056A] “For the Lord has chosen Jacob for himself, Israel for his own possession.”

> “It has been proved for the best reason,” he says, “that the Lord is kind and gracious: namely, because before he had done anything good or evil, with no preceding merits, God chose him for himself solely by his kindness. And he chose not only Jacob himself, but all Israel—that is, all his offspring, later called from Israel himself—to be his own possession and inheritance.”

No less apt for confirming the same view are the words which the holy bishop gives on Psalm 44:8, p. 388, col. 2, “Therefore God, your God, has anointed you with the oil of gladness above your companions”:

> “To others the Spirit is given by measure, but in him—that is, Christ—all the fullness of divinity rests bodily” (Colossians [Col. 0056B] 2:9). “His companions are the apostles and all others who have been chosen for the inheritance not by their own merits.”

And because the election or predestination of the saints, according to St Augustine, *On the Predestination of the Saints*, ch. 10, is the preparation of grace, while grace is the gift itself—so that whoever are delivered are most certainly delivered—

> [Note: Col. 0056D] “This predestination of the saints is nothing other than the foreknowledge and preparation of God’s benefits, by which all who are delivered are most certainly delivered.” St Augustine, *On the Gift of Perseverance*, ch. 25.

—A. N. showed himself his follower in the commentary on Psalm 64:5, p. 429, col. 1, “Blessed is he whom you have chosen and taken up; he shall dwell in your courts”:

> “Blessed is the one whom the Lord in his mercy has chosen and taken for himself out of so great a multitude of human beings. This person cannot perish, but without any doubt will receive the goods predestined for him. And he himself will dwell in his tabernacles, concerning which the Lord himself says: ‘In my Father’s house are many dwelling-places’” (John 14:2).

> [Col. 0056C] This doctrine of the free election of the righteous, which Bruno followed, appears fully consonant with the divine oracles. For Wisdom 9:17 says of God: “Who shall know your mind, unless you give wisdom and send your Holy Spirit from on high? Thus the paths of those on earth were corrected, and human beings learned the things pleasing to you. For by wisdom all who have pleased you, Lord, from the beginning were healed.”

Adhering to these words, A. N. said in his exposition of Numbers 1, p. 172, col. 1:

> “The Lord knows both the names and the number of his elect; and truly blessed are those who are numbered in God’s army and whose names are written in the book of life. It is impossible for any of them to perish.”

Indeed, these—namely, the righteous—attain salvation not only through election but also through action, whether they are called in the morning, that is, early, or in the evening, provided that they do the work to which they are called. Keeping this necessity of good works before his eyes, St Bruno taught it thus in his exposition of Psalm 64:9, p. 430, col. 1, on the words “You will delight the goings forth of morning and evening”:
