> [Col. 0057A] “Therefore the Lord delights in the departure of those who go out and flee from the company of the wicked. The morning departure is that which occurs early or in the first age of life; the evening departure is that which occurs late or in old age. Yet God receives all and gives the denarius to both first and last. Remember that Gospel in which the master of the household hires labourers for his vineyard.”

St Augustine said of those called by God: “They are moved so that they may act, not so that they themselves may do nothing.” The same holy bishop says the same in his exposition of Psalm 64:12 and in many other places.

Although St Bruno affirmed gratuitous predestination, which entails the free election of the just [Col. 0057B] and their certain salvation, attained through the gift of victorious grace, he was nevertheless very far from those heretics who say that Christ’s grace necessitates and compels. For he reconciled the efficacy of grace most admirably with freedom of choice, faithfully following Augustine’s teaching in this also. [Note: [Col. 0057C] St Augustine writes in the first book *On the Spirit and the Letter*, chapter 37: “When power is given, necessity is not imposed.” And in chapter 34: “God acts,” he says, “so that we may will and believe . . . but to consent or dissent belongs to one’s own will.” In the second book *On Grace and Free Will*, chapter 15, he shows how under grace the human will is not compelled but free, explaining the words of Ezekiel 18:31, “Make for yourselves a new heart and a new spirit”: “He who says, ‘I will give you a new heart, and I will put a new spirit within you’ (Ezek. 36:26)—how then does he who says, ‘Make for yourselves,’ say, ‘I will give you’? Why does he command, if he himself is to give, unless because he gives what he commands when he helps the person whom he commands to do it? Free will is always in us, but it is not always good: for either it is free from righteousness when it serves sin, or it is free from sin when it serves righteousness, and then it is good. But God’s grace is always good, and through it a person of evil will becomes a person of good will. Through it also the good will which has already begun to exist is increased and becomes great, so that it may be able to fulfil [Col. 0058C] the divine commandments which it wills, when it wills them very fully and perfectly.”]

For, explaining the words of Psalm 67:10, “You will set apart a voluntary rain, O God, for your inheritance,” he says: “This rain is not compelled but voluntary, because it is voluntarily given and voluntarily received. But because the Jews were unwilling to receive it, God set it apart for his inheritance.” But lest these words be taken as merely incidental remarks, they may be confirmed by two passages. In his commentary on Exodus 4:20, after explaining the Lord’s words, “I will harden Pharaoh’s heart,” he concludes thus: “Hence [Col. 0057C] it follows that the salvation of the good is due to the grace of God, who, drawing them to himself with the bridle of his mercy, does not permit them to sin even when they wish to sin. This he does not by using force, but by softening the heart and changing it for the better.”

A second and most extensive passage is supplied by the exposition of Christ’s conversation with the Samaritan woman, found in the commentary on John 4:7–11. The woman comes to Jacob’s well to draw water, where she finds the Lord resting. He says to her, “Give me a drink”; but when she hesitates that such a request should be made of her by a Jewish man, Jesus answers and says to her: “If you knew the gift of God, and who it is that says to you, ‘Give me [Col. 0058A] a drink,’ perhaps you would have asked him, and he would have given you living water.” St Bruno explains this as follows: “If you knew me, and were enlightened by the Holy Spirit—for the gift of God is the Holy Spirit—you perhaps would have asked of me, as I now ask of you; and I would have given you unfailing living water, water sufficient unto eternal life.”

By these and other words addressed to the woman, Christ kindles in her a desire for more perfect water and raises her mind to the truth which, under the metaphor of water springing up unto eternal life, he presents for belief. “Gradually,” says our author, “the Lord separates her from her own understanding, in order to draw her to a better understanding. Now somewhat separated from her former understanding, the woman no longer understands the water of that well; she asks for another water, by which, always abounding, it may no longer be necessary for her to come there [Col. 0058B] again.” Thus the Samaritan woman is drawn to Christ not by compulsion but sweetly and gently; she gives him full faith and announces him among her fellow-citizens as the promised Saviour. [Note: [Col. 0058D] By the same inward and gracious compassion and illumination, as St Augustine teaches in *On the Grace of Christ*, chapter 45, Christ aided Peter, who had denied him three times. “What is written in Luke 22:61, ‘The Lord looked upon him,’ was accomplished inwardly, in the mind, in the will. The Lord secretly came to his aid by mercy; he touched his heart, recalled his memory, visited Peter with his inward grace, and moved the inner man even to outward tears, bringing forth emotion.” And St Prosper, interpreter of St Augustine, says in book III *Against the Conferencer*: “The Lord makes the unwilling willing; by whatever means he inclines the unbelief of one who resists, so that the heart of the hearer, with delight in obedience produced within it, may rise where it was oppressed; may learn where it was ignorant; may trust where it distrusted; may will where it did not will. For Psalm 84:2 says: ‘The Lord will give goodness, and our land will yield its fruit.’”]

Bruno continues, in his exposition of John 4:44, “No one can come to me unless the Father who sent me draws him,” to describe the wonderful gentleness with which God calls human beings to do good, and the delightful impulse by which he draws them to himself: “He draws,” he says, “not by violence but by love. In this sense it is said: ‘Each man is drawn by his own pleasure’ [Virgil, *Eclogues* II.65]. But God draws no one unless he is willing and desires salvation.”

This will is stirred in us by the light of truth, by which we are enlightened; by the fire of charity, by which we are kindled; and by the hope of heavenly blessedness, [Col. 0058C] by which we are refreshed. Bruno himself strengthens us in this hope of our salvation, though we have been sinners. Citing Psalm 144:8–9—“The Lord is merciful and compassionate, patient and greatly merciful; the Lord is gracious to all, and his mercies are over all his works”—he thus extols divine mercy: “No place is left for despair after so great a repetition of mercy. Only the person who does not believe these things, and who, having heard them, nevertheless persists in his wickedness, can despair. Of such persons the Apostle says in Romans 7:32: ‘But according to your hardness and impenitent heart, [Col. 0059A] you store up wrath for yourself on the day of wrath and of the revelation of the righteous judgment of God, who will render to every one according to his works.’ Therefore his mercies are over all his works, because there is nothing in his works that can be compared with mercy. Mercy drew him down to earth and compelled him to undergo the death of the cross; mercy filled heaven and restored the fall of the angels.”

Finally, lest one who, aided by God’s mercy, acts well should attribute anything to himself, but should refer back to God’s aid whatever he does according to righteousness, Bruno offers the following exposition, p. 179, col. 2, on the cloud described in Numbers 9, which always covered the tabernacle, shining in the night and protecting it by day from the heat of the sun: [Col. 0059B] “By this cloud are signified the graces of the Holy Spirit, by which the darkness of our ignorance is enlightened and we are defended from the heat of vices and the fires of lust. For we are God’s tabernacle, of whom the Apostle says in 2 Corinthians 6:17: ‘I will dwell in them and walk among them.’ But what does it mean that at the command of this cloud the tabernacle is both pitched and moved, except that when we act well we are not under our own power, but under that of the Spirit who is in us? For by him we are governed, by him instructed, and by him directed along the straight way to our homeland.”

That Bruno remained constant in this opinion is shown by what he says in his commentary on the passage in Matthew 25: “Lord, you delivered to me two talents.” “You gave me,” he says, “understanding and activity; for you give understanding [Col. 0059C] to those who understand; you bestowed both good will and the effect of acting well. Hence the Apostle says in Romans 9:16: ‘It is not of him who wills nor of him who runs, but of God who shows mercy’—who first grants the will to act well, and then the ability to run well.” [Note: [Col. 0059D] St Bruno said all this concerning the gratuitous gift of grace under the guidance of St Augustine, who writes in *On the Predestination of the Saints*, chapter 15: “Let human merits be silent here, merits which perished in Adam; and let the grace of God reign, which reigns through Jesus Christ, the only Son of God, our Lord.” [Col. 0060D]]

But lest anyone should suppose that St Bruno, who taught so copiously and learnedly so many and such great things concerning the necessity of Christ’s grace and its properties, passed over in silence the necessity of good works for salvation, he says, among much else which I omit for brevity’s sake, the following on the words of Psalm 74, p. 459, col. 1: “When I receive the time, I will judge righteousness.” “These words,” he says, “are spoken by our Saviour and answer what precedes. ‘When I receive the time,’ he says, ‘I will judge righteousness, and I will give to each according to his merits. Those who confess me, invoke my name, and proclaim my wonders, I will reward with worthy gifts.’ This will take place in the judgment, when both good and evil stand before the tribunal of Christ and are there divided—those who confessed and praised Christ, and those who denied him.” And below in the same psalm, on the words, “A cup is in the hand of the Lord, full of pure wine mixed,” etc., he says: “This cup in the hand of the Lord is the measure of recompense. And it is rightly said to be in the hand of the Lord, because it is in his hand and power [Col. 0060A] to render to each according to his works,” etc.

## § VIII. On the Sacraments

We said above that Christ the Lord chose twelve among his disciples, named them apostles, and appointed them the first workers and ministers in establishing the Church. The Evangelists and the other sacred writers have related most fully the benevolence with which our Redeemer embraced them throughout his life, the hidden heavenly things which he communicated to them, and the commands and institutions by which he trained them to raise and establish that work. And because Jesus Christ had come full of grace and truth, and all who believed in him were to receive from his fullness, he opened the fountains of heavenly blessing, or grace, and made the apostles their dispensers. These fountains are the sacraments, through which grace is given for grace: that is, it is either first communicated to those who receive them or increased in them.

St Bruno treats baptism, the gate of the sacraments, in many places. Passing over what he says when elucidating Exodus 14, p. 64, col. 1, I shall first cite his exposition of John 3, where, extolling its efficacy, he says: “So great is the power of this sacrament that it immediately cleanses a person from every sin.”

In his commentary on Matthew 28:16—“All power has been given to me in heaven and on earth. Go therefore, teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit”—he teaches that such great power in baptism flows from Christ’s divinity and universal authority. “For he,” he says, [Col. 0060C] “who according to his divinity always received, together with the Father and the Holy Spirit, power over all things, is as man the one who lately suffered and who rules both heaven and earth; and he is now believed to be God and Lord, not of the Jews alone but of all nations. Now,” he says, “there is no distinction: ‘He who believes and is baptized shall be saved.’ Teach all; baptize all, whether they are Jews or Gentiles.”

Moreover, both in the exposition of Leviticus 9 and in that of Numbers 7, our author recalls the promises which those being baptized ought to make: to renounce the devil and all his pomps and works. In Deuteronomy 7 he says that one still held by original sin, and therefore accursed, should not remain [Col. 0060D] under the curse; but on that same day, once he has recognized the sinfulness of his death, should be buried in the water of baptism. He also discusses baptism and confirmation appropriately when explaining Numbers 19, p. 186, col. 2, where it is written: “Whoever touches the corpse of a human being and is therefore unclean for seven days shall be sprinkled with this water on the third and seventh day, and thus shall be cleansed. If he is not sprinkled on the third day, he cannot be cleansed on the seventh.” St Bruno comments as follows: “Whoever is born from Adam has touched a human corpse, because before Adam became a corpse and subject to the laws of death, [Col. 0061A] he is not recorded to have begotten anyone. Therefore, as far as he is concerned, he is unclean for seven days, because unless he is regenerated by the water of baptism he is never clean. Hence it is said here that such a person should be sprinkled with this water on the third day, so that, baptized under a threefold immersion, he may deserve to be enlightened by the Lord. He is also sprinkled on the seventh day, so that through the laying on of hands he may be confirmed by the seven graces of the Holy Spirit. But why can one who has not been sprinkled with this water on the third day not be cleansed on the seventh, except because no one is confirmed by a bishop who has not first been baptized in the Trinity?”

From this it follows that in Bruno’s day baptism was still administered by a threefold immersion and the invocation of the most holy Trinity, and that it ought to precede confirmation [Col. 0061B] conferred by a bishop. But St Bruno treats confirmation and its effect explicitly and quite learnedly in his treatise *On the Sacraments and Mysteries*. After discussing baptism, he writes: “Now confirmation alone remains, which is ordered to be performed by bishops and in which the fullness of the mystery of the entire Christian religion is completed. For in baptism remission of sins is given through the Holy Spirit. But here the same Spirit is invoked to come and deign to defend and inhabit the very house which he has sanctified. For the apostles themselves received the Holy Spirit after baptism, whom indeed they had already received in baptism itself for the remission of sins. Then, by breathing upon them, they received [Col. 0061C] the power of binding and absolving from sins; and they received the same Holy Spirit again on the day of Pentecost, for the perfection of all power and knowledge.” He teaches that confirmation is particularly signified by this, and says that it cannot be repeated because it has its effect fully and perfectly.

Bruno considers the sacrament of baptism, or regeneration by water and the Holy Spirit, by which Christ’s blood is applied, so necessary that he declares that all persons, including infants, perish if they die without it. His teaching is as follows, in his exposition of Psalm 118, p. 561, col. 2: “I considered all the transgressors of the earth sinners.” “All human beings,” he says, “were made transgressors in Adam, who, transgressing the law imposed upon him, approached the tree forbidden to him. In that transgression all perish who have not been redeemed by the blood of Christ. But those who have been redeemed become transgressors if they do not keep the law given to them.”

If what the holy bishop of Segni taught concerning these two sacraments, namely baptism and confirmation, agrees perfectly with Catholic doctrine and fully confirms the Church’s tradition in their use, still more excellent and distinguished are the things which he wrote in various places in his works concerning the most holy sacrament of the Eucharist, and set forth earlier at the Roman council [Col. 0062A] against Berengar. Before all else, it is fitting to cite his most splendid exposition of Leviticus 16, p. 157, col. 1, where God promises Moses that he will appear in a cloud above the tabernacle. “[Note: [Col. 0061D] See the entire commentary on Exodus 29, where he treats the sacrifice of the calf and the two rams, whose immolation is interpreted as signifying the offering [Col. 0062D] of the body and blood of Christ the Lord.] The Lord,” he says, “formerly appeared in the cloud and in darkness because he was afterwards to appear veiled by the covering of flesh; for that cloud signified Christ’s flesh. And now he appears in a cloud above the oracle, because in the sacrament he is seen upon the altar under another appearance. Yet it is permitted neither always nor to everyone to approach this oracle, this altar, and sacrament. First it is necessary to offer a calf for sin and a ram as a whole burnt offering—that is, one must believe that Christ the Lord was immolated for our sins and suffered bodily in his entirety [Col. 0062B] upon the altar of the cross.”

Having just described the symbol of the most holy Eucharist and its signification, he now speaks more plainly of it and teaches how it is consecrated in his commentary on the words of Psalm 93: “May the Lord remember every sacrifice of yours, and may your rich whole burnt offering be made acceptable.” “For Christ himself is the great priest according to the order of Melchizedek, who by wonderful power changes bread and wine into the substance of his body and blood, and gave them to his disciples, saying: ‘Take and eat; this is my body; and this is the cup of the New Testament in my blood.’ But on the following day, after doing this, he offered himself for us upon the altar of the cross.”

But an even greater confirmation of the Catholic faith comes from the incontrovertible authority supplied by his commentary [Col. 0062C] on Leviticus 8, p. 141, col. 1, where mention is also made of the celebrant priest’s hands stretched out over the host and the cup to be consecrated. “[Note: [Col. 0062D] See also what he sets forth in his commentary on Leviticus 1, p. 126, col. 2.] And though bishops,” he says, “and priests have their hands stretched out and raised over Christ’s body and blood, yet there is one high priest, Jesus, who sanctifies and blesses, by whose ineffable power bread and wine are converted into the substance of his body and blood. Moreover, he poured out his blood around the altar, because Christ offered us his blood to drink. For the altar is the Church, which is wholly sprinkled and made drunk with Christ’s blood.”

If St Bruno drew from the figures and symbols of the Old Testament such clear and significant testimonies [Col. 0062D] for affirming the transubstantiation, in the sacrament of the altar, of the body and blood of Christ the Lord, what more luminous teaching should we not expect to hear in his commentaries on the Gospels? There he so vigorously defended Christ’s real presence after the consecration of bread and cup. See how he expounds this ineffable mystery while explaining the words of Matthew 26: “While they were eating, Jesus took bread and blessed it, and gave it to his disciples, saying: ‘Take and eat; this is my body.’” Bruno explains here what Christ meant when elsewhere, namely in John 6:54, [Col. 0063A] he said: “Unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man and drink his blood, you shall not have life in yourselves.” “Behold,” he says, “the priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek changes bread and wine, by ineffable power, into the substance of his body and blood. For just as then he was alive and speaking, yet was eaten and drunk by his disciples, so now too he remains whole and incorruptible, and is daily drunk and eaten by his faithful in the sacrament of bread and wine. For unless bread and wine were changed into his flesh and blood, he himself would never be eaten or drunk bodily. These things are changed into those; those are eaten and drunk in these. How this happens is known by him alone who can do all things and knows all things. For he spoke in person, [Col. 0063B] and now speaks through his ministers: ‘This is my body’; and so great is the power and efficacy of his word that what is spoken comes to be immediately. Likewise, when he says, ‘This is my blood,’ the wine is at once changed into his blood. And taking the cup, he gave thanks and gave it to them, saying: ‘Drink of this, all of you; for this is my blood of the New Testament, which shall be shed for many for the remission of sins.’ ‘This,’ he says, ‘is my blood, which is to be shed’: this is not one thing and that another, but this and that are one and the same. Tomorrow, therefore, that blood which you now drink and see in the cup will be shed from this side of mine.”

The same Catholic doctrine shines forth in the commentary on John 6:51: “I am the living bread which came down from heaven,” etc. “If anyone eats of this bread, he shall live forever; [Col. 0063C] and the bread which I will give is my flesh for the life of the world.” “Now,” he says, “with the Lord himself explaining, we understand what this bread is. This bread is the flesh of Christ, which was immolated upon the altar of the cross for the life of the world. The Church eats it, and therefore does not die but lives forever. For the bread and wine placed upon the altar are sanctified by a heavenly blessing at the priest’s word and are essentially changed into Christ’s flesh and blood, so that the substance is one and the same both of that flesh which was born of the Virgin and of that which was made from bread. This great and wonderful sacrament began at the time when our Saviour, blessing the bread and wine, said to his disciples: ‘Take and eat; this is my body. And this is the cup of the New Testament [Col. 0063D] in my blood.’”

Since in the Mass not only a sacrament but also a sacrifice is performed, our author, most learned in these doctrines, affirms in his commentary on Job 1, p. 222, col. 2, that it is performed and renewed daily by priests. There it is said that the holy man was accustomed to offer whole burnt offerings for each of his sons every day. “Job offered whole burnt offerings for each,” he says, “because our Saviour offered himself both for all and for each and every one of the faithful, and does not cease daily to offer himself through his ministers.” A little earlier he had also said concerning the offering of the ram as a whole burnt offering, etc.: “This is that whole burnt offering which is daily performed in the holy Church. For Moses—that is, Christ—offers the ram as a whole burnt offering, because even though it is performed through the ministry of priests, he himself nevertheless immolates and sacrifices his flesh and blood. For it is not the priest’s voice but his own which says: ‘This is my body,’ and, ‘This is the cup of the New Testament in my blood, which shall be shed for you and for many for the remission of sins,’” p. 141, col. 1.

No one will deny that Bruno said these things about the most holy Eucharist together with many holy Fathers. But his teaching concerning Viaticum—that is, the reception of Christ’s body in the final peril of life—is distinctive. It shows that from the most ancient time the Church was accustomed to carry it to faithful persons dangerously ill. Explaining Deuteronomy 15, p. 198, col. 1, where it is said that a servant must not be sent away without provisions for the journey, he writes: “See [Col. 0064B] how good is the Lord, who does not permit even wicked and ungrateful servants to depart empty, but gives them viaticum from the flocks, the threshing-floor, and the winepress. For he understands this sacrament and this name, and does not fail to know what this viaticum signifies. Therefore he urges those repenting at the final hour to receive this viaticum, so that they may be borne safely through their entire life up to the judgment-seat of the Judge.”

While St Bruno rightly extolled the dignity and power of the Eucharistic sacrament, he did not fail to warn Christians that those who approach the sacred table should first take care to be cleansed from sins, lest they partake unworthily of the body and blood of the Lord. Thus, in Leviticus 5, citing Paul’s words in 2 Corinthians 6:1, “We exhort you not to receive the grace [Col. 0064C] of God in vain,” he says, p. 135, col. 2: “That soul appears to sin in things consecrated to the Lord through which entire faith is not applied to the sacraments; for when, insofar as it can, it does not receive grace from them, it certainly commits a very great sacrilege.” He urges this purity still more strongly upon priests, saying: “Let them not approach the altar unless washed; water is near, tears and repentance are near.” Thus in Exodus 30, p. 116, col. 1.

It should therefore not seem surprising that the holy bishop so frequently commends repentance and teaches that Christ’s passion gives it the power to remit sins. See p. 132. But lest anyone suppose that Bruno speaks only of repentance of the heart and considers it sufficient for cleansing the conscience, he deals specifically with sacramental confession in his commentary on Leviticus 7, p. 142, col. 1. “For the Lord wills,” he says, “that we give and disclose our sins to priests, so that we may be filled with their counsels and teaching. Let us give them our fat: let us confess our sins to them; let us tell them what evil our flesh, fattened by wantonness, has done. It belongs to them to burn, to consume, and to destroy sins.”

Again, explaining Psalm 61, “Pour out your hearts before him,” he makes clear to whom confession should be made. “Whatever,” he says, “you have in your heart, reveal and make known to him; and thus, as it is written in James 5:16: ‘Confess your sins to one another and pray for one another, that you may be saved.’ For you confess to God what you confess to his vicars, that is, to bishops and priests. But the person who displays no sign of repentance conceals his sin. Yet in order that one may be cleansed from sins, it is not enough to confess one’s sins to a priest; one must obtain absolution.” [Col. 0065A] Accordingly, St Bruno, explaining Leviticus 13, p. 152, col. 1, confirms this truth: “Why, after repentance has been performed, is a person absolved and reconciled, unless because he is washed and cleansed by the priest’s absolution? Let penitents hear this: their sins are not blotted out, because, persisting in sins, they always add sins to sins.”

Nor will it be superfluous to recount what he adds at the end of the same chapter concerning the necessity of sacramental absolution, on the command to wash even clean garments. “Why,” he says, “are things which are clean washed a second time? Except because, although a person is clean through repentance, nevertheless, unless he has been reconciled and absolved by a priest, he still abstains from the sacraments as unclean. For although he is clean, he is not regarded as clean until he participates with the other faithful in the Church’s sacraments. Therefore he is washed first by repentance, and second by reconciliation and absolution.”

No one fails to see that the heretics raved when they attempted to abolish sacramental confession, calling it a modern invention and proclaiming that repentance of heart was sufficient. Although our author offered such a distinguished [Col. 0065C] testimony concerning sacramental confession—that is, the secret accusation of sins—not only in the passages cited above but also in his exposition of Psalm 31, p. 357, col. 1, he did not forget public penance. Sinners were required to undergo this for graver public offences, in order to obtain reconciliation from the Church according to the prescribed discipline still in force in Bruno’s day. [Note: [Col. 0065D] In this passage St Bruno mentions public penance for public offences, which had to be expiated both by punishment and by example before the penitent was absolved. [Col. 0066D]]

Taking an image from the reconciliation of the leper described in Leviticus 14, p. 153, col. 1, he says: “The priest goes out from the camp to reconcile the leper, because even to this day we see our bishops go out through the doors of the Church to reconcile sinners. But the leper is neither received nor cleansed, because neither ought the sinner who has not done penance for sin to be reconciled. For repentance is to weep for sins committed and not to commit the sins that ought to be wept for.” [Col. 0065D]

No passage occurs to me in which St Bruno treats extreme unction; and he has very little concerning marriage in his commentary on Genesis 2 and John 4. I pass these over, since much must be said concerning orders, of which he wrote so copiously and learnedly that I can scarcely embrace even the principal heads. Since, however, through this sacrament, whose author, like that of the others, was Christ the Lord, a hierarchy is established in the Church—that is, the assumption and appointment of certain faithful persons to sacred ministry and to the propagation of the truth of his law—I shall first [Col. 0066A] treat the Church and then the different grades of orders.

## § IX. On the Church

We understand and profess the Church to be the society of the faithful, subject in spiritual matters to their own particular pastors or bishops, and especially to the Roman pontiff, established as visible head in the universal Church. Of old, the first worshippers of God and those descended from Abraham, the first father of believers, represented the Church; now the Church, of which we are members, rejoices in Christ as its author, and, established in his steadfastness, is sustained by his governance.

“For,” says St Bruno in his exposition of Genesis 2, p. 10, col. 2, “as Eve was made from one rib taken away while Adam slept, so, while Christ slept in the sleep of death [Col. 0066B] on the cross, blood flowed from his side which redeemed and built the Church. He redeemed it by freeing the whole human race from condemnation through his blood; and he built the Church by granting his grace and his Spirit to the faithful, establishing commandments, and promising an eternal reward to those who obey.”

At the beginning of the Church’s birth, says our author in his exposition of Exodus 34, p. 123, col. 1, the apostles alone, called by the Lord, received the faith. He strengthened them by teaching, examples, and miracles for so great a work; and through their ministry, or apostolate, he gathered from every part of the world—so St Bruno himself teaches in *Genesis*, p. 18, col. 2—different nations as it were into one Church. [Col. 0066C] Nor were several Churches made, even though many were founded in different regions of the world, as our author aptly notes in his commentary on the Song of Songs. For when the sacred writer had previously called them vineyards, under which name Churches are understood, and afterward spoke of a vineyard in the singular number, he signified that however many vineyards, that is, Churches, there may be, they constitute one vineyard.

“Many vineyards,” he says, “are many Churches; but the Synagogue is one. The apostles left it, as it is written in Acts 13:46: ‘It was necessary first indeed to speak the word of God to you; but because you rejected it and judged yourselves unworthy of eternal life, behold, we turn to the Gentiles.’ It may also be read as a question: ‘Have I not kept my vineyard?’ Certainly I have kept it. But because he first used ‘vineyards’ in the plural and afterward ‘vineyard’ in the singular, he signified the unity of the Church, which, though divided according to the character of places, is one in faith and love.” [Col. 0066D]

St Bruno affirms the Church’s unity in two other places. First, speaking of the different chambers made by Noah in the ark, he says that they signify the many Churches founded throughout the world, which are contained, like separate rooms, within the same house. “The Church,” he says in *Genesis* 8, p. 17, col. 2, “is without spot and wrinkle. By the chambers he signifies the individual Churches, which, divided among provinces and bishoprics, are contained within the universal Church [Col. 0067A] as separate rooms within a house.” The other passage occurs in his commentary on Exodus 2, p. 49, col. 1: “Even if, because of the diversity of places, there are many Churches in this world, nevertheless in the unity of faith there is believed to be only one Catholic and universal Church.”

The holiness and excellence of this same Church is also asserted by our author in his commentary on Job 42, p. 298, col. 2: “Neither the Synagogue, nor idolatry, nor any other sect can be compared with the beauty of the Church. For it is she who has neither spot nor wrinkle. And she indeed receives an inheritance among her brethren—that is, among the choirs of angels, who are sons of the same inheritance as she.”

[Col. 0067B] We likewise confess the Church to be apostolic, founded and propagated by the apostles. Although, as St. Maximus of Turin says, they obtained equal grace of holiness before the Lord, nevertheless one among them was chosen by him as prince of all and appointed the chief foundation upon which he built his Church.

That St. Bruno splendidly affirmed this truth is evident from two passages. The first is found in his commentary on Exodus, chapter XXXIII, p. 122, col. 2. Having related Peter’s celebrated confession of Christ’s divinity, he calls Peter’s faith—the faith revealed to him by the heavenly Father—the rock or foundation upon which Christ was to build the Church. “Peter’s faith,” he says, “is called the rock. [Col. 0067C] Thus, when Peter said to the Lord, in Matthew, chapter XVI, ‘You are the Christ, the Son of the living God,’ he immediately confirmed that faith and said: ‘I say to you that you are Peter’; that is, ‘Upon this faith of yours, by which you call me the Son of the living God, I will build my Church.’”

The other passage, in the commentary on the aforesaid chapter of Matthew, agrees with this: “Let us consider what this means: ‘And upon this rock I will build my Church.’ Upon this rock, which you have now laid as the foundation of faith; upon this faith which you have just taught, saying, ‘You are the Christ, the Son of the living God’; upon this rock and upon this faith I will build my Church.”

Now, because St. Bruno maintains that Peter’s faith is the rock upon which Christ the Lord promised to build his Church, he intended to indicate Peter’s own person, from whom that illustrious testimony to Christ’s divinity proceeded, and especially to mark his election: that, before the other apostles, he should be the Church’s chief foundation. For Jesus did not first say that he would build his Church upon faith in general, but upon Peter’s faith, which Peter himself had confessed and in which the eternal Father had revealed to him the mystery hitherto hidden [Col. 0068A] from human beings.

That this must entirely be referred to Peter’s person, as affirming Christ’s divinity, follows from what has already been said and is more clearly inferred if Christ’s words are received in their true sense. Christ must not be understood to have wished to build his Church upon Peter’s material person—that is, upon his bodily and spiritual nature—which is inert of itself and does nothing, but upon Peter’s faith. For just as the Church consists by faith, so it is said to be founded upon the person of Peter, who possesses the faith that is a stable and firm foundation for sustaining the Church’s structure.

That this was Bruno’s meaning is clearer from what he immediately adds: “The Apostle, agreeing with this statement, says in I Corinthians [chapter III; the printed text reads XXXII]: ‘No one can lay another foundation besides that which has been laid, which is Christ Jesus.’ As though he said: ‘There is no other foundation except that rock which Peter laid as a foundation when he said, “You are the Christ, the Son of the living God.”’”

Indeed, that the Church is preserved through being founded upon the strength and steadfastness of this rock—namely, Peter—and of his successors in the same preeminence and dignity of the apostolate, is also demonstrated by Christ’s oracle when he said to Peter: “I will pray for you, Peter, that your faith may not fail.” For that firmness and inerrancy of the Church’s faith, founded by Christ in Peter, established for it a character of truth and a distinctive property inherent in it and destined to endure perpetually.

Lest this interpretation of the divine words be transferred to [Col. 0068C] another meaning, one should keep before one’s eyes what the same St. Bruno plainly adduces in his commentary on John, chapter XXI. There he most clearly affirms the supreme authority and power, in the universal Church, of Peter and his successors—authority handed to him by Christ and not communicated to the other apostles. For when Christ had three times tested Peter’s love and always heard him steadfast in it, he entrusted to him the feeding not only of his lambs but also of his sheep, saying: “Feed my lambs; feed my sheep.” On this St. Bruno comments:

“First he entrusted the lambs to him, then the sheep, because he made him not only a shepherd but the shepherd of shepherds. Therefore Peter feeds the lambs and feeds the sheep; he feeds the children and feeds the mothers, because besides lambs and [Col. 0068D] sheep there is nothing in the Church. The sheep, therefore, are the prelates and bishops, successors of the apostles, divinely appointed; under the supreme head, namely the Roman pontiff, they ought to feed and govern their flock.”

[Note: [Col. 0067D] These excerpts appear to be from the author of the sermon for the feast of the Apostles Peter and Paul, attributed by the better critics to St. Eucherius of Lyons, although published under the name of Eusebius of Emesa. “First,” he says, “he entrusted the lambs to him, that is, to Peter; then the sheep, because he made him not only a shepherd but the shepherd of shepherds. Therefore Peter feeds the lambs and the sheep: he feeds the children, [Col. 0068D] and he feeds the mothers; he governs both subjects and prelates. He is therefore shepherd of all, because besides lambs and sheep there is nothing in the Church.” The most distinguished Bossuet, Bishop of Meaux, used this authority in his celebrated address delivered to the assembled French clergy in 1682, in order to establish the Roman pontiff’s power of governing the whole Christian flock.]

Finally, in his commentary on Psalm LXIX, St. Bruno calls St. Peter the greatest of the apostles; he again asserts that Christ the Lord entrusted to him the care of strengthening his [Col. 0069A] brethren, and confirms his primacy and his full authority in the universal Church.

How Peter founded the Roman Church and established his see in it Bruno teaches in his commentary on the words of Exodus, chapter XXII, p. 80, col. 1, “If anyone seduces a virgin not yet betrothed,” etc. “Blessed Peter,” he says, “was a good seducer, who converted the Roman multitude to the love of faith and righteousness. For he found her like a virgin, free and not yet betrothed or handed over to a husband; he slept with her and begot many children from her. For he slept with her when he devoted himself to preaching and begot children by the seed of the word; afterward he endowed her with faith, [Col. 0069B] knowledge, and virtues, and strengthened her by the grace of the Holy Spirit, because both bridegroom and dowry pleased the virgin’s father.”

Thus, according to Bruno, Peter established the Roman Church, chosen by him as his bride, after rescuing her from impious idol worship and illuminating her with the heavenly rays of truth; he established her in the true religion of God, the supreme ruler, and in knowledge of Christ the restorer, adorning her with every endowment of knowledge and virtue. And in order that this inheritance which he had established might remain perpetually with his successors in the apostolic see, he chose to die at Rome in the most glorious martyrdom of the cross, imitating Christ his master, and left her his own blood as though it were a written instrument ratifying his will.

Since our Bruno was a most holy bishop [Col. 0069C] and conducted himself as an example of every kind of episcopal perfection, it is not surprising that, in expounding Exodus and Leviticus, he treated so extensively of the election, duties, and virtues of bishops. But lest I exceed the limits of this preliminary discourse, I shall cite only a few of the many passages, especially those contained in the Commentary on Exodus.

First, then, we should hear what he teaches in explaining the words of Exodus, chapter XXIX, p. 112, col. 2: “The holy garment which Aaron uses shall belong to his sons after him, that they may be anointed in it and their hands consecrated.” “For you,” he says, “bishops and priests, are Aaron’s sons, if indeed you imitate him; and you are brothers of Moses—of that Moses, certainly, who says in Psalm XXI, 23: ‘I will declare your name to my brothers.’ Therefore you possess Aaron’s garment; you are clothed with glory, honor, and the adornment of every virtue. You possess the breastpiece and the ephod; you are anointed with the grace of the Holy Spirit; your hands also are consecrated to make Christ’s body and blood. For you use this garment for seven days and are never stripped of it. For there are only seven days; whatever is done for seven days is done for all time.”

I may also recount how the same St. Bruno describes the election and ministry of bishops in explaining Exodus, chapter XXVII, p. 101, col. 2: “That the lamp may burn continually in the tabernacle of testimony [Col. 0070B] outside the veil.” “Aaron and his sons,” he says, “place this lamp; those who perform the office of the first priest and of his successors arrange it, consecrate it, and establish it.

[Note: [Col. 0069C] This rule conforms to the decree, or canon, promulgated at the Roman council under Pope Siricius: ‘Let no one dare to ordain without the knowledge of the apostolic see.’ See Observations on Fleury’s *Ecclesiastical History*, vol. I, p. 299. This rule was so firmly maintained by the Roman pontiffs that St. Leo the Great, in his letter to the bishops of the province of Vienne, complained of Hilary, Bishop of Arles, because he had not kept it. “Hilary,” he says, “went beyond bounds, intending to disturb the condition of the Churches and the concord of priests by novel presumptions; wishing to subject you to his own power so that he would not permit himself to be subject to the blessed apostle Peter, claiming for himself the ordinations of all the Churches throughout Gaul and transferring to himself the dignity owed to metropolitan bishops; even diminishing, with arrogant words, the reverence due to the most blessed Peter himself. Although, above the others, the power of binding and loosing was entrusted to him, nevertheless the care of feeding the sheep was entrusted to him in a more particular way. Whoever judges that primacy should be denied to him can in no way diminish his dignity; but, puffed up by the spirit of his own pride, he casts [Col. 0070C] himself down into hell.” With such authority ringing out, what cogent argument can those offer who strive to assail [Col. 0070D] the supreme power of the Roman pontiffs in the ordination of bishops? If they bring forward the apostles as legal precedent and example, since they ordained bishops wherever there was need, all authors reply that the apostles were equipped by the Lord with an extraordinary mission and power, extraordinary privileges, and the working of miracles; and therefore it is not surprising that, at the beginning of the Church, they performed episcopal ordinations. Yet it may more truly be said that they did this with the consent of St. Peter, their head, before they separated from him in order to publish the Gospel throughout the whole earth. For once Peter himself had been appointed, by Christ’s authority, as head of the Church, the Church had to be governed as a body—and is so described in the Gospel—so that its members must altogether agree with the head itself. Are governors of cities appointed in any kingdom without some authority from the sovereign prince? The same may be affirmed of their earliest successors.]

“The lamp is chosen by the people and presented to the pontiffs; but by the bishops it is consecrated, ordained, and placed in its see. And the lamp must not cease, before God and until it departs from this miserable and dark life, to preach to and enlighten God’s people until morning; so that, once this night is ended, the Sun of righteousness may rise for it and it may enter that day of which the Psalmist says in Psalm LXXXIII, 10: ‘For one day in your courts is better than thousands.’”

Here one should note not so much the practice of electing bishops, still in force in the Church in Bruno’s time, and of their consecration, as the fact that consecrating bishops acted in the place of the supreme pontiff. They were not permitted to proceed to such a consecration unless they possessed the mandate of that same supreme pontiff, that is, apostolic letters by which they fulfilled his office. Nor shall I pass over in silence the other particular feature of episcopal consecration mentioned by Bruno: namely, that before bishops are consecrated, they are required to answer concerning the faith and swear that they will never depart from it or from the Church’s rules. For, explaining the words of Leviticus, chapter VIII, p. 141, col. 2, “He offered also the second ram in the consecration of the priests; [Col. 0071A] Aaron and his sons laid their hands upon its head,” etc., he says: “Moses in this place, who consecrates the priests, can signify a certain pontiff, through whose ministry bishops and priests are consecrated. At the beginning of consecration he offers the ram if he fully instructs those to be consecrated concerning the faith. Thus they themselves lay their hands upon the ram’s head, because in some manner they swear and confess that they believe all things about which they are questioned.”

St. Bruno also does not omit to state what the duties of bishops are and what offices belong to Levites. In Leviticus, chapter VI, p. 174, col. 1, he says: “It belongs to bishops to handle and perform the greater sacraments of the Church, namely confirmation and the conferral of orders. Levites, however, and the other lesser orders ought faithfully to labor and toil in outward offices, so that no one may be found useless or idle, but the obedience of the lesser orders may promptly follow the command and direction of their superiors.”

Since bishops are established in such high dignity and excellence of duties, how they should order their lives so as to shine like lights in the Church may be learned from many passages in which St. Bruno discusses the matter. I prefer the passage in which he describes the conduct they ought to maintain, explaining the words of Exodus, chapter XXVIII, p. 105, col. 1: “You shall make also a hyacinth-blue robe of the ephod,” etc. “Because the ephod,” he says, “was placed over this robe, it is therefore called the robe of the ephod. The whole [Col. 0071C] pontiff was covered by it, and therefore it had an opening for the neck, by which even the head might be covered. By it we understand the holy and undefiled conduct of a bishop: that he may be wholly clothed in such holy life and excellent conduct that nothing bare, unbecoming, or unadorned may appear in him. Hence the whole robe is said to have been hyacinth-blue, so that the pontiff clothed in it might be thought to be not earth but heaven, not a human being but God. For hyacinth, as we have often said, signifies heaven because it is the color of the air.”

Since preaching the word of God is especially incumbent upon bishops, the holy Bishop of Segni commends it to them in the same place. Having cited the words, “Aaron shall wear it in the office of ministry, that its sound may be heard when he enters and goes out from the sanctuary before the Lord,” he says: “Pontiffs must cry out without interruption; they must always preach, sound the bells of their voices, and call the people to faith, baptism, and repentance. Whether he enters the sanctuary [Col. 0071D] or goes out from the sanctuary, he must do this. For as long as he is in the church, when he sees the people around him—for the people are the sanctuary—it is fitting for him always to resound and instill words of edification into their ears. Although it is good to do this everywhere, it ought especially to be done where the people are accustomed to come to receive the sacraments. If a bishop does this, he shall not die; but if he does not do it, he shall die. What does ‘he shall die’ mean? It does not seem to be said of ordinary death, for we shall all die. It must therefore be understood of another death, from which may almighty God deign to snatch and free us.”

To these should be added what our author teaches in his commentary on Matthew, chapter V, “Nor do they light a lamp and put it under a bushel,” etc.: “A lamp is lit in order to shine; a bishop is ordained in order to enlighten others. For the lamp is the bishop, and the light is the grace of the Holy Spirit or evangelical preaching. Therefore let him who has been placed upon the Church’s lampstand see that he does not put under a bushel the grace of the Holy Spirit by which he has been enlightened; let him see that he does not bury in the earth the talent entrusted to him.”

A bishop’s teaching, moreover, must be sound and orthodox. For even if he is adorned with some virtues and performs some good works, yet teaches wrongly, he betrays his office in everything he does well and becomes guilty before the Lord. Explaining the command that the pontiff should wear the breastpiece joined to the ephod, Bruno draws these lessons: “For just as,” he says, p. 104, col. 2, “the breastpiece signifies preaching, so the ephod signifies burden and work. If a bishop teaches well but acts badly, or conversely acts well but teaches badly, his ephod and breastpiece are not joined. We read that very many heretics acted well indeed but taught badly. Fasting, keeping vigils, giving alms, and similar things are good works. We have heard that the bishops of the Manichaeans, Arians, and Donatists [Col. 0072C] did these things; but because they taught wrongly, although in doing these and similar things they seemed to possess the ephod, they wholly lacked the breastpiece. For if they had possessed it, they would not have preached irrational—that is, false and erroneous—things.”

And since St. Bruno set out to convey a perfect idea of the episcopate, he also found in the golden plate on which “Holy to the Lord” was written, worn by the pontiff on his forehead, an occasion to discuss a bishop’s wisdom. “This plate,” he says on Exodus, chapter XXVIII [the printed text reads XXVI], p. 106, col. 1, “was above the tiara, because wisdom is higher than all ornaments in a pontiff and shines more brightly. And although he possesses the other ornaments, if he does not possess wisdom, there is nothing upon him upon which ‘Holy to the Lord’ may be written. This is the name of a pontiff; one who is not designated by it is no pontiff. This star is set upon the pontiff’s forehead so that it may never be hidden, may be seen by all, may enlighten all, and may shine upon all who are in the house.”

Bishops should not shine only in teaching and wisdom; in a sense they must take upon themselves the people’s sins and continually implore God for the people. St. Bruno teaches this in his exposition of the same passage, Exodus, chapter XXVIII, p. 106, col. 1: “Aaron shall bear the iniquities of the things which the children of Israel have offered and sacrificed.” “When the people offer gifts to priests for the blotting out of sins,” he says, “what else do the priests bear in those gifts but the sins of the people? In their gifts the people lay down the burdens [Col. 0073A] of their sins; priests, by contrast, are burdened with sinners. Let this burden be the duty of priests: that, praying for sinners and worthily fulfilling their office, they may always strive to appease God’s indignation and wrath.”

Above all, a bishop must excel in the most unblemished morals. If he ought to sanctify others, he must devote himself wholly to his own holiness. Our author aptly indicates what he must do in commenting on Exodus, chapter XXIX, p. 111, col. 2: “You shall place all these things upon the hands of Aaron and his sons, and shall sanctify them, lifting them up before the Lord.” “Then,” St. Bruno says, “he is sanctified when he receives the sacred law and the divine volumes for meditation and teaching, and promises to keep them not with his lips only but with his whole heart. He lifts them up before the Lord because, both in life and in teaching, he presents himself in such a way that his services deserve to be performed on high and to be seen and received by God. For he does not lift himself or his gifts on high who disfigures and drags down his life and soul by the contagion of vices.” He says the same in his commentary on Leviticus, chapter VI, p. 137, col. 2.

Here an open path would seem available to me for examining that great question concerning simoniacal ordinations: whether they should be regarded as invalid or merely unlawful. But since the most distinguished Pietro Lazzari has written most learnedly on the question in his notes on Bruno’s commentary on John, chapter X, and since I shall have many other matters to bring forward in my observations on the treatise of the same holy bishop, *On the Corrupt State of the Church*, I shall now set out only briefly the state of the controversy.

Holy men flourishing in the eleventh and twelfth centuries, who sought to defend the purity and holiness of the sacred ministry, lamented that the Church was infected far and wide by the stain of simony. Some of them, including our Bruno, maintained that simoniacs’ ordinations were wholly null and void. Relying on the authority of Holy Scripture, they said that Christ the Lord told the apostles in Matthew, chapter X: “Freely you have received; freely give”; and that St. Peter pronounced a divine curse upon Simon Magus, who offered money in order to receive the Holy Spirit and the grace of miracles: Acts, chapter VIII, 20, “May your money perish with you, because you thought that the gift of God could be possessed with money.”

Second, they recalled that many councils had condemned simony and treated simoniacs as heretics. Third, they asserted the saying of St. Leo the Great, cited by Gratian, Part II, Cause 1, Question 1, Canon 1: “If grace is not given or received freely, it is not grace. But simoniacs do not receive freely; and if they do not receive it, neither can they give it to anyone.” Reason also seemed to support them: since the ministry of the Church is holy and appointed for the performance of sacred acts, no one should be admitted to it unless shown to have been called by God—a calling which cannot be presumed in simoniacs. Nevertheless, as we shall say, the Church condemns simoniacal ordinations as unlawful and subjects simoniacs to canonical penalties; yet it regards orders [Col. 0074A] conferred simoniacally as valid and denies that they should be repeated.

Bruno also does not fail to discuss the ordination of priests. He maintains that it is performed by bishops not only through consecration, that is, anointing with chrism, but also by the touch of the book of the divine Scriptures, through which, according to eleventh-century discipline, priests received authority to expound and preach God’s word. Thus the holy bishop says in his commentary on Leviticus, chapter VIII, p. 142, col. 1: “The fact that he handed all these things together to the priests signifies that, after priests have been consecrated, they must receive a book from the hand of the pontiff, so that they may have authority to expound and preach the word of God.”

In the same place he also admonishes us priests that, so long as we are in this life, we must always be consecrated and sanctified and progress toward what is better. “Let us therefore remain,” he says, “day and night—that is, at all times—in the tabernacle; let us observe and keep what he himself commanded, lest we die.”

St. Bruno also admonishes Levites, or deacons, concerning how they should conduct themselves toward bishops and priests and what service they ought to render in the Church. Having cited the context of Numbers, chapter III, “And the Lord spoke to Moses, saying: Bring the tribe of Levi near, and make it stand before Aaron the priest, that it may minister to him,” etc., he addresses the Levites as follows, p. 173, col. 1: “Understand these things, Levites; open your eyes and see. Let pride not puff you up. Know that you are ministers of bishops and priests, and not merely ministers, but gifts given to serve and obey, and to comply with their admonitions and commands. If you do otherwise, you shall die.”

Because God chose the tribe of Levi for the ministries required in sacred acts, our author says in his commentary on Numbers, chapter I, p. 172, col. 2, that there is a great difference between the order of clerics, signified by the tribe of Levi, and the rest of the people. “For it,” he says, “is set over the tabernacle of testimony; it holds primacy over the whole Church; it carries its vessels and ceremonies, the tabernacle itself, and all its implements, because it rules, orders, and directs the whole Church and its sacraments.”

Therefore, since God willed certain persons to be specially consecrated and dedicated to himself and entrusted sacred things to their administration, “no one but these,” St. Bruno continues, “dared approach in order to take down, set up, or in any way arrange the tabernacle, because whoever among outsiders approached was put to death.” Secular persons and laypeople, therefore, are forbidden to meddle in sacred things or usurp ecclesiastical offices.

The Church thus consists of persons devoted to the sanctuary and of the entire multitude of believers, who in baptism have given their name to Christ, retain the same faith and sacraments, and profess that through these they are renewed in godliness. They therefore believe that Jesus Christ is true God and true man; that he suffered and died for us, rose again, descended to hell to free the souls of the righteous, and finally returned gloriously with them to heaven. Whenever occasion offered, Bruno took care to draw the foundations of this faith from the sacred Scriptures and to teach clearly what must be believed.

## § X. On Jesus Christ the Redeemer

Following St. Bruno’s teaching, we have spoken above of the truth of Christ’s coming, or of the incarnation of the divine Word, who became human in form in order to rescue humankind from destruction, raise it to his sonship and inheritance, and grant it possession thereof. Now, following the same teacher, we shall endeavor to set forth what properties must be acknowledged in Christ and what were his principal deeds.

Bruno most plainly confesses Christ’s divinity when, explaining the words of Exodus, chapter XXIII, p. 83, col. 1, “And my name is in him,” he adds: “For the Father’s name is in the Son, because the Son, like the Father, is God.” Still more striking is the passage in chapter XXXIII of the same book, p. 121, col. 1. Recounting God’s speech to Moses from the cloud, he says: “But what is the pillar of cloud except the incarnate Word? For as the Lord spoke and was seen in the cloud, so God spoke and was seen in a human being. They saw the cloud; they saw the humanity; they heard the voice, yet did not recognize God. For if they had recognized him, they would never have crucified the Lord of glory.”

Our author also treats Christ’s true humanity most eloquently in many passages, of which we shall adduce only a few. In Genesis, chapter XXII, p. 28, col. 2, he explains how Isaac, to be sacrificed by his father Abraham, bore the figure of Christ. “Allegorically,” he says, “Abraham, whose name is interpreted ‘father of many nations’ or ‘exalted father,’ signifies God the Father, of whom it is written in Psalm CXII: ‘The Lord is exalted above all nations.’ Isaac, however, signifies his Son Jesus Christ, who himself became obedient to the Father even unto death. The altar signifies the cross on which he was sacrificed. The ram, sacrificed in Isaac’s place, is Christ’s flesh. For Christ is God and man: according to divinity he is immortal and impassible; according to humanity, passible and mortal. Therefore, while Christ is in the flesh, the ram alone is sacrificed, the lamb alone is slain, the flesh alone is crucified; for Christ did not suffer according to divinity.”

Bruno confirms the same truth in explaining the words of Psalm LXXII, “Remember this creature of yours,” saying, p. 458, col. 1: “He seems to speak to the divinity, commending to it the humanity which it assumed; he calls it a creature so that our Savior may be believed to be true God and true man. And it was entirely fitting that he who had hitherto spoken so much of the power of his divinity should say something also of his humanity, thereby removing an occasion from those heretics who believed him to be not a human being [Col. 0076A] but God.”

He had already taught this doctrine in his commentary on Psalm II: “The one whom the Jews call Christ,” he says, p. 301, col. 2, “we call king. Christ our Lord is God and man. According to his humanity, he was appointed king and lord not only by the Father but also by himself and by the Holy Spirit. For according to divinity he was neither made nor created; according to humanity he created and made himself.”

The exposition of the words of Psalm XVII, “The groanings of death found me,” agrees with this: “When he says,” he states, p. 328, col. 1, “that groanings of death and the feelings of human suffering came upon him, he shows that he is a true human being and not a phantom, as certain heretics preached [Note: [Col. 0075D] The Manichaeans say that the Word of God is a human being, not a true one but one of mere likeness, insofar as they say that the Son of God assumed a phantom body. St. Thomas, *Summa Theologiae*, III, question 16, article 1.]; but in truth [Col. 0076B] he was himself taken, bound, crucified, and put to death.”

St. Bruno taught the same doctrine concerning the reality of Christ’s humanity in his exposition of the words of Psalm CVIII, p. 537, col. 2, “And my heart is troubled within me.” “This,” he says, “belongs to Christ’s humanity. For who but a human being, as it is written in Mark XIV, 33, ‘began to be distressed and sorrowful’? His humanity did what belonged to it, and his divinity what belonged to it; for unless he had done this, who would have believed him to be human? If he had displayed only the nature and power of divinity, no one would have believed him to be human. Therefore it was very necessary for our Savior to show that these affections were in him.”

St. Bruno likewise affirmed, p. 302, col. 1, that Jesus Christ, according to divinity, is Son of God not by adoption but substantially. For, he says, the Father himself testified to this when he said in Luke, chapter III, verse 23: “You are my beloved Son; in you I am well pleased.”

Because the twofold nature of Christ, divine and human, may be proved ever more fully from His twofold will—which the Monothelites of old denied—A. N. does this most abundantly in explaining Psalm LXVIII, *Save me, O God*, etc. “When praying before the Passion,” he says, p. 443, col. 1, “he had said to the Father: ‘Father, if it be possible, let this cup pass from me’; he immediately added: ‘Nevertheless, not my will but yours be done.’ For beyond doubt he willed what he asked for; but he willed it thus, if the Father Himself should will it. Therefore, if he asks for something and does not receive what he asks, let no one dare say on this account that his will was not evident [Col. 0076D]. Nor is it unfitting that a changeable nature should have a changeable will. For we must not doubt that he assumed everything that is ours, apart from sin. But when he says: ‘Save me, O God, for the waters have entered even unto my soul’; and many other things that follow, the Lord spoke them not with his mouth, but by the intention of his heart.”

Christ, moreover, had a human will which naturally shrank from suffering and death; yet it was so subordinated to the divine will that it fully consented to undergo the Passion. Since A. N. also acknowledged a divine will in Christ, he consequently professed that whatever Christ willed was wholly in His power. For, explaining the first verse of Psalm LXIII, *Hear, O God, my prayer*, etc., he says, p. 426, col. 1:

“We have often already said that whenever our Savior prays for something, asks something, and seems to need something, the whole matter must be referred to his humanity. That humanity itself does not pray for itself but for us, because whatever is in his will is in his power; therefore for him to pray was to will.” And below: “He had no need to pray long, since his will was heard so promptly. For in him alike were both the will and the effect of the will; nor could he will anything before possessing what he willed. Christ had this most complete power of his will because he was God and man.”

Saint Bruno had said in his Commentary on Exodus, chapter XII, p. 58, col. 1, that Christ’s Passion is signified in the Old Testament through figures and enigmas; yet he did not thereby exclude the plain testimonies in the Old Testament that foretold Christ’s Passion and death. Since, then, many sacraments or mysteries are contained in figures and mystical significations, he endeavored ingeniously to bring them forward and elucidate them.

I shall first set forth his exposition of Exodus, chapter XXIV, p. 84, col. 2, on the passage where Moses erected an altar and commanded twelve calves to be sacrificed upon it.

“Therefore Moses, rising early in the morning, built an altar at the foot of the mountain; because the Jews, who are sacrificed through Moses, early in the morning prepared a cross for Christ the Lord on Mount Calvary, at the foot of Jerusalem and Mount Zion [Col. 0077C]: for the altar signifies the cross. Upon this altar Christ was sacrificed. But because none of the twelve tribes can excuse itself from Christ’s death, twelve calves are sacrificed for the twelve tribes. And although there was one calf, because one Christ was sacrificed, nevertheless, because each tribe—indeed every individual person—is liable in full, Moses commanded twelve calves to be sacrificed. One Christ was indeed crucified and sacrificed; yet everyone who consented to his death killed him; he is guilty of the murder of the whole Christ. And although not all laid hands upon Christ, all the Jews nevertheless killed him by their consent.”

Nowhere, however, did A. N. treat Christ’s Passion with such fullness as in his exposition of chapter XXIX of the same book of Exodus, p. 107, where the rite of sacrificing the ram is prescribed. I could reproduce his entire interpretation here; but for our purpose that part is enough in which the sum of Christ’s life is gathered together and His most sorrowful death proclaimed. Speaking of the ram’s entrails and feet cut into pieces, he says:

“These things—that is, the entrails and feet of the ram—we place upon the cut-up flesh and upon its head; because, after we have distinctly shown that Christ God was born of the Virgin, lived among men, gave sight to the blind, cleansed lepers, raised the dead, and performed the other deeds which he did, then finally, from all these things, we ought also to add and render this: that he suffered for us and, because of our sins, endured the most shameful death [Col. 0078A] and the ignominy of the cross, etc. But what he adds, ‘And you shall offer the whole ram upon the altar,’ is as though he said: you shall always keep in memory, heart, and mind not only Christ’s divinity and humanity, but also his Passion, resurrection, ascension, and whatever has been written concerning him. For we have said that this altar signifies the mind and heart of man.”

According to Bruno’s opinion, p. 148, col. 1, Christ died in the thirty-third year of His age, an opinion in which many distinguished writers and chronologists agree.

Enough has been said thus far concerning Christ’s Passion and death; we must now speak of His resurrection, concerning which Holy Scripture contains many most splendid testimonies [Col. 0078B]. Thus, in Job, chapter XIX, we read: “I know that my Redeemer lives, and that on the last day I shall rise from the earth.” On this Saint Bruno says in his commentary: “O how great is the hope of resurrection! These words alone suffice against all who deny the resurrection: ‘whom I myself shall see,’ he says. What does ‘I myself’ mean? It means: in this flesh, in this essence, in this person. And not another through a change of flesh, but one and the same through the recovery of his own flesh.”

Further, explaining the Psalmist’s prophecy in Psalm XL, “I slept and took my rest, and rose again,” he says, p. 380, col. 2: “Christ’s death was sleep: he slept as long as he willed, and rose when he willed; for had he not willed it, he would never have fallen asleep.”

And since in the same psalm Christ is said to have entreated the Father to raise Him—“But you, have mercy on me and raise me up, and I will repay them”—Saint Bruno teaches, p. 381, col. 1, how the Prophet is to be understood: “This prayer of Christ’s humanity was inward; it was in the heart, it was in the will alone. He had no need of words for praying, since he possessed all things according to his will. Therefore these things were written for our sake; for if they had not been written, they would not have come to our knowledge.”

Before Christ rose from the dead, however, and during those three days in which His body rested in the tomb, He Himself descended with His soul and divinity into hell, in order to free the souls of the righteous from that prison and place of darkness. Saint Bruno recognized this Catholic truth as foretold [Col. 0078D] in the words of Job, chapter XIV: “Who will grant me that you may protect me in hell?” He explains them thus, p. 248, col. 2:

“I know that I shall descend into hell; but who there, if not you, will protect and free me from the punishments of torments? The time appointed for mercy was Christ’s Passion; for then, descending into hell, he snatched away and freed the souls of the righteous, according to Hosea, chapter XIII, 14: ‘O death, I will be your death; I will be your bite, O hell.’”

You will find the same teaching confirmed in the exposition of Psalm XV, 10: “For you will not abandon my soul in hell, nor will you allow your Holy One to see corruption.” “For,” he says, p. 325, col. 2, “the divinity descended into hell together with the soul, yet did not abandon the body in the tomb. The soul could be separated from the body; the divinity could not, because God is everywhere and contains all things. For it would have been utterly unworthy that that most holy flesh should see any corruption—a flesh born of the Virgin without any corruption and living in this world without any sin.”

Likewise, on Psalm LIII, “You have granted him the desire of his soul,” and “The Lord is the protector of my soul,” he says, p. 407, col. 2: “For who else ought to receive it except the divinity itself, to which it was ineffably united? For immediately when our Savior gave up the spirit, that most holy soul, together with the divinity, penetrated the gates of hell; and, having despoiled hell, led forth with itself the souls of the saints who were held captive there.”

Saint Bruno teaches the same in his commentary on Psalm LXVIII, on verse 16, “Let not the deep swallow me up, nor let the pit close [Col. 0079B] its mouth over me.” “Here,” he says, p. 444, col. 2, “it is clearly shown that this prayer belongs not to the body but to the soul: for the soul alone of our Savior descended into hell, signified by this deep pit. It could not indeed be held there; but, having bound the devil and despoiled hell, it ascended thence in great victory.”

He has similar statements on Job, chapter XLI.

> [Note: [Col. 0079D] O times! O morals! Who would believe it? In these days, when so many ravings of heretics have been overthrown and extinguished by the Church, the teacher of truth, there are still subverters of orthodox doctrine who dare to recall them from the ashes. One of these recently raised a controversy concerning Christ’s descent into hell. Against him, therefore, we first set the Apostles’ Creed, which contains the confession of this descent: “He descended into hell.” Second, let him hear Saint Augustine’s expression of this truth in Epistle 164, formerly 99, chapter 5, no. 14: “Let us hold most firmly what faith possesses, strengthened by the most solid authority: that Christ . . . . . was in hell.” The same holy Doctor places the contrary opinion among heresies in *On Heresies*, heresy 79. Third, Holy Scripture contains many testimonies which cannot otherwise be expounded and understood, as Saint Bruno and the other Holy Fathers explain them, unless that Catholic dogma is admitted. It is indeed absent from the Nicene Creed because the Fathers did not wish to include in it every article of faith. See Thomas Aquinas, *Summa Theologiae*, II–II, q. 1, art. 9, ad 4; Cardinal Gotti, *Theologia*, vol. XVI, dissertation 1, §3; and Nicoli’s *Exposition of the Creed*. See also the most learned Giovanni Vincenzo Patuzzi, O.P., who defended in a special work the article of the Apostles’ Creed, “He descended into hell,” against certain heterodox writers. [Col. 0080D]]

The same author next asks how Christ’s prediction in Matthew, chapter XII, 40, is to be understood: “As Jonah was in the belly of the whale for three days and three nights, so shall the Son of Man be in the heart of the earth for three days and three nights.” For if Christ’s body was not laid in the tomb until the evening of the day of Preparation—that is, before the Sabbath of the Paschal solemnity [Col. 0079C]—and He rose very early on the next day, called the Lord’s Day, how can it be true that He lay in the tomb for three days and three nights? Saint Bruno answers in Sermon II on the Lord’s Resurrection:

“Therefore the Son of Man was in the heart of the earth for three days and three nights. For on the night when he was seized by the raging Jews rushing upon him, from the time when he himself said, ‘If you seek me, let these go their way,’ our Savior was in their power. Likewise, during the other two nights following that one, in which his body was guarded until the Lord’s Day lest he should rise, his body alone was in their power. The three days are likewise counted as Friday, the Sabbath, and the beginning of the third day, on which the Creator and Lord of the world rose from the dead very early in the morning [Col. 0079D]. It is a very common practice of all Scriptures sometimes to put the whole for a part and the part for the whole.”

[Col. 0080A] Christ did not ascend into heaven immediately upon rising; rather, as Luke testifies in Acts, chapter I, He associated with His apostles for forty days, speaking to them of the kingdom of God—that is, of the Church, which He left them to establish and spread. He first confirmed them in faith in His resurrection; afterward He taught them whatever was to be revealed concerning mysteries and sacraments, appointed them new teachers of His law, sent them into the whole world to spread it, and finally, having conferred upon them the power of the Holy Spirit, bestowed the full power to forgive sins and to bind.

Bruno found this institution of the apostolate prefigured in Numbers, chapter XXVI, where God commanded Moses to lay his hands upon Joshua’s head [Col. 0080B] before Eleazar and the multitude of Israel, and to give him a share in his glory. He elucidated this thus, p. 192, col. 2: “For Christ too is recorded to have done this: before ascending into heaven, he appointed the apostles as his vicars and the leaders of the whole Church; and, granting them a share of his glory, commanded them to perform signs and mighty works in his name.”

A. N. also speaks excellently on the words of Genesis, chapter XXIV, p. 85, col. 1: “Moses and Aaron, Nadab and Abihu, and seventy elders of Israel went up and saw the God of Israel.” In this event he affirmed that the Lord’s ascension was signified.

“Moses,” he says, “after the covenant had been ratified, went up together with the elders of Israel to see God. This signified that, after the lamb had been sacrificed, Christ’s blood poured out, and the new covenant ratified, the gate of heaven is opened, and Jesus the great priest enters the Holy of Holies; and in the heavenly palace God is seen by human beings [Col. 0080C].”

Since, as has often been said, all Christ’s deeds are found foretold in the Psalms, we find His ascension into heaven predicted in Psalm LXVII, verse 19: “Ascending on high, he led captivity captive; he gave gifts to men.” On this A. N. says, p. 439, col. 1:

“Here God and our Lord, ascending on high—first indeed upon the cross and then into heaven—led captivity captive, as it is written in John, chapter XII, verse 32: ‘When I am lifted up from the earth, I will draw all things to myself.’ All were captives of the devil, but many—not all—were made captives of Christ. Many are still held in captivity; if they had willed it, they would not be in captivity. But he gave gifts to men, and very great gifts, when he sent the Holy Spirit [Col. 0081A] to the apostles and gave them such grace that they spoke in the languages of all peoples and healed infirmities.”

Long before, Saint Bruno, explaining the words of Psalm XLVI, “God went up with a shout of joy, and the Lord with the sound of a trumpet,” had described the great joy and exultation of the angels when they saw Christ the Lord ascending into heaven, and came to meet Him, applauding and blessing Him in His triumph. It is worthwhile to reproduce his exposition, p. 393:

“The Lord ascended in jubilation—that is, in the great joy and gladness of the apostles, who saw him ascend in such glory and such power. Or it was in the jubilation of the angels, all of whom, we must not doubt, came to meet him in highest exultation. Their voices and praises, though we do not know what they were like, since they were most excellent, may be understood through the sound of the trumpet. And who could ever say or conceive how great was the joy in heaven when Christ the Lord ascended into heaven? I seem to see all the angels and archangels humbly adoring that most glorious humanity of our Savior and giving thanks for so great and such a victory over the most proud enemy, thus overcome.
