And I think all this is signified in these words, which say here: ‘In jubilation and in the sound of a trumpet.’”

The Father, therefore, received the Son, Saint Bruno had said in his commentary on Psalm III, p. 303, col. 2, glorified Him as He returned to the Father incarnate and made man, and exalted Him to the seat of His majesty. “Where did He receive Him? In that loftiest and most splendid secret place of His glory. For although God is everywhere [Col. 0081C], there is nevertheless some place where He has revealed His glory more clearly and manifestly.”

## § XI. On the Coming of the Holy Spirit

Christ had promised the apostles that, once He had returned to His Father, He would send them the holy Paraclete, who would fill them with every truth, power, and kind of grace. A figure of this wondrous divine manifestation, as A. N. notes, had preceded it when God appeared to Moses on Mount Sinai and, while the people of Israel listened, gave him His commandments amid thunder, lightning, and flashes, as a testimony to His heavenly power and majesty. The comparison is excellent and highly suited to proving the harmony of the two Testaments.

Bruno’s exposition on Exodus, chapter XIX, p. 70, col. 1, is as follows:

“Now the third day had come; morning had grown bright, and behold, thunder began to be heard, lightning to flash, a very dense cloud to cover the mountain, and the blare of a trumpet sounded with great force. See,” says the holy bishop, “how well the two Testaments answer each other, and how fittingly the same event is celebrated in each. In Acts of the Apostles, chapter I, 12, it is written: ‘Then they returned to Jerusalem from the mountain called Olivet; and when they had entered the upper room, they went up, where Peter and John, James and Andrew, Philip and Thomas, Bartholomew and Matthew, James son of Alphaeus, Simon the Zealot, and Judas son of James were staying. All these persevered unanimously in prayer with the women [Col. 0082A], and Mary the mother of Jesus, and his brethren.’ This most holy gathering is called the Church; this is called Mount Zion. Upon this mountain the Lord descended, preserving in some manner the likeness and the time at which He ascended Mount Sinai. For Moses says: ‘Now the third day had come, morning had grown bright, and thunder began to be heard, lightning to flash,’ etc. Therefore let us also say: ‘Now the third month had come, and Pentecost—that is, the fiftieth day—had grown bright; and, as the blessed evangelist Luke writes in Acts, chapter II: “Suddenly there came from heaven a sound as of a mighty rushing spirit, and it filled the whole house where they were sitting. And divided tongues, as of fire, appeared to them and rested upon each of them; and they were all filled with the Holy Spirit [Col. 0082B] and began to speak in various tongues, as the Holy Spirit gave them utterance.”’ For behold, in both cases a sound is heard and fire is seen. But in the former there is a dark cloud; in the latter, the splendor of most brilliant light appears, because the former was shadow and figure, whereas the latter is truth. For what the thunder there signifies is here the voices of the apostles; what the flashing lightning there signifies is here miracles shining everywhere; and the very dense cloud covering the mountain signifies the apostles watering the Church with saving rains. The trumpet’s loud blare signifies the preaching of all the teachers resounding far and wide.”

A. N. then explains why the Holy Spirit appeared under the form of fire, and why divided tongues were seen resting upon each apostle:

“Now,” he says in Sermon II on the Holy Spirit, “let us see what that fire and those tongues which appeared over the apostles signify, when, as the Evangelist says, all were gathered together in one place. Hebrews XII, 29: ‘For our God is a consuming fire.’ Therefore the Holy Spirit fittingly appeared in fire, in order to consume sins, illuminate the eyes of the mind, and inflame the whole person with the love of God. This is the baptism which John the Baptist promised when he said: ‘I baptize you with water, but another comes after me, who will baptize you with the Holy Spirit and fire,’ Luke, chapter III, 17. The Holy Spirit also had to appear in tongues, since He Himself speaks in the apostles; for who speaks except the tongue? This office belongs to no other member [Col. 0082D]. Those who speak with this tongue need not consider how or what they shall speak. Thus, having received this tongue, the apostles spoke the mighty works of God.”

## § XII. On Charity

Since that fire which God sent upon earth descended for no other reason than to set human hearts aflame, Saint Bruno, who burned with it throughout his life, seized the opportunity afforded by interpreting Leviticus, chapter VI—where it is commanded that the fire always burn upon the altar, and that the priest take care to place wood upon it lest it be extinguished—to state elegantly, p. 136, col. 2:

“This fire, which never fails upon the altar but ought to burn continually, signifies the unceasing ardor of love in the hearts of the faithful. For if this fire is absent from the understanding, the entire office of the priest will be wholly useless. Therefore let the priest diligently strive to nourish continually the fire of love and place wood upon it every day: let him remember the mercy of God; let him remember what God has done and what He has promised to give those who love Him. For with these and similar pieces of wood gathered from the forest of Holy Scriptures, this fire is kindled and inflamed with the love of God. Upon this fire, therefore, O priest, place the holocaust, that you may offer God a sacrifice of praise; for this is the fat of peace offerings, by whose richness you delight God. This is the perpetual fire which shall never fail on the altar. ‘Many waters could not quench charity,’ Song of Songs VIII, 7.”

Happy, then, are those souls which, kindled with heavenly fire, will burn with it continually until life’s end, and which, passing into eternal happiness—where the other gifts will cease—will find that charity never fails, but becomes purer and more ardent throughout eternity [Col. 0083B].

Saint Bruno nevertheless teaches, in Exodus, chapter XXV, p. 87, col. 2, that the saints who enjoy the vision of God will not possess beatitude perfect in every respect until, souls and bodies reunited, the entire multitude of saints is raised together above the heavens. Nor, immediately after death, will the righteous who die in charity gain entrance into heaven if something of guilt remains to be expiated.

## § XIII. On Purgatory, and on the Veneration and Invocation of Saints

It is more than sufficiently known that one of the errors of the Greek schismatics was the denial of the existence of purgatory: that is, a place in hell appointed for the souls of the righteous who still have either venial sins or the debt of punishment due for forgiven sins to expiate [Col. 0083C]. Against them, therefore, the ecumenical Council of Florence defined that purgatory must be admitted as a Catholic dogma. Accordingly, in order to confirm the definition of the Fathers of Florence and to show how rightly modern heretics—Luther, Calvin, Zwingli, and others—seem also on this ground to have been proscribed, I shall set forth what Saint Bruno thought of this Catholic doctrine.

Thus, explaining Leviticus, chapter XXII, p. 126, col. 2, he says: “After this life the righteous are offered to God and received immediately into the fellowship of the saints, or later, if perhaps they need purgatory. For not all who are saved are received into blessedness as soon as they have died [Col. 0083D].”

A. N. repeats the same point in explaining the words of Psalm XXXI: “Blessed is he to whom the Lord has not imputed sin.” “Therefore,” he says, “let penitents rejoice because their sins have been forgiven them; nevertheless, let them fear, because they do not know whether the punishment of sin has also been remitted to them. On whatever day they are converted, if they have been worthily converted, they will be saved; but the fire remains. Sin has been forgiven, but not the punishment for sin. We read that certain persons shone forth through miracles after death and yet were assigned to purgatory. Of these there can be no doubt both that their sins were forgiven and that the punishment for sin was not forgiven. Of such persons it is said, 1 Corinthians III, 15: ‘If anyone’s work is burned up, he shall suffer loss; but he himself shall be saved, yet as through fire’ [Col. 0084A].”

Since, moreover, Holy Scripture, tradition, and the pronouncement of the Church assure us that some righteous persons are to be regarded as among the saints—that is, among the inhabitants of heaven—their invocation will be pious and useful. Saint Bruno teaches this in his commentary on Job, chapter XI, p. 244, col. 1:

“The saints rise when, laying aside the flesh, they die; for then they first receive immortal life. But how do they rise? Like the morning star, that is, bright and immortal. Then they have confidence, hope being set before them, because they undoubtedly attain the things for which they had hoped. Very many will entreat their countenance, because they desire to become such persons; as it is said of the Church: ‘All the rich among the people will entreat your face’—or they desire to come to that place where they may see them and be joined with them [Col. 0084B].”

That their painted images, and especially those of the Blessed Virgin Mary, ought to be honored with a certain veneration and devotion, Saint Bruno likewise suggests in his commentary on the same Psalm XLIV:

“Not only shall the daughters of Tyre adore your Son, but they shall also entreat you and render their vows to you. For if we understand this of her face and image, it will not be unfitting; since wherever she is painted, we ought all to venerate her.”

## § XIV. On the Eternity of the Punishments of Hell

We find Saint Bruno asserting another Catholic dogma: namely, the most miserable lot of the wicked, who, dying in grave sin, are condemned to the eternal punishments of hell [Col. 0084C]. Against the Origenists, who denied the eternity of fire and punishments in hell, the holy bishop established this truth by explaining Job, p. 239, col. 2: “A fire which is not kindled shall devour him; he who is left in his tent shall be afflicted.”

“For,” he says, “that fire is inextinguishable, and once kindled needs no further kindling. But he who is left in the tent of his flesh shall always be afflicted, because flesh and soul shall be tormented eternally.”

In his commentary on Psalm II, p. 352, col. 2, he likewise says: “The impious and sinners condemned in judgment shall no longer find mercy.” Saint Bruno sets forth many other matters pertaining to theological doctrine, not so much in his commentaries on the two Testaments as in his remaining writings. If I wished to bring forward each of them [Col. 0084D], I would extend this introductory discourse too far. Nevertheless, I shall note several matters of greater importance.

## § XV. On the Authority of Holy Scripture and Tradition

A. N. teaches how highly divine writings—that is, the books of both Testaments—are to be valued in Exodus, chapter XXXIV, p. 119. Having quoted the Apostle’s words in Romans, chapter VII, 8, “I did not know concupiscence unless the law had said: ‘You shall not covet your neighbor’s property,’” the holy bishop says:

“Therefore let us believe the testimony of the law, which, because it always speaks truth and never lies, is not without reason called testimony. No one dares contradict this testimony; the authority of the law is its final proof. It was written by the hand of God, the work of God, the Scripture of God. There is nothing human in it; it is wholly divine, wholly composed by God dictating and writing it, and therefore full of truth and authority [Col. 0085A].”

Saint Bruno also establishes the authority of tradition both in matters of faith and in rites established by the Church for administering the sacraments, in two places. With regard to the understanding of mysteries, he says in his Commentary on Exodus, p. 89, col. 2, that we ought not to believe otherwise than the holy Fathers taught and believed, for their doctrines must be retained as divinely revealed; nor may anyone presume to know more than they declared must be believed.

“Let the faith of the saints, therefore, suffice us; nor should we seek further concerning those things which have been divinely revealed to them. And since we are unable to understand ourselves and the things within us, let us not labor to extend ourselves to things above us [Col. 0085B].”

From the same source—that is, from tradition—the same holy bishop taught that observance of sacred rites is to be derived, in his treatise *On the Sacraments and Mysteries*. Treating baptism, he says that, for the validity of the sacrament—that is, for obtaining its power and grace—water and the Spirit, namely the invocation of the most holy Trinity, are necessary, constituting its matter and form.

“But since other things were added later, they may not be omitted. Therefore these alone,” he says, “can suffice for the sacrament of baptism; but our holy Fathers, who established those things by the Spirit of God, wished to provide for us not only in those matters which pertain to the power of the sacrament, but also in those which pertain to signification. Water and the Spirit suffice for the perfection of baptism; the other things which are added pertain to signification. For the apostle Philip did not have oil and chrism when he baptized the eunuch. Yet these things are not to be omitted, which have been added by the careful ordering of the saints in order to signify something [Col. 0085C].”

The rite and administration of sacred things, therefore, which the Church received through tradition, had a certain divine origin insofar as the holy Fathers, inspired by God, established them and left the Church itself as their guardian. Hence no private individual may omit or alter them, since the authority of tradition acquires greater weight from the consent of the Church.

## § XVI. On the Authority of the Church in Doctrine of Faith

[Col. 0085D]

The consensus of the Church in doctrines containing the dogmas of faith has always carried the greatest weight. By this a great difference is established between the world and the Church itself: the former is agitated by continual change and variety in the sciences, in laws, and in principles of government; whereas the latter enjoys firmness and stability. For although heretics sometimes arise who, like stormy winds, strive to shake and tear her apart, nevertheless they do not prevail, nor can they overthrow her firmness and stability, since the concord of orthodox doctrine and the united resolve of holy bishops and priests to preserve the deposit of faith [Col. 0086A] always resist them and render their efforts futile.

St Bruno sets this out at length in his Commentary on Psalm LXV, p. 432, explaining the words: “Who turned the sea into dry land; they shall pass through the river on foot; there shall we rejoice in him.” “By the sea,” he says, “let us understand the world, but by dry land the Church. The former is stirred by storms and tempests; the latter always remains firm and stable. The sea is turned into dry land when Gentiles and idolaters pass over to the Church and receive the faith of Christians. By rivers, moreover, because ‘many waters’ signify many peoples, are denoted the various peoples and nations of this world. We do not fear to enter rivers which we can cross. Therefore, when holy preachers, bishops, and priests preach among peoples securely and without fear [Col. 0086B], then we may say that they pass through rivers on foot. Where there was formerly fear, there joy is proclaimed. There, therefore—that is, among the peoples signified by the rivers—the saints now rejoice in one and the same thing, that is, all together and in common. The joy of all is shared, because their faith is shared: no one contradicts another, but all alike praise and bless Christ.”

The same holy bishop acknowledges that councils employ every force capable of breaking heretical errors, p. 370, ch. 1, where, explaining the words of Psalm XXXVII, “Their bow is broken,” he says: “The bow of heretics is broken, because all their heresy and deception have been condemned in many councils.” Concerning the First Council of Nicaea, he had already said, in chapter XIV on Genesis, p. 24, col. 1, [Col. 0086C] that the Arian heresy had been condemned by it and the Catholic faith confirmed.

Whether, therefore, the Church is assembled in general councils or dispersed, whenever she teaches something or defines it as a rule of belief, she must be heard and believed, since, as we have from the Apostle, 1 Timothy 3:15, she is established by God as the pillar, etc., and foundation of truth. How great the Church’s power is, and with what divine gifts she shines adorned, St Bruno represents in the cloud that descended upon Mount Sinai, in which, in Exodus chapter XXIV, the glory of the Lord is said to have appeared: “The cloud,” he says, p. 85, ch. 2, “which covered Mount Sinai is the fullness of all knowledge and wisdom, which descended upon the Church and showed the glory of the Lord to appear in it; because [Col. 0086D] the power of miracles and the grace of the Holy Spirit do not abandon the Church until the consummation of the age, according to what the Lord says: ‘I am with you always, even unto the consummation of the age.’”

Thus fortified by these privileges and prerogatives, and always assisted by the protection of her divine author, the Church exercises full authority over her children, that she may instruct them, keep them in truth, and make them perfect observers of the commandments. In order that faith might be placed in the preaching of the apostles, Christ declared that he spoke through their mouths, and thus confessed that those who heard them heard himself teaching, Luke 10:16: “He who hears you hears me”; and that those who despised them despised the Redeemer himself: “He who despises you despises me” [Col. 0087A].

Our author continues, in his commentary on this passage of Luke, confirming by events the promises which he says the Lord had made to them. For, as stated above, the Lord had sent the apostles two by two before his face, into every city and place to which he himself was about to come. “But now,” says St Bruno, “having returned, they joyfully reported to the Lord, who knows all things, those things which not they themselves, but he in them, had accomplished. For they rejoiced in the name of Christ, whose power they had experienced. They also rejoiced in the immense grace bestowed upon them by the Lord, because they not only healed infirmities, but even commanded demons and saw them subject to themselves.”

Besides evangelical preaching and the showing of signs, by which their mission was confirmed, the apostles exercised this power, and left it to be exercised by their successors, not so much by persuasion as by authority specifically entrusted to them, in order that they might separate the evil from the good and subject them to their judgment. Our author shows this law prefigured in Leviticus chapter XIII, p. 149, ch. 1, discussing the discernment of leprosy reserved to priests. For just as a leper, once recognized, was by God’s command separated from the rest of the community, so one known to be infected by spiritual leprosy must be separated from the fellowship of the faithful. But this discernment and sentence of separation belongs to the Church, and no one may arrogate it to himself. Let Bruno be heard, explaining in the same place the various kinds of excommunication:

“To bishops and priests alone the Lord has given power, with respect to the soul, to condemn and [Col. 0087C] absolve. But he sins who judges that some leper and sinner ought to be separated from communion with him before he has been judged by bishops and priests. Let the leper therefore be brought to the priest. For thus the Lord says: ‘Show yourselves to the priests,’ Luke 17:14. Let the priest examine him and inquire diligently whether it is leprosy. For leprosy has its signs; it cannot be concealed and is easily recognized. Who, indeed, doubts that an adulterer, murderer, perjurer, sacrilegious person, thief, or robber is a leper? When, therefore, the priest has found such a person, let him change his judgment neither through fear nor through love. Let him declare him to be a leper, and let him be separated according to the priest’s judgment—according to his, indeed, not another’s; for it is his office to judge him, and his office to separate him.

[Col. 0087D]

“How is he to be separated? For this separation occurs in many ways: some are separated from the body and blood of Christ; others from entrance into the Church; others from communion with the faithful. They are also separated from certain foods and drinks and other pleasures of the flesh, so that they may no longer lawfully use things which they formerly used lawfully.”

But what the Church ought to judge concerning heretics St Bruno declares in his Commentary on Numbers chapter XV, p. 183, ch. 2. After speaking of the different kinds of sacrifice for expiating the different kinds of guilt, he comes to the sin of pride and says: “But the soul which has committed something through pride, whether he is a native or a stranger, because he has rebelled against the Lord [Col. 0088A], shall perish from the people of God. We understand this clearly concerning the heretic, and for this reason he is rightly called a rebel. For it is great pride for someone, while the whole Church protests and sets forth the dogmas of faith, to wish to rebel against her and stubbornly defend his own opinion. Such a person, therefore, shall perish, whatever his rank, whatever his order, whatever his condition and religious profession.”

To perish from the people of God is the same as to be separated from the assembly of the faithful by a sentence of excommunication and expelled from communion with the Church. This is clear from Bruno’s following interpretation of the man whom the Israelites led outside the camp and stoned because he had gathered wood on the Sabbath. “By this,” he says, p. 183, ch. 2, “we are given to understand that [Col. 0088B] those who violate God’s covenant and refuse to keep and observe with the other faithful the ordinances of the Church of God ought to be driven from the Church, condemned by all, and excommunicated; for he is overwhelmed by as many stones as there are assenting persons by whom the excommunication is confirmed.”

If these things are rightly and deservedly affirmed concerning the judgment and power of bishops and priests, they must be affirmed still more of the high priest and bishop of bishops. Since the cognizance of graver cases is reserved to him in the Church, he may use the power of the keys entrusted to him by Christ the Lord whenever he judges it expedient. Although, when treating of St Peter, prince of the apostles, we have already adduced many very weighty testimonies from Bruno concerning the supreme authority of the Roman pontiff over the universal Church, [Col. 0088C] the following statements of the Bishop of Segni in his treatise *On the Unleavened Sacrifice* are most appropriate for confirming them still further.

For the Greeks, who consecrate with leavened bread, objected to the Latins that we eat unleavened bread with the Hebrews in the Jewish manner, since we celebrate the sacrifice with unleavened bread. St Bruno replies: “Far be this from the Catholic, apostolic, and Roman Church, which is called and shown to be the head, foundation, and mirror of all Churches; which God and our Lord Jesus Christ deigned to build by himself, specially promising his beloved disciple, the apostle Peter, when he said in Matthew XVI: ‘You are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my Church, and the gates of hell shall not prevail against [Col. 0088D] it; and I will give you the keys of the kingdom of heaven.’ And again, Luke chapter XXII: ‘I have prayed for you, Peter, that your faith may not fail; and when you have at length turned, strengthen your brethren.’”

Since the holy bishop wrote this treatise at the request of Benedictine monks who had a monastery at Constantinople, he concludes his work by addressing them: “Therefore, most beloved brethren, stand manfully in the fellowship and firm support of the orthodox pillar, and let no one, by persuasive words, separate you from the custom of the holy Catholic and apostolic faith of the aforesaid see, the mother Church of Rome. For, according to Augustine, the most eloquent teacher and African bishop, there is no other see in heaven or on earth more worthy or more preeminent than that held by the Roman [Col. 0089A] Church. Hold fast to her, love her with a pure heart, and do not depart from her unity, since it is written, Proverbs 22:28: ‘Do not transgress the boundary which the ancient Fathers have set’; and Ecclesiastes 10:8: ‘He who breaks down a hedge shall be bitten by a serpent’—that serpent, namely, which cast Adam out of paradise, from whose pestilential mouth may the Lord always deliver you.”

Since these things concerning the apostolic see have been said not in ambiguous words but in open and certain expressions, it cannot be doubted [Col. 0090A] that this is the constant and firmly established judgment of the holy Fathers in every age: that the doctrine of this supreme see must be held as the rule of faith, and therefore that no one may depart from it or refuse obedience to it. Truly pitiable are those who choose to be blind amid so great a light, and who, driven by an evil spirit, flee from the embrace of their most loving mother and drag themselves and all whom they seduce to eternal ruin.

[Col. 0089A]

LIFE OF ST BRUNO, OR BRUNON, OF ASTI, BISHOP OF SEGNI AND ABBOT OF MONTE CASSINO. Published in Book IV, chapter 33, of the *Chronicle of Monte Cassino* by Peter the Deacon, as it had been arranged by Leo, bishop and cardinal of Ostia; but, prevented by death, he had been unable to complete it, as Peter himself attests in his dedicatory epistle to Rainald, abbot and cardinal.

[Col. 0089]

[Col. 0089B] The most blessed Brunus, or Bruno, fortieth abbot of this monastery, held office for three years and ten months. He was born in the province of Liguria, of the distinguished lineage of the people of Asti; yet from infancy he possessed still more distinguished virtues, and from boyhood had been adequately educated in liberal studies. He became a canon of the bishop of Asti. Then, leaving homeland and parents out of desire for the kingdom of heaven, he hastened here, so that under the monastic habit he might serve God more freely; but he first came to the city of Rome. At that time Urban II presided over the universal Church.

It happened that, at the very time when this man was making his way to this place, the bishop of Segni departed this life. The Roman pontiff, seeing him aflame in spirit, said to him: “Just as the calmness [Col. 0089C] of the sea often brings danger to sailors, so also for monks withdrawn from the world’s tempest, rest and security themselves are accustomed to bring a most destructive shipwreck. Therefore you ought to obey our injunctions and endeavor to govern the care of the Church of Segni, which we lay upon you, with a devotion and diligence proportionate to your knowledge and wisdom.”

When he gave no assent whatever to these words, the pope ordered him to proceed to the aforesaid city and, having there ordained him bishop in the Roman pontiff’s stead, to go where he wished. Then the aforesaid man arrived there and strove to fulfill the charge imposed upon him; meanwhile the same pope secretly sent letters to the people of Segni, instructing them to have him ordained bishop. When these things came to his knowledge, he left the Church of Blessed Mary in the silence of the dead of night [Col. 0089D] and took flight.

While he was striving to carry out his plan, at a certain crossroads a virgin stood near him, adorned in imperial robes, whose face shone like the sun. When he asked her what and who she was, and where she was going, she answered: “Know that I am the bride from whom you are not rightly fleeing. Therefore I command you, on behalf of God Almighty, to return to the Church. Beware that you do not wish any further to resist God’s will.” Having said this, she vanished. Struck by these words of the holy virgin [Col. 0090B] and recognizing God’s will in his ordination, Bruno yielded and ascended the episcopal chair amid the rejoicing of all.

Once ordained, however, he remained fixed in his former intention. Thus, when an opportunity presented itself, under the aforesaid Abbot Oderisius he came to this place and, to the tears of those who had accompanied him and suspected nothing of the kind, became a monk. The people of Segni, deeply grieving his absence, approached Pope Paschal II and begged him in tears to compel Bruno to resume the care of their bishopric, rather than permit one so mindful only of his own concerns to dwell quietly in the monastery of Monte Cassino [Col. 0090C], removed from the world’s tempest.

Moved by their words, the pontiff sent vigorous men from his side, who commanded Bruno, on behalf of the apostolic see, to attend to the care of his sheep and always to adhere to the Roman pontiff in ecclesiastical cases. They further rebuked and reproved him for having dared, without permission from the apostolic see, to seek a monastery—a place in which the pope would by no means allow him to remain. To this Bruno replied in writing through friendly bishops and cardinals:

“All who belong to the Roman Church undoubtedly know that, unless the madness of the schismatics were raging against the Church, I would have carried out in deed many years ago what I have now done. But now, since Peter is holding the helm in the Roman Church and the whole Church of Christ our God rejoices throughout the world, the storms of the winds are now silent and the seas rest in calm. Therefore I am bound to render what I once vowed to God. For it is better not to vow than to vow and not fulfill it. But if anyone should perhaps object that I ought not to have relinquished a bishopric once received [Col. 0091A], I will freely reply: there are many who have not abandoned the rights of their bishopric and yet are among those on the left, as the Lord says in Hosea 2: ‘They were princes, and I knew them not; they became judges, and not by my Spirit.’ But it is certain that those who have left the episcopate with right intention rejoice everlastingly in Christ in eternal happiness. Nor do I lack examples of saints whose footsteps I have followed, who, leaving the tumult of the world, attained a peaceful life. Therefore through you I earnestly beseech the supreme pontiff that henceforth he trouble me no more; and I humbly ask that he not compel me to leave the peaceful harbor to which, with Christ as pilot, I have come.”

Since he could not by any argument bend either the apostolic pontiff or the people of Segni, the aforesaid Abbot Oderisius asked the pope to permit the aforesaid man to serve God in this monastery under the monastic habit. The pope listened to his prayers and relented.

After this, the pope sent him with Bohemond into Gaul. Acting in the Roman pontiff’s place, he held a synod in those regions according to ecclesiastical tradition. From there he returned to Rome, and on the forty-fourth day after the deposition of Abbot Otto he returned to this monastery; the brethren placed him over the governance and care of this abbey. The same apostolic pontiff later came to this place and declared publicly to that assembly not only that Bruno was worthy to be abbot, but also that he would be a worthy successor to himself in the apostolic see [Col. 0091C].

It must not be supposed that this man lived here idly, since he expounded for us such and so many books of Scripture. We take care to set forth a summary of those which have come into our hands: on Genesis, Exodus, Leviticus, Numbers, Deuteronomy, the Psalter, Isaiah, the Song of Songs, Judges, and Revelation. He composed sixty-nine sermons on the feasts and Sundays of the whole year, and one hundred and forty-five homilies.

At this same time Adenulfus, Lando, and Atenulfus, counts of Aquino, intoxicated by diabolical frenzy, entered the castle of Terame through the treachery of peasants [Col. 0091D], compelled the inhabitants of that castle to swear fealty to them, and began to plunder the towns belonging to the monastery. When this was reported to the aforesaid abbot, he sent to the counts and attempted to admonish them to restore the castle to the monastery and desist from such great injustices and depredations. They would not even allow his warning to be heard, but threatened that they would do worse day by day.

Then the abbot, after taking counsel with the brethren, separated these sacrilegious men from the thresholds of the Church; and immediately summoned Prince Robert and invited him to recover the castle. Robert assembled a very large army, came against the same castle, and began to besiege it by every means. After he had remained there in hostile array for [Col. 0092A] fifteen days, the same counts sent word to the abbot that, if he would allow them to leave with their arms, they would restore the castle itself without any dispute. The abbot agreed, and the aforesaid castle returned to this monastery’s possession on the Ides of August, in the year of the Lord 1108. For that castle the abbot paid the prince of Capua 200 pounds.

In October the same apostolic pontiff came here and, taking our abbot with him, proceeded to Benevento to celebrate a synod. Following in the footsteps of his predecessors, he decreed there that, if anyone received an ecclesiastical benefice from the hand of laymen, both giver and recipient should be deprived of communion. He also censured secular and costly garments and prohibited clerics from using such attire. When [Col. 0092B] he had come to Capua, at the request of the same abbot he solemnly dedicated the Church of St Benedict, which Abbot Desiderius had rebuilt within that city; he also placed there relics of the garments of the most holy Father Benedict. He then came to this monastery and returned to Rome.

At this time Duke Roger, by decree, granted to Blessed Benedict that the monastery’s livestock should pay no tax to himself or his successors, as they had been accustomed to do, anywhere within the territory of Mount Gargano; and that from the church called Passari as far as the bridge of Salpi and as far as the sea, the sheep should have permission to pasture, with a penalty of ten pounds of gold imposed. At that time Laydulfus, son of Count Pandulf of Presenzano, in the presence of the same [Col. 0092C] abbot, declared that he gave up his entire share in the castle of Mortula, Casa Fortini, Cucuruzzo, and Rocca de Bantra, under a penalty of one hundred pounds should he seek to revoke this. John, bishop of the see of Trivento, together with Robert son of Tristan, lord of the castle of Limessano, also offered to this place the Church of St Illuminata within the boundaries of that same castle, with all its churches and appurtenances.

In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1110, indiction 3, in the month of June, on the sixth day of that month, a comet appeared. Then, on the third day before the Ides of February, Emperor Henry arrived at the city. The pontiff therefore sent to meet him. When Henry had ascended the upper steps of the church of St Peter, the lord pope was present there with the bishops and cardinals [Col. 0092D]. After entering the basilica, the two sat down. The pontiff requested the restoration of ecclesiastical right. Henry withdrew with the bishops and princes. Meanwhile the pontiff and those with him were held under guard. At last he was allowed with difficulty to ascend to the altar of Blessed Peter for the celebration of the solemn Mass. When Mass had been completed, the pontiff was compelled to descend from his seat; he sat below, before the Confession of St Peter, with the brethren, and there he was kept under guard by soldiers until night. At last he was led with the brethren to lodgings outside the church’s atrium.

A great multitude of clergy and laity was captured with him. He also ordered boys and people of various ages, who had gone out to meet him with flowers and palms, some to be slaughtered, others stripped, some beaten, and others bound. Meanwhile John of Tusculum [Col. 0093A] and Leo, bishop of Ostia, when they saw that the pope had been captured, withdrew into the City in plebeian dress.

When the Romans heard that the pope was captive, such an uproar, grief, and indignation seized their hearts that they immediately killed all Germans who had entered the city, whether for prayer or for any other business. On the following day they went out from the city, joined battle, killed very many of the emperor’s army, seized their spoils, and began a fiercer fight against the Teutons. They nearly drove them from the portico, threw the emperor himself from his horse, and wounded him in the face. When the Germans saw themselves hard pressed by the Romans, they withdrew to their camp. The Romans, greatly emboldened, [Col. 0093B] all bound themselves by oath against the emperor.

When these things were reported to the emperor, that same night he fled from the portico in such fear with his whole army, taking the apostolic pontiff with him, that they left behind not only their baggage but also many companions in their lodging. After two days he ordered the pontiff to be stripped of his sacred vestments; when this had been done, they dragged him away in chains, proceeding as far as Soracte. The pontiff, with two bishops—the bishop of Sabina and the bishop of Porto—and four cardinals, was held at the castle of Trebicum; the other cardinals were held in custody at Corcodisum.

Thus, while the emperor was daily ravaging the Romans’ lands and testing their resolve by money and trickery, God gave the people such constancy that [Col. 0093C] he could obtain no agreement from them, not even by promising the release of the pope and cardinals. Seeing, therefore, that things had turned out otherwise than he had expected, he began to affirm by oath that, unless the pontiff complied with him, he would kill or mutilate, by cutting off their limbs, both the pontiff himself and all those whom he held in chains. But since he could not bend the pontiff’s constancy to this, he finally agreed after full deliberation to free all whom he had captured, provided that he could secure provision for himself from the pontiff in the future.

The pontiff, however, preferred to lay down his life rather than violate the rights of the Church, although Henry asserted that he sought not the Church’s rights or any offices, but only the regalian rights. A grave danger of schism was set before him, threatening nearly every Church of the Latins [Col. 0093D]. Yet overcome by the tears and sighs of his children, he dissolved wholly into tears. “I am compelled,” he said, “for the peace and liberation of the Church, to endure that which, in order not to endure it, I was prepared even to shed my life’s blood.”

Accordingly, by the pope’s word an oath was sworn in this manner: that he would no longer disturb the emperor; that he would confirm to the emperor, under anathema, a privilege concerning the presumed and rashly claimed right of the Church, namely, that the emperor should invest bishops and abbots freely elected without simony with ring and staff, and that a bishop thus invested should freely receive consecration from the archbishop to whom it belonged. But if anyone were elected by people and clergy and not invested by the emperor [Col. 0094A], he should be consecrated by no one. After the pope had confirmed these terms by oath, the emperor in turn swore that he would safely bring the pontiff with the bishops and cardinals, and all who had been captured with or for him, as well as the hostages, within the gates of the Transtiberine city; and that he would neither capture them nor permit them thereafter to be captured.

The emperor was crowned on the next day. After the coronation, when the solemnities of Mass had ended, the emperor returned to his camp, while the pontiff returned to the City. From this point scandals of dissension and schism began to arise in the Roman Church.

At this same time, while our abbot Bruno was solemnly dedicating the Church of St Thomas the Apostle outside the castle of Vallefredda, a certain woman afflicted by an unclean spirit was brought to him. Moved by compassion for [Col. 0094B] her affliction, after prayer he gave the suffering woman to drink water in which he had washed his hands, and immediately cast the evil spirit out of her.

The aforesaid abbot, joined by Guala, bishop of Reggio, Robert of Palestrina, and other cardinals, earnestly pressed the aforementioned pontiff to annul the privilege which he had granted to the emperor and bind him with the bond of anathema. Those who had been imprisoned with him said: “What we said before, we say now; what we preached before, we preach with one voice; and what we condemned before, we condemn.” Others, however, not only did not condemn what had been done against the Catholic Church, but even shamelessly endeavored to defend it.

While the apostolic Church was shaken by dissensions of this kind, [Col. 0094C] the pontiff was told that the aforesaid man had been the leader and standard-bearer of that discord and scandal. When the abbot heard this, seizing an opportunity, he said to him:

“My enemies tell you that I do not love you and speak ill of you; but they lie. For I love you as my father and lord, and while you live I wish to have no other pontiff, as I have promised you together with many others. Yet I hear my Savior saying to me: ‘He who loves father or mother more than me is not worthy of me’ (Matthew 10); and likewise the Apostle: ‘If anyone does not love the Lord Jesus Christ, let him be anathema’ (1 Corinthians 16). Therefore I ought to love you, but I ought to love still more him who made both you and me. Nothing must ever be preferred to so great a love.

“I do not approve that covenant—so foul, so violent, so treacherously made, so contrary to every piety and religious obligation. Who indeed could approve that by which faith is violated, the liberty of the Church is lost, the priesthood is abolished, the one and unique door of the Church is closed, and many doors are opened through which whoever enters is a thief and a robber? We have the canons; we have the enactments of the holy Fathers handed down from the times of the apostles to your own. We must walk the royal road and turn aside from it neither to one side nor to the other. The apostles condemn and separate from the communion of the faithful all those who obtain the Church through secular power. For laymen, however religious they may be, have received no authority to dispose of the Church [Col. 0095A]. This is the holy ordinance of the apostles; whoever contradicts it is not Catholic. Everyone who maintains heresy is a heretic. No one can say that this is not heresy, which the holy and apostolic Church calls heresy in many councils and condemns together with its authors.”

Such an address between the pontiff and the abbot supplied fuel for envy and hatred. Among other things which the pontiff then said concerning the abbot was this: “Unless I remove him from the administration of the monastery, he will, by his arguments, take from me the governance of the Church.” Therefore he sent the abbot a letter forbidding him any longer to be both bishop and abbot, because the apostolic see could no longer tolerate a bishop presiding over so celebrated a monastery. He also sent letters to the brethren through Leo, bishop of Ostia and monk of this abbey [Col. 0095B], ordering them no longer to obey the man, but to elect themselves an abbot according to God and the Rule; otherwise, he himself would appoint abbots in all the cells of the monastery.

When the abbot heard this, he called the brethren together and began to explain the disagreement which had arisen between himself and the supreme pontiff over ecclesiastical matters. He also urged them that, if they wished to have an abbot whom he himself chose, he would protect and defend them and this place to the full extent of his power. There was then in the monastery a brother named Peregrinus, a Ligurian by nationality, skilled in worldly cunning, upon whom Bruno intended to impose the burden of government. When the brethren learned this, they told the abbot that, as long as he wished to preside over them by the right of an abbot, they would all obey him as lord and father; but if he relinquished that charge, they would by no means allow anyone else to exercise the election owed to them by the precept of the Rule, but would themselves, according to ancient custom, appoint an abbot.

When Peregrinus heard this and thought he could carry out his purpose by force, he summoned armed soldiers to his aid to guard the monastery. On the following day, while the brethren entered the church peacefully to celebrate Mass, a multitude of raging men, armed with weapons, suddenly confronted them and demanded to know who they were who refused to fulfill the abbot’s will. The brethren, taking this very grievously and indignantly, rushed upon them with one accord and drove them from the monastery. When this was reported to the abbot, he immediately went up to the monastery. Calling the brethren to himself, he said: “I do not wish a scandal to arise because of me between you and the Roman pontiff [Col. 0096B].” Placing the pastoral staff upon the altar, he said: “Take back what you gave me.” Having granted absolution to the brethren, he returned to his bishopric.

There, living in holy conduct until the time of Oderisius II, abbot, he happily passed to the Lord on the day before the Kalends of September [31 August]. He was buried in the city of Segni, in the Church of St Mary, Mother of God and Virgin. Even today the Lord deigns to work miracles at his memorial through the merits of his intercession.

Girard, forty-first abbot of this monastery, descended from the most noble stock of the Marsi, was elected abbot by the unanimous consent of the brethren after Otto’s death, when Bruno, having become abbot in the manner related above and, at the Roman pontiff’s command, having left the care of the monastery, had returned to his bishopric [Col. 0096C].

[Col. 0095C]

COMMENTARY ON THE LIFE OF ST BRUNO OF ASTI, BISHOP OF SEGNI

PREFACE.

[Col. 0095C] Misfortune is commonly ascribed to the condition of men if they were born and lived in periods called obscure, uncultivated, and of the lowest age. I readily grant that a certain prerogative of distinction and honour belongs to an age in which the more humane letters and intellectual disciplines flourished most brilliantly, and in which more outstanding writings by learned men appeared; hence those who prospered in those fortunate days are judged happy and blessed. From this eminent seat, however, those are commonly cast down who, through the vicissitudes of time, were born when learning was declining toward sunset, and who, with good studies almost neglected, had no eminent models set before their eyes. Yet because virtue and wisdom rise more gloriously in proportion as the way to them is more difficult—being acquired by greater exertion and native ability—I cannot agree with those who presume to judge men’s merits from the reproach attached to their age. [Col. 0095D]

I undertake to repel this prejudice, or the unworthy opinion entertained by some concerning Saint Bruno of Asti, bishop of Signi; and I maintain that he ought to be placed among the more illustrious bishops, the more celebrated doctors, and the Fathers who have deserved best of the Catholic Church. As regards wisdom, I would have praised not merely that wisdom which is human and in which many pagan philosophers excelled, but that which is from above, descending from the Father of lights (James II.17), and which, as most wise Solomon teaches in Ecclesiasticus I.11, “God pours out upon men according to His gift, and grants it to those who love Him.”

Indeed, if Saint Bruno’s commentaries on the divine books [Col. 0096C] are weighed impartially; if his theological treatises are examined; if his exposition of mysteries and sacred rites, and the abundant harvest of his homilies and sermons, are considered, the holy bishop of Signi must be numbered among the more illustrious teachers of divine doctrine. What wonder, then, if this lamp, so shining, did not remain hidden under a bushel, but, placed upon a lampstand, poured out its brightness over the whole house of God (Matthew V.15); if he refuted heretics and heresies; if he discharged the chief ecclesiastical dignities and offices; if he everywhere won for himself the affection and esteem of foreign peoples; if more celebrated writers left eminent testimonies to his holiness and learning; if many supreme pontiffs held him in high regard?

When I mention these supreme pastors of the Church, let Saint Gregory VII, Victor III, Urban II, and Paschal II be kept in mind: men most renowned for learning, prudence, and greatness of spirit, who preserved Peter’s ship safe and uninjured while it was tossed by great waves. This was the man who came to the aid of the Church, suffering under the Simoniacal plague; who did not fear human powers when they strayed from the straight path; who fought invincibly for sacred rights; who, like a most sturdy wall, exposed himself for the safety of the sanctuary. If anyone reflects upon these matters, which we have briefly gathered together and shall treat more fully in his Life, he will judge Saint Bruno worthy not of a mediocre reputation, but of comparison with the greatest and holiest men. [Col. 0096D]

The episcopal see itself in the city of Signi, over which he presided for so many years, also lends him great distinction. It was a notable municipality of the Roman commonwealth, populous and very strongly fortified, [Col. 0097A] so that Gaius Marius chose it for winter quarters with his army while intending to attack Sulla, and stationed his camp in that most secure place. Signi is also reckoned among the foremost cities of Campania: it renounced false deities, professed the Christian religion, and was adorned with episcopal dignity. Certainly, in the time of Saint Symmachus, who held several councils at Rome, Sanctulus and Justus, bishops of Signi, are found subscribing the synodal decrees; and many bishops conspicuous for holiness and learning made that see illustrious.

The fame of the city of Signi is increased by Saint Vitalian, Roman pontiff, whom it gave birth to, and who most holily governed the Roman Church from 1156 to 1169; he is called the co-apostle of the English because, by sending evangelical ministers into that island, he first brought there the light of the Catholic faith. The Senate and People of Signi (*S. P. Q. S.*) placed the following inscription beneath his marble image in the principal church of Signi, for the perpetual remembrance of so great a pontiff and fellow citizen. [Col. 0097B]

Another title to the praise of the city of Signi may be drawn from the fact that Roman pontiffs, often compelled to leave the City because other towns of their dominion had rebelled or were insufficiently safe, chose it as their residence. They considered themselves adequately defended not so much by the advantages of its site—for the city stands on the summit of a lofty mountain—as by the loyalty of its inhabitants. Finally, Signi’s glory was increased further because Alexander III solemnly celebrated the canonization of Saint Thomas, archbishop of Canterbury, and Lucius III that of Saint Bruno, in the principal church of the same city, having summoned bishops from all Campania [Col. 0097C] and with many cardinals of the Holy Roman Church present.

## COMMENTARY ON THE LIFE OF SAINT BRUNO

[Col. 0097]

### CHAPTER I. On the homeland and birth of Saint Bruno

Those who wish to set forth the histories of ancient times with greater order and scrutiny of truth are at once held in doubt at the threshold of their work if they find the earliest writers of them disagreeing among themselves. This has certainly happened to me while writing the acts of Saint Bruno, bishop [Col. 0097D] of Signi, since Peter the Deacon, a monk and continuator of the Chronicle of Monte Cassino begun by Leo of Ostia, differs very greatly from the anonymous author, said to have been a canon of Signi, not so much in identifying Bruno’s homeland and parents as in many matters comprised in his deeds.

For the Cassinese chronicler wrote that Bruno was born in the province of Liguria, from an illustrious stock of citizens of Asti. The Anonymous writer, however, relates that Bruno’s birthplace was Solero, a town in the territory of Alessandria, and that his parents, Andrew and Willa, possessed no distinguished nobility of birth. Yet the position of the Cassinese writer is strongly defended by many arguments by Philip Malabayles, a Cistercian abbot, in his inquiry concerning the Life of Saint Bruno, published by Maurus Marchesius, a monk, together with the aforesaid writers. He accordingly contends that Bruno was born at Asti and descended from a family, surnamed Astensi, highly illustrious in blood and in lordship over the castle of Solero.

Ferdinand Ughelli, Arnold Wion, Matthew Lauretus, Mabillon, Ferrarius, Lucentius, and many others who have embellished Bruno’s acts seem to have adopted the same opinion. Yet it matters little to the glory of his name whether the people of Asti or of Solero claim him as their fellow citizen, since it is not one’s homeland or a splendid lineage, but eminent and illustrious virtues and deeds, that make a man worthy of praise. Nevertheless, I do not think it should pass unnoticed that the Solero family, most distinguished among the Allobroges, claims Saint Bruno as its own and has customarily assumed his name, as though hereditary in the family, for a long time.

> **Note:** [Col. 0097D] Bruno, an Asti native and descended from the Solari or Soleria family, is affirmed by many writers: Ecclesia, in the catalogue of Piedmontese writers, p. 42; Ughelli, *Italia Sacra*, col. 1236, [Col. 0098D] vol. I; Rosoti, *Syllabarium scriptorum Pedemontanorum*, p. 127; Leiser, in *Historia poetica et poemata medii aevi*; and others. Conversely, others have reported that Saint Bruno was born at Solero, of an Asti family; these, as well as the former writers, are listed by the distinguished Count Giovanni M. Mazzuchelli of Brescia, vol. II, part IV, p. 2227. They are Possevino, vol. I, *Appendix fac.*; Einsinger; Gabriel Busselin, in *Historia universalis*; Porta, *Alexandria illustrata*, p. 220. Soprani and Oldoini, however, number Bruno among Ligurian writers. Both opinions have their defenders. Writers called Bruno “of Asti” either from Asti as his birthplace, or because Solero, where many hold that he was born, was then situated in the diocese of Asti. [Col. 0099D]

In what year Bruno was born, although the biographers make no [Col. 0099A] mention of it, may nevertheless be inferred from the year in which he was ordained bishop of Signi. This occurred after the Roman council, as we shall show below. That synod was convened by Saint Gregory VII in 1079, without dissent; and since Bruno refuted the heretic Berengar in it and gave other proofs of singular learning, prudence, and holiness, it may be inferred that he was then about thirty-five years old and flourishing at the age at which he could most suitably discharge the episcopal office. These points being established, it will be clear that Bruno’s birth should be assigned to the forty-fourth year after the millennium.

> **Note:** [Col. 0099D] Corrado Corradi, O.P., who in 1694 published in octavo a brief compendium in Italian of the deeds of Saint Bruno, places his birth in the forty-eighth year after the millennium [Col. 0100D]. We nevertheless do not depart from our opinion, because it accords better with the calculation of the years of Bruno’s life.

### CHAPTER II. On Bruno’s education and studies

A custom had already become established from the time of Saint Benedict among noble persons—as Saints Placid and Maurus attest—of placing their children under his discipline, so that they might receive the holier rudiments of Christian devotion and be instructed in good letters. Since the disciples of the holy patriarch were then flourishing especially in the monastery of Saint Perpetuus near Asti, Andrew and Willa, Bruno’s parents, entrusted him while still a child to those eminent religious men for instruction, having discerned in him the first signs of an excellent natural disposition. [Col. 0099B]

I do not know whether those set over his education admired more in the young Bruno his intellectual capacity for acquiring the disciplines, or his greater zeal for gaining heavenly wisdom; for he pursued with the utmost eagerness whatever could perfect and adorn mind and soul. Having completed among the Benedictines the course of humane letters, Bruno was sent by his parents, who held great hopes concerning him, to the university of Bologna, the most celebrated in all Italy, to acquire higher learning.

I judge it superfluous here to mention the remarkable brilliance by which Bruno immediately distinguished himself among his peers, or his diligence and assiduity in attending his teachers. For that Bruno united this supreme application of mind with an exceptional natural ability is shown not so much by all the honours and degrees conferred on him by the heads of the university, as by the outstanding fruits of his studies which he brought to light and which we have undertaken to collect and publish anew. In these writings, all who have discussed them have most fully shown that he had acquired a profound understanding of the divine Scriptures, extensive knowledge of Hebrew and Greek, [Col. 0099C] and a treasury of universal learning. [Col. 0099D]

After Bruno’s parents recalled him to Asti, he himself composed a short commentary on the Psalms in order to comply with the wishes of his bishop Ingone, as he himself testifies in the preface to the Apocalypse. Although Bruno’s writings have been treated in the prolegomena, it was permissible to mention these matters in order that it may be certain that, after completing his studies at Bologna, he returned to his homeland equipped with more distinguished attainments. Some writers, such as Corradi, have doubted this return and taught that he proceeded directly from Bologna to Rome; but their opinion must be wholly rejected. [Col. 0100A]

### CHAPTER III. On Bruno’s first dignities

A second, not insignificant disagreement occurs among the biographers. Some affirm that he was a canon of Asti; others, a canon of Siena; and others wish him to have held that dignity in both cities. Those who argue for Bruno’s canonry at Asti adduce the authority of Peter the Deacon, and say that an exceedingly ancient image of Bruno, preserved among the canons of that cathedral, represents him as a young man dressed in a canon’s garments. They likewise mention a similar statue, erected in a chapel dedicated to him beyond all memory. They also say that the name Bruni or Bruno is recorded in some very ancient documents preserved in the canons’ archive. Furthermore, they add that it is by no means unreasonable that Ingone, a bishop eminent for holiness and learning, should have wished Bruno to be enrolled among the canons [Col. 0100B] of his church, so that he might shine there like a star and pour upon his people the light of exceptional wisdom.

> **Note:** [Col. 0100D] He governed the Church of Asti from 1072 to 1079.

As was said above, Bruno had already produced his first interpretation of the Psalms, by which he had demonstrated to that same bishop how deeply he was versed in sacred studies. Others, however, maintain that Bruno was a canon at Siena.

> **Note:** [Col. 0100D] “Marcus Antonius Scipio, in his eulogies of the abbots of Monte Cassino, states plainly,” as Malabayles says, “that Bruno, after completing his course of studies, now somewhat older, went down into Etruria and served for some time as a canon in the principal church at Siena, with the great approval of the brethren.” Crillerius must be corrected, for he calls our Bruno a canon of Signi, not of Siena.

For Bruno himself says of himself in the same preface to the Apocalypse: “For the canons of Siena, among whom I myself lived as a canon, whatever sort of canon I may have been, I expounded the Song of Songs as best I could.” The defenders of this opinion are not unaware that some have interpreted this passage as referring to the sustenance which those canons supplied to Bruno while he lived at Siena, rather than to his actually holding a canonry among them. But many reject such an interpretation as far too unworthy of so great a man, and allow the words no other sense than that Bruno, having been admitted there to a canonry, made his manner of life wholly conform to that of those canons. [Col. 0100C]

For at Asti, as at Vercelli, canons then lived regularly within cloisters like monks and served in complete dedication to the principal church. At Siena, however, the canons may have been governed by different institutions, and therefore it is likely that Bruno adopted no different manner of life from theirs.

> **Note:** [Col. 0101D] The canons of Asti professed the Rule of Saint Benedict, contrary to the opinion of Pennotti, who wrote that they were governed according to Saint Augustine’s institution. Thus Gattula, part I, p. 372, *Historia Casinensis*.

The Cassinese chronicler gives a clear testimony that Bruno was a canon of Asti, and Ughelli follows him; conversely, the Bollandists judge that, because of his exceptional merits in virtue and learning, the canons of Siena made Bruno their colleague. Others reconcile the two views thus: Bruno, having returned [Col. 0101A] to his homeland, was a canon there for some years; afterward, perhaps through a desire or vow to seek Monte Cassino, he left Asti and set out toward Rome. But when he came to Siena, he did not wish, as an unknown man, to proceed farther. For Rudolph, bishop of that city, highly commended for holiness and learning, and the canons—some of whom perhaps had known him as a fellow student and friend at Bologna, or knew him already celebrated by report—endeavoured to retain him among themselves by conferring a canonry upon him. At their request, Bruno subsequently expounded the Song of Songs. [Col. 0101B]

Corradi relates the matter differently. He says that Bruno, moved by the renowned piety and wisdom of the bishop of Siena, visited him. When the bishop questioned him about certain theological matters before some of the principal ecclesiastical men, they admired not merely his eloquence and wealth of learning, but also his singular modesty and graciousness; and, though he resisted because he had proposed for himself another kind of more perfect life, they wished to enrol him among the canons of the principal church. Corradi also adds that Bruno was ordained priest by the bishop of Siena, held the dignity of canon there for six years, and gave striking proofs of piety and a most blameless life. [Col. 0101C]

This does not conflict with the age at which Bruno is said to have gone to Rome, if we suppose that he spent some years in a canonry at Asti and others in one at Siena. For, as stated above, he is shown to have been more than thirty years old at episcopal ordination. Some object that no document survives at Siena showing that Bruno was a canon there; but no one is ignorant how much, and what kind of, material the ravages of time and the vicissitudes of wars have everywhere carried off and destroyed. Since Bruno’s own testimony is available, his authority is sufficient for all.

Nor should I omit the devotion toward Saint Bruno, transmitted to the canons of Siena from their forebears, [Col. 0102A] and their annual liturgical celebration of his feast-day. This can be supposed to have been granted by Roman pontiffs only upon established acts showing that Saint Bruno had been a canon of the metropolitan church. To these considerations I add the most distinguished and learned Lord Tiberius Burghesi, archbishop of Siena—may God preserve him long and safe in that see—and also certain canons of that Church devoted to Saint Bruno, who, as soon as this recent edition of his works became known to them, wished to acquire it for themselves.

### CHAPTER IV. On Bruno’s journey to the City

Having left the homeland and parents whom we love most dearly, in order to seek Monte Cassino and devote himself there wholly to the spiritual life, Bruno could not be detained by the Sienese from remaining steadfast in his purpose of renouncing the world. He therefore took leave of the bishop of Siena and his fellow canons, who bore his departure with sorrow, and came to Rome to pay devout and reverent homage to the thresholds of the holy apostles and the memorials of the more celebrated martyrs.

> **Note:** [Col. 0101D] “Corradi relates that Bruno was sent to Rome by the bishop of Siena to transact certain important affairs.”

Yet Bruno could not remain unknown there, but became known to Saint Peter Igneus, bishop of Albano and cardinal.

> **Note:** [Col. 0101D] Saint Peter, born at Florence from the most noble family of the Aldobrandeschi, is highly celebrated in the annals of the Church. From childhood he was a disciple of Saint John Gualbert and an eminent ornament of his congregation, because he twice passed unharmed through a blazing fire in order to expose the wickedness of the Simoniacs. [Col. 0102D]

Peter wished him to lodge with him and did not cease to render him every service, overcome by the presence and conversation of so remarkable a man. As Peter associated familiarly with Bruno and increasingly admired in him the breadth of his wisdom and his most holy character, he commended him to Gregory VII, the supreme pontiff, and declared him very useful to the Church, especially in those days [Col. 0102B] when mighty waves were assailing it.

The pontiff, inflamed with a desire to see Bruno, summoned him to himself. Having spoken with him at length about the state of the Church and especially about the heresy of Berengar, who had long been utterly overthrowing Catholic doctrine concerning the sacrament of the altar, Bruno argued so wisely and aptly before the pontiff for the refutation of the error that he far exceeded Gregory’s exceptional expectations. Let us briefly recall here the esteem which Bruno had won from Peter Igneus and Pope Gregory, themselves eminent for such learning and holiness.

> **Note:** [Col. 0102D] From Bruno’s Life of Pope Saint Leo IX it is clear how great was his familiarity and association with Pope Gregory VII.

Thus, although one hundred and fifty bishops summoned to the council were present at Rome, Bruno himself was chosen, [Col. 0102D] *Ecclesiastical History*, book LXIX, year 1079, to dispute with Berengar in that synod. From Fleury we learn that Alberic, a monk of Monte Cassino, was assigned to Bruno; but neither Binius, Ughelli, nor Spondanus mentions him.

### CHAPTER V. On the disputation with Berengar at the Roman council

In February 1079 Gregory VII held a council at Rome [Col. 0103A] in the church of Saint Saviour, attended by 150 bishops, among whom the more distinguished were Henry, patriarch of Aquileia; Peter Igneus of Albano; Anselm of Lucca; Landulf of Pisa; and Rainerius of Florence. The principal cause of this assembly was Berengar’s relapse into the same heresy.

> **Note:** [Col. 0103D] For he had abjured his error at the Council of Vercelli in 1053, in the presence of Saint Leo IX; again at the Synod of Tours in 1054; and once more at the First Lateran Council under Nicholas II in 1059.

He denied Christ’s real presence in the sacrament of the Eucharist. For this he had already been condemned in three councils, and was now striving to defend himself by new sophistries and arguments. Writers of that age acknowledge that Berengar of Tours, archdeacon of the Church of Angers, possessed acute intelligence and was thoroughly trained in the school of the Peripatetics. Men otherwise learned and versed in sacred letters and theological disciplines declined to engage this adversary, because, being unpractised in disputations, they did not wish to expose themselves [Col. 0103B] to the tricks and sophistries of a captious man.

> **Note:** [Col. 0103D] “At the same time, while Blessed Gregory VII was residing in the Lateran palace, a very serious question concerning the sacrament of the body and blood of our Lord Jesus Christ was being debated with a certain Master Berengar, who held insufficiently faithful views concerning that sacrament. No one was found who dared to dispute with that master concerning the sacrament of so great a mystery, because that master was too highly practised in the conflict of questions, etc.” Anonymous. Severinus Binius, in his notes on this council, writes: “The acts of his Life testify that Saint Bruno, who shortly afterward was created bishop of Signi, disputed against Berengar in this council.” Vol. X, col. 380, Paris edition, 1671. Pagi likewise asserts this under the year 1079, no. 3, and praises him for having refuted Berengar. [Col. 0104D]

The difficulty of so great a contest did not frighten Bruno. He cheerfully entered the arena, with present not only the pontiff and bishops but the entire Roman clergy. The contest between Bruno and Berengar was long. When Bruno had refuted and successfully crushed everything more subtle and ingenious that the heresiarch had devised, Berengar yielded in defeat, publicly condemned his heresy in the council, and promised to profess the orthodox faith concerning the most holy Eucharist. This victory won Bruno great glory and renown; and the pontiff and Fathers congratulated him with festive acclamations, easier to conceive in the mind [Col. 0103C] than to recount.

Gregory showed how highly he valued Bruno not only by words, but from that time resolved to promote him to episcopal dignity.

> **Note:** [Col. 0104D] “The acts of his Life testify that Saint Bruno, or Brunon, renowned in this century for learning and holiness, disputed against Berengar in this council; shortly afterward, though unwilling, he was made bishop of Signi, compelled by divinely manifested visions.” Spondanus, under 1079, Gregory VII, year 7. Theophilus Raynaud, too, in *On Good and Bad Books*, part I, Erot. 10, §2, p. 277, calls Saint Bruno of Signi a great combatant against Berengar under Gregory VII.

### CHAPTER VI. On Bruno’s election as bishop of Signi

The Church of Signi in Campania was vacant after the death of its shepherd Erasmus. Gregory, in the fifth year of his pontificate, resolved to give Bruno to it as successor. He discussed the matter with Cardinal Peter Igneus, bishop of Albano, so that Peter might exhort Bruno—whom Gregory had perceived to be most averse to honours and vehemently desirous of Cassinese retirement—to undertake the burden.

Hardly had Peter Igneus made Gregory’s intention known to Bruno when Bruno declared himself unworthy of so great an honour. With prayers and tears he begged Peter to dissuade the pontiff from his decision and to allow him to consecrate himself to the religious life he had vowed under Saint Benedict’s discipline. For he said that it was exceedingly difficult to serve God amid worldly cares and anxieties, but not when separated from the world and in solitude, where all things draw one to God and there are many inducements to devotion. What holy men do must be judged to be done only in a holy and upright way. [Col. 0103D]

The pontiff had already designated Bruno bishop, but refused to compel by command one whom he loved greatly. He therefore arranged with the bishop of Albano that he should take his candidate with him and make known to him the pontiff’s order directing him to preside over the election of the bishop of Signi. Peter Igneus and Bruno set out from Rome and arrived at Signi by night. [Col. 0104A]

In private, the bishop of Albano summoned the canons and chief men of the city. He addressed them concerning the election of their shepherd, highly commending the man whom they would hear preaching in the morning, and made known to them the pontiff’s desire. Scarcely had day dawned when a very great crowd of people and the entire clergy assembled at the principal church of the Blessed Virgin Mary. After the customary prayers had been said, Bruno mounted the pulpit and spoke concerning concord and peace in election with such grace and abundance of speech that he seized all in admiration and joy. On the following day the election was held, in which Bruno was chosen bishop by unanimous consent and vote. But this unexpected election of himself so affected him with grief that he resolved to flee from Signi by night.

Yet because it was God’s will, not human will, that Bruno should undertake the governance of that Church, his resistance was finally overcome by miraculous signs. The Cassinese chronicler and the Anonymous writer bear witness to these. “When such things,” says Leo of Ostia, “had come to his knowledge, he left the church of Blessed Mary in the silence of the dead of night and took flight. But while he was striving to carry out his plan, at a certain crossroads there stood before him at a distance a virgin adorned in imperial dress, whose face shone like the sun. When he asked her whence she came, what and who she was, and where she was going, she answered: ‘Know that I am the bride from whom you are not rightly fleeing. Therefore I command you, on behalf of God Almighty, to return to the church; and beware of wishing any longer to resist God’s will.’ Having said this, she vanished.” [Col. 0104B]

Struck by these events, Bruno, recognizing through the breath of so great a Virgin and through God’s will in his appointment, [Col. 0104C] yielded and ascended the episcopal throne, to the rejoicing of all. The Anonymous writer adds that after his election Bruno came to Rome with the holy cardinal of Albano and delegates from Signi. When Gregory received them before him, he rejoiced greatly and commanded that the elect should receive sacred ordination according to custom. The same author relates further prodigies and new visions appearing to Bruno on successive nights, confirming that it was God’s will that he should join the Church of Signi to himself as his bride. Bruno obeyed them most humbly and was at last ordained bishop by the pontiff himself. Thus the Anonymous writer, followed by Corradi.

Two things should be noted here. First, the Cassinese chronicler says nothing of Bruno’s disputation with Berengar, although it is celebrated by all writers. Second, he erred in assigning Bruno’s elevation to the episcopate to Urban II rather than to Saint Gregory VII, as more reliable documents testify. These and many other matters which the Cassinese chronicler omitted but the Anonymous writer and other authors related sufficiently show that the former did not write an accurate history of Saint Bruno. [Col. 0105A]

### CHAPTER VII. On Bruno’s deeds in the episcopate
As soon as he could, Bruno left Rome and went to Segni. I pass over all the demonstrations of joy with which he was welcomed by all the citizens, in order at once to set before the reader’s eyes the image of his virtues and the excellence of his deeds. From his earliest youth [Col. 0105C] he had wholly conformed himself to monastic discipline and had always diligently maintained it; in this very respect, therefore, he could appear as an exemplar of eminent holiness. Yet Bruno also strove to display the particular virtues of a bishop, concerning which the anonymous writer bears splendid testimony:

> “First,” he says, “in accordance with the apostolic command (1 Tim. 3:2), he began to show himself blameless in all things: sober, chaste, humble, gentle, and kind. Likewise, in his gait, bearing, dress, and every movement, he never offended anyone’s sight; rather, he always regulated all his actions and words with a modest gravity. For he was truthful in speech, just in judgment, prudent in counsel, discerning in command, [Col. 0105D] and distinguished in every kind of moral uprightness.”

By night and day he took the greatest delight in devoting much time to prayer; every day he offered the holy sacrifice with the deepest devotion; he accustomed himself to cultivate his mind through the reading of the most holy Fathers, and to omit nothing that might contribute to a greater increase in him of heavenly grace and wisdom. Since he joined to zeal for personal righteousness a wonderful solicitude for fulfilling the pastoral office, he formed his clergy above all in the best manners; he laboured to draw the people away from vices and daily to inflame them toward Christian virtues by sermons; and if any quarrel or discord arose in the city, he settled it with the greatest humanity. If I turn to works of charity, I shall say that he showed himself a most loving father of the poor: for whatever [Col. 0106A] he possessed, he generously supplied to them, reserving scarcely the necessities for himself. These matters are related at length by the same anonymous writer, from whom I shall cite a few things:

> “In works,” he says, “of charity and almsgiving he was so attentive that he seemed to think of nothing else. He clothed the naked, fed the hungry, received pilgrims with hospitality, and took care to assist all the needy alike.”

For wards and widows found protection with Bruno; the sorrowful, the sick, the abandoned, orphans, and those crushed by calamities found consolation and relief. He had become all things to all, because, as the Apostle says, he desired to gain all for Christ (1 Cor. 9:22). But because in the Lord’s field there are always thorns and thistles which cannot be wholly rooted out, the Church of Segni too [Col. 0106B] was infested by these harmful weeds, and not all the labours of its excellent cultivator succeeded in bringing them back to better fruitfulness.

Among these wicked men of Bruno’s flock was one Adulphus, count of Vico, as they say. The bishop had already often and most lovingly, like a father, admonished him to correct his most depraved conduct and to fear the justice of almighty God. But since he was one of those who become worse when treated kindly, and hated his fatherly admonition, he wickedly resolved to remove him from the midst. It happened one day that Bruno, returning from Rome to Segni, accompanied by some clerics, was passing through Vico. Adulphus came to meet him and, with feigned compliments, invited him to spend the night in his house. The bishop thanked him but could not be diverted from [Col. 0106C] his intended course. Therefore the wicked count, seeing that he had been thwarted, ordered his retainers to seize Bruno and the clerics, hold them bound, and cast them into prison.
