To increase their distress and affliction, guards were placed over them—worthless men who, as he himself relates in his *Exposition of Psalm 54*, p. 410, were inflamed against him by envy and rage. Always exposed to their eyes, he was permitted to do nothing without them.

> “When on one occasion,” he says, “I had been taken captive, certain men were assigned to guard me, who hated me more than the others did. They were indeed always with me; they sat beside me; without them I could do nothing.”

After the holy prelate had spent several days [Col. 0106D] in filth and destitution of every necessity, he was at last grievously tormented by burning thirst and asked for a cup of water to be brought to him. Water was brought; Bruno blessed it; and when he wished to taste it, he found wine. This miracle was repeated twice more, and began to be proclaimed everywhere. Adulphus himself, struck with amazement and fear, not only restored his bishop and the clerics to liberty but most humbly asked forgiveness, which he immediately obtained. Before departing, however, Bruno admonished the count to do penance for his crime and change his wicked life into a Christian one.

The Casinensian chronicler passed over all these highly commendable events concerning Bruno, but the historian of Segni committed them to memory. Having returned to Segni, Bruno applied himself [Col. 0107A] with the greatest diligence to the customary duties of his pastoral office, and gave thanks to God because he saw piety flourishing among the clergy and good morals among the people. Yet he continually pondered the beloved solitude of Monte Cassino and envied those monks who, freed from every earthly care, could aspire to God with their whole mind, delight in Him, and be refreshed in the contemplation of heavenly things.

Before concluding this chapter, however, some observations remain to be made. First, in his own Church of Segni, he consecrated an altar dedicated to the Blessed Virgin Mary, depositing in it many relics of saints. He also performed another consecration at Capua: that of the sacred building of Saint Angelo in Formis, at the request of Otto, abbot of Monte Cassino, who had erected it in honour of St Nicholas. The Bollandists acknowledge that before Bruno entered the Order of St Benedict, he administered the Church of Segni for twenty-three years. In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1089, on 8 July, in the twelfth indiction, St Bruno, whom Urban II had among his household prelates, subscribed the constitution of that pope by which he confirmed to the clergy and people of Velletri all their customs and privileges.

> [Note: [Col. 0107C] Such a constitution of Urban II is printed in book III, pp. 204 ff. of the *History of the City and Church of Velletri*, by the distinguished Alexander Borgia of Fermo, archbishop and illustrious author of many other works, uncle of the aforesaid cardinal. [Col. 0107D]]

A copy of this papal diploma survives in the archive of the Church of Velletri. The most distinguished prelate Stephen Borgia, Secretary of the Sacred Congregation for the Propagation of the Faith, now most deserving cardinal of the Holy Roman Church, supplied me with a copy. The subscription of St Bruno is striking, and reads as follows; a facsimile of the same hand is also presented.

[Col. 0107B] Three years later, on the day before the Nones of September, St Bruno was present as assisting bishop to the same Urban II at the consecration of the church of the monastery of St Benedict at Cava; by papal command he consecrated the abbot’s private chapel, as appears from Muratori, vol. VI of the *Italian Writers*, pp. 238 and 240.

## CHAPTER VIII. Bruno’s passage to the monks of Monte Cassino

Bruno bade farewell to his Church and embraced the institute of St Benedict in the monastery of Monte Cassino. But the writers of his life disagree as to how and when this occurred. Peter the Deacon, who entirely omitted the deeds of the holy bishop during his episcopate—

> [Note: [Col. 0107D] Fleurus says the following concerning Peter the Deacon in *Ecclesiastical History*, book LXVI, under the year 1111: “Leo of Marsi, a monk of Monte Cassino and later Cardinal Leo of Ostia, set forth the Chronicle of the monastery of Monte Cassino in three books. Peter the Deacon, [Col. 0108C] librarian of the same monastery, added a fourth; [Col. 0108D] he began with the year 1087, under Abbot Oderisius, and continued to the year 1136. This book, however, was not written with the same trustworthiness and diligence as the preceding ones.” Many other writers held the same opinion along with the most distinguished Muratori.]

—having scarcely said a word of his ordination, immediately states that Bruno departed from Segni with a few citizens, all wholly unaware of their bishop’s [Col. 0107C] intention, and went to Monte Cassino. The Casinensian chronicler did not record the year in which Bruno entered the monks of Monte Cassino, but merely related that Bruno earnestly requested Abbot Oderisius to receive him among the monks, without consulting the Apostolic See at all.

The anonymous writer describes the matter otherwise, and affirms that it happened under Pope Paschal II. He says that, when Bruno lay seriously ill in Apulia, whither Paschal had taken him, he disclosed his desire to devote himself to the Benedictine institute in the solitude of Monte Cassino, and said that nothing would be more welcome to him than to be granted this permission if he recovered. Pope Paschal [Col. 0108B] therefore, lest Bruno’s illness should be increased by sorrow, acceded to his wishes, provided only that he would always remain near him and, should it be necessary, be at hand in every matter.

Paschal was created Roman pontiff in the year 1099. Six years later, namely in January 1105, Bruno, bishop of Segni, appears as a subscriber in a parchment document preserved in the archive of Monte Cassino and published by Erasmus Gattula in the *Additions to the History of Monte Cassino*, part I, p. 222. It states that Robert, count of the Calatini, through the hands of Lord Bruno, bishop of Segni, granted to Oderisius, abbot of Monte Cassino, partly as a gift and partly for money paid, the town of Pontecorvo; Bruno was also present at payment of the price. The adoption of Bruno’s monastic [Col. 0108C] profession must therefore be placed at the end of 1105 or the beginning of the following year, 1106; for in that same year he was sent by Paschal to Gaul with Bohemond, prince of Antioch, as we shall say below.

When, by divine assistance, Bruno had recovered his health and obtained the Apostolic approval, he went to Monte Cassino and, as the anonymous writer reports, “was received with great honour both by Abbot Oderisius, who then presided over that monastery, and by all the brethren of the same Church; and there, having made profession according to the Rule of St Benedict, he received the religious habit.”

We cannot agree with Peter the Deacon’s account that the people of Segni complained before Pope Paschal that they had been left without a pastor; that Paschal sent vigorous men from his side, who in the name of the Apostolic See commanded Bruno to return to his Church and reproved him for abandoning the administration of his bishopric without papal consent [Col. 0109A]. For how can it be supposed that Bruno, most learned in sacred canons and combining no less holiness with learning, would leave his Church, his bride, without consulting the Roman pontiff—an act certainly forbidden to him—and entrust to no one the care of the flock committed to him? Since, therefore, the authority of the anonymous writer in this matter appears more consistent with Bruno’s learning and holiness, we judge that he should be followed rather than Peter the Deacon.

> [Note: [Col. 0109D] The most distinguished Jean Mabillon partly agrees and partly disagrees with what has been related thus far. He places Bruno’s resignation of the bishopric of Segni in 1104, whereas we demonstrate that it occurred at least a year later. Yet, against Peter the Deacon’s assertion, he acknowledges that Bruno, having fallen ill in Apulia, whither he had gone with Pope Paschal II, obtained permission—if God granted him health—to seek the solitude of Monte Cassino and there profess the religious life. He nevertheless follows the Casinensian chronicler in relating that Paschal, at the earnest request of the people of Segni for their pastor, sent messengers to command Bruno by the authority of the Apostolic See immediately to return to his Church. This command occasioned the letter Bruno wrote to Paschal, begging him not to remove him from his purpose. Mabillon further adds that it was not so much Bruno’s prayers as those of Abbot Oderisius that finally moved Paschal to permit him for a time to remain at Monte Cassino in monastic habit; but shortly afterwards he sent him to Gaul with Bohemond, prince of Antioch, and assigned him other embassies, of which there will be discussion later. See vol. V of the *Benedictine Annals*, book LXX, p. 471.]

Meanwhile, the eyes of all the monks were turned toward Bruno; they admired his exceptional [Col. 0109B] charity, his constant devotion to prayer, and his profound humility joined to wisdom, and the whole house was filled with the fragrance of Bruno’s holiness.

“After five years had elapsed,” to use the words of Erasmus Gattula, “during which he lived as a simple monk, Otto, who had succeeded Oderisius in the prelacy, having died, St Bruno was chosen abbot by the common counsel of the brethren.” Hardly had this election become known at Rome when Paschal came to Monte Cassino and, in the assembly of the brethren, declared not only that the government of that most celebrated monastery had deservedly been entrusted to Bruno, but also that Bruno was worthy to succeed him in the Apostolic See, as Peter the Deacon attests.

Who could believe these things if Bruno had left the Church of Segni without the pope’s knowledge? The pope therefore held Bruno in great esteem; [Col. 0109C] for this reason he frequently summoned him, either to consult with him on the weightier affairs of the universal Church or to commit some task to him. These facts ought to be recalled so that, if any disputes which later arose between the two are recounted—as everyone agrees once occurred between Pope Stephen and Cyprian—we may say that they sprang not from ill feeling but from adverse circumstances. Each strove to serve God’s cause, but they did not contend for it in the same manner. Paschal, shepherd of the entire Christian flock, had before his eyes peace and unity, lest another schism arise; Bruno, however, laboured to assert and defend the rights of the Roman Church and the immunity of the episcopate from lay power.

[Col. 0109D] While, therefore, the holy Bishop Bruno governed the monastery of Monte Cassino, besides regular observance—of which he was always a most watchful enforcer both by word and example—he recovered, as [Col. 0110A] Peter the Deacon relates, certain territories and goods of the monastery which had been usurped by some counts of Aquino, by means of the arms of Robert, prince of Capua. He also annexed to the monastery other possessions acquired through the generosity of the bishop of Trivento, and omitted nothing that might advance a greater zeal for holiness and increase its revenues. The documents which I shall recount in chronological order demonstrate this.

For in 1108 Otto, son of Walter, swore homage—commonly called *homagium*—and liege service to Bruno, as prelate of Monte Cassino, and to the monks, for the castle of Pesco Costanzo, possession of which was granted to him. In the same year, while Bruno governed Monte Cassino, Landulf, son of Pandulf, count of Teano, gave castles and possessions to the monastery; the archive of Monte Cassino possesses the grants written on parchments, and they are found among the documents published by the aforementioned Erasmus Gattula.

To these I add another acquisition made by the monks of Monte Cassino under the same Abbot Bruno, in January 1109. Robert, lord of the Castle of Limosano, held by hereditary right the church of St Illuminata of Pesco Maggiore; he ceded it, with all its rights, to the same monastery. At that time John Celsus, bishop of Trivento, possessed certain rights over this same church; with the consent of his canons, he freely renounced them “out of brotherly love for the venerable bishop and abbot Bruno.” Gattula also published this charter in his *History of Monte Cassino*, p. 421. It was sealed with two seals, namely those of the bishop and the count, as may still be seen.

Finally, the reputation [Col. 0110C] of Bruno’s holiness and that of the monks of Monte Cassino had grown so greatly that Duke Roger of Apulia, imitating his father’s piety toward St Benedict and his disciples, confirmed to Bishop Bruno and the monks possession of Monte Cassino and renounced the right of ownership “which we used to possess,” as the diploma says, “over the estates of St Benedict, namely over the abbot’s chamber, the cellar, and the infirmary of the brethren—a right of ownership which belonged to us by virtue of the lordship of Monte Gargano.”

Likewise, in the same diploma—which Lord Giovanni Battista Federici, director of the archive of Monte Cassino, discovered as an autograph among many parchments with no small labour—Duke Roger affirmed a previously granted right “to lodge and pasture all the flocks of the monastery from [Col. 0110D] the church called Passari as far as the Salpi bridge [lacuna]. And again as far as the sea. Given at Capua, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1110, the twenty-fourth year of the duchy, in November, indiction IV.” This diploma, which we have seen and which is furnished with a leaden seal, escaped Gattula’s diligence.

From these matters, therefore, it is evident that although St Bruno governed the monastery of Monte Cassino for only three years and ten months, he greatly enlarged its revenues and dominion, so that the monks themselves acknowledge St Bruno as highly deserving in this respect. During the time Bruno lived at Monte Cassino, he carried out certain embassies; these must be discussed in the following chapter.

## CHAPTER IX. Bruno’s embassies

He who had been most acceptable to St Gregory VII, and had acquired no less favour with Urban II, Victor III’s successor, will be seen also to have been wholly in the favour and confidence of Paschal II. I shall first speak of Bruno’s journey into Gaul [Col. 0111B], then of the embassies he discharged in Paschal’s name.

After Urban had settled ecclesiastical affairs in Italy upon the extinction of Guibert’s schism, he resolved in 1095 to go to Gaul, where many matters required his presence and authority. He took with him among the Italian bishops Daimbert of Pisa and Bruno of Segni, employed them in all affairs, and was accustomed to do nothing without them; so highly did he value their loyalty and prudence.

Urban convened the Council of Clermont, over which he presided. After thirty-two canons had been enacted for the restoration of ecclesiastical discipline, the matter of war against the Saracens was addressed: they occupied the holy city of Jerusalem and raged with every cruelty against Christ’s faithful. The sign of the cross [Col. 0111C] was given to those ready to depart for the East and enroll in Christian military service, so that they might wrest the holy places from the hands of the barbarians, restore religion and worship, and free an innumerable multitude of souls from servitude. This was the beginning of the most celebrated expeditions of Christian princes against the Turks. Their leaders included Hugh the Great, brother of Philip king of the Franks; Godfrey of Bouillon; Bohemond the Norman; and Raymond, count of Toulouse, who stirred up many other princes to accomplish the same undertaking.

After Urban had achieved much at Clermont, he proceeded to Tours, where likewise he held a council for the same cause. When it was concluded, he consecrated the magnificent church of that monastery. With the bishops of Lyons, Pisa, and Segni assisting, he adorned the church of the monastery of Cluny with a similar consecration. There, as the most distinguished Jacques Sirmond testifies, a monument still survives recording that the inner chapel for the sick was consecrated by Bruno, bishop of Segni.

After accomplishing these and other matters in Gaul, Urban set out for Rome. At Bruno’s request he turned aside to Asti and there solemnly dedicated the greater church of that city, in the year, as is said, 1096. The memory of this sacred ceremony is recorded in a marble inscription placed above the principal door of the church:

> To the greater glory of God and of the Mother of God assumed into heaven: Urban II, Supreme Pontiff, with St Bruno, bishop of Segni, accompanying him on the journey and, as a former canon of this cathedral, acting as intercessor, dedicated this basilica, newly built on the old site.

I now come to the embassies which Bruno carried out in the name of Paschal II. The first of these was to Gaul, accompanying Bohemond, prince of Antioch.

> [Note: [Col. 0111D] “In the year 1106, on the seventh day before the Kalends of June, a council was held at Poitiers, at which Duke Bohemond was present. Bruno, legate of the Holy Roman Church, brought him there, held the council, and confirmed the way to the Holy Sepulchre.” From the Chronicle of St Maxentius, commonly called the Chronicle of Maillezais; Philippe Labbe, p. 217, vol. II of the *New Library of Manuscripts*. Jacques Sirmond likewise treats of St Bruno’s embassy to Gaul in his notes to Epistle 14, book XI, of Godfrey, abbot of Vendôme and cardinal of St Prisca: “The embassy of Bruno, bishop of Segni in Campania, falls in the year of Christ 1106. For the Chronicle of St Albinus records that Duke Bohemond came to Gaul in this year; Bohemond was accompanied, by Paschal’s order, by Bruno as legate. Peter the Deacon and Abbot Suger are authorities for this; they also mention the synod held by him at Poitiers.” St Ivo of Chartres likewise fully agrees. In Epistle 164 to Godfrey of Blois, he reproves him because, against the advice of Bruno, legate of the Holy Roman Church, without any compulsion and indeed although the legate dissuaded him, he had resigned his abbey and given the first vote in the election of Maurice. Relying on these very clear testimonies, Gattula says that Baronius and Mabillon were mistaken in placing Bruno’s embassy to Gaul in 1104. Spondanus also mentions this embassy of St Bruno in these words: “Moreover, Peter the Deacon in the Chronicle of Monte Cassino testifies, and Ivo of Chartres frequently mentions, that Paschal sent to Gaul with Bohemond St Bruno, bishop of Segni—although he had now laid down the burden of the episcopate and taken monastic habit at the monastery of Monte Cassino—and that he held a synod.” Yet Spondanus too did not reach the correct date of this embassy, since he placed it under the year 1105.]

Having been captured by the Saracens, Bohemond had vowed that, if he escaped his chains, he would travel for religious devotion to the tomb of St Leonard at Noblat in Limousin. Once his vow was fulfilled, Bohemond came to Rome and asked the pope to send with him to Gaul some man distinguished in rank and prudence. For this work [Col. 0112C] Bruno was summoned from Monte Cassino. The pope also charged him to convene a council at Poitiers and preside over it as legate of the Apostolic See.

Bruno and Bohemond departed from Rome and first went to Noblat. There the prince of Antioch gave thanks to St Leonard, his deliverer, and hung at his altar the silver chains with which he had been bound.

> [Note: [Col. 0112D] Vol. X of the *Councils*, p. 728, Paris edition, 1671.]

They then went to Poitiers, where on the seventh day before the Kalends of July, in 1106, the Second Council of Poitiers was held, with Bohemond present. Suger, who attended, calls it full and celebrated.

> [Note: [Col. 0112D] See Pagi, vol. II, p. 554, Antwerp edition, 1717.]

After several enactments had been published, Bruno, the papal legate, spoke with such eloquence concerning supplies to be sent to the Holy Land that very many Frenchmen, equipped with arms, migrated to the East [Col. 0113A], while others supplied a great quantity of gold. When these matters had been concluded and Bruno had acquired great renown in Gaul, he returned to Italy. His embassy being approved by the pope, he with difficulty obtained permission to return to his former solitude at Monte Cassino. But he was allowed to enjoy it only for a very short time. Paschal, intending to go to Benevento to hold a council, came to Monte Cassino and wished to take Bruno with him.

At this synod many excellent measures were enacted. Chief among them was the prohibition against ecclesiastical persons wearing costly and secular garments; an anathema was also pronounced against simoniacs and against those who received investitures of ecclesiastical benefices from the hands of laymen. Since Pope Paschal had experienced Bruno’s skill and consummate prudence in affairs of such importance, [Col. 0113B] he gave him a second embassy to carry out in Sicily.

Roger was prince of the Sicilians. With the greatest courage he had driven the Saracens from that island, restored churches everywhere, and restored the worship of the Christian religion. Whether he had requested a legate of the Holy Roman Church, or Paschal knew that many matters in those churches required correction and restoration, the pope judged that a task of such consequence would be most successfully managed if entrusted to Bruno. Nor did his expectation deceive him. Bruno travelled through the entire province, cut down the evil weeds—that is, rooted out vices and corrupt customs—prescribed canonical enactments to be observed by clerics and priests, attended to the sanctity of the churches and the splendour of sacred worship, and finally made every successful inquiry into the means by which divine worship, the exemplary virtue of priests, [Col. 0113C] and the religion of the people might flourish and shine ever more brightly.

But Bruno was sent as legate not merely to restore these things. He was also to stir the Sicilians to holy war against the Mohammedans, obtain ample assistance from them, and urge Roger himself to undertake the journey to Jerusalem for the glory of the Christian name. Having completed this embassy, Bruno returned to Rome and then to Monte Cassino, where he was received with the greatest joy by the monks over whom he presided.

But because other matters were being prepared for the holy abbot and bishop, concerning which people’s opinions would differ, heaven confirmed his holiness by a remarkable miracle. Bruno was solemnly consecrating a church in the village of Vallefredda, dedicated to God in honour of the Apostle St Thomas, [Col. 0113D] when a woman grievously afflicted in extraordinary ways by an evil spirit was brought before him. Those standing around earnestly begged him, moved by compassion, to free her. The holy bishop prayed briefly, then ordered the possessed woman to drink water in which he had washed his hands during the rite. As soon as this was done, the woman was freed from the demon before everyone’s eyes. Public thanks were offered to God, and there was no one who did not invoke Bruno’s protection when they saw him endowed with heavenly gifts. This remarkable miracle may be seen painted, for its perpetual remembrance, in the chapel of the greater Church of Segni dedicated to St Bruno the bishop.

## CHAPTER X. On investitures

[Col. 0114A]

Those to whom Cardinal Baronius, Spondanus, Pierre de Marca, Natalis Alexander, and Cardinal Noris—men of great merit in ecclesiastical history—are not unknown will not consider it necessary that, when I must deal with investitures because of the disagreement which arose between Pope Paschal II and Bruno, bishop of Segni, I should begin the question from its origin. It will be enough to recall the privilege granted by Paschal II to Emperor Henry V, not voluntarily but under the greatest force and fear. By it, he allowed Henry to confer certain tokens of possession of temporal goods upon those admitted to the sacred ministries of the Church.

Since ecclesiastical discipline, established by ancient councils [Col. 0114B] and confirmed by later enactments, opposed Paschal’s concession, differing opinions concerning it emerged. Some said that the canonical laws must be observed; others thought that in these circumstances Paschal’s privilege should be defended. Bruno, then abbot of the monastery of Monte Cassino and bishop of Segni, was counted among the former. His holiness and consummate prudence in action would remain not slightly clouded unless the truth of the matter, freed from alleged facts, were brought into the light.

For I shall not imitate Matteo Laureto, Malabaile, Ughelli, Ferrari, Corradio, and others who, in writing Bruno’s deeds, omitted this controversy altogether. Care must be taken for Bruno’s excellent reputation, and the accusations brought against him must be refuted and repelled. Yet, lest I become more prolix than the occasion requires, [Col. 0114C] I shall reduce the matter to three points.

First, Bruno’s accusers derive their ground for attacking him from Peter the Deacon of Monte Cassino, who wrote in book IV, chapter 33, of the *Chronicle of Monte Cassino* that Bruno complained to Paschal about the privilege granted to Henry and used harsh words to the pope in demanding its repeal. Second, they attack the holy bishop because he said that this privilege contained heresy. Third, they accuse him because through him the dispute concerning it became so inflamed that Paschal feared he might be deposed from the papal see.

I do not hesitate to assert at once that the first accusation is to be dismissed as worthless. Peter the Deacon indeed assumes that Bruno came from Monte Cassino to Rome before the council held by Paschal; but the contrary is demonstrated [Col. 0114D] by the letters which he wrote to Peter, bishop of Porto, to the cardinals of the Holy Roman Church, and to Pope Paschal himself—letters already published by Baronius and others, and which we too shall publish in the second volume. For if Bruno had been in Rome either before or after Paschal’s return to the city, what need was there for him to commit to letters his opinion concerning the investitures granted to Henry, when he could have pursued the matter in person? In fact, the conversation reported by Peter the Deacon is expressed in the same terms in Bruno’s letter to Paschal. First, to be sure, he refutes the calumny of his enemies that he did not love the pope and spoke ill of him; then he explains why he judged the Church injured by the granting of the concession, and why he said that it must wholly [Col. 0115A] be revoked and eliminated.

This testimony is completely overthrown by the most eminent Baronius, who, in vol. XII of the Roman edition, 1607, under the year 1111, p. 83, writes as follows:

> But those matters which Peter the Deacon of Monte Cassino affirms to have been transacted in a mutual conversation between Bruno, or Brunon, and Paschal were conducted rather by letters than by Bruno’s personal presence. For there survive Bruno’s own letters, addressed to Paschal in precisely these words, and longer letters of the same tenor, together with other letters of his written at that time on the same subject to the bishop of Porto. Drawn from the Cassinese library, I shall not hesitate to reproduce both here word for word and to repeat what has been said.

Some may wonder that Natalis Alexander, though an accurate writer, followed not the father of ecclesiastical annals but Peter [Col. 0115B] the Deacon in this account, and presented the letter written to Paschal as a speech delivered in his presence.

[Note: [Col. 0115C] The distinguished Cassinese historiographer, Dom Abbot Erasmus Gattula, reproduced the same letters of St Bruno on p. 371 ff.; and especially calls the letter which the holy bishop sent to Pope Paschal one “full of reverence and zeal.” He further observes that Bruno displayed singular reverence toward the Holy See when he declared that Paschal’s constitution condemning investitures had issued from the apostolic source. He then appends the letter of St Ivo of Chartres to Henry, abbot of Angers, no. 233, [Col. 0115D] and that of Geoffrey to the same Pope Paschal, book I, letter VII; from these it is evident that those very distinguished men fully agreed with Bruno concerning the privilege of investitures.

Concerning this letter of Geoffrey of Vendôme, Jacques Sirmond writes in his notes:

> After mentioning at the outset the pact, or privilege, extorted by Henry through force and fear on the third day before the Ides of April, A.D. 1111, he says: “Although necessity seemed to excuse this act of Paschal’s—since otherwise, as he himself alleges in his letter to Guy of Vienne, the enslavement of the Church, the inward captivity of its members, and destruction threatened to the city and Italy seemed imminent—it was nevertheless so universally disapproved that it nearly provoked open schism. Consequently prudent and judicious men, who deeply resented the violation of the Church’s rights—among them this Geoffrey of ours and others whose letters survive—did not cease to urge and press Paschal to annul by public decree the pact which he had made unwillingly and himself voluntarily condemned. This indeed he did [Col. 0116C] at the following Lateran synod, when he again revoked Henry’s investitures.”]

Yet the very distinguished Dom Rémi Ceillier fully agreed with Cardinal Baronius in his *General History of Sacred Authors*, vol. XXI, p. 101, Paris edition. His words are these:

> Bruno was still at Monte Cassino in 1111, when Emperor Henry compelled Pope Paschal II to grant him the right of investiture. All the cardinals who had been taken prisoner with the pope disapproved of his conduct. Bruno himself gave evidence of his displeasure. He was represented to the pope as the principal instigator of the disturbance stirred up in Rome on this occasion. Bruno wrote to the pope and to Peter, bishop of Porto, who had subscribed [Col. 0115C] the concession made to the emperor; but his letters did not at all appease Paschal, etc.

Ceillier’s agreement with Baronius is therefore to be valued more highly than Peter the Deacon’s little story, which is shown to rest on an assumption and will appear still more plainly so below. It is one thing to remind a superior of some failing; [Col. 0116A] it is another to challenge him face to face and injure his dignity. The former is permissible, if done modestly and temperately; the latter is wholly to be condemned. Since earlier popes and councils had condemned investitures and their corrupt use, those who opposed these newly granted ones, recognizing the same danger, were defending the Church’s rights and pontifical decrees. Bruno therefore is not to be blamed if he was among them, since he supported a good and holy cause, necessary in those times.

[Note: [Col. 0116C] Orderic Vitalis, book X, p. 762, says that Robert of Paris and several other bishops and cardinals held the same opinion as St Bruno concerning the privilege of investitures granted by Paschal II to King Henry, and held that it must be regarded as null. The author of the *Ecclesiastical History* published at Paris in 1740, p. 40, confirms the same.]

I do not know, however, why Bruno seemed to some to be the principal author of the condemnation of the privilege—unless perhaps because, while the others objected, he surpassed them in holiness and learning [Note: [Col. 0116C] See Pagi, vol. II, p. 555.], and his judgment was therefore held in the highest regard. Also prominent in this controversy were [Col. 0116B] John of Tusculum, John of Vercelli, Robert, bishop of Paris, and Gaula, bishop of Reims, who openly rejected the concession of investitures. Moreover, “scarcely had the pope returned to the city when, as the same Peter the Deacon relates, scandals of dissension and schism began to arise in the Roman Church.”

[Note: [Col. 0116C] Pagi confirms the same at the place cited: “When Paschal [Col. 0116D] returned to the city, he found the cardinals and all the Roman clergy alienated from him and strongly disapproving the compact which he had made with Emperor Henry contrary to the decrees of his predecessors, having consulted only a few cardinals.” Therefore, “in this same year 1111,” Baronius writes, “Paschal II, having returned to the city, sent letters to the entire Catholic world concerning what had been done with Henry. In them he excused himself on the ground that, in order to avoid the evils threatening and to redeem the Church’s peace, he had yielded thus for a time.”]

Bruno, absent and residing at Monte Cassino, cannot be called the mover or inciter of these disturbances; rather, zeal for opposing sides and differing opinions about the privilege produced them.

The second charge against St Bruno—namely, that he called Paschal’s privilege a heresy—is no less easily refuted than the preceding one. Let us inspect the letters which he wrote and examine the conciliar acts; from these it will be clear what he thought and what he did.

[Note: [Col. 0116D] See Labbe, *Acts of the Councils*, vol. XII, p. 767.]

In his letter to Paschal, he first recalls [Col. 0116C] Paschal’s constitution, by which he condemns and excludes from the communion of the faithful all clerics who receive investitures from the hand of a layman and all who lay hands upon them. He then proceeds:

> For this constitution is that of the apostles [Note: [Col. 0116D] St Bruno knew perfectly the enactments of the apostles and councils. The following are relevant. Canon 31 of the Apostles provides: “If anyone, employing secular authorities, obtains a church through them, let him be deposed and cast out, together with all who communicate with him.” Likewise, from the Council of Antioch: “If anyone obtains the Church of God through secular rank, [Col. 0117D] let both he and those ordained by him be cast out; and in every way let them be separated from communion and be under anathema, as Simon Magus was by Peter.” Similarly, in the Roman synod attended by 240 Fathers under Pope Nicholas I, the foregoing decrees were confirmed: “Whoever among secular princes and powerful men, or of any other lay rank, attempts to act against the common, harmonious, and canonical election of ecclesiastical order, let him be anathema until he obeys and consents to what the Church has shown itself to desire concerning the election and ordination of its own pastor.”], and yours is holy, catholic; whoever contradicts it [Col. 0117A] is not Catholic. For only those are Catholic who do not contradict Catholic faith and doctrine. Conversely, heretics are those who obstinately oppose Catholic faith and doctrine.

Is this not the doctrine of all orthodox Christians: that error in faith and obstinacy in will constitute heresy? What else did St Bruno teach? But, properly to understand these matters, those calamitous times must be recalled. It was not Guibert’s schism alone that ravaged the Church; clerical incontinence, simony, usurpation of ecclesiastical goods, and the tyrannical domination of the powerful were subverting everything completely. To these evils under which the Church suffered was added the fact that certain persons, as Bruno himself says in his letter to Peter, bishop of Porto, [Col. 0117B] imprudently tried to defend investitures, although they knew that these had been struck by anathema. Since investitures opened to simoniacs, incontinent clerics, usurpers, and wicked clerics a door to every crime, Bruno called that concession, or privilege, a heresy in this sense.

We do not deny that heresy, properly speaking, can only be dissent from some dogma of the faith, together with persistence in that dissent; but improperly, and as it were by analogy, he is guilty of heresy who tears the Church apart or allows it to be torn apart. Let Cardinal Baronius be heard on the year 1112, concerning the case of Paschal II:

> It is not heresy to grant investitures themselves, which is the one thing Paschal II did. But it is heresy—that is, it is false doctrine, contrary to good morals and [Col. 0117C] the sacred testimonies of the Fathers—to introduce this into the Church.

John, archbishop of Lyons, had already taken this position in his letter to Daimbert, archbishop of Sens, which is letter 233 to Henry, abbot of Angers. John writes:

> And although we do not consider exterior investitures made by laymen to fall very properly under the name of heresy, to hold that they should be made and ought to be made is an undoubted heresy.

Ivo’s agreement is clear from these words:

> Concerning investitures of churches made by laymen, I praise and confirm, so far as lies in me, the judgment of my predecessors Gregory and Urban. Whatever name this kind of usurpation may properly bear, I call schismatic the opinion of those who wish to defend lay investitures [Col. 0118A]. Nor do I say this against the lord pope, because he wrote to me in certain letters that he did what he did under compulsion and that he still forbids what he had forbidden.

It was in these senses, certainly, that Bruno called the privilege in question a heresy. He knew well the violence inflicted upon Pope Paschal in order to obtain that concession. Paschal sinned neither by intention nor by evil doctrine; rather, his courage failed when he saw so many and such great calamities threatening himself and his people.

I think, however, that those historians were deceived who, having not investigated all—or at least the principal—writers of this age and trusting too readily to one source of lesser reliability, reported that Bruno at a Roman council, with Paschal himself presiding, when the entire assembly of Fathers rejoiced because the pope had revoked the privilege [Col. 0118B] and pronounced a sentence of condemnation upon it, could not restrain himself from again declaring aloud that the privilege was a heresy. I shall show this to be sheer invention.

Paschal held two Roman councils for the condemnation of investitures: the first in 1112, the other in 1116. The alleged incident certainly did not happen at the first. William of Malmesbury reports that John, bishop of Tusculum, and Bruno of Segni, although they were in Rome, were absent from the council on the day when the privilege was condemned; but they were present on the following day, when the decree of proscription was read, to which all assented and which all praised.

[Note: [Col. 0117D] The edict published at this synod reads:

> That privilege—which is no privilege (for it ought not to be called a *privilegium*, but a *pravilegium*, an evil privilege)—extorted by the violence of King Henry from the lord Pope Paschal for the liberation of captives and of the Church, we all, gathered in this holy council with the same lord pope, condemn by canonical censure and ecclesiastical authority, by the judgment of the Holy Spirit; we wholly annul it and completely excommunicate it, so that it may have no authority or force whatever. It is condemned because that privilege contained the provision that one canonically elected by clergy and people should be consecrated by no one unless first invested by the king; this is contrary to the Holy Spirit and canonical institution.

> When this document had been read, the entire council cried out: “Amen, amen. Let it be done, let it be done.”]

Thus Severinus Binius notes concerning this council:

[Note: [Col. 0118D] The same is also narrated by Fleury, under the year 1112, no. 12: “Bruno of Segni,” he says, “like the two cardinals Peter of St Sixtus and Alberic of St Sabina, though staying in Rome on the day when the privilege was condemned, was absent from the council; nevertheless, he approved the act of condemnation.”]

The same is confirmed by an Angers manuscript, whose words [Col. 0118C] Stephen Baluze reproduced in his additions to Pierre de Marca, book VII, chapter 20, and Cardinal Noris in his *History of Investitures*, col. 448:

> Bruno of Segni and John, bishop of Tusculum, though they were in Rome that day, did not attend the council; afterwards, when the condemnation of the privilege had been read, they consented and praised it.

At the second synod, therefore, in 1116, Paschal again confessed his wrongdoing and confirmed the proscription of the privilege in this address:

> After the Lord had done with his servant what he willed, and had delivered me and the Roman people into the hands of the king, I saw daily plunderings, burnings, killings, and adulteries. I desired to avert these and similar evils from the Church and the people of God; and what [Col. 0119A] I did, I did for the deliverance of God’s people. But I acted as a man, who am dust and ashes. I confess that I acted wrongly; but I ask all of you: pray for me to God, that he may forgive me. That evil document made in the tents, which because of its perversity is called a *pravilegium*, I condemn under perpetual anathema, so that it may never be held in good memory by anyone; and I ask you to do the same.

Then all cried out: “Let it be done, let it be done.”

After these words of the pope, the abbot of Ursperg relates that Bruno said aloud:

> Let us give thanks to almighty God, because we have heard Pope Paschal, who presides over the present council, condemn with his own mouth that privilege which contained heresy.

But what fair judge would consider a matter of such importance sufficiently secure on the testimony of Ursperg alone [Col. 0119B], when Suger, abbot and participant in the council, is entirely silent about it despite writing a full history of it? What if Cardinal Baronius himself makes absolutely no mention of that speech of Bruno? He reports Paschal’s retraction, or recantation, just given, but then adds:

> In another Vatican manuscript, which agrees with the foregoing, this is added: Then, as the Fathers rose from the assembly, thanks were given to God and the pope because, the truth having been made clearer, the cause of scandal and dissension was removed. Twelve archbishops, one hundred and fourteen bishops, fifteen cardinal-priests, and eight cardinal-deacons consented—all of whom joined the condemnation of the same privilege—together with abbots and an innumerable multitude of clergy and laity.

See vol. VII, Vatican edition, 1607, p. 93.

Reason likewise persuades us that Ursperg’s account must be regarded as nothing but invention. For if Bruno had harbored anything hostile toward Paschal, he had had an opportunity in the first synod to say whatever he wished; but, as we have said, he deliberately chose not to attend it with John, bishop of Tusculum, lest his presence be burdensome to Paschal, as Cardinal Noris judges, and lest he seem to encourage those seeking the revocation of the privilege. I pass over the remainder of the story, because it rests on no sufficiently firm foundation and is wholly inconsistent with Bruno’s exceptional virtue and his obedience toward Pope Paschal. It is well known that Ursperg is considered by many to be a writer of [Col. 0119D] doubtful reliability. Consult Natalis Alexander, in the article cited, no. 11. Since the opponents offer nothing solid, nothing of proven authority, the second accusation wholly collapses; and we hope to establish the same concerning the third, which we now undertake to refute.

The question is whether Bruno, by his speeches or letters, rebuked Paschal so strongly over the granted privilege and pressed so insistently for its revocation that the pope, overcome by fear, said—as Peter the Deacon reports:

> If I do not hasten to remove him from the abbacy, it will come to pass that by his arguments he will take the Roman pontificate away from me.

The same chronicler supports [Col. 0120A] this story, teaching that Paschal sent Leo, cardinal-bishop of Ostia, with a letter to the monks of Monte Cassino, ordering them to choose another abbot and commanding that Bruno, released from that governance, return to govern the Church of Segni.

Two contemporary French writers, whom Cardinal Noris, at the place cited, p. 443, calls distinguished—namely Hildebert, bishop of Le Mans, and Abbot Suger—have recorded a very different account of Paschal’s retaining or resigning the pontificate. From Terracina, where Paschal was staying to avoid the Roman tumults, he wrote on 5 July 1111 to John of Tusculum and John of Vercelli:

> For the salvation of our soul we are considering, and shall endeavor to amend, the act which we committed for our brothers and sons, on account of the destruction of the City and [Col. 0120B] the whole Church, so that it may be evident that whatever in me is earthly has likewise been corrected for the Church.

Suger accordingly states in his *Life of Louis the Fat* that Paschal, repentant of his deed, really did resign the pontificate; and, after settling the affairs of Rome as best he could, withdrew into the wilderness:

> By this act the pope gave certain proof: when he had in some fashion released the brethren, the pillars of the Church, for its defense and restoration, and had restored such peace to the Church as he could, he fled to the solitude of the wilderness, and would have remained there permanently had not the violence of the universal Church and the Romans compelled him to return.

[Note: [Col. 0119] *Spicilegium*, vol. IV, p. 249; Hildebert, *Works*, p. 111, book II, letter 22.]

Hildebert, however, notes the retreat into solitude that Paschal chose for himself:

> Renouncing home, country, possessions, and office, he migrated to the island of Pontia, to be mortified in the flesh.

The same author further adds that Paschal, overcome by the unceasing prayers and tears of the cardinals and the whole Roman people, again assumed the helm of the Apostolic See and summoned a council to be held at Rome in the following year. This was indeed the council, as I said above, held in 1112.

In this great conflict of writers, we shall examine to whom greater credence should be given. First, we have already noted that Peter the Deacon very often falls into omissions and fabrications of many matters. Secondly, what he says about Paschal’s fear of losing the pontificate because Bruno, abbot of Monte Cassino, opposed him and was trying by his arguments to alienate people from him, is far too [Col. 0120D] absurd and injurious both to Paschal and to Bruno. For first, it is clear that nothing more foolish could be alleged. What? If Paschal feared that Bruno, abbot of Monte Cassino, would deprive him of the pontificate by his arguments, could he have disregarded those same arguments once Bruno had returned as bishop to the Church of Segni? Did Bruno’s change of place alter his arguments? The allegation also insults Paschal, as though he doubted the love and obedience of the universal Church, which recognized him as true pope, and could not otherwise revoke the privilege, the cause of dissension. It also gravely disparages Bruno—a man of conspicuous holiness and merit, and holder of eminent offices—by representing him as likely to abandon the pledge he had given Paschal when he wrote to him: “While you live, I wish to have no other pope.”

On the other hand, the writings of Suger and Hildebert are commonly accepted as sincere, and what they relate about Paschal at this crisis contains nothing inconsistent with his highest virtue. Indeed, his voluntary resignation gains him greater veneration.

[Note: [Col. 0121D] Mabillon adhered more closely to these writers than to the rest; I shall cite here his very weighty testimony:

> When Paschal entered the City, the remaining cardinals strongly disapproved of that pact. But when the pope pleaded the state of necessity to excuse his action and perceived that they could not easily be appeased, he gave place to their anger and withdrew to Campania. Meanwhile the aforesaid cardinals, holding an assembly at Rome together with John of Tusculum, annulled the act as wholly contrary to the decrees of earlier popes. When the pope, then at Terracina, learned of this, he wrote to them: he praised their zeal indeed, but said that their act seemed to have been done not canonically, not from charity, but from rivalry: “Whatever manner it may finally have been done,” he said, “we nevertheless, trusting in the divine mercy, are considering for the salvation of our soul and shall endeavor to amend the act which we committed for our brethren and sons, on account of the destruction of the City and the whole province.”

> Mabillon then mentions the accusation made before the pope against Bruno, bishop of Segni and abbot of Monte Cassino, as having acted as leader and standard-bearer in that conflict; Bruno endeavored to clear himself by letters sent to Paschal and to Peter of Porto. See Mabillon, *Benedictine Annals*, book V, year 1111, p. 550, and Pagi, at the place cited.]

For when they say that Paschal, for the peace and concord of the faithful and in grief over the concession yielded to Henry, repented of his action, considered resigning the pontificate, and actually did so, they bear witness to a notable and very rare example of magnanimity and render him praiseworthy for all posterity.

The report of Hildebert and Suger concerning Paschal’s resignation [Col. 0121B] of the Roman pontificate is confirmed by Geoffrey of Viterbo, *Chronicle*, part XVII, in these verses, published by Cardinal Noris, p. 446; Geoffrey also says that Paschal repeated it at the Roman council of 1112:

> The grieving pope raises laments and swiftly summons  
> the whole Church throughout the world to the City by his letter.  
> When it had assembled, he disclosed Caesar’s acts.  
>
> Then he said: “O Fathers, take note of the document from Caesar,  
> and make whatever decrees concerning these things seem right.  
> Command also that I shall no longer be pope.  
>
> I have perceived that your evils have come through my sins;  
> I have judged myself worthy to be deprived of office.  
> I too, he said, must be deposed, lest you perish.”  
>
> So he spoke, cast aside the mitre, and left the mantle.

[Col. 0121C]

> “Let the Church order without me whatever it pleases,” he said,  
> “and let it itself judge according to the pope’s custom.”

The agreement of these writers regarding Paschal’s voluntary resignation of the Roman pontificate ought to prevail over the sole testimony of Peter the Deacon, whom we have shown can very often be convicted of errors and omissions. But it is said that Bruno truly did relinquish the government of the Cassinese monastery and returned to Segni to administer his own church; therefore it cannot be doubted that Pope Paschal, through Leo of Ostia and through letters written to Bruno himself and to the monks, ordered him to resign the abbacy of Monte Cassino, as Peter the Deacon likewise records. This remaining part of the history supplies the material for the following [Col. 0121D] chapter, where we reserve its examination.

## CHAPTER XI. On the Resignation of the Abbacy of Monte Cassino

[Col. 0122A]

In order that something certain may be established concerning this celebrated event, I think two points should first be stated. First, Pope Paschal never allowed Bruno to lay aside the insignia of the episcopate.

[Note: [Col. 0122D] “Bruno was always bishop of Segni, and however insistently he sought to be relieved of that church, the pope never wished to accept his resignation.” Fleury, vol. XIV, book LXV, year 1111.]

From this it is clear that Paschal intended at some time to restore him to his own Church. Secondly, the people of Segni always complained to the pope of their pastor’s absence and repeatedly offered their prayers that he might compel the bishop to return to the discharge of his office.

Meanwhile, the controversy arose over the privilege granted by Paschal to Emperor Henry, which was discussed in the preceding chapter. Since Bruno had been denounced to him as one of the chief opponents of that concession, the pope, thinking that the governance of the celebrated and powerful monastery of Monte Cassino added greater fame and authority to Bruno, commanded him to return to Segni. Peter the Deacon certainly records the matter thus:

> Accordingly Pope Paschal sent a letter to Abbot Bruno, forbidding him any longer to be both bishop and abbot. The Apostolic See would no longer endure that a bishop should preside over so celebrated a monastery. He also sent letters to the brethren through the bishop of Ostia, a monk of this monastery, commanding them no longer to obey that man.

Mabillon, in vol. V, p. 559 of the *Benedictine Annals*, followed the Cassinese chronicler in this account, though neither Ferrari nor Ughelli did so. Ferrari, in his catalogue of the saints of Italy, highly esteemed by the Bollandists, attributes Bruno’s return to his own Church to the petitions and prayers [Col. 0122C] of the people of Segni, saying: “At the people’s urging, he is compelled to return to his Church.” Ughelli, however, assumes that a controversy arose between Paschal and Bruno over whether it were better to exercise the episcopal office or preside over a community of monks. Since the pope upheld the former, Bruno, overcome by his arguments and reverence for him, relinquished the government of the abbey after three years and ten months there and returned to his former see, for which he had been ordained.

I would pass over in silence, along with many writers, the dissension full of tumult and bitterness which Bruno’s departure from Monte Cassino is said to have aroused, unless the reports published about it harmed the exceptional integrity of the holy bishop and the eminent reputation of the monks. Let us hear Peter the Deacon once more. He relates that the monks [Col. 0123A] of Monte Cassino, when Bruno proposed to them as abbot a certain monk, a Ligurian by nationality named Peregrinus, were deeply disturbed and unanimously said that if Bruno wished to retain the government, they would gladly obey him as before; but if he were prepared to relinquish it, he should leave them free, in accordance with St Benedict’s rule, to elect for themselves whichever abbot they wished.

He further adds that the monks’ agitation, lest Peregrinus, an ambitious and exceedingly crafty man, should prevail, grew so intense that Bruno, overcome by fear, went down to the lower monastery. Meanwhile, when Peregrinus brought armed soldiers inside the enclosure of the monastery, in order to obtain by force what he could not achieve voluntarily, all the monks rose together and attacked the insolent band with such force [Col. 0123B] that they completely drove them from those buildings. Finally Peter the Deacon concludes the story thus:

> When this was reported to the abbot, he went up to this monastery and, summoning the brethren to him, said: “I do not wish scandal to arise between you and the Roman Church on my account. Therefore receive the pastoral staff which you gave me.” Immediately placing it on the altar, granting the brethren absolution, he returned to his bishopric.

You will not find a word of this conflict in Mabillon. He does indeed mention the letter sent by Paschal to Leo, bishop of Ostia, in which Paschal instructed Bruno to resign the abbey and the monks to elect another abbot. He summarizes the whole affair in these words:

> Bruno did what lay in his power to have another elected in his place; [Col. 0123C] but as the brethren steadfastly resisted, the holy bishop is reported to have addressed them with the words given above from Peter the Deacon: “I do not wish that on my account …,” etc.

After this Mabillon rebukes Peter the Deacon for having omitted many things in his *History* and falsely reported others, vol. V, book LXV, p. 139.

[Note: [Col. 0123D] The most learned Tiraboschi also demonstrates that Peter the Deacon fell into a manifest factual error and an anachronism in Appendix 1, p. 451, vol. I of the *History of the Abbey of Nonantola*, Modena edition, 1784 [Col. 0124D]. Before him Cardinal Noris, *History of Investitures*, p. 438, reproved the same chronicler for similar errors.]

But we can place no faith in the anonymous writer of Segni on this matter. He ascribes Bruno’s departure from the government of Monte Cassino to a conspiracy of the monks against their bishop, accusing them of violently and disgracefully expelling him. We judge his account to be a fabrication: first, because the anonymous writer lived more than seventy years after Bruno and neither confirms what he wrote about this event by the testimony of any contemporary author nor derives it from anything other than popular opinion, than which nothing is more uncertain—or else he was excessively indulgent toward the people of Segni, who bore ill will toward those very religious men because they had kept their pastor with them for so long against the people’s wishes. Secondly, who would believe a writer who contradicts himself? The anonymous author is convicted of this error—which, according to the canons of criticism, is very grave—because, though a little earlier he had commended the monks, saying that “most of them, moved by the Spirit of God [Col. 0124A] and distressed at the injury to their Father, would gladly have recalled him, had they not feared to act contrary to apostolic commands,” he afterwards says that the same monks, prompted by diabolical suggestions, formed a conspiracy against the holy abbot and expelled him from the monastery not only with insults but even with beatings, in an unbridled and irreverent spirit.

Thirdly, everyone knows that this account has already been excellently refuted by Dom Philip Malabayle and Erasmus Gattula, whom we mentioned above; and all writers who have elucidated the Cassinese Chronicle after Peter the Deacon have completely dismissed it as a calumny. Finally, with the Bollandists we say that every suspicion of such a crime must be rejected, as unworthy and injurious to Bruno’s holiness and to the excellent reputation of the Cassinese [Col. 0124B] monks.

## CHAPTER XII. On Bruno’s Return to the Church of Segni
When Bruno was received back by the people of Segni, the joy and applause with which they welcomed him, now that they saw him restored to them, may be inferred from the sadness and grief with which they had lamented his absence for many years, while he was bound by other obligations. Peter the Deacon places his return in October 1111. And so it must have been, for in the following year he attended the Second Lateran Council, celebrated by Paschal II, as is clear from his subscription.

Although Segni is not so far from Monte Cassino, and its citizens could not infrequently see and consult their holy bishop, and although “every year,” as the anonymous writer says, “while he remained in the monastery, they received chrism and holy oil from his hand [Col. 0124C], because they revered him with most affectionate devotion,” nevertheless they ardently desired his presence. Out of the love with which they regarded him, they demanded that, being present, he should provide for the spiritual welfare of the whole diocese.

Saint Bruno immediately resumed his former manner of life; and, fulfilling each duty of the pastoral office most abundantly, he seemed to cause a new splendour of virtues and a new order of things to arise and flourish again in the Church of Segni. Bruno’s renown had indeed spread widely, not only in Italy but also in Gaul, where in his legations he had successfully conducted affairs of the greatest importance; so that bishops again and again chose him as judge of their disputes and acquiesced in his decision.

[Col. 0124D] He himself recounts a serious quarrel that arose between the bishop of Siponto and the bishop of Benevento. When the case had been brought before him, although the archdeacon of the Church of Benevento advanced his bishop’s cause too shrewdly and violently, nevertheless, because the weight of the arguments favoured the bishop of Siponto, Bruno adjudged the case to him. [Note: [Col. 0124D] Commentary on chapter XXV of Deuteronomy, p. 211.]

That Bruno acted as reporter and judge in another case is evident from a bull of Paschal II, the ninth in volume II of Maynard’s collection. In this constitution the pope confirmed to the monks of Monte Cassino, against the abbess of St Mary in the city of Capua, the cell of Cingla, where the following is said concerning Bruno:

> “When Bruno, bishop of Segni, had returned and spoken, they declared that the lord pope’s judgment seemed reasonable and just to them, and that it ought to be held valid, as having been conducted according to canonical order.”

The same judgment had already been rendered by Urban II, from which the aforesaid abbess had appealed. This constitution is found dated on the Kalends of April, A.D. 1102, in the pontificate of Paschal II. It is probable that Bruno decided many other cases of this kind which, like those we have mentioned, the writers of his life omitted.

Bruno again went to Rome, as we said in the preceding chapter, and attended the Third Lateran Council, which Pope Paschal celebrated in 1116 [Col. 0125B] in order to settle the disputes which still troubled the Church over investitures. There again he condemned and struck with anathema that very privilege.

Two years later Paschal died, namely on 16 January 1118; and after twelve days John, chancellor of the Holy Roman Church, was given as his successor, chiefly through the efforts of Peter, cardinal-bishop of Porto. He was given the name Gelasius II. How mournful were the beginnings of Gelasius’s pontificate—so that, scarcely crowned, he fled Rome and sought protection among the Gauls—is related at length by ecclesiastical writers. They also report that, before the first year of his pontificate was completed, he was seized by pleurisy and gout and died most piously in the celebrated monastery of Cluny.

When Hugh, archbishop of Vienne, went to that same monastery on business concerning Gelasius [Col. 0125C], and found him to have died a few days before, the cardinals and bishops unanimously elected Hugh himself supreme pontiff, and he was called Calixtus II. I have thought it worthwhile to recall these matters in order also to mention the singular joy felt by Bruno upon hearing of Hugh’s election to the Roman pontificate. In Gaul he had known him as one highly distinguished by nobility of birth, piety, and learning, and had dealt with him familiarly.

Another cause of joy came to the holy bishop of Segni in the reconciliation of Emperor Henry V with the Catholic Church. For Henry at last renounced investitures and surrendered them to Pope Calixtus; Calixtus absolved him from censures and received him into communion with the Roman See. This is attested by Geoffrey of Viterbo, *Chronicle*, p. 17, and Otto of Freising, *Chronicle*, book VII, chapter 16. In the fifth year of Calixtus’s pontificate Bruno paid the debt of human nature and exchanged his earthly dwelling for a heavenly one, as the more trustworthy documents attest.

## CHAPTER XIII. On the death of Saint Bruno

There is not one opinion among writers concerning the year in which Saint Bruno departed this life [Col. 0126A]. Matthew Lauretus, in his notes on the above-mentioned *Chronicle of Monte Cassino*, which he himself published at Naples in 1616, thinks, according to his calculation, that Bruno’s death should be assigned to 1125. His reason is that Angelo Rocca, in the book *On the Canonization of Saints*, testifies that a bull concerning the canonization of Saint Bruno by Lucius III in the year of the Lord 1183 was preserved in Rome in the library of the Fathers of the Congregation of the Oratory; and, since this solemn act is referred to the fifty-eighth year after the holy bishop’s passage to the higher regions, it follows that he died in 1125.

But no copy of such a bull exists in that library, as I myself have inquired, and no one testifies to having seen it. The anonymous writer more truly recorded the year of Bruno’s blessed falling asleep:

> “He passed to the Lord,” he says, “on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of August, in the fifth year of Calixtus II, and in the forty-fourth year of his own episcopate.”

These chronological marks indicate not 1125 but 1123. For the fifth year from Calixtus II’s accession to the chair of Saint Peter was in progress when Saint Bruno closed his final day on 18 July 1123; nor can this date be postponed further.

There is also the unanimous agreement of the more accurate writers, who affirm that he began his episcopate under Saint Gregory VII in 1079, as we said in the first chapter: namely, in the year in which he contended victoriously against Berengar at the Roman council concerning the sacrament of the most holy Eucharist. If, therefore, forty-four years spent in the episcopate are added from the beginning of this inauguration, it is plainly proved that his mortal life cannot be extended beyond 1123.

[Note: [Col. 0125D] That Saint Bruno’s actual day of death was the fifteenth day before the Kalends of August is confirmed by a manuscript of Monte Cassino recently examined by the distinguished director of that archive, Don Giovanni Battista Federici. Since it contains the Martyrology of Usuard, and its writing seems, from the form of the characters, to have been executed about the year 1050, in the time of the celebrated Abbot Desiderius, an entry was added on 23 July commemorating Saint Bruno, in these words: “On the same day, the deposition of Saint Bruno, bishop and confessor.” This addition must be believed to have been made after Lucius III, Supreme Pontiff, celebrated his solemn canonization. [Col. 0126D]]

Finally, since it is acknowledged in another appendix to the acts that Honorius III erected an altar to Saint Bruno [Col. 0126C] and consecrated it with his own hands, and since the year from Bruno’s death is expressly said to have been the hundredth, it again follows that he passed into immortality in 1123. This is further confirmed because, as the same appendix asserts, that year, 1223, was the seventh of Honorius’s pontificate, since he was elected pope in 1216; and this agrees with the date of that consecration.

Bruno was now nearly eighty years old, and greatly weakened in strength by the austerity and labour of his life, when it pleased God, as the anonymous writer testifies, to reveal to him that his departure from this life was not far off. Warned by this foreknowledge, he burned all the more with heavenly love, desiring to be dissolved and to be with Christ. Therefore he devoted himself continually to prayer and refreshed his people frequently with the nourishment of God’s word.

[Col. 0126D] Having then been seized by a grave fever, he took to his bed. As his weakness increased and he was afflicted by greater languor, he summoned clergy and people to himself and left them his final instructions for a Christian life. Since his failing strength did not permit him to rise, he asked to be carried from his bed to the window. There, gathering his last breath, he preached with such force and such an outpouring of love that all burst into tears, overcome by sorrow at his approaching death.

To console the people of Segni, [Col. 0127A] the holy bishop promised them two things: first, that his patronage before God would always be present with them; secondly, that they would never again fall under tyrannical domination. Subsequent events proved these prophecies true. At last, when his illness threatened death, Bruno asked for the last sacraments to be administered to him; and, producing most fervent acts of love for God, he rendered his most pure soul to its Creator in the seventy-sixth year of his age. These things we have received from the anonymous writer; the other authors seem to have thought it enough to say that he died most holily.

[Note: [Col. 0127D] Cardinal Baronius, after mentioning Bruno’s resignation of the abbacy of Monte Cassino and his return to the Church of Segni, adds: “There, living in holy conduct until the time of Oderisius II, abbot, he happily passed to the Lord on the day before the Kalends of September. He was buried in the city of Segni [Col. 0128D], in the church of Saint Mary, Mother of God and Virgin; and even today the Lord deigns to work miracles in remembrance of him, through the intercession of his merits.”]

While the funeral rites for the holy bishop were being performed in the church of the Blessed Virgin Mary, where his body was buried, God confirmed his holiness by many miracles. These are recorded by the anonymous writer, the *Chronicle of Monte Cassino*, and Ferrarius from a very ancient breviary [Col. 0127B]. I shall not linger over describing them, since Angelo Toti, canon of Segni, adorned the Life of Saint Bruno, published by himself at Rome in 1783, with these same wondrous signs.

## CHAPTER XIV. On the virtues of Saint Bruno

Bruno must have shone with the greatest virtues, since he won for himself the favour and love of so many eminent men and supreme pontiffs. We have already said with what goodwill Saints Gregory VII and Peter Igneus embraced him, and what splendid proofs of their affection they gave him. The testimony of Saint Leo IX must likewise be held in very high esteem: when he appeared to John, bishop of Tusculum, he commanded him to urge Bruno of Segni [Col. 0127C] to write Leo’s deeds.

Well known also to everyone was his close friendship with Peter, the distinguished bishop of Anagni. To oblige him, Bruno illuminated the Pentateuch with his commentaries and handed down to posterity a compendium of Peter’s most holy life. Saint Peter departed this life in 1105, and Paschal II enrolled him among the saints, chiefly moved by Bruno’s testimony.

He who spent his early youth in the school of higher perfection, and who, fired by its desire, resolved to abandon all earthly things and devote himself to God alone, must be said already to have laid the firmest foundations of every virtue. Who inspired in him flight from the world, contempt of honours and riches, and perpetual self-denial, if not heavenly grace, which anticipated him with its blessings from early morning, so that he might shine in the Church as an example of outstanding holiness? Since these things take their origin from humility, how greatly Bruno cherished this virtue was shown by his constant effort.

Nor need I recall the canonries at Asti and Siena which he relinquished, or the entirely contemptuous name which he earned among those citizens. These were only the first signs of his humble spirit; far greater things [Col. 0128A] carry us away in admiration. Bruno arrived in Rome unknown, intending to seek Monte Cassino. By divine prompting, Saint Peter Igneus, cardinal, sought him out; he received him as a guest in his house and highly commended him to Saint Gregory VII.

Chosen above all others to contend at the Roman council for the Catholic faith against the heretic Berengar, Bruno refuted him with such force of eloquence and learning that, once truth had been laid bare and every error removed, he compelled him to recant and seek pardon. The more difficult the contest, the more glorious was Bruno’s victory. Adorned with the praises of all the Fathers, he saw an open path prepared for him toward higher ranks in the Church. Indeed, Gregory named him bishop of Segni; and though he firmly refused this dignity, repeated miracles alone persuaded him to undertake it.

Bruno felt an even greater conflict against his humility from the legations and distinguished offices which both Urban II and Paschal II very often entrusted to him. Therefore, to escape the fame of his name resounding everywhere, he hid himself in the solitude of Monte Cassino. Yet even there he could not long remain a private monk. The more he concealed himself, the more honours pursued him; hence, by the unanimous votes of all the monks, he was chosen archimandrite of Monte Cassino and compelled to preside over that most celebrated monastery.

Some writers—among whom I may name Bellarmine, Oldoini, Teissier, Martène, and Mabillon—have written that Bruno was admitted among the cardinals of the Holy Roman Church. But because more certain evidence of this dignity’s having been conferred upon him is lacking, one may at least conjecture that, when it was offered, he humbly refused it.

From this singular virtue, which Bruno loved intensely, must be believed to have flowed his complete abstinence from the softer conveniences of life. He always lived content with moderate and frugal food, worn clothing, and scarcely necessary furnishings. Thus we find Bruno greatly commended by Gallic writers because, while others during the time of their legation possessed much gold and, when their legation ended, were robbed on the road by brigands, these same brigands, hoping for the same booty, attacked Bruno as he returned from Gaul. But finding on him nothing except a small travelling allowance, they departed disappointed.

[Note: [Col. 0128D] See Pierre de Marca, *On the Concord of Priesthood and Empire*, book V, chapter 50, no. 8.]

Mindful, moreover, of the saying of Gregory the Great, who taught that leaving all things behind is not sufficient for complete perfection unless the following of Christ the Lord is added, Bruno strove wholly to conform himself to this teaching. Since our Saviour made himself both teacher and example of love for enemies, for while hanging from the tree he asked the Father to forgive his crucifiers, the bishop of Segni showed himself a perfect imitator of such love and beneficence.

It had been too little for him to forgive Count Adulphus of the little town the injury and sufferings of imprisonment inflicted upon him [Col. 0129A]. When the count fell from great power and abundant wealth into utter need and misery, Bruno never failed him, but generously supplied all his necessities.

It is difficult to repay our enemies with benefits; but it is much more difficult to restrain one’s spirit and act generously toward those who plot against one’s good name and reputation for integrity. That Bruno was attacked by such persons is evident from his letters both to Pope Paschal and to the cardinals of the Holy Roman Church. In them he indeed repels the calumnies brought against him—that he was planning to remove Paschal from the throne, supporting Paschal’s adversaries, and disturbing the entire Church—yet he always treated as brothers those whom he knew to be hostile to him. Neither in speech nor in writing did he utter anything that displayed diminished charity or goodwill [Col. 0129B].

Therefore, since he loves his enemies and does good to those who persecute him, and is, according to Christ’s teaching, a most beloved son of the Father who is in heaven, no one will doubt that Bruno earned for himself the most abundant rewards of this sonship.

As regards zeal for the purity of Christian faith, holiness of morals, the worship of God and the saints: the councils over which Bruno presided, the offices he held, and the writings he published will be his everlasting testimony that he promoted these with all his strength. Considering these things and those previously stated, I am carried away by a singular and truly noble courage in Bruno. He spared himself no labour; he undertook and successfully completed every arduous business among many nations and before great princes. He also opposed an unconquered spirit to injuries, detractions [Col. 0129C], and threats from hostile men.

Because Bruno was conscious that he sought nothing but God’s glory, he pursued it fearlessly by defending truth and justice, recalling the wicked to a better way of life, and supplying timely counsel. What wonder, then, if envy accused him as a disturber of the Church, as a partisan, or as too stubbornly attached to his own opinion? Such is the fate of nobler virtues: those who hate them sprinkle them with abuse and represent them as opposite vices. But as the sun disperses clouds and does not permit them to rob it of its light, so virtue, flashing far and wide with its own splendour, repels everything opposed to it.

Much more might be added [Col. 0129D] concerning faith, hope, and charity, which are chiefly and supremely required in a holy man. Yet since the entire life of Bruno, whose deeds we have thus far recounted, shines especially through these virtues, and since they are confirmed by the illustrious teachings set forth more fully in chapters 1, 2, and 3 of book II of the *Sentences*, we judge that proof is unnecessary.

## CHAPTER XV. On the wisdom of Saint Bruno

Saint Bruno clearly understood that sacred Scripture contains, besides the revelation of divine mysteries and legislation, treasures also of human learning. He therefore omitted nothing by which he might adorn himself with those disciplines that cultivate the mind and perfect the soul. Accordingly, his writings abundantly testify that he pursued dialectic, ethics, history, chronology, rhetoric [Col. 0130A], and even poetry.

The holy bishop calls such disciplines handmaids of the supreme mistress, namely the knowledge of God, whose hidden things are more successfully investigated with their aid and communicated to others for apprehension. In many places he indeed refutes the sophisms and captious arguments used by heretics to deceive the unwary. He teaches that reasoning should be employed as a touchstone, not to conceal error, but to disclose and prove truth.

He very frequently lays down moral precepts which are not only wholly consistent with Gospel commands, but are drawn from the more approved ethical writers—Plato, Aristotle, and Seneca—whom he seems to have cherished greatly. He likewise applied himself to sacred history, seeking first to acquire it from the divine books and then from reading Philo, Josephus, and other Hebrew writers. He joined secular history to it, being accustomed to employ the rites, fables, and sayings of pagan authors whenever he perceived that they could contribute anything useful to his subject.

When we collected his writings, we discovered that the holy bishop was by no means ignorant also of natural history. For whenever he treats plants, trees, stones, or animals, he fittingly describes their properties, powers, and character, so that he appears to have drawn them from the storehouses of Theophrastus, Pliny, Dioscorides, and other similar authors.

I shall further call Bruno an accurate chronologist, since we shall show that, in the reckoning of years—in which so many and such great writers have erred—he agrees with the more reliable chronologists [Col. 0130C]. Nor, in writing, when occasion required, did he neglect the charm and elegance of poets, especially in his exposition of the *Song of Songs*, in order to conform himself to the imagery and allegorical utterances of the sacred writer.

I confess, indeed, that Bruno adopted certain popular opinions and inventions of some persons; but writers of that age must be excused, since the rules of criticism had not yet supplied light and guidance for writing. Some authors affirm that our Bruno delighted in poetry. Examples may be the verses read in his exposition of Psalm 150, as well as those of various metres in which the holy commentator embraced the more beautiful passages of the *Song of Songs* [Col. 0130D].

Whether Saint Bruno was an eloquent orator will be clearly shown by his speeches—namely, his homilies and sermons.
