Yet these studies, which enlighten the mind and delight the soul, did not draw him away from cultivating more serious disciplines, for he is known to have been highly proficient in canon and civil law. Indeed, why did the supreme pontiffs entrust so many legations to him unless they knew how greatly Bruno excelled in knowledge of the canons, and with what prudence and learning he rendered judgment in the more difficult cases?

I shall mention here only a few instances among many. When he was exercising the office of papal legate in Gaul, a marriage-dissolution case was brought before him. Mathildis, wife of Galleran, chamberlain to Philip the Fat, sought the dissolution, and both parties were absent. Bruno instructed the bishop of Paris to summon each party to the case on a suitable day. Before him, once force and serious fear had been proved, the case was judged in Mathildis’s favour. These facts occur in letter 161 of Saint Ivo of Chartres to Humbald, bishop of Auxerre.

At the Council of Poitiers, over which Bruno presided as legate of the Holy Roman Church, he deposed Archbishop Bertrand, convicted of simony, and installed in his see Richard, cardinal and abbot of Saint Victor. Finally, we may say that Bruno also took jurisprudence as his companion, because a manuscript in the archive of Monte Cassino contains a concise collection of certain civil laws. With these resources [Col. 0131B] Bruno fulfilled the episcopal office to the greatest glory and the benefit of his people, and he enriched the Church with his most learned writings.

Among these writings, many authors deeply lament his lost commentary on Isaiah. For to no prophet were the mysteries and sacraments of the divine Redeemer revealed more profoundly and abundantly; and therefore their interpretation and exposition cannot be attempted except by one possessing the broadest knowledge of divine things and having consulted the most highly esteemed earlier interpreters. Bruno is said to have taken Saint Ambrose especially as his guide among these. But since we still lack the expositions of both holy Fathers, we cannot enjoy their wisdom and labour. We nevertheless entreat those in charge of the greatest libraries to devote every care to recovering these monuments of sacred learning [Col. 0131C].

## CHAPTER XVI. On Saint Bruno’s love for the Order of Saint Benedict

No interpreter of Saint Bruno’s deeds has hitherto treated of his love and esteem for the most holy institute of Benedict. Yet, since throughout his life his affection for that body of monks was singular and exceptional, we have rightly and properly resolved to pursue the subject in this special dissertation.

Indeed, Bruno was born of noble family; he was not offered by his parents as a child, but entered freely and as an adult. He was not compelled by a meagre patrimony, nor was he obscure in the world, nor attracted by hope of dignities. Rather, he was already distinguished by a double canonry, ordained bishop of a prominent see, and highly esteemed by the supreme pontiffs for his eminent wisdom. That he embraced the monastic profession with the utmost desire and preferred this manner of life to all others must surely be ascribed only to his being won over by the most approved virtues of Saint Benedict, which he saw imitated by Benedict’s sons.

This also may have moved so distinguished a man: the measured observance of Benedict’s rules pleased him, since each monk could apply himself to his own spiritual advancement and, without lacking necessary resources, was permitted to cultivate more serious studies and transmit his nocturnal labours to posterity. Saint Bruno showed this in deed. Having relinquished the administration of the bishopric of Segni and been received as a monk in the solitude of Monte Cassino, he wrote the greater part of his works [Col. 0132A]. We have already said how much he deserved from the Church by enriching it with learned commentaries on sacred Scripture; and we judge it unnecessary to praise this again here.

But what especially carries us away in admiration of him is that he so soon became, as it were, a prodigy of holiness, so that after only a few years of regular profession all the monks, in agreement, entrusted to him the supreme government of the monastery. Those who were adorned with such dignity were held in such high esteem by the Roman Church that they not only became cardinals and bishops, but were even raised to the supreme pontificate.

Not to mention more ancient examples, in those very times there were the celebrated Abbot Desiderius, afterward called Pope Victor III; Gelasius II; Leo of Ostia; and Abbot Rainald, cardinals; as well as many others who illumined no less the monastery of Monte Cassino than the Benedictine Order as a whole.

Since Bruno shone exceptionally in wisdom and holiness, by which he won the love and reverence of great princes, it was not difficult for him to obtain many benefactions from them—not to provide for his own comforts, but to increase the revenues and resources of Monte Cassino. How often, too, praises of Saint Benedict resounded from his lips! At one time he said that the Holy Spirit had spoken through Benedict and that Benedict’s sayings should be held in the highest esteem; so in sermon IV, book II of the *Sentences*. At another he extolled Benedict’s humility because he gloried in woollen and humble garments and used poor furnishings; this is in sermon 19 of the same book, entitled *On Abstinence*.

Elsewhere, calling Benedict not infrequently “his father,” he did not hesitate to place him among the chief pillars of the holy Church—namely the apostles Peter, James, and John—and among the first martyrs, Stephen and Lawrence: book I of the *Sentences*, chapter 4. He also compared Benedict with the prodigies of austerity and abstinence, Anthony, Paul, and Hilarion: book II of the *Sentences*, chapter 9.

Moreover, in sermon 2 *On Confessors*, book VI of the *Sentences*, he called Saint Benedict wiser than Solomon:

> “Not with the wisdom of this world, which is folly with God, and to which he never wished to draw near; but with that wisdom which is true and leads a human being to eternal life.”

In the same sermon [Col. 0132D] he describes the entire institution of his holy father in such pre-eminent and vivid colours that, since it was preserved whole and inviolate in Bruno’s day, this single testimony refutes whatever hostile writers have invented against Benedictine monks. Setting before himself the image of the queen of Sheba, who entered the house of King Solomon and was amazed on seeing such order, splendour, and dignity in all things, he relates the following most eloquently:

> “Oh, if that queen of Sheba had come to Saint Benedict and had heard wisdom from his mouth; if she had seen his servants, his ministers, his sons and brothers, his tables and his food—how all things are ordered, how well arranged; how all have one heart and one soul, and no one says that anything is his own, but all things are common to them; how all love one another, how all obey one another; what love, what charity, what affection is among all! If, I say, that queen of Sheba—so prudent, so wise, so devout, so dedicated to God—had been able to see all these things, she would truly have lost her whole spirit, because she would have deserved to receive the grace of the Holy Spirit.”

From this, I think, arose Bruno’s great hesitation when his return to the Church of Segni was under discussion. The holy conduct of Saint Benedict’s devoted sons held him; so did their perfect observance of the best rules, the balanced distribution of prayers and studies, and the complete tranquillity of a mind devoted to God. Therefore papal authority and the never-ceasing prayers of his people were necessary before he would leave the monastery of Monte Cassino and return to the exercise of the episcopal office [Col. 0133B].

## CHAPTER XVII. On the canonization of Saint Bruno

Scarcely had Bruno passed from his earthly to his heavenly homeland when frequent miracles made his tomb glorious and renowned. This is plainly attested by the chronicler of Monte Cassino and by the anonymous writer. Accordingly, he began to be venerated and regarded as a saint, not only in the Church of Segni but also by the monks of Monte Cassino.

But God, who wished his servant to be adorned with heavenly honours, moved Pope Lucius III—when Bruno’s fame and renown, remarkable miracles, and the crowds of people coming daily to implore his patronage were increasing—to honour him, according to ecclesiastical decrees, with the name and cult of the saints in a solemn rite and celebration, after his virtues and miracles had been proved.

Although the pope could have performed this religious act at Rome, he himself went to Segni, accompanied by thirteen cardinals whose names are recorded beneath the bull of canonization, in order that it might be more solemn. In the cathedral church where Bruno’s relics were kept, he enrolled him by apostolic authority in the register of the saints. In the same church there is a marble monument of this canonization, which reads as follows:

> **TO THE ETERNAL MEMORY OF BLESSED BRUNO, WHOM LUCIUS III, SUPREME PONTIFF, IN AN ASSEMBLY OF CARDINALS AND BISHOPS AT SEGNI, IN THE CHURCH OF BLESSED MARY, WHERE HIS DEAD BODY RESTED, ORDERED TO BE ENROLLED AMONG THE SAINTS IN THE FIFTY-EIGHTH YEAR AFTER HIS DEPARTURE. THE SENATE AND PEOPLE OF SEGNI.**

The Bollandists demonstrate that the author of the appendix to the *Chronicle of Monte Cassino* erred concerning the year of this celebration, asserting that it was performed by Lucius III in the fortieth year after Bruno’s death and in the time of Bartholomew, bishop of Segni. Both assertions are false. The first is false because the election of Pope Lucius III occurred on 29 August 1181, and therefore, since this date is fifty-eight years after Bruno’s passage to heaven, his canonization cannot have taken place in the fortieth year after his death, but in the fifty-eighth—during the first year of Lucius III’s pontificate.

The second assertion is no less false, because Bartholomew is associated with Lucius III and called bishop of Segni, although he was nearly seventy years later than that pontiff, as is clear from Ughelli’s catalogue. Peter, however, was made bishop of Segni by Alexander III, the fourth bishop after Bruno.

Another illustrious sign of honour and special veneration ought not to be omitted. Honorius III came to Segni for this purpose, accompanied by three cardinals—Peter, bishop of Palestrina; Nicholas, bishop of Tusculum; and Andrew, bishop of Porto—that he might with his own hands consecrate an altar dedicated to Saint Bruno. He placed in it many relics of the holy apostles, martyrs, and virgins.

Among the supreme pontiffs who deserved especially well of Saint Bruno, I shall also count Gregory XIII, who granted in 1584 to the diocese of Segni that psalmody and Mass should be celebrated on the feast of Saint Bruno with the double rite and octave. This is evident from the letters of Cardinal Sirleto dated 11 June 1584, in the thirteenth year of Pope Gregory. Since, then, so many Roman pontiffs adorned the holy bishop of Segni in life and after death with most distinguished dignities and honours, those writers who handed down not his praises but detractions to posterity should be held of no account.

## CHAPTER XVIII. On the cult of Saint Bruno
Before Bruno was solemnly enrolled among the saints, as we said in the preceding chapter, the Church of Segni and the monks of Monte Cassino paid him particular devotion and honour. But after his sacred canonization [Col. 0134C] by Lucius III, and as miracles frequently shone forth at his tomb, the people of Segni became so inflamed with love and trust toward the holy bishop that they chose him as their principal patron and protector. Accordingly, not only the citizens but also the neighbouring peoples eagerly contributed great quantities of gold, so that the larger church in which his sacred ashes were venerated might be restored more fittingly and adorned with precious furnishings.

It happened, however, that when all Campania was invaded and devastated in 1557, while Paul IV occupied the Roman see, by hostile forces commanded by the Duke of Alba, the city of Segni suffered the same calamity: its possessions were plundered and burned. Since military licence left nothing untouched by fire, robbery, and devastation [Col. 0134D], the silver casket in which the relics of St Bruno were kept, together with the silver bust containing his sacred head, suffered the same violence. Yet the head was removed from its shrine, wrapped in linen, and thrown into a certain tomb. Whatever human skill could repair, the people of Segni took care to restore as quickly as possible. But they were plunged into the deepest grief because they lacked the more precious memorial of their most beneficent Father, and had no indication where they might seek it.

Long after the devastation of Segni, on 10 July 1626, when a certain tomb in that same church was opened, behold: in the darkness a great light shone forth, wonderfully illuminating the linen covering [Col. 0135A] in which the holy bishop’s head was wrapped. As soon as this remarkable miracle became known to the bishop, by his order, amid the joyful exultation of clergy and people, the sacred head was raised and placed in a place of honour. In order that the miraculous discovery of St Bruno’s head might be established by public records, authorization was sought from the Sacred Congregation of Rites at Rome; suitable witnesses were summoned for examination, and by oath confirmed the miracle which they had seen. Once everything had been duly completed and proved, nothing remained for the restoration of public veneration to the venerable head except for the bishop of Segni to issue a written decree.

When Bishop Peter Corbellis delayed this longer than was proper, a new miracle compelled him to complete the matter. The same Peter kept the sacred head [Col. 0135B] upon a table in his private chamber; but one evening, when night’s darkness had come on, as he was writing that decree, the sacred head again appeared to him surrounded by shining rays which filled the whole room with splendour. I do not know whether fear or wonder was greater in Bishop Peter, since he had been so slow to decree public honours for Bruno’s head. At last, on the third day before the Ides of November [11 November] 1703, he restored them with the greatest solemnity and amid the rejoicing of all the citizens. A marble monument erected in the principal church records all these matters.

> WHILE THE MOST HOLY CLEMENT XI SAT AS SUPREME PONTIFF, THE VENERABLE HEAD OF ST BRUNO, BISHOP OF THIS CHURCH—STRIPPED OF ITS SILVER SHRINES AND GEMS BY IMPIOUS SOLDIERS IN THE DESTRUCTION OF THIS CITY IN THE YEAR 1557, CAST INTO A TOMB, AND MIRACULOUSLY FOUND IN 1626 SURROUNDED BY DIVINE LIGHT—WAS AT LAST, BY DIVINE INSPIRATION, IN RESPONSE TO THE EARNEST PRAYERS OF THIS CLERGY, CITY, AND DIOCESE, RESTORED TO ITS FORMER VENERATION BY THE MOST ILLUSTRIOUS AND MOST REVEREND LORD PETER, COUNT OF CORBELLIS, OF FANO, REFERENDARY OF BOTH SIGNATURES, AND BISHOP OF SEGNI, AFTER A WEIGHED PROCESS, PROOFS, MIRACLES, AND THE OPINIONS OF THE MOST EMINENT CARDINALS OF THE HOLY ROMAN CHURCH AND THEOLOGIANS, TO THE GREAT JOY OF THE CITY OF SEGNI, IN THE YEAR OF SALVATION 1703, ON THE THIRD DAY BEFORE THE IDES OF NOVEMBER.

Therefore, since the people of Segni know that heaven has given them a patron through so many and such great miraculous signs [Col. 0135D], they have hitherto bestowed most generously whatever can contribute to his honour and glory; and this same piety and generosity is passed down from fathers to sons. The people of Segni themselves experience the benefits with which the holy bishop repays such worship: they repeatedly have his patronage present whenever they implore him with suppliant vows for clear skies, timely rains, or the repelling of storms.

How splendidly St Bruno’s feast is celebrated on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of August [18 July], with the gathering of peoples and every sort of solemnity, preceded by the nine-day observances by which the citizens anticipate and render more holy so great a celebration, I cannot relate briefly [Col. 0136A], and therefore pass over. But the people of Asti and Solero also—who, as we said, contend with one another in claiming St Bruno as their fellow citizen—honour him in their churches, where altars have been erected in his honour, with every ecclesiastical observance and festive procession on the anniversary of his passage to heaven. At Siena also, in whose cathedral church, as we said, Bruno was a canon, his memory is celebrated on 18 July with the Office and Mass under the double rite, and he is held in special veneration.

### Decree of Cardinal Sirleto granting to the city and diocese of Segni the Office of St Bruno, Bishop of Segni, from the Common of Confessor-Bishops, with proper lessons approved by that most learned cardinal

We, William Sirleto, priest-cardinal of the title of St Lawrence in Panisperna [Col. 0136B], make known and attest that our most holy lord Gregory, Pope XIII, by an oral decree made to us, granted and gave permission to the bishop and clergy of Segni to recite publicly and privately, in choir and outside it, within the city itself and the diocese of Segni, the following Office of St Bruno, bishop and confessor, under the double rite with an octave.

> Given in the Apostolic Palace, at the place of our residence, 11 June 1584, in the thirteenth year of the pontificate of our most holy lord Gregory, Pope XIII.
>
> **LESSON I.** Bruno was born at Solero in Insubria, not far from the city of Asti, of honourable and devout parents, Andrew and Scylla. While still very young, he was entrusted for instruction to the religious men of the monastery of St Perpetuus in the diocese of Asti [Col. 0136C], and made remarkable progress in every branch of ecclesiastical learning. He was then sent to Bologna for study; having applied himself excellently both to secular and divine letters, he obtained the title of doctor. When he travelled into Etruria, wishing to visit the bishop of the city of Siena, whose name was then most celebrated, he was kindly received by him and, to the public joy of all, admitted into the college of canons of the greater church.
>
> Subsequently, when sent to Rome by the bishop on necessary business, at the time when Gregory VII governed the Church and a grave controversy had arisen concerning the sacrament of the Eucharist with Berengar, who held wholly erroneous opinions, the pontiff, moved by Bruno’s reputation, asked him—after others had tried in vain—to confront Berengar alone [Col. 0136D] and, having convicted him by arguments and by truth itself, finally recall him from error. Trusting in God’s help, Bruno undertook the task with great courage and successfully accomplished it.
>
> **LESSON II.** The pontiff, having observed Bruno’s steadfastness and been moved by his virtues, said to Peter, cardinal-bishop of Albano, by whom Bruno had been kindly received as a guest: “I commend this man to you in the highest degree, for he will be of great service to the Church.” Thus, having received holy orders at Rome and been consecrated by the supreme pontiff himself, Bruno was made bishop of the Church of Segni, though against his will. That Church received him with the incredible joy of all, and public thanks were given to God for having granted them such a shepherd [Col. 0137A].
>
> But he immediately set about healing the ailments of his flock. Above all, he was seized by Adolphus, formerly count of Segni, and cast into chains. The place of his imprisonment was the castle of Vico, not far from Mount Lepinus, where Segni itself was founded. There, after suffering many grave and cruel hardships, he was tormented by most intense thirst and ordered water drawn from a nearby well to be brought to him. When he tasted it, he discovered it to be wine of a better quality. He rebuked the man who had brought it for offering wine instead of water. But the man, pleading innocence upon oath, was ordered likewise to bring cold water; and, at the bishop’s blessing, the water was repeatedly changed into wine. Struck by this miracle, Count Adolphus, conscious of his crime, lest by continuing in sin [Col. 0137B] he should heap guilt upon guilt and incur the hatred of good men to his great disgrace, released the bishop from custody.
>
> **LESSON III.** St Bruno was very diligent in reading and meditating upon sacred Scripture, as his outstanding writings show. For he wrote on the five books of Moses, the Book of Judges, the Books of Kings, the Psalms of David, the Song of Songs, the prophet Isaiah, Job, and the Apocalypse. He also published 155 homilies which he delivered to the people, and sixty-nine sermons, in which both his learning and piety shine forth. Paschal II held his holiness and wisdom in such high regard that he entrusted him with legations to Gaul and Sicily, where he both regulated the churches and restored moral discipline. He honourably attended the great Lateran synod [Col. 0137C], at which he strove with invincible vigour for the repeal of the laws that the Roman pontiff had issued under compulsion from Emperor Henry V.
>
> Having held the episcopate for thirty-four years, he departed this life at Segni on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of August [18 July] in the year 1125, aged seventy-three, after performing many miracles. Later, in the year of the Lord’s Nativity 1183 [Col. 0138A], fifty-eight years after blessed Bruno’s death, Lucius III, Supreme Pontiff, enrolled him among the saints at Segni. In his honour, Honorius III, in the year of salvation 1223 and the seventh year of his pontificate, personally dedicated an altar with his own hands in solemn rite, assisted by Peter of Palestrina, Nicholas of Tusculum, and Andrew, cardinal-bishops.

We consider it appropriate here to report the decree of the Alexandrian synod of 12 November 1618, issued by the command of Lord Erasmus Pallavicini, bishop of that city and nuncio of the Apostolic See to Ferdinand II, Emperor of Austria. It reads as follows:

> Antiquity established, and custom has not been abolished in these times, that the deeds of illustrious men should be committed to public history, so that they may live perpetually in the world insofar as possible. Following this approved custom [Col. 0138B], we endeavour to commend to the memory and likewise to the veneration not only of you but of all posterity a man distinguished not merely by secular achievements, virtues, and human learning, but also instructed in divine disciplines and enjoying eternal glory. He rightly remains in human memory and is honoured with worthy veneration, since he has passed to the joys of the angels.
>
> Therefore, since blessed Bruno, bishop of the city of Segni, derived his glorious origin from the town of Solero in this diocese—and we know that this very city was built from its contribution—it has seemed fitting to us that, as an expression of devotion, the Office of so great a saint should be recited throughout the Alexandrian Church. Accordingly, by this present decree we order that on the feast of the saint himself [Col. 0138C], customarily celebrated from the Roman Martyrology on 18 July, the Office of that same St Bruno, bishop and confessor, be observed under the double rite with an octave. This Office shall be observed without exception both in church and outside it, publicly as well as privately; and accordingly we decree that it be entered each year in the Calendar.

[Col. 0137C]

## Testimonies of Ecclesiastical Writers concerning St Bruno

### I. Peter the Deacon, monk of Monte Cassino, *On the Illustrious Men of Monte Cassino*, chapter 34

Bruno, bishop of Segni and abbot of Monte Cassino, a most distinguished and illustrious defender and doctor of the Church, among the many outstanding monuments of his intellect, wrote—at the request of the canons of Segni—an exposition of the Psalter, Genesis [Col. 0138D], Exodus, Leviticus, Numbers, Deuteronomy, the Song of Songs, and Judges.

> **Note:** [Col. 0137D] In the preface to his commentary on the Psalms, St Bruno gives a different account of those who urged him to expound the Psalms. Having spoken of the first exposition, he refers to the other as follows: “Asked therefore by friends, and especially by the venerable Abbot Peregrinus, I took pains that this too, like the former, should have its own interpretation.” This is the commentary on the Psalms included in this volume. Peter the Deacon was therefore mistaken in saying [Col. 0138D] that the exposition of the Psalms had been prepared at the request of the canons of Segni.

> **Note:** [Col. 0138D] In chapter 2 of Prolegomenon I, where it was stated that Peter the Deacon, among the recorded works of St Bruno, made no mention of his commentary on the prophet Isaiah, this should have been added in this catalogue, which was the more appropriate place for such a mention. In the Life of the same saint, however, we acknowledge that Peter the Deacon called him an expositor of Isaiah.

He also composed the following sermons: *On the Praises of the Church at the Dedication of a Temple*; *On Paradise*; *On Noah’s Ark*; *On the Tabernacle of the Covenant*; *On Solomon’s Temple*; *On the Woman through Whom the Church Is Signified*; *On the City of Holy Jerusalem*; *On Basilicas Dedicated by Bishops*; likewise, *On the Gospels*; *On the Ornaments of the Church*; *On Faith*; *On Hope*; *On Charity* [Col. 0139A]; *On the Four Virtues*; *On Humility*; *On Mercy*; *On Peace*; *On Patience*; *On Chastity*; *On Obedience*; *On Abstinence*; *On the Adornment of the Church*; *On the New World*; *On New Heavens*; *On the Sea and New Fishers*; *On New Trees*; *On New Animals*.

On the feast of feasts, that is, the Holy Trinity: three sermons; *On the Nativity of the Lord*; *On the Circumcision*; *On the Epiphany*; *On the Octave of the Epiphany*; *On Palm Sunday*; *On the Lord’s Supper*; *On Easter*; *On the Ascension of the Lord*; *On Pentecost*; *On the Nativity of St Mary*; *On the Annunciation*; *On the Purification*; *On Her Assumption*. Three sermons on virgins; three sermons on martyrs; seven sermons on martyrs; a homily on the feasts of confessors; another on the feast of St Benedict; with two sermons on pontiffs; four *On the Holy Angel*; five homilies on the apostles; three homilies on several martyrs; three homilies on one martyr; *On the Dedication of a Church*; *In Advent of the Lord*; on the second Sunday [Col. 0139B] of Advent; two on the third Sunday, *On the Annunciation of the Blessed Virgin Mary*; on the fourth Sunday of Advent; on the vigil of the Nativity of the Lord; three homilies on the day of the Lord’s Nativity; on St Stephen; on St John the Evangelist; on the feast of the Innocents; on the first Sunday after the Lord’s Nativity; on the octave of the Lord’s Nativity; on the Epiphany; on the first Sunday after Epiphany; on the third, fourth, and fifth Sundays; on the Purification of St Mary; on Septuagesima; on Sexagesima; on Quinquagesima; on Ash Wednesday and the hair-shirt.

From the sixth weekday and Saturday at the beginning of Lent up to the Lord’s Supper: forty homilies. On the Lord’s Supper; Holy Saturday; the feast of Easter; Monday, Tuesday, Wednesday, Thursday, and Friday; and Saturday in Easter week; the first, second, third, and fourth Sundays after Easter week; in the major procession; on the feast of the apostles Philip and James; on the Finding of the Holy Cross; on St Michael; on the Ascension of the Lord; on the first Sunday after the Ascension of the Lord; on Pentecost; on the first Sunday after the octave of Pentecost; on the second, third, and fourth Sundays; on St John the Baptist; on the vigil of the apostles Peter and Paul [Col. 0139C], and on their feast-day. Twenty-four homilies on the first Sunday after the Nativity of the Apostles. On St Lawrence; the Assumption of St Mary; St Matthew; the vigil of St Andrew; and his feast-day.

He also composed a sermon on St Scholastica; a sermon *On the Translation of St Stephen from the City of Constantinople to the Roman Fortress*; verses in praise of St Mary; a homily on the beheading of St John the Baptist; and one on the Nativity of St Mary. He lived in the times of Emperors Henry IV and V. He was buried in his episcopal see near the city of Segni.

### II. Sixtus of Siena, *Actuarium in the Sacred Library*, p. 513, with additions by P. Pius Milante, O.P., Naples edition, 1742

St Bruno, or Brunus, an Italian Ligurian of distinguished Astesan blood, first bishop of Segni or Signi, then, after resigning the episcopate, a monk of Monte Cassino, and afterwards elected abbot by the unanimous will of all the brethren, governed for three years and ten months; but he was compelled by Paschal II, Roman Pontiff, to return to his episcopate. He wrote commentaries on the Pentateuch, Job, the Psalter, the Canticle of Zechariah, 164 homilies or sermons, and many other theological works. All these, as Cave writes, were collected into one body and restored to their author through the study and care of Mauro Marchesi, and printed at Venice in two folio volumes in 1651. He fell asleep in the Lord in 1125, on the day before the Kalends of September [31 August].

### III. Robert Cardinal Bellarmine, with the Supplements of Philip Labbe, Venice edition, 1727, p. 351

Mauro Marchesi, a monk of the Cassinese Congregation from Palermo, seeks to prove by many arguments in the historical dissertation prefixed to the published works that the book *On the Praises of the Church*, and all those immediately following it, which the Carthusians claim for their most holy patriarch, belong not to him but to Bruno, bishop of Segni and cardinal of the Holy Roman Church [Col. 0140A].

Among Bruno’s writings is mentioned a *Life of Pope St Leo IX*, more extensive than that written by Wibert, the archdeacon, published by Sirmond in 1615 together with the *Life of Charles the Good, Count of Flanders*.

Among those who mention Bruno, above all, are Peter the Deacon in the Cassinese Chronicle; Cardinal Baronius in volume XII of the *Annals*; Marcus Antonius Scipio in his eulogies of the abbots of Monte Cassino; Ferdinand Ughelli in volume I of *Italia Sacra*, under the bishops of Segni; and Philip Malabayla in his inquiry concerning the birth, canonicate, and withdrawal from Monte Cassino of St Bruno. They state that he died on 18 July in about 1125 and was enrolled among the saints by Lucius III. Dom Luc d’Achery published, in volume XII, p. 79, of the *Spicilegium*, St Bruno’s work *On the Consecration of a Church*, more fully than in the Venetian edition made by Marchesi.

### IV. Jacques Le Long, *Exegetical Library*, p. 654

Bruno, a Ligurian from the city of Asti, of the Solero family, a Benedictine, abbot of Monte Cassino, then bishop of Segni, died in 1123. His works are:

1. A commentary on the Pentateuch.
2. On Job.
3. On the Psalter according to the Vulgate version.
4. On the Song of Songs.
5. On the Apocalypse.

These works were published in two volumes at Venice in 1651, and in the Lyons *Library of the Fathers*. 6. On the Book of Judges. 7. On Judith. 8. On Isaiah. 9. On the four Gospels, at Paris in the Library of St Victor, MS 815, and at Turin in the library of the Duke of Savoy.

The commentaries on the Book of Judges and on Isaiah are preserved in the library of the Carthusians’ monastery of St Bartholomew [Col. 0140C] near Anagni.

He wrote another work, namely a commentary on the Psalms, as he himself attests in its preface: “When I was a young man, I expounded the Psalter according to another translation.” This is explained by the anonymous author of his Life prefixed to the printed works: “Asked,” he says, “by certain men from beyond the Alps, he ran through the Psalter according to the Gallican translation in a concise exposition.”

St Bruno the German of Cologne, founder of the Carthusians, died in 1101. His works are: 1. An exposition of the Psalms of David. 2. Commentaries on all the Epistles of Paul, published in folio at Paris in 1509, again at Paris in 1524 in folio, and at Cologne in 1611 and 1640. There are those who deny that these works belong to our Bruno and maintain that they should be ascribed to the man of Asti.

The 144 homilies or sermons of St Bruno were wrongly ascribed to Eusebius of Emesa, Eucherius of Lyon, or others.

[Col. 0140D] *Treatise on the Canticle of Zechariah*; *Treatise on the Incarnation of the Lord*; *Treatise on the Subject of Unleavened Sacrifice*; a short work *On the Sacraments, the Mysteries of the Church, and Ecclesiastical Rites*; *Life of St Peter of Anagni*; *Life of Pope St Leo IX*, to which is added an answer to the question, “Why is the state of the Church corrupt?”; six books of *Sentences*. Luc d’Achery published the short work *On the Consecration of a Church*, *Spicilegium*, vol. XII, p. 79.

### V. Ferdinand Ughelli, Cistercian Abbot, *Italia Sacra*, on the Bishops of Segni, vol. I, p. 1236

St Bruno, born at Asti of the most noble Solero family, lords of the castle of Solero, had Andrew and Scylla as parents. He was cultivated in the first disciplines at the Benedictine monastery of St Perpetuus [Col. 0141A], then pursued higher studies at Bologna, namely canon law and jurisprudence. Elected a canon of Asti, he went to Rome during the pontificate of Gregory VII and, in a public Roman council, by disputation rebuked and defeated Berengar, who held impious views concerning the sacrament of the altar. Consequently, as a reward of honour and of this celebrated victory, he was made bishop of Segni by the supreme pontiff.

He governed that Church most wisely for many years, until, moved by a desire for a more tranquil and contemplative life, he resigned his burden and professed as a monk of Monte Cassino in 1104. In that capacity Paschal II sent him to Gaul, where, according to Peter the Deacon, book IV, chapter 33, he is said to have celebrated a famous synod; Ivo of Chartres often mentions this legation. On returning thence to the cloister in 1107, after the death of Abbot Otto, he was elected abbot of Monte Cassino by the consent of all the monks on the Ides of November [13 November]. He governed for three years and ten months. When these had elapsed and it was disputed between him and Pope Paschal [Col. 0141B] whether it was preferable for him to preside over the monastery or to exercise the episcopal office, overcome by reverence for the pontiff, he resigned the abbacy and returned to the Church of Segni, which he afterwards governed, as he had before, with the highest praise for piety.

In his leisure Bruno wrote wisdom; for these monuments of his are still to be seen at Monte Cassino:

One book on Genesis; one on Exodus; one on Judges; one on the Psalms; one on the Apocalypse; six books of *Sentences*; sermons for Sundays and saints’ days; various homilies. He produced another exposition on the Psalms, as he himself acknowledges. A manuscript codex of this exposition exists with Abbot Hilarion Rancatus. He exchanged this life for the heavenly one under Calixtus II, in 1125, on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of August [18 July]; he was enrolled among the saints by Lucius III in the fifty-eighth year after his death. Baronius records his commemoration in the Roman Martyrology on 18 July. More concerning him may be found in Leo of Ostia, *Cassinese Chronicle*, book IV, chapter 31, and in the letters of Paschal, but in the year 1226 [Col. 0141C]. Pope Honorius III personally dedicated an altar to St Bruno in that same cathedral. Bruno himself consecrated an altar of the Blessed Virgin Mary in the same cathedral, as an ancient inscription records.

### VI. François Combefis, volume I of the *Library of Preachers*, p. 8, Paris edition, 1662

St Bruno, an Astesan by birthplace, bishop of Segni and abbot of Monte Cassino, was the author of those homilies that were long published under the name of Eusebius of Emesa and inserted in the final Cologne edition of Alcuin’s Homiliary. Mauro Marchesi of Palermo, monk of the Cassinese Congregation, proves this in his dissertation on Bruno and the books written by him, prefixed to the Venice edition of his works of 1631.

As for the six books of *Sentences*, the first of which is *On the Praises of the Church*, found inscribed to the most holy patriarch of the Carthusians in certain manuscripts of the Grande Chartreuse—and from which six lessons for the Office of that same holy patriarch have also been drawn—I find it difficult to agree with Marchesi [Col. 0141D]. Manuscripts conflict with manuscripts. Peter the Deacon, affirming in book IV, chapter 31, of his work *On the Illustrious Men of the Monastery of Monte Cassino*, where he carefully enumerates the books of Bruno of Asti, makes no mention of this great and, as it were, crowning work, but instead cites that final homiletic work of pseudo-Eusebius and sermons.

> **Note:** [Col. 0141D] It is manifest that Combefis either suffered a lapse of memory or had not read the testimony of Peter the Deacon concerning the works of St Bruno which we placed first. He did not indeed call them books of *Sentences*; [Col. 0142D] but he listed the individual titles of the chapters or sermons. How greatly Combefis erred here is sufficiently clear from what we have set forth in the Prolegomena and in the Life.

The affinity of style, in which Marchesi thinks he finds support, perhaps works more against him. The most holy patriarch may have mentioned the great St Benedict in titles, since, as the singular patron, model, and guide of monastic life, Benedict was the one from whom he, a new founder of a new religious militia, had borrowed many things. If these considerations seem slight, and one prefers to stand with the other Bruno—who pressed domestic examples and teachings upon his own people and adapted his style to the circumstances of his time and his hearers—I do not contend; let it be so as far as I am concerned. Bruno lived as bishop for more than forty years, of which he spent some years as a monk and some as abbot at Monte Cassino. He died in 1101.

### VII. Natalis Alexander, *Ecclesiastical History, Twelfth Century*

Bruno, born at Asti among the Insubrians from the most noble Solero family, most renowned for holiness and learning, refuted the heresiarch Berengar at the Roman synod in 1079. Subsequently made bishop of Segni by Gregory VII, who presided over that synod, he exercised the pastoral office for several years with the highest praise. Then, drawn by the desire for contemplation, he went to Monte Cassino [Col. 0142B], professed the religious life, and was elected abbot of Monte Cassino. But, at the people’s urging, he was ordered by apostolic authority to return to his Church, and about 1125 passed into immortal life. He was enrolled among the saints by Lucius III, supreme pontiff.

Among the many outstanding monuments of his intellect, he wrote, at the request of the canons of Segni, an exposition on the Book of Judges, the Psalter, and the Song of Songs. He also composed a great many sermons, including the 134 enumerated by Peter the Deacon in his book *On Illustrious Men*, which Theodore Petraeus, a member of the Cologne Charterhouse, published in volume III of the works of St Bruno, patriarch of the Carthusians. That they are not his is demonstrated both by Peter the Deacon’s authority and by other records. St Bruno, bishop of Segni and abbot of Monte Cassino, is called by Peter the Deacon “a most illustrious defender and doctor of the Church.” Dom Luc d’Achery published in volume XII of the *Spicilegium* the expositions of Bruno, bishop of Segni, *On the Consecration of a Church*, addressed to Godfrey [Col. 0142C], bishop of Maguelonne; likewise, *On the Consecration of Chrism* and *On the Meaning of Priestly Vestments*.

### VIII. Arnold Wion, a Belgian, monk of St Benedict of Mantua, in the work entitled *Tree of Life*, part I, p. 19, Venice edition, 1595

St Bruno, or Brunus, of distinguished Astesan blood, first bishop of Segni, then, after resigning the episcopate, a monk of Monte Cassino, was afterwards, following the death of Otto, the forty-fourth abbot, elected the forty-fifth abbot on the Ides of November [13 November] 1107 by the unanimous will of all the brethren. He governed for three years and ten months. When those had elapsed, compelled by Paschal II, he laid down the abbacy on the Ides of September [13 September] 1111 and returned to his episcopate, where, persevering in holy conduct until the end, he passed to the Lord [Col. 0142D] on the day before the Kalends of September [31 August].

Since he flourished no less in learning than in holiness, he wrote several works, namely:

On Genesis; Exodus; Leviticus; Numbers; Deuteronomy; the Song of Songs; Judges; the Psalms; Isaiah; and the Apocalypse.

Six books of *Sentences*, which are in the library of Monte Cassino on parchment; sixty-nine sermons on Sundays and the principal feasts of the year, in four books. The first, *On the Praises of the Church*, contains nine sermons; the second, *On the Ornaments of the Church*, contains twelve sermons; the third, *On the New World*, ten sermons; the fourth, *On the Principal Feasts of the Year*, thirty-six sermons. [Col. 0143A] These were in my possession on parchment, but I gave them as a gift, for friendship’s sake, to Dom Constantine of Syracuse, a Benedictine monk of Catania.

One hundred and fifty-five homilies on various subjects, which are the same as those described by Possevino.

### IX. Antonio Possevino, Society of Jesus, *Sacred Apparatus*, p. 243, Cologne edition, 1608

Bruno, or Brunus, a Ligurian of distinguished Astesan blood and a holy man, was first bishop of Segni; then, after resigning the episcopate, a monk of Monte Cassino; afterwards, following the death of Otto, the forty-fourth abbot, he was elected the forty-fifth abbot in 1107 by the unanimous will of all the brethren. He governed for three years and ten months. When these had elapsed, compelled by Paschal II, in the fourth year, on the Ides of September [13 September], he relinquished the abbey and returned to his episcopate, which he administered holy until he passed to the Lord on the day before the Kalends of September, in 1125. He wrote:

[Col. 0143B] One book on Genesis; one on Leviticus; one on Numbers (and these three are manuscript books in the library of Monte Cassino); one on Deuteronomy; one on the Song of Songs; one on Exodus; one on Judges; one on the Psalms; one on Isaiah; and one on the Apocalypse.

Six books of *Sentences*, preserved on parchment in the library of Monte Cassino; sixty-nine sermons on Sundays and the principal feasts of the year, in four books. The first is *On the Praises of the Church* and contains nine sermons. The second, *On the Ornaments of the Church*, contains twelve sermons. The third, *On the New World*, contains ten sermons. The fourth, *On the Principal Feasts of the Year*, contains thirty-six sermons. Constantine of Syracuse, a Benedictine monk of Catania [Col. 0143C], received all these as a gift from Arnold Wion.

He further wrote homilies on various matters, of which the following manuscripts are preserved by Arnold:

On the first Sunday of Advent, beginning: “Two disciples.”

On the second Sunday of Advent, beginning: “To those who ask.”

On the third Sunday of Advent, beginning: “John the Baptist.”

On the fourth Sunday of Advent, beginning: “For all thought.”

On the Friday of the Ember Days, beginning: “The Virgin full of God.”

On the vigil of the Nativity of the Lord: “But first it must be asked.”

### X. William Cave, *Literary History of Ecclesiastical Writers of the Hildebrandine Age*, p. 539, Cologne edition, 1720

Bruno, a Lombard by birth, born in the village of Solero among the Insubrians from a distinguished Astesan lineage, son of Andrew and Willa, began his training in piety and learning; he then went into Etruria and was admitted among the canons of Siena. From there he came to Rome and disputed before Gregory VII against Berengar at the Roman synod of 1079; he was soon designated bishop of Segni. Since he strongly resisted the pontiff in that matter, Gregory, by a certain pious stratagem, surrounded him and compelled him to accept the burden imposed. He flourished especially around the year 1087.

In 1096 he attended the Council of Tours. After spending many years in the episcopate, overcome by a longing for solitude, he fled to Monte Cassino in 1104. The people of Segni sought the return of their bishop by earnest petitions to Pope Paschal. Compelled by pontifical authority, he returned to his see. In the same year he was sent by the pontiff [Col. 0144A], first to Roger, Count of Apulia, and then, together with Bohemond, prince of Antioch, into Gaul, where he held the Council of Poitiers. In 1107 he returned to Monte Cassino and was elected abbot of that monastery, Pope Paschal approving the election and bestowing upon him this eulogy: that he was most worthy to receive the helm of the Christian commonwealth when the pope’s life should end. In the fourth year, by the pontiff’s command, he resigned the office of abbot and returned to the people of Segni; finally, in 1125, on the day before the Kalends of September [31 August], he fell asleep in the Lord, in the forty-fourth year of his episcopate.

**Works**

Commentaries on the Pentateuch; a commentary on Job; a commentary on the Psalter; a commentary on the Song of Songs; a commentary on the Apocalypse; 144 homilies or sermons wrongly ascribed to Eusebius of Emesa [Col. 0144B] or Eucherius of Lyon; a treatise on the Canticle of Zechariah; a treatise *On the Incarnation of the Lord*; a treatise on the subject of unleavened sacrifice; a short work *On the Sacraments, the Mysteries of the Church, and Ecclesiastical Rites*; a *Life of Pope St Leo IX*; an answer to the question, “Why is the state of the Church corrupt?”; a *Life of St Peter, Bishop of Anagni*.

Six books of *Sentences*: *On the Praises of the Church*; *On the Ornaments of the Church*; *On the New World*; *On the Feast of Feasts*; *On the Praises of the Blessed Virgin*; *On Martyrs, Confessors, etc.*

These short works are also included among the works of Bruno the Carthusian.

The works of Bruno, collected into one body, restored to their author, and illustrated with notes by Mauro Marchesi, monk of Monte Cassino, were published at Venice in 1651 in two folio volumes [Col. 0144C], and afterwards in the *Library of the Fathers*, vol. XX, p. 294.

Luc d’Achery published more fully Bruno’s short work *On the Consecration of a Church* in volume XII, p. 79, of the *Spicilegium*.

### XI. Louis Ellies Dupin, *Library of Writers*, etc., Paris edition, vol. X, p. 159

Bruno of Asti, a canon of the cathedral church of that city and afterwards also a canon of Siena, came to Rome during the pontificate of Gregory VII and, in his presence, disputed against Berengar. For this reason he was rewarded with the bishopric of Segni. He withdrew to Monte Cassino while Paschal II governed the Church; Paschal took his departure badly and recalled him in order to send him as legate of the Apostolic See into Gaul and Sicily. He served for several years as archimandrite of Monte Cassino, but finally returned to his episcopate [Col. 0144D], where he ended his life in 1123.

This author’s works were published at Venice in 1651 by Mauro Marchesio, a monk of Monte Cassino, and divided into two volumes. The first contains commentaries on the five books of Moses, on the book of Job, the Psalms, the Song of Songs, and the Apocalypse; in these commentaries he chiefly pursues the moral rather than any other sense. The second volume comprises 144 sermons, most of which had been published under the name of Eusebius of Emesa or Eucherius of Lyons. It also contains a treatise on the Canticle of Zechariah; a treatise *On the Incarnation* and *On the Burial of Christ the Lord*, dealing with the time during which that same Lord remained in the tomb; a treatise *On the Use of Unleavened Bread against the Greeks*; and, furthermore, an exposition of certain ecclesiastical rites. Likewise, it contains a Life of Pope Leo IX, with an appended treatise *On the Corrupt State of the Church*, in which he discusses ordinations performed by heretical or schismatic bishops; also a Life of St Peter, bishop of Anagni; two letters, one to Peter, bishop of Porto, the other to Paschal II; six books of *Sentences*, or various moral sermons, which were ascribed to Bruno, founder of the Carthusians, but which Marchesio claimed for Bruno of Segni—not so much on the testimony of Peter the Deacon as from their conformity of style, their frequent commendations of the Rule of St Benedict, which he professed, and because he calls himself commentator on the book of the Apocalypse, which Bruno the Carthusian did not expound. Added to these was a commentary on the Psalms by Otto, a monk of Monte Cassino, dedicated to the holy bishop. The treatise *On the Sacraments*, or *On the Rites of the Church*, likewise composed by Bruno, was printed by Luc d’Achery as a new discovery, although it had already appeared in the Venetian edition.

XII. Augustine Calmet, *Sacred Library*.

[Col. 0145B] Bruno, born at Solero in the diocese of Asti—whence his name “of Asti”—lived in the eleventh century and died in 1120 or 1125. He is also called Bruno of Segni because he was raised to the episcopal chair of the Church of Segni in the Roman territory. Afterwards he withdrew to Monte Cassino, where he was installed abbot of that monastery. There survive from this writer commentaries on the Pentateuch, Job, the Psalms, Isaiah, the Song of Songs, and the Apocalypse, printed in the *Library of the Fathers*. He is believed to have been the author of a commentary on the Epistles of St Paul and of certain other works published under the name of St Bruno, founder of the Carthusian order. His works were brought together into one body through the efforts of Mauro Marchesio, dean of Monte Cassino, in 1651. He adheres especially to the moral and allegorical sense.

XIII. Johann Albert Fabricius, *Latin Library of the Middle [Col. 0145C] and Later Ages*, with additions by Giovanni Domenico Mansi, Padua edition, 1754, p. 287. The complete works of St Bruno of Asti, published by Marchesio, are described.

The six books of *Sentences*, which do not differ from those which the Carthusians attributed, in volume III of his works, to St Bruno their founder, must be recognized as the work of St Bruno of Segni, as the anonymous writer of Melk recognized in chapter 83.

Besides these works found in the collection of his writings, Bruno is reported to have written still-unpublished commentaries on Judges, Judith, and Isaiah, as Jacob Le Long states in his *Library*. Peter the Deacon also mentions his verses in praise of the Blessed Virgin Mary. The most learned Mansi further adds: in the Riccardiana Library there is a twelfth-century manuscript containing an unpublished short work of St Bruno of Asti, *On the Valiant Woman*. In it is also found an exposition of the Song of Songs greatly differing from that printed in the *Library of the Fathers*, of which work a fragment is supplied by the distinguished Lami in the catalogue of that same library; he further adds two still-unpublished letters by the same author.

XIV. Remigius Ceillier, *History of Sacred Writers*, book XXI, p. 101.

At the request of St Peter Damian, Bruno illustrated Isaiah and the Apocalypse with his commentaries, but that labor on Isaiah still lies hidden in darkness. His commentary on the Apocalypse is divided into seven books according to the number of churches or bishops.

P. Le Long mentions Bruno of Asti in the *Historical Library of the French*, p. 654, where he speaks of two unpublished commentaries by this same St Bruno on the books of Judges and Judith. Peter the Deacon, monk of Monte Cassino, mentions only the commentary on Judges. St Bruno likewise wrote the Life of St Peter, bishop of Anagni. See the Bollandists, 13 August. He also published a treatise on the state of the Church in the eleventh century, which is found with his other works in volume XX of the Lyons edition of the *Library of the Fathers*, issued by the Annisson firm. His works are highly commendable for their stylistic polish and elegance, and likewise for the learning and solid piety with which they generally abound.

XV. Giovanni Battista Mari Romani, canon of Sant’Angelo in the Fish Market. Note on Peter the Deacon.

St Bruno was born at Asti from the most noble Soleri family. Gregory VII made him bishop of Segni as a reward for his virtues and learning, because he had defeated in public disputation at a Roman council Berengar, whose opinions concerning the sacrament of the altar were impious. Then, touched by a desire for the contemplative life, he laid aside the burden of the episcopate and professed himself a monk of Monte Cassino in 1104. Thereafter, by the unanimous vote of all the monks, he was elected abbot of Monte Cassino on the Ides of November, 1107; he governed there for three years and ten months. When these had elapsed, overcome by reverence for the pope, he returned to the Church of Segni, which he had accepted most unwillingly.

But lest we lessen the praises of so great a teacher through deficiency of talent and an insufficiently fortunate pen, we leave him to be praised by others. Bruno’s shorter works, divided into two volumes, appeared at Venice in 1651 through the care and labor of Dom Mauro Marchesio, dean of Monte Cassino, and were also elucidated with scholia. Although not all the works listed in the catalogue of our Peter are read there, many which Peter passed over are included. Some manuscripts survive at Turin in the most noble and celebrated library of the most serene Duke of Savoy—especially a commentary on all four Gospels—as well as some in the library of the most illustrious Lord Charles de Montchal, archbishop of Toulouse, as Philip Labbe writes in his *New Library of Manuscript Books*, p. 195. Perhaps time, which conceals public things and reveals hidden things, will, through God’s mercy, soon enrich the world with treasures so great.

Consult the supplement concerning ecclesiastical writers by Aubertus Miraeus under “Bruno,” and the most distinguished Theophilus Raynaud of the Society of Jesus, *On Bad and Good Books*, part I, problem 10, under Eusebius of Emesa and Bruno the Carthusian, fols. 131 and 138. Bruno ascended from the valley of miseries to the mountains of eternity in 1125, on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of August [18 July], having been renowned for many miracles both in life and death. He was afterwards enrolled among the saints by Lucius III, as may be seen in the marble inscription displayed in Segni Cathedral. See also the introduction to the aforesaid published shorter works of St Bruno. The complete works of St Bruno of Asti are reprinted in the Lyons edition of the *Library of the Fathers*, vol. XX, p. 1294.

XVI. Giovanni Maria, Count Mazzuchelli, vol. II, part IV, p. 2227.

Bruno of Asti, descended from the Solari or Soleri family, is said by many writers to have been of that lineage: Ecclesia, in his catalogue of Piedmontese writers, p. 42; Ughelli, *Italia Sacra*, vol. I, col. 1236; Rosotti, *Syllabus of Piedmontese Writers*, p. 127; Leiferius, in his history of medieval poetry and poems; and others. Conversely, other writers say that this same Bruno was born from an Asti family: Possevino, vol. I of the *Sacred Apparatus*, pp. 253 and 383; Ciacconius, in the *Library*, col. 458; Cave, *Ecclesiastical History*, p. 539; Milantes, vol. I of the *Library of Sixtus of Siena*, p. 513; the supplement to the *Library of the Saints*; Einsinger; and others. Gabriel Busselin, however, in his *Universal History*, Porta in *Alexandria Illustrated*, p. 220, and Quadrius, vol. II, say that Bruno was born in the town of Solero. Soprani and Oldoini number him among Ligurian writers. Oldoini and Teissier call St Bruno a cardinal and state that he governed the monastery of Monte Cassino for three years and ten months.

The authors who wrote about St Bruno of Asti [Col. 0147A] are Baronius, *Ecclesiastical History*, XII, and his notes on the *Martyrology*; Leo of Ostia, *Chronicle of Monte Cassino*, book IV, chapter 31, and its continuator Peter the Deacon; the anonymous author of Melk, *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, chapter 83; the Bollandists, *Acts of the Saints* for July; Philip Malabayla, *Inquiry into the Birth, Canonry, and Withdrawal to Monte Cassino of St Bruno*; Le Long, *Sacred Library*, vol. II, p. 654; and Legipontius, vol. II of the *Literary History of the Order of St Benedict*, p. 210, and [Col. 0148A] vol. III, p. 129. The works of St Bruno, collected and annotated by Abbot Dom Constantine Cajetan while he was at Rome, were afterwards published by Marchesio. See Armellini, part II, *Library of Monte Cassino and the Benedictine Order*, p. 105.

St Bruno’s exposition of the Gospels is found among the Latin manuscript codices of the Royal Library of Paris, codex 2510; his shorter works are preserved in codex 2311 of the same library.

[Col. 0147A]

# EXPOSITION ON THE PENTATEUCH OF ST BRUNO OF ASTI, BISHOP OF SEGNI

1 You asked me, sweetest Father and fellow bishop Peter—whose affection for me has always overflowed so abundantly that you ought rightly not to have asked but commanded me—to expound the book of Genesis for you. But because I was hindered by many matters which, as you yourself know well, it was not proper to avoid, I have been unable until now to fulfill your request. I preferred for a time to appear disobedient to you, whom I knew to be ready to forgive, rather than fail to do those things which, had I not done them, would have made me appear blameworthy even to you. At last, therefore, though late, I have done what you commanded by asking.

From the beginning of the book through the construction of Noah’s ark, since these matters seemed more difficult, I considered it entirely necessary to expound everything continuously. From there to the passage in which Jacob blesses his sons with their respective blessings, I have prefixed brief historical notices to each chapter and appended allegories, quite concisely, wherever exposition seemed needed. You will also find Jacob’s blessings, since they too seemed to contain some difficulty, arranged in a continuous exposition. Receive, then, what you asked for; let it be a pledge of affection, and always remember me in your prayers.

## THE EXPOSITION OF GENESIS BEGINS

[Col. 0147]

## CHAPTER ONE

[Col. 0147B]

> “In the beginning God created heaven and earth.”

[Note: [Col. 0147C] Manuscript of Santa Croce Minor in the Laurentian Library.]

“In the beginning,” he says, “and before every creature, God created heaven and earth.” The Psalmist also bears witness to this, saying: “And thou, O God, in the beginning didst found the earth, and the heavens are the works of thy hands” (Ps. 101:26). Therefore God did not create heaven before earth, but created heaven and earth together. Hence also: “He who lives for ever created all things together” (Ecclus. 18:1). For even if God is related in that same book to have made everything in six days, it must nevertheless not be doubted that he created all things from nothing simultaneously. He created at once the very matter of all things, from which he afterwards commanded the remaining things to be made at distinct times, as he willed.

Let it therefore be said: In the beginning of all creatures God created heaven [Col. 0147C] and the things contained in it—namely, angels and the heavenly powers—and earth, already, as it were, pregnant and about to give birth, the material and mother of all things arising from it. It is clear, therefore, that although things which now seem to come into being may be first in time, earth was not first by nature.

> “But the earth was empty and void, and darkness was upon the face of the deep; and the Spirit of God moved over the waters.”

The earth was empty because, being like unformed matter, it did not yet bear within itself the forms which we now see. It was also void because no one inhabited it. But why is it not similarly said of heaven that it was empty and void, unless, as I suppose, it had angels as inhabitants immediately in its very creation? Therefore, although earth contained naturally within itself all things made from it, it is nevertheless rightly called empty and void because nothing had yet been made from it in time.

“And darkness was upon the face of the deep,” because light had not yet been made to illuminate that new creation. By “the deep” is understood the lofty profundity of heaven and earth, wholly filled with darkness. But the Spirit of God moved over the waters because, like a good craftsman, he was already planning to make the abundant variety of creatures which we see.

[Note: [Col. 0148C] St Bruno followed the opinion of St Ambrose, who in book I, chapter 18, of the *Hexaemeron*, after setting aside other opinions, says: “We, in agreement with the judgment of the saints and faithful, understand this to be the Holy Spirit, so that the working of the Trinity may shine forth in the constitution of the world.”]

For example, when we are about to construct a house, we contemplate the material of the timbers with eyes and mind, assigning some for beams, others for columns, and others for other purposes. Moreover, the fact that he had said nothing above about the creation of water and yet introduced it in his account as though it had already been created clearly shows that by the name “earth” all things contained in the earth are to be understood, such as fire and water; and by the name “heaven,” everything heaven contains, such as air, whose creation is not separately described.

> “And God said: Let there be light. And there was light. And God saw the light, that it was good; and he divided the light from the darkness. And he called the light Day, and the darkness Night.”

It is evident that there is no interval between God’s speaking and acting. Thus he said, “Let there be light,” and light was made. And what is God’s speaking other than his willing?

[Note: [Col. 0149D] Monte Cassino manuscript: “than to make.”]

For he accomplished all things not by crying aloud or moving his lips, but indeed by willing. But what is this light, said to exist before the sun, moon, and stars? Hear what follows: “He called the light Day, and the darkness Night.” Thus “light” stands for day. Good, then, is the light which, separated from darkness, illuminates the forms and colors of things. We can scarcely discern this light, because we are suffused with the greater light, namely that of the sun. It follows:

> “And evening and morning came: one day.”

Some understand evening and morning to mean night and day. Since, omitting the nights, Scripture enumerates all the days in order, they wish to understand both day and night under the single name “day.” But the order of speech is remarkable: evening is placed before morning, as though God had begun to work not in the morning but in the evening. For if it had said, “Morning and evening came: one day,” perhaps there would be no question. But because it places evening between two mornings, it may be doubted to which of them it refers. If evening refers to the preceding morning, the whole night is undoubtedly omitted; if to the following morning, the whole day is passed over and only the boundaries of night are given. Accordingly, “evening and morning came: one day” would more suitably have been called “one night.” Yet because divine providence created night not for labor but for rest, there is no inconsistency in giving only the boundaries of the day in God’s work, which was certainly accomplished not at night but by day.

For if in this passage we understand one day to mean, as they wish, the entire period of day and night, God unnecessarily divided the two from each other and, having divided them, gave them different names: for he called the light Day and the darkness Night.

[Note: [Col. 0149D] Same manuscript of Santa Croce Minor.]

Therefore no day consists of night and day. Since what is described here is not dreams seen at night but works accomplished in the day, it was necessary to enumerate days, not nights.

[Note: [Col. 0149D] Same manuscript of Santa Croce.]

Thus in the beginning God made heaven, earth, and light. When these had been accomplished, evening came; and, the preceding morning continuing into it, one day was made. At that time he divided light from darkness; when that day was finished, evening came. For he did not make night in the day, but commanded it to come into being in its proper order after the day.

The statement “one day was made,” rather than “the first day,” means this: “first” and “second” are relative terms, and neither can exist without the other. Since, therefore, the second did not yet exist, it was one day; nevertheless, that one could not yet be called first. Having arranged these matters according to the letter, let us also see what they signify allegorically.

> “In the beginning God created heaven and earth.”

[Note: [Col. 0150D] See Augustine, *City of God*, book XI, chapter 32, for his view concerning the “beginning” in which God is said to have made heaven and earth.]

In what beginning? Certainly in him who said, “I am the beginning, who also speak unto you” (John 8:26). “For all things were made through him, and without him was made nothing” (John 1:3). In this beginning God created from the outset the entire fabric of the world and the very ranks of angels. In this same beginning, at the end of the ages, having assumed flesh, he begot, created, and restored to a new and original nature heaven and earth, the apostles and the Church, the righteous and sinners, Jews and Gentiles, by the word of preaching, the water of baptism, and the illumination of the Holy Spirit.

Yet the earth was still empty and void; the Church was still barren and without children. The prophet also, consoling her in her barrenness and promising fruitfulness, said: “Rejoice, barren woman who dost not bear; break forth and cry aloud, thou who dost not travail; for more are the children of the desolate than of her who has a husband” (Isa. 54:1; Gal. 4:27).

But why empty and void? Because darkness still lay upon the face of the deep. No one understood the Scriptures, since they were deep and shrouded in the darkness of ignorance. In order that they may be understood, “deep calls to deep” (Ps. 41:8). Christ removed this darkness when he opened the apostles’ understanding so that they might understand the Scriptures. For if the Jews understood them, they would flee to the Church; but because, as the Apostle says, “even to this day, when Moses is read, a veil is laid upon their hearts” (2 Cor. 3:15), they are unable to understand them. But when the fullness of the Gentiles has entered, then, the veil having been removed, Israel will be saved (Rom. 11:25). Nor will our earth thereafter be called empty and void, inhabited as it will be by the fullness of so many children. The following words teach how this occurs.

> “And the Spirit of the Lord moved over the waters.”

For what we understand by “the deep,” we likewise understand by “the waters.” These are the waters springing up into eternal life: whoever drinks them will never thirst (John 4:14). Of them it is said: “All you who thirst, come to the waters” (Isa. 55:1).

[Note: [Col. 0150D] Monte Cassino manuscript: “But how these things occur. So that the mention of the Trinity might be complete, he says, ‘And the Spirit moved over the waters.’ St Augustine teaches the same in the cited book and passage of the *City of God*.”]

Over these waters the Holy Spirit moved; by the brightness of his illumination, driving darkness away, he illuminated them and made them drinkable and intelligible. Hence it fittingly follows:

> “And God said: Let there be light. And there was light.”

As if he said: Darkness has been driven away; earth has been illuminated; therefore let there be light, let ignorance perish. “Arise, be enlightened, O Jerusalem, for thy light has come” (Isa. 60:1). This light, this conscience inspired in believers by the Holy Spirit, pleased the eyes of the heavenly majesty; therefore he separated it from darkness. Hence the Apostle: “For what participation has light with darkness? What portion has a believer with an unbeliever? What agreement has Christ with Belial?” (2 Cor. 6:15). And elsewhere: “After a first and second admonition, avoid a heretical man” (Titus 3:10). God signified this separation when he divided light from darkness.

> “God also said: Let there be a firmament in the midst of the waters, and let it divide waters from waters. And God made the firmament and divided the waters that were beneath the firmament from those that were above the firmament; and it was so. And God called the firmament Heaven. And evening and morning came: the second day.”

If, as is true, the firmament was made in the midst of the waters, there can be no doubt that waters were everywhere. But if they were everywhere, I ask, where were they drawn together, leaving so vast a space of heaven and earth empty? It is clear, therefore, that they did not then possess their present density, but filled everything like mist and clouds. The firmament said to be in the midst of the waters is not that which God is said to have created in the beginning—for otherwise heaven would have been created twice—but rather that which revolves without ceasing and in which the sun, moon, and stars appear.

There is also a heaven above this one, of a far more worthy and excellent nature. Wishing to ascend above it, the ancient enemy said, “I will ascend into heaven” (Isa. 14:13). For he was in heaven when he said these things, but, desiring to ascend higher, he spoke thus. Whether the upper waters, with the firmament interposed, also changed their nature, I would not easily say. When these things had thus been accomplished, evening came; joined with its morning, it makes the second day. But this is according to the letter. Let us hear what these things signify spiritually.

> “Let there be,” he says, “a firmament in the midst of the waters, and let it divide waters from waters.”

What is the firmament but the apostles? Hence the Psalmist says: “The heavens declare the glory of God, and the firmament proclaims the work of his hands” (Ps. 18:1). This firmament guards and strengthens us; it provides the rains and light of salvation; it divides the lower waters from the upper. The waters beneath the firmament are the New Testament; those above the firmament are understood as the Old Testament. But how do the apostles divide these waters? Do you wish to hear how? The Law commands every person to circumcise the flesh of his foreskin. By contrast, the Apostle says: “I, Paul, tell you that if you are circumcised, Christ will profit you nothing” (Gal. 5:2). You see, then, how great is the division and how great the intervening firmament which prevents waters from being joined to waters.

The words here, “And God called the firmament Heaven,” also appear appropriate to the apostles, for they conceal and preserve heavenly mysteries. Hence the Apostle says: “I heard secret words which it is not permitted for a human being to speak” (2 Cor. 12:4).

> “And God said: Let the waters under heaven be gathered together into one place, and let the dry land appear. And it was so. And God called the dry land Earth, and the gatherings of the waters he called Seas.”

This place into which the waters are gathered means seas, lakes, and rivers, and that very deep from which we see springs of water flow through certain hidden veins of the earth. Thus, by divine providence, the waters were gathered into one place so that they might neither cover the surface of the earth as before, nor yet fail everywhere to make its dryness fruitful with their moisture.

[Note: [Col. 0151D] Same manuscript of Santa Croce in the Laurentian Library.]

God also gave names quite suited to the things themselves, calling the dry land “Earth” and the gatherings of waters “Seas.” *Terra*, “earth,” is said to derive from *terere*, “to wear down,” because human beings and all animals continually wear it down by cultivating and treading upon it. But *mare*, “sea,” derives from *amaritudo*, “bitterness,” because we find it salty and bitter. But this is according to the letter; now let us consider its meaning:

> “Let the waters which are under heaven be gathered together into one place, and let the dry land appear.”

We have explained above that this place into which the waters were gathered—seas, lakes, and rivers—means either the two volumes of the New and Old Testaments, or the apostles and teachers of the Church. For in them is contained the fullness of all wisdom and knowledge, which is signified by the name of waters. The words “and let the dry land appear” seem, however, to belong more to history than to allegory. But why did God, changing its name, call the earth dry land, unless he was already signifying that the holy Church would be scourged, crushed, trodden underfoot, and afflicted in many ways?

He called the gatherings of waters “seas,” because although to know and understand the sacred Scriptures is sweet and pleasant, to do what they command is bitter and harsh. For the sea takes its name from bitterness. To fast, keep vigils, and abandon all the delights of this world—who does not find that bitter? Yet these are the commands of the sacred Scriptures; rightly, therefore, are they signified by such a name.

> “And God saw that it was good. And he said: Let the earth bring forth green grass bearing seed, and fruit-bearing trees yielding fruit according to their kind, whose seed is in itself upon the earth. And it was so. And the earth brought forth green grass bearing seed according to its kind, and trees yielding fruit, each having seed according to its own species. And God saw that it was good. And evening and morning came: the third day.”

These matters, which are sufficiently clear according to the letter, we see accomplished spiritually in the Church of the saints. What is meant by the earth except the Church? What by green grass and fruit-bearing trees, except the examples and teaching of the apostles and prophets? These are ever green and living; they ever bear fruit, and according to their kinds and species produce diverse fruits and seeds. For they have implanted naturally within themselves a seed which is always scattered and never fails, always sprouts and always grows.

Consider how long ago this book was published. See how many volumes it has produced from itself. Consider its fruits and seeds, namely its teaching and precepts: how living and powerful they are. You will find some fruits in the Old Testament and others in the New. As many teachers, so many seeds and varieties of fruits.

The words, “And God saw that it was good,” mean as though he had said: He enabled us to see and understand that he created nothing except what is good. Evening came, night passed, morning came, and with its night the third day was completed. Thus some understand this passage. But if it is understood allegorically, it may be said in this way: when the end of this present and laborious life has come, there will be evening and morning—an evening indeed for those who are cast down from light and happiness into darkness and miseries, but morning for those who are transferred from this unhappy and wretched life to perpetual light and eternal joys. It follows:

> “And God said: Let there be lights in the firmament of heaven, and let them divide day from night; and let them be for signs and seasons, and days and years, so that they may shine in the firmament of heaven and illuminate the earth. And it was so. God also made two great lights: the greater light to rule the day, and the lesser light to rule the night; and the stars. And he placed them in the firmament of heaven, to shine over the earth and to rule day and night, and to divide light from darkness. And God saw that it was good. And morning and evening came: the fourth day.”

[Col. 0153D] The two lights are understood to be the sun and moon, placed in the firmament of heaven, which divide day and night. They also serve us as signs of fair weather and rain, and wherever in the world we may be, they indicate to us the regions of the world. Sailors understand how necessary these signs are: suddenly driven into the deep by winds, they would not know where to steer without the signs of heaven. They also give other signs, of which the Gospel says: “There will be signs in the sun, moon, and stars” (Luke 22:25). They determine seasons, days, and years; since it is easy to see how this occurs, let us pass on to other matters.

He calls the sun the greater light, because it holds dominion by day; the moon the lesser light, because we see it preside over the darkness of night. The stars also, differing in brilliance and magnitude, are set in heaven and provide us both light and signs. But this is according to the letter. Spiritually, however, the two great lights—the sun and moon—signify the New and Old Testaments: the New is understood as the greater and the Old as the lesser.

“For the Law,” as the Apostle says, “was ordained through angels by the hand of a mediator” (Gal. 3:19). But speaking of the New Testament, he says: “In these last days he has spoken to us in his Son” (Heb. 1:2). And again: “If the ministry of death, engraved in letters, was in glory, how much more will the ministry of the Spirit be in glory?” (2 Cor. 3:7). And shortly afterwards: “For what was glorified in part was not glorified because of the surpassing glory” (ibid., 10). From these and similar passages it is clearly gathered that the New Testament is greater than the Old.

Set in the firmament of heaven—that is, firmly adhering in the breasts of the apostles and teachers—these divide day and night and preside over day and night. Day and night signify the Church and the Synagogue, the people of the Gentiles and the people of the Jews. Thus the New Testament presides over the day because it illuminates the holy Church with the rays of its splendor and, by marking out the path of the right way, separates her from the gloom of night, darkness, and error.

But the moon, dim and pale, presides over the night and darkness because the Old Testament displays a dim and dark light to the Jewish people, ever dark and blind. “Blindness has happened in part to Israel.” Hence, when Moses received the Law, cloud and darkness covered the whole mountain of Sinai.

[Note: [Col. 0153D] Same manuscript of Santa Croce in the Laurentian Library.]

These, then, divide day and night; nevertheless, they illuminate both lands, govern both churches, and shine fixed in heaven—that is, in the hearts of the apostles. They also give us signs by which we may avoid the assaults and snares of enemies; they determine days and years,

[Note: [Col. 0154D] Same manuscript: “seasons.”]

declaring that visible things are fleeting and transitory, while invisible things are eternal, and therefore urging us to despise the former and truly seek the latter. Hence the Psalmist says: “One day in thy courts is better than thousands” (Ps. 83:11). And again: “But thou art the same, and thy years shall not fail” (Ps. 101:28).
