Thus these most brilliant lights of heaven are for us signs, seasons, days, and years. God also made the stars and placed them in the firmament, that they might shine over the earth, rule day and night, and divide light from darkness. By them we may understand the individual books of the prophets and apostles. Enlightened by these books, the teachers of the Church, signified by the name “heaven,” illuminate our earth and the holy Church. When, therefore, we see this firmament so elegantly adorned with sun, moon, stars, and every beauty, what shall we think of that higher heaven, where the orders of heavenly spirits gaze in wonder upon the very Sun of righteousness? It follows:

“And there was evening, and there was morning: the fourth day. God also said: ‘Let the waters bring forth creeping creatures with living souls, and birds above the earth beneath the firmament of heaven.’ And God created the great sea-creatures, and every living and moving soul which the waters had brought forth according to their kinds, and every bird according to its kind. And God saw that it was good; and he blessed them, saying: ‘Increase and multiply, and fill the waters of the sea; and let birds multiply over the earth.’ And there was evening and morning: the fifth day.”

A double kind of animal arises from the waters: one, namely, which lives upon the waters and cannot live apart from them; the other, which, flying, seeks the heights and feeds upon the nourishment of the earth. And marvellous is the order of the divine arrangement: before he created animals, he made herbs and fruit-bearing trees, so that, as soon as they arose, they might find from what to live. Man, however, was created last, and all these things were given him by God for use. Great sea-creatures are said to exist in the farther part of the sea, so huge that they surpass the size of mountains. But how diverse and manifold are the species and kinds of the other fish and birds cannot be told. Blessing them all, God commanded them to fill the waters and the lands by multiplying; and this blessing has prevailed so greatly that they increase daily and none of them can perish utterly.

But what do we understand metaphorically by the waters except baptism? And what by the fish and birds which arise from them except the people of the faithful, who are regenerated by the waters of baptism? Some of these, taking up the wings of wisdom, knowledge, and the other virtues, strive to fly even to heavenly things. Among them heretics and philosophers display the likeness of troublesome birds, since they often fly higher than is necessary and, rejoicing in plunder, most greedily shed the blood of souls. By the rest, however, who are not separated from the waters, we understand the simple people: though they do not know how to fly by wisdom and empty philosophy, they nevertheless live in such a way that they deserve to be presented by the fishers of the Church at Christ’s banquet. The great sea-creatures also signify rulers; but among fish, as among birds, there are some who live by plunder in the manner of robbers. They signify those who, although they have received Christ’s faith and name in baptism, yet, living the life of tyrants and wicked persons, are counted among unclean animals. [Note: The same Laurentian manuscript: “Those who, although they have received the faith in baptism and the name of Christians, yet [Col. 0156D] [live the life] of wicked persons,” etc.] God rightly blessed these, because none except the baptized deserve Christ’s blessing. It follows:

“And God said: ‘Let the earth bring forth the living soul according to its kind: cattle, creeping things, and beasts of the earth according to their kinds; cattle, and every creeping thing of the earth according to its kind.’”

Here a question arises. Since God created all things for man, why were so many poisonous, deadly, and hostile-to-man creatures made? The answer is that, if man had not sinned, all things would obey his rule: a serpent would harm him no more than an eel; the wolf, no less than the sheep, would serve him. But after he had in pride become disobedient to his Creator, he began also to be despised by the animals themselves. They were unwilling to obey one whom they saw disobedient to him by whom they had been subjected to man’s dominion; and those creatures which had first been made for service were afterward turned into instruments of punishment.

This is also asked: why did God not create the world before, through such immense and infinite stretches of time? What sudden change of mind befell him who cannot change? But this question seems useless, because if it had pleased God to do it earlier or later, one might nevertheless ask why he acted then and not at another time. There is no change in God, to whom nothing new happens, and to whom past and future are present; before he made the world, he already held it made in the disposition of his mind. Nor, when he creates something, is he moved in any respect, because, as regards himself, he does nothing new. Rather, because before time he ordained how and in what place or time things were to be ordered, he commands them to come to pass. Therefore the world existed before it was made: in God’s disposition it never had any beginning. For God has never not possessed what he possesses; otherwise he would be subject to accidents, if he were now to determine to do something which he had not previously determined. Therefore the Apostle John says: “What was made in him was life” (John 1:4). For all things that come to be in time lived and flourished in him before time. Hence it is rightly said: “He who lives for ever created all things together” (Ecclus. 18:1). He created all things together because he ordained together when and how all things should come to be. Therefore, when heaven and earth came to be at their appointed time, nothing new happened to God, because what was then happening in time had long been ordained with God to happen then. But because it is dangerous and difficult to dispute concerning these matters, let it suffice that we have said this much.

Spiritually, however, we understand the earth as the holy Church. [Note: From the Cassinese manuscript.] By the living soul we understand the multitude of all the faithful, which lives because in baptism it rose with Christ. The cattle signify those who mercifully bear the burdens of others, concerning whom the Apostle says: “Bear one another’s burdens, and so you will fulfil the law of Christ” (Gal. 6:2). Creeping things are those who love earthly things more than heavenly ones; and therefore, clinging to these with their whole body, they scarcely ever direct the eyes of the mind to heaven. The beasts of the earth signify those who do not think of higher things, do not entangle themselves in questions, but always need the guidance and governance of others. Since our earth—that is, the holy Church—has brought forth all these and regenerated them in the waters of baptism, it is called good. This is what is meant when it says: “And God saw that it was good.”

“And he said: ‘Let us make man in our image and likeness, and let him rule over the fish of the sea, the birds of heaven, the beasts, every creature of the earth, and every creeping thing that moves upon the earth.’ And God created man in his own image; in the image of God he created him; male and female he created them.”

God, it says, saw that it was good, and said: “Let us make man.” Therefore it is God who speaks. Does he speak to angels? Far be it! For man was not created by angels; otherwise there would be not one Creator but many, whereas God alone is the Creator of all. Thus it is written: “The terrible and mighty Creator of all” (2 Macc. 1:24); and again: “You made all things in wisdom” (Ps. 103:24). If, therefore, it is true—as it cannot be denied—that God alone created all things, whom was he inviting when he said, “Let us make man”? Let us hear, then, what is said at the beginning of this book: “In the beginning God created heaven and earth.” You have, therefore, God—that is, the Father; and you also have the beginning—that is, the Son, for he himself says: “I am the beginning, who also speak to you” (John 8:25). But what follows? “And the Spirit of God was borne over the waters.” Thus you also have the Holy Spirit.

That not the Father alone created heaven, but the Son and Holy Spirit also together with him, the Psalmist declares: “By the word of the Lord the heavens were established, and by the Spirit of his mouth all their power” (Ps. 32:6). But the whole Trinity—that is, God and his Word and his Spirit—is one God; and he says, “Let us make man,” not seeking help outside himself, but disposing all things within himself together with his Son and the Holy Spirit. [Note: That a Trinity of persons is proved from this passage is the opinion of many holy Fathers: thus Saint Basil, Homily 9 on Genesis; John Chrysostom, Homily 8 on Genesis; Augustine, *The City of God*, book 16, chapter 6; Cyril of Jerusalem, *Against Julian*, book 1. Their authorities are reported by Petavius, *On the Trinity*, book 2, chapter 7. Calmet agrees in his comments on this passage, where he says that the words, “Let us make man in our image and likeness,” express consultation and deliberation among several persons.]

For God spoke once, because he disposed all things together, nor does he need afterward to dispose anything further. When, therefore, the time, hour, or moment arrives at which something, ordained before time, is to be made, while God remains in his own immovability, his very disposition proclaims in an ineffable voice: “The time has come; it is the hour; let it now be made, and let that appear as made which was ordained before time to be made now.” Therefore let the Jews either believe in the Trinity or find other creators of man besides God.

But since, as we have said, we have considered who spoke and to whom he said, “Let us make man,” [Note: The same Cassinese manuscript.] let us also see in whose likeness man was made. “In our image,” he says, “and likeness.” Although image and likeness are different things, in this place image and likeness signify the same thing. Thus man was made in God’s likeness: wise, just, good, immortal, and incorruptible; for God is such. [Note: “Therefore God made man,” says Augustine, “in his own image and likeness. For he created for him such a soul as, by reason and understanding, would be superior to all terrestrial animals, swimming creatures, and birds, which have no mind of that sort. And when he had formed the man from earth’s dust and had breathed into him the soul of which I have spoken—or rather, had made it by breathing, and had willed that this breath which he made by breathing (for what else is breathing than making breath?) should be the human soul—he also made for him a wife, from a bone removed from his side, as a helper for begetting offspring.” Augustine, *The City of God*, book 12, chapter 23.]

Yet man lost immortality when he sinned and in this became unlike God, although nothing is in every respect like God. Therefore, whenever we sin, we lose God’s likeness. Only those have God’s likeness who rationally preserve wisdom, justice, goodness, and the other virtues like these. It is a great honour for man to cleave to the virtues by which he appears to be like God.

But since it is said, “God created man in his own image,” and then added, “in the image of God he created him,” this may also be understood to mean that God gave man a bodily image such as he had ordained before time that the Son, who is certainly God, would one day assume. Thus not only our inward but also our outward person would in some manner be like God. Nor was it enough for God that he had made man in his likeness; he moreover set him over every creature beneath heaven.

With these matters thus arranged, let us consider their meaning. Who, I ask, is this man who has God’s likeness and to whom the fish of the sea, the birds of heaven, the beasts, every creature of the earth, and all creeping things are subject? Although some rightly understand him to be Christ, I think that he is the order of apostles and teachers, together with the rest who hold authority in the Church of God. They are called prelates because others are subject to them; and because they have God’s likeness, all honour them as superior. For the Apostle possessed God’s likeness when he said: “Be imitators of me, as I also am of Christ” (Phil. 3:17). To these are subject the fish of the sea—that is, those regenerated in the waters of baptism; the birds of heaven—that is, philosophers and wise persons; the beasts—that is, the unlearned and undisciplined; every creature of the earth—that is, persons of whatever sex, race, nature, or condition; and all creeping things. For when lovers of the world and those who cling to earthly pleasures serve them, then even creeping things undoubtedly honour them. But because among the Church’s teachers some have manly strength and others womanly softness, it is rightly said that “male and female he created them.” It follows:

“And God blessed them and said: ‘Increase and multiply, fill the earth and subdue it; and rule over the fish of the sea, the birds of heaven, and every living thing that moves upon the earth.’”

These matters have been explained above: God blessed them, it says, and then, adding the blessing itself, says: “Increase and multiply”—namely, in wisdom, virtues, and the offspring of holy children.

“And God said: ‘Behold, I have given you every herb bearing seed upon the earth, and all trees which have within themselves the seed of their own kind, that they may be for food to you, to every animal of the earth, to every bird of heaven, and to all things that move upon the earth and in which there is a living soul, that they may have them for food.’”

These also have been explained at the place where it says: “Let the earth bring forth green herb and fruit-bearing tree.” As these things were given literally as food to every animal of the earth, so, according to the spiritual understanding, these delights are prepared not only for the wise and teachers but also for all who wish to use them. Hence the Apostle says: “I am debtor to Jews and Greeks, barbarians, wise and unwise” (Rom. 1:14). And the Lord says in the Gospel: “Go into all the world; preach the Gospel to every creature” (Mark 16:16). “For whatever things were written were written for our instruction” (Rom. 15:4). Who, then, should perish of hunger when such abundant and great riches have been set before them? It follows:

“And it was so; and God saw all the things which he had made, and they were very good. And there was evening and morning: the sixth day.”

When God had made all things and, on the sixth day, on which all things were completed, looked upon them, he saw all things to be good: where then was evil, where was the devil himself, prince of evil? Had he not yet fallen—the one of whom it is said: “He did not stand in the truth, and from the beginning he was a liar” (John 8:44)? Or perhaps on the very day on which man was made he envied man’s glory and, by giving fatal counsel, lost his own dominion together with his goodness? For the condemnation of man and devil is read as occurring together, not one before the other. For when the woman said, “The serpent deceived me, and I ate,” the Lord immediately cursed the serpent, saying: “You shall be cursed among all animals and beasts of the earth.” He also said to the woman: “I will multiply your pains”; and to Adam: “Cursed is the earth in your work” (Gen. 3:13, 17). I have found nothing certain about these matters in the books of the apostles and prophets, and I have learned that the teachers of the Church have held differing views; I leave their discussion to others. Yet I say that, even if he had fallen earlier, it could nonetheless be said: “God saw all things that he had made, and they were very good.” All the things he had made were indeed very good, because even in the devil himself there still remains good what God had made.

## CHAPTER II

“And so the heavens and the earth and all their adornment were completed. And on the seventh day God completed his work which he had made, and he rested on the seventh day from all the work which he had accomplished. And God blessed the seventh day and sanctified it, because on it he ceased from all his work which God created in order to make.”

When it says, “God completed on the seventh day his work which he had made,” it should not be understood as though he made something on the seventh day, but that when that day began all things were complete, and it was the limit after which nothing remained to be completed.

But allegorically, what do the six days signify except the six ages of the world? The first age extends from Adam to Noah; the second from Noah to Abraham; the third from Abraham to David; the fourth from David to the Babylonian captivity; the fifth from the Babylonian captivity to Christ; and the sixth from the coming of the Lord to the end of the age. During these God does not cease to work, as Truth himself says in the Gospel: “My Father works until now, and I work” (John 5:17). For who but he made those things which we see continually come into being? Although in six days he made the seeds of all things, nevertheless those seeds cannot themselves produce anything unless he commands and wills it. [Note: The same Laurentian and Cassinese manuscripts.] “For, as the Apostle says, neither he who plants is anything nor he who waters, but God who gives the increase” (1 Cor. 3:7). He first ordained, then created; afterward, from the things he had created, he caused all that comes to be to arise.

This third operation of God will not cease until this sixth day—that is, the last age—first comes to an end. When it is finished, all things will become new, and thereafter nothing new will come to be. But when heaven then becomes new and earth new, when the brightness of the moon becomes like the brightness of the sun and the brightness of the sun becomes sevenfold, what appearance do we suppose the earth will then have? [Note: The same manuscript.] After that universal conflagration, it will not be necessary for it to produce herbs and fruit-bearing trees as before, since there will be no one to use them. Or perhaps only those things will exist which, in coming into being and dying, will need no further renewal? But since perhaps it is superfluous to ask this, let us pass to other matters.

“And he rested on the seventh day from all the work which he had accomplished.” Of this day it is written: “For one day in your courts is better than thousands” (Ps. 83). This day will have no end, nor will any night follow it; for, unlike the other days, it is not said of this one: “And there was evening and morning: the seventh day.” Why is this? Because, even if it has a morning, it will not decline toward evening. God blessed this day. What does “he blessed” mean except that he gave it every delight, every joy, and every blessing? Thus God blessed and sanctified it. O wonderful sanctification, after which no one will be able to sin! It follows: because on it he had ceased from all his work which God created in order to make. For he created in six days in order to make during the six ages what no one knows how he has ordained. [Note: The same manuscript.]

“These are the generations of heaven and earth when they were created, in the day on which the Lord made heaven and earth, and every shrub of the field before it arose upon the earth, and every herb of the region before it sprouted. These,” he says, “are the generations of heaven and earth when they were created.” Do you wish to hear when? “In the day on which the Lord made heaven and earth.” What then? Did he create all things in one day and not in six days? He created them in one day because he made the matter of all things together; and he created them in six days because from that matter he formed all things into diverse kinds. Yet he still creates daily, while he multiplies some things by generating them from the others. We have spoken sufficiently of these matters above. It follows:

“For the Lord God had not rained upon the earth, and there was no man to cultivate it; but a spring rose from the earth, watering the whole surface of the earth. Therefore the Lord God formed man from the mud of the earth, breathed into his face the breath of life, and man became a living soul.”

If it is understood that the Lord had not rained upon the earth before man was made, and that a spring watered it, this seems not very relevant, since in those very few days the earth does not seem greatly to have needed either rain or irrigation by springs. It may therefore be understood that throughout the whole first age until the Flood God did not rain, but that a spring rising from the earth watered it at a suitable time, as the Nile is said to do throughout Egypt even to this day.

The inserted words, “and there was no man to cultivate it,” are a recapitulation. Since the author had said little about the creation of man, who was made on the sixth day, he now returns to that same day in order to speak more fully about the same man. “The Lord God formed man from the mud of the earth”: behold the material of the flesh. “And breathed into his face the breath of life”: behold the soul. “And man became a living soul.” The whole man consists of soul and body, but he stated the material of the body and did not state that of the soul. For Moses almost everywhere, passing over invisible things, speaks only of visible things. Hence he gave an account not of what is above heaven but of what is beneath heaven. [Note: The Laurentian manuscript: “what happens beneath heaven.”] For he awaited him who said: “He who is of the earth speaks of the earth; he who comes from heaven is above all” (John 3:32).

There are many things whose material we do not know, and many things which God created not from something but from nothing. Of what material were the heavens made? Of what, the earth? Whence the waters, whence the angels? Since we do not know the creation of souls, let us at least know this: although the soul was breathed by God, it is nevertheless not a part of him, as heretics pretend; for he could not condemn a part of himself to punishments. Whether God created all souls together; whether, as flesh arises from flesh, souls arise from souls; or whether he breathes them into the body already formed in the mother’s womb, is no small question. [Note: The same manuscript.] But of the first man it is said that God created him from the mud of the earth, and then it is added that he breathed the breath of life into his face. If other persons also have souls in a manner like this, it is not inappropriate. [Note: Thomas Aquinas, *Summa Theologiae*, Part I, question 90, articles 3 and 4, proves that the human soul is created immediately by God and united to the body already formed, because the natural perfection of human nature requires that it be joined to it as its form.]

“Now the Lord God had planted a paradise of delight from the beginning, in which he placed the man whom he had formed, to cultivate it. And the Lord God brought forth from the ground every tree beautiful to see and pleasant for food. He also placed in the midst of paradise the tree of life and the tree of the knowledge of good and evil. And a river went out from the place of delight to water paradise, and from there it divided into four heads. The name of one is Phison: it is that which goes around the whole land of Havilah, where gold is produced; and the gold of that land is excellent; there too are found bdellium and the onyx stone. The name of the second river is Gehon: it is that which goes around the whole land of Ethiopia. [Note: The river Phison is the Ganges; Gehon is the Nile.] The name of the third river is Tigris; it flows toward the Assyrians. The fourth river is Euphrates.”

How greatly the Lord loved man may easily be understood also from this: he had prepared for him such a dwelling-place that, if he had not sinned and had begotten children in a most chaste marriage without any concupiscence, then, once the number of the elect had been completed, he would ascend to the heavenly Jerusalem without tasting any bitterness of death and would enjoy eternal blessedness, differing from the angels neither in merit nor number.

Among the other trees of paradise—whose scent, taste, beauty, and power no one can describe—the Lord also placed the tree of Life, to which he gave such a nature that whoever tasted of it could not die. He also placed the tree of the knowledge of good and evil; after the first human beings ate from it, they immediately understood what good things they had lost and what evils they had incurred. For every contrary is better known through its opposite. Thus the sick extol health with great praises, though while healthy they seldom spoke of it. So too, after these persons sinned, seeing how much danger and peril hung over them, they began to admire the good itself—which they had previously not known—much more than before. [Note: The same manuscript.] Therefore it is called the tree of the knowledge of good and evil because, in the first transgressors, it taught us how good it is to keep God’s commands and how evil and dangerous it is not to obey them.

But of what taste and delight do we suppose that river to be which goes out from the place of delight? If, as philosophers relate, there are rivers in the regions of the East more pleasant to drink than every other beverage, what kind of river shall we say this is which proceeds from paradise? But this is according to the letter; now let us consider the meaning. The paradise of delight which God planted from the beginning signifies the holy Church. It is rightly said to have been planted from the beginning, because he chose it before the world’s foundation. “Paradise” is interpreted as “garden of delights.” But who can enumerate its delights? The living bread alone which is eaten in it surpasses every delight.

What is the tree of Life except Christ? For he himself says: “He who eats my flesh and drinks my blood shall live for ever” (John 6:53). And again: “If they do these things in the green tree, what shall be done in the dry?” (Luke 23:31). And the Psalmist says: “He shall be like a tree planted beside streams of water” (Ps. 1:3). Solomon also, speaking of Wisdom, which is Christ, says: “She is a tree of life to those who lay hold of her; and blessed is he who holds her fast” (Prov. 3:18).

The tree of the knowledge of good and evil, however, is transgression of God’s commands. For when he says, “You shall not kill; you shall not commit adultery; you shall not steal; you shall not bear false witness against your neighbour; you shall not covet your neighbour’s property” (Luke 18:25), man is thereby forbidden to approach that tree. But if a person does all these things, he will experience in dying what good it is to observe them and what evil it is to transgress them. The river going out from paradise is understood as evangelical teaching. Its taste was experienced by him who said: “How sweet are your words to my palate, more than honey and the honeycomb to my mouth” (Ps. 118:103). It divides into four heads because the four books of the Gospels, written from it, water the whole world with the waters of divine speech.

See how the very names of the rivers agree with the four Gospels. Phison is interpreted as “invocation of the mouth.” The Gospel changed the mouths of all nations, so that they no longer praise many gods but worship and venerate one God in truth. [Note: The same Cassinese manuscript: “worship one God in Trinity.”] Gehon means “breast,” because evangelical preaching filled the breasts of the faithful with wisdom and made them stronger against enemies. Tigris received its name from swiftness, because the Gospel rapidly filled the whole world at once. Euphrates means “fruitfulness,” because the teaching of the Gospel makes the holy Church fruitful and abundant in every good thing.

“Therefore the Lord took man and placed him in the paradise of delight to cultivate and keep it; and he commanded him, saying: ‘From every tree of paradise eat; but from the tree of the knowledge of good and evil do not eat, for on whatever day you eat from it, you shall die by death.’” [Note: Adam was punished with death by sinning; he would not have been subject to it if he had remained innocent. “It is established,” says Augustine, *The City of God*, book 13, “that bodily death itself was inflicted upon us not by a law of nature but as the penalty of sin.”]

Man, made outside paradise, is placed in paradise. And because idleness is the enemy of the soul, he is commanded to work, lest he live idly. Let those who inhabit sacred and religious places hear this and understand how greatly they ought to guard themselves against the devil’s snares, since they know that man was tempted and overcome not outside paradise but in paradise. All the trees of paradise are given to man for food, but the tree of the knowledge of good and evil alone is forbidden him, so that we may understand that we should use only those things which the Lord commands to be done and abstain from those things which he forbids to be done.

“You shall love the Lord your God and your neighbour as yourself; honour father and mother” (Matt. 22:27). These are the apples; these are the fruits which he commands us to eat. “You shall not kill; you shall not commit adultery,” and so forth: these are the things from which he commands us to abstain. “On whatever day you eat from it, you shall die by death.” [Note: The Cassinese manuscript: “Whenever we act contrary to these things, we incur that sentence of death which says: ‘On whatever day you eat from it, you shall die by death.’”]

Adam died as soon as he ate, not because he immediately departed from this life, but because he received within himself the condition by which he would one day depart; had he not sinned, he could never have died at all. We too die when we do such things, because by sinning we are separated from the life which is Christ. Death is the loss of life.

“And God said: ‘It is not good for man to be alone; let us make for him a helper like himself.’” [Note: The same Cassinese manuscript: “like himself.” The manuscript of the library of Monte Amiata: “a helper like himself.”] “Therefore, when the Lord God had formed from the ground all the animals of the earth and all the birds of heaven, he brought them to Adam to see what he would call them. For whatever Adam called each living soul, that is its name. And Adam gave their names to all the animals of the earth, all the birds of heaven, and all the beasts of the earth.”

Tell us, Adam, in what schools did you learn these things? Who taught you to give names so fitting to things? For you were not made blind and foolish, as some rave; nor did sin open your eyes. Rather, you were created a perfect and wise man, but by pride you greatly diminished both your own perfection and ours. And the creatures rightly receive names from him whom they ought to obey and serve. [Note: Thus it is found in Ecclesiasticus, chapter 17, where, after mentioning the woman formed from the first man Adam, it says: “He created for them knowledge of spirit; he filled their hearts with understanding; he showed them good and evil,” etc.]

[Col. 0164D] “But for Adam no helper like himself was found.” [Note: [Col. 0164D] The same manuscript: “a helper similar to him.”] Therefore the Lord God cast a deep sleep upon Adam; and when he had fallen asleep, he took one of his ribs and filled up the flesh in its place. [Note: [Col. 0164D] The same Monte Amiata manuscript: “The Lord God applied the rib to him, which Adam had taken,” etc.] And he built the rib which he had taken from Adam into a woman, and brought her to Adam. And Adam said: “This now [Col. 0165A] is bone from my bones and flesh from my flesh; she shall be called woman [virago], [Note: [Col. 0165D] The same Cassinese manuscript: “because.” Monte Amiata manuscript: “she was taken from man.” The same manuscript: “a man shall leave his father.”] because she was taken from man. Therefore a man shall leave father and mother and shall cleave to his wife, and the two shall be one flesh.” [Note: [Col. 0165D] The same manuscript: “Now both were naked.”] Now both were naked—Adam, namely, and his wife—and they were not ashamed.

For Adam, made in the likeness and image of God, had nothing like himself among the creatures. Woman was therefore made, to assist him both in the propagation of children and in other necessities. But, so that there might be greater love between them, woman was made not from elsewhere [Note: [Col. 0165D] Both the Laurentian and Cassinese manuscripts correct the edition, which reads “creation.”] but from the man’s rib. Hence it comes about that men, pursuing their own rib with a certain natural love, desire to cleave to woman as though to their own flesh. Those who, with divine assistance, can overcome in themselves the impulse of this love, as men who have conquered their own [Col. 0165B] nature by struggle, are rightly preferred to other people.

Moreover, when the rib was removed, its place was filled not with bone but with flesh, so that from this also we may know ourselves to be weaker and softer. But who could deny that Adam was filled not only with the spirit of wisdom but also with that of prophecy, when, as soon as he saw the woman, he said: “This now is bone from my bones and flesh from my flesh”? For although the woman was made while he slept, nevertheless, not while dreaming but through God’s revelation, he recognized both his bone and his flesh in her. Hence he adds: “She shall be called woman [virago], because she was taken from man.” For, insofar as woman was made from the man’s rib, every human being is one flesh not more with his wife than with every woman. Yet the two are one flesh through a certain natural [Col. 0165C] union of pleasure and the love of unity.

Explaining this passage in his epistles, the Apostle says: “This is a great mystery; but I understand it in Christ and in the Church” (Eph. V, 12). In a certain manner Christ left the Father when he emptied himself, taking the form of a servant. Hence he himself says: “I came forth from the Father and came into the world” (John XVI, 28). He also left his mother, namely the Synagogue, which, according to his humanity, was his mother just as it was the mother of the other Jews. But he cleaved to his wife, because, as the Apostle says, “he betrothed to himself a glorious Church, without spot or wrinkle” (Eph. V, 27). The two are one flesh because Christ is the head of the Church.

[Col. 0165D] Let us therefore follow the Apostle and explain allegorically what we have said. “He cast,” he says, “a deep sleep upon Adam”; for Adam signifies Christ. Hence the Apostle: “The first man is earthly, from the earth; the second man is heavenly, from heaven. As we have borne [Col. 0166A] the image of the earthly man, let us bear also the image of the heavenly” (I Cor. XV, 47). Adam’s sleep foreshadowed Christ’s death. For just as, while Adam slept, one rib was removed and the Church was made, so, when Christ slept upon the cross in the sleep of death, blood flowed from his side, and both redeemed and built the Church. [Note: [Col. 0165D] “Adam sleeps so that Eve may be made; Christ dies so that the Church may be made. Eve is made from the side of the sleeping Adam; when Christ has died, his side is pierced by the lance, so that the sacraments may flow forth by which the Church is formed.” [Col. 0166D] Augustine, *Tractates on John*, tract. 9, no. 10.]

It follows: “Now they were naked and were not ashamed.” Why should those be ashamed who knew nothing shameful in themselves, in whom there was no stirring of the flesh, and in whom no member moved against their will? They were no more aroused by looking upon their sexual organs than by contemplating their eyes or hands. [Note: [Col. 0166D] “Adam, preserving the dignity of angelic decency, was indeed naked of worldly clothing, but clothed in the splendor of immortality. His eyes looked upon nothing evil; his heart entertained no shameful thought. Among modest minds, nakedness itself was clothed.” Maximus of Turin, Homily 85, Roman edition, p. 286.] It follows:

## Chapter III

“Now the serpent was more cunning than all the animals [Col. 0166B] of the earth which the Lord God had made; and he said to the woman: ‘Why has God commanded you not to eat from every tree of paradise?’ The woman said to him: ‘We eat of the fruit of the trees which are in paradise; but of the fruit of the tree which is in the midst of paradise God commanded us not to eat, nor to touch it, lest perhaps we die.’”

It may be understood that the serpent possessed this quality—not only through the devil’s inspiration, who dwelt in it, but also in its own nature, by God’s grant—of being more cunning than all the animals. But the evil spirit, being invisible, could not show himself to the woman except through some form. For if, as the Apostle says, “Satan himself transforms himself into an angel of light” (II Cor. XLI, 13), it was easy [Col. 0166C] for him to transform himself into a serpent. [Note: [Col. 0166D] The holy Fathers commonly teach that in the temptation of the woman the devil employed a real serpent as his instrument; Natalis Alexander proves this against Cajetan, dissertation 3, art. 3, *History of the Old Testament*.]

Indeed, the woman might there have recognized the deception, since she heard the serpent speaking contrary to its nature, had she not known that all God’s creatures were good and suspected no evil anywhere in anything. For she had heard from no one that anyone had been deceived. What evil, then, could she have suspected, especially when it was not the serpent which appeared, but the devil himself speaking to her so cunningly in the serpent? As though ignorant, he questions her and asks why God had commanded that they should not eat from every tree of paradise. For he wished to know whether they remembered God’s command, so that, by sinning knowingly and willingly, they might incur greater divine indignation.

But what did the woman answer him? [Col. 0166D] “We eat,” she says, “of the fruit of the trees of paradise; but of the fruit of the tree which is in the midst of paradise we do not eat, lest we die.” Well do you speak, woman: remain in this; keep faith. You know what sort of tree it is, you know that it is forbidden to you, and you know both sin and [Col. 0167A] the punishment of sin. If you touch it, there can be no excuse; and if there is one, it will be useless. It follows:

“But the serpent said to the woman: ‘You shall by no means die. For God knows that on whatever day you eat from it your eyes shall be opened, and you shall be like gods, [Note: [Col. 0167D] The same Monte Amiata manuscript: “and you shall be as gods.”] knowing good and evil.’ Therefore the woman saw that the tree was good for food, beautiful to the eyes, and delightful in appearance; and she took of its fruit and ate, and gave it to her husband, who ate, and the eyes of both were opened.” [Note: [Col. 0167D] The same Monte Amiata manuscript: “their eyes.”]

“You shall not die,” says the serpent, “if you eat; rather, when the eyes of your mind have been opened, you too shall see invisible things, and you shall be like gods”—like the angels in heaven, because you do not see [Col. 0167B] how much superior they are to you and therefore do not know it. “You shall be,” he says, “like gods”; but in what respect? “Knowing good and evil.” For knowing belongs not to bodily eyes but to the eyes of the mind; when we open our physical eyes, we do not become wiser. Otherwise fools and those deprived of understanding would be blind.

But did the angels know good and evil while the first human beings still did not know what was good and what was evil? If they did not know this, they were foolish; but if they were such, they were not made in the image and likeness of God. For they are said to possess God’s likeness chiefly in this, that they are rational; rationality is the discernment of good and evil. Therefore, being rational, they knew good and evil; in this respect, then, they did not differ from the angels.

Here too the devil’s cunning [Col. 0167C] persuasion is evident. Since that tree, called the tree of the knowledge of good and evil, might by its very name have frightened them from presuming to approach it, he wickedly interpreted the name itself: “You shall be,” he says, “like gods, knowing good and evil.” That is as though he said: You shall know everything—whatever is useful or useless, prosperous or adverse, whatever can benefit or harm you; you shall know all things. [Note: [Col. 0167D] St Thomas teaches that the devil assailed the first human being in three ways, *Summa Theologiae*, III, q. 41, art. 4: “First,” he says, “he prompted the mind of the first human being to eat the forbidden tree, saying: ‘Why has God commanded you [Col. 0168D] not to eat from every tree of paradise?’ Second, he tempted him through vainglory, when he said: ‘Your eyes shall be opened.’ Third, he brought the temptation to the height of pride, when he said: ‘You shall be like gods, knowing good and evil.’”]

But the devil lies, because that tree was not called the tree of the knowledge of good and evil because it was to bestow all these things; rather, good and evil are put for just and unjust. But what will you do, unhappy woman? Whom will you believe, God or the devil? God says: “On whatever day you eat from it, you shall die the death.” The devil says: “You shall by no means [Col. 0167D] die.” But the one is truthful, while the other has been a liar from the beginning. Yet you believed him—to your own harm and ours. You saw the tree, and, delighted by it in taste and sight, ate from it; you gave it to your husband; you were deceived and deceived another. He also ate, and the eyes of both were opened.

Then were not your eyes open, Adam? How, then, when you saw the woman, did you say: “This now is bone from my bones and [Col. 0168A] flesh from my flesh”? What sort of eyes, then, were opened to you? Certainly the eyes of the mind. For then you first understood how great a good you had lost and how great an evil you had incurred.

“And when they knew that they were naked, they sewed fig leaves together and made coverings for themselves. And when they heard the voice of the Lord God [Note: [Col. 0168D] In the Monte Amiata manuscript: “in the midst of the tree of paradise.”] walking in paradise in the breeze after midday, Adam and his wife hid themselves from the face of the Lord God in the midst of paradise.” For previously they were naked and were not ashamed; but after they sinned, they perceived in their members a certain movement of concupiscence, which they were ashamed to see in one another. And though they had previously been naked, they did not recognize their nakedness in themselves, because their very bright flesh [Col. 0168B] before sin was more pleasant to behold than any garment.

But why, after sewing fig leaves together, did they make themselves a girdle? Perhaps because these were the first leaves they came upon; or perhaps because they were larger than the others then present. For fig leaves are said to grow in the regions of the East which exceed the breadth of a shield. Fig leaves have in them a certain roughness that naturally causes itching. Thus they signify that those very bodily parts which they covered were ever troubled and disturbed by a certain heat of concupiscence. It follows:

“And when they heard the voice of the Lord God walking in paradise, Adam and his wife hid themselves.” What voice of the Lord? Perhaps one threatening and denoting their error because they had sinned; or perhaps they were ashamed to appear before him because they were naked. But why is he said to have walked in the breeze? One who seeks the breeze shows that he has endured the heat of burning. Hence we are given to understand that the first human being’s sin had moved the Lord to heat and anger—not that such passions are in God, but because his will cannot be signified except by human affections. The fact that it was after midday signified their death and decline: for they were drawing near to death, because they were hurrying from joy to sorrow. They also left this to us as though by inheritance: that when we sin, we hide ourselves and always strive to conceal our crimes by a certain impious excuse. It follows:

“And the Lord God called Adam and said to him: [Col. 0168D] ‘Adam, where are you?’” O most merciful Lord, who wills not the death of the sinner but life: for he always calls those who stray to repentance. What does he say? “Adam, where are you?” He speaks not because he does not know the place, but because he has compassion for Adam’s ruin—as though saying: “Adam, where are you? Into what misery you have fallen; from how great a glory into how great an abyss you have been plunged!” Adam says: “I heard your voice in paradise and was afraid, because I was naked, [Col. 0169A] and I hid myself.” [Note: [Col. 0169D] “To Adam, hiding and concealing himself from the Divinity, it is said: ‘Adam, where are you?’ Not because Adam could be hidden from the Lord’s sight, but because no place is safe or secure for a sinful conscience while it fears discovery.” St Maximus, Homily 53, p. 166.]

“I heard your voice,” he says; “I perceived your wrath and indignation, and I was afraid.” Why? “Because I was naked”: because I was ready for punishments, because I had lost that garment of righteousness in which I had been clothed and neither feared nor was ashamed. Therefore I hid myself. But where shall I flee from your face? “For if I ascend into heaven, you are there; if I descend into hell, you are present” (Ps. CXXXVIII, 8). To him he said:

“Who told you that you were naked, unless” it was because you “ate from the tree of which I commanded you not to eat?” As though he said: If you had not eaten the forbidden tree, you would never have known in your members the shameful nakedness; but because you ate, you now see another law in your members resisting the law of your mind (Rom. VII, 23). Therefore [Col. 0169B] you hid yourself; therefore you were ashamed. And Adam said:

“The woman whom you gave me as a companion gave me from the tree, and I ate.” As though plainly saying: It is true, Lord; I cannot deny it. But the fact that I ate was caused by the woman. But what woman? The one whom you gave me as a companion. O unhappy man, created in such wisdom, how did you so quickly lose your understanding? You impute your sin not to yourself but to God, so that because he gave you a woman as companion, he himself should be the principal cause of your fall?

“Then he said to the woman: ‘Why have you done this?’ She said: ‘The serpent deceived me, and I ate.’” Both ate; neither asks pardon, but they excuse their sin. Therefore they incur not forgiveness but the punishment of a curse. This is what he feared who said: “Do not incline my heart [Col. 0169C] to an evil word, to make excuses for excuses in sins” (Ps. CXL, 4).

“And the Lord said to the serpent: ‘Because you have done this, [Note: [Col. 0169D] The same Monte Amiata manuscript: “you are cursed.”] you shall be cursed among all animals and beasts of the earth. You shall crawl upon your breast, and you shall eat earth all the days of your life. I shall place enmities between you and the woman, and between your seed and her seed; she shall crush your head, and you shall lie in wait for her heel.’”

For not only the evil spirit, signified through the serpent, but also the serpent itself is cursed and hated by everyone more than all earthly animals. The ancient enemy crawls upon his breast, because he tramples down and scatters all his counsel and wisdom, which indeed is contained in the sinner; and he does not leave those whose breasts he possesses, but reigns, walks, and rules proudly in them. He eats earth all his days because he insatiably torments with eternal punishments the sinners whom he deceives.

There are enmities between the devil and the Church, [Note: [Col. 0169D] Christ warned Peter concerning this enmity, saying: “Simon, Simon, behold, Satan has sought you [Col. 0170D] that he might sift you like wheat; but I have prayed for you, that your faith may not fail” (Luke XXII, 31).] which is signified by the woman, and between the seed and children of each, because, thinking different things, [Col. 0170A] desiring different things, and pursuing different things, they can never have peace and concord with one another. The Church crushes his head because, foreseeing the beginning of his cunning plot, she immediately scatters his counsel, ingenuity, and guile at its very outset. But he lies in wait for her heel because, unless she walks uprightly and advances firmly along the path of good work, he at once attacks her and strives to trip and cast her down as she wavers.

“To the woman also he said: ‘I shall multiply your afflictions and your conceptions; in pain you shall bear children; you shall be under your husband’s power, and he shall rule over you.’” Understood according to the letter, these words need no exposition. You will recognize that the Church’s afflictions have been multiplied if you recall the prisons, chains, [Col. 0170B] scourges, and various other tortures of the saints. The prophet testifies that her conceptions are multiplied, saying: “Rejoice, barren woman; break forth and cry aloud, you who do not bear, because the children of the deserted woman are many, more than those of her who has a husband” (Gal. IV, 27). She bears in pain, as the Lord himself says: “When a woman gives birth, she has sorrow” (John XVI, 21). She is under her husband’s power because no one but Christ rules over her.

[Note: [Col. 0170D] The same Monte Amiata manuscript: “But to Adam he said.”] “But to Adam he said: ‘Because you listened to the voice of your wife more than to mine, and ate of the tree [Note: [Col. 0170D] The same manuscript: “from which I commanded you not to eat.”] concerning which I commanded you not to eat, the earth shall be cursed in your work. With toil you shall eat from it all the days of your life; it shall bring forth thorns and thistles for you, and you shall eat the plants of the earth. By the sweat of your face you shall eat your bread, until you return to [Col. 0170C] the earth from which you were taken; for you are dust, and to dust you shall return.’”

No excuse, he says, will help you. Because you obeyed the woman by despising my commands, the earth shall be cursed in your work—but not in mine. [Note: [Col. 0170D] “If anyone does good, it is from God; if evil, it is from the human being himself, because God is not the author of evil.” Fulgentius, *To Monimus*, ch. 19.] For when you act wrongly, it is your work; but when you act rightly, it is not yours but mine. Therefore the earth—that is, your flesh—is cursed not in my work but in yours. You ate of the forbidden tree: it is your work. And who does not know what blessing the earth lost in this work, since it is clear that it would of its own accord have supplied everything necessary to everyone, had the first human beings not performed this act?

Hence it adds: “With toil you shall eat from it all the days of your life.” Had you not sinned, you would have abounded in every good thing [Col. 0170D] without toil. But because you sinned, it will not yield even the due reward of labor; rather, “it shall bring forth thorns and thistles for you, and you shall eat the plants of the earth,” because you made evil use of paradise’s delights. “By the sweat of your face you shall eat your bread,” because in pride you despised rest, “until you return to the earth from which you were taken,” because you will not, as you thought, be a god; rather, “you are dust, and to dust you shall return.”

[Col. 0171A] “And Adam called the name of his wife Eve, because she was the mother of many living persons.” Eve is not the mother of all living beings, but only of human beings. Yet because only human souls among the other earthly creatures cannot die, human beings alone are rightly called living.

“God also made garments of skins for Adam and his wife, and clothed them.” In this he showed them to be mortal, because he clothed them in the skins of dead animals. Thus, as persons condemned, they displayed in their very clothing the curse to which they were subject, wearing the signs of their condemnation as though for reproach. Hence it adds:

“Behold, Adam has become as one of us, knowing good and evil.” This is to be understood ironically, [Col. 0171B] as though he said: Behold, man has even been diminished in his dignity, since in pride he wished to be more than a human being.

“See, therefore, lest perhaps he stretch out his hand and take also from the tree of life and live forever.” For just as by tasting the tree of the knowledge of good and evil he subjected himself to the laws of death, so also, had he taken from the tree of life, he could, after recovering the immortality which he had recently lost, have lived forever. [Note: [Col. 0171D] St Thomas explains this passage differently, II–II, q. 164, art. 2: “It must be said that if man after sin had eaten of the tree of life, he would not thereby have recovered immortality; but by the benefit of that food [Col. 0172D] he could have prolonged his life further. Hence the statement, ‘he shall live forever,’ is taken in the sense of a long time. It was not expedient for man to remain longer in the misery of this life.”] Therefore what follows came about:

“And the Lord sent him out from the paradise of delight, to till the earth from which he was taken. And he drove out Adam, and set before the paradise of delight the Cherubim and a flaming, turning sword to guard the way to the tree of life.” [Col. 0171C] *Cherubim* is interpreted “fullness of knowledge.” It signifies the apostles and the teachers of the Church, in whom the treasures of wisdom and knowledge are hidden. When someone is cast out because of sin from paradise—that is, from the holy Church—he is forbidden by them to presume to approach the tree of life, that is, to partake of Christ’s flesh.

This sword is shining and flaming, bright and without rust: one struck by it is either enlightened or burned. Hence the Apostle says: “To some we are an odor of life unto life; to others, an odor of death unto death” (II Cor. II, 16). It is also turning, ready and swift to strike: it strikes sinners all around it, condemning poor and rich alike.

## Chapter IV

[Col. 0171D]

“Now Adam knew Eve his wife, and she conceived and bore Cain, saying: ‘I have acquired a man through God.’” “I,” says Eve, “have been placed under my husband’s power because of transgression; now, through the begetting of sons, I possess a man.” Hence it is understood that we ought to be subject and obedient in equal measure to both parents.

“And again she bore his brother Abel. Abel was a shepherd of sheep, and Cain a farmer.” Cain, whose name is interpreted “possession,” undertook to cultivate and possess [Col. 0172A] the earth. But Abel, whose name means “mourning,” fed sheep, signifying Christ, whose sheep we are and whom the Jews, his brothers according to the flesh, killed with an impious death, ever to be lamented.

“After many days it came to pass that Cain offered gifts to the Lord from the fruits of the earth; Abel also offered from the firstborn of his flock and from their fat. And the Lord looked upon Abel and his gifts, but upon Cain and his gifts he did not look.” For the Lord looks not so much upon the gifts offered to him as upon the desire and mind of those offering them. Therefore here too he is said to have looked first upon the offerers, that is, upon the disposition in which they offered, before looking upon their gifts.

But how could Cain know that God had not looked upon his gifts, [Col. 0172B] unless he saw that his brother’s sacrifice was consumed by fire coming from heaven, whereas his own was not? The same is read concerning the sacrifices of Abraham, Manoah, and Elijah. For holy men believed that their sacrifices pleased God when they saw them consumed by fire sent from heaven.

“Cain was exceedingly angry, and his face fell.” Cain is angry not so much because his own gifts are despised as because his brother’s gifts are received. There is no doubt that this occurred through the fever of envy. Great, therefore, is envy—the cause of the first murder.

“And the Lord said to him: ‘Why are you angry, and why has your face fallen? If you do well, [Col. 0172C] will you not receive? But if you do ill, sin will immediately be present at the door; yet its desire shall be under you, and you shall rule over it.’” As though he said: Do not be angry or grieved; do not be inflamed by the torches of envy. Abel has committed nothing against you. You too should act well, so that you may receive good things. For if you act wickedly, or even if you merely think of doing evil, the devil is at hand: the prince of sin stands before the door, so that, once he has entered the dwelling-place of your heart, he may bring your evil will through to its effect.

Yet its desire shall be under you: it will come with your assent and depart with your resistance. If, therefore, you resist, all its appetite and desire will be in vain. But if you consent, you will not rule over it; rather, it will rule over you. “For whoever commits sin is the slave of sin” (I John III, 41).

[Col. 0172D] “And Cain said to his brother: ‘Let us go out.’ And when they were in the field, Cain rose up against Abel his brother and killed him.” Cain signifies the Jewish people, while Abel signifies Christ. For they then indeed went out when the Jews drew Christ outside the city in order to crucify him.

“And the Lord said to Cain: ‘Where is your brother?’ He answered: ‘I do not know. Am I my brother’s keeper?’ And he said to him: ‘What have you done? The voice of your brother’s blood cries to me from the earth. Now [Col. 0173A] therefore you shall be cursed upon the earth, which opened its mouth and received your brother’s blood from your hand. When you cultivate it, it shall not give you its fruits, but shall bring forth thorns and thistles for you. You shall be a wanderer and fugitive upon the earth.’”

When Cain was asked where Abel was, he answered that he did not know, because the Jews also, when questioned about who Christ is and where he is, say that they do not know, whether from fear or ignorance. Hence in the Gospel they ask: “If you are the Christ, tell us plainly” (John X, 24). And elsewhere: “Who this man is, we do not know” (John IX, 29). To them he says: “You know both me and where I am from” (John VII, 28).

But what do we suppose Abel’s blood cried then, except what the souls of the saints are said to cry: “Avenge our blood, [Col. 0173B] O our God” (Apoc. VI, 10)? Yet Christ our Lord says compassionately: “Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they do” (Luke XXIII, 34). Hence, the Apostle testifies that Christ’s blood speaks better things than Abel’s blood (Heb. XII, 24). Even now Christ’s blood cries from the earth, because worthy remembrance of his passion is made daily in the Church. This is the earth which, opening its mouth, thirstily drinks daily the blood of Christ, which [Note: [Col. 0173D] The same Cassinese manuscript: “of those Jews themselves.”] the impious people of the Jews did not fear to shed. Therefore it is cursed throughout the earth and is held in reproach and derision by all.

It is a wanderer and fugitive upon the earth because, scattered everywhere, it never possesses the place of its own dominion.

[Col. 0173C] “Cain said to the Lord: ‘My iniquity is greater than I can deserve forgiveness for. Behold, you drive me out today from the face of the earth, and I shall be hidden from your face; I shall be a wanderer and fugitive on the earth, and everyone who finds me will kill me.’” These words are full of despair. “My iniquity is greater than I can make satisfaction or repentance for, so as to deserve indulgence and pardon from you. I shall be cast out from the land of the living; I shall be hidden from your face and shall no longer deserve to see you. Moreover, even in this land of pilgrimage I shall be everywhere a wanderer and fugitive, and shall be unable to possess not only heavenly but even earthly things without fear and sorrow.”

These words also apply to the Jews, who, expelled from their inheritance, are wanderers and fugitives everywhere. Because they do not feel themselves illuminated by the divine countenance, [Col. 0173D] they fear being killed by all. This might perhaps already have happened to them had not he whom they killed, Christ our Lord, prayed for them, saying: “Do not kill them, lest my people ever forget” (Ps. LVIII, 12).

“And the Lord said to him: ‘It shall not be so; but whoever kills Cain shall be punished sevenfold.’” Another translation has: “He shall pay sevenfold vengeance,” [Col. 0174A] which is understood more plainly. This means as though he said: It shall not be as you wish. You shall not die now, nor shall everyone who finds you kill you. You shall be preserved for a long time and reach the seventh generation. Whoever kills you shall pay seven acts of vengeance in your case—that is, [Note: [Col. 0173D] The Laurentian manuscript: “from full and complete anguish and tribulation.”] he shall free you from full and complete tribulation. For the number seven signifies perfection.

Thus Cain endured penance for his fratricide for a long time; at last, as the story goes, he was killed by Lamech in the seventh generation. In this way Lamech paid seven acts of vengeance upon him, when, death intervening, he freed him from all the distresses which he had suffered up to that time through seven generations. But if it is said, “he shall be punished sevenfold,” as our translation has it, it must be understood that Lamech sinned more greatly than Cain and therefore is held worthy of a greater punishment. Lamech already knew that Cain had been condemned for murder; Cain, however, had heard of no one before him condemned for such a cause. Thus Cain’s punishment might have corrected Lamech, whereas Cain had no preceding example by which to be instructed. And as the Gospel says: “The servant who knows his master’s will and does not do what is worthy shall be beaten with many stripes; but the one who does not know and does not do it shall be beaten with few” (Luke XII, 47). “He shall be punished sevenfold” means nothing other than that he shall be punished altogether abundantly and severely.

“And the Lord placed a sign upon Cain, so that everyone who found him should not [Col. 0174C] kill him.” This sign is said to have been a trembling of the limbs, because, like a madman or a melancholic, he moved people to pity for his misery. [Note: [Col. 0173D] St John Chrysostom on this passage, Augustine, *Against Faustus*, II.12, Jerome’s letter to Damasus, and Theodoret, *Questions on Genesis*, q. 42, held the same opinion, following the Septuagint translators. In place of the words, “You shall be a wanderer and fugitive upon the earth,” they translated, “You shall be groaning [Col. 0174D] and trembling,” etc.; and, showing the trembling of all his limbs, the repulsiveness of his face, and the squalor caused by the bite of a guilty conscience, they said that God placed a sign upon Cain so that he might be distinguished from other people and no one should kill him.]

For who would wish to kill one who seemed to suffer things worse than death itself? The Lord likewise gave the Jews the sign of circumcision, by which they are distinguished from all nations; and though they are subject to all nations and ever given over to fear and contempt, there is no one who wishes to kill them.

“And Cain went out from the face of the Lord and dwelt as a fugitive in the land toward the eastern region of Eden.” For one goes out from the face of the Lord who does not merit the regard of his mercy. [Note: [Col. 0174D] Both manuscripts correct the edition, where it reads: “measures.”] This aptly applies to the Jews, who flee from Christ the Lord and dwell in the world as wanderers and fugitives. Because they are devoted to pleasure and are mindful not of the setting but of the rising—that is, not of everlasting death but of present life—they are rightly said to dwell toward the eastern region of Eden. For *Eden* is interpreted “pleasure” or “delight.”

But we have resolved not to introduce into this work matters in which only the historical narrative is related, or which do not seem to pertain much to the subject, in order to expound them allegorically, [Col. 0175A] so that the volume may be shorter and we may dwell longer on matters more necessary.

“Listen to my voice, wives of Lamech; give ear [Note: [Col. 0175D] The same Monte Amiata manuscript: “my speech.”] to my words: for I have killed a man to my wound, and a young man to my bruise; [Note: [Col. 0175D] The same Monte Amiata manuscript: “Vengeance shall be given sevenfold for Cain, but for Lamech,” etc.] vengeance shall be given sevenfold for Cain, but for Lamech seventy times seven.”

Lamech, the first bigamist, had two wives, to whom he reveals what a great crime [Note: [Col. 0175D] The same Laurentian manuscript: “what crime.”] he had committed. The Hebrews relate that when Cain was once, according to his custom, wandering alone among thickets in a forest, Lamech, skilled in archery, shot an arrow at a sound. Thinking that he had killed some wild animal, he found Cain killed by his wound. Moved by grief, he also killed a certain young man who was with him, either to conceal the matter [Col. 0175B] or because the deed had been done at that young man’s urging. This, they say, is what is meant by “I have killed a man to my wound”—that is, Cain—“and a young man to my bruise,” that is, in my anger and indignation.

But whether he killed him in this manner or another, it is clear that Lamech killed Cain. What follows—“vengeance shall be given sevenfold for Cain, but for Lamech seventy times seven”—is the sentence of a prophet judging. Perhaps “sevenfold” is itself the same as “seventyfold,” because each number signifies perfection. But if we understand that a greater punishment was, or will be, exacted from Lamech than from Cain, we think this is so because Lamech ought at least to have been deterred by the example of Cain’s condemnation from committing murder. For he had already heard that Cain had incurred God’s indignation and wrath for fratricide; perhaps he had also heard that Cain had been divinely marked, so that no one should presume to kill him contrary to God’s command. He sinned greatly, therefore: neither the sign imposed upon Cain, nor the example of condemnation, nor the voice of God threatening and forbidding could restrain him from murder.

## Chapter V
“This is the book of the generation of Adam, in the day when God created man: he made him in his likeness; male and female he created them, and blessed them, and called their name Adam in the day when they were created.” This, he says, is the book of Adam’s generation, in which it is fully set out how he was begotten and created. And lest Adam be thought perhaps older than Eve, it says that they were created on one day; [Col. 0175D] for both were created in one and the same day, and called by one name, namely Adam. For Eve was made together with Adam—not as a person, but as material; there are indeed two persons, but one material. Finally, the first rib, from which the woman was made, was created together with Adam and in Adam; and because that rib was a part of Adam, while the whole man was called Adam, rightly that rib too—or rather, the woman in the rib—was called Adam. This is what is meant by: “and he called their name Adam.”

But where it is said that Enoch began to call upon the name of the Lord, this should be understood to mean that, after Abel’s death, he invoked God more worthily and served him. Concerning Methuselah, however, the corruption of the books of the scribes has produced so great an error that many have maintained that he lived after the Flood, although it is clear that only five souls were saved in the ark. The easiest solution to that exceedingly difficult question, then, will be to say that the books are corrupt in the number of his years. [Note: The Samaritan codex makes Methuselah’s life 240 years shorter than does the Hebrew text and the Septuagint, which extend it to 969 years. See Natalis Alexander, *Dissertation VIII on the Years of the Patriarchs*.]

## CHAPTER VI

“But Noah, when he was five hundred years old, [Col. 0176B] begot Shem, Ham, and Japheth. And when men began to multiply upon the earth and had begotten daughters, the sons of God, seeing the daughters of men to be beautiful, chose wives for themselves from among all whom they had chosen.”

In this passage some have dangerously erred, supposing the sons of God to be either angels or demons who, delighted by the appearance of women, descended to earth and—something even to say is impious—lay with them; from this, they say, there arose a certain kind of demons called incubi. We, however, understand the sons of God to be the sons of Seth, the first of whom was Enoch, of whom it is written that he began to call upon the name of the Lord. [Note: This is also the view of John Chrysostom, Theodoret, Augustine, and other Holy Fathers: namely, that this passage of Scripture is to be understood thus—not as speaking of angels, who are nowhere called sons of God, but of the sons of Seth, worshippers of the true God, who joined themselves in carnal love to the daughters of Cain. See Natalis Alexander, *Dissertation VII*, part 1, *Old Testament*.]

Those are sons of God who do God’s will; the daughters of men are understood to be those descended from Cain’s stock. Behold once again women [Col. 0176C] become the cause of men’s ruin: those who ought to have begotten children for God, enticed by women’s beauty, beget giants for the world. Such proud and mighty offspring do the sons of God produce whenever they unite themselves with the daughters of men—that is, with heretical and philosophical perversity.

“And God said: My spirit shall not remain in man forever, because he is flesh; and his days shall be [Note: The same manuscript: one hundred and twenty years.] one hundred and twenty years.” If in this passage “spirit” is understood as that of which it is written, “he breathed into his face the breath of life” (Gen. II, 8), it is surely a divine threat: that the man who refused to obey the life-giving and never-dying soul should die in corruptible and passing flesh, [Col. 0176D] which always lusts against the spirit.

Others understand it as if he said: “The spirit of my wrath and indignation shall not remain in man forever”; that is, I shall now take vengeance upon man, but I shall not take vengeance forever. Why? Because he is flesh: because he is changeable, because he is of fragile material. Therefore I shall have mercy upon him, as is fitting, and his days shall be [Col. 0177A] one hundred and twenty years. This does not mean that no person lived longer afterward, but that so many days were granted to humanity for repentance until the Flood; had they repented worthily during them, the Flood would not have occurred. But because people persisted in their wickedness, when twenty years had been cut off from the number and one hundred completed, the Flood came. For God—whom nothing can ever escape—knew that those who had remained unconverted for a hundred years would nevertheless have remained in their wickedness even had they lived the remaining twenty years. Rightly, therefore, those who accomplish nothing in the number do not come to the number.

“Now giants were upon the earth in those days. For after the sons of God went in to the daughters of men, and they bore children,” it is understood, this race of human beings [Col. 0177B] was born. For every rational and moral creature, “of either sex, of whatever nature, whether in number of limbs or in bodily size, either increases or diminishes”; and man does not descend from any stock other than Adam’s. “And these,” indeed, “are mighty men of old, men of renown.” [Note: This assertion is common among the Holy Fathers against those who wrongly imagined that giants were begotten from the intercourse of demons with women. See Augustine, *City of God*, book XV, ch. 9; Cyril of Alexandria; Theodoret; and others cited by Natalis Alexander.]

“God, seeing that the wickedness of men was great upon the earth, and that every thought of the heart was continually intent upon evil, and foreseeing the future, repented that he had made man upon the earth, and was inwardly touched with sorrow of heart. ‘I will destroy,’ he said, ‘man whom I have created from the face of the earth, from man even to animals, from creeping things even to birds of the air; for I repent that I have made them.’”

God, he says, saw that man—whom he had made in his [Col. 0177C] image and likeness, and for whom he had created the other animals of the world and everything necessary for this life—had turned wholly toward evil. He therefore says that he repents of having created man, although he cannot repent. For God cannot repent, suffer grief, or become angry; nevertheless, when he performs the work of one repenting, grieving, or angry, he is said to repent, grieve, and be angry, although he himself undergoes no change, since his nature is unchangeable.

When he says, “I repent that I made man,” it is as though he said: Because man has transgressed my commandments, I shall show myself toward him as though I repented of having made him. For what one repents of having made, [Col. 0177D] one is pleased to destroy. Therefore, whenever we speak of God or introduce him as speaking, because we cannot speak of him otherwise, we use human words and human affections. [Note: Since God is unchangeable by nature, how can he be said to repent that he made man? “It must be understood metaphorically,” says St Thomas, *Summa Theologiae*, I, question 19, article 7, “according to our likeness.”]

It follows: “But Noah was just and perfect in his generations; he walked with God and begot three sons, Shem, Ham, and Japheth. Now the earth was corrupt before the Lord and filled with iniquity. And when God saw that the earth was corrupt—for all [Col. 0178A] flesh had corrupted its way upon the earth—he said to Noah: The end of all flesh has come before me; the earth is filled with their iniquity, and I shall destroy them with the earth.”

Noah, he says, was a just and perfect man: not with respect to consummate justice and perfection, but in his generations; among that generation of men none at that time was so perfect. But what else is it to walk with God except to follow God and keep his commandments? And when the earth is said to have been corrupt, it was corrupted solely by man’s corruption and sin—not because either the earth itself or earthly animals committed anything by which the earth might properly be called corrupt. For “all flesh” in this passage means nothing other than all humankind. [Note: “Here he used flesh for the earthly human being, in whom the enticement of the flesh corrupted his way.” Ambrose, *On Noah and the Ark*, ch. 5, no. 12.]

Yet all things made for man are rightly destroyed together with man. This is what he says: “The end of all flesh has come before me”; that is, it so pleases me, it is so ordained by me, that all flesh should come to an end, and that people should be destroyed together with the earth and with the things made for man. For in this way God destroyed the earth itself: it was much more fertile before the Flood than afterward. Hence, after the Flood, meat is said to have been granted to man for food.

“Make yourself an ark of smoothed timbers; you shall make little chambers in the ark and coat it inside and outside with pitch. And thus you shall make it: the ark shall be three hundred cubits long, fifty cubits wide, and thirty cubits high.” [Col. 0178C]

We understand this ark to be the holy Church, outside which whoever is found will perish. The ark is built of smoothed timbers because the holy Church too is built of those who have been well hewn and squared by the sword of the Spirit, adorned in character and virtue and beautified with every grace, and who are known to have nothing crooked or defective; the Church is without spot or wrinkle. By the chambers he signifies the individual churches, which, divided among provinces and bishoprics, are contained within the universal Church like rooms within a house.

All the timbers and the entire ark are commanded to be coated with pitch, so that the whole Church, bound together by the bond of charity, cannot be divided by any heresy or discord. For pitch signifies charity, [Col. 0178D] without which the Church can neither stand nor endure. Pitch is said by nature both to join unlike woods inseparably and to preserve them forever incorrupt. It is rightly commanded to be applied inside and outside, because true love is held within through the affection of the heart and outwardly displayed through works of mercy.

The ark is three hundred cubits long because the length of the Church extends from the beginning of the first age to the end of the final age. For three hundred cubits make six fifties, by which we understand the six ages: the first, from Adam to Noah; the second, from Noah to Abraham; the third, from Abraham to Moses; the fourth, from Moses to David; the fifth, from David to Christ; the sixth, from Christ to the end of the age. These are signified by the six water jars whose water Christ changed into wine. Thus the Church’s length is as great as the extent of this life.

Its width is rightly said to be fifty cubits, so that it may be found equal to each age. For the Church’s width is as great as the breadth of the world. Thus the Lord commanded the apostles, saying: “Go into the whole world; preach [Col. 0179B] the Gospel to every creature” (Mark XVI, 20). And because the Law is given on the fiftieth number, the Holy Spirit is sent, an inheritance is restored to its owners through the year of Jubilee, and David, repenting in the fiftieth Psalm, obtained mercy, this ark is not without reason divided according to this number. For these are the greatest and principal causes by which the Church’s length and width grow and are enlarged.

The Church is also thirty cubits high, because Christ, when he attained this age of his full maturity, was baptized and began his preaching. Of this age the Apostle says that “we shall meet the Lord, unto a perfect man, unto the measure of the age of the fullness [Col. 0179C] of Christ” (Eph. IV, 13). Let the Church therefore glory that it reaches this height, in which our Savior displayed the mark of the perfect man.

“You shall make a window in the ark, and in one cubit you shall complete its top. But you shall place the door of the ark low down in its side; you shall make upper rooms and three stories in it.” What do we understand by the window except teachers and apostles, who illumine the holy Church and deserved to hear from the Lord, “You are the light of the world” (Matt. V, 14)? Every house without windows is dark and without light. Rightly, therefore, the apostles are called windows, through whom the light of heavenly wisdom and the brightness of doctrine shone upon us.
