The Church is completed in one cubit because all its perfection consists in unity: it has one heart and one soul—“one Lord, one faith, one baptism, one God and Father of all” (Eph. IV, 5–6)—and, tending toward one glory, one blessedness, and one rest, obtains the reward of one and the same denarius. The door, placed low down in the side, is he who said, “I am the door; whoever enters through me shall be saved” (John X, 9). Whoever does not enter through this door is a thief and a robber. It is placed low down in the side because, through the humanity of flesh assumed below, joined to the side of his bride, he provided all with a way of entrance.

The upper rooms and three stories—or, as another translation has it, [Note: St Maximus of Turin uses the same version when, in Sermon 6 on Lent, p. 450, he says: “For the ark, the Church, is threefold, because it contains the mystery of the Trinity. For when Scripture says that it was two-chambered and three-chambered, it plainly shows that it is distinguished by the threefold grace of the Godhead.”] two-chambered and three-chambered—may indeed signify many other things. It is unnecessary to explain everything that follows. We shall therefore give only a brief general exposition, introducing allegories only where necessary.

It follows that the Lord will bring the waters of the Flood upon the earth and destroy all flesh, and will establish a covenant with Noah, commanding him, upon entering the ark, to take with him two by two of every living creature, together with food by which they may live. Under an allegorical interpretation, this signifies that the holy Church is continually shaken and troubled by the storms of adversities and the waters of disturbances; and, while sinners perish in eternal condemnation, the saints have made this covenant with the Lord: that they should not fear those who kill the body, because he will not abandon or forsake them, but will be with them until the consummation of the age. The statement that Noah took all kinds of animals into the ark signifies the coming together in the Church of the diversity of all nations. Every food that may be eaten is the whole doctrine of both the New and Old Testaments.

## CHAPTER VII

“Noah therefore did everything that God commanded.” For, entering the ark with his sons, wife, and women, he brought in with him everything God had commanded: [Col. 0180C] of clean animals, seven and seven; but of unclean animals, two and two. “Seven and seven” is understood as though he had been commanded to bring in seven, and no more, of each kind; but only two of the unclean are taken aboard, so that the seed may be preserved. Seven of the clean, however, are taken in both so that their seed may likewise be preserved and so that, when Noah comes out of the ark, something may remain to be offered to the Lord.

Therefore, at the beginning of the day, at first dawn, when day was already breaking, Noah entered the ark, together with his sons, his wife, and the wives of his sons. Nor should anyone wonder how Noah could gather so many animals into one ark and through one door, since he who made all things effortlessly and from nothing easily gathered all things together into one, likewise without effort. It is greater to create than to gather. To me it does not seem more marvelous than that our Lord Christ, through a few apostles, gathered into one Church so many nations from all parts of the world—nations so wild and so divided.

When he says, “All the fountains of the great deep were broken open, and the floodgates of heaven were opened,” this seems to mean that water, boiling upward not only through the hidden channels of the earth, filled the world, but also that the water above the firmament, bursting through certain [Col. 0181A] windows of heaven, inundated the earth. Yet it may more rightly be understood that the entire air, which is frequently called heaven, was dissolved into waters falling in an extraordinary manner. [Note: The sources from which so great an abundance of water burst forth in Noah’s Flood are identified by Natalis Alexander, “On the Universality of Noah’s Flood,” article 4, single page, vol. I.]

The Flood occurred for forty days and forty nights because this number seems sufficient both for the blotting out of sins and for suggesting repentance. It also contains within itself the fullness of the New and Old Testaments, since it is composed of four and ten: four tens, or ten times four, make forty.

## CHAPTER VIII

“And the Lord remembered Noah, and all the living creatures and all the cattle that were with him in the ark; he brought a spirit over the earth, and [Col. 0181B] the waters diminished.” God, who never forgets, is said to remember when he has mercy upon sinners. He brought a spirit—that is, a wind of clear weather—over the earth, which we may perhaps understand as the north wind. [Note: Ambrose thought otherwise. “I do not think,” he says, “that this was said so that we should understand wind by the name Spirit, for wind could not dry up the Flood.” He concludes: “There is therefore no doubt that that Flood was checked by the invisible power of the divine Spirit, by a heavenly operation, not by a blast. Yet no one will deny that God could have given that power to the wind.”]

If anyone wonders where so great a flood of waters went back, let him first consider where it came from; yet both are difficult to know. Nevertheless it is written: “The Lord founded the earth upon the seas and prepared it upon the rivers” (Ps. XXIII, 6). And again: “Let there be a firmament in the midst of the waters, and let it divide waters from waters” (Gen. I, 6). The waters are therefore many, since heaven and earth are contained in them.

“And when forty days had passed, [Col. 0181C] Noah opened the window of the ark that he had made and sent out a raven; and it went forth and did not return until the waters dried up from the earth.” What does this raven signify except sinners? If they are ever separated from the Church through schism, heresy, or other sins, they persist in their wickedness, love the glory and spaciousness of the world, and neglect to repent so as to be reconciled to mother Church. Just as that bird is unchangeable in colour, so they are unchangeable in mind.

“He also sent a dove after it, to see whether the waters had now ceased; and when it found no place where its foot might rest, it returned to him in the ark, for the waters were over the whole earth. He stretched out his hand, took it, and brought it into the ark.” The dove represents those of whom the Lord said: “Upon whom shall my spirit rest, except upon the humble and quiet person, trembling at my words?” (Isa. LXVI, 2). If such people at any time leave the Church for any reason, they hasten to return to it as swiftly as possible. They think that they can have no rest after leaving such a mother. They return of their own accord, carrying peace and an olive branch in their beak. For what else is it to carry an olive branch in the mouth except to show peace in one’s words? It is rightly said that this olive had green leaves, so that such peace may be believed to be living, true, and not feigned.

The raven does not do this; the heretic scorns to do it; the proud, excommunicated from the Church, despise to do it. But why, after the third sending, does the dove no longer return to the ark, except because, when the flesh is dissolved, the waters have ceased, and all adversities have failed, it finds a greater rest for itself? The third sending, therefore, is the dissolution of this mortal flesh. Thus Rachel had sent forth those children of hers of whom it is said: “Rachel weeping for her children, and refusing to be comforted, because they are not” (Jer. XXXI, 15). What does it mean to say, “because they are not”? [Note: The Laurentian codex: “Except because they are no longer in this life, because they are with God, because [they possess] heavenly goods, etc.”] Except that they are not in this life, because they cannot leave heavenly goods [Col. 0182B] in order to return again to these perishable and transient things.

“And Noah, opening the roof of the ark, looked and saw that the surface of the earth was dry.” Although he could sufficiently have learned this through the window, he preferred to climb upon the roof in order to look, because the higher anyone ascends through the degrees of virtues, the more he looks down upon the waters and adversities of this world [Note: The same codex: “looking down upon the adversity of the waters.”] and promises himself hope of future prosperity.

“Go out from the ark: you and your wife, your sons and your sons’ wives with you.” Behold, men go out of the ark with women, although they entered the ark separately from women. This is because ecclesiastical men [Note: Here *ecclesiasticus* has the same meaning as “religious” and “God-fearing,” as those in the Church of God ought to be.] devote themselves to prayer at one time, and at another, as the Apostle says (1 Cor. VII), [Col. 0182C] return to one another, so that husband may render the marital due to wife and wife to husband, lest Satan tempt them because of their lack of self-control.

“Then Noah built an altar to the Lord; and, taking from all the clean cattle and birds, he offered burnt offerings upon the altar. And the Lord smelled a sweet savour and said to him: I will never again curse the earth because of men; for the inclination and thought of the human heart are prone to evil from its youth. Therefore I shall not [Note: The same M. A. codex: “strike every living creature, as I did.”] strike every living thing as I have done to all the living creatures of the earth.”

Because all flesh had corrupted its way and the whole world had been purified by the waters of the Flood, it was necessary that a burnt offering be made to God from every kind of clean animal, so that he who had been offended by all might be appeased by the sacrifice of all. Man alone was not sacrificed in this offering, because Christ, the true Lamb who takes away the sins of the world, remained to be sacrificed in his own time.

Yet because Noah was just, God took pleasure more in his devotion and pious will than in that smoke of animals; hence it is said: “And the Lord smelled a sweet savour.” No unclean animal is offered to God, because only the holy and those cleansed from sins please God. The statement that he will not curse the earth because of men is explained immediately afterward when he says: “Therefore I shall not strike every living creature as I did.” What, then, is it in this passage to curse? It is to strike or destroy.

And the reason is added: “For the inclination and thought of man are prone to evil”; human nature itself is fragile and pitiable, and unless protected by God’s help, easily slips into sin. It therefore appears worthy of receiving mercy. But why does he say, “from his youth”? Because one who sins in infancy and childhood does so more through ignorance [Col. 0183B] than through conscious thought and intention.

“All the days of the earth, seedtime and harvest, cold and heat, summer and winter, night and day, shall not cease.” How briefly and beautifully he has set forth every variation of the seasons, so as both to give us hope of a settled life and to remove the fear of a flood.

## CHAPTER IX

“And God blessed Noah and his sons and said to them: Increase and multiply and fill the earth; and let your fear and dread be upon all the animals of the earth and upon all the birds of the air, with everything that moves upon the earth. All the fish of the sea are delivered into your hand, and everything that moves and lives shall be food for you: as green herbs [Col. 0183C] I have given you all things, except that you shall not eat flesh with blood.”

Just as above the curse signifies destruction, so here the blessing signifies multiplication; and this blessing has been so powerful that it operates effectively everywhere even to this day. But what is there that does not fear man, before which the fearsome countenance of man does not appear? What is so fierce and untamed that it is not either conquered or domesticated by human skill? If understood allegorically, the saints increase daily and are a terror not only to men but even to demons themselves. And because everything that moves and lives is given to us for food and delivered to us as green herbs, let those who forbid us to eat meat be ashamed, and let them themselves, because they are weak, eat vegetables.

“For, according to the Apostle, all things are clean to the clean; but to the defiled and unbelieving nothing is clean” (Rom. XIV, 20). Just as all nations may receive the grace of faith, as was shown to the blessed apostle Peter (Acts X, 11), so it is not sinful to eat every food. Certain things, however, are harmful; some produce scandal; some are unpleasant or unpalatable; and these are not accepted as food even by Catholics. Custom also rejects many things which would not be sinful if consumed. For blessed John ate locusts, which are not even customary food among the Gentiles.

But when he says, “except that you shall not eat flesh with blood,” this belongs more to figure than to the letter. It is no sin to eat blood; it is forbidden by the apostles in the Acts of the Apostles solely in order that Jews coming to faith should not be scandalized (Acts XV, 29). Hence the Apostle says that he would rather not eat meat or drink wine than cause his brother to stumble (1 Cor. X, 28). Allegorically, to eat flesh with blood is to associate with heretics and criminal men who persist in their iniquities. Such people, therefore, should not be admitted to ecclesiastical communion before they are separated from blood. The prophet wished to be diminished in this blood when he said: “Deliver me from bloodguiltiness, O God, my God” (Ps. L, 16).

[Col. 0184B] “For I shall require the blood of your souls from the hand of every beast; and from the hand of man, from the hand of a man and his brother, I shall require [Note: The same M. A. codex: “his soul.”] his life. Whoever [Note: Likewise: “his blood shall be shed.”] sheds human blood, his blood shall be shed; for man was made in the image of God.”

Perhaps these are the beasts of whom the Psalmist said: “Do not deliver to beasts the souls confessing you” (Ps. LXXIII, 19), so that the death and blood of a human being may be required not only from men but even from demons themselves. We may also understand beasts as heretics and tyrants, who never cease to destroy God’s people by cunning and cruelty. This blood is required from the hand of man, just as Abel’s blood is required from the hand of Cain. Hence the Lord also says in the Gospel: “From that generation shall be required all righteous blood shed upon the earth, from the blood of righteous Abel to the blood of Zechariah son of Barachiah” (Matt. XXIII, 36).

It follows: “From the hand of a man I shall require the life of a man, and from the hand of his brother I shall require his life.” For we are all brothers: it is the Lord’s judgment. No one, therefore, will kill his neighbour and brother with impunity. Hence it is added: “Whoever sheds human blood, his blood shall be shed.” This does not mean that every murderer is killed temporally, but that unless he comes to his senses and repents, he will receive eternal death for the death he has caused. And this is fitting, for man was made in the image of God. Whoever, therefore, does not fear to shed human [Col. 0184D] blood should at least reverence in him the image of God.

“God also said this to Noah and to his sons: Behold, I shall establish my covenant with you and with your seed after you.” God established this covenant with Noah and every living creature: that he would no longer bring the waters of the Flood upon the earth. So that this might be believed firm and doubted in no way, he also established a sign to remain at all times between God and humanity as a testimony: namely, the rainbow. Seeing it, God would remember his covenant; and when man saw it, recognizing that God was not forgetful of him, he would be consoled, all fear expelled, by the brightness of so great a testimony. [Note: Ambrose thinks that the rainbow formed by the refraction of solar rays in a dewy cloud should not be taken as the sign promised by God to Noah, but that it signifies “the power of the invisible God, which, according to the divine will, governs through the appearance of this rainbow both stretching and relaxing—his mercy and power—which permits neither all things to be confused by excessive dissolution nor burst apart by excessive eruption.” *On Noah and the Ark*, cited passage, ch. 27, no. 104.]

And because the world was first judged by water and will again be judged by fire, the rainbow displays two principal colours: green, signifying water, and red, signifying fire.

“Now the sons of Noah who came out of the ark were Shem, Ham, and Japheth; from them the entire human race was dispersed.” [Note: The same M. A. codex: “the human race.”] It then follows that Noah planted a vineyard and, drinking, became drunk and lay naked in his tent. Ham saw him and mocked him, informing his brothers. They took a cloak and covered their father, not seeing their father’s shame; therefore they are blessed by their father, while he is subjected to curse and servitude.

But what do we understand by Noah except Christ, and by his vineyard [Col. 0185B] except the Jewish people? “For the vineyard of the Lord of hosts is the house of Israel” (Isa. V, 7). He drank its wine, namely the cup of death, of which he said to blessed Peter: “The cup which the Father has given me—would you not have me drink it?” (John XVIII, 11). Thus drunk with such a cup, he fell asleep when, bowing his head, he gave up his spirit.

But what nakedness, what shameful and mockable thing did his son Ham—that is, the Jewish people—see in him? What did they see that they should grieve over, be ashamed of, and desire to cover? Namely, that which Jews reproach us with to this day. They cast in our teeth the death of our Savior and the disgrace of the cross: that they worship the living God while we worship a dead man—a man captured, bound, scourged, spat upon, crowned with thorns, [Col. 0185C] given vinegar to drink, and finally crucified. These are his shameful things; these are what we blush to see; these are what we strive to cover with the cloak of reasons and the testimony of the prophets.

Hence the Apostle says: “Christ died once for our sins” (1 Pet. III, 18)—“but in that he lives, he lives to God” (Rom. VI, 10). He himself, covering his nakedness, said: “O foolish and slow of heart to believe all that the prophets have spoken! Was it not necessary that Christ should suffer thus, rise from the dead, and so enter into his glory?” (Luke XXIV, 25). Such nakedness therefore requires such a covering.

These two brothers are Gentiles: they are Greek and Latin. For in these two languages the glory of God is proclaimed and [Col. 0185D] Jewish obstinacy is overcome.

## CHAPTER X

“But Noah, awakening from the wine, when he learned what his younger son had done to him, said: Canaan is cursed; he shall be a servant of servants to his brothers.”

Canaan was the son of Ham, from whom sprang the Canaanites, Hittites, Jebusites, Hivites, Amorites, and the rest who inhabited the land of promise and resisted God’s people. The Israelites killed some of them and subjected others to servitude, so that the saying might be fulfilled: “He shall be a servant of servants to his brothers.” Therefore Ham is not cursed, but Canaan, from whom these peoples derive their origin.

Canaan is interpreted “merchant,” and by him we understand the Jews, who, because they bartered their Lord for thirty pieces of silver, serve in servitude among every nation; deservedly they are called not merely servants but servants of servants. It follows: “And he said: Blessed be the Lord God of Shem; let Canaan be his servant. May God enlarge Japheth, and may he dwell in the tents of Shem; and let Canaan be his servant.”

From Shem—whose name is rightly interpreted “named”—was born Abraham and the whole Hebrew people; from him arose the patriarchs [Col. 0186B] and prophets. From him too, according to the flesh, our Savior and all the apostles derive their origin; it is beyond doubt that not only the Canaanites but all nations serve them. Therefore, in his blessings he says that Japheth shall dwell in the tents of Shem—that is, either in the churches founded by the apostles or in those dwelling places of which the Lord said: “In my Father’s house are many dwelling places” (John XIV, 2).

For from Japheth, whose name is interpreted “breadth,” sprang the Gentile people, who ruled not only the Canaanites but all nations.

## CHAPTER XI
The subject is how Noah’s sons came to the plain of Shinar and, wishing to make a famous name for themselves, began to build there a tower whose summit would touch heaven. [Col. 0186C] But the Lord, coming down, confused their language so that they could not understand one another; hence that place is called Babel, which means “confusion.” And so they were scattered throughout all the lands. [Note: [Col. 0186D] The same manuscript: “were divided.”] For all spoke one and the same language, which we certainly believe to have been Hebrew. [Note: [Col. 0186D] Natalis Alexander shows that this was the more common opinion of the Holy Fathers, *History of the Old Testament*, proposition IV, and teaches that this language was coeval with the world itself.] But pride and vain glory confused it; and whereas all the nations of the world had been able mutually to understand one another, now, within a small tract of land, they are unable to understand one another, as though irrational creatures. For God always hates pride; therefore he humbles the proud and exalts the humble. Thus the devil also, when he wished to raise his throne above the heights of heaven, was cast down. [Note: [Col. 0186D] The Laurentian manuscript here corrects a very corrupt edition.]

Therefore the Lord came down upon the mountain—or rather, he did not come down, since he is everywhere. For one who comes down is not where he comes down from. He came down, then, not in himself, but through angels subject to him. Therefore, calling them, he said: “Come, let us go down and confuse their language there”; that is, “Go down; bear me with you; possess my power and authority within yourselves; do in my name whatever shall be useful and necessary.” Thus the Lord came down.

[Col. 0187A] “These are the generations of Terah. Terah begot Abraham, Nahor, and Haran. Moreover Haran begot Lot. And Haran died before Terah his father, in the land of his birth, in Ur of the Chaldeans.” The Hebrews relate that Haran, because he refused to sacrifice to idols, perished after being handed over to the fire by the Chaldeans before his father—that is, in his father’s sight. For *Ur* means “fire.” Abraham too, for the same reason, was thrown into fire and delivered by God’s help; and with his father, wife, and nephew Lot he fled, intending to go into the land of Canaan. They came as far as Aram and dwelt there. [Note: [Col. 0187D] All critics reject this narrative as a fable, although it had some credibility with Jerome, whose footsteps Bruno followed. See Ludovico Vives, notes on book XVI, chapter 15, of *The City of God*.]

## CHAPTER XII

“But the Lord said to Abraham: ‘Go out from your land, from your kindred, and from your father’s house [Col. 0187B] and come into the land which I shall show you; and I shall make you into a great nation and bless you.’” At the beginning of his address, the Lord commands Abraham to do a most difficult thing. In this Abraham’s faith is especially commended: immediately leaving his home, he obeyed the command of the one commanding him. Abraham is not permitted to dwell long in one place, but is always moved from place to place, so that we may readily understand that we are strangers in this world and have here no abiding city, but seek the city to come (Heb. 13:14). But when he says, “And in you all the kindreds of the earth shall be blessed,” this means in the seed that shall arise from you—namely, in Christ—from whom, in whom, and through whom all are blessed, and without [Col. 0187C] whom no one is blessed.

“They went out from Aram in order to go into the land of Canaan,” which they had earlier purposed to reach. “And the Lord appeared to Abraham and said to him: ‘To your seed I shall give this land.’ And he built there an altar to the Lord who had appeared to him, and invoked his name.” Since the Lord himself says, “No man shall see me and live” (John 1:18), and the Apostle says, “No one has ever seen God” (1 John 4:12), how is it said that the Lord appeared to Abraham? The Lord did not appear to Abraham in himself—that is, in his own substance, which is indeed ineffable and invisible—but through an angel. [Note: [Col. 0187D] This is also the opinion of St Augustine, who says in book XVI, chapter 29, of *The City of God*: “It belongs indeed to divine power and to the invisible, incorporeal, and unchangeable nature, without any alteration of itself, to appear even to mortal eyes—not through that which it is, but through something subject to it. And what is not subject to it?” [Col. 0188D]] Having heard so great a promise, Abraham, though poor and a stranger, was neither unbelieving nor ungrateful; at once he built an altar and [Col. 0187D] gave God thanks for what had been promised, leaving, clearly, a great example to posterity.

“And there was a famine in the land. Abraham went down into Egypt and asked his wife to say that she was his sister, lest he should be killed on account of her beauty.” The woman was therefore taken into Pharaoh’s house, for which reason the Lord struck him with very severe plagues. [Col. 0188A] Twice Sarah was carried off because of her beauty, but, with the Lord protecting her, she was not violated. Thus we read in the book of Esther (Esth. 2): for six months such women were anointed with myrrh, and for six months with certain other perfumes, before they were brought before kings. During this period, therefore, as it is written, the Lord rebuked kings on their account; and the woman was always returned untouched and undefiled to her husband. Some think that both Pharaoh and Abimelech were struck with severe afflictions in the private parts of their bodies, so that, for as long as they had Sarah with them, they could not have intercourse with women. Hence, once they knew the cause, they did not resist but most willingly returned her to her husband.

## CHAPTER XIII

[Col. 0188B] Let no one blame Abraham as though he had compelled his wife to lie, so that, being his wife, she falsely said that she was his sister. In fact, as Abraham himself admits, Sarah was his sister by their father, though not by their mother; for they both had one father, but not the same mother. If anyone maintains that this is false because it was written above, “Terah took Abraham his son and Sarah his daughter-in-law” (Gen. 11:31), and did not say “his daughter,” Abraham defends himself by that saying: “You are all brothers, for one is your Father who is in heaven” (Matt. 23:9); it is the Lord who speaks. According to this, therefore, both Abraham and Sarah are shown to have one [Col. 0188C] father, even if not one mother.

## CHAPTER XIV

Next follows how Lot was captured and how Abraham, having counted his three hundred and eighteen household-born servants, delivered him. Further, how Melchizedek, king of Salem and priest of God Most High, brought forth bread and wine, blessed him, and received tithes. For Abraham, whose name means “exalted father,” signifies the holy Church. And what is Melchizedek but Christ, of whom the Apostle speaks most fully in the Epistle to the Hebrews? Abraham—that is, almighty God—therefore took his three hundred and eighteen household-born servants, that is, the three hundred and eighteen priests whom he gathered at the Council of Nicaea, and through them delivered Lot—that is, the holy Church—which was already declining into heresy. [Col. 0188D] [Note: [Col. 0188D] Not that the whole Church could fall away from the Catholic faith, contrary to Christ’s promise made to Peter: “I have prayed for you, Peter, that your faith may not fail” (Luke 22:32); rather, the Arian heresy had begun to prevail.] Having slain the rulers and condemned heretical perversity, he confirmed the Catholic faith.

Over this victory Melchizedek—that is, Christ our Lord, king of peace and righteousness—rejoicing, he who first offered himself in sacrifice to God the Father, from that time onward, his enemies having been overcome and the priesthood confirmed, does not cease daily through his servants to offer bread [Col. 0189A] and wine—that is, his flesh and blood—to God the Father. Christ receives tithes from the Father because he assumed flesh on account of the tenth drachma, and came into this world on account of the hundredth sheep—which is itself also a tenth. But it should be known that allegory sometimes follows the history, and sometimes the interpretation of names. Hence Abraham, whose name means “exalted father,” is greater than Melchizedek according to the interpretation of the name, but lesser according to the history. Therefore the Apostle, speaking of these matters, says (Heb. 7): “Without controversy, the lesser is blessed by the greater,” indicating the lesser Abraham, whom Melchizedek blesses. Christ also, though equal to the Father according to divinity, is lesser than the Father insofar as he was made [Col. 0189B] a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek.

## CHAPTER XV

Again the word of the Lord came to Abraham, promising him an heir and a seed comparable to the stars. “Abraham believed God, and it was reckoned to him as righteousness” (Rom. 4:3). Abraham and his wife were already approaching old age, though the Lord repeatedly promised him a son and yet did not give him one. Abraham knew that God could not lie; therefore, against hope, he believed in hope. Faith overcame nature; believing that nothing was impossible to God, and at God’s command, he did not despair of having a son at any age. Because he believed thus, because he had this faith, it was reckoned to him as righteousness. Therefore faith produces righteousness (Rom. 4:3): not circumcision but [Col. 0189C] faith makes a person righteous, for Abraham had not yet been circumcised.

“And the Lord said to him: ‘I am the Lord who brought you out of Ur of the Chaldeans to give you this land, that you may possess it.’ But he said: ‘Lord God, how may I know that I shall possess it?’ And the Lord answered: ‘Take for me a three-year-old heifer, a three-year-old she-goat, and a three-year-old ram, and also a turtledove and a dove.’” By these animals the whole offspring of the Jews, and all who descend from Abraham’s stock, are signified. By the heifer is signified that part of the people which, serving the Lord, humbly bore the yoke of the law; by the she-goat, the other part, transgressing, sinful, and serving idols; by the ram, the leaders of the people—that is, judges, kings, and princes. By the turtledove and dove, however, he signifies prophets and priests. They are aptly said to be three years old, because the kingdom, strength, and power of the Hebrews endured, flourished, and thrived through three ages, as through three years. The first age was from Abraham, to whom these things are shown, to David; the second from David to the Babylonian deportation; the third from the Babylonian deportation to Christ. Each of these ages has fourteen generations. In this sacrifice, then, God showed Abraham how great and what kind of a people would arise from his stock, how long [Col. 0190A] it would reign, and how great the adversities it would suffer.

“He took all these things, divided them down the middle, and placed each half opposite the other; but he did not divide the birds. And birds of prey came down upon the carcasses, and Abraham drove them away.” The birds are rightly not divided while the others are, because unity and concord reign only among spiritual and Catholic men, who are understood through the birds. But the birds of prey descending upon the carcasses are vices and evil spirits, which always seek, with insatiable greed, to tear apart and rend the people of God. But Abraham drives them away; by him we understand holy and apostolic men, who always protect and defend the holy Church from their snares.

“And when the sun was setting, a deep sleep fell upon [Col. 0190B] Abraham, and a great dark terror seized him. And it was said to him: ‘Know beforehand that your seed shall be a stranger in a land not its own; they shall subject them to slavery and afflict them for four hundred years. Yet I shall judge the nation whom they shall serve, and afterwards they shall come out with great possessions. But you shall go to your fathers in peace and be buried in a good old age. In the fourth generation they shall return here, for the iniquities of the Amorites are not yet complete up to the present time.’”—“When,” he says, “the sun was setting,” and night was already approaching, “a deep sleep fell upon Abraham.” Since, as often happens, he saw strange and dreadful things, “a great dark terror seized him.” For he could not but be frightened when such things were shown him by divine revelation, even though in sleep. “Therefore it was said to him: ‘Know,’” says the angel speaking to him, “and know long before it comes to pass, that ‘your seed shall be a stranger in a land not its own,’” that is, in Egypt, “and the Egyptians shall subject them to slavery and afflict them for forty years.” This is narrated more fully in Exodus. “Yet I shall judge the nation whom they serve,” because he powerfully afflicted all Egypt with ten plagues; but the Hebrews, having despoiled Egypt, went out with great possessions. “But you shall go to your fathers in peace,” that is, peacefully and quietly, “and be buried in a good old age”; but they themselves “shall return here in the fourth generation.” This is true [Col. 0190D] if generations are counted not according to Judah but according to Levi. “For the iniquities of the Amorites are not yet complete”—for “sin, when it is completed, brings forth death” (Jas. 1:15). Therefore let the filthy become still filthier, lest perhaps he should turn and be healed. For he is wicked who refuses to repent; and the longer he is awaited by the Lord, the more deserving he is of a greater punishment, and he shall have no excuse.

“And when the sun had set, there was a dark gloom; and a smoking furnace and a lamp of fire appeared, passing between those divisions.” The setting of the sun, which is the end of the day, signifies the end of this age. [Note: [Col. 0189D] So also Augustine, *The City of God*, book XVI, chapter 5.] The dark gloom is that of which it is said: “The sun shall be darkened, and the moon shall not give its light” (Matt. [Col. 0191A] 24:29). There are also the darknesses which the wicked shall suffer in hell. The smoking furnace and lamp of fire are the conflagration of this age, by which the whole world will be terribly set ablaze at the last judgment. The fire is rightly said to have passed between those divisions, yet not to have consumed the carcasses, because, once judgment has been completed and all have been made immortal, the fire will be able to pass through them but will not be able utterly to burn and consume them. But if by the setting of the sun Christ’s death is understood, and by the gloom the darknesses that occurred at his passion, what are the furnace and lamp of fire but the Holy Spirit, who descended upon the apostles on the fiftieth day and passed through them? It follows:

“On that day he made a covenant with Abraham, saying: [Col. 0191B] ‘To your seed I shall give this land.’” He then describes the boundaries of the land which he would give him. For when such great mysteries had been revealed, and nothing remained by which Abraham could doubt, a covenant is fittingly made with him and the future inheritance is described.

## CHAPTER XVI

Here follows the account that Abraham, at his wife’s request, lay with her handmaid Hagar and begot Ishmael; but when Sarah, her mistress, afflicted her and she fled from her presence, she was warned by an angel and returned to her mistress. The Apostle explains what is to be understood by these two women: “These are the two covenants” (Gal. 4:24), wishing Sarah to be understood as the Church and Hagar as the Synagogue. Hence Isaac signifies the children of the Church, but Ishmael the children of the Synagogue. Hagar bore before Sarah, because the Synagogue bore before the Church. How the Church afflicted the Synagogue—unless perhaps by preaching the faith of Christ, which it refuses to hear—I do not know. Yet the Synagogue is also temporally afflicted in many places by the children of the Church, by paying taxes and performing other services of subjection. The angel who warns Hagar to return to her mistress signifies the teachers of the Church, who very often urge the Jews to turn to faith in Christ and to the Church. Therefore Hagar shall return to her mistress, if not now, yet at some time, because “when the fullness of the Gentiles has entered, then all [Col. 0191D] Israel shall be saved” (Rom. 11:25). But what follows concerning Ishmael, that he was “a wild man, and his hand against all, and the hand of all against him,” does not apply to the historical account. But since, as has been said, Ishmael signifies the children of the Synagogue, it is clear that he agrees and is at peace with no nation. For while he strives to defend the law and circumcision, he is attacked not only by Christians but also by the other nations; and since every religion except his own displeases him, he contends with all in verbose disputation. Therefore all hate his tents, all abhor the synagogues of the Jews—those who wish indeed to contend but refuse to yield to truth and [Col. 0192A] reason.

And Hagar said: “Surely here I have seen the back parts of him who sees me.” [Note: [Col. 0191D] The Laurentian manuscript: “Surely here I have seen the back parts of him who sees me; therefore she called that well, ‘of the living one, and of him who sees me.’”] Hagar, fleeing, is warned by the angel to return to her mistress; perhaps recognizing that this would benefit her, she says: “You are God, who have heard me, as though you had given me healthful counsel”; and she added: “Surely here I have seen the back parts of him who sees me.” It has also been said that Hagar signifies the Synagogue, and the angel the teachers of the Church. Therefore let Hagar say, let the Synagogue say: “True, O teachers, are the things you say; you announce what is beneficial to me. Therefore I shall return to the Church; I shall return to my mistress. For I see what I saw: I see Christ my Lord; I see his back parts, though I despised his front. He is present in this place, and I did not know him; he passed by, and now I know him—whom, indeed, I should not have known unless [Col. 0192B] I had come to the well.” Thus the Samaritan woman deserved to know him at the well. This well is the New Testament. Read the Gospel if you wish to know Christ. This well is called the well of the living one and of him who sees me: of the living one, because the Synagogue thought him dead; and of him who sees me, because, although it had grievously offended him, he nevertheless always looked upon it mercifully.

## CHAPTER XVII

A lengthy history is then described: God appeared to Abraham, made an everlasting covenant with him, and, adding one letter, called him Abraham; and he promised him the entire land of Canaan as an everlasting possession. He also changed Sarai’s name [Col. 0192C] and called her Sarah. Moreover, he commanded Abraham to circumcise the flesh of his foreskin. “For the male who is not circumcised shall perish from among his people.” Abraham fittingly grew in name when a son was promised to him, in whom he was to inherit all nations. Hence it is said: “Your name shall no longer be called Abram, but your name shall be Abraham, because I have made you father of many nations.” Sarai, however, who is called “our princess,” had her name conversely shortened, so that she is no longer called “our princess” but simply “princess”; for such is the meaning of Sarah. As we have said, she signifies the Church, which is princess not of one people but of all nations. Concerning Abraham’s circumcision, the Apostle says in the Epistle to the Romans that “he received the sign of circumcision, a seal of the righteousness of faith” (Rom. 4:11). Circumcision, therefore, is a sign, and it is also a seal of the righteousness of faith. It is a sign so that the people who were to be scattered among all nations might be recognized by all. But it is a seal of righteousness so that, through the removal of that superfluity, the children of the Church might understand that they cannot otherwise be faithful and righteous unless, with all their members circumcised, they cast away from themselves everything superfluous and harmful. The Jews are circumcised in one member, but we in all our members. A circumcised foot does not run [Col. 0193A] toward evil. A circumcised hand does not strike the innocent. A circumcised tongue does not speak falsehood. A circumcised ear does not wish to hear detraction. Hear, finally, what is written: “Circumcise your hearts and your bodies” (Joel 2:13). And blessed Stephen, speaking to the Jews, said: “Stiff-necked, and uncircumcised in hearts and ears, you always resist the Holy Spirit” (Acts 7:51). These things alone suffice against those who wish to understand everything literally; or, if they do not suffice, let them cut off their ears and cut their hearts—which we have heard no one has done to this day. Therefore either they do not understand this, or, if they understand, they neglect to do it.

## CHAPTER XVIII

Concerning the three men who appeared to Abraham: [Note: [Col. 0193D] “Three men appeared,” etc. St Ambrose, book I of *On Abraham*: “He believed that these three men, of whom the present discourse treats, represented the most holy persons of the Trinity.” Other Fathers—such as Irenaeus, book III, chapter 6, and book IV, chapter 23; Tertullian, book II *Against Marcion*, chapter 27; Justin, in the *Dialogue with Trypho*; and Hilary, book IV *On the Trinity*—held that two were angels and that the third was the Son of God, the second person of the Trinity. The Church seems to have embraced this view in its office, where it repeats the verse, not found in Scripture but in the Holy Fathers, as in Augustine, book II *Against Maximinus*, chapter 6, article 3: “He saw three and worshipped one.” [Col. 0194D]]

Meeting them, he worshipped and said: “Lord, if [Col. 0193B] I have found favor in your eyes, do not pass by your servant; but I shall bring a little water, and let your feet be washed.” When they consented, Abraham took butter, milk, and a calf which he had cooked, and set them before them. After they had eaten, they said that when a year had elapsed, at the same time Sarah would have a son. Then they rose and went toward Sodom, while Abraham was seeing them on their way. And the Lord said to him: “The outcry of Sodom and Gomorrah is multiplied, and their sin is exceedingly grievous; therefore I shall go down there.” So the two angels went to Sodom, but Abraham remained standing and spoke with the Lord. Abraham always grows in faith, and always deserves to learn greater things concerning God. [Note: [Col. 0194D] The greatly erroneous edition is corrected from the Laurentian manuscript.] For behold: what had before then been unknown to all, he beholds God in Trinity and worships him in unity—not because he saw the Trinity itself, but because through what he saw he deserved to know God in Trinity and unity. Thus, though he saw three, he worshipped only one and called only one “Lord.” For of this the Lord says in the Gospel: “Abraham your father rejoiced that he might see my day; he saw it and rejoiced” (John 8:56).

For angels, when they wish, assume a body from the air, by which they may be seen, touched, speak, eat, and drink. For as air is body, so also are bodies which are assumed from the air. They put these on temporarily, and, after putting them off, are immediately dissolved again into the same air. The angel [Col. 0193D] Raphael, speaking to Tobias, says: “Peace be with you; do not fear. For when I was with you by the will of God, I seemed indeed to be with you and to eat and drink, but I use invisible food and drink which cannot be seen by human beings” (Tob. 12:17). According to this statement, then, let those to whom it seems impossible that angels should eat and drink understand that the other angels also eat and drink. Moses nevertheless testifies that they ate, saying: “And when they had eaten, they said to him: ‘Where is Sarah your wife?’ He answered: ‘Behold, she is in the tent.’ And he said to him: ‘Returning, I shall come to you at this time, and Sarah your wife shall have a son.’ When she heard this, Sarah laughed.” Menstruation had now ceased for her; the time of her monthly flow had passed, after which, by the law of nature, it is impossible for a woman to bear. Hence Sarah is rebuked by the Lord for laughing. Although Abraham himself is also said above to have laughed, he is not rebuked, because he laughed not in doubt but in wonder; for he knew that nothing was impossible for God.

There follows the sin of the Sodomites and Gomorrahites, which, because of its magnitude, [Col. 0194B] is called an outcry. Thus it is said also of Cain’s sin: “Behold, the blood of your brother cries out to me from the ground” (Gen. 3:10). Sins, therefore, cry out; nor can they be hidden according to human wishes. They always press upon and trouble the ears of God. Yet wonderful is the Creator’s patience: he does not immediately punish, nor, rashly believing the accusing outcry, does he condemn them, though he knows all things; rather, he comes down and sees whether the reports concerning sinners are true—giving human beings a great example, namely, that no one should rashly pronounce judgment. This is what is said: “I shall go down and see whether they have fulfilled in deed the outcry which has come to me, or whether it is not so, that I may know.” Therefore the two angels turned from there and went to Sodom. But Abraham [Col. 0194C] remained standing and spoke with the Lord, and by his prayers obtained from him that, if even ten righteous persons had been found there, those cities would not be destroyed. Unhappy, then, and already near destruction is the city which, abounding only in sinners, did not deserve to have holy and righteous men.

## CHAPTER XIX

The two angels therefore came to Sodom. Lot invited them—or rather, compelled them—to lodge with him. But the men of the city violently surrounded the house in order wickedly to abuse them. To prevent this, Lot offered his two daughters. But while they still continued importunately, from the least to the greatest, they were struck with blindness. Lot, with his wife and daughters, went out following the angels. [Col. 0194D] But his wife, looking back, was turned into a pillar of salt. Great is the virtue of hospitality, through which the patriarchs themselves are shown to have pleased the Lord. Great is the iniquity of the Sodomites, who do not blush so shamelessly to defile even unknown men. But what shall I say of Lot, who, to protect his guests, did not spare his own daughters? [Note: [Col. 0194D] Ambrose excuses this offering of the daughters in order that no more criminal act might be committed against the angels. “For although,” he says, “that impurity too was shameful, yet it was less contrary to nature to have intercourse than to sin against nature.” *On Abraham*, book I, chapter 6, no. 52.]

Allegorically, the two angels are the two Testaments; for through their proclamation we have received whatever wisdom and knowledge we possess. By their sentence the wicked are condemned; by their counsel the good are delivered. But the Sodomites signify heretics, who always try to adulterate the word of God, and, abusing both Testaments by wrongly understanding and expounding them, strive wickedly to violate them. Lot, however, whose name means “turning aside,” signifies the holy Church, whose constant concern is to turn away from evil and do good. By his two daughters, I think, are signified our flesh and the property we possess. The saints of God despise these daughters; they expose them, I say, to fury, and prefer to be deprived of them rather than sin against God’s law or fail to defend the purity of the Testaments. But what [Col. 0195B] is signified by Lot’s wife, except that foolish people among Christians who, neglecting to persevere in good, easily lapse back into former sins? To such persons the Lord says: “No one who puts his hand to the plough and looks back is fit for the kingdom of God” (Luke 9:62). The woman was fittingly turned into a pillar of salt, so that through her example she might furnish the others with wisdom lest they suffer such things. Lot also rightly wished to bring out with him his two sons-in-law, because we ought, if we can, to deliver from death even those whom we love in the flesh. But they were unwilling to leave Sodom; therefore they perished with the entire city.

What does it mean that “the sun had risen over the earth and Lot entered Zoar,” except that, when the Sun of righteousness, the Lord Jesus Christ, comes for judgment and holy men are received into Zoar—that is, into the heavenly homeland—fire will immediately descend upon Sodom, namely that fire which is to burn the whole world? [Col. 0195C] For Zoar means “small”: “Many are called, but few are chosen” (Matt. 20:16). Zoar, therefore, is small because the elect are few. [Note: [Col. 0195D] He teaches the same elsewhere, as in the homily on the Septuagesima, the homily on the Second Sunday after Pentecost, and book I, chapter 2, of the *Sentences*, *On Noah’s Ark*. Many other Fathers hold the same view; their testimonies were collected by Petrus Franciscus Fogginius in the book entitled: *The Fathers of the Church on the Small Number of Adult Believers Who Shall Be Saved*, etc.] Let no one doubt that judgment takes place before the fire.

Lot went up from Zoar and dwelt on a mountain. His two daughters also, thinking that no men remained on earth, took counsel together; making their father drunk, they lay with him, conceived by him, and bore Moab and Ammon. Here history alone is narrated. This appears impossible to some because they do not believe that someone can lie with a woman unknowingly. But we know that semen is sometimes emitted unknowingly in sleep; and if it were received into a generative womb, we do not doubt that it could produce offspring. Nor do we think Lot, who could become drunk, sinned less than the daughters, who were prompted not by the impulses of lust but by love of children, lest the human race should utterly perish. [Col. 0195D] [Note: [Col. 0196D] Ambrose has the same account in *On Abraham*, chapter 6, no. 56.]

## CHAPTER XX

It follows that Abraham departed from there [Col. 0196A] and came into the southern land. There also, as above, he said that Sarah was his sister. Abimelech therefore took her, on account of which he himself, his wife, and his maidservants were afflicted by the Lord. This was explained above, where Sarah was said to have been taken by Pharaoh for the same reason. But when it is said that, “Abraham praying, God healed Abimelech, his wife, and his maidservants, and they bore children,” this is what we said above: they had been afflicted in their genitals so that they could not have intercourse with one another. Hence it is added: “For God had closed every womb of the house of Abimelech because of Sarah, Abraham’s wife.” For as long as he desired to misuse another man’s wife, he could not use his own.

## CHAPTER XXI

[Col. 0196B] The Lord visited Sarah, and she bore a son at the time which God had foretold to her. Abraham called his name Isaac, which means “laughter” or “joy.” Hence she says: “God has made laughter for me; whoever hears shall laugh with me.” And again she says: “Who would have believed that Abraham would hear that Sarah was nursing the son whom she bore him, now that he was already old?” Therefore the child grew and was weaned, and Abraham made a great feast on the day of his weaning. A great feast is fittingly held on the day of weaning, so that, separated from milk, he may find great delights to enjoy. Hence the Apostle says: “I gave you milk to drink, not solid food” (1 Cor. 3:2). Why? “For you were not yet able” (ibid.). But what is said of those who have been weaned? “We speak wisdom among the perfect” [Col. 0196C] (1 Cor. 2:6). This is the great feast; this Abraham, this the Apostles, prepare for their children, now weaned and torn away from the breasts.

“And when Sarah saw the son of Hagar the Egyptian playing with Isaac, she said to Abraham: ‘Cast out the slave-woman and her son, for the son of the slave-woman shall not be heir with my son Isaac.’ Therefore Abraham rose early, took bread and a skin of water, placed it on Hagar’s shoulder, gave her the boy, and dismissed her. When she had gone away and wandered in the wilderness of Beersheba, and the water was now exhausted, she placed the boy beneath one of the trees there.” But the Lord, having compassion, heard the boy and showed her a well of water. I think Ishmael had provoked Isaac to a shameful and dishonorable game, at which Sarah was so impatiently indignant. For because he desired to deprive him of his birthright, he incited him to disgraceful acts. We have said above that Sarah signifies the Church and Hagar the Synagogue; the Apostle himself testifies to this (Gal. 4:25). Literally, I believe that the Synagogue was rejected with her son when Jerusalem was captured and the Jews were scattered among all nations. Spiritually, however, it was cast out when, because the Jews refused to hear the word of God, [Col. 0197A] the Apostles turned to the Gentiles. Hence the Apostle says: “It was necessary that the word of God should first be preached to you; but because you have rejected it and judged yourselves unworthy of eternal life, behold, we turn to the Gentiles” (Acts 13:47). The Synagogue was therefore cast out; it carried bread and a skin of water—that is, the law and the prophets—with which to feed its adulterous children. For the Jews carry and read these everywhere, but do not understand them. It follows:

“When she had gone away and wandered in the wilderness of Beersheba,” etc. [Note: [Col. 0197D] The sense, mutilated in the edition, is supplied from the same Laurentian manuscript.] The Synagogue wanders, then—indeed, wanders. But where does it wander? In the wilderness. In what wilderness? In the wilderness of Beersheba, that is, beside the well of abundance; for this is the meaning of Beersheba. By the well of abundance we may understand the Church, around which the Hebrews dwell in many places, or the law itself which they carry. They wander around it because they misunderstand it. This may readily be proved from the fact that whenever they dispute with us, they quickly fail, quickly have nothing to offer, and quickly the water in their skin dries up; but our water does not dry up, because it is the Spirit who speaks, whom no one can resist. It follows:

“When the water in the skin was used up, she cast the boy beneath one of the trees,” etc. For whenever the Jews fail in disputation, whenever they do not find in the Law and the Prophets suitable testimonies to bring forward against the Christian faith, then the water dries up in their skin. This indeed benefits them when, pierced with compunction, they turn to Christ [Col. 0197C; Note: Col. 0198D: The Laurentian manuscript, with which the Cassinese agrees]. Hence it follows that “the Lord heard the voice of the boy, showed him a well of water, filled the skin, and he drank.” We understand this well to be the holy Church, the New Testament, and the Gospels. Therefore, Jews, come here; approach here weeping and repentant; drink from this water; fill the skin of the Law from this source; and apply spiritual understanding to the dry letter. For although you will not do this now, you will nevertheless do so at some time, as the Apostle says: “When the fullness of the Gentiles has entered, then all Israel will be saved” (Rom. 11:25). Then Hagar—that is, the Synagogue—will fill the skin and give living, new water to the thirsty and dying Ishmael—that is, the Jewish people—water which she will draw from the Church’s ever-full and ever-abundant springs.

[Col. 0197D] Concerning Abraham and Abimelech’s making a covenant with one another, that they should not harm each other; and concerning the restoration of the well which Abimelech’s servants had violently taken away; and Abraham’s giving Abimelech sheep, oxen, and seven ewe-lambs: for Abraham means “father of many nations,” whereas Abimelech means “my father is king.” What, then, are we to understand by these two fathers except soul and flesh? If they agree with one another, having nothing soft or effeminate, but possessing all that is manly and masculine, they are rightly called fathers rather than mothers. Hence Truth itself says: “If two of you agree concerning anything they ask, it shall be done for them” (Matt. 18:19). But since the soul possesses understanding, counsel, and reason, which the flesh does not possess, they cannot otherwise agree in turn unless the flesh follows the soul.

Therefore Abraham, a holy and spiritual man, signifies the soul; Abimelech, however, a carnal and worldly man, denotes the flesh. Abimelech’s servants—that is, the gluttony, drunkenness, lust, and similar things of the flesh—are understood as those which serve the flesh alone. By the well which these most wicked servants took away from Abraham—that is, from the soul—we understand the fountain of wisdom, which cannot exist together with them. Hence it is written: “Wisdom shall not enter into a malicious soul, nor dwell in a body subject to sins” (Wis. 1:4).

Therefore, once the well of wisdom has been restored to the soul and the flesh has now been subdued, Abraham—that is, the soul—gives to Abimelech—that is, to the flesh—sheep, so that it may live simply; and oxen, so that it may no longer serve vices, but, bearing Christ’s yoke, which is sweet, may begin to labor in his field. Moreover, he gives it seven ewe-lambs, that is, the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit, which are always a testimony of the covenant [Note: Col. 0198D: The text is corrected from the same Laurentian manuscript], so that it may no longer allow its servants to wage war against the soul. This agreement was properly made with Phichol, commander of the army, intervening; for Phichol, whose name means “mouth of all,” signifies wisdom, which both makes the tongues of infants eloquent and without which true peace and concord cannot exist.

## Chapter XXII

[Col. 0198C]

“After these things had been done, God tested Abraham and said to him: Take your only son, whom you love, Isaac, and go into the land of vision; and there offer him as a burnt offering upon one of the mountains which I shall show you.”

Abraham is commanded to sacrifice his son on that mountain upon which Christ the Lord was crucified. For the mountain of vision is Zion, which itself is interpreted “vision” or “watching-place.” Although the two events did not occur in the same place, they occurred on the same mountain, so that God might most fittingly show what he wished this sacrifice to signify.

Isaac is therefore led to the victim; and although he could have resisted, he nevertheless willingly permits himself to be bound and laid upon the altar. Josephus indeed says this: he was already of such an age that, if he wished, he could easily have overcome his father; but after he learned that God had commanded this, he willingly gave himself up to be sacrificed, lest he resist God’s will. Which of the two, then, Abraham or Isaac, is more praiseworthy in this matter is not easily apparent. Abraham, however, hoped that his son would immediately rise again if he were slain, since he knew that God could not lie. For how could the nation compared to the stars of heaven be born from Isaac if he did not rise after death?

Abraham is therefore forbidden to kill the boy. He calls him “boy,” however, according to the customary manner of speaking, just as those advanced in age were also accustomed to be called boys. “Then Abraham, looking back [Note: Col. 0199D: Manuscript of the Biblioteca M. A.: ‘He saw a ram behind him,’ etc.], saw a ram caught by its horns among the brambles; and, taking it, he offered it as a burnt offering in place of his son.” Abraham is praised for his deed, blessed by the Lord, and promised an unconquerable offspring, in whom all nations should be blessed. By this offspring Christ is understood: whoever is not blessed in him is not blessed.

Allegorically, Abraham—whose name is interpreted “father of many nations” or “exalted father”—signifies God the Father, of whom it is written: “The Lord is exalted above all nations” (Ps. 112:4). Isaac, however, signifies his Son Jesus Christ, who himself became obedient to the Father unto death. The altar signifies the cross upon which he was sacrificed. The ram sacrificed in Isaac’s stead [Col. 0199B] is Christ’s flesh. For Christ is God and man: according to divinity, immortal and incapable of suffering; according to humanity, capable of suffering and mortal. Therefore, with Christ placed upon the cross, the ram alone is sacrificed, the lamb alone is slain, the flesh alone is crucified; for Christ did not suffer according to divinity. This, therefore, is the reason why a ram was sacrificed in place of Isaac.

And the brambles clinging about the ram’s horns and head—do they not seem to you to be the thorny crown upon the Savior’s head? But what does it mean that the Lord says to Abraham: “Now I know that you fear God”? Did he not know before? It is as though he said: Now, by testing and proving you, I have come to know you—that is, I have made known to all nations that you fear the Lord. For unless Abraham had been tested, his obedience would not have been known.

## Chapter XXIII

Sarah lived one hundred and twenty-seven years and died. Abraham, having bought a field, buried her in the double cave, in which Adam and Eve, Abraham and Sarah, Isaac and Rebekah are said to have been buried, and to which Jacob was brought from Egypt. What, then, do we understand by the double cave in which the bodies of the patriarchs rest, except the heavenly homeland? It is called double because it bestows double blessings upon the saints. Hence it is written: “They shall possess double things in their land” (Isa. 61:7). There, until the Judgment, the souls alone will enjoy blessedness; after the Judgment, however, souls and bodies will enjoy eternal blessedness. [Col. 0199D] Rightly, therefore, the holy man, filled with the Spirit of God, wished to bury his wife not in the tombs of the Canaanites but in this most noble cave.

## Chapter XXIV

After this it is related how Abraham commanded his servant to place his hand beneath his thigh and swear that he would take no wife for his son Isaac except from among his own kindred. The servant therefore did what he had been commanded: he took ten camels from his master’s herd, loaded them with all his master’s goods, and, traveling into Mesopotamia, found Rebekah, daughter of Bethuel, son of Nahor, Abraham’s brother. She had come to the well to draw water. He gave her earrings and bracelets, vessels of gold and silver, and garments as gifts, and took her as a wife for his master.

Let us therefore say what Abraham’s thigh, Isaac, the servant, Rebekah, the well, the ornaments given to her, and her relatives signify. What do we understand by Abraham’s thigh—whence, as the evangelist Matthew describes (Matt. 1), Christ derives his origin according to the flesh—except humanity? Great, therefore, is this oath made upon the flesh of the Creator of the world.

That Isaac signifies Christ the Apostle testifies, saying: “He does not say, ‘And to seeds,’ as though to many, but as though to one: ‘And to your seed,’ which is Christ” (Gal. 3:16). The ten camels are the multitude of the prophets, said to be ten because the number ten contains within itself all numbers: ten means all. It was therefore highly fitting that all the prophets should be brought for Rebekah’s conveyance. The camels go laden because the riches of the prophets are great. But who is this servant who leads them? Who, I ask, except the company of the apostles, and especially Paul, servant of Jesus Christ? These find Rebekah; these find the holy Church; these find patience. For this is the interpretation of Rebekah. She is the one to whom the Lord says: “By your patience you shall possess your souls” (Luke 21:19).

But let Moses say what kind of person Rebekah was: “A girl exceedingly beautiful, a most lovely virgin, unknown to man.” Such, therefore, is the Church, having neither spot [Col. 0200C] nor wrinkle. She had come to the well; she had come to draw water. But what did she find? The servant of Abraham, the servant of Christ, finds those who bore living and unfailing water. Thus the Samaritan woman too, when she came to the well to draw water, found Christ there promising living water. But Rebekah is much better than the Samaritan woman: from the latter water is scarcely drawn by entreaty, whereas Rebekah promises it of her own accord. The former says: “How is it that you, being a Jew, ask to drink from me, a Samaritan woman?” (John 4:9). The latter says: “Drink, my lord; for I will also give drink to your camels.”

But why do they ask water from those to whom they had come to give water, except so that, in the most insignificant thing and one that is most abundant, they might test what mercy and charity they have toward their neighbors—persons to whom they are to entrust Christ’s mysteries? For it is said that whoever gives even a cup of cold water to his neighbor shall not lose his reward (Matt. 10:42).

After Rebekah has been proved obedient, patient, and merciful, earrings are given her, so that, adorned with them, she may become fit and ready to hear the word of God. Christ sought such ears, and ears thus adorned, when he said: “He who has ears to hear, let him hear” (Luke 8:8). The ears of the Church are rightly adorned first, and then through them one comes to the remaining members, because they were the first to meet the coming Word of God. Therefore the Psalmist, beginning with the ears, says: “Hear, daughter, and incline your ear” (Ps. 44:12). Once these are adorned, one comes to the hands, by which works are understood; for it is not enough to have heard unless the things heard are also fulfilled in deed. Hence the Lord himself says: “Blessed are those who hear the word of God and keep it” (Luke 11:28). And the Apostle: “Not the hearers of the Law,” he says, “are righteous before God, but the doers” (Rom. 2:13).

When these things have thus taken place, she is asked whose daughter she is, and she says: “I am the daughter of Bethuel, son of Nahor and Milcah.” Bethuel is interpreted “virgin of God”; Nahor, “rest of light”; Milcah, “his queen.” What, then, is the virgin of God, of whom Rebekah glories that she is the daughter, except she of whom the Apostle says: “But that Jerusalem which is above is free, and she is our mother” (Gal. 4:26)? And John says of her: “I saw the holy city, the new Jerusalem, coming down from heaven from God, prepared as a bride adorned for her husband” (Rev. 21:2).

Rebekah is therefore the daughter of this virgin; the Church is her daughter, dwelling and living in this life. But what is Nahor, “rest of light,” except God the Father, in whom he rests who is called Light from Light? And what is Milcah, “his queen,” except Christ, the power of God and the wisdom of God? Rebekah, then, sprung from such parents and such a lineage, enriched with great gifts, carried upon the vehicle of the prophets, and betrothed to Christ the Lord, is brought to him. For she is built upon the foundation of the apostles and prophets. What, however, do the vessels of gold and silver and the garments given to Rebekah signify [Col. 0201C] except the teaching, examples, character, life, conduct, and instruction of the apostles and prophets, by which the holy Church, taught and adorned, pleases the Lord?

At that time Isaac had gone out into the field to meditate. When Rebekah saw him, she descended from the camel and covered herself with a mantle. He brought her into the tent of Sarah his mother and took her as his wife, loving her so greatly that he tempered the grief which had come upon him through his mother’s death.

At that time, I say, when the apostles began to preach and led the Church to Christ her Lord, Christ the Lord had gone forth from the Father and come into the world, of whom it is written: “After this he was seen upon earth and conversed with men” (Baruch 3:38). But why had he come? To meditate. For it had been said of him: “His will was in the law of the Lord, and in his law he shall meditate day and night” (Ps. 1:2). Hence also animals that do not chew the cud are called unclean. He had come, therefore, to meditate; that is, he had come in order to teach us to meditate, to chew over the Scriptures, and to understand them spiritually.

Therefore it is said here that he walks along the way leading to the well whose name is “of the living and seeing one.” This well is the Holy Spirit, who enables us to understand the Scriptures spiritually. He walked, therefore, along the way—not along that which leads to the letter, upon which the Jews walk, but along that which leads to the Spirit, upon which the Church proceeds—because “the letter kills, but the Spirit gives life” (2 Cor. 3:6). It is called the well “of the living” because it enlightens the eyes of the mind; and because it makes one see, it is called “of the seeing one.” Filled with this water, this Spirit, Christ said: “The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because he has anointed me; he sent me to preach the Gospel to the poor” (Luke 4:18).

That Rebekah, on seeing him, descended from the camel is a sign of fear and humility. That she covered herself with a veil means either that she blushed or wished to appear more becoming. The more familiarly holy persons approach God, therefore, the more they ought to humble themselves in order to please him and adorn themselves more fittingly.

He brought her into the tent of his mother and took her as his wife, because he began to love the Church with the love with which he had previously loved the Synagogue. For when the latter fell, the former arose. Hence it is added: “And he loved her so greatly that he tempered the grief which had come upon him through his mother’s death.” This best of sons grieved more over his mother’s death than over his own, when, hanging upon the cross, he said: “Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing” (Luke 23:34). For his mother according to the flesh was the Synagogue, because Christ was born from the Jewish stock.

## Chapter XXV

It follows that Abraham took another wife named Keturah, by whom he had many sons. He gave all that he possessed to Isaac; but to the sons of his concubines he bestowed gifts and separated them from Isaac. It must not be supposed that the holy man, beloved by God, took other wives for the sake of lust. Rather, since he was called a father, he wished also in reality to be the father of many sons. Moreover, he signified that God has one holy wife, who bears him legitimate sons worthy of the inheritance, and many concubines, who bear illegitimate sons to be cast out from the inheritance—such as Jews, pagans, and heretics.

Hence it is fittingly added: “For he gave to his son Isaac all that he possessed; but to the sons of his concubines he bestowed gifts.” For Christ himself says: “All things which the Father has are mine” (John 16:15). If they are his, then they are ours. “For,” as the Apostle says, “we are heirs of God and fellow heirs with Christ” (Rom. 8:17). To the sons of the concubines he bestowed gifts [Col. 0202D; Note: These are the Gentiles, who, on account of certain moral virtues, have been enriched with temporal goods, knowledge, and much glory]: namely temporal goods, the substance of the world, understanding and reason, skill in many arts, and many other outstanding goods. They misuse these and are separated from Isaac. “For what fellowship has light with darkness? Or what share has the faithful person with the unbeliever? What agreement has Christ with Belial?” (2 Cor. 6:15). It is the Apostle who speaks. It should be noted, moreover, that he calls these women both wives and concubines.

Abraham lived one hundred and seventy-five years, and, failing, died in a good old age, since nothing blameworthy is found in his life. [Col. 0203A] Isaac and Ishmael buried him in the double tomb. After his death God blessed Isaac his son, who lived beside the well named “of the living and seeing one of all things,” because, devoted to wisdom and righteousness, he meditated upon God’s Law day and night. Abraham outlived Isaac’s taking of a wife by thirty-five years.

Isaac was forty years old when he took a wife. Because she was barren, he prayed to the Lord for her, and she conceived. “But the little ones struggled in her womb. Therefore she went to consult the Lord, who answered and said: Two nations are in your womb, and two peoples shall be divided from your belly; one people shall prevail over the other, and the elder shall serve the younger. So they were born; but Esau came out first, red and entirely hairy like a skin; the other came out holding his brother’s heel in his hand, and therefore was called Jacob.”

For in the Gospel the Lord says: “Ask and you shall receive; seek and you shall find; knock and it shall be opened to you” (Luke 11:9). It is clear, therefore, that God wishes to be asked, and hastens by prayers what he will do. Rebekah was barren, yet destined to bear; she would not have given birth unless Isaac had prayed to the Lord for her. Their struggle while still little ones in the womb signified the discord which they and their children would have.

But where did Rebekah go to consult the Lord, except that, according to customary practice, she offered sacrifice and sought an answer? She received the answer that the elder would serve the younger and one people prevail over the other. This does not mean that Esau himself served Jacob, but that Jacob’s children, down to Christ’s birth, afflicted and overcame not only Esau’s children but all the surrounding nations. Read the ancient histories and you will find this.

After Christ’s birth, however, it is no longer Jews but Christians who are called Jacob’s seed and his children; and to them, according to both letter and spirit, not only Esau’s children but also the Jews themselves and all nations are subject. Let the Apostle declare that, after Christ’s birth, it is no longer Jews but Christians who are called Jacob’s seed: “For not all who are from Israel are Israelites; nor are all who are Abraham’s seed children, but ‘In Isaac shall your seed be called’” (Rom. 9:6); that is, not the children of the flesh are the children, but the children of promise are reckoned as the seed. And in the Gospel it is said: “God is able from these stones to raise up children to Abraham” (Luke 3:8). And the Lord says to the Jews: “If you were Abraham’s children, you would do the works of Abraham” (John 8:39). From these things, therefore, it is clear that Jews are no longer called Jacob’s seed, but Christians are.

They also now hold Esau by the heel, because the Jews cannot by any means escape them or their servitude. By the birthright which Esau sold, however, the priestly dignity is understood. Jacob is rightly said to have bought it, because the holy Church, figured by Jacob, now possesses this dignity, while the Jews remain without Law, king, or priesthood. For the sake of bread and a dish of lentils, for the advantage of earthly wealth, lest perhaps they should lose their place, the Jews cried: “We have no king but Caesar” (John 19:15). By this utterance they denied Christ; by it they lost both priest and priesthood. Fearing that, unless they killed Christ, they would lose their place and nation, they lost everything by killing him.

But Jacob and the children of the Church hunger and thirst, and, selling not merely bread and a dish of lentils but even all that they possess, they purchase this dignity and grace. Wretched Jews, who lost so great a dignity and who, though they had been firstborn above all, see others standing above themselves in priestly dignity! How much better it would have been for them to hunger and fast than for it to be said of them, once wickedly filled: “The beloved grew fat and kicked; he grew fat, thick, and bloated; he forsook God his maker and departed from God his savior” (Deut. 32:15).

## Chapter XXVI

It follows that, when famine arose over the land, Isaac went to Abimelech, king of the Philistines, and said that Rebekah was his sister. But when the reason was discovered, Abimelech ordered that no one should dare touch her. “He sowed in that land and found a hundredfold in that very year. God blessed him, and he became very rich. Therefore the Philistines envied him and stopped up all the wells which the servants of Abraham his father had dug, filling them with earth, so that Abimelech himself said: Depart from us, because you have become far more powerful than we.”

He departed, but the dispute about the wells did not cease until Abimelech came and made a covenant with him. Isaac knew that his father had been a wise man; following his example, he thought it foolish, where there is a means of escaping danger, to commit oneself to chance and fortune. For if he had said that Rebekah was his wife, it might have happened that he would be killed. He preferred, therefore, to say that she was his sister, lest he stand in suspense between the two possibilities; for he knew that Abraham had done likewise. So too should we act in doubtful circumstances.

Moses did not wish to pass over in silence so memorable and rare an event: namely, that Isaac deserved to gather one hundred measures from a single measure of seed. For the Lord says in the Gospel: “The seed fell into good ground and bore fruit, one thirtyfold, another sixtyfold, another a hundredfold” (Matt. 13:8). Thus he shows that Isaac was a righteous and perfect man, since he deserved to gather the hundredfold fruit.

But who are Abraham’s servants who dig wells and seek water with such labor in every place? Who also are the Philistines who stop them up and fill them with earth? The servants of Abraham—of the greater Abraham—are the prophets, apostles, and teachers. They dig wells; they search the Scriptures; they expound the sacred books spiritually; casting aside the veil of the letter, they offer us living water. The Philistines, whose name is interpreted “falling through drink,” are heretics, Jews, and philosophers. Drunk with false and heretical teaching, falling like madmen and drunkards through the cup of madness and falsehood, they strive to close and stop up not only other wells but even the very streams of teaching from the four Gospels [Col. 0205A].
