But because in some things they agree with us, they are said not to have disputed over certain wells.

By Abimelech’s covenant with Isaac, let us understand the very same thing that we explained above concerning his covenant with Abraham. [Note: Col. 0205D: The same Laurentian and Cassinese manuscripts.] Just as Isaac here signifies the soul, as he did above, so Abimelech signifies the flesh. Let Abimelech come to Isaac; let flesh come to soul; let it hear what is written: [Note: Col. 0205D: Isa. 46:8. The Vulgate reads: “Return, transgressors, to the heart.”] “Return, sinners, to the heart.” Let them make a covenant, agree together, and now follow not merely carnal but also spiritual understanding; let them drink water from the springs of Israel. If they do this, they will no longer desire to stop up Abraham’s wells; and his servants will not cease to dig wells.

For how many wells Jerome dug, how many Augustine, how many Ambrose, so that the place in which these dwell—that is, the Church—may rightly be called Beersheba, that is, the well of satiety [Note: Col. 0205D: Both manuscripts correct the edition].

## Chapter XXVII
“Now Isaac had grown old, and his eyes were dim, so that he could not see; and he called his son in order to bless him.” But Jacob intervened at Rebekah’s counsel, wrapped in goatskins so as not to be recognized, bringing a dish and inviting his father to eat. After Isaac had touched and kissed him and perceived the fragrance of his garments, he blessed him, saying: “Behold, the scent of my son is like the scent of a full field which God has blessed. May God give you, from the [Col. 0205C] dew of heaven and from the richness of the earth, abundance of grain, wine, and oil; may peoples serve you and tribes adore you. Be lord of your brothers, and may the sons of your mother bow down before you. Whoever curses you shall be cursed, and whoever blesses you shall be filled with blessings.”

For what are we to understand by Isaac but the Jewish people, also called by another name, the Synagogue? And by Esau, but Jews living carnally? And by Jacob, but Christ and the Church, of which he himself is the head? Isaac grew old when, with the advent of baptism, circumcision began to cease; for what grows worn and old is near destruction. His eyes became dim, and he could not see, because beneath the veil of the letter he did not recognize the spiritual meaning. [Col. 0205D] Indeed, even while speaking with Christ, he did not know who he was, his eyes being blind. Therefore he called Esau—he called his carnal sons—and commanded him, as usual, to bring him something from his hunting.

The Synagogue is never satisfied with victims and burnt offerings, never with the blood and sacrifices of animals. Christ was present, whose words are sweeter than honey and the honeycomb; the Lamb who takes away the sins of the world was being sacrificed. Yet the Synagogue still sought flesh; it still sacrificed and ate goats. Isaac, then hungry, [Col. 0206A] signified this. The Lord cries: “I will not take calves from your house, nor goats from your flocks” (Ps. 49:9). Again: “What is the multitude of your sacrifices to me? says the Lord. I am full; I do not desire the burnt offerings of rams, the fat of fattened animals, or the blood of calves, lambs, and goats” (Isa. 1:11). Yet Isaac speaks; the insatiable Synagogue asks: “Bring me something from your hunting.”

While the Synagogue daily hungered after these sacrifices, Jacob came—Christ came. But how did he come? Do you wish to hear how? Wrapped in goatskins: that is, in the likeness of sinful flesh. “For he emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, made in the likeness of men, and found in appearance as a man” (Phil. 2:7). This was the first [Col. 0206B] clothing of humankind, when the first man was expelled from paradise. Thus clothed, Christ came, bearing with him two excellent kids: one for sin and the other as a burnt offering—namely, his flesh and blood. By these original sin is loosed and God is appeased from indignation.

Rebekah, whose name means “much patience,” cooked these kids. Thus it was through much patience that Christ permitted himself to be cooked and slain for us; for unless he had possessed much patience, he would not have allowed himself to be crucified by the Jews. “For,” as the Apostle says, “he loved us and gave himself for us” (Eph. 5:2). He was offered because he himself willed it, and he suffered by his own patience. For concerning this kid it had been said: “Do not cook a kid in its mother’s milk” [Col. 0206C] (Exod. 23:19). The kid, therefore, is cooked, but not in its mother’s milk, when Christ is killed—rather, after he has been weaned.

What does it mean that Isaac kisses and touches Jacob and delights in the fragrance of his garments, except that Christ, in the presence of his flesh, both spoke and lived among the Jews, and for a time they delighted in the fragrance of his knowledge and in the miracles he performed? For it is written (Matt. 14:36) that even his garments healed the sick; and all who touched him were made whole from whatever infirmity held them. Isaac blesses Jacob and does not recognize him, because to this day the Jews bless Christ, though they do not understand whom they bless. All the Scriptures are full of blessings: the patriarchs and prophets wrote blessings concerning Christ. As Jews read these, they bless Christ even unwillingly.

> [Note: “Christ our Lord is blessed even from the mouth of Jews—though they err, yet chant the Law and the Prophets; that is, he is truly spoken of, while another is thought to be blessed, whom they in their error await.” Augustine, *City of God*, book XVI, ch. 38.]

For they suppose that they bless another Christ, who is none other than Antichrist. For just as Jacob signifies Christ and the Church, of which he is the head, so Esau denotes Antichrist and the carnally living Jews, who are his members. When he comes, when he returns from hunting, he will restore all the ceremonies and sacrifices of the Law. But before he comes, let us hear how [Col. 0207A] Isaac blesses Jacob.

“Behold,” he says, “the scent of my son is like the scent of a full field which the Lord has blessed.” The Lord himself also says: “I am the flower of the field and the lily of the valleys” (Song 2:1). Therefore the fragrance of Christ is like that of a field filled with lilies, roses, and other sweet scents. By these we understand virtues and the gifts of the Holy Spirit, with which he was anointed above his companions. Hence it follows: “May God give you of the dew of heaven.” What is the dew of heaven but the spirit of wisdom and understanding, the spirit of counsel and strength, the spirit of knowledge and piety, and the spirit of the fear of the Lord? (Isa. 11:2). Christ abounds in such dew.

> [Note: The corrupt text of the edition is corrected at this point.]

By the richness of the earth are understood all the better things possessed by the earth—that is, by the Church. Hence there is added: [Col. 0207B] “Abundance of grain, wine, and oil.” By these, through which people are nourished and live, we understand faith, hope, and charity; or else the apostles and teachers, who feed us with spiritual food. Concerning faith it is said: “Without faith it is impossible to please God” (Heb. 11:6). Concerning charity: “God is charity” (1 John 4:16), by which Christ loved us and washed us from our sins in his blood (Rev. 1:5). Concerning hope: “For by hope we were saved” (Rom. 8:24). That peoples should serve him, tribes adore him, that he should be lord of his brothers, and that the sons of his mother—that is, of the Church or Synagogue—should bow before him, is so manifest as not to need exposition. For he says: “As I live, says the Lord, every knee shall bow to me, and every tongue shall confess” (Isa. 45:23). And the Apostle says: “Therefore God also exalted him and gave him the name above every name, that at the name of the Lord every knee should bend—of heavenly, earthly, and infernal beings” (Phil. 2:10).

While these things were taking place, Esau came. For he will come at the end of the age with a great multitude of Jews. He has not yet come, because the Synagogue has not yet ceased from blessing Christ: it blesses him openly through the good, and in the Holy Scriptures even through those who are not good. Therefore he will come bringing food and offering sacrifices. But Isaac will not receive those sacrifices; those foods will not please the patriarchs and prophets. Isaac has already received Jacob’s food; the Synagogue of the saints is already filled with Christ’s sacrifices.

But because it is written: “In those days Judah shall be saved, and Israel shall dwell securely” (Jer. 33:16); and, “when the fullness of the Gentiles has come in, then Israel shall be saved” (Rom. 11:25); and, “Though the number of the children of Israel be as the sand of the sea, a remnant shall return to the Lord” (Rom. 9:27): because this, I say, is written, we must necessarily believe that Esau—that is, the Jewish people—will not be wholly deprived of the father’s blessing. Rather, all who turn to the Lord will receive the blessing [Col. 0208A] of the Synagogue, that is, of the patriarchs and prophets.

From Christ’s birth until that time, Esau wanders in hunting and seeks food with great labor; then he will turn, and then, groaning, weeping, and repenting, will deserve to hear: “Your blessing shall be in the richness of the earth and in the dew of heaven from above.” This has been explained above. And because he repented, he will receive the same blessing as his brother.

What follows—“You shall live by the sword”—belongs to Esau according to the letter, because he was a hunter. “And you shall serve your brother,” because the Israelite people ruled around him. “And the time will come when you shall shake off and loose his yoke from your neck.”

> [Note: The same Laurentian manuscript corrects and supplies the edition. The Cassinese manuscript reads: “And the time will come when you shake off and loose the yoke from your neck.” All this was fulfilled according to the letter; and it greatly harms the Jews that they shook their brother’s yoke from their necks.]

All this was fulfilled according to the letter, and it greatly harmed the Jews that they shook their brother’s yoke [Col. 0208B] from their necks. For his yoke is sweet and his burden light (Matt. 11:30). Yet this must be understood: not everything narrated by history is to be expounded allegorically; otherwise it would not be history.

## CHAPTER XXVIII

“Esau therefore hated Jacob and thought of killing him. But these things were reported to Rebekah.” Yet by whom were they reported except by him who alone knows human thoughts and never forsakes those who hope in him? Therefore, by command of his father and mother, Jacob set out for Mesopotamia to his uncle Laban.

“When he had come to a certain place and wished to rest there, he took one stone and, placing it [Col. 0208C] beneath his head, slept in that same place. And in a dream he saw a ladder standing upon the earth, whose top touched heaven, with angels ascending and descending by it, and the Lord leaning upon the ladder and saying to him: I am the Lord God of Abraham your father and the God of Isaac; the land in which you sleep I shall give to you and to your seed, etc. When Jacob awoke from sleep, he said: Truly the Lord is in this place. How dreadful,” he said, “is this place! This is none other than the house of God and the gate of heaven. Rising therefore in the morning, he took the stone which he had placed beneath his head, set it up as a pillar, and poured oil upon it,” vowing that he would give tithes from all things if the Lord protected him and supplied what was necessary for life.

Let us therefore say what the stone, the ladder, and the angels signify. That stone upon which Jacob slept is Christ, [Col. 0208D] who is called a stone in many places. John the Evangelist also, reclining upon his breast, deserved to see no lesser things than Jacob. Therefore let all who desire to see heavenly things sleep upon this stone, for “blessed are the dead who die in the Lord” (Rev. 14:13).

The ladder which touched heaven signifies the linked sequence of virtues and good works.

> [Note: See Augustine, *City of God*, book XVI, ch. 38.]

For as one ascends by certain rungs on a ladder to higher places, so those advancing from virtue to virtue [Col. 0209A] “shall see the God of gods in Zion” (Ps. 84:7). The angels ascending and descending by this ladder signify holy men, who ascend to the heavenly kingdoms by the degrees of virtues and good works; thus one goes to the stars. But why do the angels appear not only to ascend but also to descend, except because holy men cannot be without sin in this life? “If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us” (1 John 1:8). Therefore, whenever the saints sin, they descend this ladder.

It is fitting that the Lord should appear standing, leaning or firmly supported upon this ladder, in order to teach us also that we should always lean upon the staff of virtues. For this is not a reed staff, easily broken; whoever leans upon it can stand securely. Jacob, waking from sleep, said: “Truly the Lord is in this place,” where I heard him speaking, where I rested while sleeping upon him, and I did not know it. Therefore, if I sinned by not showing this stone fitting reverence, I did so in ignorance. “How dreadful is this place,” where God deigns to dwell; “this is none other than the house of God and the gate of heaven,” where angels dwell and the ladder of the saints is seen.

“He therefore set up the stone as a pillar,” venerating in the stone him who was signified by that stone. Since God had anointed him with the oil of gladness above his companions, Jacob likewise poured oil upon it. Then he says: “And this stone which I have set up as a pillar shall be called the house [Col. 0209C] of God.” For that stone signified Christ’s flesh, in which all the fullness of divinity dwelt bodily. Of it it is written: “Wisdom has built herself a house.”

> [Note: The same Laurentian manuscript.]

The wisdom of the Word built itself a house, namely the flesh which it assumed, because “the Word was made flesh and dwelt among us” (John 1:14). And “he hewed out seven pillars”: that is, the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit, which always support this house.

The law concerning tithes had not yet been written, and already Jacob promised that he would give tithes. Abraham too is recorded as having done this. By this he wished wonderfully to signify that, since man is the tenth—for there are nine orders of angels—people should send their tithes there as a pledge of themselves, where they hope that they themselves will come as tithes.

## CHAPTER XXIX

Jacob departed from there and came to a certain well, beside which three flocks of sheep lay. There, because he had learned that Rachel would come with the flock, he waited for her; and, after watering the flock, he kissed her. Then he came to Laban and served him seven years for Rachel and another seven for Leah. We must therefore say what Jacob, Laban, and his daughters signify.

Jacob signifies Christ for many reasons, especially in this place because he was a shepherd. Laban, whose name means “white,” denotes the world; their names appear quite suitable to them. For who does not admire the brightness and beauty of this world? Leah, because she had weak eyes and because her name means “laborious,” represents the Synagogue or the active life. Rachel, however, who had a beautiful face and whose name means “sheep,” represents the Church or the contemplative life.

Let us therefore follow the order. Jacob comes to the well. This well seems to me to be the knowledge of the New and Old Testaments. The three flocks of sheep are the Jews, Samaritans, and heretics, for these three drink from this well. Fittingly, the well is shut by a great stone: namely, the one of whom it is written, “He shuts and no one opens; he opens and no one shuts” [Col. 0210B] (Rev. 3:7)—“He is the lion from the tribe of Judah, who opened the book and loosed its seven seals” (Rev. 5:5).

Jacob stood beside the well, and the flocks of sheep stood there; but because Rachel had not yet come, the well remained shut. For the well is shut as long as Christ has not begun to speak. Rachel comes, the well is opened, the sheep are watered, the faithful are baptized, Christ speaks and preaches. This is what is meant by the words: “And he kissed her.” Of this kiss it is said: “Let him kiss me with the kiss of his mouth” (Song 1:1).

That Rachel reported Jacob’s arrival to her father Laban indicates that the holy Church proclaimed Christ’s advent to this world. At her proclamation, Laban runs to meet him: for through the Church’s preaching the whole world is converted to Christ. Jacob served seven years for Leah and seven for Rachel because, either in person or through his servants, our Lord Christ serves this world throughout this last age, which revolves in seven days, in order to join faithful souls to himself. “For he did not come to be served, but to serve” (Matt. 20:28).

Why is Leah introduced in place of Rachel except because the active life comes before the contemplative? Preaching, baptizing, and giving alms belong to the active life; unless these come first, no one will delight in the contemplation of God. For who will contemplate what he does not know? It follows:

“Now when the Lord saw that Jacob despised [Col. 0210D] Leah, he opened her womb, while her sister remained barren.” The Church was indeed barren at the beginning, whereas the Synagogue had already borne innumerable children. The active life always bears children for God; the contemplative life benefits itself alone. Leah has weak eyes; Rachel has a beautiful face, but is barren. Rachel, setting everything else aside, desires to see God alone; Leah directs the dim eyes of her mind toward God in such a way that she does not lose the necessities of this life.

## CHAPTER XXX

But why is it that these holy women, from an excessive desire for children, bear children not only by themselves but also [Col. 0211A] through maidservants?

> [Note: Augustine observes that, “because at that time no law forbade several wives for the sake of multiplying offspring, Jacob also took the woman to whom alone he had pledged the faith of a future marriage.” *City of God*, book XVI, ch. 38.]

It is because the holy Church both baptizes and begets children not only through the righteous and Catholics, but also through sinners and heretics. Yet these are not called the children of the maidservants, because, whoever performs the baptism, the Church alone is mother.

It follows that Reuben went out into the field and found mandrakes, which he gave to his mother Leah. In exchange for them Rachel permitted her sister to have Jacob sleep with her that night. Mandrakes are said to have this nature: they induce sleep, resemble the human form, and grant fertility to a barren woman. This indicates that holy men, clinging to the embrace of God alone, are sometimes, as though weighed down by heavy sleep, closing the eyes with which they contemplated God. Then, imitating the image of other human beings and unwilling to be wholly useless and unfruitful to this life, they take upon themselves the management and administration of earthly matters.

This too was done by the Apostle, who, like Rachel, was caught up into the third heaven, but immediately thereafter, like Leah, descended to marital intercourse and said: “Let the husband render the debt to his wife, and likewise the wife to her husband. The husband has no authority over his own body, but the wife does; and the wife has no authority over her own body, but the husband does” (1 Cor. 7:3). Because the contemplative life acts in this way after the example of the active life, it is not without reason said that Rachel bought these mandrakes from her sister. But because she granted her husband to Leah for only one night, she signified that she would not long remain estranged from his contemplation.

Jacob dwells differently with Leah and with Rachel: with the former carnally, with the latter spiritually. To the woman by whom he begets children he makes himself visible. Therefore Rachel, receiving the mandrakes—that is, taking temporary charge of earthly matters—conceived and bore a son. “Rejoice, therefore, barren woman who does not bear; break forth and cry aloud, you who do not travail; for the children of the desolate are more numerous than those of her who has a husband” (Gal. 4:27).

It follows concerning Jacob’s request of Laban: that whatever among the sheep and goats was reddish, spotted, or variegated should be given to him as his wages. When Laban had granted this, and Jacob saw in dreams that all the variegated and spotted males were mounting the females, he took [Col. 0211D] branches of poplar, almond, and plane tree, stripping part of their bark and leaving part with the bark; and he placed them in the watering troughs where water was poured out, so that when the flocks came to drink, they might conceive before them.

For philosophers say that in conception nature follows the outward sight, and that what sight contemplates externally [Col. 0212A] nature produces internally.

> [Note: Many modern philosophers hold that a disturbance of the mother’s imagination cannot be the cause of spots or other marks appearing in offspring. This view is especially maintained after the English philosopher Blondel, who wrote a metaphysical and physical dissertation on this subject. Blondel appears to use very powerful anatomical arguments in proving the point; yet how many things remain unknown concerning the physical operations and affections of human beings! Sacred Scripture in this place does not explicitly attribute that effect to the excited imagination of the parents; but the ordinary manner of speaking seems to suggest it.]

Accordingly, in the conception of mares or dogs, some people customarily place males of excellent breed before their eyes. They report that a certain woman gave birth to an Ethiopian child because, at the time when she conceived, she looked upon its painted image on a wall. This seems sufficiently plausible from the things just related.

But what do the channels through which the water was poured out signify except the teachers of the Church, from whose mouths, as from channels, streams of wisdom and knowledge flow? And what do the branches signify except lengthy discourses and extended sentences of Scripture? They are stripped of bark on the side according to which they are spiritually understood. But on the side left with bark are those Scriptures [Col. 0212B] expounded according to the letter and surface alone. Because they always grow and never fail, they are deservedly said to have been green. Some of them, according to the nature of the poplar and plane tree, provide the shade of refreshment and sweetness for those burning with the heat of vices; others, like the almond tree, provide sweetness and a pleasant flavor.

In the sight and understanding of these, the sheep of the holy Church, nourished by the good shepherd, conceive the seed of the Word of God and bear children of many varieties. Of these it is written: “All the glory of the king’s daughter is within, clothed round about in fringes of gold with varieties” (Ps. 45:13). The children of the Church are not of one color; rather, according to the diversity of virtues, jewels of different colors, as it were, shine forth in them. Jacob foresaw this [Col. 0212C] from the time when in dreams he saw only variegated males mounting the females. This variety is found not only in the teachers and masters of the Church, but in the congregations themselves.

## CHAPTER XXXI

Next it is related that Jacob fled from Laban and, with his wives, children, and all the possessions he had acquired, returned to the land of his birth. Laban pursued him for seven days and overtook him on Mount Gilead. Warned by the Lord not to say anything harsh against Jacob, he made a covenant with him and returned to his own place. [Col. 0212D] Jacob, however, went on his way.

We have said that Laban signifies this world. Therefore Jacob fittingly flees from Laban with his wives, children, and all his possessions, and returns to the land of his fathers, so as to give us an example that we should not love the world or the things that are in the world. Let us therefore flee the world’s servitude with all our [Col. 0213A] friends and relatives whom we can save by example or admonition. Let us return to the land of our fathers, the land flowing with milk and honey, the land inhabited by Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. Let us bring with us our possessions, disposing of them rightly, so that they may serve God and not the world.

Let us not fear Laban—that is, let us not fear this world, which pursues us for seven days, that is, at all times, in order to subject us to its service. For God will not allow us to be tempted beyond what we can bear (1 Cor. 10:13). Let us make a covenant with Laban, a covenant with the world’s delights and pleasures, so that neither they may return to us nor we to them. Let Gilead be witness of this covenant. Gilead means “heap of testimony,” by which we understand the Holy Scriptures, in which the testimonies of the saints are heaped together. These separate us from the world; these separate us from the vanities of this age. Blessed, therefore, is the person who stands beside Gilead, believes the testimonies of the saints, and meditates upon the law of the Lord day and night.

## CHAPTER XXXII

Jacob went on the way he had begun, and angels of God met him. When he saw them, he said: “These are the camps of God.” He sent messengers to Esau in order to find favor with him. Moreover, he offered him gifts, that if he could not appease him with prayers, he might at least do so with gifts. When everyone had been sent ahead and he remained alone in the camp: “Behold, a man wrestled with him until morning. When he could not overcome him, [Col. 0213C] he touched the sinew of his thigh, and it immediately withered. And he said to him: Let me go, for dawn has come. He answered: I will not let you go unless you bless me. He said: What is your name? He answered: Jacob. But he said: Your name shall no longer be called Jacob, but Israel; for if you have been strong against God, how much more shall you prevail against men? Jacob asked him: Tell me by what name you are called. He answered: Why do you ask my name?”

> [Note: The Cassinese manuscript adds: “which is wonderful?”]

“And he blessed him in the same place. Jacob called the name of that place Phanuel, saying: I have seen the Lord face to face, and my soul has been saved. Immediately after he crossed Phanuel, the sun rose upon him; but he limped on his foot.” For this reason the children of Israel do not eat the sinew that withered in Jacob’s thigh.

Jacob fittingly encountered angels after he had separated from Laban, because those who leave the world are immediately counted in God’s army; and those who flee the camps of the age deserve to see and dwell in the camps of God. Nor should anyone disdain to seek peace from the rulers and secular men of the world, since holy Jacob, to whom God had promised assistance, strove so humbly to appease Esau with both prayers and gifts. “For God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble” (Jas. 4:6).

What does Jacob signify here except the Jewish people, which derives its origin from him? And what does the angel signify except Christ? Of him it is written: “The Lord, the ruler whom you seek, shall suddenly come to his holy temple, and the angel of the covenant whom you desire” (Mal. 3:1). If we wish to understand the angel’s wrestling with Jacob only literally, does it not appear ridiculous? What benefit was there in the angel’s fighting with Jacob, especially when it is said that he could not overcome him? Who could believe this? Finally, why does he make him limp and bless him?

This angel, therefore, is Christ, and for that reason is called now a man, now an angel. Taking flesh and coming into the world, he wrestled with Jacob until morning, because the Jews did not cease persecuting him until the hour of the resurrection, which occurred early in the morning. [Col. 0214B] Christ wrestled with the Jews because by admonishing, acting, and rebuking them he very often provoked them to anger. The Jews wrestled with Christ by plotting, accusing, mocking, and persecuting him in many ways.

When he could not overcome them—he could not, indeed, because he would not: “for he was offered because he himself willed it” (Isa. 53:7); but he did not will to conquer through the flesh, because he had come to redeem the flesh—he touched the sinew of his thigh, and it immediately withered. Thus Christ both blessed Jacob in part and did not bless him in part. He blessed the sound foot; he did not bless the lame foot. He blessed the apostles and the other believers; he did not bless those who crucified and persecuted him. Thus in one respect Jews are blessed, but in another [Col. 0214C] they limp. Hence it is said: “Foreign sons have lied to me; foreign sons have grown old and have limped from their paths” (Ps. 18:45).

To this day the Jews limp on one foot, accepting the Old but not the New Testament.

> [Note: Augustine presents the same interpretation more briefly in the cited book of *City of God*, ch. 39.]

Therefore, because Jacob is divided into two—the believing and the unbelieving—one part of him, namely the part that limps, wrestles with Christ; the other seeks Christ’s blessing. The part that wrestled proudly withered, but the other, because it strove to hold him in devotion, is blessed. Christ is held not by force but by love. Why is Jacob struck not wholly but only in part, except because not the whole Jewish people but only a part was hostile to him? Hence the Apostle says: “Blindness has happened in part [Col. 0214D] to Israel” (Rom. 11:25).

Why does he say, “Let me go, for dawn has come”? He says this, surely, to the good, who after dawn—after the resurrection—deserved to hold him in this world for forty days. Thus, as though he were being held, he said: “It is expedient for you that I go; unless I go, the Paraclete will not come to you” (John 16:7). Nor do they let him go until he blesses them. Thus the Evangelist says: “And, lifting up his hands, he blessed them. And it came to pass, while he was blessing them, that he departed from them and was carried up into heaven” (Luke 24:50).

The good part alone, therefore, held him; it alone is blessed; it alone, its name changed, is called Israel. Israel means “a man seeing [Col. 0215A] God.” To this part alone it is said: “For if you have been strong against God, how much more shall you prevail against men?” For he was strong against God insofar as he held him so long until he blessed him. Moses likewise held him when the Lord said: “Let me go, that I may destroy this people and make you into a great nation.” Unless he were being held, he would not have said, “Let me go.” The saints prevailed against their enemies because “through faith the saints conquered kingdoms” (Heb. 11:33).

Jacob said: “I have seen the Lord face to face, and my soul has been saved.” For Jacob saw the Lord not in his own substance, since he is invisible, but through the angel who spoke to him. The apostles also saw Christ: first according to his humanity, and afterward through the contemplation of spiritual understanding.

## CHAPTER XXXIII

When Jacob heard that Esau was coming to meet him, he divided his children and wives, saying: “If Esau strikes one company, the other will be saved.” Having sent the flocks ahead, he placed the maidservants and their children first, Leah and hers second, and Rachel and Joseph last. In doing this Jacob signified the persecutions of the Church and the contests of the martyrs. The saints were first deprived of their property and possessions, as the Apostle says in praise of some: “For you received with joy the plundering of your goods” (Heb. 10:34). When tyrants could not prevail in this way, they took [Col. 0215C] their homes and families; but when the saints could not be overcome even thus, they applied tortures to their bodies, signified by Leah, hoping thereby to reach Rachel—that is, the soul.

But because the Lord had said: “Do not fear those who kill the body, because they cannot kill the soul” (Matt. 10:28), leaving everything else, they strove to defend the soul alone. Job also signified this: he first lost all his possessions, then his sons and daughters, and afterward, grievously afflicted throughout his body, he took care to preserve his soul alone, concerning which the Lord had said to Satan: “Nevertheless, preserve his soul” (Job 2). Hence the Psalmist says: “May the Lord keep [Col. 0215D] you from all evil,” and immediately specifies: “May the Lord keep your soul” (Ps. 121:7).

Leah, therefore, is neglected for Rachel’s sake; the maidservants and their daughters are neglected for Leah’s sake; the flocks and every possession are neglected for the maidservants’ sake. For the flesh too must be neglected for the soul’s sake; the entire household for the flesh’s sake; and private household must be preferred to every possession.

## CHAPTER XXXIV
After Esau, having seen Jacob, returned to Seir, and Jacob came and dwelt near the city of Salem, Dinah, Leah’s daughter, went out to see the women of that country. Shechem, son of Hamor, prince of that land, seized her and lay with her. Therefore Simeon [Col. 0216A] and Levi, Dinah’s brothers, greatly angered and having chosen a suitable time, entered the city; and, after killing everyone, rescued their sister.

For what do we understand by Dinah except all simple and carnal persons, who, having bleary eyes like their mother, can very easily be deceived? And what by Shechem, whose name is interpreted “shoulder,” except heretics, who, like strong men, strive to carry into their own flock all whom they can deceive? Shechem is rightly called the son of Hamor; for *Hamor* is interpreted “ass,” and thus this shoulder and this ass bear many into eternal perdition. Heretics, therefore, because they are sons of an ass, cannot possess sound and rational understanding.

Dinah goes out to see the women [Col. 0216B] of that land because simple persons are separated from the Church, delighting to hear the doctrines of heretics and philosophers. They are at once captured and deceived, and transferred into the flock of heretics; whence it comes about that a soul betrothed to God begins to be the devil’s whore. But marvelous is the craftiness of heretics! It is not enough for them to have carried off one soul; rather, they direct their attention against the whole Church. They therefore get themselves circumcised and pretend that they wish to adopt the religion of the saints, so that, living among the saints, they may more easily deceive them. This is what Shechem and Hamor say: “If we circumcise our males, imitating the rite of the nation, their property, their cattle, and everything that they possess will be ours.” They are thus circumcised not for religion’s sake, but in order to subject the household and all its possessions to themselves.

But what do Simeon and Levi do? What do priests and Levites do? What do bishops and teachers of the Church do? They take up the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God; they gather together, attack the conventicles of heretics, expose heresies, uncover pretences, and, from greatest to least, either carry people off or kill them. They kill them because, striking them with anathema, they condemn them to eternal death; but they carry off those whom they can convert from heretical depravity to Christ’s faith. Thus they rescue Dinah and reconcile simple souls to the Church. That this vengeance pleased God is proved by the fact that the terror of the Lord seized all the surrounding cities, and they [Col. 0216D] did not dare pursue those who were departing. That Jacob is said to have been displeased seems rather to concern the historical narrative.

## CHAPTER XXXV

After this the Lord commanded Jacob to go up to Bethel and dwell there. Jacob ordered his household to cast away the foreign gods, purify themselves, and change their garments. They therefore gave him the gods that they had and the earrings that were in their ears. He buried them beneath the terebinth which stands beyond the city of Shechem.

For Bethel is interpreted “house of God.” Those who had meanwhile been heretics rightly go up there. Before they ascend, they cast away foreign gods, because no one who serves foreign gods dwells in the Lord’s house. Moreover, they are purified and change their garments [Col. 0217A] so that, baptized in soul and body, they may deserve to put on Christ. Jacob buries both the gods and the earrings in the earth, so that they may be understood as dead and may no longer appear to deceive people. But why are earrings buried with them, unless so that no one may thereafter presume to trouble human ears with their memory? Earrings are ornaments of ears, by which hearing is understood. For ears that do not hear are not adorned. Thus Jacob, circumcising the ears of his household, wished them to be deaf and without hearing for listening to the praises of gods. Hence it is written: “Their memory has perished with a sound” (Ps. 9:8). For if there is no one to hear, both the sound and the proclamation and the memory perish.

He therefore came to Bethel and, having built an altar there, called [Col. 0217B] the name of that place “house of God.” “At the same time Deborah, Rebekah’s nurse, died and was buried at the foot of Bethel beneath an oak; and the name of that place was called ‘Oak of Weeping.’” At the same time, he says, when Jacob went up from Bethel, Deborah, Rebekah’s nurse, died, because the Synagogue died at the time when Christ began to build and inhabit the house of the Lord—that is, the Church. *Deborah* is interpreted “bee.” Of her the Lord says: “They surrounded me like bees” (Ps. 117:12).

Deborah was Rebekah’s nurse because the Synagogue nourished the Church when it was little and nursing. For it taught us both the Law and the Prophets, and whatever we have of the Old Testament we received from it. The place in which Deborah—that is, the Synagogue—was buried [Col. 0217C] is called the Oak of Weeping, because the Synagogue, placed in outer darkness, has for its shade and refreshment weeping and gnashing of teeth. For when the wicked pass from excessive heat to waters of snow, it would have been better for them always to remain under the sun than to pass beneath the shadow of that oak, which compels them, by its excessive cold, both to weep and gnash their teeth.

“Jacob departed from there and came to the land which leads to Ephrath. When Rachel was giving birth there, she began to be endangered by the difficulty of the childbirth. Therefore she called her son Belom, that is, ‘son of my sorrow’; but his father called him Benjamin, that is, ‘son of the right hand.’”

Rachel fittingly gave birth in the place where the Holy Church had its beginning, concerning which it is written: “We heard of her in Ephrath” [Col. 0217D] (Ps. 131:6). Ephrath is Bethlehem itself, where Christ our Lord was born according to the flesh. Rachel dies while giving birth to her son because the Holy Church gives birth by dying. Paul was beheaded while giving birth; Peter was crucified while giving birth. For how was he not giving birth by dying, when, placed upon the cross, he was begetting children through preaching? At no time did the holy martyrs beget more children for the Lord than when they were suffering. Thus the Lord says in the Gospel: “A woman, when she gives birth, has sorrow” (John 16:21).

She calls her son Belom, “son of my sorrow,” because she bore him in sorrow—that is, in death—and in afflictions. But his father called him Benjamin, “son of the right hand.” For if Christ is called the right hand [Col. 0218A] and Jacob signifies Christ, then Christ’s children are children of the right hand. Hence it is also said of Benjamin that he used either hand as his right hand. But at Rachel’s death there was no weeping, because the Holy Church tends by dying not toward grief but toward joy. Deborah, however, is wept for—and weeps herself—an aged, decrepit, contemptible woman, of whom Jeremiah says: “She has wept bitterly in the night, and her tears are on her cheeks; among all her beloved there is none to comfort her” (Lam. 1:2).

## CHAPTER XXXVI

It follows that, when one hundred and eighty years had been completed, Isaac died, and his sons Esau and Jacob buried him in the double cave. Then the sons of Esau and their chiefs are recounted; likewise the sons of Seir and their chiefs. As for the statement, “This is Onan, who found hot waters in the wilderness while he was feeding the asses of Zibeon his father,” it should be understood as though it said: This Onan, by his art and ingenuity, discovered how a mule might be born from an ass and a mare; or, taken literally, he found waters, which are difficult to find in the wilderness.

## CHAPTER XXXVII

“Joseph, when he was sixteen years old, was feeding flocks with his brothers, still a boy; and he accused his brothers before his father of a very grave offence. Israel loved Joseph and made him a richly ornamented, many-coloured tunic.”

In a dream he saw himself binding sheaves with his brothers in the field; and his sheaf rose [Col. 0218C] and stood, and was worshipped by his brothers’ sheaves. When he told this to his brothers, they answered: “Will you indeed be our king, and shall we be subject to your dominion?” He also saw another dream, which he related to his brothers: “I saw in a dream, as it were, the sun, moon, and eleven stars worshipping me.” When his father heard and understood this, he said: “Shall I, your mother, and your brothers worship you upon the earth?” His brothers therefore envied him.

Joseph, whose name is interpreted “increasing,” signifies Christ, whose kingdom and dominion increased so greatly that it filled the whole world. John says of him: “It is necessary that I decrease, but that he increase” (John 3:30). While still [Col. 0218D] a boy, he sat in the midst of the elders, heard them and questioned them; and all marveled at his answers and teaching (Luke 2:46). Thus our Joseph too, still a boy, fed the flock.

The statement that Joseph accused his brothers before his father of a grave offence uses the plural for the singular: he did not accuse all his brothers, but only Reuben, who had lain with Bilhah, his father’s concubine. But will Christ ever accuse anyone? The Apostle says: “Who shall bring an accusation against God’s elect? Christ, who justifies. Who is he that condemns? Christ Jesus, who died—indeed, who also rose again—who also intercedes for us” (Rom. 8:34). If, therefore, it is established that Christ intercedes with the Father for us, there is no doubt that [Col. 0219A] he also accuses and condemns the wicked.

The father made for this beloved son a many-coloured tunic, by which we understand the flesh with which divinity was clothed. His sheaf, full of the finest grain and intended to nourish the whole world, is worshipped by his brothers’ sheaves, because “at the name of Jesus every knee shall bow, of those in heaven, on earth, and under the earth” (Phil. 2:10). Moreover, the sun, moon, and eleven stars worshipped him, because kings, rulers, the whole Church, and all his disciples worship and venerate him.

[Note: Col. 0219D. The Codex of Monte Cassino omits “eleven.”]

How, then, according to the letter, could the moon worship Joseph, since Rachel, understood by the moon, had already died?

[Note: Col. 0219D. Something is lacking through the copyists’ ignorance.]

His brothers therefore envied him, and the Jews were already thinking of killing him, because his dreams, admonitions, and teaching [Col. 0219B] seemed contrary to them, and they feared that such a one, as a righteous king, would rule over them. Thus they said: “Come, let us kill him, for he is useless to us and contrary to our works, and he professes to have knowledge of God; he calls himself the Son of God” (Wis. 2:13).

After this, at Jacob’s command, Joseph went to visit his brothers who were feeding flocks. When they saw him from afar, “they planned to kill him and said to one another: Behold, the dreamer is coming; come, let us kill him and cast him into an old cistern.” As soon as he came to his brothers, they stripped him of his long, many-coloured tunic; afterward, at Judah’s counsel, they sold him to the Ishmaelites.

For after the Jews saw [Col. 0219C] the signs and miracles Christ performed, and that all the people revered and followed him, the chief priests and Pharisees, moved by zeal and envy, “assembled a council, how they might seize Jesus by deceit and kill him” (John 11:47). Then, “when the devil had put it into the heart of Judas, son of Simon Iscariot, to betray him” (John 13:2), he went to the chief priests, and they gave him thirty pieces of silver. Thus those who did not differ in name were also alike in deed: one Judah sold Joseph, the other Judas sold Christ.

“For Judah said to his brothers: Behold, the Ishmaelites are passing by; come, let him be sold.” His brothers agreed and sold him for twenty pieces of silver. Joseph, because he was of lesser merit, was rightly sold for a lesser price. By Reuben, who strove [Col. 0219D] to free Joseph, we understand that part of the people which did not consent to the Savior’s death. By the goat-kid which they killed we signify Christ’s death; by the tunic which they dipped in its blood, Christ’s flesh made bloody with his own blood. Joseph is therefore delivered from death if his tunic is bloodied, because Christ suffered according to the flesh, though according to divinity he cannot die.

## CHAPTER XXXVIII

As for what follows concerning Judah’s sons, who were wicked in the sight of the Lord and were killed by him, and concerning Judah himself, who lay with his daughter-in-law, we leave its exposition to others, not thinking it especially fitting to insert human crimes into spiritual mysteries. Yet, since all things that were written were written for our instruction, let us fear to do such things, lest by doing them we suffer like punishments.

Indeed, were it not for the fact that Judah’s firstborn was wicked, his second son could signify the Jews and heretics, who, envying their firstborn brother—that is, Christ—do not wish to cast into the ears of hearers that seed of the word through which truth, which is Christ, may arise in their hearts. Instead, they spill it on the ground, where they know no fruit can come from it. This is done so that a son may not be raised up in the brother’s name. For according to the Law, if anyone took his brother’s wife as his own wife, he begot children not for himself but for [Col. 0220B] his brother.

[Note: Col. 0219D. The erroneous edition is corrected from the same Laurentian codex.]

## CHAPTER XXXIX

Joseph was taken down into Egypt, and Potiphar, Pharaoh’s eunuch and commander of the army, bought him and placed him over all that he possessed. He himself knew nothing except the bread that he ate; but because he refused to sleep with his mistress, he was accused by her, as was supposed, and sent to prison. Then, at Pharaoh’s command, he was brought out of prison and appointed by him as overseer; he delivered all Egypt from famine. Therefore, in the Egyptian language, they called him “savior of the world.”

What Joseph’s self-restraint was may easily be recognized from the fact that, though he presided over great wealth, content with necessities alone, he ate only bread. Thus he proved a vigorous master of vices, especially of lust, which is conquered by nothing more effectively than mortification of the flesh. So Daniel too, with those three most noble youths, was content with bread and vegetables. Yet under the name “bread” every kind of food may be understood; hence the Gospel says: “When Jesus entered the house of a certain ruler of the Pharisees on the Sabbath to eat bread” (Luke 14:1). Thus, the statement that he knew nothing except the bread he ate means that, delighted by no glory, honor, or riches, he used only what his body required.

But since Joseph signifies Christ, and Christ was sold only once, what did Joseph’s second sale signify in Christ? Our Lord Christ was sold once in himself, but many times in his faithful people. Therefore he says to the disciples: “He who hears you hears me; and he who despises you despises me” (Luke 16). And to Saul, who persecuted him: “Saul, Saul, why do you persecute me?” (Acts 9:4). Likewise: “What you did to one of the least of mine, you did to me” (Matt. 25:40). Thus Christ, in his servants, is scourged, arrested, sold, and killed.

For at one time tyrants had issued this law: whoever informed against a Christian should have that Christian’s property. Led by this greed, wicked people everywhere diligently sought Christians. Thus Christians were sold through their own possessions.

[Note: Col. 0220D. The same codex remedies the faulty edition.]

But to whom did they sell them except Potiphar, the prince of Pharaoh, by whom the devil is understood? *Potiphar* is interpreted “a mouth bending down to learn.” When holy martyrs were brought before judges, they were immediately examined: who they were, where they came from, whether slaves or freeborn, and of what religion. In this way Potiphar, bending his mouth down to learn, questioned them about everything in a subtle examination. When they declared themselves Christians, he immediately set before them, so far as he could, all their possessions, promising riches, honors, and dignities if they would consent to his will.

[Note: Col. 0221D. Perhaps the author derived this fabrication from Hebrew tales.]

This Potiphar is said to have bought Joseph for shameful uses because he was handsome and fair of face; for that reason, by a divine judgment, he was made a eunuch through the withering of his testicles. [Col. 0221B] He was afterward made priest of Heliopolis, and Joseph later took his daughter as wife. This seems quite applicable to tyrants, who, desiring to defile and corrupt the faith of the saints, are reported to have been struck by the Lord in many ways—especially those who attempted to violate consecrated virgins.

But what do we understand by Potiphar’s wife except idolatry? Because Joseph and the holy martyrs refused to consent to her, they were condemned, as though sacrilegious and adulterous, to prison, death, and exile. Israel committed fornication with this harlot, of whom it is said: “Israel committed fornication after the gods of the nations” (Judg. 8:27).

The saints, therefore, placed in prison, found God their helper even there; he never abandons [Col. 0221C] those who hope in him. Although Joseph—sold, accused, and sent to prison—could signify all martyrs, he principally signifies those who lived in the time of Diocletian and Maximian. They pursued idolatry so vigorously that whoever refused to sacrifice was immediately handed over to prison or exile, or punished with various tortures.

After them came the Emperor Constantine the Great, to whom God deigned to reveal in a vision the pool of piety, in which both he himself and the whole world were cleansed from the leprosy of vices. Joseph is sought; Sylvester is sought, to interpret the king’s dreams. Joseph is drawn from prison; Sylvester is brought out of the hiding places in which he had concealed himself for a long time. He interprets dreams, explains mysteries, and becomes the emperor’s friend—more so than Joseph was Pharaoh’s.

Joseph was declared second in Pharaoh’s kingdom and received a ring, a robe, and a golden necklace about his neck. Sylvester, however, deserved to be the first to receive from Constantine all the insignia of the Roman Empire, which Roman pontiffs use to this day on great feast days. Hence pontiffs wear the chlamys and the purple.

[Note: Col. 0221D–0222D. In Bruno’s time this opinion was still current, based on Canon 14, Distinction 96; in a later period that canon was listed among the apocrypha. It is cited by the distinguished Sebastiano Berardi, vol. I, dissertation 1, §5, *On Archiepiscopal Insignia*, who calls it very ancient. Yet this in no way impairs the supreme dignity of the Roman pontiff in the Church, since, as Spondanus says under the year 324, no. 28, pontiffs had already used a crown or golden plate and other insignia of their high priesthood. See Anastasius the Librarian, *Life of St. Sylvester*, Roman edition of 1731, vol. I, p. 27.]

If Joseph is called savior of the world because he delivered Egypt alone from famine, why should Sylvester not also be called savior of the world, since he refreshed the whole world with the bread of God’s word and spiritual nourishment? Potiphar’s daughter was entrusted to Joseph; the holy and universal Church to Sylvester. Sylvester is said to have done far more than Joseph. The one is read to have opened granaries, the other churches. The one granted slavery to the Egyptians; the other granted freedom to Christians.

And when Jacob, with his sons and grandsons, his whole household and family, is joyfully brought in wagons to Joseph in Egypt, does this not seem to signify that, at Sylvester’s wish and Constantine’s command, all the saints returned with glory and honor to their homes from the prisons and exiles in which they had been held? For if, as is true, wherever two or three are gathered in Christ’s name he himself is in their midst, who would dare deny that our Joseph too was led with his saints out of prison and exile? It would be lengthy to compare every detail individually. Let it suffice for us to have said this: Pharaoh, through love of Joseph, did not benefit the Israelites more at that time than Constantine, through favor for Sylvester, afterward benefited Christians.

Passing over St. Bruno’s exposition in the next seven chapters, he comes to Chapter XLVII, which he elucidates together with the remainder, especially the final chapter, where the individual predictions made by the dying Jacob to his sons are elegantly and copiously explained.

## CHAPTER XLVII

Israel therefore came into Egypt, blessed [Col. 0222C] Pharaoh, dwelt in the land of Goshen, increased, and multiplied exceedingly; and all the days of his life were one hundred and forty-seven years. When he saw that the day of death was drawing near, he called his son Joseph and said to him: “If I have found favor in your sight, place your hand under my thigh and swear to me that you will carry me out of this land and bury me in the tomb of my fathers.” Joseph swore; and when he had sworn, Israel worshipped God, turning toward the head of his bed.

Israel, he says, came into Egypt because our Lord Jesus Christ, coming into this world, blessed Pharaoh and all the rulers of this world who do not refuse to obey the merits of the saints. And he increased in it so greatly that his dominion was extended from the rising and setting of the sun, from the north and from the sea.

## CHAPTER XLVIII

What it signifies that Joseph swore beneath his father’s thigh has already been explained above, where Abraham’s servant too is said to have sworn beneath his thigh. The statement, “Israel worshipped the Lord, turning toward the head of his bed,” signifies that the head of his bed was toward the east, in the direction in which he was accustomed to worship God, since even from that time he venerated Christ the Lord as the Sun of righteousness.

The Apostle, following another translation, says of this: “By faith Jacob blessed the two sons of Joseph and worshipped the top of his staff” (Heb. 11:21). The sense is that Jacob, worn out by old age and leaning upon the top of his staff, worshipped God; not that Jacob worshipped the staff itself, or the scepter of Joseph his son.

[Note: Col. 0223D. See Cornelius a Lapide, *Commentary on Hebrews*, chapter 11.]

## CHAPTER XLIX

When this had been done, Joseph was told that his father was ill. Taking his two sons Manasseh and Ephraim, he went to him; Jacob appointed them his heirs, so that they might divide the inheritance equally with [Col. 0223B] his own sons. When Joseph brought them near to their father, Jacob crossed his hands and blessed them, placing his right hand upon the head of Ephraim, who was on his left, and his left upon the head of Manasseh, who was on his right. Joseph, greatly distressed by this, attempted to transfer his father’s right hand to the head of Manasseh, who was older. But Jacob refused and said: “I know, my son, I know. This one too shall become a people and shall multiply; but his younger brother shall be greater than he, and his seed shall grow into nations.”

He blessed them at that time, saying: “By you Israel shall be blessed, and it shall be said: May God make you like Ephraim and Manasseh.” And he placed Ephraim before Manasseh.

Joseph had brought his sons to his father so that Manasseh, the elder, stood on the right and Ephraim on the left. The holy man, full of the Spirit of God, crossed his hands and, as it were, made with his own arms the sign of the cross over them. He blessed them, praying the God of his fathers and the angel who rescued him from all evils—in whom he understood both the Father and the Son—to bless them, to cause his own name and those of his fathers Abraham and Isaac to be invoked over them, so that they might prove worthy to be called sons of such fathers.

These two tribes became very numerous. Ephraim ruled over the ten tribes; and it was a proverb in Israel that, whenever someone wished good things for another, he would say in blessing: “May God make you like Ephraim and Manasseh.” The statement, “He placed Ephraim before Manasseh,” is as though it said: He appointed, established, and commanded that Ephraim should henceforth be greater than Manasseh. So John the Baptist says in the Gospel: “He who shall come after me has been made before me” (John 1:27).

Jacob said to Joseph his son: “Behold, I am dying, but God will be with you and will bring you back to the land of your fathers. I give you one portion beyond your brothers, which I took from the hand of the Amorite with my sword and my bow.” Nowhere above do we read that Jacob violently took land from the Amorites; but because it is said here, it may be understood to have happened. Or, if it is not understood in this way, it is a prophecy of the future: he speaks as though he had already done what he knew Joseph’s sons would do. Perhaps this is the estate of which the Gospel says: “Jesus came to a city of Samaria which is called Sychar, near the estate which Jacob gave to Joseph his son” (John 4:5).

## CHAPTER L

“Jacob called his sons and said to them: Gather together [Note: Col. 0224D. The Vulgate reads: ‘That I may tell you what will happen to you in the last days. Gather together,’ etc.] and hear, sons of Jacob; hear Israel your father. Gather together, that I may tell you what shall happen to you in the last days. Reuben, my firstborn, you are my strength and the beginning of my sorrow, first in gifts, greater in rule. You have been poured out like water; you shall not increase, because [Col. 0224B] you went up to your father’s bed and defiled his couch.”

Reuben, Leah’s son, was the firstborn. He, Gad, and the half-tribe of Manasseh possessed all the land which the children of Israel seized before they crossed the Jordan. Leaving behind wives, children, flocks, and all their equipment, they marched unencumbered and armed before their brothers. Therefore Jacob now says to Reuben: “You are my strength,” for, if you lead and fight, I shall conquer; “and the beginning of my sorrow,” because you lay with Bilhah, your father’s concubine. Hence he says afterward: “Because you went up to your father’s bed and defiled his couch.” “Beginning of my sorrow,” therefore, is as though he said “my greatest sorrow.” “First in gifts,” either because he is first to be blessed, or because he first received an inheritance. “Greater in rule”: he would indeed have been greater in rule had he not lost his birthright because of the sin mentioned above.

“You have been poured out like water,” not considering where you were rushing, conquered by lust’s frenzy; and therefore you shall not increase. For if he is not to increase, how will he be greater in rule? He ought to have been greater; but because he fell headlong without reflection and did not restrain the force of his outpouring, he shall neither increase nor be greater. Thus Moses too, blessing him, says: “May Reuben live and not die, and may he be few in number.” It may also be understood thus: You shall not increase in sins—that is, add sins to sins; you have sinned: be still.

Since it is said above: “Gather together, sons of Israel, that I may tell you what will happen to you in the last days,” it seems to refer literally to Reuben but allegorically to the whole Jewish people, so that these are the words of the Lord speaking: “Reuben, my firstborn.” Thus it is written: “Israel is my firstborn son.” God at one time loved this people as a firstborn son before all nations. “Beginning of my sorrow”: that is, you are my chief and greatest sorrow, both for other reasons and because you killed my most beloved Son. “First in gifts,” because I entrusted to you the Law, manna, and spiritual gifts. “Greater in rule,” because so long as you were faithful, no nation could overcome you—or indeed resist you. “You have been poured out like water,” overwhelming and destroying all enemies, or even multiplied beyond number. You shall not increase; rather, as you feared, the Romans will come and take away your place and nation. Why is this so? “Because you went up to your father’s bed and defiled his couch”: that is, by teaching, examples, and violence, you defiled and corrupted many souls betrothed to the Lord. And because the Father is in the Son and the Son in the Father, each is, as it were, called the other’s bed.

“Simeon and Levi are brothers, weapons of iniquity for warfare. Let not my soul enter into their counsel, nor my glory be in their assembly; for in their anger they killed a man, and in their will they undermined a wall. Cursed be their anger, because it is stubborn, [Col. 0225B] and their indignation, because it is harsh. I will divide them in Jacob and scatter them in Israel.”

Because, as we read above, Simeon and Levi, brothers, deceitfully killed Shechem and Hamor on account of their sister Dinah, they are called weapons of iniquity for warfare. Their gatherings and counsels, full of fury, wrath, and indignation, could not be appeased even by those who made satisfaction and sought pardon. Therefore Jacob prays that his life and glory may never come under their counsel and power; or, alternatively, that he may never trust the counsels of men who could perpetrate so great a crime by deceit and pretence. He adds concerning this: “For in their anger they killed a man”—namely Shechem and Hamor—“and in their will they undermined a wall,” destroying their entire city or preparing an entrance for themselves to enter it. “Cursed be their anger, because it is stubborn,” that is, implacable; “and their indignation, because it is harsh,” unable to be softened. It should be noted that he curses not them but their anger and indignation, so that after the curse these might no longer be able to remain in them. “I will divide them in Jacob and scatter them in Israel.” Simeon received an inheritance within Judah’s allotment and dwelt among Judah’s sons. But cities to dwell in were given to Levi from all the tribes.

Spiritually, however, by Simeon and Levi we understand all the Jews, especially the priests and Levites: weapons of iniquity for warfare, who plotted conflict all day long; who, after forming a wicked plan, killed the man—namely Christ—in their fury; “and in their will undermined the wall,” that same one who fortified and defended Jerusalem. Therefore they were divided in Jacob and scattered in Israel: that is, throughout all lands, if by Jacob we understand the Church, which is spread throughout the whole world.

“Judah, your brothers shall praise you. Your hand shall be upon the necks of your enemies, and the sons of your father shall bow down before you. Judah is a lion’s whelp; from the prey, my son, you have gone up. You have lain down in rest like a lion, and like a lioness—who shall rouse him? The sceptre shall not be taken away from Judah, nor a ruler from his thigh, until [Col. 0226A] he comes who is to be sent; and he shall be the expectation of the nations. Binding his colt to the vine, and, O my son, his she-ass to the vine-stock. He shall wash his robe in wine, and his cloak in the blood of grapes. His eyes are more beautiful than wine, and his teeth whiter than milk.”

For the tribe of Judah, because it possessed the Temple, the Law, and the prophets, always deserved praise above the others. The books of Kings testify how its hand held the necks of its enemies. There too it is found how the whole people bowed before and revered David and the other kings descended from him. Judah is called a lion’s whelp because of the strength possessed by that people. He went up to the prey, laying waste all the surrounding cities. He rested like a lion and [Col. 0226B] like a lioness, because, so long as it kept the Law given to it, all feared to disturb its rest and peace or make war against it. Hence it is added: “Who shall rouse him?”—that is, by provoking him to war.

“The sceptre shall not be taken away from Judah, nor a ruler from his thighs [Note: [Col. 0225D] The Vulgate reads: “nor a ruler from his thigh.”], until he comes who is to be sent, and he shall be the expectation of the nations”: this is a clear prophecy concerning Christ. For he is the one whom all nations awaited, and by whom they were delivered from everlasting death. From the time when the tribe of Judah began to reign—that is, from the time of David—it had a king from no tribe other than its own. But the statement, “The sceptre shall not be taken away from Judah,” must be understood thus: not that it would never at all be taken away—for when carried into captivity it did not always have a king—but [Col. 0226C] that this dignity would not be taken from this tribe and given to another tribe which was to rule over it. For whenever a king died, the sceptre was indeed removed; nevertheless royal dignity and honour remained in that tribe as something natural and hereditary. Thus, after the death of any king, and after the return from captivity, a king from this tribe of Judah was chosen without any dispute. This continued, as Jacob foretold, until Christ’s coming. For then Herod reigned in Judaea, though by fraud; yet he had a wife from the tribe of Judah, and through her possessed both kingdom and sceptre.

What follows—“Because he shall bind the colt and she-ass to the vine, and because he shall wash his robe and cloak [Col. 0226D] in wine”—seems, in the literal sense, to signify that he would enjoy peace and rest: that he might sleep safely beneath his vine, and possess such an abundance of wine that, if necessary, it would suffice even for washing clothes.

Spiritually, however, we understand Christ through Judah: him whom not only his brothers, but every creature, praises and blesses; whose hand is upon the necks of his enemies, because no one can resist him. The sons of his Father also worship him—namely, angels and human beings. He himself is the lion’s whelp, the strongest of all beasts, who fears no encounter with any other.

It is said that when a lion’s whelp is born, it lies as though dead and sleeping, without moving, until the third day; but on the third day it is awakened from sleep by a certain roar and by the voice of its parent. Christ, speaking of himself, says: “I slept and began to sleep, and I rose again, because the Lord sustained me” (Ps. 3:6). I slept in the tomb; on the third day I rose again, [Col. 0227A] awakened from sleep by the voice of the Father. Hence it is added: “You lay down in rest like a lion and like a lioness: who shall rouse him?” Surely the Father, who will not abandon his soul in hell; or he himself, since he has power to lay down his life and to take it up again.

And the words, “From the prey, my son, you have gone up,” are what is said elsewhere: “Christ, ascending on high, led captivity captive” (Eph. 4:8). For, ascending the cross, he seized the prey from the devil’s hand [Col. 0227B]—that is, the whole world.

But what does he mean by, “Binding his colt to the vine”? What is meant by the vine, and what by the colt? “For the vineyard of the Lord Sabaoth is the house of Israel” (Isa. 5:7); but the colt is the wanton and unbroken Gentile people. He therefore bound the colt to the vine, joining Jews and Gentiles in one faith, that there might be one fold and one shepherd.

“And, O my son, his she-ass to the vine-stock.” “I,” says the Lord, “am the true vine, and you are the branches” (John 15:5). The she-ass is the Synagogue, which, in that part of it which believed, the Lord joined and bound to himself with an indissoluble bond. Thus Paul called the children of this she-ass inseparably bound to this vine: “Who shall separate us from the love of Christ? Shall tribulation, or distress? For I am certain that neither [Col. 0227C] death nor life shall separate us from the love of God which is in Christ Jesus” (Rom. 8:35). If, therefore, the colt is bound to the vine—that is, to the Synagogue—and the she-ass, that is, the Synagogue, is bound to the vine-stock, then the colt also is bound to the vine-stock.

“He shall wash his robe in wine, and his cloak in the blood of grapes.” Christ’s robe and cloak are his flesh, which the soldier’s spear pierced, and immediately blood and water came forth. Hence it is said: “Who is this who comes from Edom, with garments dyed from Bozrah? This one, beautiful in his robe” (Isa. 63:1). It should be noted that wine is called blood because wine is changed into blood.

“His eyes are more beautiful than wine, and his teeth whiter than milk.” Christ’s eyes are understood to be the prophets, who deserved, through the penetrating sharpness [Col. 0227D] of their minds, to see the mysteries of the Church even to the consummation of the age. These are more beautiful than wine because, fervent in spirit, they cleansed and expelled from themselves all superfluous and harmful things; for wine too is purified by fermenting and bubbling. The teeth are the apostles, who, by chewing over and explaining the difficult and harder matters of the Scriptures, nourished us as infants. They are whiter than milk because, made whiter than snow, no stain of sin appears in them.

“Zebulun shall dwell on the shore of the sea, and at the harbour of ships, extending as far as Sidon.” This seems to be a description of his allotted inheritance rather than a blessing, though this very allotment was given him as a blessing. Of it it is written: “At the [Col. 0228A] first time the land of Zebulun and the land of Naphtali was lightened” (Isa. 9:1). For these two tribes lived beside the Sea of Galilee. Hence Matthew says: “When Jesus heard that John had been handed over, he withdrew into Galilee; and, leaving the city of Nazareth, he came and lived at maritime Capernaum, in the borders of Zebulun and Naphtali” (Matt. 4:13). Christ spent much time in Galilee, which was formerly the dwelling-place of the holy apostles Peter, Andrew, James, and John. Accordingly Naphtali is deservedly called “a hind let loose, giving words of beauty.” For the apostles are hinds, to whom, when they were sent by the Lord, it was said: “Go into all the world; preach the Gospel to every creature” (Mark 16:15). Read [Col. 0228B] and see what words of beauty they gave. Great, then, is the blessing of Zebulun and Naphtali, because they deserved to have such great men.

“Issachar, a strong ass, dwelling within the boundaries; he saw that rest was good, and that the land was excellent; and he put his shoulder to bearing, and became tributary in service.” Issachar dwells within the boundaries because, as is written in the book of Joshua, Ephraim lies to the south and Manasseh to the north, and they meet on the east in the tribe of Issachar, so that Issachar is the boundary of both. But because we can say little here according to the letter, let us turn to allegory.

Issachar, the strong ass, signifies the teachers of the Church, because they bear the burden of the whole Church [Col. 0228C]. These dwell within the boundaries: between the active and contemplative life. At one time they devote themselves to prayer; at another they supply the needs of the faithful. Since they know that the rest of heavenly blessedness is good, and know also that this land—that is, the holy Church—is excellent, they put their shoulders to bearing and labour with all their strength so that they may bring this land over to that rest. Therefore they became servants in tribute. For, as the Apostle says, they became all things to all people in order to gain all; and, as tributaries of all and debtors to all, they serve everyone by admonishing, rebuking, and correcting. When the Apostle says, “I am debtor to Greeks and barbarians, to wise and foolish” [Col. 0228D] (Rom. 1:14), does he not seem to you to pay tribute to all? It follows:

“Dan shall judge his people, like another tribe of Israel. Let Dan be a serpent in the way, a horned serpent in the path, biting the horse’s hoofs, so that its rider falls backward. I shall await your salvation, O Lord.” Samson, who judged the people courageously and vigorously and afflicted the Philistines, came from the tribe of Dan. From this tribe also, as is reported, Antichrist is to be born; the remaining words that follow should be understood of him.

“Let Dan,” he says—that is, Antichrist—“be a serpent in the way,” so that, in likeness to the ancient serpent, he may destroy and deceive by the poison of his deceit a people walking in the way of God’s commandments. [Col. 0229A] But what kind of serpent? “A horned serpent in the path.” Cerastes means “horned.” Read Daniel, and you will find how Antichrist is signified by horns. In the Apocalypse also he is described as having two horns like a lamb’s, by which his hypocrisy and false humility are understood. This serpent will be horned because he will display royal dignity, and will convert more people to himself by horns and violent strength than by action or speech. For “he sits in ambush with the rich in secret places, to kill the innocent” (Ps. 10:8).

“Biting the horse’s hoofs” [Note: [Col. 0229D] Codex of Monte Cassino: “For what is meant by the horse except the world? What by its hoofs,” etc.]. What, then, is signified by its hoofs except the end of the world? For the hoofs are the final part of the body. This serpent therefore bites the horse’s hoof, because Antichrist, appearing at the end of the world, will devour by biting the lovers of the world.

[Col. 0229B] “So that its rider falls backward.” The riders of this horse may be understood as kings, princes, and all the powerful people of this world, to whom this world is subject and by whom, as it were by riders, it is ruled and governed. These will fall backward; but one who falls backward does not see where he falls. They are rightly said to fall backward because they do not understand what punishments await them after the fall of death. But since the end will follow not long after these things, and the Lord will come in his majesty to judge, he therefore added: “I shall await your salvation, O Lord,” looking not at all toward Antichrist, who himself too will fall backward with the rest.

“Gad, girded, shall fight before him.” Before whom? Surely before Israel. The tribe of Gad [Col. 0229C], having received a possession beyond the Jordan, went before its brothers, fully equipped and armed. Moses had commanded this. It follows: “And he himself shall gird himself behind”; that is, Israel too, girded and ready for war, will follow after him.

If this is understood spiritually, Gad, girded for battle, signifies Christ, of whom he had just said: “I shall await your salvation, O Lord.” And through Gad we understand the apostles, who, fearing nothing and ready for battle, preached Christ’s name even among his adversaries. But he, as a good commander, followed after them, aiding them with signs and miracles. Thus it is written: “And they went forth and preached everywhere, while the Lord worked with them and confirmed the word by the signs that followed” [Col. 0229D] (Mark 16:20). The Saviour himself also says: “Without me you can do nothing” (John 15:5). This, then, is what is meant by: “And he himself shall gird himself behind.”

“Asher, his bread is rich, and he shall provide delights for kings.” This does not proceed according to the letter, unless perhaps it signifies the fertility of the land. Spiritually, however, Asher, whose name means “blessed,” signifies the Church. Its bread is Christ, who says: “I am the living bread, who came down from heaven” (John 6:42). Of this bread it is written: “May the Lord remember all your sacrifice, and may your burnt offering become rich” (Ps. 19:4). By this bread not bodies but [Col. 0230A] minds are filled. He shall provide delights for kings—that is, for bishops and priests, who by heavenly blessing prepare this bread upon the table of the altar. This bread provides delights for those who themselves taste and understand its flavour. “Taste,” he says, “and see that the Lord is sweet” (Ps. 33:9).

“Naphtali, a hind let loose, giving words of beauty.” This was explained where Zebulun is blessed. For these two tribes lived beside the Sea of Galilee, where our apostles were accustomed to fish. Let the whole blessing, therefore, be referred to them.

“Joseph, an increasing son, an increasing son and beautiful in appearance.” Joseph is rightly called an increasing [Col. 0230B] son, because he grew so great that he was called the saviour of the world, lord of Egypt, and father of Pharaoh. His son Ephraim likewise ruled over the ten tribes, with Judah and Benjamin alone following the house of David. He was also beautiful in appearance, and Potiphar and his wife burned intensely with desire for his beauty. Hence Egyptian women and daughters of the nobility, whenever they passed by in order to look at him, climbed upon the wall. This is what he says: “The daughters ran about upon the wall,” in order to admire his beauty, “and those who had arrows quarrelled and envied him.” What are those who have arrows, except soldiers and the other powerful men of Egypt? When they saw a foreigner and captive raised above them, they quarrelled among themselves—as is customary—because they endured such things, and perhaps also quarrelled against the king himself out of envy.

Yet their conduct did little good, because Joseph managed everything with vigilant and strong counsel and administration. Hence it is added: “His bow rests in strength.” He was strong in hand and strong with the bow; therefore he did not fear adversaries who rose against him. It follows: “And the bonds of his arms and hands were loosed by the hands of the Mighty One of Jacob.” [Col. 0230D] The Psalmist says: “They humbled [Col. 0230C] his feet in fetters; but afterwards the king sent and released him, the ruler of peoples set him free and dismissed him” (Ps. 104:18).
