That this happened by God’s will alone and by the intervention of Joseph’s merits is made clear when he says, “by the hands of the Mighty One of Jacob”: that is, the merit or power of both Jacobs brought about Joseph’s release.

“From there came forth the shepherd, the stone of Israel.” From there, I say—that is, from Jacob—the shepherd came forth, surely the good shepherd. For he himself says: “I am the good shepherd” (John 11:14). According to the flesh, he was born from Jacob’s seed. Let it then be said: from there the shepherd came forth. Which shepherd? Israel. Which Israel? The Stone. Therefore the first Israel did not come forth from Jacob—for otherwise Jacob would have come forth from Jacob—but that Israel came forth from Jacob who is called the Stone, by whom we understand Christ. Of him it is written: “The stone which the builders rejected has become the head of the corner” (1 Pet. 3:7).

From this point he speaks to Joseph, saying: [Col. 0231A] “The God of your father shall be your helper, and the Almighty shall bless you.” This can by no means be understood of Christ; for his Father has no lord—indeed, he himself is God of gods and Lord of lords. Therefore this and the rest that follows should be understood of Joseph.

It follows: “With blessings of heaven above and blessings of the abyss lying below. May the Almighty,” he says, “bless you.” But with what blessings? “With blessings of heaven above.” Isaac likewise blessed him, saying: “May God give you of the dew of heaven”; and “with blessings of the abyss lying below,” that is, abundance from the richness of the earth. For, compared with heaven, the earth is called an abyss.

By the blessings of heaven we may understand the blessings of God and the angels [Col. 0231B]; by the blessings of the abyss, those of the prophets and patriarchs. Prophets are called abysses because of the depth of their spiritual understanding. Hence it is written: “Abyss calls to abyss” (Ps. 41:8), that is, the apostles call the prophets as witnesses.

“With blessings of breasts and womb”—understand, “May the Almighty bless you.” If these blessings are understood literally, both saying and hearing them seem quite absurd and shameful. Yet according to the letter, the blessing may be understood as a wish for both many children and abundance of provisions. But what is meant by the breasts except the two Testaments? Hence the Church is told through Solomon: “Your two breasts are like two twin fawns of a gazelle” (Song 4:5). [Col. 0231C] These breasts sufficiently provide milk for all believers. By these breasts the Church’s children are nourished; in these blessings are contained those by which all peoples are blessed.

But what is meant by the womb except baptism? By this womb all are regenerated and born into the Church; nor are those counted among her children who are not regenerated through this womb. “Unless one is born again of water and the Holy Spirit, he cannot enter the kingdom of God” (John 3:5). Here are received those blessings by which both soul and body are cleansed of sins. Nowhere does a human being receive greater blessings than in this womb. Great, therefore, are the blessings of breasts and womb, by which we are born and nourished.

But why are the breasts mentioned first, and then [Col. 0231D] the womb? Unless because we are conceived by the breasts but born from the womb? Conception precedes birth; preaching precedes baptism. It is a wondrous generation, in which a person is first suckled and then born. For who in the primitive Church came first to baptism before being instructed in the mysteries of faith?

It follows: “The blessings of your father have been strengthened,” that is, have become strong and effective. Joined to the blessings of his fathers, they cannot fall in vain until the desire of the everlasting hills comes; as though he said: These blessings, my son, are sufficient for you at present. In the meantime live content with them [Col. 0232A] until he comes who is desired by all nations, with whose blessings no blessings can ever be compared. For he is the seed in whom all nations shall be blessed; he is the desire of the everlasting hills—that is, of the patriarchs and prophets, of whom it is said: “The mountains leaped like rams” (Ps. 113:4); likewise: “Mountains and hills shall sing praises before the Lord”; and again: “His foundations are in the holy mountains” (Ps. 86:1). For he is the one into whom angels desire to look.

May these blessings be upon the head of Joseph and of those who imitate Joseph, and upon the crown of the Nazarite among his brothers. Joseph was a Nazarite, as the firstborn of Rachel and one consecrated to God from infancy. “For every male opening [Col. 0232B] the womb shall be called holy to the Lord” (Luke 2:23).

“Benjamin, a ravenous wolf: in the morning he shall eat the prey, and in the evening divide the spoils.” Jerusalem is situated in the tribe of Benjamin; there also the Temple and altar were built. Benjamin is called a ravenous wolf because of the altar, upon which sacrifice was offered daily without interruption, and which nevertheless, like a ravenous wolf, could not be sated with all sacrifices. For the multitude of priests and Levites was so great that many animals scarcely sufficed for their daily expense. Such a sacrifice is therefore called prey. This prey they ate in the morning after the offering; in the evening, however, the priests and [Col. 0232C] Levites divided among themselves the spoils, that is, the skins of the animals.

Allegorically, Benjamin signifies the apostle Paul, who drew his origin from that tribe. Thus he himself says: “For I too am an Israelite, from the tribe of Benjamin” (Rom. 11:1). Like a ravenous wolf, he persecuted the holy Church with great fury and made such slaughter everywhere that even the apostles feared his cruelty. Hence he says: “For I am the least of the apostles, unworthy to be called an apostle, because I persecuted the Church of God” (1 Cor. 15:9).

“Morning and evening” means the same as “first and afterward.” First he ate the prey by persecuting, devastating, and tearing apart the Church; for it is said: “Those who devoured Jacob.” But afterward he divided Christ’s spoils by preaching, distributing sacred orders, and ordaining bishops and priests throughout bishoprics and churches. [Col. 0232D] [Note: [Col. 0231D] (178–79) Saint Augustine has the same passage in his sermon *On the Saints*.]

“Jacob spoke these things and blessed his sons with their own blessings; and, having finished the commands by which he instructed his sons, he gathered his feet upon the bed and died.”

O how precious in the sight of the Lord is the death of his saints! For behold Jacob, a holy man dear to God, spoke as long as he wished; and, as though death and life were in his power, he died when he wished. He lived one hundred and forty-seven years. They embalmed and buried him, as he had commanded his son, in the double cave. There Abraham and Sarah, Isaac and Rebecca, Jacob and Leah, and, as is reported, the greatest Adam [Col. 0234A] were buried; there also the bones of Joseph, carried from Egypt by the children of Israel [Note: [Col. 0232]], were laid.

[Col. 0233] Here ends the exposition on Genesis by the Venerable Bruno, bishop; thus the Laurentian Codex.

# THE EXPOSITION ON EXODUS BEGINS

[Col. 0233]

[Col. 0233A] As I am about to expound the book of Exodus [Note: [Col. 0233D] *Exodus* is a Greek word, from ἔξοδος, having the same meaning as the Latin *exitus*, “departure”; as in Psalm 113: “At the departure of Israel from Egypt.” This book, therefore, contains the narrative of the Israelites’ departure from Egypt under the leadership of Moses.], I invoke almighty God as my helper. I believe that by his finger not only the two tables contained in this volume, but also the whole book, was written and published.

# CHAPTER ONE

[Col. 0233B] “These,” he says, “are the names of the sons of Israel who entered Egypt with Jacob; each entered with his household. Reuben, Simeon, Levi, Issachar, Zebulun, and Benjamin; Dan and Naphtali, Gad and Asher. Thus all the souls of those who came forth from Jacob’s thigh were seventy-five [Note: [Col. 0233D] The Vulgate has seventy; hence Saint Bruno seems to have used another version, to which he adapted his interpretation.]. Joseph, however, was in Egypt; and when he had died, together with all his brothers [Note: [Col. 0234D] Codex Bibl. M. A.: “And all that generation, the children of Israel increased and, as it were sprouting, multiplied.”], and all his kindred, the children of Israel increased, multiplied like sprouting grass, grew exceedingly strong, and filled the land.”

These details are prefaced so that one may understand from how few persons, as from seeds, so great a multitude of people grew. Those alone who were able to go forth to war, from twenty years upward, were numbered as six hundred and three [Col. 0233C] thousand, five hundred and sixty-six men; and we do not doubt that those not counted were much more numerous. For the number of the good always increases and multiplies.

But when it says, “All the souls who came forth from Jacob’s thigh were seventy-five,” this cannot stand unless it signifies sons and grandsons of both sexes, or unless we understand as included those already dead and those not yet born. For Genesis says that all the souls of Jacob’s house who entered Egypt were seventy; this certainly is not true unless the two sons of Judah already dead—Er and Onan—and the two sons of Joseph born in Egypt are counted with the rest.

From this [Col. 0233D], certain heretics seem to confirm their error, who hold that souls descend by propagation, because they are said to have gone forth from Jacob’s thigh. But a part is put for the whole, and the whole human being is called “soul” by privilege of the greater part. It is as if he had said: All the human beings who came forth from Jacob’s thigh were seventy souls.

“Meanwhile a new king arose over Egypt, who did not know Joseph, and said to his people: Behold, the people of the children of Israel is numerous [Col. 0234A] and stronger than we are; come, let us oppress it wisely.” This king is the devil, the king of darkness indeed, because Egypt is interpreted as “darkness.” And he does not know Joseph—that is, he does not love him. For this is the sense in which it is said: [Col. 0234B] “Amen, I say to you, I do not know you” (Matt. 25:12). Joseph is Christ, the true Saviour of the world, who delivered not only Egypt but also the whole world from famine. Hence he himself said: “Come to me, all you who labour and are burdened, and I will refresh you” (Matt. 11:28).

The black king, the king of darkness, persecutes and strives to oppress his people because it seems numerous and strong. “Come,” he says, “let us oppress it wisely.” What is “wisely” except cunningly and craftily? He adds why they ought to do this: “Lest perhaps it multiply; and, if war should arise against us, it may join our enemies”—by whom God himself and the angels are understood. It follows: “And, having conquered us, it may depart from the land.” For then the devil truly understands himself to be conquered and defeated: when holy people depart from the land, when they flee Egypt, [Col. 0234C] when, despising earthly things, they seek heavenly things, when they pass from earthly to heavenly things.

“He therefore appointed taskmasters to afflict them with burdens.” Such as the king is, such are the overseers. Afflicted by such burdens, the Prophet said: “For my iniquities have risen above my head; and like a heavy burden they have weighed heavily upon me” (Ps. 37:5).

“And they built store-cities for Pharaoh, Pithom and Rameses.” Pithom means “mouth of the abyss,” and Rameses “moth.” What is the mouth of the abyss except the gate of hell? What is the moth except that worm which does not die [Col. 0234D]? Those therefore who serve the devil build such cities for themselves as well as for the devil: they open a pit and fall into it; their worm shall not die, and their fire shall not be quenched.

“The king of Egypt commanded the Hebrew midwives, one of whom was called Sephora and the other Puah, to kill the males and preserve the females. But the midwives feared God and did not do according to the command of the king of Egypt; instead they preserved [Col. 0235A] the males. And because the midwives feared God, he built them houses. Pharaoh therefore commanded that the males be thrown into the river and the females preserved.”

This wicked king always seeks to destroy those who are strong and able to resist his wickedness; but he loves females, whom he can readily deceive, and through whom from the beginning he subjected the world to himself. Since he first destroyed the first human being through a woman, he therefore now also seeks, through the midwives who fear God, to kill the males.

But what are the midwives who fear God and do not obey Pharaoh, except ministers of the Church? They receive those newly born in Christ, nourish and preserve them, and bring them into life. Therefore a house is built for them by him who says: “In my Father’s house are many dwelling-places” (John 14:2). Hence the Apostle says: “We know that if our earthly house of this dwelling is dissolved, we have a house not made with hands in heaven” (2 Cor. 5:1).

Nor can it be understood literally that God built houses for the midwives, unless perhaps this is understood to mean that God increased their households. Behold, however, a new plan is devised again: he commands all males to be thrown into the river. This is, of course, the river which was turned into blood, in which not even the fish themselves could live. By it we undoubtedly understand the false teaching of philosophers and heretics; whoever falls into it will be suffocated in the blood of wickedness and deceit.

# CHAPTER II

[Col. 0235C]

At that time Moses was born. When his father could no longer conceal him, he placed him in a basket of rushes and sent him into the river. Pharaoh’s daughter took pity on him, received him, and adopted him as her son.

Josephus relates concerning Moses that, while he was still a child and Pharaoh’s daughter joyfully brought him to her father, a certain priest of idols cried out: “This is the one who will destroy Egypt.” Rising up, he wished to kill him; but immediately the girl took the child and fled. He is said to have been of such great beauty that whenever he went out through the city, men and women alike, leaving necessary business behind, eagerly ran to look upon him.

Moses therefore grew up [Col. 0235D]; and, surpassing everyone in wisdom and strength, he became commander of the army. Thereafter he managed everything successfully and defeated all the enemies around him. Although he could have been lord of Egypt had he wished, he preferred to live humbly with his brothers. Hence the Apostle says: “By faith Moses, when he had grown great, refused to be called the son of Pharaoh’s daughter” (Heb. 11:24).

What does Moses signify except Christ? Of him Moses himself says: “The Lord will raise up for you a prophet from among your brothers, like myself; you shall hear him” (Deut. 18:15). For Christ too, out of fear of Herod, was carried into Egypt by his parents. There the land of Egypt—which we understand as Pharaoh’s daughter—protected and nourished him with his parents for a time as though he were her own. Then [Col. 0236A] he returned to the land of Judah, fulfilling the prophecy: “Out of Egypt I called my son” (Hos. 11:2; Matt. 2:15).

In those days Moses went out to his brothers and saw their affliction. He also saw an Egyptian striking a Hebrew; killing the Egyptian, he hid him in the sand. Likewise Christ our Lord, coming into this world to visit his brothers—that is, the whole human race—killed many Egyptians, that is, evil spirits; deprived them of power and cast them out of possessed bodies. They are rightly hidden in sand, so that we may understand by this that evil spirits can neither hide nor dwell in sandy, barren, and fruitless ground.

On the next day, when Moses saw two Hebrews [Col. 0236B] quarrelling and rebuked the one committing the wrong, the latter answered angrily: “Who appointed you ruler and judge over us? Do you wish to kill me as you killed the Egyptian yesterday?” This report reached Pharaoh, and he sought to kill Moses. Moses therefore fled and came to the land of Midian.

Likewise, when Christ frequently rebuked the Jews for their wickedness and called them to the way of salvation, they in return laid snares, watched him, accused him, and intended to kill him. Hence he said: “Whoever is of God hears God’s words; therefore you do not hear, because you are not of God” (John 8:47). He therefore left the Jews, as he himself says: “Behold, your house shall be left to you desolate” (Luke 13:35). And he came [Col. 0236C] to the land of Midian, that is, to the Gentiles.

The priest of Midian had seven daughters, through whom we understand all the Churches of this world. This number frequently signifies universality in Holy Scripture. They had come to the well to water the flocks, but shepherds came and drove them away. Moses therefore arose; Christ too arose and delivered the Churches from the hand of the shepherds—that is, from the violence of philosophers and heretics. Moreover, he watered the flocks, saying to his disciples: “Go, teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit” (Matt. 28:19).

Although, because of the diversity of places, there are many Churches in this world [Col. 0236D], yet in the truth of faith only one catholic and universal Church is believed to exist. Of it it is said: “One is my dove, my perfect one, my immaculate one” (Song 6:8). Therefore Moses took not all these maidens as wives, but only one, fittingly called Zipporah, since *Zipporah* means “beauty.” She is the one of whom the Apostle says: “That he might present to himself a glorious Church, having neither spot nor wrinkle” (Eph. 5:17). She is the one addressed in the words: “If you do not know yourself, O most beautiful among women, go,” etc. (Song 1:8).

After a long time the king of Egypt died—the one, namely, who sought to kill Moses. When he had died, the children of Israel cried to the Lord, and he heard them.

# CHAPTER III

[Col. 0237A]

“Moses was tending the sheep of Jethro, his kinsman, the priest of Midian. And when he had driven the flock into the inner part of the desert, he came to the mountain of God, Horeb; and the Lord appeared to him in a flame of fire from the midst of a bush, and he saw that the bush was burning and was not consumed.”

Now the mysteries begin; now the sacraments are revealed. This is Moses’ first vision; here he first begins to speak with God. But what is signified by the bush, if not the blessed Virgin Mary, who arose from the thorny and sinful race of the Jews as a beautiful and fragrant rose springs from the roughness of the brier? She appeared burning, yet was not burnt, because, overshadowed by the Holy Spirit, she conceived without fleshly concupiscence, without the heat of lust. For this is what the Angel says: “The Holy Spirit shall come upon you, and the power of the Most High shall overshadow you” (Luke 1:35). Thus there was fire in the bush, radiance in the virgin, light in Mary—the light which says: “I am the light of the world” (John 8:12), “the true light, which enlightens every person coming into this world” (John 1:9).

Moses wished to come nearer, to see why the bush was not consumed; but because he was not yet fit to know such great mysteries, it was said to him: “Do not come near here”—that is, do not seek things beyond you; do not investigate the virgin’s chastity or Christ’s incarnation—“take off the sandals from your feet.” Why is this? For the place in which you stand is holy ground. On holy ground it is not permissible to wear sandals, nor to be clothed in the skins of dead animals; for this reason Adam, when he departed naked from Paradise, was clothed in a girdle of skins.

And the Lord said: “I am the God of your father, the God of Abraham and the God of Jacob. I have seen the affliction of my people in Egypt, and I have heard their cry, and I have come down to deliver them. Come therefore, and I will send you to Pharaoh. Do not fear: I shall be with you, and this shall be the sign that I have sent you.” That is: recognize from this that you have been sent by God, because God will always be with you, and whatever signs and miracles you wish to perform, he will always work through you and in you. “And when you have brought my people out of Egypt, you shall sacrifice to the Lord upon this mountain”: that is, upon Horeb, the mountain of God, whose name means “raven.” By it we understand the people of the Gentiles, from whom and among whom the great and singular sacrifice is daily offered to the Lord. For to this raven the Apostle says: “You were once darkness, but now you are light in the Lord” (Eph. 5:10).

“And Moses said: I shall go to the children of Israel and say to them: The God of our fathers has sent me to you. If they say to me, What is his name? what shall I say to them? And the Lord said to Moses: I am who I am. Thus shall you say to the children of Israel: He Who Is has sent me to you.”

A wonderful name! Is not heaven? Are not earth, sea, angels, and human beings? Or is it because it is written: “All nations are as though they were not; so are they before him”? What does it mean when it says, “He Who Is has sent me to you”? Let him say it, then, who always is; who is always the same; who never began to be; who never ceases to be; who gives being to all; who is not changed from his own being into being or non-being. He who is thus named has sent me to you. For this name belongs to no other; it is the name of God alone.

“And the Lord said to Moses: Thus shall you say to the children of Israel: The Lord God of our fathers, the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob, has sent me to you. This is my name for ever, and this is my memorial from generation to generation.”

Behold, now there is a more familiar name, and one which the Hebrews cannot say that they do not understand. Both the old and the new generation know this name; the Synagogue understands it, and so does the Church. “Go therefore, and tell the children of Israel that I have seen their affliction and will bring them out of the land of Egypt. And you and the elders of Israel shall go in to the king of Egypt and say to him: The Lord God of the Hebrews has called us; we shall go a three days’ journey through the wilderness, that we may sacrifice to the Lord our God.”

What is the three days’ journey? What is the wilderness? “Behold,” says David, “I fled far away and remained in the wilderness” (Ps. 54:8). Therefore the Church of the Gentiles is the wilderness; here offerings are made, here sacrifice is offered; outside it there is no place for true sacrifice. The journey of three days signifies faith in the Trinity: by the first day one comes to the Father, by the second to the Son, and by the third to the Holy Spirit. This suffices for those who come to sacrifice: it is not right to stop short of it or proceed beyond it. For whoever acts otherwise will not have his sacrifice accepted.

The Jews come as far as the Father. There were heretics who believed in the Father and the Son but did not receive the Holy Spirit. There were also those who believed in many gods, like the Gentiles who worshipped idols. None of these, therefore, came to the appointed boundary of faith; consequently their sacrifice is abominable. It follows:

“But I know that the king of Egypt will not let you go, except by a mighty hand. For I shall stretch out my hand and strike Egypt with all my wonders, which I shall perform in their midst.”

Truly, the judgments of God are a great abyss. He knows that Pharaoh will not release them, yet commands him to release them; in this way God’s justice and Pharaoh’s iniquity are revealed. He does not wish violently to take away what is possessed by another, though unjustly; he exercises his own right, lest perhaps he be said to have acted unjustly in what he is about to do against the Egyptians. Finally, he also makes his own people more cautious by revealing to them the things that are to come.

“After these things,” he says, “I shall give this people favour in the sight of the Egyptians. A woman shall ask her neighbour for vessels of silver and gold and for garments, and you shall despoil Egypt.”

This seems unjust to some: that God’s people should seize things by deception. But because God himself commanded it to be done, what justice commands to be done cannot be unjust. For it had not yet been said: “Love your enemies” (Matt. 5:44); indeed, the law then was that later promulgated: “You shall love your neighbour and hate your enemy” (ibid., 5:43). If, then, those who afflicted them, oppressed them under the heavy yoke of slavery, and unjustly held not only their possessions but their very persons, were enemies, why should that be called unjust which appears to be done justly? For justice is that which gives each person what is his due. Where there is neither judge nor justice, vengeance is necessary.

Yet, understood in a particular sense, this seems to contain a great mystery. Although we flee Egypt—that is, this violent and dark world—nevertheless, if we judge that it contains anything good, useful, or honourable, such things ought to be embraced, taken, and retained. For lovers of the world often possess literary learning, honourable manners, and skill in many arts. We have received many things from poets and philosophers which are greatly to be embraced and loved. To seize, possess, and retain these—to despoil Egypt by means of them—is not a sin.

## Chapter IV

“But Moses said: They will not believe me, nor listen to my voice; rather, they will say: The Lord has not appeared to you.”

Moses’ unbelief is referred to the whole people. In himself he shows how hard and continually unbelieving that people was. They will not believe without signs, because “the Jews seek signs and the Greeks seek wisdom.” “For a wicked and perverse generation seeks a sign” (Matt. 16:4). Therefore it follows:

“And the Lord said to Moses: What is that which you hold in your hand? He answered: A rod. And the Lord said: Throw it upon the ground. He threw it down, and it became a serpent, so that Moses fled.”

Moses is questioned for no other reason than that he may be bound by his own answer. For he himself confessed that he held the rod which, when immediately changed into a serpent, he feared. This is a sign—a wondrous sign. Let him who will not believe words believe the sign.

But what is signified by the rod except God’s correction? Hence it is written: “Your rod and your staff, they have comforted me” (Ps. 22:4). Again: “The rod of uprightness is the rod of your kingdom” (Ps. 44:7). And Solomon says: “He who spares the rod hates his son” (Prov. 13:24). And the Apostle: “What do you wish? Shall I come to you with a rod, or in mercy and gentleness?” (1 Cor. 4:21).

This rod is turned into a dragon for those who, often corrected, refuse to amend themselves. Since they prove incorrigible, they at last feel the wrath and indignation of divine vengeance raging against them. Hence the Psalmist says: “You shall rule them with a rod of iron, and break them like a potter’s vessel” (Ps. 2:9). Thus divine correction is a rod to some and a dragon to others: it chastises some mercifully and strikes others incurably.

Moses, however, takes hold of its tail, and the serpent is changed into a rod, because there is a righteous man who, by his prayers, averts the vengeance threatening sinners. When God, the God of vengeance, is appeased from anger, the raging dragon is changed into a rod. David held the tail of this serpent when, seeing the angel striking, he cried: “It is I, Lord, who have sinned; I have acted wickedly. These, who are sheep, what have they done? [Note: Col. 0239D: The Vulgate reads: ‘Turn, I pray, your hand against me and against the house of my father.’] I pray, let your anger be turned away from your people” (2 Sam. 24:17). Likewise Phinehas, of whom it is written: “Phinehas stood up, and the scourge ceased” (Ps. 105:30). So too this Moses, to whom the Lord says: “Let me alone, that I may destroy this people.”

“And the Lord said again: Put your hand into your bosom. When he had put it into his bosom, he brought it out leprous as snow. Put your hand back into your bosom, he said. He put it back, and brought it out again, and it was like the rest of his flesh. If they do not believe you or listen to the word of the first sign, they will believe the word of the following sign.”

Moses’ hand signifies the people of the Hebrews; his bosom, the land of promise. “Put your hand into your bosom,” he says; that is, lead the people into the promised land. Moses then drew his hand out of his bosom, signifying that the people, because of their sins, were to be led into captivity. Hence the hand appeared leprous: for unless it had been leprous, it would not have been drawn out of the bosom; unless the people had sinned, they would not have been led into captivity.

But what does the Psalmist say? “Why, Lord, do you turn away your hand and your right hand from the midst of your bosom unto the end?” (Ps. 73:11). This is what follows: “Put your hand back into your bosom”; that is, lead the people back from captivity into their own land. For when the people, led into captivity, confessed whenever they had sinned and, doing penance, implored God’s mercy, they were immediately heard by the most merciful Lord; and those who had been cast out of their homeland as leprous returned cleansed through repentance. Hence it follows: “He put it back, and brought it out again, and it was like the rest of his flesh.”

Thus those who were not corrected either by the rod, by the serpent, or by severe discipline were at least compelled by expulsion from their homeland to return to repentance. But if not even thus they were converted, and still persisted in their malice, the sword of divine vengeance pursued even those who had been cast out, so that, continually falling, they wallowed in their own blood. And this is what is said: “If they do not believe you or listen to the word of the first sign, they will believe the word of the following sign.”

“But if they do not believe even these two signs, nor listen to your voice, take water from the river and pour it upon dry ground; and whatever you draw from the river shall be turned into blood.”

When it says, “If they do not listen to the word of the first sign,” this is what the Lord says in the Gospel: “If you are unwilling to believe my words, believe the works” (John 10:38). Signs also speak in their own way; and people believe signs no less than words. But what is meant by the river water and by the dry ground? “Many waters are many peoples” (Rev. 17). Water is taken from the river when some part is separated from the whole. It is poured upon the earth when it is led away from the place of its habitation to other nations. It is changed into blood if it falls struck down by the swords of enemies.

This is what Ezekiel is commanded to do (ch. 5:1): shave his head and beard, take scales, and divide the hair into three parts; burn one part with fire in the midst of the city, cut another down with the sword, and scatter the third to the wind—after the Lord says that he will send out the sword. The prophet’s beard is the people of the Jews: one part perished in the midst of Jerusalem by fire and famine; another was slain by swords in the same place; while the third, poured out over the earth and scattered among all nations, was nowhere able to escape the sword of divine vengeance.

“And Moses said: I beseech you, Lord, I have not been eloquent from yesterday and the day before yesterday; and since you spoke to your servant, I am more impeded and slow of tongue. [Note: Col. 0241D: This passage, greatly corrupt in the edition, is corrected from the Laurentian manuscript.]”

“I have not been eloquent from yesterday and the day before yesterday” means all past time. Every wisdom and eloquence fails when compared to that highest and incomparable wisdom and eloquence. This often happens among human beings as well: someone who thought himself wise, when reasoning with a wiser person, immediately learns through conversation what he lacks and how much he needs to learn.

“And the Lord said to him: Who made the human mouth? Or who formed the mute and deaf, the seeing and the blind? Was it not I?” “I,” he says, “made all; I bestowed particular gifts upon each person; I created the eloquent and the mute, the wise and the foolish. I have not lost my power; I do what I will. Go, therefore; and I shall be in your mouth. I shall teach you what to say, and neither wisdom nor eloquence will be lacking to you.” But Moses says: “I beseech you, Lord, send whom you will send,” and entrust so great a task to someone else.

“The Lord, angry with Moses, said: Aaron your brother is a Levite; I know that he is wise and eloquent.” He was a Levite because he was the firstborn. “Speak to him,” he says, “all my words, and I shall be in your mouth and in his mouth. He shall speak for you to the people”; and because he is fluent and eloquent, he will fulfil the office of your mouth. It belongs to priests, therefore, to speak to the people. But you shall be, in matters pertaining to God, like a messenger and mediator.

Moses went to Jethro, his kinsman, and said to him: “I shall go into Egypt to see my brothers.” And Jethro said: “Go in peace.”

“And the Lord said to Moses: Return to Egypt, for those who sought your life are dead.”

It is evident, then, that Pharaoh alone was not seeking to kill Moses. All the kings of Egypt were called Pharaohs. Thus another Pharaoh was now ruling the Egyptians, succeeding the one from whom Moses had fled.

“Moses therefore took his wife and sons, set them upon an ass, and returned to Egypt. And the Lord said to him: [Note: Col. 0241D, Codex of the Library of Monte Amiata: ‘See that you perform before Pharaoh all the portents [printed *offensa*, evidently *ostensa*] which I have placed in your hand: I shall harden his heart, and he will not release the people.’] See that you perform before Pharaoh all the signs which I commanded you to perform; I shall harden his heart, and he will not release the people.”

What is this, Lord? You will harden his heart? “For, as the Apostle says, you have mercy on whom you will, and harden whom you will” (Rom. 9:18). But if you harden him—and no one can resist you—what fault is there in Pharaoh? Why is he punished because he does not release the people, when he cannot release them because he is hardened? By whom? By you. For you say: “I shall harden his heart.”

It must therefore be understood otherwise. When it is said, “I shall harden his heart,” it is as if he said: I shall permit his heart to be hardened; I shall impose no force upon him; let him be wholly left to himself and do what he wishes, so that, whether he acts well or badly, it may all be attributed to himself and not to me. Wretched is the person thus left to his own will.

[Note: Col. 0241D: Free choice is established. God cannot be the author of evil; if a person falls away from the good—that is, from justice—God, if he so wills, leaves that person in his perverse will and does not draw him back from perversity to justice.]

From this, then, it follows that the salvation of the good is God’s grace: drawing them to himself with the bridle of his mercy, he does not allow them to sin even when they wish to sin. Yet he does this not by applying force, but by softening the heart and changing it for the better. The destruction of the wicked, however, is justice; for “whatever a man sows, that shall he also reap” (Gal. 6:2). Human nature is never so inclined toward evil that it can act well only under compulsion.

[Note: Col. 0242D: Although human nature has been wounded through original sin, its goodness has not been so consumed that it can act well only under compulsion. For it possesses the capacity for good action. See Natalis Alexander, Dissertation 26, section 3, against the Manichaeans.]

From this it is evident how unjust Pharaoh was: so often scourged, confronted with so many miraculous signs, he was not moved by a single sign or by the natural good within him toward mercy. The Lord therefore did not choose to soften him, lest someone perhaps think him good when of his own accord he was so wicked and unjust.

“Go, say to Pharaoh: Israel is my firstborn son. I said to you: Release my son; and you refused. Behold, I shall kill your firstborn son.”

Israel is God’s firstborn son, not by nature but by grace. For this nation, chosen by God before all others, was beloved above all. When all Egypt’s firstborn were killed, then the Lord also killed Pharaoh’s firstborn; for God is no respecter of persons.

While Moses was on the journey, at a lodging place, the Lord met him and wished to kill him. “Zipporah immediately took a very sharp stone and circumcised the flesh of her son’s foreskin; she touched his feet and said: You are a bridegroom of blood to me.”

From this we may understand that Moses had already been instructed concerning the circumcision of his son; but because his mother lived under another law, perhaps resisting, he either could not do it or neglected it. Thus she, the mother who lived under another law, is no longer merely instructed but in a sense compelled to circumcise him. For if he had brought his uncircumcised son to his brothers, all of whom were circumcised, he might, as a violator of God’s covenant, have caused them scandal.

Zipporah therefore took a very sharp stone—and the rock was Christ—and circumcised her son’s foreskin. By this rock both Jews are circumcised and people are baptized. For the Apostle says: “All of you who were baptized into Christ have put on Christ” (Gal. 3:27). We have set forth the matter of circumcision most fully in the book of Genesis. It follows:

“And she touched his feet and said: You are a bridegroom of blood to me.”

Why did the stone touch his feet, except because circumcision and baptism are useless if, after baptism or circumcision, one’s feet are not established upon the rock? Hence the Psalmist says: “He brought me out of the pit of misery and the miry clay, and set my feet upon a rock” (Ps. 39:3).

When she says, “You are a bridegroom of blood to me,” she seems to speak with feminine tenderness, as though saying: This benefit I receive from union with you: that I shed the blood of my children. But if Zipporah is understood to have said this to the Lord, it will be explained thus: A new kind of marriage, in which children are begotten from blood; a wondrous bridegroom, to whom children are begotten either from water or from blood.

“And he let him go, after she had said: You are a bridegroom of blood to me”—not because she said this, but “because of the circumcision.” For that was why he had come: not to attend to the woman’s words, but that the boy might be circumcised.

## Chapter V

Moses came, therefore, and related to his brother everything he had heard. Together they came to the elders of Israel; Aaron spoke what the Lord had commanded, performed the signs, and the people believed. All rejoiced and, bowing down, worshipped.

We are moving on to greater matters; therefore we do not wish to labour over the exposition of the narratives, lest perhaps, as is the custom of some, we make difficult things which are plain in themselves. Then they came to Pharaoh and told him to release the people. He refused to hear this, but afflicted them more harshly than before. This happened by God’s providence, so that both Pharaoh’s malice and God’s power might become known.

## Chapter VI

“The Lord spoke to Moses, saying: I am the Lord, who appeared to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob as God Almighty, and I did not make known to them my name Adonai.”

What does this mean: the Lord appeared to the patriarchs, showed them that he was God Almighty, and yet did not make known to them his name, Adonai? By these three patriarchs, from whom all Jews derive their origin, we ought to understand the entire people of the Jews. But God’s name is Jesus Christ.

[Note: Col. 0243D, the same Laurentian manuscript: “For he is called both Name and Speech and Word.”]

For he is also called the Word. “Behold,” says the prophet, “the name of the Lord comes from afar” (Isa. 30:27). But the Jews did not know him, “for if they had known him, they would never have crucified the Lord of glory” (1 Cor. 2:8). Their malice blinded them, according to the saying: “Blind the heart of this people, that seeing they may not see and hearing they may not understand” (Isa. 6:10).

Adonai means “Lord God.” The Saviour speaks to his disciples, saying: “You call me Teacher and Lord, and you speak rightly, for so I am” (John 13:13). Again: “If anyone says anything to you, say that the Lord has need of them” (Matt. 21:3). This ignorance, therefore, belongs not to the patriarchs but to the patriarchs’ offspring. The Lord made his name known to them, and did not make it known: he made it known according to themselves, but not according to their members; he made it known to the first, but not to the last.

In the same way he promises them the land of promise, yet it is not given to them. “To you,” says the Lord, “I shall give this land”—to you, and not to you; to you in your seed, but not to you personally. It may also be understood thus: “I did not make known to them my name Adonai,” because I showed myself to them not as Lord but as Father. But now, in delivering you and afflicting the Egyptians, all nations will know what manner of king and Lord I am. Hence it is often said: “I am the Lord your God,” and again: “You shall know that I am the Lord.”

## Chapter VII

“And the Lord spoke to Moses, saying: I am the Lord.” This is what he said just above: Adonai. This is the name which he did not make known to the patriarchs—that is, to the patriarchs’ children. It follows: “Speak to Pharaoh what I shall say to you.” And Moses said: “Behold, I am of uncircumcised lips; how will Pharaoh hear me?”

He is of uncircumcised lips who speaks superfluous, vain, and useless things; but one is circumcised who knows how to ask and answer reasonably. What can the Jews say to this, when they hear of an unheard-of circumcision of lips? And, that I too may speak with uncircumcised lips, would that they would circumcise their noses as well, so that they might now cease from useless circumcision.

“And the Lord said to Moses: Behold, I have made you a god to Pharaoh,” by granting you such power that you may afflict him according to your will, and that he may be astonished at the signs and miracles you perform and be unable to harm you in any respect. “And Aaron your brother shall be your prophet,” so that, because he himself is fluent and eloquent, he may speak for you to Pharaoh.

“But I shall harden his heart.” This has been explained above. Similar to it is what is said: “Do not lead us into temptation” (Matt. 6:13). Likewise Pharaoh could have said: “Do not harden my heart, Lord.” God neither hardens nor leads anyone into temptation; but because it lies within his power both to soften a hardened person and to restrain one going into temptation, he is therefore said to harden and to lead into temptation.

Thus Moses and Aaron did as the Lord commanded. Aaron took the rod before Pharaoh and his servants, and it was changed into a serpent. Enough has been said above about the rod and its transformation. The rod appropriately began the signs, because, as we said, it signifies God’s correction. Moses therefore came to Pharaoh not with a sword, but with a rod. Thus, had Pharaoh wished to repent, he could easily have recognized from this that the Lord is ready to forgive. But because he was unwilling to repent, the rod was changed into a serpent, so that he might understand that, being worthy of greater punishments, he should expect the torments of greater correction. Thus one who is not corrected by the rod is handed over to the dragon—that is, the devil—to be punished.

“Pharaoh then summoned wise men and sorcerers, and they too, by Egyptian incantations and certain secret arts, did likewise. Each cast down his rod, and they were changed into dragons; but Aaron’s rod swallowed their rods.”

Unhappy Pharaoh! When he should have humbled himself, he fled to the fabrications of his own deception, attempting by the false things which he himself performs to prove untrue what the Lord says. Tyrants are often recorded to have done this: when they saw signs and miracles which God performed through his martyrs, they thought the martyrs magicians and enchanters. We likewise read that the Jews said to our Saviour: “By Beelzebub, prince of demons, he casts out demons” (Luke 11:15). Nor is it surprising that sorcerers could do this through their incantations and the devil’s art, since Satan himself, as the Apostle says, “transforms himself into an angel of light” (2 Cor. 11:14). But Aaron’s rod swallowing their rods signifies that nothing can resist divine vengeance.

“And the Lord said to Moses: Pharaoh’s heart is hardened; he refuses to let the people go. Go to him in the morning; behold, he will go out to the waters. Tell him to release the people. But if he despises to listen, take the rod and raise it over the waters of Egypt, over its streams, marshes, and pools, that they may be changed into blood and the fish may die.”

This is the first plague with which the Lord struck Egypt. The Lord scourged Egypt with ten plagues, signifying the ways and the reasons for which he afflicts the whole world. Because the number ten contains all numbers in itself, ten is often taken for all.

Hence it is said in the Apocalypse concerning the saints: “They shall have tribulation for ten days” (Rev. 2:10), that is, for all days. For ten, one hundred, and one thousand, unless resolved in and through themselves, have nowhere further to grow; therefore, though finite, they are often taken for infinite. The ten plagues therefore signify all the plagues with which, because of the hardness of our heart, we are scourged by the Lord in this world.

Every person may be called Pharaoh who, hearing God’s commandments through the teachers of the Church, makes light of them and resists them with hardened heart and mind. He holds God’s people in slavery when a person does not permit the five bodily senses and the powers of the soul to serve God. This is God’s people, oppressed under the heavy slavery of the body. While it lives in populous Egypt, surrounded by a multitude of vices and evil spirits, it cannot sacrifice to God. It therefore wishes to go into the wilderness, seek a secluded place, and escape the society of the wicked—not bodily, but mentally. For whoever is separated from vices and evil spirits, wherever that person may be, is in the wilderness: he is deserted, left behind, and set apart in mind and spirit from the evil people; he is now alone with God. Let us consider the rest.

“The Lord said to Moses: Go to Pharaoh; behold, he will go out to the waters.” What do the waters signify here, if not the foolish wisdom of this world, of philosophers and poets? Because it declares pleasure to be the highest good, praises the world’s glory, honours, and delights, and does not reprove vices and fleshly lusts, Pharaoh and all lovers of the world run to it, thirst for it, and desire to drink it. Therefore Moses, carrying the rod of correction and powerfully stretching out his strong hand, changes it into blood.

He changes it into blood because Christ our Lord and his disciples have shown by true reasoning how poisonous, dangerous, foul, and full of the filth of sins it is. Whoever therefore does not wish to die and fears to perish should flee these waters and not receive this teaching; for those who drink it die. This was signified by the fish which died in Egypt’s river.

The sorcerers who perform signs like Moses signify hypocrites, because they too, like the Church’s teachers, condemn the learning of philosophers and poets. Of them the Lord says: “The scribes and Pharisees have sat upon Moses’ seat” (Matt. 23:2). But they do all their works not for God’s praise but for the sake of shameful gain and to be seen by people.

They dug for water around the river of Egypt because, having learned the truth, they no longer wished to drink it. To dig for water is to seek the fountain of wisdom purely and sincerely. This fountain is properly dug beside the river, because it is found only in the divine Scriptures. This blood lasted for seven days, because the aforesaid learning of philosophers, changed into blood and sin, will henceforth never be received by Catholic men; for there are only seven days. Thus “seven days” means all days. But Pharaoh refused to release the people.

## Chapter VIII

“And the Lord said to Moses: Say to Aaron: Stretch out your hand over the rivers, streams, and marshes, and bring forth frogs upon the land of Egypt. Aaron stretched out his hands over the waters of Egypt, and frogs came up and covered the land of Egypt.”

[Note: Col. 0245D: Saint Augustine briefly surveys all the plagues inflicted by God upon Pharaoh and the Egyptians in *The City of God*, book XVI, chapter 43.]

In the first plague philosophers and poets perished, together with all their learning, and pagan rites were destroyed. But behold, in this second plague frogs bubble forth: heretics arise, troubling all by their talkativeness and defiling everything by their uncleanness. They do not come from elsewhere, but rise from the waters, because by misunderstanding and perversely interpreting the Scriptures, they conceive errors there and become heretics there. First philosophers and poets, and then heretics, deceived the world by erroneous wisdom. They are therefore placed in the order in which they followed one another in time.

Heretics are rightly signified by frogs because heretics trust not in reason but in talkativeness. The sorcerers also did the same by their incantations, already signifying that hypocrites would imitate the examples of the saints with a certain semblance.

[Note: Col. 0247D, Codex of Santa Croce in the Laurentian Library: “by a certain pretence.”]

“Pharaoh said: Pray to the Lord that he may take away the frogs from me and my people, and I shall release the people that they may sacrifice to the Lord. And Moses prayed, and the frogs died.”

This is what sinners do even today: when they are in straits, they pray to the Lord, whose generosity they immediately forget. The death of the frogs signifies the destruction of heretics.

“But Pharaoh, seeing that respite had been granted, hardened his heart and did not release them, as the Lord had commanded. And the Lord said to Moses: Speak to Aaron: Stretch out your hand and strike the dust of the earth, and let it become gnats throughout all the land of Egypt. They did so, and gnats came upon people and beasts, and all the dust of the earth was changed into gnats.”

Some call *sciniphes* gnats; others, very small flies, in distinction from the dog-fly. But what do these *sciniphes*, which troubled both people and beasts with excessive vexation, signify if not care and anxiety over temporal things? When you see someone labouring, running about, sweating, and hurrying with such anxious mind for the sake of transitory and fleeting wealth, do not *sciniphes* seem to you to sting and follow that person? They arise fittingly from the dust of the earth, because this sort of care and anxiety invites people toward earthly and fleeting goods.

These are found both in people and beasts because they weary both the wise and the foolish. Even beasts, in the literal sense, would not be wearied unless such anxiety existed. For it forces oxen to plough, horses to rush into war, and other beasts to be weighed down by burdens. Wishing to free us from this anxiety, the Lord said: “Do not be anxious, saying, What shall we eat? or What shall we drink? or What shall we wear?” (Matt. 6:31).

Among the plagues by which the world is struck, this third plague vexes it more than any other. The sorcerers wished to make *sciniphes* as well, but could not—not because making frogs or serpents is more difficult, but because they can act only where God permits them to act. Hence they themselves say: “This is the finger of God,” understanding that this power is God’s hand, able so suddenly to restrain them from their customary activity.

“Then the Lord said to Moses: Say to Pharaoh: Let my people go; otherwise I will send upon you, and upon [Col. 0248A] your servants and your people, and into your house, every kind of fly. And it came to pass thus. Most grievous flies came into Pharaoh’s house and over all the land of Egypt, and the land was ruined by flies of this kind.” For what do we understand by the flies except the spirit of fornication, that lust which is itself the foulest of all vices? Of this the Apostle says: “Every sin which a man commits is outside the body; but he who commits fornication sins against his own body” (1 Cor. 6:18). Hence it is also said here that the land was ruined by flies of this sort. For what does it mean that the heat of lust corrupts the earth—that is, our flesh? There are many kinds of this lust; therefore the flies too are said to have been of different kinds. Since they are called most grievous, it is made known how extensively [Col. 0248B] this vice rages among human beings. By these flies the adulterer, the fornicator, the sodomite, and every practitioner of lust are stung, harassed, inflamed, pursued, and corrupted.

Yet these flies were not in the land of Goshen, where the children of Israel lived, because holy men repel every assault of lust from themselves by fasts, vigils, prayers, and the mortification of the flesh. “And Pharaoh called Moses and Aaron and said to them: Go, sacrifice to your God in this land. And Moses said: It cannot be done so; for shall we sacrifice to the Lord our God the abominations of the Egyptians? If we slaughter before them those things which the Egyptians worship, they will stone us.” He calls them “the abominations of the Egyptians.” Wonderful is the prudence of the man who, before the king himself, [Col. 0248C] calls his gods abominations; for the Egyptians worshipped not only goats, sheep, and cows, but many other monstrosities. “We shall go three days’ journey into the wilderness and sacrifice to our God, as he commanded us.” What the journey of three days signifies has been explained above.

“And Pharaoh said: I will let you go; only do not go far away. Pray for me.” Consider, Pharaoh, what your strength and power can accomplish: you ask the Prophet himself to entreat the Lord for you, that he may drive away the flies from you and your people. The rod still strikes you, and you cannot bear it; what if he should rain fire from heaven? Do not harden your heart further; do not deceive God’s servants any longer, lest perhaps, if they cease praying for you, both you and your people perish. And Moses went out from Pharaoh [Col. 0248D] and prayed to the Lord, and the flies perished. But Pharaoh’s heart was hardened, and he would not let the people go. The Pharaoh who is more often hardened is therefore more often scourged. It follows:

## CHAPTER IX

“But the Lord said to Moses: Go, say to Pharaoh: Thus says the Lord: Let my people go; otherwise behold, my hand shall be upon your fields, and upon your horses, asses, camels, cattle, and sheep: a very grievous pestilence. Therefore the Lord fulfilled his word the following day, and all the animals of the Egyptians died; but of the animals of the children of Israel not one at all perished.” What, then, [Col. 0249A] do we understand by these things just enumerated except outward possessions? When the Lord suddenly takes these away from sinners, it is either a test or a punishment. Thus he is read to have dealt with blessed Job, who, though suffering, nevertheless gave thanks patiently, saying: “The Lord gave; the Lord has taken away” (Job 1:21). For the holy man recognized God’s mercy even in this: that God struck not him, but what was his. Therefore, when a person is scourged in outward things, let him give thanks, turn back, and repent. Indeed, let him acknowledge the mercy of him who so mercifully calls him to repentance. For the Lord corrects every son whom he receives (Heb. 12:7). Blessed is the person whom the Lord corrects. Let him not be hardened like Pharaoh, but, confessing that he has sinned, let him seek pardon, lest punishment perhaps rage even [Col. 0249B] against his soul. Hence it is written: “May the Lord keep you from all evil; may the Lord keep your soul” (Ps. 120:7).

This is the fifth plague, by which a person is struck in what he possesses, not in himself. “And Pharaoh’s heart was hardened, and he did not let the people go. And the Lord said to Moses and Aaron: Take handfuls of ashes from the furnace; let Moses scatter them into the sky before Pharaoh, and let them become dust over the whole land of Egypt. For there shall be wounds and swelling blisters upon people and animals throughout all the land of Egypt. And it came to pass thus. Nor could the magicians stand before Moses because of the wounds which were upon them.” Behold, not animals alone, but human beings themselves are struck, so that those who do not feel the rod may at least be corrected by torments. What is meant by the furnace except affliction? And what by ashes except a people already scorched by the long-burning fire of affliction? Therefore ashes are taken from the furnace and scattered into heaven, because the prayers of afflicted people are heard in heaven. And rightly are ashes scattered into heaven through the hands of Moses, because through the hands of Christ and the saints every people is presented to the Lord.

The wounds and swelling blisters, dreadful to see and unbearable to endure, signify those future torments with which no torments can compare. These torments await those who persevere with hardened heart in their wickedness to the end. This plague comes upon both people and [Col. 0249D] animals, because wise and foolish, noble and lowly, rich and poor alike are afflicted by divine retribution. For fools stand in relation to the wise as animals do to human beings. The magicians could not stand before Moses because of the wounds, because, like lepers and unworthy of the sight of Christ, driven out beyond the camp, they shall not dwell in the city of the saints. “And the Lord hardened Pharaoh’s heart, and he did not let them go.”

There follows the sixth plague, in which, as in the others, Pharaoh is warned to let the people go. If he scorns to do so, the Lord threatens to send all plagues upon him and his people, and to rain exceedingly great hail, such as has not been in Egypt from the day it was founded until the present. Therefore Moses commands that people and the things which are [Col. 0250A] outside be gathered indoors, lest they die. But why does Moses first warn Pharaoh to let the people go, and then announce every plague to him before it happens? Is it not because Christ, who is understood through Moses, and his disciples, whom Aaron signified, first called the people to repentance and then proclaimed to them the evils of the world to come and the torments of hell? They were, as it were, raining hail upon them when they set forth the torments prepared in hell for the devil and his angels. They sent forth darting lightning when, like burning missiles, they slew vices and evil spirits in human hearts by the sayings of Scripture. Fire also accompanied it, because the brightness of signs and miracles followed their preaching, so that those unwilling to believe words might at least, enlightened, terrified, and pierced in heart by the fire and splendour of miracles, turn to the Lord.

Everything that is outside perishes, because whoever is separated from the faith and fellowship of the saints, and is found outside the Church, shall perish in judgment. Therefore Moses commands that everything be gathered together, lest things remaining outside should perish through the carelessness and negligence of teachers. But when he says, “For this reason I have placed you, that I may show my strength in you and that my name may be proclaimed in all the earth,” it must be understood as though he said: For this reason I endure your hardness, and therefore spare you so often: that through you my strength may be displayed; that whenever I will, I overcome you, and, once overcome, permit you to recover strength again, so that my name may be proclaimed [Col. 0250C] in all the earth—he to whom every creature is obedient, whose miracles are without number, whom no one can resist with impunity, who commands not armed soldiers but locusts and gnats to overcome kings and rulers, no less than thunderbolts and flies.

“And Pharaoh sent and called Moses and Aaron, and said to them: I have sinned even now; the Lord is just, repaying me according to my deeds and punishing according to my sins. I and my people are wicked, though the Lord has shown mercy to us so often and we have not acknowledged it. Pray to the Lord, that the thunders and the hail may cease; and I will let you go, and you shall by no means remain here any longer.” You would have been blessed, Pharaoh, if you had carried this declaration through; if you had done as you say; if you had not hardened your heart [Col. 0250D] further. And Moses prayed to the Lord, and the hail ceased.

“Therefore Pharaoh’s heart and the hearts of his servants were hardened, and he did not let the people go.” The fact that the late crops were not damaged may signify the salvation of the later, Christian people.

## CHAPTER X

After this, when Pharaoh, though warned as before, had refused to let the people go, and when Moses had announced that locusts would come and Pharaoh had despised the warning, “Moses stretched out his rod over the land of Egypt, and the Lord brought a scorching wind throughout that day and night; and when morning came, the scorching wind lifted up the locusts, which rose over the whole land of Egypt and covered it, devastating [Col. 0251A] everything. Thus the grass of the land and whatever fruit the hail had left were devoured.”

For what do we understand by locusts, which descend like the ranks of commanders, formed into an army and laying waste everything, except the multitude of vices and evil spirits? The scorching wind lifts and carries them, because every vice and evil spirit is borne along by the violent and impetuous spirit of pride. For pride is the beginning of every sin: it carries vices, lifts demons up, and exalts sinners. Filled with this swelling, inflated by this wind of pride, that proud one said:

> “I shall ascend above heaven;  
> and above the stars of heaven I shall exalt my throne;  
> I shall sit on the mount of the covenant,  
> on the sides of the north,  
> and I shall be like the Most High.”

[Note: [Col. 0251D] The Vulgate has: “I shall ascend into heaven; above the stars of God I shall exalt my throne; I shall sit upon the mount of the covenant, on the sides of the north; I shall ascend above the height of the clouds; I shall be like the Most High” (Isa. 14:13).]

Thus locusts fly; thus vices and evil spirits are carried along. Every disobedience is pride; whoever sins is disobedient. Thus every sin is borne along by the wind of pride. These are the locusts that devour everything, gnaw away at it, scatter all things, and leave nothing beautiful or green upon the trees. Thus they become barren and fruitless, useful for nothing else except to be cut down and thrown into the fire. But this happens only in the land of Egypt, in Pharaoh’s kingdom, in the land of darkness, which is not illuminated by the rays of the sun of righteousness. It follows:

“Therefore Pharaoh hastily called Moses and Aaron and said to them: I have sinned against the Lord your God and against you; but now forgive my sin this once also, and entreat the Lord your God to take away this death from me.” Thus, whoever you are, if you perceive the army of locusts devouring your land—if you perceive luxury, avarice, discord, desire, fornication, gluttony, drunkenness, vainglory, anger, and other things like these, which are understood through the locusts, devastating and destroying your flesh—run quickly, run to Moses; beseech Christ to spare you and forgive your sin. But do not afterward harden your heart like Pharaoh, lest you too perish in Pharaoh’s likeness. Hear the Prophet saying: “Today, if you hear his voice, do not harden your hearts” (Ps. 94:8). The fact that, at Moses’ prayer, all the locusts were lifted by the wind and cast into [Col. 0251D] the Red Sea, where they perished, is to be understood thus: the vices and evil spirits that formerly pursued a people now repenting and confessing that they had sinned are, at Christ’s command, wholly wiped out in baptism. “And the Lord hardened Pharaoh’s heart, and he did not let the children of Israel go.”

“But the Lord said to Moses: Stretch out your hand toward heaven, and let darkness come upon the land of Egypt, so dense that it may be felt by touch. Moses stretched out his hand toward heaven, and dreadful darkness came over all the land of Egypt for three [Col. 0252A] days. No one saw his brother, and no one moved from the place where he was. But wherever the children of Israel lived, there was light.” Behold, those who follow the king of darkness—though so often warned and scourged, though seeing so many signs and miracles, yet still persevering in evil with hardened heart—are enveloped in darkness, see nothing, and remain motionless like stones, that they may at least understand through outward darkness the blindness of their own heart.

[Note: [Col. 0252D] Bruno appears to adhere to those Fathers who maintain that hardened sinners, as punishment for their obstinacy, are deprived altogether of every light and assistance of grace.]

Of this darkness the Apostle says: “You were once darkness, but now you are light in the Lord” (Eph. 5:10); and John says: “Everyone who hates his brother is a murderer and remains in darkness” (1 John 3:15). Whoever, then, does not wish to remain in darkness, having expelled vices, should follow the light—the light, namely, which says: “I am the light of the world” [Col. 0252B] (John 8:12). But because Moses signifies Christ, his hand, which he stretches toward heaven, can signify Christ’s hands stretched out in heaven. For in Christ’s Passion darkness also came for three hours; thus we may rightly understand those three hours to have been signified by these three days. The people of God do not endure this darkness, following him who says: “He who follows me does not walk in darkness” (ibid.).

Pharaoh called Moses and Aaron and told them to go and sacrifice to the Lord with their children, leaving the rest behind. Moses would not go without the flocks, lest anything perhaps be lacking for sacrifice. “And Pharaoh said: Depart from me, and take care not to see my face again. On whatever day you appear before me, you shall die. [Col. 0252C] But he said: It shall be as you have spoken: I shall not see your face again.” What does Moses mean when he says, “I shall not see your face again”? Later he did see him and speak with him. But because “to see” frequently means “to show mercy” in sacred speech, it can be understood as though he said: I shall no longer look upon your face; I shall no longer have mercy on you; I shall no longer urge you to let the people go; nor shall I pray to God for you any more.

## CHAPTER XI

“And the Lord said to Moses: I shall yet bring one plague upon Pharaoh and Egypt; and afterward he will let you go and will compel you to depart. Therefore tell all the people that every man should ask his friend, and every woman her neighbour, for vessels of silver and gold; and the Lord [Col. 0252D] will give his people favour before the Egyptians.” What this signifies has been explained above; it is easier to return there than to repeat the same things again.

Moses was a very great man in the land of Egypt before Pharaoh and all the people. He was great in words, great in miracles, great in steadfastness; and great because he bore the figure of Christ. And he said to Pharaoh: “At midnight I shall enter Egypt, and every firstborn shall die, from Pharaoh’s firstborn, who sits upon his throne, to the firstborn of the maidservant who is at [Col. 0253A] the mill, and all the firstborn of the animals [lacuna]. And all these servants of yours shall come down to me and bow before me, saying: Depart, you and all the people subject to you.” We shall explain these matters in what follows, namely in the place where they are fulfilled. “After this we shall depart.” And he went out from Pharaoh exceedingly angry. This is a good anger, by which pride is conquered, folly overcome, an unrepentant heart recalled to repentance, though fruitlessly, and God’s people freed from most grievous bondage.

## CHAPTER XII

“And the Lord said to Moses and Aaron in the land of Egypt: This month shall be for you the beginning of months; it shall be first among the months of the year.” This month, he says, is the beginning of the other months; among us it is called March. But let it be first for you—that is, greatest and chief—among the months of the year, because greater mysteries are performed in this month than in the others.

“Speak to the whole assembly of the children of Israel and say to them: On the tenth day of this month let each take a lamb for his families and households. But if the number is too small to be sufficient for eating a lamb, he shall take his neighbour, who is joined to his household, according to the number of souls sufficient for eating the lamb. The lamb shall be without blemish, male, one year old; according to this rite you shall also take a kid. And you shall keep it until the fourteenth day of this month, and the whole multitude of the children of Israel shall sacrifice it at evening.”

On the tenth day the lamb and the kid are taken and kept until the fourteenth day of the same month, and then they are sacrificed. Since the tablets of the Covenant had written upon them ten words—that is, ten chief commandments—in which the whole Law was, as it were, contained, the whole Old Testament is therefore frequently understood through ten. Since there are four Gospels, in which the New Testament is enclosed, the New Testament is therefore denoted through four. Thus the tenth day denotes the Old Testament, while the fourth after the tenth denotes the New. The lamb is taken on the tenth day, but kept to be sacrificed until the fourteenth, because Christ’s Passion, signified in the Old Testament through figures and enigmas, was at last truly fulfilled in the New. There Christ is shown; here he is sacrificed. There he is signified; here he is offered. There, finally, the sacrifice of the lamb is narrated; here Christ’s Passion is proclaimed.

For the Old Testament came to its end at the time when Christ our Lord said to his disciples: “Amen, I say to you, I shall not henceforth drink of this fruit of the vine until that day when I drink it new with you in my kingdom” (Matt. 26:29). Therefore the old wine is set aside and the new is promised—not because the old Law is utterly destroyed, but because it is understood in a new and spiritual sense; [Col. 0254A] and this is in the kingdom of God, which is the Church.

Christ is both lamb because of his innocence and called a kid because of the likeness of sinful flesh. Of him it is said: “Behold the Lamb of God, behold him who takes away the sin of the world” (John 1:29). And likewise of him it is said: “Do not boil a kid in its mother’s milk” (Exod. 23:19). We ought to invite our relatives and neighbours to eat this lamb, so that the love by which we desire the salvation of all may become known. For every Christian is our neighbour, as is everyone who is not far from the Church. This lamb is without blemish, because it is written: “He committed no sin, nor was deceit found in his mouth” (1 Pet. 2:22). He is also male and one year old, because he has nothing soft, nothing feminine, [Col. 0254B] nothing subject to corruption, nothing that experiences a carnal stirring.

The lamb is eaten in households, but the kid is sacrificed by the whole multitude. By this are most plainly signified both the sacrifice now continually received in the Church and that sacrifice offered upon the altar of the cross by the frenzied Jews. Though this and that are one and the same, they are performed differently. Therefore they kill the kid, reckoning the Saviour of the world among the wicked and sinners, as it is written: “And he was numbered among the wicked” (Luke 22:37). Likewise: “Unless this man were an evildoer, we would not have handed him over to you” (John 18:30). But because we believe the Son of God to be innocent, holy, just, and without any stain of sin, [Col. 0254C] we both sacrifice and receive the spotless lamb.

[Note: [Col. 0253D] Because Christ, holy and innocent, wished to become for us a victim on the cross, he is represented in the spotless lamb to be sacrificed and eaten; because the same Lord was to be handed over to death by the Jews as though impious, he assumed the figure of the kid, to be sacrificed in the same [Col. 0254D] Paschal solemnity, but in different ways because of the differing representation.]

Therefore, although both lamb and kid are sacrificed, only the lamb is eaten by the people. That sacrifice is received in this, because this is most truly changed into that. For that would never be eaten unless this were changed into that. This is the change wrought by the right hand of the Most High. The whole multitude of the children of Israel sacrificed the kid—but when? At evening, because Judas the traitor at about this time spoke with the Jews, sold Christ, and received the money; and on the following day our Saviour gave up his spirit at about the evening hour, that is, after the ninth hour. Hence the Psalmist says: “The lifting up of my hands is an evening sacrifice” (Ps. 140:2).

But since our Lord was crucified on the eighth day before the Kalends of April, and this sacrifice of the lamb had occurred on the day before he was crucified, how is it true that the lamb is said to have been sacrificed on the fourteenth day of the aforesaid month? For the Jews do not reckon months as we do, but determine the beginnings of months according to the new moon.

[Note: [Col. 0254D] The Jews reckon months from the renewal of the moon, but we from the course of the sun.]

It follows:

“Then they shall take of the lamb’s blood and place it upon both doorposts and upon the lintels of the houses in which they shall eat it.” Those place the lamb’s blood upon both doorposts who receive him with mouth [Col. 0255A] and heart. But those who either receive him unworthily or, receiving him, do not believe it to be Christ’s blood, place the blood upon only one doorpost. Of them the Apostle says: “He who eats and drinks unworthily eats and drinks judgment upon himself” (1 Cor. 11:29). Therefore, receiving with our mouths and believing in our hearts that it is Christ’s blood, let us place it upon both doorposts and receive him both in body and mind. When we make the sign of the cross upon our foreheads, then we place Christ’s blood upon the lintels of our houses. It follows:

“And they shall eat the flesh at night, roasted with fire, with unleavened bread and wild lettuces.” In this passage we understand the same thing through both the flesh and the unleavened bread, [Col. 0255B] and rightly he gives both, because this flesh is made from the bread. Those eat it with wild lettuces who receive it with a contrite and humbled heart and, sharing the bitterness of the cross, somehow taste it upon the palate of their heart. “You shall not eat any of it raw, nor boiled in water, but only roasted with fire.” For if the flesh of the lamb is eaten either raw or boiled in water, it is apt easily to upset the stomach; but if roasted, it both strengthens and is received more eagerly.

Therefore, whoever does not distinguish this flesh from other meats, does not understand it to be sweeter than every food, and, as though disdaining it, does not believe it offers salvation and life to those who receive it worthily—such a person eats this flesh either raw or boiled in water. But he eats it roasted with fire who, believing that life is in it, receives it most eagerly and, in receiving it, shares Christ’s Passion.

[Note: [Col. 0255D] By receiving the sacrament of the Eucharist, we share in Christ’s Passion.]

For the Lord himself says: “He who eats my flesh and drinks my blood has eternal life” (John 6:55). Moreover, this flesh is not raw, because Christ suffered; nor is it boiled in water, because he was crucified not secretly but openly, before all who saw. Flesh gives off a scent when it is roasted; Christ’s Passion also gives off a scent.

“You shall eat its head with its feet and entrails, and nothing of it shall remain until morning.” The head of Christ, as the Apostle says, is God; his feet, which touch the earth, signify his flesh, which was taken from the earth. And what do his entrails signify except all hidden things and profound mysteries? Therefore, those eat his head with his feet and entrails who believe him to be both God and human, and receive worthily and faithfully whatever is written concerning him. For it is not enough to believe him both God and human, unless, receiving the entrails as well, we believe without doubt that he was born of a virgin, circumcised, truly suffered, rose again on the third day, and all the other things written about him. Therefore it is added: “Nothing of it shall remain until morning.” Let all be received; let all be believed; let nothing of [Col. 0256A] this lamb remain that is not enclosed within the breast of faith.

Morning signifies the end of this life, because Christ, the sun of righteousness, shall appear; and when darkness is driven away, night shall be no more. Then there will be no time for conversion or for eating the lamb’s flesh, because those who begin to believe then shall hear with the foolish virgins: “Amen, I say to you: I do not know you” (Matt. 25:12).—“If anything remains, you shall burn it with fire.” What remains is what cannot be eaten, such as the skin and bones. The lamb’s skin is Christ’s flesh: how this is united to God, how the Word became flesh, can neither be said nor understood. But who can eat, or, so to speak, gnaw the bones, so as to comprehend how he was begotten by the Father before all ages, even by investigating it for a very long time, if this were permitted, and forever? There are also many other things which, since they cannot be eaten and understood, should be burned with the fire of love and faith.

[Note: [Col. 0255D] Here it should be noted how many prescriptions Moses laid down concerning the manner of eating the Paschal lamb; all of them signified the spiritual purity and disposition with which believers of the new law ought to approach in order to eat the flesh of the true Lamb, whose sacrifice is mystically renewed daily in the Church.]
