For it is enough to believe when understanding is not granted. More people eat this flesh by believing than by understanding. Let those who can eat; but those who cannot, let them believe and burn it with the fire of love. It follows:

“And thus you shall eat it: you shall gird your loins, have sandals on your feet, hold staffs in your hands, and eat in haste. For it is the *phase*, that is, the passage of the Lord.” To gird the loins is to restrain lust with the girdle of chastity and continence. Hence the Lord himself says: “Let your loins be girded” (Luke 12:35). [Col. 0256C] They have sandals upon their feet who, as though prepared to go elsewhere, recognize that they are pilgrims in this world. Such persons, running the way of God’s commandments, walk safely and without fear—well shod, as it were—over serpents and scorpions. Let them hold staffs in their hands, so that they may be able to defend themselves from adversaries rushing upon them.

You have humility: it is a staff to you, for by it you conquer pride. You have chastity: this too is a staff by which lust is overcome. But why say more? As many virtues as you have, so many staffs you have. Thus should one who comes to eat this flesh be prepared, fortified, and armed. You shall eat it quickly and in haste, so that when the Lord comes, you may already be full and satisfied, lest you begin to believe then, when you ought to be delivered through faith. For there must be no delay in receiving faith: “Watch therefore, because you know neither the day nor the hour” (Matt. 25:12).

“And I shall pass through the land of Egypt that night and strike every firstborn in the land of Egypt, from human being to beast; and upon all the gods of Egypt I shall execute judgments—I, the Lord.” For once the lamb had been sacrificed and Christ the Lord crucified, after Jesus bowed his head and gave up his spirit, all the firstborn in the land of Egypt died, because [Col. 0257A] original sin perished throughout the whole world in all those who believed and were baptized, so that sin, which began through the tree of desire, might be destroyed through the tree of the cross. For as many people as there are, so many original sins there are; each person is born with his own, which could not be wiped out except by Christ’s blood and the water of baptism. Rightly, moreover, are all firstborn struck, from human being to beast, because without respect of persons all original sins are destroyed in every nation, sex, and age. “For everyone who calls upon the name of the Lord shall be saved” (Rom. 10:13). The Lord executed his judgments upon all the gods of Egypt because, through the intervention of his death, hell is despoiled, temples fall, and throughout the nations the worship and religion of the gods are abhorred.

“And the blood shall be for you as a sign in the houses in which you are; and I shall see the blood and pass over you, and there shall not be in you a destroying plague when I strike the land of Egypt.” Of this sign the apostle John says: “I saw the Lamb standing upon Zion, and with him one hundred forty-four thousand, having his name and the name of his Father written upon their foreheads” (Rev. 14:1). He also saw twelve thousand sealed from every tribe of the children of Israel. There is nothing in these to be struck, because, receiving the Lamb’s blood upon both doorposts and eating his flesh with both mouth and heart, they have dedicated their whole selves, inwardly and outwardly, to the Lord. [Col. 0257C] It follows:

“You shall have this day as a memorial, and you shall celebrate it as a solemn feast to the Lord throughout your generations, in perpetual observance.” Thus the Lord himself commanded his followers, saying, “Do this in remembrance of me” (1 Cor. 11:24), when he spoke of this sacrifice. Therefore the Apostle also says: “For as often as you eat this bread and drink the cup, you proclaim the Lord’s death until he comes” (ibid., 26).

“You shall eat unleavened bread for seven days.

[Note: [Col. 0257D] The most learned Mazochius observes in his *Spicilegium* on Exodus, chapter 12, that the divine command given to the Hebrews concerning abstinence from leavened bread for the seven days of Passover was such that it had force not only at that time, or chiefly at that celebration, but permanently—that is, so that they should celebrate Passover every year by the same rite.]

On the first day there shall be no leaven in your houses; whoever eats leavened bread, that soul shall perish from Israel, from the first day until the seventh.” This is what the Apostle says: “A little leaven corrupts [Col. 0257D] the whole lump. Purge out the old leaven, that you may be a new dough, as you are unleavened; for Christ our Passover has been sacrificed. Therefore let us feast, not with old leaven, nor with the leaven of malice and wickedness, but with the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth” (1 Cor. 5:7). And the Lord says in the Gospel: “Beware of the leaven [Col. 0258A] of the Pharisees, which is hypocrisy” (Luke 12:1). For not only the old and corrupt understanding of the Law, but every corruption and every perversion of mind, can be called leaven.

[Note: [Col. 0257D] Manuscript of Santa Croce at the Laurentian Library: “For Christ calls hypocrisy leaven, [Col. 0258D] while the Apostle calls malice and wickedness leaven.”]

By contrast, he calls unleavened bread sincerity and truth. We are commanded to eat unleavened bread for seven days, so that during all the time in which we live and are in this world we may be nourished by the food of sincerity and truth, so that sin may not reign in our mortal body and we may not serve the desires of the flesh. For because the world was made in seven days and revolves and endures through seven, all time is frequently understood through seven days. “On the first day,” he says, “there shall be no leaven

[Note: [Col. 0258D] The same manuscript: “There shall be no leavened bread.”]

in your houses.” The first day of this solemnity is every occasion on which we approach [Col. 0258B] to partake of

[Note: [Col. 0258D] The same manuscript: “to receive.”]

Christ’s flesh and blood. Therefore, although we ought at all times to live in sincerity and truth, on the day above all when we receive Christ’s flesh and blood, no leaven of malice and wickedness should be in our houses. Let us therefore be cleansed from every sin on this day, lest we receive Christ’s flesh unworthily. “For whoever eats and drinks unworthily eats and drinks judgment upon himself” (1 Cor. 11:29). This is what he means when he says: “Whoever eats leavened bread, that soul shall perish from Israel, from the first day until the seventh day”—that is, throughout the whole time of this solemnity.

“**The first day shall be holy and solemn, and the seventh day equally venerable with the same festivity; you shall do no work on them, except what pertains to eating [Col. 0258C], and you shall observe unleavened bread.**” What the first day is has already been said. We understand the seventh to be that of which the Apostle says: “There remains therefore a sabbath-rest for the people of God” (Heb. 4:9). How venerable this is, those know who glorify with the Lord in the heavenly Jerusalem, free from every care and anxiety. On both solemnities no work should be done, except what pertains to eating [Note: [Col. 0258D] Mazochius likewise teaches, in *Spicil. in Exod.*, p. 37, that the Gentiles received from the Hebrews the custom of observing feast days, and that cessation from work was especially observed by servants.], concerning which the Savior himself says: “My food is to do the will of my Father who is in heaven” (John 4:34). This is forbidden at no feast: to give alms is God’s will; to clothe the naked is God’s will; and always to perform whatever belongs to mercy and piety is God’s will and the food of the soul. [Col. 0258D] Therefore, if the soul is nourished and fed by these and similar things, and if on feast days it is permitted to do only those things by which the soul is nourished, then we are not forbidden to do good on feast days. Thus, on these solemnities we ought to do no work except what pertains to eating, so that the soul may lack its food on no day. But when he says, “**And you shall observe [Col. 0259A] unleavened bread,**” he plainly indicates how sincerely and chastely he wishes us to live.

“**On this very day I shall lead your host out of the land of Egypt, and you shall keep this day throughout your generations as a perpetual observance.**” For on the very same day on which our Lamb was sacrificed, hell was despoiled and the whole world was delivered from the devil’s bondage. Therefore the Church keeps this day solemnly at all times, by a perpetual rite. “**In the first month, on the fourteenth day of the month at evening, you shall eat unleavened bread until the twenty-first day of the same month at evening.**” This calculation cannot stand unless it is understood according to the Hebrews. For this solemnity often passes through the entire first month in such a way that it falls wholly within [Col. 0259B] the month of April; whereas among the Hebrews it is never celebrated except on the fourteenth day of the first month. Immediately after that celebration, on the next following Sunday, our celebration also takes place. It follows: “**For seven days leaven shall not be found in your houses.**” This confirms what has been said. It repeats it for the purpose of committing it most firmly to memory.

“**Moses then called all the elders of the children of Israel and said to them: Go, take an animal for your families, and sacrifice the Passover; dip a bundle of hyssop in the blood which is on the threshold, and sprinkle from it the lintel and both doorposts. Let none of you go out through the door of his house [Col. 0259C] until morning.**” When this animal is to be taken has been discussed above. It remains for us to speak of the hyssop. For the Psalmist says: “You shall sprinkle me with hyssop, and I shall be cleansed” (Ps. 50:9). Hyssop naturally grows among rocks; and “the Rock,” says the Apostle, “was Christ” (1 Cor. 10:4). Therefore hyssop grows in Christ—a good herb, hyssop, which grows in Christ—and rightly so, because no herb touches Christ’s blood except that which grows in Christ. For the Church alone is born and reborn in Christ; the Church alone is founded in Christ. This, then, is the hyssop which touches and sprinkles Christ’s blood. It is not without reason called a bundle, because it both binds and gathers many within itself. This bundle, therefore, is dipped in Christ’s blood, is drenched with Christ’s blood, [Col. 0259D] and sprinkles the lintel and both doorposts with Christ’s blood, because the holy Church is protected inwardly and outwardly by this blood. For it is on the threshold—that is, at the entrance of the house, namely in the mouth—and, sprinkled on both doorposts, sanctifies both soul and body. But the command that no one should go out through the door of his house until morning seems to signify that we should dwell faithfully in the holy Church until the end; whoever is found outside it [Col. 0260A] will perish with the Egyptians at the Lord’s command.

“**And it came to pass at midnight that the Lord struck every firstborn in the land of Egypt, from the firstborn of Pharaoh, who sat upon his throne, to the firstborn of the captive woman who was in prison, and every firstborn of the beasts. Then a great cry arose in Egypt; and Pharaoh called Moses and Aaron by night and said: Go, sacrifice to the Lord as you know, and, as you go, bless me.**” [Note: [Col. 0259D] The Vulgate reads otherwise: “And Pharaoh rose by night, and all his servants, and all Egypt; and a great cry arose in Egypt, for there was no house in which there did not lie a dead person. And Pharaoh, having called Moses and Aaron by night, said: Rise, and go out from among my people, you and the children of Israel; go, sacrifice to the Lord, as [Col. 0260D] you know. Take your sheep and your herds, as you requested, and depart; and bless me as you go.”]

For what are we to understand by Pharaoh’s firstborn but that first and greatest sin by which the first human being was deceived in Paradise? Since it brought the greatest devastation upon the world, it is described as sitting, like a king after a great triumph, [Col. 0260B] upon Pharaoh’s throne. By the captive woman, who was in the flesh, we should understand the multitude of souls held in hell on account of original sin. But by the maidservant who was at the mill [Note: [Col. 0260D] The faulty edition is corrected from the manuscript of S. Croce in the Laurentian Library.], he intended the whole multitude of human beings subject to this laborious life, as though turning the mill of days and revolving the wheel of months and years. Christ slew the firstborn of these, because, by destroying with his blood the original sins not only of the living but also of the dead and of those not yet born, he reconciled all things to God the Father. Therefore a very great cry arises in Egypt: the devil groans with all his wickedness, grieves over such great spoil taken from him, and now [Col. 0260C] has no hope in the souls of the saints. And when Pharaoh says, “As you go, bless me,” this must be understood as: As you go, deliver me from this danger. “**The Egyptians pressed the people of Israel to leave the land of Egypt quickly, saying: We shall all die.**”

“**The people therefore took the dough before it was leavened, and, binding it in their cloaks, put it on their shoulders; and they asked the Egyptians for vessels of silver and gold and for a great quantity of clothing. And the Lord gave them favor in the sight of the Egyptians, so that they lent these things to them; and they despoiled Egypt.**” [Note: [Col. 0260D] The same manuscript, M. A., reads “the Egyptians,” as does the Vulgate.] For the people leaving Egypt carry incorrupt dough without leaven, because, when we are about to celebrate Passover, we ought to use new and sincere [Col. 0260D] food. For since in this feast we pass from the Old Testament into the New, everything ought to be sincere, new, and incorrupt for us, so that, transformed by the water of baptism and the new law, we may strip off the old human being with its deeds and put on the new, created according to God in righteousness and holiness of truth (Col. 9:3). But what the despoiling of Egypt signifies has already been said above.

[Col. 0261A] “**The children of Israel set out from Rameses for Succoth.**” Rameses is interpreted “moth,” or “he thundered joyfully.” Therefore, the people leaving Rameses—that is, leaving the devil’s bondage, where the moth of every corruption was laying waste—thundered joyfully, since they came to Succoth, which is interpreted “tabernacles,” saying with the Psalmist: “How beloved are your tabernacles, O Lord of hosts! My soul longs for and faints away in the courts of the Lord” (Ps. 83:1). For as soon as a person leaves Egypt—that is, the manner of life of this world—he comes joyfully to Succoth, that is, to the tabernacles of the Church. Here he makes unleavened bread for himself; here he prepares new food for himself, so that, abandoning the leaven of malice and wickedness, he may live on the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth.

“**The dwelling of [Col. 0261B] the children of Israel, who had remained in Egypt, was four hundred and thirty years. When these were fulfilled, on the same day the whole host went out from the land of Egypt. This night is to be observed; the children of Israel ought to observe it throughout their generations.**” This is the night to be observed, followed by so joyful a day, on which Christ, coming forth from the tomb, illumined the world by his resurrection.

“**The Lord said to Moses and Aaron: This is the ordinance of the Passover: no foreigner shall eat of it.**” Here *Phase* signifies the lamb that was sacrificed. No foreigner may eat of it: neither a heretic, nor a Gentile, nor a false Christian. It is given to the sons of the Church alone to eat; all others [Col. 0261C] are foreigners. “**But every purchased slave shall be circumcised, and then he shall eat.**” Who is this purchased slave? Let the Apostle speak: “For you were bought at a great price; glorify and bear God in your body” (1 Cor. 6:20). Therefore we are purchased slaves, because these words are addressed to us. Accordingly we may eat this Lamb, but only if we have first been circumcised. Our circumcision, however, is required not in the foreskin alone but in all our members; for Moses above complained that he was uncircumcised in lips. How all the members are circumcised, we explained in Genesis when treating Abraham’s circumcision.

“**The resident alien and the hired servant shall not eat of it.**” [Col. 0261D] A resident alien is every person whom the Church has not begotten; a hired servant is one who serves the Lord not from sincere affection or for the salvation of his soul, but for payment and gain. Of such persons the Lord says: “But the hired servant flees, because he is a hired servant” (John 10:13). If evil shepherds are hired servants, and a hired servant may not eat of this Lamb, how will evil shepherds be permitted to eat what they are not permitted to eat? “**You shall eat it in one house; you shall not carry any of its flesh outside; nor shall you break a bone of it.**” For if the Lamb is taken according to houses and families, as he said above, how is it eaten in one house? The one house is the Church, outside which there is no place for the true sacrifice. And because it is written, “Do not give what is holy to dogs” (Matt. 7:6), [Col. 0262A] it is said here: “You shall not carry any of its flesh outside.” The blessed Evangelist John explained what follows, “Nor shall you break a bone of it,” saying: “The first indeed broke the legs, and those of the other who was crucified with him. But when they came to Jesus, seeing that he was already dead, they did not break his legs, so that the Scripture might be fulfilled: ‘You shall not break a bone of it’” (John 19:32–33).

“**The whole assembly of the children of Israel shall do this. But if any of the sojourners wishes to join your settlement and to keep the Lord’s Passover, every male belonging to him shall first be circumcised; then he shall celebrate it rightly, and he shall be as a native of the land. But if anyone is uncircumcised, he shall not eat of it. The same law shall be for the native and for the settler who sojourns [Col. 0262B] among you.**” It is clear, therefore, that a person is rejected or chosen not by the dignity of his nation but by the merit of holiness; for God is not only the God of the Jews but also of the Gentiles. Whoever therefore wishes to enter the settlement and fellowship of the saints, to be circumcised with the new circumcision, and to be baptized, let him approach the flesh of the Lamb and eat. It should be noted, however, that on the very day on which the lamb is eaten, the people depart from Egypt, because there is no fellowship of light with darkness, nor of Christ with Belial (2 Cor. 6:15).

## CHAPTER XIII

“**The Lord spoke to Moses, saying: Consecrate to me every firstborn that opens the womb among the children of Israel, both among human beings and among animals; for all are mine.**” Since the Lord had just killed all the firstborn of the Egyptians, he accordingly dedicated all the firstborn of the children of Israel to himself, so that it might never slip from their memory that the firstborn of Egypt had been destroyed. Moses said to the people: “**Today you go out in the month of new fruits,**” because, when the earth has first been released from frost, it begins to produce fresh grass. “**You shall enter a land flowing with milk and honey,**” which, because it signifies the land of the living, is more fertile than every other land. “**There you shall observe this sacred rite in this month: for seven days you shall eat unleavened bread, and there shall be nothing leavened in your houses.**” What this signifies has been sufficiently stated. It follows:

[Col. 0262D] “**And you shall tell this to your son on that day, saying: This is what the Lord did for me when I came out of Egypt; and it shall be like a sign on your hand and like a memorial hanging before your eyes.**” What we hold in our hands and have before our eyes we do not easily forget. “**And when the Lord brings you into the land which he swore to give you, you shall set apart every firstborn for the Lord, whatever is of the male sex. You shall exchange the firstborn of a lamb for a sheep; but if you do not redeem it, it shall be killed.**” We exchange the firstborn of a lamb for a sheep when, by reproving, rebuking, watching over, and admonishing, we convert some foolish and undisciplined person to sheep-like simplicity. But if this person is not redeemed, he shall be killed: if he does not repent and does not believe the teachers of the Church, he shall die the death.

“**But you shall redeem every firstborn of a human being among your sons with a price.**” The firstborn of a human being is faith, without which it is impossible to please God. This is the first of all virtues to be born in the minds of believers; this is first produced by priests in the hearts of Christians. But because faith without works is dead, it must be redeemed with a price. Have you been baptized? You have faith. Do you cease from good work? Your faith dies. Therefore, if faith is idle and dead in those who refrain from good works, how much more must faith be judged dead in murderers, adulterers, sacrilegious persons, and even perjurers? For the Apostle says: “Whoever does not care for his own, and especially for members of his household, has denied the faith and is worse than [Col. 0263B] an unbeliever” (1 Tim. 5:8). Faith must therefore be redeemed not once but many times; for unless it were redeemed, since we see it die so often, very few would be those for whom it would suffice to have purchased it once. Thus we ought to give the greatest thanks to God, who established for us this law concerning the redemption of our dearest firstborn, without whom we cannot please him. Let it then be redeemed—but when? After one month. For the firstborn were offered to the Lord after one month; therefore they must be redeemed after one month. What we redeem, we show to have been ours. After we offer our faith, then, if it has become alienated from us through sins, it must be redeemed. But at what price? At five shekels of silver, certainly. I understand the five shekels of silver to mean the five senses of the body, which are indeed silver when, through their devout use, they are made worthy to be placed among God’s treasures. Therefore faith is redeemed by five shekels, because even if a person has been a sinner, once he begins to serve God with all the powers of mind and body, with his inward and outward senses, he will no longer be called an unbeliever. Let our firstborn, then, live for God and never die for him who killed the firstborn of the Egyptians for our sake.

The Lord did not wish to lead the people through the land of the Philistines, which was near at hand, lest perhaps, if war arose against them, they should quickly return to Egypt; instead, he led them around through the wilderness by a long route. By this he intended to signify that the way leading to the homeland is neither short [Col. 0263D] nor easy, but that we must enter the kingdoms of heaven through many tribulations. Finally, the more ardently awakened we are in God’s service and the farther we withdraw from this world, the less we fear the wars of rising vices. But if, on coming into the land of the Philistines, which is near Egypt, we devote ourselves to drunkenness and pleasure—for *Philisthiim* is interpreted “those falling by drink”—we are easily defeated in battle and return to Egypt. That the children of Israel went up armed from Egypt signifies that, from the moment we leave the world, we must always fight, armed on the right and on the left, against vices and evil spirits. It follows:

“**The pillar of cloud by day and the pillar of fire before the people by night never failed.**” [Col. 0264A] One protected them from the heat of the sun, while the other protected them from darkness. This pillar is the grace of the Holy Spirit, which both protects us from the heat of vices and illumines us lest we be enveloped in the darkness of errors. Of this pillar it is said to blessed Mary: “The Holy Spirit shall come upon you, and the power of the Most High shall overshadow you” (Luke 1:35). Setting out from Succoth, they encamped at Etham, on the outermost borders of the wilderness. *Ethan* is interpreted “foolish navigation.” Rightly, therefore, one comes from Succoth—that is, from the tabernacles—to Etham, because once a person has come to the Church and has been baptized, he ought not to sit idle, but to sail with the apostles amid the perils of this sea. And while he is still stationed on the outermost borders of the wilderness, because he has not yet reached the dangerous places of the desert, [Col. 0264B] let him begin to prepare his soul for temptation.

## CHAPTER XIV

The children of Israel, setting out, came opposite Atharoth, which lies between Migdol and the sea, opposite Baal-zephon. Atharoth is interpreted “crown,” Migdol “tower,” and Baal-zephon “having a watchtower.” Therefore the people come from Etham to Atharoth because, having begun their voyage and advancing through certain stages of virtue, they come to the crown, hoping, if necessary, to be able to die for Christ’s name. This crown lies between Migdol and the sea—that is, [between] faith and baptism—because one comes to the crown through the strength of faith and the grace of baptism. It looks [Col. 0264C] toward Baal-zephon because God’s people, mindful of the Church of watchers, never forget holy preaching; and therefore they do not fear those who kill the body, since they cannot kill the soul.

Pharaoh was told that the people of Israel had fled, and his heart was changed; and he pursued Israel with the entire army of the Egyptians. When the Hebrews saw them, they were greatly afraid. The Lord said to Moses: “Why do you cry to me? Raise your staff, stretch out your hand over the sea, and divide it.” When Moses did this, the sea was divided and dried up, and the children of Israel entered through the midst of the dry sea. The water was like a wall on the right and on the left. The Egyptians pursued and entered after them. But the angel of the Lord, [Col. 0264D] who went before the camp of the children of Israel, together with the cloud placed himself in the middle between the Egyptians and the Hebrews, so that throughout the whole night they could not approach one another. The morning watch had now come; at the Lord’s command Moses stretched out his hand over the sea, the waters returned to their former place, and all the Egyptians died.

For what is Pharaoh with the entire army of the Egyptians but the devil with the whole host of demons? What are the Hebrews but the Christian people? And what is the Red Sea but the water of baptism? The Egyptians therefore pursue the Hebrews and die there, because vices and evil spirits, pursuing Christians up to baptism, perish and fail when their strength is lost. [Col. 0265A] Then Moses and the children of Israel sang this song to the Lord and said:

## CHAPTER XV

“**Let us sing to the Lord, for he has been gloriously magnified**” [Note: [Col. 0265D] The manuscript of Monte Amiata reads: “for he has been gloriously honored.”], destroying enemies with such power. “**He cast horse and rider into the sea.**” The horse is pride; the rider is the devil. Lifted up on this horse, he rushes furiously into battle, and all his host is driven by this horse into every crime. “**The Lord is my strength and my praise,**” through whom I am strong and praiseworthy. “**And he became salvation to me,**” saving and delivering me by his blood. “**This is my God, and I shall glorify [Note: [Col. 0265D] The manuscript of S. Croce in the Laurentian Library reads: “And I shall glorify him.” [Col. 0266D] “The God of my father, and I shall exalt him.”] him. The Lord is like a warrior.**” Everywhere he fights [Note: [Col. 0266D] The Cassinese manuscript reads: “he fights for us and conquers in battle.”] and conquers for us. His name is Almighty, to whom [Col. 0265B] nothing is impossible. “**Pharaoh’s chariots,**” of whom we have just spoken, “**and his army**”—that is, the multitude of all vices—“**he cast into the sea,**” that is, he destroyed them in baptism. For as many as are the vices, so many also are the chariots on which the devil rides. “**His chosen princes were submerged in the Red Sea,**” because original sin and idolatry perished in baptism. “**The depths covered them; they went down into the deep like a stone,**” so that they may appear no more. We pass over the rest, because it needs no exposition.

“**The peoples rose up, and they were enraged.**” This is a prophecy concerning the future: the peoples of whom there will be mention below rose up to fight against them. “**And they were enraged,**” because, although they had a stronger army and greater resources, they could not resist them. [Col. 0265C] “**Pains seized the inhabitants of Philistia,**” as they saw an unconquerable people rising against them. “**Then the princes of Edom were troubled,**” hearing of this people’s strength; “**trembling seized the mighty men of Moab,**” who were now almost despairing of safety. “**All the inhabitants of Canaan grew numb,**” struck by a terror greater than fever. Hence Moses, rejoicing and exulting, says: “Thus, Lord, thus may it always be: let dread and terror fall upon them through the greatness of your arm. Let them become motionless like a stone, until your people pass over, O Lord, until this people whom you have possessed passes over. You will bring them in and plant them upon the mountain of your inheritance,” of which you swore to [Col. 0265D] our fathers. “**In your most secure dwelling, which you, O Lord, have made.**” This seems to refer more to the heavenly Jerusalem than to this Jerusalem, into which God’s people are to be brought. Of it he further says: “**Your sanctuary, O Lord, which your hands established,**” by which heaven is understood, where are the Holy of Holies. “**The Lord shall reign for eternity and beyond.**” How can this either be said or conceived? “The Lord shall reign for eternity and beyond”: what can I say? I have said “for eternity”; I have nothing to say beyond it. Had I known anything beyond eternity, I would have said something beyond eternity. Therefore he said: “The Lord shall reign for eternity.” What is “for eternity”? Always and without end.

“**For Pharaoh’s horseman entered the sea with his chariots and horsemen;**” this is a cry of triumph, “**and the Lord brought back the waters of the sea upon them. But the children of Israel walked on dry ground through its midst.**” Then Mary the prophetess, Aaron’s sister, took a tambourine in her hand, and all the women who belonged with her went out after her with tambourines and dances, saying: “Let us sing to the Lord, for he has been gloriously magnified; he cast horse and rider into the sea.” What, indeed, is Mary but the holy Church? She sings with the tambourine because she praises God in the mortification of the flesh. Since tambourines are made from the skins of dead animals, they often signify the mortification of the flesh. The other [Col. 0266B] women follow her with tambourines and dances, because they too subdue the flesh and serve the Lord in the beautiful and orderly arrangement of life; for in a chorus persons stand in order and sing in harmony. Of these women the Psalmist says: “Virgins shall be brought to the king after her” (Ps. 14:15), that is, after Mary. Our virgin derives her name from her; and because, after her Son, she is the head of the whole Church, not without reason do the other women with tambourines follow her as she plays the tambourine.

“**Moses and Aaron led Israel from the midst of the Red Sea, and they entered the wilderness of Shur.**” Why is it that Israel comes into the wilderness as soon as it comes out of the sea, except because the Christian people, immediately upon baptism, enter a narrow and perilous [Col. 0266C] way and are tempted by the devil in likeness to their Savior? Thus Christ too is led from baptism into the wilderness to be tempted by the devil. That the Red Sea signifies baptism the Apostle makes clear, saying: “And all were baptized in the cloud and in the sea” (1 Cor. 10:1). What are “in the cloud and in the sea” except “in water and Spirit”? “For unless one is born again of water and the Holy Spirit, he shall not enter into the kingdom of heaven” (John 3:5).

“**They walked for three days through the wilderness and found no water. They came to Marah, but they could not drink the waters of Marah because they were bitter; and the Lord showed Moses a piece of wood, which, when he cast it into the waters, they were changed into sweetness.**” The three ages from Abraham to Christ are understood by these three days, during which the people, walking through the wilderness, through a trackless and waterless land, could not find water. For he had not yet come who said: “If anyone thirsts, let him come and drink, and rivers of living water shall flow from his belly” (John 7:37). The Hebrews had waters but did not find them, because they possessed the Law but did not understand it. At length, after the third day had passed—that is, in the third age—they came to Marah; they came to the mountain of Myrrh and the hill of Thur; they came to the place and time of bitterness, when the Lord was crucified. [Col. 0267A] There they found waters, because “blood and water came out from his side” (John 18:34). Then the veil of the temple was rent and the Scriptures were opened. These, indeed, are the waters which, because they were at first bitter, the people could not drink. Moses therefore cast wood into them, and they were changed into sweetness. This wood is the wood of the cross; by it every water [Note: [Col. 0267D] In St Augustine, *Questions on Exodus*, question 56, that water is called Merra because it was bitter; and he says that, after wood was cast into it, it became sweet, and that the wood prefigured the glory and grace of Christ’s cross. St Maximus likewise gives this interpretation in Homily 3, *On Lent*, p. 116, from which I quote these few words: “The sacrament of the wood removed the harshness borne by the harmful water.”]—every bitterness of the Scriptures—is changed into sweetness. For when Scripture says, “Love your enemies; do good to those who hate you” (Luke 6:27), to whom does this water not seem bitter? Who would wish to drink and accept it? Yet, mindful of Christ’s cross and Christ’s passion—he who died for the ungodly and prayed for the unjust and sinners—we follow the Master’s example; the waters become sweet, we love our enemies, and pray for persecutors. Therefore we are always commanded to carry the cross: so that, always mindful of it, nothing that divine Scripture commands may seem bitter or impossible to us. For it commands nothing more bitter to us than Christ’s cross. Let the bitterness of the Law be overcome by the bitterness of the cross; and, contemplating Christ’s torments, let us not feel these transitory torments. Thus all waters become sweet when they have been drunk with the wood. Rightly, moreover, after crossing the sea the people come to Marah, because one who has just been baptized is pierced by Christ’s passion and considers sweet, through the desire of drinking, the things that formerly seemed bitter. “There he established for him commandments and judgments, and there he tested him.” Where? At Marah—that is, in the bitter waters [Col. 0267C] made sweet by the wood of the cross. For where, if not in the sacred volumes, are commandments and judgments established? There we are instructed and judged; there we are tested by God; from there we receive the precepts of testing, by obeying which we are crowned and by disobeying which we are condemned.

“**They came to Elim, where there were twelve springs of water and seventy palm trees, and they encamped beside the waters.**” They come from Marah to Elim, which is interpreted “ram,” because after Christ’s passion the Church received the apostles as teachers. The twelve springs of water and seventy palm trees are understood as the twelve apostles and the seventy disciples of Christ. From these springs flowed water by which the whole world is refreshed [Col. 0267D] and watered [Note: [Col. 0268D] Bruno agrees with St Maximus of Turin, who most eloquently illustrates and explains this same passage in Homily 5, *On Lent*.]. Since palms signify victory, those are rightly called palms who through faith conquered kingdoms. But Christ’s disciples were twelve and seventy-two, so that the number twelve might be completed seven times, and that by this number also we might understand that they were filled with every grace of the Holy Spirit.

## CHAPTER XVI

[Col. 0268A]

“**They set out from Elim, and the whole multitude of the children of Israel came to the wilderness of Sin, which is between Elim and Sinai.**” *Sin* is interpreted “jar,” through which measure is understood. Rightly, therefore, the people come from Elim to the wilderness of Sin, because after the Church came to the apostles, it found the measure by which it should live. For it heard the Gospel, where it is said: “With whatever measure you measure, it shall be measured back to you” (Matt. 7:2).

Then follows the account of the people’s murmuring: “**Would that we had died by the hand of the Lord in the land of Egypt, when we sat over pots of meat and ate bread to the full. And the Lord said to Moses: Behold, I shall rain bread from heaven for you; let each person gather from it as much as is sufficient to eat, a gomor for every head. But on the sixth day let them gather double what they were accustomed to gather on each of the other days.**” The people murmured, exasperated and unbelieving; and although they had many herds of cattle and flocks of sheep, they nevertheless wished death upon themselves for the sake of meat. For they desired the flesh of birds, which they had been accustomed to eat in Egypt. Birds are very plentiful in Egypt and around the Nile. Hence no one ought to doubt that desiring more sumptuous foods [Note: [Col. 0268D] The manuscript of S. Croce in the Laurentian Library reads “more sumptuous fare.”] is sinful. But one gomor is given for every head, so that they may understand that they are equal by nature and live content with only what is sufficient for them, gathering no more through anxiety about tomorrow; for neither did the one who gathered more have [Col. 0268C] more, nor did the one who gathered less have less. It is indeed better to gather less and have abundance than to gather more and labor to no purpose. On the sixth day double is gathered, because on the seventh it is not found. We too must now prepare that by which, after this life, we may be able to live in the sabbath-rest [Note: [Col. 0268D] The same manuscript adds: “Whatever a person has sown, that also shall he reap” (Gal. 6:7).].

“Then the Lord said to Moses: ‘Speak to the children of Israel: In the evening you shall eat meat, and in the morning you shall be filled with bread; and you shall know that I am the Lord your God.’ So it came to pass in the evening that quail came up and covered the camp; and in the morning dew lay all around the camp. When it had covered the surface of the earth, there appeared in the wilderness something small, like that pounded with a pestle, resembling hoarfrost upon the [Col. 0268D] ground. When the children of Israel saw it, they said to one another, ‘Manhu?’—that is, ‘What is this?’—for they did not know what it was.”

For in this place meat and bread signify the same thing. Divine Scripture is both flesh and bread: flesh, indeed, according to the letter; bread, however, according to the spiritual understanding. Thus Elijah received meat in the evening, [Col. 0269A] but bread in the morning, because Scripture is understood first according to the letter and afterwards according to the Spirit. For bread descended from heaven, whereas birds rose from the earth; and because it is not difficult, nor a matter of profound learning, to understand the Scriptures according to the letter, the birds are said to have flown close to the earth.

This too should be observed: even to this day, when we read the Scriptures, we do not cease to say *manhu*. For, questioning each individual statement, we say: “What is this? What does this signify? How is this or that interpreted?” This bread too is reported to have possessed every flavour according to the desire of those using it; by this it was indicated that divine Scripture was to be understood in many diverse ways. For heretics themselves also bend it to their own interpretation.

[Col. 0269B] Yet its principal taste was like fine flour with honey. For what is sweeter than honey? What is more strengthening than wheaten bread? Therefore a sound understanding of Scripture ought both to be sweet to taste and strong for nourishing and strengthening; for weak food nourishes weak humours.

That manna was gathered according to the measure of a gomor is what the Apostle says: “Do not think more highly than you ought to think, but think unto sobriety” (Rom. XII, 3). For sound understanding does not exceed its measure, whereas the heretic is not contained within measure. Heretics always speak lofty things and, exceeding the measure of faith, transgress the boundaries established by the Fathers. Each person may gather from this bread only as much as can suffice for daily food. This too the Lord commanded us [Col. 0269C] to pray: “Give us this day our daily bread” (Matt. VI, 11). This signifies nothing other than that our Catholic faith, content with truth alone, should cast away every superfluity.

For God has set a shortened word upon the earth. But what was superfluous—that is, what was kept for the following day—teemed with worms and decayed; and when the sun grew hot it melted away. For all the superfluous learning of heretics, illuminated by the light of truth, vanishes and fails. Therefore it is commanded that nothing of it be left until morning, because what is left is superfluous. It is indeed better for it to melt away in the fields than, once gathered, to rot; for it is better that divine Scripture remain unused in sacred [Col. 0269D] volumes than that, gathered in the hearts of heretics, it should be defiled by perverse interpretation.

What does it mean that on the sixth day that is gathered by which one lives through the seventh, except that we must prepare in this life the means by which we may live in the life to come? Moses is commanded to fill a gomor from it, set it before the Lord, and preserve it as a memorial for all generations. By this we may plainly understand that the sound and spiritual interpretation of the Scriptures is never to be set aside in any generation. “Heaven and earth shall pass away, but the words of God shall not pass away” (Matt. XXIV, 35).

Now the children of Israel ate manna for forty years, until they came into an inhabited land. [Col. 0270A] What do the forty years signify except the works of both Testaments? For this number consists of ten and four: ten times four, or four times ten, makes forty. [67] By ten is understood all that time in which the Old Testament was observed according to the letter; by four, that in which faith in the four Gospels is held. Therefore the children of Israel ate manna for forty years, because holy and spiritual men understood the Scriptures spiritually both in the New and in the Old Testament.

This food will not fail until we come into the inhabited land and the land of the living; for after we arrive there, the Scriptures will no longer be necessary for us. For God will be all in all. Hence the Apostle says: [Col. 0270B] “Whether tongues, they shall cease; whether knowledge, it shall be destroyed” (I Cor. XIII, 8).

## Chapter XVII

“Therefore the whole multitude of the children of Israel set out from the wilderness of Sin by their stages, according to the word of the Lord, and encamped at Raphidim, where there was no water for the people to drink. They quarrelled with Moses and demanded water.”

Raphidim is interpreted “soundness of judgment.” Sound judgment is: “You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, and your neighbour as yourself” (Matt. XXII, 37)—and, “What you do not wish for yourself, do not do to another” (Tob. IV, 16)—and similar precepts. Therefore the people came from the wilderness of Sin to Raphidim because, after receiving from the apostles a measure for living, and recognizing that the same measure by which they [Col. 0270C] had measured would also be measured back to them, they immediately turned to sound judgment, resolved to love God and their neighbour, and to injure no human being.

[Note: [Col. 0269D] The printed edition is corrected from the Cassinese manuscript.]

The lack of food and drink which the people then suffered bodily signified that which people now suffer spiritually, concerning which the Lord threatens certain persons, saying: “I will send upon you famine and thirst—not a famine of bread nor a thirst for water, but for hearing the word of the Lord” (Amos VIII, 11). Hence it is said in Ezekiel: “I will make your tongue cling to your palate, and you shall not be able to speak, because they are a provoking house” (Ezek. II, 6). On account of the people’s sins, the tongue of teachers is often silent. Concerning the Jewish people also, under the figure of a vineyard, the Lord says: [Col. 0270D] “I will command my clouds not to rain rain upon it” (Isa. V, 6).

“And the Lord said to Moses: ‘Go before the people, take the rod in your hand, and go. Behold, I will stand before you there upon the rock of Horeb; you shall strike the rock, and water shall come out of it, that the people may drink.’ And Moses did so before the elders of Israel.”

That both these things and those said above must be understood spiritually is made clear by the Apostle, who says: “For our fathers were all under the cloud, and all passed through the sea, and all were baptized into Moses in the cloud and in the sea; and all ate the same spiritual food, and all drank the same spiritual drink. For they drank from the spiritual rock that followed them, and that rock was Christ” (I Cor. X, 1). [Col. 0271A] Who, then, will understand literally things which the Apostle declares to be spiritual?

Moses therefore came with the whole multitude of the children of Israel to the rock, because the chief priests, with the entire multitude of the people, seized Christ. But the Lord stood there before the people upon the rock and was not seen, because God, remaining in a man, was not recognized. But what do we understand by the rod with which the rock is struck twice, except the reed and the spear? Once our rock, struck with a reed, did not give waters; but struck a second time with a spear, blood and water came forth. Some, however, wish to understand by the twofold striking of this rod the two beams of the cross.

And he called the name [Col. 0271B] of that place “Temptation,” because of the quarrel of the children of Israel and because they tempted the Lord, saying: “Is God among us or not?” So too the Jews, tempting Christ, said: “If you are the Christ, tell us plainly” (John X, 25). Likewise: “If he is the Son of God, let him now come down from the cross, and we will believe him” (Matt. XXVII, 43). And again: “If you are king of the Jews, save yourself” (Luke XXIII, 37). For what else did they signify by these words except: “Is God among us or not?” Truly God is not in you, because you cast God away from yourselves. And as he himself says: “Your house is left to you desolate” (Matt. XXIII, 38). Yet God was in you, because he who remained among you and spoke to you was God.

“Then Amalek came and fought against Israel [Col. 0271C] at Raphidim. And Moses said to Joshua: ‘Choose men, and go out to fight against Amalek. But Moses, Aaron, and Hur went up to the top of the hill; and when Moses raised his hands, Israel prevailed; but if he lowered them a little, Amalek prevailed.’”

What does Amalek, interpreted “a brutish people,” signify except the multitude of vices? Joshua, the minister of Moses, fights against these with chosen men because holy and Catholic men always wage war against vices. Moses stands on the summit of the hill, holding the rod of God in his hand, because bishops and rulers of peoples, established in the higher seats of the Church, bear in their hands the rod of correction and guidance.

Moses raises his hands, and Israel prevails: priests and bishops raise pure hands to God with prayers, and victory is given to the faithful. Moses lowers his hands, and Amalek prevails: the holy cease from prayer, and vices and sins reign among the people.

[Note: [Col. 0271D] St Maximus of Turin, Homily 2 *On the Cross*, interprets this same passage of Scripture similarly.]

By these things it is readily understood how necessary it is that rulers of the Church should always entreat the Lord for the people. Hence the Apostle says: “Obey your leaders and submit to them, for they keep watch as those who will render [68] an account for your souls” (Heb. XIII, 17).

But Moses’ hands were heavy. “Therefore they took a stone and placed it beneath him, and he sat upon it. Aaron and Hur supported his hands on either side, and it came about that his hands did not grow weary until sunset.” [Col. 0272A] Moses’ hands, he says, were heavy, because the hands of priests too are often weighed down by the burden of sins. Evil spirits labour greatly to hinder the prayers and hands of the holy.

Aaron and Hur, perceiving this, placed a stone beneath him, upon which Moses sat, so that, established upon the firm rock, he might remain steadfast and unshaken. But what do we understand through Aaron, whose name is interpreted “strong mountain,” except him of whom it is said: “The Lord is strong and mighty; the Lord mighty in battle” (Ps. XXIII, 8)? And what through Hur, who is called “fire,” except the Holy Spirit, who appeared to the disciples in fire? Rightly, therefore, Aaron and Hur support Moses’ hands lest they grow weary, because it is Christ our Lord and the grace of the Holy Spirit that causes the hands, virtues, and works of the saints to stand and not [Col. 0272B] fall.

Thus Moses’ hands did not grow weary until sunset, because the one sustained by Christ and the grace of the Holy Spirit perseveres in good works without any weariness until death. By the setting of the sun we understand the end of day and of life. Blessed is he whose hands are supported by such helpers.

And Joshua put Amalek and his people to flight by the edge of the sword. Yet Joshua’s victory, and the overcoming of vices and evil spirits, must not be ascribed to Joshua but to Moses; not to the people but to the prayers of the saints. Hence it adds: “Write this for a memorial in a book, and deliver it into the ears of Joshua, for I will blot out the memory of Amalek from under heaven.” It is commanded that this be written in a book, entrusted to memory, and delivered into Joshua’s ears so that whoever, after the likeness of Joshua, overcomes spiritual enemies may attribute the victory not to himself, but to the merits and prayers of the saints and to God who has mercy and gives help. For he himself fights and conquers; he himself blots out the memory of Amalek from under heaven; he himself destroys the multitude of vices.

“And Moses built an altar and called its name, ‘The Lord is my hearing,’ saying: ‘Because the hand of the throne of the Lord, and there shall be war of God against Amalek from generation to generation.’” Moses rightly erected an altar to the Lord after the victory, that he might give thanks to him who heard him and granted the power of victory. Accordingly, he gave the altar the name “The Lord is my hearing,” that is, “The Lord heard me”; [Col. 0272D] and he immediately adds: “Because the hand of the throne of the Lord,” that is, the power and strength of the saints, in whom the Lord sits and dwells as though in his own seat; “and there shall be war of God against Amalek,” that is, against vices and evil spirits, from generation to generation, because they will never have peace or concord with one another.

## Chapter XVIII

“When Jethro, priest of Midian and kinsman of Moses, had heard all that the Lord had done for Moses and for Israel his people, he took Zipporah, Moses’ wife, whom he had sent away, and his two sons, and led them to Moses. They greeted one another and rejoiced.”

[Col. 0273A] Jethro offered burnt offerings and sacrifices to the Lord, and gave Moses advice that he should appoint tribunes, centurions, commanders of fifties, and commanders of tens to judge the people: namely, men who were capable, feared the Lord, possessed truthfulness, and hated greed; while Moses himself should attend to the more serious matters. Moses did as he advised.

That Moses, who spoke continually with the Lord, did not reject the useful advice of Jethro, his kinsman, although he was a Gentile, provides an example to churchmen and to those established in high rank: they should not disdain to accept good and useful counsel from inferiors, even if they are sinners. Hence the Apostle says: “Do not be wise in high things, but consent to the humble” (Rom. XII, 16).

What kind of judges they ought to be he comprehends in a sufficiently concise statement, when he urges that men be chosen who are capable, fear the Lord, are truthful, and are without greed. For upright judgment is greatly hindered and disturbed whenever one of these things is lacking.

That Christians ought not indiscriminately or rashly to share fellowship with everyone may readily be understood from this: Jethro did not eat with the elders of the children of Israel until he had offered burnt offerings and sacrifices to the Lord. Hence blessed John says: [Col. 0273B] “If anyone comes to you and does not bring this doctrine, do not receive him into your house or say to him, ‘Greetings’; for he who says to him, ‘Greetings,’ shares in his evil works” (II John I, 10–12).

## Chapter XIX

“In the third month after Israel’s departure from Egypt [Note: [Col. 0273D] The Vulgate reads: ‘from the land of Egypt.’], [Col. 0273C] on this day they came into the wilderness of Sinai. For, setting out from Raphidim and arriving at the wilderness of Sinai, they encamped in that place. There Israel pitched its tents opposite the mountain.”

The same day, he says, on which Jethro departed from them, the children of Israel set out from Raphidim and encamped in the wilderness of Sinai. Raphidim, as we have said, is interpreted “soundness of judgment.” Therefore the people come from Raphidim into the wilderness of Sinai because, after churchmen have embraced sound judgment and promised to keep God’s commandments, they are led on to greater things: both to hear God speaking and to receive more fully the graces of the Holy Spirit. [69] For at Sinai the children of Israel received the law and heard God speaking in cloud and darkness. [Col. 0273D]

“But Moses went up the mountain. And the Lord called him from the mountain and said: ‘Thus shall you say to the children of Israel: You yourselves have seen what I did to the Egyptians, how I bore you upon eagles’ wings and took you to myself.’”

That God carried the children of Israel upon eagles’ wings is not literally true, unless it is perhaps understood metaphorically. For, since eagles fly higher than other birds, they are said to have been raised upon eagles’ wings because earthly dangers could not harm them.

“If, therefore, you hear my voice and keep my covenant, [Col. 0274A] you shall be my special possession above all peoples; for all the earth is mine”: that is, I shall love you, as my own and special people, more than the other nations. And although all the earth is mine, you alone shall be to me a priestly kingdom and a holy nation, because neither the devil, nor vices, nor tyrants, but the Holy Spirit, priests, and virtues shall reign over you and within you.

“Moses came and, having summoned the elders of the people, set before them all the words which the Lord had commanded. And all the people answered together: ‘All that the Lord has spoken, we will do.’”

We ought to understand that everything said to that people was said to us.

[Note: [Col. 0273D] These words refer to the Apostle’s statement in Rom. XV: “Whatever things were written were written for our instruction” [Col. 0274D]. Since we have been endowed by God with gifts far greater than those of the Hebrews, let us endeavour to render him every faith and obedience.]

For we too, if we wish and with his assistance, are [Col. 0274B] a holy nation and a priestly kingdom: renouncing the devil and his works, we have promised to serve God faithfully. Therefore let us hold to faith and keep our promises, because we have a gracious and faithful Lord, whom we shall not regret having served.

“And when Moses had reported the words of the people to the Lord, he said to him: ‘Now I shall come to you in the darkness of a cloud, so that the people may hear me speaking with you and may believe you for ever.’” The fact that the Lord spoke with Moses in the darkness of a cloud already signified the mystery of his incarnation. For just as he then spoke with Moses, yet was not seen because he was veiled by the darkness of the cloud, so later, speaking with the Jews, he could not be seen because he was veiled by the covering of flesh. Of this cloud it is written: “Behold, the Lord shall ascend upon a light cloud [Col. 0274C] and shall enter Egypt” (Isa. XIX, 1).

“And the Lord said to Moses: ‘Go to the people and sanctify them today and tomorrow; let them wash their garments. Let them be ready for the third day, for on the third day the Lord shall come down before all the people upon Mount Sinai. You shall set boundaries all around and say to them: Take care that you do not go up the mountain or touch its boundaries.’”

What do “today and tomorrow” signify except the present time and the time to come? Therefore the person sanctified today and tomorrow is sanctified at all times. To wash garments is to cleanse the flesh from the stains of sins. Since the soul is clothed with flesh, garments signify flesh. Of these garments it is said: “Let your garments be white at all [Col. 0274D] times” (Eccl. IX, 8).

By the third day is understood the third month after the immolation of the lamb, on which both the Lord then descended upon Mount Sinai and, later, the Holy Spirit descended upon Christ’s disciples, making them perfect through the fullness of all knowledge.

Boundaries are set around Mount Sinai because Mount Zion too has its boundaries, beyond which those who are called may not proceed. That Sinai here signifies Zion, hear the Apostle saying: “For you have not come to a tangible mountain and burning fire and tempest and darkness, but you have come [Col. 0275A] to Mount Zion and to the city of the living God.”

[Note: [Col. 0275D] The same manuscript of Santa Croce at the Laurentian Library reads: “For you have not come to the tangible and accessible fire and tempest and darkness and storm and sound of a trumpet,” etc.; [Col. 0276D] “but, on the contrary, you have come to Mount Zion,” etc. The Cassinese manuscript agrees.]

(Hab. XII, 18.) Whoever strives, without being called, to ascend to ecclesiastical ranks and honours undoubtedly approaches the forbidden boundaries of the mountain and shall surely die. Hence it adds: “For everyone who touches the mountain shall surely die. No hand shall touch him, but he shall be crushed with stones or pierced with spears; whether beast or man, he shall not live. When the trumpet begins to sound, then they shall go up the mountain.”

Things that are near are touched with the hand; things that are distant are struck with stones or spears. This signifies that judgment against such persons will occur not in the present but in the future: as though stones and spears were to come upon them from afar, because they are not struck now, but after this [Col. 0275B] life will be condemned to eternal punishments. “Whether beast or man, he shall not live,” because whether a foolish or wise person should presume such things, he will be liable to the danger of death. For we see many both foolish and endowed with worldly wisdom boldly attempting, though not called, to climb the heights of this mountain. Therefore let them wait until they are called; let them wait until the trumpet sounds. This is what is said: “When the trumpet begins to sound, then they shall go up the mountain”: then they shall go up, when, having been invited, they are told: “Friend, go up higher” (Luke XIV, 10).

“And Moses came down from the mountain to the people and sanctified them. When they had washed their garments, he said to them: ‘Be ready for the third day, and do not approach your wives.’” O how greatly those must abstain from unlawful things to whom even lawful things are forbidden. Of such persons the Apostle says: “Those who have wives should be as though they had none” (I Cor. VII, 29).

“The third day had now arrived; morning had dawned; and behold, [70] thunders began to be heard, flashes of lightning shone, a very thick cloud covered the mountain, and the blare of the trumpet sounded with great force.” [Col. 0275C] See how well the two Testaments correspond with one another, and how fittingly Pentecost is celebrated in both.

It is written in the Acts of the Apostles: “Then they returned to Jerusalem from the mountain called Olivet. And when they had entered the upper room, they went up where Peter, John, Andrew, Thomas, Bartholomew, Matthew, Philip, James of Alphaeus, Simon the Zealot, and Judas of James were staying. All these persevered with one accord in prayer, with the women and Mary the mother of Jesus and his brothers” (Acts I, 12). [Col. 0275D]

This most holy gathering is called the Church; it is called Mount Zion. The Lord descended upon this mountain, maintaining in some manner a correspondence also with the time at which he descended upon Mount Sinai. “For,” Moses says, “the third day had now arrived; morning had dawned; and thunders began to be heard, flashes of lightning shone,” and so forth. Let us therefore say as well: the third month had now arrived, [9] and Pentecost—that is, the fiftieth day—had dawned; and [Col. 0276A] as the blessed evangelist Luke writes: “Suddenly there came from heaven a sound like that of a rushing mighty wind, and it filled the whole house where they were sitting. Divided tongues like fire appeared to them and rested upon each one of them. They were all filled with the Holy Spirit and began to speak in different languages, as the Holy Spirit gave them utterance” (Acts II, 2).

For behold, in both accounts a sound is heard and fire is seen. But in the former a dark cloud appears, while in the latter the splendour of most brilliant light; for that was shadow and figure, but this is truth. What there are thunders, here are the voices of the apostles; what there are flashing lightnings, here are miracles shining everywhere. The very thick cloud which covered the mountain is the apostles, watering the Church with saving [Col. 0276B] rains. The trumpet’s loudly resounding blast signifies the preaching of all teachers, thundering far and wide.

“The people who were in the camp were afraid. And when Moses led them out from the place of the camp to meet God, they stood at the foot of the mountain. But the whole mountain smoked, because the Lord had descended upon it in fire, and smoke ascended from it as from a furnace.”

This fear was one of awe and reverence. The statement that “they came from the place of the camp to meet God at the foot of Mount Zion” corresponds to what is said in the Acts of the Apostles: “When this sound occurred, the multitude came together and was confused in mind” (Acts II, 6). The people gathered from all Jerusalem at the foot of Mount Zion—that is, at the place where Zion, namely the holy Church, was being built, as it were, by foundations already laid. For there were the apostles; there was the mother of Jesus; there, in seed and beginnings, was the whole Mount Zion. And they were confused in mind, namely through fear and astonishment. Hence it is said here too that [Col. 0276C] “all the people in the camp were afraid”; for this fear signified that fear.

But the whole mountain smoked because the Lord had descended upon it in fire, and smoke rose from it as from a furnace. For the prophet Joel foretold this, saying: “In those days I will pour out my Spirit upon all flesh, and your sons and daughters shall prophesy,” and so forth, “and I will give wonders in heaven above and signs on earth below: blood and fire and vapour of smoke” (Joel II, 28). Those whom so great a fire of the Holy Spirit had kindled could not but burn and smoke. Just as smoke shows that fire is present, so the steadfastness of their words and the diversity of languages showed that the Holy Spirit burned in the hearts of the apostles. Blessed are those hearts filled with this fire; blessed are those who deserve to burn in this way!

All were astonished and marvelled, saying: “Are not these who speak Galileans? And how is it that we hear each one of us [Col. 0277A] speaking in our own language?” (Acts II, 8). Thus this smoke outwardly showed how great and what kind of fire was burning inwardly.

It continues: “And the whole mountain was terrible, and the sound of the trumpet gradually increased in strength and stretched out more prolongedly. Moses spoke, and the Lord answered him.” To whom would this mountain—that is, the assembly of apostles—not have seemed terrible, when he heard men formerly ignorant and scarcely proficient in one language now speaking in every language? The sound of the trumpet gradually grew and was prolonged further, because the voice and preaching of the apostles, gradually advancing, increased and was heard farther and farther, until “their sound went forth into all the earth, and their words to the ends of the world” (Ps. XVIII, 5). This is the trumpet [Col. 0277B] to which it is said: “Cry aloud; do not cease; raise your voice like a trumpet” (Isa. LVIII).

“But Moses spoke, and the Lord answered him,” because when the apostles preached, the Lord answered by teaching their hearts. For it was not they themselves but the Lord who spoke in them.

“And the Lord descended upon Mount Sinai, on the very summit of the mountain, and called Moses to its peak.” The Lord stands on the summit of Mount Sinai, by which Zion is understood, concerning which he says: “But I have been appointed king by him over Zion, his holy mountain” (Ps. II, 6). There he calls Moses to its very summit; by Moses the apostles are understood, who, having been appointed rulers over the whole Church, occupy higher [Col. 0277C] seats than the rest.

“And he said to him: ‘Go down and solemnly warn the people, lest perhaps they should wish to cross the boundaries in order to see the Lord, and a very great multitude of them perish.’” To cross the boundaries is to usurp ecclesiastical dignities contrary to God’s will. Let each person therefore remain in his own rank, and not wish to cross a forbidden boundary before he is called.

[71] “Let the priests also and the people who approach the Lord be sanctified, lest he strike them.” This is what the Apostle says: “Therefore many among you are weak and sickly, and many sleep. For if we judged ourselves, we should certainly not be judged” (II Cor. XI, 30). Let him who presumes to approach the Lord without sanctification fear lest he be struck.

[Col. 0277D] For King Uzziah approached and was struck with leprosy; the sons of Aaron approached and fell dead; Dathan and Abiram approached and the earth swallowed them; Uzzah approached the ark and, struck by the Lord, perished. It continues:

“Go down, and you shall come up, you and Aaron with you. But let not the priests and the people cross the boundaries or come up to the Lord, lest perhaps he destroy them.” Let priests hear this and, content with their own boundaries, not presume to go up where Moses and Aaron alone are commanded to ascend. For bishops are permitted to ascend more highly than priests, and bishops perform certain matters of God’s mysteries which the other priests are not permitted to perform. [Col. 0278A] Moses went down to the people and told them everything. So too the apostles told us everything that they heard from the Lord.

## Chapter XX

“And the Lord spoke all these words: ‘I am the Lord your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt and from the house of bondage.’”

When the Lord spoke these words, the whole people heard. These are the ten words of the Law, in which the whole Law is contained. He first spoke them on the mountain with everyone listening; afterwards he wrote them twice upon tablets of stone, because Moses, in anger, had broken the first tablets. At the beginning of the address he teaches them who he is, saying: “I am the Lord your God,” whom you ought rightly to obey and believe, because “I brought you out of the land of Egypt and from the house of bondage.”

“Thou shalt have no strange gods before me.” This is the commandment by which all gods are cast away and the one true God is commanded to be worshipped—the God who is everywhere, before whose sight every creature stands. And therefore he says, *before me*, because whoever is not before him is nowhere. For this commandment both the holy Apostles and the other martyrs were put to death. It is rightly placed first, since it was necessary to defend it before the others.

The second commandment is: “Thou shalt not make unto thyself any graven image,” by which every cult of idols and images is abolished. [Note: [Col. 0277D] Castus Innocens Ansaldus, O.P., in his book entitled *On the Sacred and Public Cult among the Pagans of Painted Panels, against the Greek Schismatics*, demonstrates with great learning that this passage of Exodus is to be understood thus: not only lofty sculptures are forbidden, but also paintings and low reliefs, called anaglyphic works.] Nor shalt thou make any likeness of that which is in heaven above, such as the sun, moon, and stars; or of that which is on earth beneath, such as Saturn, Jupiter, and Mercury; nor of those things which are in the waters, such as Neptune and the Nymphs; nor of those under the earth, such as Pluto, Charon, Cerberus, and the like. All these things deceived paganism worshipped; and, because it could not see them, it worshipped their images.

“For I am the Lord thy God, mighty and jealous”: and because I am mighty, I can avenge myself; and because jealous, I shall render deserts in both respects. For “jealous” may be understood both of one who loves and of one who hates. “Visiting the iniquity of the fathers upon the children unto the third and fourth generation of them that hate me, and showing mercy unto thousands of them that love me and keep my commandments.” If a son is good, he shall not bear his father’s iniquity; but if he is evil, he shall endure punishment for both his own iniquity and his father’s. But if the father too is good, and the son has not departed from his father’s goodness, he shall be enriched with far greater blessings on account of his father’s goodness. Hence the seed of Abraham was loved by the Lord; hence also the kingdom is not wholly taken away from the tribe of Judah for David’s sake.

“Thou shalt not take the name of the Lord thy God in vain; for the Lord shall not hold him guiltless that hath taken the name of his God vainly.” Here every lie is removed, and it is enjoined that the grace of God not be received in vain. For each is guilty: both he who swears in Christ’s name and does not keep his oath, and he who is called a Christian in Christ’s name and does not keep Christ’s faith. Indeed, whoever does not keep what he either affirms or denies takes the Lord’s name in vain, and, as though holding it cheap, counts it as nothing. But when the Lord’s name is entrusted to thee as a pledge, remember the pledge and do not forswear thy promise.

“Remember that thou keep holy the Sabbath day.” Thus it is said: “Sanctify a fast.” To sanctify the Sabbath is not to cease from good works. For, although the Sabbath is holy in itself, a person becomes holy by acting well. “Six days shalt thou labour, and shalt do all thy works”—that is, works for thine own benefit. For when thou actest wickedly, thou dost not do thine own works but the devil’s. “But the seventh day is the Sabbath of the Lord thy God: thou shalt do no work therein.”

Christ was reproached as doing wrong because he performed many things on Sabbaths. For on the Sabbath he commanded the man whom he had healed: “Take up thy bed and walk” (John 5:8). Christ therefore understood the Sabbath differently from the Jews. Because it is said, “Ye shall do no work therein,” they thought that even a good work done on it was a sin. Mocking their folly, God’s Wisdom said: “Is it lawful to heal on the Sabbath?” (Luke 14:3). On no day, indeed, do we read that our Saviour healed as many persons as on the Sabbath. Hence it is understood that he keeps the Sabbath better who works more goodness, mercy, and compassion on it.

But ought we to do good and keep Sabbath on only one day of the week? For those who turn from evil and do good every day have Sabbath every day. For what did resting from works signify except that one ought to rest from sins? Therefore let it be said: “It is the Sabbath: thou shalt do no work therein, thou, nor thy son, nor thy daughter, nor thy manservant, nor thy maidservant, nor thy beast, nor the stranger within thy gates.” For all these can do harm, and in all these ways we sin. Not only if my son, my servant, or the stranger in my care steals, kills, or commits other offences through my negligence is it sin to me; but also, if my beast causes injury to others, it ought to be imputed to me.

For in six days God made heaven and earth, the sea and all that is in them, and rested on the seventh day; therefore the Lord blessed the seventh day, or Sabbath, and sanctified it. Let us therefore rest every day and do nothing evil, so that all our days also may be blessed. “For,” as the Apostle says, “those days are evil in which evil works are done” (Eph. 5:16). All our days, therefore, are turned into Sabbath if in all of them we rest and cease from evil. Yet I do not say this in order to deny that on feast days we ought also to abstain from lawful things, since whatever is done contrary to the ordinances of the saints is sin. [Note: [Col. 0279D] St Bruno alludes to the holy canons which, at certain times and on feast days, forbid the celebration of weddings, dancing, and hunting, which are otherwise lawful. [Col. 0280D]]

“Honour thy father and thy mother, that thou mayest be long-lived upon the land which the Lord thy God shall give thee.” This is a great commandment: to him who observes it both the land of habitation and long life are promised. Although its literal sense edifies the mind and is full of devotion, it nevertheless appears to signify something greater. Our Father is he to whom we say daily, “Our Father who art in heaven” (Matt. 6:10); and our mother is the holy Church, which bore us to the Lord through water and the Holy Spirit. If we honour these, we fulfil all the commandments of the law. Whoever sins dishonours the Lord, who forbids everyone to sin; and whoever injures his neighbour in any respect acts against the Church, of which he himself is a member and son. Therefore “honour thy father and thy mother” is the same as: “Thou shalt love the Lord thy God with all thy heart, and thy neighbour as thyself” (Matt. 22:37).

“Thou shalt not kill; thou shalt not commit adultery; thou shalt not steal; thou shalt not bear false witness against thy neighbour. Thou shalt not covet thy neighbour’s house; thou shalt not desire his wife, nor servant, nor maidservant, nor sheep, nor ox, nor ass, nor anything that is his.” These five commandments concern one’s neighbour, while the five above concern God. Although these are contained in the others and could readily have been understood in them, God nevertheless chose to state them by name and specifically, because people sin more frequently in these matters. Since they hear these things forbidden above all others, they ought to avoid and flee them more carefully.

Concerning covetousness the Apostle says: “I had not known that covetousness was sin, unless the law had said: Thou shalt not covet” (Rom. 7:8). For how can that fail to be sin which is almost universally the cause of sin? Covetousness makes fornicators, adulterers, thieves, and robbers; many other things spring from this root, and if it is cut down, they will cease together with it.

“But all the people heard the voices, and the lamps, and the sound of the trumpet, and saw the mountain smoking; and, terrified and shaken with fear, they stood afar off, saying: Speak thou to us and we will hear; let not the Lord speak to us, lest perhaps we die.” [Note: [Col. 0280D] Thus the Vulgate and manuscript biblical codex M. A.] This mountain signifies the Apostles, who burn inwardly with the fire of the Holy Spirit and therefore seem outwardly to smoke. Of them it is said: “Touch the mountains, and they shall smoke” (Ps. 143:5). They would not smoke unless they burned; smoke therefore stands for fire. By the voices and sound of the trumpet heard upon the mountain is understood the word of preaching, resounding everywhere through the mouths of the Apostles. “For,” as Truth itself says, “it was not they who spoke, but the Holy Spirit in them” (Acts 6:10). The lamps are the brightness of miracles.

The Jews were terrified and shaken with fear, because, coming to the Apostles, they said: “What shall we do, brethren?” To them blessed Peter said: “Repent, and let every one of you be baptized” (Acts 2:38). For what else was it to say, “What shall we do, brethren?” than what the people said to Moses, “Speak thou to us, and we will hear”? Both proceed from fear. “What shall we do?” they say. “Speak; give counsel: let not the Lord speak to us, lest perhaps we die.” Those who would not believe while the Apostles spoke will one day hear the Lord himself speaking and pronouncing the sentence of death. Fearing this, therefore, they say: “Speak thou to us: what shall we do? Give counsel, show the way; let not the Lord speak to us, let him not be angry with us. We have sinned; we ask forgiveness.”

“And Moses said to the people: Fear not; for God has come to test you, that his terror might be in you and that ye might not sin.” This is what Peter also said: “Repent, and let every one of you be baptized.” Fear not: God has come not to destroy you but to save you. For if he had not come and spoken, ye would have had no sin; now ye shall have no excuse for your sins. Ye have been tested; ye have been called; ye have seen signs and miracles. Therefore do not sin; turn back and fear the Lord. It follows:

“And the people stood afar off, but Moses drew near unto the darkness wherein God was.” What is meant by this darkness but the obscure and profound knowledge of the Scriptures, according to the words: “Dark water in the clouds of the air” (Ps. 17:12)?
