The people stand far from it, while Moses alone enters it, because only holy and spiritual men understand the secret mysteries of the Scriptures and there find God. Nor should it be believed that the whole people understood those things which were then revealed to Moses in that darkness.

“And the Lord said further to Moses: Thus shalt thou say to the children of Israel: Ye have seen that I have spoken to you from heaven.” The Lord did not speak from heaven but from the mountain—unless perhaps by “heaven” we understand the air, which is often called heaven. Thus it is said, “The birds of heaven” (Ps. 8:8), although birds certainly do not ascend into heaven.

“Ye shall not make gods of silver, neither shall ye make gods of gold for yourselves.” Let the avaricious hear this, who worship and venerate gold and silver as gods. Hence avarice is called the service of idols (Gal. 5:20). “Ye shall make me an altar of earth.” An altar of earth is a human being, since man was made from earth. Upon this altar he receives Christ’s flesh and blood; upon this altar is made that sacrifice of which the Psalmist speaks: “A sacrifice unto God is a contrite spirit” (Ps. 50:19). Hence it is added: “And ye shall offer upon it your holocausts and your peace offerings.”

Upon this altar we make God favourable and merciful toward us by offering sheep and oxen. We offer sheep when we vow patience and simplicity to God. We offer oxen when we humble ourselves beneath Christ’s yoke. He commands this to be done not in Jerusalem alone, but in every place where remembrance of his name shall be, because we have an altar everywhere. Indeed, we ourselves are altars, and the victims which we offer, because we do not receive them from elsewhere but bear them within ourselves.

“But if thou shalt make me an altar of stone, thou shalt not build it of hewn stones.” An altar is made of stones when the Church is built from unfruitful and sinful persons. Hence it is written: “God is able of these stones to raise up children unto Abraham” (Matt. 9:9). Yet this altar is not built of hewn stones, because God is no respecter of persons; rather, in every nation he who fears God and works righteousness is acceptable to him. Hence the Apostle says: “See, brethren, that not many noble according to the flesh, not many mighty, nor many wise, are among you. But God hath chosen the foolish things, to destroy wisdom; and God hath chosen the weak things, to confound the strong” (1 Cor. 1:26).

If the Apostles had exhorted and preached only to the wise, rich, noble, and powerful, they would then have sought to build an altar out of hewn stones. But because such people desired earthly things more than heavenly, they considered the Apostles’ preaching and Christ’s Passion folly. Thus the Apostle says: “We preach Christ crucified: unto the Jews indeed a stumbling block, and unto the Gentiles foolishness” (ibid., 23). Therefore it is added: “For if thou lift up thy tool upon it, it shall be polluted.” What is meant by the tool but the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God? This tool is lifted over the altar to slay the victim when teachers preach among the people Christ’s Passion and how the Lamb was sacrificed on the cross. But the tool—that is, the preaching of the saints—lifted over such an altar is polluted when it is treated by them with contempt and mockery. Hence the Lord himself says: “Give not that which is holy to dogs, neither cast ye your pearls before swine” (Matt. 7:6).

It follows: “Thou shalt not go up by steps unto my altar, lest thy shame be uncovered.” Behold another altar now, loftier than the rest; yet ascent to it by steps is forbidden. This altar is faith in the Trinity. He ascends to it by steps who believes and understands that there is greater and lesser in the Trinity. Let us therefore ascend plainly, and not by steps, to this altar, believing the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit to be equal. Arius ascended to the altar by steps; and thus his shame—his foolish and impious heresy—was revealed to all nations. For, ascending, he fell; and with his entrails spilled out, he perished shamefully by an unheard-of death.

## Chapter XXI

“These are the judgments which thou shalt set before the children of Israel. If thou buy a Hebrew servant, he shall serve thee six years; in the seventh he shall go out free for nothing. With what garment he entered, with the same let him go out; if he had a wife, his wife also shall go out with him.” What is signified by the Hebrew, whose name means “one passing over,” except those who pass over to the Church and to the catholic faith? Our Lord Christ—signified by Moses, to whom these words are addressed—bought them with his precious blood. But because the world was made in six days and consists of six ages, the entire duration of this life is often understood by six years or days. Thus he serves for six years who serves throughout his whole life.

Some serve faithfully and never wish to depart from the service and slavery of their Lord. Others, however, although they appear to serve and dwell in the house of their Lord, which is the Church, throughout their lives, nevertheless bear their servitude heavily. Of such people it is said: “In the seventh year he shall go out free for nothing.” Good and merciful is the Lord, who, although he knows his servant to be faithless and wicked, nevertheless does not drive him from his house. He waits for the seventh year, waits for the end of the week and the end of life. If even then he turns back in repentance and does not love harmful freedom, he may still dwell with his Lord; otherwise, he shall depart free, but with an evil freedom. For only those are free who serve the Lord.

He goes out free for nothing because the Lord retains none of his money or substance. Hence it is added: “With what garment he entered, with the same let him go out.” He came poorly clothed and departs poorly clothed, because he lost that white garment which he received in baptism. He is clothed with his former garment, the clothing of his former manner of life. Of this garment the Church says: “I have put off my tunic; how shall I put it on?” (Song 5:3). Whoever speaks thus does not wish to withdraw from God’s service.

“If he hath a wife, his wife shall go out with him.” Let an evil wife follow an evil husband. This wife signifies vain religion and the foolish wisdom of this world. She bears and nourishes wicked children, children of vices; from her arise the covetous, the proud, and robbers. Therefore let her, so impious, be cast out from the inner chambers of the Church.

“But if his master hath given him a wife, and the woman hath borne sons and daughters, the woman and her children shall be his master’s, but he himself shall go out with his own garment.” No violence is done to any servant; none is kept against his will. If he wishes to depart, let him leave the household garments and take back his own, namely those of which we have just spoken above. To this servant his master gave a wife—sound knowledge and ecclesiastical religion—which bore sons and daughters, by whom honourable conduct and virtues are understood. For Christian religion bears such sons and daughters. This woman and her children do not follow the ungrateful and fugitive servant; rather, when he departs, she remains with him to whom she had been given when the servant then promised faith.

“But if the servant shall say: I love my master, and my wife and children; I will not go out free: then his master shall offer him to the gods, and he shall be brought to the door and the doorposts, and his ear shall be pierced with an awl, and he shall be a servant for ever.” A good servant is one who loves his mistress—such a religious wife—and such excellent sons and daughters, and prefers to remain a servant with them rather than, leaving them, depart into freedom. For not all servants are evil. The good servant is he to whom it is said: “Well done, good and faithful servant; enter thou into the joy of thy Lord” (Matt. 25:21).

This servant, therefore, the master offers to the gods: that master, surely, who set upon his own beast the man wounded by robbers, brought him to an inn, and cared for him. But to what gods, except bishops and rulers of the Church? For if sons of kings are called kings, why should sons of God not be called gods? The Psalmist says: “I have said: Ye are gods, and all of you sons of the Most High” (Ps. 81:6). These gods are also called the door and the doorposts, because, standing at the entrance of the Church, they bring all who come into the Church inside. Therefore the good servant is rightly said to be offered to the gods and brought to the door and doorposts, because everyone who loves Christ and Christian religion desires always to cling to them and continually receives, with the watchful and ever-open ear of his heart, the words of life flowing from them; “for he who is of God hears the words of God” (John 8:47). Hence it is added: “And he shall pierce his ear with an awl, and he shall be a servant for ever.” Those ears are open and pierced which always desire to hear God’s word. Conversely, those ears are closed of which it is said: “Like the deaf asp, stopping her ears, which will not hear the voice of the charmers” (Ps. 17:6). Let us therefore stand at the door and doorposts; and, lifting up our pierced and open ears, let us hear the Lord saying: “He that hath ears to hear, let him hear” (Mark 4:23); and blessed John: “He that hath an ear, let him hear what the Spirit saith to the churches” (Rev. 2:29). The awl with which the ears are pierced signifies the inspiration of the Holy Spirit.

“If any man sell his daughter to be a servant, she shall not go out as maidservants are wont to go out.” She who above was a wife is now called a daughter. Christian religion is a wife when it bears children, and a daughter when it is itself begotten by others. It is begotten by preachers in the hearts of hearers. Thus it is said here: “If any man sell his daughter.” A preacher sells his daughter—that is, Christian religion—when in some manner he begets it at the price of faith. It is rightly called a maidservant, because it is given to no one without the price of faith: no one is baptized unless he first promises faith.

But she does not go out as maidservants are wont to go out; rather, she is given in chastity, taken in honour, and received religiously—well clothed, well arranged, and well adorned, so that she may rightly please her purchaser. If she displease the eyes of her master to whom she has been entrusted, let him dismiss her; but he shall have no power to sell her to a foreign people if he has despised her. [Note: [Col. 0283D] The Cassinese codex reads: “he shall not have power.”] Many have been baptized and received Christian religion with love, but by living wickedly and falling into shameful acts plainly show how displeasing it is to them. They grow angry and flee if they are exhorted to act rightly. Such persons dismiss her because they do not wish to live and dwell with her.

But they have no power to sell her to a foreign people, because he who despises her is not permitted to impart or preach her to others, according to the words: “But unto the sinner God said: Why dost thou declare my righteousness, and take my covenant in thy mouth?” (Ps. 48:16). Hence also the Apostle says: “Thou that preachest that men should not steal, dost thou steal? Thou that sayest men should not commit adultery, dost thou commit adultery? Thou that abhorrest idols, dost thou commit sacrilege?” (Rom. 2:22). Therefore only those should sell and impart Christ’s faith to others who love it and do not wish to depart from it.

“But if he hath betrothed her unto his son, he shall deal with her according to the manner of daughters.” This son is the mind, which proceeds and is born from the womb of the heart. If, therefore, he betroths her to his son and joins her to his mind through a chaste and sincere love, he shall deal with her according to the manner of daughters: endowing her well, adorning her well, treating well the mother of the household, and appointing her mistress of the whole house.

“But if he take another for him, he shall provide the maiden with marriage, clothing, and the price of chastity; if he do not these three things, she shall go out freely without money.” In these words are most clearly marked those who afterwards fall away from sincere and true religion into hypocrisy and love of the world. Forgetting their former love and drawn far from the embrace of their former wife, they take and join another wife to their son—that is, to their mind and desire. They pursue covetousness, heap up riches, surrender themselves to worldly pleasures, and love things perishable and transitory. And because they acquire much through the religion of their former wife, pretending that they still possess and retain her, they praise her, exalt her, preach her, and adorn and clothe her with an arrangement of words. This is to provide marriage for the maiden, clothing, and not to deny the price of chastity.

They provide marriage for her when, praising her, they declare her worthy to be received by men, while testifying that legitimate children cannot be born from another woman, nor a lawful marriage be made with another. They give her clothing when they adorn her with an arrangement of words. They give the price of chastity when they praise her chastity, modesty, and conduct; and by doing these things they are believed to be not hypocrites and pretenders but true and religious Christians. But if he does not do these three things and cannot feign what we have just mentioned, she shall go out freely and without money, because he will lose religion and will not gain money. We see many such people who, separated from the religion of their first way of life, and unable to deceive, appear outwardly as they are inwardly.

“He that striketh a man with intent to kill, shall die the death.” Everything written either in the Old or in the New Testament, when it cannot be understood literally, must be understood spiritually. Some murderers kill bodies, others souls. Heretics and flatterers kill souls; because they do this willingly, unless they repent, they shall die an eternal death. The same should be understood, by analogy, also of murderers of the body.

“But he that did not lie in wait, but God delivered him into his hand, I will appoint thee a place to which he must flee.” This is said of those who kill a person not willingly but by accident. They are permitted to flee to cities of refuge, in which they must remain until the high priest dies. There were six cities, evenly spaced from one another, in which such murderers were safe. But what are the six cities except the six days in which work is permitted? And what is the high priest except Christ? Murderers therefore fled to these cities so that, as long as they remained in this life, they might not live idly in these cities—that is, in these six days—but, subduing the flesh by hard penitence, might strive earnestly to escape the danger of death. Hence those found outside them were killed without penalty, because sinners found without penitence shall also be condemned.

He remained in the city until the high priest died, because before Christ’s Passion, even after penitence had been completed, no one was permitted to return to the heavenly country. [Note: [Col. 0285D] All the Fathers of the Church, from the earliest centuries onward, adhering to the divine oracles, have confessed that, when Christ the Lord, conqueror of death and the devil, returned to the Father’s throne, the gates of Paradise were opened; and that before this divine Saviour’s triumph and entrance into heaven none of the just was granted entry into that heavenly dwelling, but all the just were held in Abraham’s bosom until Christ came to free them from that prison and lead them with himself to heavenly blessedness. I shall cite one witness for all: St Maximus of Turin, sermon 44, the first on the Ascension of the Lord, p. 514, Roman edition, 1784, says: “Therefore, brethren, let us rejoice and exult in the Lord, because today Christ, passing beyond the heights of heaven, ascended to the inconceivable majesty of the Father’s throne; and the man whom the envy of the malignant enemy had driven and cast out from that first dwelling-place of Paradise, he placed in the country of angels, and made the exile of Paradise a citizen of heaven.” St Bruno is therefore to be numbered among the holy Fathers who affirm this catholic truth, since he confirms the same thing elsewhere. [Col. 0286D]]

“If anyone deliberately kill his neighbour by ambush, thou shalt pluck him away from my altar, that he may die.” Everywhere it must be understood: unless he makes satisfaction and performs worthy penitence. Death too, as above, must be understood in a twofold sense.

“He that striketh his father or his mother shall die.” Although it is a great sin to strike one’s father or mother, I understand something greater here. I think that father and mother mean God and the Church. Whoever slanders these or strikes them by the dart of his tongue in blaspheming them shall be subject to the sentence of death. The same happens to one who curses father or mother; unless this is understood of God and the Church, the sentence appears very severe. To curse the Church may be understood as speaking wickedly of it.

“He that stealeth a man and selleth him, being convicted of the crime, shall die the death.” Roman laws likewise make provision concerning this, and such people are called *plagiarii*—kidnappers. To steal and sell a person is to separate some Christian by diabolical cunning from Christ’s faith and religion and subject him to the devil’s slavery.

“If men quarrel, and one strike his neighbour with a stone or fist, and he do not die but lie in bed; if he rise and walk outside upon his staff, he that struck him shall be innocent; nevertheless, he shall restore his labour and the expenses for physicians.” The words, “he that struck him shall be innocent,” mean as if it said: “He shall not die.” Although he has sinned, it is not a sin extending to death. By those who quarrel with one another may be understood those who dispute arrogantly about the divine law. If one overcomes the other and leads him sophistically into error, yet the matter is not one of faith and is not such that the soul is endangered, he who struck him shall be innocent—that is, he who caused his neighbour so to err shall not die. Yet he ought to appease him with words and, either himself or through some wise person, bring him back to the knowledge of truth.

“He that striketh his manservant or maidservant with a rod, and they die in his hands, shall be guilty of the crime.” This appears to be said of teachers of the Church. It often happens that a pastor of the Church strikes too harshly with the rod of correction a sinful manservant or maidservant—that is, a man or woman subject to him—by exaggerating their offences, threatening future torments, and imposing the severe penitence of the canons. If they die in his hands—that is, if, because of the enormity of their crime and the unbearable burden of penitence, he perceives that they despair of forgiveness, and does not strengthen them with gentler words and the remedy of compassion—he shall be guilty, like one who kills a sick person by treating him wrongly.

“But if he survive one day or two, he that is his money shall not be subject to punishment.” If, I say, he survive one day or two—that is, if in the pastor’s presence he shows no sign of incapacity or despair and accepts the lashes of correction and penitence, but then, departing, loses confidence on that same or the following day that he can perform penitence and obtain forgiveness—the pastor shall not be subject to punishment. Why so? Because he is his money: he is subject to him, and it belonged to him to rebuke, exhort, and reprove him in season and out of season. He shall die in his own iniquity who, after surviving for one or two days, when he could not endure penitence, did not return to him and ask mercy.

“If men quarrel, and someone strike a pregnant woman, and cause an abortion, but she herself live, he shall be liable to damages according to what the woman’s husband demands and the judges determine.” The men who quarrel signify experts in the law disputing among themselves about Holy Scripture. The pregnant woman is the soul which has already received in the womb of the heart the seed of the word and preaching, but has not yet formed it by perfect understanding or committed it to memory. Therefore, while the men quarrel and dispute among themselves about laws, the pregnant woman is struck and miscarries because, amid their debate, while the soul does not know whom it ought to believe, it loses the word of God which it had conceived, still imperfect and unformed.

The striker, therefore, is liable to damages according to the judgment of the husband and the judges, because such a person shall be judged according to the judgment of God, who is the soul’s husband, and of the Apostles. For the Lord says: “Woe to him through whom scandal cometh” (Matt. 18:7). And the Apostle says: “I would they were even cut off who trouble you” (Gal. 5:12). But if her death follows—that is, if, after losing the seed, the soul dies in error—he shall render soul for soul, so that he who kills a soul may die in soul. Here he plainly shows that he was speaking of the soul under the figure of the woman.

“Eye for eye, tooth for tooth, hand for hand, foot for foot, burning for burning, wound for wound, bruise for bruise.” Explaining this briefly, the Lord says: “With what measure ye measure, it shall be measured to you again” (Matt. 7:2). This does not mean that one who here blinds an eye shall there lose an eye, but that for this and similar deeds a fitting punishment shall be repaid to him.

[Col. 0288C] “If any man strike the eye of his manservant or maidservant and make them one-eyed, he shall let them go free for the eye which he put out.” A lord strikes the eye of a manservant or maidservant when some prelate, by teaching error, wounds one of his subjects in the eye of the soul. He makes him one-eyed if, by his evil teaching, he separates him from the light of truth. Such a servant owes him no submission, but goes out free, lest by remaining longer he become wholly blind.

Likewise, if he knocks out the tooth of his manservant or maidservant, he shall let them go free. The same thing is understood by tooth as by eye. For to knock out a tooth is to tear violently and deceitfully from the mouth of the heart that sound understanding by which the bread of the divine utterance is chewed.

“If an ox strikes a man or a woman and they die, it shall be stoned, and its flesh shall not be eaten; but the owner of the ox shall be innocent.” By oxen, priests are understood: those who bear Christ’s yoke, cultivate his field, and make the holy Church fruitful by ploughing and preaching. Of them it is said: “You shall not muzzle an ox while it treads out the grain” (1 Cor. 9:9). Therefore, as many priests as there are, so many oxen a bishop has; indeed, he himself too is an ox. Thus an ox strikes a man or woman with its horn when some priest, by cursing, by the horn of pride, and by heretical teaching, kills the inward person through speech—indeed, by wounding and striking. Such an ox is stoned when, after a council of many saints has assembled, it is struck and condemned by the judgments of very many [Col. 0289A], as though by many stones. For by as many tongues as it is condemned, by so many stones is it overwhelmed. Its flesh, however, is not eaten, because its carnal and heretical opinion is not received. Such oxen were Arius, Montanus, Manichaeus, Novatus, and Jovinianus, who slew many with their proud horns. The owner of the ox remains innocent only so long as he does not know the ox’s wickedness. But if, knowing it, he consents, he too shall be killed, because not only those who commit such things, but also those who consent to their commission, are worthy of death. This is what he says: “But if the ox was accustomed to gore yesterday and the day before yesterday, and they warned its owner”—for it can happen that an ox is a gorer while its owner does not know it—“and he did not confine it, and it kills a man or a woman, the ox shall be stoned and its owner also shall be killed” [Col. 0289B]. For here it is said through the prophet: “If you do not announce it to him—that is, to the wicked person—nor speak to him so that he may turn from his wicked way and live, that wicked person shall die in his iniquity; but I shall require his blood at your hand” (Ezek. 3:18). Bishops must therefore take great care that no heresy be preached in their churches.

“But if a price has been imposed upon him, he shall give for his life whatever has been demanded.” A price is imposed upon a bishop when penance is enjoined upon him for negligence concerning those subject to him. Therefore he is commanded to give whatever is demanded for his life, because penance has no force unless the penitent entrusts his whole self to the judgment of the person who gives him penance [Col. 0289C]. “Likewise, if it strikes a son or a daughter with its horn, it shall be subject to the same judgment.” Hence it is clear that, as regards safeguarding the faith, a prelate ought to have the same concern for all those subject to him as for his own children. “If it attacks a male or female slave, he shall give thirty shekels of silver to the master.” By a slave in this place we understand Gentiles and persons of another religion. Although they are numbered among God’s servants, they are not numbered among God’s children; for only those are children of God of whom it is said: “But to all who received him, he gave power to become children of God” (John 1:12). By the thirty shekels we understand the threefold knowledge of the Decalogue. Thus the owner of the ox gives thirty shekels of silver for the redemption of the slave or female slave, because the bishop turns the whole fullness of the law toward faith in the Trinity and, by applying rational medicine, heals those whom the ox had previously wounded [Col. 0289D].

“If anyone opens a pit, or digs one and does not cover it, and an ox or ass falls into it, the owner of the pit shall pay the price of the animals; but what is dead shall be his.” Who else seems to be signified by this man except one who lies in wait for his brother out of inveterate hatred and, persisting in hatred, keeps the pitfall of his snares open until he catches and kills his neighbour in it? Since he has carried his wicked intention through to its effect, he pays the price of the animals: either he expiates his sin by harsh penance, or he himself shall be killed for it. Hence it is added: “But what is dead shall be his,” because that death will be imputed to him, and to no one else, as though hanging about his neck, as the saying goes [Col. 0290A]. He too digs and opens a pit who disputes before simple persons about profound questions of faith. If he has opened the pit, then either by suddenly ceasing from such disputation, or by satisfying his hearers to such an extent that everything seems plain and nothing profound remains there, he shall pay for whatever goes astray and perishes there.

“If one man’s ox wounds another man’s ox, and it dies, they shall sell the living ox and divide the price; but they shall divide between them the carcass of the dead one.”

[Col. 0290B] “‘If,’ he says, ‘my ox wounds your ox’: that is, if someone from my people, infected with the poison of heretical perversity, wounds and kills by seduction someone from your people, let us sell the living ox and divide the price—that is, let us meet together and, handing the heretical man over to Satan, condemn him to eternal death; and let us equally divide the price of his condemnation and the recompense we receive from the Lord, so that, having been equal in condemning him, we may be equal in the recompense that we shall receive on his account.’ [Note: This passage is supplied from the codex of Santa Croce in the Laurentian Library, Col. 0289D.]” But let us divide the carcass of the dead one between us, because both have sinned, both have been negligent, and both have a share in the ox’s carcass and sin. For I ought to have guarded mine more carefully, and you yours [Col. 0290C]. “But if he knew that the ox was accustomed to gore yesterday and the day before yesterday, and its owner did not guard it, he shall give ox for ox and receive the carcass whole.” For if a bishop had previously learned that a man from his flock was preaching heretical doctrines, and neither rebuked him nor restrained him from that perversity, he shall give ox for ox: his own life shall answer for the life of the person who had been led astray and deceived. Hence it is added: “And he shall receive the carcass whole,” because the entire guilt for that person’s death shall fall back upon the bishop.

## 78. CHAPTER XXII

“If anyone steals a sheep or an ox and kills or sells it, he shall restore five oxen for one ox and four sheep for one sheep.” Since oxen provide greater usefulness than sheep, they rightly deserve a greater punishment in the literal sense, although some prefer to read this chapter in the opposite way. For just as priests are understood by oxen, so the remaining multitude of human beings is understood by sheep. Indeed, according to the canons, one who kills a priest or injures him is subject to a greater penalty than one who inflicts injury or death upon other people [Col. 0290D]. To steal, kill, or sell a sheep or ox is, on whatever pretext, to separate a Christian person from faith in Christ and from God. But what is meant by the five oxen except the five bodily senses? And what by the four sheep except the four elements of the body? The same thing is therefore understood by oxen and sheep, because in both cases the human body alone is figured. Thus anyone who, pierced in heart because of a soul which he has killed and separated from God, subjects the five senses of his body to Christ’s yoke and gives his whole self to lamentation and penance, undoubtedly restores five oxen for one ox. But anyone who turns the four elements of his body to all simplicity and compels them to serve God alone for the guilt he has committed, surely gives the Lord four sheep for one sheep [Col. 0291A].

“If a thief is found breaking into or digging through a house, and, having received a wound, dies, the striker shall not be guilty of blood. But if he does this after sunrise, he has committed homicide, and he himself shall die.” [Col. 0291B] He seems to distinguish between manifest and non-manifest theft and thief. A manifest thief is one who steals by day, a non-manifest thief one who steals by night; and according to human laws, manifest theft is punished more severely. Here, however, the reverse is the case: whoever kills a thief by day is guilty, but one who kills him by night is innocent. I understand this thief, who breaks into and digs through a house at night, to be the devil, who always strives secretly and by snares to corrupt and destroy the house of our body, which is also called the temple of God, so that he may steal and carry off from us the treasure of virtues and good works. If anyone finds him, perceives that his house is being plundered, and kills him, he shall not only be innocent but shall moreover deserve a reward [Col. 0291C]. He is easily found by those who recognize his snares. But because a human being is a visible creature, he is said to steal after the sun has risen—that is, in daylight and openly. If anyone kills such a person in revenge for his possessions, loving neither his own flesh nor his neighbour more than his money, he too shall die in soul. Judges, however, are not bound by this law, since everything they do, they do from love of justice. Thus the Apostle says: “For he does not bear the sword without cause; for he is God’s avenger” (Rom. 13:4). It follows: “If he does not have what he must restore for the theft, he himself shall be sold.” The person who has nothing with which to make restoration for theft is so wicked and impious that he does not know how to repent. For theft and all other sins are redeemed by penance, and without penance no sin can be redeemed [Col. 0291D]. Therefore he is sold, handed over to the devil, and cast into prison; he shall not leave it until he pays the entire debt. “If what he stole is found alive with him, whether ox, ass, or sheep, he shall restore double.” He restores double because he returns what he stole and, if he is converted, also performs harsh penance for his sin; or, if he is incapable of conversion, he shall be crushed by a double breaking.

“If anyone damages a field or vineyard and lets his animal loose to graze another’s property, he shall restore, in proportion to the damage, whatever best thing he has in his own field or vineyard.” This can be understood of heretics, who let loose their proud, unbridled, luxurious, and insatiable animal—that is, their own mind—into God’s field and vineyard, which is the Church, to ravage and graze upon it [Col. 0292A]. “Their throat is an open grave” (Ps. 13:3). In proportion to the damage, they restore whatever best thing they possess in their field, because for this crime they lose their very soul, which is better than everything they possess. That the human person himself is called a field, hear the Apostle saying: “For you are God’s cultivation” (1 Cor. 3:9). A human being is called both field and vineyard because he produces both the grain of good work and the wine of sacred speech.

“If a fire breaks out and finds ears of grain, and catches heaps of produce or standing crops in the fields, the one who kindled the fire shall make good the damage.” The Lord says in the Gospel: “The field is the world” (Matt. 13:38) [Col. 0292B]. If the world is a field, what are ears of grain, heaps of produce, and standing crops in the fields except human beings? Thus a fire that breaks out catches ears of grain, heaps of produce, and standing crops in the fields when the fury of indignation and hatred disturbs an entire people and compels it to burn and boil with love of warfare. The person who first kindled the fire and became the chief cause of discord shall make good the damage of this conflagration.

“If anyone entrusts money or a vessel to a friend for safekeeping, and it is stolen from the person who received it, if the thief is found, he shall restore double.” By the person who lends money to a friend, no one can better be understood than Christ, who says: “You are my friends if you do what I command you” (John 15:14) [Col. 0292C]. Money means faith and true knowledge; vessels are human beings, in whom God’s treasures are stored. Hence the Apostle is called a vessel of election. The friend to whom money is lent signifies the prelates and teachers of the Church, because God entrusted his money—faith and doctrine—and his people to them for keeping. He rightly entrusts money first and vessels afterwards, because without faith and doctrine no one should be a guardian of souls. These things are taken from their guardians by theft when people, deceived by the errors and snares of heretics or malicious spirits, are separated from faith in Christ. But since some thieves are found while others remain altogether hidden, it follows: “If the thief is found, he shall restore double.” Heretics can indeed be found; malicious spirits, however, since they are by nature invisible, can neither be found nor compelled to give account [Col. 0292D]. Heretics restore double because, having been converted to the faith, they bring about the conversion also of those whom they deceived; in addition, they perform penance for their offences. But if they persist in wickedness, they nonetheless restore double, because the Lord shall crush them with double breaking. It follows:

“If the thief is concealed, the master of the house shall be brought before the gods and shall swear that he did not stretch out his hand against his neighbour’s property in order to commit fraud, whether concerning ox, ass, sheep, garment, or anything by which damage may be inflicted. The case of both parties shall come before them, and if they judge against him, he shall restore double to his neighbour” [Col. 0293A]. For even today we see that, if someone from the people dies wickedly and in a grave crime, the entire accusation is turned against the bishop: they cry out that he is a murderer through whose fault and negligence that soul has perished and been stolen from God. Then the bishop should run to the gods, hasten to the canons, and there hear apostles, teachers, and holy Fathers speaking and laying down judgments; and if he cannot defend himself by their judgment, he must pay the loss. But how will he defend himself except by an oath? An oath, however, is one’s own conscience. Each person is defended by his own conscience as though by an oath. Hence the Apostle says: “But it is a very small thing to me that I should be judged by you; I am conscious of nothing against myself, but I am not thereby justified” (1 Cor. 4:3–4). If, therefore, your conscience tells you—if it swears this, for it swears if it does not lie—that you often warned, often entreated, and often taught that person to turn away from evil, and he refused to believe you, you are indeed defended by your conscience from having committed fraud concerning your neighbour’s property. But are you thereby acquitted? The Apostle says: “But I am not thereby justified” [Col. 0293B]. It can happen that one who did not commit fraud nevertheless sinned through negligence. Await judgment, therefore; and although your conscience defends you, yet if the judges decide against you, restore double. To restore double is both to do penance for one’s sin and, in the future, to exercise great watchfulness and care lest anything of the kind occur. Something proper and distinct may be understood in the ox, ass, sheep, and garment: by the ox, priests; by the ass, fools; by sheep, the simple; and by the garment, the adornments of faith [Col. 0293C].

“If anyone entrusts to his neighbour an ass, ox, sheep, or any animal for safekeeping, and it dies, is injured, or is captured by enemies, and no one sees it, an oath shall be taken between them that he did not stretch out his hand against his neighbour’s property.” Whoever did not sleep over the preceding chapter readily understands this one. Only this should be noted: guardians are not liable in the case of those who die, are injured, or are violently carried off by enemies of themselves, because bishops are likewise not held accountable for those who perish without their fault or negligence [Col. 0293D]. Yet an oath is required if no one saw it, under which condition spiritual guardians seem to be released. For who would dare say that no one saw it, when God and Lord himself, who entrusted his possessions to them for safekeeping, saw what happened? Truth itself is their witness that they sinned in this loss; and since they are defended by conscience, the testimony of their conscience is accepted, and they are not compelled to make restoration. This is what he says: “And the Lord shall accept the oath, and he shall not be compelled to restore.” But if it was stolen, he shall restore the loss to its owner. What is stolen must be restored because negligence is clearly recognized there; things carefully guarded are not stolen [Col. 0294A]. “If it has been eaten by a beast, he shall bring to him what was killed, and he shall not make restitution.” This too perishes not through negligence but through violence: for our enemy the devil goes about like a roaring lion, seeking whom he may devour. What was killed is brought to its owner so that, seeing the carcass, he may believe that the animal was eaten by a beast. If this is understood spiritually, the bishop’s conscience alone is accepted as proof, and the bishop’s conscience alone is believed.

“But if he borrows any of these things from his neighbour, and it is injured or dies while its owner is absent, he shall be compelled to restore it. But if the owner is present, he shall not restore it, especially if it had been hired for the wages of its labour.” An injured or dead animal is restored by the recipient when its owner is absent because it is not believed to have been injured or dead without the recipient’s fault. But if the owner is present, the animal is not restored, because he himself knows that it was injured or died without fault on the recipient’s part [Col. 0294B]. This may be proved from the fact that if the person who borrowed the animal killed it while the owner was present, he would nonetheless be compelled to restore it, just as if he had done so in the owner’s absence. Hence it is clear that restoration of the animal is commanded solely on account of fault and bad keeping: where there is no fault, there is no restoration. I have said this because our Lord, from whom we have received on loan and hire these animals that we guard, is always present; nevertheless, if any of them are injured or die without our fault, he shall not compel us to restore them [Col. 0294C].

“If anyone seduces a virgin not yet betrothed and sleeps with her, he shall endow her and have her as his wife. But if the virgin’s father refuses to give her, he shall pay money according to the customary dowry which virgins receive.” There are good seducers and evil seducers. Concerning good seducers the Apostle says: “As deceivers and yet true” (2 Cor. 6:8). Christ was such a seducer, of whom the Jews said: “We know that that deceiver said, while still alive” (Matt. 27:63); and: “Some were saying, ‘He is good’; but others, ‘No, rather he deceives the crowds’” (John 7:12). What need is there to speak of evil seducers? They are evident. Thus blessed Peter was a good seducer, who converted the multitude of the Romans to love of faith and righteousness [Col. 0294D]. [Note: Saint Peter, coming to Rome, took it as a virgin free for marriage; and from it he begot very many children of faith through the preaching of God’s word and the grace of the Holy Spirit.] For he found it like an unoccupied virgin, not yet betrothed or given to a husband; he slept with it and begot many children from it. He slept with it when he devoted himself to preaching and begot children by the seed of the word. Afterwards he endowed it by strengthening it with faith, knowledge, virtues, and the grace of the Holy Spirit; and he had it as his wife because both the bridegroom and the dowries pleased the virgin’s father.

It follows: “But if the virgin’s father refuses to give her, he shall pay money according to the customary measure received by virgins.” If, I say, such a seducer is displeasing to the virgin’s father, then although he has seduced, defiled, corrupted, and endowed her, he cannot have her as his wife [Col. 0295A]. Simon Magus seduced, violated, and corrupted the Roman people, joining it to his love through many magical delusions as though through great dowries. Yet because he displeased not only the father of this virgin but also almighty God, the Father of all, he was certainly unable to have her as his wife. Nevertheless, for his unlawfully and wickedly contrived dowries, he paid the whole sum and price, because for his wicked presumption he was handed over to eternal fires.

“You shall not permit sorcerers to live. Whoever has intercourse with a beast shall surely die. Whoever sacrifices to gods shall be killed, except to the Lord alone.” Those upon whom the law inflicts bodily death are signified to be condemned to everlasting death unless they repent [Col. 0295B]. Intercourse with a beast can be understood as association with heretics and the unclean. “You shall not grieve or afflict a stranger, for you yourselves were strangers in the land of Egypt.” This is what is said: “Do not do to another what you do not wish done to yourself.” Strangers are those who understand that they have another homeland, as the Psalmist says: “For I am a stranger with you in the land, and a sojourner, as all my fathers were” (Ps. 38:13). Whoever afflicts such persons acquires condemnation for himself. “You shall not harm widow or orphan. If you harm them, they shall cry out to me, and I shall hear their cry; my wrath shall be angered, and I shall strike you with the sword, and your wives shall become widows and your children orphans.” Although it is very pious to understand this as concerning all widows and orphans, I think that this widow is the Church, of which it is written: “Blessing, I shall bless her widow” (Ps. 131:13) [Col. 0295C]. Orphans are those whose ancient father, the devil, has died; reborn through water and the Holy Spirit, they have become children of God. Whoever harms them should await God’s vengeance. [Note: The faulty edition is corrected from the codex of Santa Croce in the Laurentian Library, Col. 0295D.]

“If you lend money to my poor people who dwell with you, do not press them like an exactor, nor oppress them with usury.” Avaricious moneylenders should understand that this was written because of them: “If you take your neighbour’s garment as a pledge, return it to him before sunset; for it alone is what covers the clothing of his flesh, and he has no other thing in which to sleep. If he cries out to me, I shall hear him, because I am merciful” [Col. 0295D]. Therefore the garment is commanded to be returned to persons so poor that they have nothing else with which to cover themselves. By the garment we may also understand all the other things by which wretched people support life; if these are taken from them, it is a grave sin. For constrained by want, they surrender not only their clothing but themselves to slavery; and, what is still harsher, compelled by necessity, they are forced to give as a pledge even the most shining garment of faith itself, received in baptism—the garment with which the soul alone is clothed, and without which it has nothing to cover its nakedness and shame [Col. 0296A]. Whoever receives this garment proves that he has no brotherly love unless he returns it before sunset—that is, before the wretched person reaches the end of day and life—and releases him from such an obligation. For when he cannot pay the price and you refuse to relinquish it from avarice, he is suddenly taken from this life and you are delivered to the exactor on his account. Let those hear this who at last allow persons whom they have unjustly imprisoned to depart after taking their word that they will bring money; since they cannot obtain the money and fear to return to prison, they certainly incur the danger of eternal condemnation.

“You shall not speak ill of gods, nor curse the ruler of your people.” The gods are the apostles and teachers of the Church; those who speak ill of them are persons such as Jews and heretics [Col. 0296B]. The ruler of our people is Christ; whoever curses him shall be cursed.

“You shall not delay to offer your tithes and firstfruits.” We are commanded to give tithes because we ourselves are the tithe. We are the tenth drachma for which the woman rejoices when she has found it; by these tithes the number of the elect shall be completed. We give firstfruits because the Lord struck the firstborn of Egypt and original sins. “You shall give me the firstborn of your sons.” This firstborn is Christ, of whom it is said: “Who is the firstborn of the dead and the ruler of the kings of the earth” (Rev. 1:5). Israel gave him as a gift, because blessed Mary, born from Israel’s own line, offered him to the Lord in the temple. “You shall do likewise with oxen and sheep” [Col. 0296C]. If we understand prelates by oxen and subjects by sheep, it is clear that the whole Church consists in oxen and sheep. Their firstborn are understood to be only those who follow the faith and example of the saints, because among all brothers only the firstborn hold primacy. “For seven days it shall be with its mother; on the eighth day you shall give it to me.” By seven, as we have often said already, the whole present life is understood; the eighth day, on which Christ rose, is the day of judgment, on which we too shall all rise. Hence certain psalms are entitled “for the eighth.” Thus the firstborn is with its mother for seven days because holy persons do not depart from the breasts of the Church as long as they live. But on the eighth day they are given back to the Lord, because when this life has ended, immediately after the resurrection of the flesh they are presented to the Lord [Col. 0296D]. “You shall be holy men to me; you shall not eat flesh that has been tasted by beasts, but shall throw it to the dogs.” What are beasts except heretics? And what is flesh tasted by beasts except either Scriptures corrupted by them or sinners corrupted by them? We should not eat such flesh, because we should neither receive their doctrines nor commune with those violated by them; rather, we should throw them to dogs and robbers such as they themselves are.

## CHAPTER XXIII

[Col. 0297A]

“You shall not accept a lying report; you shall not join your hand so as to bear false witness for the ungodly.” For one who lies and one who willingly listens to liars without rebuking them sin in almost the same way. The person who joins his hand to the ungodly is one who follows him and bears false witness on his behalf. How great a sin it is to bear false witness is apparent from the fact that the Lord wrote it on the tablets of stone among the Ten Commandments.

“You shall not follow a crowd in doing evil.” But because they are many and you cannot restrain them, at least do not provide assistance or consent to their wicked acts. “Nor in judgment shall you acquiesce in the decision of the wicked so as to depart from the truth.” For a person does not cease to sin by acquiescing in a false judgment and departing from truth merely because the judgment of falsehood is rendered by many [Col. 0297B]. “You shall also have mercy on the poor person in his cause.” For in every matter mercy should be shown especially to those who seem most to need mercy.

“If you meet your enemy’s ox or wandering ass, bring it back to him.” Our enemy is the divine word, which always commands things contrary to us—that is, to our flesh. Although this good enemy of ours always afflicts and persecutes our flesh, nevertheless, if we see his ox or ass—that is, some learned or unlearned person—going astray, we ought to bring him back to it, so that he may receive its saving commands and not depart from its full stalls. If we perceive that our own flesh, previously subjected to its yoke or repeatedly bearing a burden like its ass, is now wearied and fleeing or wandering, we should bring it back to it and fulfil whatever it commands us, whether to fast, keep vigil, or do anything else [Col. 0297C].

“If you see the ass of one who hates you lying beneath its burden, you shall not pass by, but shall lift it up with him.” This is what the Apostle says: “Bear one another’s burdens” (Gal. 6:2). An ass lies beneath a burden when a sinner is weighed down by the weight of sins. Hence the Psalmist says: “For my iniquities have gone over my head, and like a heavy burden they have weighed heavily upon me” (Ps. 37:5). Therefore the ass is the human body. If persons who hate you and are your enemies are seen by you lying beneath such a burden, do not pass by; lift them up and help them. Give them counsel and assistance by which they may be able to lay down so great a burden [Col. 0297D]. Remember that Samaritan who placed on his own animal the man wounded by robbers. In the salvation of souls, no one should give heed to enmities or hatred. “You shall not turn aside in judgment concerning the poor, but shall always judge without respect of persons. You shall flee falsehood; you shall not kill the innocent and just,” because God is against the ungodly. [Note: This is added by the codex of Santa Croce in the Laurentian Library, Col. 0297D.]

“You shall not accept gifts which blind even the prudent and overturn the words of the just.” It is God who speaks and cannot lie. Therefore whoever does not wish to be blinded and overthrown should not willingly accept gifts [Col. 0298A].

## 82

“You shall not be troublesome to a foreigner, for you know the souls of strangers, because you yourselves were strangers in the land of Egypt.” This has been said above, but is repeated here so that it may be held more firmly.

“For six years you shall sow your land and gather its fruits; but in the seventh year you shall let it go and give it rest, so that the poor of your people may eat, and whatever remains the beasts of the field may eat. Thus shall you do with your vineyard and olive grove. For six days you shall work; on the seventh day you shall cease, so that your ox and ass may rest and the son of your female slave and the stranger may be refreshed.” We have often already said that the six years, six days, and six ages signify the time of our working, because God completed all his work in six days and rested on the seventh [Col. 0298B]. Therefore the seventh year and seventh day stand for rest, in which ox, ass, slave, female slave, and stranger shall have rest in the heavenly Jerusalem—not these things themselves, but what they signify shall dwell there. The prudent reader understands what they signify. Then will be fulfilled what is written: “They went forth and wept, casting your seed; but they shall come with rejoicing, carrying their sheaves” (Ps. 125:6). But what is said here, “so that the poor of your people may eat, and whatever remains the beasts of the field may eat,” must be understood only literally. Thus for six years our land, vineyard, and olive grove are worked, because in this present life we ought to exercise our flesh, so that we may bear fruit for God: the grain of good work, wine which gladdens the human heart, and oil of mercy and piety [Col. 0298C]. But in the seventh year it rests, because after this life blessedness and rest follow. “Keep all that I have said to you, and you shall not swear by the name of foreign gods, nor shall it be heard from your mouth,” for people are accustomed to swear by them. Therefore, so that they may neither worship nor venerate such gods, they are forbidden to swear by their name.

“Three times in every year you shall celebrate feasts for me.” A person celebrates feasts three times in one year if he worships God in unity and Trinity. The Jew does not understand this, because although he celebrates feasts three times a year, he does not acknowledge the mystery of the Trinity. “You shall observe the feast of unleavened bread; for seven days you shall eat unleavened bread, as I commanded you, at the time of the month of new things, when you came out of Egypt” [Col. 0298D]. This is the first feast; when and how it ought to be celebrated we have explained sufficiently carefully above.

“You shall not appear before me empty-handed.” Those people appeared before the Lord three times a year with gifts; but we are before God’s countenance and in his presence. You ought never to be empty and without gifts. Hence the Apostle says: “Pray without ceasing; give thanks in all things” (1 Thess. 5:17) [Col. 0299A]. Whoever does this is neither empty nor without a gift. “And the feast of the firstfruits of your work, whatever you sow in the field.” This second feast was celebrated when, beginning to reap for the first time, they offered firstfruits to the Lord.

“And also the feast at the end of the year, when you have gathered all your fruits from the field.” This third feast was held on the first day of September, concerning which it is written: “Sound the trumpet at the beginning of the month, on the notable day of your feast” (Ps. 80:4). This month appears to be at the end of the year because, once the fruits of the entire year have been gathered, people again begin from the beginning to sow and, as it were, renew the year. Concerning these feasts, if life remains with us, we hope to say more in Leviticus [Col. 0299B]. “Three times in the year all your males shall appear before the Lord your God.” Males alone are commanded to be presented to God, because the Almighty receives and beholds nothing feminine, nothing soft, nothing given over to pleasure and luxury.

“Thou shalt not sacrifice the blood of my victim upon leaven.” For leaven, as the Apostle testifies, signifies corruption, sin, and wickedness. By the blood of the victim we understand Christ’s blood. He therefore commanded that the blood of the victim should not be sacrificed upon leaven—that is, that Christ’s blood should neither be received nor offered by the unrighteous. For the blood of the victim is sacrificed upon leaven when Christ’s blood is either consecrated by unrighteous priests or handed over for the unrighteous to drink. “The fat of my festival shall not remain until morning.” For all fat belonged to the Lord, and was always burned upon the altar as a sweet fragrance. Concerning this fat the Psalm says: “Let my soul be filled as with fat and richness” (Ps. LXII [63], 6). And again: “May the Lord remember all thy sacrifice, and may thy burnt offering become rich” (Ps. XIX [20], 4). But that the burnt offering may become rich, and may delight God both in taste and in fragrance, let no victim ever be offered without fat; let him who sacrifices never forget the fat. Do not keep it until another day, for you do not know whether you will reach another day. Burn it today; today render to the Lord a sweet fragrance. Let the festival not be lean; let not the victim be without fat. For a victim without fat is what service without faith is. For the Apostle says: “I beseech you by the mercy of God, that you present your bodies as a living sacrifice, holy, pleasing to God—your reasonable service” (Rom. XII, 1). Therefore, when you sacrifice in this way, when you mortify the flesh, do not forget the fat: let your sacrifice grow rich and fragrant. “Break thy bread to the hungry, bring the needy and homeless into thy house; when thou seest one naked, cover him, and do not despise thine own flesh” (Isa. LVIII, 7). This is the fat; this is the richness of your festival. Thus let the sacrifice become rich, and thus let it be kindled by the fire of charity into a sweet fragrance.

83. “Thou shalt bring the first fruits of the produce of thy land into the house of the Lord thy God” [Col. 0300A]. For man is earth, because he was made from earth; and his first fruits may be called faith, hope, and charity, because, born from baptism, he first bore fruit in these above all things. Without them, moreover, he cannot make an offering in the house of the Lord. But if by “land” we understand the Church, then the first fruits will be the apostles, whom Christ, bringing into the Father’s house, says: “Father, I will that where I am, they also may be with me” (John XVII, 24).

“Thou shalt not boil a kid in its mother’s milk.” For our Saviour, in the likeness of sinful flesh, was a kid. While he was still hanging at the Virgin Mother’s breast, wicked Herod wished to kill him. To him it is now said: “Thou shalt not boil a kid in its mother’s milk”; that is, do not kill Christ while he is still an infant at the breast and a little child. Cease from thy folly, for thus it was ordained by the Lord.

“Behold, I will send my angel, who shall go before thee, guard thee on the way, and bring thee into the place which I have prepared. Observe him, listen to his voice, and do not think him to be despised; for he will not forgive when thou hast sinned, and my name is in him” [Col. 0300B]. The one whom he had just called a kid he now calls an angel, of whom it is written elsewhere: “And at once the Lord whom you seek, and the Angel of the covenant whom you desire, shall come into his holy temple” (Mal. III, 1). Therefore he says: “My name is in him.” For the Father’s name is in the Son, because the Son, like the Father, is God. This Angel, sent by the Father, goes before us, guards us, and brings us into the eternal tabernacles. For these things are said concerning us, as the Apostle says: “All these things happened to them in figure” (I Cor. X, 11). We must observe him, hear him, and obey him, because he will not forgive one who sins—that is, one who has become hardened in sin.

“But if thou hearest his voice and dost all that I say, I will be an enemy to thine enemies and will afflict those who afflict thee; and my angel shall go before thee, and I will bring thee to the Amorite, the Hittite, the Perizzite, the Canaanite, the Hivite, and the Jebusite, whom I will destroy.” By these nations are understood vices and evil spirits, whom the Lord crushed, drove from the land flowing with milk and honey, and expelled from the Church abounding in the sweetness of spiritual graces [Col. 0300D].

“Thou shalt not worship their gods, nor serve them; thou shalt not do their works, but shalt destroy and break in pieces their statues.” Whoever has read the sufferings of the holy martyrs will find that they did this; and for this reason they were put to death by the impious through diverse torments. “And ye shall serve the Lord your God, that I may bless thy breads and thy waters, and remove infirmity from thy midst.” For this reason sins and iniquities are removed from our midst, from our soul and heart: because the breads of the word of God which we eat, and the waters of baptism by which we are washed, are blessed by the Lord with an effective blessing.

“Thy land shall not be barren or sterile.” For it was said to the first man: “When thou hast tilled the earth, it shall not give thee its fruit, but shall bring forth thorns and thistles for thee” (Gen. III, 18) [Col. 0301A]. Now, by contrast, fruitfulness is promised to our land, so that we also, who are earth, may always abound in spiritual gifts and reap eternal life from the Spirit. That land is not barren in which the harvests of virtues spring up and grow. “I will fill up the number of thy days.” For it is written: “Men of blood and deceit shall not halve their days” (Ps. LIV [55], 24), because they neither live here as long as they hope to live, nor attain the days of eternal blessedness. But the days of the saints will be fulfilled, because through the predestination by which they were predestined before the ages they shall live for ever.

> Note: [Col. 0301D] Thus the corrected reading in Codex S. Crucis in the Laurentian Library.

[Col. 0301B] “I will send my terror before thee, and will slay every people into whose land thou shalt enter.” Those peoples whom they conquered signified vices and sins, which we also overcome. Indeed, this battle is so much stronger because the enemies themselves are stronger—stronger, certainly, because they are invisible. “And I will turn the backs of all thine enemies before thee, sending hornets beforehand, which shall drive out the Hivite, the Canaanite, and the Hittite before thou enterest.” Although it may be understood that through hornets and wasps some portion of that land was abandoned by its inhabitants, yet the greater part was overcome by great and harsh battles.

“I will not drive them out from before thee in one year, lest the land be reduced to a wilderness and wild beasts increase against thee; little by little I will drive them out from before thee, until thou hast increased and possessest the land” [Col. 0301C]. We understand these things according to the letter; if some idle person expounds them allegorically, we do not object.

“I will set thy bounds from the Red Sea to the sea of the Philistines, and from the desert to the river; I will deliver the inhabitants of the land into your hands and drive them out before you.” By these four boundaries the four quarters of the world may be understood. From them, after the gods of the nations and evil spirits have been expelled, the holy Church now holds and possesses them in peace under Christ as its leader. Hence it is written: “And he shall rule from sea unto sea, and from the river unto the ends of the earth” (Ps. LXXI [72], 8).—“Thou shalt not make a covenant with them, nor with their gods” [Col. 0301D]. The Jews did not heed this. But we, worshipping neither the rites nor the gods of the nations, serve and adore one God, who said: “Thou shalt worship the Lord thy God, and him only shalt thou serve” (Matt. IV, 10).—“They shall not 84 dwell in thy land, lest perhaps they cause thee to sin against me, if ye serve their gods, who would certainly be a stumbling-block to thee.” For this reason, when the Jews were often led into captivity, they themselves know how much stumbling they endured. We likewise, since we understand these nations to be vices, whose gods are surely evil spirits, must not permit them to dwell in our land [Col. 0302A]. Let us cast them out of our flesh, lest they compel us also to serve their gods and lead us into the stumbling-block of great temptation. For as long as vices dwell in our land, we cannot avoid their snares; therefore the Apostle says: “Let not sin therefore reign in your mortal body” (Rom. VI, 12).

## CHAPTER XXIV

“He also said to Moses: ‘Ascend unto the Lord, thou and Aaron, Nadab and Abihu, and seventy elders of Israel, and ye shall worship from afar. Moses alone shall ascend unto the Lord; they shall not approach, nor shall the people ascend with him.’” Moses, the lawgiver and mediator of God’s people, signifies Jesus Christ, the mediator of God and men, giver of both Testaments [Col. 0302B]. Aaron, whose name is interpreted “strong mountain,” represents the apostles, concerning whom it is said: “Its foundations are in the holy mountains” (Ps. LXXVI [87], 1). Nadab is interpreted “willing,” and through him the martyrs are figured, who freely gave themselves over to death for Christ. Abihu, however, whose name is interpreted “my father is he,” signifies bishops and priests, who, like fathers, beget others in baptism. Hence the Apostle says to the Corinthians: “For in Christ Jesus I begot you through the Gospel” (I Cor. IV, 16). The seventy elders are understood as Christ’s seventy disciples. All these are commanded to ascend to the Lord and worship from afar. Yet Moses alone, ascending to the Lord, draws near to him, because “no one has ascended into heaven except he who descended from heaven, the Son of Man who is in heaven” (John III, 13) [Col. 0302C]. The Son alone draws near to the Father; he alone sits at the Father’s right hand. “For no one knows the Father except the Son, and anyone to whom the Son wills to reveal him” (Luke X, 22). One therefore ascends, and yet all ascend; but he alone ascends, because no one has ever ascended with him or in likeness to him.

“Moses therefore came,” after he had spoken with the Lord, “and related to the people all the words and judgments of the Lord. And all the people answered with one voice: ‘All the words which the Lord has spoken, we will do.’” For the Lord never judges a person according to what he was or will be, but according to what he is. He saw what these men would become; nevertheless, he received them as they then were before God [Col. 0302D], not as they would afterwards become.

> Note: [Col. 0301D] Another reading in Codex S. Crucis in the Laurentian Library: “For he knew that afterwards they would worship the golden calf; nevertheless, they were not then before God such as they would afterwards become” [Col. 0302D].

“Moses wrote all the words of the Lord; and, rising early in the morning, he built an altar at the foot of the mountain, and twelve pillars for the twelve tribes of Israel. He sent young men from the children of Israel, and they offered burnt offerings and sacrificed twelve calves as peace offerings to the Lord.” Moses wrote the Lord’s words so that they might not be handed over to oblivion through the passage of time. And because a testament is confirmed by the death of the testator, while this testator could not die, something had to be done by which that testament might be confirmed. It was therefore confirmed by the blood of calves [Col. 0303A], until the one signified by the calves should come. Hence the Apostle says: “Where there is a testament, the death of the testator must necessarily intervene; for a testament is confirmed in the dead; otherwise it is not yet valid while he who made the testament lives. Hence not even the first covenant was dedicated without the shedding of blood” (Heb. IX, 16).

Therefore Moses, rising early, built an altar at the foot of the mountain, because the Jews, who are signified by Moses, early in the morning, upon Mount Calvary at the foot of Jerusalem and Mount Sion, prepared the cross for Christ the Lord; for the altar signifies the cross. Upon this altar Christ the Lord was sacrificed. But because none of the twelve tribes can excuse itself from Christ’s death, twelve calves are sacrificed for the twelve tribes. Although there was one calf, because one Christ was sacrificed, yet because every tribe—indeed, every individual person—is wholly liable, Moses commanded twelve calves to be sacrificed. One Christ was indeed crucified and sacrificed; nevertheless every person who, assenting to his death, killed him, is wholly a murderer of Christ. And although not all laid hands upon Christ, all the Jews nevertheless killed him by consent.

We may also understand the twelve calves as the twelve apostles, who in Christ’s Passion were grieved, scandalized, and in some manner sacrificed. Hence the Apostle says: “If Christ died for all, then all died. But Christ died for all, so that those who live might live no longer for themselves but for him who died and rose again for them” (II Cor. V, 15) [Col. 0303C]. Thus there was one calf with reference to the one sacrificed; and there were twelve—indeed, far more than twelve—with reference to those who suffered with him and those who killed him. “Young men from the children of Israel” were sent, by whom we understand all the Jews assenting to Christ’s death. “And they offered burnt offerings and sacrificed peace offerings to the Lord,” by which God was reconciled to the world and the whole world reconciled among itself. But what victims? Twelve calves. For each person sacrificed one calf, because whoever rendered help toward Christ’s death is reckoned wholly guilty of Christ’s death.

“Moses therefore took half the blood [Col. 0303D] and put it into bowls, but poured the remaining part upon the altar.” The Church drinks this blood; it was shed among all nations for the cleansing of the whole people. The part poured upon the altar signifies that part of Christ’s blood which, flowing from his hands and feet, stained the wood of the cross. “Taking the book of the covenant, he read it in the hearing of the people. And they said: ‘All that the Lord has spoken we will do, and we will be obedient.’ Then he took the blood, sprinkled it upon the people, and said: ‘This is the blood of the covenant which the Lord has made with you concerning all these words.’”

After the people had heard the law given to them, understood the covenant which he had made with them [Col. 0304A], and promised that they would keep the law and preserve the covenant, Moses immediately took the blood, sprinkled it upon the people, and confirmed the testament, saying: “This is the blood of the covenant which the Lord has made with you concerning all his words.” This also Christ did: confirming the New Testament, he took the cup and said: “This is the cup of the New Testament in my blood, which shall be shed for you and for many for the remission of sins” (Luke XXII, 21). Everything that Moses said signified what Christ later accomplished.

“Moses, Aaron, Nadab, Abihu, and seventy of the elders of Israel ascended, and they saw the God of Israel; and under his feet was, as it were, a work of sapphire stone, and like heaven when it is clear” [Col. 0304B]. Moses’s ascent with the elders of Israel to see God after the covenant had been confirmed signified that, after the lamb had been sacrificed, Christ’s blood shed, and the New Testament confirmed, heaven’s gate is opened; Jesus, the great Priest, enters the Holy of Holies; and God is seen by human beings in the heavenly palace. “For where the body is, there will the eagles be gathered” (Luke XVII, 37).

Now “under his feet was, as it were, a work of sapphire stone.” Sapphire has the colour of a clear sky; hence it is added: “and like heaven when it is clear.” Whoever therefore desires to approach God, see God, and draw near to God’s feet should flee darkness, drive away clouds, cast out disturbances of the mind, become wholly tranquil and wholly serene, like heaven and unlike earth, so that, wholly bright and pure [Col. 0304C], he may deserve the fellowship of angels.

It follows: “Nor did he lay his hand upon those who had withdrawn far away.”—“For salvation is far from sinners” (Ps. CXVIII [119], 155); and those who flee God and, dragged away by the cords of sins, withdraw far from him are unworthy of his protection. “And they saw God, and ate and drank.” God, who is invisible by nature, in some manner allows himself to be seen when he displays his power in some likeness. Thus Moses testifies above that he saw him in the burning bush. But that these men ate and drank, unless it is understood of the sacrifice mentioned above, I cannot tell. The food and drink of the saints, and of those who see God, is the contemplation of the supreme Good.

[Col. 0304D] “The Lord said to Moses: ‘Ascend unto me upon the mountain, and remain there; and I will give thee two tablets of stone, and the law and commandments which I have written, that thou mayest teach the children of Israel.’” Whoever desires to see, address, and hear the Lord should ascend the mountain, draw near to heaven, and rise wholly above earthly pleasures. Moses, by ascending the mountain so often, signified this. But the fact that the children of Israel receive the law and commandments written upon stones shows their hardness and unbelief. They were stones, and therefore deserved to receive hard commandments fashioned upon stones.

“Moses and Joshua his minister arose; and, ascending the mountain, he said to the elders: ‘Wait here until we return to you. You have Aaron and Hur with you. If any question arises, you shall refer it to them’” [Col. 0305A]. For Moses, ascending the mountain, left deputies in his place to settle disputes, questions, and disagreements among the people in his stead.

“When Moses had ascended, a cloud covered the mountain, and the glory of the Lord dwelt upon Sinai, covering it for six days. But on the seventh day he called him from the midst of the darkness.” Moses in this passage signifies the apostles and teachers; Mount Sinai signifies Mount Sion, that is, the holy Church. For as Moses received the law on Mount Sinai, so the apostles and teachers received it on Mount Sion. The cloud which covered the mountain is the fullness of all knowledge and wisdom, which descended and rained upon the Church [Col. 0305B]. “And the glory of the Lord dwelt upon Sinai, covering it with a cloud for six days,” because the power of miracles and the grace of the Holy Spirit do not leave the Church until the consummation of the age, according to what the Lord says: “Behold, I am with you all days, even to the consummation of the age” (Matt. XXVIII, 20). The six days, as we have often said, signify this whole laborious life. “But on the seventh day the Lord called Moses from the midst of the darkness,” because, when the labours and days of this life are ended, the Lord will call his faithful ones to himself from this world, full of darkness and gloom.

“The appearance of the glory of the Lord was like a burning fire upon the summit of the mountain in the sight of the children of Israel.” The glory of the Lord is whatever glorifies the Lord. For if, seeing fire, you glorify the Lord, then fire is the glory of the Lord. Likewise the sun, moon, and stars are the glory of the Lord, because in them [Col. 0305C] the Lord is glorified; and so also are all other things. “And Moses entered into the midst of the cloud, ascended the mountain, and was there forty days and forty nights.” The Old Testament is not without reason obscure and profound, since it was given in cloud and darkness; that cloud foreshadowed this obscurity which we now perceive. And since we too are beginning, in some manner, to enter the cloud and deeper darkness of this book, let us beseech almighty God, who dwells in inaccessible light, that he may deign to reveal to us in light what he gave Moses in darkness.

Nor is it without mystery that the law was given in forty days. The number forty consists of four and ten: four times ten and ten times four make forty. In ten, therefore, understand the Old Testament; in four, the New Testament, since the former is contained in the Ten Commandments and the latter in the four Gospels. Thus the forty days signify that both Testaments are one, that one is given in the other, and that neither can exist without the other—just as four and ten cannot exist without one another in forty. For each Testament becomes new if we understand it spiritually.

## CHAPTER XXV

[Col. 0306A]

“And the Lord spoke to Moses, saying: ‘Speak to the children of Israel, that they may take first fruits for me from every person who offers willingly; you shall receive them. And these are the things which you shall receive: gold, silver, bronze, blue, purple, twice-dyed scarlet, fine linen, goats’ hair, rams’ skins dyed red, blue skins, shittim wood, oil for preparing lamps, spices for ointment and sweet incense, onyx stones, and gems for adorning the ephod and breastpiece.’”

The Lord commands Moses to receive, for the use of the tabernacle, the first fruits and offerings of those who offer them to the Lord freely and willingly. For God loves no offering except that which is offered with heartfelt devotion and desire [Col. 0306B]. These are the first gifts which the children of Israel offered to the Lord; hence they are not improperly called first fruits. “These,” he says, “are the things which you shall receive: gold, silver, and bronze.” Gold stands for wisdom; hence it is written: “A desirable treasure rests in the mouth of the wise” (Prov. XIV, 33). And the Apostle says: “We have this treasure in earthen vessels” (II Cor. IV, 7). Silver signifies purity of speech; hence the Psalmist says: “The words of the Lord are pure words, silver tried by fire” (Ps. XI [12], 7). Bronze, because it sounds more clearly than other metals, signifies fluency and eloquence. Hence the Apostle says: “Though I speak with the tongues of men and of angels, but have not charity, I have become as sounding bronze or a tinkling cymbal” (I Cor. XIII, 1).

Gold, silver, and bronze are therefore brought together for the building of the tabernacle, because wisdom without truth and eloquence is evil and useless. Thus it is written of the wise without truth: “They are wise to do evil, but they do not know how to do good” (Jer. IV, 21) [Col. 0306C]. Of many wise men lacking eloquence it is also said: “Many dogs, unable to bark” (Isa. LVI, 10). And again: “He who hides grain is cursed among the peoples” (Prov. XI, 26). Likewise: “Hidden wisdom and concealed treasure—what profit is there in either?” (Ecclus. XX, 32). God’s tabernacle therefore has gold, that is, wisdom; it has silver, that is, purity of speech; and it has bronze, that is, fruitfulness of eloquence. Such a building should have such material.
