It follows: “Blue, purple, twice-dyed scarlet, and fine linen.” Josephus too, in explaining these, said that they signify the four elements. By blue, which is the colour of the air, he intended the air to be signified; by purple, water, because it is dyed from the blood of fish, which arise from water and live in water. By scarlet, because it is wholly fiery and blood-red in colour, he intended fire to be signified; and by fine linen, earth, because it springs from the earth. He intended thereby to signify that human beings themselves are the material of God’s tabernacle: and as man is constituted from these four elements, so God’s tabernacle is constituted from human beings [Col. 0307A].

Alternatively, by these four most noble materials are understood the four principal virtues, in which all other virtues are contained and without which they are shown to be vain and useless: prudence, justice, fortitude, and temperance. Blue, having a heavenly and divine colour, signifies prudence, which descends from heaven from God, according to the saying: “All wisdom is from the Lord God” (Ecclus. I, 1). Purple, with which kings and princes are clothed, signifies justice. Hence those clothed in purple are told: “Love justice, you who judge the earth” (Wis. I, 1). Scarlet, being blood-coloured, signifies fortitude, by which the holy martyrs, fighting even unto blood, proved most steadfast in Christ’s faith. Fine linen, however, which springs from the earth, signifies temperance. For as earth is in the middle of all the elements and receives all the elements into itself, so temperance moves among all the virtues, reconciles them all, and joins them together.

These things, placed in God’s building, look to one another and reciprocally supply each other with comeliness and beauty. Let gold look to silver: let the wise person not speak without purity of expression. Let silver look to gold: without wisdom, even what is pure and true should not be spoken [Col. 0307B]. For speaking what is true is not always fitting and useful; and at times telling a lie does less harm than telling the truth. Let gold and silver also regard bronze, so that neither wisdom nor truth may be idle. They are idle if they are not spoken or set forth, if they are not heard through the sound of bronze and voice. Let bronze likewise attend to gold and silver: whoever is fluent and eloquent should remain silent without wisdom and truth.

Likewise prudence, justice, fortitude, and temperance, understood through blue, purple, scarlet, and fine linen, should agree and mutually follow one another, because any one of them without the others is useless. Solomon was wise, but because he lacked fortitude, he was overcome by women. King Uzziah was just, but because he lacked temperance, he was killed by enemies. Samson was the strongest of all, but poor in wisdom, and he lost his eyes. But what shall I say of temperance? Unless it is fortified by the help of the other virtues, it easily compels a person to deny God and truth [Col. 0307D]. Yet it is the seasoning of the others; without it all the rest seem vain and foolish. Let us consider what follows.

“Goats’ skins, rams’ skins dyed red, blue skins, and shittim wood.” These too are commanded to be offered for the construction of the tabernacle. They offer goats’ hair, so that penitents who come from sin may not lack the hair-shirts with which they are to be clothed. They offer rams’ skins dyed red, so that the martyrs too may find clothing. They offer blue skins, with which all prelates, clothed thereby, may contemplate heavenly things alone. But what do we understand by shittim wood, said to be strong and incorruptible, except holy men, who because through faith they conquered kingdoms obtained eternal promises? Shittim is fittingly interpreted “thorns,” since holy men enter the kingdoms of heaven through many tribulations [Col. 0308A]. Shittim is also the place concerning which it is said in the Book of Numbers: “At that time Israel was dwelling in Shittim” (Num. XXV, 1). The remaining matters which follow we leave to be explained in their proper place. Now let us discuss what is immediately at hand.

“And they shall make me a sanctuary, and I will dwell in their midst. According to every likeness of the tabernacle which I shall show thee, and of all the vessels for its service, so shall ye make it.” By sanctuary he means the whole tabernacle, which he commands to be made according to the likeness shown to Moses on the mountain [Col. 0308B]. It may reasonably be said that these things were revealed to Moses by the Lord not merely through words but by a certain spiritual vision. The whole tabernacle is divided into two parts: the Holy Place and the Holy of Holies. Hence the Apostle says: “The first tabernacle was made, in which were the candlestick, the table, and the setting forth of the loaves, which is called the Holy Place” (Heb. IX, 12). Beyond the veil was the second tabernacle, called the Holy of Holies, having a golden censer and the ark of the covenant, covered on every side with gold; within it were a golden vessel containing manna, Aaron’s rod which had blossomed, and the tablets of the covenant. I have set these matters forth beforehand so that, as we are about to speak of the ark, we may more easily understand what they signify.

“Make an ark of shittim wood, whose length shall be two and a half cubits, its breadth a cubit and a half, and its height likewise a cubit and a half; and thou shalt overlay it with the purest gold within and without” [Col. 0308C]. What do we understand by this ark but the Catholic Church? Not, however, the Church which still dwells in this world and suffers many injuries, but that Church which, having passed beyond the veil of heaven, now dwells and abides in the Holy of Holies. Of it the Apostle says: “But that Jerusalem which is above is free, which is our mother” (Gal. IV, 16). And concerning this ark the Apostle John says: “And the temple of the Lord was opened in heaven, and the ark of his covenant was seen in his temple” (Apoc. XI, 19).

This ark is joined and built from shittim wood—that is, strong and incorruptible wood, thorn-wood with which Christ is crowned. For Christ’s crown is the saints, because for them he fought, conquered, and was crowned. Every dimension of this ark seems to contain something imperfect, because in both length and breadth it has a half, and in height a half-cubit. This is because that noble and heavenly ark is not yet perfect, nor will it be perfected until the consummation of the age. Every day some are built into it; every day stones—that is, the souls of saints—are borne there by angels, and its walls are built from them.

> Note: [Col. 0307] Codex S. Crucis in the Laurentian Library: “something is built in it.”

Hence the Psalmist says: “Deal favourably, O Lord, in thy good will with Sion, that the walls of Jerusalem may be built” (Ps. L [51], 20) [Col. 0309A]. Therefore the Lord says to the souls of the saints: “Wait yet a little time, until the number of your brethren is filled up” (Apoc. VI, 11). For the saints will not have perfect blessedness until, their souls joined to their bodies, the entire multitude of saints is raised together above the heavens. Then indeed, when all things have been perfected, there will be nothing by which this ark may grow and nothing by which it may fear diminution. Then it will have no half, because “when that which is perfect has come, that which is in part shall be done away” (I Cor. XIII, 10).

It is overlaid inside and outside with the purest gold because it will outwardly display through preaching the brightness of wisdom which it possesses inwardly. Those who hide the wisdom given them are overlaid within, but not without [Col. 0309B]. For when the Apostle says, “He speaks wisdom among the perfect” (I Cor. II, 6), he signifies that they are overlaid with gold both within and without.

“And thou shalt make upon it a golden crown round about.” What does the ark’s being crowned all around mean, except that the multitude of saints, signified by this ark, has now, when the battle is completed and the enemies overcome, been crowned by God for victory and triumph? “For,” says the Apostle, “no one will be crowned unless he has competed lawfully” (II Tim. II, 3). And again: “I have fought the good fight, I have finished the course, I have kept the faith; henceforth there is laid up for me the crown of righteousness” (II Tim. IV, 7). Thus the whole ark is crowned, and every person who is in the ark is crowned, because individuals each have their own crowns and all together have one crown [Col. 0309C].

“Thou shalt make also four golden rings, which thou shalt place at the four corners of the ark: let two rings be on one side, and two on the other.” The four rings are the four principal virtues, without which this ark can neither be moved nor carried. They are placed at the ark’s four corners, so that it may have prudence on one side, justice on another, fortitude on one side, and temperance on another. The four Gospels too are understood through the four rings. Since they shine with the brilliance of wisdom, they are not improperly compared with gold; through their preaching this ark is built, lifted, and carried.

“Thou shalt also make bars of shittim wood, and overlay them with gold; and thou shalt put them through the rings at the sides of the ark, that it may be carried by them. They shall always remain in the rings and shall never be removed from them” [Col. 0309D]. What do the bars signify except teachers? They are of shittim wood, being strong, enduring, and unfailing. They are said to be covered with gold because they shine with the light of wisdom. They are passed through the golden rings so that the ark may be carried by them, because, enveloped in the sayings of the Gospels, they must be ready to lift the ark. Thus they are rightly commanded always to remain in the rings and never be withdrawn from them, so that whenever the ark must be lifted, no delay may be found in them.

To lift the ark is to extol and preach in words the virtues, triumphs, glory, honour, and blessedness of the saints. The Apostle lifted the ark when he said: “Things which eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor have entered into the heart of man, which God has prepared for those who love him” (I Cor. II, 9) [Col. 0310A]. Christ also not only lifted it, but exalted it above the heavens, when he said: “Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven. Blessed are the meek, for they shall possess the earth” (Matt. V, 3), and so forth. Therefore let the bars not be separated from the rings; let teachers not depart from the Gospels. Let them always be at hand, always ready to carry the ark and preach the Gospel, so that they may be able to give an account concerning whatever they are asked; lest perhaps they seek the rings and do not find them at the moment when they must answer and lift the ark.

“Then you shall put into the ark the testimony which I shall give you.” Understand this testimony to be the Law which the Lord wrote on the two tablets of stone. It was placed in the ark because it was entrusted to the hearts of the saints. And rightly the Law is enclosed in the ark, while the Gospel is set around it on the four sides: for the rites and ceremonies of the Law lie hidden, but the precepts of the Gospels are spread and preached through the four quarters of the world. In this ark, as the Apostle says, there was “a golden urn containing manna” (Heb. 9:4), by which we understand Christ, full of the sweetness of all wisdom and knowledge. There was also Aaron’s rod which had budded—that is, the Virgin Mary, who, though barren and without seed, bore a son.

[Col. 0310C] “You shall also make a mercy-seat of the purest gold: its height shall be two cubits and a half, and its breadth a cubit and a half.” He calls the mercy-seat the oracle by which the ark was covered. [Note: [Col. 0309] The erroneous edition is corrected from codex S. Cr. in the Laurentian Library.] Rightly, moreover, the ark is the collection of holy souls and blessed spirits, and is called a mercy-seat, because, ever beholding above themselves God’s clemency and propitiation, they obtain not only what they ask and pray for, but whatever they desire. For they can will nothing other than what they know the Lord wills. And therefore, if they desire anything, they desire it in such a manner that they do not depart from God’s will.

The mercy-seat is also of the purest gold, because God grants propitiation so wisely that He is never deceived in granting it: for He is never propitiated except toward one who repents. Human beings, however, are often well disposed toward those toward whom they ought not to be well disposed. And because God is not propitiated always, nor toward everyone, He also placed something incomplete in the dimensions of the mercy-seat—namely, a half and a half.

“You shall also make two golden cherubim, wrought in relief, at either side of the oracle; and one cherub shall be on one side of the oracle and the other on the other side; they shall cover both sides of the mercy-seat, spreading their wings and covering the oracle.” What else ought we to understand by the two cherubim than the two Testaments? For *cherubim* is interpreted “fullness of knowledge,” and the fullness of knowledge is contained in these two. They are rightly said to be golden and wrought in relief, because [Col. 0311A] they shine with wisdom and cannot be formed upon the anvil of the heart without great labor.

One cherub is on one side of the oracle and the other on the other side, because no one can come to the oracle except through them. No one will find God propitious unless he first receives from them the teachings of faith. Even before they were written, Abraham and the other patriarchs taught these things; for all divine wisdom flowed from here. They cover both sides of the mercy-seat so that the mercy-seat itself, and whatever lies beneath it—that is, the ark and its poles, the Church and its teachers—may be filled with wisdom and knowledge; and, seeing their wings, men may learn to fly, because healing is in their wings and all their sayings bear human beings upward to heavenly things. By these wings they fly; by these they descend into human hearts.

“They shall look toward one another, their faces turned toward the mercy-seat by which the ark is to be covered; in it you shall place the testimony which I shall give you. From there I shall command you, and speak to you above the mercy-seat, and from the midst of the two cherubim which shall be upon the ark of the testimony, all the things which I shall command through you to the children of Israel.”

That the cherubim look toward one another signifies the friendship and harmony of the two Testaments; both testify and say the same thing. Their faces are turned toward the mercy-seat which covers the ark, so that they may be seen and known by all, and that there may be no one in the ark and congregation of saints for whom their countenance is foreign and unknown. [Col. 0311C] Let those hear this who neglect to meditate upon the holy Scriptures.

In this ark, as he had said above, the testimony is commanded to be placed, by which the tablets of the covenant are understood, so that holy Church may never forget the Law given to her. And because there are two Testaments, namely the Old and the New, therefore he commanded the Testament to be placed in the ark twice. It follows: “From there I shall command you, and speak to you”; that is, whenever I speak to you, whenever I command anything to the children of Israel through you, seek me there; find me there; from there I shall speak to you. From where? Above the mercy-seat and from the midst of the two cherubim.

Therefore, whoever wishes to speak with God, let him come to the cherubim; let him hasten to the Testaments of the Scriptures, and there he will find the Lord both speaking and showing mercy. Do you wish to hear the Lord speaking in the cherubim? “I,” he says, “am the Lord your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt; you shall have no strange gods besides me” (Lev. 11:45). And in the New Testament: “I am the door; if anyone enters through me, he shall be saved” (John 10:9). Thus God speaks from the midst of the cherubim.

“You shall also make a table of setim wood, two cubits in length, one cubit in breadth, and one cubit and a half in height; and you shall overlay it with the purest gold.” After the construction of the ark, Moses is commanded to make the table, which signifies the very same thing that we have just said the cherubim signify. For the table in this place is understood as divine wisdom, concerning which it is written: “You have prepared a table before me” (Ps. 22:5). And again: [Col. 0312A] “Let their table be made a snare before them” (Ps. 68:22).

For divine Scripture is called *cherubim* because it is the fullness of all knowledge and, flying swiftly with certain wings, suddenly fills all things; and it is called a table because it feeds the soul with many and diverse delights. This table is made from setim wood, which is strong and incorruptible, and thereby signifies divine Scripture as eternal and unfailing.

This table is perfect in length and breadth, without diminution, because it has no half in length or breadth. In height, however, it has a half, and therefore seems imperfect in height; for something must always be added to the half in order for a cubit to be completed, whereas a cubit lacks nothing. Rightly, indeed, this table has no diminution in length and breadth, because until the consummation of the age—which is its length—it will sufficiently supply spiritual food to all who come to it. Likewise in breadth, by which it is spread throughout all the bounds of the world, it has nothing lacking and abundantly refreshes all.

But when it stretches upward, so as to speak of higher things—of God, of unity and Trinity, and of how the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son—it cannot fully instruct and satisfy us; therefore this table seems to have great diminution in height. For blessed Paul, caught up into the heights, says that he heard certain things which he does not dare place upon this [Col. 0312C] table: “For I heard secret words which it is not lawful for a human being to utter” (2 Cor. 12:4). What it is not lawful to utter is not lawful to write; and what is not lawful to write is not placed upon this table. For this table is divine Scripture. It is plain, then, how much diminution this table possesses in height. Yet it is overlaid with the purest gold, because it shines throughout with the most sincere splendor of wisdom and knowledge. It follows:

“You shall make for it a golden rim round about, and for the rim itself an engraved crown, four fingers high, and above it another small golden crown.” Why is this table commanded to have a rim? Is it itself going to speak and say, “Lord, you shall open my lips, and my mouth shall proclaim your praise” (Ps. 50:17)? Certainly it says this, because whoever says it says it through the table; indeed, the table says it not through itself but through others. Those, therefore, through whom it says this are its lips.

You indeed—you, apostles—are the lips of this table; you are golden lips around it, devouring all its delights. You, golden lip, blessed Paul, what do you say? Do you wish to hear what? “We speak wisdom among the perfect” (1 Cor. 2:6). Truly this is a golden lip. And that, too, is a golden lip from which it is said: “In the beginning was the Word” (John 1:1). What was it that I wished to say? All the apostles are golden lips. Forgive me, God, forgive me, who presume, with polluted lips, to speak of golden lips.

And for the rim itself he made an engraved crown, [Col. 0313A] four fingers high. Therefore not the table but the rim is crowned. For what king was ever as worthy of a crown as the apostles? Who defeated so many enemies? Who overcame so many kingdoms? Who so often triumphed over his adversaries? Concerning this crown the Apostle said confidently: “Henceforth there is laid up for me a crown of righteousness” (2 Tim. 4:8).

Thus the rim has an engraved crown, carved and varied, fashioned with much artistry, because through many labors the apostles received the palms and crowns of victory. This crown is said to be four fingers high because, having overcome the four regions of the world, the apostles purchased it at the price of their blood. Thus the size of the crown grew in proportion to the extent of their kingdoms. For rulers of the world also, in ancient times, customarily placed upon themselves as many diadems as the kingdoms they conquered.

He also made another small golden crown above it. Therefore they possess the first crown because they conquered the world; the second because they overcame vices. Thus the apostles and teachers of the Church deserve two crowns: one for those whom they convert to the faith, concerning which the Apostle says: “Therefore, my most beloved and most desired brothers, my joy and my crown, stand thus in the Lord, beloved ones” (Phil. 4:1); the other for vices and evil spirits overcome—a crown with which Christ’s confessors are crowned.

“You shall also prepare four golden rings and place them at the four corners of the same table, by each of its feet. The golden rings shall be beneath the crown, that poles may be passed through them and the table carried.” What the four golden rings and the poles signify in the construction of the ark has been said above. The four rings are the four principal virtues; the poles are bishops and teachers. These rings are at the four corners so that they may first meet all who come to the table. For one is unworthy of the food of this table who refuses to enter through these rings. This is the narrow gate of which it is said: “Enter through the narrow gate which leads to life” (Luke 13:24).

Whoever, therefore, is not held by these rings—that is, whoever does not preserve prudence, justice, courage, and temperance—makes himself unworthy of this table. Through these rings, then, let the poles pass; let bishops and teachers be held chained and joined to these virtues. Let them never depart from them, never forget prudence, courage, or temperance. For by these poles the table is carried, because the people are nourished by bishops who bring the provisions of spiritual sustenance. That the rings are placed beneath the crown means that all who adhere to the rings are worthy to be crowned.

It follows: “You shall also make the poles of setim wood and cover them with gold, for carrying the table.” Blessed are the bishops if they understand this: if they know themselves to be setim wood, wood strong and incorruptible; if, covered with gold, they shine [Col. 0314A] with the splendor of virtues and with the light of wisdom and knowledge.

“You shall also prepare dishes, bowls, censers, and cups, in which drink-offerings are to be offered, of the purest gold.” What shall we sinners do, called to offer drink-offerings, when God commands all these things to be made of the purest gold? By this are understood the lower ranks of the Church. For all these are vessels of ministry in which sacrifice was offered. Therefore our God, who says, “Be holy, because I am holy” (Lev. 11:44), wills that not bishops alone, but also deacons, subdeacons, and all other ministers of the Church and altar, should shine both in doctrine and in life.

“And you shall place upon the table the loaves of presentation before me always.” I take these loaves to be all the volumes of the holy Scriptures. Moses placed five loaves on this table, of ineffable savor and beauty. Christ, although he placed them all—for “he is the living bread who came down from heaven” (John 6:59)—nevertheless offered four principal loaves, with which no delights can be compared. Isaiah too placed loaves, and Jeremiah, and all the prophets. Blessed Paul also placed his loaves, whose quality need not be praised. But who can enumerate all who brought loaves to this table?

Even now loaves are being placed upon this table. For he himself says: “And you shall place upon the table the loaves of presentation before me always.” “Always” was not added without reason; for what is always done is done at every time. But because I am not worthy to place loaves upon this table, I pray to you, Lord Jesus, that you may at least allow me to fill my belly from those which have been placed there. Let what has been said about the table suffice; now let us consider the lampstand.

“You shall also make a lampstand of the purest beaten gold: its shaft, its branches, its cups, and its knobs and lilies proceeding from it. Six branches shall come forth from its sides, three from one side and three from the other. Three cups like nuts shall be upon each branch, with knobs likewise and a lily; and likewise three cups in the likeness of a nut upon the other branch, with knobs and a lily. This shall be the work of the six branches which are to proceed from the shaft. But upon the lampstand itself there shall be four cups in the form of a nut, knobs upon each, and lilies. The knobs shall be beneath two branches in three places, making the six branches proceeding together from one shaft. Thus both the knobs and branches shall be from it, all beaten work of the purest gold. You shall also make seven lamps and place them upon the lampstand, that they may shine toward the front.”

We have set forth the whole lampstand so that its form may first be understood literally, and the manner in which it was made may be known. [Col. 0315A] Its shaft was continuous up to the top, and at four places upon it there were four cups in the form of nuts, which perhaps we may now call [term uncertain]. Above these were knobs—that is, certain small wheels—and above the wheels were lilies in four places. There were three branches on one side of the shaft and three on the other, making six altogether. Beneath the branches were knobs; in three places they had three cups in the form of nuts, and above the cups knobs, and above the knobs lilies. Seven lamps were above: one on the shaft and six upon the branches.

We must not suppose that the Lord commanded so artistic and marvelous a lampstand to be made through Moses in order to serve an empty practical purpose, but to intimate a great mystery. This lampstand is Christ, who said: “No one lights a lamp and puts it under a bushel, but upon a lampstand, so that it may give light to all who are in the house” (Luke 11:33). It is rightly made of the purest gold, because Christ our Lord, the power of God and the wisdom of God, is wholly pure and unstained by any contagion of vices: he committed no sin, nor was deceit found in his mouth.

By the shaft of this lampstand we understand the Lord’s body; by the branches proceeding from this shaft, and the seven lamps burning upon them, the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit with which our Savior was filled. Hence it is said through the prophet: “A rod shall come forth from the root of Jesse, and a flower shall rise from his root; and the Spirit of the Lord shall rest upon him: the spirit of wisdom and understanding, the spirit of counsel and might, the spirit of knowledge and piety, and the spirit of the fear of the Lord shall fill him” (Isa. 11:1).

These, therefore, are the seven lamps placed upon the lampstand and giving light toward the front, because, as will be said below, the lampstand stood on the other side opposite the table. The whole table is illuminated by these lamps, and every place which these lamps do not illumine is dark. The four cups in the shaft signify the four Gospels, the whole, complete, and perfect knowledge of which is contained in the Savior’s breast, since they also flowed forth from it.

The Gospels are fittingly compared with cups, because, as they offer drink and pour out everywhere the wine of faith, the whole world has been filled and made drunk by them. Four knobs were placed above the cups because each Gospel bears [Col. 0315D] and supports the whole world. For the knobs signify the roundness and circumference of the whole world. Though there is only one world, nevertheless, because there are four Gospels by which it is sustained and governed, the whole and complete world is assigned to each Gospel. And this is not without reason, because each Gospel by itself would suffice for the whole world’s faith, instruction, and salvation.

Although by the four knobs the four parts of the world—East, West, North, and South—may also fittingly be understood, so that one part of the world is assigned to each Gospel; and thus each cup will have its own proper sphere. It remains to speak of the lilies: just as each cup has its own sphere, so each sphere has its own lily above it.

[Col. 0316A] But what are the lilies except the flowers of virtues, the fragrances of good works, and the white-clad host of saints? These lilies first appeared above the spheres when the cups of Gospel preaching began to sprinkle and pour upon the world. I myself think the upper sphere to be the choir of bishops. Since that sphere was nearer the lamps, it signified that bishops are illumined by greater mysteries and receive more light and understanding. Let the second sphere be understood as the choir of priests and other ranks, which is below the bishops and does not approach the brightness of the light so closely. The third, that of all laypeople, who adhered not only to bishops but also to all the ecclesiastical orders set above them, shows that all orders of the Church partake in some measure of the gifts of the Holy Spirit.

Having described everything belonging to the shaft of the lampstand, let us now consider its branches. Each branch had three cups, and as many knobs and lilies. The three cups are the three kinds of wisdom: physics, that is, natural philosophy; ethics, that is, moral philosophy; and logic, that is, rational philosophy. From these three parts of wisdom, as from three cups—or rather, as from three rivers—all wisdom flows; by them the whole world is watered and made drunk.

Each branch, therefore—that is, each gift of the Holy Spirit—has these three cups, because whatever the grace of the Holy Spirit touches, it can fill with the fullness of all knowledge. For it bears these cups, by which it satisfies all who thirst. Hence Truth itself says: “Whoever believes in me, as Scripture says, rivers of living water shall flow from his belly” (John 7:38). The Evangelist immediately explains this: “But he said this concerning the Spirit, whom those who believed in him were to receive” (ibid., 39).

The three cups adhere to the branches because wisdom is from the Lord God and cannot be possessed without the grace of the Holy Spirit. He also gives wisdom to the wicked, he who “makes his sun rise upon the good and the evil” (Matt. 5:45). Let the same understanding apply to the knobs and lilies as above. Thus, to state it briefly: the lampstand is Christ’s body; the four cups are the four Gospels; the knob is either the world [Col. 0316D] or its power which encompasses the whole world; the lily is his divinity, or the fragrances of virtues; and the seven lamps are the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit. It follows:

“The snuffers also, and the vessels in which what has been snuffed is extinguished, shall be made of the purest gold.” Unless these lamps burned sluggishly and slowly in some persons, they would certainly have no need of snuffers. For snuffers are applied to lamps so that they may shine more brightly. There is someone in the Church to whom the spirit of wisdom has been given; if he is sluggish in preaching and instruction, his lamp needs a snuffer so that it may shine more clearly.

The snuffer is charity. Those who possess it cannot be idle, according to the saying: “The charity of God urges us on” (2 Cor. [Col. 0317A] 5:14). This cleans and snuffs lamps that burn sluggishly and slowly; and in vessels prepared for that purpose it extinguishes and destroys the sluggishness and slowness which it removes from them, so that in this way every trace of darkness may be wholly cleansed from the lamp.

I myself think these vessels—if, indeed, they ought to be called vessels, for they have not been given a name—to be care and concern. Whoever possesses this has wholly extinguished sluggishness and slowness in himself; because he is always concerned, his lamp is never darkened. Such was the Apostle who said: “Apart from the things which are outward, there is my daily pressing concern, the care of all the churches” (2 Cor. 11:28). He burned so brightly that he had no need of a snuffer.

“The whole weight of the lampstand, with all its vessels, shall be one talent of the purest gold.” Seven times ten, or ten times seven, makes seventy. This lampstand possesses the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit not only in its lamps but also in its very weight. Hence we believe that the body of the Lord was fashioned by the working of the Holy Spirit, and we confess that our Savior himself and the Holy Spirit are of the same weight and equality. It follows: “Receive and make according to the pattern which was shown you on the mountain.” He makes him attentive and admonishes him to look carefully, because great are the things that appear here, but far greater those which lie hidden.

With these matters thus arranged, let us approach the construction of the tabernacle with the tools of the Holy Spirit.

## CHAPTER XXVI

[Col. 0317C]

“Now the tabernacle shall be made thus: you shall make ten curtains of twisted fine linen, blue, purple, and twice-dyed scarlet, varied with embroidered work.” What these signify we have already said above. By these are signified the four elements and the four principal virtues. Fine linen, because it grows from the earth, signifies earth; blue, because it has the color of the air, stands for air; purple, because it is dyed with the blood of fish, signifies water, since fish too are born from water; scarlet, because it is of a fiery and red color, is taken for fire.

Since human beings are composed of these four elements, the entire material of these curtains is human beings. For if the walls of the Church are constituted from human beings, why should the curtains of the tabernacle not also be woven from human beings? For the Church and the tabernacle are the same. Let the threads in the curtains therefore be what are called stones in the walls of the Church.

The curtains from which this tabernacle—that is, holy Church—is constructed are as many as the nations of the Gentiles. They are said to be ten because the number ten contains all numbers within itself; therefore ten means the same as all. The apostles wove these curtains. Hence blessed Paul, the teacher of the Gentiles, supported himself by the craft of tent-making. The apostles wove as many curtains as there are peoples or cities converted to the Lord.

The apostles placed twisted fine linen in the curtains when they turned earth—that is, earthly and sinful persons—from worldly pleasures toward Christ’s love and faith. They placed blue when they urged people to contemplate and love heavenly things alone. They placed purple when they called them to the grace of baptism. They placed scarlet when they exhorted them to burn with the fire of the Spirit and to love God and neighbor. Scarlet is twice dyed because the charity and fire of love kindled toward God extends also toward one’s neighbor. If you love God alone, you are dyed once; if your neighbor alone, you are dyed once; but if you love God and your neighbor, you are both scarlet and twice dyed: scarlet because you burn with the fire of love, and twice dyed because you redden with a double love.

These curtains are made with embroidered work, so that they themselves may fly and may teach all who look upon them to fly. For these curtains are made here, but they ought not remain here for long. They shall take wings as eagles; they shall fly and not grow weary.

“Each curtain shall be twenty-eight cubits in length and four cubits in breadth. All the coverings shall be of one measure.” Why is the length of the curtains twenty-eight cubits, except because in twenty-eight each Testament is doubled? For twice ten and twice four make twenty-eight. Each Testament is doubled when it is first understood according to the letter and then spiritually. Rightly, therefore, the length [Col. 0318C] of the curtains is twenty-eight cubits, so that every part of the Church may extend itself so far as to be able to understand each Testament both according to the letter and spiritually.

Whoever does not receive both Testaments cannot be a curtain, for all curtains are of one measure. Therefore every people, every sect, every soul which does not receive both Testaments, does not extend itself to embrace both, and does not believe that both must be understood in a double sense, will by no means be woven into the curtains of the Church.

The breadth of the curtains is four cubits because the Law and the Prophets are compressed into the four Gospels. For God has made a shortened word upon the earth. Therefore, since one cannot understand everything, let one at least extend oneself by four [Col. 0318D] cubits and understand the brevity of the Gospel.

“Five curtains shall be joined one to another, and the other five shall adhere in a similar joining.” That the curtains are divided into two parts signifies the two walls of the Church: one coming from circumcision, the other from uncircumcision. Hence Christ is called the cornerstone, joining in himself the two walls, namely Jews and Gentiles. The curtains are joined to one another, whereby we understand the peace, concord, and charity of the saints.

“You shall also make blue loops on the sides, at the outer edges of the curtains, that they may be joined together. Each curtain shall have fifty loops on either side, so arranged that loop may meet loop and one may be fitted to the other.” He had said that five curtains were to be joined to one another; now he explains how they are to be joined. Each curtain had fifty loops along its length on both sides, by which it was joined to the curtain placed beside it. These loops were blue, that is, of heavenly and airy color; by them we understand virtues, which certainly have not an earthly but a heavenly origin. For we possess no virtue unless it comes from there.

By these loops the curtains are joined; by these they are coupled to one another. Therefore, O human being, whoever you are, if you wish to be a curtain, receive these loops so that you may be joined to another curtain like yourself. If anyone does not desire to be a curtain of this tabernacle, or cannot be a curtain, let him at least be some part of it. Whatever it is, because it is in the curtain, let it have a loop; and if not all of them, at least one or two.

Faith is an excellent loop, without which no curtains are joined. Since the Jew does not possess this, he is not joined to me; for the Jew has no loop to which my loop may be joined. Likewise the heretic, because he lacks this loop, is not joined to the Christian. “For what,” as the Apostle says, “has faith in common with unbelief? What fellowship has light with darkness? What agreement has Christ with Belial?” (2 Cor. 6:15).

Charity too is a loop, and such a loop that curtains coupled by it cannot be wholly separated. There are also many other loops: justice, prudence, courage, temperance, peace, patience, humility, kindness, gentleness, generosity, self-control, chastity, and concord. But who can enumerate them all? These loops meet each other, kiss each other, embrace each other, and hold each other when a just person loves a just person, a prudent person a prudent person, a strong person a strong person, a modest person a modest person, a patient person a patient person, and a merciful person a merciful person, embracing each with the arms of charity.

If lovers of the world had possessed these loops, they would surely not hate, persecute, kill, or scourge one another; nor would one provoke another by such great injuries. It is thus evident that they either are not among the curtains of the Church or are there without loops. For when in one congregation of saints you see many people so consenting with one another and joined by the bond of charity that they are thought to be not many but one person, do you not see how these loops meet one another and mutually hold each other? Hence it is said in the Acts of the Apostles: “The multitude of believers had one heart and one soul” (Acts 2:32).

“You shall also make fifty golden rings, by which the curtains’ veils are to be joined, that one tabernacle may be made.” It has been said how five curtains on one side and five on the other were to be joined. It remains to say how these two parts are to be joined to one another so that one tabernacle may be made from them, and there may be one fold and one shepherd. Therefore, he says, “You shall make golden rings, by which the curtains’ veils”—that is, the two parts—“may be joined together.”

Above he commands blue loops to be made, but here golden rings, because Jews may be bound among themselves, and Christians among themselves, by the bonds of virtues. The golden rings signify the books of both Testaments; why they are called golden has often been said. Jews and Christians are joined by these books because they preach one faith, confess one God, and all the books were given by one God. For I would not believe the Jews unless the law of the Gospel agreed with them; nor would Jews believe us unless the Gospels agreed with the Law.

Therefore, because all the books of the New and Old Testaments agree among themselves, these two veils—that is, circumcision and uncircumcision—are joined together. While the books of the two Testaments, like certain rings, meet one another in harmony and agreement, they bind and unite Jews and Christians in one faith. The number of the rings itself also corresponds to the number of the books. There are forty-two books of the Old Testament and six of the New; if Paul’s Epistles and the Catholic Epistles, contained in two volumes, are added, all the books make fifty. For the book of Ruth, as Jerome says, is counted in the book of Judges; and Ezra and Nehemiah are compressed into one volume. Therefore there are rightly fifty rings, since there are fifty books. Let this suffice concerning the curtains. Now let us consider the goat-hair coverings.

“You shall also make eleven goat-hair cloths for covering the roof of the tabernacle. The length of one cloth shall be thirty cubits, and its breadth four. The measure of all the cloths shall be equal.” Just as by the curtains we understand learned and religious men, so by the goat-hair cloths we understand secular persons and sinners. In the former, blue, purple, scarlet, and fine linen shine; in the latter the rough, shaggy, prickly hairs of goats bristle, because the former are adorned with virtues but the latter deformed by vices and sins.

The goat-hair cloths are more numerous than the curtains and are also longer, because sinners are more numerous than the righteous and are raised higher in riches and honors. Hence Truth itself says: “Many are called, but few are chosen” (Matt. 22:14). These cover the roof and defend the tabernacle against the assaults of hail and rain, because if we were all monks [Col. 0320D] and priests, the Church would easily be trampled by Saracens and robbers. Hence the Apostle commands prayer for kings and all others who are placed in high station, and says that the more contemptible members are more necessary.

That the curtains and goat-hair cloths are equal in breadth, namely four cubits, shows that all the righteous and unrighteous hold the same faith of the Gospels. It follows:

“Of these, join five separately, and couple six to one another, so that you double the sixth covering at the front of the roof. You shall also make fifty loops on the edge of the other covering, so that it may be joined to the other.” For, just as the curtains, so too the coverings are joined; their explanation, therefore, will suffice here as well. But the sixth covering, which exceeds the curtains, is doubled in the middle at the [Col. 0321A] front of the roof, and half covers the rear of the tabernacle—not because one covering is divided in this way, for otherwise the whole tabernacle would be covered by a single covering, but because one covering was added in order that all the curtains might be covered by the coverings. The loops, moreover, signify the same thing both in the coverings and in the curtains. The two parts of the coverings are the two walls of the Church, of which we have already spoken.

These two parts, however, are joined by fifty bronze clasps, just as the two parts of the curtains are joined by fifty golden rings. For golden rings and bronze clasps are the same thing: they signify, as we have said, the fifty books of both Testaments. But in joining the curtains they are golden, because there they join teachers and religious men; here, however, they are bronze, because they unite the unlearned and sinners, who attend not so much [Col. 0321B] to the gold and wisdom that shine in them as to bronze—to the sounding letter and the simple history. Of these it is added: “You shall make fifty bronze clasps, by which the loops shall be joined, so that one covering may be made out of all”; and there may be in them one flock and one shepherd.

“But what remains of the coverings prepared for the roof—that is, the one covering which is additional—you shall use half of it to cover the rear of the tabernacle. And one cubit shall hang down on one side and another on the other side, being the excess in the length of the coverings, protecting both sides of the tabernacle.” The fact that the coverings exceed the curtains at the front and rear of the tabernacle, and on either side, signifies that at the beginning of the Church, at its final consummation, [Col. 0321C] and now, while they remain in this world, the wicked are always more numerous than the good. Yet because the covering is doubled at the front of the tabernacle and covers its rear, it signifies that the holy Church needs greater protection at its beginning and at its end, because it suffered greater tribulation at the beginning and will suffer greater tribulation at the end.

For concerning its first persecution the Lord says: “The hour is coming when everyone who kills you will think that he is offering service to God” (John 16:2). But concerning the last he says: “Then there will be tribulation such as has not been from the beginning of the world until now, nor will be” (Matt. 23:21). Let this suffice concerning the coverings.

“You shall also make another covering for the roof out of skins of rams dyed red, and over this another covering [Col. 0321D] out of hyacinth-colored skins.” For the tabernacle—that is, the holy Church—had three coverings: the first of haircloth, the second of red skins, the third of hyacinth-colored skins. Since haircloth is fitting for sinners converted to repentance, the haircloth signifies penitents. But because martyrs are reddened by their own blood, the dyed-red skins signify martyrs. Hyacinth, however, because it has an airy, sky-blue hue, is used to signify heaven.

Therefore, since repentance was imposed upon sinners converted to the faith immediately at the very beginning of faith, not without reason was their first covering haircloth. But when some of them, having immediately undertaken penance, were dragged [Col. 0322A] off to punishment and beheaded even before they could be baptized, what else did they put on after haircloth but red skins? And because, leaving their body wrapped in red skins, their soul at once penetrated the secrets of heaven, it received as a third covering hyacinth-colored skins. Let the first garment therefore be repentance and haircloth, the second martyrdom, the third heaven. These matters having been briefly explained, let us consider the boards.

“You shall make boards standing before the tabernacle from setim wood, each of which shall be ten cubits in length and one cubit and a half in width.” By the boards, as will be shown most clearly in what follows, are signified all the books of the New and Old Testaments; for as many as the boards are, so many are the books. They stand before the tabernacle, so that they may always be seen by those who are in the tabernacle [Col. 0322B], because we ought always to have the volumes of the sacred law before our eyes.

These boards are made from setim wood, which is interpreted “thorn,” because the sayings of the holy books always prick and rebuke sinners. They are ten cubits in length because they teach us the ten commandments of the law and exhort us to observe them. Nor could they have greater length, because in those ten commandments is contained the fullness of the entire law; whoever observes them will lack nothing 95 for perfection. They are a cubit and a half in width because every book is imperfect in itself, and in order that its half-cubit may be completed, it requires [Col. 0322C] the supplement of another; hence they summon one another in turn as testimony. For the Gospels themselves are confirmed in many places by the law and the prophets. Oh, how often blessed Paul is necessary in expounding this board which we are now considering! Let board therefore be joined to board, and let all the intermediate and incomplete cubits be completed by conjunction with others. Hence it is added: “On the sides of the board let two mortises be made, by which one board shall be joined to another board.” For the boards are joined to one another, as it were, by mortising, because the sacred volumes agree with one another so harmoniously in certain places that they appear to say precisely the same thing.

“Of these there shall be twenty on the southern side, which [Col. 0322D] faces south; you shall cast forty silver bases for them, so that two bases may be placed beneath each board at its two corners.” There are forty-two books in all of the Old Testament, since Ruth is counted among the books of Judges and Nehemiah among the books of Ezra. Of the New Testament there are six books: namely, the four Gospels, the Acts of the Apostles, and the Apocalypse; the rest are called not books but Epistles. Thus all the books of both Testaments number forty-eight; and there are likewise forty-eight boards by which the tabernacle is enclosed. See, therefore, how fittingly books are understood by the boards.

Twenty boards are placed on the southern side, so that, with the number ten doubled, we may know that the whole law must be understood in a twofold way: first according to [Col. 0323A] the letter, and then spiritually. Had the Jews understood this alone, they would today not be Jews but Christians. Let us, then, understand both the law and the prophets according to the letter and spiritually, and place beneath each board these two bases by which it may be held and supported. This is what he says: “Let two bases be placed beneath each board at its two corners.” For the two bases are the two understandings, namely letter and spirit. They hold and support each board, because without these two understandings we cannot hold or bear the books of the sacred law.

These bases are silver because they are pure and true. For that silver signifies purity and truth of utterance, hear the Psalmist: “The words [Col. 0323B] of the Lord are pure words, silver tried by fire” (Ps. 11:7). These bases are placed at the corners so that, if either one is removed, the board cannot stand. Thus the board falls unless both support it. Let those hear this who wish to understand the Scriptures either only according to the letter or only spiritually; and while they place the board upon only one base, let them beware lest they themselves fall together with the board.

“On the second side of the tabernacle, which faces north, there shall be twenty boards, having forty silver bases; two bases shall be placed beneath each board.” Whoever does not understand this should read again the explanation given above.

“But on the western side of the tabernacle you shall make six boards.” These six boards are the six books of the New Testament. [Col. 0323C] They are fittingly placed on the western side because, when the sun had already turned toward setting, they were issued after all the others and in the last age. “For we are those,” says the Apostle, “upon whom the ends of the ages have come” (1 Cor. 10:11). Blessed are those eyes which deserve to see these boards and to know their skillful arrangement.

“And again you shall make two others, which shall be erected at the corners behind the tabernacle.” If these two are erected behind the tabernacle, then certainly the six must stand at the front of the tabernacle. It is therefore clear that the six boards of the New Testament stood at the very entrance of the tabernacle. And rightly so, because unless one enters through these, no one enters the tabernacle except as a thief and robber. For in these boards our Savior is portrayed, crying: [Col. 0323D] “He who does not enter the sheepfold through me, but climbs in by another way, is a thief and a robber” (John 10:1). And again: “I am the door; if anyone enters through me, he shall be saved” (ibid., 9).

But I think that the two boards erected behind the tabernacle are the two books of Maccabees, for they occupy the last place in the whole Old Testament. They are fittingly placed behind the tabernacle because, in those times, the law lay trampled down and hidden, and no one was permitted to inspect the boards or devote himself to reading; all the Jews were compelled, abandoning their own laws, to turn to Gentile customs.

“They shall be joined together from below to above, and one fastening shall hold them all together. The same joining shall also be preserved for the two [Col. 0324A] boards which are to be placed in the corners; and together there shall be eight boards, their bases being sixteen silver bases, reckoned as two bases for each board.” What their joining and fastening signify has already been said: they signify the harmony and strength which all the volumes of the divine law possess among themselves. For all say one thing, all preach one faith, all praise and magnify one God. This is their fastening: all agree from below to above, from the last to the first. From the Apocalypse to Genesis they agree in preaching one faith and one God.

But in saying that the same joining is to be preserved also for the two boards, he assigns authority to the two books of Maccabees [Col. 0324B] and places them in the canon together with the rest. And quite rightly, since in them the power and might of God are more fully narrated.

“96 You shall make five bars of setim wood to hold the boards on one side of the tabernacle, and five others on the other side, and the same number for the western side; they shall be inserted through the middle of the boards from end to end. You shall overlay the boards with gold and cast golden rings in them, through which the bars may hold them together; and you shall cover the bars with plates of gold.” What, indeed, are signified by the five bars but the five senses of the body? They are made from setim wood and covered with golden plates when they begin to perceive not carnal things but spiritual ones; in this way they become incorruptible [Col. 0324C] and shine like gold—indeed, more brightly than gold.

There are five bodily senses: sight, hearing, taste, smell, and touch. Without them the boards of the tabernacle—that is, the volumes of the divine law—cannot stand. For all would already have fallen and failed unless they were seen with the eyes of mind and body; unless they were heard with the ears of heart and head; unless they were perceived as sweet by the inner and outer palate and taste; unless the fragrance of their understanding delighted us; unless their touch, striking the heart, stirred it and kindled it to love of the heavenly light.

[Col. 0324D] These, therefore, are the five bars inserted through golden rings when the aforesaid senses, enveloped in the splendid sayings of the sacred books, do not permit the divine law either to fall or to be consigned to oblivion. For as many as the sayings are, so many are the golden rings; and the bars are inserted through as many rings as the understanding is enveloped in sayings, being inserted from end to end through all the boards. The fact that all the boards are overlaid with gold signifies that all divine books shine with the light of wisdom and knowledge. Let this suffice concerning the boards.

“And you shall erect the tabernacle according to the pattern shown you on the mountain.” Moses saw the pattern for erecting the tabernacle; yet how it is erected is not stated. For the tabernacle will be erected when, all things having been perfected, holy Church is exalted above the heavens. Nevertheless, let us say how we think this tabernacle was erected according to the letter. [Col. 0325A]

There were forty-eight boards by which the tabernacle was enclosed, and above them were curtains twenty-eight cubits in length. The width of the tabernacle was equal to the length of the curtains. There were ten curtains in all. Each had a width of four cubits, which, joined together, make forty cubits—for four times ten makes forty. Either, then, the tabernacle was forty cubits long, or its length was reduced to thirty cubits by ten cubits of the curtains hanging at the rear. I think that ten cubits of the curtains hung behind the tabernacle because the boards over which the curtains were stretched were ten cubits long. Above the curtains [Col. 0325B] lay the coverings, one cubit of which hung down on one side of the tabernacle and another on the other side. This occurred because the coverings were two cubits longer than the curtains. Moreover, if the tabernacle had been more than thirty cubits long, it could not have been enclosed by the boards. For there were twenty boards on one side of the tabernacle and twenty on the other, each one cubit and a half wide; joined together, these make only thirty cubits.

“You shall make a veil of hyacinth, purple, twice-dyed scarlet, and twisted linen, woven with embroidered work and beautiful variety. Hanging it before four columns of setim wood, which [Col. 0325C] shall themselves be overlaid with gold, and shall have golden capitals and silver bases. The veil shall be inserted by rings, and between them you shall place the ark of testimony; thus the sanctuary and the Holy of Holies shall be divided.” This veil, placed between the Holy of Holies, signifies heaven, as the Apostle testifies. For he says: “Christ, having appeared as high priest of the good things to come, through a greater and more perfect tabernacle, not made by hands, that is, not of this creation, and not through the blood of goats or calves, but through his own blood, entered once into the Holy Places, having found eternal redemption” (Heb. 9:11). Explaining this still more plainly, he says: “For Jesus did not enter into holy places made by hands, copies of the true things, but into heaven itself, that he might now appear [Col. 0325D] before the face of God for us” (ibid., 24).

Concerning hyacinth. Hyacinth is a plant or flower; hyacinth is also a gemstone. Both the flower and the stone are blue in color, a color which we often see in clouds illuminated by the sun. We behold hyacinth in heaven, because the sky displays the hyacinth color. We also see, in some fashion, purple and scarlet in the radiance of the stars; and the whiteness of linen sometimes appears in the moon. Our eyes themselves show us with what beautiful variety the sky is woven.

The veil itself, which divided the tabernacle, was woven with such variety not without great mystery. [Col. 0326A] For the hyacinth woven into the veil preached, if not by speech then by color, that earthly things should be despised and heavenly things loved. Those who saw the purple—if indeed they understood what they saw—were kindled by it to love justice. For purple signifies justice, which only kings were permitted to wear. Hence Wisdom says to them: “Love justice, you who judge the earth” (Wis. 1:1); and for this reason Roman pontiffs also use it. Purple is therefore given to those whose right it is to administer justice among the people.

Scarlet, wholly blood-red and twice dyed with the flaming color of charity, summoned people to martyrdom and strengthened them with such great courage that they did not hesitate to die not only for God and the defense of the faith, but even one for another. Twisted linen [Col. 0326B] exhorted them to afflict the flesh and to love bodily brightness and chastity. This veil, therefore, was made with embroidered work, so that it might teach souls to leave earthly things and fly toward heavenly things.

This veil, then, which thus preaches, admonishes, teaches, and persuades, is the preaching of the Gospel. Hence it is said to hang before four columns, by which we understand the four Evangelists: Matthew, Mark, Luke, and John. The veil hangs before them because it is depicted by them, varied by them, preached by them, sustained and carried by them.

These are the pillars of the Church, made from no other wood than setim wood, strong and incorruptible wood, because these are they of whom it is said: “But the righteous shall live forever” (Wis. 5:16). [Col. 0326C] These columns are overlaid with gold because no wisdom or knowledge can be compared with the preaching of the Evangelists. They have golden capitals, in which a desirable treasure rests. And truly, they are golden heads from which flowed words so golden, so radiant, so clear, and so precious. Hence it is said through the Psalmist: “The commandment of the Lord is bright, enlightening the eyes” (Ps. 18:9); and again: “Your word is a lamp to my feet and a light to my paths” (Ps. 118:105).

And since silver signifies the truth of speech and purity of expression, according to the words, “The words of the Lord are pure words, silver tried by fire” (Ps. 11:7), these columns are said to stand on silver bases. [Col. 0326D] The Evangelists never depart from truth; they never speak falsehood. Whatever they say is true, just, holy, pure, and most worthy of belief. Unhappy Jews, who contradict these columns and do not heed the silver bases upon which they stand.

The veil, therefore, is inserted through rings because Gospel preaching is held fast, bound to the sayings of Christ. This veil divides the tabernacle and separates the New from the Old Testament; it shows how heaven differs from earth, and the righteous from sinners.

[Note: [Col. 0325] Cassinese codex: “This, however, shows how heaven differs from earth, and the righteous from sinners.”]

It follows:

“You shall place the mercy seat upon the ark of testimony in the Holy of Holies, and the table outside the veil, [Col. 0327A] and opposite the table the lampstand on the southern side of the tabernacle.” The table stood on the northern side. All these matters have been explained above. The mercy seat is placed upon the ark when the regard of divine mercy looks upon the Church in order to aid it. The table is placed outside the veil because knowledge of sacred utterance is not jealously hidden from anyone, but satisfies all who desire to approach it with thanksgiving.

[Col. 0327B] The lampstand is placed opposite the table so that the dishes laid upon it may be seen, because without Christ’s illumination divine Scripture cannot be understood. For he is “the true light that enlightens every person coming into this world” (John 1:9). And because God shall come from the south, the lampstand is placed on the southern side. But because evils shall be unleashed from the north over the whole earth, the table is placed in the northern part. We ought especially to fortify that place through which we fear enemies may break in upon us.

“You shall make a curtain at the entrance of the tabernacle out of hyacinth, purple, twice-dyed scarlet, and twisted linen, with embroidered work. And you shall overlay with gold five columns of setim wood, before which the curtain shall be drawn; their capitals shall be golden and their bases bronze.” By this curtain made at the entrance of the tabernacle we understand the glorious choir of the apostles, to whom were granted the keys of heaven and the Church, the power of loosing, and the authority to open and close the gates of Paradise.

This tabernacle is made of hyacinth because, as has often already been said [Col. 0327C], hyacinth signifies heaven. The apostles are heavens, of whom it is said: “The heavens declare the glory of God” (Ps. 18:1). They are also purple, because purple signifies kings. The apostles are kings: they shall judge the twelve tribes of Israel, clothed in purple. Of them it is said: “The princes of the peoples have gathered together with the God of Abraham” (Ps. 46:10).

They are also twice-dyed scarlet because, by confessing God and teaching their neighbor, they deserved to be stained by the shedding of their own blood. Scarlet is dyed when martyrdom is undertaken for God and for one’s neighbor.

[Note: [Col. 0327D] Cassinese codex: “Scarlet is twice dyed when someone undertakes martyrdom for God and for his neighbor.”]

They are also twisted linen, being whitened by virtues and made whiter than snow, strengthened by great courage in battles; for linen is twisted in order that it may become stronger. The apostles’ [Col. 0327D] strength and virtue were shown to be greater in proportion as they were more harshly tortured by tyrants. These, indeed, are those winged and many-eyed cherubim who bear the whole Church.

But the five columns which he commanded to be overlaid with gold signify the five books of Moses.

[Note: [Col. 0328D] The edition is corrected at this point from the Laurentian codex.]

They are overlaid with gold when they are understood spiritually. For through these five books we understand all the commandments of both Testaments. If the whole law is signified by the ten words, why should not the whole law be signified by the five books in which those same words are contained? The curtain was drawn and stretched before these five columns [Col. 0328A] because wherever the holy apostles were, they always had the law and the prophets before them and in their minds. The curtain was stretched before the columns because it always looked toward the columns.

The capitals of the columns are golden because their voice and preaching shine with the splendor of wisdom and knowledge. Their bases are bronze because they resound with a clear and well-sounding ring; bronze rings more clearly than all other metals. Therefore, just as gold signifies wisdom, so bronze signifies the sound of the voice. The columns rightly have golden capitals and silver bases, because Gospel preaching and the volumes of the divine law shine with wisdom and everywhere resound in fame and sound.

## Chapter XXVII

[Col. 0328B] “You shall make an altar from setim wood, five cubits in length and the same in width—that is, square—and three cubits in height. Horns shall rise from its four corners, being part of it itself, and you shall cover it with bronze.” Having finished the tabernacle, he begins to speak of the altar; and by the altar he signifies almost the same thing as he signified by the tabernacle. For it is the custom of prophets to signify one and the same matter in different ways. This can be plainly seen in the book of Revelation, where one and the same vision is repeated seven times in different figures.

Here the altar signifies the Church. Why it is said to be made of setim wood is not unknown to one who has read what precedes. This altar is square because the holy Church extends and spreads through the four regions of the world. [Col. 0328C] The Psalmist briefly enumerates them when he says: “From the rising of the sun and its setting, from the north and from the sea” (Ps. 106:3).

It has five cubits on each side because the faith and commandments of these five books suffice for every part of the Church. If they are understood spiritually, the whole Old and New Testament is contained in them. Moses is placed before all other volumes because they embrace all the rest within themselves and are held to be, as it were, firstborn among them all. They therefore rightly hold primacy over the others, since they are first by their very origin.

Yet I do not place them above the Gospels, because both flowed from one and the same source. The two collections would even agree in number, except that Deuteronomy is repeated, because its name is interpreted “second law.” [Col. 0328D] The second law is indeed the New Testament, just as the first law is called the Old Testament; for there are only two Testaments. This book called Deuteronomy is between the two, since it repeats the one and signifies the other. But if it signifies the latter, wherever this book is found which is called the second law, there also are the Gospels. Therefore either the books of Moses are not four, or their fifth book is understood to be the second law, that is, the Gospel.

This altar is also three cubits high because, when the Church is raised upward, it is enough for it to measure three cubits—that is, to believe in and worship the Father, the Son, and [Col. 0329A] the Holy Spirit. Do not measure beyond this, for it is not permitted to go further; if you advance further, or if you fail even to advance this far, you will no longer belong to this altar.

It follows: “The horns at the four corners shall be part of it.” The four horns signify the four regions of the world: East, West, North, and South. These four horns are from the altar itself because the four regions of the world are not from elsewhere but from the Church itself. The whole altar is covered with bronze because the whole Church does not cease to sing and rejoice in God’s praises in a clear and harmonious voice. It is she to whom it is said: “Cry aloud, do not cease; lift up your voice like a trumpet” (Isa. 58:1). We have already often said that bronze resounds more clearly and more loudly than other metals; hence it is frequently understood as the sound of the voice and holy preaching.

[Col. 0329B] “And you shall make for its use basins to receive ashes, tongs, flesh-hooks, and fire-pans.” Evil is that basin of which it is said: “Moab is the basin of my hope” (Ps. 107:10). But these are good basins, which serve the altar, cleanse the altar, and receive the altar’s ashes. By them are understood priests, who wipe the altar of God—which is the Church—clean of every defilement, receive into themselves the ashes and sins of others, and, having received them, cast them far from the Church. They receive them in order to destroy them, not to retain them. Of such it is said: “They shall eat the sins of my people” (Hos. 4:8).

They also hold tongs, by which they draw coals from the fire. To draw coals from the fire is to help and console with brotherly charity [Col. 0329D] those who are burned by the fire of tribulation and distress. Consolation and assistance are the tongs by which the afflicted are delivered from fire and distress. Thus the Apostle says: “For as the sufferings of Christ abound in us, so through Christ our consolation also abounds” (2 Cor. 1:5). And the Psalmist: “According to the multitude of my sorrows in my heart, your consolations made my soul glad” (Ps. 93:19).

We understand the same thing by flesh-hooks and tongs. For to draw boiling meat from a pot with a flesh-hook is the same as to snatch burning coals from the fire. Meat in a pot and coals in a fire signify all faithful people constrained by tribulations. Do you wish to be a flesh-hook? [Col. 0329D] It is indeed good to be such a flesh-hook: console the sorrowful, assist the wretched, help the needy, open prisons, free captives. These are the meats which our flesh-hook draws out.

But what are the fire-pans, except those who, fervent in charity, pursue hospitality and willingly receive with all humanity everyone whom they know to be afflicted for Christ’s name or to burn with love for him? For if Christ’s coals signify 99 faithful people who are afflicted and fervent in charity, whoever receives them is a fire-pan.

[Col. 0330A] “You shall make all its vessels of bronze, and a bronze grating in the form of a net. At its four corners shall be four bronze rings, which you shall place beneath the ledge of the altar; and the grating shall reach to the middle of the altar.” All the vessels of the altar are made of bronze so that all the children of the Church, signified by the vessels, may praise, preach, and bless God in a clear and harmonious voice. For unless vessels signified saints, the Apostle would not be called a vessel of election.

What is the bronze grating but Gospel preaching? Why it is called bronze has often already been stated: the very clear sound of this bell filled the whole world.

[Note: [Col. 0329D] The edition is purged of errors from both the Laurentian and Cassinese codices.]

It is rightly commanded to be made in the form of a cross because it is drawn by fishermen. For of it the Lord says to the apostles: “Cast the net on the right side of the boat, and you will find; therefore they cast it, and enclosed a great multitude of fish” (John 21:6). [Col. 0330B] Because Gospel preaching catches and holds every kind of people as in a net, the Gospel says: “The kingdom of heaven is like a dragnet cast into the sea, gathering fish of every kind” (Matt. 13:47).

The four bronze rings placed at the four corners of the grating signify either the four Evangelists or the four principal virtues. Without these the grating—that is, Gospel preaching—cannot gather and hold in itself everyone who is in the Church; it holds that part of the Church which does not refuse obedience to Gospel preaching. The middle of the altar signifies only the portion of the good.

“You shall also make two bars for the altar from setim wood; you shall cover them with bronze plates and insert them through rings, [Col. 0330C] and they shall be on both sides of the altar for carrying it.” What this signifies has been sufficiently explained above. For it has been stated what bars, setim wood, bronze plates, and rings signify; and we think it superfluous to say the same thing repeatedly.

It follows: “You shall make it not solid, but hollow and empty within, as was shown you on the mountain.” According to the letter, this altar was made not solid but hollow and empty so that it could be carried more easily. According to its meaning, however, it is hollow and concave in order that it may receive and contain within itself God’s treasures.

But what is the reason that the whole tabernacle, with its boards and columns, is made of silver, while the altar, which seems worthier and more excellent, is built of [Col. 0330D] bronze? It is that divine Scripture judges each thing precious or cheap not according to its material,

[Note: [Col. 0330D] From the Laurentian codex the text of the edition is here rendered more correct and complete.]

but according to what it signifies of God. Bronze, in itself, is indeed cheaper than gold; but according to its signification it is more precious. For wisdom, if kept hidden in the heart, is gold; but if it is brought forth from the heart to the ears of hearers, it is bronze. Therefore, by as much as holy preaching is better than hidden wisdom, by so much, according to its signification, bronze is better than gold. Hence the saying: “Hidden wisdom and concealed treasure: what profit is there in either?” (Ecclus. 20:32).

This altar is therefore rightly made [Col. 0331A] of bronze, because it belongs chiefly to ministers of the altar to preach. Everyone is permitted to possess both gold and wisdom; but not everyone is permitted to touch the altar and preach in the Church. Let this suffice concerning the altar; now let us come to the court of the tabernacle.

> “You shall also make the court of the tabernacle: on its south side, facing noon, there shall be hangings of fine twisted linen; one side shall extend one hundred cubits in length, with twenty pillars and as many bronze bases, whose capitals and their fillets shall be of silver.”

There is indeed a great difference between the court and the tabernacle. For the tabernacle is woven of blue, purple, twice-dyed scarlet, and fine linen; but the hangings of the court are made of fine twisted linen alone [Col. 0331B]. Moreover, in the tabernacle the pillars, boards, and other things were of gold and silver; but in the other, almost everything was made of bronze. What, then, do we understand by the court? For the tabernacle and the court signify, in a certain manner, different things. The tabernacle, as I suppose, chiefly denotes the primitive Church, which from Christ’s Passion until the time of Emperor Constantine was constructed, for the most part, out of holy martyrs. From that time until the coming of Antichrist, however, the whole Church is called the court of this tabernacle. Hence, in an unusual way, the court of the tabernacle is much larger than the tabernacle itself. Therefore the court of the tabernacle is the Church of confessors, which from the time of the aforesaid ruler [Col. 0331C] has spread among all nations.

Its hangings are made of fine twisted linen because it is sufficient for us to mortify and discipline the flesh and preserve the brightness and purity of mind and body. For no one is clothed in scarlet; no one is now made bloody by bloodshed. It is now sufficient to be washed in baptism, clothed in linen, and wear white garments, according to the saying: “Let your garments be white at all times” (Eccles. IX.8). The hangings on the south side were one hundred cubits long; likewise, on the north there were hangings of the same number of cubits, for that was the total length of the court. But why is it said to have been one hundred cubits long? Ten, one hundred, and one thousand are perfect numbers: they may indeed be repeated, but they cannot be increased beyond themselves. For if [Col. 0331D] you count up to ten, unless you begin again from the beginning, you have nothing further to say; and the same is true of one hundred and one thousand. Thus to say “one hundred cubits” is the same as saying “many cubits”: the finite is put for the infinite. The court extends one hundred cubits in length because its length will be as great as the duration of this life; for the court and the world will have one boundary.

There are twenty pillars on one side of the court and twenty on the other, so that all who are in the court may, on both sides, see, read, and understand the Law in its twofold sense. For the Law is doubled when it is understood both literally and spiritually. Since there are ten words of the Law, the whole Law is very often signified by ten. Therefore, because ten and ten make twenty, we find the Law understood in two ways in twenty [Col. 0332A]. Let the Jews, then, read twice ten, that they may understand the whole Decalogue once; otherwise they will not know what the twenty pillars signify. What the twenty pillars on one side signify, the twenty on the other side signify also. Let the south believe, if it will not believe the north; indeed, let it believe both, because both say the same thing, so that every word may stand in the midst of two or three witnesses. That the pillars had bronze bases—what this signifies has often already been said.
