They had silver capitals with their fillets because they not only spoke, but spoke truthfully and purely; they attended not merely to the sound of the letter, but to spiritual understanding and purity of expression. For sound is understood in bronze, but purity of speech in silver [Col. 0332B]. Let no one wonder that the pillars speak: we have said that the Law is signified by pillars; begin to read it, and you will discover how it speaks.

> “In the breadth of the court, which faces west, there shall be hangings for fifty cubits, with ten pillars and as many bases.”

Let us measure as far as fifty, and go no farther; there let us stand, there let us remain, if we wish both to possess freedom and to recover our lost inheritance. For the fiftieth year is called the jubilee, in which, by command of the Law, freedom was restored to slaves and a lost inheritance to its proper owners; and that entire year was kept by all in joy and festive jubilation. Rightly, therefore, Holy Church reaches this number by extending herself [Col. 0332C], and, having so extended herself, remains there: rejoicing in freedom, exulting in inheritance, resting from every servile and evil work, she appoints a solemn day “in dense array, even to the horn of the altar.” The ten pillars with their bases signify the ten words of the Law. Thus the court has the Law and commandments on every side, that it may learn wisdom, fear to sin, and know what it ought to believe. For the whole court is supported, as it were by pillars, by these ten commandments of the Law. Since these commandments are at times represented by doubled pillars, they signify that they ought to be understood in two ways; and ten signifies nothing other than twenty, except that twenty in some fashion expounds ten. For whenever we double the Decalogue, we signify a double understanding.

[Col. 0332D]

> “Also, on that breadth of the court which faces east, there shall be fifty cubits; of these, hangings of fifteen cubits shall be assigned to one side, with three pillars and as many bases.”

It has already been said what the fifty cubits signify. It remains, therefore, to say what these two hangings signify, which are placed on either side at the entrance of the tabernacle. These two hangings are the two peoples, namely Jews and Gentiles; for from these two the court of the tabernacle is filled. They are the two walls joined in the building of the Church by the one cornerstone. Hence the Apostle says: “For he is our peace, who made both one” (Eph. II.14). Each hanging is fifteen cubits long, for there are that many Gradual Psalms. This number consists of an even and an odd number, namely seven and eight; hence it is written: “Give a portion to seven, and also to eight.” Seven denotes this life, which revolves in seven days; but eight denotes that other blessed and immortal life which will begin on the eighth day when all rise again. For on that day the resurrection of all will occur, on which Christ the Lord rose. You give a portion to seven when you render the dues of this life; you give a portion also to eight when you bestow the proper dues upon the other life as well. When you eat and drink, you give a portion to seven; but if you fast and keep vigil, you give a portion to eight. If you labor for your livelihood, you give a portion to seven; but if from your rightful and personal labors you give alms, you give a portion to eight. Rightly, therefore, the hangings before the court [Col. 0333B] of the tabernacle are made fifteen cubits long, so that all who come there, seeing both seven and eight, may understand from the very number of the cubits and the very dimensions of the hangings how they ought to live in this life. Let them give a portion to seven and a portion to eight, and thus pass through temporal goods without losing eternal ones.

The three pillars set on each side—that is, the six pillars which were in the two hangings—signify the same thing that, when speaking of it, we said the six boards at the entrance of the tabernacle signify: namely, the six books of the New Testament. Rightly, indeed, the New Testament is placed at the front both in the tabernacle and in the court of the tabernacle, because through it one enters the Church. For just as all the aforementioned pillars signify the Old Testament [Col. 0333C], so all those placed here, whether at the sides of the court or at the entrance itself, denote the New Testament, concerning which there follows:

**101**

> “At the entrance of the court there shall be a hanging of twenty cubits, of blue, purple, twice-dyed scarlet, and fine twisted linen, worked in embroidery. It shall have four pillars with as many bases.”

The very material indicates what we should understand by this hanging; for nowhere else in the whole court is blue, purple, or scarlet used. Therefore this hanging, placed at the entrance of the court, and that placed at the entrance of the tabernacle signify the same thing; the exposition of the latter can therefore suffice for this. The choir of apostles is signified, who guard the gates of the Church, hold the keys, open and shut, bind and loose, and first lead souls to faith and then the souls of the faithful into the heavenly kingdoms [Col. 0333D]. The hanging has four pillars and as many bases, through which the four Gospels with their writers are understood. For what else are the apostles but the four Gospels? They preached, that is, their Master’s teaching. Even their bases—the Gospel writers themselves—were with them, came from them, and lived among them. That this hanging is said to be twenty cubits long means that the holy apostles, expounding the entire Old Testament in two ways, literally and spiritually, made it agree and harmonize with the four Gospels. For the pillars of the four Gospels cannot otherwise sustain this hanging [Col. 0334A] unless the meaning of both Testaments agrees.

All the pillars of the court round about were covered with plates, and had silver capitals and bronze bases. In the bronze plates and bases are displayed the voice and sound of preaching; in the silver capitals, purity of expression and truthfulness of speech. This has been sufficiently explained above. Yet by the bases of the pillars we may understand the holy preachers, who, bearing the books and precepts of both Testaments as though they were pillars, filled the world with the clear sound and utterance of preaching. It follows:

> “The court shall occupy one hundred cubits in length and fifty in breadth; its height shall be five cubits.”

This too has been explained. For in repeatedly commanding the bases to be made of bronze, he seems to fashion bells for the Church—not bells that tinkle, certainly, but bells that speak rationally and summon peoples to faith in Christ. The height of this court was five cubits, by which the five books of Moses may be signified; when rightly understood, they raise the whole Church upward and toward heavenly things.

> “You shall make all the vessels of the tabernacle for every use and ceremony, both its pegs and those of the court, of bronze.”

Everything is made of bronze, that all together may praise, preach, and bless God in a loud and harmonious voice. It follows:

> “Command the children of Israel to bring you the purest oil from olive trees, beaten with a pestle [Col. 0334C], so that a lamp may burn continually in the tabernacle of testimony, outside the veil which hangs before the testimony. Aaron and his sons shall set it in place, and it shall shine before the Lord until morning. This shall be a perpetual observance through their generations among the children of Israel.”

Oil is brought by the children of Israel when a man full of the grace of the Holy Spirit, compassion, and mercy is chosen by the whole people. It is taken from olive trees—that is, from the teaching and assembly of the saints—so that he may love peace and imitate the sweetness and savor of the holy Fathers. Let him be pure in life and morals, indeed most pure and, as the Apostle says, irreproachable. Let him also be beaten with a pestle: not delicate, not idle, but proven by patience amid tribulations and injuries. Such a man is chosen [Col. 0334D] so that the lamp may always burn in the tabernacle of testimony: that the tabernacle may never be without a lamp, never without light, and the people never without a bishop and teacher. For he is the lamp; let him also be full of oil, filled with mercy and compassion.

This lamp must burn outside the veil, that people may see it, that it may enlighten all and, according to the Gospel, shine upon all who are in the house. But outside which veil? Outside that veil which hangs before the testimony, which closes off the testimony and conceals from us the divine mysteries. Those who, overshadowed by a veil, are unable to shine are shut behind this veil. Aaron and his sons set this lamp in place: those who hold the office of the first priest and of his successors appoint, consecrate, and establish it. The lamp is chosen by the people and presented to the bishops; it is consecrated, ordained, and placed in its seat by bishops [Col. 0335A]. Let it shine before the Lord until morning; and until he departs from this wretched and dark life, let him not cease to preach to and enlighten God’s people, so that, when this night has ended, the sun of righteousness may rise for him and he may enter that day of which the Psalmist says: “For one day in your courts is better than thousands” (Ps. LXXXIII.10). This observance shall be perpetual among all generations of the children of Israel; and this rule concerning the lamp of the tabernacle and the choosing of a bishop must always be kept.

## CHAPTER XXVIII

> “Bring near to yourself Aaron your brother with his sons [Col. 0335B] from among the children of Israel, that they may serve me in the priesthood: Aaron, Nadab and Abihu, Eleazar and Ithamar. You shall make holy garments for Aaron your brother, for glory and beauty. And you shall speak to all who are wise of heart, whom I have filled with the spirit of prudence, that they may make the garments of Aaron, in which, being sanctified, he may minister to me.”

“Make,” he says, “a holy garment woven with virtues and holiness, fashioned with wisdom and holiness for glory and beauty.” For whoever is clothed in this garment is clothed in glory and beauty. Hence it is said of the Savior: “The Lord has reigned; he has put on beauty; the Lord has put on strength and girded himself with power” (Ps. XCII.1). Those wise and understanding men make this garment, to whom the Lord himself says: “I will give you a mouth and wisdom, which none of your adversaries will be able to resist or contradict” (Luke XXI.15). The holy apostles made this garment, teaching us by their words how we ought to be clothed and adorned [Note: [Col. 0335D] The edition is corrected from the Cassinese codex.], so that we may appear worthy to minister to God. It was not human wisdom, however, but the Holy Spirit who had filled them, that taught them. In these garments Aaron, being sanctified, is to minister to the Lord; unless clothed in them and first sanctified, he is not to minister to the Lord. To you, O bishops; to you, O ministers of the Church, these things are said: you are Aaron, you are sanctified, and you may put on these garments and enter the Holy of Holies.

> “These are the garments which they shall make: the breastpiece, the ephod, the close-fitting linen tunic, the turban, and the belt. They shall make holy garments for Aaron your brother and his sons, that they may serve me in the priesthood.”

We shall expound these separately below. It should be noted, however, that the Lord commands holy garments to be made not only for Aaron but also for his sons. For not only bishops, but also their sons—that is, priests of a lower order—ought to be clothed in holy garments. For they too minister to the Lord, approach the altar, touch the sacraments, and exercise the priesthood.

> “They shall receive gold, blue, purple, twice-dyed scarlet, and fine linen.”

We have said above that these signify either the four elements according to Josephus—earth, water, fire, and air—or the four principal virtues: prudence, justice, fortitude, and temperance [Col. 0336A]. It has often been said that gold stands for wisdom. We have explained why each of these things signifies what it does. A bishop ought to wear gold in his garments, so that he may shine altogether with wisdom and knowledge. Let him also bear blue and always meditate upon and contemplate heavenly things; let him bear purple as an observer of justice; let him bear scarlet, that he may never forget love; let him bear linen, that he may be white in chastity and possess moderation and discernment in all things.

The bishop also bears blue in another sense, praying to God for favorable conditions of air and sky; he bears purple, supplicating concerning floods of water; he bears scarlet, entreating against excessive drought and the heat of the sun; and he bears linen when, by his prayers, he turns the barrenness of the earth into fruitfulness. It follows:

> “They shall make the ephod of gold, blue and purple, twice-dyed scarlet, and fine twisted linen, in embroidered work.”

Concerning this ephod the Savior says to his disciples: “Take my yoke upon yourselves, and learn from me, because I am meek and humble of heart. For my yoke is sweet and my burden light” (Matt. XI.30). For where, except upon the shoulders, is a yoke or burden carried? Let us therefore put on the ephod, that we may have strong shoulders for bearing burdens [Col. 0336C]. That bishop has no ephod who does not gladly carry the burdens he has undertaken; on the contrary, that bishop has an ephod of whom it is said: “Like a shepherd he shall feed his flock; he shall gather the lambs in his arm, carry them in his bosom, and himself bear those with young” (Isa. XL.11). Therefore let the bishop have an ephod and never forget the burden he has assumed. Let him lift up weak and weary sheep, lay them upon his shoulders, and bring them back to pasture, that he may confidently say: “I have become like a beast of burden before you, and I am always with you” (Ps. LXXI.23).

This ephod is made of gold, blue, purple, twice-dyed scarlet, and fine twisted linen, because the bishop cannot bear the burden of the office laid upon him except through wisdom, signified by gold; heavenly contemplation, signified by blue; royal and kingly authority, signified by purple [Col. 0336D]; strong love of God and neighbor, figured in twice-dyed scarlet; and purity and chastity of mind and body, signified by linen. But if the bishop is distinguished by these colors and virtues, he will be able, with God’s help, to carry the burden. For the bishop carries a greater burden in proportion as there are more persons for whom he will render an account. Hence the Apostle says: “Obey your rulers and be subject to them, for they keep watch over you as those who will render an account for your souls” (Heb. XIII.17).

Look, then, O bishop, at the burden you carry; look at the ephod. You see gold there: devote effort and zeal to wisdom. You see blue: look upon heaven and contemplate heaven. You see purple: preserve justice. You see twice-dyed scarlet: if necessary, let the blood of martyrdom dye you for love of God and neighbor. You see fine twisted linen: subdue, discipline, and afflict the flesh, that it may serve the spirit and become ever whiter and purer [Col. 0337A]. The ephod is made in embroidered work and varied with many colors, so that by its outward beauty the bishop may more easily understand what he ought to be inwardly; for all his glory is from within.

**103**

> “It shall have two joined edges at the tops of both sides, so that they may come together as one.”

The ephod was long enough to extend over both shoulders of the high priest; it had, however, a short and moderate breadth. Its upper and lower edge were joined together at the tops on both sides, so that one continuous edge was formed from the two. For when the two borders met each other at the tops on either side, they were joined together so skillfully that one seemed to be made from two. What else, then, do we think is signified by this, except that our whole life should be so continued in good works that the end accords with the beginning, and that we do not abandon before the end the good we have begun? The two edges come together as one when the first and last stages of our life meet in perseverance in good. It follows:

[Col. 0337C]

> “Its woven work and all the variety of its workmanship shall be of gold, blue, purple, twice-dyed scarlet, and fine twisted linen.”

The outward garment displays inward glory, and the ephod itself shows what kind of shoulders it presses upon. Gold signifies wisdom; blue, heavenly and angelic life; purple, royal authority; twice-dyed scarlet, love of God and neighbor; and fine twisted linen, chastity and mortification of the body. Let the bishop bear these things, be adorned by them, and shine through them; without this variety he must not approach God’s altar.

> “You shall take two onyx stones and engrave upon them the names of the children of Israel: six names upon one stone and the other six upon the other, according to the order of their birth. With the work of an engraver and the carving of a gem-cutter you shall engrave them with the names of the children of Israel, enclosed in gold and set around; and you shall place them on both sides of the ephod, as a memorial of the children of Israel. Aaron shall bear their names before the Lord upon both shoulders for remembrance.”

Take, he says, two onyx stones, which are both beautiful in appearance and sufficiently durable to retain writing, and larger than other such stones can be found; and engrave upon them the names of the children of Israel. Names are written for this purpose: that they may not be consigned to forgetfulness and that readers may be instructed. Therefore the bishop should always remember the ancient Fathers and recall how they lived and served God; let him imitate [Col. 0338A] their life, follow their teaching, and hold fast to their works. The twelve sons of Israel are the twelve sons of Christ. Bishops ought always to keep in their minds the names and remembrance of these men, and imitate their character, teaching, and life; therefore it is said here that Aaron is to bear them for remembrance.

How shall he bear them before the Lord? Surely so that the Lord may be moved to mercy through their intercession. The bishop should not go without them; let him carry them with him, have them as intercessors, and say: “Have mercy, O God; have mercy on your people, that the one who does not trust in his own merits may be delivered through the intercessions of your apostles.” These stones containing the names of the saints are enclosed and surrounded by gold, because God’s saints shine with the light of every wisdom and knowledge.

[Col. 0338B]

> “You shall also make the breastpiece of judgment in embroidered work, according to the weaving of the ephod: of gold, blue, purple, twice-twisted scarlet, and fine twisted linen. It shall be square and doubled, a span in length and a span in breadth.”

What the breastpiece signifies may be understood from its very name and from the place where it is put. It is placed upon the breast of the high priest to guard the treasure of the heart and the repository of wisdom. Unless the Psalmist had this breastpiece upon his breast, he could never have said: “I have hidden your words in my heart, that I may not sin against you” (Ps. CXVIII.11). Where the breastpiece is, there also are reason, wisdom, and knowledge; for this is what the breastpiece signifies. Therefore where these things are not in the breast and heart, the breastpiece ought not to be placed; for if it is placed there, it is useless, like a seal guarding nothing [Col. 0338C].

It is called the breastpiece of judgment, that the one who uses it may judge reasonably, judging nothing rashly, carelessly, or disorderly. This breastpiece is made in embroidered work and set off by beautiful variety, so that the breast may be adorned with many virtues and all may be governed in one harmony and concord. The breastpiece has the same weaving that we said the ephod has. Thus it too is made of gold, blue, purple, twice-dyed scarlet, and fine twisted linen, so that the same radiance of virtues may shine in the heart through knowledge and upon the shoulders through action. For the bishop ought both to do what he understands and understand what he does. Hence, as will be shown below, the breastpiece and ephod are joined to one another. Both are of one and the same weaving when teaching and action agree.

The breastpiece is square because it is completed by four virtues, as by four corners: prudence on this side, justice on that; fortitude on this side, temperance on that. These adorn both the breastpiece and the bishop’s breast. Blue, purple, scarlet, and linen signify these four virtues. It is also doubled, on account of the active and contemplative life, or on account of the twofold understanding of the holy Scriptures. A bishop who does not possess this doubleness cannot govern the people entrusted to him as he ought. It measures a span in length and breadth [Col. 0339A], both that it may cover the extent of the breast and that it may be enclosed in God’s palm and hand, according to the saying: “The king’s heart is in God’s hand” (Prov. XXI.1); and the Psalm: “Into your hands I commend my spirit” (Ps. XXX.6).

**104**

> “You shall set in it four rows of stones. In the first row shall be a sardius, topaz, and emerald; in the second, carbuncle, sapphire, and jasper; in the third, ligure, agate, and amethyst; in the fourth, chrysolite, onyx, and beryl. They shall be set in gold according to their rows and shall bear the names of the children of Israel. Each stone shall be engraved with one of the twelve names, according to the twelve tribes.”

There are twelve stones because there are twelve patriarchs and as many apostles, from whom the remaining multitude of faith and religion derives its origin [Col. 0339B]. They are rightly called precious stones, because in the building of the Church they shine before all others in both wisdom and holiness. These stones are placed in the high priest’s breastpiece so that his heart and breast may always be enlightened by the teaching, faith, character, virtues, and examples of patriarchs and apostles, and so that the bishop, always seeing and reading their names, may seek their manner of life, embrace their life, and follow their faith.

Three stones are placed in each of four rows because faith in the Trinity was spread through the four Gospels by the apostles’ ministry. Although individual names are engraved upon individual stones, each person is nevertheless adorned not merely by individual stones but by all of them. For each imitates the color, splendor, and beauty of all. All seem red through martyrdom, green through faith, aflame through love, bright through heavenly contemplation, white through chastity, and black through repentance [Col. 0339C]. In short, there is nothing in colors, character, splendors, virtue, wisdom, or beauty that cannot be found in the holy apostles.

> “You shall make on the breastpiece chains of purest gold, linked to one another, and two golden rings, which you shall place on each upper end of the breastpiece. You shall join the golden chains to the rings at its edges, and fasten the ends of the chains to two hooks on each side of the ephod, facing the breastpiece. You shall also make two golden rings, which you shall place at the lower ends of the breastpiece, on the edges opposite the ephod and facing its back; likewise two other golden rings, to be placed on each side of the ephod below, facing the front of the lower joining, so that it may be fitted to the breastpiece. The breastpiece shall be bound to its rings and to the rings of the ephod by a blue cord, so that the made joining may remain and the breastpiece and ephod may not be separated from one another.”

Understand the literal arrangement of all this as follows. The breastpiece had two rings at its two upper ends, to which two corresponding rings of the ephod were attached; two small chains were joined to the two rings of the breastpiece. In addition, there were two other rings below on either side of the ephod [Col. 0340A], through which a blue cord was drawn. This cord held two further rings of the breastpiece, and thus bound the breastpiece and ephod reciprocally to each other so that they could not be separated.

What the breastpiece and ephod signify has been stated. Let us say what it signifies that they are thus joined so that they cannot be separated from one another. The breastpiece and ephod are joined when a bishop’s preaching and action agree well together. For teaching and preaching are signified by the breastpiece, while burden and action are signified by the ephod. If a bishop teaches well but acts badly, or, conversely, acts well but teaches badly, his ephod and breastpiece are not joined.

Concerning those who teach well and act badly, Truth itself says: “The scribes and Pharisees sit on Moses’ seat; therefore observe and do whatever they tell you, but do not act according to their works. For they say and do not do; they bind heavy and unbearable burdens and lay them upon the shoulders of men, but they themselves will not move them with their finger” (Matt. XXIII.2). Such men had the breastpiece but not the ephod; for if they had had the ephod, they would not merely touch other people’s works with a finger but would carry them upon their own shoulders.

We read that very many heretics acted well but taught badly. Fasting, keeping vigils, giving alms, and similar things are good works. We have heard that bishops of the Manichaeans, Arians, and Donatists did these things [Col. 0340C]; but because they taught wrongly and preached error, although by doing such things they seemed to make an ephod, they had no breastpiece at all. For if they had had a breastpiece, they would not have preached irrational—that is, false and erroneous—things. Therefore he bears the ephod and breastpiece mutually joined and bound together who both acts well and teaches well.

But what are we to understand by the rings, small chains, and blue cord by which they join the breastpiece, except hope and love, wisdom and the other virtues? Those who possess these cannot cease from the doctrine and practice of truth. By these, as by certain fastenings, preaching and action are joined together; they follow one another and harmoniously render mutual service [Col. 0340D]. It follows:

> “Aaron shall bear the names of the children of Israel in the breastpiece of judgment upon his breast, when he enters the sanctuary, as a perpetual memorial before the Lord.”

The names, conduct, life, and memory of the saints should always be in the high priest’s breast and heart, that by their judgment, teaching, and example he may teach and do everything. Let him also have the names of the whole people written in his heart, that, always remembering all, he may intercede with God for all.

**105**

> “You shall put in the breastpiece of judgment doctrine and truth, which were upon Aaron’s breast when he entered before the Lord; and he shall bear the judgment of the children of Israel upon his breast before the Lord always.”

Let bishops hear this and attend to it most carefully [Col. 0341A]. Let them consider what it signifies that doctrine and truth are placed upon Aaron’s breast. That bishop has no breastpiece on his breast—indeed, has neither heart nor breast—in whose heart there is no doctrine and truth. For what will he teach without doctrine? What will he judge without truth? It is called the breastpiece of judgment so that doctrine may be in the breastpiece and truth in judgment.

Therefore let the bishop always look upon his breastpiece, always upon his own breast. This book—the entire Law of both Testaments—is sufficient there. He has knowledge in his breast, provided that he understands what he has in his breast. But how could the breast fail to understand what is in the breast? How could that heart fail to see what presses upon it with its weight? The breastpiece is placed so near, directly over the heart, that the heart may easily understand what it intends and signifies. The breastpiece stands over the heart like a teacher over a disciple; it cries aloud with wondrous voice, if only there is someone to hear. It admonishes the eyes of the heart, asks that they be turned toward it, that they look and read, read and understand what gold, blue, purple, scarlet, and linen signify; what the twelve stones signify; what the names inscribed upon them signify; and what doctrine and truth signify. If the bishop understands this, there is nothing belonging to his office that he does not understand. This is what that Wise Man signified when he said: “For in the robe that reached to his feet was the whole world, and the great deeds of the fathers were engraved in four rows of stones” (Wis. XVIII.24). It follows:

“Make also the robe of the ephod wholly of violet-blue, in the midst of which above there shall be an opening for the head, and [Col. 0341C] a woven border all around its edge, such as is usually made at the extremities of garments, so that it may not easily be torn.” Since the ephod was placed over this robe, it is called the robe of the ephod. The high priest was wholly covered by it, and therefore it had an opening near the neck, by which the head too might be covered. By it, moreover, we understand the holy and pure conduct of a bishop: he is to be so wholly clothed in a holy life and excellent conduct that nothing bare, unbecoming, or unadorned may appear in him. Hence the whole robe is said to have been violet-blue: when the high priest was clothed in it, he was thought to be not earth but heaven, not man but God. For violet-blue, as we have often said, signifies heaven because it is of an airy colour. The Apostle was clothed in this garment when he said: “Our citizenship is in heaven” (Phil. III.20). He said this while still living on earth; but because he lived a heavenly and angelic life, he rejoiced that, clothed in violet-blue garments, he was already in heaven. Hence the apostles are also called the heavens, because they are clothed in such garments. This robe has an opening for the head, so that, covering the entire head, it may not permit sight and hearing, taste and smell—the faculties contained in it—to roam through unlawful and harmful things. It also has a woven border all around, such as is customarily made at the extremities of garments, so that it may not easily be torn. By this is understood perseverance in good works, concerning which it is written:

“He who perseveres to the end shall be saved” [Col. 0342A] (Matt. X.22). For then the robe—that is, holy conduct—is interrupted when a person is separated from the work he began by any occasion whatever.

“But at the lower edge, around the feet of the same robe, you shall make, all around, things like pomegranates of violet-blue, purple, twice-dyed scarlet, and twisted linen, with bells interspersed among them, so that there shall be a golden bell and a pomegranate, and again another golden bell and a pomegranate.” Pomegranates are full of bright and sweet grains arranged in regular order. By them we may understand the Church of the saints and congregations established throughout the whole world, in which Christ’s faithful are kept united in harmony, peace, and love. By the bell, however, evangelical preaching [Col. 0342B] is understood; hence the bells are said to be golden. Gospel preaching shines with the light of wisdom. The pomegranates are made of violet-blue, purple, twice-dyed scarlet, and twisted linen, because gatherings of saints are built from human beings and virtues alone. For we have often already said that by these four colours are understood either the four elements of which man consists or the four principal virtues. They are placed among the pomegranates beside the bells, so that no church may lack either a preacher or preaching. For then the bells ring among the pomegranates when, in the assembly of the faithful and amid the churches, the voices of preachers and teachers are heard. It follows:

[Col. 0342C] “And Aaron shall wear it while performing the ministry, so that its sound may be heard when he enters and leaves the sanctuary in the presence of the Lord.” High priests, therefore, must cry out without interruption; they must always preach, make the bells of their voices sound, and call the people to faith, baptism, and repentance. Whether they enter the sanctuary or leave it, they ought to do this; for as long as they are in the church and see the people around them—for the people are the sanctuary—they ought continually to cause words of edification to resound and be instilled in their ears. Although it is good to do this everywhere, it ought especially to be done where God’s people customarily come to receive the sacraments. If a bishop does this, he shall not die; [Col. 0342D] but if he does not, he shall die. What does “he shall die” mean? This does not appear to refer to the common death, for all of us shall die. It must therefore be understood of another death, from which may almighty God deign to rescue and deliver us. It follows:

“You shall also make a plate of the purest gold, on which you shall engrave, with the work of an engraver: Holy to the Lord. And you shall bind it with a violet-blue band, and it shall be upon the tiara, hanging over the high priest’s forehead.” Do you wish to recognize the high priest? Look upon his forehead and read the inscription; read: “Holy to the Lord.” Thus the high priest’s forehead is inscribed. Great indeed is the reverence due to that house which bears such an inscription. Yet this title is written only upon gold, and upon the purest gold. What is gold? Wisdom; for this has already been stated above. [Col. 0343A] But since not every wisdom is pure—for the wisdom of the world is foolishness before God—therefore “Holy to the Lord” is written upon the purest gold. Let wisdom therefore shine upon the high priest’s forehead: that wisdom which he who is true Wisdom promises to his disciples, saying, “I will give you a mouth and wisdom which none of your adversaries shall be able to resist or contradict” (Luke XXI.15). Those who do not have this golden plate lack a great ornament indeed. This plate is bound with a violet-blue band, by which we understand a holy and heavenly life and contemplation of God. Divine wisdom cannot be held without this violet-blue band, for it is written: “Wisdom shall not enter into a malevolent soul” (Wis. I.18). [Col. 0343B] This plate was upon the tiara because wisdom is superior to all ornaments in a high priest and shines more brightly: it is to be sought first; it is to be regarded. Though he may have the other ornaments, if he does not have wisdom, there is nothing in him upon which “Holy to the Lord” may be written. For this is the high priest’s name; whoever is not marked by this title is not a high priest. This star hangs over the high priest’s forehead so that it may never be hidden, may be seen by all, may illuminate all, and may shine upon all who are in the house.

“And Aaron shall bear their iniquities, which the children of Israel shall have offered and sacrificed in all their gifts and offerings.” For if it is written of our Saviour: “Truly he himself bore our sins [Col. 0343C] and carried our iniquities [Note: [Col. 0343] Isa. LIII.4. The Vulgate reads: ‘Truly he himself bore our infirmities and carried our sorrows.’],” when the people offer gifts to priests for the removal of sins, what else do the priests bear in the gifts but the people’s sins? In their gifts, therefore, the people lay down the burdens of their sins; the priests, conversely, are burdened with sins. Let this then be the burden of the priests’ office: praying for sinners and worthily fulfilling their ministry, let them strive always to appease God’s indignation and wrath.

“The plate shall always be upon his forehead, so that the Lord may be propitious to them.” The high priest must always wear the golden plate, so that by its sight and presence the people may be enlightened. Let him bear the plate on his forehead, bear the lamp on his face, and always bear wisdom openly [Col. 0343D]; let him teach and preach, persist at all times, whether convenient or inconvenient, so that God may be propitious to him.

“You shall bind the tunic with linen, and make a linen tiara.” The tunic and tiara are woven of linen because holy conduct, and the glory and crown of the head, are preserved by purity and mortification of the flesh. Even though the bishop is clothed in the robe of good conduct, even though, having overcome vices, he is crowned with a linen tiara, nevertheless, unless by subduing the flesh and by chastity he binds both firmly, he can easily lose both tiara and tunic. Hence the Apostle says of himself: “Thus I fight, not as one beating the air; but I chastise my body and reduce it to slavery, lest perhaps, having preached to others, I myself should become reprobate” [Col. 0344A] (I Cor. IX.26). It follows:

“You shall also make a girdle with embroidery.” For the Lord says in the Gospel: “Let your loins be girded” (Luke XII.35). Whoever is girded is girded with a belt. The belt, moreover, is chastity. He is girded with a belt who binds his flesh with the girdle of chastity, lest, indulging lust, it wander loosely through unlawful things. The belt is made with embroidery because chastity makes a person light and agile for flight.

“Moreover, for Aaron’s sons you shall prepare linen tunics, and girdles, and tiaras for glory and honour; and you shall clothe Aaron your brother and his sons [Col. 0344B] with all these things, and consecrate the hands of them all and sanctify them, so that they may exercise the priesthood for me.” Linen tunics, which through much labour and frequent washing in water are brought to the brightness of whiteness, signify, as we have said above, mortification of the flesh and purity of chastity. Therefore tunics, girdles, and tiaras—which themselves were also of linen—seem to signify almost the same thing. In this one may most clearly understand how greatly chastity and bodily continence please the Lord. This is the glory and adornment of the high priest; with these the ministers of the Church ought to be clothed, adorned, and glorified. Their hands are consecrated so that they may apply themselves to good works and neither touch nor do what is evil and unclean [Col. 0344C].

“You shall also make linen breeches, to cover the flesh of their nakedness from the loins to the thighs; and Aaron and his sons shall use them when they enter the tabernacle of testimony or approach the altar to minister in the sanctuary, lest, guilty of iniquity, they die. It shall be an everlasting ordinance for Aaron and his offspring after him. You shall do this also, that they may be consecrated to me in the priesthood.” Behold, again the virtue of chastity is commended in the breeches. They are commanded to be made of linen because chastity is signified by linen. Those priests do not have breeches who do not cover the flesh of their nakedness, who neither restrain nor curb the shameful parts of the flesh, so that they may in any way feel their sexual members. [Col. 0344D] Therefore the breeches cover both the loins and the whole thigh, because the greater stimulation of the flesh is felt there. For if that part of the body is carefully guarded, there is no means by which bodily chastity may be corrupted. Therefore let ministers of the Church always have breeches, since they do not enter the tabernacle only at intervals, but are always in God’s temple; indeed, they themselves are God’s temple. Let them never subject themselves to fleshly pleasure; let them always have their loins girded, lest they die. Let this be for them an ordinance not temporary but everlasting; let them keep this law and never forget the breeches and chastity.

## CHAPTER XXIX

[Col. 0345A]

“Take a calf from the herd [Note: [Col. 0345D] From the same Laurentian manuscript the edition is corrected, which begins this chapter with words that are the end of the preceding chapter], two unblemished rams, unleavened loaves, and a cake without leaven, mixed with oil; likewise unleavened wafers anointed with oil. You shall make them all of wheaten flour and, having placed them in a basket, offer them: the calf, moreover, and the two rams.” This calf is understood to be Christ our Lord, because, deriving his origin according to the flesh from the herd of holy patriarchs and prophets, he was sacrificed for our sins. This is the fatted calf which that most kindly father ordered to be killed for joy at the return of his son. What we say is very well known. This calf and the two rams will be treated most fully below. By the unleavened loaves, the cake without leaven, and the unleavened wafer, we understand an incorrupt life, holy conduct, and the integrity of both the inner and outer person. They are all understood as unleavened so that they may not be in the leaven of malice, but in the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth. They are also anointed with oil, namely the grace of the Holy Spirit, by whose anointing all good things increase and are perfected. But since we shall speak more fully of all these things later, let us for the present be silent concerning them.

“And you shall bring Aaron and his sons to the entrance of the tabernacle of testimony. When you have washed the father with his sons in water, and when, being baptized, they are cleansed from all sins [Note: [Col. 0346D] In the manuscript of the Library of Monte Amiata and in the Vulgate the words ‘and when, being baptized, they are cleansed from all sins’ are absent], you shall clothe Aaron in his [Col. 0345C] garments,” so that, having put off “the old man with his deeds, he may put on the new man, who is created according to God in righteousness and holiness of truth” (Eph. IV.22). What the garments are with which he ought to be clothed follows in the enumeration: “That is, the linen garment, the tunic, the ephod, and the breastpiece, which you shall bind with the girdle; and you shall place the tiara upon his head, and the holy plate upon the tiara, and pour the oil of anointing upon his head, and by this rite he shall be consecrated.” Clothe him, he says, in the linen of chastity, the tunic of holy conduct, and the ephod of good works; to these let the breastpiece of teaching, truth, and every wisdom be inseparably joined. Hence both are commanded to be bound with a girdle. “And you shall place the tiara,” that is, the crown of victory, on his head, [Col. 0345D] so that the strength of which he is capable may be recognized. “And the holy plate upon the tiara,” so that the flash of wisdom may shine on his forehead. “And you shall pour the oil of anointing upon his head,” so that, wholly anointed with the grace of the Holy Spirit and sanctified in mind and body, he may be able to appear worthy before God. Since these things have already been explained above, we pass over them briefly.

You shall also bring forward his sons and clothe them in linen tunics: “You shall gird Aaron, that is, him and his children, with a girdle, and place mitres upon them; and they shall be my priests in an everlasting religious observance.” We have often already said [Col. 0346A] that linen signifies purity and cleanness of the flesh, because there is no garment so often washed, so often immersed in water, and brought to whiteness and its own cleanliness. Therefore not only Aaron but also his sons are commanded to be clothed in linen tunics, because all who minister to God ought both to be adorned with virtue and bound with the girdle of chastity. Thus the Lord says in the Gospel: “Let your loins be girded” (Luke XII.35). For the sacramental signification of this, he also commands that mitres be placed upon them, because mitres too are made of linen. The same thing, therefore, is signified by linen tunics, girdles, and mitres. He who is clothed in the garment of chastity is rightly girded as a man and crowned as a victor. These, then, are God’s priests, preserving an everlasting religious observance.

“After you have consecrated their hands, you shall bring the calf before the tabernacle of testimony.” Since the tabernacle has been made, the altar built, the priestly garments prepared, and the priests clothed, it now remains in due order to speak of sacrifice. Therefore let it be said: After you have initiated and consecrated their hands, so that they may be clean and worthy to touch God’s sacrifice, you shall also bring the calf before the tabernacle of testimony. This calf, as we have said above, is Christ. Moses, however, sometimes signifies Christ; at other times he stands for the whole people of the Jews, because, as leader and prince of all, he bore within himself the counsels of all. [Col. 0346C] Thus Moses—that is, the Jewish people—brought forward the calf before the tabernacle of testimony when, after giving thirty pieces of silver, the Jews seized Christ and led him to the high priests; since he was judged and condemned by their judgment, the following is added:

“And Aaron and his sons shall lay their hands upon its head, and you shall slaughter it before the Lord, by the entrance of the tabernacle of testimony.” For whom do Aaron and his sons signify except Annas and Caiaphas, and the priests, Levites, scribes, and Pharisees? They laid their hands upon the calf’s head because they did not fear to lay hands upon Christ the Lord, crying and saying: “According to the law he ought to die, because he made himself the Son of God” (John XIX.7). Hence the Apostle also says: “The head of Christ [Col. 0346D] is God” (I Cor. XI.4). Therefore they lay hands upon Christ’s head who both deny that he is God and endeavour to suppress his divinity. They slaughtered him before the Lord because the Lord was always personally present at his death. This was by the entrance of the tabernacle of testimony because, although he suffered outside the city gate, he was nevertheless judged and condemned in the city and near the temple.

“And, having taken some of the calf’s blood, you shall put it with your finger upon the horn of the altar.” What does the altar signify but the cross? And what do the horns of the altar signify but the horns of the cross? The calf’s blood was therefore placed upon the altar’s horns because Christ’s blood, flowing from his fingers and hands, made the horns of the cross bloody. You shall pour the remaining blood at its base; the base of this altar signifies that part of the cross which was fixed in the earth. The remaining blood is therefore poured at the base of the altar because all that blood of Christ which dripped from his feet and flowed from his side reached the base of the cross as it ran down. It follows:

“You shall also take all the fat which covers the entrails, the lobe of the liver, the two kidneys, and the fat upon them, and offer it as incense upon the altar.” What are the entrails, the fat, and those things adhering to the heart—which lie hidden, as it were invisible, in secret—but Christ’s love for us, and his mercy and compassion? [Col. 0347B] Christ our Lord offered these upon the altar of the cross, burning them as an odour of sweetness, when he prayed for his persecutors and said: “Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing” (Luke XXIII.34). The Psalmist also speaks of this, saying: “Let my soul be filled as with fatness and richness” (Ps. LXII.6). Again: “May the Lord remember your sacrifice, and may your burnt offering be made fat” (Ps. XIX.4). Again, the three youths in Daniel say: “As in a holocaust of rams and bulls, and as in thousands of fat lambs, so may our sacrifice be made” (Dan. III.40). Why is all fat commanded to be offered, and why is a fat burnt offering praised? Lean flesh without fat gives off no odour when roasted and provides no flavour when eaten. This fat, however, must be understood as belonging not to the body but to the spirit, not to the flesh but to the mind. The fatness of the soul is faith, hope, charity, and the gathering of all virtues. These give off a sweet fragrance; these please the Lord in every sacrifice; and without them no sacrifice is acceptable. With this fat were fattened those of whom it is said: “All the fat ones of the earth have eaten” [Col. 0347C] (Ps. XXI.30). Christ therefore offers his fat; he offers a joyful and rich burnt offering; he offers fragrance and the savour of sweetness. For he himself is the mountain of God, a rich and fertile mountain. The fragrance of this fat fills both heaven and earth. It follows:

“But you shall burn the calf’s flesh, its hide, and its dung outside the camp, because it is for sin.” In explaining this, the Apostle makes clear that all this must be understood of Christ, saying: “For the bodies of those animals whose blood is brought into the holy places for sin are burned outside the camp; therefore Jesus also, that he might sanctify the people through his own blood, suffered outside the gate” (Heb. XIII.11). Then the calf’s flesh, hide, and dung were burned outside the camp when Christ our Lord, hanging on the cross outside the gate, suffered a harsh death for our sins [Col. 0348A]. Let no one, when he reads of the calf’s dung, shrink from the thought that the dung too signifies Christ: by this dung our earth is enriched; by this dung both our flesh and our soul are made fertile. I think that the same thing is signified by the calf’s dung and by the uncovered shameful parts of the patriarch Noah. The calf’s dung, therefore, signifies the disgrace of the cross. In this the Apostle glories, saying: “But far be it from me to glory except in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ” (Gal. VI.14). Our calf, therefore—that is, the Word of God—has flesh by which we are nourished. Hence he himself says: “He who eats my flesh and drinks my blood has eternal life” (John VI.55). He also has a hide, which, unless it is stripped from the surface of the letter [Col. 0348B], prevents us from approaching the flesh and the spiritual understanding. When we ourselves say these things, we in some manner flay the calf—that is, the Word of God. For what the hide is over the flesh, ignorance is over the letter. [Note: [Col. 0347D] The Cassinese manuscript rightly corrects the edition, where “disgrace” is read instead of “ignorance.”] Let what has been said about the calf suffice.

“You shall also take one ram, upon whose head Aaron and his sons shall place their hands. When you have slaughtered it, you shall take some of its blood and pour it around the altar. You shall cut the ram itself into pieces, and, having washed its entrails and feet, place them upon the cut flesh and upon its head, and offer the whole [109] ram as incense upon the altar.” Although one and the same thing is understood by both the calf and the ram, since each signifies Christ’s passion, nevertheless there is a difference. The calf signifies that death of his concerning which the Apostle says: “Christ died once for our sins; he dies no more; death shall no longer have dominion over him [Note: [Col. 0347D] The Vulgate reads: ‘But if we have died with Christ, we believe that we shall also live with Christ, knowing that Christ, having risen from the dead, dies no more; death shall no longer have dominion over him. For in that he died, he died to sin once; but in that he lives, he lives to God’]” [Col. 0348C–D] (Rom. VI.9). The ram, however, represents that sacrifice of his which is now daily and devoutly offered by priests in holy Church in remembrance of him. Therefore there the blood is placed upon the altar’s horn, whereas here it is poured only around the altar. He says, then: “You shall also take one ram, upon whose head Aaron and his sons shall lay their hands.” In this place Aaron and his sons signify the bishops and priests of holy Church; above they signified the ministers of the Synagogue. Aaron and his sons lay their hands upon the ram’s head when high priests and priests raise pure hands to consecrate Christ’s body. He uses the head for the whole body, because the head is the principal part of the body. “When you have slaughtered it,” he says, “you shall take some of its blood and pour it around the altar,” so that it may be received by the faithful both with mouth and heart. This altar can be understood most fittingly as the human mind and heart. The blood is therefore poured around the altar because, continually touching minds and hearts, Christ’s blood and passion will never be erased from the faithful’s memory. Our hearts always swim in his [Col. 0349A] blood, and his blood and passion always move about our mind. Hence the Lord himself says: “Do this in remembrance of me” (Luke XXI.19). It follows:

“You shall cut the ram itself into pieces.” We cut the ram into pieces when we expound individually and by separate propositions all that has been written concerning the Saviour: now speaking of his ineffable birth, now of his preaching, now of the miracles he worked by his word alone, now of his passion, now of his resurrection, now of his ascension.

“And, having washed its entrails and feet, you shall place them upon the cut flesh and upon its head, and offer the whole ram upon the altar.” What do its feet and entrails signify but his end and passion? The feet are the end of the body; to see the entrails, however, is terrible. Therefore what is signified by the calf’s dung is signified by the ram’s entrails and feet. We wash the ram’s feet and entrails when we prove that Christ the Lord suffered not from weakness but willingly; when, from his own testimony, we show that he willingly endured spittle, scourges, the crown of thorns, and all the disgrace of the cross—for these are his entrails: “For he was offered because he himself willed it” [Col. 0349B] (Isa. LIII.7). For he had power to lay down his life and to take it up again. Hence he said: “Unless a grain of wheat falls into the earth and dies, it remains alone; but if it dies, it brings forth much fruit” (John XII.24). When we say this, we wash his feet and entrails and show that those things which appeared in him weak, feeble, and contemptible were noble, strong, and admirable. We place these—that is, the ram’s entrails and feet—upon the cut flesh and its head because, after we have separately shown that Christ, though God, was born of a virgin, lived among human beings, gave light to the blind, cleansed lepers, raised the dead, and did the other things that he did, then at last we ought to place and add to all these things that he suffered for us and endured, because of our sins, the most shameful death and the disgrace of the cross. This is the proper order [Col. 0349C] of preaching: cutting our ram—that is, the Word of God—into pieces, beginning with the head and placing that head first, we say: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God” (John I.1). This is the ram’s head. Then, explaining the other members in order—after expounding that he became man, was born of a virgin, lived with human beings, and similar matters written about him—we should at last come to his passion and add the disgrace of the cross after all things and above all things. This is to place the ram’s feet and entrails upon the cut flesh and upon the head. John the Evangelist is known to have done this. For after he had said, “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God,” he proceeds, setting forth Christ’s teaching and miracles piece by piece, and at last adds his passion and the disgrace of the cross over all the rest [Col. 0350A]. The further words, “And you shall offer the whole ram upon the altar,” mean as much as if he said: You shall keep always in memory, heart, and mind not only Christ’s divinity and humanity, but also his passion, resurrection, ascension, and everything written concerning him. For we have said that this altar signifies the human mind and heart. Whenever, therefore, with a contrite spirit and a contrite and humbled heart, we lovingly remember our Saviour and preach him to others, we sacrifice the whole ram upon the altar of the heart. For the Lord’s offering is an odour of sweetness; indeed, no offering of ours is sweeter to God than the love, devotion, and affection by which we are moved concerning his remembrance and sigh in his sweetness. Filled with this sweetness, the Psalmist said: “My soul thirsted for the living God: when shall I come and appear before the face of God? My tears were my bread day and night” [Col. 0350B] (Ps. XLI.3).

“You shall take the other ram also, upon whose head Aaron and his sons shall lay their hands. When you have sacrificed it, you shall take some of its blood and put it upon the tip of the right ear of Aaron and his sons, and upon the thumbs of their right hands and right feet. And you shall pour the blood around the altar.” [Col. 0350C] This third offering is that of which the Psalmist speaks, saying: “Precious in the sight of the Lord is the death of his saints” (Ps. CXV.15). The calf, then, as we have said, signifies Christ’s passion; the first ram, the sacrament of his body and blood, which is daily offered everywhere in the Church; but this second ram signifies the sufferings and torments of the apostles and martyrs. Of this ram it is written: “Bring to the Lord, sons of God; bring to the Lord the sons of rams” (Ps. XXVIII.1). Again: “The mountains leapt like rams” (Ps. CXIII.4). Of this offering the Apostle also says: “For I am already being poured out, and the time of my departure is at hand” (I Tim. IV.6). Again: “I beseech you, through the mercy of God, to present [Col. 0350D] your bodies as a living sacrifice, holy and pleasing to God, your rational service” (Rom. XII.1). The Lord himself also said to the sons of Zebedee: “Can you drink the cup which I am about to drink?” (Matt. XX.22). When they replied that they could, he said: “You shall indeed drink my cup” (ibid.); that is, you too, suffering for me, shall be God’s burnt offering and sacrifice. Aaron and his sons therefore laid their hands upon this ram’s head because, at the instigation of high priests and priests—signified by Aaron and his sons—hands were laid upon the apostles immediately after Christ’s passion. First they killed Stephen and James; afterwards they persecuted the Church everywhere with great cruelty. They laid their hands upon the ram’s head when they afflicted the primitive Church with varied and numerous torments. We have said above that Aaron and his sons sometimes signify the high priests and priests of the Jews, and sometimes our bishops and priests: they signify the former when they act wickedly, the latter when they do some good; the former when they persecute the saints, the latter when they are consecrated by the Lord. Hence it follows: “When you have sacrificed it, you shall take some of its blood and place it upon the tip of the right ear of Aaron and his sons.” Behold: Aaron and his sons, who just now signified Jewish high priests and priests, now signify our bishops and priests. Since they have nothing left-handed, the ram’s blood is commanded to be placed upon their right ear, hand [Col. 0351B], and foot. The Jews, however, do not have the right ear which blessed Peter cut off from the servant Malchus. The saints have nothing left-handed; hence the Lord says in the Gospel: “Let not your left hand know what your right hand does” (Matt. VI.23). The ram’s blood touches our ears when we delight to hear the sufferings of the martyrs. But because it profits very little merely to hear unless we also imitate their deeds, hands too are stained with blood, so that we may follow them both in action and, if need be, in suffering. It touches the feet also, so that we may not be reluctant to preach to others the good example which we derive from them, according to the Apostle’s words: “How beautiful are the feet of those who proclaim peace, who proclaim good things!” (Rom. X.15). The fact that blood touches the tip [Col. 0351C] of the ear means that the ears of the saints will never be closed to God’s word until the final consummation of the age. And because the Jewish people too will open their ears to hear God’s word near the end of the world, the tip of Aaron’s ear is not without reason said to have been touched. To touch the tip of the ear is to call the last and furthest people to repentance. The ram’s blood is poured around the altar because the minds and hearts of all delight in the sufferings, steadfastness, and blood of the holy martyrs. Whether we understand the altar as the whole Church or as each person’s mind, the martyrs’ blood is poured upon it because the martyrs’ sufferings are recounted to the minds of the faithful. It follows:

“And when you have taken some of the blood that is upon the altar, and some of the oil of anointing, you shall sprinkle Aaron and his garments, his sons, and their garments.” The blood from the altar and the oil of anointing are sprinkled upon Aaron and his garments because the sufferings of the holy martyrs and the grace of the Holy Spirit, by which they were anointed, are handed on to all bishops and priests for preaching and imitation. Imitation pertains to Aaron; preaching pertains to his garments. For while the martyrs’ blood is seen upon the garments, the garments themselves in some fashion preach the martyrs’ sufferings. But when Aaron is both stained with blood and anointed with oil, then the priest both imitates martyrdom and is strengthened by grace. That priest [Col. 0352A] is not stained with the martyrs’ blood who disdains to imitate the martyrs’ sufferings; if he also neglects to preach their martyrdoms, then without doubt he has not received their blood even upon his garments. For our garment is the flesh, since the soul is clothed in this garment. Therefore, when with the tongue of the flesh we preach the martyrdoms of the martyrs, we in some fashion bear their blood upon our garment. This blood is taken from the altar of our heart, because what we have in our heart, that we do and teach,
“After they themselves and their garments have been consecrated, you shall take the fat from the ram, and the tail, and the fat [111] which covers the vital organs, and the membrane of the liver, and the two kidneys, and the fat which is upon them, and the right shoulder, because it is the ram of consecration; one cake of bread, a wafer [Col. 0352B] sprinkled with oil, and a flat cake from the basket of unleavened bread which is set before the Lord.”

“After they themselves,” he says, “and their garments have been consecrated,” so that they may imitate the life of those whose persons and garments are sprinkled with blood, “you shall take the fat from the ram,” and the rest which follows. For it is not enough that we be sprinkled with the ram’s blood alone, unless we also receive from the ram its fat, tail, fat covering the organs, and the other things set down here; because we ought to embrace and imitate not only the sufferings of the martyrs but also their life, character, and wisdom.

Take, therefore, the fat—not of the flesh, I say, but of the mind. For the mind’s fat is justice, prudence, temperance, and fortitude: with this fat the soul is made rich. Take also the tail, so that you may be like those of whom he speaks, and persevere in good work [Col. 0352C] even to the end. “For he who perseveres unto the end, he shall be saved” (Matt. 24:13). For the tail stands for the end, because the tail is the end of the body.

Take also the fat which covers the vital organs. The vital organs are the hearts, for life is there. Thus, by the heart’s fat are understood wisdom and knowledge. Lean is the heart which is not made fat by this fat. Take also the membrane of the liver, that you may leave nothing of the fat behind. For all the fat of this ram is good. According to physicians, digestion belongs to the liver; hence they call it the master of the household, because by its function the other parts are nourished. But a lean, sick, and feeble liver cannot digest foods. What, then, is the membrane of the liver [Col. 0352D] except that understanding by which, through rumination, we digest the meanings of the holy Scriptures? Food that is not digested is useless; Scripture which is not understood is fruitless. Therefore, that our liver may grow fat, let us take this membrane of its liver.

Likewise take the two kidneys and the fat which is upon them, so that your kidneys may be such as were the kidneys of the saints. “Let your loins be girded” (Luke 12:35). Where desire rules, say to the Lord with the Psalmist: “Test me, O God, and try me; burn my kidneys and my heart” (Ps. 25:2). But because chastity of the flesh is useless unless chastity of mind is also possessed, he commands that the fat upon the kidneys also be taken. Chastity is fat when neither the flesh is corrupted by fornication nor the soul by heretical perversity or [Col. 0353A] the love of vices.

Take also the right shoulder. Hear the Apostle saying: “Bear one another’s burdens, and thus you will fulfil the law of Christ” (Gal. 6:2), so that, as you do not shrink from bearing Christ, you may not shrink from bearing your neighbour. For that bishop has no shoulders who is unwilling to bear others’ burdens. This is the ram of consecration, because by this ram Aaron and his sons are consecrated.

“You shall also take one cake of bread, a wafer sprinkled with oil, and a flat cake from the basket of unleavened bread which is set before the Lord.” By the cake of one bread, the wafer, and the flat cake we understand faith, hope, and charity. For as bread ranks among all foods, so faith is first and greatest among all virtues: “Without faith it is impossible to please God” (Heb. [Col. 0353B] 1:6). It is given first; it is received in baptism; whoever does not have it has nothing.

It is a cake of one bread because faith too is one. Thus the Apostle says: “One Lord, one faith, one baptism” (Eph. 4:5). But why a cake? A cake expresses the likeness of a crown; by faith one comes to the crown. Hence, after the Apostle had said, “I have fought the good fight, I have completed the course, I have kept the faith” (2 Tim. 4:7), he immediately added: “Henceforth there is laid up for me a crown of righteousness” (ibid.).

The wafer, however, signifies hope. Whatever we fry in the pan, whatever we roast on the gridiron, whatever afflicts us in diverse tribulations—all this is wrought by hope for future blessedness. Hence the Apostle also says: “If we hope for that which we do not see, [Col. 0353C] we await it through patience” (Rom. 8:25). What, moreover, does the breadth of the flat cake signify but charity, of which it is written: “Your commandment is exceedingly broad” (Ps. 116:96)? For upon this commandment “hang all the law and the prophets” (Matt. 24:40).

All these things are both unleavened and smeared with oil, because they are sincere and incorrupt and filled with the grace of the Holy Spirit. Faith which is not catholic, and faith which is dead without works, is neither unleavened nor smeared with oil. All these things, moreover, are placed and gathered in the basket of unleavened bread; by this basket we understand this book—the book, I mean, of Exodus. For in this book the Lord commanded Moses both to gather and to write all these things, and thus ordered him to hand them down to Aaron and his sons [Col. 0353D]. Therefore, since Aaron and his sons signify bishops and priests, to whom is this basket—that is, this book—to be understood as handed down, except to bishops and priests? For all these things have been entrusted to us for reading, meditation, teaching, and observance. Hence it follows:

“And you shall put all these things upon the hands of Aaron and of his sons, and you shall consecrate them, lifting them up before the Lord.” A bishop is consecrated when he receives the sacred law and the divine books for meditation and teaching, and promises to keep them not merely with his lips but with his whole heart. He lifts them up before the Lord because, both in life and teaching, he presents himself in such a manner that his services deserve to be borne upward and to be seen and received by God. For he does not lift up on high either [Col. 0354A] himself or his gifts who, through the contagion of vices, disfigures and brings low both his life and his soul. It follows:

“You shall receive the gifts from their hands and pour them out upon the altar as a whole burnt offering, an exceedingly sweet fragrance before the Lord, [112] because it is his offering.” Unless these things had pleased the Lord, he would by no means have commanded Moses, his mediator and in a certain sense his vicar, to receive them; for what Moses receives is also received by God. They are burned upon the altar so that they may yield a sweet fragrance and please the Lord. For the Apostle says: “We are the good fragrance of Christ to God: to some, a fragrance of life unto life; to others, a fragrance of death unto death” (2 Cor. 2:15).

When, by preaching, we pour into the minds of the faithful those things which have been said above [Col. 0354B], then we empty the basket upon the altar of the heart, and burn in a fragrance of sweetness those things which had been laid up in it. God is pleased by this fragrance, and all to whom this fragrance comes delight in it. For this is an offering to the Lord. Hence the Psalmist says: “Sacrifice to God a sacrifice of praise” (Ps. 49:14). When, therefore, the aforesaid basket is poured out upon the altar—that is, upon the minds of the faithful—when the book is expounded and holy Scripture preached, then a sacrifice of praise is offered to God. Therefore, when God’s priests offer such a sacrifice, when they preach to the people, when they kindle and set aflame the minds of the faithful, then their offerings become an exceedingly sweet fragrance to the Lord. [Col. 0354C] It follows:

“You shall also take the breast from the ram by which Aaron was initiated, and you shall consecrate it, having lifted it up before the Lord; and it shall fall to his portion. You shall consecrate also the breast of consecration and the shoulder which you have set apart from the ram by which Aaron and his sons were initiated; and they shall fall to the portion of Aaron and his sons, by a perpetual right from the children of Israel, because they are firstfruits and beginnings from their peace-offerings, which they offer to the Lord.”

The ram by which Aaron was initiated and consecrated is the one of which we have spoken until now. Aaron receives its breast and shoulder because bishops and priests ought to bear in their breast the counsels of all, and upon their shoulders the burdens of all. Those who eat the breasts and shoulders of so many animals [Col. 0354D] ought to be wise and strong—if one may so speak—broad-breasted and broad-shouldered. For this reason, bishops and priests, breasts are given to you, lest you lack a place in which to lay up God’s treasure. You also possess shoulders, that you may be able powerfully to bear the burdens of the whole Church. But priests who eat consecrated shoulders and breasts must take care that they possess shoulders and breasts which are holy and just. For a holy breast utters holy things, and iniquity does not climb upon holy shoulders. These, moreover, are counted among the firstfruits and therefore belong to the priests, because all firstfruits are given to the priests by the people.

“The holy garment which Aaron wears shall be possessed by his sons after him, that they may be anointed in it and [Col. 0355A] their hands consecrated. For seven days the high priest who has been appointed in his place from among his sons, and who enters the tabernacle of testimony to minister to the Lord in the Sanctuary, shall wear it.”

For you, bishops and priests, are Aaron’s sons—provided you imitate Aaron—and brothers of Moses, namely of that Moses who said: “I will declare your name to my brothers” (Ps. 21:23). You, therefore, possess Aaron’s garment; you are clothed in glory and beauty and in the ornament of every virtue. You possess the breastpiece and ephod; you are anointed with the grace of the Holy Spirit. Your hands also are consecrated for making the body and blood of Christ and for doing every good and honourable thing. For seven days you wear this garment, because you wear it on all days [Col. 0355B] and never strip it off. There are only seven days; what is done for seven days is done at all times.

“But you shall take the ram of consecration and boil its flesh in a holy place; Aaron and his sons shall eat it.” We have said that by this ram is understood the multitude of all the apostles and martyrs. Bishops, priests, and their sons eat their flesh—not as those of whom it is said: “For they have devoured Jacob” (Ps. 78:7). We eat the flesh of the apostles and martyrs because they are our bread, our food, and our refreshment. We live by their examples, are nourished by their teaching, and are filled by their words and deeds. We boil their flesh [Col. 0355C] in a holy place because we meditate in a faithful heart upon their writings, teaching, and examples, and chew them over with sound understanding. But heretics do not boil this flesh in a holy place, because in the dung-heap of a heretical heart they corrupt all things by understanding them wrongly. Let us therefore follow the examples of those by whose bread we are filled.

“They shall eat, in the vestibule of the tabernacle of testimony, the breads which are in the basket, so that it may be a propitiatory sacrifice and may consecrate the hands of those who offer it.” We have already eaten the flesh of the ram; let us eat also the breads which are in the basket. Each food is good and pleasant to eat. We have heard the life and teaching of the apostles and martyrs; let us hear also [Col. 0355D] the things contained in this basket, that is, in this book. We have heard the new things; let us hear also the old. For good is the one who brings forth from his treasure new things and old.

We ought to eat these breads in the vestibule of the tabernacle and in a holy place, so that we do not give what is holy to dogs or scatter pearls before swine. Let us eat them in a holy place; let us dispense and expound them in the assembly of the faithful. Why is this so? That there may be a propitiatory sacrifice; that the Lord’s name may not be blasphemed; that neither ministry may be disparaged; and that the hands of those who offer may be consecrated. “If you offer rightly but do not divide rightly, [113] you have sinned” [Note: [Col. 0355] The Vulgate reads thus: “If you do well, will you not be received? But if you do ill, sin will immediately be present at the door?”] (Gen. 4:7). For just as one must consider [Col. 0356A] what one offers and to whom one offers, so one must also consider where one offers. Hence it continues: “A foreigner shall not eat of them, because they are consecrated.”

The greater mysteries of the Scriptures ought to be handed down to the faithful alone. For what fellowship has the faithful person with the unbeliever? Therefore let faith be preached to unbelievers; but if anyone is converted, let him draw near and eat. “For a foreigner shall not eat of them. But if anything remains of the consecrated flesh or of the breads until morning, you shall burn the remains with fire; they shall not be eaten, because they are consecrated.” I think this is what was said above concerning the Paschal lamb: “If anything remains, it shall be burned with fire” (Exod. 12:10). For not everything can be eaten, because it is not possible to understand everything. Much will remain [Col. 0356B] until morning; and before this night—this life, full of darkness and ignorance—comes to an end, the sun of righteousness will rise before all the mysteries of the holy Scriptures are understood. Therefore, let what cannot be understood be burned in the fire of faith, entrusted to the Holy Spirit, and believed with firm love of charity. For the remains were forbidden to be eaten for no other reason than that we should refrain from probing and investigating matters which are not open to the understanding and which God’s wisdom has willed to remain hidden: how the Word became flesh; how the Son of God was begotten either from the Father or from the mother; how the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son; and many other such matters—none of which has ever been revealed to any human being in this life.

“You shall do upon Aaron [Col. 0356C] and his sons all the things which I have commanded you. For seven days you shall consecrate their hands, and each day you shall offer a calf for sin, for expiation.” What does “you shall consecrate their hands for seven days” mean? Hear, bishops; hear, priests: let no day be omitted. Your hands must be consecrated every day. For there are only seven days; therefore, whoever is consecrated for seven days is consecrated on all days. The hands of the one who always guards his hands and works are consecrated on all days, so that they may be clean, do no evil, and persist in every good work.

He also offers a calf for expiation each day who never forgets the passion of the only-begotten Son of God. This calf [Col. 0356D] is Christ. While we keep in mind his birth, teaching, works, miracles, cross, scourges, passion, crown of thorns, and the other things which he endured for us, we offer God a great sacrifice for the expiation of sins. This calf is also offered each day for expiation because, until the consummation of the age, the holy Church will not cease to offer daily the sacrament of Christ’s body and blood.

“And you shall cleanse the altar when you have sacrificed the victim of expiation, and anoint it for consecration.” We showed above, when we spoke of it, that this altar signifies the Church. For since [Col. 0357A] the mind of each faithful person is called an altar, much more should the whole Church be understood and called an altar. This altar must be cleansed as often as a victim of expiation is sacrificed upon it. “For he who eats and drinks this victim unworthily eats and drinks judgment to himself” (1 Cor. 11:29). These are the Apostle’s words. This altar is cleansed by repentance, tears, almsgiving, and works of mercy. It is anointed for consecration with the oil of piety and the grace of the Holy Spirit; for by this oil the Church is consecrated. It follows.

“For seven days you shall expiate the altar and consecrate it, and it shall be the Holy of Holies; everyone who touches it shall be consecrated.” It has often already been said that the seven days signify all time. [Col. 0357B] What is consecrated at all times and progresses toward the better is holy—indeed, the Holy of Holies. Everyone who touches this altar is consecrated, because whoever embraces the Church’s religion and is touched and pierced in heart by the examples of the saints undoubtedly becomes holy.
