“This is what you shall do upon the altar: two year-old lambs continually every day, one lamb in the morning and the other in the evening; a tenth part of fine flour mixed with beaten oil, a quarter of a hin in measure, and wine for a libation in the same measure for one lamb.” Although the two lambs signify one and the same thing—for they signify that Lamb who takes away the sins of the world—Christ was nevertheless sacrificed daily in the Church in one way and on the cross in another. Here [Col. 0357C] he is sacrificed by the faithful with piety; there he was sacrificed by the Jews with cruelty.

Indeed, our Lamb was sacrificed both morning and evening. For Christ our Lord was judged, condemned, scourged, spat upon, bound, struck with blows, and subjected to many insults by the Jews in the morning; but in the evening, hanging upon the cross, he gave up his spirit. Hence the Psalmist says: “Let my prayer be directed as incense in your sight; the lifting up of my hands, the evening sacrifice” (Ps. 140:2). Let us too sacrifice two lambs, and morning and evening be mindful of Christ’s cross and passion, so that by the sacrifice of remembrance and compunction which we offer in the morning, we may remain safe from every adversity throughout the day; and that which [Col. 0357D] we perform in the evening may keep us safe from every assault of vices throughout the night. This is what “morning and evening” means: day and night, at all times.

Let us also offer a tenth portion of fine flour; let us offer wine in the same measure. O wondrous mystery! This is the sacrifice of Melchizedek; this is the sacrifice of our high priest—the high priest indeed to whom it was said: [114] “You are a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek” (Ps. 109:5). Christ offered fine flour and wine; we too daily sacrifice fine flour and wine. For bread strengthens the heart, and wine gladdens the human heart. This fine flour—this marrow of wheat, this living bread that came down from heaven—is mixed with beaten oil because, by the operation of the same Holy Spirit [Col. 0358A], this bread is changed into Christ’s flesh; and by that Spirit’s overshadowing and inspiration Christ was born of the Virgin.

But in commanding a tenth and a fourth to be brought, he seems most plainly to signify that God receives no one’s offering who does not receive the New and Old Testaments. Therefore, in faith in both Testaments and with the oil of the Holy Spirit, let us offer bread and wine; and the lamb is joined to them because these are changed into the flesh and blood of the Lamb.

“But you shall offer the other lamb in the evening according to the rite of the morning offering and according to what we have said, as a sweet fragrance; it is a sacrifice to the Lord, a perpetual offering throughout your generations.” Since both lambs signify one and the same thing, they are offered in the same rite both evening and morning. This sacrifice becomes a perpetual offering because this offering will not cease in the holy Church until the consummation of the age. But where it is made follows:

“At the door of the tabernacle of testimony before the Lord, where I shall appoint to speak to you; there I shall command the children of Israel, and the altar shall be consecrated in my glory. The tabernacle of testimony also shall be consecrated with the altar, and Aaron with his sons, that they may exercise the priesthood for me; and I shall dwell in the midst of the children of Israel and shall be their God, that they may know that I am the Lord their God, who brought them out of the land of Egypt, that I might dwell among them—I, the Lord their God.”

The sacrifice is made at the door of the tabernacle because there are the priests; indeed, they themselves are the door, and the remaining multitude of the faithful enter the tabernacle through them. [Col. 0358C] The sacrifice is made at the door so that, at the very entrance of faith and upon receiving baptism, those regenerated in Christ may at once become partakers of Christ’s body and blood. Hence a basin is placed beside the altar, in which the priests wash. This will be discussed in what follows.

## Chapter 30

“You shall also make an altar for burning incense, of shittim wood, one cubit in length—that is, square—and two cubits in height; its horns shall rise from it. You shall cover it with the purest gold, both its grating and its walls round about and its horns.”

The altar mentioned above signifies the whole Church; this one signifies Christ’s humanity. Thus, because of the sweet fragrance offered upon it, it is called the altar of incense. Only the high priest was permitted to approach it in order to sacrifice, because it signified the humanity of the one and highest priest. The Church had perceived the fragrance of this altar when she said: “Draw me after you; we shall run in the fragrance of your ointments” (Song 1:4). Isaac too, perceiving its fragrance, said: “Behold, the fragrance of my son is as the fragrance of a field full of blessing, which God has blessed” (Gen. 27:27). This is that flower of the field and lily of the valleys, upon whom rest the seven graces of the Holy Spirit.

This altar is of shittim wood, wood that is strong and incorruptible. Hence the Psalmist, speaking of him, says: “You will not give your Holy One to see corruption” (Ps. 15:10). *Setim* means “thorn”; and we read that this altar was crowned with thorns [Col. 0359A]. It is square, as befits that which is firm, stable, and immovable. This is the firm rock upon which the Church is founded. It rises two cubits in height because it is constituted, as it were, by two cubits: God and man. It has one cubit in breadth because Christ, God and man, is one. Finally, because the Son is in the Father, the Father in the Son, and the Holy Spirit proceeds from both, this altar is not improperly measured by three cubits.

The horns proceed from Christ because all his power and strength come neither accidentally nor from elsewhere, but our Saviour always possesses them in himself naturally and substantially. It is covered with the purest gold because he shines not only with the light of wisdom and knowledge but is himself the source of all wisdom, and the one with whom it always was and who is before all ages. This is the house which Wisdom is said to have built: “Wisdom has built herself a house; she has hewn out seven pillars” (Prov. 9:1). Since, therefore, this whole house is built by wisdom, the whole altar is fittingly covered with the purest gold.

Since, moreover, by the grating made in the manner of a net his preaching is understood, who can worthily say with how great a light of wisdom and knowledge this grating shines? This is the net which the Lord commands the apostles to cast on the right side of the boat. It follows:

“You shall make for it a little golden crown round about, and golden rings beneath the crown on each side, so that bars may be put into them and the altar carried. You shall also make [Col. 0359C] the bars of shittim wood and overlay them with gold.”

This altar is crowned, as the Psalmist testifies concerning the God-man: “You made him a little lower than the angels; you crowned him with glory and honour” (Ps. 6:8). And again: “You placed upon his head a crown of precious stone” (Ps. 20:4). This crown is a little golden crown because it was wisely acquired. What are the four golden rings—for there are as many rings as corners of the altar—but the four Gospels? By these the altar is lifted and carried, because through evangelical preaching Christ’s name and glory were borne throughout the lands. But by whom? Certainly by the holy apostles and evangelists, bishops, and doctors of the Church. These are the bars [Col. 0359D] by which the altar is carried; they pass through the golden rings—that is, the Gospels—and, wrapped in their teachings, are not separated from them. Of them it is written: “You ride upon your horses, and your chariots are salvation” (Hab. 3:8). They are called both bars and horses; fittingly they are said to be of shittim wood, as strong, incorruptible, and eternal. They are overlaid with gold because they shine with much light of wisdom.

“You shall place the altar opposite the veil hanging before the ark of testimony, before the mercy-seat by which the testimony is covered, where I shall speak to you.” The altar is placed opposite the veil, and not within it, so that it may be seen by all and fill and pervade all with the fragrance of incense burned upon it. This is what the Lord says: “I have spoken openly [Col. 0360A] to the world; I have always taught in the synagogue, where all the Jews assemble” (John 18:20). The altar stands before the mercy-seat because Christ our Lord never forgets propitiation and mercy; he always looks toward the mercy-seat and always shows mercy to those who come to him. The Lord speaks there; he speaks in him, because he himself is God and Lord. It follows:

“And Aaron shall burn fragrant incense of sweet fragrance upon it in the morning, when he arranges the lamps; he shall burn it also when he sets them in place in the evening: perpetual incense before the Lord throughout your generations.” Aaron himself is Jesus, our high priest and priest, who upon the altar of his assumed flesh delighted all around him with the fragrant odour of every incense through the renown of his fame. He did this morning and evening. What are morning and evening? All time. Morning is the beginning of day, evening the beginning of night; morning stands for day and evening for night, while day and night signify all time. Thus morning and evening Aaron arranged and set in place the lamps, because Christ our Lord illumined his faithful at all times through the teaching of the Word, the wonder of virtues, and the diversity of graces. The hearts of the faithful are illumined by such lamps.

“You shall not offer upon it incense of another composition, nor an offering, nor a victim, nor pour libations.” Nothing foreign, corrupt, or defective, [Col. 0360C] nothing of inferior doctrine, shall be offered on this altar, because Christ our Lord “committed no sin, nor was deceit found in his mouth” (1 Pet. 2:22). This altar gives forth nothing but justice, piety, gentleness, charity, wisdom, concord, peace, and the like; such is the fragrance poured out from it, such are the incenses that smell sweet. Since the Apostle says, “We are the good fragrance of Christ to God in every place” (2 Cor. 2:15), what a fragrance must Christ himself be!

“And Aaron shall make atonement upon its horns once in the year with the blood offered for sin; and it shall be propitiated upon it throughout your generations; it shall be the Holy of Holies to the Lord.” Once our high priest Jesus Christ, upon the horns of this altar—that is, in the humanity which he had assumed from his virgin mother—made intercession to the Father for the sins of the Jews when he said: “Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing” (Luke 23:34). He himself is priest, himself victim, himself altar; in his own blood “he entered once into the holy places, having obtained eternal redemption” (Heb. 9:12). By this sacrifice, by the prayers of this high priest, the Lord has been propitiated for all generations. What follows—“It shall be the Holy of Holies to the Lord”—must be understood of the altar. For Christ’s body is the Holy of Holies, because by it all other things are consecrated. So much concerning the altar.

“And the Lord spoke to Moses, saying: When you take the sum of the children of Israel according to their number, each shall give to the Lord a price for his soul, [Col. 0361A] and there shall be no plague among them when they are counted. This shall every one give who passes into the name: half a shekel, according to the measure of the sanctuary. A shekel has twenty obols. Everyone who is included in the number, from twenty years old and upward, shall give the price.” [Note: [Col. 0361] Codex Casinensis: “Everyone,” he says, “who is included in the number, who is enrolled in the Lord’s portion both in deed and in name, shall bring,” etc.]

Everyone, he says, who is numbered—that is, who passes into the name, who is enrolled in the people of God in deed and in name—shall bring a price; he must not be empty or without a gift, because the redemption of one’s own soul is wealth. But what shall he give? Half a shekel. A shekel has twenty obols; therefore he shall give ten obols. But why ten? Do you wish to hear why? Because there are ten words of the law: by this price each person redeems his soul. You have not killed: you have given one shekel. You have not committed adultery: you have given two shekels. You have not committed theft: you have given three shekels [Col. 0361B], and so with the rest. For you give as many shekels as commandments you keep. Hence they are commanded to be given according to the measure of the sanctuary. For the law is in the sanctuary. In the sanctuary the Decalogue is found and measured.

They give the price from twenty years old and upward because the price of the one who does not double ten is not received; because he does not understand the Testament in a twofold sense; because he does not approve the exposition according to letter and spirit of both Testaments. Here the Jews, and here also the Manichaeans, are condemned.

“The rich man shall add nothing to half a shekel, and the poor shall diminish nothing; and you shall give the money received, which has been collected from the children of Israel, for the uses of the tabernacle of testimony, that it may be a memorial of them before the Lord and that he may be propitious to their souls.” The rich man adds nothing to half a shekel, because there is nothing further for one who observes the ten [Col. 0361C] words of the law to do. The poor person ought to diminish nothing, because “whoever offends in one point has become guilty of all” (Jas. 2:10). All this money, however, is to be given for the uses of the tabernacle of testimony, so that whoever keeps the commandments of the law may do so not for popular favour but for the soul’s benefit, and may always keep in mind: “Amen, I say to you, they have received their reward” (Matt. 6:10). Such persons are useless to the tabernacle of testimony, because Jerusalem’s walls are not built from them.

“And the Lord spoke to Moses, saying: You shall also make a bronze basin with its base for washing; you shall place it between the tabernacle of testimony and the altar, and water having been put into it, Aaron and his sons [Col. 0361D] shall wash their hands and feet in it when they are about to enter the tabernacle of testimony and when they are about to approach the altar, in order to offer incense upon it to the Lord, lest perhaps they die. It shall be an everlasting ordinance for him and for his seed throughout their generations.”

What do we understand by the basin but baptism? What by its base but faith? The basin is bronze because baptism is not given without sound and the voice of confession: “For with the heart one believes unto righteousness, but with the mouth confession is made unto salvation” (Rom. 10:10). Hence others intercede by promising faith for little children who cannot speak [Col. 0362A]. The basin is placed between the tabernacle and the altar, so that whoever desires to enter the tabernacle or approach the altar may first be washed with water and regenerated by the sacrament of baptism.

Formerly Aaron with his sons, but now our priests with the entire multitude of the faithful, wash in this basin. For all of us are either priests or sons of priests. They washed hands and feet; we wash the whole body and cleanse it from every stain of vice—although the person needs only to wash the feet. Yet we too wash ourselves daily by repentance for sins, tears of compunction, and works of piety and mercy. For this too is a basin in which priests who are about to approach the altar must daily wash and be cleansed, lest perhaps they die [Col. 0362B]. Therefore, if they fear death, let them wash lest they die; let them not approach the altar unless washed. Water is near; tears and repentance are near. Thus David and Peter were cleansed, for otherwise it is not permitted to be baptized again.

“And the Lord spoke to Moses, saying: Take for yourself the choicest spices: five hundred shekels of first-quality and selected myrrh; half as much, that is, two hundred and fifty shekels, of aromatic cinnamon; likewise two hundred and fifty shekels of calamus; but five hundred shekels of cassia by the weight of the sanctuary; and a hin-measure of olive oil.” By these four aromatic substances are understood the four principal virtues, often mentioned already: prudence, justice, fortitude, and temperance. If the oil [Col. 0362C] of the Holy Spirit is mixed with these, an ointment of wonderful composition is made, and whoever has been anointed with it is consecrated without any doubt. This ointment gave our Saviour his name, so that Christ is called from *chrism*; hence he himself says: “The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because he has anointed me; he has sent me to preach the Gospel to the poor” (Luke 4:18). It follows:

“And you shall make holy anointing oil, an ointment compounded by the work of a perfumer; and with it you shall anoint the tabernacle of testimony and the ark of the covenant, the table with its vessels, the lampstand and its utensils, the altar of incense and of whole burnt offering, and all the furnishings pertaining to their service; you shall consecrate them all, and they shall be the Holy of Holies; whoever touches them shall be consecrated. You shall anoint Aaron [Col. 0362D] and his sons and consecrate them, that they may exercise the priesthood for me.”

“The tabernacle itself,” he says, “and whatever is in the tabernacle, you shall anoint with the ointment mentioned above, because whatever is anointed with it becomes the Holy of Holies. For what is to be understood by the tabernacle and the things within the tabernacle has been stated above.”

“Human flesh shall not be anointed with it, and you shall make no other according to its composition, because it has been consecrated and shall be holy to you. Any man who shall prepare such a thing, or shall give any of it to a stranger, shall be cut off [Col. 0363A] from his people.” Human flesh, he says, shall not be anointed with it; for this ointment belongs not to the flesh but to the mind. But what does “human” mean? Were not Aaron and his sons human beings? For in Holy Scripture “men” are often understood to mean the wicked and sinners, according to the saying: “But you shall die like men” (Ps. 81:7). And the Apostle says: “When one says, ‘I am of Paul,’ another, ‘I am of Apollos,’ another, ‘I am of Cephas,’ are you not men?” (1 Cor. 1:12). Therefore this ointment belongs not to sinners but to saints; not to carnal persons but to spiritual ones. It is assigned to priests alone, to holy and spiritual men alone. Hence it is added: “And according to its composition you shall make no other.” For heretics, and especially Simoniacs, strive to make something according to its composition, [Col. 0363B] since from the same ingredients and with the same sacramental words they ordain their own bishops and priests, confer holy orders, and sell the other sacraments of the Church for a price—doing this, however, for strangers, as they themselves are strangers and alien to the Catholic faith. Therefore they are cut off from the people of God and separated from the fellowship of the saints. These are those whom our Saviour cast out of the temple. Thus far concerning the ointment.

“And the Lord said to Moses: Take for yourself spices—stacte, onycha, sweet-smelling galbanum, and the clearest frankincense; all shall be of equal weight. And you shall make incense compounded by the work of a perfumer, carefully blended, pure, and most worthy of consecration.” What, indeed, are these four fragrant ingredients, by whose natural power wounds are treated and healed, but the four Gospels? All are of equal weight, because they possess one and the same truth and authority. They are all blended together so that what is not found in one Gospel may be discovered in another; and, while in some matters they correspond mutually with one another and in none disagree, they produce a very sweet fragrance. Onycha, however, which is translated “claw” or “nail,” is not well known among our people. But when these things are expounded to the peoples with due order, reason, and in accordance with the truth of what has been written, then surely there results from them incense compounded by the work of a perfumer, carefully blended, pure, and most worthy of consecration. The Apostle was the most skilful [Col. 0363D] perfumer of this composition: he laid a foundation as a wise architect; speaking wisdom among the perfect, he became all things to all people, that he might gain all. Breathing out the fragrance of this incense, he said: “But thanks be to God, who gave the pledge in our hearts” (2 Cor. 5:5), and “[who] makes manifest through us in every place the fragrance of the knowledge of himself, among those who are being saved and among those who are perishing. For to some we are a fragrance of life unto life; to others, a fragrance of death unto death” (2 Cor. 2:14).

[Col. 0364A] “When you have crushed all these things into the finest powder, you shall place some of it before the testimony of the tabernacle, where I shall appear to you; the incense shall be most holy to you.” For then we crush all things into the finest powder when, closely investigating the meanings of the Gospels and repeatedly breaking them up by meditation, we bring them to spiritual understanding. For just as spices give forth a sweeter scent when they are ground, so Holy Scripture provides a sweeter fragrance the more it is meditated upon and broken up. We place this incense before the testimony of the tabernacle when we prove the New Testament by the testimony of the Old Testament. In a sense the New Testament stands before the Old, while it awaits the latter’s testimony in its own defence. For just as the Gospel is the testimony of the Church, so the law is the testimony of the tabernacle; and there indeed—that is, in the testimony, in the sacred books—the Lord appears to Moses, because we know God through the instruction of the Holy Scriptures. Do you wish to see God? Do you wish to know him? Do you wish to hear him speaking? Read the Gospels; read Exodus; read the books of Moses; read the apostles and prophets. For here the Lord will appear to you; here you will know his power and might. Hence the Psalmist says: “Seek the Lord and be strengthened; seek his face always” (Ps. 104:4). This incense is most holy because the Gospels possess much greater authority than the Song of Songs.

> [Note: [Col. 0363D] What the commentator says here concerning the authority of the Gospels in comparison with the Song of Songs is not to be understood with respect to the foundation of faith, which is equal in all the sacred books, but with respect to the matters treated in the Gospels. Since these are, generally speaking, clear and very frequently furnish rules for conduct, whereas the contents of the Song of Songs are exceedingly full of mystery, therefore, as regards practice, so to speak, what the Gospels provide is far more useful and more generally applicable than what is contained in the Song.]

“You shall not make such a composition for your [Col. 0364C] own uses, because it is holy to the Lord. Any man who makes something like it in order to enjoy its fragrance shall perish from his people.” Hear this, hypocrites; hear this, avaricious people: because you expound the Scriptures and preach the Gospels not for God’s praise or for the edification of souls, but for deadly purposes—for the sake of abounding in riches and filling your purses—and make this holy composition unholily for yourselves. For through the Psalmist the Lord says to you: “But God said to the sinner: Why do you recount my righteousness and take my covenant into your mouth?” (Ps. 49:16). Therefore you shall perish; you shall be cast out from the people of God, you who unlawfully enjoy the fragrance of the holy composition. For you are forbidden to make such a composition, [Col. 0364D] to spread this fragrance, and to compound this incense. And let this suffice concerning the incense.

## CHAPTER XXXI

“And the Lord spoke to Moses, saying: Behold, I have called by name Bezalel, son of Uri, son of Hur, of the tribe of Judah; and I have filled him with the Spirit of God, with wisdom, understanding, and knowledge in every kind of work, to devise whatever can be made in gold, silver, bronze, marble, precious stones, and various kinds of wood. And I have given him as a companion Oholiab, son [Col. 0365A] of Ahisamach, of the tribe of Dan; and in the heart of every skilled person I have placed wisdom, that they may make all the things which I commanded you: the tabernacle of the covenant, the ark of testimony, and the things mentioned above.” Bezalel means “shadow of God,” by whom we understand the apostles. Having all their hope beneath the shadow and protection of almighty God, they feared no heat of tribulations and adversities. The Lord called these by name because from among thousands he chose very few, as he himself says: “You did not choose me, but I chose you” (John 15:16). For one who is called by name is chosen not by chance but by providence.

These are sons of Uri, son of Hur. Hur and Uri are interpreted as “fire” or “light.” Therefore the apostles are sons of Christ, while Christ is the Son of God, because [Col. 0365B] Christ is fire from fire, light from light. They are rightly said to be of the tribe of Judah, because it is written of them: “The princes of Judah, their leaders” (Ps. 67:28). For Judah means “confession,” [that is, acknowledgment or profession]; and the apostles died in confession of Christ and for Christ. To him—that is, to Bezalel—is given as a companion Oholiab, whose name means “my protection.” His father, however, signifies bishops and teachers, whose protection is God, the Father and Creator of all. Oholiab is the son of Ahisamach, which is said to mean “strengthening his brother.” But he who strengthens his brother is Christ, who always and everywhere grants strength, power, and steadfastness to his own brother, namely the Christian. Hence he says to his disciples: [Col. 0365C] “I will not leave you or forsake you” (John 14:18); and again: “Behold, I am with you all days, even to the end of the age” (Matt. 28:20). Elsewhere he says: “Therefore be prudent as serpents and simple as doves” (Matt. 10:15). By saying these and similar things, the Lord strengthens his brothers.

Thus Oholiab is son of Ahisamach—that is, son of Christ, who, as we have said, strengthens his brothers. He is deservedly said to be of the tribe of Dan, since Dan means “judging”; for to these the Lord granted the judgment of the whole world. Therefore you bishops and teachers, you sons of him who strengthens his brothers, you sons of Ahisamach, consider that you are companions of Bezalel, whom the Lord called by name; companions of the apostles, whom [Col. 0365D] Christ first called to the faith, on whom he bestowed names, and whom he chose from all as princes of all. The Spirit of God—the Spirit of wisdom, understanding, and every kind of knowledge—filled them so that they might construct the tabernacle of God, which is the Church, with marvellous skill and ineffable teaching. You bishops, teachers, and all learned men have been given as their companions, helpers, and fellow-workers. Therefore build the house of God; apply yourselves, labour, pray, and say: “In your good pleasure deal kindly with Zion, O God, that the walls of Jerusalem may be built” (Ps. 50:19). Since we have sufficiently expounded above the tabernacle, ark, table, lampstand, and all the things enumerated here, let it suffice that we have touched upon these matters.

“And the Lord spoke to Moses, saying: [Col. 0366A] Speak to the children of Israel and say to them: See that you keep my Sabbath.” Moses has already spoken sufficiently above concerning the Sabbath, and we too have expounded it sufficiently. The observance of the Sabbath is not repeated so often without cause, nor does the Lord say without cause: “See that you keep my Sabbath.” Keep, he says, my Sabbath; keep my rest. Rest as I do; rest, I say, from evil; cease from iniquity. For this is what the Sabbath rest signifies. He celebrates the Sabbath badly who abstains from good works. For Christ too worked on the Sabbath—namely, those things which it was lawful to do on the Sabbath. The Jews misunderstood this badly and said: “This man is not from God, because he does not keep the Sabbath” (John 9:16). [Col. 0366B] It is therefore lawful to do good on the Sabbath. Whenever we sin, we violate the Sabbath; but so long as, doing good, we refrain from evil, we keep the Sabbath, rest with God, and lawfully observe the festal day. Therefore we must keep Sabbath for God not on one day with the Jew, but at every time.

“And the Lord gave Moses, after completing such words on Mount Sinai, two stone tablets of testimony, written by the finger of God.” Since the Jews were always hard, stony, and unbelieving, they deserved to receive the law written upon stones, so that at least through the hardness of the stones they might understand the hardness of their own hearts.

## CHAPTER XXXII

“When the people saw that Moses delayed coming down from the mountain, they gathered against [Col. 0366C] Aaron and said: Arise; make gods for us to go before us. For we do not know what has happened to this man Moses, who led us out of the land of Egypt.” You say, foolish and senseless people, to Aaron: “Make gods for us.” Does Aaron know how to make gods? Why do you not rather say to Aaron: “Be a god to us”? For if Aaron creates gods, Aaron is better than the gods. Wait a little until Moses comes, and he himself will teach you what God is. For Moses came, Christ came down, and taught what God is; for the people did not yet know what God was.

“And Aaron said to them: Take the golden earrings from the ears of your wives, sons, and daughters, and bring them to me. And the people did what he [Col. 0366D] commanded, bringing the earrings to Aaron. When he had received them, he fashioned them by casting and made from them a molten calf. And he said: These are your gods, Israel, who led you out of the land of Egypt.” But what are earrings except ornaments of the ears? And what are ornaments of the ears except hearing? For ears which do not hear are not adorned at all. Therefore, in making the calf, the Hebrews lose their hearing; for had they heard rightly, they would not proclaim the calf. Hence the Lord himself says: “Israel, if you listen to me, there shall be no new god in you, nor shall you worship a foreign god” (Ps. 80:10). This is what Jacob signified when, at the root of Shechem near the terebinth, he buried the earrings of his children together with the idols of the land. But what are you saying, Israel? “These are your gods who led you out of [Col. 0367A] the land of Egypt”? Did oxen open the Red Sea for you? Did oxen give you manna? “You changed your glory into the likeness of a calf that eats hay.” What is hay? Let the prophet say: “Truly the people are hay” (Isa. 40:8). Therefore this calf eats the people. Flee the calf, lest it devour you.

“When Aaron saw this, he built an altar before the Lord and cried out with the voice of a herald: ‘Tomorrow is a solemn festival of God.’ Rising early in the morning, they offered burnt offerings and peace offerings. And the people sat down to eat and drink, and rose up to play.” Aaron built an altar before the Lord, but not for the Lord. For the Lord beholds all things. This heightens the evil. Hence the Psalmist says: “Against you alone have I sinned, and done evil [Col. 0367B] before you” (Ps. 50:4). “Though you were present and saw it, I did not fear or blush to do evil.” Aaron therefore sinned greatly in giving his consent to so great a crime. Those bishops and priests also sin greatly—who were then indeed signified by Aaron—if they favour a sinful people and do not rebuke their folly.

“And the Lord spoke to Moses: Go, descend; your people, whom you led out of the land of Egypt, has sinned. They quickly departed from the way which you showed them.” The people, he says, has sinned—now no longer mine, because it chose another god for itself. Your people, he says, whom you love, for whom you always intercede, has sinned; indeed, it is neither mine nor yours, because it has despised [Col. 0367C] both me and you. “Your people” must therefore be understood ironically.

“And again the Lord said to Moses: I see that this people is stiff-necked. Leave me, that my anger may burn against them and I may destroy them; and I will make you into a great nation.” This people, he says, is hard, proud, and stubbornly stiff-necked; it can neither be restrained nor held in check by the reins of law and righteousness. Leave me, then; do not intercede for it. Let your prayer now cease, for it holds me back; it turns aside my indignation; standing between us, it does not permit me to strike and destroy them. We must observe, therefore, how powerful are the prayers of the saints, which alone restrain God and appease his indignation and wrath. Moses, however, seeking not his own glory but being concerned for the people, prayed to the Lord, saying: [Col. 0367D] “Why, Lord, does your fury burn against your people? Let your wrath rest; remember Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, from whom these people derive their origin.” And the Lord was appeased and did not destroy his people.

“And Moses returned from the mountain, carrying the two tablets of testimony, written by the hand of God on both sides and made by the work of God.” The writing of God was also engraved upon the tablets. Thus they are called tablets of testimony because they testify what God wills and does not will, and give us testimony of his will. For the Apostle says: “I did not know that covetousness”—that is, he means, was sin—

> [Note: [Col. 0367] The mutilated passage here in the edition is supplied from the Laurentian manuscript.]

> “—unless the law said: ‘You shall not covet your neighbour’s [Col. 0368A] property’” (Rom. 7:8).

The law therefore gives testimony that covetousness is sin. Let us therefore believe the testimony of the law, which, since it always speaks truth and never lies, is not undeservedly called testimony. For no one dares contradict this testimony: the authority of the law is final proof. It was written by the hand of God, the work of God, and the writing of God; nothing in it is human. It is wholly divine, wholly composed with God dictating and writing; therefore it is full of truth and authority. Why, then, are the tablets written on both sides, except that the testimonies of the law may be read and understood in two ways? For the law has a twofold meaning. It follows:

“When he came near to the camp, he saw the calf and the dances.” In anger he threw the tablets from his hand [Col. 0368B] and broke them at the foot of the mountain. Moses is angry and breaks the tablets; the people sin and the tablets are broken; the people sin and the law is destroyed. Why was this done? For if Moses had not broken the tablets, he would not have spared the people. And what good was it that he had appeased God by prayer, if he himself then killed them by the command of the law? For the law says: “Whoever sacrifices to gods shall be put to death, except to the Lord alone” (Exod. 22:20). Therefore he did not wish to come to the sinful people with the tablets, with the rigour of the law; rather, he broke the tablets, set aside the law, and spared the sinful people. Whenever, therefore, out of regard for mercy, a bishop pities some sinner and fears that he may fall into worse things, then in a sense he breaks the tablets and lays aside [Col. 0368C] the severity of the law. Indeed, I do not think it a great sin thus to break the tablets and sometimes to abandon the law’s strictness for the sake of mercy. Hence Moses is nowhere reproved by the Lord for breaking the tablets.

But hear what follows: “Taking the calf which they had made, he burned it and ground it into powder, scattered it in water, and gave the children of Israel drink from it.” This shows at whom Moses was angry: he was angry with the calf and tried to destroy the sin. Therefore he ground the calf into powder, put it into water, and gave it as drink to the children of Israel. But why did he put it into water? Why did he give the children of Israel drink from it? Perhaps so that they might drink the calf as hay, because the calf eats hay. The Jews drink, however, because they are greedy and [Col. 0368D] avaricious; they drink the gold of the idol because they are idolaters and sacrilegious. Thus this deadly drink, this teaching of idolatry, penetrated their inward parts so deeply that they could scarcely ever be torn away and separated from the worship of idols. This calf and this drink of the calf signified the calves of Samaria and the idolatry of the ten tribes. For the ten tribes became drunk with the powder of the calf—that is, with the teaching of Jeroboam’s idolatry in Samaria—when scarcely two tribes in Judaea gave heed to the law and the prophets.

“When Moses saw that the people had been stripped bare (for Aaron had stripped them for the shame of their filth and had set them naked among their enemies), standing in the gate of the camp, he said: ‘Whoever belongs to the Lord, join me.’” After Moses, [Col. 0369A] as was fitting, rebuked Aaron for his sin, and did not wish so great a crime to go wholly unpunished—especially because, as the Apostle says, “All these things happened to them in figure, but were written for our correction” (1 Cor. 10:11)—he commanded each person to kill his brother, friend, and neighbour. And on that day twenty-three thousand persons fell. For the people had been stripped of the protection and weapons of God, and had been set naked among their enemies because of the shame of their filth—that is, the calf which they had worshipped. Enemies lived all around them; if they had known that this people had sinned so, offended the Lord so, was so bereft of strength, and lacked God’s armour and every aid, they could easily have destroyed them all. Aaron had stripped them of God’s protection and weapons because he had consented to their making of the idol.

[Col. 0369B] Therefore Moses commands those who belonged to the Lord, who had not worshipped the idol, who had not lost their weapons, to gird themselves with swords and kill their brothers and neighbours. When they promptly fulfilled the command, Moses said to them: “You have consecrated your hands today to the Lord, every one of you against his son and his brother, that a blessing may be given to you.” A blessing is rightly given to them, and their hands and works are consecrated to the Lord and by the Lord, because they obey Moses, avenge the injuries done to God, and, led by zeal for God in killing idolaters, spare neither sons nor brothers. This is what the sons of Levi did, who are recorded in Genesis as having avenged the violation of their sister Dinah. Moses then returned [Col. 0369C] to the Lord and said: “I beseech you, Lord, this people has committed a great sin and made gods of gold for themselves. Either forgive them this offence, or, if you will not do so, blot me out of the book which you have written.” The Lord answered him: “Whoever sins against me, I shall blot him out of my book.” Moses speaks thus as a man; out of an excessive affection of love he says: “Either spare them, or destroy me together with them.” The Apostle likewise says: “I too wished to be anathema from Christ for my brothers” (Rom. 9:3). Hence even to this day King Hezekiah is reproved by the Jews because he prayed only for himself and for all the people, saying: “The word of the Lord is good; let peace and truth be in my days” (4 Kings 20:19).

[Col. 0369D] But when he says, “Blot me out of the book which you have written,” this is to be understood as: “Blot me out of your remembrance.” For the names of all the saints are written, as it were in a book, in the mind of God; unless they sin unto death, they cannot be erased from it. This is the book of life, in which one who is written lives eternally and without end. Hence the Lord says: “Whoever sins against me, I shall blot him out of my book” (Exod. 32:33). Moses therefore confidently said: “Blot me out of your book,” because he knew that he had committed no sin and was not ignorant that God can do nothing unjustly. It follows:

“But go now and lead this people to the place of which I spoke to you. My angel shall go before you; but on the day of vengeance I shall visit this sin of theirs. Therefore the Lord struck the people because of the guilt of the calf which Aaron made.” When the Lord struck the people [Col. 0370A] because of the guilt of the calf—unless perhaps this means what is read above, that twenty-three thousand fell in one day—is nowhere stated here. The day of vengeance may be understood either in this life or in the next.

## CHAPTER XXXIII

“And the Lord spoke to Moses: Go, ascend from this place, you and your people, whom you led out of the land of Egypt, to the land which I swore to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, saying: ‘To your seed I shall give it’; and I shall send my angel before you. For I shall not go up with you, because the people is stiff-necked, lest perhaps I destroy you on the way.” I shall send, he says, my angel before you; but you shall no longer have my own presence as you have had until now. For you have corrupted yourself by denying me and worshipping the [Col. 0370B] calf; you have committed a most grievous sin. But this is said to Moses in the person of the whole people. He gives the reason why he does not wish to go before them: “Because,” he says, “the people is stiff-necked; and I cannot bear those who are proud and carry their necks high. Thus it may easily happen that, if I am present with you, I shall destroy you on the way.”

But what is this, that Truth speaks thus? What is this, that he now promises not to do what he will do? The words of God are conditional: when he is sometimes moved by the prayers of the saints, he seems to act contrary to what he had said. Hence, although he now says to the people, “I shall not go up with you,” he nevertheless later goes up with them. Thus he goes up with them and does not go up with them: with them, because his substance is not changed; [Col. 0370C] not with them, because through repentance the people becomes other than it was. Hence it is added: “When the people heard this most grievous word, they mourned, and no one put on his customary adornment.” For in a sense this penitent people mourning was another people; the people which worshipped the calf was another. Therefore the Lord went up with this people, but not with that one. It is true, then, that he both went up with it and did not go up with it.

“And the Lord said to Moses: Say to the children of Israel: You are a stiff-necked people. Once I shall go up in the midst of you and destroy you. Now put off your adornment, that I may know what I shall do to you. Therefore the children of Israel put off their adornment at Mount Horeb.” For the Lord often took vengeance upon that people and often afflicted it with many tribulations, delivering them now to the Philistines, now to the Assyrians, now to the Chaldeans, [Col. 0370D] and now to other nations. Yet he quickly had mercy upon them: he did not destroy them, but brought them back to their homeland. Therefore, when it says here, “Once I shall go up in the midst of you and destroy you,” this may be understood of both comings of our Saviour. In his first coming he destroyed them by depriving them of power, kingdom, priesthood, and prophetic oracle; moreover, by delivering them to the Roman army, he subjected them to all nations. But how he will destroy them in the second coming requires no exposition. The children of Israel put off their adornment and clothed themselves in garments of penitence so as to soften God’s indignation. They did this at Mount Horeb, “Horeb” being interpreted “raven,” a colour quite familiar to penitents. When he says, “That I may know what I shall do to you,” it means: “That I may make you know my will and what I shall do to you now that you repent.”

[Col. 0371A] “Moses also took the tabernacle and pitched it far outside the camp, and called its name the tabernacle of the covenant.” If this is understood of the tabernacle which Bezalel and Oholiab made, it is an anticipation; otherwise Moses pitched the tabernacle before the tabernacle had been made, which cannot be. He pitched it outside the camp because salvation is far from sinners. It is called the tabernacle of the covenant because there God established a covenant with the people. There too the law was laid down, in which the whole covenant was contained; there judgments are delivered, questions resolved, and the Lord speaks with Moses; there the pillar of cloud is seen by all. [Col. 0371B] But what is the pillar of cloud except the incarnate Word? For just as the Lord spoke and was seen in the cloud, so God spoke and was seen in a human being. They saw the cloud; they saw the humanity; they heard the voice, yet did not recognise God. For had they recognised him, they would never have crucified the Lord of glory. Of this cloud it is said through the prophet: “Behold, he shall ascend upon a light cloud and enter Egypt” (Isa. 19:1); by this we understand that flesh which Christ took from the Virgin Mary.

“But the Lord spoke to Moses face to face, as a man is accustomed to speak with his friend.” He spoke face to face and present to present: he was asked and answered; [Col. 0371C] they heard and understood one another in turn. For this is how a human being speaks to his friend. Moses did not otherwise see the face of God, who is certainly invisible and cannot be seen with fleshly eyes. When Moses returned to the camp, his minister Joshua, son of Nun, a youth, did not depart from the tabernacle. Neither does Joshua depart from the tabernacle nor Jesus from the Church: “Behold,” he says, “I am with you all days, even to the end of the age” (Matt. 28:20). This is the youth; this is the son of one year; this is that little one who is greater in the kingdom of heaven; this is the minister of Moses; this is he who came to minister, not to be ministered to, and to give his life as a ransom for many. Hence he himself says to Moses—that is, to his disciples, who are now signified by Moses: [Col. 0371D] “But I am in the midst of you as one who ministers” (Luke 22:27).

“Moses said to the Lord: You command me to lead this people out, yet do not tell me whom you will send with me, especially since you have said: ‘I know you by name, and you have found favour before me.’” Since he had said above, “My angel shall go before you,” Moses asks that the angel himself be named and more expressly identified. For one angel is set over each nation by God. Hence Michael the archangel is said to belong especially to the Jewish nation, as is written in Daniel: “There is no one who helps me in all these things except Michael the archangel, your prince” (Dan. 10:21). He is speaking to the Jews. [Col. 0372A]

But what does he mean when he says: “Especially since you have said, ‘I know you by name’”? For it is no great matter to know someone by name: who is there whom God does not know by name? If, then, he knows all by name, why did he say to Moses: “I know you by name”? What does “I know you” mean? What does “by name” mean? “I know you” sometimes means “I love you.” Thus the Lord will say to certain people at judgment: “Amen, I say to you, I do not know you” (Matt. 25:12), that is, “I do not love you.” Thus in this passage, “I know you” means “I love you.” How can this be proved? By the phrase “by name.” Consider your name: why are you called Moses? Certainly because you were [Col. 0372B] taken from water.

> [Note: [Col. 0371] What is added here has been taken from the Laurentian manuscript; the Cassinese manuscript supplies it as well.]

But why, when all the Hebrew infants were perishing in the Egyptian waters, were you alone taken up so that you might not perish? Who did this, if not I? Interpret your name, therefore, and from the name itself you will understand that I know you, that I have loved you, and that from the beginning you found favour before me.

“If, therefore, I have found favour in your sight, show me your face, that I may know you and find favour before your eyes. Look upon your people, this nation.” Show me your face, he says, so that thereby I may understand that I have found favour before your eyes. Show me, that I may know you, see you, and understand you. What does this mean? For if the Lord spoke with Moses face to face, why does Moses desire that God’s face be shown to him? It is one thing to speak face to face and another to see a face. One can speak face to face with someone and neither see nor [Col. 0372C] be seen by him; this often happens at night. Therefore Moses spoke face to face and personally with the Lord; yet there was something—indeed, very much—that he desired to know and see concerning God. For it belongs properly to God neither to be seen nor understood in this life.

“And the Lord said: My face shall go before you, and I shall give you rest.” The face of the Lord goes before the person whom the face of the Lord follows: the Psalmist says, “Seek his face always” (Ps. 102:4). If, then, it always follows and always goes before, it is never found and never fully seen. And Moses said: “Unless you yourself go before us, do not lead us out from this place. For how shall it be known that I and your people have found favour in your sight, unless you walk with us, so that we may be glorified above all the peoples who dwell upon the earth?” [Col. 0372D] As though he said: “Go before us and help us, not through an angel, not through a minister, not through a messenger, but through yourself.” It is very remarkable that Moses speaks as though God were not personally present everywhere, and asks for God’s presence. Although God is personally present everywhere, he does not appear present to those whose prayers and cries he does not hear. Moses therefore asks that God may so go before the people, and be so personally present always, that he may always assist them in all their needs.

[Col. 0373A] “And the Lord said to Moses: I shall do this thing also which you have spoken. For you have found favour before me, and I know you yourself by name.” We expounded this above and showed how he both goes before them in person and does not go before them. “And Moses said: Show me your glory. He answered: I shall show you all good, and I shall call in the name of the Lord before you; and I shall have mercy on whom I shall will, and I shall be gracious to whom it pleases me. Again he said: You cannot see my face, for no human being shall see me and live.” It is clear, then, what Moses sought; had he obtained it, he could not have lived. The Lord therefore provided better for Moses than Moses did for himself: “I, the Lord,” he says, “shall show you all good. I shall [Col. 0373B] show myself to you—not now, indeed, but at some time.”

For it is written in the Gospel that, when the Lord was transfigured on the mountain, Moses and Elijah appeared speaking with him; then the Lord showed Moses all good. Then too the Lord called in the name of the Lord before him. We have this from the blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, for he said: “Lord, it is good for us to be here” (Matt. 17:4). “Here,” he says, “is the good state of being, where you have shown Moses yourself, who are all good.” But what follows—“I shall have mercy on whom I shall will, and I shall be gracious to whom it pleases me” (Exod. 33:19)—means this: “You pray for your people; you entreat for persons whose hearts and thoughts you do not know. ‘I know whom I have chosen; I shall have mercy on whom I shall will’” (John 13:18), for I will nothing but [Col. 0373C] good.

“And again: ‘Behold,’ he says, ‘there is a place beside me; you shall stand upon the rock. And when my glory passes by, I will place you in a cleft of the rock, and I will protect you with my right hand until I have passed by. Then I will take away my hand, and you shall see my back; but you cannot see my face.’” This may perhaps be understood literally: that Moses, placed somewhere, learned something more subtle concerning the Lord’s majesty. And because he says, “You shall see my back,” perhaps he showed him the mystery of the Incarnation. Moses also saw God’s back at that time when, on the mountain, with the Lord transfigured, he deserved to behold the incarnate Word. This is called his “back,” because it occurred in the latter time and in the final age. [Col. 0373D]

Allegorically, however, by Moses we understand the apostles, who both spoke with the Lord and were called friends of God by the Lord himself. Moses stands upon the rock; and the rock was Christ, because the holy apostles were established and founded in faith in Christ. They are placed not only upon the rock, but also in the cleft of the rock, because, standing at the entrance of faith and at the gateway of the Church, they introduce others into the Church and into faith in Christ. For faith is called a rock. Thus, when Peter said to the Lord, “You are the Christ, the Son of the living God” (Matt. 16:16), the Lord immediately confirmed his faith, saying: “And I say to you that you are Peter” (ibid., 18), that is, upon this faith of yours, by which you call me the Son of the living God, [Col. 0374A] “I will build my Church” (ibid.).

Therefore Peter, together with the other apostles and Peter himself, was in the cleft of the rock—that is, at the gate and entrance of faith—since the confession of faith was proclaimed by them, upon which the whole Church was founded. The Lord protected these with his right hand; he fortified them with his strength and power, because, as he himself says, he lost none of them (John 17:12). And when the Lord passed by and, going up from the Mount of Olives, ascended into heaven, lifting up his hands—for it is thus written in the Gospel, that he was borne into heaven with uplifted hands (Luke 24:50)—he showed them his back: he showed them his glorified humanity and flesh. For these were his “back,” since afterward he no longer associated bodily with them. They saw his [Col. 0374B] back because, as long as he could be seen, they followed him with their eyes as he went. Hence the angels say to them: “Men of Galilee, why do you stand looking into heaven? This Jesus, who has been taken up from you into heaven, will so come as you saw him going into heaven” (Acts 2:11).

But they did not see his face, because it was not revealed to them in what manner “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God” (John 1:2). For this is the face of God.

## CHAPTER XXXIV

“And afterward: ‘Cut for yourself,’ he says, ‘two stone tablets like the former ones, and I will write upon them the words which the tablets that you broke contained.’” The breaking of the tablets was the abolition of the Law according to the letter; their being written again signifies the New Testament. For if it is understood spiritually, it is written holily in both Testaments.

“Be ready in the morning, so that you may immediately ascend Mount Sinai and stand with me on the summit of the mountain. Let no one ascend with you, and let no one be seen anywhere on the whole mountain. Let not even oxen or sheep graze opposite it. Therefore he cut two stone tablets like those which had been before, and, rising by night, ascended Mount Sinai as the Lord had commanded him, carrying with him the two tablets.” That Moses signifies the apostles is clear. Thus Moses alone ascends the mountain to receive the Law, and no one is seen on the whole mountain, because at the beginning of the Church’s birth, the apostles alone, called by the Lord when no one had yet embraced his faith, ascended Mount Zion, the mountain of faith; and they received faith in Christ not on stone tablets, but in faithful hearts. Yet the fact that Moses was alone on the mountain, that no one was seen on the entire mountain, and that neither oxen nor sheep grazed opposite it, signified that the Law given there, veiled for a time beneath the letter, would be understood by either none or few. [Col. 0374C–D]

“And when the Lord descended in a cloud, Moses stood with him, invoking the name of the Lord. As he passed before him, he said: ‘Ruling Lord God, merciful and gracious, patient and abundant in mercy, and true, who preserves mercy unto thousands; who removes iniquity, wickedness, and sins; and before you no one is innocent by himself. You repay the iniquity of fathers to their children and grandchildren, to the third and fourth generation.’ And Moses quickly bowed down to the earth and worshipped, and said: ‘If I have found favor in your sight, Lord, I beseech you, go with us—for this is a stiff-necked people—and remove our iniquities and sins, and possess us.’”

“No one,” he says, “is innocent before you by himself,” because not even an infant of one day is without sin. Hence the Psalmist says: “For I was conceived in iniquities, and in sins my mother bore me” (Ps. 50:6). One therefore becomes innocent through you who is not innocent in himself, because you alone can make clean one conceived from unclean seed. [Col. 0375A]

But the Lord repays the fathers’ iniquity to the children if the children do not depart from their fathers’ iniquity. Otherwise, “The son shall not bear the iniquity of the father” (Ezek. 18:20). Moses asks the Lord to go with the people and to possess them, because, being stiff-necked, they need an owner and ruler. [Col. 0375B]

“The Lord answered: ‘I will make a covenant, and, before all who see, I will perform signs such as have never been seen on earth or among any nations, so that the people among whom you are may behold the terrible work which I shall do. Observe all that I command you today.’” By the covenant which he promises to make, we must understand these commandments or precepts set forth below. Let anyone who wishes to know the Lord’s signs and terrible works read the other books of Moses. [Col. 0375C]

“I will drive out before you the Amorite, the Canaanite, the Hittite, the Perizzite, the Hivite, and the Jebusite. Beware lest you ever make friendship with the inhabitants of that land, which would be your ruin; rather, destroy their altars, break their images, and cut down their groves. Do not worship a foreign god. The Lord—his name is Jealous—is a jealous God.”

The devil, who is also envious and does not cease to persecute God’s people, is called jealous and emulous: for he loves in order to destroy; he emulates in order to kill. Hence the Apostle says to certain people: “They are zealous for you, but not rightly; rather, they wish to deceive you, so that they may glory in your flesh” (Gal. 4:17). [Col. 0375D] The matters that follow have already been explained above and require no exposition.

“And when Moses came down from Mount Sinai, he held the two stone tablets of the testimony and did not know that his face was horned from his converse with the word of the Lord. But Aaron and the children of Israel, seeing Moses’ horned face, were afraid to come near. Called back by him, Aaron and the leaders of the synagogue returned; and after he had spoken, all the children of Israel also came to him, and he commanded them all that he had heard from the Lord on Mount Sinai.”

Moses, he says, was horned and did not know it; his face shone, and he did not know it. [Col. 0376A] Whence are these horns, Moses? Whence this great splendor, which the people cannot bear, if not from fellowship with God’s word? This splendor is that of the letter: the understanding of the letter alone still shines in your face. If, then, the understanding of the letter shines so brightly, what will the understanding of the Spirit do? This is what the Apostle says: “For if the ministry of death, inscribed in letters upon stones, came in glory, so that the children of Israel could not look upon Moses’ face because of the glory of his countenance, which is being abolished, how much more shall the ministry of the Spirit be in glory?” (2 Cor. 3:7).

For that which was glorified was not glorified in this respect, because of the surpassing glory. So great is the glory of the New Testament; so great is the splendor of those who understand the Scriptures spiritually—“those who have been taught shall shine like the brightness of the firmament”—that what was glorified in the Old Testament appears wholly unglorified. What, indeed, do the Jews understand clearly? “For blindness has happened in part to Israel” (Rom. 11:15). Moses calls the people, and those who fear to approach recognize his voice, because the voice contains only the sound of the letter. They fear his face, because where the eyes are, there is splendor; there is spiritual understanding, gleaming like the sun’s rays. They therefore return to Moses; they return to the letter that kills; they return to the sound of the voice, because, fearing the shining face and spiritual understanding, they had previously refused to come near. Hence it continues:

“When he had finished speaking, he put a veil over his face.” He put a veil over his face because they were afraid to see it. This is what the Apostle says: “Even to this day, when Moses is read, a veil is placed before the eyes of the Jews [Note: Col. 0375: The Vulgate reads: ‘a veil is placed over their heart’]” (2 Cor. 3:15). [Col. 0376C] For when Moses—that is, the Law of Moses—is read before the Jews’ eyes, the veil of the letter is placed upon them; looking only at the veil and attending only to the letter, they cannot see what lies beneath the veil. For their eyes are weak, and they fear to see the splendor. But we, beholding the glory of the Lord with unveiled face, desire always to look not so much upon the veil as upon that which is beneath the veil.

## CHAPTER XXXV

“Therefore, when the whole multitude of the children of Israel had been assembled, he said to them: ‘These are the things which the Lord commanded to be done: you shall work for six days; the seventh day shall be holy to you. It is the Sabbath, the Lord’s rest. Whoever does work on it shall be put to death. You shall not kindle a fire in any of your dwellings on the Sabbath day.’”

We have already said much above concerning the Sabbath, and it is superfluous always to say the same thing; but to seek a new exposition of it every time seems superstitious. Let no one kindle a fire on the Sabbath; let no one sow quarrels and discords, by which the faithful people may be inflamed to anger and fury. But I give thanks to almighty God, who has brought me thus far, as I think, by a straight path through this dark and very dense forest. For everything that follows [Col. 0377A] to the end of the book has already been both narrated and explained above. To almighty God be honor and [Col. 0378A] glory, power and dominion, now and always and unto all ages of ages. Amen.

[Col. 0377] Here Saint Bruno closes his Commentary on Exodus and omits the five remaining chapters.

# THE EXPOSITION OF LEVITICUS BEGINS

[Col. 0377]

## ADMONITION

Since the exposition of the following book of Leviticus, published by Dom Maurus Marchesius, is very corrupt in many places and much inferior in Latin style and learning to the commentary communicated to us from a Cassinese manuscript of excellent quality by the most reverend Dom Thomas Capomatius, the present abbot of Monte Cassino, we judged it fitting to enrich our collection with the latter. Therefore we have taken the first six chapters from it entire, and have partly supplemented and partly corrected the rest.

## PREFACE

[Col. 0377B]

After the exposition of Genesis and Exodus, let us proceed, in the order in which they were written, under Jesus’ guidance, to Leviticus. For the explanation of this work I invoke God the almighty Father and his Son Jesus Christ together with the Holy Spirit, and humbly entreat that he may deign to fill my mind also, for the exposition of this book, with the same Spirit by which he filled Moses’ mind for writing.

In this volume Moses—or rather, the Holy Spirit through Moses—treats most fully of sacrifices. If these are understood spiritually, without doubt sins are removed, God is appeased, and pardon is granted to sinners. Although all Jewish sacrifices in some fashion foreshadow Christ’s passion and death, some properly and spiritually signify that great and unique sacrifice which Jesus himself, victim and priest, offered to God the Father upon the altar of the cross; some signify that sacrifice which is daily performed by priests in the Church in remembrance of him; some the sufferings of the holy martyrs; others the mortification of our flesh itself; and still others contrition of heart and spirit.

For the burnt offerings of those animals whose blood is carried by the high priest into the Holy Places, and whose flesh is not eaten but burned outside the camp, properly proclaim Christ’s passion, as the Apostle testifies. For he says: “For the bodies of those animals whose blood is carried into the Holy Places by the high priest are burned outside the camp” (Heb. 13:11). [Col. 0377C] Explaining this, he immediately added: “So also Jesus, that he might sanctify the people, suffered outside the gate” (ibid., 12). Since, God willing, we shall say much concerning these matters below, it does not seem necessary to say more at present. Let us now come to the words of the book itself.

## CHAPTER I

“And the Lord called Moses and spoke to him from the tabernacle of testimony, saying: ‘Speak to the children of Israel, and say to them: Any man among you who offers a victim to the Lord from cattle—that is, offering victims from oxen and sheep—if his offering is a burnt offering, he shall offer an unblemished male from the herd at the entrance of the tabernacle of testimony, to make the Lord favorable to himself.’”

This man who offers victims to make the Lord favorable to himself seems to me to be the Christian people, who do not cease daily to sacrifice, in remembrance of Christ, a calf from the herd of the patriarchs, not only upon the visible [Note: Col. 0377D: Another Cassinese manuscript reads: “of the Church.”] altar but also upon the invisible altar of the mind. Therefore a male and unblemished calf, taken from Moses’ herd, is commanded to be offered, because the Jewish people sacrificed to the Lord for the sins of the whole world Christ our Lord, “who committed no sin, nor was deceit found in his mouth” (1 Pet. 2:22), coming in the flesh from the flock of patriarchs and prophets. [Col. 0378B–C]

Thus Moses, the Jewish people, and the Church sacrifice one and the same calf: Moses by signifying, the Jews by sinning, the Church by commemorating. But since not every offering is a burnt offering, it says: “If his offering is a burnt offering.” For when the whole offering was burned, it was called a holocaust. The calf is led to the entrance of the tabernacle of testimony because Christ our Lord also was seized by the Jews and then led to the high priest, who lived before the entrance and in the courts of the temple itself.

But since we too sacrifice this calf, it seems necessary to say how it is also led by us to the entrance of the tabernacle of testimony. The Apostle indicates that we are God’s tabernacle, saying: “For the temple of God is holy, which you are” (1 Cor. 3:17). If therefore we are the temple and tabernacle of God, what is the entrance of this tabernacle? I understand faith to be its entrance, through which Christ enters the tabernacle of our breast, as through a door. Hence the Lord himself says: “Behold, I stand at the door and knock. If anyone opens the door to me, I will enter in to him and dine with him, and he with me” (Rev. 3:20). [Col. 0378D–0379A]

Therefore we offer the calf at the entrance of the tabernacle when we read Christ’s passion in our mind and believe it by faith. For the Lord himself says: “Do this in remembrance of me” (1 Cor. 11:24). Hence it continues:

“And he shall lay his hands upon the head of the victim, and it shall be accepted and shall avail for his expiation.” It is difficult to understand this of the Jews, for whom Christ’s death was not beneficial but harmful. But let us [Note: Col. 0379D: Another Cassinese manuscript reads: “let us lead and offer.”] lead our calf to the entrance of the tabernacle; indeed, by believing, eating, and drinking, let us bring him into the very tabernacle of our breast. Let us lay our hands upon his head; let us touch him with the hands of faith; by touching let us believe, and by believing say: “My Lord and my God” (John 20:28). For this is how faith touches; thus the Apostle Thomas is said to have touched. To touch is to believe.

Blessed John, touching his head, said: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God” (John 1:1). Believe that Christ is God, and you touch his head: “For,” says the Apostle, “the head of Christ is God” (1 Cor. 11:4). Believe that he is man, and you touch his feet. If, therefore, you have touched him in this way—if you believe Christ to be the head and beginning of all creatures—your victim will be accepted, and your offering will avail for your expiation. [Col. 0379B]

First, then, touch the calf’s head; afterward sacrifice it, lest, when you sacrifice Christ as though he were a calf, you forget that he is God and man. You see the child Jesus; you see a calf one year old. Do not regard his age; do not say with the Jew: “You are not yet forty years old.” Touch the calf’s head; believe in his divinity. Say with the evangelist: “In the beginning was the Word.” For the divinity of this calf is Christ’s head. Since, therefore, it has been said what the tabernacle is, what the entrance of the tabernacle is, what the calf is, and what it is to lay hands upon the calf’s head, it remains now for the priests to come, pour out his blood, skin him, cut up his limbs, arrange them upon the altar, place fire beneath them, and accomplish the whole burnt offering for the benefit and advantage of those making the offering. All this pertained to the priest alone.

For this is what it says: “And the sons of Aaron, the priests, shall offer [Col. 0379C] his blood and pour it around the altar, which is before the entrance of the tabernacle; and, when the victim’s skin has been removed, they shall cut its limbs into pieces and place fire upon the altar, arranging a pile of wood beforehand; and they shall arrange upon it the pieces that have been cut up, namely the head and all that adheres to the liver, after the entrails and feet have been washed with water. The priest shall burn them upon the altar as a burnt offering and a sweet-smelling odor.”

Who, then, are these sons of Aaron to whom these special offices are assigned? To believe, to touch the calf, to lead it to the entrance of the tabernacle, to put its blood upon each doorpost, to eat Christ’s flesh, and to drink his blood: these things have been granted to all the faithful. But to remove the victim’s skin, cut its limbs into pieces, and do the rest that follows has been specially granted to bishops and priests.

Bishops and priests, therefore, are sons of Aaron—of that Aaron whose name is most fittingly interpreted “strong mountain”: “A mountain curdled, a rich mountain, a mountain in which it pleased God to dwell” (Ps. 67:16). You, bishops and priests, are sons of this Aaron. Come, then, and sacrifice; pour out the calf’s blood around the altar. For what else do you do whenever you give us to drink the blood consecrated through your ministry, except that, like Aaron’s sons, you pour out the blood around the altar [Col. 0380A–B] of our heart?

You remove the victim’s skin when, taking away the veil of the letter, you expound spiritually the things that remained hidden. You cut the limbs into pieces when you explain, part by part and by individual meanings, the mysteries of the whole victim. You place fire beneath the altar because by expounding all these things you kindle our hearts to love God. Such fire kindled the hearts of those who heard the Lord himself expounding the Scriptures, and said: “Was not our heart burning within us while he spoke to us on the way and opened the Scriptures to us?” (Luke 24:32).

For this fire to burn, it is first necessary to arrange a pile of wood upon the altar. By these pieces of wood we understand faith, hope, patience, humility, and the remaining abundance of virtues. Unless this wood has first been arranged upon the altar of the heart, the fire of charity and the love of God cannot burn [Note: Col. 0379: The same Cassinese manuscript reads: “And the love of God cannot burn there.”]. But after the altar—that is, the hearts of the hearers—has been warmed by the fire of charity, then let the priests arrange above it the pieces that have been cut up, namely the head and all that adheres to the liver. For divine mysteries should be revealed to those whose hearts already seem inflamed with the desire to hear and to act. [Col. 0380C]

Bishops must first arrange the calf’s head upon the altar, because in their sermons they should teach hearers before all else that Christ is man and God, the head and beginning of all creatures. Indeed, narrating in order his passion, resurrection, and ascension, they should arrange them in Christian minds as upon an altar. Blessed John followed this order of preaching: beginning from the head, he first treated Christ’s divinity. “In the beginning,” he says, “was the Word, and the Word was with God” (John 1:1). Afterwards he came down to his humanity and works, as though to the feet. These are the calf’s limbs: so they should be cut up, arranged, expounded, and placed upon the altar of heart and mind.

But what should we understand by the things adhering to the liver—namely its fat and richness—except that exceeding mercy and compassion of our Savior, by which he prayed even for his enemies, saying: “Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing” (Luke 23:34)? [Col. 0380D–0381A] This fat, this richness, healed and cured our wounds. Of it the Psalmist says: “May the Lord remember all your sacrifice, and may your burnt offering be made rich” (Ps. 19:4). These things are announced to us so that we may be more inflamed with love of God and more earnestly moved to implore Christ’s compassion and mercy.

What, then, is the meaning of what follows in the passage: “the feet and entrails having been washed with water”? Must we wash Christ’s feet and entrails, he who is now in heaven, to whom nothing foul or unclean ever adhered, who committed no sin and in whose mouth no deceit was found, and who was the author and perfecter of all purity? Certainly all these things are true and infallible. Yet the Jews do not believe them, but judged and still judge him as a sinner and a blasphemer. Therefore we must wash and, in some fashion, cleanse him: that is, we must proclaim him holy, innocent, and just.

But how shall we rightly prove all this and persuade the Jews of this truth? He himself teaches us: “Which of you,” he says, “will convict me of sin? For the ruler of this world comes, and has nothing in me” (John 8:46). When holy preachers arrange and set forth these and similar matters in this way, and good hearers understand and believe them, a burnt offering of fragrance and sweetness is made to God. [Col. 0381B] It follows:

“But if the offering is a burnt offering from small livestock, from sheep or goats, he shall offer a one-year-old animal without blemish, and he shall sacrifice it at the side of the altar that faces north before the Lord; and the sons of Aaron shall pour its blood around the altar,” and the rest, as above.

For we understand the same thing by the calf, the lamb, and the kid. Christ is a calf because he is the greater victim; a lamb because he is gentle, innocent, and meek; and a kid because of the likeness of sinful flesh. He is one year old and without blemish: chaste, pure, and without sin. The fact that the altar faces north signifies that our hearts ought always to be watchful against the devil’s snares. “For evils shall be opened from the north upon all the inhabitants of the earth” (Jer. 1:14). But God shall come from the south; the devil has placed his seat in the north. [Note: Col. 0381D: What follows is found in another Cassinese manuscript.] The remaining matters [Col. 0381D] have not been expounded because they were just now expounded above in the calf’s burnt offering.

“But if the burnt offering to the Lord is from birds, from turtledoves or young pigeons, the priest shall offer them upon the altar; and, twisting the head back toward the neck and tearing the place of the wound open, he shall cause the blood to run down upon the base of the altar.”

It is fitting that, after Christ’s mysteries, this passage should show how we too ought to sacrifice and offer ourselves to the Lord. By the turtledove and pigeon we understand chastity of soul and body, and patience. For the turtledove is a most chaste animal, keeping unbreakable fidelity to its companion whether alive or dead; the pigeon, however, lacks gall and bitterness. Thus the turtledove fittingly signifies chastity, and the pigeon patience.

Therefore the priest offers upon the altar of our heart a turtledove and pigeon when he instructs us both to possess and to preserve chastity and patience. The great priest Jesus offered a turtledove when he said: “Let your loins be girded” (Luke 12:35); and a pigeon when he spoke of patience, saying: “In your patience you shall possess your souls” (Luke 21:19). We therefore possess a turtledove, we possess a pigeon; indeed, we ourselves have now become turtledoves and pigeons—provided, however, that we keep both chastity and patience. [Col. 0382A]

The head being twisted back toward the neck signifies that one who has become chaste and patient ought also to be modest and humble. Such persons should not walk with neck held high, but with head humbly bowed. Then, by tearing open the place of the wound, he causes the blood to run down upon the base of the altar, because a holy person devoted to God does not hide his sin but casts it forth. He then makes the blood run down around the altar when he does not put the remembrance of his sins away from his own heart, but, like a turtledove and pigeon, does not cease to groan and weep for those sins. Thus the Psalmist made blood run down around the altar of his heart when he said: “For I know my iniquity, and my sin is always before me” (Ps. 50:4). That blood signifies sin is so customary an interpretation that it needs no examples. It follows:

[Col. 0382C] “But he shall cast the crop of its throat and its feathers near the altar, toward the eastern side, in the place where ashes are customarily poured out.” What is signified by the crop of the throat except gluttony of the belly? What by the feathers except lightness of conduct, pride, and instability of mind? It is good for a person to cast these away and reject them. But where should they be cast?
