Near the altar, for the altar is the heart, as has often been said. What is separated from the heart is consigned to forgetfulness. Therefore these things are rightly cast not upon the altar but near the altar, so that, forgetting them, a person may not return to them again.

They are commanded to be cast toward the eastern side, so that, forgetting the things behind with the Apostle, we may stretch forward toward what lies before. For we always travel from sunrise toward sunset. Whatever we do not take with us toward sunset, we leave behind our backs by casting it toward the eastern side. Sunset is the end of life. Let these things be poured out in the place where ashes are customarily poured out—that is, where superfluities are cast away—because they are superfluous and useless. [Col. 0382C–D]

“And he shall break its little wings, but shall not cut them off or divide them with iron.” He commands the little wings of the turtledove and pigeon to be broken, lest chastity and patience be able to fly away and separate from us. Attend carefully to what is said. You have become a turtledove and pigeon: do not fly away; do not be wandering and unstable. Break your little wings, because they are harmful; but do not cut them off, because they are natural. Although you do not fly, you do not lose the nature of flying; although you do not sin, you still have the power to sin. But you cease to fly for God—that is, to sin—according to the saying of Ecclesiasticus: “He was able to transgress and did not transgress, to do evil and did not do it” (Ecclus. 31:10). [Col. 0383A] It follows:

“And he shall burn it upon the altar, upon wood with fire placed underneath: it is a burnt offering and an offering of most sweet odor to the Lord.” The fire by which all things must be burned is the fervor of charity. This is the fire of which the Lord says: “I came to cast fire upon the earth” (Luke 12:49). A good mind, sincere affection, sound understanding, and a contrite spirit are the wood kindled by this fire. But where? Upon the altar of the heart, certainly. For the heart in which this wood has been arranged and has burned with this kindled fire is a burnt offering and an offering of most sweet odor to the Lord.

This is especially so if the priest, by teaching, preaching, and admonishing, has arranged above it the turtledove, pigeon, and the other matters mentioned above—that is, chastity and patience. Such an altar is always burning, but especially when it is inflamed by the priest’s voice and spirit. Hence the Lord says through the prophet: “I created the smith and the one who blows coals in the fire” (Isa. 54:16). It follows again concerning that sacrifice which the holy Church everywhere offers in remembrance of Christ’s passion, and which is therefore made from fine flour and called a memorial. [Col. 0383B–C]

## CHAPTER II

“When a soul offers an offering of sacrifice to the Lord, his offering shall be of fine flour; he shall pour oil upon it, put frankincense on it, and bring it to the sons of Aaron the priest. One of them shall take a full handful of the flour and oil, together with all the frankincense, and shall place it as a memorial upon the altar, an odor most sweet to the Lord.”

This chapter treats figuratively of that sacrifice which the holy Church everywhere consecrates in remembrance of Christ’s passion; hence the present offering is made from fine flour. This fine flour was made from that grain of which the Savior said: “Unless a grain of wheat falls into the earth and dies, it remains alone” (John 12:24). This fine flour was ground for us from the Jews, of whom the Psalmist says: “The Lord will break the millstones of lions” (Ps. 57:7). [Col. 0383C–D]

A soul offers this—that is, some good and spiritual person, one who follows the desires of the soul rather than those of the body—because with a contrite heart and contrite spirit he remembers Christ’s passion. He pours oil over it, marveling at Christ’s compassion and mercy: though he was ground like grain by the wicked, though he was crucified by the Jews, yet pouring forth the oil of compassion and gentleness, he did not cease from mercy. When he healed the ear of Malchus’ servant and prayed the Father to forgive the Jews, did not Christ then abound in the oil of mercy? [Col. 0384A]

He adds frankincense to the fine flour when he reflects within himself why the Father took such delight in his Son’s passion. Concerning this frankincense the Psalmist says: “Let my prayer be directed as incense in your sight” (Ps. 140:2). When the soul mentioned above considers these things and cannot discover the reason by itself, it brings all together—namely fine flour, oil, and frankincense—to the sons of Aaron the priest. That is, it brings them to its prelates, bishops, and doctors of the Church, to be instructed by them in their understanding. Hence the passage continues: “One of them shall take a full handful of the flour and oil, together with all the frankincense, and shall place the memorial upon the altar, an odor most sweet to the Lord.” [Col. 0384A–B]

Hear this, bishops, and see that no exception among bishops is made here. Someone comes with his offering and wishes to ask a bishop about his doubt. Therefore, the bishop who cannot answer his question and does not receive his offering for sacrifice—that is, for exposition—will not be that “one” of whom it says here: “one of them.” The fact that he takes not all the fine flour, but a full handful of it, means that a bishop ought to expound not everything, but only those things which pertain to the salvation of souls and which hearers can understand and grasp.

Receiving all these things, then, the bishop places the memorial—that is, something to be remembered and understood—upon that person’s heart. For unless all things that pertain to the salvation of souls are placed upon the altar of the heart, and made a memorial, such a burnt offering will not exist. Unless this sacrifice were placed upon the altar of the heart, it could be consigned to forgetfulness and would not be a memorial. Such an offering becomes an odor most sweet to the Lord. It follows: [Col. 0384B–C]

“What remains of the sacrifice shall belong to Aaron and his sons: it is most holy among the Lord’s offerings.” The command that whatever remains of these things be left as the priest’s portion clearly shows that those mysteries which hearers cannot grasp or understand ought to be stored away and concealed in the breast and treasury of priests, according to the saying: “I have hidden your words in my heart, that I may not sin against you” [Col. 0384D] (Ps. XVIII [19]:11). For these remnants from the Lord’s offerings are most holy.

What has been said concerning fine flour should also be understood of loaves, cakes, and wafers, since these too are made from grain and fine flour. Therefore, things having one material should have one meaning also: for they signify the flesh of the Lamb—namely, that Lamb who takes away the sins of the world. Whether they are baked in an oven, fried in a pan, or roasted on a griddle, they always signify Christ’s Passion; for Christ’s cross was oven, pan, and griddle. Therefore all who endure sufferings undergo the affliction of the cross, as the Lord himself indicated when he said: “Whoever wishes to come after me, let him deny himself, take up his cross, and follow me” [Col. 0385A] (Matt. V [5]:13), understanding every suffering in the cross alone.

The addition of oil to all these things signifies that Christ did not cease to show mercy even in his very Passion. Christ always pours out oil, by which he both has mercy and heals. These things are entrusted to the hands of priests, because they are required to expound them. The wafers are divided into small pieces when the whole mystery of Christ is carefully expounded, sentence by sentence and part by part. A memorial is placed upon the altar when this same mystery is implanted in the hearts of the hearers. All these things are unleavened and without leaven, because our Lamb is spotless, innocent, and without sin, and because the Lord accepts nothing corrupt or stained. It follows:

“Every offering presented to the Lord shall be made without [Col. 0385B] leaven; nor shall any leaven or honey be burned in the Lord’s sacrifice.” Leaven is removed from the sacrifice because it is corrupt and corrupts the whole mass, as the Apostle says. Honey, however, is excluded because it is sweet: the flesh of the lamb is commanded to be eaten not with the sweetness of honey, but with the bitterness of wild lettuces.

“Whatever sacrifice you offer, you shall season with salt; nor shall you take away the salt of the covenant of your God from your sacrifice. In every offering you shall offer salt.” Salt stands for wisdom. Hence the Lord also says to his disciples: “You are the salt of the earth” (Matt. V [5]:13). For as food is seasoned with salt, so sacrifice is seasoned with wisdom. Whoever sacrifices to the Lord but does not understand what he does makes, as it were, a sacrifice without salt. The inward priest is the understanding [Col. 0385C] that propitiates the Lord by sacrificing upon the altar of the heart. This salt, which is to be used in the sacrifice, is called the salt of the covenant because God commanded this to be done, and the people repeatedly promised that they would observe it. Let this suffice concerning the sacrifice of fine flour; let us now proceed to explain mystically the offering of firstfruits.

“But if you offer a gift of your firstfruits to the Lord from ears of grain still green, you shall roast them with fire and crush them in the manner of spelt; and thus you shall offer your firstfruits to the Lord, pouring oil over them and placing frankincense upon them, because it is an offering to the Lord. Of it the priest shall burn, as a memorial of the gift, a portion of the crushed spelt and oil, and all the frankincense” [Col. 0385D].

This passage appears to be understood of catechumens. When they come to the Church, they ought to be questioned concerning their purpose, steadfastness, and faith. For the Prophet says: “Unless you believe, you shall not remain” (Isa. VII [7]:9). These people offer to the Lord the firstfruits of their produce—that is, the first rudiments of faith—not indeed from wheat and solid food, but from ears still green, when they promise that they will nevertheless believe what is said to them by those priests, even though they do not understand it.

Let us consider what it means to roast ears with fire and crush the new produce in the manner of spelt. I think it signifies nothing else than that they now believe the sacraments of faith in the ardor of charity, without yet examining them fully. Whoever examines them carefully crushes them not merely in the manner of spelt, but into the fineness of flour [Col. 0386A]. They pour oil over them when, together with faith, they promise mercy and kindness. They place frankincense upon them when, renouncing the devil, they promise to adhere to virtues and good works. Since these are fragrant to the Lord, they bear the likeness of frankincense.

After catechumens have offered the Lord this offering of their faith, it remains for the priest to teach them and enable them to understand greater things. Let him therefore take a portion of the crushed spelt and oil, and all the frankincense, and begin to sacrifice—that is, let him begin to labor in their instruction. Here it should be noted that the law commands the priest to take only a portion of the crushed grain, so that he may not clearly set forth all its parts at once. Even if the priest cannot teach them all the mysteries of the Christian faith, [Col. 0386B] it is enough for him to explain some part of them; for to unfold all the hidden things of our faith seems either impossible or at least difficult.

But the law commands that none of the oil or frankincense be diminished, because they can be fully instructed in the practice of mercy and in giving a good example. Nor is it surprising that teaching catechumens, explaining the sacred doctrines to them, and imparting knowledge of the Scriptures should here be called sacrifice, since God receives this work as a sacrifice dear to himself. Thus he says through the Psalmist: “The sacrifice of praise will honor me” (Ps. XLIX [50]:23). And the Apostle says: “Through him let us continually offer to God a sacrifice of praise, that is, the calves of lips confessing his name” (Heb. XIII:15).

## Chapter III

[Col. 0386C]

“But if his offering is a sacrifice of peace offerings, and he wishes to offer from the herd, he shall offer before the Lord a male or female without blemish; and he shall place his hands upon the head of his victim, which shall be slain at the entrance of the tabernacle.”

Here it should incidentally be noted that in the first sacrifice Christ without blemish was represented under the figure of calf and lamb; next, in the turtledove and dove, we ourselves were offered in sacrifice; afterwards Christ was figuratively slain in fine flour and loaves; and now, finally, we ourselves are commanded to be slain, so that we may understand that it is necessary for us often to suffer for Christ, who often suffered for us.

This present victim is rightly called a peace offering [Col. 0386D], because through it we are purified with God and joined to him again. Therefore, if anyone wishes to offer a peace offering from the herd in the priestly or regular order, whether male or female, let that person keep himself or herself unblemished from every vice, so as to be offered worthily. For what is understood by the ox but the priestly or regular order, according to the Apostle’s saying: “You shall not muzzle the ox while it treads out the grain” (I Cor. IX:7)? In this order, certainly, both holy men and devout virgins are understood. For women dedicated to God labor, indeed, in his field.

Hear this, therefore, you who approach holy orders. Hear, you who offer yourselves for the service of God. If you are spotless, approach confidently; but if not, do not presume to approach. Place your hand [Col. 0387A] upon the head of your victim—that is, restrain the pride of your flesh. Observe the Apostle placing his hand upon his victim, for he says: “I chastise my body and bring it into servitude” (I Cor. IX:27). Slay it at the entrance of the tabernacle, so that those who are in the tabernacle may see you and, “seeing your good works, glorify your Father who is in heaven” (Matt. V [5]:16). Let others see your fasts; let them see how, by sacrificing, you wear down and afflict your flesh, so that they may take an example from your holy manner of life. Come, devout young men; come, chaste virgins, to God’s holy tabernacle. For there the sons of Aaron await you; there prelates and priests await you, desiring to receive you into their fellowship, to purify you, [Col. 0387B] to consecrate you, and to offer you.

“And the sons of Aaron the priest shall pour the blood around the altar, and shall offer from the peace offering as an offering to the Lord,” etc. It is clear that blood signifies sins, according to Ezekiel’s saying: “If you do not declare his iniquity to him, I shall require his blood from your hand” (Ezek. III [3]:18). The altar, however, signifies the mind and heart. Thus priests pour around the altar the blood of one who longs to enter the priestly or regular order and be numbered among the oxen, when they admonish such persons to remember their sins and keep them around the circuit of their heart, so that they may always say: “My sin is always against me” (Ps. L [51]:5).

Then the Lord commands that the fat of the victim and all its richness be offered and burned, because the flesh grows proud through fatness and rushes into lust and every shamefulness. Hence elsewhere it is said: “The beloved grew fat and kicked” (Deut. XXIII [32]:15); and therefore the Apostle forbids us to be found in revelry and drunkenness. Elsewhere he says: “Make no provision for the flesh in its desires. And do not become drunk with wine, in which is debauchery” (Eph. V:18). This, then, is the reason why it is especially necessary that the fatness of our body be reduced, burned, and destroyed. For while the flesh is worn down by fasts, the soul grows fat, its seat becomes visible, and a sacrifice acceptable to God is made. Therefore let the spirit be kindled, so that the flesh may grow cold in the fires of vices [Col. 0387D].

To kindle this offering, let us gather wood—that is, let us follow the examples of the righteous, considering how they lived and how, by fasts and vigils, they made all bodily fatness thin. If this wood is kindled upon the altar of our heart, it will cause every harmful fatness to be burned up. It follows:

“If they offer a lamb before the Lord, they shall place their hand upon the head of their victim, which shall be slain in the vestibule of the tabernacle of testimony. And the sons of Aaron shall pour its blood around the altar, and shall offer the fat and the whole tail with the kidneys, and the rest, as above.”

The rite in the slaughter of the lamb signifies the same as we have noted above; only in the difference of the victim is some distinction found. For by the ox we understand a teacher and priest; by the lamb, a gentle and simple person; by the goat, a sinner. Therefore, whether anyone offers ox, lamb, or goat, let that person place a hand upon the head of the victim—let him restrain his pride, chastise it, and slay it. This, however, must be done only beside the tabernacle: that is, according to the ordinances and laws of the Church. Whoever departs from the Church gains no benefit from any sacrifice, [Col. 0388A] abstinence, or mortification of the flesh; therefore every victim is commanded to be brought to the tabernacle.

Thus the sons of Aaron kill us and pour out our blood, for only the priests of the Church wash us from sins and offer sacrifices for us. For he was a son of Aaron and a priest of the Church who said: “Put to death your members that are upon the earth” (Col. III:5); and again: “You are dead, and your life is hidden with Christ in God” (ibid.). But why do they pour out our sins upon the altar, except that they may be consumed by fire and always kept in remembrance? How priests offer the fat, kidneys, and all richness has already been stated above. Finally, why does the Lord command the tail to be offered? He himself teaches this in the Gospel, saying: “Whoever perseveres to the end shall be saved” (Matt. XXIV:13).

“All fat shall belong to the Lord by a perpetual statute, throughout your generations and in all your dwellings. You shall eat neither fat nor blood.” Since there is good fat and bad fat, how can all fat belong to the Lord? Good fat is that by which the soul grows rich and receives strength, of which the Psalmist says: “May my soul be filled as with marrow and fatness” [Col. 0388C] (Ps. LXII [63]:6). Bad fat is that by which the soul, made gross, grows proud; of this the same Psalmist says: “Their iniquity came forth from fatness” (Ps. LXXII [73]:2).

Therefore all fat must be offered to the Lord: the good fat of the soul, that it may be inflamed with holy desire; and the evil fat of the body, that it may be destroyed by repentance. Thus the fat of the soul is offered to God in the pan of the heart when the conscience of sins is set on fire by heavenly love. But the fat of the body is sacrificed to God when the flesh is subdued by the rigor of repentance. Thus all fat belongs to the Lord.

Next, fat is commanded to be burned and blood poured out, so that neither may be eaten [Col. 0388D]. But attend to the reasoning. Blood must not be eaten because in it the cause of sin is understood. Yet fat must be offered upon the altar: that is, all harmful fatness must be burned up and destroyed in a contrite heart. This is what is meant by the statement: “The fats with which the breast is covered and the lobe of the liver shall be offered upon the altar.” But why the lobe of the liver? The lobes of the jecur—that is, the liver—appear to have the likeness of coagulated and dead blood. Therefore blood and the form of blood are to be placed upon the altar, so that not only sin, but even the appearance of sin, may be utterly destroyed.

## Chapter IV

“The Lord spoke to Moses, saying: Speak to the children of Israel. If a soul sins through ignorance regarding the sacrifice, and does anything among all the commandments of the Lord which he commanded not to be done: if the priest who is anointed sins, causing the people to offend, he shall offer to the Lord for his sin an unblemished calf, and shall bring it to the entrance of the tabernacle of testimony before the Lord; he shall place his hand upon its head and slay it before the Lord. He shall also take some of the calf’s blood and bring it into the tabernacle of testimony.” [Note: [Col. 0389D] Another reading has: “into the tabernacle of the sanctuary.”]

As the law speaks with distinctions, so we also ought to speak with distinctions: first concerning the priest who sins through ignorance and his expiation, and afterwards concerning the people whom the priest’s ignorance led into error. Thus this soul—or priest—who sinned through ignorance by leading the people [Col. 0389B] into error signifies Caiaphas, or some other priest of the Jews. For the words of the context are especially suited to Caiaphas. He not only sinned himself, but caused others to sin, leading the people into sedition and to the killing of Christ, and saying: “It is expedient for you that one man die for the people, lest the whole nation perish” (John XI:50). John immediately adds: “Therefore from that day they planned to kill him” (ibid.). Thus it appears that he is the priest who both sinned and caused the people to offend.

Moreover, in the Evangelist’s addition, “He did not say this of himself” (ibid.), it is clearly indicated that he sinned through ignorance. For the sin of the priest who offends through ignorance, a calf is offered, whose blood is brought into the tabernacle by the high priest. The Apostle says of this: “For the bodies of those animals whose blood is brought into the sanctuary by the high priest for sin are burned outside the camp; therefore Jesus also suffered outside the gate, that he might sanctify the people through his own blood” [Col. 0389C] (Heb. XIII:11).

Accordingly, following this interpretation of the Apostle, we must understand the entire sequence of this offering as referring to Christ sacrificed upon the altar of the cross. Taking our matter from the Apostle’s own words, let us expound more fully what he left undeveloped or stated briefly.

This soul which sinned through ignorance is understood as Caiaphas. First, therefore, we must inquire how Caiaphas is meant where it is said that he should offer to the Lord an unblemished calf for [Col. 0389D] his own sin. For these words seem incapable of being applied to him. Christ was killed not for his sin, but unto his sin, through Caiaphas’s persuasion; nor did Caiaphas then think that an unblemished calf was being killed, but a man worthy of death. Yet, since Christ the Lord died to discharge Adam’s sin, sin pertains equally to Caiaphas and to all humankind. It is certain that Christ was sacrificed for Caiaphas’s sin; thus Christ’s death removed original sin, while Caiaphas’s sin brought in actual sin.

[Note: [Col. 0389D] Another Cassinese manuscript reads: “It is certain that Christ was sacrificed also for Caiaphas’s sin. Caiaphas therefore offers Christ for his own sin, but because he did this impiously,” etc.]

Thus Caiaphas sacrifices Christ [Col. 0390A] for his original sin; but by doing this impiously, he incurs actual sin. He brings him to the door of the tabernacle of testimony because, according to Caiaphas’s counsel, Christ was brought to a trial of death. He places his hand upon Christ’s head when he strives to assail and conceal Christ’s divinity, in which God is the head. He indeed slays him by nailing him to the cross, when through persuasion and counsel he hands him over to be killed.

By the blood’s being brought into the tabernacle, I think it is understood that, when Christ had died, his shed blood penetrated even heaven and there stood before the face of God the Father on our behalf, as Paul says: “For Jesus did not enter into holy places made by hands, copies of the true ones, but into heaven itself, now to appear before the face of God for us” (Heb. IX:12). He entered, [Col. 0390B] therefore, not to sprinkle the blood of calves or goats, but to obtain for us forgiveness of sins through his own blood.

“And when he has dipped his finger in the blood, he shall sprinkle it seven times before the Lord, facing the sanctuary.” The priest’s sprinkling blood seven times toward the sanctuary after dipping his finger in it specifically teaches that Christ’s blood is sprinkled for the washing away of sins until the end of the world. For what is done seven times is done throughout all time, since the whole course of time is bounded by only seven days. Christ’s blood is therefore fittingly sprinkled seven times because it is offered by priests until the consummation of the age. This is done before the veil of the sanctuary: that is, in the presence and majesty of the eternal Father [Col. 0390C].

“And he shall put some of the same blood upon the horns of the altar of most pleasing incense to the Lord, which is in the tabernacle of testimony; but he shall pour all the remaining blood at the base of the altar of burnt offering, at the entrance of the tabernacle.” These two altars certainly represent two peoples. For not only was the people of the Gentiles, who then began to believe, redeemed by Christ’s blood; he also liberated the earlier people, the Jewish people, from hostile slavery. The redeemed souls of both peoples testify to this when, giving thanks, they sing: “You have redeemed us, O God, by your blood from every tribe, people, and nation” (Rev. V:9). Therefore the blood of the victim touches two altars because Christ’s blood redeemed two peoples [Col. 0390D].

“The fat of the liver with the kidneys, as it is removed from the calf of the peace offering, he shall burn upon the altar of burnt offering,” etc. What is indicated by the calf’s fat except Christ’s mercy? What is shadowed forth by the altar of burnt offering except the human heart? Therefore the fat of the calf is placed upon the altar when the human heart is imbued with God’s mercy and loving-kindness and, following Christ’s own example, becomes merciful toward its neighbors. Peter says: “Christ suffered for us, leaving you an example, that you may follow [Col. 0391A] in his footsteps” (II Pet. II [1 Pet. II]:21). Therefore, just as loving-kindness and mercy toward humankind abounded in Christ’s inward parts, so our hearts, anointed with this fat of mercy, must abound toward our neighbors.

“But he shall carry outside the camp the skin and all the flesh, with the head, feet, entrails, dung, and the rest of the body, and shall burn them upon a pile of wood, etc.; they shall be burned in the place where ashes are poured out.” Here the Apostle’s words alone suffice for explanation, when he treats of the animals burned outside the camp: “Jesus,” he says, “suffered outside the gate, that he might sanctify the people through his own blood. Therefore let us go out to him outside the camp, bearing his reproach” (Heb. XIII:12). Paul speaks aptly here: for the pile of wood and Christ’s reproach were the cross, upon which his body was burned. Therefore the whole calf is burned outside the camp because Christ’s whole body suffers outside the gate. Let this suffice concerning the priest who sins through ignorance. Let us proceed to the people deceived by ignorance and the manner of their expiation.

“But if the whole assembly of Israel has acted in ignorance and done what is contrary to the Lord’s command, and afterwards has understood its sin, it shall offer a calf for sin and bring it to the entrance of the tabernacle of testimony. And the elders of the people shall place their hand upon its head before the Lord.” In what the people and assembly sinned has been stated above: for they killed the same calf, with the same intention [Col. 0391C] as the priest. Therefore whatever is said there concerning the priest’s victim is to be understood here concerning the people’s victim.

Peter testifies that the people, like the priest, sinned through ignorance: “And now, brothers, I know that you acted through ignorance, as did your fathers” (Acts III:17). Likewise Paul says: “For if they had known, they would never have crucified the Lord of glory” (I Cor. II:8). This can also be proved from Christ’s testimony, when he prayed to the Father for them, saying: “Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing” (Luke XXIII:34).

[Note: [Col. 0391D] “Even among that unbelieving people there are and have been many for whom the Lord mercifully prayed, that they might be converted from their error and saved; and what he prayed for, he effectively obtained and accomplished.” St Remigius of Lyons, *On the Three Epistles*, book XIX.]

Moreover, the elders of the people also place their hands upon the calf’s head, clearly showing that they, together with the priests, wished to conceal Christ’s divinity. Thus in his killing they are counted with the priests, as Scripture says: “The chief priests and elders of the people took counsel that they might seize Jesus by deceit and kill him” [Col. 0391D] (Matt. XXVI:4).

As for the statement that their offence is cleansed when the priest prays for them and sprinkles the calf’s blood before the Lord against the veil of the temple, it must be understood not of the priest mentioned above, who sinned through ignorance, but of him of whom the Psalmist says: “Therefore God, your God, has anointed you with the oil of gladness above your companions” [Col. 0392A] (Ps. XLIV [45]:8). For he, dipping his finger in his own blood, brought it into the tabernacle of heaven itself, because, as the Apostle says: “Through his own blood he entered once for all into the holy places, having obtained eternal redemption” (Heb. IX:12).

“But if a ruler sins and does one of the many things forbidden by the law of the Lord through ignorance, and afterwards understands his sin, he shall offer to the Lord an unblemished male goat from the goats.” After treating of the high priest of the Jews and their people, let us explain something concerning the rulers of the Church—that is, bishops—and their subjects. Paul testifies in his own case that such persons sometimes offend even through ignorance, when he says that he was formerly a blasphemer. Yet, because he acted through ignorance [Col. 0392B], he shows that he obtained mercy.

It may likewise fittingly be affirmed that Peter, prince of the Church, sinned through ignorance; for a person is said not to know when he entirely forgets what he ought to do. Now if Peter had not forgotten his Master’s word when he denied him, it would have been pointless to write that he afterwards remembered; for the Evangelist says: “And Peter remembered the word of Jesus which he had spoken” (Luke XXII:61), etc. Moreover, how many rulers of the Church sin not only ignorantly but knowingly? If such persons understand that they have sinned, they are bound to offer a victim to the Lord. They are said to understand this when they are restrained from the sins they committed earlier through repentance.

These persons offer a victim to the Lord—that is, a victim, or an unblemished goat for sin—when each offers to the Lord his own self, now corrected. It is from the goats because it is from Adam’s stock, from a sinful stock, from the stock that says in all its offspring: “I was conceived in iniquities, and my mother conceived me in sins” [Col. 0392C] (Ps. L [51]:6). Therefore each person offers himself to the Lord as a goat when he ceases to sin and begins to repent worthily.

[Note: [Col. 0392D] Reading of another Cassinese manuscript: “But one offers oneself to the Lord who ceases to sin and begins to repent worthily.”]

Thus the goat, named because of sin, is now presented unblemished through repentance.

“And he shall place his hand upon its head. And when he has slain it in the place where the burnt offering is customarily slain before the Lord, because it is for sin, the priest shall dip his finger in the blood of the sin offering, touching the horns of the altar of burnt offering and pouring the remainder at its base.” What the laying on of hands and the smearing of blood upon the altar’s horns signify has already been stated above. I think, therefore, that offering a goat by killing it signifies the same as afflicting oneself in repentance. For one who is afflicted in heart is rightly said to kill oneself before God, since, as Scripture says, “man sees the face, but God looks upon the heart” [Col. 0392D] (I Kings XVI [1 Sam. XVI]:7).

Here the Lord calls “priest” the one whom he previously called “ruler,” to show of what ruler he speaks [Col. 0393A].

[Note: [Col. 0393] The same aforementioned Cassinese manuscript: “The one whom he had previously called ruler, he now calls priest, so that it may be understood more clearly of what ruler he speaks.”]

The pouring out of blood and the staining of the altar with blood indicate that he both expels sin and stores the memory of sin in the heart, according to what we read: “My sin is always against me” (Ps. L [51]:3). The burning of the fat has already been explained above.

“And the priest shall pray for him, and it shall be forgiven him.” The priest prays for the ruler; the priest prays for himself. Certainly it seems contrary that the same person should be priest and ruler, since a ruler governs with strictness, whereas a priest exercises mercy with gentleness. Thus one presides, in a sense, forcibly; the other intercedes mercifully. Yet they fittingly coincide in one ruler who is also priest, since he who has sinned outwardly through severity inwardly groans in sorrow. Then the priest prays for the ruler: when, for the matters in which he sinned outwardly by commanding, he groans inwardly while sacrificing [Col. 0393B].

“But if a soul of the people of the land sins through ignorance, doing anything among those things forbidden by the law of the Lord and thus offending, and does not know its sin, it shall offer an unblemished female goat and place its hand upon the head of the victim,” etc. This soul from the people of the land, which sins through ignorance, represents each subject. It is now clearly shown how proper an order is observed in delivering the commandments. For when the text dealt with the old Church—that is, the people of the Jews—it treated first of the high priest and afterwards of the people. But when it treats of the ministers of the new Church, the same proper order of discourse is observed. After treating of the ruler or bishop to be sanctified, it fittingly passes to the expiation of the subjects.

Therefore this soul of the people of the land, or each subject, frequently sins through ignorance, because good is easily despised by a person and evil chosen in place of good. Such a person is commanded to offer a female goat for sin; this occurs when one mortifies one’s own flesh through rigorous repentance. Perhaps for this reason the manner of repentance is clearly shown, while its fixed duration is not indicated, so that one may understand that one must repent as long as one does not separate blood from the heart [Col. 0393D].

Whoever wishes to know how serious it is to sin through ignorance should carefully consider the canons set forth above. From the penalty found there to have been imposed upon oneself, one will immediately perceive the gravity of the fault. For one who is commanded to keep a hand upon the victim—that is, to restrain the pride of the flesh by repentance—to pour blood around the altar of the heart—that is, to shape one’s heart by continual remembrance of sins—and to burn up all fatness, is certainly not assigned a slight penance.

## Chapter V

“If a soul sins and hears the voice of one swearing, and is a witness, either because that person saw it or knows of it, then, unless he reports it, he shall bear his iniquity.” It is well known that the Jews sinned against this commandment of the law, since, though they heard the voice of the one swearing so often, they concealed it. What voice of one swearing do we understand here, if not that which they and we have often heard concerning Christ the Lord: “The Lord has sworn and will not repent: You are a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek” [Col. 0394A] (Ps. CIX [110]:5)? Though they heard this voice often, they not only did not proclaim it, but took care to conceal it. Because they did not preach Christ’s kingdom and priesthood, they will bear their iniquity.

Nor should we suppose that this was said only concerning the Jews; it must be understood as said concerning all the Lord’s words. For everything he has said is seen to be an oath, since it is always found firm and stable, as he himself said: “Heaven and earth shall pass away, but my words shall not pass away” (Matt. XXIV:35). Whoever knows or hears God’s will and does not do it shall be beaten with many stripes. For no one judges and proclaims better what one knows or hears than the person who practices what the Lord commanded with assurance. For something is more effectively commended by doing it than judged by preaching it.

“If you do not forgive,” says the Lord, “the sins of people against you, neither will your heavenly Father forgive you your sins” [Col. 0394B] (Matt. VI:15). This indeed is an oath, which only those rightly understand and proclaim who forgive the sins of those who sin against them.

“A soul which touches anything unclean—whether something killed by a beast, or dead of itself, or any creeping thing whatever—and has forgotten its uncleanness, is guilty and has sinned” [Col. 0394C]. This passage teaches that uncleanness comes from three things: from what has been killed by a beast, from what has died of itself, and from contact with creeping things. From this example we must surely take instruction concerning the purity of our souls.

Thus the person killed by beasts is rightly understood as anyone deceived by heretics. Hence the Psalmist asks that the faithful be delivered from heretics, saying: “Do not hand over to beasts the souls confessing you” (Ps. LXXIX [80]:19). But one dies by oneself who, by one’s own will, plunges into some heresy or grave sin. By the creeping thing, which lies prostrate upon the earth with its whole breast and is never raised upward, there is undoubtedly signified one who desires earthly things with every effort of the soul and never considers heavenly things.

Thus, whenever the soul is joined to the company of heretics, it is cast into danger of death; whenever it joins itself with such sinners, it incurs uncleanness. For whoever touches pitch will be defiled by it. Here, to touch such people signifies nothing else than believing them, communicating with them, and imitating their deeds.

“And if it touches anything of a person’s uncleanness, according to every impurity by which one is customarily defiled, and afterwards, having forgotten it, comes to know it, it shall be liable to guilt” [Col. 0395A]. After treating of association with heretics, the discourse turns to their doctrines. For the person polluted by uncleanness signifies one who has already become a heretic. Such a person’s teaching is uncleanness and pollution; it is, as it were, wickedly implanted as seed when another person becomes a heretic through communion with that person.

“A soul that swears and utters with its lips that it will do something either evil or good, and confirms the same by oath and word, and afterwards, having forgotten, understands its offence, shall do penance for its sin and offer from the flocks a ewe or a female goat; and the priest shall pray for it and for its sin.” What does swearing here that one will do evil signify, except promising God that one will afflict one’s flesh by repentance and wear it down with fasts? And who swears to do good except one who binds oneself to observe God’s commandments, according to the Psalmist’s saying: “I have sworn and resolved to keep the judgments of your righteousness” [Col. 0395B] (Ps. CXVIII [119]:106)?

Therefore one is said to forget the oath one made who does not perform what one promised to God. Such a person, who shows oneself forgetful by failing to practice what one vowed, should show oneself mindful by doing penance. What penance one must do is indicated by the letter of the text when it says: “Let one offer a ewe,” etc. For one offers an unblemished ewe to the Lord who keeps oneself unharmed from every wickedness of sins. Therefore, in order that the soul may make itself a simple ewe, it must entirely abstain from every sinful occasion [Col. 0395C]; it will perform no small penance.

“If, however, he is unable to offer an animal from the flock, let him offer to the Lord two turtledoves or two young pigeons, one for sin and the other for a burnt offering; and let him give them to the priest, who, first offering one for sin, shall twist back its head,” etc. Behold, the letter of the Law provides for the poor, while the spiritual understanding remains unchanged. 135 For this reason, according to the letter, a turtledove and a pigeon are substituted for a ewe or goat, so that the ordinance concerning sacrifice may be wholly observed even by the poor. Yet, according to the spiritual understanding, the same substitution is made, so that the same thing is understood through the turtledove and pigeon as through the ewe and goat. For what is signified by the turtledove, continually lamenting, except afflicted flesh? And what is designated by the simple pigeon except the innocence of the ewe? Thus, he offers a turtledove in place of the goat and a pigeon in place of the ewe, who afflicts his flesh by penitence and keeps his spirit unstained by every deceit. Hence it is now clear that, in this substitution, provision is made for the poverty of the poor without altering the rite of sacrifice. These birds, by which flesh and spirit are signified, are commanded to be given to the priest, so that the penitent may thereby learn to commit his whole self to the priest’s judgment. The priest offers the turtledove for sin when, in prayer, he presents before God the affliction of the flesh.

[Col. 0396A] “He shall twist back its head toward the feathers, so that it remains attached to the neck and is not wholly torn away. And he shall sprinkle its blood upon the side of the altar.” The priest twists the bird’s head back toward the feathers when he urges the penitent to walk with head bowed, to blush for sins, and by no means to be proud. In the command that the head is not to be violently detached from the neck but must remain attached there, I think this is signified: namely, that the humility of mind which each person must henceforth possess should appear voluntary rather than forced. The altar is moistened with the blood of this first bird when the penitent’s heart is troubled by remembrance of sins. “But he shall burn the other as a burnt offering.” The priest burns the other bird as a burnt offering when, by his words and [Col. 0396B] counsels, he wholly inflames the penitent’s mind with love for God.

“If his hand is unable to offer two turtledoves or two young pigeons, he shall offer for his sin a tenth part of an ephah of fine flour; he shall put no oil upon it, nor add any frankincense, because it is for sin; and he shall give it to the priest, who, taking from it a full handful, shall burn it upon the altar as a memorial of him who offered it, praying and making atonement for him; but he himself shall have the remaining part as an offering.” Behold, again more earnest attention is given to the poverty of the poor, and yet the rite of sacrifice is not altered. For the same thing is signified by fine flour as by the goat and the turtledove. The command that a tenth part of an ephah of fine flour be offered [Col. 0396C] seems to look toward the Gospel passage in which that woman—by whom Mother Church is understood—rejoices at finding one of ten lost drachmas. For the Church loses one of ten drachmas when one of the faithful commits sin; but she rejoices that she has found it when the sinner is presented before the priest with a contrite heart. Thus one who, by sin, becomes a lost vessel and, according to the Psalmist, becomes, according to the Psalmist, a lost vessel from a drachma, is restored by contrition of heart from a lost vessel into a found drachma through contrition of heart. “He shall put no oil upon it, nor add any frankincense, because it is for sin,” etc. He offers fine flour without oil for sin who removes from every delight his flesh, which penitence wastes away. Likewise, he adds no frankincense who [Col. 0396D] separates it from every sweetness, so that it may seem rather putrid from stripes than anointed with the finest ointments. For he offered fine flour without oil and without frankincense for sin who said of his own penitence: “My wounds have putrefied and corrupted because of my foolishness” (Ps. 37:6).—“And let him give it to the priest,” etc. The penitent gives the fine flour to the priest when he commits his whole self to his authority. The priest burns part of this flour on the altar when he offers the penitent’s affliction to God by his prayers. But he reserves a part for himself when he mortifies and afflicts himself with fasting on the penitent’s behalf. It is fitting that the priest should regard it as a very great offering that he may support the sinner by penitence of his own, lest [Col. 0397A] like the Pharisee, he hear said of himself that he lays heavy burdens upon others’ shoulders but does not move them with his own finger. For when he is said to eat the sins of the people, he is at least bound to share in their remission.

“If a soul, through error, transgressing the sacred rites, sins in things consecrated to the Lord, it shall offer for its trespass an unblemished ram from the flock, worth two shekels according to the weight of the sanctuary; and it shall restore what damage it has caused and add a fifth part besides, giving it to the priest, who shall pray for it by offering the ram, and it shall be forgiven.” This passage seems to deal with sacrilegious persons, whose crime is reckoned by all as capital. If restitution is imposed upon them as punishment [Col. 0397B] and they are commanded besides to pay a fifth part, they nevertheless do not seem to be punished as they deserve. But among the sacrilegious, he sins more gravely who irreverently empties divine mysteries of their content. Hence the Apostle warns us to flee this capital crime, exhorting us thus: “We exhort you not to receive the grace of God in vain” (2 Cor. 6:1). Thus that soul seems to sin in things consecrated to the Lord through which whole faith is not applied to the sacraments. For, while it does not receive from them the grace it is able to receive, it certainly commits the greatest sacrilege. Here it is commanded to offer an unblemished ram—not just any ram, but one bought for two shekels. By the ram is understood that very person formerly called sacrilegious, who, as soon as he withdraws from error through penitence, immediately assumes the character of an unblemished ram. He is bought for two shekels when he is formed by the precepts of the two Testaments. For if he still does not give full faith to each Testament and its words, he does not assume the form of the unblemished ram. He alone is bought for two shekels of sanctuary weight who is instructed [Col. 0397C] by the words of the two Testaments and completely delivered from his error. He properly repays the damage he caused when he undergoes penitence for sins committed. Finally, he adds the fifth part besides when he sins with none of the five senses.

## Chapter VI

[Col. 0397D] “And the Lord spoke to Moses, saying: Command Aaron and his sons. This is the law of the burnt offering: it shall burn upon the altar all night until morning; the fire shall be from the same altar. The priest shall be clothed in a linen tunic and linen breeches; he shall take up the ashes which the devouring fire has cast out, and, placing them beside the altar, shall put off his former garments; clothed in others, he shall carry them outside the camp and cause them to be consumed to ashes in a very clean place. But the fire upon the altar shall always burn; the priest shall nourish it, laying wood upon it every morning, and, after placing the burnt offering above it, shall burn the fat of the peace offerings.” In order that what is here set forth concerning the rite of the burnt offering may be spiritually understood by each of us, we must recall the Apostle’s saying: [Col. 0398A] “The temple of God is holy, which temple you are” (1 Cor. 3:17). If, therefore, we ourselves are God’s temple, let us seek within ourselves an altar and a priest fit for kindling the burnt offering. We understand, then, the altar to be the human heart and the priest to be the intellect; hence that intellect is clothed like a priest in a hyacinth-blue tunic which confesses that all it understands has been received from above, according to the saying: “All wisdom is from God” (Ecclus. 1:1). If it is found sincere and chaste, it is said to be clothed in linen breeches, in which the observance of chastity is indicated and the keeping of the Law is signified. It becomes an altar when it continually kindles within itself the fire of love and charity; by that fire, searching the divine Scriptures and learning in them the divine commandments, it inflames for God a most acceptable burnt offering of thanksgiving and confession, by which it greatly appeases and delights him. This burnt offering is commanded to be kindled throughout the whole night so that it may be understood to be done throughout the whole course of life. This fire is said to be from the same altar so that the love by which our heart is kindled may be understood to arise in and proceed from the heart.

“He shall take up the ashes which the devouring fire has cast out, and place them beside the altar,” etc. You hear that the devouring fire burns the burnt offering and turns it wholly into ashes. The love of learning God’s wonders and of seeking truth in some manner masters the deep mysteries of Scripture and brings them to ease of understanding. For this is to burn the burnt offering: [Col. 0398C] to penetrate the mysteries of the holy Scriptures. Therefore the priest takes up these ashes and places them beside the altar when he commits wholly to heart and memory whatever the intellect can discern and understand through inquiry. Afterwards, having put off his former garments and put on others, he carries the ashes outside the camp and causes them to be consumed to ashes in a very clean place. Attend carefully to what is said: he wishes the priest to go outside the camp; he wishes the ashes of the burnt offering to be carried outside. But for what purpose except that he may burn them again? He is therefore clothed in other garments when prepared for this work. But what are these garments without which the intellectual priest cannot carry the ashes outside? I think [Col. 0398D] these garments are letters, words, and utterances. Unless he is clothed with them, he seems unable either to go outside or to make anything understood. For who would ever understand what the intellect does within unless it, clothed in speech, brought itself outward through tongue and conversation? Thus clothed, the priest carries the ashes outside the camp—ashes, I say, because, if he carried out Scripture still untouched and unmeditated, perhaps he would have nothing to say. He burns again outside the ashes that have been carried forth when he expounds in words the mysteries of God which he penetrated within; and this is done in a very clean place, that is, in the congregation of righteous people. For it is written: “Do not give what is holy to dogs, nor cast pearls before swine” (Matt. 7:6). [Col. 0399A] This priest consumes the ashes of the burnt offering to ashes when he explains the difficulties of the holy Scriptures unto full understanding. But this fire, which never fails on the altar and ought to burn continually, establishes in the hearts of the faithful the ardor of unceasing love. For if this fire is absent from the intellect, the entire office of the priest will be wholly useless. Therefore let the priest carefully strive continually to nourish the fire of love and lay wood on it daily: let him remember God’s mercy; let him remember what God has done and what he has promised to bestow on those who love him. From such wood and similar wood gathered from the forest of the holy Scriptures, this fire is kindled and most greatly inflamed toward love of God. Therefore, O priest, place [Col. 0399B] the burnt offering upon this fire, so that you may sacrifice to God a sacrifice of praise. For this is the fat of the peace offerings, by whose richness you soothe God. This is the perpetual fire which will never fail upon the altar, because “many waters cannot quench charity” (Song 8:7).

“This is the law of the sacrifice and drink offerings which the sons of Aaron shall offer before the Lord and before the altar. The priest shall take a handful of the fine flour, 137 mixed with oil, and all the frankincense placed upon the flour, and burn it upon the altar as a memorial of most sweet odor to the Lord. Aaron and his sons shall eat the remaining part of the fine flour without leaven, and shall eat it in the holy place of the tabernacle.” [Col. 0399C] No distinction is to be sought between sacrifice and drink offering, since both have one and the same meaning. For when sacrifices were anciently made from fine flour, drink offerings were immediately most pleasing to God. By the sons of Aaron, to whom these instructions concerning drink offerings are given, the bishops and priests of the Church are fittingly signified. They are said to offer these drink offerings before the Lord because they always stand in God’s presence and are illuminated by his inward illumination. What is signified by fine flour, frankincense, and oil has already been explained in the preceding chapter. The priest is commanded to offer not all the flour but a full handful, so that by preaching he may reveal to the people only those divine secrets which he knows can suffice for their understanding. But the remainder is commanded to be [Col. 0399D] eaten by Aaron and his sons—that is, by those alone who continually exercise themselves in study of the sacred volumes. To eat it without leaven means nothing else than both to receive and teach these mysteries without the error of perversity. They are commanded to eat it not anywhere, but in the holy place of the tabernacle—that is, in a secret place where the incapable may not hear. Priests do this when they discuss among themselves alone the doctrine and precepts of the Law. For they themselves are sanctuaries and tabernacles of God, in which all these things remain fittingly hidden. And because this part of the fine flour also seems to pertain to the sacrament of faith, it is commanded that it be eaten entirely without leaven and corruption, lest anyone, eating incautiously, fall upon some passage which, if the soul understands it perversely, exposes itself to the danger of error. Hence the text fittingly adds: [Col. 0400A] “Only males of Aaron’s stock shall eat it.” For “males” here means the wiser and stronger, by whom the commandments of God are better understood and more religiously observed. To these alone it is permitted to examine and know what the rest are not permitted even to hear. Then follows: “Everyone who touches them shall be sanctified.” He touches firmly who puts into practice what he faithfully believes. For merely to believe is to see; but to do what is believed is to touch. It follows:

“The Lord spoke to Moses, saying: This is the offering of Aaron and his sons, which they ought to offer to the Lord on the day of their anointing. They shall offer a tenth part of an ephah of fine flour in a perpetual sacrifice, [Col. 0400B] half of it in the morning and half in the evening, fried in a pan and mixed with oil.” If, then, by Aaron and his sons we understand bishops and priests, this offering certainly seems to concern bishops and priests. They must offer it on the day of their anointing, that is, throughout the whole time of their life; hence it is commanded to be offered as a perpetual sacrifice. For that is not offered perpetually which is offered on only one day, unless that one day itself is understood to be perpetual. Therefore the bishop and priest ought to be anointed and sanctified not on one day only but every day, and to become better than himself. They offer a tenth part of an ephah of fine flour. For what do we understand by fine flour except the priest’s flesh? When this is ground and afflicted in the mill of compunction, it nourishes [Col. 0400C] others by its good example as though with a certain food. He who offers the tenth part offers himself wholly, because every human being is a tenth. Hence the Gospel calls the drachma the tenth. The Apostle also says of Levi: “He who receives tithes has himself been tithed” (Heb. 7:9). Therefore the sons of Aaron are rightly called tithes. But because morning and evening signify day and night, the priest must offer half of his offering in the morning and half in the evening, so that by day and by night, and at every time, he may not cease from this immolation. Of this it is further said: “It is fried in a pan and mixed with oil.” How this offering is fried in the pan of the heart, mixed with the oil of heavenly anointing, is understood only by those accustomed to offer it. But once this frying begins to grow hotter through the fervent fire of the Spirit, the human being, as though outside himself and in some manner raised higher, no longer seems to belong to his own power. [Col. 0400D] The priest who lawfully succeeds the father offers it hot to the Lord as a sweet odor. And the whole offering shall be burned upon the altar; for every sacrifice of priests is consumed by fire, and no one shall eat of it. This, indeed, we understand better by experiencing it than by explaining it. For what is surrounded on every side by the fire of the Spirit, wholly burned, wholly fried, and wholly anointed with oil cannot fail to be hot. But when it says, “No one shall eat of it,” I think this means that the priest should offer so holy an offering to the Lord not for display, as hypocrites do, but in secrecy and in the inner chamber of the heart. Therefore he ought to offer it when his mind is free, both in time and place, for heavenly contemplation. It follows:

[Col. 0401A] “This is the law of the victim for sin. In the place where the burnt offering is offered, it shall be sacrificed before the Lord. It is most holy. The priest who offers it shall eat it in a holy place, in the court of the tabernacle. Whatever touches its flesh shall be sanctified. If a garment is sprinkled with its blood, it shall be washed in a holy place; but the earthen vessel in which it was cooked shall be broken; if it is bronze, it shall be scoured and washed with water. Every male of priestly stock shall eat its flesh, because it is most holy.” 138 [Col. 0401B] I understand this victim, by which sins are remitted and which it is permitted only to the priest and the males of his stock to eat, to be that which is daily sacrificed in the holy Church by priests. This male is indicated not by sex but by faith, wisdom, strength, and constancy: one who does not readily believe the serpent and so yield to heretics. “Whoever touches its flesh shall be sanctified”; for this is what the Lord himself says: “He who eats my flesh and drinks my blood has eternal life” (John 6:55).—“If it is sprinkled with its blood, it shall be washed with water.” Why is a garment, sanctified by contact with the blood, washed with water, unless because those regenerated in the holy Church by the water of baptism are cleansed by the sprinkling of Christ’s blood alone? Therefore blood flowed together with water from the side of our Savior. [Col. 0401C] The earthen vessel in which it was cooked is broken; the bronze one is scoured and washed with water. For we are vessels in which Christ’s flesh is cooked, provided that we are mindful of his passion. Thus he himself says: “Do this in remembrance of me” (1 Cor. 11:24). The Apostle explained this, saying: “For as often as you eat this bread and drink the cup, you proclaim the death of the Lord until he comes” (ibid., 26). Therefore we must be broken, scoured, and washed; for these three signify one and the same thing. He who is afflicted and worn down by penitence and compunction is indeed broken, scoured, and washed. Yet under different aspects we ourselves are both earthen and bronze vessels: earthen indeed because we are from the earth; hence the Apostle says, “We have this treasure in earthen vessels” (2 Cor. 4:7); [Col. 0401D] bronze because we sound out clearly in the praises of God, for nothing rings more clearly than bronze. It is permitted to eat of this victim, which is wonderfully made in remembrance of Christ; but of that which Jesus himself offered upon the altar of the cross, it is permitted to no one, considered in itself, to eat. The seventy disciples misunderstood this when Christ offered them his flesh to eat, and, scandalized, went back. For they thought they had to eat bodily the flesh of Christ which they saw, not sacramentally, but cut into pieces. Concerning this it is further said: “For the victim slain for sin, whose blood is brought into the tabernacle of testimony to make atonement, shall not be eaten in the sanctuary, [Col. 0402A] but shall be burned with fire”—namely, with the fire of the Passion. This has been sufficiently expounded above by the testimony of the Apostle. It follows:

## Chapter VII

“This also is the law of the victim for trespass: it is most holy. Therefore, where the burnt offering is slain, there also the victim for trespass shall be slain; its blood shall be poured around the altar. From it they shall offer the tail and the fat which covers the vital parts, the two kidneys and the fat beside them, and the membrane of the liver with the kidneys; and the priest shall burn these upon the altar: it is incense to the Lord for trespass. Every male of priestly stock shall eat this flesh in a holy place, [Col. 0402B] because it is most holy. As the victim is offered for sin, so also for trespass; one law shall govern both victims.” Although *peccatum* (“sin”) and *delictum* (“trespass”) are often used interchangeably for the same thing, sin differs from trespass. To act against a commandment is sin; not to do what the commandment requires is trespass. He who kills acts against the commandment which says: “You shall not kill” (Exod. 20:13). But he who does not honor his father and mother neglects and abandons the commandment which commands: “Honor your father and mother” (ibid., 12). Thus *delictum* seems, as it were, to be called *derelictum* (“something abandoned”), because the commandment is abandoned. Since one law governs both victims, let there be one exposition for both. The blood of this victim is poured around the altar so that [Col. 0402C] our hearts may always swim in Christ’s blood and we may never forget his Passion. Hence we are also commanded to offer its tail; for the tail is the last part of the body. The Savior himself offered this when he said: “It is finished”; and immediately, says the Evangelist, “bowing his head, he gave up the spirit” (John 19:30). Therefore let us always remember this ending, this extremity, this tail, in which Christ gave up his spirit for us. Let us offer his fat, richness, and kidneys; let us speak, preach, and praise his piety, mercy, chastity, and continence. For this is the sacrifice of praise. “And a sacrifice of praise,” he says, “shall honor me” (Ps. 49:23). We pass briefly over these matters, since they can readily [Col. 0402D] be understood from what has been said above. It follows:

[Col. 0402D] “The priest who offers the victim of the burnt offering shall have its skin; and every sacrifice of fine flour which is baked in an oven, and whatever is prepared on a griddle or in a pan, shall belong to the priest by whom it is offered, whether mixed with oil or dry; it shall be divided in equal measure among all the sons of Aaron.” Let importunate and insatiable priests hear this, those who refuse to share ecclesiastical revenues with others. But since by the victim of Christ we understand the Word of God and the wisdom of God, what do we signify by the skin except the letter by which spiritual understanding is covered? For just as the Word and wisdom of God were once hidden in flesh, so now, unless the skin and covering of the letter are removed, they do not appear. [Col. 0403A] Therefore the priest who offers the victim shall have its skin. If this is understood of Caiaphas, who delivered Christ to death, it is clear; for he, like the other Jews, considered nothing in the divine Scripture but the skin and the letter. This skin is also very necessary to us, since flesh is difficult to eat unless the skin is first known. Therefore we always have readily at hand and in our power the skin, the letter, and the history. It follows:

“This is the law of the victim of peace offerings which is offered to the Lord. If the offering is for thanksgiving, they shall offer unleavened loaves mixed with oil, unleavened cakes anointed with oil, cooked fine flour, and small cakes mixed with oil.” Since God is reconciled to us by all victims, almost [Col. 0403B] all victims can be called peace offerings. But if offerings are made for thanksgiving [Note: [Col. 0403D] Codex Casinensis: “if the offering is made”], so that we may wish to give the Lord thanks for such great benefits received from him, let us offer loaves, cakes, cooked fine flour, and small cakes: all unleavened and without leaven, and all moreover anointed with oil. For we ourselves are all these things. The Apostle says of us: “Purge out the old leaven, that you may be a new dough, as you are unleavened” (1 Cor. 5:7). If, therefore, we are unleavened, incorrupt and sincere, let us offer ourselves to God, so that the image of God may be rendered to God. For God delights in such food. As sinners are the food of the devil, so the saints are the food of God: all anointed with oil, all touched by the grace of the Holy Spirit, all suffused with God’s mercy. It follows:

[Col. 0403C] “They shall also offer leavened loaves with the victim of thanksgiving, which is sacrificed for peace offerings. Of these, one shall be offered to the Lord as firstfruits, and shall belong to the priest who pours out the blood of the victim; its flesh shall be eaten on the same day, and nothing of it shall remain until morning.” Who are these leavened loaves offered with the victim of thanksgiving? Surely they are those two thieves crucified with the Lord. “Of these, one shall be offered to the Lord as firstfruits”: as firstfruits indeed, because in Christ’s Passion he believed first; hence he deserved to hear from the Lord: “Today you shall be with me in paradise” (Luke 23:43). This is what is meant by: “And it shall belong to the priest who pours out the blood of the victim.” This loaf belongs to that priest [Col. 0403D] who poured out for us no blood other than his own, and whose flesh shall be eaten that same day. On what day? Certainly on the day on which the victim is offered. Therefore it shall be eaten every day, since the victim is offered every day. What, then, is meant by what follows: “Nothing of it shall remain until morning”? What is this morning? It is the end of this night, of this life, and the beginning of that day on which the sun of righteousness shall arise. Then it will not be time to eat this flesh; then it will not be time to turn to faith. For to believe is to eat. Do you wish to eat this flesh? Believe, and you have eaten. It follows:

[Col. 0404A] “If anyone offers a victim by vow or freely, it shall likewise be eaten the same day. But if anything remains for the next day, it may be eaten; whatever the third day finds, fire shall consume. If anyone eats of the flesh of the victim of peace offerings on the third day, the offering shall become void and shall not benefit the offerer; rather, whatever soul has defiled itself with such food shall be guilty of transgression.” This victim, like the preceding one, signifies Christ. For Christ offered himself both by vow and freely: by vow because he had thus disposed and ordained, and before the ages predestined concerning himself; freely because he is almighty. But what are the two days on which it is permitted to eat this flesh? And what is the third day on which it is forbidden? I understand the two [Col. 0404B] days to be the two Testaments, in which this flesh is eaten because it is believed and understood through their revelation, illumination, and teaching. The first day is this book which now teaches us these things, under whose teaching Moses, Aaron, and many others ate Christ’s flesh. The second day is the Gospel, in which Christ is much more openly sacrificed and believed, eaten and drunk. Let us now come to the third day—but let us not eat on it, so that we may not believe it, because it is dark: without sun and light, wholly blind and erroneous. By it we understand the depraved teaching of heretics, in which many blasphemies concerning Christ are uttered. Therefore, if anyone sacrifices, believes in, and eats Christ according to this teaching, it will profit him nothing; [Col. 0404C] rather, whatever soul defiles itself with such food and errs by believing these things shall be guilty of transgression. Berengar was indeed such a day, for by philosophically disputing about Christ’s body and blood, he led us to impossibilities. But what we do not comprehend by reason, we consume with the fire of Spirit and charity, believing not so much arguments as the faith and authorities of the saints. Hence it is also said here: “Whatever the third day finds, fire shall consume.” Against heretics whom we cannot resist by reason and arguments, we resist by faith, authority, and the fire of charity. It follows:

[Col. 0404D] “Flesh which touches anything unclean shall not be eaten, but shall be burned with fire; whoever is clean shall eat of it.” Whoever believes heretics will not be transferred into the body of the Church, but will be burned with eternal fire. What it is to touch something unclean has already been explained above.

“A defiled soul that eats of the flesh of the victim of peace offerings, offered to the Lord, shall perish from its people [Note: [Col. 0403] Codex of the library of Monte Amiata: ‘shall perish from his people,’ and likewise below]. And whoever touches the uncleanness of a human being, or of an animal, or of anything that can defile, and eats of such flesh, shall perish from [Col. 0405A] its people.” The Apostle briefly expounded this when he said: “For whoever eats and drinks unworthily eats and drinks judgment upon himself, not discerning the body of the Lord” (1 Cor. 11:29). We have expounded it briefly because we speak [Col. 0405B] to the watchful and have resolved to hand these things on only to males of Aaron’s stock.

“And the Lord spoke to Moses, saying: Speak to the children of Israel: You shall not eat the fat of ox, sheep, or goat. You may use for various purposes the fat of a carcass that died of itself and of an animal seized by a beast. Whoever eats fat that ought to be offered in incense to the Lord shall perish from his people. You shall also not take the blood of any animal [Note: [Col. 0405D] The same Monte Amiata codex: ‘you shall not take’] as food, whether of birds or of cattle. Every soul that eats blood shall perish from its people.” Although these matters have been sufficiently expounded above, let us nevertheless say a few words about them. He seems here to speak not of the fat of flesh but of the fat of the soul. The soul’s fat and richness are wisdom, faith, charity, and the other virtues. For that soul is fat which abounds in these, just as, conversely, that is lean which lacks them. Blood stands for the soul because blood is the seat of the soul. Hence later in this same book it is said: “The soul of all flesh is in the blood” [Note: [Col. 0405D] According to the ancient opinion, blood was said to be the seat [Col. 0406D] of the soul; now the seat of the soul is variously debated. Many agree that it is in the brain.]. Therefore the Lord forbids the eating of fat and blood according to that sense in which it is said: “For they have eaten Jacob” (Ps. 78:7). For to eat in this sense is nothing other than to persecute, destroy, and kill. Thus it is a great sin to eat fat and blood. But it is permitted to use in various ways the fat of an animal that died of itself or was seized by a [Col. 0405C] beast, because the learning of heretics and philosophers is often useful to us in many respects. The learning of Aristotle, Priscian, and Origen is often necessary to us. It follows:

“Whoever offers a victim of peace offerings to the Lord shall offer with it its sacrifice, that is, its drink offerings. He shall hold in his hands the fat of the victim and the breast. When he has consecrated both as offerings to the Lord, he shall give them to the priest, who shall burn the fat upon the altar. But the breast shall belong to Aaron and his sons.” Every victim is a peace offering because through it we reconcile God to ourselves; and by drink offerings we understand every unleavened thing. Therefore a victim of peace offerings should not be offered without drink offerings, because a victim will not profit if it is not offered in the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth. But why does the Lord command that the fat and breast which a person has consecrated and vowed to God be given to the priest? The Lord wishes us to give and open our breasts—that is, our hearts—to priests, so that they may be filled by their counsels and teaching. Let us give them our fat: let us confess our sins to them; let us tell them what evil our flesh, fat with wantonness, has done. It belongs to them to burn the fat; it belongs to them to set sins ablaze and destroy them.

“Also the right shoulder from the victims of peace offerings shall be given to the priest as firstfruits. He who offers the fat [Col. 0406A] and blood of the sons of Aaron shall himself have the right shoulder as his portion. For I have taken from the children of Israel the breast of elevation and the shoulder of separation from their victims of peace offerings, and have given them to Aaron and his sons by a perpetual law from all the people of Israel.” The right shoulder is given to priests because they ought to be strong for bearing the sins of others. The breast is also given to them because those who fill the breasts of others ought not themselves to be without a breast. Therefore let the whole people run to them as to their own breast, as to the treasury of wisdom, and drink thence in thirst. This is what the breastpiece and the ephod signify. He calls it the “breast of elevation and shoulder of separation” as though saying “the exalted breast and the separated shoulder.” What follows—[Col. 0406B] “This is the anointing of Aaron and his sons in the ceremonies of the Lord, on the day when Moses offered them,” etc.—is the heading of what follows.

## Chapter VIII
“Then the Lord spoke to Moses, saying: Take Aaron with his sons, their garments, the oil of anointing, the calf for sin, two rams, and the basket with unleavened bread; and assemble the whole congregation at the entrance of the tabernacle. Moses did as the Lord commanded. When the whole multitude had assembled before the doors, he said: ‘This is the word which the Lord commanded’ to be done.” And at once he brought forward Aaron and his two sons. “When he had washed them, he clothed the high priest in a linen tunic, girding him with a belt and clothing him [Col. 0406C] in a hyacinth-blue robe; over it he placed the ephod, fastening it with a girdle and fitting it to the breastpiece, in which were doctrine and truth. He also covered his head with the turban, and on it, opposite the forehead, placed the gold plate consecrated for sanctification, as the Lord had commanded him. He also took the oil of anointing, with which he anointed the tabernacle and all its furnishings.”

For what Aaron with his sons signifies; what the calf and the two rams signify; what the oil of anointing, the garments, and the other things enumerated here signify—we have explained these matters sufficiently carefully and fully in Exodus. Let us here say something briefly concerning the calf and the two rams.

“He offered,” it says, “the calf for sin; and when Aaron and his sons had placed their hands upon it, he slew it, caught its blood, and, dipping his finger, touched [Col. 0406D] the horns of the altar all around. When it had been expiated and sanctified, he poured the remainder of the blood at its base. But the fat that was upon the entrails, the membrane of the liver, and the two kidneys with their fat he burned upon the altar; the calf itself, with its skin, flesh, and dung, he burned outside the camp, as the Lord commanded.”

For this calf, which is offered for sin, is Christ our Lord, sacrificed for our iniquities. Aaron and his sons placed their hands upon its head, because the high priests, priests, scribes, and Pharisees did not fear to lay hands upon him and to deny God. One portion of his blood touches the horns of the altar; another is poured at its base, because one portion of Christ’s blood stained the horns of the cross, while another portion flowed down to the ground below. But all his fat and richness are burned upon the altar, so that that prophetic saying may be fulfilled: “May the Lord remember every sacrifice of yours, and may your burnt offering become fat” (Ps. 19:4). O rich sacrifice, by whose fragrance the world is filled and every sickness healed! But the calf with its skin, flesh, and dung is burned outside the camp, because, as the Apostle says, Jesus “suffered outside the camp, in order to sanctify the people through his own blood” (Heb. 13:12). This concerning the calf. Let us now consider the ram:

“And he offered the ram for the burnt offering. When Aaron and his sons had placed their hands upon [Col. 0407B] its head, he slew it and poured its blood all around the altar. Cutting the ram itself into pieces, he burned its head, limbs, and fat in the fire. Having first washed the entrails and feet, he burned the whole ram together upon the altar, because it was a burnt offering of most pleasing fragrance to the Lord, as he had commanded him.”

This is that burnt offering which is made daily in the holy Church. For Moses—that is, Christ—offers the ram as a burnt offering; for although it is performed through the ministry of priests, he himself offers and sacrifices his flesh and blood. For the voice that says, “This is my body,” and, “This is the cup of the New Testament in my blood, which shall be shed for you and [Col. 0407C] for many for the remission of sins” (Luke 22:19–20), is not the priest’s voice but his own. By this utterance the entire sacrifice is offered and sanctified.
