Therefore it continues: “When Aaron and his sons had placed their hands upon its head, he slew it.” Aaron and his sons lay on their hands, while Moses sacrifices it, because although bishops and priests hold their hands outstretched and raised over Christ’s body and blood, there is nevertheless one high priest, Jesus, who sanctifies and blesses; by his ineffable power bread and wine are changed into the substance of his body and blood.

He poured its blood all around the altar, because Christ also offered us his blood to drink. For the altar is the Church, wholly [Col. 0407D] sprinkled and made drunk with Christ’s blood. Christ the Lord burned the ram itself, cut into pieces—its limbs, fat, and feet, after the entrails had first been washed—and consumed it upon the altar when, beginning with Moses and the other prophets, he interpreted for his two disciples the Scriptures concerning himself. Thus they too, sensing that the altar of their heart was burning with the burnt offering placed upon it, said: “Was not our heart burning within us while he spoke on the road and opened the Scriptures to us?” (Luke 24:32). Beginning with Moses, perhaps he expounded to them these very sacrifices, in which his death and passion were so plainly signified.

To wash the entrails is to show, by providing reasons, that those things which were thought shameful and dishonourable are necessary and honourable. This indeed he did when he said: “O foolish and slow of heart to believe all that the prophets have spoken: was it not necessary for Christ to suffer thus?” (Luke 24:25). For it seemed shameful, dishonourable, and utterly dreadful to them that the Son of God could have suffered and died.

The third sacrifice follows, in which we are instructed how bishops and priests ought to be consecrated.

“He offered,” it says, “the second ram in the consecration of the priests. Aaron and his sons placed their hands upon its head. When Moses had slain it, he took some of the blood and touched the tip of Aaron’s right ear, and likewise the thumb of his hand and of his foot. He also brought forward Aaron’s sons. When he had touched [Col. 0408B] the tip of each one’s right ear, and the thumbs of the right hand and foot, with the blood of the ram that had been slain, he poured the rest all around the altar.”

Moses in this passage, since he consecrates the priests, can signify a high priest through whose ministry bishops and priests are consecrated. At the beginning of the consecration he offers a ram if he thoroughly instructs those to be consecrated in the faith of Christ. Accordingly, they themselves place their hands upon the ram’s head, because in a sense they swear and confess that they believe all the things concerning which they are questioned.

The high priest touches the right ears, hands, and feet of each of them with the ram’s blood, so that their hearing, action, and preaching may be cleansed and sanctified by Christ’s blood: that they may have ears to hear; hands sanctified for doing good and for making Christ’s body; and feet that are beautiful for preaching peace and preaching good things. They are touched at the extremities because it is not the one who has begun, but “the one who perseveres to the end, that one shall be saved” (Matt. 10:22). He pours the remaining blood around the altar of their heart, so that, always mindful of Christ’s passion, they may take up their cross and follow him.

It continues:

“But he separated the fat, the tail, and all the fat which covers the entrails, and the membrane of the [Col. 0408D] liver, and the two kidneys with their fat, and the right shoulder. Then, taking from the basket of unleavened bread which was before the Lord, he took loaves without leaven, an oil-mixed cake, and wafers; he placed them upon the fats and the right shoulder, and handed them all together to Aaron and his sons.”

What are we to understand by the basket containing the unleavened breads except this book and the other volumes of the sacred Scriptures? In them, surely, the individual sayings are breads, cakes, and wafers by which they are nourished. Since these proclaim mercy and contain no error, they are fittingly called both mixed with oil and unleavened. These are placed upon the fats and the right shoulder because the meaning of the fats and the right shoulder is explained and understood by the sayings of the sacred Scriptures. That Moses handed all these things together to the priests signifies this: after priests have been consecrated, they ought to receive the book from the high priest’s hand, so that they may have authority to expound and preach the word of God.

[Note: [Col. 0409D] Formerly the ordination of priests was effected solely through the laying on of hands; at a later period the anointing with chrism was added, and later still the touching of the book of the Gospels, which Eugenius IV prescribed in the Decree for the Armenians.]

“After they had raised these things before the Lord, he took them again from their hands and burned them upon the altar of burnt offering, because it was an offering of consecration, a sacrifice to the Lord as a pleasing fragrance.”

[Note: [Col. 0409D] The edition is supplemented from the Cassinese manuscript.]

Those who are consecrated raise the things just mentioned before the Lord when they promise to keep them both in speech and in heart. Then Moses, the Lord’s vicar, receives all things again from their hands and burns them upon the altar as a pleasing fragrance, signifying that this whole act is pleasing to the Lord and sweetly fragrant to him. It continues:

“He also took the breast, raising it before the Lord [Col. 0409B] from the ram of consecration as his own portion, as the Lord commanded him. Taking the ointment and the blood that was upon the altar, he sprinkled Aaron and his garments, and his sons and their garments.”

Moses claims the breast for himself because high priests ought to be strong in mind and wise. Great indeed must be the breast of one who has to preserve and store up such great mysteries. But why does Moses raise the breast before the Lord, unless so that our hearts and breasts may always be raised up to contemplate heavenly things? Ointment and blood are sprinkled upon the priests and their garments, so that they may be cleansed and sanctified inwardly and outwardly; that they may appear outwardly such as they are inwardly; and that they may provide good things not only [Col. 0409C] before God but also before all people. For the ointment is the grace of the Holy Spirit. Concerning the blood the Apostle John says: “He loved us and washed us from our sins in his blood” (Rev. 1:5). It continues:

“And when he had sanctified them in their garments, he commanded them, saying: Cook the flesh before the entrance of the tabernacle, and eat it there. Eat also the breads of consecration which have been placed in the basket, as the Lord commanded me, saying: Aaron and his sons shall eat them. Whatever remains of the flesh and the breads shall be consumed by fire.”

The priests cook and eat the flesh before the entrance of the tabernacle because, in the assembly, in penitence, and in the hearing [Col. 0409D] of the faithful, they read and expound the divine Scriptures, teaching others to cook them, eat them, and understand them. The same is to be understood concerning the breads, of which we spoke above. Whatever remains is consumed by fire—the fire, surely, of the Holy Spirit, the fire of faith and charity—which often causes us to believe what we are unable to understand.

“You shall not leave the entrance of the tabernacle for seven days, until the time of your consecration is completed. For consecration is completed in seven days, as has now been done, so that the rite of sacrifice might be fulfilled. You shall remain in the tabernacle day and night, observing the Lord’s ordinances, lest you die.”

Those who are commanded not to leave the tabernacle for seven days—for there are no days except seven—ought never to leave the tabernacle. For this tabernacle is the Church, which priests never leave except by sinning; but all heretics have left it by sinning and [Col. 0410B] by pride.

[Note: [Col. 0409D] This passage, where St Bruno says, “Priests leave the Church when they sin,” is not to be understood in the same way as when he subsequently speaks of heretics. Nor could it have been unknown to Bruno that sinners too are members of the Church, since he has often said above that sinful Christians are to be cleansed by priests and are to receive penitence from them for their sins [Col. 0410D]. Therefore, when he says that priests leave the Church by sinning, he means only that they leave the tabernacle, as he says in the same place—namely, that they lose the holiness necessary for a priest ministering in the tabernacle.

This is more than sufficiently confirmed by what the same commentator teaches in the following chapter 12 concerning the threefold separation of sinners; in his commentary on Numbers, chapter 18; and finally in his exposition of verse 29 of Psalm 17: “In the ecclesiastical body,” he says, “the good and the evil, the righteous and sinners, the perfect and imperfect, the wise and foolish, are all contained.”]

Consecration is completed in seven days because, as long as we are in this life, we ought always to be consecrated, sanctified, and to advance toward what is better. Let us therefore remain day and night—that is, at every time—in the tabernacle; let us observe and keep what he himself commanded, lest we die. For whoever guard this tabernacle well do not die, but rather pass from death to life.

143. CHAPTER IX

“The Lord said to Aaron: Approach the altar and sacrifice for your sin; offer the burnt offering and make supplication for yourself and for the people. When you have slain the victim for the people, pray for it, as the Lord commanded. And Aaron immediately approached the altar [Col. 0410C] and sacrificed the calf for his sin. His sons brought him its blood; dipping his finger in it, he touched the horns of the altar and poured the remainder at its base.”

All these things have been stated and explained above. Moses nevertheless wished to speak of them after the consecration of the priests. But Aaron in this place seems to signify the high priests of the Jews, who crucified Christ our Lord for their own sin—indeed their own, because it was original sin. Yet lest the people subject to them too should be thought innocent of Christ’s death, he therefore added: “His sons brought him its blood.” The people also brought Christ’s blood to the high priests when they accused him, declared that he was guilty of death, and cried, “Crucify, crucify!” [Col. 0410D] Since Christ’s blood was shed through the priests’ plotting, the priest is therefore said to have dipped his finger in the blood. What the horns of the altar and its base signify, as also all the fat and richness, and the skin and flesh burned outside the camp, has been sufficiently explained above. It continues:

“He sacrificed also the victim of burnt offering, and his sons brought him its blood, which he poured all around the altar. They brought the victim itself, cut into pieces, with its head and every individual limb, and he burned all these things upon the altar with fire, after first washing the entrails and feet with water.”

But this victim of the burnt offering is the same as the preceding one; yet the priest who offers this and that one does not seem to be the same. The former sacrifices with cruelty; the latter, with compassion. For Aaron differs from himself: at one time he signifies the high priests of the Jews; at another, any minister of the Church. He also signifies [Col. 0411B] Jesus himself, greatest of all priests.

Now I wish, by way of example, to offer this victim of burnt offering. Let my sons therefore bring me the blood of this victim; let them bring the victim itself cut into pieces, together with its head and individual limbs. But how will they bring it? Do you wish to hear how? Let them come to me and ask what this blood signifies: this is to bring the blood. Let them also ask what the victim signifies, what the pieces signify, what the head and the other limbs signify. If I explain each of these things to them individually, then I sacrifice the victim upon the altar of their heart and kindle them in love for Christ through faith and charity. These matters too have already been explained above. It continues:

“And offering for the sin of the people, he slew the goat; when the altar had been expiated, he made the burnt offering, adding to the sacrifice the libations which are offered together, and burning them on the altar apart from the rites of the morning burnt offering.”

To offer a goat for the people’s sin is to teach and admonish the people to restrain and afflict by penitence the flesh that is wanton and sinful, and not to permit it to wander through unlawful things. The altar is expiated if the heart is cleansed from depraved thoughts; unless it has been cleansed, a burnt offering acceptable upon it cannot be made. Hence the Psalmist says: “Create in me a clean heart, O God” (Ps. 50:12). The libations offered together are understood to be the breads and the other unleavened things. Therefore those to whom we give the remedy of penitence ought to be admonished to live in the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth [Col. 0411D].

We are commanded to keep all these things apart from the rites of the morning burnt offering, which must indeed be kept inviolate in themselves. By the rites of the morning burnt offering he means those things which, at the beginning of our faith, we promised to the Lord, when we renounced the devil and all his pomps and works. True penitence, therefore, consists in observing these rites of the morning burnt offering, afflicting and mortifying the flesh for past sins, provided that afterward we live in the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth. It continues:

“He also sacrificed the ox and the ram, the people’s peace offerings. His sons brought him their blood, which he poured around the altar. But the fat [Col. 0412A] of the ox and the ram, the tail, the kidneys with their fat, and the membrane of the liver they placed upon their breasts.”

By the ox and the ram we may understand either Christ our Lord or the holy apostles. We sacrifice them when we preach their torments and sufferings. Our sons bring us their blood when they ask us about their sufferings; we pour it around the altar of their heart when we explain all things to them and encourage them, according to the apostles’ example, not to fear death for Christ. And because the breasts of teachers disclose divine mysteries all the more abundantly the more they are pressed by questions, they placed upon the breasts of the ox and ram the fat, the tail, the kidneys, and all their richness.

In a certain manner, the one who asks me about the tail and fat of the ox places the tail and fat upon my breast. Until I satisfy him, my breast and heart are burdened and wearied by no slight weight. What these things signify has already been stated above. It continues:

“And Aaron separated the right shoulders, raising them before the Lord, as Moses commanded.” 144. He separates them because they are his own. For a shoulder is necessary to one who must bear the entire weight and the sins of the entire people. But he raises it before the Lord so that he may seek not his own interests, but those of Jesus Christ; so that with the Apostle he may say: “I live; yet no longer I, but Christ lives in me” (Gal. 2:20). For when he says this, [Col. 0412C] his limbs are no longer his own, but belong to him whom he serves.

It continues: “When the burnt offerings had been completed, Moses and Aaron blessed the people; and the glory of the Lord appeared to the whole multitude. And behold, fire came forth from the Lord and consumed the burnt offering and the fats which were upon the altar. When the crowds saw this, they praised the Lord, falling upon their faces.” Perhaps he calls this fire the glory of the Lord.

CHAPTER X

“Aaron’s sons Nadab and Abihu took their censers, put fire in them, and placed incense upon it, offering before the Lord strange fire which had not been commanded them. Fire came forth from the Lord, devoured them, and they died before the Lord.”

This is what the Apostle says: “If anyone preaches to you a gospel other than that which you have heard and received, let him be anathema” (Gal. 1:9). Those who preach to the Church things contrary to faith and not contained in God’s law offer strange fire and strange incense before the Lord. Arius offered such fire and such incense; therefore he died and was condemned to eternal fires.

“But Moses spoke to Aaron and to Eleazar and Ithamar, his sons: Do not uncover your heads and do not tear your garments, lest perhaps you die.”

This is a sign of grief and sadness. But the damnation of the wicked ought rather to be a cause for rejoicing than sorrow. Hence it is written: “The righteous shall rejoice when he sees the vengeance of the wicked” (Ps. 57:11).

“The Lord also said to Aaron: You and your sons shall not drink wine or anything that can intoxicate when you enter the tabernacle of testimony, lest you die; for it is an everlasting commandment throughout your generations. And that you may have knowledge to distinguish between holy and profane, between polluted and clean, and may teach the children of Israel all my ordinances which the Lord spoke to them through the hand of Moses.”

Even when understood literally, these things edify the mind. For drunkenness is a great sin: besides overthrowing the senses, it also provokes lust. Hence the Apostle: “Do not become drunk with wine, in which is lust” (Heb. 5:18). This is the drunkenness of the body; but far worse is drunkenness of the mind. For our mind is filled and intoxicated with anger, indignation, hatred, and pride. Intoxicated by these, it is easily deceived and cannot distinguish between holy and profane, polluted and clean. Therefore, because we are always in God’s tabernacle, we must flee every drunkenness, lest we die.

“Moses spoke to Aaron and to his sons who remained: Take the sacrifice which remains from the Lord’s offering, and eat it without leaven beside the altar, because it is the Holy of Holies. You shall eat it in a holy place, because it has been given to you and your sons from the Lord’s offerings, as was commanded me. The breast also [Col. 0413C] that was offered, and the shoulder that was separated, you, your sons, and your daughters with you shall eat in a most clean place. For they have been reserved for you and your children from the peace offerings of the children of Israel.”

The sacrifice which remains from the Lord’s offering signifies the entire sequence of the holy Scriptures. This sacrifice is called a sacrifice of praise. It remains to us from the Lord’s offering because, although wicked people killed Christ and his disciples, they could not erase their memory or the many volumes written in their praise.

[Note: [Col. 0413D] Julian the Apostate undertook this among other measures against the Christian religion: he sought out all records of the divine Scriptures and consigned them to flames.]

The priests eat this sacrifice without leaven—that is, without any heretical perversity or any corruption—beside the altar, that is, in the holy Church, [Col. 0413D] in the assembly of the faithful, in the council and congregation of the righteous. There God’s mysteries are revealed; there the mysteries of the New and Old Testaments are expounded. For it is written: “Do not give what is holy to dogs, nor cast pearls before swine” (Matt. 7:6). They also eat the breast and shoulder, so that they may become wise and bear one another’s burdens. For in the breast are the heart, mind, and wisdom; upon the shoulders we bear burdens. Aaron, his sons, and his daughters are permitted to eat this sacrifice, because no believer is forbidden to praise God, devote himself or herself to wisdom, and bear the burdens of others.

It follows from this that, when Moses looked for the goat that had been offered, he found it burned up; and he was angry with the priests because they had not eaten it. By this he seems to have wished to signify nothing else than that penitents who afflict themselves for their sins over a long time should not be held in contempt or neglected, but should be received humbly and joyfully and reconciled to the body of the Church. For what is it to eat the goat except to reconcile sinners to the Church? Thus the Apostle Peter ate them, to whom it is said: “Slay and eat” (Acts 10:13). The goat is burned up if the remedy exceeds due measure and causes the sinner to despair. Therefore this goat must not be burned up, but cooked temperately. Thus far concerning the sacrifices.

CHAPTER XI

[Col. 0414B] “The Lord spoke to Moses and Aaron, saying: Say to the children of Israel: These are the animals which you shall eat among all the living creatures of the earth. Everything that has a divided hoof and chews the cud you shall eat; but whatever has a hoof yet does not divide it, such as the camel and the rest, you shall not eat, and you shall count it among the unclean. Likewise the hyrax and the hare are unclean, because although they chew the cud, they do not divide the hoof. So also the swine, which divides the hoof and chews the cud.”

We must therefore say what it is to divide the hoof, to chew the cud, and to eat. The hoof is divine Scripture, by which the feet of the soul are protected for walking. This hoof is divided into letter and spirit, or also into the New and Old Testaments. What is chewing the cud except carefully investigating holy Scripture, breaking it down most minutely by the understanding of the heart, and, by repeatedly turning it over for a long time, bringing it to spiritual understanding?

The Jews neither divide the hoof nor chew the cud, because they neither receive both Testaments nor understand spiritually by meditation what they receive. Swallowing the letter alone and whole, they taste nothing but the letter. The Manichaeans, although they understand certain things spiritually by chewing the cud, nevertheless do not divide the hoof, because they do not receive the Old Testament. The Ebionites, on the contrary, receive both; but because they wish to observe circumcision together with baptism and all the ceremonies of the law, they either do not wish, or do not know how, to chew the cud. [Col. 0414D] All these, therefore, are unclean; and we are forbidden to eat them, to bring them into the ecclesiastical body, and to mingle them with it. And although blessed Peter was told, “Slay and eat” (Acts 11:7), he nevertheless ought not to eat these. For one who wishes to be sanctified must guard against every uncleanness of the soul. For thus it is written there: “What God has sanctified, do not call common” (Acts 10:15).

“These are the creatures born in the waters which it is lawful to eat. Everything that has fins and scales, whether in the sea, rivers, or ponds, you shall eat; but the rest shall be polluted for you.”

Only those fish which have fins and scales are said to leap above the water. By them we understand those who always seek higher things and desire heavenly things—

[Note: [Col. 0415D] Another Cassinese manuscript: “and contemplate heavenly things.”]

—and who, although battered by many storms of adversity, nevertheless say with the Apostle: “Our citizenship is in heaven” (Phil. 3:20). But the rest, who lie hidden beneath the waves, always seek what is lower and deep, and are raised by no desires toward things above and heavenly; they are not without reason called unclean and separated from the body of the Church. “There is no part for the faithful with the unbeliever, no fellowship of light with darkness” (2 Cor. 6:15).

“These are the birds which you shall not eat and which are to be avoided by you: the eagle, griffon-vulture, osprey, kite, and vulture according to its kind; every kind of raven according to its likeness; the ostrich, owl, gull, and hawk according to its kind; the horned owl, cormorant, ibis, swan, pelican, purple gallinule, heron, and plover according to its kind; also the hoopoe and the bat.”

Nearly all these live by prey and plunder and cruelly lie in wait for other animals. In them thieves, robbers, sacrilegious persons, and all plunderers are excluded from the body of the Church. The raven kind is rejected because it is never washed clean of its inborn and natural blackness. It signifies sinners who persevere in wickedness and do not know how to repent. But what do we understand by the ostrich, which indeed has wings but cannot fly, except hypocrites? Though they bear the likeness of goodness, they refuse to do good. What by the owl, which flees light and loves night, except those who follow the prince of darkness and flee Christ, the sun of righteousness? “For everyone who does evil hates the light” (John 3:10). Yet this creature, like the horned owl, lives by prey and plunder. The hoopoe, however, a most filthy animal, nests in dung; by it we understand prostitutes and adulterers. What has been said concerning the owl is also to be understood concerning the bat.

“Every winged creature that walks upon four feet shall be abominable to you. But whatever walks upon four feet and has longer hind legs upon which it leaps over the earth, you shall eat: such as the locust according to its kind, the attacus, the *ophiomachus*, and the grasshopper, each according to its kind. But whatever among winged creatures has only four feet shall be detestable to you.”

What do birds signify except wise persons? What do the four feet signify except the four elements from which a human being is composed in the body and without which he cannot move? Those walk on four feet who obey the body alone, which, as we have said, consists of four elements. Such were the Epicureans—indeed, such still are those who proclaim bodily pleasure to be the highest good. But if two longer hind legs are added to them, [Col. 0416A] by which they leap upon the earth and raise and lift themselves from lower to higher things, they will no longer be counted among unclean animals.

For the two legs are the two Testaments, longer, indeed, than all the feet; since by their faith and teaching the human spirit is lifted above the very heavens and as far as the throne of God. Therefore, whatever among winged creatures has four feet and, descending to earth by bodily necessity, walks upon them—if it then leaps by these legs and raises itself to higher things and begins to fly—will not be abominable or unclean. For whenever we serve the body, we walk upon earth with four feet. For the four elements carry us; we ought to obey them not for pleasure but for necessity. Therefore, always leaping and always fleeing, let us not remain in one place or be occupied with transitory food. This is what locusts do; this is also what the Apostle admonishes, saying: “Make no provision for the flesh in its desires” (Rom. 13:14). It continues:

“Whoever touches their carcasses shall be polluted and unclean until evening. And if it is necessary for someone to carry one of them dead, he shall wash his garments and shall be unclean until sunset.”

What do their carcasses signify except their dead works and mortal sins? Concerning these the Apostle says: “Let us not again lay the foundation of repentance from dead works” (Heb. 6:1). Whoever imitates and performs their dead works touches their carcasses; he is polluted and shall be unclean until evening. What is “until evening”? Evening here seems to signify the end of sin rather than the end of the day. For sin has its rising and setting; sin has its morning and evening. Blessed is the person whose sin has now reached evening; blessed is the one whose sin has reached its end and setting. For such a person, because he ceases to sin, because every sin in him has perished and died, is now clean.

By those who carried the carcasses of unclean animals, I think those are signified who, although approaching penitence and strongly accusing themselves of their past sins, nevertheless carry their burdens even unwillingly—

[Note: [Col. 0415D] From the Cassinese manuscript: “By those who carried the carcasses of animals, I think those are signified who, although they repent of their sins, nevertheless still bear their weight, while they are forced unwillingly to endure the stirrings of a depraved habit which they have not cast off.”]

—because they cannot yet wholly cast out and uproot their depraved habit and the very stirrings of sin. Such persons must wash their garments, because it is fitting that they cleanse their flesh and works through fasts and vigils, almsgiving, tears, and prayers. Yet they shall remain unclean until sunset—that is, until all that stirring, every heat of depraved desire, and the entire desire to sin dies and is extinguished within them. Sunset and evening signify the same thing. It continues:

“But whatever walks upon hands, among all living creatures that go on four feet, shall be unclean [Col. 0417A] to you. Whoever touches their carcasses shall be polluted until evening.”

In the literal sense this seems to be said of the bear, monkey, and similar animals; for these are four-footed and walk upon hands. Moses, however, speaks concerning quadrupeds. Animals which walk upon hands press their hands and eyes, and their entire face, down toward the earth. They signify those people who despise the good things above and eternal things, and who with every effort and action, every gaze of the mind, and the whole intention of the heart, love only earthly and transitory things. The Apostle speaks to them, saying: “If you have risen with Christ, seek the things that are above, not the things upon earth” (Col. 3:1). Indicating that these too are unclean, he says: “If anyone called a brother is a fornicator, [Col. 0417B] or covetous, or an idolater, or a reviler, or a drunkard, with such a one do not even take food” (1 Cor. 5:1). But what it is to touch their carcasses and carry their dead bodies we have just explained above. It continues:

“And whatever any part of their carcasses falls upon shall be defiled—whether a wooden vessel, a garment, skins, or haircloth; and whatever is used for any work shall be dipped in water, and shall be unclean until evening; and afterward it shall be clean. But an earthen vessel into which any of these things falls shall be defiled, and therefore must be broken.” For not only persons who touch the carcasses of unclean animals, but also vessels, garments, and similar things upon which they fall, are defiled, since we sin not only willingly but also unknowingly. For what is it to touch a carcass with the hand except to sin knowingly and willingly? But what is it for a carcass to fall upon something except to sin either unknowingly or unwillingly? Human beings, being rational, touch carcasses; but they fall upon vessels and garments, as upon things without reason. By the former, therefore, we may understand teachers and wise persons; by the latter, the unlearned and foolish. For as a human being differs from a garment, so the wise differ from the foolish. But since folly and ignorance excuse no one, these too must wash their garments and be unclean until evening. What does “until evening” mean? That is, until the end and completion of sin. But an earthen vessel is either broken by repentance and saved, or broken by an iron rod and condemned. It follows:

“Every food which you eat, if water has been poured upon it, shall be unclean; and whatever of such carcasses falls upon it shall be unclean; whether ovens or cooking-pots, they shall be destroyed, and they shall be unclean. But springs, cisterns, and every collection of waters shall be clean. Whoever touches their carcass shall be defiled.” By food, every liquid, springs, cisterns, and collections of waters, we understand nothing better than the books of the holy Scriptures. For these are food and drink for us. But if the water of defiled vessels falls upon these, and they are corrupted by the perversion of unclean people—who ought to be called not so much human beings as horses and mules, in whom there is no understanding—they shall be defiled and unclean. For what do we understand by these vessels, whose water poured over our food and drink corrupts and defiles them, except heretics, Jews, and pagans? If their accursed superstition is mixed with our faith and evangelical teaching, it makes it unclean and defiled. This is what he says: “Every food which you eat, and every liquid which is drunk, if water from any unclean vessel has been poured upon it, shall be unclean.”

But by ovens and cooking-pots, in which and upon which bread and other foods are cooked, teachers of the Church may be understood, in whose breast spiritual foods are prepared and made intelligible and fit to be eaten. These are deservedly destroyed and cast down from their dignities if they allow anything unclean and defiled to fall into themselves. It follows:

“If it falls upon seed, it shall not defile it. But if anyone has drenched the seed with water, and afterward it has been touched by carcasses, it shall immediately be defiled.” Here by “seed” he seems to mean those who, though called to faith, have not yet been baptized or sown in the field of the Church. If something defiled falls upon them, it is not defiled—unless it was clean; for dung is not defiled by dung. But if anyone has drenched the seed with water, it is immediately defiled by what is unclean, because after a person has been baptized—having been cleansed from every defilement—he can be defiled if he touches what is unclean.

[Col. 0418C] “If an animal which it is lawful for you to eat has died, whoever touches its carcass shall be unclean until evening; and whoever eats anything from it or carries it shall wash his garments and be unclean until evening.” A clean animal dies when some Christian is excommunicated for his crimes or separated from the Church because of heresy. Therefore, whoever participates with him or receives his deadly, that is, dead teaching, shall be unclean until, having undertaken repentance, he has made satisfaction. This is what “until evening” means, for evening is the end of sin.

“Everything that creeps upon the earth shall be abominable to you and shall not be taken as food. Whatever four-footed creature walks upon its breast, and has many feet, or drags itself upon the ground, you shall not eat, because it is abominable.” What creeping things signify has already been said above. Creeping things adhere to the earth with their whole body more than other animals; by them we rightly understand the covetous and avaricious, and those given over to every luxury and pleasure of the flesh. They go with as many feet as the vices by which they are dragged along the earth. And because they scatter all their counsels and think of nothing but transient and earthly things, walking upon their breast they press the earth with heart and breast. But the Apostle commands that one should not even take food with such persons. Hence no one ought to doubt that they are unclean. Let what has been said concerning clean and unclean animals suffice.

## CHAPTER XII

[Col. 0419A]

“And the Lord spoke to Moses, saying: Speak to the children of Israel, and say to them: If a woman, having received seed, bears a male child, she shall be unclean seven days, according to the days of the separation of her monthly flow; and on the eighth day the infant shall be circumcised. But she shall remain thirty-three days in the blood of her purification; she shall touch no holy thing, nor enter the sanctuary, until the days of her purification are fulfilled.”

The Jews observed these things according to the letter, but they do not understand what the letter signifies. For what sin does a woman commit in giving birth, that she should be called unclean? As certain doctors of the Church have written, if a woman entered the church immediately after childbirth to give thanks to God, she would not sin. But because he did not simply say, “If a woman bears a male child,” but added with considerable care, “If, having received seed, she bears a male child,” there is no doubt that this was said to distinguish the Blessed Virgin Mary, who bore the Savior without a man’s seed.

> [Note: [Col. 0419D] Not without great significance, and prophetically, is it said in this law concerning women to be purified after their childbirths, if they had given birth from seed received from a man; for the Blessed Virgin Mary alone was to bear Christ the Savior without it.]

Spiritually, this woman seems to be the Synagogue, which, having received the seed of the divine Law, gave birth to a male as often as it performed some good work; for a male child is a good work. And although it had borne a male and produced many children of good works, nevertheless, in the likeness of a menstruating woman, it was unclean for seven days. These seven days signify the entire span of time from Moses to Christ’s incarnation; when that week was finished, the Lamb was born who takes away the sins of the world, of whom it is written: “Who loved us and washed us from our sins in his blood” (Rev. 1:5).

Nevertheless, although the week has ended and Christ has been born, the Synagogue has not yet been completely cleansed, because Christ’s blood has not yet been shed. Therefore let her remain still for thirty-three days in the blood of her purification; let her await the day—indeed, the thirty-third year. For in that year Christ was sacrificed, without whose blood the world could not be cleansed and washed.

> [Note: [Col. 0419D] Bruno’s opinion concerning the year of the death of Christ the Lord—namely, that he underwent death fixed to the cross in the thirty-third year of his age—is called the older, more common, and truer opinion by the most learned Johann Lorenz Berti, *Compendium of Ecclesiastical History*, vol. I, ch. 13, p. 67 [Col. 0420D]. Augustine Calmet, Muratori, Gordon, and others also agree with it. Christ suffered in A.D. 29, in the first year of the 202nd Olympiad, in the seventy-fourth year of Julius Caesar’s correction, P. J. 47 42, under the consuls Rubellius Geminus and C. Fusio Geminus.]

That a day is used for a year you will find in Ezekiel, where it is said: “A day, I say, for a year, son of man, I have given you” (Ezek. 4:6). The seven days signify both all time and some definite portion of time. Why they signify all time we have often said already. But because months and years are also parts of time, they are often used for some portion of time. Why the infant is circumcised is very well known; but why on the eighth day must be explained. For the eighth day is itself also the first. On it the world began; on it Christ rose; and on it the universal resurrection shall occur. Then the circumcised will not merely be circumcised, but, having been wiped clean of all sins, pure and spotless, they shall receive forever the holy name and the inheritance.

“But if she bears a female child, she shall be unclean for two weeks according to the manner of her menstrual flow, and she shall remain sixty-six days in the blood of her purification.” The Synagogue bears a female as often as it works iniquity. For this daughter the Synagogue is unclean for two weeks: one, namely, before Christ’s incarnation; the other after his preaching, death, and resurrection, so long as it remains in its unbelief. For through these two weeks the whole of both that time and this time is signified. Unless, therefore, it ceases to bear an unclean daughter and wholly turns itself to faith in Christ, it will be reckoned no less unclean than if it were a menstruating woman.

> [Note: [Col. 0420D] Codex Casinensis: “wicked” (*iniquam*).]

We shall speak of the menstruating woman in what follows. But sixty-six days are given them for purification; through them we may understand all the days up to the consummation of the age. For this number consists of sixes, and the number six often denotes in sacred discourse the perfection of good work, because the Lord performs his work in six days: “He saw all the things that he had made, and they were very good” (Gen. 1:31). During all these days, therefore, the Synagogue can be purified, because throughout all of them it is permitted to do good work. And lest perhaps it should say, “It is not lawful to heal on the Sabbath,” no Sabbath is included among these days, for the Sabbath is not contained in six days. [Col. 0420C] This whole number, moreover, is composed solely of sixes.

“And when the days of her purification have been fulfilled, for a son or a daughter she shall bring a lamb of a year old for a burnt offering, and a young pigeon or a turtledove for sin, to the door of the tabernacle of testimony; and she shall hand them over to the priest, who shall offer them before the Lord and pray for her, and so she shall be cleansed from the flow of her blood.” The Synagogue, then, or some child of the Synagogue, brings a year-old lamb as a burnt offering if, recognizing that he has sinned, he preaches or reveres Christ’s passion—not by killing the Lamb now, but by eating him; not by condemning him, but by adoring him; not by persecuting him, but by believing in him. He also brings a young pigeon or a turtledove for sin. Where? To the door of the tabernacle. For what purpose? That he may hand them to the priest. Why? “That he may offer them before the Lord and pray for her, and so she shall be cleansed from the flow of her blood.”

For what is signified by the young pigeon but the patience and innocence of soul and body? And what by the turtledove but the chastity of both persons? He offers these for sin who, repenting of sins, promises to live innocently and chastely. This is done through the counsel of priests—

> [Note: [Col. 0421D] Codex Casinensis: “by the counsel of priests.”]

—who always stand at the door of the tabernacle, opening for others the gate of piety and faith, and presenting to God by their prayers holy vows and good desires. But when it says, “And so she shall be cleansed from the flow of her blood,” it signifies that the woman needs cleansing not because she gave birth, but because she sinned.

> [Note: [Col. 0421] The same codex: “It indicates that a woman must be cleansed in this way not because she gave birth, but because she sinned.”]

“But if she cannot offer a lamb, let her offer two turtledoves or two young pigeons, one for a burnt offering and the other for sin.” In this provision the poor are cared for, and the meaning is not changed. For Christ is also the turtledove—indeed, the head of the turtledove, that is, of the Church—and the young pigeon, because he is the Son of the Church. For the Virgin Mary is the daughter of the Church, and Christ himself is her Son. Therefore a person offers two turtledoves or two young pigeons: namely, Christ and himself—Christ as a burnt offering and himself for sin—meditating on Christ’s passion and mortifying and afflicting himself. But if anyone wishes to understand only a human being in both the lamb and the birds, the allegory is plain and requires no labor.

## CHAPTER XIII

“And the Lord spoke to Moses and Aaron, saying: A man in whose skin and flesh there has arisen a variety of color, or a pustule, or something as though shining—that is, a spot of leprosy—shall be brought to Aaron the priest, or to any one of his sons, who, if he sees the leprosy in the skin, the hairs changed to a white color, and the appearance of the leprosy itself lower than the remaining skin and flesh, shall judge it a spot of leprosy; and at his discretion the man shall be separated.”

Just as bodily leprosy has certain signs, so spiritual leprosy has manifest indications. By the leprosy of the body, Moses wished to show us the invisible leprosy of the soul, setting forth evident proofs of each leprosy. Therefore, when a person recognizes that there is a leprous spot in his soul, let him bring it to Aaron and his sons; let him bring it to bishops and priests. For it is better that he bring himself than that he be brought by others; better that he accuse himself than that he be accused by others. But whether the soul is first brought to the priest by itself or by another, it must first be judged by him before it is condemned by the judgment of others. For the power to condemn and absolve according to the soul has been given by the Lord to bishops and priests alone. Therefore the person sins who thinks that a leprous person and sinner ought to be excluded from communion before he is judged by bishops and priests.

Let the leper, then, be brought to the priest. For thus the Lord says: “Show yourselves to the priests” (Luke 17:14). Let the priest examine him and inquire carefully whether it is leprosy. For leprosy has its signs; it cannot be concealed and is easily recognized. Who, indeed, doubts that an adulterer, murderer, perjurer, sacrilegious person, thief, or robber is leprous? When the priest finds such a person, let him change his judgment neither through fear nor through favor. Let him say that he is leprous, and let him be separated according to the priest’s judgment—according to his, certainly, not another’s. It belongs to him to judge and to separate him.

How is he to be separated? For this separation occurs in many ways. Some are separated from the body and blood of Christ; others from entrance into the Church; others from the communion of the faithful. They are also separated from certain foods and drinks and from other pleasures of the flesh, so that they may no longer lawfully use things which they had previously used lawfully. It follows:

“But if there is a shining whiteness in the skin, not lower than the remaining flesh, and the hairs are of their former color, the priest shall confine him seven days. On the seventh day he shall examine him; and if the leprosy has not increased or passed beyond its former limits in the skin, he shall shut him up again for another seven days. On the seventh day he shall examine him. If the leprosy is dimmer and has not increased in the skin, he shall cleanse him, for it is scab; and the man shall wash his garments and shall be clean.”

These things must be understood concerning one about whom an evil report is spread on some occasion. A shining whiteness appears in the skin when a shameful report concerning someone is announced by others to his disgrace and shame. But if it is not true and cannot be proved, the supposed blemish is not lower than the flesh, because the man remains sound in the matters of which he is accused. For if the blemish were lower and had made, as it were, a hollow in the flesh, it would have given a clear and unquestionable sign of leprosy. The hairs too are of their former color because, as far as he himself is concerned, the soul has not lost the appearance of its beauty, although it is discolored by the detractions of others.

The priest shall therefore confine him for seven days and examine him on the seventh day. By seven days is understood any period during which a person accused is given a respite in order to clear himself. Since his case is still pending and not yet determined, he seems, as it were, confined and not wholly in possession of his freedom. But the seventh day is understood as that on which, once the respite has ended, the whole case ought to be concluded and the accused person declared innocent, if no accuser then appears and the accusation cannot be proved by any manifest evidence. This is what he says: “If the leprosy has not increased or passed beyond its former limits.” For the leprosy would appear to increase and pass beyond its former limits if what had first been alleged were afterward proved true.

If, I say, this occurs, he shall again shut him up for another seven days, giving him a respite as before. I think this is done so that either the case may not remain unexamined or the accusers may not pretend that they were unable to appear by the appointed time. But if neither accusers are present nor, when the priest examines him, the leprosy appears more dim and has not increased in the skin—that is, if the report which had first been openly spread subsides because accusers and judges are lacking—he shall cleanse him, because it is scab. What does “he shall cleanse him” mean except that he shall judge him clean? It was not leprosy but scab; not a crime but the appearance of a crime. Let the person wash his garments: let him clear himself by oath or in some other way, so that he may be believed to be what he is.

We often see this happen to God’s priests. Hence the holy Fathers rightly wished accusations against priests to be difficult. It follows: “But if, after he has been seen by the priest and restored to cleanness, the leprosy grows again, he shall be brought to him and condemned as unclean.” This is as though it said: If after the priest’s judgment he does not keep himself guarded and the leprosy of the committed crime appears through certain proofs, he shall again be brought to the priest; then, condemned as unclean, he shall lose even the designation by which he had previously seemed clean.

[Col. 0423B] “If a leprous spot is in a person, he shall be brought to the priest, and the priest shall see him. When there is a white color in the skin, and it has changed the appearance of the hair, and living flesh itself appears in the swelling, it shall be judged a very old leprosy, rooted in the skin. Therefore the priest shall pronounce him defiled and shall not shut him up, because the uncleanness is evident.”

This must be understood of the leprosy of that crime which, through evil practice and habit, is so manifest that it cannot possibly be concealed. Such a person is to be accused and brought to the priest. He is brought by an accusation; hence accusers are called informers (*delatores*), as though they bring and carry others forward. The priest shall see and examine him, and when he observes most certain signs in the color, the hairs, and the living flesh itself, he shall not confine him or give him any respite. Rather, he shall declare him defiled—that is, judge him defiled—because the uncleanness is evident and requires no proof. For living flesh in the leper indicates that he sinned knowingly and willingly. But the change in color and hairs indicates a very old leprosy.

“But if a spreading leprosy breaks out in the skin and covers all the flesh from head to foot, everything that falls under the sight of the eyes, the priest shall examine him and judge him to be affected with a very clean leprosy, because he has wholly turned white; and therefore the man shall be clean.” Behold another kind of leprosy, by which we understand madness and frenzy. For we often see the mad and frenzied rush into crimes, and while, their reason being lost, they suppose that they are doing something good, they commit murders and many other acts. Therefore, when the priest sees that a person is wholly and entirely afflicted by this leprosy of illness, and sees in him nothing of knowledge or reason, he shall judge him to be affected with a very clean leprosy; and therefore the person shall be clean. For how can he fail to be clean from sin when he does not understand what he does? Such persons are not assigned repentance for their sins—indeed, for acts which are not their own—because where there is no will to sin, there ought to be no punishment for sin.

Therefore, although the Jews had not lost reason and understanding, the Lord nevertheless speaks of them as though they were mad and frenzied, saying: “Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing” (Luke 23:34). They did not know because they did not wish to know; but from these persons knowledge has been taken away not by the will but by illness. Hence he adds: “But whenever living flesh appears in him, then by the priest’s judgment he shall be defiled and reckoned among the unclean. For living flesh, if sprinkled with leprosy, is unclean.” The person who lacks the reason and knowledge proper to a living human being ought to be reckoned not living but dead. If living flesh—that is, irrational perception—should be restored to him, and he should afterward fall into some crime, then by the priest’s judgment he is to be condemned as defiled and unclean. For living flesh—that is, a person devoid of his senses and reason—if he commits some evil, it ought not to be imputed to him; for he does not act voluntarily and must not be judged as consenting to sin.

“But if it turns again to whiteness and covers the whole person, the priest shall examine him and decree him clean.” If a person is again overtaken by his former illness and habitual madness, he is indeed leprous; but because he does not discern, even if he sins, he is nevertheless clean and without sin.

“Flesh and skin in which an ulcer has arisen and has been healed, and in the place of the ulcer a scar has appeared, white or reddish, the person shall be brought to the priest. When he sees that the place of the leprosy is lower than the remaining flesh and the hairs have turned white, he shall pronounce him defiled; for a spot of leprosy has arisen in the ulcer.” This is to be understood of sinners who, after repentance has been performed and the wound of sin healed, relapse into sin like a dog to its vomit. For what is a healed ulcer except sin erased by repentance? In the scar on the skin, manifest signs of leprosy appear when that sanctification itself is abolished by a return to sin. This person, therefore, being brought to the priest, because the leprosy is manifest and he cannot in any way defend himself, has nothing remaining but condemnation, because he is guilty.

There is no need everywhere to explain every point individually, since they may easily be understood from what has been said above. It follows: “But if the hair is of its former color, the scar somewhat dim, and the neighboring flesh not lower, he shall confine him seven days; and if it has increased, he shall adjudge him leprous. But if it remains in its place, it is the scar of the ulcer, and the man shall be clean.” By these things we understand that, if no certain and manifest signs of sin have yet appeared against an accused person, and, after a respite has been granted, no accusers appear and the evil report becomes dimmer—subsiding, as it were, no longer sounding as openly as before, nor increasing—the person must be judged clean and innocent.

“Flesh and skin which fire has burned, and which when healed has a white or reddish scar, the priest shall examine it; and behold, if it has turned white and its place is lower than the remaining skin, he shall pronounce him defiled, because a spot of leprosy has arisen in the scar.” This too, like the preceding passages, is understood of one who returns to sin after repentance has been performed. Although all sins set a person on fire with a certain fire of desire, it is especially characteristic of lust to burn through desire. If, therefore, the fire of lust has burned flesh and skin—that is, has wounded the body and the soul consenting to it—and afterward, when the person has been healed by repentance, he returns to sin and commits the same acts again, the priest shall examine him. If he sees in him the most certain signs of leprosy—that is, if the flesh has turned white and the place of leprosy is lower than the rest of the flesh, for these are the most certain signs—he shall condemn him, because leprosy has followed again after repentance.

“But if the color of the hairs has not changed, nor is the spot lower than the remaining flesh, and the appearance of the leprosy itself is somewhat dim, he shall confine him seven days, and on the seventh day he shall examine him. If the leprosy has increased in the skin, [he shall pronounce] him [unclean]; but if the whiteness remains in its place and is not very clear, it is the spot of a burn; and therefore he shall be cleansed, because it is the scar of a burn.” Whoever has carefully heard the preceding matters can easily understand these also; for here, as there, the same full respite of seven days is given. The number seven admits no diminution. Therefore the respite of seven days signifies that complete and entire respite ought to be given to the accused. If after it the appearance of leprosy remains in its place and, when the respite has ended, the evil and shameful report subsides, the person is to be judged clean and innocent, because it was not leprosy but the appearance of leprosy; not a burn but the resemblance and spot of a burn. For the difference between being and being said to be is as great as that between leprosy and an appearance of leprosy, and between a burn and the spot of a burn.

“A man or woman in whose head or beard leprosy has sprung up, the priest shall examine them; and if the place is lower than the remaining flesh, and the hair is yellow and finer than usual, he shall pronounce them defiled, because it is leprosy of the head and beard.” This kind seems to concern faith. For what is meant by the head except the mind? And what by the beard except the face? For the place of the beard is the face. Unless beard is understood as face, the interpretation cannot stand, since women do not have beards. Therefore leprosy in the head is error in the mind; but leprosy in the face is sin openly displayed, for what is in the face is not hidden. Whoever believes and understands wrongly concerning God himself and the Christian faith has leprosy in mind and head; but whoever makes known to others what he himself wrongly believes carries leprosy in his face as well as in his head.

When the priest sees such persons and recognizes in them certain and manifest signs of leprosy, he shall condemn them because they are guilty. But if manifest signs do not appear, he shall confine him as above. Then, if after the granted respite he discovers nothing certain, the person shall be shaved and shut up again. A person is shaved and cleansed apart from the place of the blemish when he is absolved in all other respects but is held only in the matter of which he has been accused. But if after the second respite the report has subsided, no witnesses of proof are present, and no indications appear, the priest shall cleanse him—that is, judge him clean—and, his garments having been washed, he shall be clean, purifying himself by oath or in any other way. But if after correction the person begins openly to preach and defend his heresy, no further signs need be sought, because he is to be considered guilty and unclean.

“A man or woman in whose skin a whiteness appears, the priest shall examine them. If he finds a somewhat dim whiteness shining in the skin, let him know that it is not leprosy but a blemish of white color, and that the person is clean.” He sets forth only one sign, which is found not only in leprous persons but also in the healthy; by it we understand an evil report, which, if it is merely vague, should not be rashly believed. For we have often heard even just and innocent people unjustly defamed.

[Col. 0426B] “A man from whose head the hairs fall, being bald, shall be clean; and if the hairs have fallen from his forehead, he is bald in front and clean.” Here too, as above, he is judged clean, because no one is condemned on the basis of one sign alone, especially an ambiguous one. Loss of hair often occurs not only to leprous persons but also to the healthy.

“But if a white or reddish color has arisen in the baldness or front baldness, and the priest sees this, he shall condemn him as afflicted with unquestionable leprosy which has arisen in the baldness.” Here two signs are given: one ambiguous, namely baldness; the other manifest, namely the color in the baldness. This person is therefore rightly condemned, as one condemned by manifest judgment. These matters can also be interpreted otherwise, but for the present this is sufficient. It follows:

[Col. 0426C] “Therefore whoever has been marked with leprosy and separated at the discretion of the priest shall have torn garments, an uncovered head, and a mouth covered with a garment; he shall cry that he is defiled and unclean at all times, because he is leprous and unclean; he shall live alone outside the camp.” This penance is given to lepers: after they have been separated at the priest’s discretion—for otherwise they are not separated—they are to have torn garments, which are indeed a sign of grief and sorrow. Thus we read that Jacob and many others tore their garments. They are also to have an uncovered head, so that they may reveal the secrets of their heart. For the head is frequently taken for the mind and heart. Hence the Psalmist: “Hope in him, all you congregation of the people, and pour out your hearts before him” (Ps. 61:9). And again: “I said: I will confess my injustices against myself to the Lord” (Ps. 31:3). These are words of an uncovered head.

They are also to have their mouth covered with a garment: “Praise is not becoming in the mouth of a sinner” (Ecclus. 13:9). Let them therefore be silent and not preach, because “God said to the sinner: Why do you recount my justices?” (Ps. 49:16). He to whom this is said is commanded to cover himself. But let them cry that they are defiled and unclean at all times; for the more a sinner accuses himself and confesses his crimes to the Lord, the sooner he obtains pardon from the most merciful Lord. “For if, as the Apostle says, we judged ourselves, we should certainly not be judged” (1 Cor. 6:31). Let them live outside the camp, lead a harsh and rugged life, flee amusement and gladness, and adopt a solitary and unfamiliar way of life. It follows:

“A woolen or linen garment that has leprosy in the warp or the woof, or indeed a skin or anything made from skin, if it is marked by a white or reddish spot, shall be considered leprosy and shown to the priest. Having examined it, he shall confine it seven days; and on the seventh day, examining it again, if he finds that it has increased, it is persistent leprosy. He shall judge the garment, and everything in which it is found, to be defiled; and therefore it shall be burned in flames.”

We rightly say that this garment is the flesh with which every soul is clothed.

> [Note: [Col. 0427D] Thus according to another Casinensis manuscript.]

Of this garment the Apostle says: “Put off the old man” (Eph. 4:24). And the Church in the Song of Songs: “I have taken off my tunic; how shall I put it on?” (Song 5:5). And the prophet says: “A garment mixed with blood shall be for burning, and fuel for the fire” (Isa. 9:5).

In married persons the garment is woolen; in virgins and the continent it is linen; in all the rest it is of skin. For wool comes from flesh and clings to flesh; linen is outside the flesh and foreign to it; but skin is dead flesh. Of the married person it is said: “He shall cleave to his wife, and the two shall be one flesh” (Eph. 5:31); but virgins, being as it were far from the flesh, do not follow pleasures of the flesh. The rest, like dead flesh, feel their own corruption and do not understand it.

Although the leprosy of this garment is manifold, the greatest and principal meaning is fornication, concerning which the Apostle says: “Every sin whatever a person commits is outside the body; but he who commits fornication sins against his own body” (1 Cor. 6:18). This vice exceeds all bodily vices so greatly that, in comparison with it, the rest appear almost not to exist. This leprosy, therefore, because it often corrupts not only fornicators and adulterers but also virgins, continent persons, and married persons, is found in woolen, linen, and skin garments. Its signs are a white or reddish spot. For fornicators are often detected by pallor and blushing, because they are affected both by fear and by the fire of love.

When the priest sees such a garment and finds it so defiled, he shall confine it seven days—namely, reckoning seven years for its cleansing in penance. For not without cause did the holy Fathers establish this number of years for penitents. For concerning Cain the Lord himself says: “Whoever kills Cain shall be punished sevenfold” (Gen. 4:15). When these years have been completed, if the person is worthy, let him be absolved, washed, and reconciled. For why is a person absolved and reconciled when his penance has been completed, except because by the priest’s absolution he is washed and cleansed?

But if, after the seven days of which we have also spoken above, the priest finds that the leprosy has increased, he shall judge the garment defiled, because the leprosy is persistent; and therefore it shall be burned in flames. Let penitents hear this, in whom sins are not erased if they increase daily, because those who persist in sins always add sins to sins. Let them hear what is said: “And therefore the garment shall be burned in flames”; and let them remember that saying of the Gospel: “Go, you cursed, into eternal fire” (Matt. 25:41), and that of the prophet: “Their worm shall not die, and their fire shall not be burned” (Isa. 66:24).

“What if he sees that it has not increased? He shall give orders that they wash the thing in which the leprosy is, and he shall shut it up for another seven days. And when he sees that its former appearance has indeed not returned, though the leprosy has not increased, he shall judge it unclean and burn it with fire, because the leprosy has spread over the surface of the garment, or throughout it.” If, he says, after penance has been undertaken, the sin which ought to have been erased has increased, nothing remains but condemnation. But if it has not increased, yet has not been erased—for although the person has ceased from sin, he has nevertheless not done penance—the leprosy must be washed, the same penance imposed again, and it must be shut up for another seven days, so that what he sinned during the first seven may at least be corrected in these following seven days. But if even after these seven days the priest sees that the former appearance has indeed not returned, though the leprosy has not increased, he shall judge it unclean, as one who despises the canons: although he has ceased from sin, he has nevertheless either neglected or failed to take care to render fitting satisfaction by penance. For one who scorns to erase sin either does not understand himself to be a sinner, or shows that he fears no punishment for sin. It is not enough for a person to abstain from evil unless he also does good. Hence it is written: “Turn away from evil and do good” (Ps. 36 [37]:27). Therefore, whoever ceases from sin must also do penance for sin; otherwise, even if the stain does not grow, the garment does not recover its former appearance. The priest burns such a garment with fire because he judges the sinner unwilling to do penance worthy of eternal fire. But what does it mean when he says that the leprosy has spread over the surface of the garment, or throughout it, when above he said that the leprosy had not increased? It has not increased, indeed, because the person has not returned to sin; yet it has spread over the whole surface of the garment because, in that which has not been erased, it still covers the whole garment.

“But if the place of the leprosy is darker after the garment has been washed, he shall tear it out and separate it from the whole. But if, in the places which were previously stained, a wandering and shifting leprosy appears again, it must be burned with fire; if it ceases, he shall wash those things which are clean a second time, and they shall be clean.” The place of leprosy is darker after the garment has been washed if, after undertaking penance, the sinner conceals what he has done and how he has lived. Therefore let the place be torn out and separated from the whole; let it plainly appear whether anything hidden within remains: thus it must be broken open, if he confesses. But if leprosy appears again in those places, and the person is unconvertible, neither ceasing from sin nor doing penance, he must be rebuked and condemned; he must be judged worthy of fire and punishment. But if it ceases, he shall wash those things which are clean a second time, and they shall be clean. Why are the things which are clean washed a second time, unless because, although a person is clean through penance, yet unless he has been reconciled and absolved by the priest, he still abstains from the sacraments as unclean? For although he is clean, he is not seen to be clean unless he shares in the Church’s sacraments together with the other faithful. Thus he is washed first by penance, and secondly by reconciliation and absolution. Thus far concerning leprosy; now let us consider its cleansing.

## CHAPTER XIV

“And the Lord spoke to Moses, saying: This is the rite for the leper when he is to be cleansed. He shall be brought to the priest; and the priest, going outside the camp, when he finds that the leprosy has been cleansed, shall command the person being purified to offer for himself two living sparrows, lawful for food, cedarwood, scarlet thread, and hyssop. He shall order one of the sparrows to be sacrificed in an earthen vessel over living waters; but he shall dip the other, alive, together with the cedarwood, scarlet, and hyssop, in the blood of the sparrow that has been sacrificed. With this he shall sprinkle the person who is to be cleansed seven times, so that he may be rightly purified; and he shall release the living sparrow to fly away into the field.”

The priest goes out from the camp to reconcile the leper, because even today we see our bishops go out through the doors of the church to reconcile sinners. Yet the leper is not received or cleansed, because neither should a sinner who has not done penance for sin be reconciled. For penance is to weep over sins committed and not to commit things that should be wept over. Peter wept and was cleansed; David also wept and was cleansed. Paul mourns the Corinthians who sinned and did not do penance. Thus Samuel mourned for Saul. This satisfaction is brief and easy: “Turn away from evil and do good” (Ps. 36 [37]:27). Begin to weep, but from the heart; say while weeping: “Father, I have sinned against heaven and before you; I am no longer worthy to be called your son. Make me as one of your hired servants” (Luke 15:18–19). This is true reconciliation; thus the leper is cleansed, thus the sinner deserves pardon. Hear what the Lord says: “Quickly bring out the first robe and clothe him” (ibid.). “Quickly,” he says: let there be no delay. “For in whatever hour the sinner is converted and groans, he shall live and shall not die” (Ezek. 33:11).

The person being purified offers for himself two sparrows—not just any sparrows, but living ones, lawful for food. What are the two sparrows but body and soul? Of these the Prophet says: “Our soul has escaped like a sparrow from the snare of the hunters” (Ps. 123 [124]:7). Rightly, therefore, he offers two sparrows, so that he may restore to the Lord not a part but his whole self: no longer dead, no longer liable to sins. And because formerly he was unclean, it was not lawful to eat his sparrows; but now, because he is clean, he offers such sparrows as may lawfully be eaten and received into the body of the Church.

But why does he offer cedarwood, scarlet, and hyssop with the sparrows? Cedarwood is by nature incorruptible and fragrant; scarlet is fiery and red; and hyssop naturally grows on rock. Let the person being reconciled therefore offer cedarwood, so that henceforth he may lead an incorrupt and fragrant life; let him offer scarlet, that he may be kindled by the fire of the Holy Spirit and charity; and let him offer hyssop, that with firm roots he may cling to that rock of which the Apostle says: “And the rock was Christ” (1 Cor. 10:4).

One of the sparrows is sacrificed in an earthen vessel, by which we understand the body; because it is made from earth, it is fittingly ordered to be sacrificed in an earthen vessel. He used “earthen” and “clay vessel” so that we may plainly understand that the body is signified by this sparrow. This is said to occur over living waters, for “the letter kills, but the spirit gives life.” Thus we too must afflict our body, so that we may be dead to the flesh but alive in spirit. But he shall dip the other sparrow, alive, with cedarwood, scarlet, and hyssop, in the blood of the sacrificed sparrow. For the living sparrow is the soul, which, being immortal, cannot die. It is dipped in the blood of the sacrificed sparrow so that the soul may never forget those sins which the body has committed; for blood stands for sin. But because remembrance of sins is sometimes helpful and sometimes harmful—it is helpful if it is done in order that sins may be erased, but harmful if the mind, taking delight in them, desires to return to them—therefore the soul is not dipped in the blood without cedarwood, scarlet, and hyssop, so that while it is dipped, it may remain incorrupt, burn with love, and cling to the rock.

With this blood the person who has been cleansed is sprinkled seven times; for what is done seven times is done always. Therefore a person is sprinkled seven times with his own blood, so that he may always remember his sins. But when it says, “And he shall release the living sparrow to fly away into the field,” this means that the soul must never again be enclosed in prison, conquered by the flesh, or restrained by mere will. Let it be mistress; let it be free; let it fly into the field and search the Scriptures. For there are flowers there, there are fragrances there. Let it say with Isaac: “Behold, the fragrance of my son is like the fragrance of a full field which the Lord has blessed” (Gen. 27:27). It follows:

“And when the man has washed his garments, he shall shave all the hair of his body and wash himself with water; and, being purified, he shall enter the camp. Yet he shall remain outside his tent for seven days; and on the seventh day he shall shave all the hair of his head, his beard and eyebrows, and all the hair of his body.” Behold, the person who is reconciled washes his garments so that no one may henceforth recoil from him and, as all look on him, he may appear no longer leprous but clean. He shaves all the hair of his body, so that nothing superfluous and useless may remain in him. He is also washed with the water of confession of a good vow and priestly blessing; wholly purified, he enters the camp and is reconciled to the Church, so that joy and exultation arise. Our holy mother calls together her friends and neighbors, saying: “Rejoice with me, because I have found the drachma which I had lost” (Luke 15:9). Behold, he has entered the camp; yet he remains outside his tent for seven days, that is, he must live free from every desire of this age until the end of his life, until on the seventh day, which is the last, he is found wholly purified after once more shaving his head and all the hair of his body.

“And after washing his garments and body again, on the eighth day he shall take two unblemished lambs, a year-old ewe without blemish, three tenths of fine flour mixed with oil for a sacrifice, and separately a sextary of oil.” When the first week has ended, the second begins, since the eighth day is the beginning of another week. In this week, therefore, as in the first, the person is washed and offers another sacrifice by which he is purified. But in this sacrifice no longer sparrows but a lamb is sacrificed, “who takes away the sins of the world.” The first lamb is Christ; the second is the choir of apostles: both, indeed, sacrificed. The year-old and spotless ewe is the Church, having neither spot nor wrinkle; because it consists in its entirety of three parts—Asia, Africa, and Europe—three tenths of fine flour are joined to it. Of these the Gospel says: “The kingdom of heaven is like leaven, which a woman hid in three measures of flour” (Luke 13:21). This flour is mixed with oil because the Church is anointed by the grace of the Holy Spirit. The sextary of oil, moreover, which is added, is ordered in what follows to be offered with the first lamb. Literally, three tenths are made if you take three sextaries from thirty sextaries. It follows:

“And when the priest purifying the man has placed him and all these things before the Lord at the entrance of the tabernacle of testimony, he shall take the lamb and offer it for a trespass offering, together with the sextary of oil; and, after presenting them all before the Lord, he shall sacrifice the lamb in the holy place where the victim for sin and the burnt offering are customarily sacrificed.” It should be noted that the preceding sacrifice is offered not only by the priest but also by the person to be cleansed. Here, however, the sacrifice is offered not by the person to be cleansed but by the priest alone. For it was not fitting that the person being cleansed should offer this sacrifice. The priest places the person being purified before the entrance of the tabernacle, so that he may readily hear and see the things done in the tabernacle. Then he offers the lamb and the sextary of oil, praising, proclaiming, recalling, and explaining Christ’s passion: how the righteous one died for the ungodly, the Lord for servants, so that they might not die; how abundantly he overflowed with oil, how he abounded in compassion and mercy, when he prayed even for those crucifying him, saying: “Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing” (Luke 23:34). This is the sacrifice of praise by which sins are erased, by which the person being cleansed is kindled to the love of God and stirred to compassion and mercy.

[Col. 0432A] “And the priest, taking some of the blood of the victim sacrificed for trespass, shall put it upon the tip of the right ear of the person being cleansed, and upon the thumbs of his right hand and foot.” Hearing is understood in the ear; action in the hand and foot. Therefore Christ’s blood touches the ear, that it may be clean and always open to hear the word of God, according to that saying: “He who has ears to hear, let him hear” (Luke 8:8). And because, as the Apostle says, “It is not the hearers of the law who are righteous before God, but the doers of the law who shall be justified” (Rom. 2:13), it also touches hand and foot, so that he may both act well and run in the way of God’s commandments. Since the left and adverse side ought not to know what the right does, it touches only the right side, as though he had no left side. It touches the extremities so that he may persevere to the end.

“And from the sextary of oil he shall pour some into his own left hand, dip his right finger in it, and sprinkle seven times before the Lord. What remains of the oil in his left hand he shall pour upon the tip of the right ear of the person being cleansed, and upon the thumbs of his right hand and foot, upon the blood poured out for the trespass offering, and upon his head; and he shall pray for him before the Lord.” The priest works with both hands, because through the weapons of righteousness on the right and left he is neither broken by adversities nor raised up by prosperity. He carries the oil in his left hand and sprinkles it with his right; and this seven times, before the Lord. The priest sprinkles oil seven times before the Lord because he always and at every time intercedes for sinners. What is oil but the prayers of the saints?
