By this oil the indignation of the heavenly Judge is softened and appeased. He carries the oil in his left hand because, so long as he is in this life, he never ceases from mercy. He fittingly sprinkles it before the Lord with his right hand, because with a hand, as it were, powerful and strong, he directs all his action toward God.

He pours the remainder upon the right ear, hand, and foot of the person being cleansed, so that he may hear and understand the meaning of: “I desire mercy, and not sacrifice” (Hos. 6:6), and: “Be merciful, as your Father also is merciful” (Luke 6:36). Let the ear hear this, and let hand and foot delight in it, so as to practise compassion and mercy. In these two members nearly all our action consists. The priest also pours oil upon the blood of the victim and upon the head of the person being cleansed: upon the blood because all that blood, rich in compassion and mercy, was shed for compassion and mercy alone; upon the head, that the human mind may be enriched by this anointing, according to: “But when you fast, anoint your head” (Matt. 6:17). Contrary to this is: “Let not the oil of the sinner anoint my head” (Ps. 140 [141]:5).

> [Note: [Col. 0431D] The edition is corrected from the Cassinese manuscript. “Yet even with regard to the remission in the holy Church of crimes themselves, however great, God’s mercy is not to be despaired of by those who do penance according to the measure of each sin.” (Augustine, *Enchiridion*, ch. 22).]

Thus let the person anointed know and understand that he has been saved by the oil of mercy, delivered by mercy, reconciled by mercy; and therefore let him say: “I will sing forever of the mercies of the Lord” (Ps. 88 [89]:2). Let us also say: “Who is wise, and will keep these things, and understand the mercies of the Lord?” (Ps. 106 [107]:43).

“And he shall make the sacrifice for sin. Then he shall sacrifice the burnt offering and place it upon the altar with its libations, and the man shall be duly cleansed.” In this burnt offering the lamb, the ewe, and the three tenths of fine flour are sacrificed, because the faith, hope, charity and mercy, patience and humility, piety, wisdom, and holy conduct of the holy apostles and of the whole Church are praised, proclaimed, and recounted, and are sacrificed in a sacrifice of praise and jubilation. By these the person is instructed and taught, so that he may know what he should do, what he should believe, what he should follow, what he should flee, and how thereafter he ought to conduct himself in the assembly of the faithful. If he understands well and acts faithfully, he will be clean.

“But if he is poor and his hand cannot find the things that have been named, he shall take a lamb for a trespass offering, that the priest may pray for him; a tenth of fine flour mixed with oil for a sacrifice; a sextary of oil; and two turtledoves or two young pigeons, of which one shall be for sin and the other for a burnt offering; and on the eighth day of his purification he shall offer them to the priest.” As regards the signification, the poor appear to offer no less than the rich. He offers, indeed, but does not sacrifice; sacrifice belongs to the priest. This is the lamb of whom we spoke above, who takes away the sins of the world. This tenth part of fine flour is divided above into three tenths. This sextary of oil, which is sacrificed with the lamb, is God’s mercy. The two turtledoves or two young pigeons are the two sparrows of whom we spoke above. Since we have recently explained these things and the rest which follows concerning this sacrifice, it is enough to have said this briefly.

There follows concerning a leprous house: its owner reports to the priest that something like a plague of leprosy appears in his house; the priest orders everything to be brought outside and the house shut up for seven days. If on the seventh day he sees that the leprosy has increased, he shall remove the stones in which the leprosy is and put other stones in their place; he shall scrape the house inside and throw its dust outside the city into an unclean place. But if, after these measures, the priest enters and discovers that the leprosy has returned, it is a persistent leprosy and the house is unclean. They shall immediately destroy it and cast its stones, timber, and all its dust outside the camp into an unclean place. Let us explain this briefly, since it can easily be understood from what has been said.

If therefore, whoever you are, you see something like a plague of leprosy in your house—if you discover the teaching of heretical perversity in your authority, household, or flock—report it to the priest; report it to the assembly and congregation of saints. For nothing is to be judged rashly; let everything be done with reason and order. Therefore the priest and the order of saints command that everything be brought outside and that all the people separate themselves from those whose knowledge and teaching appear leprous. Let the house be shut up for seven days; let the mouths of those who seem to speak wrongly be stopped; let them be forbidden to sow this teaching among the people, until the priests have most carefully examined and judged whether it is sound or leprous. But if on the seventh day—the day appointed to settle this matter—they see that the leprosy and heresy have increased, for they increase when they are most openly disclosed, let them remove the stones in which the leprosy is: let them condemn the opinions in which the heresy lies. Let them put other stones in their place, that is, let them teach the doctrine and opinions of the Catholic faith after all heretical perversity has been removed. Let them scrape the house inside, root out every error from their hearts and minds, and cast all the dust, all the darkness and uncleanness of that leprosy, outside the city and beyond the boundaries of the Church.

But if after all this—may it not happen!—the leprosy returns, and the priest finds that those recently cleansed have again been defiled with heretical perversity, it is a persistent leprosy and the house is unclean. Hence the Apostle says: “After a first and second admonition, avoid a heretical person, knowing that such a one is perverted” (Titus 3:10–11). Let such a house therefore be destroyed, and let its stones, timber, and all its dust be thrown outside the town. Let heretics be condemned, excommunicated, and anathematized; and let them be expelled from the Catholic Church together with their doctrine and heresies. This is done in an unclean place, for every place outside the Church is unclean.

“Whoever enters the house while it is shut up shall be unclean until evening; and whoever sleeps in it or eats anything in it shall wash his garments.” For as long as the house is shut up, so long is the heretic separated from and excommunicated by the Church. What is it to enter it but to participate and communicate with him? Whoever does this shall be unclean until evening—not the evening of the day, but that of sin. When sin is ended through penance, then it has come to its evening and end. But what is it to sleep in it but in some manner to rest in and delight in its teaching? For the person who is deceived by it and loses understanding also sleeps in it. Thus such people are fittingly called senseless, to whom the Apostle says: “Awake, you who sleep, and arise from the dead, and Christ shall enlighten you” (Eph. 5:14). Whoever is filled and satisfied with its madness eats in it. Let him therefore wash his garments, do penance, and hear what is written: “Let your garments be white at all times” (Eccl. 9:8).

“But if the priest, entering, sees that the leprosy has not increased in the house after it has been demolished, he shall purify it, health having been restored, and for its purification he shall take two sparrows, cedarwood, scarlet, and hyssop, and sacrifice one sparrow in an earthen vessel over living waters,” etc. All this has been both written and explained in the first cleansing of the leper.

## CHAPTER XV

“The Lord spoke to Moses and Aaron, saying: Speak to the children of Israel and say to them: A man who suffers a discharge of semen shall be unclean, and he shall then be judged subject to this defect when at every moment it clings to his flesh and the foul fluid increases. Every bed on which he sleeps shall be unclean, and every place where he sits.” This too is understood according to the same interpretation as that concerning the leprous house. For this man is the heretic, whose shameful doctrine, sown by him in the ears of many as unclean seed, tends to produce many persons in the same heresy. Therefore, when that seed of wicked preaching adheres at every moment to his flesh—that is, to his mouth—while he does not cease to disseminate his heretical teaching, he shall be judged subject to this defect. Then whatever he touches will be unclean, for whoever is led astray by him will be unclean. Whoever therefore believes him and imitates him must wash his garments, do penance, and thus through confession and repentance shall be unclean only until evening; because after not a long time but a brief interval, as it were of a single day, namely from morning until evening, this kind of sin shall be forgiven him by the people. To sit upon his bed, couch, or saddlecloth is to accept, praise, and preserve the heresy itself.

“If the one who suffers this condition is healed, he shall count seven days after his cleansing; and after washing his garments and his whole body in living waters, he shall be clean. On the eighth day he shall take two turtledoves or two young pigeons, come before the Lord at the entrance of the tabernacle of testimony, and give them to the priest, who shall make one a sin offering and the other a burnt offering.” If the person suffering this condition is healed, he shall count seven days after his cleansing. The seven days stand for the whole period of penance, during which the penitent ought to wash his sins in living waters—that is, in spiritual works, almsgiving, fasts, prayers, and tears: living works able to obtain life and salvation. But on the eighth day, that is, after completing the penance of seven days, he shall take two turtledoves or two young pigeons, and the priest shall pray for him, and he shall be cleansed. Having first been cleansed in two ways, namely through the penance of contrition and satisfaction, as though two young birds had been offered, he is afterwards absolved. He must hold those two turtledoves or young pigeons in his hands in order to offer them to the Lord; after he has been reconciled to God and cleansed, he must cling to him continually and persevere in right living, as has already been said above.

“A woman who, when her monthly period returns, suffers a flow of blood shall be separated for seven days. Whoever touches her shall be unclean until evening, and whatever she sleeps or sits upon during the days of her separation shall be defiled.” This can be understood both of one soul and of the whole church of the wicked. For whoever persists in sins suffers a flow of blood. The soul which suffers this whenever the month returns—for months always return—does not fear to repeat sin. Therefore whoever always commits sin always flows with blood. For it is clear that blood signifies sin. She is separated for seven days because, unless she repents and ceases to sin, she must never be reconciled to the Church. Whoever touches her—touching means imitating—will be unclean. One explanation is sufficient both for the man who suffers a discharge of semen and for the woman who suffers a flow of blood, for each signifies almost the same thing and can be understood of the same matter; hence the offering and purification of both are one.

## CHAPTER XVI

“The Lord spoke to Moses: Speak to Aaron your brother, that he may not enter at every time into the sanctuary within the veil before the propitiatory, by which the ark is covered, lest he die; for I shall appear in a cloud over the oracle. Unless he has first done this, he shall offer a calf for sin and a ram for a burnt offering. He shall be clothed in a linen tunic, cover his private parts with linen breeches, gird himself with a linen girdle, and place a linen mitre upon his head. These are holy garments; after he has washed, he shall clothe himself with all of them.”

The Lord formerly appeared in cloud and darkness because afterward he was to appear clothed in the veil of flesh; that cloud signified Christ’s flesh. The Lord also now appears in a cloud over the oracle, because in the sacrament he is seen under another form upon the altar. Yet it is not permitted always or to everyone to approach this oracle, this altar, and sacrament. First it is necessary to offer a calf for sin and a ram for a burnt offering: that is, it is first necessary to believe that the Lord Christ was sacrificed for our sins and suffered bodily in his entirety upon the altar of the cross. Since the Jews and unbelievers do not believe this, they do not approach this propitiatory; for they believe that he suffered, but not for sin in a burnt offering. But although we believe these things, this is not yet sufficient unless we add what follows.

Let us therefore be clothed in linen garments, so that, wholly white and whiter than snow, we may preserve in every way the purity and chastity of the inner and outer person. These garments are holy; therefore all are made of linen, concerning which we spoke sufficiently in Exodus. He places the linen mitre upon his head who turns his eyes away lest they behold vanity. For the five bodily senses are active in the head; if they have this mitre upon them, they will be chaste and unstained. Therefore not only the priest but the whole people must be clothed in these garments if they wish to approach the sacrament of Christ’s body and blood. Not only virgins but also the continent and the married can possess chastity. It follows:

“And he shall receive from the whole multitude of the children of Israel two goats for sin and one ram for a burnt offering. And when he has offered the calf and prayed for himself and his house, he shall make the two goats stand before the Lord at the entrance of the tabernacle of testimony; and, casting lots over each, one lot for the Lord and the other for the scapegoat, he whose lot comes out for the Lord shall offer it for sin. But the one whose lot comes out for the scapegoat he shall set alive before the Lord, that he may pour out prayers over it and send it into the wilderness.”

Both the goat and the ram signify Christ. The goat is set forth because of the likeness of sinful flesh; the ram, being of the sheep-kind, is spoken of him who was led like a sheep to slaughter. Therefore the first goat is a mystery of Christ; the other is Antichrist. The former came out by lot for a burnt offering to the Lord for sin; the second goat, after many prayers—indeed, curses—is sent into the wilderness. For the Jews, scattered throughout the world, seem to carry this goat with them, because according to them he is the Messiah whom they expected; and, still expecting him, they draw that goat with them through the different regions into which they have been scattered.

“After these things have been duly celebrated, he shall offer the calf and, praying for himself and his house, sacrifice it. Taking a censer, which he has filled with coals from the altar, and grasping in his hand prepared incense, he shall enter through the veil into the holy place, so that, after placing the spices upon the fire, their cloud and vapour may cover the oracle which is above the testimony, and he may not die. He shall also take some of the blood of the calf and sprinkle it with his finger seven times before the Lord toward the propitiatory, on the east.”

After, he says, the priest has put on the garments mentioned above; after he has divided the two goats by lot—for this is the order—let him offer the calf and, praying for himself because he too is a sinner, and for his house, that is, the people subject to him, sacrifice it. Above, it is offered—that is, led to the tabernacle; here it is not merely offered but also sacrificed. This is not done without incense and a sweet fragrance. Whoever prepares Christ’s sacrament, whoever approaches to receive his flesh and blood, ought to be fragrant with upright conduct and the sweetness of virtues. Therefore the priest, taking the censer—the censer is the breast—must fill it with coals from the altar, that he may be kindled with the fire of the Holy Spirit and charity. Then, after placing spices upon the fire, he must pass through the veil and enter the holy place, lifted wholly in mind and spirit above heaven; by the vapour of virtues and fragrance of holy prayers, he must propitiate God both for himself and the people. Hence it adds: “And taking some of the blood of the calf, he shall sprinkle the propitiatory seven times before the Lord toward the east.” The calf’s blood is sprinkled seven times toward the propitiatory because, until the consummation of the age, Christ’s blood intercedes to the Father for us every day. It follows:

“And when he has slaughtered the goat for the sin of the people, he shall bring its blood within the veil, as was commanded concerning the blood of the calf.” Because the goat and the calf signify the same thing, they are sacrificed with one and the same rite. It follows:

“Let no person be in the tabernacle when the high priest enters the sanctuary to pray for himself, his house, and the whole assembly of Israel, until he comes out.” This appears to be commanded so that all may keep silence during that holy contemplation, as though the high priest alone were present, so that without noise, tumult, or any disturbance he may pour out pure prayers to God.

“But when he has gone out to the altar which is before the Lord, he shall pray for himself and his house, and pour the blood of the calf and goat upon its horns all around; and sprinkling it seven times with his finger, he shall expiate and sanctify it from the uncleannesses of the children of Israel.” This altar is the Church, whose four horns signify the four regions of the world. The altar is sprinkled seven times with blood because, until the consummation of the age, the whole Church is expiated and sanctified by Christ’s blood. Therefore, whether the high priest is within or without, whether he practises the active or contemplative life, he must always pray both for himself and for the people.

“After he has cleansed the sanctuary, the tabernacle, and the altar, he shall then offer the living goat; placing both hands upon its head, he shall confess all the iniquities of the children of Israel, all their offences and sins. Having called these down upon its head, he shall send it into the wilderness by the hand of a man prepared for this purpose.” Once all things have been cleansed and the sacrifice completed, the high priest places both hands upon the head of the living goat, so that he condemns and curses it, with every power at his disposal, as guilty of all iniquities together with the devil, its head. For not only our high priests, but also those of the Jews, in the sacred books, though without understanding, condemn Antichrist daily. Reading about him in the Psalms without understanding, they constantly say (Ps. 9 and following): “His mouth is full of cursing, bitterness, and deceit; under his tongue are toil and pain; he sits in ambush with the rich in secret places, that he may kill the innocent.” And a little later: “Break the arm of the sinner and the wicked man.” Of him the Apostle also says: “Unless the falling away comes first and the man of sin, the son of perdition, is revealed—he who opposes and exalts himself above everything called God or worshipped, so that he sits in the temple of God, showing himself as though he were God” (2 Thess. 2:3–4). The man prepared for this service, through whom Antichrist is sent into the wilderness, is the Jewish people, who, scattered among all nations because of their iniquities, worship, proclaim, follow, and venerate him.

“When he has borne all their iniquities into a solitary land and has been sent away into the wilderness, Aaron shall return to the tabernacle of testimony; and, having laid aside the garments in which he had first been clothed when entering the sanctuary, and leaving them there, he shall wash his flesh in a holy place and put on his own garments [Col. 0439A].” For Antichrist bears all the iniquities of the children of Israel into hell, into the wilderness, into a solitary land, because on account of those whom he deceived he will be consigned to eternal fires and will endure the punishment deserved by his wickedness. There he will be abandoned and forsaken, tormented and scourged. Then Aaron will return to the tabernacle of testimony, because, having recognized the truth, the Jewish priests will be converted to the faith and to the Church. There, having laid aside and left their former, symbolic garments, they will wash their flesh in the water of baptism and put on their own garments, so that, stripped of the veil of the letter and adorned with the truth—which is Christ—they may live in the holy Church, not in the oldness of the letter but in the newness of the Spirit. Likewise, concerning him “who sends away the scapegoat, [Col. 0439B] he shall wash his garments and his body with water, and then shall go out into the camp.” For we said above that this man is the Jewish people. Hence it is clear that, at the consummation of this world, not only the priests and experts in the law but the whole Jewish people will abandon Antichrist; converted to the faith and reborn through the water of baptism, they will be joined to the camps of the Church. Thus the Apostle says: “When the fullness of the Gentiles has entered, then Israel shall be saved” (Rom. XI.25).

“But the calf and the goat which had been sacrificed for sin, and whose blood was brought into the sanctuary in order that atonement might be completed, they shall carry outside the camp and burn with fire both their skins and their flesh and their dung.” [Note: [Col. 0439] The same, Codex of Monte Cassino: “Wherever these things are mentioned, they are explained solely by the exposition of the Apostle, who says.”] For whenever these matters occur, the Apostle’s exposition alone ought to suffice, when he says: “For the bodies of those animals whose blood is brought into the holy places by the high priest are burned outside the camp. Therefore Jesus also, that he might sanctify the people through his own blood, suffered outside the gate” (Heb. XIII.11). By these words of the Apostle it is shown most plainly that by the calf and the goat we must understand Christ’s Passion. And whoever burns them shall wash his garments and flesh with water, and then enter the camp. Great indeed is God’s mercy proclaimed in this statement, because even to those who killed him, if they are reborn from water and the Holy Spirit, forgiveness, pardon, and entrance into the Church are promised.

[Col. 0439D] “In the seventh month, on the tenth day of the month, you shall afflict your souls and do no work, whether native-born or a stranger residing among you. On this day there shall be atonement and cleansing for you: you shall be cleansed before the Lord from all your iniquities. For it is a sabbath of rest, and you shall afflict your souls by a perpetual observance.” What, then, is the seventh month and the tenth day of the month, except the last day of all months? For seven is last among days, and ten among numbers. As all days are contained in seven, so all numbers are contained in ten. Therefore, the fact that the Jews [Col. 0440A] afflicted themselves on this day, did no work, and, making atonement, cleansed themselves from all their iniquities, signified that final day: on it, whoever now afflicts himself will not be afflicted; on it every worldly operation will cease; on it, healed, atoned for, and renewed from every corruption and iniquity, they will receive eternal blessedness. For it will be a sabbath of rest, of which the Apostle says: “A sabbath-rest remains for the people of God” (Heb. IV.9). For according to the letter it cannot be that the tenth day of the seventh month always falls on a sabbath.

“But the priest who has been anointed and whose hand has been consecrated, and who performs the priestly office in place of his father, shall put on the linen robe and holy garments, and shall make atonement for the sanctuary of the Covenant and [Col. 0440B] the altar, and for the priests and all the people. And this shall be an everlasting ordinance for you, that you may pray for the children of Israel and for all their sins once a year.” For this was done once a year in figure, because it had to be done once in truth. For the great Priest Jesus—who was anointed with the oil of gladness above his companions, and who succeeded his father Melchizedek in the priesthood, as it is written: “You are a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek” [Ps. CIX.5]—will make atonement for and sanctify all things once, namely when he makes a new heaven and a new earth; when that “creation, which was subjected unwillingly to vanity, will be delivered from bondage to corruption into the liberty of the glory of the children of God” (Rom. VII.21). Then he will put on the linen robe and [Col. 0440C] holy garments, because he will appear in glory and majesty. [Note: [Col. 0439D] Codex of Monte Cassino: “and in the majesty of the Father.”] For he once appeared in such garments to the three disciples on the mountain when transfigured.

## CHAPTER XVII

Here the Lord commands that no sacrifice be offered except at the door of the tabernacle of testimony, wishing to remove from the people every occasion for sacrificing to idols. This is what he says: “And they shall no longer sacrifice their victims to demons, with whom they have committed fornication.” Yet this may also signify that there is nowhere any place for a true sacrifice outside the Church. He also forbids eating the blood of any animal, because the soul is in the blood, and blood must be offered upon the altar for its expiation. Now the statement, “The soul of the flesh is in the blood [Col. 0440D],” is as though he said, “The life of the flesh is in the blood,” so that *soul* is understood as *life*: for flesh cannot live without blood. What, then, is it to eat blood except to take life from the flesh? Let murderers hear this and fear to eat and drink blood, since “the Lord will abhor the man of blood and deceit” (Ps. V.7). It follows:

“Any man of the children of Israel, and of the strangers residing among you, who takes in hunting or bird-catching a wild animal or bird which it is lawful to eat, shall pour out its blood and cover it with earth.” Whoever understands what the two [Col. 0441A] flocks of sheep are, and what the one fold and one shepherd are, also understands who are the children of Israel and who are the strangers residing among them. These take a wild animal or bird by hunting or bird-catching when they convert heretics or philosophers to the faith by evangelical preaching. They pour out the blood and cover it with earth because they wash away their sins in the water of baptism, so that, as though dead and buried, they may appear no more. Hence the Psalmist says: “Blessed are those whose iniquities have been forgiven and whose sins have been covered” (Ps. XXXI).

“The soul that eats an animal which died of itself or was taken by a beast shall wash its garments and itself with water, and shall be unclean until evening; but if it does not wash, it shall bear its iniquity.” An animal that died of itself [Col. 0441B] is anyone who does not have that life which speaks in the Gospel, saying: “I am the way, the truth, and the life” (John XIV.6). One taken by a beast is he who has been deceived by heretics. To eat such persons is to receive them, commune with them, and imitate them. Whoever does this should wash himself inwardly and outwardly with water, do penance, and remain unclean until evening. What “until evening” means, we have often said already.

## CHAPTER XVIII

Next comes the matter of shamefulness and incest. Since the whole Church understands and observes these things according to the letter, it seems either useless or superfluous to seek another interpretation in them. It is very difficult, indeed, to give an account of them, unless perhaps God prohibited such [Col. 0441C] unions so that the bond of love might extend also to strangers. For no one needs to be bound to his relatives by another bond in order to love them more, since a mother ought to love them greatly solely from the kinship of blood. Let him therefore be joined to others whom he does not yet love, so that through a certain affinity he may begin to love and cherish them. [Note: [Col. 0441D] Other reasons may be offered for this divine law prohibiting marriages between blood relatives and relatives by marriage. The chief reason is drawn from the words of the command itself, which repeatedly declares that the nakedness of one’s brother, father, sister, mother, uncle, and so on is not to be uncovered: by these words due honor toward parents and those most closely descended from them is commanded to be preserved, as toward those in the third and fourth degree of consanguinity. Another reason may be given: namely, lest, if permission for marriage is granted to relatives who often live together in the same house, an occasion for unchaste love be provided before marriage is contracted.] Whether, then, for this reason or another, if God prohibited such 160 unions, they are very much to be feared and avoided, because he himself prohibited them. Hence he says here: “Keep the laws and judgments which, if a man does them, he shall live by them: I am the Lord.” This is as though he said: “The man who does not do them shall die.” Whatever we pass over, we pass over because it has either been explained above or is easy to understand, [Col. 0441D] as here concerning the peace-offering, of which enough has been said earlier. It follows:

## CHAPTER XIX

“When you reap the crops of your land, you shall not shear the surface of the earth all the way to the ground, nor gather the ears that remain; nor shall you collect in your vineyard the clusters and fallen grapes, but shall leave them for the poor and strangers to pluck.” Although these [Col. 0442A] words, understood literally, are full of piety and mercy, they may nevertheless signify something else. Where there are no strangers and poor persons, to gather the harvest very carefully and shear down to the ground seems to be no sin. We think that these poor persons are poor not in possessions but in knowledge, while strangers are those newly converted to the faith. The land is the Church, and its crops are the books of the holy Scriptures. Whoever expounds the sacred Scriptures most profoundly shears these crops to the very ground. Whoever gathers the remaining ears and fallen grapes searches and investigates more carefully, repeating again and again those things which he seemed to have passed over less cautiously. This ought to be done among the wise and those rich in understanding. [Col. 0442B] But among the poor and unlearned, it suffices to reap and expound only the letter and surface. We should not burden them with the full harvest and customary food; rather, for instruction in the faith, we should leave them a few words, as it were a few ears. Of these the Apostle says: “I gave you milk to drink, not solid food” (I Cor. III.2). But concerning the wise he says: “We speak wisdom among the perfect” (I Cor. II.6). Thus these harvests are to be sheared to the ground in one place, but in another only at the surface.

“You shall not curse the deaf, nor place a stumbling-block before the blind.” The deaf and blind are not only Jews and Gentiles, but all who refuse to hear and understand the truth. We should not curse these, but call them to the faith by humble admonition. To place a stumbling-block before them [Col. 0442D] is to do something in their presence by which they may reasonably be scandalized. Whoever does not understand this should read the Apostle’s Epistle to the Romans, where he says: “Let us therefore no longer judge one another; but judge this rather, that you do not place a stumbling-block before your brothers” (Rom. XIV.13).

“You shall not make your cattle mate with animals of another kind. You shall not sow your field with diverse seed. You shall not wear a garment woven from two materials.” These seem to signify nearly the same thing. Whoever makes his own cattle mate with animals of another kind permits, on whatever pretext, the foolish and unskilled persons whom he ought to govern to be corrupted by heretics. Whoever sows God’s field with diverse seed [Col. 0442D] mixes error with the Catholic faith by preaching in the Church. Whoever wears a garment woven from two materials is clothed partly with Catholic and partly with heretical faith. For when the Apostle says, “Put on the Lord Jesus Christ” (Gal. III.27), what does this mean except, “Put on faith in our Lord Jesus Christ”? Therefore the garment is faith.

“If a man lies with a woman in sexual intercourse, who is a slave and also marriageable, yet has not been redeemed by a price nor granted freedom, both shall be beaten, but shall not die, because she was not free.” For, as it is written, “Everyone who commits sin is a slave of sin” (John VIII.34), any soul guilty of crime is a slave, even if she is marriageable, a daughter of the Church, and reborn through the water of baptism. Unless, therefore, she is redeemed by the price of repentance and freed from sin, so that she is no longer a slave but free, one must not lie with her, because such a union is unlawful. “For what fellowship has light with darkness? What participation has Christ with Belial?” (I Cor. VI.15). Yet such a union often occurs: even religious men associate with wicked persons when they seem to attach themselves to them and flatter them. But what does “both shall be beaten, but shall not die” mean? Let them, therefore, be beaten by voluntary penance so that they may not die; for unless they are so beaten, they will die. Not only the person who sins must be beaten, but also he who shares in that person’s sin through communion with him—as happens through fellowship with excommunicated persons. Let those who commune with the excommunicated hear this. “But for his offence he shall offer to the Lord, at the door of the tabernacle of testimony, a ram; and the priest shall pray for him, and his sin shall be forgiven.” He offers a ram who slaughters and sacrifices foolish simplicity. For had he not been foolish, he would never have lain with a soul whom he knew to be a slave of iniquity. It follows:

“When you have entered the land and planted fruit-bearing trees in it, you shall remove their foreskins. [Col. 0443C] The fruits which they put forth shall be unclean to you, and you shall not eat from them until the fourth year. All their fruit shall be sanctified in praise to the Lord; but in the fifth year you shall eat their fruit, gathering the fruits 161 which they produce.” The Apostle had planted such trees when he said: “I planted, Apollos watered, but God gave the growth” (I Cor. III.6). He removed their foreskins when he said: “Owe no one anything except to love one another; for he who loves his neighbor has fulfilled the law. You shall not commit adultery, you shall not kill, you shall not commit fornication, you shall not bear false witness, you shall not covet your neighbor’s property” (Rom. XIII.8), and similar things; for these are the foreskins to be removed. For until these have first been removed, all the fruit they put forth will be [Col. 0443D] unclean, and therefore will not be eaten until the fourth year. The four years are the four Gospels; any trees not watered by their water and teaching are unclean, and neither their fruits may be eaten nor their faith and words accepted. But once the fourth year has passed—that is, once the teaching of the four Gospels has been received most fully—all the fruit of the aforesaid trees will be sanctified in praise to the Lord. Therefore it is lawful in the fifth year to eat the fruit and gather the produce, because once the four years are complete both trees and fruits have been sanctified.

“You shall not eat flesh with blood.” To eat flesh with blood is to reconcile a sinner to the Church without repentance [Col. 0444A] and sanctification. “You shall not practice divination or observe dreams.” The Church of the faithful ought to believe not in auguries and divinations but in the commands of the divine law and the words of prophets and apostles. Dreams have caused many to err; therefore dreamers and inventors of falsehoods should not readily be heard. “Nor shall you cut your hair in a circle, nor shave your beard.” For if, as we have often said, the mind is the head of the soul, what are the hairs of this head except thoughts? Some of these are good and some evil. Therefore let us not cut the hair in a circle, lest perhaps we cut away good thoughts together with the evil; rather, when evil thoughts alone have been cut out by the roots, let the good ones spread and grow. Concerning evil thoughts, that we may cut them down, [Col. 0444B] the Psalmist says: “Blessed is he who shall seize and dash your little ones against the rock” (Ps. CXXXVI.9). But concerning good thoughts, that they may be permitted to grow, he says: “The thought of man shall confess to you, and the remnant of thoughts shall keep festival for you” (Ps. LXXV.11). We ought not shave the beard, so that we may appear as men rather than women, and imitate the strength of men rather than the softness of women. Hence we rightly customarily call holy women—who often surpass men in strength of mind—bearded. But the fact that men of our order shave their beards has another meaning: they wish to understand these and similar matters more spiritually than literally, and to be strong men rather than merely appear such. Therefore let the beard grow inwardly for us [Col. 0444C] and be shaved outwardly. The inward beard grows without hindrance; but the outward, unless shaved, produces many inconveniences and is cultivated for beauty only by very idle and vain men. We pass over many matters that seem easy.

## CHAPTER XX

Here he commands that anyone who gives any of his offspring to the idol Moloch be killed. *Moloch* is interpreted “our king,” and in it may be signified all the monstrous forms of idols, under whose rule unhappy people thought themselves secure. He named one idol so that what is commanded in one instance might be observed in all. Had he not done this, the Psalmist would never have said: “They sacrificed their sons [Col. 0444D] and daughters to demons” (Ps. CV.37).

“The soul which turns aside to magicians and soothsayers and commits fornication with them, I will set my face against it and destroy it from among its people.” The soul which is joined to God through faith commits fornication if, turning to the ministers of demons, it believes their empty superstitions. For how does one not commit fornication when one’s whole faith is corrupted? Unless these and the other sins for which a person is commanded to be killed are removed by worthy repentance, the soul is destroyed according to the higher understanding. Therefore the canons forbid anyone who has committed any of these acts to approach holy orders.

## CHAPTER XXI

[Col. 0445A]

“And the Lord said to Moses: Speak to the priests, the sons of Aaron, and say to them: Let not a priest be defiled by the deaths of his fellow-citizens, except only by those of his blood-relations and near kin—namely, his father, son, brother, and virgin sister who is not married; but neither shall he be defiled by the ruler of his people.” For there is not one death common to all fellow-citizens, but many deaths by which a priest must not defile himself. Greed kills one person; pride slays another; lust destroys another; discord puts another to death. Let the priest therefore flee such deaths. There is also another death which the priest of the Jews certainly could not avoid: namely that by which his father and mother, son [Col. 0445B] and daughter, and all his kindred die. This is original sin, from which no one at all could ever be cleansed before Christ’s incarnation. Except for this single death, by which all are necessarily defiled, God’s priest is defiled by no other death or greater sin. Although a human being can live without fault, he nevertheless cannot live without sin. But because a sister who is married seems, beyond original sin, to have contracted another sin also through pleasure of the flesh, he forbids the priest to be defiled by this death and sin as well; and this is what he says: “by his brother and virgin sister.” The priest approaches the death of his relatives because he too is subject to the same death. But when he says, “Neither shall he be defiled by the ruler of his people,” I understand this of that [Col. 0445C] ruler of whom the Lord himself says: “For the ruler of this world comes, and has nothing in me” (John XIV.31). His death is pride, despair, and evil will. It follows:

“They shall not shave their head or beard, nor make incisions in their flesh; they shall be holy to their God and shall not defile his name. For they offer the incense of the Lord and the bread of God, and therefore they shall be holy. He shall not take as wife a prostitute or a base harlot, nor one divorced from her husband, because he is consecrated to his God and offers the bread of presentation. Therefore he shall be holy, because I, who sanctify you, am holy.” To shave the head and beard and make an incision in the flesh were signs of grief and sorrow. Priests of idols also once used to sacrifice to their gods by this rite. Hence Jeremiah says: “Their priests sit with torn tunics, with heads and beards shaven, their heads uncovered” (Baruch VI.30). Concerning incision of the flesh, you will find this in the books of Kings. But what do we understand by a prostitute, a base harlot, and a woman divorced from her husband, except a soul corrupted by heretics, defiled by demons, and rejected by God? A priest ought not join himself to this soul, because children born from her are not legitimate but bastards. Hence the Lord himself says: “By their fruits [Col. 0446A] you shall know them” (Matt. VII.16). Therefore priests who are consecrated and ought not to be defiled should flee the fellowship of such persons. They also offer the bread of presentation, which the Lord himself forbids to be given to dogs.

“The daughter of a priest, if she is discovered in prostitution and violates her father’s name, shall be burned with flames.” [Note: [Col. 0445D] The edition is corrected from the same codex.] Every soul is truly the daughter of that priest whose priesthood remains forever according to the order of Melchizedek, in whose name we have been reborn and baptized. Therefore the daughter discovered in prostitution, or in violation of the faith, is the soul seduced by heretics, which has denied the faith of Christ her father and so violated his name—of whom it is written: “You shall not take the name of your God in vain” (Exod. XX.7). Therefore she shall be burned with flames: namely, the flames of eternal [Col. 0446B] fire.

“The high priest—that is, the chief priest among his brothers—upon whose head the oil of anointing has been poured, whose hands have been consecrated to the priesthood, and who is clothed in holy garments, shall not uncover his head or rend his garments; he shall not enter in to any dead person at all, nor shall he be defiled by his father or mother. Nor shall he go out from the holy things, lest he defile the sanctuary of the Lord; for the oil of the holy anointing of his God is upon him: I am the Lord.” Other priests were not forbidden from the death of their relatives, but the highest priest was permitted to approach no dead person whatsoever. Why is this? Because Jesus, the greatest of all priests, [Note: [Col. 0445D] The edition is purged of errors from the same codex.] alone was born without sin and alone lived in the world incapable of sin. He himself did not experience in himself the death of his father and mother: his father David, whose son he is very often called; and his mother, the Synagogue, from which he was born according to the flesh. The death and sin of these, I say, he did not experience. He is indeed greatest among his brothers, of whom he says: “I will declare your name to my brothers” (Ps. XXI.23). He also signifies that he has been anointed with the oil of gladness, saying: “The Spirit of the Lord is upon me; therefore he has anointed me and sent me to preach the Gospel to the poor” (Luke IV.18). He is clothed in holy garments—namely, majesty and strength. Hence the Psalmist says: “The Lord has reigned; he has put on majesty; the Lord has put on strength [Col. 0446D] and girded himself” (Ps. XCII.1). His head is not uncovered because his divinity has not been seen by human beings; for, as the Apostle says, “God is the head of Christ” (I Cor. XI.3). Nor are his garments rent, because his faith is not divided. Indeed, according to the letter, the soldiers are recorded as saying of his garment: “Do not tear it, [Note: [Col. 0446D] Codex of Monte Cassino: “But let us cast lots whose it shall be.”] but let us cast lots for it, whose it shall be.” Unhappy Caiaphas, who tore his garments (Matt. XXVI), was forgetful of this command. It follows:

“He shall take a virgin as wife; a widow, divorced woman, defiled woman, or prostitute he shall not take, but a maiden from his own people, lest he mingle the stock [Col. 0447A] of his race with the common crowd of his nation; for I am the Lord who sanctifies him.” This is that virgin of whom the Apostle says: “I have betrothed you to one husband, to present you as a chaste virgin to Christ” (II Cor. XI.2). And again: “That he might present to himself a glorious Church, having neither spot nor wrinkle nor anything of that sort” (Eph. V.27). The widow, divorced woman, defiled woman, and prostitute is the Synagogue, which, having forsaken so great and such a husband, has repeatedly committed fornication after the gods of the Gentiles. Therefore he takes a maiden from his own people, a people obedient to him—for every people is his—lest he mix his offspring and race with prostitutes, that is, unbelievers.

“And the Lord spoke to Moses, saying: Speak to Aaron. Any man in your family from his seed [Col. 0447B] who has a blemish shall not offer bread to his God, nor approach his mercy.” The Lord teaches us what sort of priests ought to be chosen for ministry at the altar: “Let them,” he says, “be without blemish.” Unless by blemish we understand crime, the command seems in a way impossible, since no one is without sin. “If he is blind, if lame, if he has a small, large, or crooked nose, if he has a broken foot or hand, if he is hunchbacked, if he has bleary eyes, if he has a white spot in the eye, a continual itch, a scab upon his body, or a hernia.” A blind person is one who wrongly understands [Note: [Col. 0447] The same Codex of Monte Cassino: “Who applies perverse interpretations to the holy Scriptures.”] the sacred Scriptures, as Jews and heretics do. The lame person is one who does not walk with a straight step on the way of God’s commandments; of these it is said: “They limped away from your paths” (Ps. XVII.46). Therefore the Apostle says: [Col. 0447C] “Let us walk honorably as in the day” (Rom. XIII.13). The nose discerns smells: if it is small, it does not perceive fully; but if large, it exceeds measure. Those to whom the Apostle says, “Do not become children in understanding, but be little children in malice” (I Cor. XIV.20), had a small nose; those to whom he says, “Do not think more highly than you ought to think, but think soberly” (Rom. XII.3), a large one. But a crooked nose judges both good and evil to have a good smell, and is more shameful and worse because it is crooked. Whoever has a broken foot or hand, languishing through idleness alone, neither says nor does anything good. Thus he lies about, serving the body and loving nothing except idleness and pleasures; rightly he is removed from the priesthood. The hunchbacked man, ignorant of heaven, looks only at the earth [Col. 0447D]; by him we may understand the greedy and covetous person, whose every hope and desire concerns earthly and passing things. A bleary eye, though it sees, is outwardly ugly and is ashamed of itself: such are those we see in the Church who have acuteness of intellect but waste away through the sickness of a shameful life. Conversely, the eye having a white spot certainly demonstrates that it sees nothing; by it are understood those who are not ashamed to sin, and whoever sees their deeds does not doubt that they are blind. Whoever has a continual itch is always restless, labors and is wearied; the itch grows and is not cured. Such are [Col. 0448A] lovers of worldly dignities: the more they devote themselves to this vice, the more fiercely they burn, labor, hurry, and grow weary. Nothing is enough for them, because, having a continual itch, they are never healed of it. Hence the Lord himself says: “How difficult it is for a rich man to enter the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. XIX.24). But what do we understand by a scab, which grows secretly and almost imperceptibly, then suddenly invades and occupies the surrounding places—whence it also received its name—except lust? If lust has settled in the heart even merely through thought, it continually grows and corrupts the whole person. What do we understand by those with hernias except hypocrites and lovers of vain glory, who are sterile in producing children? They do their works to be seen by people, desire to be considered good, and do not wish to be such; yet they boast of themselves as most fruitful. But what follows—“Nevertheless he shall eat of the breads offered in the sanctuary”—is to be understood thus: although one who has blemishes cannot be a bishop, he is nevertheless permitted to eat of spiritual bread and food. Many receive Christ’s flesh and blood who cannot become priests. For no one who has had a blemish—that is, who has committed a crime—ought to become a priest even after penance has been performed, although after penance he may lawfully partake of the Church’s sacraments. Hence it adds:

## CHAPTER XXII

“Any man of your stock who approaches those things which have been consecrated and which the children [Col. 0448C] of Israel offered to the Lord, if uncleanness is in him, shall perish before the Lord.” It says, “in whom uncleanness is,” not “in whom it was.” For if he has been cleansed by repentance, he may not indeed perform the sacraments, but he may approach the sacraments. This it explains still more plainly, saying: “A man of the seed of Aaron who is leprous or suffers a flow of blood shall not eat of the things sanctified to me until he is healed.” Notice that it says, “until he is healed.” This is said not of every kind of uncleanness but of a crime already committed, from which he is healed by repentance. “No foreigner shall eat of the consecrated things; a priest’s resident lodger and hired servant shall not eat of them. But one whom the priest has bought, and one born in his house, shall eat [Col. 0448D] of them.” Because a foreigner is not a child of the Church, while a resident lodger and hired servant serve the Lord not from love but for temporal gain, they are rightly excluded from consecrated things. “For whoever eats and drinks unworthily eats and drinks judgment upon himself” (I Cor. XI.29). But those whom the priest has bought—of whom the Apostle says, “You were bought at a great price” (I Cor. VI.20)—and those who faithfully guard his household, may approach and eat.

“If a priest’s daughter has married any man of the people, she shall not eat of the consecrated things or of the firstfruits. But if, widowed or divorced and without children, she returns to the house of her father [Col. 0449A], she shall be fed with her father’s food as she formerly was when a maiden.” Who this priest is is clear: every soul reborn through the water of baptism is his daughter. If she marries any man of the people—that is, if she joins herself to a heretic or unbeliever—she immediately becomes alien to spiritual food and Christ’s sacraments. But if she rejects the companionship of heretics, abandons error, returns to the Church, and leaves behind all the children and works of heretical perversity, she will again be fed with the food of her heavenly Father, who casts out none who comes to him. Here God’s great mercy is proclaimed; no occasion for despair is given to anyone. “The sinner, in whatever hour he turns, shall live and shall not die” (Ezek. XXXIII.11).

“Whoever eats of the consecrated things through ignorance [Col. 0449B] shall add a fifth part to what he ate and give it to the priest in the sanctuary.” This is the same as the foregoing. If, by error in the observances, he sins concerning things consecrated to the Lord, he shall restore the loss he has caused and add a fifth part, delivering it to the priest. What is here said to be “through ignorance” is elsewhere said to be “through error.” To eat here means to destroy and dissipate, according to the saying: “For they have devoured Jacob and laid waste his dwelling-place” (Ps. LXXVIII.7). The Apostle too says: “If you bite and devour one another, beware lest you be consumed by one another” (Gal. V.15). Whoever, through ignorance or error, eats consecrated things forgets the divine law, commits sacrilege, and scatters and dissipates the goods of the Church. Whoever does this [Col. 0449C] should restore the loss and add a fifth part. What is it to add a fifth part except to humble oneself before the priest’s judgment and make satisfaction to the Church? A human being is called the fifth part because there are five bodily senses, without which one can neither sin nor repent. Or else because the goods of the Church are divided into four parts: whoever has sinned concerning tithes, firstfruits, or other things consecrated to the Lord shall make full restitution—of which, as we have said, there are four parts—and add a fifth, that is, deliver himself to the priest, ready to obey his judgment in all things. For he possesses nothing greater than himself that he can deliver to the priest as restitution for the loss. Thus he restores five parts, having sinned in four.

[Col. 0449D] It follows concerning this: whoever offers to the Lord a holocaust or a sacrifice of peace offerings, whether he offers it voluntarily or in fulfillment of a vow, must offer a male without blemish, and there must be no blemish in it. If it is blind, broken, scarred, or has boils, scab, or mange, he must not offer it to the Lord. For the Lord teaches us in the Gospel what we ought to offer him, where, speaking of tribute and seeing Caesar’s image, he says: “Render therefore to Caesar the things that are Caesar’s, and to God the things that are God’s” (Luke 20:25). If, then, we are God’s image; if we ought to offer ourselves to God, let us wash away the stains of sins, because God does not receive what is unclean and blemished. “Blessed therefore are the undefiled in the way, who walk in the law of the Lord” (Ps. 118 [119]:1).

[Col. 0450A] For they do not offer the blind, who wish the eyes of their mind to be illuminated by the light of faith; nor do they offer the broken, who wish the bones of the inner human being to be firm and sound, lest they fail while running in the way of God. For the bones of the soul are its virtues. Nor indeed should we offer those things that have either a scar, boils, scab, or mange. Rather, as commanded above, let us offer ourselves clean and sincere, without any stain of sin. Nothing leavened is to be offered to the Lord; by this every corruption of soul and character is prohibited. He has used “scar” for “wound,” according to the saying: “My scars have become putrid and corrupted” (Ps. 37 [38]:6). Otherwise, if, after the wound has already healed, they bear a scar, they do not please the Lord: it is repentance not yet perfected. It follows:

[Col. 0450B] “An ox or a sheep whose ear and tail have been cut off you may offer voluntarily; but a vow cannot be discharged by such animals.” What is voluntarily given is not demanded as though owed. Hence the Apostle says: “Each one as he has determined in his heart, not grudgingly or of necessity” (2 Cor. 8:7). But vows, even unwillingly, we must fulfill: “Vow and render to the Lord your God” (Ps. 65 [66]:12). Thus animals that are diminished may be voluntarily offered, because the things we do voluntarily, although we do not do them perfectly and fully, are nevertheless accepted by God. But a vow cannot be discharged by them, because whatever we vow we must perform whole and without any diminution. It is therefore better not to

[Col. 0450C] vow than to take something away from a vow and, as it were, cut something off.

“From the hand of a foreigner you shall not offer bread to your God, nor anything else that he may wish to give; for all these things are corrupt and blemished, and you shall not accept them.” A foreigner is one who is not of the Church; God hates the gifts of the ungodly, and offerings of such persons are not to be accepted.

“When an ox, sheep, or goat has been born, it shall be under its mother’s udder for seven days; but on the eighth day and thereafter it may be offered to the Lord.” Whatever a person’s condition, if he has remained for seven days under the udder of mother Church and has not departed from her faith and teaching, he may be offered to the Lord on the eighth day and thereafter; for there are only seven days.

[Col. 0450D] Therefore one who remains under the udder for seven days does not depart from that udder as long as he lives. Such a person may thus be offered to the Lord on the eighth day—that is, immediately after this life—and be received into the assembly of the saints; or thereafter, if perhaps he needs purgation. For not all who are saved are received into blessedness immediately upon dying. But what it says, “Mothers shall not be sacrificed on the same day with their young,” means as if it said: Although the children of the Church are sacrificed and pass on daily, nevertheless their mother lives and endures, and does not cease to bear children. It follows:

“If you sacrifice a victim in thanksgiving to the Lord, so that it may be acceptable, you shall eat it on the same day; nothing shall remain until the morning

[Col. 0451A] of the next day.” Although the Apostle says, “I give thanks to God always for you” (Phil. 1:3), nevertheless the victim of thanksgiving is sacrificed and wholly eaten in one day—one day being understood as the whole span of time 165. During this day, therefore, we ought to give thanks, serve God, sacrifice ourselves, and receive the cup of salvation, because after this life there is no place for repentance. For that person sacrifices a victim in thanksgiving who, mindful of God’s benefits, says with the Psalmist: “What shall I render to the Lord for all that he has rendered to me? I shall receive the cup of salvation and call upon the name of the Lord” (Ps. 115 [116]:3). It follows:

## CHAPTER XXIII

“These are the feasts of the Lord, which you shall proclaim holy.

[Col. 0451B] For six days you shall do work; the seventh day, because it is the Sabbath rest, shall be called holy; you shall do no work on it. It is the Sabbath of the Lord in all your dwellings.” We have spoken sufficiently in Exodus about the Sabbath, which we rightly celebrate when we turn away from evil and persevere in good. There were also other feasts that the Jews observed most solemnly; although they did not always occur on the Sabbath, they were nevertheless called Sabbaths. Hence the Gospel says: “It came to pass on the second-first Sabbath” (Luke 6:1), that is, on the second principal Sabbath. For the first principal Sabbath was in March; the second, when they offered sheaves of ears of grain; and the third was observed in the seventh month. There were three first—that is, principal—

[Col. 0451C] Sabbaths, at which every male appeared before the Lord. Concerning the first, in which Passover is celebrated and the lamb is eaten with unleavened bread, enough has been said in Exodus. Let us now speak of our first Sabbath, that is, the second principal feast.

“When,” he says, “you have entered the land which I shall give you, and have reaped the grain, you shall bring the sheaves of ears, the firstfruits of your harvest, to the priest. He shall lift up the bundle before the Lord, that it may be acceptable for you on the day after the Sabbath, and shall consecrate it. And on the same day on which the sheaf is consecrated, an unblemished lamb of one year shall be slain as a holocaust to the Lord; and libations

[Col. 0451D] shall be offered with it: two tenths of fine flour mixed with oil, as a sweet-smelling offering to the Lord, and also a libation of wine, a fourth part of a hin.” For the Lord says in the Gospel: “The harvest indeed is plentiful, but the laborers are few. Pray therefore the Lord of the harvest that he may send laborers into his harvest” (Matt. 9:37). The harvests, then, are understood as peoples; the laborers, as the apostles. The Lord sent them to reap where they themselves had not sown. Let it therefore be said: When you have reaped the grain and gathered the sheaves of the faithful into God’s ark, which is the Church, you shall bring the firstfruits of your harvest to the priest. For the firstfruits were those who believed in the primitive Church; the apostles themselves offered these in person to the priest, that is, they rendered them to the Lord, who lifted up

[Col. 0452A] the bundle before the Lord. For he himself says: “When I am lifted up from the earth, I shall draw all things to myself” (John 12:32). No one is lifted up except by him and through him. He appropriately used “bundle,” because “many are called, but few are chosen” (Matt. 22:14). This was done on the day after the Sabbath, which is now called the Lord’s Day by the Lord himself; thus even then this day seemed, in a certain way, to take precedence away from the Sabbath. And on that very same day the lamb was slain as a holocaust, because at one and the same time the people are saved and Christ is sacrificed. Hence he further adds: “And libations shall be offered with it, namely two tenths of fine flour mixed with oil.” By these we understand the two peoples, Jews and Gentiles, who were indeed sprinkled with oil because they deserved to receive

[Col. 0452B] God’s mercy and the gifts of the Holy Spirit. And lest so great a sacrifice should be completed in one day only, cakes and wine were also offered daily, signifying the bread and wine which, through the ministry of the priest, are daily changed into Christ’s flesh and blood.

“You shall not eat bread, parched grain, or porridge from the harvest until the day on which you offer from it to your God.” Unless an unbeliever is first converted so that he may be offered to the Lord, we cannot bring anyone into the body of the Church. For this is what eating signifies here, as was said to blessed Peter: “Kill and eat” (Acts 10:11). There are therefore unclean harvests also, and they must not be eaten unless first offered to the Lord and washed in baptism.

[Col. 0452C] “You shall therefore count from the day after the Sabbath, on which you offered the sheaves, seven full weeks, until the day after the completion of the seventh week—that is, fifty days—and thus you shall offer a new sacrifice to the Lord from all your dwellings: two loaves of firstfruits, from two tenths of leavened fine flour, which you shall bake as firstfruits to the Lord. And with the loaves you shall offer seven unblemished lambs of one year, one calf from the herd, and two rams; and they shall be a holocaust, with their libations, a most sweet odor to the Lord.” For all these feasts seem to signify nearly the same thing. Hence, although it is not said in one manner, one sacrifice is nevertheless offered in all: whether a lamb, calf, or goat is sacrificed for sin, it signifies Christ’s passion.

[Col. 0452D] Likewise the harvests, loaves of firstfruits, and two rams are people offered to God. For it is the prophets’ custom often to repeat the same thing in different words. All the Jewish feasts signified this solemnity of ours, of which it is said: “Appoint a solemn day amid the throngs, even unto the horn of the altar” (Ps. 127 [118]:7). We celebrate the feast not three times a year but throughout the whole year, if we cease from servile and wicked work and persevere in good work. The seven 166 weeks precede this feast of ours because “we are those upon whom the ends of the ages have come” (1 Cor. 10:11). For from Christ’s passion the fiftieth

[Col. 0453A] day and the year of Jubilee are celebrated in the Church, since we have been freed from slavery and the inheritance of the heavenly homeland has been restored. In this great solemnity, therefore, let us offer a new sacrifice to the Lord from all our dwellings, for the old things have passed away. But what shall we offer? Two loaves of firstfruits; for in these two loaves the whole Church consists. The two loaves are the two peoples, namely Jews and Gentiles. From all those whom he had created, the Lord chose these for himself as firstfruits and tithes. They are rightly said to be of leavened fine flour, because, as the wicked do, so also the good derive their origin from the mass of sin. With these loaves are offered seven unblemished lambs, by which we can understand nothing better than the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit,

[Col. 0453B] without whom no one is offered to God. They are rightly called lambs and unblemished, because they make human beings innocent and unblemished. Let us also offer a calf, that we may always be mindful of Christ’s passion. Let us also offer two rams, and, for the honor of God and the edification of the whole Church, praise the two chief apostles; for the Lord delights in such a sacrifice, and delights to hear praise of himself and of his own, and their triumphs. It follows:

“You shall also offer a lamb and a goat for sin, and two lambs of one year as a sacrifice of peace offerings; and when the priest has lifted them up with the loaves of firstfruits before the Lord, they shall fall to his use.” Here the sacrifice is indeed doubled, but the meaning is not changed: what is understood through the calf is also understood through the lamb

[Col. 0453C] and goat; and what is signified through the two rams is signified through the two lambs.

“In the seventh month, on the first day of the month, you shall have a Sabbath, a memorial with trumpets sounding; it shall be called holy. You shall do no servile work on it, and you shall offer a holocaust to the Lord.” He calls the first day of this month a Sabbath, not because it was always a Sabbath, but because they observed it as a Sabbath: on it they sounded trumpets, offered a holocaust, and did no servile work, because these things signified this feast of ours, in which we cease from evil and praise God with voice and heart, always offering a holocaust of praise and rejoicing.

[Col. 0453D] “And the Lord spoke to Moses, saying: On the tenth day of this seventh month there shall be a most solemn Day of Atonements, and it shall be called holy; you shall afflict your souls on it and offer a holocaust to the Lord. Every soul that is not afflicted on that day shall perish from its people; and whoever does any work, I shall destroy from its people; for it is a Sabbath of rest, and you shall afflict your souls on the ninth day of the month,” etc. “Likewise, from the fifteenth day of this seventh month there shall be the feast of tabernacles for seven days to the Lord.” We have said that this month signifies the final age, which is last among the ages as the seventh day is last in the week. The whole month is therefore rightly observed as festive, because it signifies the Church’s festive time.

[Col. 0454A] It is wholly festive: joyful in its beginning, middle, and end. For the tenth is used for the end, because in every number the tenth is its end and limit; the fifteenth day is in the middle of the month. Since, therefore, the first, tenth, and fifteenth days of this month are celebrated, the whole month is shown to be festive by the distinction of its greater parts. For he calls not only the seventh day, but also the seventh month and the seventh year, Sabbath, because rest and solemnity were observed in all these. This is that solemnity in which once a year the high priest entered the Holy of Holies. Since it signified this acceptable time and these days of salvation, we must now make atonement, now afflict our souls, now sacrifice a holocaust:

[Col. 0454B] for the person who is not now afflicted will perish; the person who is not now purified by repentance will perish; and so will the person who does not sacrifice offerings of praise. For now is the Sabbath of rest, in which we ought to rest and cease from every iniquity. We therefore celebrate this Sabbath from evening until evening, and persevere in rest from every evil until the end, until the last day. “From evening until evening” is to be understood as from Christ’s first coming until Christ’s second coming. For Christ’s birth was the end and evening of the sixth age, and the morning and beginning of the seventh. This age, however, will have its evening and end together with this world. Thus far concerning the tenth day; now let us consider the fifteenth:

[Col. 0454C] “From the fifteenth day of this seventh month there shall be the feast of tabernacles for seven days to the Lord. The first day shall be called most solemn and most holy; you shall do no servile work on it, and for seven days you shall offer holocausts to the Lord. The eighth day likewise shall be most solemn and most holy, and you shall offer a holocaust to the Lord; for it is an assembly and gathering; you shall do no servile work on it.” What has been said, and these same words, all refer to the same thing. On the first day of this month they sounded trumpets, because at the beginning of this age the great voice of preachers rang out throughout all lands. For of this day it is written: “Sound the trumpet at the beginning of the month, on the distinguished day of your solemnity” (Ps.

[Col. 0454D] 10 [81]:4). But on the tenth day that great feast was observed in which the high priest alone, not without blood, entered the Holy of Holies to make atonement for the people. And on the fifteenth day of the same month 167 was the feast of tabernacles, in which the children of Israel lived in tabernacles for seven days. What did all these things signify except that we, in this seventh month, in this final age, ought to praise God with the trumpet of mouth and heart; expiate body and soul from all sins; and live peacefully in the tabernacles of the Church for seven days—that is, for as long as we live—and serve God? These are the tabernacles of which the Psalmist says: “How beloved are your tabernacles, O Lord of hosts; my soul longs for and faints for the courts of the Lord”

[Col. 0455A] (Ps. 83 [84]:2). The first and eighth days of this solemnity are most celebrated. On them, as on the others, we ought to cease from servile work and offer to God the sacrifice of praise, the calves of our lips. Hence the Apostle says: “Through him therefore let us always offer to God a sacrifice of praise, that is, the calves of lips confessing his name” (Heb. 13:13). They are most celebrated days because at the beginning of the faith the apostles and martyrs shone forth, and in the last days Jews and Gentiles alike, having known the truth, will be converted to faith. Hence the eighth day is called the day of assembly and gathering, because then the greatest assembly of saints will be gathered into the Church. It follows:

“On the first day you shall take for yourselves the fruit of the most beautiful tree, branches of palm trees, and boughs of thickly-leaved trees,

[Col. 0455B] and willows from the torrent; and you shall rejoice before the Lord your God and celebrate the solemnity for seven days in the year.” The most beautiful tree is that of which it is written: “He shall be like a tree planted beside streams of water, which shall yield its fruit in its season” (Ps. 1:3). And indeed our Lord Christ is the most beautiful tree, whose most sweet and delightful fruits the holy apostles gathered on the first day, immediately at the beginning of the Church’s birth. Of these the Psalmist says: “How sweet are your words to my palate, sweeter than honey and the honeycomb to my mouth” (Ps. 118 [119]:103). By the branches of palm trees, the boughs of thickly-leaved trees, and the willows from the torrent—from which shelters were made against the burning heat of the sun—we rightly understand

[Col. 0455C] the examples and exhortations of the saints, and words of consolation. Hence the Apostle says: “Whatever things have been written were written for our instruction, that through patience and the consolation of the Scriptures we might have hope” (Rom. 15:4). These matters concerning the feasts have been stated briefly.

## CHAPTER XXIV

It follows concerning the purest oil, which Aaron placed in lamps upon the lampstand from evening until morning before the Lord. We have said enough about this in Exodus. For the lampstand is Christ, whose lamps with oil signify the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit, by which the tabernacle of the whole Church is illuminated. It follows:

“You shall also take fine flour and bake from it twelve

[Col. 0455D] loaves, each having two tenths; you shall set six of them on either side upon the purest table before the Lord, and place upon them the brightest frankincense, that the bread may be a memorial of the Lord’s offering. They shall be changed every Sabbath before the Lord, received from the children of Israel by an everlasting covenant; and they shall belong to Aaron and his sons, that they may eat them in a holy place.” This fine flour is the writing and knowledge of sacred law; from it were baked and arranged twelve loaves—that is, the preachings and discourses of the twelve apostles. These are aptly signified by the twelve baskets filled in the Gospel from the fragments of the five loaves. For each has

[Col. 0456A] two tenths, which expound the entire Decalogue of the Law in a twofold way, namely according to the letter and according to spiritual knowledge. If the ten words of the Law were understood according to the letter only, the apostles would have made their loaves from one tenth. These loaves are placed upon the purest table because they are added, as certain expositions, upon the teaching of both Testaments, which is signified by the table. And the brightest frankincense is appropriately placed upon them, because apostolic teaching is sweet to the taste and delightful in fragrance. Hence the Apostle says: “We are Christ’s good fragrance to God in every place, among those who are saved and among those who perish; to some we are an odor of life unto life, to others an odor of death unto death” (2 Cor. 2:15).

[Col. 0456B] They are changed every Sabbath because on every feast and whenever the people assemble as one, the teaching of the apostles must always be expounded, recited, and in a manner renewed. Aaron and his sons eat them in a holy place, because bishops and priests ought always to meditate upon these things and expound them in the assembly of the faithful. It follows:

“Behold, the son of an Israelite woman, whom she had borne by an Egyptian man among the children of Israel, quarreled in the camp with an Israelite man. And when he had blasphemed the name of the Lord and cursed him, he was brought to Moses; and they put him in prison until they should know what the Lord would command. Then, at the Lord’s command, all who had heard laid their hands upon his head, and all the people stoned

[Col. 0456C] him.” I understand this man, born of a believing mother and an unbelieving father, who quarrels against an Israelite, that is, a Catholic, to be a heretic: his mother is the Church, and his father is the devil. For, born in the Church and seduced by the devil, he has become the son of him whose works he performs. Thus the Lord himself says: “You are of your father the devil” (John 8:44). This man quarrels in the camp against an Israelite because the heretic, disputing against a Catholic in the Church, does not fear to blaspheme and curse God. Therefore he is sent to prison,

168

separated from the communion of the faithful; bishops assemble, a council is held, accusers are present, they lay their hands upon his head, they convict him, he is stoned by all the people, cursed and condemned, and judged worthy of death by the entire

[Col. 0456D] council. All cast stones at him who confirm the sentence of condemnation against him.

## CHAPTER XXV

[Note: The edition is corrected and supplemented from the same Cassino manuscript.]

It follows concerning the seventh year, which, like the seventh day and the seventh month, was held wholly most solemn: they did not sow the field or prune the vineyard, but all things that the earth bore of its own accord were common. They were not gathered by anyone as private property, but all received them solely as common blessing for food. By the seventh year we understand the same thing that we said was signified by the seventh day and seventh month.

[Col. 0457A] The seventh year signifies this seventh and final age, in which the Church keeps Sabbath in God’s praises, resting from servile and wicked work, despising worldly and transient things, not thinking of tomorrow, and using one common food prepared without labor. This is also understood of the future life, for the rest of which promised to us we labor in this toilsome life as though in six years. “For what a man has sown, as the Apostle says, that shall he also reap” (Gal. 6:7). It follows:

“You shall also count for yourself seven weeks of years, that is, seven times seven, which together make forty-nine years. And you shall sound the trumpet in the seventh month, on the tenth day of the month, at the time of propitiation, throughout all your land.” What was said concerning the seventh year, seventh month, and seventh day must be understood concerning the fiftieth year.

[Col. 0457B] They sounded the trumpet in the seventh month, on the tenth day of the month, namely the month in which the forty-ninth year ended; and, once all the fruits of the earth had been gathered, the fiftieth year, which was also the Jubilee, began. The sound of the trumpet was the proclamation of the Jubilee. In this year the land rested, all observed feast and joy, bondage was dissolved, liberty was granted, and every person returned to his former possession. This year began spiritually when Christ our Lord redeemed the world from the devil’s bondage by his blood and restored to us our first possession; he opened the gates of paradise to his faithful. Its blessedness is awaited after the seventh

[Col. 0457C] week of years, when the year of Jubilee and praise, the year of rest and blessedness, will begin for the saints.

“If your impoverished brother has sold you his little possession, and his kinsman wishes to do so, he may redeem what that man sold.
