But if he has no near relative, and he himself can find the price for redemption, the fruits shall be reckoned from the time when he sold it, and he shall pay to the buyer what remains; thus he shall receive back his possession. But if his hand does not find enough to repay the price, the buyer shall retain what he bought until the year of Jubilee; for in it every sale shall return to its owner and former possessor.” How full these words are of reason and fairness, mercy and compassion. For it is not the possession but the time of its fruits that is sold; not the land but the fruits of the land.

[Col. 0457D] Thus neither purchaser loses his price nor seller his possession; provision is made for both. The abundance of the one supplies the poverty of the other; conversely, the poverty of the latter makes the former’s abundance abound all the more. No one is deceived in such a sale, in which there is both a term and a condition. The Jubilee is the term; the condition is that the usufruct itself may at any time be redeemed. Here, therefore, no interest accumulates, nor does an avaricious moneylender seize another’s property, because both time and fruits are reckoned. In matters where God’s mercy

[Col. 0458A] and compassion are so plainly commended, it is superfluous to seek another allegory.

“Whoever sells a house within city walls shall have the right to redeem it until one year is completed. If he does not redeem it and the course of the year has elapsed, the buyer and his descendants shall possess it forever, and it cannot be redeemed, even in the Jubilee. But if it is in a village, a house without walls, it shall be sold under the law of fields. If it has not been redeemed, it shall be restored to the Lord in the Jubilee.” We may understand the walled city as the Church, and the village without walls as that which is outside the Church. For concerning the wall of the Church it is written: “The city of our strength is Zion, the Savior; a wall and bulwark shall be set in it” (Isa.

[Col. 0458B] 26:1). In this city, whoever is established in the Church and commits a crime sells his house. Hence the Apostle says in the person of some: “For the Law is spiritual, but I am carnal, sold under sin” (Rom. 7:14). One year is understood as this entire present life. Therefore, whoever by sinning has sold his house, his flesh, and himself to the devil cannot redeem it even in the Jubilee unless, before the year of this life ends for him, he redeems it through repentance. Here Jubilee means the last day, when the saints, liberated from the slavery of corruption, will be transferred to their first possession and to the glory of the children of God.

169

But those who sin in the village and outside the Church, because they are not defended by the wall of God’s protection,

[Col. 0458C] even if they cannot first redeem their house and flesh, sold to the devil in many ways, nevertheless receive it in the Jubilee. But unbelievers do not have the Jubilee. Whatever day someone is freed from bondage is a Jubilee for that person. Therefore a person has a Jubilee on whatever day he is baptized. In this Jubilee that house which was sold in a village and outside the Church returns to its owner, because then the person is freed from the devil’s bondage. Yet this Jubilee can occur only once; the other jubilees occur as often as sins are absolved through repentance and liberty is restored. But the statement, “The dwellings of the Levites which are in cities can always be redeemed, whereas their suburban lands

[Col. 0458D] must never be sold,” is sufficient to understand in its literal sense alone. Ecclesiastical buildings may indeed be leased for rent for the Church’s own benefit, but they may never be wholly alienated. This is because they are in cities and are not easily concealed or consigned to oblivion; but suburban lands, because they are far from human view, cannot safely be sold even temporarily and conditionally. They therefore have a perpetual possession and must in no way be alienated.

Those, however, who have sold themselves to someone may be redeemed by themselves or by others.

[Note: The same Cassino manuscript corrects the edition at Col. 0457D.]

For they are held not as slaves but as tenants or hired laborers,

[Col. 0459A] a matter in which God has made sufficiently merciful provision: the person sold is bound only to restore the price, while the purchaser, upon receiving the price, suffers no loss. Would that Christians observed these rules, so that the rich might assist the poor without burdensome interest, and the poor might render services to the rich without losing their possessions! For we have often seen a small sum borrowed suddenly devour the entire substance of the poor.

## CHAPTER XXVI

There follows a very lengthy discourse in which the Lord promises many benefits to the children of Israel if they obey him and keep his commandments; conversely, if they are disobedient, he threatens them with many evils. Anyone who carefully reads their histories will be able to understand that all these things happened to them according to the letter. “But they were written,” as the Apostle says, “for our correction, upon whom the ends of the ages have come” (1 Cor. 10:11). Since these matters are sufficiently easy in themselves,

[Col. 0459B] there is no need to dwell upon them longer. Concerning those who have vowed themselves to God, as in the following chapter.

## CHAPTER XXVII

“A person who has made a vow and promised his soul to God shall pay its price according to valuation. If it is a male, from twenty years up to sixty years, he shall pay fifty silver shekels, according to the sanctuary standard; if a female, thirty. But from the fifth year up to the twentieth, a male shall pay twenty shekels, a female ten,” etc.

[Col. 0459C] The Lord indeed says: “Vow and render to your God” (Ps. 75 [76]:12); yet here he permits vows to be redeemed. I do not understand this to apply to every vow, especially since it is said concerning the soul itself. Therefore, one who fails in a vow should redeem the vow and pay the price according to valuation. “According to valuation,” indeed, because sex, age, and means must be considered in paying the price. Men are to be judged differently from women, infants and children differently from adolescents and young men, the elderly and poor differently from the rich and wise, and the unwise differently from all these. Although there is more and less in the price, equality nevertheless exists in the satisfaction. The person who pays five shekels does not make less satisfaction than the one who pays fifty. Thus the Lord himself testifies that the woman who put two small coins into the treasury

[Col. 0459D] put in more than all the rest (Luke 21:1), for she had no more to give. Thus in assigning penances one must consider age, strength, knowledge, resources, condition, intention, and similar factors. For there are many who neither drink wine nor eat meat, yet do not make as much satisfaction as those who use these in sobriety according to their bodily condition and need. Thus the Apostle praises those who eat everything, as also those who eat vegetables, and those who judge every day, as also those who judge one day before another (Rom. 14:21). Therefore the male who is strong, from twenty up to sixty years—for at this age one is vigorous—shall pay fifty shekels; that is, he should make satisfaction by a greater and more perfect penance.

[Col. 0460A] This is according to the sanctuary standard, that is, according to the judgment of the priests. But the woman, who is more delicate and lacks something of masculine strength and knowledge, shall pay thirty. Although this number differs from the former in quantity, it is not inferior in the redemption of the soul. For a soul is redeemed by thirty shekels just as by fifty. Christ was baptized at thirty years of age, sanctifying the waters; on the fiftieth day the apostles are baptized in the Holy Spirit and fire. Hence the Lord himself says: “But you shall be baptized in the Holy Spirit not many days hence” (Acts 1:5). By so many shekels, then, is the soul redeemed which is cleansed in one way or another and released from sins. It is enough for the soul,

170

if it is redeemed for so great a price as that for which the Savior himself was sold.

[Col. 0460B] Likewise, both the vow and the soul are most perfectly redeemed by twenty shekels, because one who doubles the Decalogue of the Law by understanding and observance has nothing further with which to make satisfaction. Solomon also indicates that the redemption of fifteen shekels is perfect, saying: “Give a portion to seven, and also to eight” (Eccl. 11:2); for this number consists of these parts, through which the present and future life are signified. One gives a portion to each life who passes through this one in such a way as not to lose the other. Why the two together signify one is well known. Let us now come in order to the ten shekels, by which, because the ten words of the Law are understood, the soul is redeemed better by no other price than this. He also perfectly redeems his soul who pays five shekels for its redemption, that is, who gives the five senses of his body over to serving the Lord.

[Col. 0460C] It remains for us now to speak of three shekels and to show that there too redemption is perfect. For two shekels signify soul and body, while the third signifies all our possession. One who gives himself and everything back to the Lord makes perfect satisfaction. Of him the Lord says: “If you wish to be perfect, sell all that you have and give to the poor” (Matt. 19:12). It is clear, therefore, that the redemption of the soul, although it differs in amount, does not differ in the perfection of payment.

“If he is poor and unable to pay the valuation, he shall stand before the priest, and he shall give as much as the priest estimates and sees that he is able to pay.” [Col. 0460D] For this poverty seems to be not of temporal riches but of knowledge and virtues, and it must be judged according to the discretion of a prudent priest. This is what the Lord says: “The servant who did not know his master’s will and did not do what was worthy of it will be beaten with few stripes” (Luke 12:48). Hence sins committed by the delirious and insane are not imputed to them.

“But an animal that may be sacrificed to God, if anyone has vowed it, shall be holy and may not be exchanged”—that is, neither a better for a worse nor a worse for a better. “But if he exchanges it, both that which has been exchanged and that for which it was exchanged are consecrated to the Lord.” For no animal except a clean one is sacrificed to the Lord. [Col. 0461A] [Note: At Col. 0461D the edition is supplemented from the Cassinese codex.] But what is a clean animal except a good work, clean from every malice? Whoever has vowed such a work must perform it and may not exchange it. For making a vow and swearing are closely related and very similar. But if someone offers something else in place of what he vowed, imagining that he has thereby discharged his vow, he is mistaken. Rather, what is done as the redemption of the vow belongs to the Lord—that is, it will be accepted by the Lord—and the vow itself must moreover be fulfilled. Therefore holy vows must be performed, but wicked vows must be redeemed. Hence it continues:

“But if it is an unclean animal that cannot be sacrificed to the Lord, and someone has vowed it, it shall be brought before the priest. The priest, judging whether it is good or bad, shall set its price; and if he is able to pay it, he shall add a fifth part beyond the valuation.” What is an unclean animal except an evil work? Since the Lord does not receive it, it cannot be sacrificed to him. And just as it is evil to vow such a thing, so also it is evil to do it. Yet if anyone has vowed something of this kind, let him come to the priest and disclose his vow to him. If the priest recognizes it as evil, he shall set the price by which it may be redeemed; for it is better that it be redeemed than carried out. This price is the satisfaction of penitence. If the one who offers it wishes to pay this price, he shall add a fifth part above the valuation, performing penitence, which consists in the five senses of the body. Such a vow was made by those who vowed that they would neither eat nor drink before they had killed the Apostle.

[Col. 0461C] “If a man vows his house and consecrates it to the Lord, the priest shall consider whether it is good or bad; and it shall be sold according to the price fixed by him. But if the one who made the vow wishes to redeem it, he shall give a fifth part above the valuation, and he shall have the house.” Although this was spoken literally, it can nevertheless signify something spiritually. For in divine speech one is often called both a house, a temple, and a tabernacle. Hence it is clear that there is no believer who has not vowed and consecrated his house to God, since through faith and baptism he has committed himself to the Lord. The priest considers this house, whether it is good or bad, and fixes the price at which it is sold [Note: At Col. 0462D the same Cassinese codex supplements and corrects the edition]; for a good house is sold in one way, and [Col. 0461D] a bad house in another.

A good house is sold to God for the price of virtues. But concerning the bad one is said what the Apostle says: “I am carnal, sold under sin” (Rom. 7:14). The one, therefore, is cleansed so that it may shine; the other is devastated so that it may fall. If the one who made the vow wishes to redeem it, he shall give a fifth part above the valuation and shall have the house. Therefore whoever has lost his house by sinning can possess it again only by repenting and making satisfaction. For such a house is lost through sinning; but whoever vows well should render what he vowed. Such a vow does not need redemption. It would need redemption, however, if it had not been fulfilled or if, after being fulfilled, it had been violated.

[Col. 0462A] “But if he vows a field from his possession and consecrates it to the Lord, the price shall be estimated according to the measure of seed. If the land is sown with thirty measures of barley, it shall be sold for fifty silver shekels. If he vows the field immediately from the year in which the Jubilee begins, it shall be valued at its full worth. But if after some time, the priest shall calculate [p. 171] the money according to the number of years remaining until the Jubilee, and they shall deduct from the price. But if the one who vowed the field wishes to redeem it, he shall add a fifth part of the estimated money and shall possess it.”

These matters, and the rest which follows concerning possession of fields, should be understood literally. It was necessary for many reasons that they should be written. By fixing the price, error, fraud, disputes, and entreaties are removed, and the greed of priests is restrained. All these things commonly occur among buyers and sellers; but they cannot occur here, because the price, the time, and the manner of sale are determined, so that it may neither be bought more dearly nor sold more cheaply. Finally, he commands that a fifth part be added above the valuation, so that one who has vowed his possession to the Lord may not have a great desire to redeem it, knowing that it will cost him more to redeem.

For from the beginning, before it was consecrated to the Lord, a man could redeem the possession that he had vowed. It was sold to him more dearly than to others because others bought not the possession itself but only its usufruct, whereas he redeemed the possession itself by hereditary right. For once something had been consecrated to the Lord, it could no longer be sold or redeemed; other possessions returned to their own owners at the Jubilee. Anyone, therefore, could give his own possession to the Lord, but could not sell it to others and alienate it completely. Thus it was very necessary to write these things, so that, having spoken above concerning other possessions, he might not remain silent also about the Lord’s possessions, lest someone perhaps think there was no difference between them. It follows:

[Col. 0462C] “But if he wishes to redeem it, and it has been sold to someone else, the one who made the vow shall no longer be able to redeem it. When the day of Jubilee comes, it shall be consecrated to the Lord, and the consecrated possession shall belong by right to the priests.” This is what we have just said: the man who had sold his field could immediately redeem it at the beginning. But if it had first been sold to another—though it was sold not as a possession, but in usufruct—the one who made the vow could no longer redeem it. When the Jubilee arrived, it belonged by right to the priests, as though consecrated to God.

“But if a purchased field, not sanctified to the Lord from the ancestral possession, is involved, the priest shall calculate the price according to the number of years until the Jubilee, and the one who vowed it shall give it to the Lord. But at the Jubilee it shall return to the owner who sold it and had it as the lot of his possession.” Since no one could purchase another’s field by hereditary right, if anyone vowed to the Lord a field whose usufruct he had acquired, and which he did not possess from the estate of his ancient forefathers, it did not therefore become the Lord’s permanently; rather, when the Jubilee came, it returned to the former owner who had sold it and whose inheritance it had been. The man who had purchased it and vowed it to the Lord had, of course, the right to redeem it until the Jubilee.

Having expounded all those matters in this most profound book that seemed to require exposition, let us give thanks to our Lord Jesus Christ. Whoever follows him does not walk in darkness, but is illumined by the splendor of the true light. To him, together with the coeternal Father and the Holy Spirit, belong honor and glory, kingdom and dominion, might and power, now and always, and through the infinite ages of ages. Amen.

Here ends the book of Leviticus.

THE EXPOSITION OF NUMBERS BEGINS.

[Col. 0463]

172 CHAPTER I.

[Col. 0463B]

“The Lord spoke to Moses in the wilderness of Sinai, in the tabernacle of the covenant, on the first day of the second month, in the second year after their departure from Egypt, saying: Take the sum of the whole congregation of the children of Israel by their kindreds and houses, and the names of every male, from twenty years old and upward, of all the strong men of Israel; and you shall number them by their companies, you and Aaron. And there shall be with you the leaders of the tribes and houses in their kindreds, whose names are these.”

Whoever has heard our Lord Jesus Christ saying in the Gospel, “Even all the hairs of your head are numbered” (Matt. 10:30), ought to understand what is signified by the numbering of God’s people. For the Lord knows both the names and the number of his elect; and truly blessed are those numbered in God’s army, whose names are written in the book of life. It is impossible for any one of these to perish. Therefore only males and strong men, from twenty years old and upward, are not without reason numbered in this place. Those whom sex, age, and strength commend are fittingly summoned to fight and to engage the enemy.

But why from twenty years upward, except because twenty is twice ten? For the Ten Commandments contain the fullness of all knowledge. Whoever has doubled them and understands them both according to the letter and spiritually will be able securely both to dispute and to fight against Jews and heretics. But those who have anything less than this number are easily overcome in such a contest. To be twenty years old also means to understand the knowledge of the divine law in a twofold manner. But one who puts into practice what he understands seems to possess something even beyond twenty.

But what is signified by Moses and Aaron, who both number the warriors and choose twelve leaders over them, except Christ our Lord? For he is both lawgiver like Moses and priest like Aaron. He also chose twelve leaders for his army, whom he named apostles, saying to them in the Gospel: “You did not choose me, but I chose you” (John 15:16). Let this suffice concerning this chapter.

“The Lord spoke to Moses, saying: Do not number the tribe of Levi, nor include their sum with the children of Israel; but appoint them over the tabernacle of testimony, all its vessels, and everything pertaining to its rites. They shall carry the tabernacle and all its utensils, they shall minister, and they shall camp around the tabernacle.” The tribe of Levi is indeed numbered, as will later be shown; but the total of its number is not placed with the others, because this tribe is devoted to greater mysteries. For the clerical order, signified by this tribe, differs greatly from the rest of the people. It is set over the tabernacle of testimony; it holds authority over the whole Church; it bears its vessels and rites, the tabernacle itself, and all its utensils, because it governs, orders, and disposes the whole Church and its sacraments.

Therefore, not without reason, because these are the ministers and guardians of the whole tabernacle, they pitch their tents closest around the tabernacle itself. After them, the rest of the multitude encamps, each according to the order assigned to him. No one besides them dared to approach for taking down, erecting, or in any way arranging the tabernacle, because any outsider who approached was put to death. If our kings and rulers understood this, they would not usurp ecclesiastical offices.

CHAPTER II.

This same very well-arranged order of the camp appears to signify something great. For the tabernacle was pitched in the middle; nearest around it the Levites encamped. Then on the eastern side Judah pitched its tents; Issachar and Zebulun were counted in its army, and they always set out first by their companies. On the south the children of Reuben placed their camp, with Simeon and Gad numbered among them. On the western side were the camp of the children of Ephraim, together with Manasseh and Benjamin. But on the north Dan encamped, and beside him Asher and Naphtali; these always set out last.

Thus it is rightly said of the Church: “Beautiful as the moon, chosen as the sun, terrible as an army arrayed in battle-order” (Song 6:9). Nothing in it ought to be done disorderly, improperly, rashly, or confusedly. Let each remain in his own order; let one who is inferior not place himself before his superior.

173 CHAPTER III.

“The Lord spoke to Moses, saying: Bring near the tribe of Levi and make it stand before Aaron the priest, that they may minister to him and keep watch; and that they may observe everything pertaining to the worship of the multitude before the tabernacle of testimony, and guard the vessels of the tabernacle, serving in its ministry. You shall give the Levites as a gift to Aaron and his sons, to whom they have been given by the children of Israel. But you shall appoint Aaron and his sons over the service of the priesthood. Any outsider who approaches to minister shall die.”

Understand these things, Levites; open your eyes; see to it that pride does not puff you up. Know that you are ministers of bishops and priests, and not merely ministers, but gifts given to serve, to obey, and to comply with their counsels and commands. For if you act otherwise, you shall die, just as the outsider who approaches to minister shall die.

“The Lord spoke to Moses, saying: I have taken the Levites from the children of Israel in place of every firstborn that opens the womb in Israel, and the Levites shall be mine. For every firstborn is mine. From the day when I struck the firstborn in the land of Egypt, I sanctified to myself everything firstborn in Israel; from man to beast, they are mine: I am the Lord.”

In the firstborn of the Egyptians whom the Lord struck, he signified that by his blood and by the water of baptism he would destroy first and original sin in all the faithful. In their place he claimed for himself all the firstborn of the children of Israel, because, original sin having been destroyed, he showed that he loves faith—which is the first and greatest principle of Christian religion, and through which the soul that was dead is made alive—and that it pleases him. For just as all die through that sin, so all are made alive through this virtue, according to the saying: “The righteous shall live by faith” (Gal. 3:11).

But because not all who possess faith are worthy and fit for the sacraments of the Church, only the Levitical tribe is chosen by God to serve in the tabernacle in place of the firstborn, so that, as this tribe was one in lineage, so the entire clerical order might be one and the same in religion. Signifying this, the Apostle commands bishops, presbyters, and deacons to be without blame.

The Lord next commands Moses to number all males of the tribe of Levi from one month old and upward, and likewise to number all male firstborn from one month old and upward among the other tribes of the children of Israel. But because the firstborn of all Israel were more numerous than the males of the tribe of Levi alone, he commanded that all those in excess, then and thereafter, be redeemed after one month for a price of five shekels. A shekel contains twenty obols.

What does it mean that males alone are numbered, except that those are counted in God’s army who are neither of feminine frailty nor easily deceived like Eve? They are numbered from one month old and upward, signifying that this whole army consists only of believers. For after one month all firstborn were brought to the temple and offered to the Lord by their parents. Since, therefore, they are not given to God before one month, they are rightly not counted in God’s army before one month. They are thus numbered after one month: that is, after they have been joined to the Church, given back to God, and already cling to him by faith.

Hence they are redeemed after one month, because before one month they are of no value: they have neither been brought to the temple, nor offered to God in the temple, nor joined to the Church. The firstborn are redeemed with five silver shekels, by which these five books of Moses are signified. They are rightly called silver because they are pure and true, corrupted by no falsehood, according to the saying: “The words of the Lord are pure words, silver tested by fire” (Ps. 11:7).

These shekels are received by the priests according to the measure of the sanctuary if they are understood in a twofold way, that is, literally and spiritually. Hence they are said to contain twenty obols, because in this number the words of the law are doubled. There are ten, and if they are understood twofoldly they contain in themselves the whole fullness of the divine law. But if they are not doubled, such shekels will not be according to the measure of the sanctuary.

Those who are redeemed should not suppose that they are thereby immediately free from the service of the tabernacle. They are free from service at the altar, but not from service altogether. For by giving the five shekels, they have promised to receive, hold, and observe the faith, knowledge, and teaching of these five books. Let us therefore redeem our firstborn; let us redeem our faith. It needs redemption because without works it is dead. Let us give five shekels for it; let us render these five books to the Lord—not only by reading, but also by believing and acting, and by holding to teaching and faith.

CHAPTER IV.

There follows the command which the Lord gave Moses to number the children of Levi, namely those from thirty years old upward to the fiftieth year, and to assign to each the service he was to perform in the temple. He commanded, therefore, that the sons of Kohath should carry the ark of testimony and the table of the presentation, upon which the loaves always lay; that along with it they should carry the censers, mortars, cups, and bowls; the lampstand with its lamps, tongs, snuffers, and all the vessels of oil necessary for trimming the [p. 174] lamps; likewise the golden altar, and also the other altar with all its vessels. These, indeed, were the burdens of the sons of Kohath.

But the sons of Gershon carried all the curtains of the tabernacle and of the court of the tabernacle, the covering, the tent, and the cords. The sons of Merari carried the boards, bars, columns, and bases. All these things were done according to the command and arrangement of Aaron and his sons. They themselves erected the tabernacle; when the camp was to move, they themselves entered the tabernacle and the holy of holies, took down the tabernacle itself, wrapped the ark, the table, the lampstand, and the other burdens of the sons of Kohath in a hyacinth-blue cloth, and commanded them to carry them thus wrapped.

Since it is clear in itself that bishops ought to devote themselves to contemplation and to handle and administer the greater sacraments of the Church, so the Levites and the other lesser orders ought faithfully to labor and toil in outward offices, so that no one may be found useless or idle, but the obedience of the lesser may immediately follow the commands and disposition of the greater. What the ark of the covenant, the table and lampstand, the curtains and boards, the columns and the other things signify, we have explained most carefully in Exodus.

That all these are carried wrapped outwardly in a hyacinth-blue cloth signifies, I think, that every faithful soul, whether in prosperity or adversity, should both live and display a holy, heavenly, and angelic life. For such a cloth wrapped the man who, while still living on earth, said: “Our citizenship is in heaven” (Phil. 3:20); for hyacinth imitates the color of heaven.

But why are these numbered from the thirtieth to the fiftieth year, except because ministers of the Church ought to be strong and prudent in age and wisdom? For especially in these years does life flourish—youth, namely, which is chief among the ages. There are twenty years from the thirtieth to the fiftieth, and we have already said sufficiently what is signified by this number. In his thirtieth year our Savior was baptized and began to show, by teaching and work, the power of his majesty.

CHAPTER V.

“The Lord spoke to Moses, saying: Command the children of Israel to cast out from the camp every leper, every one who has a discharge of seed, and every one defiled by the dead. Cast out both males and females from the camp, lest they defile it while they dwell among you.” Every unbelieving and criminal soul is leprous, especially one infected by Simoniacal and heretical depravity. To have a discharge of seed is to sow error among the people. One defiled by the dead means a person who has touched the corpse of a dead man; and by this no one is better understood than the murderer of body and soul. Such persons should be expelled from the Church, lest they defile it by dwelling with it: “Whoever touches pitch shall be defiled by it” (Ecclus. 13:1); and, “Evil conversations corrupt good morals” (1 Cor. 15:35).

[Col. 0468A] “When a man or woman has transgressed the commandment of the Lord and committed an offense, they shall confess their sin and restore the principal, adding a fifth part to the person against whom they sinned. But if there is no one to receive it, it shall be given to the Lord and shall belong to the priest, except for the ram offered for expiation, that it may be an acceptable sacrifice.”

This chapter plainly shows that the confession of those who seize the property of others is useless and their penitence fruitless unless they restore it in full and make satisfaction for the injury. For touch is the fifth among the senses, and thefts and robberies are committed through it. Therefore robbers restore this fifth part when they promise that they will no longer deceitfully touch what belongs to another.

It is fitting that, if there is no one to receive these things, they are given to the Lord, because all things are his and everything is owed to him by right. He receives the disposition of the penitent; he closes the door of pardon to no one who repents and wishes to make satisfaction. These things belong to the priest because it pertains to him both to receive penitents and to remove sins by his intercessions. What is signified by the ram offered for expiation, except that anyone who sins in this way must, after making satisfaction, live innocently, so that he may no longer be a ravening wolf but a ram, harming no one? Otherwise neither the sacrifice will be acceptable nor the penitence fruitful.

“If a spirit of jealousy stirs a husband against his wife, whether she has been defiled or is charged upon false suspicion, he shall bring her to the priest and offer an oblation for her: a tenth part of a satum of barley flour. He shall not pour oil upon it nor put incense on it, because it is a sacrifice of jealousy, an offering investigating adultery.”

This jealous husband can be understood as Christ Jesus, whose wife is not only the Church but also each individual soul. He is called jealous, that is, suspicious, not in himself, who knows all things, but according to us, who are his members. For he says that he is hungry, thirsty, naked, and sick, not because his omnipotent nature undergoes any of these things. Thus he is jealous in us just as he is hungry, thirsty, naked, and sick.

Jesus himself is stirred in us by a spirit of jealousy when, for love of him, we are stirred against someone whom we consider suspect in the Catholic faith. We must bring such a person to the priest—that is, to a council of bishops and priests—and offer an oblation for that person. What oblation? A tenth part of a satum of barley flour. There are ten words of the Law, and I think that their [p. 175] tenth part is this flour. Thus the satum of flour signifies the entire book of the Law, while each individual commandment signifies a tenth part of the satum. For example, “You shall not commit adultery” (Exod. 20:14). This commandment, then, is offered here; it is recited in the council; it is brought against the woman accused of adultery.

Such flour is rightly called barley flour because it is received with sad throats of the heart from both sides. For who willingly either discusses heresies or hears them discussed? No oil is poured upon this flour, nor incense placed on it, because no one ought to offer mercy or an assent of sweetness to such an accusation; rather, it should appear horrible and foul to everyone. Let those hear this who anoint heretics with flattery and who delight in their words as in some sweet fragrance.

“The priest shall therefore bring her and set her before the Lord, and he shall take holy water in an earthen vessel and put into it a little dust from the floor of the tabernacle.” [Note: The Vulgate reads, “Therefore the priest offers her,” etc.]

What is signified by holy water except examples from the holy Scriptures? What is meant by an earthen vessel except the human body? Hence the Apostle, filled with such water, said: “We have this treasure in earthen vessels” (2 Cor. 4:7). The little dust, however, is the body of Christ, taken from the floor of the tabernacle—that is, from the flesh of the Virgin, in whom he dwelt for a time as in a tabernacle.

Therefore the priest—that is, some devout and wise man—brings and sets before the Lord the aforesaid flour, namely the offering of jealousy or accusation, because he discloses in the council everything of which the woman is accused. Then he takes holy water in an earthen vessel, because he gathers all the proofs of the Catholic faith in the treasury of his breast. Into these he mixes a little dust from the floor of the tabernacle, by which we understand Christ’s incarnation from the Virgin. When these things have thus been arranged, the priest recites both the accusation against the woman and afterwards the creed of the Catholic faith. This is what he says:

“When the woman has stood before the Lord, the priest shall uncover her head and place upon her hands the sacrifice of remembrance and the offering of jealousy.” The woman stands before the Lord because the person accused stands in the presence of the priests. Her head is uncovered when the priest’s questions reveal what she holds in her mind and what faith she professes. Then the sacrifice of remembrance—that is, the Catholic faith—and the offering of jealousy—that is, the accusation of the crime—are placed upon her hands: that is, they are recited to her openly and plainly. Excommunication then follows, so that if she believes otherwise or devises one thing in place of another, she may be subjected to the curses that follow. And this is what follows:

“But he shall hold the most bitter waters, in which he has placed the curses with an imprecation, and shall adjure her and say what follows.” “He,” that is, the priest who recited in the council both the woman’s accusation and the creed of faith, shall hold the most bitter waters. By these we understand the written instrument of examination, wholly set down with curses and anathema. He will give these waters to the woman to drink, because he will read aloud this whole curse while she hears and understands. When it has been recited, the woman—that is, the soul accused concerning faith—will answer: “Amen, amen,” that is, “Let what you say happen, if I hold a faith other than the faith which you hold.”

Yet first the priest shall take a handful from what is offered and burn it on the altar. We have already said above that this sacrifice signifies the creed of faith. We take from it a handful when we separate some part from the whole, especially the part concerning which the soul was accused. We burn this on the altar of the accused person’s heart after we have persuaded that person by arguments both to hold, believe, and love this article of faith.

Then the priest shall take from her hand the sacrifice of jealousy, raise it before the Lord, and place it upon the altar. Above we said that the sacrifice of jealousy was the tenth part of a satum of flour when we expounded the tenth commandment of the Law—namely, the commandment, “You shall not commit adultery” (Exod. 20:14). We call it tenth not according to order, but according to number. The priest takes it from her hand when he shows that she has not committed adultery. He raises it before the Lord and places it on the altar, making all who are present hear it with their ears and understand and believe it in their hearts.

That after drinking the waters the woman’s belly swells and her thigh decays, if she is guilty, signifies, I think, that after a heretic has been excommunicated and condemned, all strength of begetting and bringing forth is removed from that person’s teaching and preaching; it appears useless, empty, and foul to everyone. For just as women beget and bring forth by the belly and thigh, so heretics beget and bring forth their adulterous offspring by teaching and preaching.

CHAPTER VI.

“The Lord spoke to Moses, saying: Speak to the children of Israel and say to them: When a man or woman makes a vow, that they may be sanctified and wish to consecrate themselves to the Lord, they shall abstain from wine and from everything that can intoxicate. They shall not drink vinegar from wine or from any other drink, nor anything pressed from the grape; they shall not eat fresh or dried grapes. During all the days in which they are consecrated [p. 176] to the Lord by their vow, they shall eat nothing that can come from the vine, from the dried grape even to the grape-stone.”

Before they are sanctified and baptized, all Christians make this vow; for when they come to faith, they renounce the devil and all his works and all his pomps. What else is it not to drink wine and everything that can intoxicate, except to abstain from vices and sins by which the soul, intoxicated, loses sense and reason and every virtue and strength? Hence he rightly commands them to reject not only wine but also grapes and everything that can come from the vine, even to the grape-stone, so that we may sin neither in deed nor even in thought.

“Throughout the whole time of his consecration, a razor shall not pass over his head, until the day is fulfilled on which he is consecrated to the Lord. He shall be holy, with the hair of his head growing.” We call the mind the head of the soul, and the hairs of that head signify holy thoughts. This Nazirite ought always to be adorned and never deprived of them. Whoever always thinks good things does not easily sin, for evil thoughts are the cause of sinning, according to the saying: “For from the heart proceed evil thoughts, adulteries, thefts, murders” (Matt. 13:19). Let the hairs of the mind grow, let good thoughts grow, by which the Nazirite may always be adorned and protected. It follows:

“Throughout all the time of his consecration, he shall not go in to a dead person, nor be defiled at the funeral even of his father, mother, or sister.” To go in to a dead person is to commit a mortal and criminal sin. Whoever imitates the evil examples of parents is defiled by the funeral of father and mother, brother and sister. By this figure we are commanded to separate from our body all members that scandalize us. Hence the Lord also said to one wishing to defile himself at his father’s funeral: “Let the dead bury their own dead; but go and preach the kingdom of God” (Matt. 8:22). Let us therefore flee death and follow life: “I,” says the Lord, “am the way, the truth, and the life” (John 14:6). It follows:

“But if someone suddenly dies before him, the head of his consecration shall be defiled; and he shall shave his head on the day of his purification; on the seventh day he shall shave it.” Someone suddenly dies before him when, at the devil’s suggestion, he commits some sin through which the soul dies, though that soul is before him and within him. Then the head of his consecration is defiled when his mind and his holy mode of life become abominable and filthy.

He immediately shaves it, so that in the cutting of the hair itself he may show by what grief and what penitence he is inwardly constrained. For it is not fitting that someone should appear handsome in outward hair who has inwardly made his mind bald by sinning. Nor should one be ashamed to repent who was not ashamed to sin. In shaving his head, he shows that he has committed a crime, for otherwise a Nazirite was not permitted to shave his head. What else, then, is shaving the head except manifesting sin through penitence?

The one who is shaved immediately and on the same day is the person who, led at once by penitence, does not delay to turn to the Lord or put it off from day to day. He is shaved again on the seventh day so that, as he began, so he may persevere in penitence to the end. “For whoever perseveres to the end, that one shall be saved” (Matt. 24:13). Hence David says: “My sin is ever before me” (Ps. 50:4). For the seventh day is the last day. Thus one is shaved on the first and on the seventh day who, from the time of sinning onward, never ceases to repent. Let the person who commits a crime always appear shaven, always penitent and grieving; let him not pretend to be a Nazirite and righteous person when by sinning he has lost righteousness.

“In the eighth day he shall offer two turtledoves and [Col. 0472A] two young pigeons to the priest at the entrance of the tabernacle of testimony. The priest shall make one a sin-offering and the other a burnt-offering, and shall make intercession for him, because he sinned in connection with the dead; and he shall sanctify his head on that day and consecrate to the Lord the days of his separation, offering a year-old lamb as a sin-offering. Yet the former days shall be void, because his consecration was defiled.”

Although the day of judgment is called the eighth day (and for this reason certain psalms are entitled “for the eighth”), nevertheless every day may be an eighth day, because, once the week of this life is ended, the soul is separated from the body. On this day the Nazirite—who, although he has sinned, has nevertheless erased his sins by worthy repentance—offers to Jesus the great priest two turtledoves, or two young pigeons, that is, chastity and innocence of body and soul. This takes place at the entrance of the tabernacle of testimony, that is, at the entrance to the heavenly kingdom. The priest also makes one offering for sin and the other as a burnt-offering, because through these he both remits the man’s sins and reconciles him to God the Father, making intercession for him. For, as the Apostle says, he always intercedes for us with the Father (Rom. 8:34). Then indeed he reconciles him, sanctifies him, and consecrates him to the Lord, offering a year-old lamb. For because, after sinning, he lived humbly in repentance and innocently like a lamb, he deserved by the lamb’s innocence to be released from sin. Therefore, let one who wishes his repentance to bear fruit live as a lamb: humbly and innocently.

But the statement, “Yet the former days [Col. 0472C] shall be void,” seems to be what the Lord says through Ezekiel: “But if the righteous man turns away from his righteousness and commits iniquity, none of the righteous deeds that he did shall be remembered” (Ezek. 18:24). If, therefore, a righteous man sins and does penance, he will indeed be saved—not because he was righteous, but because he did penance. Thus the days of his former righteousness do not without reason appear to have been lost.

What follows concerns that Nazirite who lived without fault throughout his life and persevered in good works to the end. Such was the Apostle, who says: “I am conscious of nothing against myself” (1 Cor. 4:4). He commands that bishops and priests of this kind be chosen. It follows:

[Col. 0472D]

“This is the law of the consecration: when the days which he had determined by vow are completed, he brings him to the door of the tabernacle of the covenant, and offers his oblation to the Lord: a spotless year-old lamb as a burnt-offering, a spotless year-old ewe as a sin-offering, and a spotless ram as a peace-offering.”

The vows of our Nazirites, however, are not made for a time, but are fulfilled together with their lives. For when the saints pass from this life, then they enter the gates of the heavenly palace; then the great priest Jesus Christ offers their oblations to the Lord, because he commends their holy life and good conduct and reconciles them to the Father. By the lamb, the ewe, and the ram—in which the whole kind of sheep is contained—we understand perfect innocence, [Col. 0473A] humility, and simplicity. Therefore he who lived in these qualities and did not depart from these virtues is rightly offered with them. Since God delights in and is appeased by such a sacrifice, and forgives sins, it is rightly called both a burnt-offering, a sin-offering, and a peace-offering.

The priest shall therefore offer before the Lord a basket of unleavened breads mixed with oil, unleavened cakes anointed with oil, and the libations belonging to each offering; and he shall make both the sin-offering and the burnt-offering. But he shall sacrifice the ram as a peace-offering, offering at the same time the basket of unleavened bread and the libations due according to custom. For in all these things, which are unleavened and without leaven, is signified the holy, sincere, and incorrupt life of the Nazirite, who lived not in the leaven of malice and wickedness [Col. 0473B] (1 Cor. 5:8), but in the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth. Since all his works never lacked mercy and piety, they are rightly represented not merely as unleavened, but also as anointed with oil.

Christ the great priest offers these things for the Nazirite, because, commending him by such qualities, he renders the Lord gracious toward him in every respect. For he himself said: “Whoever confesses me before men, I also will confess before my Father” (Matt. 10:32). Therefore, whether someone offers for us a ram or unleavened bread, let it be understood as the commendation of our innocent and sincere life. It follows:

“Then the Nazirite shall shave, before the door of the tabernacle of the covenant, the hair of his consecration; and the priest shall take his hair [Col. 0473C] and place it upon the fire that is under the sacrifice of the peace-offerings. He shall take a boiled unleavened shoulder of the ram, an unleavened cake, a grape from the basket, and one unleavened wafer, and give them into the hands of the Nazirite before his head has been shaved; then, receiving them back from him, he shall raise them before the Lord. And they shall be for the priest after they have been sacrificed, like the breast that was commanded to be set apart.”

When the vow has been fulfilled and the Nazirite is shaved, this is not, as above, a sign and display of grief or repentance; rather, it is so that his hair may be placed in the sacrifice of the peace-offerings, in order that he may please God not only by works but also by thoughts. For we have said that good thoughts are signified by the hair; they are, indeed, the seasoning of the whole sacrifice, because God looks upon the heart.

But the fact that the priest takes the shoulder of the ram, the cake, and the wafer and gives them into the Nazirite’s hands, then receives them back and raises them before the Lord, seems to signify that whatever good we possess we have received from Christ, through whom we shall at last render both ourselves and our goods to God. Hence the Apostle says: “For what do you have that you did not receive? And if you received it, why do you boast as though you had not received it?” (1 Cor. 4:7).

You have a shoulder, by which you bear the works of others; you have an unleavened cake and wafer, namely incorrupt faith and knowledge, which feed and nourish you. Do not boast as though these were your own, because you have received them from elsewhere. Therefore you ought to render them to the priest as things not your own, since they belong to him—as does the breast that was commanded to be set apart. For from Christ’s [Col. 0474A] breast proceed the preaching of the Gospel, our faith, and every good work of ours. Therefore all things are his. And although all may rightly do good, not all may preach the Gospel; consequently it is said of the breast that it was commanded to be set apart.

What, then, is meant by what follows: “After these things the Nazirite may drink wine”? Since above we signified vices and sins by wine, this wine must be another: namely, that by which the soul, made drunk, forgets all its troubles and all the tribulations it suffered here. Of this the Psalmist says: “They shall be intoxicated with the abundance of your house, and you shall give them drink from the torrent of your delight” (Ps. 35:9). Let this suffice concerning the Nazirite.

## Chapter VII

[Col. 0474B]

There follows the account of the twelve princes who offered to the Lord six wagons and twelve oxen, by which the tabernacle and all its burdens might be carried. These were indeed very necessary, since the Levites could hardly carry the burdens and all the equipment of that tabernacle. It does not seem necessary to seek an allegory in these things. An allegory must necessarily be sought where the letter commands something either useless or altogether lacking reason.

“And the Lord said to Moses: Let the leaders each offer gifts on successive days for the dedication of the altar. On the first day Nahshon son of Amminadab, of the tribe of Judah, offered his oblation. In it they made a silver dish weighing [Col. 0474C] one hundred and twenty shekels; a silver bowl of seventy shekels, according to the weight of the sanctuary, both full of fine flour mixed with oil for a sacrifice; a small mortar of ten gold shekels, full of incense; a bull from the herd and a ram for a burnt-offering; a goat for sin; and for the sacrifice of peace-offerings, two oxen, five rams, five he-goats, and five year-old lambs. This was the offering of Nahshon son of Amminadab.”

Every believer may be called a tabernacle, according to the Apostle’s saying: “For the temple of God is holy, and you are that temple” (1 Cor. 3:17); and likewise an altar, because in him a sacrifice acceptable to God is made. This altar is dedicated when a person is converted to faith and consecrated to the Lord through baptism. For this dedication the leaders of the Church—namely bishops and priests—offer gifts, because they instruct one newly converted, who begins service in Christ’s army, with the commandments of the law, the teachings of faith, examples of the saints, and a rule of life.

For what is signified by the dish and the small mortar, each made from numbers of ten, but this book of the Law, which consists of ten commandments? Count the number in each case, and you will find the number ten everywhere. These are rightly said to be filled with fine flour mixed with oil and with incense, because this book and its teaching abound in the anointing of the oil of the Holy Spirit, mercy, and piety, and are full of the fragrance of most sweet understanding. Since the whole book shines with the light of wisdom and knowledge, the vessels are not without reason said to be golden and silver [Col. 0475A]. The shekels are reckoned by the measure of the sanctuary, because all the commandments of the Law have been weighed in the balance of truth and righteousness.

Moreover, the aforementioned leaders offer for the dedication of this altar a bull from the herd, a ram, and a year-old lamb as a burnt-offering, because they announce to the newly converted the passion of Christ, the Lord’s labours, and his innocence. This bull, taken from the herd of patriarchs and prophets, cultivated the field of the Church and sowed it with the seed of the Word. This ram, led to sacrifice, did not open his mouth. This is the Lamb who takes away the sins of the world. Therefore we follow his examples by labouring, suffering, and living innocently.

Nor should anyone think it absurd that a goat is also said to be offered for sin, because for our sins he was numbered among the wicked. They also offered two oxen in the sacrifice of peace-offerings, five rams, five he-goats, and five year-old lambs, so that the new soldier might learn by these both to labour and to govern the senses of his body. For we have two oxen, namely soul and body, by which we bear Christ’s yoke, which is sweet, and sweat in his field. If these two agree within us, whatever we ask, as the Evangelist says, we shall obtain. We also have five senses, through which we make peace with God—provided they are innocent and clean. For all the animals are clean. To sacrifice he-goats, however, is to kill and overcome lustful inclination by mortifying the flesh. The other leaders likewise offered similar gifts and sacrifices. Let this one exposition, therefore, suffice for all.

## Chapter VIII

There follows the lampstand, which is commanded to be placed on the southern side, so that it may shine upon the table placed to the north. This lampstand is Christ, of whom we spoke sufficiently in Exodus. It is rightly placed in the south, because “God comes from the south, and the Holy One from Mount Paran” (Hab. 3:3). We also treated in the same book of the table, by which the teaching of both Testaments is signified. Yet it is neither understood nor illuminated unless by the light of this lampstand. It is placed in the north, where Scripture records that the seven devils are. Therefore whoever encounters the devil in battle must first approach this table and be refreshed by its provisions [Col. 0475D].

Then the Lord commanded Moses to take the Levites from the midst of the children of Israel, purify them, sprinkle them with water of purification, and have them shave every hair of their bodies. Then they were to take two oxen; and, with the entire multitude of the children of Israel gathered, the children of Israel were to lay their hands upon the Levites. Aaron was to offer them before the Lord, that they might serve in his ministry. The Levites also were to lay their hands upon the heads of the oxen, of which Moses offered one for sin and the other as a burnt-offering, praying for them. Thus purified, the Levites afterwards entered the tabernacle.

That the Levites were then purified, sprinkled with hallowed water, and shaved of all bodily hair signified [Col. 0476A] that our Levites too, and the entire order of clerics, ought to be purified from every stain of vice, washed from every crime, and cleansed from every superfluous and depraved thought. The children of Israel also lay their hands upon them, so that the Levites may understand how great a burden and labour they undertake. For those who bear the hands of all must labour for all; and what the hands of all ought to have done in the tabernacle, those alone must do who have received the hands of all upon themselves.

Aaron offers them to God, because it belongs to bishops both to consecrate the other orders and to offer them to God. But what are the two oxen upon whose heads the Levites lay their hands, except body and soul? For those who wisely tame their body and soul and restrain them from every evil desire surely hold their hands upon the heads of these oxen. The Apostle was a wise tamer of these, saying: “I chastise my body and bring it into slavery” (1 Cor. 9:27). If they have been thus tamed, Moses—that is, our Saviour—offers one for sin and the other as a burnt-offering, so that by their sacrifice sins may be absolved and God’s grace received.

We intended to speak briefly in this book about sacrifices, because in Leviticus we discussed them most fully. Nor do we suppose these matters will be difficult for those who, passing through that book, arrive at this one. After this purification, the Levites enter the tabernacle, because those purified in this way are worthy both of the tabernacle of the Church and of heaven.

Finally, at the end of this [Col. 0476C] chapter, the Lord commanded that Levites should serve in the tabernacle from their twentieth year until their fiftieth, and afterwards should become guardians of the vessels. For in the fiftieth year, that is, the jubilee, every slave is restored to freedom; in it the Levites too begin to rest from labour. It was necessary that they should labour in youth and tame the flesh, so that they might more readily overcome the pleasures of the flesh. At this age, however, because strength is already failing and natural heat diminishing, they are commanded to rest. Yet they guard the tabernacle and what is in it, because it often happens that virtues acquired by labour are lost through idleness. We must guard the tabernacle of our body and whatever virtues are in it, because at every age we can sin, and the devil, a cunning thief, always lies in wait for us [Col. 0476D].

## Chapter IX

The Lord commanded the children of Israel to keep the Passover at its appointed time, that is, on the fourteenth day of the first month. But those who are unclean through contact with a human soul, or are far away on a journey, because they cannot do this at its proper time, should do it on the fourteenth day of the second month at evening, with unleavened bread and wild lettuces.

Why is the Passover—that is, the immolation of the lamb—held only on the fourteenth day? Is it not because no one ought to approach Christ’s flesh and blood who has not yet been enlightened by the light of the ten days of the Old Testament and the four of the New? For the words of the Law are ten, and the Gospels four; by their light and faith the world is illuminated. Therefore no one is worthy to keep the Passover who has not been enlightened by this light and these days.

To be defiled through a human soul is the same as to be defiled through a dead person; this has already been stated and explained above. Those are far away on a journey who, because of the sins in which they persevere, have become far removed from the religion of the Church and from God. Of them the Psalmist says: “Salvation is far from sinners” (Ps. 118:133). They cannot keep the Passover with the others, because “whoever eats and drinks this unworthily eats and drinks judgment upon himself, not discerning the body of the Lord” (1 Cor. 11:29). Let them first be cleansed and return to God and to the Church, and then eat.

We pass over these matters because they were discussed most fully in Exodus. [Note: [Col. 0477D] Nothing in this edition is more corrupt than this passage; we supply and emend it by the light of the Laurentian manuscript, with which the Cassinese manuscript agrees.] A foreigner and a stranger may eat of this sacrifice; by them we understand Gentiles converted to the faith.

There follows the cloud which always covered the tabernacle. At night it gave light, and by day it protected from the heat of the sun. By it are represented the graces of the Holy Spirit, by which the darkness of our ignorance is enlightened and we are defended from the heat of vices and the burning of luxury. For we are the tabernacle of God, of whom he himself says: “I will dwell in them and walk among them” (2 Cor. 6:17). But what does it mean that, at this cloud’s command, the tabernacle is both pitched and moved? It means that when we do good, we are not under our own power but under that of the Spirit who is in us. For by him we are governed, taught, and directed along the straight way to our homeland [Col. 0477C].

## Chapter X

“The Lord spoke to Moses, saying: Make for yourself two beaten silver trumpets, at whose sound the camp may move, the people gather, the army prepare for battle, and on the Kalends and other festivals they may be sounded over burnt-offerings.”

By the two trumpets we may understand the two Testaments; why they are called silver is plain, for silver signifies purity of speech. They are beaten, because every day they are fashioned on the anvil of our heart by the hammer of the Holy Spirit; for beaten work cannot be made without hammer and anvil. When we learn the commandments of the Testaments, we feel the tongues of teachers striking our hearts as a hammer. By these trumpets the apostles and teachers summoned peoples from every part of the world to the Church; by them they teach us to prepare for wars, to fight against enemies, and to overcome both vices and evil spirits. By their sound we also learn how we should live, how we should run in the way [Col. 0478A] of God’s commandments, and how we should offer God sacrifices of praise and rejoicing. For their sound is differentiated according to the capacity of the hearers, so that each person may readily recognize in them what he ought to do.

Here Moses urges Hobab, son of Raguel and his kinsman, to travel with him. Hobab says: “I will not go, but shall return to the land in which I was born.” Moses replies: “Do not leave us; for you know in what places we ought to pitch camp in the wilderness, and you will be our guide.” Why does Moses wish to appoint as guide of the army a Gentile man when the Lord himself was its guide? He knew that a vain and proud man would not accept counsels for his own salvation unless he were won by certain praises and gentle persuasions. Hence we are given a rule: it is not sinful to turn powerful and proud people toward justice and truth even by flattery. [Note: [Col. 0477D] Since a little above St Bruno said that Moses used praises and gentle persuasions with Hobab, a vain and proud man, in order to induce him to comply, here, where he says that it is not sinful to turn powerful and proud people toward justice by “flatteries,” he must be understood to have used *adulationes* in the sense of gentle persuasions. Such words differ from one another. According to ancient writers, *adulatio* commonly denotes soothing speech joined with falsehood; *blandimentum*, by contrast, may be employed without prejudice to truth. [Col. 0478D]]

“And they set out from the mountain of the Lord on a journey of three days, and the ark of the covenant of the Lord went before them for three days, providing a place for the camp. The cloud also was over them as they went.”

What is the journey of three days but faith in the Trinity? On the first day one comes to the Father, on the second to the Son, on the third to the Holy Spirit. This is the extent of the way: one may neither stop short nor go beyond it; otherwise the ark that goes before is left behind and the faith of the Church is not held. Those who walk in this way are always overshadowed by the cloud and grace of the Holy Spirit.

## Chapter XI

[Col. 0478C]

“Meanwhile a murmuring of the people arose, as if they were grieving over their labour, against the Lord. When he heard it, he was angry, and the fire of the Lord was kindled against them and devoured the farthest part of the camp. When the people cried out to Moses, Moses prayed to the Lord, and the fire was extinguished.”

Of this the Apostle says: “Do not murmur, as some of them murmured and perished by the destroyer” (1 Cor. 10:10). All these things happened to them as figures, but were written for our correction. Let us therefore be corrected, lest we likewise perish. For this fire signifies eternal fire, which will burn the impiously murmuring and those who speak against God—except only those who, led by repentance, flee to Christ, signified by Moses, and deserve to be protected by his help [Col. 0478D].

There follows the account of the people weeping from desire for meat and wishing to be in Egypt, because cucumbers, leeks, onions, and garlic came to their minds. Therefore the Lord was greatly angered, and the matter also seemed intolerable to Moses. The Lord thus gave them [Col. 0479A] meat, sending them a multitude of quails for food; they flew around the camp at a height of two cubits above the ground.

What is this, foolish and senseless people? You abound in heavenly bread and desire onions and garlic? You reject manna and long for meat? The allegory is plain. For even to this day the Jewish people follow the letter that kills, not the Spirit that gives life; in the Law they seek a carnal, not a spiritual, understanding. Christ came; the living bread came down from heaven. He gave manna, food that does not perish but remains unto eternity, containing every delight and every savour of sweetness. He gave Gospel preaching; he opened the understanding of his disciples so that they might understand the Scriptures. This, then, is manna, by which our inward person is both refreshed and fattened.

Those who wish to understand the commandments of the Law only according to the letter—what else do they eat but cucumbers, melons, leeks, onions, and garlic? In these are also signified the writings of heretics, philosophers, and poets. Therefore this history records that not only the Jews but also the mixed multitude which had gone up with them from Egypt wept from the same desire.

Let us, then, not seek quails flying close to the earth, nor follow a carnal understanding which is not raised above the earth; but let us learn to fly after that eagle which says: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God” (John 1:1). The Lord was therefore rightly greatly angered, and the matter rightly seemed intolerable to Moses. For who can endure that manna should be rejected and onions and garlic chosen? Who can easily bear that a people delivered with such labour from such harsh slavery should wish to return to Egypt merely to eat garlic?

But let us see what follows: “The meat,” he says, “was still in their teeth, and such food had not yet failed; and behold, the anger of the Lord was stirred against the people, and he struck them with an exceedingly great plague.” Thus it is evident that those whose evil desires God grants are altogether unhappy; perhaps he would not have killed them if he had not given them the meat they wickedly sought. Let us therefore ask the Lord not to grant us an answer when we ask for something wickedly. “For,” says the Apostle, “all these things happened to them as figures” (1 Cor. 10:11) [Col. 0479D].

Now the Lord commands Moses, distressed by such great evils among the unbelieving people, to choose seventy-two men from the elders of Israel, who may bear the burden of the people with him, so that he alone is not weighed down. When this had been done, “the Lord came down in a cloud and, taking from the Spirit that was in Moses, gave it to them. When the Spirit rested upon them, they prophesied and did not afterwards cease.” These seventy-two men most plainly signify the seventy-two [Col. 0480A] disciples of Christ, whom God filled not from another Spirit but from that Spirit which was in Christ—whom Moses then signified. Filled with it, they preached Christ’s mighty works and did not thereafter cease from preaching.

## Chapter XII

Miriam and Aaron spoke against Moses because of his Ethiopian wife, saying that the Lord had spoken not only to Moses but also to them. Therefore the Lord was greatly angered, for Moses was the meekest man of all people. The Lord said to Aaron and Miriam: “Why were you not afraid to speak against my servant Moses, who is most faithful in all my house? I speak with him mouth to mouth, openly; he sees God, not through riddles and figures. But to the other prophets I shall appear by dream and vision.” Angered against them, he departed; the cloud also withdrew, which was above the tabernacle. And behold, white leprosy like snow appeared upon Miriam. Moses prayed for her, saying: “Lord God, I beg you, heal her.” The Lord replied: “If her father had spit in her face, ought she not at least to be covered with shame for seven days? Let her be separated outside the camp for seven days, and afterward let her return.”

Let us consider the meaning. Moses signifies Christ; his Ethiopian wife, the Church gathered from sinners; Miriam, the Jewish people; and Aaron, the Jewish high priests and priests. For the Jewish people and high priests often spoke against Christ, saying that God had spoken to them too in the writings of the prophets and that they ought to be believed rather than Christ, who, loving and embracing an Ethiopian wife as it were, ate with tax collectors and sinners. Therefore the Lord said to them, as persons professing to believe in Moses: “If you believed Moses, you would surely believe me also, for he wrote of me” (John 5:46).

That Christ was the meekest of all men may be understood from the fact that, like a lamb led to sacrifice, he did not open his mouth, and he prayed even for those who crucified him. He was most faithful in the house of God, which is the Church, because he did not hesitate to give himself over to death for it. And in saying that he sees God openly and not through riddles [Col. 0480D] and forms, the text most plainly teaches that it spoke not of Moses but, in the figure of Moses, of Christ. For when Moses desired to see the Lord, the Lord himself says to him in Exodus: “No human being shall see me and live” (Exod. 33:20). And John the Apostle says: “No one has ever seen God” (John 1:18). Our Moses also says: “No one has seen the Father except the Son, and anyone to whom the Son chooses to reveal him” (Matt. 11:27). It is therefore clear that the first Moses saw God only through riddles and forms.

[Note: [Col. 0479D] St Thomas proves by several arguments that, while living, a human being cannot see God’s essence by the natural light of the intellect. First, some likeness on the side of the faculty of intuition must exist, by which the intellect is capable of seeing God; but the wayfarer lacks this power. Second, because in the state of which we speak a human being understands or perceives nothing except through created species and images, these cannot represent an immaterial and simple nature—which God is—nor can they in any way lead to a vision of his substance. Third, because the divine essence is unbounded, containing in itself in a pre-eminent manner whatever can be signified or understood by a created intellect, the human being here lacks a proportionate means for seeing God. It will be otherwise, however, for one enjoying heavenly blessedness: there the intellect, strengthened by the light of divine glory, will see God as he is, according to Psalm 35: “In your light we shall see light.” Thus the Holy Doctor, *Summa theologiae*, I, question 12, article 2 and following. With regard to the Moses of whom St Bruno speaks, it may be said that according to God’s ordinary providence he did not see the divine essence, though this cannot be said of an extraordinary gift of divine light, which God could also have bestowed.] 

What follows—that [Col. 0481A] the Lord departed from them in anger and the cloud withdrew from the tabernacle—what else do we think it signifies except that the Father and the Holy Spirit likewise forsook the Jews when they spoke against our Saviour and refused to believe in him? Then white leprosy like snow appeared upon Miriam, because from that time the impious Jewish people were defiled by the stains of their own unhappiness. For them, just as Moses prayed for Miriam, Christ prayed, saying: “Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing” (Luke 23:34).

Yet the Synagogue remains outside the camp, because the seven days have not yet been completed for her return to the Church: “For when the fullness of the Gentiles has entered, then Israel will be saved” (Rom. 11:25). Then these seven days will be completed, because there are only seven days. To spit in the father’s face means to despise a prelate of the Church who publicly and plainly rebukes and excommunicates one of his subjects for misdeeds. Such a person is covered with the shame of seven days if he is ashamed of his sins until perfect repentance, or even for as long as he lives [Col. 0481B].

## Chapter XIII

Then it is narrated that Moses, by the Lord’s command, sent twelve men from among the leaders of Israel out of the wilderness of Paran, where the people then remained, to inspect the land of promise. It was the season when early grapes could be eaten. They went, explored the land, and cut off a branch with its cluster of grapes, which two men carried on a pole [Col. 0481C]. They returned after forty days, bringing also pomegranates and figs. Displaying the fruits of the land, they said to the children of Israel:

“We came to a land that truly flows with milk and honey, as may be known from these fruits. But it has very powerful inhabitants and great, walled cities; therefore we cannot possibly go up against this people, because it is stronger than we are.”

But Caleb and Joshua said: “Let us go up and possess the land.” Therefore the whole multitude wept throughout that night, wishing to appoint themselves a leader and return to Egypt.

## Chapter XIV

“When Caleb and Joshua, having torn their garments [Col. 0481D] in grief, encouraged them, and they themselves were now about to stone them, the glory of the Lord appeared over the covering of the covenant before all.”

I would understand these twelve leaders to be the twelve apostles, were it not that they feared, dissuaded the people from ascending into the land of promise, and became the cause of their ruin and death. Another interpretation must therefore be sought. But let us now understand by them all the leaders of the Church, that is, bishops; by Caleb and Joshua, the good alone; and by the rest, all the others. For the number ten, because it contains all numbers within itself, sometimes signifies many, sometimes all. Here, indeed, ten remain, only two being removed from the twelve.

By these ten evil leaders, therefore, let us understand all evil leaders of the Church. For all, both good and evil, praise the land of the living; all extol its glory and blessedness and place before the ears and eyes of their hearers, through preaching, the fruits of its happiness. But because they live badly, they repel people from it by the bad example of their conduct. Of these the Lord says: “Since they have the key of knowledge, they themselves are unwilling to enter, and do not permit those who wish to enter” (Luke 11:52). When the evil perish, therefore, only good leaders enter the land of the living.

“And the Lord said to Moses: ‘How long will this people speak against me? How long will they not believe me?’ And he wished to kill them; but Moses prayed for them, saying: ‘God is patient and of great mercy, taking away iniquity and crimes, and leaving no one innocent, visiting the sins of fathers upon children to the third and fourth generation. Forgive, I beg you, the sin of this people.’ And the Lord said: ‘I have forgiven according to your word. As I live, the whole earth shall be filled with the glory of the Lord. Nevertheless, all who have seen my majesty and the signs that I performed, and have now tested me [Col. 0482C] ten times and have not obeyed my voice, shall not enter the land of promise.’”

Because the Lord is patient, waiting long for sinners, he does not punish immediately; because he is merciful, he takes away the iniquities and crimes of those who turn through repentance. Yet he leaves no one innocent, because no human being shall be justified in his sight. He visits the sins of fathers upon children to the third and fourth generation only in those who imitate their fathers in iniquity and crime; otherwise a son shall not bear his father’s iniquity.

The Lord forgave the people’s sin on account of Moses his servant, but he did not remit the punishment of sin. For all who had been numbered from twenty years old and upward died in the wilderness during those forty years because of this sin. In this is proved true the saying: “The Lord does not take vengeance twice for the same thing.” In saying, “those who have now tested me ten times,” he uses a finite number for an infinite one; “ten times” means “many times,” because this number contains all numbers within itself.

## Chapter XV

[Col. 0483A]

“Then the Lord spoke to Moses, saying: Speak to the children of Israel, and say to them: When you have entered the land of your dwelling, which I shall give you, and you make an offering to the Lord as a burnt offering or a peace-offering [Note: The word “peace-” is absent from the Vulgate.], in fulfilling vows, or freely offering gifts, or on your solemn festivals, burning a sweet-smelling odor to the Lord, from cattle or from sheep: whoever sacrifices a victim shall offer a sacrifice of fine flour, a tenth part of an ephah, mixed with oil amounting to a fourth part of a hin; and he shall give wine of the same measure for poured libations, with the burnt offering or victim, for each lamb. For rams there shall be a sacrifice of two tenths [Col. 0483B] of fine flour, mixed with a third part of a hin of oil; and he shall offer wine for a libation, a third part of the same measure, as a sweet-smelling odor to the Lord. But when you make a burnt offering or sacrifice from cattle, fulfilling a vow, or give peace-offerings to the Lord, for each ox you shall offer three tenths of fine flour mixed with oil, amounting to half a hin, and wine of the same measure for poured libations, as an offering of most sweet odor to the Lord. Thus you shall do for each ox, ram, lamb, and kid. Both native-born persons and foreigners shall offer sacrifices by the same rite: one command and judgment shall be for you and for the strangers of the land.”
