Let us consider the meaning. Why are the children of Israel now told that, before they arrive at the land of promise, they should offer fine flour, oil, and wine with every burnt offering, unless [Col. 0483C] it is because they did not possess these things in the wilderness? They are therefore commanded that, when they have abundance of them, whoever sacrifices a lamb should also offer a sacrifice of fine flour, a tenth part of an ephah, and a fourth part of a hin of oil and wine. He who sacrifices a ram should offer with it two tenths of fine flour and a tenth part of a hin. But he who offers an ox to the Lord should offer with it two tenths of fine flour, and a full hin of wine and oil.

Let us not seek this burnt offering and these sacrifices outside ourselves. If we wish, we can find all these things within ourselves. We are the lambs, rams, and oxen; we are also the fine flour and the tenths; we too are drenched with oil and wine [Col. 0483D]. Therefore we offer all these things if only we offer ourselves to the Lord. If you wish to be a ram and a lamb, be innocent, patient, and meek. If you wish to be an ox, submit and humble yourself beneath Christ’s yoke, and labor steadfastly and confidently in the field of the Church. If you wish to be fine flour, be wholly white and without leaven; and the more you are ground and afflicted, the whiter and more beautiful you will become.

A tenth is called a human being because [Col. 0484A] he himself is the tenth drachma; he is also the hundredth sheep. This tenth of fine flour—that is, a human being, unleavened, sincere, and uncorrupted—is wholly drenched within and without with the oil of the Holy Spirit and the wine of evangelical preaching. By this oil we have been healed, and by this wine we have been made drunk. Although several tenths are enumerated here, all nevertheless signify the same thing. For two tenths signify no more here than one, nor three more than two. One denotes the whole multitude of believers; two, the people of the Jews and the Gentiles; and three, the corresponding three parts of the world—Asia, Africa, and Europe. [Note: Above, in the exposition of Leviticus, chapter XIV, we saw that St Bruno made the same division of the world, since America, the fourth part of the globe, was not discovered until the end of the fifteenth century and was added to the dominion of the kings of Spain. These princes, especially Catholic ones, through apostolic men brought those peoples, still barbarous and idolatrous, to the Christian faith and attached them to the Holy Roman Church. Therefore the world is now said to be divided into Asia, Africa, Europe, and America.]

Here the Lord commands the children of Israel to offer firstfruits to him from their threshing floors and also from their foods and cooked dishes. By this I readily understand mercy toward the poor [Col. 0484B] and generosity in almsgiving. It follows that, if the whole multitude sins through ignorance, it shall offer a calf from the herd as a burnt offering of most sweet odor to the Lord, together with its sacrifice and libations as the ceremonies require, and a goat for sin; and the priest shall pray for them, and they shall be forgiven.

I think that this sin is that by which the children of Israel killed Christ—a deed which he himself showed to have been done through ignorance, saying: “For they do not know what they are doing” (Luke 23:34). And the apostle Peter says: “And now, brothers, we know that you acted through ignorance, as did also your rulers” (Acts 3:17). Let them therefore repent and offer the calf—the very one whom they killed—by washing, preaching, believing, [Col. 0484C] drinking, and eating; so that, delighted by such a sacrifice, the Lord may say: “A sacrifice of praise will honor me” (Psalm 49:23). But what is to be understood by sacrifice, libations, and ceremonies, we have just explained above when speaking of fine flour, oil, and wine.

To offer a goat for sin is to burn sinful flesh with the fire of repentance, so that it may be released from sin. The priest is the mind, which, doubled upon the altar of the heart and offering the victim of compunction, deserves to be heard both for itself and for others. For sin through ignorance is chiefly the fault of the mind; therefore by its intervention let it come about that we are heard. But if one soul sins unknowingly, it shall offer [Col. 0484D] a yearling she-goat for its sin, and the priest shall pray for it [Note: The errors of the edition are corrected from the Laurentian manuscript.], as above. This concerns every person who errs unknowingly and understands and believes otherwise than truth is. Having recognized his sin, he should therefore offer a she-goat, which, since it is of the same kind, signifies the same thing that we have just said the male goat signifies.

But the soul that has committed something through pride, whether [Col. 0485A] native or stranger, because it has rebelled against the Lord, shall perish from its people. This is plainly to be understood of a heretic, and for this reason he is rightly called rebellious. For it is great pride, when the whole Church protests and sets forth the doctrines of the Catholic faith, for anyone to wish to rebel against it and stubbornly defend his own opinion. Such a person shall perish, whatever his nation, rank, condition, or religious profession.

It follows concerning the man whom the children of Israel led outside the camp and overwhelmed with stones because he had gathered wood on the Sabbath. This teaches that those who violate God’s covenant and refuse to keep and observe the ordinances of God’s Church together with the other faithful ought to be expelled from the Church and condemned and excommunicated by all [Col. 0485B]. For he is overwhelmed by as many stones as there are assenting persons by whom the excommunication is confirmed.

“Moreover the Lord said to Moses: Speak to the children of Israel and say to them that they should make fringes for themselves at the corners of their garments, placing blue bands upon them; when they see these, they shall remember all the Lord’s commandments and shall not follow their own thoughts and eyes, committing fornication through various things, but, rather, remembering the Lord’s precepts, shall do them.”

This chapter needs no lengthy exposition, since the one who wrote it has himself explained it. He commanded them to place blue bands in the fringes so that these might be a sign by which, remembering the heavenly commandments, they would not think vain and useless things [Col. 0485C]; for hyacinth has the color of heaven. Let the blue bands, then, be holy and chaste thoughts, which, interwoven with the fringes—that is, with the sayings of God’s commandments—may guard our eyes from every fornication. Of the fornication of the eyes the Lord says: “Whoever looks at a woman in order to desire her has already committed adultery with her in his heart” (Matthew 5:28).

## CHAPTER XVI

It follows concerning the rebellion which Korah, Dathan, and Abiram made against Moses and Aaron, wishing to claim the priesthood for themselves, with the agreement of two hundred and fifty men among the elders of the Synagogue. The earth opened and swallowed these men, while fire consumed the rest, who held censers and offered incense [Col. 0485D]. Then the Lord commanded Eleazar, Aaron’s son, to take up the censers lying in the fire, hammer them into plates, and fasten them to the altar, so that, seeing them, the children of Israel might always remember this deed and might not presume to approach the priesthood established solely for Aaron’s sons.

Whenever we read that the Lord punished the children of Israel for their iniquities, we should always remember the Apostle’s saying: “All these things happened to them figuratively; but they were written for our correction” (1 Corinthians 10:11). Therefore let every person fear to raise sedition against bishops and the rulers of the Church, and let him fear unjustly to seize for himself things that do not belong to him; for whoever does this blasphemes God. Hence it is said here: “If they go down alive into hell, you shall know that they have blasphemed the Lord” [Col. 0486A].

Why the censers, hammered into plates, are to be fastened to the altar has been explained by the one who wrote it: “For what letters are to those who read, these plates are to those who do not know the Law.” Thus one has them fastened around the altar of the heart if one does not forget them. Would that our kings and princes, would that simoniacs and invaders of the Church, had had these plates fastened to the altar of their hearts and had not forgotten the death of Korah, Dathan, and Abiram! But he who says that these censers were sanctified by the deaths of persecutors signifies that the holy Church is defiled by cohabitation with simoniacs and invaders, and that their separation is thereby signified.

## CHAPTER XVII

[Col. 0486B] Here the Lord commanded Moses to take one rod for each tribe, with each person writing his name upon it. Aaron, however, was to write his own name upon the rod of Levi and place them in the tabernacle of the covenant. The priesthood was to belong to the one whose rod had sprouted. Let us also pray to our Lord Jesus Christ that he may make our rods and our governance sprout, lest we be found dry and fruitless in his house. For he is no pontiff whose rod does not sprout. This miracle may be raised against those who deny that a virgin could give birth: for it is no more wonderful for a virgin to give birth than for a dry rod in a single night to sprout flowers and fruit.

## CHAPTER XVIII

“Then the Lord said to Aaron: You and your sons, and your father’s house with you, shall bear the iniquity of the sanctuary; and you and your sons together shall bear the sins of your priesthood. But also take with you your brothers from the tribe of Levi, the scepter of your father, and let them stand ready and minister to you; nevertheless, they shall not approach the vessels of the sanctuary or the altar.”

These things pertain to priests and to whatever is within the veil. For not only bishops and priests, but also the other orders of clergy bear and carry the iniquity of the sanctuary and the sins of the entire Church. It is indeed a great and burdensome load to carry. It would be most necessary that those who bear the iniquities of others and are commanded to relieve others of sin’s burden should themselves be free of their own iniquities. We ought always to be very anxious, since we are commanded to mourn both our own iniquities and those of others [Col. 0486D]. Levites, however, are forbidden to approach the vessels of the sanctuary and the altar, lest perhaps they presume rashly to usurp what belongs to bishops.

“Then the Lord said to Aaron: Every offering and sacrifice, and whatever is given back to me for sin and transgression, and is placed in the Holy of Holies, shall be yours and your sons’; you shall eat it in the sanctuary. Only males shall eat of it, because it is consecrated to you.”

For just as all tithes belonged to the Levites, so all firstfruits, offerings, and sacrifices belonged to the priests. In this, as in the other matters, it is signified that all greater mysteries pertain to them. They ate it [Col. 0487A] in the sanctuary because we ought to expound the more hidden divine mysteries in the assembly of the faithful, where there are only males—that is, those stronger in faith and understanding. For this is consecrated and dedicated to the priestly order alone.

“But the firstfruits which the children of Israel have vowed and offered I have given to you and to your sons and daughters by a perpetual right; whoever is clean in your house shall eat from them.”

By “firstfruits” one may understand not only the first things, but also the better things. Hence in Exodus we read of firstfruits of gold, silver, and precious stones. Therefore all firstfruits belong to priests [and] to their sons and daughters, because whatever is faithful, holy, religious, and outstanding in virtues and morals belongs to priests and to those who are generated and regenerated by them [Col. 0487B] through the water of baptism. Whether male or female—that is, whether perfect or less perfect—all share one faith and one doctrine. Only heretics are separated from this participation, because they are unclean, although they too are children of priests.

The Lord commands that all firstborn things and every unclean animal be redeemed, while clean ones are not redeemed. [Note: Casinensis manuscript: “That all firstborn things belong to the priests; but the firstborn of human beings and every animal,” etc.] Their blood the priest shall pour upon the altar, their fat he shall burn, but their flesh shall be his, like the consecrated breast and shoulder. What do we understand by firstborn things except faith and the soul, which are plainly first, chief, and dearer things? These are said to belong to priests because through their ministry both faith and souls [Col. 0487C] are offered to God. For no one is baptized unless he first offers his faith and soul to priests. An unclean animal is redeemed because violated faith and soul are restored at the price of repentance. [Note: The edition is corrected here from the Laurentian manuscript.] But clean things are not redeemed; they are offered, because what is free and subject to no slavery has no need of redemption. Their blood is poured upon the altar because their life and soul are rendered to God. God delights in their fat, by which the strength and fortitude of the soul are signified. But their flesh belongs to priests, as do the consecrated breast and shoulder, because it belongs to priests to preach the lives of the saints, give counsel, and bear burdens.

We have already spoken above of the firstborn of human beings [Col. 0487D], who are redeemed after one month for five shekels, so that, after being baptized and offered to God, they may entrust the five senses of their body to priests in such a way that they no longer serve pleasures but God. Levites too are commanded to offer firstfruits: namely, a tenth part of the tithes offered to them by the people. Hence it is clear that firstfruits do not always mean something first. We give tithes because we ourselves are tenths: we are the tenth drachma and the hundredth sheep. What is a hundredth is a tenth; we are also the tenth order, because [Col. 0488A] there are nine orders of angels. Therefore, since we give tithes, we commend ourselves as it were as tenths in the Lord’s tithes. We pass briefly over these matters because we have spoken of them above.

## CHAPTER XIX

“Then the Lord spoke to Moses and Aaron, saying: This is the ordinance concerning the victim established by the Lord: command the children of Israel to bring you an unblemished red heifer of full age, which has borne no yoke. You shall hand it over to Eleazar the priest, who shall lead it outside the camp and sacrifice it in the sight of all; dipping his finger in its blood, he shall sprinkle it seven times toward the doors of the tabernacle, and shall burn it in the sight of all, [Col. 0488B] delivering to the flames its hide and flesh, its blood and dung.”

What is understood by this heifer except Christ’s flesh? It is rightly called red, being stained with its own blood. It is of full age because the Lord suffered in youth. It has no blemish, because, as is written of our Savior: “He committed no sin, nor was deceit found in his mouth” (1 Peter 2:22). Hence it is said not to have borne a yoke, by which slavery to vices is signified. And because our Lord was delivered by the people to the priests and their rulers, this heifer too is commanded to be handed over to Eleazar.

That it is led outside the camp and sacrificed in the sight of all, and together with hide, flesh, blood, and dung is given to the flames, the Apostle has explained, saying: “For the bodies of those animals whose blood is brought into the sanctuary by the high priest are burned outside the camp. Therefore Jesus also, in order to sanctify the people through his own blood, suffered outside the gate” (Hebrews 13:11).

But what should we think is signified by the priest’s dipping his finger in its blood and sprinkling it seven times toward the doors of the tabernacle? Perhaps this: that the Jews, crying out, said, “His blood be upon us and upon our children” (Matthew 25:27). It was rightly done seven times, because parents, children, grandchildren, and all descended from them are held liable under this curse until the consummation of the age. For there are only seven days, and what is done seven times is understood to be done on all days [Col. 0488D].

The priest shall also cast cedar wood, hyssop, and scarlet twice dyed into the flame that consumes the heifer; then, after washing his garments and body, he shall enter the camp, and he shall be unclean until evening. Cedar wood, which is incorruptible and fragrant by nature, signifies the saints. Hyssop, which naturally grows upon rock, denotes those whose foundation is Christ. Scarlet twice dyed likewise signifies those inflamed with love of God and neighbor. Thus these things are rightly placed together with the heifer in the flame, and are inwardly kindled by a great fire through reading and remembering it [Col. 0489A]. For cedar wood, hyssop, and scarlet are burned with the heifer as often as those signified by them, remembering Christ’s Passion, are tormented by the fire of grief and sorrow. This may fittingly be understood of the apostles and the others who were present at his Passion.

By the priest who sacrifices the heifer and the man who burns it are most rightly signified not only Caiaphas and the wicked people then living, but the whole Jewish people and all their priests who succeeded them both in descent and in wickedness. They shall indeed be unclean until evening, by which the end of this world is understood. Then they shall wash their garments; then the water of baptism shall cleanse their countenance inwardly and outwardly; then they shall enter the camp and be converted by faith to the Church, according to the words: “They shall return at evening” (Psalm 58:15); “In those days Judah shall be saved” (Jeremiah 23:6); and “When the fullness of the Gentiles has entered, then Israel shall be saved” (Romans 11:25) [Col. 0489B].

“But a clean man shall gather the ashes of the heifer and pour them out outside the camp in a most clean place, that they may be kept for the multitude of the children of Israel for water of sprinkling, because the heifer was burned for sin. And when the one who carried the heifer’s ashes has washed his garments, he shall be unclean until evening.”

What is signified by the ashes of the heifer except Christ’s remains? And what his remains are, the evangelist says: “After he had eaten, he took the remains and gave them to them, and said: These are the words which I spoke to you while remaining [Col. 0489C] with you” [Note: The Vulgate reads: “And when he had eaten before them, he took the remains and gave them to them. And he said to them: These are the words which I spoke to you while I was still with you”] (Luke 24:43).

These remains, that is, Christ’s words and the evangelical preaching which he left to his disciples as he ascended to heaven, were gathered by the clean man—that is, the apostolic assembly. It should be noted that neither the priest nor the man who burns the heifer, but only the one who gathers the ashes, is called clean. Therefore the apostles carry the heifer’s ashes, that is, apostolic preaching, outside the camp of the Jews and pour them out in a most clean place, that is, in the Church of the Gentiles, no longer wishing to give what is holy to dogs or cast pearls before swine.

Christ’s words are much more for us a means of preservation, sprinkling, and cleansing [Col. 0489D] than those ashes were for the children of Israel. But why is this man, chosen as clean, called unclean after carrying ashes that are themselves clean and washing with water? Perhaps because he is clean in comparison with others, but, with regard to perfection, is not clean as long as he lives. For who shall boast that he has a clean heart? Even the stars are not clean in God’s sight. Whoever is clean still needs to wash his feet (John 13:10). The Lord himself says this.

“Whoever touches a human corpse and is therefore unclean for seven days shall be sprinkled with this water on the third and seventh days, and thus shall be cleansed; if he has not been sprinkled on the third day, he cannot be cleansed on the seventh.”

Whoever is born from Adam touches a human corpse, because Adam is not recorded to have begotten anyone before he was a corpse and subject to the laws of death. Therefore, with respect to himself, every person is unclean for seven days, because unless he is regenerated by the water of baptism he is never clean. Hence it is said here that such a person should be sprinkled with this water on the third day, so that, baptized under triple immersion, he may deserve to be enlightened by the Lord. He is sprinkled also on the seventh day, so that through the laying on of hands he may be confirmed by the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit. Why can one who has not been sprinkled with this water on the third day not be cleansed on the seventh [Col. 0490B]? Because no one is confirmed by a bishop who has not first been baptized in the Trinity.

“Everyone who touches the corpse of a human soul and has not been sprinkled with this mixture shall defile the tabernacle of the Lord and perish from Israel, because the water of expiation has not been sprinkled upon him; he shall be unclean, and his uncleanness shall remain upon him.”

What do we understand by the corpse of a soul except heretics, who are dead not in body but in soul? To touch their corpse is to acquiesce in their impieties. Whoever does this, unless he has been sprinkled and cleansed by the water mentioned above—that is, by evangelical doctrine—shall defile the Lord’s tabernacle, leading others into error; he himself shall perish, be unclean [Col. 0490C], and retain his uncleanness, as Truth himself says: “Whoever believes and is baptized shall be saved; but whoever does not believe shall be condemned” (Mark 16:16). It follows:

“This is the law concerning a man who dies in a tent. All who enter his tent, and all the vessels that are there, shall be unclean for seven days. A vessel that has no lid and fastening upon it shall be unclean.”

The tent is the Church, in which no one dies except a Christian; and he dies if he separates himself from the Catholic faith. Whoever is in this man’s tent and joins himself to his faith and fellowship shall be unclean. Hence those vessels are rightly called unclean in this passage [Col. 0490D], because they have neither lid nor fastening: all are unclean whose ears have not been closed to the faith and doctrine of this dead man. But what the seven days signify we have often already said.

“If anyone in a field touches the corpse of a slain man, or of one who died naturally, or his bone, or a grave, he shall be unclean for seven days.”

As the tent signifies the Church, so the field signifies things outside the Church. Therefore seven days—that is, all days—are unclean for those outside the Church: either because by being born they have touched the corpse of the first man, whom the devil killed, [Col. 0491A] or because, clinging to many sinners, they have themselves destroyed themselves. To touch a dead person’s bone is to receive any portion of a heretical man’s teaching. But one touches the grave of the dead who venerates and receives his entire book, full of stench and decay. Let us hear how these also ought to be cleansed.

“They shall take ashes from the burning of the sin-offering and put living water upon them in a vessel. Then a clean man, having dipped hyssop in it, shall sprinkle from it the whole tent, all the furnishings, and the people defiled by such contamination; and in this manner the clean man shall cleanse the unclean on the third and seventh day. Having been expiated on the seventh day, he shall wash himself and his garments, and shall be unclean [Col. 0491B] until evening.”

We think that the Apostle took from this passage what he says: “He who knew no sin, he made sin for us” (2 Corinthians 5:21). For just as here “the ashes of sin” means the ashes of the heifer burned for sin, so there “sin” means a victim for sin. In placing living waters upon the ashes, they were in some manner indicating life-giving doctrine through those ashes. This water is sprinkled with hyssop by a clean man, because whoever preaches this doctrine must be clean and rooted and founded upon that rock of which it is said: “And the rock was Christ” (1 Corinthians 10:4). Hyssop naturally grows upon rock.

Thus the clean man cleanses the unclean man [Col. 0491C] and everything belonging to him: namely, his faith, understanding, knowledge, doctrine, and the tent of his soul—that is, his body. What is meant by the third and seventh days has already been said above. Why one so expiated washes again and is unclean until evening has also already been said; there is no need to repeat the same things often.

## CHAPTER XX

It follows concerning how, when the people came into the wilderness of Zin and water failed, they turned in rebellion against Moses and Aaron. By the Lord’s command, after gathering the entire multitude before the rock, they said: “Can we bring water out for you from this rock?” And he struck the rock twice with the rod, and very abundant waters came forth. Then the Lord said to Moses and Aaron: “Because you did not believe me, to sanctify me before the children of Israel, you shall not bring this people into the land which I gave them.”

This passage shows most plainly how much faith can accomplish and how much unbelief can harm. We explained this in Exodus. Although this miracle and that one are not the same, their exposition is the same; indeed, that exposition seems to belong more to the present passage than to the earlier one. We must be greatly afraid lest we too be unbelieving, when we see such great men brought into so severe a predicament on account of unbelief in one matter. Yet this happened for their benefit and as an example to us [Col. 0492A]. For useful is that death which releases a person from labor and brings him into joy and rest.

Aaron therefore went up Mount Hor and there, by the Lord’s command, died. *Hor* means “light”; he therefore fittingly dies upon the mountain of light, fleeing darkness and hastening toward the brightness of glory.

## CHAPTER XXI

The Canaanite heard that Israel had come, fought against him, conquered, and carried off spoil from him. But Israel, binding itself to the Lord by a vow, said: “If you give this people into my hand, I shall destroy its cities.” The Lord handed the Canaanite over to it, and Israel killed him and overthrew his cities. This Canaanite is the devil, who fought against us in the first man [Col. 0492B], conquered, and took no small spoil from us when he deprived us of immortality itself. All of us who come to faith, renounce him, and take up arms against him are bound by a vow against him. Therefore we kill him and overthrow his cities as often as we convert unbelievers to faith and sinners to repentance.

Then it is narrated that the people, now wearied by travel and labor, murmured against Moses. Therefore the Lord sent fiery serpents among them, which killed them. Moses prayed for them, and the Lord commanded him to make a bronze serpent, so that those struck might be healed by looking upon it. Of this serpent the Lord says: “As Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness, so must the Son of Man be lifted up, that [Col. 0492C] everyone who believes in him may not perish but have eternal life” (John 3:14).

Therefore look upon the serpent—that is, believe in Christ. The fiery serpents signify evil spirits, which are more wicked than all living things and surpass all in the fire and frenzy of credulity. They destroy souls and have most power against those who do not cease to murmur against Christ and slander him by living wickedly. Therefore, those struck by these serpents should run not to the serpent, but to the likeness of the serpent; let them run to him who committed no iniquity and yet was numbered among the wicked: “who appeared in the likeness of sinful flesh, in order that he might condemn sin in the flesh through sin” (Romans 8:3); who is now lifted up upon the wood of salvation to cast down him who earlier climbed onto the wood of desire [Col. 0492D].

Then the people came to the Arnon, at the borders of the Amorite: “For the Arnon is the boundary dividing the Moabites and Amorites. Hence it is said in the book of the wars of the Lord: ‘As he did at the Red Sea, so he shall do at the torrents of the Arnon. The cliffs of the torrents have bent down, that they might rest at Ar and lie upon the borders of the Moabites.’”

This, he says, was written in the book of the wars of the Lord, which we do not have: namely, that just as the children of Israel emerged victorious at the Red Sea while the Lord fought for them, so they would conquer at the torrents of the Arnon. He metaphorically calls the Amorites cliffs because they were hard and strong. Yet, after these were conquered and humbled, the children of Israel rested within their borders [Col. 0493A], that is, within the boundaries of the Amorites and Moabites. For the Lord had commanded the children of Israel not to touch the children of Moab and Ammon, who were Lot’s sons; likewise, not the children of Esau, who lived in Seir and Edom.

“From that place the well appeared, concerning which the Lord spoke to Moses: Gather the people together, and I shall give it water. Then Israel sang this song: ‘Rise up, O well; sing to it. The well which the princes dug, which the leaders of the multitude prepared in the giver of the law and with their staffs.’”

This well is the New Testament, which the leaders of the Church—that is, the apostles and teachers—prepared, dug, and expounded in the lawgiver. [Note: Casinensis manuscript: “In the teacher of the Law,” that is, as Christ taught them, he who is teacher of the Law. “Prepared,” etc.] But hear this, those who have staffs, when it says, “with their staffs”: either cast away your staffs or dig wells. For in saying that these leaders dug the well with their staffs, it commands those who have staffs—that is, the governments of the Church—to search out the depths of the holy Scriptures and provide living water to all who thirst [Col. 0493B]. What we said above was signified by the Canaanites whom Israel destroyed is likewise signified by Sihon king of the Amorites and Og king of Bashan. Therefore that exposition suffices here as well.

## CHAPTER XXII

It follows concerning Balaam, who, led by greed, went to Balak son of Zippor in order to curse the children of Israel. Although the Lord had at first forbidden him to go there, seeing, of course, his eagerness to go, he later permitted him to depart, yet forbade him to curse the people. Unhappy, then, are those whose evil desires the Lord grants. And because the greedy are easily deceived by covetousness, Balaam is warned by both the miracle of the speaking donkey and the voice of the angel of the very thing that had been commanded before.

Balaam went, and because he did not dare to curse, he found another way not to lose the money promised him. I have said this so that the greatness of greed’s evil may be understood. Let someone else expound Balak’s words and Balaam’s sacrifices; I do not care to labor over them. Let us therefore expound only those things Balaam seems to have said by the spirit of prophecy.

## CHAPTER XXIII

“From the tops of the rocks I shall see him; from the hills I shall behold him. The people shall dwell alone and shall not be counted among the nations. Who can number Jacob’s dust or know the number of Israel’s offspring? Let my soul die the death of the righteous, and let my last end be like theirs.”

For in that people Balaam saw, not by his own spirit but by the Spirit of God, the whole Church already; hence he desired to die the death of the righteous and become like it: “Blessed are the dead who die in the Lord” [Col. 0494A] (Revelation 14:13). What are meant by the high rocks and hills, except the lofty, difficult, and figurative sayings of both Testaments? Let whoever desires to see and contemplate the life, conduct, glory, blessedness, and other qualities of God’s people draw near to these, see them, and read them. For in this mirror the beauty of the Church is seen.

And this people shall dwell alone. Where? Certainly in the land of the living. It shall not be counted among the nations that die without baptism; and because it is innumerable, it is called dust.

“Again Balaam took up his parable [Note: [Col. 0493D] To “take up a parable” is to pour forth utterances under the prompting of the Spirit. The Hebrew word *mashal* was especially effective in the sententious genre. That this Balaam, moved by the higher Spirit, uttered his blessings or curses may also be understood from the fact that, sent to curse the Israelites, he blessed them; for he could not attempt anything except where the Spirit impelled him. Mazocchi, *Spicilegium ad Numeros*, ch. 23.] and said: ‘Stand, Balak, and listen; hear, son of Zippor. God is not like a man, that he should lie, nor like a son of man, that he should change. Has he spoken, then, and will he not do it? [Col. 0494B] Has he declared it, and will he not fulfill it? I have been brought to bless; I cannot prevent the blessing. There is no idol in Jacob, nor is an image seen in Israel. The Lord his God is with him, and the royal trumpet-shout of victory is among him. God brought him out of Egypt; his strength is like that of a rhinoceros. There is no augury in Jacob, nor divination in Israel. In their proper times it shall be said to Jacob and Israel what God has done. Behold, the people shall rise like a lioness and lift itself up like a lion. It shall not lie down until it has devoured the prey and drunk the blood of the slain.’”

Why, foolish [p. 189] Balaam, do you so often test God, whom you yourself testify, as God, can neither lie nor change? It should have sufficed you that he spoke once, whose will is changed neither by sacrifice nor by a change of [Col. 0494C] places. Hence it is clear that you do not bless God’s people willingly, but because you cannot prevent the blessing. You grieve because there is no idol in Jacob; and therefore, by your accursed counsel, it came about that they later sacrificed to Baal-peor. The Lord brought him out of Egypt, whose strength is like that of a rhinoceros, because by his singular omnipotence he surpasses all things, just as this animal, with its single horn, throws down whatever it attacks. And although there is now no idol in Jacob, yet in its own time it shall be said of him that he made gods of gold, silver, and wood. Read the prophets, and you will find that this was said of Israel. This people is compared to a lion, and is said to have devoured prey and drunk blood. Whoever does not understand this should read both these books and the books of Kings [Col. 0494D] and Maccabees, in which he will find how much blood it shed.

## CHAPTER XXIV

“Again Balaam took up his parable and said: Balaam son of Beor has spoken; the man whose eye is stopped up has spoken [Note: [Col. 0494D] The Vulgate reads “whose eye is stopped up,” as also in the edition of St Bruno; but in the Venetian Bible printed in 1542, edited by Isidore Clarius, one finds here and below, “whose eye is opened.”]; the hearer of God’s words has spoken, he who has beheld the vision of the Almighty, who [Col. 0495A] falls, and thus his eyes shall be opened: How beautiful are your tents, Jacob, and your tabernacles, Israel! Like wooded valleys, like watered gardens beside rivers, like tents which the Lord has pitched, like cedars near waters. Water shall flow from his bucket, and his seed shall be in many waters. His king shall be taken away because of Agag, and his kingdom shall be removed. God brought him out of Egypt; his strength is like that of a rhinoceros. They shall devour the nations that are his enemies, break their bones, and pierce them with arrows. He lay down and slept like a lion, and like a lioness—who would dare rouse him? Whoever blesses you shall himself be blessed; whoever curses you shall be accounted under a curse.”

For Balaam says of himself that he is stopped up and blinded, whose eyes are not [Col. 0495B] opened even in his downfall and condemnation. For there is no one whose eyes, for knowing the truth, are not opened even after death. By “tabernacles,” however, he means gatherings of people, individual churches; because they abound in virtues, wisdom, and holiness, they are compared to a shady valley, a watered garden, and cedars. Water flows from his bucket—from the breast of him from which unfailing wisdom always streams. His seed shall be in many waters: this signifies that from that people there shall come offspring among many nations. “His king shall be exalted above Agag.” For Saul was the first king of this people; as is read in the books of Kings, he fought against Agag king of Amalek. Raised up in pride because of him, he preserved Agag, as though for the glory of his triumph, and was disobedient to God, who had commanded that all Amalek be destroyed, from man [Col. 0495C] to beast. Hence he also lost his kingdom, so that thereafter no king would arise from his line. The story is long; whoever reads it will understand these matters more clearly.

“Taking up his parable again, he said: Balaam son of Beor has spoken; the man whose eye is stopped up has spoken, who, falling, has open eyes: I shall see him, but not now; I shall behold him, but not near. A star shall rise from Jacob, and a rod shall arise from Israel; it shall strike the leaders of Moab and lay waste all the sons of Seth; and Idumea shall be his possession, Seir shall yield as an inheritance to his enemies; but Israel shall act valiantly. From Jacob shall come one who rules and destroys the remnants of the city.”

Since Balaam sins knowingly, he therefore says most rightly of himself [Col. 0495D] that, falling, he has open eyes; just as, conversely, one falls with closed eyes who sins unknowingly and in ignorance. But what he says—“I shall see him, but not now; I shall behold him, but not near”—may be understood of the Last Judgment, when both good and evil alike shall stand before Christ’s tribunal. Immediately adding concerning this, he says: “A star shall rise from Jacob,” because the whole world shall be enlightened; “and a rod shall arise from Israel,” because the ignorance of fools shall be corrected. Let all this be understood of Christ, who, deriving his origin according to the flesh from Israel, rules over all the nations of the world. He himself shall destroy the remnants [Col. 0496A] of the city—namely, Jerusalem—whose remnants are all the wicked, once only the good have been brought into its buildings.

This may also be understood literally of David, where it says: “A star shall rise from Jacob, and a rod shall arise from Israel,” and so forth. For among that people he was more illustrious than all kings in both strength and holiness. He struck Moab and measured it with a line, leveling it to the ground. Seek this in the books of Kings. “He also laid waste the sons of Heth,” by whom we ought to understand the Canaanites and the others who had formerly inhabited the land of promise. Rebecca too speaks of them in Genesis, saying: “I am weary of life because of the daughters of Heth; and if Jacob takes a wife from the stock of this land, I do not wish to live” (Gen. 27:46).—“And Idumea became his possession,” [Col. 0496B] as it is written: “He placed garrisons in Idumea, established a stronghold, and all Idumea became David’s servant” (2 Sam. 8:14). Seir also is in Idumea.

“And when he saw Amalek, he took up his parable and said: ‘Amalek is the beginning of the nations; his end shall be destruction.’” David overcame these also, as he did the others. “He also saw the [p. 190] Kenite and, taking up his parable, said: ‘Your dwelling-place is indeed strong; but if you place your nest in the rock, and are chosen from the stock of Cain, how long will you be able to remain? For Assyria shall take you captive.’” What else should we seek here, since we know that they were taken captive by the Assyrians? “Taking up his parable again, he spoke: ‘Alas! Who shall live when [Col. 0496C] God does these things? They shall come in triremes from Italy, overcome the Assyrians, lay waste the Hebrews, and at last perish themselves also.’” We see that this too has been fulfilled. For we know that the Romans were brought over the sea in ships and subjected these and many other nations to their empire. I would say that they have now perished, if I did not think that they are yet to perish more grievously.

## CHAPTER XXV

“Now Israel was dwelling at that time in Shittim [Note: [Col. 0495D] Mazocchi has *Cethim* in the same cited place, where he teaches in what region these Cethites lived—the people who migrated to Italy before Mosaic times, etc.]. And the people committed fornication with the daughters of Moab, who invited them to their sacrifices. They ate and worshiped their gods. And they were initiated into Baal-peor; and the angry Lord said [Col. 0496D] to Moses: ‘Take all the leaders of the people and hang them on gibbets before the sun, that my wrath may be turned away from Israel.’ And Moses said to the judges of Israel: ‘Let each man kill his neighbors who were initiated into Baal-peor.’”

For the Lord commands one thing, while Moses appears to do another. The Lord commanded Moses to hang all the leaders of the people on gibbets before the sun. Perhaps, however, what the Lord commands and what Moses does signify the same thing. For he seems to me to endure a great gibbet and a punishment almost intolerable who openly and knowingly kills his brother or son. For what else does “before the sun” mean except openly and manifestly? They would not have been afflicted by so great a grief if they had done this at night or unknowingly. If anyone understands this otherwise, I do not contend with him. There a multitude of twenty-three thousand people was killed. And then indeed “Phinehas stood and made atonement, and the plague ceased” (Ps. 106:30), by killing the fornicators, namely Zimri son of Salu and Cozbi daughter of Zur. Let us also kill the spirit of fornication: both by living chastely within ourselves and by giving good counsel to others, so that we may be able to appease God’s wrath. If priests do this, it will be reckoned to them as righteousness forever.

## CHAPTER XXVI

After this Moses, at the Lord’s command, laid his hands upon Joshua’s head before Eleazar the priest [Col. 0497B] and the whole multitude. Rehearsing all that the Lord had commanded, he gave him a share of his glory and appointed him leader of the people in his place. This too the Lord Christ is recorded to have done: before ascending to heaven, he appointed the apostles as his deputies and as leaders of the whole Church. Giving them also a share in his glory, he commanded them to perform signs and miracles in his name (Mark 16:17). As though having Christ’s hands upon their heads, they remained secure from every assault of power and every onset of adversity.

## CHAPTER XXVII

The exposition of this chapter, in which Joshua is chosen and appointed head of the people, is absent from the edition and is not found in the manuscript codices.

## CHAPTER XXVIII

[Col. 0497C] “And the Lord said to Moses: ‘These are the sacrifices which you must offer: two unblemished year-old lambs every day as a perpetual burnt offering; you shall offer one in the morning and the other at evening; a tenth part of an ephah of fine flour mixed with the purest oil, containing a fourth part of a hin; and you shall pour out a fourth part of wine for each lamb in the sanctuary, and you shall offer the other lamb in the same way at evening.’”

For what do we understand by the two lambs except the two Testaments, in which every sacrifice of praise and rejoicing is most fully contained? The Church offers them morning and evening—indeed, seven times a day—according to the saying: “Seven times in the day I have given praise to you” (Ps. 119:164). Yet by morning and evening, which are the [Col. 0497D] limits of the day, the whole day may most properly be understood. To these two lambs there is added a tenth part of fine flour, and a fourth part of wine and oil, because the one is contained in ten words and the other in four Gospels. Therefore the same thing is signified by the lambs as is understood by the tenth and the fourth: these are Testaments and lambs, because they harm no one and teach all to live innocently; they are also fine flour by which the soul is nourished, oil by which it is healed, and wine by which it is intoxicated. Rightly, then, such a sacrifice is commanded to be made morning and evening—that is, throughout the whole day—so that God may be praised without interruption, the people may be called to the lamb’s innocence, the soul may be satisfied with heavenly [p. 191] bread, the mind may be healed by the oil of the Holy Spirit with which it is anointed, and may be intoxicated by drinking the cup of the Gospel. And because praise is not precious in the mouth of a sinner, such a sacrifice is commanded to be made in the sanctuary—that is, in the assembly of the faithful. It follows:

“But on the Sabbath day you shall offer two unblemished year-old lambs and two tenths of fine flour mixed with oil as a sacrifice,” and the rest, as above. This sacrifice is the same as that described above. To offer two tenths is to understand the Law. It is sprinkled with oil if it is tempered by mercy; and it is tempered if it is understood spiritually, for the letter kills.

“But at the Kalends, that is, at the beginnings of the months, you shall offer a burnt offering to the Lord: two calves from the herd, one ram, seven unblemished year-old lambs, and three tenths of fine flour [Col. 0498B] mixed with oil for each calf, two tenths of fine flour mixed with oil for each ram, and a tenth of a tenth of fine flour, etc. … A goat also shall be offered to the Lord for sin, together with its libations, as a perpetual burnt offering.”

Of this sacrifice and of these calves the Apostle says: “Through him therefore let us always offer to God a sacrifice of praise, that is, calves of lips confessing his name” (Heb. 15:15). Let this sacrifice of praise, therefore, and the two calves of lips be understood as the two Testaments, without which we do not know how to move our lips in offering praise. Let us also offer one ram: let us preach Christ’s passion, who, like a sheep led to slaughter, did not open his mouth.

To this ram let us join seven lambs, that is, [Col. 0498C] the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit; we must be and remain always in him. We have often already said what is understood by the tenth. For he himself is the tenth drachma; he himself is the hundredth sheep; hence he may be called not only a tenth, but also a tenth of a tenth. For if you wished to give a tenth from one hundred sheep, you would give ten: for ten times ten makes one hundred. But the hundredth sheep is the tenth sheep of this tenth; therefore man is a tenth of a tenth. That man is called fine flour, hear the Apostle: “Purge out the old leaven, that you may be a new dough, as you are unleavened” (1 Cor. 5:7). For *conspersio* (“dough”) is used for flour. To what, after all, is leaven added but flour? What is called unleavened but bread? But whence comes bread, if not from fine flour? Therefore fine flour is man. This fine flour [Col. 0498D] is sprinkled with oil, because by God’s mercy and the grace of the Holy Spirit man is anointed, healed, and renewed.

Therefore from this fine flour—that is, from human beings—let us give three tenths for each calf, two for the ram, and a tenth of a tenth for each lamb. All signify one and the same thing. For every human being is what the two peoples are, what the three parts of the world are. Since, therefore, all are converted through the two Testaments and all are redeemed through Christ’s passion, rightly three tenths follow the calf, two the ram, and a tenth of a tenth the lamb. But why are all these things moistened with wine, unless that they may be made sweet by the flavor of spiritual understanding? For otherwise they seem tasteless and irrational. Therefore, that they may have flavor, let them be moistened by the fragrance [Col. 0499A] of spiritual exposition. But because exposition itself should also be proportionate, more wine is assigned to the calves and more to the ram than to each individual lamb. The chief and principal reason why Christ is sacrificed in the goat is that he was condemned as ungodly and crucified with thieves as though a criminal. Him whom we venerate in the lamb, the Jews abhor in the goat. Likewise, at Passover and Pentecost, and on the first and tenth day of the seventh month, he commands sacrifice. Let this, then, be the one exposition of them all.

## CHAPTER XXIX

“But on the fifteenth day of the seventh month, which shall be holy and venerable to you, you shall do no servile work on it, but shall celebrate a festival of the Lord for seven days; and you shall offer as a burnt offering of sweetest fragrance to the Lord thirteen calves from the herd, two rams, fourteen unblemished year-old lambs, and, for their libations, fine flour mixed with oil: three tenths for each calf—thirteen calves in all—and two tenths for one ram, that is, for the two rams together; and a tenth of a tenth for each lamb—fourteen lambs in all—and a goat for sin.”

What is signified by the seventh month and its first, tenth, and fifth day, why no servile work is to be done in it, and why this festival is celebrated for seven days, we have explained in Leviticus. Now let us consider the sacrifices which, in [Col. 0499C] this festival, were made without variation and in one and the same manner for seven days—except only that one calf was reduced from the number on each day. For thirteen were offered on the first day, twelve on the second, eleven on the third, and so on through the rest, until the seventh day, when only seven were offered. But what do the calves signify except the apostles? Unless they were thirteen, either Paul or Matthias would have no place among them. By these calves the entire Church was both ploughed and sown. The two rams and fourteen lambs signify the same thing. For they signify the two Testaments, which are contained in the four Gospels and the ten words. Thus they are both two and fourteen, because fourteen is made from four and ten. Likewise, the three tenths, the two tenths, and [Col. 0499D] the tenth of a tenth signify the same thing. In them every human being is signified; from this are made two and three tenths, because humanity is divided into two peoples and three parts of the world. Rightly, therefore, these tenths are joined to calves, [p. 192] rams, and lambs, so that every human being, of whatever nation and in whatever part of the world he lives, may follow and hold the faith and teaching of the holy apostles and the two Testaments. Thus the high priests offered the apostles in the calves, the Testaments in the rams and lambs, and the whole Church, spread everywhere, [Col. 0500A] in the tenths. We have spoken of these just above.

That one calf is taken away from the number each day perhaps signifies the death of the apostles, whose number, as one after another departed from this world, was in some sense reduced daily. But the rams, lambs, and tenths neither increase nor decrease, because there are always two Testaments, four Gospels, ten words of the Law, and one Church, composed from Asia, Africa, and Europe, from Jews and Gentiles.

“On the eighth day, which is most solemn, you shall do no servile work on it. You shall offer on it a burnt offering of sweetest fragrance to the Lord: one calf, one ram, and seven unblemished year-old [Col. 0500B] lambs; and you shall duly perform its sacrifices and libations for the calf, ram, and lambs individually, and a goat for sin.”

The eighth day is the same as the first; it is also called the Lord’s Day, and every Christian observes and venerates it with the greatest solemnity. On this day the world began; on this day Christ rose from the dead; and on this day too the final resurrection will occur. Hence certain psalms are entitled “for the eighth.” On this day, therefore, the whole Church more earnestly than on other days offers to the Lord a burnt offering and a sacrifice of praise, namely by praising and preaching Christ; for this is signified by the calf, the ram, and the seven lambs. Since what follows has been repeated very often, we pass it over.

## CHAPTER XXX

[Col. 0500C] “Moses reported to the children of Israel all that the Lord had commanded him. And he spoke to the leaders of the tribes of the children of Israel: ‘This is the word which the Lord has commanded: If any one of you makes a vow to the Lord, or binds himself by an oath, he shall not make his word void, but shall fulfill everything that he has promised.’”

Every vow made with an oath which is good and is not made contrary to justice must be paid. Therefore the leaders of the Church, to whom these words are addressed, ought to fulfill whatever they have vowed or sworn, because they must be so cautious both in vowing and in swearing that they swear or vow nothing contrary to justice. Hence it is added that if a girl living in her father’s house, or a man’s wife, makes a vow or oath, and her father or [Col. 0500D] husband hears it without objecting, she will be bound and must fulfill whatever she promised; but if he objects upon hearing it, she will not be bound by the oath. These fathers and husbands appear to be the leaders of the Church, whose individual wives and daughters they are. They are wives because they give birth from their seed; daughters because they are regenerated through their ministry. It belongs to these, therefore, to discern vows and judge oaths. No one, then, should presume to do whatever the teachers of the Church forbid, even if someone knows such things [Note: [Col. 0499D] Since the divine command concerning the obligation of a vow made to God is so clear, the shamelessness of certain flattering writers is detestable. In these [Col. 0500D] days they have not been ashamed to teach that secular rulers can dissolve even solemn religious vows, and consequently—horrible to say—they have opened the door for consecrated virgins [Col. 0501D] to incestuous and sacrilegious marriages.]. For unjust vows must be void.

[Col. 0501A] But the vows or oaths which these persons either approve by consent or confirm by their words must necessarily be fulfilled. Why is this so? Because whatever they say is just. Thus it comes about that every person must discharge just vows and holy promises, because there is no one to forbid their discharge and fulfillment; but all unjust vows become void. Nevertheless, anyone who knowingly swears contrary to justice, although he is not bound by an oath that the holy persons forbid, should not suppose himself thereby immediately free from sin. He ought not to have sworn what he knew to be sinful. Let him therefore repent—not because he does not carry out the oath, but because he knowingly swore contrary to justice.

“A widow and a divorced woman shall fulfill whatever they have vowed.” What if they have vowed wrongly? Evil vows must not be fulfilled; therefore let it be said: whatever good thing they have vowed. Since they are at their own disposal and are not subject to anyone’s authority, they may freely vow what they wish. Yet by them we may understand those souls which, separated from this world’s embraces and pleasures, are rejected by foolish people and held in contempt. But because such souls are wise and desire to do only good, whatever they choose to vow should be left to their judgment. If, however, a wife binds herself by a vow or oath to afflict her soul by fasting or some other abstinence, then, unless her husband forbids this immediately upon hearing it, she must fulfill it. This appears to signify only that the life of subordinates ought to be regulated by the judgment of their superiors. If superiors give assent to those making some good vow, [Col. 0501C] they can no longer recall them without danger.

## CHAPTER XXXI

There follows the account of the Midianites. The children of Israel, fighting against them at the Lord’s command, defeated them and killed them all, including Balaam and their five leaders; [p. 193] none of them remained except virgins alone. The children of Israel spared these, and they remained with them outside the camp for seven days, according to what Moses had commanded them. By these virgins, as also by the other nations opposing God’s people, we ought to understand the army of demons and the multitude of vices. But what do we understand by the five leaders except the five senses of our body? By these the aforesaid enemies come against us; by these they raise civil wars against us, attack us with our own weapons, and compel us to fight against ourselves. If, therefore, we first conquer these and kill them according to their former condition, the entire multitude of vices will suddenly collapse within us. By the virgins whom the children of Israel preserve for themselves we understand those souls which, fleeing the devil’s corruption, transfer themselves to faith in Christ and fellowship with the Church, and please God’s people because of their beauty. With these they naturally remain for seven days outside the camp, because both those who are converted from paganism to God and those through whom they are converted [Col. 0502A] remain outside the Synagogue at all times. Hence it is not said here, as before, that after seven days they return to the camp; for seven days signify all time.

“Whoever has killed a person or touched one who has been killed shall be purified on the third and seventh day. And from all the spoil—whether garment, vessel, or any implement prepared from goat skins, hair, or wood—there shall be purification.” The Jews are murderers. Everyone born from Adam has also touched one who was killed, to whom it had been said: “On whatever day you eat from this tree, you shall die by death.” Therefore, that they may be saved, they are set free on the third and seventh day, as are the other things that came from all the spoil and were snatched from the devil—whether a vessel, garment, or anything else made from goat skins, hair, or wood and prepared for some use. By these we may understand not only human beings, but also their faith, knowledge, life, morals, entire conduct, and all the furnishings of the inward person. All are purified together with the person himself.

“Gold and silver, bronze and iron, tin and lead, and everything that can pass through flames shall be purified by fire. But whatever cannot endure fire shall be sanctified by water of expiation; and you shall wash your garments on the seventh day, and, purified afterward, shall enter the camp.” By gold, silver, and the other things that can endure fire we understand those to whom God has given strength to be purified by the fire of suffering and martyrdom, although they have not been sanctified by the water of baptism. These, indeed, on the seventh day—that is, in this final age—wash their garments, their flesh, in the sacred font; and, purified, they enter not only the camp of the Church but also that of heaven.

## CHAPTER XXXII

The chapter is omitted in which, according to the Vulgate, the children of Israel fit for battle promise Moses that, leaving behind their women, little children, and herds, they will go out against their enemies to obtain the land of promise.

## CHAPTER XXXIII

Here Moses describes the forty stations which the people made until they came to the land [Col. 0502D] of promise. If anyone wished to treat these according to the interpretation of their names and the events enacted in them, he could extend the discussion at length [Note: [Col. 0502D] St Maximus of Turin treats of these in Homily 41, *On the Forty Stations*, vol. V, p. 122, Roman edition, 1784.]. But let us say a few things about the number. For forty consists of four and ten—for four times ten, or ten times four, makes forty. As we have often said, ten and four signify the Old and New Testaments, since the former is contained in ten words and the latter in four Gospels. Therefore, as they passed through forty stations to the land of promise, so we too, passing through the ten commandments of the Law and the four Gospels, under the leadership of Jesus, shall enter the land [Col. 0503A] of the living.

Blessed are those who remain and dwell in these stations. Blessed are those who delight in the sacred books of both Testaments: they always abound in manna, never lack heavenly bread, and never lack the living bread that came down from heaven. They are nourished with spiritual food; they are refreshed with water from the rock; the grace of the Holy Spirit shades them by day and enlightens them by night. They can truly say: “The Lord guides me, and I shall lack nothing; he has placed me in a place of pasture” (Ps. 23:1). They are blessed, therefore, if they do not murmur, do not test God, do not waver in faith, do not seek flesh—that is, if they do not understand the Law carnally—and do not desire onions and garlic.

But because Ramesses is interpreted “moth,” whenever we shake from ourselves the moths of vices by repentance or by any other means, let us understand that we are departing from Ramesses. Then, after vices have been overcome and the gods of Egypt have been broken, we can confidently celebrate the Passover. Since Sochoth is interpreted “tabernacles,” when we live religiously in the council and congregation of the righteous, let us know that we are in Sochoth. Since Ethan means “perfected,” whenever we complete some good work, let us rejoice that we are [p. 194] in Ethan. But because Athairoth is interpreted “crown,” as often as we triumph over some vice, so often do we encamp in Athairoth. We pitch our tents before Magdalum when we storm the towers and fortifications of the devil, for this is the meaning of Magdalum. We are in Marah if we are made bitter by the remembrance of sins [Col. 0503C] or the adversities of the world, since Marah means “bitter.” Since Elim means “ram,” we dwell in Elim when we imitate the innocence and simplicity of the apostles. Thus it is rightly said that there were twelve springs and seventy palm trees in Elim, through which the twelve apostles and the seventy-two disciples of Christ are figured. But when we invite the people to baptism and faith, we pitch tents beside the Red Sea, for they too were baptized both in the cloud and in the sea.

But let us come into the wilderness of Sin; let us approach the service of God and prepare our souls for temptation. For Sin is interpreted “temptation.” By this we shall afterward be able to pass into Dethaca, [Col. 0503D] which is interpreted “forgiveness”; for sins are forgiven to those who overcome diabolical temptations. Whenever we ferment anything and relax both hands and works toward corruption, let us grieve that we are in Alis and Raphidim. For Alis is called “to ferment,” while Raphidim means “to relax the hands.” Thus it is rightly read that water failed the people there: a people is easily corrupted and sins if it lacks the water of Gospel teaching. And then we in some manner receive the Law on Sinai when we exercise ourselves in the sacred volumes. But when we desire unlawful things, we hasten to Aseroth, the house of straits, for such is its interpretation. Thus, once the history and interpretation of the names are known, the prudent reader will readily discover the significance of each. We would indeed explain them individually, [Col. 0504A] were it not that they are easy and we are intent on brevity.

## CHAPTER XXXIV

The chapter in which the boundaries and dimensions of the land of promise are described is omitted.

## CHAPTER XXXV

“And the Lord said to Moses: ‘Command the children of Israel to give the Levites, from their own possessions, cities in which to dwell, and pasturelands around them, so that they may live in the towns, while the pasturelands may serve their cattle and beasts. These shall extend outward from the city walls all around for a thousand paces eastward, and there shall be the same two toward the south.’”

This very plainly shows that the clerical order ought to hold a higher position in the Church and rule over all others as though over its own beasts and cattle; hence they are rightly called shepherds. That the pasturelands extend for a space of a thousand paces shows that the whole compass of the world is subject to their governance and authority. For “a thousand” signifies the same as “all,” since this number is perfect and contains all numbers within itself, which can indeed be repeated within it but cannot increase it. It should be noted, moreover, that two thousand cubits are contained in a thousand paces; it is therefore established that two cubits make one pace.

“And the Lord said to Moses: ‘When you cross the Jordan and enter the land of Canaan, destroy all its inhabitants and break their images, cleansing the land.’” Therefore, we who come through [Col. 0504C] baptism to the Church should cleanse the land—that is, our flesh—from every stain of vice, and worship and adore the one true God.

“And the Lord said to Moses: Speak to the children of Israel, and say to them: When you have crossed the Jordan into the land of Canaan, designate which cities are to serve as refuges for fugitives who have shed blood unintentionally. When the fugitive has fled into them, the kinsman of the slain man shall not be able to kill him, until he stands before the assembly and his case is judged. Of the cities set apart as aid for fugitives, three shall be beyond the Jordan and three in the land of Canaan, [Col. 0504D] for the children of Israel, for resident aliens, and for sojourners alike, so that anyone who has shed blood unintentionally may flee to them. But if anyone kills a man with iron, stone, wood, or his hand, through hatred or ambush, the kinsman of the slain man shall cut his throat as soon as he finds him. But if he has done this by chance, and without hatred or enmity, then, before it is proved to have been so, the innocent man shall be released and shall not be killed; rather, he shall be returned to the city to which he fled, and shall remain there until the death of the high priest who has been anointed with holy oil.”

The three cities beyond the Jordan and the three in the land of Canaan signify the same thing; faith, hope, and charity may be understood by them. For no one can ever be secure who has not founded his house in these cities. Whoever flees to [Col. 0505A] them, moreover, shall not be killed. For if we understand the letter absolutely, so that those who kill a man voluntarily—or, what is worse, through hatred or ambush—have no help of flight in these cities, then (which it is wicked to say) we close the gates of repentance. Therefore it must be understood otherwise.

For by killers of bodies we often understand killers of souls. The killers of souls are chiefly understood to be Jews and heretics, who, by false persuasion, separate souls from faith in Christ and kill them. Among these, let us understand as sinning voluntarily, through hatred, and by ambush, those who sin in such a way that they never repent of having sinned, and never cease to will the evil which they began to will. For no one is so voluntary as the man whose will does not change. Others, however, although they sinned voluntarily, yet because they are now unwilling and repentant, let us say that they shed blood unwillingly. Thus he shed blood voluntarily who persists in the will to shed blood. Therefore, if anyone has shed blood voluntarily—that is, if he has not withdrawn from the will of shedding blood—let him die. But he who shed blood unwillingly—that is, who is now repentant and wishes that he had not shed it—let him flee to these cities, and he shall be saved. For if he receives the faith of the Church, possesses the hope of the Church, and holds the charity of the Church, he shall not die.

[Col. 0506A] But if the kinsman of the slain man finds him outside these cities, he shall immediately cut his throat. Read in the Gospel concerning the Samaritan to learn who this kinsman is, and you will find that he is Christ, who will indeed kill those whom he finds outside these cities and condemn them to eternal death. That this killer does not return to his own home until the high priest dies seems to signify, through Moses, that before Christ’s Passion no one returned to the heavenly homeland after completing repentance. Likewise, any Jews and heretics who believe that Jesus, the high priest, has not yet come, or has not died, or has not risen again, cannot return to their homeland; for Christ has not yet died for them in this sense—just as he had not yet ascended to the Father for Mary when he said: “Do not touch me, [Col. 0506B] for I have not yet ascended to my Father” (John 20:17).

But Christ has now died for us; we have now been redeemed by his death and blood. May he himself grant us to return to what is our own and, from the exile of this world, to enter the holy city Jerusalem—to him be glory and honor with the Father and the Holy Spirit, unto ages of ages. Amen.

## CHAPTER XXXVI

This final chapter of the book of Numbers, in which the children of Israel are commanded that each should take a wife from his own tribe and not pass to another, lest the tribes be confused, is omitted by Saint Bruno.

Here ends the book of Numbers.

# HERE BEGINS THE EXPOSITION OF DEUTERONOMY

[Col. 0505]

## PREFACE

[Col. 0505C]

196 Since in the other books of Moses we have spoken of what the Lord gave, it remains for us now also to speak, in this final book, of what he himself may grant. This book is called *Deuteronomy*, which is interpreted “second law,” because it signifies the New Testament as well, and the things said in the other books are in some way renewed and repeated in this one. Passing over, then, the matters expounded in the preceding books, let us undertake, with God’s help, to expound the remaining matters—not all of them, but the more difficult ones. Let us begin our exposition from this chapter.

## CHAPTER XIII

“If you hear in one of your cities, which the Lord your God will give you to inhabit, [Col. 0505D] certain persons saying: ‘The sons of Belial have gone out from among you and have turned away the inhabitants of your city in your land, saying: Let us go and serve foreign gods,’ inquire diligently, and, having carefully examined the truth of the matter, if you find that what is said is certain and that this abomination has actually been perpetrated, you shall immediately strike the inhabitants of that city with the edge of the sword and destroy [Col. 0506C] it. You shall also gather in the middle of its streets everything that is in it, and burn it, together with the city itself, so that you consume all things for the Lord your God. It shall be an everlasting mound; it shall not be built again, and nothing from that accursed thing shall cling to your hand.”

“If you hear,” he says, wherever you may be, from someone reporting to you that sons of Belial—that is, heretics, who are not held under the yoke of faith (for *Belial* is interpreted “without yoke”)—have gone out from among you and abandoned the faith of the Church, turning others with them away from righteousness and declaring foreign gods, that is, evil spirits, to be secure, inquire diligently into the matter. Once you have learned it to be true, you shall strike and destroy that entire wicked congregation with the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God. [Col. 0506D] Moreover, you shall burn with it, in its midst, all things belonging to it; that is, you shall condemn them to eternal punishments. For together with heretics, all their perverse knowledge and teaching—understood through their possessions—must be abhorred and condemned, so that it may be destroyed in such a way that it is no longer remembered. This is what he says: “It shall not be built [Col. 0507A] again, and nothing from that accursed thing shall cling to your hand.” By this you must understand that nothing from that heresy should cling to your mind and faith. It follows:

## CHAPTER XIV

“Be children of the Lord your God. You shall not cut yourselves or make baldness over the dead, because you are a holy people to the Lord your God, and he chose you to be his special people from all the nations that are upon the earth.”

Whoever wishes to belong to God should imitate God. For it is fitting that children display in themselves the image of their parents. Cutting oneself and making baldness over the dead are signs of great grief. Yet the Christian ought not to grieve, but rejoice, over the dead. For one who dies well is going to God. Therefore you grieve, woman, because your husband is going to God; you grieve, man, because your brother or son is going to God: you do not grieve rightly. Let us also see what the Apostle says: “You have died, and your life is hidden with Christ in God” (Col. 3:3). For these persons, while still living, were dead to this world.

And we often see brothers and relatives grieving over those who are dead, or even over those who desire to die in this manner; such people too do not grieve rightly over the dead. Nor does the person grieve rightly who grieves over a wicked dead person. For one ought not to grieve but rejoice at the destruction of the evil; rather, one ought to have grieved over his life, which was contrary to righteousness and goodness. Nevertheless, while such persons are alive, the saints ought both to grieve and weep for them, in the hope that they may perhaps be converted through their prayers. Thus Samuel also wept for Saul. But after [Col. 0507C] death it is fruitless to weep for them. Finally, when the Lord says: “I too will laugh at your destruction” (Prov. 1:26), who would dare grieve for one at whom the Lord laughs and rejoices? Therefore one should grieve over no dead person except the one who dies to faith and is separated from God. There follows the passage concerning clean and unclean animals, of which we have spoken sufficiently in Leviticus.

197 “Eat everything that is clean; but do not eat anything that has died of itself. Give it to the resident alien within your gates to eat, or sell it to him, because you are a holy people of the Lord your God.”

Those who observed this according to the letter will be saved, and thus through that shadow [Col. 0507D] they were the people of God, just as we now are through the truth. For according to apostolic teaching, we judge nothing unclean or common (1 Cor. 10:15). Whatever comes from the market, we eat, questioning for conscience’ sake. We also know that God is no respecter of persons (Acts 10:34). We separate no one coming to the faith from the body of the Church. The Church receives every food—that is, it brings every human being into its body.

Therefore we are the resident aliens; we buy and eat unclean things from the Jews. For the apostles were Jews, and they taught us not to believe that anything is common or unclean. They have now sold us the faith; we bought it at the price of our souls, and for it we became servants of Christ. Indeed, just as we now perish unless we eat all things, so they would then have perished if they had eaten them. For he eats all things who declares all things fit to be eaten.

“You shall not boil a kid in its mother’s milk.”

This is said to those who wished to kill Christ while he was still nursing and a child. We expounded this in Exodus.

“In the third year you shall separate another tenth from all that is born to you at that time, and you shall store it within your gates. The Levite, who has no other share or possession with you, and the resident alien, orphan, and widow, because they are within your gates, shall come and eat and be satisfied, so that the Lord your God may bless you in all the works of your hands which you do.”

Moses spoke much in the preceding books about tithes; but now he introduces another tenth, which seems far more worthy than the others. By this, I think, the spiritual understanding of the Law is signified. For there are ten words of the Law, which the Jews at first understood and observed according to the letter, giving one tenth. But when the third year arrives—that is, the third age of the world—another tenth is now given, in which the same ten words are understood spiritually.

For there are three times: the first before the Law; the second under the Law; the third under grace. This third time, which is now in progress, began from Christ’s birth. Therefore, in this third year, or third time, the teachers of the Church have stored this tenth in the storehouse of their heart. It is well said, moreover, “from all that is born at that time,” because even if the letter had been born earlier, the spiritual understanding of the letter was born in this time. The Levites live from this tenth; the order of clerics lives from this tenth; all who delight in spiritual food eat and are satisfied from this tenth. Resident aliens—that is, Gentiles coming to the faith—receive it; so do orphans and widows who abandon the most wicked father and husband, the devil. Let there then be two tithes: two understandings of the commandments.

## CHAPTER XV

“In the seventh year you shall make a remission, which shall be observed in this manner. Whoever is owed something by friend, neighbor, or brother may not demand it back, because it is the Lord’s year of remission. You shall exact it from a foreigner and stranger; but you have no power to demand it back from a fellow citizen or kinsman; and there shall be no needy or beggar at all among you.”

The seventh day and seventh year, as we have already expounded in other books, signify this last age, of which the Apostle says: “We are those upon whom the ends of the ages have come” (1 Cor. 10:11). In this last age we ought to grant remission, as the Lord says: “Forgive, and you shall be forgiven” (Luke 6:37). And again: “Unless you forgive people their sins, neither will your heavenly Father forgive you your sins” (Matt. 18:35). These, therefore, are the debts which we ought not to reclaim from our neighbor or from citizens of the Church, but forgive.

But in allowing us to reclaim them from a newcomer and stranger, he signifies that this remission does not avail the condemned and unbelieving; whether you forgive or do not forgive, he will nevertheless perish. What did it profit the Jews persisting in unbelief that the Lord said: “Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing” (Luke 23:34)? The debt, therefore, is exacted from them, since it is not forgiven. In saying, however, “There shall be no needy or beggar at all among you,” he seems to urge us toward generosity in almsgiving. It follows:

“You shall lend to many nations, and you yourself shall receive a loan from no one; you shall rule many nations, and no one shall rule you.”
