The Church has not lent from its spiritual riches, for there is no nation to which it has not preached its faith. And when all nations have received its faith, it has received the faith of no nation; and it shall at last rule over all, while no one except God shall rule over it.

“When your Hebrew brother or Hebrew sister has been sold to you and has served you for six years, in the seventh year you shall dismiss him free. And when you grant him freedom, you shall by no means allow him to depart empty-handed, but shall give him provisions from your flocks, threshing floor, and winepress, with which the Lord your God has blessed you. But if he says, ‘I do not wish to go out, because he loves you and your house, and finds himself well treated with you,’ you shall take an awl and pierce his ear at the door of your house, and he shall serve you forever. You shall do likewise to the maidservant. Do not turn your eyes away from them when you dismiss them free, [Col. 0509C] 198 because for six years he served you at the wage of a hired laborer.”

Since *Hebrew* is interpreted “one who passes over,” every person who passes from unbelief to the Church may be understood as a Hebrew. The teachers of the Church purchase these people for the Lord at a price. The six years mean the same as the six days; for there are only six days on which servile work may be done. Thus whoever serves for six years does not depart from service.

But it should be known that among God’s servants some serve voluntarily and find their service pleasing, whereas others serve unwillingly and find service burdensome. We see many such people in the Church, who do no good service voluntarily; nevertheless, they serve either from shame or fear. In the seventh year—that is, when their life’s course is completed—the Church allows them to depart free, serving no longer in any service; but it would have been better for them to continue serving than to depart free with such freedom.

See how good the Lord is: he does not even permit these evil and ungrateful servants to go away empty, but gives them provisions from the flocks, threshing floor, and winepress. For he understands this mystery and understands this name, nor is he ignorant of what “provisions for the journey” signifies. Hence he persuades even those repenting at the final hour to receive this provision, by which they may be borne safely throughout their whole life up to the judge’s seat. This provision is Christ’s body and blood. It was formerly received from flocks, but is now received from the threshing floor and winepress. Who does not understand this? Who does not know what the lamb signifies which was sacrificed at Passover? “For Christ, our Passover, has been sacrificed” (1 Cor. 5:7). Bread is received from the threshing floor and wine from the winepress, and these are ineffably converted into Christ’s flesh and blood.

There follows the good servant who, serving most willingly, never wishes to depart from his master’s service. Why is this? Because he loves him and his house, which is the Church, and always finds himself well treated with him. Therefore the Lord brings him to the door of his house and pierces his ear, that he may serve him forever. For one who is brought to the door is seen by all who are in the house. Rightly, therefore, is the good servant brought to the door, so that all may know how faithful and obedient he is, and the rest may take a good example from him; and those whose ears have not yet been pierced may have them pierced in imitation of him. The Lord sought such ears when he said: “He who has ears to hear, let him hear” (Mark 4:23).

Thus this man, because he served for six years—that is, throughout the whole course of his life—as though a hired laborer and always awaited the reward of his labor, returned well rewarded to the freedom of the heavenly homeland. He therefore served not as a slave but as a hired laborer, since wages are not given to a slave for his labor.

There follows the passage concerning firstborn animals, which, if male and without blemish, are all commanded to be sacrificed to God. We have spoken sufficiently of these in the preceding books. But what is said here—that firstborn animals with a blemish are not to be sacrificed to the Lord, but are to be eaten by those who are clean and those who are unclean—signifies that the guilty cannot indeed be elevated to the priestly order, but ought not to be separated from the body and communion of the Church. Only this must be observed concerning them: the blood of the Jews must not be eaten, but must be poured out like water upon the ground. By this it is clearly shown that, even if we communicate with the unrighteous, we ought not to consent to the sins of the unrighteous, but must vehemently reject and abhor them.

## CHAPTER XVI

What follows concerning the three festivals which the Jews observed most solemnly is not expounded here, because we have sufficiently expounded it in the other books, especially in Leviticus.

“You shall not plant a grove or any tree beside the altar of the Lord your God, nor shall you make or set up for yourself a statue, which the Lord your God hates.”

By these words all worship of idols and every superstition of unbelievers is forbidden.

## CHAPTER XVII

In this chapter he commands that every doubtful matter and all more important cases be decided by the judgment of priests; whoever arrogantly refuses to obey their sentence shall die. In this matter he briefly indicates what kind and what degree of knowledge and justice priests ought to possess, and what obedience the people ought to show toward them.

“When you have entered the land which the Lord [Col. 0511A] your God will give you, and desire to set a king over yourself, you shall appoint him from your own nation and from among your brothers. When he has been appointed, he shall not multiply horses for himself, nor lead the people back into Egypt—especially since the Lord has commanded you not to return by the same way. Nor shall he have many wives, who might entice his heart; nor shall he have weights of gold and silver at his table. After he sits upon the throne of his kingdom, he shall write for himself a Deuteronomy of this law, receiving a copy from the priests, and shall read it all his days, doing what is written in it. Nor shall he turn aside to the right or left, that he and his sons may reign for a long time.”

[Note: [Col. 0511D] This passage has here been composed partly in sense and partly in wording from the Vulgate.]

Would that our kings understood this [Col. 0511B] chapter and, having understood it, observed it, rather than afflicting God’s Church with such great evils. This may be understood not only of secular kings, but also of the spiritual kings of the Church. We ought to choose and appoint him from our own people—from a people, of course, Christian and religious—and from our brothers, that is, from the better sons of the Church.

Therefore, once a king has been appointed, let him not multiply horses for himself, rushing into battle in their proud display and crushing the humble people. By this we may understand that he ought not to be elevated through the service and counsel of the proud. David the king understood this when he said: “Some in chariots and some in horses, but we shall be magnified in the name of our God” (Ps. 19:8). Nor should he lead the people back into Egypt by word and example, turning them toward sins. He returns by the same way who returns again to the sin he had abandoned through repentance.

Nor should he have many wives to entice his heart. Solomon, disregarding this with a deaf ear, took not only many wives but foreign wives; miserably enticed by them, he is recorded to have worshipped idols. Spiritually, many wives may be understood as many sects of religion. He is forbidden weights of gold and silver at his table, because by these he is most easily raised into contempt for God and pride.

He is commanded to write and observe this book, which runs between the new and old things, so that in accordance with the Gospel he may bring forth new and old things from his treasury. He receives the model of this faith from the priests if he keeps it according to their teaching. But he turns neither to the right nor to the left who does not depart from truth and the straight path.

## CHAPTER XVIII

“The priests and Levites, and all who are of the same tribe, shall have no share or inheritance with the rest of Israel, because they shall eat the sacrifices of the Lord and his offerings, and shall receive nothing else from the possession of their brothers; for the Lord himself is their inheritance, as he said to him.”

By this statement we are commanded to leave the world and cling to God alone; and, having received God as our share, we should seek no other [Col. 0512A] share, lest while seeking another share we lose this one, which is altogether better. Great indeed is the inheritance if we inherit him who possesses all things. Those observe this who, content with necessities alone, hold all things in common. It follows:

“This shall be the priests’ due from the people and from those who offer victims: whether they sacrifice an ox or a sheep, they shall give the priest the shoulder and stomach, the firstfruits of grain, wine, oil, and a portion of the wool from the sheep’s shearing. For the Lord your God has chosen him from among all your brothers, that he and his son may stand and minister to the name of the Lord forever.”

The priests receive the shoulder from all victims so that they may understand that they are to bear everyone’s burdens, according to what the Lord said to Aaron: “You and your sons and your father’s house shall bear the iniquity of the sanctuary.” Therefore one burdened with many loads ought to have many shoulders. But why do priests receive the stomach, unless that they may cook and digest the food of the holy Scriptures and from it feed and nourish all the members of the ecclesiastical body? For in the stomach, that is, the belly, all food is digested, by which all the members of the body are nourished.

Moreover, priests receive the firstfruits of wine, oil, and wool, so that, possessing food and clothing, they may be content with these. But what sort of men do we suppose those are to whom all firstfruits are given? Yet why are they given? Do you wish to hear why? Because they are first; because they are greater; because in all things [Col. 0512C] they hold primacy, and all things ought to be subject to them. Therefore let them sit first, walk first, and let the rest of the multitude follow them. For whoever follows them does not walk in darkness, but will have the light of life.

“And the Lord said to Moses: I will raise up for them a prophet from among your brothers like you, and I will put my words in his mouth, and he shall speak to them all that I command him. But whoever refuses to hear his words, which he will speak in my name, I shall be the avenger.”

God gave many prophets to this people. Although they announced God’s commands and the way of life to them, and were like Moses in speech and miracles, they not only did not believe them, but, as the Lord says, stoned some, killed others, and subjected others to insults. This may also be understood particularly of that prophet who speaks of himself, saying: “A prophet is not without honor except in his own country and in his own house” (Mark 6:5), and so forth. The Father God not only raised him up, but raised him from the dead. He is like Moses, yet a prophet greater than Moses and Moses’ Lord. Signifying that he spoke his Father’s words, he said: “My teaching is not mine, but that of the Father who sent me” (John 7:16).

## CHAPTER XIX

There follows the passage concerning the three cities of refuge, which he commands to be divided among themselves at equal distances, so that the man who has fled because of homicide may have one nearby to which he can escape.

“This shall be the law concerning the fugitive killer whose life is to be preserved: one who strikes his neighbor unknowingly, and who is proved to have had no hatred against him yesterday or the day [Col. 0513A] before yesterday, but who went with him simply into the forest to cut wood, and while cutting wood the axe flew from his hand, and the iron slipped from its handle, struck his companion, and killed him—this man shall flee to one of the aforesaid cities and live, lest perhaps the kinsman of the man whose blood was shed, prompted by grief, pursue and seize him, if the way is too long, and strike down the life of one who is not guilty of death, because it is shown that he previously had no hatred against him.”

[Note: [Col. 0513] Manuscript of the library of Monte Amiata: “Because he is proved to have had no hatred against him, and in the cutting-down of liquors (*liquorum*; reading uncertain).”]

These three cities, as we expounded in the book of Numbers, signify faith, hope, and charity. They are divided from one another by equal distance because they come equally and together to meet those who are to be saved. The forest in which wood is cut may signify these and the other Scriptures of divine law. In this forest we cut wood simply when, with faithful intention, we set out individual statements.

It sometimes happens, however, that while speaking of these matters, we strike and kill something less fit for understanding, as though iron had slipped from the handle. The axe escapes the hand and iron slips from the handle when the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God, is uttered incautiously. Therefore those who cut wood in this forest in the presence of their brothers ought both to be skilled in cutting and to be able to hold fast the iron—the word of God—lest perhaps they say something contrary to faith or something which, because of its obscurity, produces scandal. Even those skilled in cutting this wood should not cut everything before everyone; some things ought to be expounded only in an assembly of the wise.

Therefore, if someone has struck a brother in this way and has refuge in one of the aforesaid cities, he shall not be killed. For he has refuge in the city of faith if his own conscience defends him: that he spoke unknowingly against the faith, and that he did not say it in order to turn anyone from the Catholic faith through hatred. For Jews and heretics do this; and for as long as they remain in this hatred, they have no refuge in these cities. The same is to be understood concerning [Col. 0513D] hope and charity.

The kinsman of the slain person is Christ, who is signified by the Samaritan in the Gospel. He himself kills those killers whom he finds far from the aforesaid cities. We spoke of this chapter at the end of the preceding book.

“You shall not take up and transfer your neighbor’s boundaries, which the ancients established in their possession.”

I do not know what possession we can better understand here than our faith and evangelical teaching. Whoever attempts to transfer its boundaries and strives to move them otherwise than they were established by the holy Fathers becomes liable to eternal condemnation.

## CHAPTER XX

[Col. 0514A]

Moses next exhorts the people that, whenever they go out to battle against their adversaries and see their army to be greater, they should not fear, because God is with them. As battle approaches, the priests are to stir up and strengthen the people. The officers too are to proclaim through the several companies, with the army listening:

“Who is the man who has built a new house and has not dedicated it? Let him go and return to his house, lest perhaps he die in battle and another man perform its office. Who is the man who has betrothed a wife and has not taken her? Let him go and return to his house, lest perhaps he die in battle and another man take her.”

After saying these things, they shall add the rest and speak to the people: “Who is a fearful man and faint of heart? Let him return to his house, lest he make the hearts of his brothers afraid, just as he himself is terrified by fear.” When the officers of the army have fallen silent and finished speaking, each shall prepare all his own men for battle.

These matters suit the beginning and end of the Church; they are most properly referred to times of tyrants, in which the small body of Christians fought and will fight against the innumerable army of persecutors. Moses therefore teaches how the leaders of the Church should instruct their soldiers at that time. He also exhorts the brave not to fear, and, so that they may rush confidently against the enemy, not to trust in their own strength but in God’s power: God remains in them, fights, and conquers. For he strengthened not only men, [Col. 0514C] but also virgins and women with such courage that they conquered impious emperors and overcame the invincible army of the Romans.

But what should we understand by the man who has built a new house and has not yet dedicated it, if not a Christian who, although in baptism he has put off the old man and has become new, and has already received God as an indweller in his house—that is, in himself, who is called a temple of God by the Apostle—has not yet attained that perfection by which he loves another as himself and utterly despises the world? For the person who has attained this has wholly dedicated himself anew to the Lord. But whoever lacks this is not yet fit to provoke the swords of tyrants against himself and go toward martyrdom.

Therefore let him return to [Col. 0514D] his house, remain within himself, hold the faith in secret, and be at least a good confessor, though he did not merit to be a martyr. For it is better for him to remain thus than to die in battle—to die, I say, not in body, 201 but in soul. For if he died in body, he would be a martyr. Therefore the one who denies God through fear dies in battle according to the soul.

The same should be understood of the man who has betrothed a wife and has not yet taken her. He has betrothed a wife who has promised Christian religion by faith, for offspring of good works is generated with this wife. Yet, though he has betrothed her, he has not yet taken her because he has not yet attained the perfection of faith and religion. The perfection in question is to despise the world and to love God and neighbor with one’s whole heart. Therefore both this man and the former should return to their house, lest perhaps they die in battle and another man take both the former man’s house and this man’s wife—that is, seize them.

The Apostle uses this sense when he says: “For you endure it if someone reduces you to slavery, and if someone takes” (2 Cor. 11:20), that is, if someone takes your goods from you. The Lord himself teaches us that “man” signifies the devil, saying: “An enemy man has done this” (Matt. 13:28). Thus this man takes away both house and wife from those who deny God.

“If, at any time, you approach to besiege a city, you shall first offer it peace. If it accepts and [Col. 0515B] opens its gates to you, all the people who are in it shall be saved and shall serve you under tribute. But if it refuses to make an alliance and begins war against you, you shall besiege it. And when the Lord your God delivers it into your hand, you shall strike with the edge of the sword every male in it, except women, children, beasts of burden, and the other things that are in that city. You shall divide all the spoil among the army and shall eat from the plunder of your enemies, which the Lord your God has given you.”

This may be understood not only of a single city or an entire people, but of any individual person. For every person is a city, and within it dwells no small multitude of citizens: virtues, if the person is good; vices, if bad. We approach to besiege this city [Col. 0515C] when we first attempt to convert an unbelieving person to faith in Christ. And first we offer that person peace, namely by preaching Christ the Son of God. “For he himself is our peace, who made both one” (Eph. 2:14). If that peace is accepted and the gates are opened for hearing and believing, all the people who are in that city shall be saved. For good is that people which opens its gates to the Gospel and receives Christ as he comes to it. Hence it is blessed “that all the people may be saved”—not the people who *was* in it, but the people which *is* in it. For, once the word of faith has been heard, the whole erroneous multitude immediately departs, and faith alone remains there with its own people.

This city serves the Church under tribute, because a faithful person continually pays the tribute of good works. [Col. 0515D] Would that we too might always be tributaries in this sense. By those who refuse to accept an alliance and begin to fight against the preachers, we understand those who are not readily converted, but dispute against faith and the Gospel with vain philosophy and dialectical syllogisms. Yet holy preachers should not immediately withdraw from such people. Rather, besieging them as though they were a most hostile city, they should attack them now with examples from Scripture, now with signs of miracles, now with other arguments, until, conquered, they yield and those who have assented to truth are converted from unbelief to faith. Then Christ’s warriors should at once destroy and annihilate all their males: all their syllogisms, all their arguments, and all the examples from false [Col. 0516A] writings by which they had formerly defended themselves and in which they had trusted. Thus some of them even burn their own books and confess that they have erred. But they preserve the women, children, and beasts of burden—that is, those opinions and arguments which either, like women, produce some good; or, like children, do no harm; or, like beasts of burden, are of some use. For the Gentiles possess many branches of knowledge which no one forbids Christians to possess.

To distribute the army’s spoil and divide the plunder of the enemy means nothing other than to entrust those newly snatched from the devil to catholic men, who may teach them the Christian religion fully and introduce them in every respect into the ecclesiastical body.

It follows: “Thus shall you do to all [Col. 0516B] cities that are very far from you,” and which are not among those cities whose possession you are to receive. But from those inhabitants who are given to you, you shall permit none at all to live. By those whom the children of Israel do not permit to live, we understand the army of vices, and the Jews, heretics, and all who persist in unbelief. For all these are destined for eternal death.

“When you have besieged a city for a long time and surrounded it with fortifications in order to capture it, you shall not cut down the trees from which food may be eaten, nor should you lay waste the surrounding country with axes; for it is wood, not a human being, and cannot increase the number of those fighting against you. But if any trees are not fruit-bearing but wild, and [Col. 0516C] fit for other uses, cut them down and build siege-machines, until you capture the city that fights against you.”

The same interpretation may apply both to this city and to that of which we spoke above. For what good citizens are in the former city, fruitful trees are in this one; and what evil citizens are in the former, wild trees are in this one, from which it commands siege-machines to be made. This teaches that pagans and heretics are often overcome by us through their own writings.

202

## CHAPTER XXI

“When the corpse of a slain person is found in the land which the Lord your God is going to give you, and the perpetrator of the killing is unknown, your elders and judges shall go out and measure the distances of the surrounding cities from the place of the corpse. [Col. 0516D] When they have determined which city is nearest, the elders of that city shall take from the herd a heifer which has not drawn a yoke or broken the ground with a plough. They shall lead it down to a rough and stony valley, which has never been ploughed or received seed, and there they shall cut off the heifer’s neck. Then the priests, the sons of Levi, whom the Lord your God has chosen to minister to him, shall come; and the elders of that city shall approach the slain person, wash their hands over the heifer which was struck down in the valley, and say: ‘Our hands have not shed this blood, nor have our eyes seen it. Be gracious, O Lord, to your people Israel, whom you redeemed, and do not impute innocent blood in the midst of your people Israel.’ [Col. 0517A] And the guilt of blood shall be removed from them. But you shall be free from the innocent blood that was shed, when you have done what the Lord commanded.”

This passage is very difficult to explain. Yet let us begin, and follow him who said: “Open your mouth, and I will fill it” (Ps. 80:11). By the corpse of the slain man, therefore, let us understand Christ’s body, the perpetrator of whose killing is, in a certain sense, unknown. That the Jews killed him is not unknown; yet the reason why they killed him is unknown. Pilate himself bears witness to this, saying: “I find no case against this man” (John 18:38). And the apostle Peter says: “Finding in him no cause of death, they asked Pilate to kill him” (Acts 13:28).

[Col. 0517B] It is customary speech that, when we ask concerning someone killed because of his guilt, “Who killed him?”, we answer, “His own sin.” In this sense, therefore, it is unknown who killed Christ, because there was no sin in him for which he should have been killed. What, then, must be done concerning this? “Let the elders,” he says, “and the judges of the people go out and measure from the place of the corpse the distances of the surrounding cities; and when they have discerned which is nearest, the elders of that city shall go out from there and do what follows.”

By the elders and judges of the people we understand the apostles. For they were first in the Church; they were established as judges by God and will judge the twelve tribes of Israel. The city nearest to the corpse is Jerusalem, whose elders [Col. 0517C]—that is, the patriarchs and prophets—are commanded to proclaim the death of the innocent man to all nations. The apostles announce Christ’s death in plain and easy speech; the prophets, according to their manner, through enigmas and figures. What follows will make this clear.

For the apostles measured from the place of the corpse—that is, from the city of Jerusalem—all the cities of this world, because “their sound has gone out into all the earth,” preaching Christ’s death everywhere and declaring everywhere that he was crucified without cause. Yet, for this to be believed more firmly, it was not enough that the apostles alone should say it; the elders of that same city also come forward to bear witness to it. They cannot lie, both because they are elders and because [Col. 0517D] they were nearest to the place. For there is now no part of the world in which the books of the prophets cannot be found; nowhere is there a place in which the prophets have not proclaimed Christ’s passion in their writings.

They proclaim it through allegories, just as here they speak rather obscurely of Christ under the figure of a heifer. Indeed, they speak not only in words but also in deeds. They take a heifer from the herd—that is, Christ our Lord from the flock of the patriarchs—which had not drawn a yoke or broken the earth with a plough, because our Savior, endowed with complete freedom, was subject to the slavery of no vices; and because he taught us to seek food from heaven rather than from earth. For he says: “Work not for the food that perishes, but for that which remains unto eternity” (John 6:27).

And they lead it into [Col. 0518A] a rough and stony valley—that is, to the Gentile people, made dreadful by the roughness of vices and the hardness of unbelief. This valley was never ploughed nor received seed, because before that time the Gentiles had known neither cultivators of the Church nor the seed of God’s word. “And they shall cut off the heifer’s neck there.” What does this mean? Christ was killed in Judaea, yet the heifer is slaughtered among the Gentiles. How then does the Apostle say, “Christ died once” (1 Pet. 3:18)? He died once and dies no more; yet he is said to die as often as his death is proclaimed and commemorated in the Church. Thus we are accustomed to say: “Tomorrow will be the Lord’s Nativity; tomorrow will be Easter; tomorrow will be the Lord’s Ascension,” although these occur tomorrow only by commemoration. Thus the prophets also kill the heifer among us as often as, through their writings, we remember Christ’s passion.

[Col. 0518B] They also bring the priests, sons of Levi, to this slaughter of the heifer, so that we may understand clearly that Christ’s crucifixion took place by the counsel of priests. But lest someone say, “You elders, you prophets, killed Christ, because, as is said here, you slaughtered the heifer, and your prophecy was the cause why Christ was killed,” the elders therefore come to the slain man, lift their hands over the heifer, and say: “Our hands have not shed this blood, nor have our eyes seen it.” What did they not see? Certainly the sin or cause for which he should be killed—for what does not exist [203] cannot be seen. Thus the perpetrator of the killing is unknown, since he was not known even by the prophets themselves.

[Col. 0518C] “And they come,” he says, “to the slain man.” When prophets speak of Christ’s passion, they come to the slain man; when they speak of his nativity, to the one born; when of the resurrection, to the one rising again; and so with the rest. But what does it mean that, coming to the slain man, they lay their hands upon the heifer, except that the heifer and the slain man are one and the same? Hands signify works, since works are done by hands: the cause stands for the effect. Therefore those lay their hands upon the heifer who demonstrate that all their works and the whole writing of their hands correspond to Christ the Lord.

Then they pray for the people—but for the entire people—for they pray for those whom Christ redeemed by his blood. Read the [Col. 0518D] prophets, and you will find them praying in this manner in many places. Whom did Christ redeem except those who return through faith to his grace? What follows, however—“But you shall be free from the innocent blood that was shed, when you have done what the Lord commanded”—is said especially to the Jews. Hence, after Christ’s passion, some, moved by repentance, came to the apostles and said: “What shall we do, brothers?” To them blessed Peter said: “Repent, and let each of you be baptized” (Acts 2:38). This, then, is what the Lord commands; whoever does it will be innocent of Christ’s blood.

“If you go out to battle against your enemies and the Lord your God delivers them into your hand, and you lead captives away, and among [Col. 0519A] the captives you see a beautiful woman, love her, and wish to have her as your wife, you shall bring her into your house. She shall shave her hair, trim her nails, and lay aside the garment in which she was taken captive; then, sitting in your house, she shall mourn her father and mother for one month. Afterward you shall go in to her, sleep with her, and she shall be your wife.”

This is not to be understood literally. Some interpreters have understood this woman to mean the teaching of the philosophers; but I think that she signifies the human mind, which by its nature is more beautiful than all women. Those who go out to battle against enemies are teachers of the Church; the enemies are all who do not belong to our religion. To fight against them is to show them their error [Col. 0519B] and invite them to Christ’s faith. Indeed, the Apostle says that he fought with beasts at Ephesus. They are conquered and led captive when, abandoning error, they are converted to faith.

Therefore, whenever Christ’s soldiers perceive a beautiful soul there, they love it and desire to take it as a wife—for every soul that promises Christ’s faith is beautiful. They bring it into their house, that is, into the Church entrusted to them. It shaves its hair and trims its nails because it despises and rejects whatever is useless and superfluous in it. For what is more superfluous to a human being than vices and sins? Unless one is freed from them, one cannot be saved. It also lays aside the garment in which it was captured, putting off the old person with its deeds.

But when it says, “Sitting [Col. 0519C] in his house, she shall mourn her father and mother for one month,” this means that before coming to the Church, before receiving the sacraments of baptism, she shall mourn and do penance because she imitated the wickedness of her parents. Her father was the devil, according to the Lord’s words to some: “You are of your father the devil” (John 8:44); and her mother is paganism. To mourn for one month means to do penance for the period fixed by the bishop, because a month is called a measure and number of days. To mourn for one month is likewise to mourn according to one measure and arrangement of days.

Afterward he enters to her, now baptized, and sleeps with her, and she becomes his wife because he then cleaves to her more intimately, unfolds the Church’s sacraments [Col. 0519D] to her, impregnates her with the seed of God’s word, and causes her to bring forth good works as though they were children.

It follows:

“If a man has two wives, one beloved and the other hated, and has children by them, and the first-born son belongs to the hated wife: when he wishes to divide his property among his children, he may not make the son of the beloved wife first-born and prefer him to the son of the hated wife. Rather, he shall acknowledge the son of the hated wife as first-born and give him a double portion of everything he possesses. For he is the beginning of his children, and to him the rights of the first-born belong.”

By this man we may understand a bishop. Although he governs the Church, since the Church is divided into two parts—the good and the bad—he seems to have two [Col. 0520A] wives. Both wives bear children by the bishop, because he has regenerated the children of both through the water of baptism. To bear a child, as it were, by the bishop is to baptize a child according to his teaching.

But which bishop does not love that wife—that part of his people—which faithfully serves God and does not depart from the Christian religion? And which does not regard as hated that wife which is devoted to luxury and pleasures, perjuries and murders, thefts and adulteries, and other iniquities? Nevertheless, as it is written, “The son shall not bear the iniquity of the father” (Ezek. 18:20). If a good son is born from a wicked mother, he shall not lose his birthright because of that. Likewise, conversely, if an unjust son arises from an excellent mother, he is not thereby first-born. [Col. 0520B] Therefore only the person who is good, whatever his parentage—whether the child of a murderer, an adulterer, or one infamous for another crime—should be judged first-born and worthy of priestly rank. For it is said: “The son shall not bear the iniquity of the father.”

That sons of slaves are not admitted to holy orders [204] occurs because it is not proper for the Church of God forcibly to seize what belongs to another. If their masters grant permission, no one excludes them from holy orders because of servitude. For servitude is not a sin; moreover, as soon as they are ordained, they become free. What belongs to the Church belongs to no one’s property. They receive a double portion because, according to the Apostle, “presbyters are held worthy of double honor” (1 Tim. 5:17).

[Col. 0520C] “If a man has begotten a stubborn and rebellious son, who will not obey the command of father or mother, and, though chastened, despises obedience, they shall seize him and bring him to the elders of the city and to the gates of judgment. They shall say to them: ‘This son of ours is rebellious and stubborn; he despises to heed our warnings; he indulges in revelry, luxury, and banqueting.’ The people of the city shall overwhelm him with stones and he shall die, and you shall remove evil from your midst, so that all Israel, hearing it, may fear.”

I think that this chapter signifies nothing other than that priests and bishops, who are the spiritual fathers and mothers of all others, should excommunicate and condemn to eternal death those children who do not obey their admonitions and evangelical ordinances, but instead follow errors and subject themselves to every luxury and every [Col. 0520D] iniquity. The one excommunicated is the one overwhelmed with stones by the whole people, as we have often said already. But this should not be done without due order: first let the person be brought to the elders and the gate of judgment, introduced before a council, and let what the decrees of the holy Fathers prescribe concerning that person be heard.

“When a person has sinned in a matter punishable by death, has been sentenced to death, and is hanged on a gallows, his corpse shall not remain on the wood; and you shall by no means defile your land, which the Lord your God has given you as a possession.”

According to these words, it is evident that not every person who hangs upon wood is accursed, but only one who [Col. 0521A] has been justly judged, condemned, and hanged for sins. Such a person was accursed even if not hanged on wood. Why, then, are others justly condemned for their iniquities and killed by whatever penalty, not likewise called accursed by God? Perhaps because the first human being hung upon wood when he took the forbidden fruit from the tree, for which he and the human race were condemned to death. Therefore, whoever hangs upon this wood while still bound by original sin is accursed. Hence it commands that the corpse of this accursed person not remain on the wood, but that on the very day on which such persons have understood the sin of their death, they be buried in the water of baptism.

[Col. 0521B] But we must ask why the Apostle, applying this statement to Christ, says: “Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law, having become a curse for us, because it is written: ‘Accursed is everyone who hangs upon wood’” (Gal. 1:13). But one who hangs on wood is accursed by God only after the preceding condition: “if he has sinned in a matter punishable by death.” Christ sinned in nothing; therefore this does not apply to him. Why then, O blessed Paul, did you say, “Accursed is everyone who hangs upon wood,” and not say, “Accursed by God is everyone who hangs upon wood”? Why did you not add “by God”? Indeed, why did you omit what you knew was in the Law? Certainly because Christ was cursed by a cursing people; yet by God he was not cursed, but blessed above all things. Hence the Psalmist says in his person: “They will curse him, [Col. 0521C] but you will bless” (Ps. 108:18).

## CHAPTER XXII

“You shall not see your brother’s ox or wandering sheep and pass it by; rather, you shall return it to your brother, even if he is not your neighbor and you do not know him. You shall bring it to your house, and it shall remain with you until your brother seeks it and receives it. Likewise concerning an ass, a garment, and everything belonging to your brother that was lost: if you find it, do not disregard it as though it were a stranger’s.”

This seems addressed especially to bishops and presbyters: they should take care not only of their own sheep but also of others’ if they see them wandering. For we often see, under the pretext of pilgrimage, not only laypeople but wandering monks and presbyters going astray. We know the bishops of some of these persons and do not know those of others. If we can, we should restore them by preaching and admonition to our brothers; or, if we cannot, while they remain with us we should care for them as though they were our own, lest they perish through our negligence.

“If you see your brother’s ass or ox fallen on the road, you shall not despise it, but lift it up with him.” For we are on the way of God’s commandments, on which the Psalmist, by no means weary, said: “I ran the way of your commandments” (Ps. 118:32). Our brother is Christ, who directs us to say with him: “Our Father, who are in heaven” (Matt. 6:8). For those are brothers who are the children of one father. His ass is [Col. 0522A] someone foolish, lazy, or lustful; his ox is whoever is accustomed to labor in his field. If we see such people fallen on this way—for sinners fall in many ways—we should lift them as far as we can. For we have a good helper, who is not unable even without us to lift up his own ass and ox. Let us help, therefore, that we may be helped.

“A woman shall not put on a man’s garment, nor shall a man use a woman’s garment; for whoever does these things is abominable to God.” It is not a change of clothes, as the letter appears to say, but an imitation of virtue that makes one abominable. For the hypocrite, who in strength and pleasures is a woman, pretends to be a man by putting on a man’s garment. [205] Likewise, even a holy man who outwardly displays a softness which is not inwardly present wears a woman’s garment. The Apostle [Col. 0522B] agrees with this when he says: “We provide what is good, not only before God, but also before all people” (2 Cor. 8:31).

“If, while walking along the way, you find a bird’s nest in a tree or on the ground, with the mother sitting upon chicks or eggs, you shall not take her with her young; but you shall allow her to go, keeping the young that you have caught, that it may go well with you and you may live a long time.”

If I knew that it would go well with me and I would live a long time because of this, I would search through forests for birds’ nests at any labor whatsoever. But the Jews are mistaken if they expect that, through the mercy they show to birds, it will go well with them and they will live a long time. Let this bird, then, be the apostle Paul. For the Lord himself, signifying that he is a bird, speaks to Jerusalem, saying: “How often I wished to gather your children, as a hen gathers her chicks, and you would not” (Matt. 23:37).

[Col. 0522C] This bird built both in a tree and on the ground because in lofty cities and humble places it gathered people to faith. It broods over both chicks and eggs, warming and nourishing with love, faith, and preaching both the baptized and the unbaptized—for those not yet baptized are still like eggs. Whoever, then, walking along the way, is making for the homeland and for God, take the chicks of this bird: learn from them what they themselves learned from their mother. Do not hold the bird herself; permit her to fly, so that she may nest in other places and preach in other cities. This is what the apostles did: once bishops had been ordained in cities that received the faith, [Col. 0522D] they immediately flew on to others.

“When you build a new house, you shall make a wall around the roof, lest blood be shed in your house and you become guilty when someone slips and falls headlong.”

The person who admonishes and teaches the Church entrusted to him to put off the old person, imitate the new, and walk in newness of life builds a new house. That person makes a wall around it when he urges others to hold and preserve with all their strength faith, hope, love, patience, and humility. Unless he does this and is diligent in constructing this wall, he himself will be guilty of shed blood when another falls headlong and stains God’s Church with his blood. This is what the Lord says through Ezekiel: “Unless you announce his iniquity, he indeed shall die, but I will require his blood from your hand” (Ezek. 3:18). [Col. 0523A] To fall from the roof is to fall from the height of faith and purity of mind into certain grievous sins. Bishops, therefore, must continually persist in God’s word and set the wall of holy preaching before those already falling and approaching sin.

“You shall not sow your vineyard with another seed, lest both the seed which you have sown and what grows from the vineyard alike be consecrated.” “For the vineyard of the Lord Sabaoth,” says the prophet, “is the house of Israel” (Isa. 5:7), whose seed is evangelical preaching. Therefore it must not be sown with another seed. Whatever is other is not good. How, then, can it be consecrated along with what grows from the vineyard? [Col. 0523B] Heresy, fraudulently introduced into catholic teaching, is both consecrated and not consecrated: for those who do not understand it, it is not consecrated; but for those who understand it, it is consecrated, because they receive it as though it were holy. Hence holy preachers must take great care how they introduce examples from heretics and philosophers into their sermons.

“You shall not plough with an ox and an ass together.” To plough together with an ox and an ass is to make the clean and unclean, the wise and foolish, the just and sinner equal in preaching, and to send them out together to evangelize. For one does not destroy less than the other builds.

[Col. 0523C] “You shall not wear a garment woven of wool and linen together.” The garment of the soul is the flesh: if it is chaste, it is woven of linen; if lustful, of wool. Linen signifies chastity because of its whiteness, while wool signifies lust because it arises from flesh, and lust is born from the wantonness of flesh. Therefore, whoever cannot be clothed in linen should be clothed in wool—that is, whoever cannot remain continent should marry whom he wishes, only in the Lord (1 Cor. 7:9); this is what the Apostle says. But no one should wear wool and linen together, lest either a fornicator pretend chastity or one pretending chastity commit fornication.

“You shall make cords on the fringes at the four corners of the cloak with which you cover yourself.” We explained this in the book of Numbers.

It follows concerning the man who defames his wife. [Col. 0523D] He says that he did not find her a virgin, and, wishing therefore to dismiss her, is brought by the girl’s parents before the elders of the city and to the gate of judgment. There they accuse him of wishing to dismiss their daughter, and, displaying the signs of her virginity, spread before the elders the garment. Having seized him, they beat him; moreover, they condemn him to one hundred silver shekels, which he gives to the girl’s father because he defamed a virgin of Israel. Nor may he ever afterward dismiss her. But if what he accused her of is true, the girl is to be cast out beyond the house and overwhelmed with stones.

[Col. 0524A] This girl seems to me to be the Christian religion. Whoever is joined to her with chaste love takes her as a wife. Her father is the bishop; her mother is the Church. She has already been defamed by many who, after first knowing her chastity, loved her most fervently. This occurs when someone doubts in faith and speaks against the truth and religion [206] which that person had received. Such a person, then, should be brought by the girl’s parents before the elders of the city and before the universal council, where not one elder or bishop but many are found. There the person should be condemned who has unjustly defamed the faith in which he or she was baptized and which was received from the beginning, declaring it violated.

At the same time, the girl’s parents—that is, those who had taught that person the faith and religion—should show the signs of virginity and incorruption, spread out the garment, and open the book which contains manifest proofs of the Christian faith. When the elders of the Church [Col. 0524B] have examined these and found nothing blameworthy in the girl or her parents, they should beat that person, rebuking him or her with the harsh lashes of their tongues. Further, they should condemn that person to one hundred silver shekels, by which are understood all the commandments of both Testaments. The number one hundred is perfect and therefore signifies all things, because it contains every number within itself. These shekels are called silver because of the purity of speech. The man is rightly commanded to give them to the girl’s father, so that he may make him certain, by oath or by any other means, that he will thereafter faithfully maintain and believe whatever the commandments of both Testaments enjoin. Once he has done this, he may no longer dismiss his wife.

[Col. 0524C] But if the accusation against her is true, let the girl be cast out beyond her father’s house and overwhelmed with stones. This is as if it said: if that faith and religion is found corrupt and violated, let it be cast out of the breast of the bishop who begot it; and, overwhelmed by every stone and excommunicated, let it perish.

“If a man sleeps with another man’s wife, both shall die—that is, the adulterer and the adulteress—and you shall remove evil from the midst of Israel.” The death of the flesh signifies the death of the soul, which those who commit such a crime indeed suffer.

[Col. 0524D] “If a man has betrothed a virgin girl, and someone finds her in the city and lies with her, both shall be brought to the gate of that city and overwhelmed with stones: the girl, because she did not cry out while in the city; the man, because he humbled his neighbor’s wife. And you shall remove evil from your midst.”

What do we understand by the virgin girl except one baptized in catholic faith? And by the man who betrothed her, except Christ? Hence the Apostle says: “I have betrothed you to one husband, to present you as a chaste virgin to Christ” (2 Cor. 11:2). This girl is corrupted in the city when someone within the Church seduces her by heretical depravity. Both are brought to the gate of the city—that is, before the bishops, through whom the rest of the multitude enters as through a gate—and there they are overwhelmed with stones, that is, condemned and excommunicated. For we have often already said what these stones signify.

[Col. 0525A] The girl is justly excommunicated because, while she was in the city, she ought to have cried out and disclosed to catholic men what the heretic said to her. The heretic, however, is punished because he humbled and violated his neighbor’s wife—namely, catholic doctrine, which he himself ought to have professed entire. He too is called Christ’s neighbor because, even though evil, he is nevertheless a son of the Church.

“But if a man finds in a field a betrothed girl, seizes her, and lies with her, he alone shall die. The girl shall suffer nothing and is not guilty of death. For as a robber rises against his brother and kills his soul, so the girl too has suffered; she was alone in the field, she cried out, and no one was present to rescue her.”

[Col. 0525B] If the city signifies the Church, whoever is not in the Church is in the field. If a betrothed girl, joined to God through faith, happens unknowingly to come among a crowd of heretics and there hears someone disputing falsely concerning faith, and, questioning this and wishing to understand whether it is catholic and true, finds no one present except heretics, then although she cries out loudly, no one is there to answer her with truth. Therefore, when this case comes before the bishops’ judgment, such a soul is judged innocent, because she was violated not by her own will, but unknowingly, secretly, and by robbery. But the obstinate heretic shall die—that is, be condemned to eternal death.

[Col. 0525C] “If a man finds a virgin girl who has no betrothed and, seizing her, lies with her, and the matter comes to judgment, he who slept with her shall give the girl’s father one hundred silver shekels and shall have her as his wife. Because he humbled her, he may not dismiss her throughout all the days of his life.”

It seems to me that this girl signifies grammar, dialectic, rhetoric, and the other liberal arts, which, so far as they themselves are concerned, are incorrupt virgins. This girl is said to have no betrothed because, although she may be joined to many, she becomes so properly each person’s own that what is in one cannot be in another. Hence one speaks of the grammar of Aristarchus because it was his own. So too, when you begin to learn an art, although it may be generated from another, nevertheless the art joined to your mind is yours and not another’s. Those who have deserved to take dialectic as their bride readily understand this.

[Col. 0525D] These girls, joined to Augustine, Jerome, Ambrose, Cyprian, and the other doctors, bore them many children—that is, many volumes of books. Nevertheless, those who are joined to them are commanded to give their father one hundred silver shekels. Who is their father but he of whom it is said: “All wisdom is from the Lord God, and has always been with him [207] and is before the age” (Ecclus. 1:1)? To give him one hundred shekels is to expound and understand faithfully and without error everything contained in these and other writings composed under the instruction of these arts. Otherwise, the shekels will not be silver unless they are free from every corruption. [Col. 0526A] How one hundred signifies all things we stated above. If, therefore, this matter comes to judgment—that is, before bishops, who, as wise and well-instructed sons of the Church, always devote themselves to wisdom and reading—let them faithfully understand and expound everything, and let them not reject marriages with such noble girls.

“Let no man take his father’s wife, nor uncover her covering.” For in rebuking the Corinthians concerning this, the Apostle says: “It is reported that there is such fornication among you as is not even found among the Gentiles, so that someone has his father’s wife” (1 Cor. 5:1). Moreover, since every faithful soul is the wife of God, who is the Father of all, whoever leads a soul into sin and error may be understood to corrupt the Father’s wife.

## Chapter XXIII

[Col. 0526B]

“Let no eunuch with crushed or amputated testicles, or with his member cut off, enter the Church of God.” By this is signified that no one will enter the heavenly homeland who is barren of good works and has not possessed the instruments of spiritual generation and fruitfulness.

“Let no mamzer—that is, one born of a harlot—enter the Church of the Lord, even to the tenth generation.” For what is “to the tenth generation” except to the last generation? The tenth generation is the last, because the number ten also is the final number. Therefore, one born of a harlot—that is, from the adultery of heretics—will never be joined to the Church of the saints.

“The Ammonites and Moabites also [Col. 0526C] shall not enter the Church of the Lord even after the tenth generation, forever, because they would not come out to meet you with bread and water on the way when you came out of Egypt.” What should we understand by these except vices and evil spirits, who, desiring to destroy us through hunger and thirst for spiritual food and drink, stir up wars against us by every means within their power and attempt to deceive us by every kind of cunning and fraud? Therefore, let us never make peace with them, never seek good for them, but always strive to destroy them and drive them away from us.

“You shall not abhor an Idumaean, because he is your brother, nor an Egyptian, because you were a stranger in his land. Those who are born from his third generation shall enter the Church of the Lord.” The Idumaeans are of the race of Esau [Col. 0526D] and are interpreted as “earthly.” The Egyptians, however, are called “darkness”; through them the Gentile people is signified—at first earthly and sinful, wholly black and dark. Yet those born in the third generation—that is, regenerated by a third immersion in baptism—enter the Church of God.

The third generation may also be understood as this final age, since these ages are divided into three periods: before the Law, under the Law, and under grace. Therefore, in this last age, which is the third, the Church is closed to no one; it is opened to Idumaeans and Egyptians, to earthly and sinful people, and to all nations.

“When you go out against your enemies to battle, guard yourself from every evil thing.” Our enemies [Col. 0527A] are evil spirits, by whom we are easily overcome unless we guard ourselves from vices.

“If there is among you a man who has been defiled by a nocturnal emission, he shall go outside the camp and shall not return until, toward evening, he has washed himself with water; and after sunset he shall return to the camp.” The Jews are defiled by a nocturnal dream because, dreaming the precepts of the Law in darkness and interpreting them as though in a dream, they continually become more unclean. Therefore, having gone outside the camp and been separated from God, they will not return to the camp of the Church until, coming to evening and sunset—that is, to the consummation of the age—they have been washed and cleansed by the water of baptism. “They shall return at evening” (Ps. 58:15), as the Psalmist says.

[Col. 0527B]

“You shall have a place outside the camp to which you may go for the necessities of nature, carrying a peg on your belt. When you sit down, you shall dig around you and cover with earth what has been discharged, by which you have been relieved—for the Lord your God walks in the midst of the camp to deliver you and hand your enemies over to you—and your camp shall be holy.” Dung and excretions are vices and sins. Such things must not be done in the camp of the faithful. Whatever is foul, whatever is fetid, whatever is wicked and vicious, must be driven far from the dwellings of the faithful and the camps of the saints. For the Lord, walking and dwelling there, abhors the stench of such things and will disdain to remain there. The remaining matters said here seem to belong more to narrative than to signification.

[Col. 0527C]

“You shall not hand over to his master a slave who has fled to you; he shall live with you in the place that pleases him and shall rest in one of your cities. Do not afflict him.” “Everyone who commits sin is a slave of sin” (John 8:34). The devil is this slave’s master. Therefore, if such a slave, moved to repentance, flees to us, let us not reject him or drive him from our communion; rather, let him dwell with us and live among the assembly of the saints. Let no one afflict him; let no one shamefully expose him for his sins. For what else does this accomplish except to hand him over again to the devil and bring him to despair?

“Let there be no prostitute among the daughters of Israel, nor [Col. 0527D] a fornicator among the sons of Israel.” All Christians must observe this most carefully, according to the letter in the body and according to spiritual understanding in the soul. For concerning the soul’s fornication it is said against Israel: “Israel committed fornication with the gods of the nations.”

“You shall not bring the wages of a prostitute or the price of a dog into the house of the Lord your God, whatever it is that they vowed, because both are an abomination before the Lord your God.” By these words the priests of God are forbidden to receive gifts acquired unjustly and through sin. Thus it is written: “The sacrifices of the wicked are abominable to God” (Prov. 21:27); and likewise: “He who offers sacrifice from robbery is like one who slays a son before his father’s eyes” (Ecclus. 34:24).

“You shall not lend at interest to your brother money, grain, or any other thing, but to a foreigner. To your brother, however, you shall lend without interest whatever he needs, so that the Lord your God may bless you.” These words are full of mercy and love. By them we are admonished to assist without interest those whom we ought to love as members of our own race and of the same religion. Hence moneylenders are condemned no less in the New Testament than in the Old.

Yet it is not without mystery that you may lend at interest to a foreign people, the Jews. For we have received from them at interest both the Law and the Prophets: for in interest not only what is lent, but also what has not been lent, is repaid in addition [Col. 0528B].

[Note: [Col. 0527D] Whatever is demanded above the quantity of gold repaid, so that the debt is not extinguished by what has been paid, is interest. St. Maximus has the same in Homily 105, p. 349.]

Thus it is evident that we have received the Law and the Prophets at interest, since in repaying them we render not only the letter but also spiritual understanding. For Sacred Scripture is for us money, gold, silver, food, drink, grain, wine, oil, and similar things.

“On entering your neighbor’s vineyard, eat as many grapes as you please, but do not carry any away with you.” It would be strange unless you wished to understand by this what the Lord says in the Gospel: “Do not give what is holy to dogs, nor cast pearls before swine” (Matt. 7:6), so that what are called grapes here are called pearls there. Therefore, our neighbor’s vineyard is the vineyard of Christ our Lord, which we are now harvesting and whose grapes we eat by expounding them. It is therefore clear that the greater mysteries are not to be offered outside or expounded to everyone.

“If you enter the grainfield of your friend, you shall break off ears of grain and rub them in your hand, but you shall not reap that same field with a sickle.” The grainfield and the vineyard signify Sacred Scripture. Entering this grainfield of my friend, entering this book of my Lord, I break off ears of grain and laboriously draw out its meanings; rubbing them with the hand of the soul—that is, with understanding—I separate the grain from the chaff and the spirit from the letter. But I do not reap with a sickle, because I do not readily or quickly pass through many things in exposition. The Jews reap with a sickle: reading and gathering the whole book all at once, they understand nothing. Would that they too, while reading a little, took care to understand.

## Chapter XXIV

“If a man takes a wife and has her, and she does not find favor in his eyes because of some uncleanness, he shall write a bill of divorce, give it into her hand, and send her away from his house [Col. 0528D].”

[Note: [Col. 0527D] The force of the Law was directed not toward dismissal—which was tolerated [Col. 0528D] rather than commanded—but toward the written bill. The Pharisees, failing to notice this, imagined that divorces had been commanded to them. See Matthew, chapter 19, and Mazochius, *Spicilegium on Deuteronomy*, chapter 24.]

“When she has gone out and married another husband, and he likewise hates her and gives her a bill of [Col. 0529A] divorce and sends her away from his house, or indeed dies, her first husband shall not be able to receive her again, because she has been defiled and has become abominable before the Lord.”

What should we understand by this woman, who is dismissed by her husband because of her uncleanness, except some sect of heretics? If a man wrongly joined to her recognizes her uncleanness and error through divine inspiration, he will send her away from his house—that is, from the secret place of his heart—and will write a bill of divorce and give it into her hand. For it is not enough to separate from so wicked a marriage by bare and simple words; one must also separate from it in writing and under oath. We see such a divorce carried out in this manner in the Church.

But if she marries another husband—for every heresy has many husbands—and he likewise hates and dismisses her for the same reason, or indeed dies, the first husband cannot receive her again, both because she is defiled and abominable and because he has been separated from her by the firmest written act of divorce. These things were spoken for us in signification, but for the Jews because of hardness of heart. Thus the Lord says in the Gospel: “Because of the hardness of their heart he permitted them to give a bill of divorce and dismiss their wives; from the beginning it was not so” (Matt. 19:8). Not because this was good according to the letter, but because hard hearts could not otherwise be softened. Hence it is also said elsewhere: “Because he gave them statutes that were not good” (Ezek. 20:25).

“When a man has recently taken a wife, he shall not go out to war, nor shall any public necessity [Col. 0529C] be imposed upon him.” We understand this of those who, newly coming to faith, are joined to the Christian religion so that they may beget children of good works from it and with it. They themselves ought for a time to be free and separated from ecclesiastical responsibilities, until they are found to be perfect in this religion [p. 209] and to have set their own household in order. Afterwards, however, they may go out to battle against heretics and tyrants.

“You shall not take as a pledge the lower or the upper millstone, because he has pledged his life to you.” I think that these two millstones signify the New and Old Testaments: the lower signifies the Old, and the upper the New.

[Note: [Col. 0529] St. Maximus says the same in Homily I on the Advent of the Lord.]

Scripture itself turns; it is itself expounded; it itself turns everything into flour; it itself feeds us; it itself prepares for us what we need in order to live. Therefore, let us not receive either this or that from the Church as a pledge. We have given our faith and have held nothing dearer; therefore, whatever we have received from her should be not a pledge but our own possession. For what is given as a pledge cannot always be retained, nor can we use it as we wish. Let us therefore receive these millstones not as pledges but as our own. For without them we cannot live. What could be our own if life itself were a pledge? Hence it is rightly said: “Because he has pledged his life to you.” This is as though he said: He could give you nothing better, nothing more precious; in these consist his life, his teaching, his faith, and his [Col. 0530A] soul. Hold, then, what you have; let what you have received be your own, because nothing better could be given you in this life.

“If a man is caught enticing his brother from among the children of Israel, and, having sold him, receives a price, he shall be put to death, and you shall remove the evil from your midst.” Though this may be understood according to the letter of kidnappers, it may also be understood of evil judges who, blinded by greed, pervert justice for a price, condemn innocent people, and sell them. In the death of the body, moreover, the punishment of the soul is signified.

“Take diligent care that you do not incur the plague of leprosy; but do whatever the priests of the Levitical race teach you, according to what I commanded them, and carry it out carefully. Remember, I pray, what the Lord your God did to Miriam on the way when you were coming out of Egypt.” These words concern not bodily but spiritual leprosy. The leprosy of the soul is sin; that soul is leprous which has been wounded by the stains of sin. Those incur this leprosy who refuse to believe God’s priests. Miriam too was struck by it because she spoke against Moses. The Jews too are struck by it because they speak wickedly of Christ.

The remaining matters that follow here, being full of propriety, mercy, and compassion, are sufficiently understood according to the letter and do not seem to require another meaning.

“Remember that you too served in Egypt, and that the Lord your God delivered you. Therefore I command you to do this thing. When you reap the grainfield in your field and forget a sheaf [Col. 0530C] and leave it behind, do not return to take it; but allow the stranger, the orphan, and the widow to take it, so that the Lord your God may bless you in every work of your hands.”

This is as though he said: Do not despise strangers and foreigners, because you too were a stranger in the land of Egypt. It would have been enough for the Jews to observe all these things according to the letter, although they signified something else. For although these matters are narrated here and at that time came to them for righteousness, they now minister death to them. Hence the Apostle says: “The letter kills, but the spirit gives life” (2 Cor. 3:6).

For what should we understand by this field that the Jews reap, in which they also leave sheaves through forgetfulness, except this book of the Law? They reap and gather it daily, but through forgetfulness leave behind far more than they gather before themselves with open eyes; and they leave its spiritual understanding to strangers, orphans, and widows. If we consider how many mysteries are contained in a few words, we shall find these reapers exceedingly forgetful, foolish, and ignorant of reaping: abandoning what is best, they burden themselves with chaff and empty ears.

As regards spiritual understanding, however, they are not commanded not to return to take the sheaves; rather, this is prophesied of them, because he knew that it would happen. Thus it is said: “Blind the heart of this people, and make their ears heavy” (Isa. 6:10). For those return to take the sheaves who, reading the sacred Scriptures, repeat the same things again and again, because, as someone says: “Words repeated ten times will please.” Hence animals that do not chew the cud are also said to be unclean. For what is chewing the cud except repeatedly turning over the same food?

The stranger, orphan, and widow are the Church of the Gentiles, which comes to Christ and to faith from afar and from every part of the world. This is the queen of the South, “who came from the ends of the earth to hear the wisdom of Solomon” (Luke 11:31). Concerning this widow the Psalmist also speaks: “Blessing, I will bless her widow; I will satisfy her poor with bread” (Ps. 131:15).

“If you gather the fruits of your olive trees, whatever remains on the trees you shall not return to collect, but shall leave it for the stranger, the orphan, and the widow. If you harvest [Col. 0531B] your vineyard, you shall not gather the remaining clusters, but they shall fall to the use of the stranger, the orphan, and the widow.” The same thing is understood through the olive tree and the vineyard as we have just said is signified through the field. For divine Scripture supplies us with grain, oil, and wine. In some places it is eaten with difficulty, like bread; in others it is easily drunk, like wine; everywhere, however, it heals the soul like medicine and oil.

[p. 210]

## Chapter XXV

“If there is a dispute between certain persons and they appeal to judges, those whom they perceive to be just they shall award the palm of justice; those whom they perceive to be wicked they shall condemn for wickedness. But if they judge the sinner [Col. 0531C] worthy of lashes, they shall lay him down and have him beaten before them. The number of lashes shall correspond to the measure of the sin.”

[Note: [Col. 0531D] The Codex of Santa Croce Minor in the Laurentian Library adds: “But in such a way that it does not exceed the number forty, lest your brother, shamefully lacerated, depart before your eyes.”]

Justice is confirmed in this judgment if they award the palm of justice to those who possess justice and impose a different recompense upon the unjust. The limit of correction is rightly set at forty lashes, because that discipline is perfect and complete which is fortified by the authority of both Testaments. For the number forty consists of four times ten and signifies both Testaments: four tens, or ten fours, make forty. Why the Old Testament is signified by ten and the New by four is clear. The Apostle indicates that he endured this discipline, saying: “From the Jews five times I received forty lashes less one” (2 Cor. 11:24). One was taken away from him lest he depart shamefully lacerated. They considered it more proper to subtract one lest they exceed the number established by the Law.

“You shall not muzzle an ox threshing your grain on the threshing floor.”

[Note: [Col. 0531D] Mazochius, citing Aelian, book XIV of the *Various History* [Col. 0532D], reports that the ancients were accustomed to smear the mouths of oxen with bovine dung so that they would not taste any of the grain; *Spicilegium* on Deuteronomy, chapter 25.]

The Apostle says concerning this: “Is God concerned about oxen?” (1 Cor. 9:9), indicating that this should not be understood according to the letter. These oxen are the apostles and teachers, who, threshing the grain of the holy Scriptures on the threshing floor of the Church, separate wheat from chaff and spiritual understanding [Col. 0532A] from the letter. Their mouths must not be muzzled, because the laborer is worthy of his wage. Hence the same Apostle says: “If we have sown spiritual things among you, is it a great thing if we reap your bodily things?” (2 Cor. 9:11). It is fitting that you refresh with bodily food the one who has fed you with spiritual delights.

“When brothers dwell together and one of them dies without children, the wife of the deceased shall not marry another; rather, his brother shall take her and raise up seed for his brother, and shall call the firstborn son born from her by his name, so that his name may not be blotted out from Israel.” These are the brothers of whom it is said: “Behold, how good and how pleasant it is for brothers to dwell together in unity” (Ps. 132:1). Though not in body, they all dwell together in mind and spirit.

One of them dies without children whenever a bishop, departing this life, leaves among his subjects in his Church no one who is considered worthy of his chair. Therefore someone is sought from another church, to whom the wife of the deceased may be joined. He will indeed be the deceased’s brother, not by nature but by office: one of the same goodness and humanity, of the same faith and charity, like a brother resembling his brother.

He will raise up seed for his brother, so that those whom he finds dead in sins or weighed down by evil sleep he may cause to awaken to good works. And he will call the firstborn by his name—not “firstborn” because he was born first, but because by the merit of holiness he is considered first and greatest among all those begotten by him. And this man [Col. 0532C] will be called bishop; for this is the name of the deceased, so that his name may not be blotted out from Israel, so that the Church may never lack a bishop and this name may never fail in her.

“But if he does not wish to take his brother’s wife, who is due to him by the Law, the woman shall go to the gate of the city and appeal to the elders, saying: ‘My husband’s brother refuses to raise up seed for his brother in Israel and will not take me in marriage.’ At once they shall summon him and question him. If he answers, ‘I do not wish to take her as my wife,’ she shall approach him in the presence of the elders, remove the shoe from his foot, spit in his face, and say: ‘Thus shall it be done to the man who does not build his brother’s house.’ And his name [Col. 0532D] in Israel shall be called the house of the unshod.”

Why is judgment sought before the city gate except because the judges sit there? The Lord speaks of himself, saying: “I am the door. If anyone enters through me, he will be saved” (John 10:9). Bishops sit before this gate so that, enlightened by his light, they may never stray or depart from the truth. All causes must be brought before them and decided by their judgment.

Therefore, in their presence, the woman approaches her husband’s brother; and because he refused to take her in marriage, she removes the shoe from his foot. What is removing the shoe from his foot except taking away the authority to preach the Gospel? Hence the Apostle says: “With your feet shod in preparation for the Gospel of peace” (Eph. 6:18). Moreover, she spits in his face because she publicly and plainly shows him to be contemptible and unworthy of so great an honor.

This may most rightly be understood of those who, aspiring to greater positions, disdain to preside over lesser churches. There is no doubt that such men seek not the salvation of souls but the glory of honor. It would be just for them always to be judged unshod and worthy of spitting rather than of such a marriage. This is what he says: “And his name in Israel shall be called the house of the unshod.” For who would dare shoe him, or assign him the office of one who is shod, when by the very designation of his name he shows himself to be unshod?

[Col. 0533B]

“If two men have a quarrel with each other and one begins to fight against the other, and the wife of one, wishing [p. 211] to rescue her husband from the hand of the stronger, puts forth her hand and seizes his private parts, you shall cut off her hand and shall not be moved by any mercy toward her.” These men who fight each other are bishops, who very often contend with one another over ecclesiastical affairs. The stronger of them is the one whose cause appears to have greater force because of its justice. The wife of the other may be understood not only as his whole Church but also as someone from his people.

Wishing to rescue her bishop from the hand of the stronger, such a person puts forth her hand and seizes his private parts if, unable to resist him by arguments, she assails him with insults and casts something in his face for which he ought to blush. No mercy must be shown in this matter; that most shameless hand must immediately be cut off, and that tongue firmly restrained with reins. Scripture testifies that the tongue too has a hand: “Death and life are in the hand of the tongue” (Prov. 19:21).

[Note: [Col. 0533] St. Bruno recalls the dispute that he undertook in defense of the Church of Siponto against the bishop of Benevento, as has been said in his *Life*.]

I remember that this happened to me recently. While I was disputing with the bishop of Benevento on behalf of the Church of Siponto, his archdeacon immediately tried to seize me by the private parts and began unjustly to defame me. But the proud hand of his tongue was promptly cut off; rebuked by the council, he made satisfaction, sought pardon, and obtained it.

“You shall not have in your bag differing weights, a larger and a smaller, nor shall there be in your house a larger and a smaller measure. You shall have a just and true weight, and an equal and true measure, so that you may live for a long time upon the land that the Lord your God will give you. For the Lord will abominate the one who does these things and opposes every injustice.” If the merchants of this world understood and observed these things according to the letter, they would gain not so much by deceiving through them as they would gain by observing them. But let us not have differing weights in the pouch of our heart; rather, let everything be equal and just. Let us do nothing without order, nothing without balance and a true measure. And because “there is no partiality with God” (Rom. 2:11), let us likewise show no partiality in judgment.

There follows the command that Moses gave the children of Israel: after they had settled peacefully in the land of promise, they were to blot out all Amalek from beneath heaven, because Amalek met them on the way and killed the rear of his army when the host was exhausted by hunger and labor. What should we understand by Amalek, whose name is interpreted as “brutish people” or “licking people,” except heretics? Like brute animals, they do not fear God, and they deceive those whom they can by licking them—that is, by flattering and fawning upon them.
