These meet the people of God on the way as they hasten toward the heavenly homeland; they strive to impede its journey; and because they cannot overcome the first and stronger members, they deceive and kill all the rearmost and less perfect.

But we should note that the persuasion of heretics has its greatest strength when the people are consumed by hunger and labor: hunger, of course, for hearing the word of God. Those who have been refreshed by this food do not fear the snares of heretics. Those too are easily overcome by them who, fatigued along the way of God’s commandments, are weary of continuing to run. Therefore the Church destroyed this people and, after the wars against tyrants, when it already seemed to be at peace, overcame it.

## Chapter XXVII

Moses commanded that, after the people had crossed the Jordan, they should erect huge stones; after smoothing them with lime, they were to write upon them clearly and openly all the words of this Law, so that they might enter the land flowing with milk and honey. They were also to make [Col. 0534C] an altar upon Mount Nabal from stones untouched by iron, from unshaped and unpolished rocks, and offer upon it a holocaust to the Lord their God.

Of these stones it is written: “Holy stones shall be raised upon the earth” (Zech. 9:16). Those who have already crossed the Jordan erect these stones. Joshua opened the Jordan; Jesus opened the Jordan. He himself taught us what the water of the Jordan signifies, since, having been baptized there, he commanded his disciples, saying: “Go, teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit” (Matt. 28:9). Therefore, these are the ones who erect huge stones; these are the ones who build Churches throughout the world; these convert the kings and rulers of the whole world to the faith. Smoothing these stones and solidifying them with the bond of charity, they write upon them clearly and openly—not in cloud and darkness—all the words contained in this book of the new Law. For these words, as the Apostle says, “are written not with ink but with the Spirit of God in our hearts” (2 Cor. 3:3).

Words are also written in the hearts of the Jews, but neither clearly nor openly; hence it is said of them: “Blindness has happened in part to Israel” (Rom. 11:15). And when he says, “so that it may enter the land flowing with milk and honey,” he seems thereby to signify that no one will enter the land of the living unless he has first passed through baptism and received the faith [Col. 0535A] and teaching of the new Law.

But what is signified by the altar built from unpolished stones and unshaped rocks upon Mount Nabal? Surely the Church, in which all the sacrifices of the Christian religion are daily performed. [p. 212] This altar is made upon Mount Nabal because the holy Church is constituted for the greater part among the Gentile people. Nabal is interpreted as “an ancient abyss.” There was an ancient abyss in this people because among them, from ancient times, the greater gate of hell and perdition stood open.

This altar is formed from unshaped stones and rocks untouched by iron because the holy Church is constituted not only of the righteous but also of the impious, sinful, and senseless. Those who worshipped stones, and who were hard, unbelieving, and fruitless, did not possess the form [Col. 0535B] and beauty of God, in whose image they had been made; not without reason, therefore, are they called stones. Iron had not touched them because they had not yet been hewn and shaped by the tools of holy preaching. For the one who said, “As a wise architect I laid the foundation” (1 Cor. 3:10), had not yet come to hew them.

Upon this altar a holocaust is offered to the Lord and a peace-offering is sacrificed, because sacrifices are made to him in many ways in the holy Church. It is not necessary here to say anything further concerning sacrifices, about which we have spoken much in the preceding books. But when he says, “And there you shall eat and feast before the Lord your God,” this must be understood not of bodily but of spiritual food. This food is received in the Church; this food is eaten before God: “For man does not live by bread alone, but by every word that proceeds from the mouth of God” (Matt. 4:4). Therefore, the word of God is food, and by this food the soul is nourished and made fat.

We do not expound what follows because it is easy and understood for the most part according to the letter. Having therefore passed over these matters, let us proceed to the canticle.

## Chapter XXXII
“Give ear, O heavens, to what I speak; let the earth hear the words of my mouth.” In the literal sense, heaven and earth cannot hear, since they are insensible and have no ears with which to hear. Allegorically, however, the heavens signify the righteous, and the earth sinners. Great matters, then, are to be spoken by him who summons good and evil alike—angels and men, righteous and sinners—to hear. And rightly indeed are those called heavens whose commonwealth is in heaven (Phil. 3:20). Rightly also are others called earth, because, made from earth, they love only earthly and transitory things.

[Note: Col. 535. The manuscript of Santa Croce in the Laurentian Library reads: “May my teaching thicken like rain,” etc.]

“Let my teaching thicken like rain; let my speech flow like dew.” For earth is made fruitful by rain and dew: by them it brings forth, and, having brought forth, is sustained. He therefore desires that his teaching be such that the field of the soul, moistened by it, may burst forth into the fruits of good works. “Like a shower upon the earth, and like drops upon the grass, because I shall invoke the name of the Lord.” Let my teaching, he says, be such, and let it give life, nourish, and make fruitful the minds which it waters, just as a shower and drops of rain upon herbs and grass make them grow. This is so “because I shall invoke the name of the Lord,” by whose invocation all things are sanctified and governed.

“Give magnificence to our God; the works of God are perfect, and all his ways are judgments.” Give, he says, O heaven and earth, magnificence to our God—that is, magnify him. For to magnify the Lord is to proclaim God’s magnificence. He is not magnified in any other way, since he can neither increase nor diminish. “The works of God are perfect.” God made nothing imperfect; yet we see many imperfect things which we do not doubt are God’s works. This, then, should be understood of the first creation, in which nothing was deficient and nothing corrupted in any part. Let us therefore magnify him who created all beginnings perfect.

[Col. 536B] “And all his ways are judgments.” His way is faith: by it one comes to him, but by it he judges the unbeliever. Thus this is judgment. Likewise, the impatient are judged by patience, the unjust by justice, and the impious by impiety; and so also in other matters. Therefore all his ways are judgments. “God is faithful and without any injustice, righteous and upright.” Hence it is evident that his ways are not merely judgments, but righteous judgments. Let the good therefore rejoice, and the evil fear. But what are they to fear? That “they have sinned against him.” Let the good rejoice, however, because they are “his children” and are “not in defilements.” For if they were still in defilements, they would not be his children.

Now, directing his mind to later times and contemplating in the Spirit the Jews worshipping idols and rising against Christ, he cries out, saying: “A crooked and perverse generation—do you return this to the Lord, foolish and senseless people?” Has he, he says, deserved this from you, because he has bestowed upon you the great benefits enumerated below? “Is he not himself your father, who possessed you and made and created you?” He himself, he says—whom you forsake, whom you provoke by foreign gods and stir to anger—he, and not another, is your father, who possessed you from the beginning, made you, and created you. Do you not know this? Do what follows, and you will prove it true.

“Remember the ancient days; consider each generation. Ask your father, and he will tell you; your elders, and they will say to you.” What will they say? This indeed: He whom you foolishly forsake and despise is your father, owner, and creator. Your elders testify to this. Isaiah, Jeremiah, and the other prophets confess it. And although he was Lord of all, although he held all nations in his power, nevertheless he chose you alone as his portion; you alone he wished to be the cord of his inheritance. For this is what he says: “When the Most High divided the nations, when he separated the sons of Adam, he established the number of peoples according to the number of the sons of Israel. But the Lord’s portion is his people; Jacob is the cord of his inheritance.”

See, then, how greatly you ought to love him and how faithful you ought to be to him, since out of all the nations of the world he alone received you as his inheritance. This division of nations and separation of the sons of Adam appears to be that which took place at the building of the tower—or rather, that which was in his disposition before the ages. For then the Lord established the boundaries of peoples according to the number of the sons of Israel, because he ordained that there should be as many parts of the world as he foreknew sons of Israel. For there are twelve parts of the world, and likewise twelve winds blowing from them. Since there are four principal winds, and each has two adjoining winds, one on the right and the other on the left, there can be no doubt that there are twelve. But if by the sons of Israel we signify the apostles, this must be understood thus: what they themselves divided into twelve parts in preaching throughout the world had previously been ordained by the Lord to be so.

Another translation reads: “He established the boundaries of the nations according to the number of the angels of God,” so that we may understand that as many of the elect ascend to heaven as evil angels remained there when they fell.

“He found him in a desert land, in a place of horror and vast solitude.” What does “he found him” mean except that he knew and tested him? We entirely find someone when we plainly know what he is like. And because a man is known in adversity, the Lord is rightly said to have found him in the desert. Although the Lord bestowed very many benefits upon this people, he nevertheless often tested them and provoked them to anger, as is read above. Yet he, on the other hand, always had mercy on them. Hence it follows: “He led him around, taught him, and guarded him as the pupil of his eye.” This is what is said above: “It is enough for you to go around this mountain.” And Moses says: “We went around Mount Seir for a long time.” For forty years the Lord led them through the wilderness, until all those who had previously been numbered from twenty years old and upward had died. Yet he always taught them how they ought to conduct themselves, and guarded them as the pupil of his eye. This signifies the greatest and most perfect protection. For it is a customary expression to say that those whom we love greatly we love as our own eyes.

“Like an eagle provoking its young to fly, and hovering over them, he spread his wings, took him up, and carried him on his shoulders.” Thus, he says, the Lord always guarded the children of Israel, taught them righteousness, urged them to good work, and hovered over them in the pillar of cloud and fire, as an eagle is accustomed to do over its young. He speaks metaphorically, in order to show by this how exceptionally attentive was God’s care for that people.

“The Lord alone was his guide, and no foreign god was with him.” The children of Israel therefore spoke foolishly when, worshipping the golden calf, they said: “These are your gods, Israel, who brought you out of the land of Egypt.”

“He established him upon a lofty land, that he might eat the fruits of the fields.” He now speaks of future things as though they were past. He calls the land of promise a lofty land, either because it is mountainous, or because it is more fruitful and noble than other lands, or also because it signifies the land of the living.

[Col. 538A] There he rather ate the fruits of the fields, by which both body and soul were filled. These fields are the books whose fruit we now eat by expounding them. Whoever eats this fruit well is established upon the lofty land. “That he might suck honey from the rock and oil from the hardest stone.” The Psalmist seems to explain this where he says: “He gave them the regions of the nations, and they possessed the labours of peoples, that they might keep his ordinances and seek his law” (Ps. 104:44–45). For “he established him upon a lofty land” means “he gave them the regions of the nations”; and “to eat the fruits of the fields,” “to suck honey from the rock and oil from the hardest stone,” means “to keep his ordinances and seek his law.”

Whoever wishes rightly to meditate on the sacred Scriptures must be quiet, free from every disturbance. Therefore the children of Israel were established upon a lofty land, so that, fearing no one, they might live in peace and possess the labours of peoples, in order that, all care set aside, they might seek God’s ordinances and his law. For what else should we understand by the rock and the hardest stone than this law, written upon tablets of stone? Yet from this rock and hardest stone we suck that sweetness by which the soul is filled. For divine Scripture is both food and medicine to us.

“Butter from the herd and milk from the sheep, with the fat of lambs and rams, sons of Bashan, and goats with the marrow of wheat; and they drank the blood of the grape, purest wine.” These things are true according to the letter. The children of Israel struck down Og, king of Bashan, and possessed not only his herds, sheep, lambs, and rams, but all his land. Spiritually, however, by herds, sheep, lambs, and rams we may understand the whole multitude of patriarchs and prophets. Because they were born of spiritual parents, they are rightly called sons of Bashan; for Bashan is interpreted “fatness.” They are called herds on account of their multitude, sheep on account of their simplicity, lambs on account of innocence, and rams on account of leadership. From them we receive butter, milk, and fat, because we are refreshed by their words and examples. Such food is sweet and pleasant.

But what is signified by the goats, which are sacrificed for sins in every offering, except Christ, sacrificed for our sins, as the Apostle says: “He condemned sin in the flesh through sin” (Rom. 8:3)? Thus the Jews, while sacrificing, in some sense ate Christ in the goats; we now eat him in the marrow of wheat. He rightly placed both, to show both their sacrifice and ours. That by “the blood of the grape, purest wine” the blood of Christ is signified is especially clear because he calls it not wine but blood. Thus even then that people ate Christ’s flesh and blood in a figure, whom we now eat in truth.

Therefore, whereas that people, feeling around themselves such great divine generosity and kindness, ought to have become better and more faithful to their God, from the very source from which they ought to have improved they were raised up in pride and became more wicked. Hence it follows: “The beloved grew fat and kicked; he grew fat, became sleek, and was enlarged.” O evil fatness, which causes one to kick against God! “Their iniquity came forth as though from fatness” (Ps. 71:7). The very repetition of the words displays their excessive and overflowing wickedness.

“He forsook God his maker and departed from God his saviour. They provoked him by foreign gods and stirred him to anger by abominations.” He explains this: “They sacrificed to demons and not to God, to gods whom they did not know. New and recent ones came, whom their fathers had not worshipped.” These words are plain: they signify that this people was given to idolatry, since it both forsook the one God, its maker, and worshipped new gods whom its fathers had not worshipped. “You have forsaken God who begot you and have forgotten the Lord your creator” (Isa. 51:13). The Lord saw this and, provoked to anger, was stirred because his sons and daughters provoked him.

Something similar is said in the Psalms: “If my enemy had cursed me, I would surely have endured it” (Ps. 14:13). For the more familiar someone is to us, the more we grieve if he offends us in some matter. And he says: “I shall hide my face from them and consider their latter end.” When the Lord hides his face from his servants and does not permit himself to be seen by them, this is a sign of anger and indignation. Therefore David asks the Lord, saying: “Show us your face, and we shall be saved” (Ps. 79:4). He considers their latter end because he knows how long they persist in evils, when they turn to good, and what punishment awaits them in the future.

“For they are a perverse generation, unfaithful children. They provoked me by that which was not God and irritated me with their vanities; and I shall provoke them by that which is not a people, and irritate them by a foolish nation.” This is as though he said: They provoked, irritated, and despised me; and I shall provoke, irritate, and despise them. They worshipped as God one who is not God; and I shall provoke them and receive in their place one which is not a people, so that, at least thus, they may waste away in grief when they see others holding their place and possessing their goods.

But how is the people of the Gentiles not a people? And why, if it is not a people, is it called a people by the prophets? The Apostle says: “God chose the foolish things of the world to destroy the wise; he chose the weak things to confound the strong; and the things that are not, that he might destroy the things that are” (1 Cor. 1:27). As we understand “the things that are not,” so we should understand “that which was not a people.” For those things are said among men to be as though they are not which are so small and lowly that they seem in some way not to exist. Hence, in customary speech, we are accustomed to say that what we value little is nothing.

“A fire has been kindled in my wrath, and it shall burn to the lowest parts of hell. It shall devour the earth with its increase and burn the foundations of the mountains.” By this fire all kinds of punishments may be signified by which sinners are tormented, whether in this age or in the future, because the Lord is angry with them. This fire burns to the lowest parts of hell because, as Scripture testifies, it is inextinguishable. It devours the earth with its increase: either here, literally, cities and men; or in hell, sinners together with their children and followers. The foundations of the mountains are riches and honours, in which the powerful of this age trust and by which, exalted, they grow proud; and the final fire will burn these together with their possessors.

“I shall gather evils upon them and complete my arrows in them.” For in this life the Lord gathered many evils and many tribulations upon the Jews; and what great evils he will gather upon all the wicked in the future—what need is there to say? The arrows are completed in them because no arrow and no punishment remains which does not rage against them. “They shall be consumed by hunger,” either here, besieged by enemies, or as that rich man who asked Lazarus for a drop of water. “And birds shall devour them with a most bitter bite” (Luke 16:23). This was fulfilled literally, because their corpses were often devoured by birds, beasts, and serpents, according to the words: “They gave the corpses of your servants as food to the birds of heaven, and the flesh of your saints to the beasts of the earth” (Ps. 78:2).

[Col. 540C] But allegorically, birds, serpents, and beasts signify evil spirits, who, because of the extreme savagery of the wicked, cannot be satiated by their punishments. “I shall send upon them the teeth of beasts, with the fury of those crawling upon the earth, and of serpents. Outside the sword shall lay them waste, and within terror, the young man together with the virgin, the nursing child with the aged man.” Whoever does not understand this should read the books of Kings, Joshua, and Maccabees. But if anyone wishes to understand it of the Jews now living, let him know that all, from the greatest to the least, are marked out for death and destruction.

[Note: Col. 539. The manuscript of Santa Croce Minor in the Laurentian Library reads: “Delivered over.”]

“And I said: Where are they? I shall cause their memory to cease among men.” It is as though he said: Where are those who once, joyful and exulting, filled all the cities of Judaea? They are now, certainly, in captivity and scattered throughout all lands. In this way he had said above: “I shall consider their latter end.” In saying, “Where are they?” he considers their memory. Their memory has ceased among men because those who were formerly most renowned among men are now judged worthy of no memory and no good reputation.

“But I delayed because of the wrath of their enemies, lest perhaps their foes should grow proud and say: ‘Our hand is exalted, and not the Lord has done all these things.’” These things would have happened to them earlier; but God delayed, so that their enemies might understand that they would have been unconquerable had they not departed from God. Thus, when their enemies overcame them, they would understand that it did not happen by their own strength but by God’s indignation, since he had departed from them in anger.

Thus far the Lord; now Moses speaks. “It is a nation without counsel and without prudence. Would that they were wise and understood and foresaw their latter end.” For they would not have perished if they had wisely believed in the counsel of the law and prophets. Indeed, if they had foreseen and understood what and how great things they would suffer for their iniquities, perhaps they would not have done those things.

“How did one pursue a thousand, and two put ten thousand to flight? Was it not because their God sold them and the Lord shut them up?” Understand, foolish and senseless people, that by God’s strength, not your own, so long as you were in him, you overcame an innumerable multitude of men with a few. This happened because the God of the Jews sold all their enemies to them as servants. Those who faithfully serve God in some sense purchase his benefits under service. But if “their God” is called the god of the Gentiles, this must be understood to mean that evil spirits deceive and sell their faithful followers, reckoning it great gain if they receive from God power to torment them eternally.

“For our God is not as their gods, and our enemies are judges.” Our enemies themselves testify, he says, that our God is greater than all. Thus far Moses; now the Lord continues what he began.

“Their vine is of the vine of Sodom and of the suburbs of Gomorrah. Their grape is a grape of gall and their clusters most bitter. Their wine is the gall of dragons and the incurable poison of asps.” Rightly, he says, shall I cause their memory to cease among men, as the memory of the Sodomites has ceased, from whom these derive their origin by wicked imitation. For their vine—that is, the Jewish nation and stock—imitated the vine and people of the Sodomites and Gomorrites in evil morals and wicked conduct, as a vine follows the character of another vine from which it has been planted. Its grapes and clusters are of gall and most bitter; its wine is the gall of dragons and the poison of asps, because all Jewish teaching is bitter, deadly, and incurable.

“Are not these things laid up with you and sealed in my treasures?” I have not forgotten, he says; I hold firmly in the treasures of memory the things which this nation has always done against me. “Vengeance is mine, and I shall repay them in the time appointed for this vengeance, that their foot may slip,” so that they may be able neither to stand, flee, nor resist. And this will happen quickly: “the day of destruction is near, and the times hasten to be present.”

Again Moses speaks: “The Lord shall judge his people and have mercy upon his servants.” It is as though he said: Truly the day of destruction is near; but let the good not fear, because the Lord, the righteous judge, will judge his people and, in judging, will have mercy upon his servants. What does “he will judge” mean except that he will separate them from the evil? For in this sense it is said: “Judge me, O God, and distinguish my cause.”

[Col. 542A] “He shall see that their hand has been weakened.” What does “he shall see” mean? Does he not see even now? Therefore “he shall see” means “he shall make it be seen” that the hand and power of those who formerly afflicted others mightily has been weakened; and just as two of them formerly put ten thousand to flight, so now ten thousand shall be put to flight by two. “And the confined also failed, and the remnant were consumed,” because, once the city had been captured, they were either slaughtered or sold. And then at last they shall learn that they sinned; that they worshipped gods and adored demons in vain; and that they ate in vain from their victims. For this is what he says: “Where are their gods in whom they trusted, from whose victims they ate the fat and drank the wine of libations?”

They said this; but the Lord, mocking them, says: Let your gods now rise, if they can, “and help you and protect you” in this great necessity. Since they cannot, see, know, and at last understand “that I alone am God and there is no other God besides me. I kill and I make alive.” For while he lives, not all die; when he calls, all rise again. “I strike and I heal.” The answer is: “and there is none who can deliver from my hand. I shall lift my hand to heaven and say: I live for ever.” When our Saviour, with hands raised, was taken up into heaven, he showed that he lives for ever. For no one dies there, where he ascended alive.

“If I sharpen my sword like lightning,” by which we understand eternal condemnation, “and my hands take hold of judgment,” I shall do what follows: “I shall render vengeance to my enemies and repay those who hate me.” This will occur in the judgment, when he renders to each according to his works. “I shall make my arrows drunk with blood, and my sword shall devour flesh.” In this he signifies that every kind of torment will not only come upon the wicked but will always remain upon them. “It shall be made drunk with the blood of the slain”—that is, my sword. It shall also be made drunk “with the captivity of the stripped head of the enemy.” The head of all the wicked is the devil, who will then be stripped bare because all his deceit and wickedness will be revealed to everyone. Those who have been captured and deceived by him belong to this captivity. Therefore the sword of God shall be made drunk with them.

“Praise, O nations, his people.” But someone may say: How do you command us to praise that people whom the Lord, holding them in contempt, permitted to be killed? To this he himself replies: “Because he will avenge the blood of his servants, repay vengeance to their enemies, and be merciful to the land of his people.” He would not do this if he had held them in contempt. By “land” he means the flesh, which after the resurrection, glorified, will be joined to eternal blessedness.

[Note: Col. 541. The manuscript of Santa Croce Minor in the Laurentian Library reads: “It will enjoy eternal blessedness.”]

## CHAPTER XXXIII

[Col. 543A]

“This is the blessing with which Moses, the man of God, blessed the children of Israel before his death. And he said: The Lord came from Sinai, and rose for us from Seir; he appeared from Mount Paran, and with him were thousands of saints. In his right hand was a fiery law.” These words do not proceed according to the letter. Let us therefore remember that chapter where it is said: “If, walking along the way, you find a nest in a tree or on the ground, and a bird sitting upon its young or eggs, let the bird go, but keep the young, that it may go well with you and that you may live a long time” (Deut. 22:6). Let us therefore let this bird go and keep its young. This bird is the letter, which under the covering of its wings conceals its young and eggs—that is, the spiritual sense. It nests in a tree in more difficult places, but on the ground in easier ones.

As we walk along the way of this volume, therefore, we find the nest of this bird in a tree, that is, in a difficult and lofty place. Let us let the bird go—or rather, let us compel it to fly away from here—so that we may keep its young, that is, spiritual understanding. If we do this, it will be well with us and we shall live a long time. Do you fear death? Let go of the letter that kills. Do you wish to live? Keep the children of the letter, that is, spiritual understanding. For the Spirit gives life.

The letter having been driven away, therefore, let us see what is signified by these three mountains—Sinai, Seir, and Paran. I think that by them the law, the prophets, and the Gospels are signified: by Sinai, where the law was given, the five books of Moses; by Seir, which is interpreted “rough” or “hairy,” the prophets, difficult to expound; and by Paran, which is called “fruitful,” the Gospels, because no seed has borne fruit as the seed of the Gospel has done. Therefore the Lord came from Sinai because his advent is first found in the law. He rises in Seir because his birth is revealed by the prophets. He appears on Mount Paran because he is heard in the Gospels and made manifest through miracles.

He comes, then, not alone, but with him are thousands of saints. “In his right hand is a fiery law,” by which sins are burned and minds enlightened. “He loved the peoples,” according to the words: “He loved us and washed us from our sins in his blood. All the saints are in his hand” (Rev. 1:5). Why in his hand? Because he governs them, holds them, and does not permit them to wander. “And those who approach his feet shall receive from his teaching.” Mary, the sister of Lazarus, understood this well. Moreover, by his feet the apostles are understood, who sowed his teaching everywhere.

“Moses commanded us a law,” certainly no other than that which he received from his teaching, since he also drew near. He speaks of himself as though of another: “An inheritance for the multitude of Jacob.” This would have been better for them than every inheritance, if only they had understood it; no enemies could have wrested it from them. “He shall be king with the most upright one, when the leaders of the people are gathered together with the tribes of Israel.” It is as though he said: This Lord and king coming from Sinai will indeed live among men on earth, but will not be separated from the Father. He will always be the most upright one with the Most Upright, of whom it is said elsewhere: “And the Word was with God” (John 1). The leaders of the people were gathered with the tribes of Israel when he preached in Judaea together with his disciples.

“Let Reuben live and not die, and let him be few in number.” By Reuben, who was the firstborn, we understand those who were first in that people to follow life and believe in Christ. They will live for ever and will not die as the others do. Yet they are few in number, although great in virtues and holiness; for “many are called, but few chosen” (Matt. 20:14).

“This is Judah’s blessing: Hear, O Lord, the voice of Judah, and bring him to his people. His hands shall fight for him, and he shall be his helper against his adversaries.” By Judah let us understand Christ, who according to the flesh was born from his stock. The Lord always hears his voice, according to what he himself says: “I knew that you always hear me” (John 11:42). The Lord brought him to his people because he first entered this world to call us, then hell to free us, and afterwards heaven to exalt us. The Lord will fight for him, and none can resist his hands and strength. He himself was his helper against his adversaries, by whom both the Jews and evil spirits are understood.

“And of Levi he said: Your perfection and your teaching belong to your holy man, whom you tested in temptation and judged at the waters of contradiction.” Your perfection and teaching, O God, he says, may be given and confirmed to your holy man, that is, to this priestly order, lest it again be tested and fall, but may remain perfect and wise in all things. He says this concerning himself and Aaron, who were found less perfect at the waters of contradiction, when the children of Israel, murmuring, tested God. Notice that at the beginning of his speech he accuses himself. “For the wise man is the first accuser of himself” (Prov. 18:17).

“He who said to his father and mother, ‘I do not know you,’ and to his brothers, ‘I do not recognize them,’ and did not know his sons: these kept your word and observed your covenant. They shall place your judgments upon Jacob and your law upon Israel; they shall set incense before your wrath and a whole burnt offering upon your altar.” This is what is read in Exodus: Moses commanded the sons, and as they passed through, they spared no one. By their example, therefore, the Lord’s priests, drawing the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God, should learn to spare no offender and to place love of God before every love. These men kept the word and covenant of God, and the judgments and law of Israel, by killing those who worshipped the golden calf. For it has been judged in this law of God, and in ours, that whoever worships another god or sacrifices to one shall die.

They place incense before God’s wrath because by their prayers they appease God’s anger, as by the most pleasant fragrance of incense. Aaron is also recorded to have done this: taking up the censer, he opposed himself to the flame which had already devoured the extremities of the camp. They also place a whole burnt offering upon the altar, preaching in the Church the sacrifice of praise and offering.

“Bless his strength, and accept the works of his hands. Strike the backs of his enemies, and let those who hate him not rise again.”

[Note: Col. 545. Another reading has: “Bless his first-fruits.”]

O that those who oppose God’s priests so greatly understood these words! For inasmuch as priests are blessed, so much are their enemies cursed.

“And of Benjamin he said: The one most beloved of the Lord shall dwell securely in him; he shall remain all day as though in a chamber, and rest between his shoulders.” Who is this one most beloved of the Lord? Surely the blessed Paul, who traces his origin from the tribe of Benjamin. But what sort of man should we think him to be who is called the Lord’s most beloved? Let us now see how he loves God, of whom he is said to be most beloved. He himself says: “If anyone does not love the Lord Jesus Christ, let him be anathema” (1 Cor. 16:22). Do you also wish to see how securely he dwells in him? “I am certain,” he says, “that neither death nor life, nor principalities nor powers, nor any creature shall be able to separate us from the love of God which is in Christ Jesus” (Rom. 8:38).

And Christ rests in him as though in a most pleasant chamber, as he himself says: “Do you seek proof of Christ who speaks in me?” (1 Cor. 13:3). “And he rests between his shoulders.” Such a horse, such a rider.

“Joseph also said: ‘May his land be blessed by the blessing of the Lord, [Col. 0545C] by the fruits of heaven, and by the dew, and by the deep lying beneath; by the fruits produced by sun and moon; by the summit of the ancient mountains; by the fruits of the everlasting hills; and by the crops of the earth and its fullness. May the blessing of him who appeared in the bush come upon the head of Joseph, and upon the crown of the Nazirite [Note: [Col. 0545] The Cistercian Bible manuscript, formerly of Monte Amiata, adds: “upon the crown of the Nazirite among his brethren.”].’” What are we to understand by Joseph, whose name means “increasing,” except the Christian people, who, growing and multiplying in a short time, filled the world? The land of this people is drenched with the Lord’s blessing, because from the very beginning its flesh—taken from earth and held under the curse of the first man—is blessed and sanctified in baptism. Then this people is made fruitful and satisfied by the fruits of heaven and dew, that is, by the words and [Col. 0545D] teaching of the apostles; and by the deep lying beneath, that is, by the lofty and profound understanding of the holy Scriptures; and by the fruits produced by sun and moon, through which we understand the most sweet utterances of Christ and the Church, by which our inward person is refreshed. And “by the summit of the ancient mountains,” that is, by the sublime and spiritual understanding of the prophets; and “by the fruits of the everlasting hills,” by which are signified the most sweet words of the apostles; “and by the crops of the earth and its fullness.” If these are understood of the land of the living, great and immeasurable riches are promised to it. For “every good gift and every perfect gift is from above” [Col. 0546A] (James 1:17).

But who is he who appeared in the bush, whose blessing he prays may come upon this people’s head and crown? For if that bush signifies the Virgin Mary, then surely it is Christ who appeared in the bush. This people is rightly called Nazirite, as being consecrated to the Lord from infancy among its brethren.

“His beauty is like that of the firstborn bull; his horns are the horns of a rhinoceros. With them he shall winnow the nations to the ends of the earth. These are the multitudes of Ephraim, and these the thousands of Manasseh.” For all of us, according to creation, are brothers, since we were born from the same parents. Yet the Christian people are most beautiful among all their brethren, because they alone have been reborn by the water of baptism and made whiter than snow [Col. 0546B]. They are aptly compared with a firstborn bull, as greater and stronger, and more suited than all others for labor. Their horns are unconquerable, like the horns of a rhinoceros, since nothing can withstand them.

It is not without reason, however, that horns are put in the plural, although the rhinoceros has but one horn, whence it is also called in Latin a *unicornis*, “unicorn.” The two horns are the two Testaments. Understanding these in a twofold way, this people overcomes the errors and vanities of all nations. With them it winnows the nations; with them it silences philosophers; with them it conquers Jews; with them it preaches and converts all the ends of the world. This people is divided into Ephraim and Manasseh, by whom we may understand Jews and Gentiles: the former means “fruitful,” the latter [Col. 0546C] “forgetfulness.” Both meanings fit the saints very well, since they bear good fruit and forget all their injuries.

“And he said to Zebulun: ‘Rejoice, Zebulun, in your going out, and Issachar in your tents. They shall call peoples to the mountain; there they shall sacrifice victims of righteousness. They shall suck the overflowing of the sea like milk, and the hidden treasures of the sands.’” What are signified by Zebulun, whose name means “dwelling-place of strength,” and by Issachar, elsewhere called “a strong ass,” except the holy teachers of the Church? For they are, like towers, an impregnable dwelling-place; like strong asses, they bear the burdens of others.

Thus Zebulun rejoices in his going out because, knowing himself fortified by God’s strength, he confidently goes out to battle against his enemies, and returns laden with great spoils taken from them. Issachar too rejoices in his tents, burdened by no weight of joy, when every day he offers so many souls to God. They call the people to the mountain, saying with the prophet: “Come, let us go up to the mountain of the Lord, and to the house of the God of Jacob” [Col. 0546D] (Isaiah 2:3). This is what they do when they invite the nations to faith and to the Church. There they sacrifice victims of righteousness, that is, the sacrifice of praise and offering.

They suck the overflowing waters of the sea like milk, either because they willingly endure for God’s sake the wrongs and adversities of the world, or because they rejoice to drink, through spiritual understanding, as though it were milk, the teaching of this law which seems bitter and undrinkable to others. Of this it adds: “and the hidden treasures of the sands” [Col. 0547A]. As gold is found in sand, so spiritual understanding is found in the letter.

“And to Gad he said: ‘Blessed in breadth is Gad. He rested like a lion; he seized the arm and the crown. And he saw your rulership, that in his portion a teacher is hidden away, who was with the princes of the people and carried out the righteousnesses of the Lord, his judgment with Israel.’” Jacob too, in blessing him, said: “Gad, girded for battle, shall fight before him.” What do we understand by Gad except the apostles? Girded with the sword of the Spirit, they fought their battles in the front rank.

They are blessed in breadth, either because they are sent out to preach throughout the breadth of the world: “Their sound has gone out into all the earth” [Col. 0547B] (Psalm 18:5). Though they are attacked on every side by many enemies, they rest securely like the lion of whom it is written: “The lion, strongest of beasts, fears no encounter” (Proverbs 30:30). They seized the arm and crown, subjecting to themselves all the strength and loftiness of the world. They overcame Rome, the head of the world; they converted its arms—that is, its emperors and princes—to the faith.

In their portion and rulership a teacher is hidden away, because the law and Christ—that is, the teaching of the Law and the Gospels—are laid up in their hearts. They therefore have a teacher in their heart, as the Lord says: “For it is not you who speak, [Col. 0547C] but the Holy Spirit who speaks in you.” This teacher was with the princes of the people, because by the bodily presence itself he also lived for a time with the apostles and worked righteousness and judgments in Judaea.

“And he also said of Dan: ‘Dan, a lion’s whelp, shall flow forth abundantly from Bashan.’” Samson was of this tribe; and the Antichrist will also be of it. Each is a lion’s whelp, because each is strong: the one in defeating the wicked, the other in persecuting the good. They are said to flow forth abundantly because they rush into battle with great strength. Bashan, whose name means “fatness,” signifies the land of Judah, which is said to be richer and more fertile than every other land. Both of them proceed from it.

[Col. 0547D] “And he said to Naphtali: ‘Naphtali shall enjoy abundance, and shall be full of the Lord’s blessings; he shall possess morning and midday.’” Naphtali means “breadth,” and by it we understand those who, enlarged by the love of charity, close their hands to no one but always keep them open in giving alms. They rightly enjoy abundance, because they freely bestow their goods upon others. To such persons the Lord will say at judgment: “Come, blessed of my Father, for I was hungry and you gave me food; I was thirsty and you gave me drink,” and so forth (Matthew 25:35). They shall possess morning and midday because they shall never decline into the sunset of death. To possess morning and midday is to inherit eternal light.

[Col. 0548A] “And he also said of Asher: ‘Asher is blessed in sons. May he be pleasing to his brothers, and dip his foot in oil. His shoe shall be iron and bronze. As your days of youth, so shall be your old age. There is no other God like the God of the most upright, the rider of heaven, your helper.’” What is figured by Asher, whose name means “blessed,” except the Christian people, who alone shall enjoy eternal blessedness? This people is blessed in sons, since unbelievers, even if they are sons, are not worthy of paternal blessing, because the good are shod by God.

It is pleasing to its brethren, by whom we understand the angels. It dips its foot in oil because it walks by the way of mercy. It is shod with iron and bronze because it has received from God the power to tread upon serpents and scorpions. Such power is an iron and bronze shoe. The statement that its youth and old age are alike demonstrates that its glory and blessedness are unchangeable.

“There is no other God like the God of the most upright.” This is an expression of wonder in praise of the Creator, who out of such wicked parents and such frail material converts this people, in accordance with his will, to so great an uprightness. Its helper is the rider of heaven, namely Christ our Lord, who ascended above all the heavens. For he himself says: “I will not leave you nor forsake you” [Col. 0548B] (John 14:18); and again: “Behold, I am with you until the consummation of the age” (Matthew 28:20).

“His clouds run about in magnificence; his dwelling-place is on high, and beneath are the everlasting arms. He will cast out the enemy before your face, [Col. 0548C] and will say: ‘Crush him.’” In the literal sense, it is marvelous that we see clouds laden with rain move about, carry waters, and now pour them out in due order and now hold them back. Our clouds too—the apostles and teachers—filled with spiritual waters and the doctrine of the Gospel, run about by his power and majesty; they water the field of our mind and make it fruitful with varied fruits of virtues.

His dwelling-place is on high because his seat is in heaven. Beneath, moreover, are the everlasting arms, because we know that his power and strength defend and sustain his faithful ones here. Therefore he casts out before our face the enemy, namely the devil, of whom it is said: “Your enemy the devil goes about like a roaring lion, seeking whom he may devour” (1 Peter 3:8). “To whom [Col. 0548D] he says: ‘Crush him.’” God’s speaking is acting; for “he spoke, and they were made” (Psalm 114:5). This is what the Apostle says: “May the Lord crush Satan swiftly under your feet” (Romans 16:20).

“Israel dwelt confidently and alone. The eyes of Jacob are upon a land of grain and wine, and the heavens shall grow dark with dew.” The prophet says this also: “Judah shall be saved, and Israel shall dwell confidently” (Jeremiah 33:16). Israel means “a man seeing the Lord.” This is the faithful people, who now see him with the gaze of the mind and later shall see him face to face. But how does Israel dwell confidently with the Lord? This is sufficiently clear from the fact that it always trusts in God’s protection; therefore it says: “The Lord is my helper; I shall not fear what man may do to me” [Col. 0549A] (Psalm 117:6).

“The eye of Jacob shall be alone upon a land of grain and wine.” Jacob is the same person as Israel; elsewhere it has been said what Israel signifies. In this place Jacob denotes the carnal people of the Jews. Moses therefore teaches that he sees other peoples looking upon heaven and spiritual things, but sees the Jews desiring only transient things and longing for nothing but grain and wine, under which are understood all carnal things that nourish the body. Although this vice is found in many others, it is attributed to the Jews alone because it rules them more than others.

“And the heavens shall grow dark with dew.” This too seems to be said as an addition to their iniquity and greed: although they see the heavens darkened by dew, they look only at earthly things. The Lord himself says: “If I had not come and spoken to them, they would not have sin; but now they have no excuse for their sins” [Col. 0549B] (John 15:22). They saw the heavens grow dark with dew and be covered with clouds when they perceived the apostles preaching and pouring out the rains of spiritual teaching. Yet, lowering their eyes to the earth, they took no care to raise them upward. Thus no excuse remains to them.

“Blessed are you, Israel; who is like you, O people saved in the Lord? He is the shield of your help and the sword of your glory. Your enemies shall deny you, and you shall tread upon their necks.” “Wretched,” he says, “is Jacob, whose eye looks only upon earth. But you, Israel, are blessed, because according to the meaning of your name you raise your eyes and contemplate God. Who is like you, O people [Col. 0549C] of Christians, signified by Israel, who are saved in the Lord?” That is, in him who said: “You call me Teacher and Lord; and rightly you say so, for I am” (John 13:13).

Just as the Lord has no people like this people, so the people itself shall have no lord like him. “Christ is the shield of your help and the sword of your glory.” He protects you; he defends you; he fights for you; he throws down your enemies; he is both shield and sword to you, and by his strength you glory, overcoming all enemies. Now he turns to Christ himself and speaks thus: “Your enemies, O Christ, shall deny you, and you shall tread upon their necks.” For although you are strong and mighty, although you are the Lord of hosts and king of glory, the Jews will nevertheless not fear to deny you, [Col. 0549D] saying: “We do not want this man to reign over us” (Luke 19:14); “We have no king but Caesar”; and “Not this man, but Barabbas” (John 19:15). But you, O Christ, shall tread upon their necks and humble their pride.

## Chapter XXXIV

“Therefore Moses went up from the plains of Moab onto Mount Nebo, to the summit of Pisgah opposite Jericho; and he showed him all the land of promise, saying: ‘This is the land concerning which I swore to Abraham, [Col. 0550A] Isaac, and Jacob, saying: I shall give it to your seed. You have seen it with your eyes, and you shall not cross over to it.’ And Moses, the servant of God, died there in the land of Moab at the Lord’s command; and the Lord buried him in the valley of the land of Moab opposite Phogor. No man has known his tomb until the present day.”

Why is Moses, the servant of God—who was most faithful in all his house, who spoke with God face to face, and whom the Lord knew by name—not permitted to enter the land of promise because of one sin? Moses, the lawgiver, to whom the law was given in cloud and darkness, here signifies those who understand the law only according to the letter. Enveloped in darkness, they cannot see what they read.

“For until today,” says the Apostle, “when Moses is read, a veil has been placed before their face [Col. 0550B] [Note: [Col. 0549] The Vulgate reads: “Until the present day, when Moses is read, a veil lies upon their heart”]” (2 Corinthians 3:15). Moses is therefore rightly found unbelieving precisely where he signifies an unbelieving people. He came to the rock and doubted, because it was not he who was there, but the unbelieving people then signified in him. This signification was the cause of his doubt.

What does this rock signify except the law, written on rock, given on tablets of stone, and assigned to a hard and unbelieving people? Moses came then to the rock; the unbelieving people come to the law even now. They think it dry; they think it without water, because they do not see spiritual understanding in it. They strike it once, and water does not come forth. They strike once because they pronounce and understand only the letter. Strike it [Col. 0550C] again, O Jew, and you will have water. Understand spiritually, lest you die of thirst; for Moses too gained nothing from the first blow. Why was this? Because he was still unbelieving and signified this single blow of an unbelieving people. Faith returns. He strikes again, and abundant waters come forth. Believe too, and you will have waters.

And not only this: but, what is better, you shall enter not the land of promise, which is captured so often, but the land of the living, which rejoices in complete security. This happened to Moses, who, reckoning habitation in that land as nothing, was transferred to the glory of a better land. Thus it is an admonition, not an expression of indignation, when the Lord says to him: “You have seen it with your eyes, and you shall not cross over to it,” because you are to cross over to a better land.

By this is signified that all who understand this law according to the letter do indeed see therein the delights, glory, and joy of the heavenly homeland, yet they cannot pass over to it. The Lord wished Moses’ tomb to be hidden, lest we return to the oldness of the letter, signified by Moses; rather, let us follow the life-giving Spirit, that we may live forever. May he grant this to us, he who lives and reigns as God with the Father and the Holy Spirit through all ages of ages. Amen.

[Col. 0551]

# The Exposition on Job Begins

## Preliminary Notice to the Exposition of the Book of Job

We leave to polemicists disputes concerning the age, homeland, and author of the book of Job. After what we observed in the general preface, it is enough for us, with St Gregory the Great [Note: [Col. 0551] Book I, chapter 1, on the book of Job.], to hold and faithfully believe that the author of this book was the Holy Spirit; or, with St Augustine, to say that St Job bore the great personage of prophecy [Note: [Col. 0551] Expositions on Psalm 104, sermon 4.].

To grasp the mind of St Bruno in interpreting it, one must observe that he set himself two purposes. In the first, he draws out and explains what was prophetically said concerning Christ and the Church, and shows it to have been perfectly fulfilled. In the other, he sets forth moral precepts filled with heavenly wisdom, by which he wonderfully kindles readers toward hope of future recompense. In pursuing these aims, our commentator is known to have consulted the ancient expositors of Job: namely Origen, St Jerome, and St Gregory the Great; and to have brought much from them into his own exposition.

In many places we have expounded the thought of the Angelic Doctor, St Thomas, who himself also commented on the book of Job, so that the agreement between them may furnish an argument for the correct interpretation. The holy bishop supplies no preface to this book, as to the others, but immediately begins its exposition. The text used by St Bruno agrees perfectly with the Vulgate, whose version, with few exceptions, does not differ from the Hebrew reading, as all biblical interpreters acknowledge. What manuscripts and authors furnish this testimony concerning the commentary of the bishop of Signi has already been sufficiently stated; therefore we refrain from repeating it. One point remains to be noted: when we spent the autumn vacation at Florence in 1785, we carefully compared the Marchesian edition of Job with the biblical manuscript of the Cistercian monastery of Monte Amiata, commended in the aforesaid preface, and recorded several variant readings, which we have supplied in their respective places.

## Chapter One

[Col. 0551A]

“A man was in the land of Uz [Note: [Col. 0551B] Cardinal Cajetan observes in his commentary on Job that it should properly be written *Huz*, not *Hus* [Col. 0552B], because Huz is the name of a kingdom in Jeremiah 25, and the land of Huz is said to lie in Arabia Petraea, on the border of Idumaea.], whose name was Job. And that man was simple and upright, fearing the Lord and departing from evil.”

The character of blessed Job is shown in few words. He was simple, according to the saying: “Be simple as doves” (Matthew 10:10). He was also upright, as one who walked on the royal road and turned neither to the right nor to the left. This was because he feared the Lord; for it is written: “He who fears the Lord neglects nothing” (Ecclesiasticus 7:19), and therefore it adds: “and departing from evil.” For a person does not fear the Lord if he does not depart from evil.

This is added to the fullness of Job’s praise: he is said to have lived in the land of Uz, that is, among impious persons and sinners [Col. 0551B]. Hence he himself says later: “I was a brother of dragons and a companion of ostriches” (Job 30:29). It is indeed highly praiseworthy to live innocently among the wicked.

Allegorically, although Job may be understood as the Church of all the perfect, in this place he especially prefigures Christ the Lord, who did not hesitate to undergo the cross and die for us in suffering. For Job means “suffering.” How simple Christ was is shown by the fact that “like a sheep he was led to the sacrifice, and did not open his mouth” (Isaiah 53:7). Even his enemies, commending his uprightness, said: “Teacher, we know that you are truthful, and teach the way of God in [Col. 0552A] truth, and care for no one” (Matthew 22:16). He himself feared the Lord, for upon him rested the Spirit of the fear of the Lord; he became obedient to the Father unto death. He too departed from evil: he committed no sin, nor was deceit found in his mouth; and of him it is said: “The wicked man shall not dwell beside you” (Psalm 5:6).

He lived in the land of Uz, that is, in Judaea. For Uz means “counsellor.” Concerning the Jews it is written: “The chief priests took counsel in order to seize Jesus by deceit and kill him” (John 11:47). It follows:

“And seven sons and three daughters were born to him. His possessions were three thousand sheep, three thousand camels, five hundred yokes of oxen, and five hundred she-asses, and a very great household. That man was great among all the people of the East.” Blessed Job was happy not only in righteousness and holiness, but also in the fruitfulness of offspring and abundance of every sort of wealth; indeed, he was greatest among all the people of the East. In this he very fittingly signifies Christ.

By his seven sons may be understood not only the apostles, full of the sevenfold grace of the Holy Spirit, but also the multitude of all the perfect. Thus blessed John wrote to only seven churches, as if to seven sons, by which he signified all others. Likewise, in this place seven means “many.” But what are the three daughters except the three parts of the world in which the whole Church consists: Asia, Africa, and Europe [Note: [Col. 0553D] Elsewhere the author maintains that the world is divided into four parts according to the four cardinal winds. Here, in order to adapt the interpretation to the text, he names only three, because America, the fourth part of the terrestrial globe, had not yet been discovered. We have already noted this in chapter XV of Numbers, p. 183.]? Sons and daughters differ in this: the former signify the more perfect, the latter persons who are less perfect.

Although the same thing signified by his sons and daughters may also be signified by his possessions, nevertheless the sheep may fittingly represent the simple; the camels, greater and powerful persons; the oxen, teachers of the Church; and the asses, those who gladly bear others’ burdens. By the great household we understand the multitude of all the faithful. Of the sheep it is written: “We are his people and the sheep of his pasture” (Psalm 94:7). Of the camels: “A multitude of camels shall cover you” (Isaiah 60:2). Of the oxen: “You shall not muzzle the ox treading out the grain” [Col. 0553B] (1 Corinthians 9:9). Moreover, the ass is greatly honored, since our Savior himself did not disdain to sit upon one. He desired us too to become asses when he said: “Bear one another’s burdens, and so fulfill the law of Christ” (Galatians 6:2).

The very number of the sheep, camels, oxen, and asses is not devoid of mystery. Seven and three can here signify the same thing as they signified in the sons and daughters. Five hundred, however, because this number is composed of five and one hundred, demonstrates perfection both in knowledge and in work. There are five books of Moses, in which complete and perfect knowledge is contained. The number one hundred may indeed be multiplied within itself, but cannot increase; hence it is undoubtedly considered perfect. Thus the more perfect members of the Church are rightly figured by the oxen and asses.

“That man was great among all the people of the East,” because it is also written of Christ: “There is none like you among the gods, O Lord” [Col. 0553C] (Psalm 85:8); and again: “For who among the clouds shall be equal to the Lord? Or who shall be like God among the sons of God?” (Psalm 88:7). It follows:

“His sons went and held a feast in their houses, each on his own day. And they sent and invited their three sisters to eat and drink with them.” The apostles and teachers went and held a feast in their houses because, scattered through all parts of the world, they fed both themselves and others by evangelical preaching. Each did this on his own day because not all preached at one time. While some withdraw, others still succeed them, preparing feasts for the hungry.

They sent to invite their three sisters to eat and drink with them because the teachers of the Church, by sweet persuasion, invite all parts of the world to Christ’s feast and to hear the word of God. Evangelical preaching is eaten when, because of its difficulty, it is scarcely understood by hearers [Col. 0554A]. It is drunk in plainer passages, where it is swallowed easily as water.

“And when the days of feasting had gone their round, Job sent for them and sanctified them; and, rising early in the morning, he offered burnt offerings for each one. For he said: ‘Perhaps my sons have sinned and blessed God in their hearts.’ Thus Job did on every day.” O most holy father, who had so instructed his sons that he feared only this concerning them: perhaps they had sinned in thought. But let us see this also in Christ.

The days of our feast always pass and continually succeed one another in turn. Hence we say daily: “Give us this day our daily bread” (Matthew 6:11). Therefore the most holy Job—that is, Christ our Lord—always sends to us. But what does he send? Everywhere, his grace: the Spirit of sanctification, who sanctifies us and frees us from sins. Job offered burnt offerings for each one because our Savior offered himself both for all and for every individual believer, and daily does not cease to offer himself through his ministers for our salvation.

His statement, “rising early in the morning,” shows with what great care this is done. Hence it is written: “For he has care for you” [Col. 0554B] (1 Peter 5:7); and therefore it adds: “For he said: ‘Perhaps my sons have sinned.’” Christ says this too, because, as the Apostle says, “appearing before the face of God for us, he daily intercedes” (Hebrews 9:24; Romans 8:34). To bless God in one’s heart is to think nothing evil of God [Note: [Col. 0553D] Ghisian manuscript: “But to curse God in one’s heart [Col. 0554D] is to think something evil of him.”].

“Thus Job did on every day.” For of God our Savior it is also said: “You are a priest forever” (Psalm 109:5). Christ therefore offers the burnt offering on every day—indeed, forever.

“Now one day, when the sons of God had come to stand before the Lord, Satan also was present among them. The Lord said to him: ‘Where have you come from?’ He answered: ‘I have gone round the whole earth and walked through it.’”

[223] How do the sons of God come to stand before the Lord, when they never depart from his sight [Note: [Col. 0554D] Angels are called sons of God insofar as they are made like God through participation in glory. St Thomas, lecture 11, commentary on Job.]? For the Lord says: “Their angels always see the face of my Father who is in heaven” (Matthew 18:10). Yet, because they always desire to see him, although they always stand before him, they are said to come before him as though absent.

Likewise Satan [Note: [Col. 0554D] The name *Satan* is Hebrew; in Latin, “adversary.” He is also called *diabolus*, as though “falling downward.” Cardinal Cajetan.], though cast down from the heights and unable to see God’s glory, is nevertheless said to have been present among them because he desired to be among the good angels. Thus the Apostle too says: “Our commonwealth is in heaven” [Col. 0555A] (Philippians 3:20), although it is surely not yet in heaven except by a certain affection and longing.

God speaks to Satan when he makes his will known to him; Satan speaks to the Lord [Note: [Col. 0555D] The same Cardinal Cajetan teaches that God spoke to Satan through species impressed upon his intellect, by which he made his will known.] because Satan’s wicked desires cannot be hidden from the Lord. For hearts speak to God no less than tongues do. Hence Moses says: “Why do you cry to me?” (Exodus 14:14), although Moses spoke not with his tongue but in his heart.

But what did Satan answer? “I have gone round the earth,” he says, “and walked through it.” For “our enemy the devil goes about like a roaring lion, seeking whom he may devour” (1 Peter 5:9). How continually and diligently he applies himself to fraud and deception is apparent from the statement that he had walked through the earth.

“Have you considered my servant Job, that there is none like him on earth: a man simple and upright, fearing the Lord and departing from evil?” These matters have been explained above. Christ, however, is called servant with respect to his flesh.

“Satan answered and said: ‘Does Job fear God for nothing? Have you not enclosed him and his house and all his substance round about, and blessed the works of his hands, so that his possessions have increased in the land? But stretch out your hand a little and touch all that he possesses: surely he will bless you to your face.’” See how Satan is present among the sons of God; see how he desires to stand before the Lord: namely, so that he may accuse the saints and receive power over them, since without God’s command and permission he can do nothing.

When God sees his wicked will and commands him by hidden inspiration to do or not to do something, then Satan stands before God and among the sons of God as though a servant ready to obey. With respect to God, Satan always stands before God, because his wicked will can never be hidden from God [Note: [Col. 0555D] “It should also be considered that things done through good angels are referred to God’s judgment differently from things done through evil angels. For good angels intend to refer to God what they do; [Col. 0556D] therefore it is said that the sons of God came to stand before the Lord, as though subjecting all things to divine judgment by their first motion and intention. Evil angels, however, do not intend to refer what they do to God; but, against their will, it happens that whatever they do is subjected to divine judgment or divine providence.” St Thomas, *On Job*, chapter 1, lecture 2.]. With respect to Satan, however, he is before God only when he can know God’s will by God’s prompting.

But what does Satan say? Does Job fear the Lord for nothing, when you so guard him, defend him, exalt him, bless him, and cause him to abound in all good things? It is as if he said: He does not fear you out of love, but lest he lose all these things if he ceases to fear you. Thus he adds: “But stretch out your hand a little and touch all that he possesses, and then you will see that he has blessed you not in heart but [Col. 0555D] to your face”: that is, not out of love but out of favor; not truly but deceptively; not in order to love you, but in order to seem to love you. Stretch out your hand, then; begin to scourge him, and the scourges will prove what kind of man he is.

Because the devil entertained such thoughts about Job—and such thought surely resounded in God’s ears—he is judged to have spoken these things concerning him.

“Then the Lord said to Satan: ‘Behold, all that he has is in your hand; only do not stretch out your hand against him.’ And Satan went out from the face of the Lord.” “All things,” says the Lord, “which are known to belong to Job are in your hand and power; but do not touch Job himself.” Having received this power, Satan went out from the face of the Lord—not because he is ever unseen by God, but because all his attention now eagerly turned, not to accusation but indeed to persecution.

If these things are referred to Christ, it must be understood that Satan at times believed him to be the Son of God, and at times a mere man. Hence in the Gospel they say: “We know that you are Christ” [Col. 0556A] (John 3:2); and again: “What have we to do with you, Son of God? Have you come before the time to torment us?” (Matthew 8:29). But when he saw Christ hungry, thirsty, and weary [Col. 0556B], though great and admirable, he nevertheless thought him to be nothing but a man. Therefore, if he were permitted by the Lord to tempt him, he supposed that he could stir him to sin. It follows:

> “Now when, one day, his sons and daughters were eating and drinking wine in the house of their eldest brother, a messenger came to Job and said: ‘The oxen were ploughing, and the she-asses were grazing beside them; and the Sabaeans swooped down, carried everything off, and I alone escaped to bring you the news.’” For at the time when Christ our Lord, according to the flesh, lived in Judaea, his sons and daughters—that is, the apostles and the rest who were more closely attached to him among that people—were eating and drinking the food and drink of the divine law in the house [Col. 0556C] of their eldest brother. For the house of the eldest brother is Judaea, since Israel is the eldest brother, of whom the Lord says: “Israel is my firstborn son” (Exod. 4:22). But while this was happening, and while our Saviour still remained peacefully in Judaea with his disciples, the devil, having received authority, suddenly took up arms against him and began so thoroughly to lay waste his possessions that an edict was published: if anyone confessed him to be the Christ, he was to be put out of the synagogue. Then indeed the Sabaeans first attacked, and carried off Christ’s oxen and she-asses. For “Sabaeans” means captors, by whom we understand evil spirits, who everywhere take wretched human beings captive from the kingdom of God.

> [Col. 0556D] The oxen and she-asses, however, are the priests and Levites. The former cultivate the field, while the latter bear burdens. Moses commanded the Levites to be, as it were, asses, when he ordered them alone to carry the tabernacle and all that was in it. Therefore the she-asses rightly grazed beside the oxen, because the Levites lived together with the priests on tithes and sacrifices. The devil first carried these off, because he knew that through them he could easily overcome the rest. By the servants struck with the sword [Col. 0557A] I think the angels given them by the Lord as guardians are meant. Seeing that they were transgressors plotting against Christ, these angels, struck by the sword of grief, left them. For of this sword it is written: “Iron passed through his soul” (Ps. 104:18). And likewise to the Virgin: “A sword will pierce your own soul also” (Luke 2:35). By the messenger, who alone always escapes and reports, what better can we understand than the Holy Spirit? Filled with him, our Saviour knew not only the deeds of his enemies but also their thoughts. Thus he himself often says: “Why do you think evil in your hearts?” (Matt. 9:4).

> “And while he was still speaking, another came and said: ‘Fire came down from heaven and consumed the sheep that it had struck and [Col. 0557B] the servants. I alone escaped to bring you the news.’” In order that Satan might more easily move blessed Job to impatience, he scourged him with frequent and uninterrupted blows. Fire is said to have descended from heaven so that it may not be doubted that this happened by God’s permission. [Note: [Col. 0557D] “With God permitting, demons can cause a disturbance in the air, stir up winds, and bring it about that fire falls from heaven.” St Thomas, on the cited passage.]

> Allegorically, fire descended from heaven and consumed the sheep and servants that had been struck, because the flame of indignation and hatred fell from the aforesaid priests and Levites upon the simple and undisciplined people. This flame consumed them because it separated them from justice and equity and incited them against God and their Lord. This flame also consumed the servants—not so that they ceased to exist, but so that they would no longer remain in them or with them. Hence, as Josephus relates, voices of angels [Col. 0557C] were heard in the Temple saying: [Note: [Col. 0558D] The author reports from Josephus that angelic voices were heard in the Temple crying out that their departure from those buildings was imminent.] “Let us leave these dwellings.”

> Let no one be troubled that another messenger is mentioned here—“another came”—for the Holy Spirit is both one and another: one in himself, but another in his gifts and workings. For the Apostle says: “There are varieties of gifts, but the same Spirit” (1 Cor. 12:4). Therefore, although he is one and the same, he is nevertheless called sevenfold: the Spirit of wisdom, the Spirit of understanding, the Spirit of counsel, and the Spirit of might. It follows:

> “But while he was still speaking, another came and said: ‘The Chaldaeans formed three bands, attacked the camels and carried them off; moreover, they struck the servants with the sword, and I alone escaped to bring you the news.’” [Col. 0557D] What are the Chaldaeans, whose name means, as it were, demons or fierce men, but evil spirits—or the aforesaid priests and Levites, with whom scarcely anything can be compared in ferocity and cruelty? They formed three bands, stirring up the people, Pilate, and Judas against Christ. They attacked the camels because they could deceive only those for whom it was impossible to enter the kingdom of heaven. Yet the messenger alone always escapes, because, as it is written: “The Holy Spirit will flee deceit and will not dwell in a body subject to sins” (Wis. 1:4). It follows:

> [Col. 0558A] “While he was still speaking, behold, another entered and said: ‘While your sons and daughters were eating and drinking in the house of your eldest brother, suddenly a violent wind came from the region of the wilderness, struck the four corners of the house, and it fell and crushed your children; they are dead, and I alone escaped to bring you the news.’” What the sons and daughters, and the eldest brother, signify has already been stated above. The violent wind signifies the severe and unbearable temptation of Satan which took place in Christ’s Passion. Hence it is said to have come from the region of the wilderness—that is, from the heart of the devil, deprived of every goodness and justice.

> The house is the synagogue. Its four corners are the priests and Levites, rulers and people, whom above he signified by oxen and she-asses, sheep [Col. 0558B] and camels. The wind shook these four corners and the house fell, because, when they could not resist the aforesaid temptation, the whole synagogue fell. Its collapse crushed not only the Jews but Christ’s own sons, that is, the apostles, because they too, severely tempted in the Lord’s Passion, wavered. Hence some of them said: “But we had hoped that he was the one who would redeem Israel” (Luke 24:21). And Thomas: “Unless I see in his hands the mark of the nails, and put my hand into his side, I will not believe” (John 20:25). Foretelling this temptation to them, the Lord himself also said: “Behold, Satan has demanded you, that he might sift you like wheat” (Luke 22:31). Thus they were for a time both crushed and dead, because in some manner they withdrew separated from God—than which there can be no greater death.

> “Then Job arose, tore his garment, and, having shaved his head, fell to the ground, worshipped, and said: ‘Naked I came out of my mother’s womb, and naked I shall return there.’” What grief inwardly gripped blessed Job is shown by what he did outwardly. Had he not done this, he would have been thought unconcerned. He therefore tore his garment and shaved his head—both signs of great grief. Yet grief did not overcome him so that he would say anything against God; and this openly shows how perfect he was. But what did he do? Falling to the ground, [Col. 0558D] he worshipped; in this Satan was overcome. And he said: “Naked I came out of my mother’s womb; naked I shall return there.” That is: I brought nothing into this world; when I die, I shall carry with me nothing of the things of this world. They belonged to the Lord: when he wished, he gave; when he wished, he took away. It is nothing to me. “Blessed be the name of the Lord.”

> “In all these things Job did not sin with his lips, nor did he speak anything foolish against God.” But since Job signifies Christ, let us see how these matters too apply to Christ. “Then,” he says, “Job arose.” When? Do you wish to hear when? When [Col. 0559A] the house fell; when the synagogue collapsed. Then Christ truly arose; then his kingdom and dominion increased, because, having left the Jews, he received the whole world as his inheritance, according to the words: “Ask of me, and I shall give you the nations as your inheritance” (Ps. 2:8).

> He tore his garment so that the Gentile people, to whom he was coming, might openly and plainly see him naked. This garment is the divine Scripture. It has not yet been torn for the Jews; therefore, under the veil of the letter, they cannot see the hidden Christ. He shaved his head when he cut off and separated from himself and from his body, which is the Church, the unbelieving and impious Jews, who, like shaved hairs, have always proved unsteady and unstable. Falling to the ground, he worshipped, because, as though coming unexpectedly to the Gentiles, who were earth and sinners, [Col. 0559B] he taught them to worship no longer idols but the one true God. Thus the Apostle says of the Holy Spirit: “He intercedes for us with inexpressible groanings” (Rom. 8:26): he prays, that is, he teaches us to pray.

> And he said: “Naked I came out of my mother’s womb”—that is, leaving the synagogue’s hiding-place, I appeared openly and manifestly to the Gentiles. “And naked I shall return there,” because near the end of the world I shall reveal myself to the Jewish people no longer in obscurity, but openly. “For when the fullness of the Gentiles has entered, then all Israel will be saved” (Rom. 11:25). It follows:

## CHAPTER II

> “Now it happened that one day the sons of God came and stood before the Lord, and Satan too came among them [Col. 0559C] and stood in his presence. And the Lord said to Satan: ‘Whence do you come?’ He answered: ‘I have gone around the earth and walked through it.’ And the Lord said to Satan: ‘Have you considered my servant Job, that there is none like him on the earth—a simple and upright man, fearing God and turning away from evil, and still retaining his innocence? Yet you moved me against him, that I might afflict him without cause.’”

> These matters have been explained above. The Lord struck Job “without cause” as regards the devil his accuser, because he neither lost his innocence nor had committed any sin for which he ought to suffer such things. Yet not without cause as regards God, since through this his merit and crown increased, and he left many an example of his patience. Christ too was killed both without cause and not without cause: without cause for those who thought he would not rise again, but not without cause for us, who have been redeemed by his blood. When the devil deceived the first human being—the sin for which Christ suffered—then he moved God against Christ.
