For then the Father in some manner said to the Son: You indeed shall die for this sin. It follows:

> “Satan answered and said: ‘Skin for skin; and everything that a man has he will give for his life. But stretch out your hand and touch his bone [Col. 0560A] and flesh, and then you will see that he will bless you to your face.’” As though he said: It is very customary and reasonable for things less dear and cheap to be disregarded for the sake of things more precious. Thus a person sets skin against skin, and, fearing a blow to the eye, presents his arm. He also gives everything else for his life and soul, because, lest he be killed, he thinks little of losing all his property. Thus Job too, because he is healthy and unharmed, considers as nothing whatever happens to him. Touch him in himself, therefore, and begin to afflict the flesh, which feels pain more acutely. The devil said this both of Job and of Christ, because he thought such things of both.

> “And the Lord said to Satan: ‘Behold, he is in your hand; nevertheless preserve his life.’” 226 What does “preserve his life” mean but: you cannot tempt his soul [Col. 0560B]? [Note: [Col. 0559D] “That is, do not take his life from him. God does not wholly expose his servants to Satan’s will, but according to a fitting measure, in accordance with that saying of the Apostle, 1 Corinthians 10: ‘God is faithful, who does not allow you to be tempted beyond what you can bear.’” St Thomas, in the same passage.]

> “Therefore Satan went out from the presence of the Lord and struck Job with a most grievous sore from the sole of his foot to the crown of his head. And he sat on a dunghill, scraping away the discharge with a potsherd.” Job, struck with a sore not merely grievous but most grievous, and not in one part of his body but from the sole of his foot to the crown of his head, showed how little he valued his flesh by scraping away the discharge with a potsherd and sitting on a dunghill. Such a bed and such a remedy are harsh even for those who suffer nothing. Let Satan, therefore, be ashamed, he who said: “Touch his bone and flesh, and then you will see that he will bless you to your face.”

> Christ likewise was struck with a most grievous wound—that is, condemned to the most disgraceful death—from the sole of his foot to the crown of his head, when he suffered in his whole body while hanging [Col. 0560C] upon the cross. He scraped away the discharge with a potsherd: that is, with his flesh, formerly assumed from earth but now baked in the fire of the Passion upon the cross, he destroyed the corruption of our sins. He sat upon a dunghill because he was still in Judaea, which he rightly calls a dunghill. Thus far concerns the head; what follows must be referred to the members.

> “Then his wife said to him: ‘Do you still persist in your simplicity? Bless God and die.’” As though she said: What use, she says, is your simplicity to you? It is better that you bless the Lord and die. Say something against God, so that he may be offended and in anger remove you from this life, in which you suffer things far worse than death itself.

> [Col. 0560D] “But he said to her: ‘You have spoken like one of the foolish women. If we have received good things from the hand of the Lord, why should we not also endure evil things?’ In all these things Job did not sin with his lips.” Job sometimes signifies Christ, sometimes one of the perfect, and sometimes the whole Church. In this place he can signify one who is perfect: when he was in a great persecution, his wife—that is, his flesh, which is the wife of his spirit—overcome by fear of death, urged him to deny Christ, saying: “Bless God and die.” Die, she says, eternally, lest you die now. But he rebuked her as a foolish woman [Col. 0561A] and refused to follow her advice. It follows:

> “Now when Job’s three friends heard of all the evil that had come upon him, they came, each from his own place: Eliphaz the Temanite, Bildad the Shuhite, and Zophar the Naamathite. They had agreed to come together, visit him, and console him.” Job’s three friends represent heretics. Having formed a conspiracy among themselves, because they cannot otherwise deceive the Church, they pretend that they have come to visit and console her, and to grieve over her miseries. Thus they come, each from his own place, like chosen and poisonous arrows from the devil’s quiver—as their very names show. For Eliphaz means “contempt of God.” But from where does this proud man who despises God come? Certainly from Teman, which means “the south”; for the south wind is rainy. Eliphaz, therefore, comes to the Church full of an inundation of rains, by which she may be submerged rather than satisfied.

> Bildad also means “oldness alone.” But whence does this Bildad come, who follows only the oldness of the letter, except from Shuah? And Shuah means “speaking.” Thus he comes from Shuah because he trusts not in truth but in talkativeness. Zophar, however, means “the destruction of the watchtower.” This man strives to destroy the watchtower—that is, Zion and the holy Church—and is said to come from Naamah. Naamah means “beauty.” Thus he comes from Naamah because he does not wish to endure tribulations with the saints, but desires to possess the world’s glory and beauty with lovers of the age.

> “When they lifted up their eyes from afar, they did not recognize [Col. 0561C] him; and crying aloud, they wept. Tearing their garments, they scattered dust over their heads toward heaven; and they sat with him on the ground seven days and seven nights, and none spoke a word to him, for they saw that the grief was very great.” Heretics, looking at the Church, do not recognize her, because they neither love her nor wish to imitate her works. They cry aloud and weep over her because they pretend to grieve with her. Therefore they tear their garments and scatter dust on their heads, which is a sign of grief. Heretics often pretend to sympathize with and pity the Church, as though she were sick in faith and straying from truth. Thus, as though wishing to heal her, they preach to her [Col. 0561D] the deceptions of their own error.

> The seven days and seven nights during which Job’s friends sat with him without speaking, I think to be the entire time from Christ’s Passion until the reign of the Emperor Constantine. During this time the Church was under the greatest persecution. Therefore it is rightly said here: “For they saw that the grief was very great.” In this time the heretics were silent. Although they sat [Col. 0562A] with the Church, they did not dare to speak, for they too were Christians, and feared that, if recognized, they might be killed. But after peace was granted and the Church began to speak confidently, the heretics rose up. Then councils were held against them among all peoples. Hence it follows:

## CHAPTER III

> “After this Job opened his mouth, cursed his day, and spoke: ‘Let the day perish on which I was born, and the night on which it was said: A man has been conceived.’” In this place, day and night signify the devil. For he is day when, as the Apostle says, he transforms himself into an angel of light (2 Cor. 2:14); and he is night because he is prince of darkness and blinds and darkens the eyes of the mind of those who follow him. [Col. 0562B] He was first, according to his nature, a day, created brightest and most splendid among all angels. Yet all human beings are born in this day—that is, in original sin, brought about by this day’s suggestion and contrivance. Hence David says: “For I was conceived in iniquities, and in sins my mother conceived me” (Ps. 50:6). Let this day, therefore—that is, this day’s sin—perish. [Note: [Col. 0561D] “He desires the day of his carnal generation to perish, so that his day may be counted in regeneration. Let the worldly day perish, he says, so that the spiritual day may rise.” St Ambrose, *On the Good of Death*, book 2, chapter 2.]

> This is an effect put for its cause. For it is most foolish to understand this literally, since neither has a day committed any sin nor can something which no longer exists perish in any way. [Note: [Col. 0561D] Bruno perhaps commented on this in the sense of the same St Ambrose. For Ambrose says, in his exposition of Luke, IV: “In temptation, holy Job speaks mysteries”; and in book II of *On the Interpretation of Job*, chapter 2, he says: “Sitting on dung, amid so many welts and wounds of fierce pain, his whole body covered with dreadful sores, he spoke mysteries. He did not occupy himself with a remedy for his own illness, but with sacred discourses. The words of the sick man were therefore stronger than those of persons who were not sick. Thus he spoke not the groans of the flesh and bodily weaknesses, but the utterances of the spirit, by which he might press on rather than yield.”]

> Let this day perish—or rather, it is now no longer day but night, for it has lost its brightness. Hence it follows:

> “Let that day be turned into darkness,” so that it may be called no longer [Col. 0562C] day but night. “Let God not seek it from above,” so as ever to show it mercy; “and let it not be remembered,” except to be scourged and tormented with eternal fires. Nor let it be illumined by the light of his brightness; rather, let him always show himself angry with it. Of this light it is said: “May God have mercy on us and bless us; may he make his face shine upon us” (Ps. 66:1). Let darkness and the shadow of death darken it, lest, looking upon and recalling its lost glory, it should deserve to be saved or restored to life by repenting. Therefore he adds: “Let gloom seize it”—namely, the gloom of eternal oblivion and obstinacy—“and let it be wrapped in bitterness,” of every torment and affliction. Hence the Lord says to sinners: [Col. 0562D] “Depart from me, you cursed, into the eternal fire prepared for the devil and his angels” (Matt. 25:41). It follows:

> “Let a dark whirlwind possess that night.” He rightly calls him no longer day but night, whom he sees surrounded by such darkness and thick gloom. What he says in the form of a curse must be understood affirmatively as being so. The dark whirlwind that possesses this night is he of whom the Psalmist [Col. 0563A] says: “He will rain snares upon them; fire, sulphur, and a stormy wind are the portion of their cup” (Ps. 10:9).

> “Let it not be counted among the days of the year, nor numbered among the months.” This year is the year of eternity, whose days, months, and hours consist only of saints; its sun, moon, and every brightness and illumination are Christ. Of it the Psalmist says: “In your book they shall all be written; days shall be formed, and no one among them” (Ps. 13:16). No one will be counted or named among them, because he is enveloped in diabolical darkness. “For the saints will shine like the sun in the kingdom of God” (Matt. 13:43).

> “Let that night be barren and not worthy of praise.” It will indeed be solitary, because there will be no other night. For the aforesaid year will have not nights but days alone, [Col. 0563B] because no one there will lack eternal light.

> “Let those curse it who curse the day, who are ready to rouse Leviathan.” Let those, he says, now curse him, dark and enveloped in gloom, who cursed him at the beginning, when he was still day and bright, because in pride he wished to ascend above all the heavens. But who are these except God’s angels, who at that time held him bound because they did not permit him to carry out all his wickedness? Yet in their time they were ready to rouse him. [Note: [Col. 0563] This interpretation follows the Septuagint, which rendered the word “rouse” as “subdue.” Thus Pineda on this passage.] We think this has been fulfilled, for it is written: “After a thousand years Satan will be released” (Rev. 20:7).

> “Leviathan” means “their addition.” But whose addition? Certainly that of our first parents: by promising to add to them the honour and dignity of that day, he took from them blessedness and immortality. It follows:

> “Let its stars be darkened by its gloom.” Of these stars the Apostle Jude says: “Woe to them who have gone in the way of Cain and followed the example of Balaam” (Jude 11). And shortly afterward: “These are wandering stars, for whom the storms of darkness are kept for ever” (ibid., 13). Wicked human beings, who outwardly seem to shine in strength and wisdom, are inwardly darkened by the devil’s gloom.

> “Let it await light and not see it, nor the rising of the dawning morning.” Although unwillingly, this evil spirit too awaits the day of judgment, when the Lord will come in his own brightness to judge. And [Col. 0563D] because it will then be said, “Let the wicked be taken away, lest he see the glory of God” (Isa. 26:10), he will not see the long-awaited light. The dawn, however, is the Church, of which Solomon says: “Who is this that comes forth like the rising dawn?” (Song 6:9). The Church will rise—indeed, rise again—at the judgment. Yet just as the devil will not deserve to see God’s glory, neither will he deserve to see the rising of the Church as she rises. Why is this? “Because he did not close the doors of the womb that bore me.” This womb is paradise, in which—and not in another womb—the human being was first born. The devil is said not to have closed it because he opened it. “Nor did he take away evils from [Col. 0564A] my eyes.” For, offering me in the first human being the tree of desire, he blinds me while promising to open my eyes. It follows:

> “Why did I not die in the womb?” Blessed Job, taking upon himself the person of the first human being, laments the calamity of the whole human race. The womb through which Adam went out from paradise was the devil’s first suggestion itself; if Adam had not accepted it, he would not have been expelled from paradise. He therefore says: “Why did I not die in the womb?” That is: why did I not understand that death threatened me in that very suggestion, if I consented to it? For he would have died in the womb had he separated himself from the suggestion as soon as he heard it.

> What is death except separation? A human being dies when the soul is separated from the body; one also dies to God when separated from him. Likewise, one dies to the world and to sin when separated from the world and sin. Thus the Apostle says: “I died to the world” (Rom. 7:10). Here this death is meant in the words, “Why did I not die in the womb?”—that is, why did I not flee at once upon hearing the suggestion? Every person in some sense dies to that from which he is separated. This, he says, I did not do; but, what is far worse, passing beyond the suggestion by listening to it, I came as far as delight. And although I ought here to have died by the aforesaid death, even this was not enough for me: received upon the knees and drawing near to the breasts, I tasted the milk of death and ate the forbidden fruit. This is what is said: “Why did I not perish immediately when I came from the womb? Why was I received [Col. 0564C] upon knees? Why was I nursed at breasts?” For the devil holds the sinner, as it were, upon his knees when the wretched person now stands close to the unspeakable deed. It follows:

> “For now I should sleep in silence and rest in my sleep.” If, he says, I had not listened to the devil’s suggestion; if, after hearing it, I had not delighted in that suggestion; if, delighting in it, I had not approached the touch of the forbidden tree; and if, approaching, I had at least not eaten from the fruit of desire—then I would now sleep in silence and rest in my sleep: that is, I would possess heavenly blessedness and rest. With whom? “With kings and consuls of the earth, who build solitudes for themselves.” By these words blessed Job seems to say that, if the first human being had not sinned, then in his own time, when the number of the elect had been completed, he would already enjoy the highest blessedness together with all those predestined to eternal life. Unless perhaps “time” is taken for time, or he himself for others; for “now” signifies present time. For if the first human being had not sinned, no one would ever be born unless predestined to eternal blessedness.

> Kings and counsellors mean either angels or teachers of the Church, who govern themselves and others well and provide the best counsel to all people. They build solitudes for themselves because in this age they live a solitary life, one greatly different from the life of other people. [Col. 0565A] “Or with princes who possess gold and fill their houses with silver”: by these, likewise, are meant the same teachers of the Church, who possess the treasure of wisdom and have filled the houses of their hearts with the silver of eloquence. For in Holy Scripture gold frequently signifies wisdom, and silver the purity of speech. It follows:

> “Or, like a hidden miscarriage, I should not exist; or like those conceived who did not see the light.” These words are spoken in the person of the first human being, who contains in himself both the righteous and sinners. Let it therefore be said: If the first human being had not sinned, then either all human beings would already be with the Lord now, or those who were not there would neither exist nor be—like miscarriages by comparison. For, because a miscarriage is not born in its proper time, as soon as it is born it is hidden away and, as though it had never been, does not remain at all in human memory. [Col. 0565B] [Note: [Col. 0565D] St Bruno must here be understood to speak of miscarried fetuses which, because of excessive immaturity, have not yet been endowed with a soul. For miscarried fetuses endowed with a soul subsist through that soul; and, having contracted original sin with their generation, they are under eternal damnation. Thus the celebrated Hyacinth Ceruti translated it:

> *Or would I not now be like a hidden miscarriage,*  
> *Or like an immature fetus, etc.*

> [Col. 0566D] St Thomas held the same view: “For from miscarried fetuses of this sort,” he says, “nothing permanent remains; but some die after the infusion of a rational soul, and these subsist after death according to the soul, though they do not see such light.” St Thomas, in the same passage.]

> The words “those conceived who did not see the light” mean the same thing, for they too are miscarriages. It follows:

> “There the wicked ceased from tumult.” Where? There, certainly, where I would now sleep in silence and rest in my sleep. For there the wicked—that is, evil spirits—having been cast down, ceased from the tumult and discord which they were trying to cause there. “And there those wearied in strength rested.” For there now rest the souls of the saints, who in this world wearied themselves greatly with the virtue and strength of faith against the wicked. “And [Col. 0565C] there those bound together are without trouble”—understand: there they rest. For there now rest without trouble those who, joined in faith and love in this life, suffered many troubles because they could not be divided from faith and love. Of them he further says: “They did not hear the voice of the taskmaster.” Although they endured many troubles, they did not assent to the taskmaster’s voice. This taskmaster can mean either some tyrant or the devil. For vices are the devil’s money; whoever receives it subjects himself to slavery. “The small and great are there, and the servant is free from his master.” There prelates and subjects, servants and masters, are without distinction, because all are subject to one King and one Lord. It follows:

> [Col. 0565D] “Why is light given to the wretched, and life to those who are bitter in soul?” Having considered heavenly blessedness and also the misery of this world, blessed Job, weary of this life, speaks for himself and those like him, saying: “Why is light given to the wretched?” He uses “light” for this life. Why, he says, do those who know themselves to be wretched here live here so long? Even if the world smiles upon them and they are enriched with its fleeting riches, nevertheless, contemplating heavenly things alone, they are always here in sadness and bitterness of soul, because they always long to depart from here and die. Hence he adds: “Who await death, and it does not come.” But with what desire? Do you wish to hear? “As though digging for treasure.” For the saints truly find treasure and eternal happiness when, their body having been put to death, they depart from this life. Thus the Apostle says: “I desire to be dissolved and to be with Christ” (Phil. 1:23).

> “And they rejoice exceedingly when they find the grave”—that is, when its predestined time arrives, in which the flesh is received into the grave and the soul into heaven. Even literally, those digging for treasure rejoice when they find a grave, because they often [Col. 0566B] find treasure there. It follows:

> “To the man whose way is hidden, and whom God has surrounded with darkness.” I said, he says, “Why is light given to the wretched?” But to what wretched man? Certainly to the man whose way is hidden. Our way is hidden, and we are wrapped in such darkness of ignorance that we wholly do not know what will happen to us. Therefore, one whom conscience defends should greatly desire to depart from here, lest by some chance he fall into something worse. Blessed Job says this because he desires it.

> “Before I eat, I sigh; and my roaring is like rushing waters, because the fear which I feared has come upon me, and what I dreaded has happened to me. Did I not dissemble? Did I not keep silence? Did I not rest? Yet indignation came upon me.” Before I eat, he says—before I taste the sweetness of that delight of which I now speak, before I am refreshed with the sweetness of the highest good—what else do I do here except sigh and suffer under the desire for that great banquet? “And my roaring is like rushing waters,” because the groaning of my heart does not occur without a flood of many tears. Why is this? “Because the fear which I feared has come upon me.” Since this holy man was afflicted by such great scourges, he thought that he had offended God in some matter, although he did not know in what he had offended. Thus in what follows he says: “I have sinned; what shall I do to you?” Nevertheless, considering his life and not knowing what evil he had done that he should be so afflicted, [Col. 0566D] he adds: “Did I not dissemble?” That is: when the world smiled upon me and I possessed everything, I conducted myself and took delight in all these things as though I possessed nothing. Hence he adds: “Did I not keep silence? Did I not rest?” As though he said: If I delighted in such riches, I would neither keep silence nor rest, because such riches are acquired neither in silence nor in rest, but rather through many disputes and labours. [Col. 0567A] “Yet indignation came upon me,” and I am uncertain why it came. For he believed that God was angry with him because he felt God’s scourges upon himself.

## CHAPTER IV
“Then Eliphaz the Temanite answered and said: ‘If we begin to speak to you, perhaps you will take it ill; but who can restrain a conceived utterance?’” Behold Eliphaz, whose name is interpreted as “contempt of God,” who also, representing heretics, comes from the south—for this is the interpretation of Theman—is so puffed up with showers of eloquence that he cannot keep in a conceived speech without its bursting forth. He speaks in the manner of heretics, who, though they begin humbly, break out at last into insults. But what does he say? [Col. 0567B] “Behold, you have taught many and strengthened weary hands.” This indeed is true: “Your words have confirmed the wavering, and you have strengthened trembling knees.” This likewise is true: “But now a blow has come upon you”; and this certainly cannot be denied. “And you have failed.” But this is false: for he did not fail, but fought manfully and conquered. “It has touched you, and you are troubled.” For if he had been troubled, he would by no means have said so calmly: “If we have received good things from the hand of the Lord, why should we not also endure evil things?” It follows:

“Where is your fear, your strength, and the perfection of your ways?” For he thought that Job had lost all these things because he saw him so humbled. “Remember, I beg you: who ever perished being innocent, or [Col. 0567C] when were the upright destroyed?” It is characteristic of heretics often to mix falsehoods with truths: for in this life the innocent and upright often do perish. “Rather, I have seen those who work iniquity, sow sorrows, and reap them, perish by the blast of God and be consumed [230] by the breath of His wrath.” This indeed often happens, but not always. Those sow and reap sorrows who act wickedly and receive evil in return. For God “to blow” means that He shows Himself angry against sinners in vengeance. When a man is angry, he emits a greater breath; hence a blast is taken to signify wrath.

“The roaring of the lion, the voice of the lioness, and the teeth of the lion’s cubs are broken.” By the lion he metaphorically signifies blessed Job; by the lioness, his wife; and by the lion’s cubs, his children. [Col. 0567D] By roaring he reproves cruelty, by voice loquacity, and by teeth gluttony—gluttony, indeed, because they were overwhelmed while eating and drinking.

“The tiger perished because it had no prey.” Again he calls Job a tiger. For the tiger is a most savage animal. Thus he says that blessed Job has perished because, his strength being lost, he no longer has the ability to seize prey. It follows:

“Moreover, a hidden word was spoken to me, and my ear secretly received the vein of its whisper.” Heretics always promise great things and, so that it may carry greater authority, exalt their own knowledge—just as this man now seems to do. For he says that a hidden and secret word, unknown to other people, [Col. 0568A] was revealed to him; and that he himself received, as though furtively, secretly and cleverly, the vein of this word—that is, its beginning and completion. And, in order to commend his own ingenuity more highly, he confesses that he heard it not openly but, as it were, in a whisper. Let us hear what this word is.

“In the dread of a nocturnal vision, when sleep is accustomed to seize men, fear held me and all my bones were terrified. And as a spirit passed before me, the hairs of my flesh stood on end. Someone stood there, whose face I did not recognize; an image was before my eyes, and I heard a voice like a gentle breeze.” Eliphaz seems to have said this so that the things he was about to say might carry greater authority: namely, that he might be believed not to have devised them himself, [Col. 0568B] but to have learned them by divine revelation; for many things are revealed to men in dreams through visions. When he says, “As a spirit passed before me,” it is as if he said: “When that spiritual vision passed before me while I was present and observing most attentively.” Since it was not seen all at once, it in some sense passed by, because it came to be while passing. Who, then, was that person whose face he did not recognize? He explains this immediately when he says: “An image was before my eyes.” For he saw not the reality of the thing, but its image. Thus in dreams we often see images of our friends, even though they are far away.

He heard a voice like a gentle breeze, because things appearing in dreams are heard so softly by the mind’s perception that, unless they are at once [Col. 0568C] considered by the waking person, they very easily slip from memory. Let others investigate what fear and trembling, terrified bones, and bristling hairs signify; for us these things suffice, and we do not doubt that such occurrences often happen in dreams. Now let us see what Eliphaz heard in that voice of the gentle breeze. It follows:

“Can a man be justified in comparison with God, or can a man be purer than his Maker?” Not only dreamers but also those who reflect understand this to be so. For no one is more just or purer than God. Yet it is characteristic of heretics to make difficult even things which are most easy, since, while they themselves alone—or almost alone—understand nothing, they suppose that no one but themselves understands. [Col. 0568D] Therefore Eliphaz calls hidden a word that is manifest to almost everyone. In these words he thinks to defeat blessed Job: for if Job is afflicted unjustly, he seems to be more just and pure than God who afflicts him; but since this cannot happen, it necessarily follows that Job is afflicted justly. This sophistry is answered where the Lord said above: “But you moved me against him, to afflict him without cause.” For “without cause” and “not without cause” are equivalent to “unjustly” and “justly.” Job is afflicted unjustly with respect to himself, because he committed no sin for which he ought to have been so afflicted; but justly with respect to God, who afflicts him in order to make him more illustrious, holier, and richer. It follows:

“Behold, those who serve Him are not steadfast, and in [Col. 0569A] His angels He found perversity.”

[Note: [Col. 0569D] “Behold, those who serve Him are not steadfast, and in His angels He found perversity.” This statement is plain according to the teaching of the Catholic faith. For the Catholic faith maintains that all angels were created good: some of them, through their own fault, [Col. 0570D] fell from the state of uprightness, while others attained greater glory. D. TH., in the same commentary, chapter 4.]

“How much more those who inhabit houses of clay, who have an earthly foundation.” This too is said against Job. He proves that it is impossible not to sin, since it is manifest that even angels sinned. But this is to be understood of evil spirits. Men inhabit houses of clay and have an earthly foundation because they were formed from clay and earth. Of them he further says:

“They shall be consumed as by a moth; from morning until evening they shall be cut down; and because no one understands, they shall perish forever.” For worms arise from human flesh and consume it, just as a moth arises from a garment and consumes the very garment from which it arose. Sinners too are consumed as by a moth, [Col. 0569B] because, as the prophet says, “Their worm shall not die” (Isa. 66:24). [231] They are cut down from morning until evening—that is, from the beginning of their birth until the end of life—because, as long as they are in this life, by continually acting wickedly they kill themselves. For as often as they sin, so often do they strike and cut themselves down. And because none of them understands either the evils he commits or the remedy of repentance, they will deservedly perish forever. Hence it is added: “They shall die, and not in wisdom.” The order is thus: they shall die, and not in wisdom. For those who end their life in sins and folly do not die in wisdom. “But those who remain shall be taken away from them.” The remnant of the wicked are the good, who are left by the devil’s teeth because the devil cannot overcome them. Thus it is also said that only a remnant of Israel will be saved. These will be taken away from them when it is said: “Come, blessed of my Father, receive the kingdom” (Matt. 25:34). It follows:

## CHAPTER V

“Call then, if there is anyone who will answer you, and turn to one of the saints.” How bad an opinion Eliphaz had of blessed Job is sufficiently apparent, since he hurls all these sayings against him. Because he saw him so afflicted, he thought him utterly cast off by the Lord. Therefore, although Job cried greatly to God, he nevertheless supposed that he was not heard. This is what is said: “Call then, if there is anyone who will answer you.” And what follows, [Col. 0569D] “Turn to one of the saints,” is as though he said: “Since God does not hear you because your sins require it, at least entreat one of the saints to intercede with God for you.” It follows:

“Anger kills the foolish man, and envy slays the little one.” The foolish and the little signify the same thing, since every fool is little and ignorant in understanding and self-control. Anger and [Col. 0570A] envy kill such a person because, while he envies and furiously seeks what belongs to another, he falls into the devil’s snare. But this ought not to have been said of blessed Job. It follows:

“I saw the fool firmly rooted, and immediately I cursed his beauty.” When a fool prospers in the world’s riches and dignities, he seems to stand with a firm root. Yet some wise person curses his beauty, reflecting within himself on the curse to which he is liable and how quickly he will lose this glory. Hence also the Apostle: “The natural man does not receive the things of God; but the spiritual man judges all things” (1 Cor. 2:14).

“His children shall be far from salvation; they shall be crushed in the gate, and there shall be none to rescue them.” The children of this fool are all who imitate his folly. These [Col. 0570B] shall be far from salvation, “because salvation is far from sinners” (Ps. 118:155). They shall be crushed in the gate because, at the very entrance of the kingdom, when the gates of paradise are opened, it will be said to them: “Depart, accursed ones, into eternal fire” (Matt. 25:41). “And there shall be none to rescue them,” since no one intercedes for them.

“Hungry men shall eat his harvest; the armed man shall seize him, and the thirsty shall drink his riches.” The hungry, he says, shall eat this fool’s harvest and labor. By these we understand evil spirits, whose food is wickedness and evil action; for this is their delight and refreshment. The armed man shall seize him: namely, he of whom the Lord says in the Gospel, “When a strong man armed guards his courtyard, the things which he possesses are in peace” (Luke 11:21). “And the thirsty [Col. 0570C] shall drink his riches”: this is what he has just said, “Hungry men shall eat his harvest.” It follows:

“Nothing happens on earth without cause, and sorrow does not arise from the ground.” It is as though he said: “You yourself, and not another, brought forth this affliction.” For God is just and does nothing without cause and reason. It is not the soil or the earth, but rather, he says, because we are sinners that we are afflicted.

“Man is born for labor, and the bird for flight.”

[Note: [Col. 0570D] Codex of the Library of Monte Amiata: “for flying.”]

It is as though he said: “At least acknowledge this sin of yours: that, being devoted only to pleasure and luxuries, you did not rebuke your own children for giving themselves to feasting and drunkenness.” Man is born not for rest and pleasure but for labor; hence it was said to the first man: “In the sweat of your face you shall eat your bread” (Gen. 3:19). Likewise, the bird is born for flight, and wings were therefore given to it, just as hands were given to man. But because man is both man and bird—for one part is heavy and from the earth, while another is heavenly and swift—he was born for flight according to this latter part, that is, the soul. Therefore let him not lie in the depths, but by flying contemplate heavenly things. Hence it is added: “Therefore I will entreat the Lord, and to God I will direct [Col. 0571A] my speech”; that is, I shall fly and be exalted above the heavens in mind and spirit; there I shall entreat the Lord, and there speak with Him. For when the saints implore God in their prayers, though they are bodily upon earth, in spirit they fly beyond heaven itself.

“He who does great and unsearchable things, and wonders without number.” For no one can investigate or count God’s wonders.

“He who gives rain upon the face of the earth, and waters all things with waters.” This is so wondrous that no one can investigate it. Who [232] can understand what clouds are, when they bear water, when they hold it back, and when they scatter it so wonderfully, drop by drop? If these things are understood allegorically, the Lord also gives rain—that is, Gospel preaching—upon the face of the earth, and waters all things with spiritual waters.

“He who sets the humble on high, and raises mourners to safety.” For He humbles the proud and exalts the humble.

“He who frustrates the thoughts of the wicked, so that their hands cannot accomplish what they have begun; who takes the wise in their craftiness.” [Col. 0571B] For, as the Apostle says, God has made foolish the wisdom of this world (1 Cor. 1:20). While the wise seek rational explanation, they do not believe God’s wonders; thus they contend neither that God assumed flesh, nor that a virgin gave birth, nor that one who died rose again. “And He scatters the counsel of the perverse”: that is, of the Jews and tyrants, [Col. 0571C] who, through many counsels and schemes, attempted to destroy Christ’s name and the Church.

“By day they shall encounter darkness, and at noon they shall grope as in the night.” At Christ’s passion, darkness occurred even literally. Indeed, they encountered darkness by day when they did not recognize Christ, who was most openly manifesting Himself through signs and miracles. And though all things were naked and open, they saw nothing, like blind men groping in the night. They groped at noon as in night when, while seeing His signs and miracles, they asked Him whether He was the Christ; to them He said: “If you do not believe me, believe the works” (John 10:38). “But He shall save the needy from the sword of their mouth, [Col. 0571D] and the poor from the hand of the violent man.” This is that needy and poor man of whom the Apostle says: “As having nothing, yet possessing all things” (2 Cor. 6:10). These could be conquered neither by the sword of iron nor by the sword of the mouth, because they were overcome neither by flatteries or threats nor by tortures. Why is this? It follows:

“And there shall be hope for the needy.” “For,” says the Apostle, “we were saved in hope” (Rom. 9:28). Because of their hope for eternal goods they could not be overcome. “But iniquity shall shut its mouth,” seeing them to be invincible. “Blessed is the man whom God corrects.” [Note: [Col. 0571] Solomon likewise says: “Whom the Lord loves He corrects, and as a father He takes pleasure in him” (Prov. 3:12).]

For by this means he is separated from the iniquity [Col. 0572A] that he commits; whoever is not corrected sins more securely. “Therefore do not reject the Lord’s rebuke,” because He wounds and heals; He strikes, and His hands will cure. To reject God’s rebuke is to murmur against His scourges.

“In six tribulations He shall deliver you, and in the seventh evil shall not touch you.” There are seven tribulations because there are seven days in which we are afflicted. But He set the seventh apart because it will be greater and will have an end. What these tribulations are, He adds:

“In famine He shall rescue you from death, and in war from the hand of the sword; you shall be hidden from the scourge of the tongue, and you shall not fear calamity when it comes; in devastation and famine you shall laugh, and you shall not fear the beast of the earth.” Of this famine the prophet says: “I shall send among you not a famine of bread or a thirst for water, but a famine of hearing the word of God” (Ezek. 5:17). The saints do not die from this famine. They are delivered also in war from the hand of the sword when, fighting against vices, they are able to overcome the devil’s temptations. They are hidden from the scourge of the tongue because they neither slander others nor answer those who slander them. Nor do they fear calamity when it comes, because they know that through many tribulations they must enter the heavenly kingdoms. They will laugh in devastation and famine because they will rejoice exultantly when sinners are devastated in punishments and tormented by everlasting famine. Nor will they fear the beast of the earth—that is, the devil, who devours and destroys the earthly and sinful—[Col. 0572C] because, when they depart from this world, he will be unable to harm them. It follows:

“But you shall have a covenant with the stones of the regions, and the beasts of the earth shall be at peace with you.” These are the stones of which it is said: “Living stones roll upon the earth” (Zech. 9:16); by them we understand the saints, of whom the walls of the heavenly Jerusalem will be built. Not only Job but every saint has made a covenant with them because he clings to them by the bond of charity. The beasts are understood to be impious and cruel men, who, when they consider the patience and humility of the saints, become peaceful toward them, because, terrified by divine prompting, they fear to offend them. Hence it is added:

[Col. 0572D] “And you shall know that your tent has peace, and when you visit your form, you shall not sin.” His tent has peace when it is honored even by enemies. The form of man is God and man, because man was made in the image of God and of man. Therefore that person visits his own form who loves God and man with unfeigned charity. Such a person does not sin, because the whole law is fulfilled in this alone. “And you shall also know that your seed shall be manifold, and your offspring like the grass of the earth.” His seed and offspring are all those who imitate his life and conduct. He therefore leaves many children who teach examples of right living. Hence it is added:

“You shall enter the grave in abundance, as a heap is brought in at its proper season.” The grave in which saints rest after death signifies the heavenly homeland. This man enters it in a certain abundance because he takes with him as many as are saved by his words and example. He is rightly compared to a heap, which is formed from an assemblage of many grains.

“Behold, this is so, as we have investigated it; [233] hear it, and consider it in your mind.” These are words of pride and boasting, in which he advises Job, as though Job did not understand, to consider it in his mind. Let us now hear what the saint answered him.

## CHAPTER VI

[Col. 0573B] “Then Job answered and said: ‘Would that my sins, by which I have deserved wrath, and the calamity that I suffer, were weighed in a balance: this calamity would appear heavier than the sand of the sea.’” “Would that,” he says, “just as you see the calamity I suffer, so you might be able to weigh in an equal balance the sins for which I am afflicted, if they were divinely revealed to you. You would surely then recognize how much greater this calamity is, and would see that it is heavy as the sand of the sea and inclines the scale by its weight.” Job’s friends thought he had sinned greatly because they saw him suddenly crushed and so scourged. Therefore he especially grieved because, even in the estimation of his good friends, he was stripped of his good name. This is what he says: “Therefore my words too are full of sorrow.” It is as though he said: [Col. 0573C] “My greatest grief increases from this: although I committed nothing for which I ought to suffer these things, you nevertheless think that I endure them because of sins.” It follows:

“For the arrows of the Lord are in me; their indignation drinks up my spirit, and the terrors of the Lord wage war against me.” Great, he says, is the calamity I suffer, because the Lord’s arrows and scourges are in me, by which I am afflicted in the flesh. His terrors wage war against me, by which the soul is disturbed. For torments of the soul are much graver than those of the body: I fear suffering the former more than the latter. The indignation of His arrows drinks up his spirit, because the more the flesh is afflicted, the more natural vigor fails and diminishes. Or again, the indignation of His arrows drank up his spirit because, if there was in him any spirit of exaltation and pride, it was consumed by these scourges of correction. It follows:

“Will the wild ass bray when it has grass, or will the ox low when it stands before a full manger?” It is as though he said: “You wonder that you see me so afflicted with sorrow, and do not consider of what goods I have been stripped, what evils surround me, and from how great an abundance I have been brought into how great a want. ‘For things which my soul formerly would not touch are now, through distress, my food.’” Let even the brute animals teach you: when they abound in necessities, they neither bray nor low. But this is according to the letter. Spiritually, however, the wild ass—that is, the wild [Col. 0574A] donkey, which is not only untamed but also unclean according to the law—signifies the Gentile people. By the ox the Jewish people is figured, which alone was both clean and tamed by the yoke of the law. Yet neither of these ought now to bray or low, since each has been converted to the faith; each abounds in the new grasses of the Gospels and, standing before a full manger, is satisfied with the delights of both Testaments.

This manger is divine Scripture, which was then empty when it was understood only according to the letter. These persons, therefore, are not to be preferred to blessed Job, because their lack of complaint is produced by the full manger and the consolation of the holy Scriptures. Hence the Apostle: “Whatever things were written were written for our instruction, that through patience and the consolation of the Scriptures we might have hope” (Rom. 15:4). Blessed Job did not have this consolation because the volumes of the holy Scriptures had not yet been published. It follows:

“Can that which is unsalted and not seasoned with salt be eaten? Or can anyone taste that which, when tasted, brings death?” Before the manger was full—that is, before sacred Scripture was spiritually understood—all things were unsalted, and nothing was seasoned with the salt of spiritual wisdom; thus they offered those who ate not life but death. Hence the Apostle: “The letter kills, but the spirit gives life” (2 Cor. 3:6). Therefore now neither the wild ass should bray nor the ox low, because the manger is full and nothing is unsalted or deadly. [Col. 0574C] But someone may say: “If, then, they were unsalted, how were they received by that people at that time?” To this he himself answers: “To a hungry soul even bitter things appear sweet.” Therefore that people, because it could not attain the reality of the thing, eagerly received the shadow and figure of the reality itself. Hence the same people speaks, saying:

“Things which my soul formerly would not touch are now, through distress, my food.” At the beginning of the nascent Church, when the apostles expounded circumcision and the ceremonies of the law spiritually to the Jews, they were more scandalized and unwilling to receive them. Hence, although the Apostle had said: “If you are circumcised, Christ will profit you nothing” (Gal. 5:2), he was nevertheless compelled to circumcise his own disciple. Thus, although that people had formerly been unwilling to receive or touch this teaching, which he calls food, afterward, when it received it, it became its food. It did receive it, but under distress, because unless it had been pressed, constrained, and convinced by arguments, it would not have wished to receive it. It follows:

“Who will grant that my petition may come, and that God may give me what I expect?” He then states what this petition is: “May He who began it Himself crush me, loosen His hand, and cut me down; and let this be my consolation: that, afflicting me with sorrow, He does not spare me, lest I contradict the words of the Holy One.” It is as though he said: “The Lord’s arrows are in me and His terrors wage war against me. This, then, is the one thing [234] [Col. 0575A] I earnestly desire: that He crush me, quickly cut me down, and, afflicting me with pains, not spare me; and that this may be my consolation.” It is consolation because in this manner sins are forgiven and one departs more quickly from the miseries of this life. But lest he be thought to have said this in indignation, he immediately added: “Lest I contradict the words of the Holy One.” Whoever murmurs against scourges that occur by the command of the divine will contradicts the words of the Holy One. It follows:

“For what is my strength, that I should endure? Or what is my end, that I should act patiently? My strength is not the strength of stones, nor is my flesh bronze. Behold, there is no help in me, and even those necessary to me have withdrawn from me.” According to the letter, he seems to say this: “I am distressed on every side by such hardships and inconveniences that I reasonably desire to be quickly cut down and pass from here, lest perhaps, as pains grow excessive, I may somehow be stirred to impatience or offend God even in thought. For I am a man of flesh, possessing neither the nature of bronze nor of stone; yet You, O God, do not cease to crush and scourge me. Therefore either, as I desire, quickly transfer me from here to that blessedness, or give me help that I may act patiently. ‘For there is no help in me’: therefore let help be in You for me, because I trust not in my own strength but in Your power. Moreover, ‘even those necessary to me have withdrawn from me.’ What, then, will one do who, having lost his strength, can do nothing by himself and has no one from whom he may be sustained in necessary matters?” It follows:

“He who takes mercy from his friend forsakes the fear of the Lord.” If, then, they had feared God, my friends and those necessary to me would not have withdrawn from me. It had not yet been written: “You shall love your friend” (Lev. 10:18). Yet blessed Job knew that what was not written on parchments was already written in God’s will. He adds how swiftly those necessary to him withdrew.

“My brothers passed me by like a torrent that swiftly runs through valleys.” A torrent is rainwater, which, gathered from mountains, flows down swiftly and is gone. He then adds why they did this:

[Col. 0575D] “Those who fear frost—snow shall come upon them.” It is as though he said: “They saw my affliction and, terrified with fear that they too might be afflicted with me, withdrew as though taking refuge in safer places.” But what did it profit them? “For snow shall come upon those who fear frost.” That is, those who fear suffering tribulation here with the saints will suffer tribulation in hell with the impious. For as great as the difference between snow and frost, so great is the difference between these and those torments. Of these he further says:

“At the time when they are scattered, they shall perish; and when they grow hot, they shall melt away from their place.” At the judgment wicked men, scattered abroad, will perish; and warmed by inward fires, they will melt away from their place, according to the saying: “I passed by, and behold, he was not; I sought him, and his place was not found” (Ps. 36:36). For those whose very places of torment will be uncertain shall have no place of habitation in this world. Indeed, they will pass from snowy waters to excessive heat. This is deserved, because they never walk on a straight and uniform way. This is what he says: “The paths of their steps are entangled”: entangled, indeed, because twisted. Hence it is added: “They shall walk into emptiness and perish.” They walk into emptiness because from the toil of this journey they acquire for themselves nothing but labor and death; therefore he says: “And they shall perish.” Let this be an example of the matter for you.

“Consider the paths of Theman, the ways of Sheba, and [Col. 0576B] wait a little. They have been confounded because I hoped.” Theman means “south”; Sheba, “net” or “captivity.” By these are understood heretics, who endeavor to deceive and ensnare every believer with showers of eloquence and nets of syllogisms. Such was this Eliphaz the Temanite and his two companions. Therefore let it be said: “Consider the paths of heretics, which are always erroneous and twisted. And wait a little”: for all this life is brief and will soon end.

“They have been confounded because I hoped.” The hope of the saints is the confusion of the wicked. For the saints hope to receive not only blessedness but also vengeance upon their enemies; and because their hope cannot be vain, the wicked must necessarily be confounded. Moreover, because blessed Job hoped and could not be moved from the firmness of his hope by three most eloquent men, they were confounded and disturbed by excessive shame. Hence it is added:

“They also came as far as me and were covered with shame.” Heretics come to the Church and are defeated; defeated, they are covered with shame. Job’s friends also came as far as him, because in disputation they pursued him even to the innermost recesses of his heart. And they were covered with shame because one man could not be conquered by many, nor could a sick man be conquered by healthy men. It follows:

“Now you have come, and, seeing my wound, you are afraid.” What did they fear, or what fearful thing did they see there? They saw a man severely scourged; [Col. 0576D] perhaps they were afraid that the same thing might happen to them. Or perhaps, because he had formerly been rich and powerful but was now oppressed by extreme poverty, they feared that the holy man would ask them to assist him from their own resources. The following words seem to suggest this:

[235] “Did I say, ‘Bring me something,’ or ‘Give me from your substance’? Or, ‘Deliver me from the hand of the enemy, and rescue me from the hand of the mighty’?” In such hardships and necessities good friends are accustomed to assist one another. But the greedy propose whatever excuses they can, and, when they ought to comfort their needy friend, instead rebuke him as though such things had happened through his own fault. These men seem to do this. Blessed Job wisely removes this fear [Col. 0577A] from them; then, mocking their folly, he says:

“Teach me, and I shall be silent; and if perhaps I have been ignorant of anything, instruct me.” He is greatly to be mocked who wishes to teach one wiser than himself and endeavors to correct one holier than himself. He adds why they ought neither to teach nor correct him:

“Why have you disparaged words of truth? For among you there is no one who can rebuke me so as to correct me; you merely compose speeches and cast words into the wind.” Because the will and judgment of all of them were one, although Eliphaz alone had spoken above, he recalls that they all disparaged words of truth and composed words of rebuke. Those cast words into the wind who speak not for usefulness but in self-display; since their words are idle, they are not retained in human memory, but carried away by the wind. It follows:

“You fall upon a little one and endeavor to overthrow your friend.” In calling himself little, he indicates his innocence and humility. In calling himself their friend, he shows—as though already an observer of the Gospel—that he loves even enemies and persecutors. But because he does not fear their deceits and attempts at overthrow, he adds: “Nevertheless, what you have begun, give ear to; and see whether I lie. Answer, I beg you, without contention; and judge by speaking what is just, and you will find no iniquity in my tongue, nor will folly sound from my throat.” To answer without contention is to yield at once when the truth has been heard. It follows:

## CHAPTER VII

“Man’s life upon earth is warfare, and his days are like the days of a hired laborer.” Here blessed Job indicates how we ought to serve as soldiers in this life; in this respect he presents himself as an example of how he has served. “For man’s life upon earth is warfare,” because, for as long as we are in this life, we must continually fight against vices and evil spirits with the weapons of righteousness on the right hand and on the left, so that, when the warfare is ended, we may be crowned for victory. The days of man are like the days of a hired laborer, because if he has labored well in God’s vineyard, then, this day—that is, this life—being ended, he will receive eternal life as his denarius and wage. Hence [Col. 0577D] it is added:

“As a servant desires the shade, and as a hired laborer awaits the end of his work, so I too have had empty months, and I have counted laborious nights for myself.” For the stag desires shade to ward off heat; and the hired laborer awaits the end of his work because, before the work is ended, he receives no wage. Thus the holy man also had empty months—empty of reward and empty of rest. Because he awaited the reward which he had not yet received, he regarded the world’s riches as nothing and wearied himself with labor. He did this with such longing that whenever he rested or ceased from this work because of some occupation, he counted it not as rest but as labor. This is what he says: “And I counted a laborious night [Col. 0578A] for myself.” He uses night for rest. Hence it is added:

“If I sleep, I say, ‘When shall I arise?’ And again I shall await evening, and I shall be filled with sorrows until darkness.” Because, he says, I desire not rest but labor, whenever I sleep and cease from God’s service—for he sleeps who does not serve God—I immediately return to myself and say in my heart, “When shall I arise?” To arise is to return to one’s accustomed work and contemplation. But although I do this, although I arise, although I persist in good work, still until evening, until darkness, until the end of this day and life, I shall be filled with sorrows: partly because I long for heavenly things, partly because, dwelling among the impious, I continually fear becoming worse. And this is what he says:

“**My flesh is clothed with rottenness and with the filth of dust.**” For no one who inhabits the earth can defend himself from being touched by the earth’s dust. Therefore blessed Job, signifying in himself the whole Church, says: My flesh is clothed with the rottenness of vices and with the filth of dust; because, even if I do not wish to sin, yet the sins of others defile me. Hence the Psalmist says: “Cleanse me, O Lord, from my hidden faults, and spare thy servant from those of others” (Ps. XVIII [19]:13). By our own sins we rot; by others’ sins we are, as it were, sprinkled with dust. But note that he speaks not of the spirit but of the flesh, so that we may understand not the spiritual but the carnal children of the Church, concerning whom he further adds:

[Col. 0578C] “**My skin has dried up and is drawn tight.**” For skin, which is external over the whole body and is more often defiled, signifies those who, by evil living, become more remote from contemplation of the heart and from the Church’s hidden counsels. Such persons have indeed dried up, because they are not anointed with the grace of the Holy Spirit. And they are drawn tight, because, having lost their moisture, they cannot stretch themselves out to do good. For a contracted hand does not stretch itself out to the poor. It follows:

“**My days passed more swiftly than a web is cut off by the weaver, and were consumed without any hope.**” To a lazy worker no day passes swiftly; but Job, because he wished to have laboured more, laments that his days passed too quickly. A web is cut off by the weaver when each person’s life comes to its end. [Col. 0578D] For the web of our life is woven, as it were, from threads: namely, from hours, days, and months. Blessed Job therefore grieves that, when he could, he did not labour more—if indeed he could have laboured more—because his web has not yet been cut off and he can no longer labour as he formerly did. The days already past were consumed without any hope, because nothing can any longer be done in them. Therefore, lest we lose our days, while they are present and while there is time, let us do good to all.

“**Remember that my life is wind, and my eye shall not return to see good things, nor shall the sight of man behold me.**” The days already past, he says, were consumed without any hope; but what I shall have in the future I do not know. Remember therefore, O Lord, that [Col. 0579A] my life is wind, because, like wind, it quickly passes and fails. Afflict me now; forgive sins now; because after I have passed hence, I shall not return here to see good things—that is, to do good again. For he sees good things who, turning his eyes away from evils, does not forget to do good. “Nor shall the sight of man behold me”—that is, of that Man who is God and man. God’s beholding is mercy. Therefore, him whose sins God does not forgive here, He does not behold in hell, “because in hell there is no redemption.”

“**Your eyes will be upon me** [Note: [Col. 0579D] “‘Your eyes will be upon me,’ that is, they will be. For the dead are visible to God, who beholds spiritual things; because those dead according to the spirit live, not according to the flesh, whom the sight of man cannot behold.” St Thomas, on this passage of Job.], **and I shall not remain.**” For he had just said: “Nor shall the sight of man behold me”; yet now he says: “Your eyes will be upon me, and I shall not remain.” This would surely be contradictory unless God looks upon sinners in two ways. He looks in mercy, according to the saying: “God looked upon Peter” (Luke XXII:61). He also looks in order to punish, as in this passage; and therefore it is said here: “And I shall not remain.” For sinners will not be able to stand in judgment, because, once the sentence of condemnation has been heard, they will immediately be carried off to torments. Hence he adds:

“**As a cloud is consumed and passes away, so he who descends to the lower regions shall not rise; nor shall he return any more to his house, neither shall his place know him any longer** [Note: [Col. 0579D] Codex of the Library of Monte Amiata: “As a cloud is consumed and passes away, so he who descends into hell does not rise, nor return any more, nor shall his place know him.”].” For as a cloud, driven by winds, is consumed and passes away, so sinners, driven headlong by demons into torments, shall no longer return [Col. 0579C] to their house—that is, to this world, in which they wished always to dwell. The words that follow, “Neither shall his place know him any longer,” are, in their literal sense, a repetition. It follows:

“**Therefore I will not spare my mouth; I will speak in the distress of my spirit; I will converse in the bitterness of my soul.**” Because, he says, I fear to descend into hell, so long as I remain in this life I will not spare my mouth. For one spares his mouth when he neither confesses his sins nor entreats God concerning them. The holy man speaks in the distress of his spirit and the bitterness of his soul, because “God does not despise a contrite heart and a humbled spirit” (Ps. L [51]:17); or also because, though so scourged, he does not cease to praise and entreat God. [Col. 0579D] It follows:

“**Am I the sea, or a sea-monster, that you have surrounded me with a prison?**” Since he desires to come to God, he grieves that he is shut up in prison; and it is as though he said: Those ought to have been shut up in prison who are full of bitterness and, like a sea-monster, devour and swallow others. Unless you had confined them in the prison of your power, [Col. 0580A] they would have made a great slaughter of the saints everywhere. But why am I shut up in prison? Why am I held back by flesh, when I desire nothing except to come to you? [Note: [Col. 0580D] Thus St Paul, longing, said: “I desire to be dissolved and to be with Christ” (Phil. I:3). This is the desire of the righteous.] It follows:

“**If I say: My bed will comfort me, and I shall be relieved by speaking with myself upon my couch, then you will terrify me by dreams and shake me with horror through visions.**” Therefore, he says, I desire to come to you, because I find no consolation here; indeed, not even my own mind can console me. For bed and couch signify the mind, because the whole force of the soul rests in it. But blessed Job cannot find consolation even there; because, placed in ecstasy and withdrawal of the mind, while he considers both the rewards of the good and the torments of the wicked, he is terrified, as it were, by dreams and visions, and [Col. 0580B] shaken with horror as he contemplates the torments of the wicked, so harsh and dreadful. Therefore he desires to be there where he may enjoy blessedness without any disturbance. Hence he adds:

“**For this reason my soul chose hanging, and my bones death.**” That is, so that the soul may be carried to heaven, while flesh and bones rest in the earth. He explains this, 237 saying: “**I have despaired; I shall no longer live.**” For the despair of the good differs from that of the wicked. The despair of the wicked is to have no hope of eternal blessedness; that of the good is utterly to reject this present life. Blessed Job therefore despaired because he despised this world with all its desires; and for that reason he no longer lives, [Col. 0580C] because by afflicting his flesh he puts it to death daily.

“**Spare me, O Lord, for my days are nothing.**” Because, he says, I reckon the days of this life as nothing, and, desiring to die, I have no hope in the world: spare me now. But what is this—that above he said, “Do not spare me by afflicting me with pain,” yet now says, “Spare me”—unless it means: even if you do not spare me in scourging, spare me by forgiving my sins after the scourges? Considering what man is and how fragile he is, and also how great a glory and blessedness have been prepared for him, he adds: “**What is man, that you magnify him?**” That man is magnified is not his merit but God’s grace. [Note: [Col. 0580D] “If man had no life other than that which is upon the earth, man would not seem worthy of so great a divine care concerning him. Therefore the very care which God has especially for man demonstrates that man has life after the death of the body.” St Thomas, on Job.] “**Or why do you set your heart upon him?**” Because you never forget him; for that which is consigned to oblivion is far from the heart. [Col. 0580D] “**You visit him at daybreak.**” At daybreak indeed, because as soon as he arises—as soon as he falls from the darkness and night of the womb into the light of this day—you visit him: you nourish him, guard him, and supply all things necessary for him. “**And suddenly you test him.**” Unless he were tested, the measure of his patience would not be known. For a man is tested as often as he is touched by adversity. [Col. 0581A] “**How long will you not spare me?**” You have tested me and made my patience known. Now, “**Let me go, that I may swallow my saliva.**” It often happens in severe illness that, when the throat is dry, the tongue parched, and the palate burning, the sick person cannot swallow his saliva. Thus it is as if he said: What is it, O God, that you are doing? You neither forgive sins nor cease from scourges. I know that I have sinned, but not so as to deserve such affliction. Yet because you do not cease to scourge me, I fear that the very sin I committed has not yet been forgiven. Therefore let me go, that I may swallow my saliva, so that I may at least understand by this that my sins have been forgiven. “**What shall I do to you, O guardian of men?**” What satisfaction do you command me to make, you who always guard me and do not fail to know in what things I have sinned? [Col. 0581B] “**Why have you set me contrary to yourself?**” As if he said: Show me, O Lord, what I have committed for which you judge me contrary and hostile to yourself. Terrified by fear of this, “**I have become burdensome to myself.**” Because I displease you, I have become burdensome to myself, since I too displease myself. I do not know what I had sinned; yet unless I had sinned, I would not have displeased you. Therefore, because I acted in ignorance, “**why do you not take away my sin, and why do you not remove my iniquity?**” The Apostle likewise says: “For I am the least of the apostles, who am not worthy to be called an apostle, because I persecuted the Church of God” (I Cor. XV:9); but I obtained mercy because I acted ignorantly. “**Behold, now I sleep in the dust.**” He sleeps in the dust who [Col. 0581C] grows sluggish in this body with respect to good work. For every man is dust, according to the saying: “You are dust, and to dust you shall return” (Gen. III:19). “**And if in the morning you seek me, I shall not remain.**” Morning will then come when, this night ended, the Lord comes to judge. Then whoever He seeks, whoever He questions concerning his deeds, will not stand; because in that strict judgment no one will be able to defend himself. Hence the Psalmist says: “Do not enter into judgment with your servant, O God, because no living person shall be justified in your sight” (Ps. CXLII [143]:2).

## CHAPTER VIII

“**Then Bildad the Shuhite answered and said: How long will you speak such things, and how long shall the word of your mouth be an abundant spirit?**” He says “How long?” because he was already weary of hearing him. And because he did not fully understand Job’s words, he says that he had spoken at length. “**Does God subvert judgment, or does the Almighty overthrow what is just?**” He rebukes Job for having said that his calamity was not proportionate to his sins; and, further commending God’s justice, he added: “**Even if your children sinned against him, and he delivered them into the hand of their iniquity, yet if you rise early to God and entreat the Almighty, if you walk pure and upright, he will immediately watch over you and restore the peaceful dwelling-place of your righteousness, so that your former state shall seem small and your latter state shall increase exceedingly.**” These things are indeed true, [Col. 0582A] yet he ought not to have said them against blessed Job and his children; for neither were they crushed nor was Job scourged because of sins they had committed. To rise early is to pass quickly from the darkness of vices into the light of righteousness. It follows:

“**For inquire of the former generation, and diligently investigate the memory of the fathers.**” As if he said: If you do not believe present things, recall even the past; and when you have learned that these things happened to the ancient fathers, then understand that I have not lied. “**For we are but of yesterday and know nothing, because our days upon earth are like a shadow.**” Ask, he says, those before us, because we too shall be asked by those who come after us. For we are of yesterday and have almost already ended our life; and we do not know, since our days upon earth are like a shadow, which quickly passes and perishes. Thus far is a parenthesis. Now he returns to the fathers, saying: “**And they themselves shall teach you, speak to you, and bring forth words from their heart.**” For they themselves speak to us, as it were, whenever we reflect among ourselves upon what they did, how they lived, and what befell them. It follows:

“**Can a rush flourish without moisture, or can a reed-bed grow without water? While it is still in flower and has not been plucked by hand, it withers before every herb: so are the ways of all who forget God, and the hope of the hypocrite shall perish.**” By these words he shows most plainly of whom he is speaking. Just as a rush neither flourishes without moisture nor grows without water, [Col. 0582C] so hypocrites would not be considered green with holiness or great in religion unless they appeared to stand in the waters of the Church. For they preach rightly, give alms, and persevere in prayers and fasts. These are the waters without which the soul neither flourishes nor grows. But the hypocrite is recognized because, while still in flower and held in honour by many because of the beauty and religion—even though feigned—in which he appears to stand (for this is to be in flower), he withers before every herb, even if he is not plucked by hand: that is, he very quickly ceases from good work even when struck by no adversity. Since he does everything for display, in order to be seen, praised, and honoured, he immediately withers. “For,” says the Lord, “they do all [Col. 0582D] their works in order to be seen by men” (Matt. XXIII:5).—“**His folly shall not please him, and his confidence is like a spider’s web.**” Since they have received their reward, when they come to judgment they too will be displeased that they have laboured foolishly; and all the confidence they seemed to possess will be vain and useless. Concerning them he further adds:

“**He shall lean upon his house, and it shall not stand; he shall prop it up, and it shall not rise.**” The hypocrite will then strive with many arguments to defend and support his house, that is, his body and soul. But because nothing is hidden from God, it shall not stand. It shall not stand because, cast down, it will fall into darkness. “And it shall not rise,” because it will not be raised upward among the saints. They will prop it up when they say: “Lord, [Col. 0583A] did we not prophesy in your name?” (Matt. VII:22), and similar things. It follows:

“**He appears watered before the sun comes, and his shoot goes forth in his rising.**” Many conceal their hypocrisy so thoroughly that they are believed always to be watered and drenched with the grace of the Holy Spirit; yet the Sun of righteousness will reveal that they were dry. His shoot goes forth at his rising because he begins to receive the fruit of his labour from the beginning of his pretence; for he will receive no other reward. “**His roots shall be thickened upon a heap of stones, and he shall dwell among stones.**” By rocks and stones we understand the saints, from whom the walls of the heavenly Jerusalem are built. Hypocrites dwell among them and thicken their roots, because they endeavour with all their strength [Col. 0583B] to cling to them, so that they may appear more praiseworthy through the society of the saints. For if they separated themselves from them, their hypocrisy would immediately become manifest. It follows:

“**If he is swallowed up from his place, it shall deny him and say: I do not know you.**” This will happen in judgment, when the Lord denies the hypocrites swallowed up and removed from their place—that is, from this world—saying: “Depart, workers of iniquity; amen, I say to you, I do not know you” (Luke XIII:27). Why is this so? It follows: “**For this is the joy of his way: that others may again spring up from the earth.**” For the wicked always desire that their number may increase. They are rightly condemned, therefore, who desire the condemnation of others. This concerns the hypocrite, figured by the rush; now he turns [Col. 0583C] to the simple person, saying:

“**God will not cast away the simple, nor stretch out his hand to the wicked, until your mouth is filled with laughter and your lips with rejoicing.**” As every hypocrite is a pretender, so every simple person is without pretence. God receives the latter, but never stretches out the hand of mercy to the former. Laughter and rejoicing signify joy; thus the mouths and lips of the saints will be filled with them, because they will enjoy eternal gladness and joy. “**Those who hate you shall be clothed with confusion, and the tabernacle of the wicked shall not stand.**” Because, clothed again with this flesh in which they now dwell, they will never be free from confusion, distress, and tribulation.

## CHAPTER IX

[Col. 0583D] “**And Job answered and said: Truly I know that it is so, and man is not justified when compared with God.**” Truly, he says, you speak, and no one can be compared with God, who, as you said, neither subverts judgment nor overthrows what is just. “**If he wishes to contend with him, he cannot answer him one thing out of a thousand.**” For he contends with God who criticizes His judgments. But he cannot answer one thing out of a thousand, because at the very beginning of his speech he is convicted by the perfection of divine wisdom. “For the Lord is great, and great is his power, and there is no number to his wisdom” (Ps. CXLVI [147]:5). Hence he adds: “**He is wise in heart [Col. 0584A] and mighty in strength** [Note: [Col. 0583] St Peter has embraced all these things briefly in saying: ‘Humble yourselves under the mighty hand of God’ (I Ep. III:6).].” He conquers as wise and fights as strong; therefore he adds: “**Who has resisted him and had peace?**” He speaks of that peace which surpasses all understanding; whoever does not possess it is truly punished, since he is possessed by the devil. Hence he adds: “**He removed mountains, and those whom he overthrew in his wrath did not know it.**” The mountains are the apostles. The Lord transferred them from the Jews to the Gentiles because the Jews resisted the Lord. He overthrew them in His wrath, and they did not know it, because by God’s hidden judgment they do not understand their own condemnation and God’s indignation against them. Had they understood, they would long ago have fled to the Church. It follows:

“**He moves the earth from its place, and its pillars [Col. 0584B] are shaken.**” The Lord moved the earth from its place because He separated the Jewish people from their inheritance; its pillars were shaken because the scribes, Pharisees, and other leaders, who were as pillars among them, were carried away into captivity along with the others. “**He commands the sun, and it does not rise; and he shuts up the stars as under a seal.**” In this passage the sun signifies the Gospel, by whose illumination the whole world is enlightened. The stars are teachers, of whom it is written:

“**And those who instruct many unto righteousness shall be like stars for everlasting eternities**” (Dan. XII:3).

This sun, by God’s command, does not now rise, because the Gospel is at present proclaimed neither to Jews nor to pagans. The stars also are shut up as under a seal, [Col. 0584C] because holy preachers do not now appear among unbelievers, among whom nevertheless they will shine most clearly near the end of the age. “**He stretches out his heavens and walks upon the waves of the sea.**” God stretches out the heavens when He says to His disciples: “Go into the whole world; preach the Gospel to every creature.” He walks upon the waves of the sea because, whenever He wills, He makes the storms of this world grow calm.

“**He makes Arcturus, Orion, the Hyades, and the inner regions of the South.**” He set each against each: that is, against Arcturus, Orion, the Hyades, and the inner regions of the South. By Arcturus, which stands in the height of heaven, we understand the apostles, who are certainly more exalted in the Church; by Orion, which appears girded with a sword, [Col. 0584D] tyrants; by the Hyades, which stir up rains at their rising, the other teachers of the Church, who scatter the rains of God’s word and water parched hearts. By the inner regions of the South we signify heretics. Hence Eliphaz is called the Temanite, and above we read: “Consider the paths of Teman.” For *Teman* means “South.” Therefore He who made Arcturus also made Orion: He who made the apostles made the tyrants; and He who made the teachers made the heretics. For there is one Creator of all, “who has done great and incomprehensible things, and wonders without number.” Because he could not number all things, he called them incomprehensible and innumerable. [Col. 0585A] It follows:

“**If he comes to me, I shall not see him; if he goes away, I shall not understand him.**” According to human opinion, God seems to come to us when He grants us prosperity, and to depart from us when He grants adversity.
