[Note: [Col. 0585D] “In the Scriptures God is said to come to a human being when He grants him His benefits, whether by enlightening his understanding, inflaming his affection, or benefiting him in whatever manner.” St Thomas, on this passage.] But we see neither His coming nor His going, because we do not understand why He grants prosperity and why adversity; for in this life He grants both to good and wicked persons alike. Who can understand why the good are afflicted and the wicked prosper? It follows:

“**If he suddenly questions, who shall answer him? Or who can say: Why do you do thus?**” When God suddenly begins to scourge a person, He thereby [Col. 0585B] questions him in a certain sense, because He compels him to consider why he is scourged. [Note: [Col. 0585D] “God questions a person when He brings him back to consider his conscience, either by inward inspiration or by outwardly moving him through benefits or scourges; according to the saying” Ps. X [11]: “The Lord tests the righteous and the wicked,” etc. The same St Thomas.] Yet a man does not answer God, because he does not know how to give the reason why this happens. God’s scourges sometimes punish, sometimes correct, sometimes increase merits, sometimes discharge sins, sometimes furnish the good with examples of patience, and sometimes instil fear into the wicked. But who can say to God, “Why do you do thus?” since He never does anything without reason and justice? “**God, whose wrath no one can resist.**” A person can resist God’s wrath by repenting and seeking pardon and mercy; he cannot resist it by pride. Therefore angels in heaven and saints on earth are subject to Him. Hence he adds: “**Under whom those who bear the world are bowed down.**” Those are said to bear the world [Col. 0585C] who sustain it by governing and guiding it, whether they do so carnally or spiritually. These are bowed beneath Him, because willingly or unwillingly they are humbled under Him. “**How much less am I, that I should answer him and speak with him in my own words?**” As if he said: How can I, in pride, murmur against Him even in thought, when both heavenly and earthly beings humble and bend themselves before Him? “**Even if I had anything just, I would not answer, but would entreat my judge.**” For He alone must be entreated who can be overcome neither by strength nor by argument. “**If he hears me calling, I do not believe that he has heard my voice.**” By His goodness God makes the sun rise [Col. 0585D] upon good and bad alike and sends rain upon the just and the unjust, not by hearing those who invoke Him but by governing the world according to His own ordering. [Note: [Col. 0586D] St Thomas teaches on this passage that God sometimes hears a person, not according to the request, but for that person’s advancement: when he is placed in tribulations, God does not remove them, although he entreats Him, because He knows that they are advantageous for his final salvation.] Thus, even though what we pray for sometimes happens, we do not always obtain it by prayer, because it would nonetheless have happened even if prayer had not preceded it. It may therefore be doubted, when we are heard, whether God has heard our prayer. “**For in a whirlwind he will crush me and multiply my wounds, even without cause.**” Because he does not know why he is crushed, he says that he is scourged in a whirlwind and darkness. That his wounds are multiplied without cause the Lord Himself shows when He says:

“**Yet you moved me against him, to afflict him without cause. He will not allow my spirit to rest, but will fill me with bitterness.**” Although I do not understand why all these things happen, I nevertheless do not resist, criticize, defend myself, or contradict. Why is this so? Would you hear why? “**If strength is sought, he is most strong; if the equity of judgment, no one dares bear witness for me; if I wish to justify myself, my mouth will condemn me; if I show myself innocent, it will prove me perverse.**” [Col. 0586B] Therefore he who has nothing by which he can defend his cause should not admonish the judge, but entreat him. But how could Job defend himself, when original sin alone was sufficient for his condemnation? It follows:

“**Even if I were simple, my soul itself would not know it, and I would be weary of my life.**” Whom would life not weary, when a human being is enveloped in such great ignorance that he does not even know himself? With what rashness, then, would one who does not understand what he is in himself presume to go before the all-knowing Judge to defend himself? Who can defend what he does not know? For no one is so simple that he does not, even unknowingly, sometimes act against the truth. It follows:

“**One thing I have spoken: he consumes both the innocent and the wicked.**” He spoke this not in words but in thought. God consumes both, but not in one way. He consumes one that he may become better; the other, that he may always be consumed and remain in punishments.

“**If he scourges, let him kill once for all, and not laugh at the sufferings of the innocent.**” Since, he says, He both consumes and scourges even the innocent, let Him now cease scourging innocent persons and kill once for all the one innocent person who dies only once. He said this because he knew that the world could not be freed from torments except through Christ’s Passion. It was as though God laughed at [Col. 0586D] the sufferings of the innocent when, leaving them in torments, He did not care to deliver them. Since he had begun to speak of Christ’s Passion, he continues:

“**The earth has been given into the hand of the wicked; he has covered the face of its judges.**” The earth was given into the hand of the wicked because Christ’s flesh was delivered into the power of the Jews. [Col. 0587A] Wickedness and malice covered the face of its judges, because, as it is written, “Their wickedness blinded them” (Wisdom II:21). The judges were the scribes, Pharisees, and chief priests themselves. “**But if he is not the wicked one, who then is?**” If, he says, the people who killed their Lord is not wicked, who else is wicked?

“**My days were swifter than a runner; they fled and did not see good.**” This is what the Lord says in the Gospel: “Many prophets and kings wished to see what you see, and did not see it” (Luke X:24). Blessed Job laments that his days passed so swiftly and that he was not granted to see Christ in the flesh; therefore he added: “They fled and did not see good.” Truly good indeed—and without whom nothing is good. Blessed, then, are the apostles who saw Him whom Job desired to see, and who, while placed in torments, desired death alone except for this.

“**They passed by like ships carrying fruit, and like an eagle flying to food.**” My days passed, he says, but not idly or uselessly: rather, like ships carrying fruit, certainly giving forth a good fragrance and refreshing many with pleasant and delightful food. Not only those who then lived, but we also are refreshed by his fruits and the sweetness of his sayings. An eagle, though naturally swift, flies yet more swiftly through desire for food. In this he indicates how quickly his days passed; though by this we may understand that he did not fly [Col. 0587C] in vain, since after his flight he found the food of blessedness. It follows:

“**When I say: I shall no longer speak thus; I change my countenance and am tormented with pain.**” If, he says, as I have just done, I ever commend my past life, I immediately return to myself and say in my heart: I shall not speak thus. When I have said this, I immediately change my countenance, and in changing it I am tormented with pain. For as I seemed cheerful in recalling my past deeds, so, with my countenance changed, I am tormented with pain in recollection of future torments. It is better to keep future things rather than past things in mind—unless perhaps a person remembers his sins. For what is remembrance of good deeds except exaltation of mind? Restraining this exaltation, [Col. 0587D] he says:

“**I feared all my works, knowing that you would not spare one who sins.**” As if he said: Why should my mind exalt itself over good deeds done in the past, when I ceased from sins because I feared the scourges of the Master, who does not spare one who sins? [Note: [Col. 0587D] Sinners would refrain from multiplying sins and would repent of past sins if they considered these things, with which agree the words found in Sirach, ch. V, 6: “And do not say: The Lord’s mercy is great; he will have mercy on the multitude of my sins. For mercy and wrath quickly come from him, and his wrath looks upon sinners.”] He says this not so much in his own person as in that of others, who often glory in their actions. And as if his friends answered him, saying: If therefore [Col. 0588A] God does not spare one who sins, and does not now spare you, then there is no doubt that you have sinned—to which he replies:

“**But if even so I am wicked**” (that is, as they suppose me to be), “**why have I laboured in vain?**” For he would have laboured in vain if he were such as they said he was. But the words, “knowing that you would not spare one who sins,” are to be understood of one who perseveres in sins, because “sinning” signifies the present tense.

“**If I were washed as with waters of snow, and my hands shone as most clean, yet you would plunge me into filth, and my garments would abhor me.**” As if he said: I am neither wicked nor do I maintain that I have not sinned, because no one is so washed and clean that the eyes of God’s majesty do not find a stain in him. To be washed with snowy waters is to be white like snow. Hands signify works, because works are done with hands. God in a manner plunges a person into filth when He shows that he is stained with filth. What do garments signify but the body with which the soul is clothed? This garment, because it is easily corrupted, abhors a person—that is, makes him abominable. [Col. 0588B]

“**For I shall not answer a man who is like myself, nor one who can be heard with me equally in judgment.**” However greatly washed I may be, he says, I will not defend myself before the Judge, because He is not like me, so as to be ignorant of anything; He knows me better than I know myself. This is what he said above: “Even if I were simple, my soul itself would not know it.” Finally, even if I wished—far be it!—to contend with Him, there would be no one able to hear Him and me on equal terms. For I have many equals; He has none equal or superior. Hence he adds:

“**There is no one who can rebuke both and lay his hand upon both.**” For every judge ought to be such as can rebuke each of the litigants where appropriate and, laying his hand upon both, reasonably compel them both to question and to answer. It follows:

“**Let him take away his rod from me, and let not his terror frighten me.**” Therefore, he says, I do not answer Him because I both feel in my flesh now His rod of correction and consider Him afterward as threatening worse things. Meanwhile, let Him take it away and let not His terror frighten me. For fear often weakens understanding; we see this in children, who, when they see a rod threatening them, lose through fear even what they knew. Hence he adds:

“**I will speak and not fear him; for, while afraid, I cannot answer.**” Blessed Job says these things because, defended by a pure conscience, he was conscious of no fault. Yet again, understanding that he was not scourged without cause, [Col. 0589A] though he did not know in what he had sinned, he feared that he had nevertheless sinned; and he laments this ignorance, saying:

## CHAPTER X
“*My soul is weary of my life.*” This we explained above, when he said: “Even if I were innocent, my soul itself would not know it, and therefore I should be weary of my life.” Since, therefore, I do not know myself, I shall no longer say, “I will speak and will not fear,” nor shall I speak against my Judge; but, on the contrary: “I will let my complaint against myself go forth.” For he lets his speech go forth against himself who begins to rebuke himself, according to the saying: “The righteous man is the first accuser of himself” (Prov. [Col. 0589B] XVIII, 17).—“I will speak in the bitterness of my soul.” He speaks in bitterness of soul who confesses his sins with sorrow, tears, and true repentance. “I will say to God: Do not condemn me.” Every person ought indeed to pray thus, saying to God: “Do not condemn me. Show me why you judge me so.” For why did blessed Job so greatly desire to know why he was afflicted, except that, once the fault—if indeed there were one—was known, he might desire to be afflicted still more and submit himself to greater repentance? “Does it seem good to you that you should accuse me falsely and oppress me, the work of your hands, and aid the counsel of the wicked?” Does it please you, he says, to oppress me and afflict me by false accusation? For this is what the wicked desire; this is what malicious spirits long for; this is their counsel: that a human being should perish and that [Col. 0589C] the work of your hands should appear vain and useless. “Do you have eyes of flesh, or do you see as a human being sees?” You, he says, see present, future, and past things together; you do not fail to know what I am, what I have been, and what I shall be. For you do not have fleshly eyes, which scarcely behold what lies before them; nor do you see as a human being sees. A human being sees the face, but you consider hearts. Hence he adds:

“Are your days like the days of a human being, and are your years like human times?” Nothing can be hidden from you, for you have always been, and are, and will be; and your years shall never fail. Why then do you search my sins by examination, when, if there are any, you know them perfectly? This is what he says: “That you should seek out [Col. 0589D] my iniquity and search my sin, though you know that I have done nothing wicked, and there is no one who can deliver from your hand.” Since, he says, I have done nothing wicked, release me mercifully, for otherwise I cannot be freed or rescued from your hand.

“Your hands made me and fashioned me wholly round about, and do you thus suddenly cast me down?” As though he said: Why do you account as so vile and contemptible one whom you created by your hands in such dignity? “Remember, I pray, that you made me like clay, and that you will return me to dust.” Made from earth, he says, and soon to return to earth, fragile, made of fragile material, if I have sinned, I ought to obtain forgiveness. [Note: [Col. 0589D] St David, considering these things also, said: “The Lord has had compassion on those who fear him, for he himself knew our frame. He remembered that we are dust” (Ps. CII, 14) [Ps. 103:13–14].] Such indeed was our creation in the first human being; but let us hear how the rest arise daily from him. It follows:

“Did you not pour me out like milk and curdle me like cheese? You clothed me with skin and flesh; you knit me together with bones and sinews; you granted me life and mercy, and your visitation guarded my spirit.” See, then, how orderly is this description of human creation. Consider too from how great a misery a human being begins; know your fragility, and do not be proud, dust and ashes. He who grants life and mercy to a human being is himself the one who visits and guards that person’s spirit. “Unless the Lord guards [Col. 0590B] the city, those who guard it watch in vain” (Ps. CXXVI, 2) [Ps. 127:1].

“Although you hide these things in your heart, nevertheless I know that you remember all things.” Although, he says, you conceal these things from me and I do not fully understand your will, yet I know that you remember all things, and that “your visitation guarded my spirit”; for unless you had likewise guarded it, it could not have withstood so great a temptation.

“If I have sinned, and you spared me for a time, why do you not allow me to be clean from my iniquity?”

For blessed Job was greatly concerned about his sin, and therefore he mentions it so often: If, he says, I sinned—indeed, if I sinned—then you ought to have punished me; [Col. 0590C] but because you did not do this and spared me for a time, I am uncertain whether I have sinned and what I have sinned. Why then do you not allow me to be clean from my iniquity? For if I had sinned knowingly and had not repented, I should rightly be accounted unclean and wicked. But now, if I sinned and, because you spared me, did not understand it, why do you judge me to be wicked? Would that you had not spared me, so that I might at once have understood my sin through the very correction. What, then, shall I do?

“If I am wicked, woe is me; and if righteous, I will not lift up my head, filled with affliction and misery.” For the holy man, while under scourges, fearing that he had sinned, suffered such affliction and misery in his mind that he feared to raise his head. For what is the lifting up of the head but the gladness of the mind?

“And because of pride you will seize me like a lioness, and, returning, you torment me marvellously.” If, he says, I am wicked—which may it never be—woe is me; and if proud, because of pride you will seize me like a lioness. For a lioness is caught when she falls into a pit; but the wicked and proud person will fall into a pit, and therefore will be caught like a lioness. Of this pit it is written: “He opened a pit and dug it, and fell into the hole which he made” (Ps. VII, 16) [Ps. 7:15]. But the Lord will return, because he who first came to be judged will come a second time to judge; and then he will marvellously torment the wicked [Col. 0591A] and the proud. Then what follows will take place:

“You renew your witnesses against me, multiply your anger against me, and punishments wage war within me.” If I am wicked—this is understood—and proud, for God’s witnesses are angels and apostles, by whose testimony the wicked shall be condemned. Then God’s wrath will indeed be multiplied, and punishments will wage war against the wicked, the Lord saying: “Depart from me, you cursed, into the eternal fire prepared for the devil and his angels” (Matt. XXV, 41). Considering these things, and knowing that all this evil had happened through the sin of the first human being, the holy man laments that transgression and says:

“Why did you bring me forth from the womb? Would that I had been consumed [Col. 0591B] so that no eye should see me; I should have been as though I had not been, carried from the womb to the tomb.” Since these matters were explained more fully above, let us now state them again briefly. We said that by “the womb” is signified the devil’s first suggestion; by “being consumed” and death, separation from sin. Let it therefore be said: “Why did you bring me forth from the womb?” that is, why did you permit me to give assent to the devil’s suggestion? “Would that I had been consumed,” that is, that as soon as I heard it I might have departed from it, “so that no eye should see me,” that is, so that I might not know that I was naked. Before he sinned, as though seen by no one, the human being was not ashamed of his nakedness; thus the eye first saw him when he became ashamed to be seen. “I should have been as though I had not been,” [Col. 0591C] that is, if, passing through the womb of suggestion by hearing it, I had not assented, I should have been as though I had not been tempted, because such temptation would have been reckoned as nothing. But one is carried from the womb to the tomb who, as soon as he emerges from the womb of temptation, forgets it thereafter as though already buried and entombed. Conversely, one lives in sin who does not depart from sin. Whoever finds these things obscure should return to what was said above. It follows:

“Will not the fewness of my days soon come to an end? Leave me then, that I may mourn my pain a little.” When blessed Job saw himself bruised and scourged in his whole body, and felt that his natural vital force was altogether diminished [Col. 0591D] within him—signs indeed of death—what else could he expect but death? Therefore he says: “Leave me.” Nor is it contradictory that at one time he asks God not to spare him from afflicting pain, and at another that he spare him. He wishes him also to spare him, so that, once the scourges have been removed and his faults forgiven, he may understand that nothing remains in him to be punished. For one who has no need of scourges—why should he desire to be scourged? But by saying here, “that I may mourn my pain a little,” he sufficiently makes clear why he asks to be left alone. For the mind cannot attend to prayer and contemplation when the body is exhausted by immense pains. It follows:

“Before I go, and return no more, to a land dark and covered with the gloom of death, a land [Col. 0592A] of misery and darkness, where the shadow of death dwells, and no order, but everlasting horror.” Once a human being descends into hell, he can no longer weep for his sins. Nor is he permitted to return here in order to repent again. There is there nothing but darkness and gloom, misery and the shadow of death, everlasting horror and fear. When he says that there is no order there, he means: there is nothing there pleasant either to sight or to hearing, since those things especially give pleasure which are done with reason and order.

## CHAPTER XI

“Then Zophar the Naamathite answered and said: Shall not one who speaks many words also be heard? Or shall a man full of words be justified?” He begins with rebuke; and, as though the holy man defended himself not by reason but by verbosity, he reproves him at the beginning of his speech. Hence he continues: “Will people be silent for you alone, and when you have mocked others, will no one refute you?” For fools think themselves thought foolish when they do not know how to resist the wise, and what they cannot accomplish by reason they attempt by insults or falsehood. Hence he adds: “For you have said: My speech is pure, and I am clean in your sight.” Job did not say this, although, if he had said it, he would indeed have said what was true. It follows:

“Would that God might speak with you and open his lips to you, that he might show you the secrets of wisdom and how manifold his law is, and that you might understand that far greater things are required of you by him [Col. 0592C] than your iniquity deserves.” As though he said: Since you will not believe us, would that God himself might speak to you directly and show you his wisdom, which is hidden from you, so that even thus you might desist from your folly. He calls the law of God manifold in order to show that it is difficult to understand. It is as though he said: Because you do not understand the law owing to its difficulty, you think that you endure great torments, whereas you ought to have endured far greater ones. For whatever a person who does not understand the law encounters seems unjust to him.

“Perhaps you will comprehend the tracks of God and discover the Almighty unto perfection?” He says this mockingly. To comprehend the tracks of God is to know most fully the path of his will. This is what he explains when he says: “and discover the Almighty unto perfection.” For who can know God’s wills and counsels perfectly and most fully, when even among ourselves we do not recognize one another’s intentions?

“He is higher than heaven—what will you do? Deeper than hell—how will you know? His measure is longer than the earth and broader than the sea.” This, then, is why God cannot be comprehended perfectly. For he is immeasurable; and although he is everywhere and diffused through all things, he nevertheless contains all things within himself. He is higher than heaven because he is greater than all the angels; deeper than hell because those whom, as the Higher One, he cast from heaven cannot hide themselves anywhere from his eyes.

[Col. 0593A] “If he overturns all things or gathers them together into one, who will contradict him?” Just as, he says, when he made all things, he had no helper, so, if it should please him to destroy everything, he will have no opponent. He says this concerning Job, who, lamenting his calamity, seemed to contradict God. “He himself knows the vanity of human beings, and, seeing iniquity, does he not consider it?” As though he said: Since he knows and understands all the ways in which we go astray, will he not consider iniquity or allow it to go unpunished? Who believes this except one who is vain and foolish? This is what he says: “A vain man is lifted up in pride and thinks himself born free like the colt of a wild ass.” This is true: so long as a human being persists in vanity, he does not cease to be proud, and, like an untamed animal, is restrained by no bridle from doing whatever his own will suggests. But why he says this is made clear by what follows.

“But you have strengthened your heart and spread out your hands.” To strengthen the heart is to remain fixed in the same purpose. He seems to say this because Job could not be changed by their words. When he says, “and you have stretched out your hands to God,” his meaning is: unless you humble your heart, you stretch out your hands to God in prayer in vain. Then, as though pitying Job’s folly, he adds counsel for recovering God’s grace: “If you remove from yourself the iniquity which is in your hand, and injustice does not remain in your tent, then you will be able to lift up your face without stain; you will be steadfast and [Col. 0593C] will not fear.” This is good counsel, but Job did not need it to be given to him. For, as Zophar falsely alleges, there was no iniquity in his hands—that is, in his deeds—nor did injustice remain in the tent of his body. The face is lifted up without stain when there is nothing in the conscience for which a person should blush. One is steadfast and does not fear whose mind is made firm in love. It follows:

“You will also forget misery and remember it as waters that have passed by; and at evening a brightness like noon will rise for you.” The saints forget miseries when they consider how great the blessedness prepared for them after these miseries will be; and if at any time they remember them, it is because they now await not miseries but blessedness alone. The brightness of noon rises for them at evening because, when the day of this life is ended, while saints are thought to be coming to evening and death, then the sun of righteousness rises for them and then they shine like the sun in the kingdom of God. Hence he adds: “And when you think yourself consumed, you will rise like the morning star; and you will have confidence, because hope has been set before you; and, being buried, you will sleep securely. You will rest, and there will be no one to terrify you; and very many will entreat your face.” For the saints rise when, laying aside the flesh, they die, because then they first receive immortal life. But how do they rise? Like the morning star: that is, bright and immortal. Then [Col. 0594A] they have confidence, hope having been set before them, because they attain without doubt the things for which they had hoped. And, weary and exhausted by the labours of the world up to that time, they then sleep securely and rest in eternal peace. Very many will entreat their face because they desire to become such as they are, as is said of the Church: “All the rich among the people will entreat your face” (Ps. XLIV, 13) [Ps. 45:12]; or because they long to come where they may see them and be united with them. It follows: “But the eyes of the wicked will fail, escape will perish from them, and their hope will be an abomination of the soul.” Then the eyes of the wicked will fail because it will be said to them: “Let the wicked be taken away, lest they see the glory of God”; or because they will not find the mercy which they expected. Hence he adds: “Escape [Col. 0594B] will perish from them, and their hope will be an abomination of the soul,” that is, an abhorrence of life. For the wicked will wish to die but will be unable to do so. [Note: [Col. 0593D] Ghis. codex: “but they cannot.”]

## CHAPTER XII

“Then Job answered and said: Therefore are you the only human beings, and will wisdom die with you? I too have a heart, as you do; I am not inferior to you. For who does not know the things that you know?” This is what Solomon says: “Answer a fool according to his folly, lest he seem wise to himself” (Prov. XXVI, 5). Therefore, he says, you alone are human and rational beings, while we are brute animals, and wisdom will die with you? For if it is only in you, once you die it will no longer exist. But it is not so. I too have heart and wisdom, as you do, and I am not inferior to you. Note that he says not that he is superior but equal to them, although he surpassed them in every virtue. “For who does not know the things that you know?” You, he says, exalt things and pretend that they have been revealed to you alone, though they are evident to all. For it is characteristic of fools to think that no one else knows what they know. It follows:

“He who is mocked by his friend, as I am, will call upon the Lord, and he will hear him. For the simplicity of the righteous is mocked: a lamp despised in the thoughts of the rich, ready for the appointed time.” Of this it is said in the Book of Wisdom: “These are they whom we once held in derision and made the object of reproach” (Wis. V, 3). The simplicity of the righteous is mocked [Col. 0594D] because it knows neither how to lie nor to feign nor to deceive. Yet that simplicity is a lamp, a light, the light and example of the faithful. At present it is despised in the thoughts of the rich, which are filled only with greed, deceit, and pretence. But it is ready for the appointed time, by which we understand the day of judgment; for then this lamp will shine and its glory will appear. It follows:

“The tents of robbers abound, and they boldly provoke God, though he himself has given all things into their hands.” As though he said: If then, as you think, because I am afflicted and stripped of the world’s riches, I am wicked and impious, it follows that robbers and tyrants, who [Col. 0595A] abound in these riches, are righteous and holy. For the tents of robbers abound in worldly prosperity and boldly provoke God to indignation and wrath—in plunder, thefts, murders, perjuries, and other iniquities which they commit. For they do these things against God, although they possess nothing except from God. If you do not understand this, those things themselves will teach you in your mind; and this is what he says:

“Surely ask the beasts, and they will teach you; the birds of heaven, and they will tell you; speak to the earth, and it will answer you; and the fish of the sea will relate it to you. Who does not know that the hand of the Lord has made all these things? In whose hand is the soul of every living thing and the spirit of all human flesh.” If you do not know, he says, that the tents of robbers abound, the beasts—that is, foolish people devoted only to pleasures—and the birds of heaven—that is, the wise, who fly higher on the wings of virtues—and the earth itself—that is, lovers of the world—and the fish of the sea—that is, the curious, wandering, and unstable—will teach you. Here, indeed, all are to be trusted, for they are good. Why is this so? Because they were created by God. This is what he says: “Who does not know that the hand of the Lord has made all these things?” The soul of every living thing is in the Lord’s hand because he has set a limit for every creature both to live and to die. Thus the Lord says in the Gospel: “Are not two sparrows sold for an assarion? Yet not one of them falls to the ground without your Father” (Matt. X, 29). And not only the life of other living beings, but the very spirit that is in human flesh is in God’s hand, [Col. 0595C] because without God’s will it can neither possess nor retain the spirit of understanding or other graces.

“Does not the ear judge words, and the palate of one eating the taste?” As though he said: Because you have neither ears for hearing nor palates for tasting, you judge my words badly and do not understand what savour and sweetness they possess. Nor is this surprising: you love not ancient but new wisdom. This is what he says:

“Wisdom is with the ancients, and prudence in long time.” By these we may understand God himself and his angels. “For all wisdom is from the Lord God” (Ecclus. I, 1). But the wisdom of heretics, because it does not flow from this source, is folly. That this should be understood of God is shown by what follows: “With him are strength and wisdom; he has counsel and understanding.” Since there are seven gifts of the Holy Spirit, he enumerates only four here, because whoever possesses these cannot lack the others. For one who is strong and patient, and full of counsel and understanding, undoubtedly cannot be without piety, knowledge, and fear of God. It follows:

“If he destroys, there is no one to build; if he shuts a person in, there is no one to open. If he restrains the waters, all things will dry up; and if he sends them forth, they will overturn the earth.” Why is this so? “Because strength and wisdom are with him.” God alone [Col. 0596A] destroys and builds, because, uprooting vices in the breasts of the faithful, he plants seeds of virtues. He both shuts human beings in and opens for them, because those whom he had first confined in hell he permitted to go free. Or again, because he sometimes restrains wicked persons and tyrants, and sometimes permits them to rage against the saints. If he restrains the waters of divine speech so that they do not flow everywhere, all things will dry up. The Jews and pagans are dry because they are not watered by these waters. When these waters are sent forth, they overturn the earth because they separate earthly and sinful people from iniquity. Such an overturning is beneficial. Of this the Apostle says: “As deceivers, and yet truthful” (II Cor. VI, 8), calling himself and the other apostles deceivers. Hence he adds:

[Col. 0596B] “For he knows the deceiver and the one deceived.” For the former deceives well and the latter is well deceived. A deception is good when it calls a person back from error to the way of truth. God’s knowing, moreover, is loving. Here he speaks of the Jews:

“He brings counsellors to a foolish end and judges into stupefaction.” These counsellors and judges are the Jews, who, plotting Christ’s death, did not fear to judge him, saying: “According to the law he ought to die, because he made himself the Son of God” (John XIX, 7). God brought them to a foolish end because they lost both their place and their nation through the very one by whom they thought to preserve them. Even while seeing Christ’s signs and miracles, they were turned to stupefaction and said: “We accomplish nothing; behold, the whole world goes after him. If we let him go on thus, the Romans will come and take away our place and nation” (John XI, 48).

“He loosens the belt of kings and girds their loins with a cord.” This often happens literally; for he casts down the mighty from their throne and exalts the humble. This may suitably be understood of the Jews, who were both rich and descended from royal stock.

“He leads priests away without glory and overthrows the mighty; changing the speech of the truthful and taking away the teaching of the elders.” For God deprived the Jewish priests of glory and honour and permitted their nobles to be overthrown and defeated. He changed the speech of the truthful, that is, of the prophets. And [Col. 0596D] he took from them the teaching of the elders, namely of those same prophets, because they imitate them neither in speech nor in teaching. Concerning them he further adds:

“He pours contempt upon princes, raising up those who have been oppressed.” The Lord poured reproach and contempt upon the scribes, Pharisees, and chief priests; but he raised up, exalted, and magnified the apostles, who had been oppressed by many tribulations.

“He reveals deep things out of darkness and brings the shadow of death into light.” The shadow of death was the law, because understood literally it gave not refreshment but death. He brought it into light and revealed its [Col. 0597A] depth from the darkness of ignorance when he caused it to be understood spiritually.

“He multiplies nations and destroys them, and restores those that have been overthrown to wholeness.” He multiplied nations by propagation of the race, saying: “Increase and multiply” (Gen. I, 22). And he destroyed them because he permitted them to wander for a time; and he restored to wholeness those whom he afterward called back to faith and righteousness.

“He changes the heart of the princes of the people of the earth and deceives them, so that they walk vainly by a pathless way.” The Lord says something similar concerning Pharaoh: “I will harden his heart” (Exod. IV, 21). The Lord changes the hearts of princes and in a sense deceives them when he permits them to be changed and deceived by falsehood. They indeed walk vainly by a pathless way because from their error they gain nothing but punishment and death. This can be understood not only of the Jews, but also of heretics.

“They will grope as in darkness and not in light, and he will make them wander like drunkards.” Whoever does not believe manifest truth, like a blind person groping in darkness, never comes to the light, which is Christ. This was what the Jews did: seeing signs and miracles, they said, “If you are the Christ, tell us plainly” (John X, 24). They wandered like drunkards because now they praised him, now again they reviled him.

## CHAPTER XIII

“Behold, my eye has seen all these things, and my ear has heard [Col. 0597C] them, and I have understood them all.” By saying that he has seen, heard, and understood future things, he shows that he possessed the spirit of prophecy; for it is not sufficient to see and hear unless understanding is also given. Let those, therefore, be silent who bark that they did not understand their visions.

“According to your knowledge I also know, nor am I inferior to you.” In these words both his humility and his knowledge are commended. His humility, indeed, because, although he was greater, he nevertheless did not set himself above them; his knowledge, because even the carnal sense was not hidden from him.

“Yet I will speak to the Almighty, and I desire to dispute with him [Note: [Col. 0597D] St Thomas’s elucidation of this passage will not be inappropriate: “I desire to dispute with God, not indeed because I wish to disapprove his judgments, but in order to destroy your errors. Given these errors, it would follow that I was unjust before God; hence he adds, first accusing you as fabricators of falsehood, who had devised this falsehood [Col. 0598D], that Job had led a wicked life. They had fallen into this falsehood because they erred concerning the faith by which God is worshipped, believing that recompense for merits and punishments took place in this life only.”], first showing you to be fabricators of falsehood and adherents of perverse doctrines.” [Col. 0597D] One speaks to the Almighty who entreats his mercy. But to dispute with God is to investigate his judgments closely. These rightly designate heretics, who are called fabricators of falsehood and adherents of perverse doctrines. Falsehood is said to be fabricated because it is produced without labour and amid a confusion of talkativeness.

“Would that you were silent, so that you might be thought wise.” [Col. 0598A] For if a fool is silent, he will be reckoned wise. If heretics were silent, they would certainly do less harm.

“Therefore hear my corrections and attend to the judgment of my lips.” Since your corrections, he says, are erroneous, hear my corrections, which do not depart from truth, so that you may at least receive sound judgment. “Does God need your falsehood, that you should speak deceits on his behalf?” He says this because, as though defending God’s justice, they had reproved him above. “Do you accept his person, striving to judge for God?” Those who presume to judge others’ hidden matters pretend that they have God’s face—that is, God’s sight and knowledge. This belongs to God alone. “Or will he be pleased by one whom no one can hide from? Or will he be deceived, like a human being, by your frauds? He himself will rebuke you because secretly you accept his person.” As though he said: Since God knows all things, and fraud never pleases him, he himself will rebuke you. Why? Because secretly you accept his person: secretly, indeed, because you think one thing in your heart and utter another with your voice. To the extent that a person understands God’s will, to that extent he accepts his face. Therefore those who speak wrongly even the things they understand rightly are justly reproved.

“As soon as he moves himself, he will trouble you, and his terror will rush upon you.” Although God is unchangeable, he is said to move and be angry when he exercises deserved vengeance upon sinners. This will occur at judgment, when they hear the sentence deserved by their deeds. “Your memory will be compared to ashes, and your necks will be reduced to clay.” Since human flesh is dust and ashes, the memory of the wicked is rightly compared with ashes, since it perishes and fails together with the flesh. For they are not written in the book of life. Their necks are reduced to clay because, however proud they may be, they are nevertheless earth and shall return to earth. “Be silent for a little while, that I may speak whatever my mind suggests to me.” As though he said: Do not carnally hinder what I utter spiritually; you speak with the tongue, I with the mind. “Why do I tear my flesh with my teeth and carry my soul in my hands?” One tears one’s flesh with one’s teeth who openly rebukes by one’s words what one has done carnally. One carries one’s soul [Col. 0598D] in one’s hands who is not ashamed to display and make known one’s life. Holy persons sometimes do this in order to give others an example of living well and confessing their sins.

“Even if he kills me, I shall hope in him.” He has scourged me greatly, he says; but if perhaps he should wish to add death also to the scourges, nevertheless I shall still hope in him. For I have despaired of the world; [Col. 0599A] I have no hope except in God. Let no one cast my scourges in my teeth as a reproach, for neither death nor life nor any tribulation will be able to separate me from the love of God.

“Yet I will rebuke my ways in his sight, and he himself will be my Saviour.” Let him do what he will, he says; let him scourge me as much as he will. Yet I will rebuke my ways and blame my deeds; I will not excuse myself through fear. For he sees all things, all things are before his sight, and he himself will be my Saviour. “For no hypocrite will come into his sight.” Hence it is clear that I am not a hypocrite. They will indeed come at some time, but at present they are unwilling to come because they are ashamed to confess their sins. Or again, they will not come into his sight because the angry Lord will turn his eyes away from them. “Hear [Col. 0599B] my speech and receive my riddles with your ears.” In calling them riddles, he indicates that he speaks figuratively; yet not in such a way that all things ought to be taken figuratively. “If I am judged, I know that I shall be found righteous. Who is there to judge me? Let him come—why do I waste away in silence?” As the Apostle says, he was conscious of nothing against himself; hence he says later: “In all my life my heart has not reproached me.” From this it is understood that, although he was not without sin—for he at times calls himself a sinner—he nevertheless committed no sin for which he ought to be judged unrighteous. Therefore he freely seeks a judge and asks him to come; and because he does not come, he wastes away with pain in silence, waiting and desiring to hear judgment. [Col. 0599C] This is because, if he were judged, the sin for which he was scourged would necessarily be made known to him. There was, indeed, nothing else for which he would have feared judgment. Hence it follows:

“Only two things do not do to me, and then I shall not hide myself from your face: withdraw your hand far from me, and let not your terror frighten me.” This is as though he said: Let the scourges cease, and let the terror cease as well. For because I am scourged, although I do not know what sin I have committed, yet I fear that I have sinned greatly, since I consider that you can scourge no one unjustly. Moreover, because you have not yet ceased scourging me, I greatly fear that this sin has not yet been remitted. If, therefore, I am freed from these two things, then I shall not hide myself from your face; rather, I shall of my own accord present myself before your face for judgment [Col. 0599D]. “Call me, and I shall answer you,” that is, with my conscience bearing witness for me.

“Or rather, I shall speak, and I shall confess to you my whole life and my conscience. And do you answer me”: that is, if I have omitted to confess anything, or if you find in me anything deserving punishment and scourges, show it to me. This is what he says: “How many iniquities and sins I have—show me my crimes and transgressions.” Blessed is the conscience that so confidently asks to be judged. For by the very imputation of sin, when he speaks of iniquity, sins, crimes, and transgressions as deserving punishment, he shows that he has committed no sin deserving punishment, although there may be some distinction among these.

“Why do you hide your face, and regard me as your enemy [Col. 0600A]? Do you display your power against a leaf carried away by the wind, and pursue dry straw?” God is said to hide his face from one to whom he shows himself angry. Blessed Job, however, did not consider God his enemy; but because God afflicted him, men regarded God as his enemy. It is clear, therefore, that he speaks according to human opinion. The holy man compares himself to a leaf and straw, saying that he is in no way able to resist God’s indignation and wrath. For one with whom God is angry is easily swept into hell by the onset of demons and, like dry straw, is burned there.

“For you write bitter things against me, and wish to consume me for the sins of my youth.” Since what is written remains, he says that his scourges are written down [Col. 0600B], because he feels that they in no way depart from him. But because he did not know in what matters he had sinned, he mentions the sins of youth, concerning which he was not altogether certain. For that age, weak and unknowing, easily sins; yet one who, upon reaching a more mature age, knowingly corrects what he did ignorantly should not be consumed for those sins.

“You have put my foot in the stocks, and observed all my paths, and considered the footprints of my feet.” For we are on a journey, and as long as we live we run, as it were with unbound feet, toward the end of this life. Once we have reached it, because we can run no farther, we hold our foot, as it were, in the stocks. Thus blessed Job, when he declares that his foot is held in the stocks, judges that his course has now reached its end. God considers our paths [Col. 0600C] and the footprints of our feet because he observes what we do and what examples we leave to others. For what are the footprints of feet except examples of deeds?

“I am to be consumed as though by rottenness, and like a garment eaten by moths.” For human flesh, dissolved into decay, produces worms from itself and is consumed by them, just as a moth arises from a garment and consumes the garment itself.

## CHAPTER XIV

“Man born of woman, living for a short time, is filled with many miseries.” Man is soft and fragile because he is born of woman. He lives only a short time and is filled with many miseries; miserable, therefore, is man.

“He comes forth like a flower and is crushed [Col. 0600D]; he flees like a shadow and never remains in the same condition.” In earliest life he appears tender, flourishing, and beautiful; then, with the passing of time, he is crushed by sickness and many necessities. “He flees like a shadow,” because he declines through growing old. “And never remains in the same condition,” because now he is an infant, now a child, now an adolescent, now a young man, now an old man; now healthy, now sick; now joyful, now sad; and, mutable in many other ways, he never remains in the same condition.

“And do you think it worthy to open your eyes upon one such as this, and to bring him with you into judgment?” God opens his eyes upon man because he searches his deeds and thoughts with subtle scrutiny.

“Who can make clean [Col. 0601A] one conceived of unclean seed? Is it not you who alone are?” The understood word is “clean.” Since every human being is conceived and born in original sin, he is rightly said to be conceived of unclean seed; yet he was cleansed by the blood and water of baptism by him who alone is. For since God always is, is the same, is unchangeable, and is ever present to all things and times, he alone is, because no other thing is in this way.

“Man’s days are short; the number of his months is with you. You have appointed his bounds, which cannot be passed.” In God’s providence the number of our days, months, and years is fixed; and he himself has appointed the limit to which one may come, beyond which it is impossible to go. Even if it was granted to Hezekiah through tears that he should live fifteen years longer, it had likewise been appointed by God that he should obtain this through tears and prayers. For it is written: “I have heard your prayer and your tears: behold, I shall add fifteen years to your days” (4 Kings 20:5).

It follows: “Withdraw a little from him, that he may rest, until his desired day comes, like the day of a hired laborer.”

> [Note: Col. 0601D] “As the sun is the cause of day, so God is the author of life; when the sun withdraws, day ends and night comes. By God’s withdrawal, therefore, he understands the ending [Col. 0602D] of the present life, which comes to man from God.” Thomas Aquinas, on this passage.

“Withdraw,” he says, “for a little while from your scourges, so that a man who is soon to die may be allowed to rest, until his day comes—the day whose arrival he desires no less than a hired laborer desires his own day.” For the saints desire to die and to be with Christ, so that they may receive the reward of their labor. Hence it follows:

“A tree has hope: if it is cut down, it grows green again [Col. 0601C]. If its root grows old in the earth and its trunk dies in the dust, at the scent of water it will bud and put forth foliage, as when it was first planted.” This should be understood of the tree planted beside flowing waters, which does not cease to bear the fruit of good works. This tree is cut down when a person dies. Its root grows old in the earth and its trunk dies in the dust when, through length of time, the human body is dissolved and reduced to dust. Yet, as it hopes, it grows green again and buds at the scent of water, because it will one day rise through the breath of the Holy Spirit. Of this water the Lord said: “He who believes in me, rivers of living water shall flow from his belly” (John 7:38). The evangelist immediately explains this, saying: “But this he said concerning the Holy Spirit, whom those believing in him were to receive” (ibid., 39). It will put forth foliage as at the beginning, because he will restore it to the beauty in which it was created from the beginning.

“But when a man has died, and been stripped and consumed, where, I ask, is he? As waters recede from the sea and a river is emptied and dries up, so when man has fallen asleep, he will not rise; until heaven is worn away, he will not awake or rise from his sleep.” Just as by the tree you understand [Col. 0602A] the righteous person, so by “man” understand the sinner. For of such persons it is said: “But you shall die like men” (Ps. 81:7). Thus this man, after he dies, is stripped of flesh and consumed by worms; he will not rise, awaken, or rise from the sleep of death until heaven is worn away, so that there may be a new heaven and a new earth. Man is compared to the sea and rivers because, just as when waters withdraw the place of seas and rivers remains empty, so when the soul departs the body remains dry and empty.

“Who will grant me that you protect me in hell and hide me until your wrath passes over?” That is, until your wrath is softened through Christ’s intervening death. “And that you appoint for me a time when you will remember me?” “I know,” he says, “that I shall descend into hell; but who there, except you, will protect and free me from the punishments of torments?” The time appointed for their mercy was Christ’s Passion, because when he descended to the underworld he rescued and freed the souls of the righteous, according to the saying: “O death, I shall be your death; I shall be your bite, O hell” (Hos. 13:14).

“Do you think that a dead man shall live again?” He says this in the person of unbelievers, as the following words make clear: “All the days in which I now serve as a soldier I await until my change comes.” For if he did not believe in the resurrection, he would serve as a soldier in vain and await the transformation of this flesh in vain. “For, as the Apostle says, we shall all rise, but we shall not all be changed” (1 Cor. 15:51).

“Call me, and I shall answer you; you will stretch out your right hand to the work [Col. 0602C] of your hands.” “You will call me,” he says, “because you will command me to rise from the dust of the earth. And I shall answer you, because I shall rise immediately.” The Lord will stretch out his right hand to those whom he deigns mercifully to draw to himself.

“Indeed, you have numbered my steps,” because you do not fail to know what I have done and how I have lived. “But spare my sins,” because no one will be saved except through your mercy.

“You have sealed my transgressions as in a bag, but you have healed my iniquity.” Those transgressions are in a bag which are hidden within and do not appear outwardly. They are sealed because, marked by divine eyes, they will be disclosed in their own time. But when he says, “You have healed my iniquity,” he seems to speak on account of the scourges. It follows:

[Col. 0602D] “A falling mountain crumbles away; a rock is moved from its place; waters hollow out stones; and the earth is gradually consumed by floods; and so you will likewise destroy man.” As someone has said: No one suddenly becomes utterly vile; rather, he is gradually defiled by filth, and as temptation grows, he continually becomes more vile than himself; so he falls little by little, moment by moment, until he receives the sentence of final ruin. Thus a mountain gradually falls, crumbles, and diminishes; a rock is gradually moved from its place; water gradually hollows stones; and earth is gradually consumed by flooding. Blessed is the one who always has these things [Col. 0603A] in mind and repels from himself temptation secretly entering in.

“You strengthened him for a little while, that he might pass away forever.” God strengthened man so that he might endure forever, because he made him in his own likeness, that he might live eternally. But only “for a little while,” because he soon allowed him to be conquered and to sin. Hence it adds:

“You will change his countenance and send him away.” Since he died through the loss of God’s likeness, he is indeed changed and sent away daily; for as human beauty gradually fails, dust at last returns to dust. It follows:

“Whether his children are noble or ignoble, he will not know. Yet while his flesh lives it will suffer, and his soul will mourn over himself [Col. 0603B].” Although the sinner, while he lives, does not cease laboring even by sinning for his children, whom he wishes to enrich, yet after he dies he does not know what they are like or how they fare. For his flesh suffers while he lives because, as we have said, he does not cease wearing himself out in this life. And his soul will mourn over himself because, when departing from here, he laments his sins in repentance, though without fruit.

## CHAPTER XV

“And Eliphaz the Temanite answered and said: Shall a wise man answer as though speaking into the wind, and fill his stomach with heat?” It is as though he said: You prove yourself foolish in this: you utter useless words, full of wind and swelling [Col. 0603C], and, as one enraged, answer with heat, wrath, and indignation, calling us liars, deceitful, and fraudulent. But what wonder, when you do not fear even to accuse God? This is what he says: “You argue in words against one who is not your equal, and you speak what is not profitable for you.”

Perhaps he says this because the holy man had said above: “If I am judged, I know that I shall be found righteous.” He thinks it impossible for both the one who scourges and the one who is scourged to be righteous.

“As far as lies in you, you have emptied out fear and taken away prayers before the Lord.” “As far as lies in you,” he says, “as far as appears in your words when properly considered, you do not fear God at all when you say, ‘Who is there to judge me?’ and similar things. Yet you pour out prayers before the Lord as though you had deserved well, saying, ‘But spare my sins,’ and many other things.”

“For your iniquity has taught your mouth, and you imitate the tongue of blasphemers.” “You have learned to speak in this way from nothing other than your iniquity. Iniquity teaches the mouth when evil conceived in the mind is uttered by the mouth. They imitate the tongue of blasphemers who presume to speak against God.”

“Your own mouth will condemn you, not I; your lips will answer.” This is as though he said: If you consider yourself well, you will seek no witness to your injustice except yourself. Consider what these scourges of yours signify.

“Were you the first man born, and formed before the hills [Col. 0604A]? Did you hear God’s counsel, and will his wisdom be beneath yours?” You wish, he says, as it were, to dispute with God, as though you were coeternal with him and knew his counsel and wisdom. Yet with what rashness do you dare contend against God, when you do not excel even us in wisdom and understanding? This is what he says: “What do you know that we do not know? What do you understand that we do not understand? Among us are the aged and the ancient, far older than your fathers.”

These words seem to answer the place where Job had said above: “Wisdom is among the ancients, and prudence in long duration.” It is clear, therefore, that Eliphaz did not understand his words rightly. With good reason, then, are they called riddles, since they were not understood even by those to whom Job spoke [Col. 0604B]. It follows:

“Is it a small thing for God to console you, but your perverse words prevent it?” It is as though he said: God would already have spared you, if, humbled, you had sought his mercies. But because you are proud, lift up your heart by considering yourself righteous, swell with the spirit of pride against God, and speak in such a manner, you cannot find his mercy. This is what he says: “What lifts up your heart, and why do you hold your eyes, as though thinking great things, in astonishment? Why does your spirit swell against God, that you utter such words from your mouth? What is man, that he should be without stain, and that one born of woman should appear righteous?” Here he openly rebukes Job’s words.

“Behold, among his holy ones none is unchangeable [Col. 0604C], and the heavens are not clean in his sight; how much more the abominable and useless man, who drinks iniquity like water?” Whatever is not God is changeable in some fashion. By the holy ones and the heavens we may understand those who, still living on earth, lead a heavenly and angelic life. Hence the Apostle, living thus in the world, said: “But our citizenship is in heaven” (Phil. 3:20). Even these are not clean in the sight of him from whom nothing is hidden, because while they live here they cannot be entirely without sin. What then will man do—what will the sinner, abominable and useless, do—who drinks iniquity like water, for whom sinning seems no labor, who sins until he is drunk with iniquity and filled throughout as though with waters?

“I shall show you; listen to me. What I have seen I shall relate to you. The wise confess it and do not conceal their fathers, to whom alone the earth was given, and no stranger shall pass through them [Col. 0604D].” “Lest you think,” he says, “that I lie, I shall relate to you not what I have heard, but what I have seen.” Although the wise gladly acknowledge and do not conceal their fathers—that is, they hold their fathers’ sayings in reverence and receive them as authoritative. To these wise persons alone the earth was given.

> [Note: Col. 0603D] “The earth is said to be given to the wise alone because they are masters of earthly goods, using them for their own good; but fools use them to their own harm.” Thomas Aquinas, on this passage.

“And no stranger shall pass through them,” as there is no doubt that he has now passed through you and devastated you [Col. 0605A]. If this is understood literally, it is false: the wise alone do not possess the earth, and even what they possess is often violently taken from them. But if we understand the flesh by “earth,” it is true, because they alone govern and possess their flesh well, and keep strangers—that is, vices and evil spirits—far away from it.

“All his days the wicked man is proud, and the number of the years of his tyranny is uncertain. The sound of terror is always in his ears; even when there is peace, he always suspects snares. He does not believe that he can return from darkness to light, while looking everywhere for the sword.” It is as though he said: These are the things that I have seen and know to be true. The wicked person never ceases from pride, although he is uncertain how long he will live and carry on his wickedness. Since his evil conscience continually troubles him, he is disturbed by every sound and frightened by every rumor. Thus, although there is peace, he fears snares and always believes that enemies are near. Consequently, like one in despair, he never trusts that he can return to light and peace; expecting death and the sword on every side, he fears everyone because he has offended everyone. Measuring others by himself, he believes that no one will spare him, for he himself spared no one.

“When he moves to seek bread, he knows that the day of darkness is ready in his hand. Tribulation terrifies him, and distress surrounds him, like a king prepared for battle.” By bread we understand every means of support by which we live and are sustained [Col. 0605C]. Therefore, because the wicked live solely by wickedness and plunder, when they set out to seek bread—that is, any necessities of this life—they rightly understand that the day of darkness is ready in their hand. They do not doubt that, while acting in such a manner, death, darkness, and eternal condemnation are prepared for them. Therefore tribulation and distress terrify them, because they fear not only present but also eternal punishments. A king prepared for war fears not only enemies, but also his own people, lest perhaps he be betrayed. So too the wicked person, hateful to everyone, fears not only those whom he has offended but those whom he has not offended.

“For he has stretched out his hand against God, and strengthened himself against the Almighty; he has run against him with neck erect and armed with a fat neck [Col. 0605D].” He stretches out his hand against God, strengthens himself against the Almighty, and runs and arms himself against him with erect neck and fat, proud neck, who, despairing of God’s mercy, does not fear to provoke him against himself by every crime and wicked deed. Whoever does not cease from iniquity is in some sense always at war with God.

“Fatness has covered his face, and from his sides hangs ruin.” What do we understand by the face and sides of the wicked man except his relatives and familiars, who always stand before him and do not depart from his side? They are laden with ruin and fatness because they abound in every iniquity. Hence the Psalmist says: “Their iniquity came forth as if from fat, and they have passed into the disposition of the heart” (Ps. 72:7). As is the master of the household, so are his servants.

“He will dwell in desolate cities and abandoned houses, which have been reduced to tombs.” Desolate cities and abandoned houses are assemblies of sinful people, deprived of all goodness, justice, and holiness; in them, because vices rule, the entire structure of God’s work has been destroyed—that is, reduced to tombs [Col. 0606A]. The wicked man dwells in such cities because every living creature loves those like itself.

“He will not be enriched, nor will his substance endure, nor will he send his root into the earth.” One who has none of eternal goods cannot be enriched. That rich man had become very poor when he asked Lazarus for a drop of water [Col. 0606B]. His substance will not endure, “because when he perishes, he will take none of it, nor will the glory of his house descend with him” (Ps. 48:18).

“Nor will he send his root into the earth, because the Lord will pluck him from his tent, and his root from the land of the living. He will not depart from darkness; flame will dry up his branches, and he will be taken away by the breath of his mouth.” The wicked will always be in hell and darkness. Flame will dry up their branches because eternal and unquenchable fire will torture their relatives and familiars. “He will be taken away by the breath of his mouth,” because he will be condemned for his pride and for the blasphemy that he spoke.

“Deceived by error, he will not believe in vain that he can be redeemed by any price.” The wicked person, deceived by error [Col. 0606C], has despaired and does not believe that he can be redeemed by any price. Yet not in vain, because it will happen to him according to his faith: he will never be redeemed. One who despairs of redemption can never be redeemed.

“Before his days are fulfilled, he will perish, and his hands will wither.” Since a person does not die before the day appointed, what does “before his days are fulfilled, he will perish” mean, except that by “his days” we must not understand the days appointed by God, but those which the wicked man appointed for himself when he foolishly hoped to live so long? Since he does not live as long as he hoped, the wicked person perishes before his days are fulfilled. His hands will wither because those who do not labor now will afterward be unable to labor.

“His cluster will be injured like a vine in its first blossom [Col. 0606D], and like an olive casting off its blossom.” When the saints rise at judgment and receive the first bloom and beauty of their own splendor, then the wicked, on hearing the sentence, will be injured, because they will lose the same bloom of immortality and life which they seemed to have received. For they will always be in death.

“For the assembly of the hypocrite is barren, and fire will devour the tents of those who gladly accept gifts.” Such an assembly will be injured like a vine in its first bloom because it will appear barren and without the fruit of good works. Fire will devour the tents of those who gladly accept gifts because the bodies of those who sell justice [Col. 0607A], or do everything for the reward of praise, will be delivered to eternal flames. Of them the Lord says: “Amen, I say to you, they have received their reward” (Matt. 5:16).

“He conceived sorrow and bore iniquity, and his womb prepares deceits.” For the hypocrite conceives sorrow in his mind and gives birth to iniquity in deed, because the womb of his breast always prepares deceits and snares for others.

## CHAPTER XVI

“And Job answered and said: I have frequently heard such things; you are all burdensome comforters. Will windy words ever have an end? Or is anything troublesome to you if you speak? I too could speak things like yours.” “What you say,” he says, “is not new to me [Col. 0607B], nor am I ignorant of the intention with which you say it: under the appearance of consolation you strive to deprive me of consolation itself.”

> [Note: Col. 0607] “The duty of a comforter is to say things by which grief may be eased; therefore a burdensome comforter is one who speaks things that aggravate the mind all the more.” Thomas Aquinas.

“But will these words, full of the wind of pride, ever have an end, and will they ever not depart from the truth? Or perhaps you speak in this way because speaking causes you no trouble, since I patiently endure everything. I too could speak in the same manner, if windy and idle words were free from sin.”

“And would that your soul were in place of my soul!” So that in yourselves you might know how you ought to sympathize with the afflicted.

“I too would comfort you with words, and shake my head over you; I would strengthen you with my mouth, and move my lips, as though sparing you.” “If you,” he says, “were in this affliction, I would comfort you differently with words, and shake [Col. 0607C] my head over you, because I would incline and bend my mind toward mercy. I would strengthen you with my mouth because I would establish you with words of true, not pretended, consolation. And I would move my lips, not as though reproaching and seeking to overthrow you, but as though sparing you.” Thus we ought to comfort the afflicted. It follows:

“But what shall I do? If I speak, my pain will not rest; and if I am silent, it will not depart from me. But now my pain has crushed me, and all my limbs have been reduced to nothing.” Although these things may perhaps be understood literally of Job, allegorically they are understood of the Church. Let the Church therefore say: “If I speak, my pain will not rest.” The Church suffers whether she speaks or is silent, because when she speaks the wicked are not corrected, and by her silence they sometimes become worse. Therefore, though she grieves because the wicked are not corrected, she must nevertheless speak, so that the good may become better and the wicked may have no excuse.

“But now my pain has crushed me.” “Now,” I say, “when Eliphaz speaks against me—that is, when heretics attack me—and all my limbs have been reduced to nothing,” because all the members of the Church are scandalized by their blasphemies. At times the multitude of heretics grew so great that the Catholic Church was thought to have been reduced to nothing and utterly destroyed [Col. 0608A]. Those acquainted with the Council of Rimini know this.

“My wrinkles bear witness against me, and a false speaker rises against my face and contradicts me.” The Church, as regards the good, has neither spot nor wrinkle. But because heretics and other wicked persons are children of the Church—double in speech and made old by evil antiquity—they have lost the beauty of their mother’s countenance through a wrinkled face. Therefore the holy Church is said to have wrinkles. These wrinkles bear witness against her because heretics always contradict the Church by duplicity of speech and the sophistries of syllogisms. These are false speakers and liars, stirred up by the devil in order to resist truth. Hence it adds:

“He gathered his fury against me, and threatening me, gnashed his teeth against me.” Heretics gathered their fury against the Church when, assembling from every side like madmen and raging persons, they held a council against her. They threatened her and gnashed their teeth against her because through rulers whom they had subverted they inflicted exile, death, and imprisonment upon the saints. Read the histories and you will find it so.

“My enemy looked upon me with terrible eyes [Col. 0608B].” By outward movement he indicates the affection of the mind.

“They opened their mouths against me in reproach; they struck my cheek; they were filled with my punishments.” “They opened their mouths against me,” he says, “not merely contradicting me but also heaping reproaches and insults upon me. They struck my cheek by openly and publicly insulting me.” Thus the Apostle says: “For you endure it if someone strikes you in the face” (2 Cor. 11:20). “They were filled with my punishments,” because my affliction is their refreshment.

“God has shut me up with the wicked man, and delivered me into the hands of the impious.” God permitted his saints to be afflicted and slain for a time, so that both the punishment of the wicked and the glory of the saints might thereby grow greater.

“I, once prosperous, have suddenly been crushed.” He says this because, through the persecution of tyrants and the deception of heretics, the Church lost many persons [Col. 0608C]. When they departed, she who had previously seemed full afterward appeared empty.

“He seized my neck, broke me, and set me up as his target.” At times the multitude of the wicked seized the Church’s neck because it took away from some the freedom to speak. But it could not seize the neck of the Apostle; hence he himself, bound in the Lord, says: “But the word of God is not bound” (2 Tim. 2:9). A target is set up so that it may be struck by the blows of arrows. Thus the saints had been set up as a target because they were battered on every side by the missiles of persecution.

“He surrounded me with his spears and pierced [Col. 0609A] my loins.” This is literally true, although by spears we may understand vices, by which Christ’s faithful are wounded when they incline certain minds toward lust. But because he wounds many in the loins, he used not vulneravit (“wounded”) but convulneravit (“wounded many”); hence it adds: “He did not spare, and poured out my inward parts upon the earth.” He did not spare, indeed, because he persecuted her by afflicting her outwardly and suggesting evil inwardly. He poured her inward parts upon the earth because he sometimes turned even some of the wiser persons toward earthly and secular things. Such persons are called inward parts because they are closer to her mind and heart.

“He cut me down with wound upon wound; he rushed upon me like a giant.” He cut her down with wound upon wound because he struck her inwardly and outwardly with many varieties of missiles. The malignant spirit is fittingly compared to a giant on account of his cruelty and strength.

“I sewed sackcloth upon my skin and covered my flesh with ashes.” The Church says this on behalf of those who, after sinning, have turned to repentance. But because they sinned through the devil’s suggestion, he covered them with sackcloth and ashes, since he was the cause that they should have to repent in this manner.

“My face was swollen with weeping, and my eyelids were darkened.” Literally, this may refer to the same penitents who weep for their sins. Allegorically, however, the Church’s face and eyelids are understood as her teachers, in whom greater beauty appears and who guard her watchfully. They mourn others’ sins [Col. 0609C], and grow dim by mourning because, when they see them incorrigible, they grow faint, as though wearied by their vigils. It follows:

“I have suffered these things without iniquity in my hand, though I had pure prayers to God.” Thus far the Church speaks. Now Christ speaks, as though saying: “What wonder, O Church, if the enemy afflicted you, who certainly are not without sin, when he most cruelly persecuted even me, who committed no sin?”

“O earth, do not cover my blood, nor let my cry find a place of hiding in you.” The Church is called earth because of her firmness and stability. She did not cover Christ’s blood because she has now preached his Passion and death among all the nations, and will reveal to all peoples his blood, which, as the Apostle says [Col. 0609D] (Heb. 12:24), speaks better than Abel’s blood. This cry would have found a hiding place in the Church if the Church had concealed Christ’s death.

“For behold, my witness is in heaven, and he who knows me is on high.” Of this he also says in the Gospel: “I bear witness concerning myself, and the Father who sent me bears witness concerning me” (John 8:18). Therefore he himself is my witness; he himself knows with me that I suffered without iniquity in my hand.

“My verbose friends; my eye drips toward God [Col. 0610A].” Thus far Christ speaks. From here the Church resumes the course of her discourse. “My verbose friends,” she says—that is, the heretics, who ought to have loved me—do not cease to disparage me with the abundance of their words. Therefore my eye drips, weeping not only for my own calamities but also for their errors.

“And would that a man might thus be judged with God as the son of man is judged with his companion.” In human judgment a case is examined until truth becomes known. She therefore desires such a judgment, that she may know with certainty why God permits the madness of heretics and why he does not deliver the innocence of the saints. For as far as human judgment is concerned, it seems far more just that the wicked should be afflicted than the good. Of this great misery she receives this one consolation: the present life is short, and all this tribulation quickly ends with life. This is what she says: “For behold, brief years pass, and I walk the path by which I shall not return.” This path is death, by which one who does not die more than once does not return.

> [Note: Col. 0609D] “There were some who believed that after death a human being would return again to the course of the present life. Thus it might appear that Job could have consolation, at least in that future life, in the hope of recovering earthly prosperity. Therefore, to exclude this, he adds: ‘And I walk the path by which I shall not return.’” Thomas Aquinas.

Or the Church too walks by a path from which she will not return, because after this life she will suffer no labor or distress.

## CHAPTER XVII
“My spirit is weakened, my days are shortened, and the grave alone remains for me.” As though he said: Because I desire to pass hence, to end my life, to shorten my days, I desire only the grave and death. [Col. 0610C] This may also be understood of the spirit of pride, which is continually weakened in the saints, since the spirit of humility continually grows in them. And because they are now dead to this world, they say that their days are shortened and that the grave alone remains for them. “I have not sinned, and my eye abides in bitterness.” “I have not sinned,” he says, “so as to deserve such affliction.” For the holy martyrs were afflicted not because of their sins, but because they confessed Christ. Or again, he says this with reference to the more perfect, who wept not for their own sins but for those of others. By this it is most plainly shown how fervently they burned with the fire of charity:

“Deliver me, and set me beside thee; and let any man’s hand fight against me.” Deliver me, he says, from the snares of my enemies; set me beside thee; and, as thou hast promised, do not desert or forsake me.
