Let whoever will fight against me, for, with thy help, I fear no one. “Thou hast made their heart far from instruction; therefore they shall not be exalted.” Their heart, he says—namely, that of the enemies and heretics—thou hast made far, that is, thou hast permitted it to become far from the instruction of truth. Therefore they shall not be exalted, but shall be humbled even to the lowest depths. It follows:

“He promises plunder to his companions, and the eyes of his children shall fail. He has made me a byword of the people, [Col. 0611A] and I am an example before them.” Who is this who promises plunder to his companions, and who is thus mentioned here without qualification, except the malignant spirit, so wicked that he may be recognized in evil deeds even without being named? He promises plunder to his companions because he incites and inflames the minds of the wicked toward plunder and robbery. They are indeed his companions because they do evil together with him, and his children because they imitate him. But their eyes shall fail, since their desire and expectation shall by no means be fulfilled. And indeed, not without God’s permission, he has made the Church a byword of the people and an example before them—that is, before his companions—because he oppressed the saints with such calamity that those inflicting some evil upon others would hold them up as a proverbial example of misfortune. [Col. 0611B] Hence it is said in the Psalms: “Thou hast made us a likeness among the nations” (Ps. 43:15). For no one thought he could say anything worse to his enemy than: “May I see you such as the Christians are.”

“But now those younger in time mock me, whose fathers I would not deign to set with the dogs of my flock.” Since heretics are children of the Church, there is no doubt that they are younger than she in time.

[Note: [Col. 0611D] Tertullian, *On Prescription against Heretics*, ch. 32, proves that heretics are much later than the Catholic Church, because they departed from the apostles and preached another doctrine. Thus the novelty of a doctrine is evidence of its later origin.]

Their fathers are understood to be the heresiarchs: Simon Magus, Arius, Sabellius, and Jovinian. The Church would not set these among the dogs of her flock, because she never wished to join them to the holy preachers. For such dogs guard God’s sheep, of whom it is said: “The tongue of thy dogs [shall have its portion] from the enemies, from him” (Ps. 67:24).

[Col. 0611C] “My eye has grown dim with indignation, and my limbs are reduced almost to nothing.” Because, he says, these men mock me, and thou, as though unconcerned for me, dost not avenge me; therefore my eye, angered, has grown dim. For the eyes of the Church are the bishops; when they see the wicked exalted and themselves cast down and humbled, they are at times darkened by indignation and astonished bewilderment, because they do not guard the flock entrusted to them with such diligence. Thus the limbs are reduced almost to nothing, since, when watch over subjects fails, the flocks are torn by the bites of vices.

“The righteous shall be astonished at this, and the just man shall be stirred up against the hypocrite; and the righteous shall hold to [Col. 0611D] his way, and he that has clean hands shall add strength.” This is what he had just said: that the wicked are exalted and the good humbled. The righteous shall be astonished at this, not knowing why it happens. Yet, lest the members be wholly reduced to nothing, the innocent man shall be stirred up against the hypocrite. And the righteous shall hold to his way, [Col. 0612A] which in indignation he had seemed to leave for a time.

[Note: [Col. 0611D] “And the righteous shall hold to his way, because he will not abandon it on account of the anger of zeal. For such anger does not precede reason, but follows it; and therefore it cannot separate a person from righteousness. Yet anger arising from zeal is useful, because it makes a person rise against evils with greater strength of spirit. This is what follows: ‘and he that has clean hands shall add strength,’ namely through zeal. Hence it is said in the third book of the *Ethics* that anger assists courage.” D. Thomas.]

For the righteous holds to his way when he steadfastly persists in the work of righteousness to which he is accustomed. And he that has clean hands shall add strength, because he will labour more vigorously in holy works. And he shall say:

“Therefore all of you turn and come, and I shall not find among you any wise man.” Because, he says, with the dimness of my eyes wiped away, I rise against the hypocrite and hold to my way; therefore you also, members of the Church, who had now almost been reduced to nothing, turn to the Lord and come after me—that is, be my imitators, as I too am of Christ. “And I shall not find among you any wise man,” for “the wisdom of this world is foolishness with God.” Hence the Apostle says: “If any among you seems wise, let him become foolish, that he may be wise” (1 Cor. 3:18). And elsewhere: “Not many wise, brethren, not many noble, are among you; but God has chosen the foolish things of the world to confound the wise” (1 Cor. 1:26). Thus far the Church. Now Job, whose words these are, just as he spoke specially of himself at the beginning of this discourse, so also indicates at its end that we should understand it spiritually of himself.

“My days have passed; my thoughts are scattered, tormenting my heart. They turned night into day, and again after darkness I hope for light.” My days, he says—those which I call mine because in them I lived not for myself but for the Lord, and which I spent in contemplation and service of God—have now passed. My thoughts, by which I thought not of worldly things but of eternal things, [Col. 0612C] and which tormented my heart both with compunction and tears—for “a contrite and humbled heart God will not despise” (Ps. 50:19)—these most often turned night into day for me, because they compelled me to keep watch no less by night than by day. Those thoughts of mine, I say, are scattered. For I am pressed by such afflictions that I take delight in thinking of nothing else. Thus the holy man grieves because, through bodily pains, he is deprived of so great a contemplation. But behold, “again after darkness I hope for light,” because after the weariness of this affliction I shall await light and rest. But what profit is this to me? It follows:

“If I wait, hell is my house, and in darkness I have spread my bed.” I, he says, await and endure in hope of light; but darkness is prepared for me. For I know that I shall descend into hell,

[Note: [Col. 0612D] “He calls the grave ‘hell’ according to the opinion of those against whom he disputed, who did not believe that the human soul remains after death, but held that only the body remains in the grave—which they called hell because it is situated within the earth.” D. Thomas.]

which is surely a place of darkness. “In darkness I have spread my bed.” He spread it not in himself but in the first man, because he himself was materially in Adam when Adam, transgressing God’s command, [Col. 0613A] spread a bed in darkness and hell both for himself and for the human race. “I said to corruption, ‘Thou art my father,’ and to the worms, ‘My mother and my sister.’” For what else are all our parents who have already gone before us than worms and corruption? Born from corruption, we shall return to corruption. “Where then now is my expectation, and who shall consider my patience?” If, he says, the soul is compelled to go to hell and the flesh to corruption and worms, where then is my expectation? What have I awaited? What do I find? What do I gain from all this great patience of mine? Who considers my patience? Surely he of whom it is written: “For thou considerest labour and pain.”—“All that is mine shall descend into the deepest hell; dost thou think that at least there shall be rest for me?” Whatever is lower may be called hell in comparison with what is above it. Since, therefore, that penal place is below heaven, air, and earth, he rightly calls it the deepest hell. He says that all that is his descends there, although it is plain that the soul alone descends, because he counted nothing else as his own except that which he carried with him. But when he says, “Dost thou think that at least there shall be rest for me?” he does not say it in despair, but because such rest is thought not to be rest but punishment.

## Chapter XVIII

“Then Bildad the Shuhite answered and said: How long wilt thou cast forth words? First understand, and then let us speak.” By saying that he cast forth words, [Col. 0613C] he reproves him for pride and boastfulness. And by urging him to understand, as though he had not understood, he mocks him. “Why are we accounted as beasts? And are we vile in thy sight, thou who destroyest thy soul in thy fury?” Perhaps he says this because Job had previously said: “Ask the beasts, and they shall teach thee.” And likewise: “Would that ye were silent, that ye might be accounted wise.” Since Job did not follow their judgment, they thought that he acted against his own soul; and therefore it is here said: “Thou who destroyest thy soul in thy fury.” For this entire dispute arose chiefly because blessed Job did not confess that he was afflicted either justly or on account of his sins. “Shall the earth be forsaken for thy sake, and shall rocks be moved [Col. 0613D] from their place?” As though he said: If you alone understand rightly, the whole world is in error. If that is so, the earth must be forsaken and the world perish. By rocks he means himself and the other wise men, who excel through loftiness of intellect. But Job will not be able to move them from their place, because he will not be able to separate them from the firmness of their understanding, evil though it be.

“Shall not the light of the wicked be extinguished? Nor shall the flame of his fire shine?” Though, he says, the perverse understanding of the wicked may sometimes shine and be thought true, it shall nevertheless be extinguished and dissipated. For the flame of his fire—that is, of his intellect—shall not always shine. For the fire and brightness of the mind is intellect.

“The light shall be darkened in his tent, and the lamp [Col. 0614A] that is over him shall be extinguished.” The tent of the wicked is the flesh. In it the light shall grow dark when all his understanding is proved to have been false. Moreover, the lamp which is over him shall be extinguished, because not only what he conceived in his mind, but also what he learned from the ancients and his superiors, shall be destroyed. Every erroneous kind of knowledge shall be made void. Bildad speaks truth; but he ought not to have said this against Job. It follows: “The steps of his strength shall be straitened, and his own counsel shall cast him down.” As long as the wicked man lives, he walks on the broad and spacious way of death; trusting in his own strength, he does whatever his will carries him toward. But then his steps shall be straitened, when, with hands and feet bound, he is cast into darkness. [Col. 0614B] Therefore it is added: “His own counsel shall cast him down.” For he would not be cast down had he trusted not in his own counsel but in that of the saints. “For he has put his feet into a net, and he walks in its meshes.” The wicked man has put his feet into a net, because he is held by the snares and deceptions of the devil, so that he cannot walk on the straight path. And he walks in its meshes because he passes from vice to vice, now committing adultery, now perjury, now murder. For as many as the vices are, so many are the meshes of this net. “His foot shall be caught in a snare, and thirst shall burn against him.” How great is the wicked man’s desire to sin is clear from this: though he is still held by one vice, he already burns to commit another. As though his foot were bound by lust, he is held fast, and yet he desires to seize another’s goods. “His trap is hidden [Col. 0614C] in the ground, and his snare upon the path.” For the devil sets trap and snare where he knows that the sinner most frequently passes. Whatever vice a person persists in is the path by which he runs to destruction. The devil, therefore, knows the paths; he knows the deceptions by which each person will be caught. He places one thing before the lustful, another before the avaricious, and another before the proud. “Terrors shall frighten him on every side, and shall entangle his feet.” Whoever acts wickedly can never be secure, because he fears not only God but also the people whom he has offended. He goes nowhere without dread; wherever he is, fear shakes him. “Let his strength be weakened by hunger, and want invade his ribs.” If someone is weakened by hunger, [Col. 0614D] want at once appears in his ribs. Thus the strength and ribs of the wicked shall be weakened and invaded by hunger and want, because when placed amid punishments he shall both lose strength and be unable to conceal the deprivation he suffers. So too that man who said: “Father Abraham, have mercy on me, and send Lazarus, that he may dip the tip of his finger in water and cool my tongue, for I am tormented in this flame” (Luke 16:24).

“Let death devour the beauty of his skin; let the firstborn of death consume his arms.” In the skin lies outward beauty; in the arms, strength. But death is the devil, because death came about through him. Therefore let death—that is, the devil—devour not only the beauty of his skin, that is, his flesh, but also consume his arms, that is, his soul, in which the whole power [Col. 0615A] and strength of man consists. “Let his confidence be torn from his tent, and let destruction tread upon him as a king.” For the wicked man’s confidence is this life, since in nothing does he trust so much as in this life. He is torn from the tent of his body because, when he hopes to live very long, his life is suddenly cut off. Then destruction treads upon him as a king, because he is wholly delivered into the devil’s power. Since the devil is the prince of death, he is rightly called destruction. “Let the companions of him who is not dwell in his tent; let sulphur be scattered over his tent.” Once the wicked man is removed from this life, he has no tent or dwelling except hell. By “him who is not” the devil is understood, who is said not to be because he has ceased to be good; and because God is called “He who is,” the devil is fittingly called “he who is not.” Thus Moses says: “He who is has sent me to you” (Exod. 3:14). Therefore the companions of him who is not dwell in the wicked man’s tent; by them the multitude of all demons is signified. Joined to them, he shall never again be free from affliction. Sulphur is scattered in his tent because he always remains amid stench.

“Below, his roots shall dry up; above, his harvest shall be crushed.” What is signified by below and above except the present life and eternal blessedness? Below, therefore, the roots of the wicked dry up, because in this life good works die within him; without them, it is not granted to live, as it were, without roots. Above, his [Col. 0615C] harvest is crushed, because in the other life he shall have nothing by which to live. “Let his memory perish from the earth, and let not his name be celebrated in the streets.” Let his memory perish, he says, and let it not be heard in the streets of the heavenly Jerusalem. “He shall drive him from light into darkness, and remove him from the world.” The Lord shall indeed drive him from light into darkness and remove him from the world, because he shall thrust him from this life and this world into darkness and eternal punishments. “He shall have neither seed nor offspring among his people, nor any remnant in his regions.” The seed, offspring, and remnant of this man may be understood either as his imitators or his works. But after this life these shall be neither among God’s people nor in his regions, that is, in the heavenly country. [Col. 0615D]

“On his day those who come after shall be astonished, and horror shall seize those who went before.” What is his day except the day of judgment, on which the wicked man shall be condemned and perish? We are those who come after, of whom John says: “Children, it is the last hour” (1 John 2:18). And the Apostle says: “We are those upon whom the ends of the ages have come” (1 Cor. 10:11). Those who went before are the patriarchs, prophets, and all the rest who lived from Adam to Christ. All these shall be astonished and seized with horror when they behold the multitude of the wicked being judged. For how shall they not be astonished when they see so great an army, and especially the powerful of this age, dragged so violently to death and torments? “These, then, are the tents of the wicked man, and this [Col. 0616A] is the place of him who does not know God.” What are they? Namely, to be removed from light into darkness. Wretched in every respect is he for whom such dwellings are prepared.

## Chapter XIX

“Then Job answered and said: How long do you afflict my soul and wear me down with words? You have confounded me ten times, and you are not ashamed to oppress me.” Those who had come to console him instead afflicted him and unjustly wore him down with reproofs in words. Since they had spoken five times and he had answered five times, he says that he was confounded ten times; for he grieved no less at his own words than at theirs, because they neither received nor believed his words. And what is greater still: he who was oppressed was ashamed, while those who unjustly oppressed him were not ashamed. It follows:

“Indeed, even if I have erred, my error shall remain with me. But you rise up against me and reproach me with my disgrace.” Even if I have erred, he says—that is, sinned in ignorance—my ignorance shall remain with me, since until now I cannot understand what I have sinned so as to deserve such affliction. Yet you rise up against me as though you knew those hidden matters of mine which I myself cannot know. “And you reproach me with my disgraces”: that is, you cast my disgrace and scourges in my face, and because I am scourged, you strive thereby to prove me wicked.

“At least now understand that God has afflicted me not by an equal judgment, and has encircled me with his scourges. Behold, I shall cry out, suffering violence, and no one will hear; I shall cry aloud, [Col. 0616C] and there is none to judge.” The Lord himself shows that he afflicted him not by an equal judgment when he says: “But thou hast moved me against him, to afflict him without cause.” How this should be understood has already been said above. To encircle with scourges is to afflict severely on every side. And from this, he says, understand that I am afflicted not by an equal judgment: I shall cry out and cry aloud, and there shall be none to hear or judge. For if he afflicts me justly, why does he not come to judgment? He would come if he made Job understand his fault; since he did not do so, he showed that there was no fault. It follows:

“He has hedged in my path, and I cannot pass; and he has set darkness upon my way.” [Col. 0616D] Whither did blessed Job wish to go, when he says his path was hedged in and wrapped in darkness so that he could not pass, except that with his whole mind and intention he strove to understand the fault for which he was afflicted? Therefore the darkness of ignorance was set before him, hindering his mind from learning the truth of this matter.

“He has stripped me of my glory and taken the crown from my head; he has destroyed me on every side, and I perish; and, as from a tree uprooted, he has taken away my hope. His wrath has raged against me, and he has regarded me as his enemy.” He had indeed been very glorious, because all considered him just and perfect. Yet he had been stripped of this glory, because, on account of the scourges he suffered, they now counted him among the wicked. Moreover, he complains that he had lost the crown received for victory over vices, since he seemed now not a conqueror but rather conquered. But this was not true in fact; it was so only in human opinion. He was destroyed on every side, because he had lost sheep, oxen, asses, camels, and all his possessions; and, like the trunk of a tree with all its branches torn away, he had lost all hope of future posterity, because he was bereft of sons and daughters. Therefore he complains that God is angry with him and regards him as an enemy—not because this was so, but because it appeared to be so.

“His robbers came together, made a way through me, and besieged my tent round about.” Together, he says, suddenly and furiously came [Col. 0617B] his robbers, that is, malignant spirits. They passed through me, laying waste and scattering everything. They besieged my tent round about, because after all was lost and his sons and daughters had been struck down, they also smote him from the sole of the foot to the crown of the head with a grievous wound; by the tent his body is understood. Thus far Job; the rest is spoken by Christ.

“He has made my brethren far from me, and my acquaintances, as strangers, have departed from me.” The Jews are Christ’s brethren according to the flesh, because they are from Abraham’s seed; they were his acquaintances through association and knowledge of the Law. Yet by unbelief they were made far from him, and, denying him, departed from him. Hence it follows: “My kinsmen have forsaken me, and those who knew me [Col. 0617C] have forgotten me. The sojourners of my house and my maidservants have regarded me as a stranger; I have been as a foreigner in their eyes.” By the sojourners and maidservants of his house—that is, of the Synagogue—are understood the priests and Levites, who served and more intimately guarded the sacred precincts of the Temple. Yet they regarded him as a stranger and foreigner, saying: “We do not know where this man is from” (John 9:29).

“I called my servant, and he did not answer; with my own mouth I entreated him.” By his servant he means the Jewish people, of whom Isaiah says: “Who is blind but my servant?” (Isa. 42:18). He called this people to faith not only by words but also by miracles, according to the saying: “If you do not believe me, believe the works” (John 10:38). [Col. 0617D] And he now entreated it not through prophets, as formerly, but with his own mouth, when he said: “Come to me, all you who labour and are burdened, and I will refresh you” (Matt. 11:28).—“And he did not answer him,” that is, they do not obey. “My wife abhorred my breath; and I entreated the children of my womb.” His wife was once the Synagogue. But she abhorred his breath, that is, his words. For when he said: “Before Abraham was, I am” (John 8:58); “I am the light of the world” (ibid., v. 12); “I am the beginning, who also speak to you” (ibid., v. 26); and “I am Christ” (Matt. 24:5), then the Synagogue recoiled from his breath. Hence she said: “According to the law he ought to die, because he made himself the Son of God” (John 19:8). But he entreated the children of his womb, namely the Jews, [Col. 0618A] whom he loved as sons. “Even fools despised me; when I had withdrawn from them, they spoke against me.” For the foolish scribes and Pharisees sometimes despised him in his words, though, seeing his signs, they marvelled. And when he withdrew a little from them and ceased from miracles, they spoke against him, saying: “Is not this the carpenter’s son?” (Matt. 13:55). “Those who were once my counsellors abhorred me, and he whom I loved most.” By his counsellors are understood those learned in the Law, who, as they studied the sacred books, in a sense took counsel with God. These men had formerly proclaimed Christ’s coming, but when they saw him in the flesh they did not receive him. Therefore he loved them most before—namely, when they preached the truth. Or “he whom he [Col. 0618B] loved most” may also be understood as Judas, who afterward betrayed him.

“My mouth clung to my skin, my flesh having been consumed, and only the lips around my teeth were left.” By the skin are understood the holy women, by the flesh the apostles, and by the mouth Christ. Therefore, when the flesh was consumed—that is, when the apostles fled—the mouth alone clung to the skin, because the holy women did not abandon Christ even during the Passion. To them he said: “Daughters of Jerusalem, do not weep over me” (Luke 23:28). They may also be called lips, since they first spoke in announcing Christ’s resurrection. Thus the lips were left around the teeth, because when Christ was visibly taken from them, the women adhered to the apostles. For the apostles are the teeth, by which the whole food of the Church is ground. Thus far Christ. From this point Job continues the order of his own discourse:

“Have pity on me, have pity on me, at least you, my friends, because the hand of the Lord has touched me. Why do you persecute me as God does, and are you filled with my flesh?” Because, he says, the hand of the Lord scourges me, whose strength I can scarcely endure, at least you, my friends, spare me now and pity me. Why do you persecute me as God does? Are you without sin? God alone is without sin. Since you are not without sin, why do you rebuke my sins? Rebuke your own. He feeds on another’s flesh who takes delight in another’s afflictions and detractions.

“Who will grant me that my words may be written? Who will give me that they may be inscribed in a book with an iron stylus and a plate of lead, or engraved with a chisel in stone?” The holy man desires his words to be written so that those who would come after him might take from them an example of patience. He wishes them to be written with an iron stylus, that is, with a stable and firm judgment, lest they be erased from human memory. But where? On a plate of lead or engraved with a chisel in stone—that is, in the hearts of Jews and Gentiles. For lead is cheaper than every other metal; the Jews are subject to all the nations. The Gentiles, moreover, because they worshipped idols and stones, are rightly signified by stone. But as though someone were to say: What does it profit you if your words are written, when you yourself shall be wholly ended by death? To this he replies: “For I know that my Redeemer lives”

[Note: [Col. 0619D] Christ redeemed us from sin by dying for us; yet he did not die in such a way that death swallowed him up. Though he died according to his humanity, he could not die according to his divinity. From the life of his divinity, moreover, his humanity too was restored to life by rising again, according to the final chapter of Corinthians: “For though he was crucified from weakness, yet he lives by the power of God.” D. Thomas.]

(whom the Jews thought that they had killed), “and on the last day I shall rise from the earth; and again I shall be clothed with my skin, and in my flesh I shall see God, whom I myself shall see, and my eyes shall behold.” O how great is the hope of resurrection! These words alone suffice against all who deny the resurrection. “Whom I myself shall see,” he says. What does “I myself” mean? That is, in this flesh, in this essence, in this person. Not another through a change of flesh, but one and the same person, through the recovery of this very flesh. “This hope is laid up in my bosom.” Thus, he says, I believe; thus I hope; thus I am certain of that thing which I hold in my bosom [Col. 0619B] and heart.

“Why then do you say, ‘Let us persecute him, and find the root of a word against him’?” They find a root of speech when they mark something in his words from which they may take material to speak against him. But they do this in vain, because his faith and hope cannot be moved. Moreover, while they attack him, they kill themselves. Therefore it follows: “Flee then from the face of the sword, for the sword is the avenger of iniquities; and know that there is judgment.” As though he said: While you contend unjustly against me, you do not consider the sword of divine vengeance hanging over your necks. Cease, therefore, from wickedness and flee the sword of vengeance, for the sword avenges iniquities; and know that there is a judgment in which God shall reveal all hidden things. [Col. 0619C] “Therefore judge nothing before the time, until the Lord comes, who will also bring to light the hidden things of darkness and reveal the counsels of hearts; and then each shall have praise from God” (1 Cor. 4:5).

## Chapter XX

“Then Zophar the Naamathite answered and said: Therefore my varied thoughts succeed one another, and my mind is drawn in different directions.” Therefore, he says, because you too do not doubt the future judgment, and yet, as though trusting in your own righteousness, do not cease from proud speech, my thoughts are varied. At least fear of that judgment ought to have restrained you from such great boasting. “I shall hear the teaching by which you rebuke me, [Col. 0619D] and the spirit of my understanding shall answer me.” Say whatever you wish, he says; rebuke me as much as you wish. I can indeed hear your teaching, but the spirit of my understanding, answering me inwardly, does not permit me to assent to your teaching. “This I know from the beginning, since man was placed upon earth: that the praise of the wicked is brief, and the joy of the hypocrite is like a point.” By these words he unjustly reproves blessed Job as both wicked and hypocritical. Yet these words, properly understood of the wicked and hypocrite, may be true. The praise of the hypocrite is brief, for once recognized it quickly perishes and ends wholly in this life. His joy is like a point, so brief that it scarcely appears ever to have existed. “Though his pride rise to heaven and his head touch the clouds, in the end he shall perish like dung.” By heaven and clouds we understand the teachers of the Church. The hypocrite rises to them and touches them when, through a pretence of good living, he presents himself as their equal. Yet in the end he shall perish like dung, because, though outwardly whitewashed, he is nevertheless defiled by the dung of vices.

“And those who had seen him shall say, ‘Where is he?’ Like a flying [Col. 0620B] dream he shall not be found; he shall pass away like a vision of the night. The eye that saw him shall see him no more, nor shall his place behold him any longer.” The hypocrite is aptly compared to a dream and a nocturnal vision, because whatever he did was phantom and deception. Therefore he shall not be with the saints, where he was thought to be, but shall be cast down with the wicked into darkness. Hence those who saw and knew him shall say in excessive astonishment: “Where is he?” Namely, he is there where neither place nor dwelling beholds and marvels at him, nor does any such eye see him as can be deceived by his deceptions. “His children shall be crushed by want, and his hands shall repay him his own pain.” His children, he says—that is, his imitators—shall be crushed by want and a lack of every good thing. And his hands—that is, the works he performed—shall repay him his own pain, because he shall be repaid in the same measure in which he measured. And rightly so. For as long as he lived, he never rested from evil. This is what he says: “His bones shall be filled with the vices of his youth, and they shall sleep with him in the dust.” What is meant by the bones except the more vigorous age? Therefore his bones are filled with the vices of youth, because even in old age he shall not cease from the vices which he was accustomed to commit in youth.

[Note: [Col. 0620D] The same is found in Proverbs 22:6: “A young man according to his way, even when he grows old, will not depart from it.”]

And they shall sleep with him in the dust, because at no age will he shake from himself the dust of vices, so as even late to awake for a good work. For the wicked always sleep; hence the Apostle says: “Awake, thou that sleepest; arise from the dead, and Christ shall enlighten thee” (Eph. 5:14).

“When evil is sweet in his mouth, he hides it under his tongue; he spares it and does not abandon it, and conceals it in his throat.” For when evil and iniquity were sweet and pleasant in the mouth of his heart, he did not disclose them or do penance, but hid them beneath his tongue. And he spared them, because he was unwilling to blot them out by confession. And he did not abandon them so that they might come forth through confession of the tongue; [Col. 0621A] rather, he concealed them in his throat, that is, in the secret place of his heart.

“His bread shall be changed in his belly into the gall of asps within.” His bread is changed within him into poison and the gall of asps [Note: [Col. 0621D] As though he were saying: just as food once eaten is sometimes converted into poisonous humours, so also the good things which the sinner possessed until death are turned into the bitterness of death. St Thomas.], when the very food by which his soul ought to have been given life becomes the means of its death. This happens to those who understand rightly but act wrongly. Hence the Apostle says: “To some we are an aroma of life unto life; to others, an aroma of death unto death” (2 Cor. 2:16).

“Riches which he swallowed down he shall vomit up, and God shall draw them out of his belly.” The riches of the Holy Scriptures, in which hypocrites frequently abound, they shall utterly lose at that time. Conversely, the good will receive perfectly whatever they lack. For as knowledge increases in the good, so ignorance will increase in the wicked. “The head of the asp shall rise up; the tongue of the viper shall kill him.” The devil is called both asp and viper: an asp because of the fierceness of its venom, a viper because it bursts when giving birth. For then the devil is burst with pain, when the sinners whom he had swallowed break forth from his belly and return to repentance. Whoever does not flee the head of the asp and drinks the incurable venom of evil spirits is surely killed by the tongue [Col. 0621B] of the viper; and, having been overcome and swallowed through the devil’s persuasion, how will he ever scarcely be able to come forth from its belly and escape?

“Let him not see the streams of the river, the torrents of honey and butter.” Let him not see, he says, nor understand the streams of the river—that is, the teachings of the New Testament—which abound and flow with honey and butter, because they show most openly that Christ is God and man. Honey, because it is gathered from the air, signifies divinity; butter, because it comes from flesh, signifies humanity. Or again, because it is sweet and easy, evangelical teaching may be called honey and butter.

“He shall pay for all that he has done, yet shall not be consumed.” For he shall be punished for every sin that he has committed; but because he will be immortal, he cannot be consumed utterly. He explains this as follows:

“According to the multitude of his devices, so shall he also endure. Because in crushing he stripped the house of the poor man, seized it, and did not build it up, his belly has not been satisfied.” For the house of the poor man, which the wicked violently crushed through pride, he made bare and despoiled through avarice. Yet [Col. 0621D] his belly has not been satisfied, because the desire of his greed cannot be satisfied.

“And when he has what he desired, he shall not be able to possess it.” Like the man in the Gospel who, though he had many goods, was told: “Fool, this night your soul shall be taken from you; and whose shall those things be which you have prepared?” (Luke 12:10).

“Nothing remained of his food, and therefore nothing of his goods shall remain.” This may be understood literally [Col. 0622A]: because he did not make alms even from the remnants of his food, therefore nothing of his goods remained for him.

“When he has been filled, he shall be straitened; he shall be in distress, and every pain shall rush upon him.” When, he says, he has been satisfied and filled, then he is hemmed in by many cares and anxieties; then he fears thieves and robbers, does not dare to sleep, dreads everything, and trembles lest he himself be seized. Thus every pain rushes upon him, though it would have been better for him not to be rich than always to remain in fear and distress because of riches. And since the wicked are nearer to misery and destruction precisely when they abound more in riches, he therefore adds:

“Would that his belly might be filled, that He may send upon him the wrath of His fury and rain down His war upon him.” Would that, he says, the desire of the ungodly might be fulfilled, so that, his wickedness being completed, he may be snatched more quickly to torments, and there at least experience the wrath and warfare of God’s fury, which descends abundantly upon the wicked like rain.

“He shall flee iron weapons, and fall upon a brazen bow; drawn forth and coming out of his sheath, flashing in his bitterness.” As he said above, so long as the ungodly man remains in this life, he is not without fear, pain, sorrow, and anxiety. These indeed are the iron weapons which he flees when passing from this world; but, what is worse for him, he falls upon the brazen bow—that is, impious and hard torments [Note: [Col. 0621D] “He shall flee iron weapons,” that is, the punishments of the present life, enduring them impatiently; these strike at close range like an iron sword. “And he shall fall upon a [Col. 0622D] brazen bow,” that is, upon the punishments of the future life, which strike, as it were, from afar like a brazen bow, which is unbreakable, signifying the unbreakable character of future punishments. St Thomas.]. Since those torments are hidden, they are called a bow; and since they are hard, they are called brazen. But when will this happen to them? Surely when he is drawn forth and comes out of his sheath—that is, [Col. 0622C] when his soul is drawn out from the tabernacle of the flesh. But how will he be there, except flashing—that is, burning and glowing—in his bitterness and distress? Hear what follows concerning the source of that bitterness:

“Terrors shall go and come upon him.” These terrors are evil spirits, which go and come upon him, because, trampling him without interruption, they do not allow him to have rest.

“All darkness is hidden in his eyes.” For he is hidden there where there are the shadow of death, darkness, and gloom.

“A fire that shall not be kindled shall devour him; he who is left in his tabernacle shall be afflicted.” That fire is inextinguishable, and once it has been kindled, it does not need to be kindled again. [Col. 0622D] He who remains in the tabernacle of his flesh shall always be afflicted, because both flesh and soul shall be tormented eternally.

“The heavens shall reveal his iniquity, and the earth shall rise up against him” [Note: [Col. 0622D] “That is, by heavenly power it shall come about that his iniquity, which lay hidden in life, is revealed after death.” St Thomas.]. The heavens are the apostles, and the earth is the Church. Since the wicked are condemned by their judgment, these are said to rise against them and reveal their iniquities.

“The offspring of his house shall be laid bare; it shall be carried away in the day of the Lord’s wrath.” Whatever is hidden now will then be open and manifest [Note: [Col. 0623D] The Lord also taught this truth when He said: “Nothing is covered that shall not be revealed, and hidden that shall not be known.” Luke 10:26.]. Then all things shall be brought out, because they shall be opened to all.

“This is the portion of the wicked man from God, and the inheritance of his words from the Lord.” That is, the wicked man shall receive this portion and inheritance from God not only for the things which he did wickedly, but also for what he spoke foolishly and without discipline.

## CHAPTER XXI

“Then Job answered and said: Hear, I pray, my words; repent, bear with me, and I will speak; and after my words, if it seems good to you, laugh.” Since they had spoken against the truth, he compassionately invites them to repentance. [Col. 0623B] That they had afflicted him not only by words but also by laughter is made clear when he says: “And after my words, if it seems good to you, laugh.” For fools, when they cannot otherwise avoid appearing defeated, defend themselves with laughter.

“Is my argument against a man, that I should not rightly be grieved?” I dispute against Him who is most just and can do nothing unjust. Therefore, when I consider both His justice, my own deeds, and these scourges, how should I not be grieved? I do not know why I am afflicted; yet I do know that I am not afflicted without cause.

“Attend to me and be astonished, and lay your finger upon your mouth.” Attend, he says, and consider my words; marvel and be astonished at what I have just said—namely, that God is just, that I am [Col. 0623C] innocent, and yet the scourges do not cease. The words which follow, “and lay your finger upon your mouth,” indicate that they were moved to indignation by these words and did not wish to reply.

“And when I remember, I am terrified, and trembling shakes my flesh.” Not only you, he says, but I too, when I recall and reflect upon these things, am immediately terrified and shaken with fear. But it is more astonishing that, because you see me afflicted, you think me wicked—as though no one but the wicked were afflicted and no one but the just enjoyed joy and gladness.

“Why then do the wicked live, are exalted, and strengthened with riches?” If, he says, as you maintain, God persecutes and afflicts only the wicked, why then do they live? Why are they exalted and strengthened by riches? [Col. 0623D] He proves this:

“Their offspring remains before them, a multitude of kinsfolk and descendants in their sight; their houses are secure and at peace, and the rod of God is not upon them. Their bull breeds and does not fail; their cow calves and is not deprived of her offspring; their little ones go forth like flocks, and their children leap in play. They take the timbrel and harp, and rejoice at the sound [Col. 0624A] of the instrument.” Who then would dare say that such people are not exalted and strengthened by riches? These words are to be understood literally and are so plain that they require no exposition.

It follows: “They spend their days in prosperity, and in a moment descend to hell” [Note: [Col. 0623D] “Hell is also understood as death, as St Thomas teaches here with many Fathers: ‘And in a moment they descend to hell,’ that is, to death. For all the ancients before the Redeemer’s coming descended to [Col. 0624D] hell; but some, oppressed by adversities on their journey, descended to hell not suddenly but through many bitter experiences, as Jacob said in Genesis 37: ‘I shall go down mourning to my son into hell.’ But those who flourish in prosperity until death descend to hell, as it were, in a moment.”]. It is as though he said: Although they live this life amid such great happiness, nevertheless in a moment they lose everything and are snatched away to torments, because there is no delay between death and punishment.

“They said to God: Depart from us; we do not desire knowledge of Your ways.” This also makes clear why they deservedly descended to hell. They say this to God not so much with their voice as by their actions, when, by living wickedly, they drive all justice and equity away from themselves. And these people do not desire to know His ways, [Col. 0624B] because they make for death not by the narrow path of virtues but by the broad ways of vices.

“What is the Almighty, that we should serve Him? And what profit is it if we worship Him?” Pharaoh said this also: “I do not know the Lord, and I will not let Israel go” (Exod. 5:2). And David likewise: “The fool has said in his heart: There is no God” (Ps. 13:1). “And what profit,” they say, “is it to us if we worship Him, when we see those who worship Him unhappy and those who do not worship Him happy?” Such things are said by those who contemplate not the future but the present.

“Nevertheless, because their goods are not in their hand, let the counsel of the wicked be far from me.” Everything is in God’s hand and power; when He commands, nothing shall remain to the wicked. Or again, their goods are not in their hand because they do not properly understand eternal goods.

“How often shall the lamp of the wicked be extinguished, and a flood come upon them, and He distribute the pains of His fury?” Although, he says, the wicked sometimes prosper, they do not always do so. Their lamp is often extinguished, and they lose what they loved as the light of their eyes. For each person’s lamp is what he greatly loves, whether children, riches, or honours. A flood comes upon them when God’s sudden indignation afflicts them violently. The Lord distributes to them the pains of His fury because He gives some to them in this life and reserves others for the life to come. Let us hear what happens when they come to those pains.

“They shall be [Col. 0624D] like chaff before the wind, and like ash scattered by a whirlwind.” Before they are kindled, they are chaff; once kindled, ash. The wind and whirlwind that scatter them signify the onset of evil spirits.

“God shall reserve for his children the father’s sorrow, and when He repays, then he shall know.” The holy man confirms his words not only through other wicked men, but also through him who will be most wicked of all—that is, Antichrist. His children are all who do his works. God reserves the father’s sorrow for them because, condemned together with him, they will suffer the same torments. And when God returns for judgment—He who now, having been judged unjustly, ascended into heaven—then this wicked man shall know how great a sorrow is reserved both for himself and his children.

“His eyes shall see his own slaying, and he shall drink of the wrath of the Almighty.” This is what the Apostle says: “Whom the Lord Jesus shall slay with the spirit of His mouth and destroy by the brightness of His coming” (2 Thess. 2:8). Since this will happen openly, he says that Antichrist’s eyes shall see it.

“For what concern has he for his house after him, even if the number of his months is halved?” His house consists of those whom he deceived. But after his death they will no longer belong to him, [Col. 0625B] because, once the truth is known, they will be converted to the faith, according to the saying: “Though the number of the children of Israel be as the sand of the sea, a remnant shall be saved” (Rom. 9:27). The number of his months shall be halved because he shall not live as long as he expects to live. Thus Truth itself says: “Unless those days had been shortened, no flesh would have been saved; but for the elect’s sake those days shall be shortened” (Matt. 24:22).

“Shall anyone teach God knowledge, who judges those on high?” It is as though he said: Since it is clear that both good and wicked people are sometimes afflicted in this life without distinction, and sometimes are not, who shall teach God knowledge by saying that it is not just [Col. 0625C] for good people to suffer, or that it is not just for wicked people to spend their days in prosperity? He who judges those on high ought neither to be taught nor judged by those below. But I also wish you to answer what follows.

“One man dies strong and healthy, rich and happy; his inward parts are full of fat, and the marrow moistens his bones. Another dies in bitterness of soul, without any wealth; and yet together they sleep in the dust, and worms cover them.” He shows that he has said this only of the wicked. For good and wicked people do not sleep together. Thus these words plainly show that the former is not condemned because he is rich, nor the latter justified because he is poor; rather, each is condemned because he is wicked. Therefore neither riches nor poverty, health nor sickness, [Col. 0625D] prosperity nor adversity condemns a person, but wickedness alone. He adds why he has said this:

“Surely I know your thoughts and the unjust judgments you make against me. For you say: Where is the house of the prince, and where are the dwellings of the wicked?” Because they saw all his goods dispersed and himself so grievously afflicted, they judged him wicked and unjust—as though everyone afflicted in this life were wicked. Now, however, he turns his speech to Antichrist, of whom he had begun to speak above. Although Antichrist is the most wicked of all, he shall nevertheless prosper for a time so greatly that he will sit in the temple of God, presenting himself [Col. 0626A] as though he were God. He is proved wicked by this: although he may not lose his kingdom and worldly glory before death, after death he is nevertheless wondrously dragged to torments. This is what he says:

“Ask any of the travellers, and you shall find that they understand the same things: that the wicked man is reserved for the day of destruction and led to the day of wrath.” He is preserved for a time and not afflicted in order that he may later be condemned to a greater punishment. Therefore, if Job is judged wicked because he is afflicted, it follows that Antichrist, who will prosper, should be judged just. By “travellers” he means those who, living as pilgrims in this world, journey toward the heavenly homeland. Such a traveller was he who said: “I am a stranger in the earth and a pilgrim, as all my fathers were; and [Col. 0626B] I have run the way of Your commandments” (Ps. 119:19). He understood the same thing as Job concerning Antichrist’s destruction. For he says: “He shall bow down and fall when he has ruled over the poor” (Ps. 9:10); and again, “You shall break the arm of the sinner and the wicked man” (ibid., 15).

It follows: “Who shall rebuke his way before him, and who shall repay him for what he has done?” Unless Christ? This is understood, for “He shall slay him with the spirit of His mouth.” His power is so great that human strength cannot resist him.

“He shall be brought to the graves, and shall keep watch amid the heap of the dead.” Of these graves the Lord says in the Gospel: “But the rich man died also, and was buried in hell” (Luke 16:22). There this wicked man shall keep watch amid the heap of the dead—that is, in that vast multitude of the damned—[Col. 0626C] because he shall never again have rest, and deservedly so:

“He was sweet to the gravel of Cocytus [Note: [Col. 0625D] “Since he invoked the testimony of travellers, he sets forth the truth concerning the punishments of the wicked after death under a story commonly related: namely, that [Col. 0626D] in hell, among others, there was a certain river called Cocytus, which means ‘lamentation,’ by which the souls of the wicked are destroyed.” St Thomas.]; after him he shall draw every man, and before him innumerable persons.” Cocytus, as the poets imagine, is a river of hell, whose name means “lamentation”; by it we may understand the more grievous punishments of hell. The gravel of this river consists of all those submerged in it, suffering lamentation, misery, and the other torments of hell. Antichrist was sweet to such persons because his works and teaching pleased all the wicked. He shall draw every man after him because whoever believes him shall be led with him to hell. “Man” in this place signifies sinners, according to the saying: “But you shall die like men” [Col. 0626D] (Ps. 82:7). He shall draw innumerable persons before him: for he will deceive not only those whom he finds here, but will also draw with him to torments those who now await his coming.

“Why then do you console me in vain, when your answer has been shown to contradict the truth?” He calls it “consoling” by way of derision. Their answer has been shown to contradict the truth, because it has not been proved either that only the wicked are scourged in this world or that only the just prosper.

## CHAPTER XXII

“Then Eliphaz the Temanite answered and said: [Col. 0627A] Can man be compared with God, even though he has perfect knowledge? What profit is it to God if you are just? Or what do you confer upon Him if your way is blameless? Will He rebuke you out of fear and enter with you into judgment? Is it not because of your great wickedness and your countless iniquities?” It is clear that Eliphaz has been defeated and has no answer left. He repeats what has already been said and is known to everyone, being ashamed to say something new; moreover, exceedingly angry, he breaks out into insults and abusive words. For who does not know that no one can be compared with God, that He can neither be increased nor diminished in any respect, and that He does nothing from fear? When Job openly asked to be rebuked and judged by God, he said this not as a provocation by threats, [Col. 0627B] but in prayer and action. But let us hear what Eliphaz, angry, says falsely against the holy man:

“For you have taken pledges from your brethren without cause, and stripped the naked of their clothing. You have not given water to the weary, and have withheld bread from the hungry. In the strength of your arm you possessed the land, and, being most powerful, held it. You have sent widows away empty, and broken the arms of orphans. Therefore you are surrounded with snares, and sudden terror troubles you. And did you think that you would not see darkness and would not be overwhelmed by the rush of flooding waters?” By darkness and flooding waters he means all Job’s afflictions, which rushed upon him suddenly and violently. [Col. 0627C] It is superfluous to seek an allegory in these words, since they ought to be understood literally. For it is no less a fault to seek allegory in things that must be understood literally than to wish to interpret only literally things that must be understood allegorically. Thus, when the Lord said in the Gospel, “To eat with unwashed hands does not defile a man” (Matt. 15:11), and the apostles, supposing that He had spoken parabolically, said, “Explain this parable to us” (ibid., 15), the Lord immediately rebuked them, saying, “Are you also still without understanding?” (ibid., 16).

“Do you not consider that God is higher than heaven and exalted above the tops of the stars? Yet you say: What does God know? And He judges, as it were, through darkness. [Col. 0627D] Clouds are His hiding place; He does not consider our affairs, and He walks about the hinges of heaven.” Although God is higher than heaven, He does not abandon the governance of the world. Nor is He far off, since He is everywhere. He knows all things because He made all things; neither clouds nor darkness obstruct His eyes. He considers all things and, though remaining unmoved, walks through all things.

“Do you desire to keep the path of the ages, which wicked men have trodden, who were taken away before their time, and whose foundation a river overthrew?” The path of the ages is that by which people walk who are worldly, not spiritual; because it is long and broad, it is called the path of the ages. Wicked men tread and keep this path because they love only present and [Col. 0628A] worldly things. Job too would desire to keep this path if, as Eliphaz supposed, he had grieved over fleeting goods. Wicked men are taken away before their time because they do not live as long as they hoped to live. The river and rush of death overthrow their foundations—that is, the stability of their life. Death is called a river because, once it began to flow, it has never ceased; all who enter this world drink from this river.

“They said to God: Depart from us,” and considered the Almighty as though He could do nothing, although He had filled their houses with goods. God fills the houses of the wicked with goods because He causes them to abound in worldly riches, which are indeed good in themselves.

“Let their counsel be far [Col. 0628B] from me.” Eliphaz distances himself from these words because he thought that blessed Job had previously uttered them concerning himself.

“The just shall see and rejoice, and the innocent shall mock them.” This is what the Psalmist says: “The just man shall rejoice when he sees vengeance” (Ps. 58:11). The innocent one—that is, Christ—shall mock them, according to the saying: “He who dwells in heaven shall laugh at them, and the Lord shall mock them” (Ps. 2:4), and shall say in derision: “Has not their exaltation been cut down?” For in exalting themselves, they were proud.

“And fire shall devour their remnant.” This is surely the fire of Gehenna; by “remnant” he means flesh and soul, because of all that they possessed nothing else shall remain [Col. 0628C] to them.

“Therefore submit yourself to Him and have peace, and through this you shall have the best fruits.” Submit yourself to Him, he says, and do not be proud; now have rest and peace, and by this you shall obtain the best fruits and a great reward.

“Receive the law from His mouth, and lay His words up in your heart.” Receive, he says, these words; receive this law not from my mouth but from His, for these words and sayings are His. Lay them up in your heart, therefore, and do not forget them. Eliphaz speaks truly, but arrogantly:

“If you return to the Almighty, you shall be built up, and you shall put iniquity far from your tent.” You have been destroyed, he says, because of your pride and wickedness; but if you do penance [Col. 0628D] and return to God, you shall be built up again, and all wickedness shall flee from you.

“He shall give you flint in place of earth, and torrents of gold in place of flint.” If, he says, you return to the Almighty, He shall give you the strength and firmness of flint in place of the softness and weakness of earth which you had. If you hold that strength rightly, He shall give you torrents of gold in exchange for it—that is, a great abundance of wisdom and knowledge.

“And the Almighty shall be against your enemies, and silver shall be heaped up for you.” Silver is heaped up for the person who holds both wisdom in the heart and truth in speech. Wisdom without truth is useless.

“Then you shall abound in delights in the Almighty, and lift your face to God.” He abounds in delights in the Almighty who delights in contemplating Him; [Col. 0629A] therefore it follows: “And you shall lift your face to God,” because you will now delight to behold not low and earthly things but heavenly things.

“You shall pray to Him, and He shall hear you, and you shall pay your vows.” Whoever pays vows after being heard shows that he made some vow in order to be heard. This often happens to sailors and to others in danger.

“You shall determine a matter, and it shall come to you; and light shall shine in your ways.” That is, you shall obtain what you desire and shall not err in your actions.

“For he who has been humbled shall be in glory, and he who lowers his eyes shall be saved.” According to the saying: “Everyone who humbles himself shall be exalted” (Luke 3:5). Pride is easily perceived in the eyes.

“The innocent man shall be saved; he shall be saved by the cleanness of his hands.” Both the humble and the innocent person shall be saved—not merely because he is humble and innocent, but because he is clean in all his work.

## CHAPTER XXIII

“Then Job answered and said: Even now my speech is in bitterness, and the hand of my wound is heavier than my groaning.” Because, he says, you weary me with unjust rebukes under the appearance of consolation, and the Lord’s hand does not cease to scourge me, my speech is bitter and my groaning increases all the more.

“Who will grant me that I may know and find Him, and come even to His throne? I will lay my case before Him and fill my mouth with reproaches, that I may know the words which He will answer me [Col. 0629C] and understand what He will say to me.” To know and find God, and come even to His throne, is to understand most fully His will and His hidden judgments. Blessed Job desired this because he wished to know why he was afflicted. He also wishes to lay his case before God and fill his mouth with reproaches, because he is ready to confess his whole life to Him and, in whatever matters he has sinned, to judge, condemn, and rebuke himself. But why does he desire this? So that he may know what the Lord will answer and say to him. For then the Lord would answer and speak to him, if He revealed both His will and what Job desired to know.

“I do not wish Him to contend with me in great strength, nor oppress me with the weight of His majesty. Let Him set equity [Col. 0629D] before me, and let my judgment come to victory.” No one is so just that he can defend himself if judged by the Lord in strict judgment. Hence the Psalmist says: “Do not enter into judgment with Your servant, for no living being shall be justified in Your sight” (Ps. 143:2). Who, not to speak of original sin, but even of sins committed in thought or ignorance, could defend himself if judged by the Lord according to strict justice? Job therefore wishes to be judged according to equity and mercy, a phrase taken from secular laws: *ex bono et aequo*, “according to what is good and equitable.” It is equitable that the Lord spare the humble, those who serve in good intention, who, even if ignorantly and in matters without which this life can scarcely be sustained, fall in some way into sin, [Col. 0630A] and immediately resort to repentance. If the Lord sets this equity before Job, he does not fear that his judgment will attain victory. But why is this equity denied to blessed Job, when it is denied to no sinner?

“If I go to the east, He does not appear; and if to the west, I shall not understand Him; if to the left, what shall I do? I shall not grasp Him. If I turn to the right, I shall not see Him. Yet He knows my way and will test me like gold that passes through fire.” Therefore, he says, He knows me and my way utterly. For I inquire and carefully consider with myself whether, in the east—that is, in my first age—I did anything for which I ought to have been so afflicted; and I understand neither sin nor a judge judging there for sin. Likewise I come to the west—that is, to this final stage of my life—and there too I do not see my judge judging me. And I seek the same thing not only in equable circumstances, but also in right and left—that is, in my prosperity and adversity—and do not find it. Thus, wrapped in the darkness of ignorance, I do not know myself. Yet He knows all my way and will therefore test me like gold passing through fire—that is, He will not cease either to burn or afflict me until, the rust of every vice having been smelted away, nothing faulty or unclean remains in me.

“My foot has followed His footsteps; I have kept His way and have not turned aside from it. I have not departed from the commandments of [Col. 0630C] His lips, and I have hidden the words of His mouth in my bosom.” Therefore, he says, I cannot find what I should blame in myself or for what I ought to be condemned, because, so far as I could, I have kept God’s law. My foot followed His footsteps because, walking rightly, I imitated Him by the steps of the virtues. One hides words in the bosom of one’s heart who commits them most firmly to memory.

“For He alone is, and no one can turn aside His thought; and whatever His soul wills, that He has done.” He is rightly said to be alone who always is and never changes. No one can turn aside His thought, because what He has once determined is firm and stable. Behold, His soul—that is, His power and might—has done whatever He willed. Since He is such, I rightly [Col. 0630D] followed Him, because there is no other such person whom I ought to have followed.

“And when He has fulfilled His will in me, many other like things are ready with Him.” That is, after He has afflicted me according to His will for some fault I do not know, He will, if He wishes, find other things in me for which I may again be afflicted.

“Therefore I am troubled before His face; when I consider Him, I am troubled with fear.” Since nothing can be hidden from Him, he says, I fear His strict judgment when I consider His face and knowledge.

“God has softened my heart, and the Almighty has troubled me.” He, he says, knows me well, and I cannot hide myself from Him in any way. He has not only made me, but softened my heart; and whatever good I thought that I had done, I did not do it, but He did: “It is not of him who wills, nor of him who runs, but of God who shows mercy” (Rom. 9:16). The Almighty has troubled me; why He has troubled me, though I do not know it, He nevertheless does not fail to know.

“For I have not perished because of the impending darkness, nor has darkness covered my face.” I suffer, he says, the darkness of ignorance, but not that of error. Those who suffer the darkness of error—such as Jews, pagans, and heretics—perish in it and because of it. But I have not perished or been afflicted because of such darkness, nor has the gloom of error covered the eyes of my heart.

## CHAPTER XXIV

“Times are not hidden from the Almighty; but those who know Him do not know His days” [Note: [Col. 0631D] “That is, they cannot comprehend the mode of His eternity; and because Job had said that the course of temporal things is not unknown to God, he consequently shows [Col. 0632D] how God judges temporal things, permitting the various sins of human beings, some of whom deceitfully inflict injuries upon others.” St Thomas.]. [Col. 0631B] We, he says, are not without some ignorance. God alone knows all things, seeing present, past, and future together. But those who know Him, whether angels or saints, although they know Him through faith, nevertheless do not know His days, because they do not recall them from eternity. What knowledge could comprehend the infinite? From this point he begins to recount the life and deeds of the wicked.

“Others have moved boundary-markers, carried off flocks, and fed them. They have driven away the donkey of the fatherless and taken the widow’s ox as a pledge. They have overturned the way of the poor and together oppressed the meek of the earth.” Since these things are plain in their literal sense, let us see what they signify allegorically. Both Jews and heretics move the boundaries of the faith when they persuade people to believe either more or less than the Catholic Church holds [Col. 0631C]. They carry off and feed flocks because, whenever they can steal believers from God and deceive them, they feed and nourish them with the teaching of their own error. But what are meant by the donkey and the ox, except bishops and priests, who both cultivate God’s field and bear the burdens of others? And what by the widow and the fatherless, except the Church and her children? Heretics steal and take away this ox and donkey when they overthrow someone from the priestly order. They take the ox as a pledge because, once they have deceived a prelate, they are secure about his subjects, as though they already held a pledge over them. Thus it is added: “They have overturned the way of the poor and together oppressed the meek of the earth” [Col. 0631D]. For once those who seemed rich both in faith and knowledge have been deceived, the simple and unlearned are easily overthrown and oppressed. It follows:

“Others, like wild asses in the desert, go out to their work; watching for prey, they prepare bread for their children; they reap a field not their own, and gather the vintage of the vineyard of him whom they have violently oppressed.” Others, he says, like wild asses, devoted to pleasure and luxury, carry out their own work, not God’s, through this desert of the world. They watch for prey; they apply themselves to deception; they prepare bread—that is, teaching of falsehood—for their children [Col. 0632A], namely, those who imitate them. They reap a field not their own because they lay waste God’s Church. And they gather the vintage of the vineyard of him whom they have violently oppressed. “For the vineyard of the Lord Sabaoth is the house of Israel; and as many faithful persons as heretics deceive, so many clusters, as it were, they gather from it in the vintage” (Isa. V, 7). But because Christ is truth, whoever resist truth violently oppress Christ.

“They leave men naked, taking away their clothing, who have no covering in the cold; whom the rains of the mountains drench, and who, lacking a covering, embrace the rocks.” For heretics, by taking away the garments of faith, leave naked those whom they deceive—those, that is, who have no covering in the cold, namely that cold of which it is said: “Because iniquity has abounded, the charity of many shall grow cold” [Col. 0632B] (Matt. XXIV, 12). The garments of faith are easily taken from those who lack the covering of charity, whenever the cold of iniquity comes upon them against the fire of charity. But because he said, “they leave,” we must understand those whom heretics, though overthrowing them, cannot retain, since, once their error is recognized, they return to the Church. Hence it is added: “Whom the rains of the mountains drench,” that is, whom the teaching of the saints washes and cleanses from every heresy. These persons, who were naked and had no covering—for heretics had stripped them—embrace the rocks, saying to the mountains: “Fall upon us,” and to the hills: “Cover us” (Luke XXIII, 30). For they ask the saints; they entreat the living stones to cover their nakedness [Col. 0632C] and clothe them again in the garments of faith.

“They used violence in plundering the fatherless and stripped the common people who were poor.” Because they cannot plunder or make a way through those who are stronger and rich in the treasures of wisdom, they turn to the fatherless and to the poor, unlearned common people. “From the naked and those walking without clothing, and from the hungry, they have taken ears of grain.” The naked and hungry are those whom the teaching of the faith has neither fully clothed nor satisfied. Thus they lose not the grain but the ears, because they do not yet perceive the faith they bear, nor understand what its taste is. “Among their heaps they rested at noon, though they thirst as they tread the winepresses.” By those who thirst while treading the winepresses [Col. 0632D], we may understand those who read the sacred books daily and do not understand them: for as many books as there are, so many winepresses there are. Among their heaps many heretics rest at noon; for, wearied by teachers, they delight and find rest among such people, and offer the must of their perverse interpretation to drink.

“They made men groan in the cities, and the soul of the wounded cried out; and God does not allow it to go unavenged.” These cities are the individual churches. The men groaning in them are bishops and priests, whose souls, wounded by the cruelty of heretics, cry out to God in grief [Col. 0633A]. God will undoubtedly avenge them. “They themselves were rebels against the light; they did not know its ways, nor did they return by its paths.” Heretics have always been rebels against the light—that is, Christ, who is the true light and light from light. They did not know his ways, because “all the ways of the Lord are mercy and truth” (Ps. XXIV, 11), whereas they are wicked and false. Nor did they return by his paths in order to repent of their iniquities. For repentance is not a road, but a path.

“At first dawn the murderer rises; he kills the needy and poor, and by night he will be like a thief.” For the wicked do by night what they cannot do by day; no time is free to them from wickedness. “The eye of the adulterer watches for darkness, saying: ‘No eye will see me,’ and he covers his face” [Col. 0633B]. “For everyone, as it is written, who does evil hates the light” (John III, 30). This may also be understood of the heretic, because he is an adulterer against the Church. He always watches for darkness, because, speaking ambiguously and obscurely, he fears being detected. This is what it means when it says that he covered his face: one who covers his face does not wish to be known. “He breaks into houses in the darkness, just as they had agreed together by day; and they did not know the light.” Blessed Job seems here to speak especially about his friends, of whom he spoke above.

For they had agreed among themselves to come together and visit him. When they were in daylight and prosperity, they agreed together to come to Job, who was in darkness and adversity, and diligently to break into and lay open, by their rebukes, all the houses and hiding-places of his conscience [Col. 0633C]. They did not know the light because, enveloped in the darkness of ignorance, they did not recognize the light of truth in blessed Job’s words. “If dawn suddenly appears, they regard it as the shadow of death; and so they walk in darkness as though in light.” Dawn appears to heretics when, convicted either by arguments or by examples of the saints, they recognize truth amid their errors. Yet they regard this as the shadow of death, because that from which they ought to rejoice makes them grieve even unto death. Thus they walk in darkness as though in light, for they delight in the darkness of error no less than holy Catholic men delight in the light of truth. “He is light upon the face of the water.” The surface of water is moved by every wind that blows upon it; so the wicked person is carried about by every wind of doctrine [Col. 0633D]. “Let his portion be cursed upon the earth, and let him not walk by the way of the vineyards.” Each day the Church condemns and curses heretics. The vineyards are churches, whose way is faith. Heretics do not walk by this way; for, had they walked by it, they would not be heretics.

“Let him pass from snowy waters to excessive heat, and his sin even to hell.” The wicked will have this in hell: transferred from torment to torment, they will now be tortured by cold, now by heat. “And his sin even to hell” [Col. 0634A], because, having died in sin and been condemned, he will suffer the torments of hell. “Let mercy forget him,” so that he may never find mercy. “Worms [shall be] his sweetness,” that is, whatever was sweet in him may be consumed by worms. Or, “his sweetness,” that is, the flesh which alone he loved, may be turned into worms. “Let him not be in remembrance.” This is what he just said: “Let mercy forget him.” But let him be broken like an unfruitful tree, according to the saying: “Every tree that does not bear good fruit shall be cut down and cast into the fire” (Matt. III, 10).—“For he fed the barren woman who does not bear, and did not do good to the widow.” He excessively and luxuriously fed his flesh, barren and unfruitful in every good work, but did no good to his soul [Col. 0634B], made a widow and separated from God.

“He dragged down the mighty in his strength; and when he stands, he will not trust in his life.” He dragged down, he says, the powerful of this age through the strength of his perversity; and, blinded inwardly, as long as he stands in this world, he will not believe in his life—that is, in Christ, who said: “I am the way, the truth, and the life” (John XIV, 6).

[Note: [Col. 0633D] God gave him a place for repentance, namely by postponing punishment; and this is why someone was permitted to live long in prosperity. But what God [Col. 0634D] offered him for good, he turned to evil, etc. D. THOM.]

“God gave him a place for repentance, and he abuses it for pride.” For when he should have humbled himself in repentance, he instead does not cease to grow proud. “But his eyes are upon his sins; they are raised up for a little while and shall not endure.” His eyes are not on God’s ways but upon his own ways [Col. 0634C], because, always looking upon the paths and deeds of habitual iniquity, he will never forget them. “They are raised up for a little while” in pride, “and shall not endure,” because they will quickly perish and fail. “And they are humbled like all things,” namely, earthly and transitory things. “And they shall be taken away” from the enticements of this life. “And like the tops of ears of grain” (the phrase “little by little,” and “most easily,” is understood) “they shall be crushed.” “But if it is not so, who can convict me of lying and set my words before God?” It is so, he says, as I have stated. Yet if it were not so, you could not convict me of falsehood or set my words before God, since you have been found liars and are no longer worthy of being believed.

## CHAPTER XXV

[Col. 0634D] “Then Bildad the Shuhite answered and said: Power and terror are with him, who makes concord in his high places.” If anything is to be feared, he says, he alone must be feared: by his terror and power he put the army of evil spirits to flight and made concord in his high places, confirming peace and concord among the other angels. They are not merely united and strong, but also innumerable, so that nothing can resist them. Therefore it is added: “Is there any number to his armies? And upon whom does his light not shine?” As though he said: It is indeed folly to wish to contend with him [Col. 0635A] who surpasses all things by the number and strength both of himself and of his armies; the light of whose eyes shines everywhere, from whom not only deeds but even thoughts cannot hide themselves. “Can a man be justified in comparison with God? Or can one born of a woman appear clean?” You are, he says, like other human beings, nor ought you deny that you were born from a woman, who is indeed frail and the gate of sin.

[Note: [Col. 0635D] He says this pointedly because, by the very fact that a human being is born from a woman through the concupiscence of the flesh, he contracts a stain. D. THOM.]

You are therefore not clean, nor can you be justified in comparison with God, because you said: “Let him set equity against me, and let my judgment attain victory. Behold, even the moon does not shine, and the stars are not clean in his sight; how much more rottenness, and the son of man, a worm.”

[Note: [Col. 0635D] That is, it cannot be regarded as shining with the splendor of justice if compared with divine justice, nor clean through innocence if compared with divine purity. D. THOM.]

For what is meant by the moon except the Church, and by the stars except the saints? Behold, he says, the Church and the stars of the New Testament—that is, saints renewed by the water of baptism and released from original sin—are not altogether clean before God’s eyes [Col. 0635B]. How much less so is man, rottenness, and the son of man, a worm, who has not yet been renewed in anything and remains held by the curse of the first man, to whom it was said: “Cursed is the earth in your work” (Gen. III, 17); and shortly afterward: “For dust you are, and unto dust you shall return” (ibid., 19).

## CHAPTER XXVI

“Then Job answered and said: Whose helper are you? Is it the weak man? And do you support the arm of one who is not strong? To whom have you given counsel? Perhaps to one who does not have wisdom, and have you displayed [Col. 0633C] your abundant prudence? Or whom did you intend to teach? Was it not him who made the breath?” These men, as God’s helpers, spoke for God and defended his justice. They endeavored to prove God just and Job unjust, as though God, being weak, imprudent, and ignorant, could not defend his own cause, or as though the holy man had wished to prove him unjust. He therefore describes God’s strength, prudence, and wisdom, saying:

“Behold, the giants groan beneath the waters [Note: [Col. 0635D] Behold, the giants: namely, the ancients.
