They groan, namely, in the punishments of hell; beneath the waters, that is, those who were [Col. 0636D] submerged by the waters of the Flood. And because not they alone perished, but many others with them, these likewise groan, namely, by the power of his might. D. THOM.], and those who dwell with them. Hell is naked before him, and there is no covering for destruction.” Behold, he says, giants—that is, kings and princes and the other powerful, together with those who live with them, namely their counsellors and retainers—groan beneath waters, that is, amid the government of peoples [Col. 0635D]. “For many waters are many peoples” (Rev. XVII, 27). They cannot possess or retain those whom they rule without great labor and anxiety. They groan under them, therefore, because, as though heavily burdened, they can scarcely bear and govern them. But God disposes and orders all things by a mere nod.

By hell and destruction the devil is understood [Col. 0636A], who is lower in punishments even than those whom he has destroyed. Because he cannot hide his iniquity and malice from God, he is said to be naked and without covering before him. “He stretches out the north over emptiness and hangs the earth over nothing.” Though this is true literally, we can marvel at it more than understand it. By the north is signified the one who said: “I will sit upon the mount of the covenant, in the sides of the north, and I will be like the Most High” (Isa. XIV, 13). God stretches him over emptiness by allowing him to rule those who are empty of faith, religion, and good works. He hangs the earth over nothing because he founded and established the holy Church upon the nations, whom he had previously counted as nothing, according to the saying: “All nations are as though they were not before him, and are accounted by him as nothing and emptiness” [Col. 0636B] (ibid., 40).—

“Who binds the waters in the clouds, so that they do not burst forth all at once downward.” The clouds are teachers, in whom God has bound and enclosed the water of his teaching, lest it burst forth all at once and extinguish the life rather than the thirst of the hearers. Thus the Apostle gave milk to drink to some, not solid food (I Cor. III, 2), though he speaks wisdom among the perfect. “Who holds the face of his throne and spreads his cloud over it.” The throne signifies the judicial seat. God still conceals and holds back the face of his throne because, while we remain in this world, we cannot know his hidden judgments. Hence he rightly says that a cloud of obscurity is spread over it [Col. 0636C]. “He has set a boundary around the waters, until light and darkness are ended.” By the waters he signified the knowledge of the holy Scriptures. God set a limit to this knowledge, so that it is not fully understood until light and darkness—that is, day and night—come to an end. For it is written: “God called the light day and the darkness night” (Gen. I, 5). Therefore no one will possess complete and perfect knowledge until this world first comes to an end.

“The pillars of heaven tremble and are afraid at his nod.” The pillars of heaven are the apostles and teachers of the Church, who would not endure such great things for him if they did not fear God. “By his strength the seas were suddenly gathered together, and by his prudence he struck the proud one.” God’s power and wisdom—God’s strength and prudence—is Christ. Incarnate, he struck the devil and cast him out of the kingdom that he had long possessed. Thus he suddenly gathered all seas—that is, all the nations of this world—into one faith and one Church [Col. 0636D]. “His Spirit adorned the heavens, and by the hand acting as midwife the twisting serpent was brought forth.”

[Note: [Col. 0636D] “The twisting serpent,” that is, the devil, who is compared to a serpent because of the poison of his malice and is called twisting because of his cunning. He pointedly says that the serpent was brought forth by the hand of God acting as a midwife. Just as a midwife sometimes delivers even a dead infant so that the mother may not be harmed, so God brought the devil [Col. 0637] out from among the angels in such a way that the fellowship of the good angels suffered no loss whatever. D. THOM.]

For the heavens—that is, the holy apostles—had not yet been adorned; but when the Holy Spirit came, they were immediately adorned with knowledge, diversity of tongues, and effective power [Col. 0637A]. And that twisting serpent, which deceived the first man and never proceeds by a straight path, was drawn out and expelled from the minds of believers by the hand and power of God, who circumcises his faithful ones in soul and body.

“Behold, these things are spoken of only in part concerning his ways; and since we have scarcely heard a small drop of his word, who can behold the thunder of his greatness?” This fragment, he says, and as it were a drop from that great fullness of his powers, we have heard and proclaimed. But since, as we have just said, he accomplished such great things in the weakness of assumed flesh, who will be able to behold him when he comes in his majesty and thunders the sentence of condemnation against the wicked [Col. 0637B]?

## CHAPTER XXVII

“Job also continued, taking up his parable, and said.” By calling it a parable, he indicates that something besides the literal meaning must be sought. “As God lives, who has taken away my judgment, and the Almighty, who has brought my soul to bitterness: as long as breath remains in me and the Spirit of the Lord is in my nostrils, my lips shall not speak iniquity, nor shall my tongue devise falsehood.” God took away his judgment because he thought that he ought to be judged otherwise. To speak belongs to the mouth; to devise belongs to the heart. Therefore neither the tongue of the mouth will speak falsehood nor the tongue of the heart iniquity. Why he said this he makes clear: “Far be it from me to judge you righteous; until I fail, I will not depart from my innocence” [Col. 0637C]. For he would lie if he judged righteous those who were not righteous; and if he lied, he would not be innocent. Thus he adds: “I will not forsake the justification which I have begun to hold. For my heart does not reproach me throughout all my life.” He would forsake justification if he ceased from truth, for truth justified him. His heart’s not reproaching him throughout his life shows that he sinned only unknowingly. For who reproaches what he does not know? Because he strongly resists unlawful thoughts, even if he has sometimes thought what is unlawful, his heart nevertheless does not reproach him for it.

“May my enemy fare as the wicked man, and my adversary as the unjust” [Col. 0637D]. Thus my enemy—that is, Satan—acts as a wicked man, because, insofar as he can, he afflicts me with every piety removed. And my adversary acts as an unjust man because, by scourging me, he greatly exceeds the measure of equity. This is what he does. Moreover, you also consider me a pretender and hypocrite. Thus it is added: “For what is the hope of the hypocrite, if he greedily seizes, and God does not deliver his soul? Will God hear his cry when distress comes upon him?” When the hypocrite pretends to be righteous, he greedily seizes the praise of righteousness, which is due to the righteous alone. He does this because he has no hope of eternal recompense. Therefore he is shown to be most foolish: he pretends to serve God, yet God does not deliver his soul. After this life God will not hear his cry, though he cry much: “Lord, Lord, open to us” [Col. 0638A] (Matt. XXV, 11). It follows: “Or can he delight in the Almighty? Or invoke God at all times?” Those who seek only worldly praise and glory do not delight in the Lord. Yet they do not invoke God always, but only when some adversity strikes them.

“I will teach you by the hand of God what the Almighty possesses, and I will not conceal it. Behold, you all know it; why then do you speak vain things without cause?” I will teach you, he says, and not conceal what the Almighty possesses—that is, truth, for this is always the teaching of the Almighty. But how shall I teach you? [Col. 0638B] Certainly not through myself, but through the hand of God, which is so strong that it can soften even hearts of stone. But tell me: why do you speak vain things against me without cause, when you yourselves know that what I say is true? “This is the portion of the wicked with God, and the inheritance of violent men which they shall receive from the Almighty. If his children are multiplied, they shall be for the sword, and his descendants shall not be satisfied with bread.” The wicked and violent are heretics, because they cruelly destroy souls and interpret the Scriptures by violence. Let us hear what portion and inheritance they receive from God. If his children are multiplied, he says—that is, his imitators and those generated by his teaching—they will be struck by the sword of divine vengeance. And his descendants, namely those born from these evil children [Col. 0638C], will not be satisfied with bread: the living bread that came down from heaven.

But since some heretics return to the Church while others remain in their errors, it is added: “Those who remain of him shall be buried in destruction, and his widows shall not weep.” Those, he says, who do not return to truth and persist in their wickedness shall be buried in the destruction of eternal condemnation. “And his widows shall not weep.” Whose widows? The widows of him whose children shall be for the sword. But what are his widows except souls separated from him once they have known the truth? These widows will not weep; rather, they will rejoice, because they will be with the saints in joy. “Though he heap up silver like earth and prepare clothing like mud, he may prepare it indeed, but the righteous shall wear it and the innocent shall divide the silver” [Col. 0638D]. For what are silver and clothing except testimonies from the holy Scriptures? Whoever does not abound in these is poor and naked: poor in reasoning, indeed, and naked in covering and defending himself.

It often happens that heretics compose books and assemble testimonies of holy Scripture in their own defense. When they bring these to councils for defense, they are overcome by these very things, as though by their own swords. Thus the righteous man is armed and clothed with their garments [Col. 0639A], and the innocent man reasonably expounds and distributes the riches of their sayings, which are signified by silver. “He built his house like a moth and made a shelter like a watchman.” The heretic builds his house like a moth because he builds the Church which he rules by corrupting and destroying it. “He makes a shelter like a watchman” because his building has no foundation laid. For he does not build upon the foundation of the apostles and prophets.

“When the rich man sleeps, he shall take nothing with him; he shall open his eyes and find nothing.” The rich person who places his hope not in God but in the riches of this world, once he has slept and closed his eyes in the sleep of death, will take nothing with him. He will open his eyes in the resurrection [Col. 0639B] and find nothing, because he will be oppressed by such want that he will be forced to beg for a drop of water. Hence it follows: “Want shall seize him like water, and by night a storm shall oppress him.” Placed in night and darkness, he will be oppressed by the violence and storm of every tribulation; and want will seize him as abundant and sudden water. “A burning wind shall take him and carry him away, and like a whirlwind shall snatch him from his place.” A burning wind, he says—that is, an evil spirit—will take him from this life, for it violently takes souls and burns eternally those whom it takes. Like a whirlwind and the violence of storms, it will snatch him from his place—that is, from this world, in which he dwelt for a time [Col. 0639C]. And deservedly so.

“He sends against him and does not spare; fleeing from his hand, he shall flee.” The Lord, he says, sends against him and stretches out the rod of his correction, and does not spare for a time, in order that he may spare eternally. For he corrects every son whom he receives (Prov. III, 12). But this man, who should amend himself and rejoice in God’s correction, flees from his hand like a bad pupil who does not accept discipline. He flees precisely by refusing discipline. But what does the Lord do in response? It is added: “He shall clasp his hands over him and hiss at him, looking upon his place.” This is what the Lord says through the prophet to the sinful people: “I will no longer be angry with you” (Ezek. XVI, 42), that is: do what you wish, for I shall correct you no longer [Col. 0639D]. To clasp one’s hands is to cease from scourges and slaps. Looking upon his place, he hisses at him because, considering toward what punishment and death he is heading, he mocks him as though in astonishment.

## CHAPTER XXVIII

“Silver has the sources of its veins, and there is a place for gold where it is refined.” Although heretics, of whom we have spoken much above, possess silver, they do not possess its veins and source. The vein and source of silver—that is, of the holy sayings—is truth. All divine Scripture flows from this fountain. But they do not drink from it because they interpret the Scriptures perversely. The place in which gold is refined is the Church, because outside her [Col. 0640A] neither is the treasure of wisdom rightly expounded nor are vessels made worthy of honor. Here blessed Paul, the vessel of election, was fashioned. Here all martyrs were refined by the fire of martyrdom and tribulation.

“Iron is taken from the earth, and stone, melted by heat, is turned into bronze.” Earth becomes iron and stone becomes bronze when baked in the fire of the Holy Spirit: earthly and sinful people, hard and unbelieving, receive the strength of iron and the sound of bronze, so that they may be strong in work and clear in preaching. “He has set a time for darkness, and he himself considers the end of all things.” He set a time for darkness because, at the time of his incarnation, our Savior opened the Scriptures and removed from them the darkness of ignorance. Or again: he set an end for darkness—that is, for sinners—at which they may cease from sinning and repent [Col. 0640B]. He also considers the end of all things because he does not fail to know the end toward which all things tend. When Judas was among the apostles and Paul among the persecutors, he saw the end of each.

“A torrent divides the stone of darkness and the shadow of death from the pilgrim people.” The stone of darkness and the shadow of death are the Jewish people. They are a stone because hard in belief, and darkness because blind in unbelief. Whoever humbles himself beneath it will be extinguished by its shadow as though by death. For everyone to whose teaching we bow down is a shadow to us. But what is the torrent except the river and preaching of the New Testament [Col. 0640C]? And what is the pilgrim people except the Church, which, journeying in this world, says: “For we do not have here an abiding city, but seek the one to come” (Heb. XIII, 14). The torrent therefore divides the stone of darkness and the shadow of death from the pilgrim people because the New Testament separates the Jews from the Church. In this they differ from us: they do not accept the New Testament.

“The earth from which bread sprang in its place has been overthrown by fire.” When the whole world suffered hunger for the divine word, the land of Judaea abounded in the bread of God’s word. But it was overthrown by fire in its place because it burned against Christ with zeal and the fire of envy. “Its stones are the place of sapphire, and its clods are gold” [Col. 0640D]. The stones of that land, he says, were full of sapphires because the saints who formerly lived in it imitated the face of heaven and the beauty of angels. Its clods were gold because the holy prophets were gold through wisdom and clods through the fruit of good work. “The bird did not know its path, nor has the eye of the vulture seen it.” The bird is Christ because, flying, he ascended into heaven. He is also a vulture because he descended to assume the carrion of our flesh. That land just mentioned did not know the path of this bird because the Jewish people would not believe either that Christ descended from heaven or that he ascended to heaven. This was because it did not behold sufficiently attentively the eye of the vulture—that is, it did not carefully consider the words of the prophets [Col. 0641A]. For the prophets were Christ’s eyes: through them first, and afterward through himself, he illuminated those sitting in darkness.

“The children of merchants did not tread it, nor did the lioness pass through it.” The merchants are the apostles, who earnestly sold the teaching of the Gospel everywhere for the price of faith; their children were bishops and teachers. Although the apostles trod the land of Judaea for a short time, their children did not tread it, because, leaving the Jews, they all turned to the Gentiles. The lioness is the Church, which everywhere conquers and devours both vices and evil spirits. She indeed passed by it, but did not pass through it; for she awaits the entry of the fullness of the Gentiles, and then all Israel shall be saved. “He stretched out his hand to the flint and overthrew the mountains from their roots” [Col. 0641B]. The lioness, he says, left the land and stretched out her hand to the flint because, leaving the Jews, she extended the hand of her help to the hardness of the Gentiles. She overthrew the mountains from their roots because she uprooted completely the powerful people of this world from the worship of demons.

“In the rocks he cut out streams, and his eye saw every precious thing.” In the rocks, he says—that is, in hard and stony hearts—he cut out and caused streams of knowledge or tears to abound. And his eye saw every precious thing because mysteries hidden through all ages were revealed to him. Hence it is added:

“Moreover, he searched out the depths of the rivers, and brought hidden things to light.” For the holy preacher searched out the depths of the rivers and [Col. 0641C] brought hidden things to light, because by expounding them he revealed the mysteries of both Testaments, long concealed. “But where is wisdom found? And what is the place of understanding?” This wisdom is Christ, who is called the power of God and the wisdom of God. “Man does not know its price, nor is it found in the land of those who live pleasantly.” Wretched Judas, and wretched also the Jews, by whom he was bought and sold for so cheap a price, though his price cannot be known. For if that wicked man had known his price, he would not have sold him for such a price. Wisdom is not found in the land of those who live pleasantly, because Christ does not dwell in those who are given over to the enticements and pleasures of the flesh. “The abyss says, ‘It is not in me’; and the sea says, ‘It is not with me.’” For the abyss signifies those enveloped in the darkness of error and [Col. 0641D] ignorance; Christ does not dwell in such persons. The sea signifies those who are full of gall and bitterness and stirred by a spirit of pride, who can never be at rest. “Refined gold shall not be given for it, nor shall silver be weighed in exchange for it.” Refined gold, which is the best gold, denotes the holy apostles; silver, because of the purity of speech, signifies the prophets. Yet none of these can be compared with Christ. Hence the Psalmist says: “Why do you look with suspicion upon the curdled mountains? The mountain in which it pleased God to dwell” (Ps. 67:17).

“Neither shall it be compared with the dyed colors of India, nor with the most precious sardonyx stone or sapphire.” For what are the dyed [Col. 0642A] colors of India but the philosophers of this world? Whatever beauty they possess, they display outwardly and upon the skin. But of the Church it is said: “All the glory of the king’s daughter is within” (Ps. 44:14). The sardonyx stone, being blood-colored, signifies the martyrs. Sapphire, however, signifies the holy preachers, who fly more loftily and contemplate heavenly things. “Gold or glass shall not equal it, nor shall lofty and eminent vessels of gold be exchanged for it, nor shall they be mentioned in comparison with it.” The saints are gold because of wisdom, and glass because of purity of life; for such as they are outwardly, such they are inwardly: there is nothing obscure, nothing dark in them. The lofty and eminent vessels were those of whom, when the Lord said, “Whom do men [Col. 0642B] say that the Son of Man is?” (Matt. 16:14), the apostles answered: “Some say Elijah, others Jeremiah, others John the Baptist, or one of the prophets.” For those who were thought to be Christ were indeed very great; nevertheless, none of them can be compared with Christ.

“For wisdom is drawn forth from hidden places. The topaz of Ethiopia shall not equal it, nor shall the purest dyes be compared with it.” This wisdom is drawn from hidden places—that is, from the heart of the Father. But who draws it forth except loving-kindness and mercy? Drawn by these, Christ descended to earth. Nor can topaz equal him, although it is variegated by the diversity of all colors. Likewise, neither can the purest dyes equal him. By these we understand those adorned with wisdom, knowledge, and the diversity of every virtue; for as many virtues as there are, so many colors. Such dyes are altogether pure when they are stained by no hypocrisy. Yet none of these things can equal Christ. “For who among the clouds shall be equal to the Lord? Or who among the sons of God shall be like the Lord?” (Ps. 88:7).

“From where, then, shall wisdom come? And what is the place of understanding? It is hidden from the eyes of all living things.” From where, he says, will Wisdom come? Who will reveal her to us? “Who shall declare his generation?” (Isa. 53:8). What is her place? Where does she dwell? Let Wisdom herself say: “I am in the Father, and the Father is in me” (John 10:38). Therefore she is hidden from the eyes of all living things, because no one knows her as she is. “It is hidden also from the birds of heaven. Destruction [Col. 0642D] and death said: ‘We have heard its fame with our ears.’” The birds of heaven may signify the apostles and teachers, who fly more loftily and contemplate heavenly things more subtly. Yet so long as they were in the world, this wisdom was not fully revealed even to them. Destruction and death signify the devil, who kills and destroys sinners. Yet he heard its fame, because, when overcome, he recognized Christ’s glory and power.

“God understands its way, and he knows its place. For he beholds the ends of the world and sees all things that are under heaven”—“For no one knows the Son except the Father” (Matt. 11:27). Before the ages, he arranged together with him the way of his humanity and incarnation. And he himself, though not spatially circumscribed, is its place. Hence he himself says: “I am in the Father, and the Father is in me” (John 10:38). Since nothing is hidden from God, this Wisdom beholds the ends of the world and all things under heaven, observing how they humble themselves.

“He made weight for the winds, and weighed the waters by measure.” In this passage, the winds signify either souls or light and wandering persons. God made weight for these, because he gave them the maturity and gravity of religion. Hence also: “I shall praise you among a weighty people” (Ps. 34:18). He weighed the waters by measure, because, as the Apostle says, he grants the graces of the Holy Spirit to each according to the measure of faith (Rom. 12:7). “When he gave the rains a law, and a way for the sounding storms, then he saw [Col. 0643B] it, declared it, examined it, and said to man: ‘Behold, the fear of the Lord, that is wisdom; and to depart from evil is understanding.’” He gave a law to the rains when he taught the proper order of preaching. This is the order: that the teacher should do what he preaches. But let us hear the law itself: “So let your light shine before men,” says the Lord, “that, seeing your good works, they may glorify your Father who is in heaven” (Matt. 5:16). What he signified by rain, he likewise signified by storms; and what by law, likewise by way. Yet by storms is understood that doctrine which instills terror in sinners concerning future judgment and eternal punishment. But when he says, “Then he saw it, declared it, prepared it, and examined it,” this means that he then permitted it to be seen, declared, prepared, and examined. For Christ became known when preachers began to rain. Then he said to man: “Behold, the fear of the Lord, that is wisdom; and to depart from evil is understanding.”

> [Note: [Col. 0643D] “For understanding is especially necessary to a human being for this purpose: that by understanding he may distinguish evils from goods; and, having avoided evils, may attain through the performance of good [Col. 0644D] works to participation in divine wisdom.” ST THOMAS.]

Truly this is wisdom and understanding: it alone suffices, and without it Christ, the power and wisdom of God, can neither be known nor possessed. For the one who fears God neglects nothing, and the one who departs from evil never sins.

## CHAPTER XXIX

“Job also continued, taking up his parable, and said: ‘Who will grant that I might be as in former months, according to the days when God guarded me?’” Blessed Job says these things concerning himself and the Church; [Col. 0643D] therefore he calls it a parable. Let the Church then speak—not the first and noble Church, but that which now exists and will exist until the consummation of the age. “Who,” she says, “will grant that I might now be such as I was in the beginning, when God guarded me, when he did not allow me to be overcome either by tyrants themselves, or by vices, or by evil spirits?” The Church says this according to the better sort, who, considering the Christian religion greatly diminished, lament its condition.

“When his lamp shone over my head, and by his light I walked through darkness.” Of this lamp and light it is written: “Your word is a lamp to my feet and a light to my paths” (Ps. 118:115). For the Word illumines the head—that is, the mind—so that it may understand rightly; and the feet—that is, works—so that they may be done without offense. By this light the Church walked securely in darkness, that is, among the impious and sinners, because she shone with the light both of words and of virtues. It follows:

“As I was in the days of my youth, when God was secretly in my tent, when the Almighty was with me, and my children were around me; when I washed my feet with butter, and the rock poured out for me streams of oil; when I went out to the gate of the city, and they prepared a seat for me in the square.” For the Church has now grown old in large measure [Col. 0644B] and retains, except in very few persons, neither the appearance nor the beauty which she had in the days of her youth—that is, in the time of the apostles and martyrs. Then God was secretly in the tent of her breast, because she sought to please God more by acting rightly inwardly than by displaying herself outwardly. Then also the Almighty was with her, as is shown in miracles, always so readily hearing her. Then her children were around her, of whom the Apostle says: “Do not become children in understanding, but be little children in malice” (1 Cor. 14:20). For they are called children from purity.

Then she washed her feet—that is, the teachers who carry her everywhere—with butter, because she poured into them a greater and more perfect knowledge. Butter is the fat of milk. As milk signifies moderate knowledge, so butter signifies perfect knowledge. [Col. 0644C] The rock poured out streams of oil for her because those who had first been unbelieving, hard, and stony, afterward, anointed by the Holy Spirit, poured out the oil of devotion and mercy. She went out to the gate of the city because she opened the gates of faith to those wishing to enter the holy city of Jerusalem. They set a chair for her in the squares so that she might now preach to all nations, not secretly but openly and manifestly. For the one who teaches truth openly sits upon a chair in the square. It follows:

“The young men saw me and hid themselves, and the old men rose up and stood.” The young here mean those who, by long perseverance in sins, have grown up in them. The old mean those who have commended their lives by gravity of character and religious devotion. Thus the latter stand by as devout persons; the former hide themselves as fearful persons. Even now we see adulterers, fornicators, and other criminals withdraw from the presence of bishops. “The princes ceased speaking and laid their finger upon their mouths. The leaders restrained their voice, and their tongue clung to their throat.” These princes and leaders are heresiarchs, who, convicted by the authority of Holy Scripture and true arguments, ceased to speak against the Church. Whoever does not understand this should read the many councils in which the mouths of heretics were stopped.

“The ear that heard me called me blessed, and [Col. 0645A] the eye that saw me bore witness for me, because I had delivered the crying poor man and the orphan who had no helper.” What does the crying poor man signify but the sinner imploring mercy? And what does the orphan, who had no helper, signify but an unbeliever coming to faith, in whom the devil, his wicked father, had already died? The Church delivered these, as those who saw and heard bear witness. For the Church despises the testimony of the deaf and blind.

“The blessing of one about to perish came upon me, and I comforted the heart of the widow.” For the sinner who was about to perish blesses the one through whom he is converted to repentance. The one who promises pardon and forgiveness comforts the heart of the widow: that is, of the penitent soul fleeing, after many sins, the marriage-union of the devil. “I put on righteousness, and it clothed me; my judgment was as a garment and a diadem.” “I was clothed,” he says, “in righteousness and equitable judgment as others are clothed in beautiful garments and a diadem, because I glory in these no less than they glory in those.” “I was an eye to the blind and a foot to the lame,” because those weakened inwardly or outwardly received from me no less comfort than from their own limbs.

“I was the father of the poor, and I investigated most diligently the cause which I did not know.” The Church nourishes the poor as her own children. Because she wishes to do nothing rashly, wrongly, or unjustly, she investigates with the greatest diligence a cause unknown to her. “I broke the millstones of the wicked man, and from his teeth I took away [Col. 0645C] the prey; and I said in my nest: ‘I shall die, and like a palm tree I shall multiply my days.’” To break the millstones of the wicked is to destroy the schemes of evil spirits or heretics; prey is taken from their teeth when someone already nearly deceived by them is recalled to the way of truth. The one who dies in his nest perseveres until death in that faith and religion in which he delights and rests. He multiplies his days like the palm tree, which, although it grows with difficulty, nevertheless lives long and does not lose its greenness. Thus the Church also grew greatly from a difficult and small beginning, lives for ever, and does not lose the verdure of her beauty.

“My root is spread out beside the waters, and dew shall remain in my harvest.” The roots of the saints are virtues, without which the soul does not live. These roots do not die in the saints because they stretch out toward the waters and are always watered by the grace of the Holy Spirit and the streams of Scripture. Dew remains in the harvest of the saints because, when their souls are separated from their bodies by the sickle of the divine command, they feel not heat but refreshment. “My glory shall always be renewed, and my bow shall be restored in my hand.” What is renewed is old. Therefore the Church grieves because her glory fails and grows old in some persons; but she is consoled because in others [Col. 0646A] it advances and is renewed. Likewise, her bow would not be said to be restored in her hand unless it seemed in some fashion to have lost its strength. Her bow is divine Scripture, and its individual arrows are its individual sayings. This bow is restored when the word of God is preached earnestly, and an impious person is convicted and condemned by the authority of the saints.

“Those who heard me waited for my judgment, and listened silently to my counsel.” For who would not gladly accept the judgment and counsel of the Church, except one who has no ears to hear? “They did not dare add anything to my words, and my speech distilled upon them.” Those who delight in the dripping of her doctrine do not presume to add anything to her words. But heretics add something to her words and corrupt the truth by adding. “They waited for me as for rain, and opened their mouth as for the latter rain.” As thirsty earth awaits rain, so faithful souls desire to hear the Church’s teaching. They open the mouth of their heart to it as to the latter rain, desiring to quench the dryness of their minds with such a drink.

“If ever I smiled upon them, they did not believe it, and the light of my face did not fall to the ground.” We have said that these things are spoken according to the more perfect members and teachers of the Church. How severe and grave they ought to be is shown by the fact that they should so rarely smile or display joy that, if they ever do so, people can scarcely believe they act thus from temporal gladness. The light of their face falls to the ground when they show a cheerful countenance to sinners. Hence it is written: “Have you daughters? Do not show them your cheerful face” (Ecclus. 7:26). Sinners must be instructed not to laugh but to weep.

“If I wished to go to them, I sat first; and when I sat, like a king surrounded by an army, I was nevertheless a comforter of the sorrowful.” If kings and princes understood this, they would not think that prelates of the Church ought to be subject to them. These words show the great reverence once accorded to bishops. Yet good bishops still sit as kings, surrounded by an army of the faithful hearing their teaching. They more readily comfort the sorrowful gently than terrify offenders arrogantly.

## CHAPTER XXX

[Col. 0646D]

“But now those younger in time, whose fathers I would not have deemed worthy to set among the dogs of my flock, mock me.” “Thus,” she says, “as I have said, it was with me of old; but now those younger in time, greater in pride, born in me and gone out from me—namely, heretics—mock my words. I did not deem their fathers worthy to set among the dogs of my flock,” that is, I despised to associate them with those who guard my flocks. For many heretics left the Church because they could not obtain greater dignities within it.

> [Note: [Col. 0645] “Those skilled in ecclesiastical history do not fail to know this; nor need I name Simon Magus, Novatian, Tertullian, and so forth.”]

He is associated with these dogs when he is ordained bishop. “Their strength of hands was as nothing to me, and they themselves were considered unworthy of life.” Heretics have strength of hands because they often do good works; but the Church counts this as nothing because they do not have faith, without which it is impossible to please God.

“Barren through want and hunger, they gnawed in the wilderness, wasted with calamity and misery; they ate herbs and the bark of trees, and the roots of junipers were their food.” Heretics are barren in good work because they suffer want and hunger for true doctrine. They gnaw in solitude because, in the dense forest of Holy Scripture, they violently gnaw and tear apart what they cannot understand. According to the inward man also, [Col. 0647B] they are wasted with calamity and misery because they are empty of faith and defiled by the infection of vices. They eat herbs and the bark of trees because they delight in novelty and, abandoning spiritual understanding, interpret almost everything according to the letter. For the skin and bark of the word of God is the letter. But what do we understand by the juniper, wholly filled with thorns, but the multitude of vices? Their root is pride and avarice, since the other vices derive their origin from these. Fat with this root, heretics despise the Church’s humility.

“Those who, snatching these things from the valleys, ran with shouting to them whenever they found any.” Divine Scripture, which he has just called a wilderness, he now calls a valley because it imitates not the loftiness of rhetoricians but the humility of plain speech. Heretics occupy themselves in this valley; when they find anything novel that seems to suit their errors, they immediately rush upon it from every side with shouting and joy, inserting it into their books and disputations.

> [Note: [Col. 0647D] “How highly the authority of the divine books ought to be valued may also be inferred from this: heretics themselves do not think that their errors can be more safely concealed than by sacred Scriptures which they have wrongly understood. Thus the Lutherans, [Col. 0648D] and so forth.”]

“They dwelt in the deserted places of torrents, and in the caves of the earth, or upon the gravel.” Heretics dwell among, and with, those deserted and abandoned by God. Such persons are called torrents because they do not abound in living water and unfailing doctrine. They are also called caves of the earth because serpents and evil spirits dwell in them. They are likewise called gravel because they are heavy with iniquity and swept along by the flood of every pleasure. [Col. 0647D] “Those who rejoiced among such things and considered it delight to be hidden under thorns. Sons of fools and of ignoble men, and not appearing at all in the land.” Heretics rejoice among such persons because such people are easily deceived by them. They count it pleasure to be beneath thorns because they delight in the pricks of sins. These are sons of fools and ignoble men, because unless their teachers were foolish and had degenerated from their mother’s nobility, they would not have reached such great madness. For this reason they now flee the Church and shall never appear in [Col. 0648A] the land of the living. “Now I have become their song, and I have become their byword.” He says this because they oppose the Church with foolish, empty, jesting mockery.

“They abhor me, and have fled far from me, and are not ashamed to spit in my face.” They flee far from the Church because they refuse to receive sound doctrine. They are not ashamed to spit in her face because they openly speak foul and dishonorable words against her and to her face.

> [Note: [Col. 0648D] “Long ago the Lutherans did this against the Roman Church; and certain modern writers do the same, attacking her with insults.”]

That this happens only by God’s permission is clear when it is said: “For he opened his quiver, afflicted me, and put a bridle in my mouth.” God’s permission is the quiver from which heretics and tyrants emerge like arrows and rise against the Church. [Col. 0648B] Her bridle consists of those who contradict her doctrine and words. “At the right hand of the East my calamities immediately arose.” Taken literally, this seems to say that heretics first came against her from that region of the world. Yet we may understand the East as the Father and the right hand as the Son, according to the saying: “Sing to the Lord, who ascends above the heaven of heavens toward the East” (Ps. 67:33). The Church’s calamities immediately rose against the right hand of the East because, from the very beginning, heretics began to detract from Christ, the Son of God.

“They overturned my feet and oppressed my paths as with waves.”—“For he who has been washed does not need except to wash his feet” (John 13:10). [Col. 0648C] The feet, therefore, are heretics, who cling nearer to the earth and love only earthly and passing things. Heretics overturned and tripped up such feet, and oppressed the paths of their doctrine as with waves of the sea. “They scattered my paths, laid snares for me, prevailed, and there was none to bring help.” The Lord also says: “He who is not with me is against me, and he who does not gather with me scatters” (Luke 11:23). Heretics scattered the Church’s paths because they preached another faith by which men would seek the heavenly homeland. At times they also prevailed, and there was none to bring help; this happened by God’s hidden judgment, who says: “It is necessary that scandals come” [Col. 0648D] (Matt. 18:7); and the Apostle says: “There must be heresies, so that those who are approved may become manifest” (1 Cor. 11:19).

“They rushed upon me as through a broken wall and an opened gate; they rolled down upon my miseries; I was reduced to nothing.” The Church’s wall and defense are Christ, faith, and knowledge of the Scriptures. Since this wall cannot be broken, heretics fight against the Church in vain. But when she says, “I was reduced to nothing,” she speaks according to their opinion.

“You have taken away my desire as with a wind, and [Col. 0649A] my salvation passed away like a cloud.” “You have taken away,” she says, “that is, you have permitted my desire for the salvation of all human beings to be taken away; and the salvation which I was effecting everywhere by healing has ceased and passed away.” But how? As the wind carries away clouds. Heretics are aptly compared with wind and the Church with clouds, because they rage with fury and violence, whereas the Church abundantly rains the doctrine of mercy. “But now my soul withers within me, and days of affliction have taken possession of me.” All these things must be referred to those times when heretics, and especially the Arians, most violently disturbed the holy Church.

> [Note: [Col. 0649] “It is enough to recall what Athanasius, Eusebius of Vercelli, and Hilary endured at that time in defense of the Church’s faith.”]

Then indeed were days of affliction, and the Church’s life withered within herself because she was now weary [Col. 0649B] even of living. So the Apostle also says: “We were burdened beyond measure, so that we were weary even of life” (2 Cor. 1:8).

“By night my bones are pierced with pains, and those who devour me do not sleep; in their multitude my garment is consumed, and they have girded me as with the collar of a tunic.” These things are understood literally of Job, although we interpret them spiritually concerning the Church. “In this night,” he says, “in this disturbance of such great tribulations, my mouth—the stronger members—is pierced with pains, because the pains of such devastation penetrated the hearts of the saints. Those who devour me do not sleep because heretics and evil spirits do not rest from persecuting me.” In this sense it is also said: “They have devoured Jacob” (Ps. 78:7). Because they are many, “my garment is consumed in their multitude”: that is, weaker outward members are deceived. Such persons are the Church’s garments, because they adorn her outwardly and she is easily stripped of them. They girded her as with the collar of a tunic in order utterly to suffocate her, so that she could not speak the truth. For if a tunic’s collar is tightly drawn, it completely cuts off the voice.

“I have been compared to mud and made like ashes and dust.” “I have been so trampled and afflicted,” she says, “that they consider me as worthless and contemptible as mud and ashes.” But what wonder? “I shall cry to you, and you will not hear me; I stand, and you do not regard me.” “They are proud,” she says, “because you do not hear me crying to you and do not regard me as persevering in the faith.” They also suppose themselves to hold the better part, seeing that in almost everything they are superior.

“You have changed toward me into one cruel, and by the hardness of your hand you oppose me.” Since to afflict severely belongs to a cruel person, although God is not cruel, yet because he performed the work of cruel people, he is called cruel. A hand that afflicts strongly is hard. “You raised me up, and, placing me as it were upon the wind, you dashed me down violently.” “You raised me greatly,” she says; “you exalted me with great honor and glory. I seemed no longer to walk upon [Col. 0650A] the earth, but to walk upon the wind and in the air, because people believed me to be such as I was. But now, because I have been thus dashed down, afflicted, and destroyed, even those familiar with me are afraid to believe in me.” Yet I say this not because I fear temporal death; concerning this I am certain. Hence it follows:

“I know that you will deliver me to death, where the house is appointed for every living being; yet you will not stretch out your hand to their utter destruction, and if they fall, you yourself will save them.” “I know,” he says, “that I cannot escape that death in which the house—that is, the flesh—of every living being is placed and appointed. For by this death flesh alone dies, not the soul. Yet you will not stretch out your hand to their utter destruction.” Whose? Surely those who are afflicted. Some of them at times succumb and fall through fear. But God does not permit this affliction to continue unto utter destruction and perdition, because he strengthens others with courage lest they fall, and pricks the conscience of those who fall, so that, returning through repentance, they may be saved. This is what he means when he says: “If they fall, you yourself will save them.”

“Once I wept over one who was afflicted, and my soul had compassion on the poor.” The Church also knows how to weep with those who weep and to pity the poor. “I expected good things, and evils came to me; I awaited light, and darkness burst forth.” This commonly happens to saints: before they can attain those good things which they await with all the desire of their mind, the evils of the present life come upon them and afflict them most grievously. While from day to day they desire to die and await the light of eternal blessedness, they suddenly fall into the storms of this world and the darkness of adversities.

“My inward parts seethed without any rest; days of affliction came before me.” The Church’s inward parts seethed when the heretics hidden within her, revealing their indignation and hatred, burned as they spoke against her. Days of affliction then came before her because she found fulfilled in her own time those evils which Scripture had foretold, but which she had thought would occur only after many ages. “I walked mourning; rising without anger, I cried out in the crowd.” The one who walks mourning weeps for both his own sins and those of others. The one who rises without anger and cries out in the crowd seeks not to avenge his own injuries but to establish peace and concord. “I was a brother of dragons and a companion of ostriches.” By dragons we understand tyrants and the proud; by ostriches, hypocrites. As the wings of ostriches are useless, so also are the works of hypocrites: neither the former by wings nor the latter by works are raised to heavenly things. Yet Job and the Church, dwelling among such persons, did not lose the purity of their innocence. “My skin grew black upon me, and my bones dried up with [Col. 0651A] heat.” The skin signifies outward beauty and the bones inward strength. In the heat and burning of persecution, the Church does not lose these things, though she seems to lose them. These, therefore, too are understood according to human opinion. “My harp has been turned into mourning, and my instrument into the voice of those who weep.” Since I now have no leisure for rejoicing and singing psalms, I must weep because of my distresses and tribulations. But what follows must be referred not to the Church, but only to Job.

## CHAPTER XXXI

“I made a covenant with my eyes, that I might not think of a virgin.”

> [Note: [Col. 0651D] “He begins to show his innocence by freedom from the sin of lust, which ensnares many. This sin is set in a slippery place; unless someone avoids its beginnings, he can scarcely draw back his foot from its later stages. The first stage in this sin is the sight of the eyes, by which a beautiful woman, and especially a virgin, is looked upon; the second is thought; the third, delight; the fourth, consent; the fifth, the act.” ST THOMAS.]

Beginning with chastity, he shows how perfect he was. Since thinking belongs to the mind, this must be understood of the inward eyes. For one does not sin by outward seeing if one is not inwardly moved by thought. “What portion would God have in me from above, and what inheritance the Almighty from on high?” “If,” he says, “I had been given over to lust and pleasure, I could not be numbered among God’s lot and inheritance.” “Is not destruction for the wicked man, and alienation for those who work iniquity?” “Therefore,” he says, “I did not do such things, because I did not doubt that those who do them are to be destroyed and separated from God. Does he not himself consider my ways and number all my steps?” “I cannot lie to God,” he says, “to whom all my works are manifest.”

“If I have walked in vanity, and my foot hastened in deceit, let him weigh me in a just balance, and [Col. 0651C] God shall know my simplicity.” “If,” he says, “I have walked in vanity as you think I have walked, and if, according to your opinion, my foot hastened in deceit, let God weigh me in a just balance—that is, let him make you understand my righteousness—and then you will know my simplicity. Thus the sentence is construed: ‘And God shall know my simplicity.’” God does not need a balance in order to know anything. “If my step has turned aside from the way, if my eye has followed my heart, and if a stain has clung to my hands, let me sow and another eat, and let my offspring be rooted out.” To turn one’s step from the way is not to keep the rectitude of good work. The eye follows the heart when action follows thought. A stain on the hands is sin in works. What does “let me sow and another eat” mean except that I should receive no fruit from my labors? “For whatever a man sows, that shall he also reap” (Gal. 6:8). Offspring is rooted out when virtues and good habits are torn up by the devil. It follows:

“If my heart has been deceived concerning a woman, and if I have lain in wait at the door of my neighbor, let my wife be another man’s harlot, and let others bend over her.” By these words he defends himself from the charge of fornication and adultery. “For this is wickedness and the greatest iniquity; it is a fire that devours unto destruction and roots out all offspring.” For fornication and adultery are the greatest sins, and therefore are rightly defined as a fire devouring unto destruction. Hence the Apostle says: “Every sin whatever a man commits is outside the body; but he who commits fornication sins against his own body” (1 Cor. 6:18). And again: “God will judge fornicators and adulterers” (Heb. 13:4). This vice scatters, roots out, and destroys the offspring of all virtues. Since we have heard of his chastity, let us now hear also of his humility.

“If I disdained to submit to judgment with my servant [Col. 0652B] and my maidservant when they disputed against me, what shall I do when God rises to judge? And when he examines me, what shall I answer him? Did not he who made me in the womb also make him, and did not one and the same form us in the womb?” It is as though he said: We all have one Lord; we are all servants of one Lord. He made all things; he “will render to each according to his works” (Matt. 16:27); and “with the same measure with which you have measured, it shall be measured back to you” (Matt. 7:2). These matters concern humility. Now let us consider his compassion and mercy.

“If I denied to the poor what they wished, and made the eyes of the widow wait.” By this he displays not only generosity, [Col. 0652C] but also promptness of goodwill. “If I ate my morsel alone, and the orphan did not eat of it—for compassion grew up with me from infancy, and came forth with me from my mother’s womb.” For in this he attributes the whole of his goodness, not to himself as a giver, but to God. This too could be said by him of whom it is written: “Before I formed you in the womb I knew you, and before you came forth from the belly I sanctified you” (Jer. 1:5).—“If I despised one passing by because he lacked clothing, or a poor man without a covering.” For he did not, on account of a man’s nakedness, despise the dignity of human nature. “If his sides did not bless me, and if he was not warmed with the fleece of my sheep.” For the tongue is the instrument of all the members, by [Col. 0652D] which they bless their benefactors. “If I raised my hand against the orphan, even when I saw myself superior in the gate”; that is, in judgment. For he uses “gate” for judgment, because judgments were held before the gates. “If,” he says, “I did this or that, let my shoulder fall from its joint, and my arm be broken with its bones.” So that, losing not only strength of body but also strength of soul, I may become useless in all the works by which I ought to have been saved. “For I always feared God as waves swelling over me, [Col. 0653A] and I could not bear his weight.” What else is this but that he always feared God more than all torments, even more than death itself? “For,” says Solomon, “love is strong as death” (Song 8:6). Sailors fear nothing more than the waves of the sea swelling over them. But those bear God’s weight lightly who make little of the wrath and fury of his majesty.

“If I thought gold my strength, and said to refined gold, ‘You are my confidence’; if I rejoiced over my great riches and because my hand had found very much.” In these few words he is most clearly defended from every suspicion of avarice, since he neither loved riches nor placed his hope in them. “If I saw the sun when it shone, and the moon proceeding brightly, and my heart rejoiced secretly, [Col. 0653B] and I kissed my hand with my mouth—which is a very great iniquity and a denial against God Most High.” These words also defend him from all idolatry. For I think that unbelievers formerly had this custom: because they believed the sun and moon to be gods, admiring their brightness and beauty, they kissed their own hands as though in veneration of them, hands which had offered sacrifice to such great gods. They also rejoiced in the hidden recesses of the mind and exulted in their hearts at the great and splendid brightness of their gods. But this is a very great iniquity and a denial against God Most High, because one must serve not the creature but the Creator: we ought to believe in him, worship him, and adore him.

[Col. 0653C] “If I rejoiced at the ruin of him who hated me, and exulted because evil befell him; for I did not give my throat over to sin, to seek his life with a curse.” (And by these things it is proved that he had no hatred against anyone.) “If the men of my tent did not say, ‘Who will give us of his flesh, that we may be satisfied?’” They said this because he restrained them, under strict discipline, from every iniquity. “The stranger did not remain outside; my door stood open to the traveler.” This pertains to mercy. “If I concealed my sin as a man does, and hid my iniquity in my bosom.” For he conceals and hides his sin who offers no satisfaction for it. And because the first man concealed his sin, [Col. 0653D] it descended as though hereditary upon the rest, so that they are unwilling to confess their sins.

“If I feared an exceedingly great multitude, and the contempt of my kinsmen terrified me, and I did not rather keep silence, nor go out through the door.” As though he said: If at any time my relatives and neighbors rose up against me, lest by my answers I should stir up quarrels and scandals, I preferred to keep silence and did not go out through the door—not because I feared their however great multitude, nor because their contempt, by which they despised me because they were more numerous, terrified me.

“Who will grant me a helper, that the Almighty may hear my desire, and that he who judges may himself write a book, so that I may carry it on my shoulder and bind it about me as a crown?” What other helper does blessed Job seek but Christ, [Col. 0654A] whom he himself imitates in all things as far as he can? For in Christ the desire of all patriarchs and prophets was fulfilled, since all awaited him; hence he himself says: “Many prophets and kings wished to see what you see, and did not see it” (Matt. 13:17). And he himself wrote the book—the book, surely, of the New Testament, the book of the Law. He judges it himself, who is both judge and lawgiver. “The Father judges no one, but has given all judgment to the Son” (John 5:25). Therefore Job awaited his coming and desired that his book be written—a book which, before it was written, he observed most perfectly. Hence he says that he bears it on his shoulder. For he bears the Gospel on his shoulder who, not considering burdensome the things it commands, [Col. 0654B] faithfully believes and performs them. This book is called a crown because no one is crowned without faith in it.

“By each of my steps I shall declare it, and I offered it as to a prince.” He reads the Gospel, as it were, through each of his steps, who carefully considers both his deeds and the words of the Gospels, fearing that he may have done something there reproved. He offers it as to a prince because he announces its secrets not to just anyone but to the rulers of the Church, lest perhaps he give what is holy to dogs and cast pearls before swine. “If my land cries out against me and its furrows weep with it; if I ate its fruits without payment and afflicted the souls of its farmers, then let thistles spring up for me instead of wheat and thorns instead of barley.” What are meant by the land and [Col. 0654C] furrows except the inhabitants and cultivators of the land? They would have cried out against him if they had felt themselves unjustly burdened and afflicted by him. He eats its fruits without payment who, though he provides nothing or little of governance and consolation to those subject to him, nonetheless does not reduce their revenues and service. Thistles and thorns arise instead of wheat and barley when those who expect joy and gladness encounter sorrow, sadness, and every tribulation. The words of Job are ended.

## Chapter XXXII

“Then these three men ceased answering Job, because he appeared righteous in his own eyes. And Elihu son of Barachel the Buzite, of the family of Ram, was angry and indignant.” [Col. 0654D] He was angry with Job because he said that he was righteous before God. Elihu is interpreted “My God”; by him are understood the arrogant, who, although they preach arrogantly, nevertheless do not depart from the truth of faith. Elihu is the son of Barachel because all who believe rightly receive the Church’s blessing. For Barachel is interpreted “blessing.” Yet although he believes rightly and has received blessing in the sacraments of the Church, nevertheless, because he preaches arrogantly, he is a Buzite and contemptible. For “Buzite” is said to mean “contemptible.” Who indeed would not despise the words of the arrogant? And perhaps this man would not have been arrogant had he not been of the family of Ram. For Ram is interpreted “high”; therefore, because he is high, he does not know how to speak humbly.

[Col. 0655A] “Moreover, he was angry with his friends because they had found no reasonable answer, but had merely condemned Job. Elihu therefore waited while Job was speaking, because those speaking were older. But when he saw that the three had been unable to answer, he became greatly angry.” For sometimes arrogant persons, although they are not opposed to the Church, nevertheless speak against her, because, trusting in wisdom, they rebuke the simplicity of the holy men who preside over her as though it were foolishness. Indeed, we often see scholars speaking arrogantly against bishops.

“And Elihu son of Barachel the Buzite answered and said: ‘I am younger in years, but you are older; therefore, with bowed head, I was afraid to declare my opinion to you.’” [Col. 0655B] For the Church had first to endure heretics before the arrogant, because arrogance greatly increased in many through heretics. For when heretics attacked the Church, and well-educated and intellectually fervent men within it overcame them by their arguments, and then found themselves praised by all for learning and ability, they suddenly fell into arrogance. Hence at times they spoke not so much in defense of truth as for the display of their own wisdom.

“For I hoped that greater age would speak, and a multitude of years would teach wisdom; but, as I see, there is a spirit in men, and the inspiration of the Almighty gives understanding”—that is, whatever their age may be: “Yet the Spirit breathes where he wills” (John 3:8).—“Those of long life are not wise, [Col. 0655C] nor do elders understand judgment; therefore I say: Listen to me; I too will show you my opinion. For I waited for your words, listened to your wisdom, while you debated in speech; and while I thought that you would say something, I considered. But, as I see, there is no one among you who can refute Job or answer his words.” In saying “among you,” he exalts his own opinion, as one able to refute and answer Job when they were unable to answer him.

It follows: “Lest perhaps you say, ‘We have found wisdom: God has cast him down, not man.’” You do not know, he says, why he is afflicted, because he is scourged not by man but by God, whose counsel is impenetrable. But we pass over these matters, because we do not wish to seek roughness upon level ground or carefully investigate the empty verbosity of arrogant persons. “He said nothing to me, and I shall not answer him according to your speeches.” The arrogant, lest they appear to be taught, deny that the teachers of the Church have spoken to them, as though they needed nothing of their doctrine. Yet arrogant persons do not answer the Church as heretics do, since, although they do not speak humbly, they nevertheless do not argue against the faith.

“They were dismayed and answered no more; words failed them.” This seems to be said not by Elihu but by the one who writes these things. For heretics often fear the syllogisms of the arrogant more than the sayings of the saints. “Since then I waited, [Col. 0656A] and they did not speak; they stood still and answered no more, I too shall give my part and show my knowledge.” Because, says Elihu, these men speak no further against Job, I shall now answer and make known what my opinion is. “I am full of words, and the spirit of my belly constrains me.” For arrogant persons, sometimes stirred by the spirit of arrogance, cannot keep silent even if they wish to do so. “And my belly is like new wine without a vent, which bursts new wineskins.” As though he said more plainly: I am stretched out by the force of arrogance no less than the apostles or prophets were stretched by the Holy Spirit. For the apostles were full of such new wine when, as they spoke in new tongues, the Jews said: “These men are full of new wine” (Acts 2:13). But the Holy Spirit bursts new wineskins because he is scarcely contained in a luxurious and fragile breast, not yet made drunk with the waters of faith.

“I shall speak and breathe a little, and open my lips and answer.” Arrogance indeed sounds forth in these words. For in saying, “I shall answer,” he intimates both that he will say much and that he abounds in wisdom. “I will not show partiality to a man, nor equate God with man.” Why so? “For I do not know how long I shall remain, nor whether my Maker may shortly take me away.” This life, he says, is short; I do not know how long I shall live here, and therefore, while I am here, I shall obey the truth without partiality.

## Chapter XXXIII

“Therefore hear, Job, my words, and listen to all [Col. 0656C] my speeches.” Arrogant persons always use long prefaces in order to make their hearers more attentive. “Behold, I have opened my mouth; let my tongue speak in my throat.” Behold, he says, I shall speak and shall delay you no longer; let my tongue speak to you—not loudly, but in the throat. Only attend and diligently receive my words. “My words shall come from a simple heart, and my lips shall speak a pure judgment.” For true words proceed from a simple heart; hence liars are said to speak with a double heart.

“The Spirit of God made me, and the breath of the Almighty gave me life.” Thus it is said of the first man: “God breathed into his face the breath [Col. 0656D] of life” (Gen. 2:7). He therefore puts forward his faith first, lest he be heard as one alien to the Church. “If you can, answer me and stand before my face.” How much arrogance this clause contains! “Behold, God made me, as he made you, and I too was formed from the same clay; nevertheless, let my marvel not terrify you, nor my eloquence be burdensome to you.” We were both created by one and formed from the same material, he says; nevertheless, we have no like wisdom and eloquence. For it is a marvel that God created from the same clay vessels so unlike. Yet let this not be burdensome or vexatious to you, nor let admiration terrify you.

“You said, then, in my hearing, and I heard the sound of [Col. 0657A] your words: ‘I am clean and without fault, undefiled, and there is no iniquity in me. Because he found complaints against me, he therefore regarded me as his enemy. He put my feet in the stocks; he watched all my paths.’ This, then, is the point in which you are not justified.” Some of these things Job said; some he did not say, nor did he say even those things in the sense understood by Elihu. For he did not state without qualification that he was clean, without fault, undefiled, and without iniquity; rather, he said that he had not sinned in such a way as to deserve affliction.

“I shall answer you, because God is greater than man. You contend against him because he has not answered you every word.” You would not contend with God, he says, if you considered only this: that God is greater than man—greater, surely, in wisdom, [Col. 0657B] power, justice, equity, and every other respect. Therefore believe that what he does is just, even though, because you are lesser, you cannot understand it; and do not further contend against him because he has not answered you every word—that is, because he has not allowed you to understand everything. For perfect knowledge of all things is not given to man in this life; it is reserved for us after this life. This is what he says: “God speaks once, and does not repeat the same thing a second time.” As though he said: Wait a little; the time will come when God shall speak once more, decisively, for by one utterance he shall instruct all his faithful so perfectly that they will need no second teaching.

He explains how this will happen: “Through a dream in a vision of the night, when sleep falls upon men [Col. 0657C] and they sleep in bed”—that is, in the rest prepared for them by God—“then he will open the ears of men and, instructing them, will train them by discipline.” This is what the Apostle says: “But when that which is perfect has come, that which is in part will be done away; now we see through a glass, in an enigma, but then face to face” (1 Cor. 13:10). But how will he train them by discipline? Do you wish to hear how? As though through a dream in a vision of the night. For we easily and quickly learn what is revealed to us through dreams. Hence it is clear that in that discipline, though it is perfect, we shall not labor much.

“That he may turn man away from what he has done and free him from pride, rescuing his soul from corruption, and his life from passing into the sword.” Therefore, he says, the sleep and slumber of death suddenly and unexpectedly often fall upon men, lest perhaps, as often happens, they become worse if they remain longer in this life. Hence it is said in the Book of Wisdom concerning the righteous man: “He was taken away lest wickedness change his heart” (Wis. 4:11). Thus also here: that he may turn man away from what he has done, he says, lest he do it further, and wholly rescue his soul from pride and corruption. This happens lest he pass into the sword of eternal punishment.

It follows: “He also reproves by pain upon the bed, and makes all his bones waste away.” Not only there, he says, but here too God, reproving man, instructs him by discipline. He reproves him through the pain of temporal [Col. 0658A] affliction in the bed of this body, because he himself knows what is useful to each person. And he makes all his bones waste away because he weakens all a person’s harmful strength and brings it to exhaustion. Hence it follows: “Bread becomes abominable to him in his life, and food once desired to his soul.” For bodily correction and affliction serve this purpose: they separate a person from all desires and pleasures of the flesh, so that by bread and food once desired we may understand every carnal delight.

“His flesh will waste away, and the bones that had been covered will be uncovered; his soul has drawn near to corruption, and his life to deadly things.” Correction by discipline also serves a person in this respect: his flesh—that is, carnal affection and the concupiscence arising from it—wastes away and fails, and the bones which had been covered by carnal affections are uncovered, because the virtues of the soul, which lay hidden when overcome by bodily impulses, receive strength and power. For the weakness of the flesh is the strength of the soul. And this superabundant and swollen fatness of the flesh causes his soul to draw near to corruption and deadly things. Vices are called deadly because they bring the condemnation of death.

“If there is for him an angel speaking, one out of a thousand, to declare to man his equity, he will have mercy on him and say: ‘Deliver him, that he may not descend into corruption; I have found that by which I may be propitious to him.’” A man, he says, now obtains pardon only with difficulty, until that Angel of Great Counsel comes, who, speaking for him, shall deliver him. This angel [Col. 0658C] is Christ, of whom it is said: “And immediately the ruler whom you seek, and the angel of the covenant whom you desire, will come to his holy temple” (Mal. 3:1). Interceding for us with the Father, he speaks as one of those like us because he displays to him his body, which is one body like our own bodies. For what is speaking except showing? Thus the Son speaks to the Father. The very presentation of the flesh, in that it is seen, speaks and intercedes to God.

He therefore declares the equity of man, because it is not equitable that the man for whom the Son of God became man should perish. He has mercy upon him and, in having mercy, says: “Deliver him, that he may not descend into corruption.” That is, deliver him now from sins so that afterward you may deliver him from torments. “I have found that by which I may be propitious to him”: I have found death, he says; I have found the cross; I have undertaken torments. This is man’s propitiation. Thus the Word speaks without a word, cries without a voice, and intercedes ineffably.

It follows: “His flesh has been consumed by sufferings; let him return to the days of his youth”—that is, to the dignity in which he was created, because for this purpose the flesh has been consumed by sufferings: by sufferings indeed, not by corruption. This may also be understood of our flesh. “He shall pray to God, and God shall be favorable to him; he shall see his face in joy, and he shall restore to man his righteousness.” After that Angel of Great Counsel has come, he says, man shall pray to God confidently, and God shall, through that angel’s intercession, [Col. 0659A] be favorable to man. He shall see his face in joy because, departing this life, he shall immediately be presented before God’s face in gladness and rejoicing. And he shall restore to man his righteousness—not because it is his own, but because it would have been his had he not sinned.

“Man shall look back and say: ‘I have sinned and truly transgressed, and I have not received what I deserved.’” Then, he says, man will first look back; then he will first begin to see and first open the eyes of his mind. Then he will not defend himself arrogantly, but humbly confess his sins. And, doing this, what follows will happen to him: “He will deliver his soul from going into destruction, and living, he shall see light.” Thus, delivered from death by such confession, he is transferred to life, so that everlasting light may shine upon him.

“Behold, God works all these things three times for each person, [Col. 0659B] to call their souls back from corruption and illuminate them in the light of the living.” For God delivers man and separates him from sins, reconciling him to his grace, three times: once through baptism; a second time through repentance; a third time through death. It follows: “Attend, Job, and hear me; be silent while I speak. But if you have anything to say, answer me; speak, for I desire you to appear righteous. But if you have nothing, hear me; be silent, and I shall teach you wisdom.” It is very remarkable that the Holy Spirit should deign to reveal such profound mysteries through so arrogant a man.

## Chapter XXXIV

“Then Elihu spoke these things also: [Col. 0659C] Hear my words, wise men, and you learned men, listen to me. For the ear tests words, and the throat judges foods by taste.” You, he says, who are wise—for he makes them well disposed so that they may favor his words—attend and consider my words. For as the ear alone hears and the throat perceives the flavor of food by taste, so the wise alone understand more carefully and better those things which are wisely said. “Let us choose judgment for ourselves, and among ourselves see what is better.” Observe that he first calls them wise, then invites them to discriminate in judgment.

“Because Job said, ‘I am righteous, and God has overturned my judgment. For in judging me there is falsehood, and my arrow is violent, though I have committed no sin.’” Whoever carefully reads what precedes understands that Job did not say this. “What man is like Job, who drinks mockery like water?” God says this in praise of blessed Job; Elihu, however, says it in blame, when he says “that there is none like him on earth.” He drinks mockery like water, not without some impairment of piety: he mocks and reproves God. “Who goes with workers of iniquity and walks with impious men?” For he walks with such persons who does similar things. Hence the Psalmist says: “If you saw a thief, you ran with him” (Ps. 49:18).—“For he said: ‘A man will not please God, even if he runs with him.’” This too is nowhere found in Job’s words. Thus Elihu is proved to say many things not only arrogantly but falsely.

“Therefore, men of understanding, hear me.” You, he says, who have [Col. 0660A] a heart, who understand the truth, hear me. Far be impiety from God and iniquity from the Almighty. For he will render to a man his work, and repay each according to his ways. This is what the Psalmist says: that “God is a righteous judge” (Ps. 7:12), rendering to each according to his works (Matt. 16:22).—“Indeed, God will not condemn without cause, nor will the Almighty overturn judgment. Whom has he appointed over the earth besides himself? Or whom has he placed over the world which he made?” He himself, he says, made the world, and he—not another—rules and judges it. He needs no partner or helper in creating, nor in ruling, because he is so just in all things that he cannot do anything unjustly.

“If a man directs his heart toward him, he will draw to himself his spirit and breath.” [Col. 0660B] If a man directs his heart toward God, he says, and begins to serve him with a pure and upright heart, he will immediately draw God’s spirit and breath to himself, because he will be filled with the grace of the Holy Spirit. “Spirit” and “breath” signify the same thing, although “breath” may be understood as life. In this God’s great benevolence is commended: he is so quickly inclined to mercy. “All flesh shall fail together, and man shall return to ashes.” As though he said: Those who direct their heart toward the Lord, enlivened by his spirit and life, cannot die; but all the rest shall perish, because they are dust and shall return to dust. “If therefore you have understanding, hear what is said and listen to the voice of my speech.”

Elihu always increases in arrogance, [Col. 0660C] so that he asks the most righteous and wisest man whether he possesses understanding. In this, as in all else, the great patience of the blessed man is displayed. “Can one who does not love judgment be healed? And how do you condemn, untouched, him who is righteous, who says to a king, ‘Apostate,’ and calls rulers impious?” This ought not to have been said against Job, who had so often above asked that he be judged. He loves judgment who knows that he has a just cause, because there he is defended, healed, and delivered from injury. But he condemns God, who is righteous, untouched, who reproves his judgment before understanding it. For God is touched when he answers questions put to him. He himself is so just that he flatters neither kings nor rulers; rather, according to their merits, he calls them apostates and impious. What is calling them except displaying and condemning them? For while he condemns them, he shows what they have been.

“He does not accept the persons of princes, nor acknowledge a tyrant when he pleads against the poor; for all are the work of his hands.” God does not show partiality; rather, in every nation, one who fears him and works righteousness is acceptable to him. He judges all equally because he created all. Hearing the groans of the afflicted, he destroys and condemns their oppressors; hence it follows:

“They shall die suddenly, and in the middle of the night peoples shall be disturbed, pass away, and remove the violent man without a hand.” They shall die suddenly because they shall perish by one sentence of condemnation. This will happen in the middle of the night because the day of the Lord will come like a thief in the night; it is night, indeed, because when he will come is dark and unknown to all. And they shall pass away, never to return again. Then God’s commands and judgments shall remove the impious and violent people without a hand, for God’s commands need the help of no one’s hand.

[Col. 0661A] “For his eyes are upon the ways of men, and he considers all their steps. There are no darknesses and no shadow of death in which those who work iniquity may hide; for it is no longer in man’s power to come to God in judgment.” The impious, he says, are removed because God’s eyes are not unaware what they were like. Considering the ways and [Col. 0661B] works of all, he will render to each according to his works. Before God’s eyes there are no darknesses of ignorance nor shadow of death—that is, the gloom of forgetfulness—in which those who work iniquity may hide.
