Therefore, before they are removed, let them repent and turn, because after they have been taken from here it is no longer in their power to come again to judgment. For God judges once, and his judgment is not reconsidered.

> **[Note: Col. 0661D]** Ecclesiastes should also be recalled, who in chapter 12 repeatedly exhorts man to provide for himself [Col. 0662D] before the sun is darkened and the darknesses of death come upon him.

“He shall crush many, innumerable persons, and cause others to stand in their place. For he knows their works; therefore he will bring in the night, and they shall be crushed.” The Lord daily kills and crushes many—indeed innumerable persons—and, considering their wicked works, will bring the night of eternal condemnation [Col. 0661C] upon them. Nevertheless, because the number of the elect has not yet been completed, he causes others to stand in their place.

“He struck them as impious men in the place of those who see, because they deliberately departed from him and refused to understand all his ways, so that they made the cry of the needy reach him, and he heard the voice of the poor.” The place of those who see is the Church, because not the blind but those who see and understand dwell in it. And these people, because they ought to walk in the way, see; they sin not from ignorance but voluntarily and deliberately. What they do not understand is not caused by inability but by will; for they would understand if they wished. These people, afflicting the needy and poor contrary to God’s command, make their cry come before God. Therefore, because they afflict others without compassion, they are deservedly struck as impious.

It follows: “For when he grants peace, who is there to condemn? When he hides his face, who is there to behold him—over a nation and over all men—he who causes a hypocrite to reign because of the sins of the people?” He himself, he says, struck the impious; he grants peace to the afflicted, and not just any peace, but everlasting peace. Whoever receives it fears no judgment or condemnation from anyone. But from whom else does God hide his face except those with whom he is angry? After it is said to them: “Let the impious be taken away, lest they see the glory of God” (Isa. 26:16), and they are cast headlong into hell, [Col. 0662A] it will be impossible for them to see him further. God does this over all nations and all men: that is, he delivers the righteous and condemns the impious. He causes a hypocritical man to reign because of the sins of the people; this may be understood particularly of Antichrist and generally of others. For often, because of a people’s sins, evil rulers are appointed over evil subjects.

“Since therefore I have spoken to God, I will not forbid you also. If I have erred, teach me; if I have spoken iniquity, I shall add no more. Does God require it from you because it displeased you?” He says this both arrogantly and mockingly, asking to be reproved where he knows with complete certainty that he cannot be reproved. For in what he has just said he has neither erred nor spoken iniquity; and even if he had spoken it, he asserts that the account would be required from himself, not another, and that he himself would render account for it. “For,” says the Apostle, “each of us shall give account for himself” (Rom. 14:12). This is what he says: “Does God require it from you because it displeased you?” The implied subject is “my argument,” as though you were to render account for it. For arrogant persons, when they do not hear their words praised, think that they have displeased others.

“For you began to speak, not I; but if you know better, speak. Let men of understanding speak to me, and let a wise man hear me. But Job has spoken foolishly, and his words do not sound of instruction.” As though he said: You ought to attribute my rebuking you to yourself, not to me: you began to speak, not I; what I rebuked, I heard from you, not invented myself. Nevertheless, if you know something better, whether than what I said or than what you earlier said, speak. He says “speak,” yet does not wait for him to speak. And, as though Job lacked understanding, he removes him from their conversation, saying: “Let men of understanding speak to me, and let a wise man hear me,” not this man who lacks wisdom and understanding.

He says that blessed Job spoke foolishly and without instruction because he heard him defend his righteousness. Hence, turning to God, he says: “My Father, let Job be tested to the end; do not depart from the man of iniquity, because he adds blasphemy to his sins.” What he was before the scourges, he says, is shown by the fact that, scourged for his sins, he does not cease to sin amid the very scourges. Let him therefore be tested to the end, that even so he may at some time come to his senses. “Meanwhile let him be bound among us, and then let him summon God to judgment by his words.” First, he says, let him now be bound and overcome by our arguments, so that by them he may understand that he can in no way resist God’s arguments.

## Chapter XXXV
“Then Elihu again spoke these words: ‘Does this thought of yours seem right to you, when you said, “I am more just than God”? For you said: “What is just does not please you,” or, “What profit will you gain if I sin?”’” Job did not say this: neither that he was more just than God [Col. 0663A], nor that what is right does not please God. But what did he say? “Let him set equity against me, and let my judgment attain victory.” And again: “I know that, if I am judged, I shall be found righteous.” It is therefore clear that Elihu did not understand these words properly. For even if Job were proved righteous, God would not thereby be unjust; for He was not afflicting him because of Job’s sins, but because He wished thereby to make him greater, more illustrious, and more eminent in merits. Both, therefore, are righteous: He who afflicts and he who is afflicted.

“Therefore I will answer your words, and your friends with you.” For he does not wish to answer you alone, because he had said that he would speak to the intelligent and wise: “Look up to heaven and see; contemplate the sky, which is higher than you. If you sin, [Col. 0663B] what harm will you do Him? And if your iniquities are multiplied, what will you do against Him? But if you act justly, what will you give Him? Or what will He receive from your hand?” He does not answer Job’s words as he had promised; for one does not find in the words of blessed Job, “What profit will you gain if I sin?” Yet this is the premise from which his argument proceeds. He ought not to have said these things against Job, but against someone desperate and most ready to sin.

“Look,” he says, “upon heaven and the sky: you see that it is higher than you; by no strength can you reach it. God is indeed there. Whether, therefore, you sin or act well, God remains secure: He is moved neither by gifts nor by threats. Your impiety will harm a man like yourself, and your righteousness will help the Son of Man.” To God, he says, [Col. 0663C] you can neither benefit nor harm in any respect; but if you are impious or righteous, you can harm or benefit a human being in many ways.

“Because of the multitude of oppressors they will cry out, and they will howl because of the violence of tyrants’ arms.” Human impiety, he says, can harm human beings. Yet those who suffer oppression cry out and howl to the Lord, asking Him to avenge them against the violence of oppressors and tyrants. Still, those who cry are not always heard, because they cry not faithfully but in doubt. Hence he adds: “And he did not say: ‘Where is God who made me, who gives songs in the night? Who teaches us more than the beasts of the earth, and hears us above the birds of heaven.’ There they will cry out, and He will not hear because of [Col. 0663D] the pride of the wicked.”

He has used the singular for the plural, and in one person shows how greatly doubt harms all. Let the afflicted person, he says, say faithfully: “Where is God, who made me?” Let him cry not only with his mouth but also with his heart, and firmly believe that He will not abandon the person whom He made. He “gives songs in the night”: that is, He has very often bestowed joy and gladness upon His faithful people amid great tribulations. Here perhaps the ancient fathers learned, in their prayers, to recount God’s mighty works. The Lord teaches us above the beasts of the earth and above the birds of heaven, because those who possess God’s wisdom are wiser than all lovers of the world and all philosophers.

“There they will cry out”: where? In the tribulations which they suffer from the impious. Why? Because of the pride [Col. 0664A] of the wicked who afflict them. “And He will not hear.” When God does not hear, this happens either because the request is not rightly made, or because He has determined to do better for His faithful servants by not hearing than by hearing. Thus the Apostle, when praying, was told: “My grace is sufficient for you, for power is made perfect in weakness” (II Cor. XII, 9). Therefore he is not heard, so that God’s power may be perfected.

“God, therefore, will not hear in vain, and the Almighty will consider the causes of individuals. Even when you say, ‘He does not regard me,’ be judged before Him and wait for Him; for now He does not inflict His wrath, and he multiplies words without knowledge.” God would hear in vain if He heard foolish, unjust, and senseless petitions. But because He considers the causes of individuals, He hears only what ought to be heard; for He knows [Col. 0664B] what is fitting for each case. Even when you say, “God does not regard my afflictions,” you are already being judged before Him; He is preparing to free you and to condemn your adversary. Therefore wait for Him until He comes to judgment. For now He does not inflict His wrath, nor does He greatly avenge crime. Whoever, therefore, desires perfect vindication should await the future judgment. From this it is clear that Job opened his mouth in vain, because whatever he said was empty and useless. He ought either to have awaited the future judgment, or to have prayed in such a way as to deserve to be heard.

## CHAPTER XXXVI

“And Elihu continued, saying: ‘Wait [Col. 0664C] a little, and I will show you; for I still have something to say on God’s behalf.’” Elihu had already spoken much; but swollen with the spirit of pride, he cannot be satisfied with speaking. Nor does he suppose that he has spoken too much, because he is defending God’s cause. Thus he adds:

“I will repeat my knowledge from the beginning, and I will prove my Maker righteous. For truly my words are without falsehood, and perfect knowledge will be proved to you.” It is as though he said: “Lest perhaps you think that I have lied, I will repeat my knowledge from the beginning. But you, if you have anything, answer; for I will prove my Maker righteous. And, as I said from the beginning, my words are straightforward and without falsehood, and my knowledge will be proved perfect to you.” Not only does he speak arrogantly [Col. 0664D], but he also forestalls and dismisses objections that might have been made against him. Indeed, he could not defend himself against the charge of falsehood.

“God does not reject the mighty, since He Himself is mighty; but He does not save the impious, and He grants judgment to the poor.” Since God is mighty, he says, He rejects the mighty not on account of their power but on account of their impiety. For He saves the mighty, but He does not save the impious. And He grants judgment to the poor, so that they may justly condemn those by whom they were unjustly judged.

“He will not withdraw His eyes from the righteous, and He sets kings upon the throne for ever, and they are exalted. And if they are in chains and bound with cords of poverty, He will make known to them their deeds and their crimes, because they have been violent.” You say that God will not save the impious; on the contrary, [Col. 0665A] He will not withdraw the eyes of His mercy from the righteous. He never forgets one whom He always beholds. He sets kings upon the throne for ever because He has prepared eternal seats for the princes of the Church, namely bishops and priests. There they are exalted; for those humbled here are raised and exalted there.

When these kings are afflicted in this world by imprisonment, poverty, and other miseries, God makes known to them by hidden inspiration, and brings to remembrance, the deeds and crimes which they once committed, so that, remembering them, they may endure more patiently the torments by which they do not doubt that their sins are being paid. This is what he had said above: “A man will look and say: ‘I have sinned and truly gone astray, and I have not received what I deserved.’”

[Col. 0665B] “He will also uncover their ear in order to correct them, and He will speak so that they may turn from iniquity. If they hear and observe, they will complete their days in good and their years in glory; but if they do not hear, they will pass through the sword and be consumed in folly.” God, he says, makes His faithful people aware of their sins by hidden inspiration and brings them to mind. He also uncovers and opens the ear of their mind. Why? “To correct them.” He speaks to them inwardly and invisibly, warning them to turn from iniquity. If they do this, they will complete their days in good—that is, this present life in holy conduct—“and their years in glory,” because afterwards they will be with the Lord in eternal glory. “But if they do not hear, they will pass through the sword” [Col. 0665C] of eternal vengeance, “and be consumed in folly,” because from their folly they will find nothing but death and destruction.

“The hypocrites and the crafty provoke God’s wrath; nor will they cry out when they are bound. Their soul will die in a tempest, and their life among the effeminate.” They rightly provoke God’s wrath against themselves, since they do everything with pretence and cunning, whether to deceive others or to gain honour and vain glory for themselves. These will not cry out when they have been bound, since they will not repent even at death itself. A person is bound when he is not in his own power. Therefore their soul will die in a tempest—that is, in tribulation and distress, when the hailstorm of all torments rushes down upon them. “And their life will be among the effeminate”: that is, among the idle, soft, and those devoted to luxury and pleasures.

“He will deliver the poor man from his distress, and in tribulation will uncover his ear.” [Col. 0665D] The poor man is one who does not place his hope in riches of this kind. Thus David, though rich, nevertheless calls himself needy and poor. The Lord uncovers and opens this person’s ear in tribulation, because He enables him to understand the benefit of tribulation, so that the one who knows that through many tribulations he must enter the kingdom of heaven may no longer grieve over tribulation.

“Thus He will save you very broadly from the narrow mouth, which has no foundation beneath it; and the repose of your table will be full of fatness. Your cause has been judged as that of [Col. 0666A] an impious man; you will receive cause and judgment.” The Psalmist says of this: “Let not the tempest of waters overwhelm me; let not the deep swallow me; let not the pit press its mouth upon me” (Ps. LXVIII, 16). This, therefore, is a description of hell, whose mouth is both narrow and very broad: narrow indeed because it holds those whom it receives most tightly and does not permit them to go out; very broad because it swallows many people in great multitudes. Hell has no foundation, because its vast abyss cannot be filled.

But the repose of your table is filled with fatness when, after the labours of this life, rest, a table, and refreshment with eternal food are prepared by the Lord for the saints. Hence the Gospel says: “He will gird Himself, make them recline, and, passing by, will minister to them” (Luke XII, 37). As for the words, “Your cause has been judged as that of an impious man,” he says this because Job was being most severely afflicted as though impious. But he will receive cause and judgment, because for such a cause and judgment he too will be appointed both advocate and judge, or because he will be rewarded for this with great honours and gifts.

“Therefore let not anger overcome you so that you oppress someone, nor let the multitude of places incline you.” Blessed Job did not at any time, overcome by anger, oppress anyone, although in the uprightness of discipline he corrected those subject to him. Hence he said above: “Have not the men of my tent said, ‘Who will give us of his flesh, that we may be satisfied?’” Nor let the multitude of places incline you to iniquity. For the rich and powerful often, because they possess many places [Col. 0666C], turn their eyes away from the height of justice and become more unjust.

“Lay aside your greatness without tribulation, and all the strong in might, lest you prolong the night, that peoples may rise in their place.” Those lay aside their greatness who humble themselves wholly in heart before God and do not trust in the greatness of their own righteousness. Some do this willingly and without tribulation; others refuse to do it unless afflicted with many tribulations. Also lay aside the strong in might—that is, take away from all the impious and proud who associate with you the licence and power to do evil.

“Do not prolong the night.” To prolong the night is to exalt the impious and those enveloped in the darkness of vices. Such persons ought not to be prolonged but [Col. 0666D] drawn back. Why? “That peoples may rise for them.” The peoples and multitudes of the good then increase when the impious and proud lose their strength. It follows:

“Beware lest you turn aside to iniquity; for you have begun to pursue this after misery.” Elihu thought it iniquity that blessed Job said he was afflicted more than he deserved. Who does not see how full of arrogance these words are?

“Behold, God is exalted in His strength, and none among lawgivers is like Him. Who can search out His ways? Or who can say to Him, ‘You have wrought iniquity’? Remember that you do not know His work, of which men have sung.” This is a clear prophecy concerning Christ. Yet it is very remarkable that Elihu should speak by the spirit of prophecy. “The Spirit breathes where He wills” (John III, 8). Caiaphas too prophesied. Moreover, even the ass spoke. Finally, the Sibyl [Note: Natalis Alexander discusses the Sibylline oracles, *Historia Veteris Testamenti*, vol. III, art. 4, proposition 2.] said that she was God’s prophetess:

“Behold,” she says, “God will come, exalted in the strength of His divinity; He who will appear exceedingly humble in the weakness of His humanity. And none among lawgivers is like Him. For who is like God among the sons of God?”

The givers of the Law were not Moses alone but also the other prophets. And who can say, “You have wrought iniquity”? No one can search out His works and ways. For He Himself said: “Which of you will convict me of sin?” (John VIII, 46.) Men sang of Him because the holy prophets foretold His coming and incarnation, His death and resurrection, [Col. 0667B] and all other things concerning Him. To be ignorant of His work is to depart from justice and equity.

“All people see Him, and every person beholds Him from afar.” All people see Him, as it is written: “All flesh shall see the salvation of God” (Isa. LI, 10). Yet each beholds Him from afar because, although they see a human being, they cannot see God, but can in some way understand Him as though from a distance.

“Behold, God is great, surpassing our knowledge; the number of His years is beyond estimation.” God surpasses our knowledge, because we cannot know Him as He is; or because no knowledge can be compared with His knowledge. And although He appears young among men, the number of His years is beyond estimation. [Col. 0667C] Thus He Himself said: “Amen, I say to you, before Abraham came to be, I am” (John VIII, 58).

“He takes away the drops of rain and pours out showers like streams, which rain from the clouds, which cover everything from above.” What are the drops of rain but the preachers of the Old Testament, who, compared with the teachers of the Church, seem to be but drops of rain? Christ, by His coming, took these away and caused them to cease; and through Himself and His disciples He poured out the streams of sacred speech like torrents raining from the clouds. These clouds cover everything from above because the volumes of holy Scripture, from which these rains flow, water and shade the hearts of the faithful.

“If He wills to spread out the clouds like [Col. 0667D] His tent, and to flash from above with His light, He will cover also the bounds of the sea.” If, he says, He wills to spread out the clouds—that is, evangelical teaching or the holy Apostles—when He says: “Go into all the world; preach the Gospel to every creature” (Mark XVI, 15); just as in the beginning He spread out His tent, that is, heaven; and if He wills to flash from above with His light, that is, with the illumination of miracles, He will cover also the bounds of the sea: that is, He will convert all the ends of the world to the faith. For as the tent of heaven, so also the doctrine of the Apostles contains and encloses within itself all the ends of the world.

“For by these He judges peoples, and [Col. 0668A] gives food to many mortals.” What does “by these” mean? By the Apostles and evangelical doctrine. By these all peoples are judged, as by law and judges; by these too God feeds many mortals, as by food and the mystery of food.

“He hides the light from the mighty, and commands it to return again.” This is what is said elsewhere: “God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble” (James IV, 6). Since the mighty and proud now do not see the light and truth, if they humble themselves, God—the light of the world and the truth—will immediately return to them.

“He declares concerning it to His friend that it is his possession and that he can ascend to it.” “You are my friends,” says the Lord, “if you do what I command you” (John XV, 14). Christ declared to these persons—that is, enabled them to understand—that this light is their possession, according to the words: “The Lord is the portion of my inheritance” (Ps. XV, 5). For if Christ is the inheritance of the saints, He is also their possession. But who would ever hope that he could ascend to this possession unless it were said: “And he can ascend to it”? God Himself confirms this hope, saying: “Father, I will that where I am, they also may be with me” (John XVII, 24).

## CHAPTER XXXVII

“Because of this my heart was terrified and moved from its place.” Because, he says, God exalted in His strength deigned to assume flesh and to become not merely man but the possession of human beings, my heart was terrified and, through excessive wonder, [Col. 0668C] moved from its place. A heart is in some manner moved from its place when a person is raised in ecstasy of mind. Thus the prophet Habakkuk: “Lord, I heard your report and was afraid; I considered your works and was terrified” (Hab. III, 2). It follows: “He will hear the hearing in terror of His voice, and the sound going forth from His mouth.” A man, he says, will hear the sound of His voice going forth from His mouth. But how will he hear it? “In terror.” Therefore this voice, which will be heard in terror, is that by which the Lord will say to sinners: “Depart from me, you cursed, into eternal fire” (Matt. XXV, 41).

“He Himself looks beneath all the heavens, and His light is over the ends of the earth.” “For,” says the Psalmist, “He dwells on high and looks upon the lowly in heaven [Col. 0668D] and on earth” (Ps. CXII, 6). Since He is everywhere and sees all things, no one can hide himself from His judgment.

“After Him a sound will roar; He will thunder with the voice of His strength, and it will not be investigated when His voice has been heard.” After the Lord has pronounced the sentence of condemnation and thundered with the voice of strength, the sound of those who remain after Him—that is, of all the condemned whom He will leave in punishment—will roar with pain and sorrow. Yet at that time no one may investigate God’s sentence, because there will be no opportunity to answer; as soon as the sentence is heard, they will be dragged to torments.

“God will thunder wonderfully with His voice, [Col. 0669A] He who does great and unsearchable things.” How will He not then thunder wonderfully and terribly, as though angry, over the impious—He who formerly, though gracious and peaceful, terrified the devout? For it is written that the children of Israel said: “Let not the Lord speak to us, lest perhaps we die” (Exod. XX, 19). God’s judgments are great and unsearchable, as the Apostle says: “O the depth of the riches of the wisdom and knowledge of God! How incomprehensible are His judgments, and how unsearchable His ways!” (Rom. XI, 33).

“He commands the snow to descend upon the earth, and the rains of winter, and the rain of His strength.” Before the Lord comes to judge, he says, He will send preachers over the whole earth. By snow we understand holy preachers, made white through life, character, and holy conduct. He who said, “You will wash me, and I shall be made whiter than snow” (Ps. L, 9), desired to become such snow. By winter rains and rains of strength is signified evangelical teaching. This is winter rain when it extinguishes the heat of lust and the fire of rage and hatred, for winter rains are colder. Evangelical teaching is also a rain of strength when it threatens sinners with the torments of future judgment.

“He seals in the hand of every human being, that each may know his works.” There are five bodily senses by which we perform good and evil works; these are also represented by the five talents in the Gospel. There are likewise five fingers of the hand. When we see them, we ought to remember our senses, so that we may understand what we have done and, if we have sinned through any one of them, repent.

“The beast will enter its hiding-place and remain in its den.” This beast is the devil; his den and hiding-place are all the impious, because he hides and dwells in them.

“From the inner regions comes the tempest, and from Arcturus the cold.” As Arcturus signifies the north, so “the inner regions” signify the south. Hence it is said above: “He makes Arcturus, Orion, the Hyades, and the inner regions of the south.” Since the Jews are nearer the south and the Romans the north, the south denotes the former and the north the latter. A tempest therefore comes from the south because the first persecution against the Church arose in Judaea. But from the north [Col. 0669D] comes cold, because by Roman swords or commands the holy martyrs were everywhere slain. Observe how elegantly he signifies death by cold. That this occurred not apart from God’s will is shown by the following words: “When God breathes, frost congeals, and again the waters are poured forth most widely.”

Frost increased when death temporarily reigned in the Church, while holy martyrs were dying everywhere. Thus the Apostle says: “Therefore death works in us, but life in you” (II Cor. IV, 12). But the waters were again poured out most widely because, when peace was granted from heaven, holy preachers increased and were strengthened, and began everywhere among the nations to pour out the rain of doctrine.

“The grain desires the clouds, and the clouds scatter their light; they shine round about, wherever the will of the Governor has led them, to everything which He has commanded them upon the face of all the earth—whether in one tribe, or in His land, or in whatever place of His mercy He has commanded them to be found.” This is what the Lord says to His disciples: “Lift up your heads and see the regions, which are already white for harvest” (John IV, 35). Christ’s grain, God’s harvest, now desires both to see and to hear the clouds of the Gospel and the teachers of the Church. The clouds scatter their light because they shine not only through teaching but also through miracles. They shine all around because “their sound has gone out into all the earth.” Nevertheless, they go nowhere except where the will of their Governor has led them, nor do they do anything except what He has commanded.

Whether He has willed them to be in one tribe [Col. 0670B] of the children of Israel, as they remained for some time first in Jerusalem and in the tribe of Judah; or in His land, that is, throughout the whole land of the Jews; or whether He has commanded them to be found in whatever place He wills to pity—that is, throughout the whole world.

“Listen therefore to these things, Job; stand and consider God’s miracles.” Why does he command one who could go nowhere to stand, except because he regarded him, by comparison with himself, as lying in the depths? Thus he adds: “Do you know when God commanded the rains to show the light of His clouds?” It is as though he said: “Was it revealed to you, as it was to me, when, according to God’s command and ordering, the light and power of the prophets would be revealed in their words and teaching?” Then the rains of the clouds—that is, the prophecies and books of the prophets—began to show their light, [Col. 0670C] that is, their brightness, when they could be understood spiritually.

Every day the Jews drink Isaiah’s rains, but do not understand how great was Isaiah’s brightness in seeing things to come with the eyes of his mind. But the rains of the prophets reveal their light and knowledge to us, because, as we drink them, we understand what they saw.

“Do you know the great paths of the clouds and their perfect knowledge?” I think that these great paths and perfect knowledges of the prophets are those by which, in prophecy, they came as far as Christ’s incarnation, passion, resurrection, and ascension. This may be understood most clearly of the Apostles.

[Col. 0670D] “Are not your garments warm when the earth has been breathed upon by the south wind?” Each person’s garment is his flesh; the south wind is warm. In this passage it signifies the Holy Spirit, who appeared to the Apostles in fire. Garments, therefore, become warm when the earth is breathed upon by the south wind, because when a person is touched by the breath of the Holy Spirit, his very flesh in some manner feels within itself the fire of compunction and love. It is as though he said: “If the fire and breath of the Holy Spirit had touched you, your pride would by no means have raised you against God.”

“Perhaps you made the heavens with Him, which are most solid, like bronze? Show us what we should say to Him; for we are enveloped in darkness.” He says this mockingly, as though saying: “You who contend with God, perhaps you are His equal and made the heavens with Him. Teach us, then, what we should say to Him and how we should answer Him. You alone are wise; we are enveloped in darkness and ignorance.” By the heavens we may also understand the angels and saints, who are called bronze-like and solid because they are strong in God’s love and faith.

“Who will report to Him what I say? Even if a man has spoken, he will be devoured.” Who, he says, will report to Him what I say, so that by at least this speech of mine he may defend himself? Though I may not know how to speak in comparison with greater persons, I nevertheless do not despair of being able to answer you. But what do I say of myself or of you? Even if a human being has spoken, his knowledge will be swallowed up, and, as though already buried, he will have nothing to answer. For what is a human being? Did even these people know it? Here “man” is used for wisdom. For the difference between the wise and other human beings is the same as that between a human being and other animals. Such human beings abound not in the Old Testament but in the New. Hence he adds: “But now they do not see the light; suddenly the air will gather clouds, and a passing wind will drive them away.”

Now, he says, people enveloped in the darkness of ignorance cannot discern light and truth. Now, I say; for later it will be otherwise. Just as air is suddenly gathered into clouds, by whose gloom and darkness everything is overshadowed, but as soon as the wind passes and the clouds are driven away all things return to their former brightness, so those who will come after us, freed from the darkness of ignorance, will see the truth clearly and openly.

“From the north [Col. 0671C] comes gold, and to God fearful praise.” By the north we understand those in whom the devil sat and dwelt, as he himself says: “I will sit upon the mount of the Covenant, in the sides of the north, and I will be like the Most High” (Isa. XIV, 13). Gold is the souls of the righteous, purified by the baptism of repentance and the fire of martyrdom. Fearful praise comes to God because those of whom we have just spoken, considering their sins and also considering what is written—“For praise is not fitting [Note: [Col. 0671D] The Vulgate reads ‘beautiful’ (*speciosa*).] in the mouth of a sinner” (Ecclus. XV, 9)—do not praise God without fear and trembling. It follows:

“We cannot find Him worthily; He is great in strength, judgment, and justice, and cannot be described.” In the things He has made, he says, we can in some measure know God’s greatness [Note: [Col. 0671D] The Apostle teaches the same: “The invisible things of God, understood through those things which have been made, are clearly seen—His everlasting power and divinity.” Rom. I, 20.]. For neither the greatness of His strength, nor His judgment, nor His justice can possibly be described. Who can understand with what strength He made heaven and earth? Who will recount His judgments, of which the Psalmist says: “Your judgments are a great deep” (Ps. XXXV, 7)? Who will investigate this justice: why He loved Jacob but hated Esau? It is enough, therefore, for us to believe and fear what is not given to us to understand.

[Col. 0672A] Hence it is added: “Therefore men will fear Him, and all who seem wise to themselves will not dare to contemplate Him.” Men and the wise fear Him, because “the fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom” (Ecclus. I, 26). But those who are not wise and think themselves wise—such as arrogant Jews, philosophers, and heretics—will not dare to contemplate Him, when it shall be said to them: “Let the impious be taken away, lest they see the glory of God” (Isa. XXVI, 10). Miserable wise men, then, because they will not dare to behold Wisdom itself.

## CHAPTER XXXVIII

“And the Lord, answering Job out of the whirlwind, said [Note: ‘This may indeed be understood literally: the voice of God may be said to have been miraculously formed in the air amid a certain disturbance of the air, as is recorded to have happened on Mount Sinai, Exod. XX; or as a voice came to Christ, when some said that thunder had occurred, as is read in John XII, 29. D. Thomas.].” Since Job was troubled and afflicted by scourges, the Lord is said to have answered him out of a whirlwind:

[Col. 0672B] “Who is this who wraps up counsels in unskilled words? Gird your loins like a man; I will question you, and answer Me.” Although he uttered sound judgments, he wrapped them in unskilled words because he spoke arrogantly. Since not to know God is to reject Him, the Lord plainly shows that Job rejects Him—the One whom, because He knows all things, He asks who he is. “Gird your loins like a man”: gird yourself with the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God; prepare yourself to answer. A greater battle is prepared for you; I will question you, and you are now to answer not a human being but God.

“Where were you when I laid the foundations of the earth? Tell Me, if you have understanding. Who set its measures, if you know? Or who stretched the line over [Col. 0672C] it? Upon what were its bases made firm? Or who laid its cornerstone?” These things are wonderful and astonishing even literally. Spiritually, however, they must be understood of the Church. The foundations of the Church are the prophets and Apostles; hence the Apostle says: “Built upon the foundation of the Apostles and prophets” (Eph. II, 20). God laid these foundations before the ages, because He ordained the times when and the manner in which they were to be laid.

Christ set the Church’s measures when He commanded His disciples: “Go into all the world; preach the Gospel to every creature” (Mark XVI, 15). The Church therefore has the same measure as the world. He stretched a line over it, either because He divided it through bishoprics, or because He corrected it to the form of uprightness. Where a line is set, crookedness cannot hide itself.

But upon whom were its bases, which He has just called the foundation, made firm, except upon Christ? He is not only the foundation but the foundation of foundations, according to the Apostle’s words: “For no one can lay another foundation except that which has been laid, which is Christ Jesus” (I Cor. III, 11). He Himself is the cornerstone, [Col. 0673A] joining in one faith two walls: one from the circumcision and the other from the uncircumcision. Of Him the Psalmist says: “The stone which the builders rejected has become the head of the corner” (Ps. CXVII, 22).

“When the morning stars praised Me together, and all the sons of God rejoiced.” By the morning stars may be understood either the angels, created at the very beginning of the world, or the Apostles, who first shone at the beginning of the Church’s birth. By all the sons of God may be signified the whole multitude of faithful angels. All these praise God and rejoice ineffably. For before they came to be, in God’s own purpose they were already praising and rejoicing in Him. To take an example from ourselves: when we decide to do some good thing, that very decision commends us to ourselves. What, then, can Job say concerning his own righteousness, when he has many equals and, before he came to be such, was ordained not by himself but by God?

“Who shut up the sea with doors when it burst forth as though coming from a womb? When I made a cloud its garment and wrapped it in darkness as in swaddling-clothes?” What is signified by the sea except the tyrants and powerful persons of this world? God often confines them, not with a wall but with doors, [Col. 0673B] because they cannot rage against the saints unless God opens for them the doors of raging and grants them permission to afflict the good. Thus the Lord says to His disciples: “Behold, Satan has asked for you, that he may sift you like wheat” (Luke XXII, 31).

They burst forth as though coming from a womb when, having received power, they rage with all their strength against the saints. One comes forth from the womb by force, not by reason. They are wrapped in cloud and darkness as in swaddling-clothes because, blinded by error and ignorance, they know nothing but vain, foolish, and childish things. Therefore, bound in these swaddling-clothes of infancy, they do not even have their own limbs in their power. God says that He does this because He permits it to happen; thus He says of Pharaoh: “I will harden his heart” (Exod. VII, 3).

“‘I surrounded it with my boundaries, and set bar and doors, and said: Thus far shall you come, and no farther; here you shall break your swelling waves.’” For God surrounded the aforesaid sea—that is, tyrants—with his own boundaries, because he set them a limit both for raging and for living. When they reach that limit, as though a bar had been set against them and doors shut, they can proceed no farther. There they break their swelling waves, because by death, conversion, loss of power, or some other occasion, they cease from madness and wickedness.

“‘Have you, after your birth, commanded the dawn, and shown the morning its place? Have you seized the ends of the earth and shaken the wicked out of it?’” The implied words are: as I have. For Christ, after his birth, commanded the dawn and showed the morning its place, because, after being born in time from the Virgin, he taught the Church and showed it both to what place it should come and where it ought to remain eternally. For dawn and morning signify the same thing. He also seized the ends of the earth, because God chose the weak things of the world, shaking from it the moths of vices; and not only this, but also separating and shaking out from it the wicked Jews and heretics. Of these it is added:

“‘It shall be restored as clay to a seal, and shall stand like a garment.’” Of this seal the Apostle says: “‘And he received the sign of circumcision, a seal of the righteousness of faith’” (Rom. IV.11). By the seal, therefore, let us understand those who have been sealed. They are restored like clay, because, now made like earth rather than heaven and wiped away like the clay of the streets, they are trampled underfoot by all nations. They stand like a garment because, swollen with perverse understanding, they do not draw near to Christ’s flesh and humanity; for they would draw near if they believed. Those garments which stand stiffly are coarser and, as though withdrawing from the body, cannot be fitted to it.

“‘Their light shall be taken away from the wicked, and the uplifted arm shall be broken.’” Because, he says, the Jews, stiff and proud like a garment, refuse to join themselves to Christ, their light—the God who is the light of the world, light sent especially to them—shall be taken from them. And the uplifted arm shall be broken, because formerly one pursued a thousand and two put ten thousand to flight.

“‘Have you entered into the depths of the sea, and walked in the lowest parts of the abyss? Have the gates of death been opened to you, and have you seen the dark doors? Have you considered the breadth of the earth?’” The implied words are: as I have. Here he calls the sea and abyss hell, because it is both exceedingly deep [Col. 0674C] and dark. Christ descended into it when he despoiled it. And because, as it is written, “‘I have become as a man without help, free among the dead’” (Ps. LXXXVII.5), he says that he walked there. There indeed are the gates of death, there are the dark doors, by which we may understand either the punishments of hell or malignant spirits. These gates were opened to him who enters and leaves through them in safety.

But because our Saviour, returning from there after defeating the prince of the world, sent his disciples to preach in all lands, it is therefore added: “‘Have you considered the breadth of the earth?’” For him to consider it was to convert it.

“‘Tell me, if you know all things, in what way light dwells, and what is the place of darkness, that you may lead each to its bounds and understand the paths of its house. Did you then know that you would be born, or did you know the number of your days?’” Unless the words followed, “that you may lead each to its bounds,” perhaps the place of light and darkness might be known. For the way of light is righteousness, and whatever leads us to God and to light. The place of darkness may be understood not only as hell, but also as the mind of every wicked person.

But since Judas perished and Paul was saved, no one knows perfectly the boundary of light and darkness except him alone who knows all things. For who saw Judas among the apostles working miracles and did not believe that he would come to light? Who knew Paul raging and killing the saints and did not assign him to darkness and hell? It is therefore evident that no one leads each person to his own end, and no one understands the paths of his house. For if he knew the paths, he would not be ignorant of the house; and the house is either hell or paradise.

But how can one know the end who does not know the beginning? For in God’s ordering, each person’s birth, days, years, whole life, and life’s end are ordained. When these things were being ordained—if indeed “when” can be either said or understood—there was no one who knew either his birth or the number and end of his days. This is what he says: “‘Did you then know that you would be born? And did you know the number of your days? Have you entered the storehouses of snow, or seen the storehouses of hail [Col. 0675B] which I prepared for the time of the enemy, for the day of battle and war?’”

Because he calls them storehouses, he signifies beneficial snows and hails. For what are snows and hails but the teachers of the Church? Since they are pure and white, they are called snow; but because they preach with power and authority and threaten sinners with the torments of the future judgment, they are not improperly called hail. The Lord prepared them for the time of the enemy and the day of battle and war, because they continually defend the Church against Jews, tyrants, heretics, and malignant spirits.

“‘By what way is light scattered, and heat divided over the earth?’” Let him answer: “‘I,’ he says, ‘am the way, the truth, and the life’” (John XIV.6). By this way light is scattered, as he himself says: “‘I am the light [Col. 0675C] of the world; whoever follows me does not walk in darkness, but shall have the light of life’” (John VIII.12). This way, therefore, scatters light because it is at once light and life. Heat is divided over the earth by him, because our Saviour gives to each person the measure of faith and the grace of the Holy Spirit. For he himself says: “‘Unless I go away, the Paraclete will not come to you; when I have been taken up, I shall send him to you’” (John XVI.7).

“‘Who gave a course to the most violent rain, and a way to the sounding thunder, that it might rain upon the earth, in a desert without man, where no mortal dwells, that it might fill the pathless and desolate place and bring forth green herbs?’” He calls evangelical teaching the most violent rain and thunder, because it suddenly and abundantly watered the whole world and thundered with the voice of many. The Lord himself gave this teaching its course, way, and such great efficacy that it rained upon the earth and in the desert, where not human beings using reason, but beasts and irrational animals dwelt, worshipping wood and stones. Hence the Apostle says that he fought with beasts at Ephesus.

Yet from these beasts, now converted to the faith, the pathless and desolate place—that is, the holy Church gathered from sinners—is full. In it the Lord daily brings forth and causes to abound green herbs, that is, the teaching of the New Testament, which is new and ever living and green. Of this it is added:

“‘Who is the father of rain, or who begot the drops of dew?’” For who else is the father of rain but he of whom it is said: “‘All wisdom is from the Lord God, and has always been with him and is before the age’” (Ezech. I.1). He also begot drops of dew, that is, gentle and humble teaching, of which the Apostle says: “‘I gave you milk to drink, not solid food’” (I Cor. III.2).

Evangelical teaching is called, according to differing respects, hail, storm, most violent rain, sound of thunder, rain, drop, small drop, and dew; it is also called ice and frost. Hence it follows:

“‘From whose womb did ice come forth, and who begot the frost from heaven?’” He who begot rain also begot frost and ice, because he who gave the New Testament also gave the Old. For the Old Testament, because it is cold—cold indeed because it kills—is called ice and frost; hence death too is called cold. But hear the Apostle: “‘The letter kills’” (II Cor. III.6); and again: “‘But if the ministry of death, engraved in letters on stones, was in glory, how shall not rather the ministry of the Spirit be in glory?’” (ibid., 7).

And his words, “‘Who begot frost from heaven?’” mean what is said elsewhere: “‘You have seen that I spoke with you from heaven’” (Exod. XX.22).—“‘The waters are hardened in the likeness of a stone, and the surface of the abyss is bound fast.’” The waters of the holy Scriptures—which, when spiritually understood, are easily drunk—have been hardened for the Jews not merely into ice, but even into stones; they cannot be scraped away or cleansed. The surface of the abyss is bound fast for those to whom the letter of that Testament itself is not opened. Of this abyss it is said: “‘Deep calls to deep’” (Ps. XLI.8). Its surface is the letter.

“‘Can you join together the glittering stars, the Pleiades, or can you disperse the circuit of Arcturus?’” There are seven stars called the Pleiades, very near to one another but not entirely joined. By them we understand all the Churches of the world. They are joined in faith and divided by place; but they will be more fully joined when God gathers them together within the walls of the heavenly Jerusalem. By Arcturus, which stands in the very firmament of heaven, are represented the teachers of the Church who preside over the rest; for by preaching they encompass and circle the world. The Lord will disperse their circuit when he grants them rest from such great labour.

“‘Can you bring forth the morning star in its time, and cause the evening star to rise over the children of the earth?’” The implied words are: as I can. As the morning star signifies Christ, so the evening star signifies Antichrist: the one brings day and brightness, the other darkness and night. Therefore he brought forth the morning star in its time, because “‘when the fullness of time had come, God sent his Son’” (Gal. IV.4). He will cause the evening star to rise over the children of earth because he will permit Antichrist to rule over earthly and sinful persons.

“‘Do you know the order of heaven, and will you establish its rule upon earth?’” This is what we always pray: “‘Your will be done, as in heaven, so also on earth’” (Matt. VI.10). Christ established heaven’s order, rule, and harmony upon earth, because he is our peace, who made both one. The Church is governed according to the pattern of that order.

“‘Will you raise your voice in the cloud? Will the rush of waters cover you?’” Christ raised his voice in the cloud because he often spoke obscurely and in parables. The rush of waters covered him because an abundance of the Holy Spirit and the fullness of all knowledge overflowed in his speech, according to the words: “‘Grace [Col. 0677A] has been poured out upon your lips.’”

“‘Will you send forth lightnings, and will they go and, returning, say to you, “Here we are”?’” What are lightnings but apostles shining with miracles and, by the blows and flash of their judgments, everywhere driving away vices and malignant spirits? The Lord sent them to preach. They always returned to him, because they did everything in his name; and because they were always ready to obey, they always answered him, “Here we are.” For one unwilling to obey, however often called, scarcely ever answers.

“‘Who put wisdom in the inward parts of man? Or who gave understanding to the cock? Who shall declare the ordering of the heavens, and who shall put the harmony of heaven to sleep, when dust was poured out upon the earth and clods were compacted?’” God alone gave both wisdom to man and understanding to the cock. Of this cock it is written: “‘A cock girded about the loins; there is no king who can resist him’” (Prov. XXX.32). By it we understand teachers, by whose voice others are awakened. How great was that cock which said: “‘Watch, righteous ones, and do not sin’” (I Cor. XV.34)!

The Lord also declared the order of the heavens because he formed others according to the example of the saints. For how often in the Gospel do we find: “The kingdom of heaven is like this person,” or “like that person.” He himself sometimes puts the harmony of heaven to sleep, because he will at some time command the saints’ preaching to cease and rest. But when will this happen? Do you wish to hear when? When dust was poured upon the earth. What does it mean that here he asks about the future and answers concerning the past, except that past and future are present to God? At the consummation of the age dust will be poured upon the earth, because bodies reduced to dust will be made firm again, as at the beginning. Then clods will be compacted, because that muddy earth, gathered and united together, will rise again.

“‘Will you take prey for the lioness, or fill the lives of her cubs, when they lie in dens and lurk in caves?’” Because of its strength, the Church is called a lioness; for it is written: “‘The righteous is confident like a lion’” (Prov. XXVIII.1). Her husband is that great lion from the tribe of Judah, who takes prey for his lioness. For even if preachers of God’s word spread nets, he himself inwardly converts hearts. Hence he says: “‘Without me you can do nothing’” (John XV.6). And the Apostle: “‘Neither he who plants nor he who waters is anything, but God who gives the increase’” (I Cor. III.7).

He also fills the lives of her cubs because he fulfills the desires of bishops and priests while multiplying and exalting his Church. They lie in dens and lurk in caves because, as deceivers yet truthful, they strive by many means to draw unbelievers to the faith. For what are their enticements and persuasion but certain caves and dens?

“‘Who prepares its food for the raven when its young cry to God, wandering because they have no food?’” The one whom he has just called a lioness he now calls a raven. Understanding herself as a raven, she says in the Song of Songs: “‘I am black, but beautiful’” (Cant. I.5). Hence the Apostle: “‘You were once darkness, but now light in the Lord’” (Eph. V.10). The Lord prepares for her both spiritual and bodily food when her young cry, saying: “‘Give us this day our daily bread’” (Matt. VI.11). These young wander in search of food because, in order to satisfy the soul with spiritual delights, they laboriously search the tables of the New and Old Testaments, and of the apostles and prophets.

## CHAPTER XXXIX

“‘Do you know the time when the ibexes of the rocks give birth, or have you watched the hinds in labour? Have you counted the months of their conception and known the time of their birth? They bend down to bring forth, give birth, and utter roars.’” This is what the Lord says in the Gospel: “‘A woman, when she gives birth, has sorrow because her hour has come; but when she has borne the child, she no longer remembers the anguish because of joy’” (John XVI.21).

Ibexes are small animals which give birth among rocks; when they fall from lofty crags, they catch themselves upon their horns without injury. By them we understand the apostles, who, generating children through water and Spirit in rocks—that is, in Churches—and supporting themselves by the horns and strength of faith, feared no cause of adversity. “‘The saints,’ says the Apostle, ‘through faith conquered kingdoms’” (Heb. XI.35). And the Psalmist: “‘The horns of the righteous shall be exalted’” (Ps. LXXIV.11).

The hinds in labour are all the Churches of this world. For the Church imitates the nature of hinds in many ways: it is agile, kills serpents, gives birth bent over, and utters roars in giving birth. The Apostle gave birth bent over when he said: “‘I became all things to all people, that I might gain all’” (I Cor. IX.16). He had bent himself very greatly in childbirth, who, in order to give birth to all for God, had humbled himself to all people and in all things. Nor does the Church give birth without roaring, because it does not generate children without the voice of preaching and prayer. Since it gives birth daily and will not cease to give birth until the consummation of the age, no one can count the months of that conception and childbirth.

“‘Who set the wild ass free, and who loosed its bonds? To whom I gave a home in solitude and its dwelling places in a land of salt, it despises the multitude of the city, does not hear the cry of the taskmaster, surveys the mountains of its pasture, and seeks out every green thing.’” This is understood of the more perfect persons, who, in order to serve God more freely and intimately, despise all worldly glory, flee human society, and withdraw to remote and solitary places. Let Paul, Antony, and Hilarion be examples. Like wild asses, free from every worldly servitude and loosed from the bonds of all cares, they chose homes and dwellings for themselves in solitude and in a land of salt. Since they did not depart from solitude, they are not improperly called wild asses.

They despised the multitude of the city because they sought neither honours nor dignities. Our daily taskmaster is the belly, to which, by the law of nature, we must daily pay the due of food and drink. They surveyed the mountains of their pasture and delighted more in spiritual food than carnal, receiving it from sacred books and from the examples of apostles and prophets. They sought every green thing because they desired not food that perishes but that which endures.

“‘Will the rhinoceros be willing to serve you, and will it remain at your manger?’” The rhinoceros, also called the unicorn, is a most fierce animal, by which are understood the powerful persons of this age. Let it therefore be said: Will the powerful of this age—kings, emperors, and princes—who serve me, serve you? Will they remain at your manger as they remain at mine, whom it now delights to hear the teaching of faith and evangelical preaching? Humble yourself, therefore, before me, since you know that such powerful people humble themselves before me.

“‘Will you bind the rhinoceros to plough with your rope?’” As I do? For God bound the powerful to plough, because they too, fearing to sin, sweat and labour in God’s field. A person is not bound to this plough who neither does good nor fears to sin. Thus the emperor Constantine and Justinian ploughed when they enacted laws for the defense of the Church.

“‘Or will it break the clods of the valleys after you?’” As it breaks them after me. The clods of the valleys, which prevent seed from falling upon level ground and growing, are wicked persons who oppose evangelical preaching. Emperors and princes broke them, because these people, through fear of the rulers, feared to impede the seed of the word.

“‘Do you trust in its great strength and leave your labours to it?’” God’s labour is the Church, which he acquired not only by preaching but also by dying. The Lord confidently entrusted it to the powerful of this age, because, through fear of them, others dare neither preach another faith in it nor would it dare publicly receive one even if it were preached.

“‘Will you trust it to return your seed to you and gather your threshing-floor?’” The powerful return seed to him when, after hearing and understanding the seed of the word, they perform works of righteousness, piety, and mercy; otherwise the seed has perished in them. They gather the threshing-floor—that is, the Church—when they protect and defend it by their edicts.

Let us now interpret these things concerning the blessed Apostle Paul, of whom they also appear to have been said especially. As a most strong unicorn, persecuting the Church, he was feared by all; but immediately converted, made Christ’s servant, dwelling and feeding at the manger of the Gospel, and bound by the chain of faith, he began to plough and thresh in God’s field. Hence he says: “‘You shall not muzzle an ox while it is treading out grain’” (I Cor. IX.9). He then broke the clods of the valleys, because he converted scribes and Pharisees to the faith. God, trusting in his great strength, entrusted and commended the holy Church to him. He in turn returned the multiplied seed and most faithfully gathered God’s threshing-floor.

“‘The wing of the ostrich is like the wings of the heron and hawk; it leaves its eggs on the ground; perhaps you will warm them in the dust.’” As by the rhinoceros he signifies Catholic and holy men, so by the ostrich he signifies the hypocrite. Though in the appearance of its feathers it resembles the heron and hawk, it differs from them because it cannot fly or raise itself upward by its wings. So likewise the hypocrite appears holy and righteous through pretence, yet is not raised to heavenly things by the wings of virtues.

The ostrich leaves its eggs upon the ground because the hypocrite does not take care to free those whom he has begotten for the Lord from earthly and carnal conduct: he wishes not to be good, but to appear good. God warms these eggs in the dust and gradually converts them to love of himself. For when someone still weak in faith, among sinners with whom he lives as though in dust, is warmed by the fire of the Holy Spirit and suddenly turns wholly to God, then the ostrich’s eggs are warmed in the dust.

“‘It will forget that a foot may trample them or a beast of the field crush them.’” A foot tramples eggs and a beast crushes them because the offspring of hypocrites, while lying in dust and serving the body alone, are trampled by the devil. Because the hypocrite thinks this of little account, he is said to have forgotten it.

“‘It is hard toward its young, as though they were not its own; it laboured in vain, compelled by no fear.’” A person is hard toward his children if he does not care for their salvation. He labours in vain who feigns holiness and righteousness for temporal gain and empty glory. The hypocrite does this, compelled by no fear, because he would not do it if he feared God and judgment. But this is no wonder:

“‘God deprived him of wisdom and did not give him understanding.’” This, therefore, is why the ostrich—that is, the hypocrite—labours vainly and uselessly.

“‘When the time comes, it raises its wings on high; it mocks the horse and its rider.’” The hypocrite raises its wings on high when it displays the virtues of its pretence. It does this when the time comes—that is, when it perceives that many see and praise it: “‘For they do all their works in order to be seen by people’” (Matt. XXIII.5). But what do the horse and its rider signify except the righteous man and the righteousness by which he is governed? The hypocrite mocks them because he claims for himself the glory and honour due to the righteous person and righteousness. His pretence is praised, and he is praised for feigned virtue no less than the other for true virtue.

“‘Will you give the horse strength? Will you clothe its neck with neighing? Will you rouse it like locusts? The glory of its nostrils is terror.’” This horse signifies the teachers of the Church, to whom the Lord gave strength and whom he guides and rules with the bridle of equity. He also put neighing around their necks, because it does not suffice for them merely to neigh and praise God; rather, they delight that, by praising and preaching, they may be heard everywhere. They are roused like locusts because in the greater heat of persecution they move and fly more vigorously. Locusts move and fly sluggishly in the morning but swiftly at noon.

But what does he mean by, “‘The glory of its nostrils is terror’”? The horse displays glory by the neighing of its nostrils, because it emits breath with greater force. So the teachers of the Church show that they burn inwardly in spirit when they are shaken by threats and terrors.

“‘It digs the earth with its hoof and exults boldly.’” What does the earth signify but sinners? What does the hoof signify but strength? The horse digs the earth with its hoof because holy preachers dig into and penetrate the hearts of tyrants with a strong answer. Therefore it is added: “‘And it exults boldly.’” The saints exult boldly because they do not fear those who kill the body. To them the Lord says: “‘I will give you a mouth and wisdom, which all your adversaries will not be able to resist or contradict’” (Luke XXI.25).

“‘It advances to meet the armed men, despises fear, and does not yield to the sword.’” Whoever does not understand should read the sufferings of the saints and will know that, in defense of righteousness, they set themselves against every danger.

“‘Over it the quiver will sound; spear and shield will flash.’” The preaching of the saints itself is their quiver, spear, and shield. From it judgments come forth like arrows; they strike adversaries with them as with a strong spear, and by them they protect and defend themselves, as with a shield, against Jews, heretics, and philosophers.

“‘Boiling and raging, it swallows the earth, and does not regard the trumpet’s blast as sounding.’” Holy preachers, as the Apostle says, boiling in spirit and raging with the lofty voice of preaching, swallow the earth—that is, sinners—because, calling them to faith, they bring them into the body of the Church. They do not regard the trumpet’s blast as sounding because, despite the threats of wicked people thundering and raging over and against them, they do not cease from preaching.

“‘When it hears the trumpet, it says, “Ha!” From afar it scents battle, the exhortation of commanders, and the howling of the army.’” Holy preachers say “Ha!” upon hearing the trumpet because, when they feel the tumult and madness of persecutors drawing near, they exult in confidence of victory. For “Ha!” is a cry of exultation. They scent battle from afar because, always ready to die, they await it with longing. Since this battle is brought against them not only by tyrants but also by heretics, it adds: “‘The exhortation of commanders and the howling of the army.’” By commanders are understood heresiarchs, whose army is the whole multitude of heretics. Hence the commanders exhort as though rational beings, while the rest, as though irrational, howl with sheer ferocity and cry out without reflection.

“‘Does the hawk grow feathers by your wisdom and spread its wings toward the south?’” The hawk, which each year, through southern winds, sheds its old feathers and puts on new ones, signifies the saints, who are daily renewed by the breathing of the Holy Spirit and, putting off the old man with his deeds, put on the new. “This comes about not by your wisdom but by mine.

“‘Or will the eagle rise at your command and place its nest in lofty places? It dwells on rocks and makes its home upon steep crags and inaccessible cliffs; from there it observes its food, and its eyes see from afar; its young lap blood, and wherever a corpse may be, it is immediately present.’” Eagles signify those who fly higher and contemplate heavenly things more subtly. Such an eagle was blessed John, who, approaching heaven, said: “‘In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God’” (John I.1).

“This eagle will place its nest in lofty places,” because the dwelling of the saints is in the heavenly kingdoms. There, then, the eagle will rise at God’s command. Meanwhile, it “‘dwells on rocks,’” that is, rests upon the sayings and examples of saints. Each of the prophetic books is a rock, which are called steep crags and inaccessible cliffs because the way through them is difficult and they are understood only with great labour. Not everyone is granted passage by this way.

Dwelling upon these cliffs, the eagle observes its food, because from them it sees and understands nothing but that living bread which came down from heaven. “‘Its eyes see from afar,’” because they do not yet see face to face, but through a mirror and in an enigma. Perhaps the books of the prophets are called rocks, crags, and cliffs because the Law was first written upon tablets of stone. The young of this eagle “‘lap blood’” because the children of apostles and teachers delight in Christ’s passion. This eagle is present wherever there is a corpse because, as the Gospel says: “‘Wherever the body may be, there the eagles also shall be gathered’” (Matt. XXIV.28). These matters are brief indeed, but not brief for those to whom we write.

“‘And the Lord added and spoke concerning Job: Will one who contends with God so easily be silent? Shall one who rebukes God answer everywhere?’” You said above, he says, “I desire to dispute with God.” Behold, God speaks to you; why do you not answer? Since blessed Job, having heard the reasoning, was silent, these words are spoken to him by the Lord out of great affection of love. For Job was not among those who refuse to defend truth. What he had earlier disputed, he did not do from malice but from ignorance.

“Job, answering the Lord, said: ‘Because I have spoken lightly, what can I answer? I will put my hand upon my mouth. I have spoken one thing, which I wish I had not said, and another, to which I will add no more.’” Therefore, he says, I do not answer you because, from the weight of your speech, I know that I have spoken lightly; and I desire rather to repent of my rashness by silence than to defend it. I will put my hand upon my mouth, so that by this act I may repair what I sinned by speech. I have spoken one thing and another which I wish I had not said; for I know that I shall not say them further. He says “one and another” because he sinned in thought and speech, murmuring against the scourge in heart and mouth.

## CHAPTER XL

[Col. 0683B] “Then the Lord answered Job from the whirlwind and said: ‘Gird your loins like a man; I will question you, and declare to me.’” These words have been explained above.

“‘Will you make my judgment void and condemn me, that you may be justified?’” Whoever murmurs against scourges condemns the one who scourges; and whoever calls himself righteous amid scourges makes void the judgment of the one who scourges. Unless perhaps—as in this passage—the one who is scourged understands a different reason in the one who scourges: for Job did not know why he was scourged.

“‘If you have an arm like God, and thunder with a voice like his, clothe yourself with splendour, raise yourself on high, and be glorious, and put on beautiful garments.’” God’s arm is Christ, through whom he made all things and by whose strength he overcame the devil. No one possesses such an arm. But who thunders with a similar voice, making all things merely by speaking? “‘Let there be light,’ he says, ‘and light was made. For he spoke, and they were made’” (Gen. I.3). No one’s voice is such.

Let it therefore be said: If you are like God in voice and strength, clothe yourself with the splendour of immortality; raise yourself on high—that is, ascend above all the heavens—and be glorious like him in his saints. Put on beautiful garments like him, who, clothed with light as with a garment, dwells in inaccessible light. By saying this, he leads Job to what is impossible; therefore he adds:

“‘Scatter the proud in his wrath [Note: [Col. 0683D] By the wrath of God is understood severe vengeance. D. Thomas.], and, looking upon every arrogant person, humble him’”—as I do, “‘who put down the powerful from their seat and exalt the humble.’” This will happen at the judgment, when by the brightness of his coming he will humble the proud and arrogant, concerning whom it is added:

“‘Look upon all the proud and confound them, and crush the wicked in their place.’” The place of the wicked is the place prepared for the wicked; what else is it but the place of torments? Hence it follows:

“‘Hide them in the dust, and plunge their faces into the pit.’” Those who, deprived of life and dissolved from flesh, return to dust are hidden in the dust together and uniformly. Their faces are plunged into the pit because they are cast headlong into hell, in which they are crushed and afflicted without end.

“‘And I will confess that your right hand can save you’”—if, that is, you can do the things stated. Only he who can do all these things can save whomever he wills by his own right hand and strength.

“‘Behold Behemoth, whom I made with you; he shall eat grass like an ox.’” Behemoth, he says, was far stronger and more glorious than you, yet he perished through confidence born of pride. Although he still possesses great strength, he can do nothing against my right hand and arm. Behemoth, whose name is interpreted “beast,” signifies the devil, who, abandoning angelic simplicity, declined into bestial ferocity.

“‘Behold,’ he says, ‘Behemoth, whom I made with you [Col. 0684B; Note: [Col. 0683D] ‘This expression can be understood in two ways. First, its sense may be: “Whom I made with you,” that is, whom I made like you.” This is said to exclude the error of those who, considering the devil’s malice, judged him not to be the creature of the good God. Secondly, its sense may be: “Whom I made with you,” that is, one having likeness with you in respect to the intellectual nature which is in man.’ D. Thomas.].’” With you, indeed, because I made both you and him.

“‘He shall eat grass like an ox,’” because he will devour those who, turned into the dryness of grass, have lost the greenness of faith and the flower of virtues. Of this grass the prophet says: “‘Truly the people is grass; the grass has dried up and the flower has fallen’” (Isa. XL.8).

“His strength is in his loins, and his power in his navel.” For a man’s lust is said to be in his loins, but a woman’s in her navel. The devil therefore has power and strength in loins and navel, because through lust he conquers many of both sexes. He rightly says “his,” because those members over which he rules belong to him. “He will bind his tail like a cedar; the sinews of his testicles are intertwined.” For the devil’s tail will be Antichrist, because he will come last, after all the rest [Col. 0684C]; and he is fittingly compared to a cedar because he will appear greatly exalted in great power. The devil will bind and embrace him, because he will possess him wholly; hence he is rightly called the son of perdition. His testicles are those through whom he begets children for himself and pours out the seed of his perversity and deception.

The devil’s bones are understood as his wiser and stronger servants. These are like pipes of bronze, deceiving people by their musical modulation and sweet speech; for bronze pipes give forth a sweet sound. But why should I speak of his bones, when even his cartilage, which is certainly much softer than bones, is like plates of iron? By this he indicates that even those regarded as lacking strength and power are exceedingly strong in the devil’s body [Col. 0684D]. These matters are most properly referred to the times of Antichrist, because then the devil will especially possess such bones and such cartilage.

“He is the beginning of the ways of God; he who made him has applied his sword.” The devil is the beginning of God’s ways—that is, of his works—because among all creatures he was made first. But the Lord has bent back his sword; for unless it had been folded so that it could not strike with a straight point, very few could escape the sword of his deception [Col. 0685A]. Thus he strikes, as it were, with a folded sword, because he wounds less than he desires.

“The mountains bring him grass; all the beasts of the field play before him.” Mountains signify the rich and powerful, who enter the kingdom of heaven with difficulty. They bring grass to the devil because they nourish him by their wicked actions; for the devil’s food consists of wicked deeds. All the beasts of the field play before him because all who live foolishly, voluptuously, and brutishly are his sport and delight. For, as the Gospel says, the field is the world.

“He sleeps under the shadow, in the hiding-place of the reed, and in moist places.”

[Note: [Col. 0685D] “Since he understands Behemoth as a great beast, namely the elephant, in which he places a figure of the devil, he enumerates its characteristics and says: ‘He sleeps under the shadow, in the hiding-place of the reed, in moist places.’ And because this animal does not inhabit just any sort of shade, but dense shade, he adds: ‘The shadows protect his shadow,’ so that the lower shade may be defended from heat by the upper shade.” D. Th.]

By these things he signifies the sexual parts. But why should I blush to explain what the Lord himself did not blush to say? Those places are called “shadow” [Col. 0685B] because they are concealed and covered from everyone; hence they are also called the private parts. In these, then, the devil sleeps; in these he delights and rests.

Or again, he sleeps under the shadow: that is, he dwells in those who lead an idle and pleasure-loving life. He sleeps in the hiding-place of the reed: that is, in the hearts of those who are not firm, but, like a reed, are empty of faith and every good. And he sleeps in moist places: that is, among drunkards who are continually flooded with wine. Hence the Apostle: “Do not be drunk with wine, in which is lust” (Eph. 5:18).

“The shadows protect his shadow; the willows of the torrent surround him.” His shadows are all who imitate his image and likeness. For in a shadow, in some manner, the image of a king is represented. His shadows therefore protect his shadow when many wicked people protect and defend one wicked person [Col. 0685C]. We often see a great multitude of wicked persons assembling to defend a single wicked man. The willows of the torrent surround him because those always stand by and serve him who are both unfruitful and dwell amid turbulent, rushing waters; that is, they delight to live among seditious and impious peoples. “Many waters are many peoples” (Rev. 17:15). Concerning these waters it is then added: “Behold, he will swallow up a river and will not be astonished; and he is confident that the Jordan will flow into his mouth.”

[Note: [Col. 0686D] “These words are referred to the devil, in whose figure they are spoken. They signify his presumption, by which he trusts that he can easily incorporate into himself by consent all unstable people, even if they possess some knowledge of God. To signify this, mention is made especially of the Jordan, a river in the land in which true knowledge of God was held,” etc. D. Th.]

By “river” he means the multitude of sinners, especially of Gentiles and Jews. Behemoth swallows them, and is not astonished, because he does not consider it a great matter to deceive such persons [Col. 0685D]. For he is confident that the Jordan—that is, the people of Christians and the baptized—will flow into his mouth. The Jordan signifies the baptized because baptism began there.

“In his eyes a man will take him; with stakes he will pierce his nostrils.” Up to this point he has described the strength of Behemoth; now he indicates how he is captured. When Christ’s divinity clothed itself in flesh, then Christ made himself like a hook, so that by the iron we understand his divinity, but by the bait his flesh [Col. 0686A]. Seeing this hook, Behemoth desired it, approached, and tempted it; and while he thought to capture it, he was captured. This happened “in his eyes,” because he presumed, with importunate greed, to attack him whom he had already recognized in his miracles and confessed to be the Son of God.

“And with stakes he will pierce his nostrils.” What do the stakes signify except God’s virtue and power? By these the devil’s nostrils are pierced. Though he possesses a most subtle intelligence, he is nevertheless unable fully to know and search out the secrets of our heart except through outward movements. This is drawn from dogs, which perceive the tracks of animals by the scent of their nostrils. For the devil too is a dog, according to the words: “Deliver my soul from the sword, O God, and my only one from the hand of the dog” (Ps. 21:21).

“Can you draw out Leviathan with a hook, and bind his tongue with a cord?” Behold, the devil is now called by another name.
