Leviathan, which in Latin is called *draco*, “dragon,” means “their addition.” This is by contrariety: because, while he promised our first parents an addition of light to their eyes, he took away immortality. By the aforesaid hook—that is, by the Word made flesh—the Lord drew him out from the minds of his faithful. His tongue was bound with a cord, because by faith in the Trinity, called a threefold cord, the persuasion and speech of his deception have been greatly restrained. Therefore his tongue is bound by this cord, because he is not heard even though he speaks.

“Will you put a ring in his nostrils, and pierce his jaw with a bracelet?” In this place ring and bracelet signify almost the same thing, because a bracelet too is a ring. Nostrils and jaws constricted by a ring lose the power and strength of their function [Col. 0686C]. Leviathan is therefore rightly said to be bound in his nostrils and jaws, because he cannot, to the degree of his greedy desire, either deceive the saints of God by cunning or crush them by the strength of his jaws.

“Will he multiply prayers to you, or speak soft words to you?” In the literal sense Leviathan multiplied prayers to the Lord when terrified evil spirits said: “What have we to do with you, Son of God? Have you come before the time to torment us? And if you cast us out from here, send us into the pigs” (Matt. 8:29) [Col. 0686D]. In respect of his members, he will multiply prayers at the judgment and speak soft words to him, because the wicked, who are his body and members, will beg for pardon and mercy.

“Will he make a covenant with you, and will you take him as an everlasting servant?” Supply: “as I do.” The devil makes this covenant with the Lord: that without his permission he may tempt no one, afflict no one, and that in the temptation or affliction itself he may keep the limit set by God [Col. 0687A]. According to this covenant he is called not only a servant but an everlasting servant, because he will serve under this condition not merely now, but also after this life.

“Will you make sport of him as of a bird, or bind him for your maidservants?” The devil is called Behemoth—that is, a beast—because of his savagery; Leviathan—that is, a dragon—because of his strength; and a bird because of his pride, since he wished to fly above all the heavens. But the Lord made sport of him as of a bird, because he set Christ’s humanity before him as bait, through which he captured, bound, and held him. He bound him for his maidservants, of whom the Apostle says: “Consider your calling, brothers: not many noble, not many wise, not many powerful are among you; but God chose the foolish things of the world to confound the wise; and the ignoble to confound the strong; and things that are not, to destroy things that are” (1 Cor. 1:26) [Col. 0687B]. These, then, are the maidservants for whom the devil was bound, so that he may not have power and strength against them, according to the saying: “The Lord will quickly crush Satan under your feet.”

“Friends will cut him in pieces; merchants will divide him.” This must be understood of his whole body, that is, of the entire multitude of wicked people. These friends and merchants are the teachers of the Church. They are merchants because they exchange the reward of the Gospel for the price of faith. They cut up and divide the devil’s body because every day they separate some persons from it and reconcile them through faith to the Church.

“Will you fill nets with his skin, and fish-traps with his head?” What do nets and fish-traps signify except the holy Church? In it fish are caught and dwell: those who are reborn and swim in the waters of baptism [Col. 0687C]. The skin of the aforesaid body of Leviathan consists of those who, being outwardly placed as if without poison, are more easily converted. By the head, however, the chief, stronger, and greater persons are represented. Blessed Paul was at one time the head of this body; from him the Church has been filled to a great extent. Thus the Lord fills nets and fish-traps from Leviathan’s skin and head when he brings into the Church both lesser and greater persons from that wicked multitude.

“Will you lay your hand upon him?” Supply: “as I lay mine.” “I,” he says, “so restrain him by my hand and power that without my command or permission he dares do nothing.” It is evident that you cannot do this, since you are scourged by him so violently; and this is what he says: “Remember the battle, and add no more to your speech” [Col. 0687D]. That is, consider in what battle you are engaged; repent of what you have spoken thoughtlessly and with insufficient caution; and consider what answer you will give to the Lord when you are so scourged by a servant.

“Behold, his hope will deceive him, and in the sight of all he will be cast down.” The devil will often be cast down through his hope, because he suddenly loses many of those whom he hoped to drag with himself to torments. This is shown to have happened to him in blessed Job. He will be cast down before all, because both good and evil persons will hear the sentence of his condemnation, when it is said: “Go, you cursed, into the eternal fire prepared for the devil and his angels” (Matt. 25:42) [Col. 0688A].

## Chapter XLI

“I will not rouse him as though cruelly; for who can resist my countenance?” It is as though Job were replying to what preceded, saying: Since this Leviathan is so strong and so wicked, why, Lord, do you rouse him thus against your faithful? Why do you permit him to rage thus against them? To this he replies: “I will not rouse him as though cruelly”; that is, I shall neither forget them nor permit him to rage beyond their strength, nor suffer them beyond what they can bear. Rather, I shall give them strength and power by which they may resist his malice [Col. 0688B]. For who can resist my countenance? Why, then, should the person whom I defend be afraid? I am in them; I fight in them; I am the one who guards the city.

And he says: “If you guard them, Lord, why do we see so many people punished by his deception?” And the Lord replies: “Who has first given to me, that I should repay him? All things under heaven are mine.” It is as though he said: Those whom I defend, I defend by mercy; those whom I do not defend, I leave by justice. Since all things are mine, they do not serve me as though they were mine; even if they did serve me, they would serve me not from their own substance, but from mine. Therefore those who have given me nothing beforehand ought to demand nothing from me as a debt. Of this most profound question the Apostle says: “O the depth of the riches of the wisdom and knowledge of God! How incomprehensible are his judgments, and unsearchable his ways! For who has known the mind of the Lord? Or who has been his counsellor? Or who has first given to him, and shall be repaid?” (Rom. 11:33) [Col. 0688C].

“I will not spare him, nor his mighty words framed for entreaty.” This is understood of the entire body of Leviathan—that is, of the whole multitude of wicked people. Although they entreat God with mighty and carefully composed words, he will nevertheless not spare them. For God considers not the arrangement of words but the compunction of the heart. Many members of the devil are within the Church who appear to pray to God very attentively, steadfastly, and eloquently. Yet God looks upon deeds, not words; hearts, not prayers [Col. 0688D]. Hence it is added: “Who will reveal the face of his garment, and who will enter into the midst of his mouth?” Supply: “unless I.” Since our eyes are weak, they see not the things hidden within but only the face of the garment; but God, penetrating the face of the garment, considers the thoughts of the heart itself, according to the saying: “Man sees the face, but God sees the heart.” The Lord also enters into the midst of his mouth, because whatever a person says or thinks, God is in both mouth and heart, for he searches all things. Therefore an elegantly framed entreaty does not avail a person, because “the Holy Spirit of discipline flees deceit” (Wis. 1:5).

“Who will open the gates of his face?” When Christ shattered the gates of hell and brought away the souls of the saints from there with himself, then he opened the gates behind which Leviathan had hidden his face so as not to be seen [Col. 0689A]. The gates of his face can also be called heretics, because through them, as through gates, one enters before his face and presence. Christ opens these gates when he exposes their heresies.

“Round about his teeth is terror.” Not only gates, but also the devil’s teeth are called heretics, because those whom they seize and devour they present to the devil. These teeth have terror round about them, because those taken by them are devoured by the devil. By “terror” we may also understand the swords of tyrants, by which heretics are very often fortified. If this is referred to the times of Antichrist, it is evident; for then heretics will fight with words and swords [Col. 0689B].

“His body is like cast shields, compacted with scales pressing one another.” The devil’s members are like cast shields because, being exceedingly hard and obstinate in wickedness, they repel the darts of the word of God. They are joined like scales pressing one another because, united in their wickedness, they mutually urge and press one another toward evil. We often see wicked people thus inviting one another to crime: one draws another, and violently impels one who does not wish to go.

“One is joined to another, and not even a breath passes through them; one clings to the other, and holding one another they will by no means be separated.” The scales of Leviathan, he says—that is, the same impious people of whom the devil’s body is made—are so joined to one another [Col. 0689C] and so united in wickedness that they cannot be separated from each other, nor can the breath of holy preaching pass through them. For they envy one another, and in lust, theft, robbery, murder, and similar things, none wishes to be inferior to another.

“His sneezing is the splendour of fire, and his eyes are like the eyelids of dawn.” In a sneeze the spirits are moved with such force that, even if a person wishes, he cannot restrain it. The devil’s sneeze will therefore be Antichrist, whom he will stir up against the Church with such an impulse of arrogance and pride as no one has ever come into this world. The splendour of fire follows him: that is, wrath, indignation, and the brightness of miracles, for he will perform many signs and prodigies [Col. 0689D]. His eyes will be those through whom he then reveals to sinners the ways of his wickedness. Since they will shine with wisdom and miracles, they are called the eyelids of dawn. For what is the eyelid of dawn but the manifestation of light and day? The working of miracles, moreover, can in some sense be called a manifestation of light.

“Lamps proceed from his mouth, like firebrands kindled with fire.” Lamps proceed from the devil’s mouth because the words of his deception inflame people toward delight in vices. Since these words smell sweetly to sinners and delight them, they are called firebrands [Col. 0690A]. But because evil desire sets them ablaze, they are said to be kindled with fire.

“Smoke proceeds from his nostrils, like a pot kindled and boiling.” Since spirit is emitted through the nostrils, spirit is signified by the nostrils. Smoke therefore proceeds from his nostrils because those who breathe in the spirit of his wickedness, overshadowed by the smoke of darkness and gloom, cannot bring forth truth. The devil is fittingly compared with a pot kindled and boiling, because he always burns with envy, hatred, and evil will.

“His breath makes coals burn, and flame goes forth from his mouth.” What do coals signify except people inflamed with hatred and anger? [Col. 0690B] The devil makes these burn because, by blowing upon them, he often stirs great quarrels from very small matters. Thus flame also proceeds from his mouth, because great discord is generated from his words.

“Strength will dwell in his neck, and want will go before his face.” Strength dwells in his neck because, from the time he began to be proud, he never afterwards humbled himself to repentance. Want will go before his face because, before Antichrist appears in this world, there will be a great scarcity of the divine word, as it is said through the prophet: “Behold, I will send upon you not a famine of bread nor a thirst for water, but of hearing the word of God. The members of his flesh cling together” (Ezek. 5:17). This we explained above concerning his scales; for the members of his flesh are the multitude of all wicked people [Col. 0690C]. These members cling together because they are united by perfidy and wickedness.

“He will send thunderbolts against him, and they will not be carried to another place.” The Lord will send the onset of every torment and thunderbolts against him and his members; nor will these be borne elsewhere, because these alone, and not others, will be afflicted.

“His heart will be hardened like a stone and will be compressed like a smith’s anvil.” The devil is always hardened and never humbles himself to repentance. Therefore, bound and constrained like a smith’s anvil, he will be beaten by the eternal blows of torments.

“When he is lifted up, the angels will fear, and in their terror they will be purified.”

[Note: [Col. 0689D] “When he is lifted from his place by divine power, the angels will fear in wonder at the divine power. In this wonder many effects of divine power become known to them; and therefore it is added: ‘and in their terror they will be purified.’ For, as Dionysius says, chapter 5 of *On the Divine Names* [Col. 0690D], angels are said to be purified not from impurity but from ignorance,” etc. D. Thom.]

By “angels” are meant the doctors of the Church [Col. 0690D], who are called angels in many places. Read the Apocalypse and you will find it. When they see Leviathan condemned and lifted up to be cast down, they will fear, and by that very fear will be purified, if anything of former corruption remains in them.

[Note: “For if God, as St Peter says, 2 Peter 2:4, did not spare the angels who sinned, neither does he spare people who do not repent.”]

“When the sword has seized him, he will not be able to stand, nor the spear, nor the breastplate.” It is as though he said: Although the devil has always been proud, impious, and cruel, he will nevertheless be most savage when the sword has seized him. This sword will be Antichrist [Col. 0691A], who will kill many thousands of people and separate them from God. After he has seized the devil and received him most fully into the dwelling-place of his breast, neither spear nor breastplate will be able to stand, because there will be no one able either to fight against him or to defend himself by self-government. Knowledge of the Scriptures is a spear to us when we attack others, and a breastplate when we are attacked by others.

“For he will regard iron as straw, and bronze as rotten wood.” Iron, he says—that is, the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God—and bronze, that is, the most clear sound of holy preaching, he will regard as straw and rotten wood, because no wisdom or eloquence will be able to resist him. Enoch and Elijah may also be signified by iron and bronze [Col. 0691B].

“The archer will not drive him away; the stones of the sling have become straw to him.” Every preacher of the Gospel is an archer and slinger. Preaching itself is both bow and sling; from it judgments go forth like arrows and stones to strike enemies. But Leviathan will not be driven away by them, because, through that man whom he has invaded, the son of perdition, he will despise all who oppose him and regard them as nothing.

“He will esteem the hammer as straw, and will mock the brandished spear.” He will esteem the hammer as straw because he will make light of the punishment of the future judgment, by whose heavy weight he will be crushed eternally. Moreover, he will mock God himself, whom he already sees brandishing the spear and preparing punishment [Col. 0691C]. For he has despaired and disdains to seek mercy, being prepared rather to endure every torment.

“Under him will be rays of the sun; he will spread gold beneath himself like mud.” The rays of the sun, by which the world is illumined, signify wise persons. Many of these, overthrown by Antichrist through threats, flatteries, or promises, will submit themselves to the devil’s yoke. He explains this when he says: “He spreads gold beneath himself like mud”; that is, those who appeared to shine with wisdom and virtues he will subject and cast down no less than earthy, muddy sinners.

“He will make the deep sea boil like a pot, and make it as when ointments boil.” What is the deep sea except the greater and more powerful persons of this age [Col. 0691D]? The devil will make them boil like a pot because he will stir them to such madness that any of the saints who refuses to obey the devil and worship the image of the beast, as is read elsewhere, will immediately be struck by their sword. He will make this as when ointments boil because he will turn their madness into zeal and fervour for God, and will teach that God delights, as in the sweetest fragrance of ointment, in the blood they shed.

“After him the path will shine; he will consider the abyss as growing old.” The path will shine after him because the brightness and fame of miracles will follow him. Or because, after the death of his son—that is, Antichrist—all error and darkness will be removed. He considers the abyss as growing old [Col. 0692A] because he regards hell and its punishments as already ended, harmless, and powerless; for what becomes old and aged is near to destruction. This proud being does not know how to fear; hence it follows: “There is no power on earth to be compared with him, who was made to fear no one.”

No human being can be compared with the angelic nature. Yet this may be understood according to his own opinion. For he who wished to be like God disdains to be equal to any creature. He was made to fear no one not by God but by himself; for pride made him such that there is nothing he deigns to fear. He sets himself above all things and, exalted in pride, beholds all things beneath himself as inferior. Hence he did not fear even to tell his Creator that he should worship him [Col. 0692B]. This is what he says: “He sees every lofty thing; he is king over all the children of pride.” He sees every lofty thing who feels nothing humble in himself; and he is therefore king because he rules all the children of pride. He rightly placed pride at both the root and the end of his discourse, because it is the root of all evils.

## Chapter XLII

“Then Job answered the Lord and said: I know that you can do all things, and no thought is hidden from you.” “I know,” he says, “that you can do all things and, as you have said, there is no one who can resist your countenance. No thought is hidden from you, since you have so carefully expounded the hidden wiles of Leviathan himself.”

“But who is this who hides counsel without knowledge?” Who, he says, is so foolish [Col. 0692C] that he tries to conceal his wiles from one who knows all things? “Therefore I have spoken foolishly, and things exceeding my knowledge beyond measure.” I also spoke foolishly in wishing to contend with you in judgment. For if, as is true, no one can resist you, I said vainly above: “Let my judgment attain victory.” I also spoke foolishly because I spoke against that wisdom which surpasses my knowledge beyond measure. A person is foolish who contends with one by whom he is surpassed in both power and wisdom.

“Hear, and I will speak; I will ask, and answer me.” What is “Hear, and I will speak” except: Hear my prayer and my speech? And what is “I will ask, and answer me” except: Make known to me what I desire to understand, and the things that I greatly desire to know? Just as we question God by desiring and entreating, so he answers us by hearing and granting. Hence blessed Job, as though already heard, adds: “By the hearing of the ear I heard you, but now my eye sees you; therefore I myself rebuke myself and do penance in ash and dust.” Formerly, he says, I heard, but now I see, because the difference between the knowledge of you which I formerly had and that which I now have is as great as the difference between hearing and sight. Therefore I rebuke myself, who presumed either to think or to murmur against your scourges. “And I do penance in ash and dust” [Col. 0693A]. What is it to do penance in ash and dust except to recognize oneself as ash and dust? Whoever does this does not trust in his own righteousness.

“After the Lord had spoken these words to Job, he said to Eliphaz the Temanite: My wrath is angry against you and your two friends, because you have not spoken rightly before me as my servant Job has.” In saying “before me,” he shows that they did not speak with the same intention as Job. God does not consider merely what is said. Hence Job earlier complains against them, saying: “You compose speeches only for rebuke and utter words into the wind; you fall upon an orphan and endeavour to overthrow your friend. Therefore take for yourselves seven bulls and seven rams [Col. 0693B], and go to my servant Job, and he will offer a holocaust for you.”

God’s anger is good when counsels of remedy are given by which sins are loosed and sinners converted. Blessed Job, as we said above, signifies the Church; his friends represent heretics. Therefore Job prays for his friends and offers holocausts for them, because heretics cannot escape the wrath of God’s indignation unless they return to the Church, are reconciled to it, and it offers prayers and sacrifice for them. Heretics offer bulls and rams when they mortify pride and ignorance in themselves. For the bull signifies pride, while the ram signifies ignorance and the leadership of perverse understanding. Since the number seven is perfect [Col. 0693C], he commanded them to offer seven bulls and as many rams, in order that they might destroy these vices perfectly within themselves.

It follows: “My servant Job will pray for you; I will accept his face, so that folly may not be imputed to you; for you have not spoken rightly to me, as my servant Job has.” This repeats what was said. Whenever such repetition occurs, it shows the firmness and stability of the discourse.

“So Eliphaz the Temanite, Bildad the Shuhite, and Zophar the Naamathite went and did as the Lord had spoken to them, and the Lord accepted the face of Job. The Lord also turned to Job’s repentance when he prayed for his friends.” Job therefore profited greatly: by praying for his friends he obtained pardon not only for them but also for himself [Col. 0693D]. This shows that prayer for others is something great.

“And the Lord doubled all that Job had possessed.” The prophet also says: “They shall possess double in their land” (Isa. 61:7). Yet when these great miseries are ended, near the end of the age, everything that the Church possessed or ought to have possessed will be doubled, because it will then gather into itself most fully both peoples, Jews and Gentiles, according to the saying: “When the fullness of the Gentiles has entered, then all Israel will be saved” (Rom. 11:25).

“Then all his brothers and all his sisters came to him, and all who had known him before; and they ate bread with him in his house, and moved their heads over him, and consoled him concerning all the evil that the Lord had brought upon him.” All will come to the Church who are called brothers either by the merit of faith or sisters by the frailty of flesh; indeed, all who knew it and had heard its fame. They will eat bread with it: certainly the living bread that came down from heaven, or also the knowledge of the holy Scriptures. They will move their heads over it [Col. 0694A], rejoicing with it and admiring its constancy, faith, and patience. In this place, movement of the head means exultation of mind. They will console it concerning every evil which the Lord permitted it to suffer, because the Church will then be perfectly consoled and will forget all its afflictions when it sees so great a conversion to itself of all nations flowing together [Col. 0694B].

“And each gave him one sheep and one golden earring.” What does the sheep signify except innocence? And what does the earring signify except obedience of both ears? Hence it is called a golden earring, so that hearing may be chaste and pure. No one, therefore, who wishes to console the Church should come to it without these gifts. Let him offer a sheep, so that he may be innocent; let him offer an earring, so that he may be obedient; and, because it is golden, let him understand wisely.

“The Lord blessed Job’s latter end more than his beginning.” In this place, “to bless” means to multiply. At the end the Church will be multiplied, because it will be filled with the fullness of all nations. Hence it follows:

“And he had fourteen thousand sheep, six thousand camels [Col. 0694C], a thousand yoke of oxen, and a thousand she-asses; and he had seven sons and three daughters.” What is signified by sheep and camels, oxen and she-asses, sons and daughters, was explained at the beginning of this book. We have now explained what the doubled number signifies. But the number of sons and daughters is not doubled, because however much it increased, it would signify nothing further. The seven sons are the seven churches, and the three daughters are the three parts of the world; in these the entire multitude of believers is contained. This too was explained at the beginning.

“And he called the name of one Day, the name of the second Cassia, and the name of the third Horn-of-the-Trumpet.” The holy Church, which consists entirely of these three women [Col. 0694D], is Day, because it is subject to the Sun of righteousness, according to the saying: “God made the greater light to rule the day” (Gen. 1:16). It is Cassia because it spreads a good fragrance everywhere; hence the Apostle: “We are the good fragrance of Christ to God in every place” (2 Cor. 2:15). It is Horn-of-the-Trumpet because it resounds everywhere with the clear and lofty voice of preaching, according to the saying: “Sound the trumpet at the new moon” (Ps. 80:4); and: “Praise him with the sound of the trumpet” (ibid.). *Cornustibii* is formed from *cornu*, “horn,” and *tibia*, “pipe”; both signify the voices of preachers.

“No women as beautiful as Job’s daughters were found in all the earth; and their father gave them an inheritance among their brothers.” For neither the Synagogue, nor idolatry, nor any other sect can be compared with the beauty of the Church [Col. 0695A]. It is the one that has neither spot nor wrinkle. It receives an inheritance among its brothers—that is, among the choirs of angels, who are children of the same Father as itself. Or again, sisters are admitted to the inheritance with brothers because the less perfect are joined with the perfect in blessedness [Col. 0696A].

“After this Job lived one hundred and forty years; and he saw his sons and his sons’ sons to the fourth generation; and he died old and full of days.” End.

[Col. 0695]

## Here begins the exposition of the Psalms.

[Col. 0695B] He can rightly and wisely judge who has first carefully examined the case. Thus this most illustrious Prophet, when he had said, “Judge me, O God,” immediately added, saying, “and discern my cause” (Ps. 42:1). This is as though he said: I do not flee judgment, provided that my case has first been diligently examined. But one who presumes to act otherwise often praises things that ought not rightly to be praised, and reproves things that ought not rightly to be reproved. How great this sin is, the prophet shows when he says: “Woe to those who call good evil, and evil good; who make light darkness and darkness light; who call sweet bitter and bitter sweet” (Isa. 5:20).

While I was still a young man, I expounded the Psalter [Col. 0695C] according to another translation. That translation differs in many places so greatly from this translation, which the Roman Church uses, that this translation cannot at all be understood according to the exposition of the former. [Note: [Col. 0695D] He says the same in his exposition of Psalm 99.] That former translation indeed has many expositors; but whether anyone has expounded this one, I do not know. Therefore, being asked by my friends, and especially by Peregrinus, the venerable abbot, I have taken pains that this too, like the former, might have its own exposition. Whoever carefully reads it all in order, I know, will not judge it superfluous, and will easily be able to understand how great the difference is between the first exposition and this second one.

For I am not ashamed to say what blessed Paul the Apostle and teacher of the Gentiles was not ashamed to say: “When I was a child, I spoke as a child, I understood as a child, I thought as a child; but when I became a man, I put away the things of a child” (1 Cor. 13:11). He does no injury to anyone who prefers himself to himself. That exposition is indeed very concise; but this one seems better to me. [Col. 0696B] I have not taken care to set forth many interpretations of a single matter; rather, that interpretation seemed sufficient to me which can be suitably connected with what precedes and follows. For the sayings of the prophets are such that they can be understood separately in many ways. I could have offered many examples of this, if I had judged it necessary.

I have omitted no title: I have included and expounded them all, since they seem to me very necessary for understanding the psalms. Above all, I affirm that this must be committed to memory: whenever the Prophet tells us—and, as though we were forgetful and disobedient, repeatedly commands us—to sing a new song always, to make melody always, and to hope firmly. To sing a new song is to proclaim the words of the Law and Prophets not according to the oldness of the letter, [Col. 0696C] but to expound and preach them according to spiritual understanding. Hence the Apostle says: “The letter kills, but the Spirit gives life” (2 Cor. 3:6). Thus too it is said in the Apocalypse of John: “Behold, I make all things new” (Rev. 21:5); for, when spiritually understood, all things are new.

## PSALM ONE

“Blessed is the man who has not gone in the counsel of the ungodly.”

This psalm has no title; yet it seems in some sense to be the title not only of the psalms but of all the Holy Scriptures. For a title is placed there so as briefly to suggest to us what we ought to seek and understand in the Scripture that follows. [Note: [Col. 0695D] Saint Hilary discussed most excellently the titles or inscriptions appended to individual psalms. “It seems to me,” he says, “a rash thing to overturn the inscriptions which have been handed down from their first origin to the time of Ptolemy, who reigned in Egypt after Alexander; inscriptions which the Seventy interpreters, all elders, translated into the Greek language, just as they did all the other sacred Scriptures. More than one hundred and fifty years before the Ptolemaic translation, that wondrous Ezra brought to light books full of heavenly grace, which had remained corrupted for a long time, first through the negligence of the Jews and then through the impiety of the Babylonians. If, therefore, Ezra, inspired by divine power, restored the remembrance of these volumes to those people, then these seventy men also did not translate these works into Greek without the Holy Spirit. Among the other sacred volumes they translated the inscriptions as well.”]

This is indeed what this psalm does: at its very beginning it teaches us to seek blessedness and thereby to turn away from evil and do good. For this is the goal toward which every human being tends and which he desires to attain; nor is there anyone who does not wish to be blessed. Yet perverse people, while seeking blessedness in this life, will have it neither in this life nor [Col. 0697A] in the next. They certainly would have had it, if they had trusted the counsel of this psalm and had wished to turn away from evil and do good.

Therefore, whoever desires to be blessed must not go in the counsel of the ungodly, stand in the way of sinners, or sit in the seat of pestilence. If you have heard the counsel of the ungodly, flee from it and do not go in it. For what is it to go in it except to do it and remain in it? If you have sworn to the way of sinners, do not stand there, but depart from it. If you have climbed into the seat of pestilence, come down quickly; judge nothing there, teach nothing there. For not to sin is impossible; but to persevere in sin is most unjust. [Note: [Col. 0697D] Vallicellanus manuscript: “most wicked.”] “For if we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us” (1 John 1:8).

Therefore, sinners are those who are invited to blessedness in this psalm. Only those will be able to attain it who, although they sin, nevertheless do not persevere in their sins. This is what is signified by not going, not standing, and not sitting. Thus perseverance in evil alone obstructs blessedness, and this alone is the sin that is not forgiven people, neither in this age nor in the age to come.

Behold, the Prophet has taught us what the righteous man hastening toward blessedness ought to flee. Now let us hear what he ought to do; for it is not enough for us to turn away from evil unless we also do good. But evils must first be driven out, because the ground must be cleared before it is planted or sown.

“But his delight is in the law of the Lord.”

Whatever either Testament commands to be done or not done is the law of the Lord. Therefore the righteous man, whose will and desire is to fulfil the law of the Lord, cannot remain in the counsel of the ungodly, stand in the way of sinners, or sit in the seat of pestilence. But when he says “was,” do not take it as though it had now ceased; hear what follows:

“And in his law he will meditate day and night.”

What does “day and night” mean? At every time, in prosperity and adversity. For both prosperity and adversity are especially accustomed to separate wretched people from the law of the Lord and from the keeping of his commandments. A certain young man came to the Lord; he was prosperous and possessed much wealth. When he asked how he might attain eternal life, and [Col. 0697D] the Lord told him to sell everything and distribute it to the poor, as it is written, “He went away sorrowful, because he had many possessions” (Matt. 19:22). Thus prosperity separates people from God and from God’s law.

Concerning adversities, however, it is easily understood when the Lord says that, if possible, even the elect would be led astray because of many tribulations (Matt. 24:24). It is therefore great praise for the righteous person to meditate on the law of the Lord day and night. Hence a great reward is promised him in the following verse.

“And he shall be like a tree planted [Col. 0698A] beside streams of waters.”

What is greater than to be compared to Christ the Lord? “We know,” says John the Apostle and Evangelist, “that we shall be like him, because we shall see him as he is” (1 John 3:2). “For the saints shall shine like the sun in the kingdom of God” (Matt. 13:43). The Lord himself shows that he is this tree, saying: “If they do these things in the green tree, what will be done in the dry?” (Luke 23:31). And Solomon, speaking of Wisdom, which is Christ, says: “She is a tree of life to those who lay hold of her, and whoever holds her fast is blessed” (Prov. 3:18). And in the Apocalypse: “To the one who conquers,” he says, “I will give to eat from the tree of life, which is in the paradise of my God” (Rev. 2:7).

This tree, therefore, is planted beside streams of waters. There are four rivers of Paradise, and there are four books of the Gospels, signified by those rivers. Do you wish to see the tree of life? You will find it beside streams of waters. Thus you will find Christ also in the four rivers of the Gospels. For there it is easily discerned who he is, what he is like, and how great he is. Moreover, this tree is beside streams of waters because, “to it, as it is written, all nations shall flow” (Isa. 2:2).—“For many waters,” Scripture says, “are many peoples.” [Note: [Col. 0697D] Waters are interpreted as peoples in Apocalypse 17:15; Augustine likewise in his exposition of Psalm 1.]

“Which will give its fruit in its season.”

From the time this world was made, this tree has not ceased to give its fruit: “For all things were made through him, and without him nothing was made” (John 1:3). Yet it gave its fruit most greatly and abundantly in its own season, in the time of [Col. 0698C] his incarnation and coming. Who can enumerate those fruits, gifts, riches, and delights which the Lord has granted his faithful from that time onward? Hence it is said: “He ascended on high, led captivity captive, and gave gifts to men” (Ps. 67:19).

“And its leaf shall not fall.”

These leaves are words; and Christ’s words shall not fall. For he himself says: “Heaven and earth shall pass away, but my words shall not pass away” (Luke 21:33).

“And everything whatsoever he does shall prosper.”

Everything that Christ does prospers, but it does not prosper for everyone. Hence the Apostle says: “We know that all things work together for good to those who love God” (Rom. 8).

“Not so the ungodly, not so.”

The ungodly, he says, shall not be blessed: for they will not meditate upon the law of the Lord day and night, nor will they be like a tree planted beside streams of waters. What then will they be? Hear what follows:

“Like dust which you cast [Note: [Col. 0698D] The Vulgate reads: “which the wind casts.”] from the face of the earth.”

The blessed are likened to the tree of life; but the ungodly are compared with dust, especially with that dust which is driven about by the wind of pride and, raised from the stability of the earth—that is, of the holy Church—appears nowhere. And therefore, because they are such:

“The ungodly shall not rise in judgment.”

What then does the Apostle mean when he says: [Col. 0699A] “We shall all indeed rise, but we shall not all be changed” (1 Cor. 15:51)? For who are those who will rise and not be changed, if not the ungodly and sinners? The ungodly and sinners will therefore rise, but not for judgment, for they have already been judged. They will rise, then, not in order to be judged again, but only in order to be condemned. And not only the ungodly, but sinners persisting in sins will be condemned. Then “the way of the ungodly shall perish”; that is, the ungodly will perish in their way and work, while the way of the righteous will appear praiseworthy,

“Because the Lord knows the way of the righteous,”

which leads them to the kingdoms of heaven.

## PSALM TWO. A PSALM OF DAVID

[Col. 0699B] Upon this psalm, which is second, is placed the first title, which it calls its own in order that greater authority and credence may be given to it. For who would not believe things strengthened by the authority of so great a king and Prophet? But if we look to that David who speaks in this psalm, and of whom this psalm says elsewhere, “I will hear what the Lord God speaks in me” (Ps. 84:8), then no one will remain who would dare to contradict anything.

Let this brief explanation suffice for us in all psalms marked beforehand with this title. It begins admirably from Christ’s very Passion, which we should always hold in memory, for through it we have been liberated and saved. And it rightly speaks with a certain indignation against those who did not fear to lay hands upon Christ the Lord.

“Why have the nations raged, and the peoples meditated vain things?”

We have just heard above concerning Christ that he is the tree of life, whose leaves will not fall, whose words will not pass away, and whose every work, and whatever he does, will prosper. Why then have the nations raged and the peoples meditated vain things? Why did “the kings of the earth stand,” namely Herod, Pilate, and the chief priests, and “gather together against the Lord,” the Father, “and against his Christ,” the Son? Why did they not even consider the great and such fruit which this most noble tree was then producing—raising the dead, enlightening the blind, cleansing lepers, and healing every disease and every infirmity?

Nations and peoples here signify the same thing, although by “nations” we can understand the Romans and by “peoples” the Jews, who joined together against Christ the Lord. To rage is not human but bestial; thus we understand their ferocity and cruelty in this word. All these children of iniquity therefore assembled and said:

“Let us break their bonds, and cast their yoke away from us.”

They complain that they are bound and under a yoke because their customary sins are forbidden by [Col. 0700A] Christ the Lord and his disciples. For the Lord rebuked them not only for the evil things they did but also for their wicked thoughts, as we find in the Gospel. Such is this: “Why do you think evil in your hearts?” (Matt. 9:4). Wretched people, who would not listen to the same one [Note: [Col. 0699D] Ghisianus manuscript: “the very same one.”] who was not dragging them violently but gently calling them to himself, when with fatherly kindness he said: “Come to me, all you who labour and are burdened, and I will refresh you; for my yoke is sweet and my burden light” (Matt. 11:28). What follows will deservedly happen to them:

“He who dwells in the heavens shall laugh at them, and the Lord shall mock them.”

Because, he says, they did these things and would not believe Christ the Lord, the Lord will show that they are fools and idiots worthy of mockery and derision. Such emotions are not in him, but we cannot show his will and operation otherwise than by expressions familiar to us. For when he does what angry and raging people are accustomed to do, though he is not angry, he is nevertheless said to do it in anger and wrath. [Note: [Col. 0699D] How the wrath of God is to be understood. “The wrath and fury of the Lord God must be understood not as a disturbance of mind, [Col. 0700D] but as the power by which vengeance is most justly executed.” Augustine, exposition on Psalm 1.] Hence it follows:

“Then he shall speak to them in his wrath, and in his fury he shall trouble them.”

This will be at the judgment, when he says to the ungodly and sinners: “Depart from me, you cursed, into the eternal fire prepared for the devil and his angels” (Matt. 25:41). Since in saying this he will imitate the manner of one angry and enraged, he is said to be about to speak and act in anger and fury.

“But I have been appointed king by him over Zion, his holy mountain.”

This verse belongs with the place where it is said, “For they gathered together against the Lord and against his Christ”; it is understood that he says: “But I have been appointed king by him.” Him whom the Jews call Christ, we call King. Christ our Lord and God is both God and man. According to his humanity, he was appointed both king and Lord not only by the [Col. 0700C] Father but also by himself and by the Holy Spirit. For he who according to divinity was neither made nor created, according to humanity created and made himself. Let us therefore retain this distinction in memory; it will be necessary to us in nearly all the psalms. For all things must be referred to his humanity whenever he is grieved, whenever he suffers anything, whenever he asks for anything, and the like.

“But I,” he says, “have been appointed king by him”—where? “Over his holy mountain.” For what purpose? “Proclaiming the commandment of the Lord.” Zion is interpreted “watchtower”; from that watchtower all bishops are called overseers and watchmen. Hence Ezekiel is told: “Son of man, I have appointed you a watchman for the house of Israel” (Ezek. 3:17). Although our Saviour is King of kings and Lord of lords, he nevertheless deigns to call himself king of the mountain of Zion alone. But let bishops hear why they have been ordained, why and by whom they have been appointed over Zion: certainly not to exercise tyrannical and secular power, but to keep watch and preach, and to fight against heretics and evil spirits.

“The Lord said to me: You are my Son.”

This pertains to divinity. I, he says, who according to humanity have been appointed king by God, am according to divinity his Son not by adoption but by substance. For the Father himself testified to this, saying: “You are my beloved Son; in you I am well pleased. This day I have begotten you” (Luke 3:23). God has nothing but “today,” since nothing is past or future to him, but all things are present to him. What else then could he say except “today”? For “I have begotten you today” means nothing other than, plainly stated, “I have begotten you before the ages and without beginning.” [Note: [Col. 0701D] Saint Maximus of Turin said the same thing more briefly, Sermon 36 on Easter, Roman edition of 1784, p. 491: “Christ is plainly the one day, because in him is the one eternity of divinity. He is called ‘today’ because neither a worn-out antiquity passes beneath him nor an unknown future passes beyond him.”] For the Father is eternal and the Son also eternal; but before the eternal there is nothing. “Today,” therefore, is eternity. Accordingly, when he says, “I have begotten you today,” it is as though he said, “I have begotten you before the ages and without beginning.”

It can also be understood according to humanity: the Father says to him, “I who begot you before the ages have today—that is, temporally—begotten you from the Virgin.” For he is the Father of all: he not only begot and created the humanity of his Son but also begot and created us all. [Note: [Col. 0701D] “Although that day may also be seen in prophecy as the day on which Jesus Christ was born according to his humanity, yet ‘today,’ which signifies presence—and in eternity nothing is past, as though it had ceased to be, nor future, as though it were not yet, but only present, because whatever is eternal always is—is understood in a divine sense in the saying, ‘I have begotten you today,’ whereby the most sincere and catholic faith proclaims the everlasting generation of the power and wisdom of God, who is the only-begotten Son.” Augustine, cited passage.]

“Ask of me, and I shall give you the nations as your inheritance, and the ends of the earth as your possession.”

[Col. 0701C] We said above that if the Son asks for anything, he asks not according to divinity but according to humanity. He asks, therefore, not only of the Father but also of himself and of the divinity which is in him. “And I will give you the nations as your inheritance.” The Jews, he says, rejected you, saying: “We have no king but Caesar, and we do not want this man to reign [Note: [Col. 0702D] Ghisianus manuscript: “this king to reign.”] over us” (John 19:12); therefore receive all nations as your inheritance. Hence elsewhere it is said: “All nations shall serve him, and he shall rule from sea to sea, and from the river to the ends of the earth” (Ps. 71:8). “To the ends of the earth” means the same as “the ends of the earth as your possession.”

“Rule them with a rod of iron.”

What does “with a rod of iron” mean? With a strong and irresistible command, which no one will be able to withstand. All metals are subdued by iron; all the kingdoms of the world are subjected to Christ’s command.

“And like a potter’s vessel he shall break them.”

A potter’s vessels, once broken, cannot be restored. The ungodly and sinners, once condemned in judgment, will find mercy no further.

[Col. 0702A] “And now, O kings, understand.”

Behold, God has been appointed a great, righteous, and powerful king, whom both we and all nations ought to obey. Therefore understand, and receive from him the teaching and discipline of kingship. This is what he says:

“Be instructed, you who judge the earth; serve the Lord in fear.”

To serve in fear is to carry out service diligently and to have no negligence in God’s service. Therefore kings, who have been appointed to govern the people justly and to administer justice, should exercise justice in such a way that they do not forget mercy; they should follow the restraints of divine law, not the impulse of their own hearts.

“And rejoice in him with trembling.”

Rejoice, he says, not in yourselves but in God; take delight not in honours and riches but in the Lord. Hence the Apostle says: “Rejoice in the Lord always; again I say, rejoice” (Phil. 4:4). “With trembling” is fittingly added, lest the fear of the Lord and the desire for eternal blessedness be driven out by the joy and prosperity of this world. By “kings” we should understand not only kings of nations but also bishops and all prelates of the Church. Indeed, every person can be called a king who governs himself well and orders his household well.

“Lay hold of discipline, lest the Lord be angry and you perish from the righteous way.”

Every teaching and institution of religion can be called discipline. Whoever does not receive and hold it deservedly incurs God’s wrath and indignation. Such persons perish from the righteous way because, turning aside into the way of sinners, they will not attain blessedness through the way of the righteous. Although this discipline is necessary for all people, it is especially necessary for those who ought to govern and teach others. Blessed are those who receive this discipline and trust not in the vanities of the world but in the Lord.

“For when his wrath has kindled in a short time, blessed are all, and only those, who trust in him.”

He said “in a short time” because the Lord will come quickly, after a little while, for judgment. Hence John the Apostle says: “Little children, it is the last hour” (1 John 2:18). And the Apostle says: “We are those upon whom the ends of the ages have come” (1 Cor. 10:11). We have already said above how God’s wrath should be understood.

## PSALM THREE. A PSALM OF DAVID, WHEN HE FLED FROM THE FACE OF HIS SON ABSALOM

[Col. 0702D] What “a psalm of David” signifies has been stated above. We read of David’s flight, but we do not read of Christ’s flight, because elsewhere he says concerning himself: [Col. 0703A] “Flight has perished from me.” [Note: [Col. 0703D] We do not read that Christ fled when the Jews sought him for death, as David was sought by Saul. Yet he fled to a mountain, as John 6:15 records, when the crowds wished to make him king. Thus the prophecy does not disagree with the Gospel, since Christ’s flight is understood for a different reason.] When the Jews came with Judas the traitor to seize him, he did not flee but went to meet them. To show the power of his divinity, he struck them down with a single word.

Yet he is the one to whom the Church says in the Song of Songs: “Flee, my beloved” (Song 8:14). And of his disciples it is said that, “leaving him, they all fled” (Matt. 23:36). Thus Jesus fled not in himself but in his disciples. In the same way it is said [Note: [Col. 0703D] Ghisianus manuscript: “because Jesus was baptizing,” and it is immediately said.] that he himself was not baptizing, but his disciples were.

Both Judas and Absalom, moreover, perished by a similar death, namely hanging. [Note: [Col. 0703D] The same manuscript: “died.”] David is interpreted “strong of hand,” [Note: [Col. 0703D] Saint Bruno seems to have taken this interpretation from the Venerable Bede, who in his exposition of the title of Psalm 2 says: “David is interpreted ‘strong of hand’ or ‘beloved,’ than which nothing can be more fittingly applied to almighty Christ, who is truly most strong and is to be sought with the highest desire. The Prophet speaks of his Passion, and the Lord himself will speak his own words.” We have noted this beforehand because, in the course of the psalms, our author very often commends Christ’s strength in the person of David. Cassiodorus gives the same interpretation in his exposition of Psalm 2.] while Absalom is interpreted “the father’s peace.” This seems to be said by contraries, just as the Lord says to Judas, [Col. 0703B] “Friend, for what have you come?” (Matt. 26:50), though he certainly was not a friend.

“Lord, why have those who afflict me multiplied?”

According to his humanity the Lord speaks and complains to the Father about the conspiracy of the Jews made against him—a conspiracy multiplied not only from the Romans who were there but also from the number of the disciples. Hence he says that “many rise up against him, and many say to his soul: There is no salvation for him in his God.” [Note: [Col. 0704D] This reading differs from the Vulgate, whose first part agrees with Augustine: “Many rise up against me.” But the second does not: the Vulgate has, “Many say to my soul, ‘There is no salvation for him in his God.’” Augustine, like Bruno, has: “There is no salvation for him in his God.” Cassiodorus reads so likewise.]

For already at that time he saw not only the Jews but also, throughout the whole world, kings and rulers, all wicked people, and the whole host of malicious spirits cruelly rising against his faithful, against his members, against [Col. 0703C] his body, which is the Church. Since, as is said, he himself is afflicted, troubled, and suffers persecution in each of his own, he rightly attributes to himself what happens to them and complains of their penalties as though they were his own.

“But you, O Lord, are my protector, my glory, and the one who lifts up my head.”

They lie, he says, who say, “There is no salvation for him in his God,” because the things listed here concern salvation. For the Father received the Son returning to himself, incarnate and made man; [Note: [Col. 0704D] “Protector” is said according to the form of a servant: the reception of humanity is the Word made flesh. Cassiodorus.] he glorified him and raised him to the seat of his majesty, according to the saying: “The Lord said to my Lord: Sit at my right hand” (Ps. 109:1).

It seems to me, however, that if the Church speaks in this psalm, it may be understood more fittingly. Let the Church, then, let the Christian people speak: the people whom first the Jews alone, and afterwards the whole world, began to afflict and destroy with most grievous punishments. “Lord, why have those who afflict me multiplied? Many rise against me.” Many from all the nations of this world “say to my soul: There is no salvation for her in her God.” This is what unbelievers used to say against the saints: that their God could not free them.

“But you, O Lord, are my protector and my glory, and the one who lifts up my head.” This is no slight consolation of the saints: that immediately after martyrdom they will be crowned, glorified, and received by God into eternal blessedness. For our Saviour had promised them that where he was, there [Col. 0704B] his servant would be also (John 12:26); and that where the body was, there the eagles would be gathered (Matt. 26:28); and that when he was lifted up, he would draw all things to himself. Thus the Church now says: “And the one who lifts up my head.” Our head is Christ, who ascended into heaven on the fortieth day after his resurrection.

“With my voice I cried to the Lord, and he heard me from his holy mountain.”

When, he says, I was troubled and tormented with grievous punishments by the ungodly and unbelieving, then I cried to the Lord with my voice—the voice of my heart, that voice which cries in silence and penetrates the secrets of heaven—and he heard me from his holy mountain, that is, from that most high and radiant inner sanctuary of his glory. For although God is everywhere, there is nevertheless a place where he deigns to reveal his glory more clearly and manifestly. We may also understand by this mountain Christ the Lord, in whom and from whom the voices of the saints are heard. And what wonder that he hears those for whom he even died? Hence the Apostle says: “He gave himself for us as an offering and sacrifice to God for an odour of sweetness” (Eph. 5:2). The voice of the one speaking is now fittingly introduced.

“I slept and took sleep, and I rose again, because the Lord received me.”

In these words he shows very briefly his Passion, resurrection, and ascension. How, he says, should I fail to hear the voices crying to me of those for whom I did not hesitate even to die? For this is what he says: “I slept.” Christ’s death was sleep; hence he fittingly added: “And I took sleep.” He indeed took it, [Col. 0704D] but did not sleep long. Therefore he added, [Col. 0705A] saying: “And I rose again.” By adding, “Because the Lord received me,” he shows that not many days afterwards he ascended into heaven. Now let us hear the Church, which had begun to speak.

“I will not fear,” she says, “thousands of people surrounding me.”

Many indeed rise against me, and my enemies have multiplied greatly; but I will fear no longer, even if many thousands besides these rise against me and surround me. Instead, I shall say—as I am accustomed always to say in all my tribulations—[Note: [Col. 0705D] Saint Augustine likewise, after expounding that the Prophet spoke in this psalm concerning Christ, maintains that he also uttered a prophecy concerning the Church’s enemies, of whom Christ is the head, and concerning future persecutors, from whom she was to be delivered and saved:]

“Rise up, O Lord; save me, my God.”

Holy and devout persons defend themselves with such weapons: they fight not with swords but with prayers.

“For you have struck all those opposing [Note: [Col. 0705D] “Those opposing” concerns not only death but also heretical disputes: those who, without zeal for truth, assail catholic rules with depraved doctrines. Such people are deservedly struck with blindness of mind, because they have joined themselves to perverse desires. Cassiodorus.] me without cause.”

I shall not fear, he says, because it is not fitting that I should fear. Why is this? Because you have struck—and daily strike—and at last in judgment will strike with an iron rod all those opposing me. And this deservedly, because they oppose me without cause.

“You have crushed the teeth of sinners.”

By the teeth of sinners we understand their power, their knowledge, their strength, their arguments, and everything else by which they can defend themselves or assail others. The Lord has crushed these things because he gave his faithful a mouth and wisdom which none of their adversaries could withstand.

“Salvation belongs to the Lord, and your blessing is upon your people.”

This is a taunt. Let your enemies, he says, who formerly used to say to me, “There is no salvation for him in his God,” be ashamed, as they can now most certainly see and know. “Salvation belongs to the Lord.” Then the Church, rejoicing over the crushing of her enemies and over her own salvation, turns to the Lord and says: “Let salvation be upon your people, O Lord, whom you have so honoured, to whom you have given this salvation and victory; and may your blessing be now and always, through endless ages of ages. Amen.”

## PSALM FOUR. A PSALM OF DAVID, UNTO THE END, IN SONGS

What “a psalm of David” signifies was stated in the second psalm. Someone might understand this psalm as belonging to David’s time and to the Synagogue, unless [Col. 0705D] the Apostle had said: “For Christ is the end of the law” (Rom. 10:4). He speaks of himself, saying: “I am Alpha and Omega, the first and the last, the beginning and the end” (Rev. 1:8). Therefore let these words be referred “unto the end,” that is, to the times of our Saviour, and let them be sung in the hymns [Col. 0706A] and praises of the Church, to which they seem properly and especially to belong. [Note: [Col. 0706D] This interpretation of the title is from the Venerable Bede, as is the exposition of the psalm, in which the Church is introduced as speaking to God. Cassiodorus held the same view, both in his exposition of the title and of the psalm.]

“When I called upon you, you heard me, O God [Note: [Col. 0706D] Cassiodorus has the same reading.] of my righteousness.”

This psalm is very disconnected and requires much linking. It is the Church speaking, who gives thanks to God because he heard her in her great tribulations. She endured great tribulations in the time of the Apostles and martyrs, and she will suffer them at the end of the age. “For then there shall be tribulation such as has not been and shall not be” (Matt. 24:21). You heard me, she says, not because of my merits or my righteousness; for if there is any righteousness in me, it is not mine but yours. But you are God and Lord, the creator and giver of [Col. 0706B] my righteousness.

“In tribulation you enlarged me.”

For holy Church has been enlarged more in tribulations and adversities than in prosperity. [Note: [Col. 0706D] “For tribulation is what always enlarges the Church, when confessors are made at the same time, martyrs are crowned, and the whole company of the righteous continually increases through afflictions.” Cassiodorus.] Its boundaries indeed extend from the rising and setting of the sun, from the north and from the sea. Yet now it seems to have failed in Africa and in many other parts of the world in which it was once quite glorious.

“Miserere mihi, Domine, et exaudi orationem meam.” Behold, our mother, the holy Church, teaches us both how she herself called upon God and how we ought to call upon him. This prayer is sufficient for us in all our petitions. If weakness comes upon us, or barrenness of the earth, or a raging adversary, or persecution from without, let us say: “Have mercy upon me, O Lord, and [Col. 0706C] hear my prayer”; and this suffices for one upon whom the Lord also has mercy, and whose petitions the Lord hears. What more does such a person seek?

“Children of men, how long will you be heavy of heart?” The Church seeks not her own salvation alone, but that of others also. For behold, having been heard in her tribulations, she turns to her very enemies, inviting them to faith and blessedness. Those are “children of men” who have but one generation, and who have not yet merited, through rebirth from water and the Holy Spirit, to have God as their Father. Such persons are heavy of heart, possessing hard and stony hearts, upon which the words of true faith and heavenly teaching cannot be written and retained. But as light things are drawn upward, [Col. 0706D] so heavy things are drawn downward. Let those heavy of heart therefore fear lest, through their own hardness and heaviness, they be dragged down to hell.

“Why do you love vanity, [Note: [Col. 0706D] Codex Ghisianus: “and seek.”] you who seek falsehood?” Those love vanity and seek falsehood who either worship false gods or place their hope in the riches of this world. Hence the Apostle also admonishes the rich (1 Tim. 6:17) not to think proudly, nor to hope in the uncertainty of riches.

“Know that the Lord has magnified his Holy One.” This is as though he said: Children of men, abandon false gods; abandon idols and vanities; believe in Christ, the Son of God, and you shall be saved. Know this, and do not doubt in any way that the Lord has magnified his Holy One—namely Christ, his Son—who freely died in order to deliver us from everlasting death. How the Lord magnified Christ according to his humanity, Christ himself shows when he says: “All power in heaven and on earth has been given to me” [Col. 0707B] (Matt. 28:18). And as though they, already believing, should say: We are sinners; we have worshipped idols, shed the blood of saints, and committed many thousands of sins; he will not receive us—the holy Church, our most merciful mother, strengthens them. “Do not fear,” she says; “I shall cry out and pray for you.”

“And the Lord will hear me when I cry to him. Be angry, therefore, and do not sin [Note: [Col. 0707D] Mazochius, in *Spicilegium Biblicum*, I, II, p. 177, judges that the passage may be punctuated thus: “Are you angry? Yet do not sin. Whenever you perceive that you are angry, do not break out into injury, whether in deed or in words.”].” This would not have been said unless it were sometimes good to be angry. For if hatred is sometimes good, why should anger not sometimes be good as well? Hear, then, what the Lord says: “Whoever does not hate father and mother, wife and children, and even his own life, cannot be my disciple” (Matt. 14:26). Certainly all these things, which are indeed to be loved, must be hated if they wish to draw us into [Col. 0707C] sins and separate us from God. To be angry with such things and in such a manner, therefore, is not sin; and thus he added: “And do not sin.” Be angry, he says, at your former way of life; be angry at vices and sins. In this way those were angry to whom the Apostle said: “What fruit, then, did you have in those things of which you are now ashamed?” (Rom. 6:21). And do not sin any longer, as you were formerly accustomed to sin. [Note: [Col. 0708D] Codex Ghisianus: “For not to sin is impossible; but …”] Yet there are certain sins, indeed very grave ones, from which we can easily abstain. Such is that of which the Lord says: “Israel, if you hear me, there shall be no new god in you, nor shall you worship a foreign god” (Ps. 80:10).

“What you say in your hearts, and on your beds [Col. 0707D] be pierced with compunction.” The beds of our thoughts are our hearts: there thoughts arise, there they rest, there they bear fruit—good fruit if they are good, evil if they are evil. Hence the Lord says: “From the heart proceed evil thoughts, thefts, murders, perjuries, false testimonies, and the like, which defile a person” (Matt. 15:18). Be pierced with compunction concerning these things; let them do penance for them; cut them down at their very beginning, and do not permit them to come into effect. Then do what follows:

“Offer a sacrifice of righteousness.” If you do this, then confidently [Col. 0708A] “hope in the Lord.” Hope for what? To receive those good things “which eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor have entered into the heart of man, which God has prepared” both for you and for all “who love him” (1 Cor. 2:9; Isa. 64:4). The person who judges and afflicts himself for his sins offers a sacrifice of righteousness. Hence the Apostle says: “If we judged ourselves, we certainly would not be judged” (1 Cor. 11:21). And that bodily affliction is a sacrifice, hear the same Apostle saying: “I beseech you, through the mercy of God, to present your bodies as a living sacrifice, holy, pleasing to God—your rational service” (Rom. 12:1).

“Many say: Who will show us good things?” I have told you, he says, to hope in the Lord, and I have shown what [Col. 0708B] you ought to hope for. But there are many who have no hope and say in their thoughts: Who will show us those good things? What trustworthy messenger has come from there? [Note: [Col. 0708D] Codex Ghisianus: “How are we to hope for these things?”] How can we hope or believe? Miserable are those who say such things, because these words are full of despair. But who are these people who speak so impiously? They are those “who have been multiplied by the fruit of their grain, wine, and oil.” By these three things, upon which human necessity is chiefly sustained, are signified all the fleeting and transitory goods of this world. Those who have placed their hope in such things cannot hope for eternal goods. Such was the man spoken of in the Gospel, who planned to destroy his storehouses and build larger ones, and who joyfully said to his soul: “You have many good things [Col. 0708C] stored up for many years; rejoice, therefore, and feast” (Luke 12:19). To him the Lord answered: “Fool, this night your soul shall be taken from you; and whose shall those things be which you have prepared?” (ibid., 20). Hence also the Apostle commands that we not hope in the uncertainty of riches (1 Tim. 6:17). Hence too he says that the rich cannot enter the kingdom of God. Now let us hear what the good likewise say and think.

“The light of your countenance, O Lord, is marked upon us,” they say. This is as though they said: We have been marked with the sign of Christ, enrolled in his service, enlightened by his teaching; in him we hope, and we most firmly await whatever he has promised us. We read in the Apocalypse (ch. 7) that twelve thousand from the whole multitude of the children of Israel were marked, by whom are signified the whole Church and the entire multitude of believers. This is the sign which the Prophet called *tau* (Ezek. 9:4), and whoever is not marked with it shall perish in the judgment. This sign is rightly called light, because one who does not have it is blind and walks in darkness. The will is recognized in the countenance; hence will is also called “countenance” (*vultus*). What, then, is the light of your countenance except the light of your will? According to your will, both this light and this sign came to be: [Col. 0709A] for you, the instrument of death was made; for us, it was made the cause of salvation. It follows:

“You have given joy into my heart.” This is the voice of the Church, signifying that she possesses joy at this response of the saints.

“In peace, in the selfsame state, I shall sleep and rest; because you, O Lord, have established me uniquely in hope.” Those who despairingly say, “Who will show us good things?” will have neither peace nor rest. But I, she says, shall sleep and rest in the selfsame state—that is, together and at the same time with all my children—in eternal peace. [Note: [Col. 0709D] “‘I shall sleep’ is understood to mean the end of life; ‘I shall rest’ is shown to indicate future blessedness, when rest and glorious repose shall at last be given to the saints.” Cassiodorus.] And I say this because you, O Lord, have established me uniquely in hope: that is, you have granted to me alone, as one singular, this immense hope of your blessedness.

## PSALM V. 307. FOR THE END, FOR HER WHO OBTAINS THE INHERITANCE. A PSALM OF DAVID.

[Col. 0709B]

We have explained above what “for the end” signifies; likewise, in the second Psalm, we explained how “a Psalm of David” is to be understood. She who obtains the inheritance is the holy Church. Hence the Apostle says that we are “heirs indeed of God, but fellow-heirs with Christ” (Rom. 16:17). The Synagogue lost this inheritance when, concerning our Savior who came to it, it said: “This is the heir; come, let us kill him, and the inheritance will be ours” (Mark 12:7). The testament of this inheritance was given to her in that Psalm in which it is said: “I have established a testament with my chosen ones [Note: [Col. 0709D] Saint Augustine has the same interpretation, [Col. 0710D] proving the inheritance of God promised to the Church. Cassiodorus also has the same.]”

[Col. 0709C] “Give ear to my words, O Lord; understand my cry. Attend to the voice of my prayer, my King and my God.” The Church speaks, having succeeded to the inheritance in place of the Synagogue. She teaches us how earnestly, perseveringly, and forcefully we ought to pray, by repeating the same thing so often. Hence the Gospel says that “the kingdom of heaven suffers violence, and the violent seize it” (Matt. 11:12). The Lord himself commands us to exercise this violence when he says: “Ask, and you shall receive; seek, and you shall find; knock, and it shall be opened to you” (Matt. 7:6). He also tells the parable of the man who asked his friend for three loaves, when [Col. 0709D] the friend was unwilling to give them; but, as the man persisted in his requests throughout the night, the friend finally arose because of his insistence and importunity, and gave him as many as he needed. Good petitions, however, are made not so much by the voice as by affection and desire, according to the saying: “The Lord will hear the desire of the poor” (Ps. 10:16).

“Because I shall pray to you, O Lord, in the morning you shall hear my voice.” Therefore let the one who desires to be heard pray in the morning. What, then, does this same prophet mean when elsewhere [Col. 0710A] he says: “At midnight I rose to give thanks to you” (Ps. 118:62), and: “In the nights lift up your hands in the sanctuary” (Ps. 133:3)? Certainly at no time can religious persons pray more attentively and quietly than at night. To pray in the morning, therefore, is as though he said: If you wish to be heard by the Lord, pray in the morning; flee the night, flee works of darkness, drive away vices and sins. Hear the Apostle saying: “We are children of light and of the day, not of night nor of darkness” (1 Thess. 5:5). And elsewhere: “You were once darkness, but now you are light in the Lord” (Eph. 5:10). Such night and such darkness must therefore first be abandoned, and then prayer must be made. A person comes forth from this darkness and arrives at morning as soon as he begins to do penance. For as morning is the end of night and the beginning of day, [Col. 0710B] so penance is the end of sin and the beginning of holiness and religious life.

“In the morning I shall stand before you.” Since, he says, you do not wish to hear us except in the morning, I shall leave the darkness of night as quickly as I can and hasten to morning. Then I shall stand before you like a servant ready for service. “And I shall see, because you are not a God who wills iniquity.” This, then, was why you did not hear in the night: because those who are in the night are in iniquity.

“The wicked one has not dwelt beside you, nor shall the unjust remain before your eyes.” Such persons will hear in the judgment: “Let the wicked be taken away, lest they see the glory of God” (Isa. 26:10). Whenever we say these things, we understand them only of those sinners who persevere in sins and refuse to return [Col. 0710C] to repentance. Of them the Apostle also says: “According to your hardness and unrepentant heart, you store up wrath for yourself on the day of wrath and revelation of the just judgment of God, who will render to each according to his works” (Rom. 2:5). Hence it follows:

“You have hated, O Lord, all who work iniquity; you will destroy all who speak falsehood.” He did not say, “those who have worked” or “those who have spoken,” but used the present tense to signify perseverance. Those who persevere in such things are worthy of hatred and destruction. Although every lie is a sin, we must especially understand this of heretics, and of all others who lie in order to deceive others. [Note: [Col. 0710D] Cassiodorus treats this and the following interpretation, saying that heretics who deceive others sin more gravely than those who merely depart from the commandments.] The following words also seem [Col. 0710D] to signify this.

“The Lord will abhor the man of blood and deceit.” Every murderer may be called a man of blood. But because he adds “and deceit,” this must be understood of heretics, who kill human souls through deceit and deception. Certainly the death of the soul, which heretics bring about, is far more dangerous than the death of the body inflicted by other murderers: the former is eternal, while the latter is temporal; the former separates the soul from God, the latter merely separates it from [Col. 0711A] the body. Such a person is therefore rightly abhorred by God, since he is more cruel than every wild beast.

“But I, O Lord, in the multitude of your mercy, shall enter into your house.” Behold, the Church now obtains the inheritance, as is written concerning her in the title of this Psalm. By the house of God, into which she confidently declares she shall enter, we understand the heavenly homeland and the land of the living. She says that she shall enter this house not by her own merits but through the abundant mercy of God: “He did not spare his own Son, but delivered him up for us all” (Rom. 8:32).

“I shall worship toward your holy temple in your fear.” The temple of God is Christ’s humanity, in which all the fullness of divinity dwells bodily [Col. 0711B] (Col. 2:9). We ought to worship this, as we are commanded in another Psalm: “Exalt the Lord our God, and worship the footstool [Note: [Col. 0711D] Codex Ghisianus: “of my feet.”] of his feet, for it is holy” (Ps. 93:5).—“Heaven is my throne, says the Lord, but the earth is the footstool of my feet” (Isa. 66:1). If the earth is God’s footstool, and we ought to worship God’s footstool, then we ought also to worship the earth. Yet there is no other earth that ought to be worshipped except this one alone, which the Word of God joined to himself: namely, Christ’s humanity, which in this place is called the temple of God. The saints worship it while they are in this life, and they worship it when they are there. They worship it indeed in the fear of God, because they fear and worship it as they do the Father and God himself.

[Col. 0711C] “Lead me, O Lord, in your righteousness.” I, says the Church, hasten to receive the inheritance; but while I remain in this life, I have particular need of your protection. Therefore I earnestly ask you to lead me in your righteousness and not permit me to depart from that righteousness. For behold, my enemies—evil spirits, Jews, heretics, and tyrants—strive by every means to hinder my way. “But you, because of my enemies,” lest they be able to turn me aside from the right path, “make straight my way before you.”

“Because there is no truth in their mouth; their heart is vain.” They are to be feared, he says, because they do everything by lies and deceit: truth is not in them, and their heart is empty [Col. 0711D] of every good thing.

“Their throat is an open tomb.” When a tomb is closed, it does not stink; when it is open, it displays the fullness of its stench. Such are heretics, who—would that they had always kept silent and never infected others with the stench of their heresy! But, as follows, they always “act deceitfully with their tongues,” killing and swallowing up the souls of the simple. “Judge them, O God.” Now she speaks as though angered, and, unable to endure them, invokes judgment and condemnation upon them.

“Let them fall from their designs.” Behold, she again speaks compassionately and desires their life more than their death. “Judge them, O God,” she says, unless [Col. 0712A] “they fall from their designs,” by which they trust that they can overthrow your faithful. “And according to the multitude of their impieties, cast them out.” From where and to where? From your Church into eternal fire; for this follows after judgment. And deservedly so, “because they have provoked you, O Lord.” For no one provokes the Lord and stirs him to anger as heretics do, because no one harms the Church so much. Tyrants rage against bodies; heretics, against souls.

“And let all who hope in you rejoice.” Rejoicing with spiritual and eternal joy; and this is what follows: “They shall exult forever, and you shall dwell in them.” For what joy is so great as always to have before one’s eyes the object of one’s desire and love? [Col. 0712B] “And all who love your name shall glory in you.”—“Let the one who glories,” says the Apostle, “glory in the Lord” (2 Cor. 10:17). The saints know no other glory, because they know that they possess nothing except from God in which they ought to glory. Hence elsewhere they say: “In the Lord we shall do valiantly” (Ps. 59:14).
