The Lord himself also says of himself: “If I glorify myself, my glory is nothing” (John 8:54). By this he signifies that the glory of his humanity itself had to be referred to his divinity.

“For you, O Lord, will bless the righteous, and you have crowned us with the shield of good will.” Rightly, O Lord, he says, do your saints rejoice in you, since they await such a reward from you. For they know that you will bless them with that desirable and long-awaited blessing [Col. 0712C] with which you will bless them in the judgment, saying: “Come, blessed of my Father, receive the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world” (Matt. 25:34).—“O Lord, you have crowned us with the shield of your good will.” In you, say the saints and the whole Church, we ought to rejoice and glory, O Lord, because behold, we are what we are; in you we overcome our enemies, and by you we are now crowned. We are always armed and defended by the protection and defence of your good will, as though by a strong and invincible shield.

## PSALM VI. 309. FOR THE END, IN HYMNS, FOR THE EIGHTH, A PSALM OF DAVID.

We have already explained above what “for the end,” “in hymns,” and “a Psalm of David” mean. Since this one title occurs in many Psalms, [Col. 0712D] one explanation will suffice for us. But the phrase “for the eighth” refers to the day of the final resurrection. For that day which is first is also the eighth, called the Lord’s Day, on which Christ the Lord rose from the dead. Of this day it is said elsewhere: “This is the day which the Lord has made; let us exult and rejoice in it” (Ps. 117:14). On this day God created heaven and earth and separated light from darkness; on this day, as we have just said, Christ rose; on this day he gave the Holy Spirit to the disciples; on this day, judging the world in righteousness and equity, he shall render to each according to his works.

“O Lord, do not rebuke me in your anger, nor rebuke me in [Col. 0713A] your fury.” Such emotions are not in God, but they seem to be in him when he does the things that those in whom they are accustomed to do. Yet the holy Church is always mindful of that eighth day, and always sings this Psalm in remembrance of that day. She therefore asks the Lord to rebuke her with fatherly compassion and mercy, not in anger and fury, as he will judge and condemn, on that eighth day, by a sentence so harsh and terrible, those persons [Note: [Col. 0713D] “She therefore asks that she may be rebuked before judgment, not in judgment; for whoever is rebuked there is undoubtedly condemned. It must be kept in mind that the day of judgment, because of the magnitude of its terror, is called anger and fury.” Cassiodorus.]

“Have mercy upon me, O Lord, because I am weak.” He speaks of the weakness of the soul, which is greater than bodily weakness. The following words make this clear when he says: “And my soul is greatly troubled.” As often as a person sins, so often is the soul weakened; and as often as he returns to repentance, so often does he recover from weakness. [Col. 0713B] “Heal me, O Lord, because all my bones are troubled.” The body is supported by its bones; if they fail, it cannot stand. In the same way, the soul is supported and borne by its bones; if they are troubled, it falls miserably. But what are the bones of the soul? First are faith, hope, and charity; then reason, wisdom, memory, and understanding; then the remaining virtues. These are weakened in the soul when a person commits some grave sin. The holy Church seems now to pray for those who have committed graver sins, since she says that not one or two but all the bones, and the whole soul, are greatly troubled. Although prayer must be made for everyone, it ought especially to be made for those who are held in more serious [Col. 0713C] weakness.

“And you, O Lord, how long?” How long, O Lord, he says, will you defer the remedy and not come to the aid of a soul suffering such great and severe weakness? “Turn, and deliver my soul.” As long as a person perseveres in sins, God is angry with and opposed to him. But if he turns to repentance, God is immediately appeased and deigns to regard his repentance. “Save me,” not by my merits, for there are no merits, but “for your mercy’s sake.” Save me, he says, and heal my soul, lest this weakness draw and plunge me down into death and hell. This happens to those who persevere in sins until death and neglect to embrace repentance. Such persons are worthy of no pardon, and there is nothing that can further [Col. 0713D] help them. Hence it follows:

“For in death there is none who remembers you; but in hell, who will confess you?” It is clear, therefore, that those are utterly condemned who neither retain remembrance of God nor seek pardon for their sins. And lest similar things should happen to me also, says the Church, I have done what follows:

“I have laboured in my groaning; every night I shall wash my bed; with my tears I shall water my couch.” By these words she most plainly teaches what those who have committed grave sins must do. “I have laboured,” she says, “and have diligently employed every means that the sins I committed might be blotted out; nor shall I yet cease, but every night I shall wash my bed and water my couch with tears.” By bed and couch we should understand our hearts, in which sins both arise and are contained. Hence the Lord says in the Gospel: “From the heart proceed evil thoughts, thefts, murders, perjuries, false testimonies, and the like, which defile a person” (Matt. 15:19). [Note: [Col. 0714D] “The bed is here called the place where the sick and infirm mind rests—that is, in bodily pleasure and every worldly delight. The person who strives to draw himself out of that delight washes it with tears.” Augustine, *Expositions on the Psalms*.] That bed which is defiled by such stains must therefore be washed. This was surely what the one did who said: “Create in me a clean heart, O God” (Ps. 50:11). Hence Solomon [Col. 0714B] says: “Keep your heart with all vigilance” (Prov. 4:23). Understanding this, the publican beat his breast, because he knew that the sins he had committed were in that bed of his breast. But what is it to wash one’s bed every night, 310 except to devote oneself to satisfaction and repentance for every single sin through fasting, prayers, and above all an outpouring of tears? Sins are called nights, because they are done in darkness and draw everything toward darkness. Hence the Lord says: “Everyone who does evil flees the light” (John 3:9). And the Apostle John: “Whoever hates his brother remains in darkness and does not know where he goes, because darkness has blinded his eyes” (1 John 2:11), signifying sins by darkness.

[Col. 0714C] “My eye has been troubled because of anger.” This is the eye of which the Lord says in the Gospel: “If your eye is single, your whole body shall be full of light; but if it is evil, your whole body shall be dark” (Luke 11:34). What, then, is this eye except Catholic understanding? The holy mother Church therefore says that this eye has been troubled in her because of anger. Good is the anger by which such an eye is troubled; good is the disturbance in which the holy Church glories. Of this anger it is said in another Psalm: “Be angry, and do not sin” (Ps. 4:5). The eye of the Church—that is, Catholic understanding—is angry and troubled against her enemies. By these we understand Jews, heretics, tyrants, and evil spirits, who try to separate her from truth and draw her into the error [Col. 0714D] of their perversity. Nor is it surprising that they are angry, since she has suffered from them not for a few days but now for a long time, the scandal of deception and this persecution of evil persuasion. Hence it follows: “I have grown old among all my enemies.” It is as though she said: I am weary of hearing them, and disgusted at hearing their errors. Therefore she very fittingly adds:

“Depart from me, all you who work iniquity.” [Col. 0715A] For I now have nothing in common with you. “There is no agreement of Christ with Belial, no share,” says the Apostle, “for a believer with an unbeliever” (2 Cor. 6:15). “Because the Lord has heard the voice of my weeping.” This is what she said above: “I shall water my couch with my tears.” Yet she did not previously say, “the voice of my weeping.” For the voice of tears sounds more deeply and is heard more clearly by the Lord than the voice of tongue and mouth. Hence elsewhere it is said: “Let not the pupil of your eye be silent” (Lam. 2:18).

“The Lord has heard my supplication; the Lord has received my prayer.” When one and the same thing is repeated so often, it is done so that it may be believed more steadfastly and firmly.

“Let all my enemies be ashamed and greatly troubled; let them be turned backward and be greatly ashamed very quickly.” These words may be understood both in a good and in an evil sense. As in the preceding verse, so also in this verse the same thing is repeated more than once. Yet it seems to me that the holy Church desires the conversion of her enemies rather than their death. It may therefore be understood in a good sense thus: “Let them be ashamed,” because they have fought against truth; “and let them be troubled,” against themselves and their errors. “Let them be turned backward” from the falsehood that they follow, and return to the truth which they endeavour to destroy. “And let them be greatly ashamed very quickly.” For time is short; judgment is at hand. He who gave today did not promise an uncertain tomorrow: “It is the last hour” (1 John 2:18). “We are those upon whom the ends of the ages have come” [Col. 0715C] (1 Cor. 10:11).—“Watch therefore, because you know neither the day nor the hour” (Matt. 4:42).

## PSALM VII. A PSALM OF DAVID, WHICH HE SANG TO THE LORD CONCERNING THE WORDS OF CHUSHI, SON OF JEMINI.

Shimei, son of Jera, is recorded to have cursed King David (2 Kings [Samuel] 16:6) when he fled from the face of his son Absalom; and this Psalm is thought to have been composed concerning Shimei’s words. Thus, by a changed name, he is called Chushi, perhaps because Shimei has a good interpretation, whereas Chushi has a bad one. Chushi means “Ethiopian,” while Shimei means “hearing the Lord”; Jemini means “right hand.” He is rightly called Chushi, so that he may be believed foul in mind and body, since he did not hesitate to curse so great a king and prophet. He is called the son of Jemini in order that this may be set against him: that one so wicked should have been born of a good father. [Note: [Col. 0715D] Isidore interprets this title differently, and more clearly.]

“O Lord my God, in you I have hoped; deliver me from all who persecute me, and save me.” This is the voice of the Prophet himself and of all others who [Col. 0716A] possess the same perfection. Having their hope in God alone, such persons conquered and despised all their persecutors and enemies. Although they were at times killed, they were nevertheless victors, because no kind of torment could tear them away from the steadfastness of their faith. They attributed this strength not to their own powers but to God alone, who never abandons those who hope in him.

“Lest at any time he seize my soul like a lion, while there is none to redeem or save.” Our enemy, the devil, as it is written, “like a roaring lion goes about seeking whom he may devour” (1 Pet. 3:8). Only those who, hoping in the Lord, were delivered and saved by him could escape his teeth and snares. Hence he first said: “O Lord my God, [Col. 0716B] in you I have hoped.” Then, seeking the recompense of his hope, he added: “Deliver me, and rescue me, 311 O Lord my God, if I have done this thing”—that is, the thing which this black Chushi, this Ethiopian and enemy of truth, alleges against me. “If there is this iniquity in my hands,” which he says there is, “and if I have repaid evil to those repaying me,” as he falsely claims, “let me deservedly fall,” that is, as is fitting and just, “empty before my enemies.” These are the words of Shimei, whom David himself quite properly calls Chushi by a changed name: “Come out, come out, man of blood and man of Belial; the Lord has repaid you for all the blood of the house of Saul, because you seized the kingdom in his place” (2 Kings [Samuel] 16:7). [Note: [Col. 0715D] Saint Bruno presupposes the well-known history of Shimei son of Gera, of the kindred of Saul’s house, who followed Absalom’s party and became a rebel and enemy of David. This man reproached King David himself for having shed Absalom’s blood and, after killing him, seized the kingdom. Our commentator says that this is false, from the same Holy Scripture, 2 Kings [Samuel] 16, from which [Col. 0716D] this reproach or curse of Shimei, or Chushi, is taken. But when the prophet, imploring God for help, speaks concerning himself, he says that he did not repay evil to enemies hostile to him and pursuing him to death; therefore he hoped that divine assistance would never fail him. Saint Augustine teaches in this place that these words may be used by any perfected soul that does good to its enemies.] All who read and understand the histories of the Kings [Col. 0716C] recognize that this is false. “Empty” may mean one void of strength, courage, and every virtue. Thus this imprecation seems exceedingly severe, and David certainly would not have made it unless he knew with complete certainty that he spoke the truth. It continues still concerning the same imprecation:

“Let the enemy pursue my soul and seize it; let him trample my life upon the earth, and bring my glory down into the dust.” Namely, into that dust of which the Psalm says: “which the wind casts forth from the face of the earth” (Ps. 1:4). By it are understood the impious and sinners; whoever is associated with them shall have no glory at all. The life of one whose life is trampled upon on earth by the devil is that of one who, overcome by the devil’s wicked persuasions, seeks only earthly and transitory things. [Col. 0716D] It follows:

“Arise, O Lord, in your anger, and be exalted at the borders of your enemies.” Show, he says, your anger and indignation; show your patience and power in the land of your enemies. Even then the prophet saw and understood through the Holy Spirit, [Col. 0717A] as he wrote these things, what the curse which Shimei uttered against him signified. This is the curse of which the Lord himself says: “They shall curse, and you shall bless” (Ps. 108:18). Therefore Shimei, in cursing David, signified the Jewish people, who would utter this curse against our Lord and Savior, as though he had seized the Father’s kingdom and falsely declared himself the Son of God. Against them the Apostle speaks, saying: “He did not consider equality with God a robbery” (Phil. 2:6). These, then, are the enemies of whom the Prophet has just said: “Arise, O Lord, in your anger, and be exalted at the borders of your enemies.”

“Arise, O Lord God, in the commandment which you have commanded.” The Lord commanded the children of Israel to kill their enemies [Col. 0717B] and destroy them all utterly. He therefore asks that, in accordance with this commandment, the Lord also act against his own enemies: that he kill and destroy that ungrateful, impious, and treacherous people, and associate with himself in inheritance the people of the Gentiles, who are better. This is what follows: “And the synagogue of the peoples shall surround you.” The synagogue of the peoples is the Gentile people, which formerly indeed sat in darkness, but now, enlightened by Christ’s light, surrounds him as king and Lord, worships him, and venerates him.

“And therefore return on high.” For this reason our Lord and Savior both suffered, rose again, and ascended into heaven: for he would have done none of these things had he not loved the Church. He ascended, therefore, [Col. 0717C] in order to draw her to himself, as he himself says elsewhere: “When I am lifted up from the earth, I shall draw all things to myself” (John 12:32).—“Lord, judge the peoples.” Let them no longer have, he says, that judge and king whom they were accustomed to have; but judge altogether yourself, you who are a righteous judge and judge all things with equity. “Judge me, O Lord.” Judge me, he says, you who know the secrets of my heart; and make others understand that I am not such a man as Hushai said that I was. This will happen at the judgment, when the purity and innocence of this most blessed man will be revealed both to Saul himself and to all others. Judge, therefore—but how?

“According to my righteousness and according to the innocence of my hands, upon me.” Happy is the conscience [Col. 0717D] that bears such testimony concerning itself. But why did he say, “upon me”? For if our hands—by which, of course, we understand the bones of our hands—are innocent, they are certainly upon us. Our innocence, then, is greater than we ourselves; for without innocence we are miserable, but happy if we possess it.

“Let the wickedness of sinners be brought to an end, and direct the righteous man, O God who searches hearts and kidneys.” This may be understood thus: David himself speaks particularly of himself, asking that the wickedness of the sinners who at that time were persecuting him together with his son Absalom may be consumed and quickly ended; and that he himself, who is righteous [Col. 0718A] and innocent, may be guided to the helm of his kingdom. When he says, “God searches hearts and kidneys,” it is as though he said: You see all things; nothing is hidden from you; you know that what I say is true. God searches kidneys and hearts because he understands what we have in our heart and what is in the kidneys, where lust rules.

“Righteous help is from the Lord, who saves the upright in heart.” He says this in thanksgiving, as though already heard and restored by the Lord to his kingdom. The upright in heart are those who, turning neither to the right nor to the left, remain firm and steadfast in the truth. Their opposites appear to be those of whom it is said: “With heart and heart they spoke evil.”

[Col. 0718B] “God is a righteous, mighty, and longsuffering judge: is he angry every day? Unless you turn back, [Note: [Col. 0717D] Cassiodorus has the same reading.] he will brandish his bow.” The prophet proved this in his own case: God is a righteous judge, and therefore he said, “My righteous help is from the Lord.” Hence he says elsewhere that God “will render to each according to his works” (Ps. 61:13). He certainly would not do this if he were not a righteous judge. “And mighty” is appropriately added, so that, once judgment has been given, whether people wish it or not, they may abide by and keep what has been judged. But lest he should seem too strict and severe, he added, “and longsuffering”; for he does not punish immediately, but waits for sinners with great patience, because “he does not will the death of the sinner,” as the Prophet says, “but rather that he turn and live” (Ezek. [Col. 0718C] 33:11). Hence it follows: “Is he angry every day?” For if he were not longsuffering and patient, he would be angry every day—indeed, every hour and moment—because sinning is so frequent among us. Yet, although he is so gracious and patient, unless you turn back, there will be no further excuse—this is understood. For as he himself says: “If I had not come and spoken to them, they would not have sin; but now they have no excuse for their sins” (John 15:22). Hence it continues:

“He has brandished his sword.” This sword is understood as the divine utterance and evangelical preaching, of which it is said: “For the word of God is living and more piercing than any two-edged sword” (Heb. 4:12); [Col. 0718D] and elsewhere: “And the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God” (Eph. 6:17). The holy preachers are armed with such a sword, concerning whom it is said: “And two-edged swords are in their hands” (Ps. 149:6). The Lord will brandish this sword when he says to his disciples: “Go, teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit” (Matt. 28:19). What excuse, then, can there be? “Their sound has gone out into all the earth, and their words unto the end of the world” (Ps. 18:5).

“He stretched his bow and made it ready; and in it he prepared instruments of death; he made his arrows for the burning.” The same thing is signified both by the sword and by the bow. [Col. 0719A] Our Savior stretched and made ready this bow—that is, the teaching of the two Testaments—when he opened the book sealed with seven seals and gave his disciples understanding, that they might understand the Scriptures. [Note: [Col. 0719D] This kind of interpretation is entirely from Augustine. For he says: “I would gladly take that bow to be the Holy Scriptures, in which the hardness of the Old Testament has been bent and tamed by the strength of the New Testament, as by a kind of bowstring. From it the apostles are sent out as arrows, or divine proclamations are shot forth.” Cassiodorus commented thus.] The instruments of death which bear this bow are the apostles and teachers, of whom the blessed apostle Paul, himself a vessel of election, says: “To some we are an odor of life unto life; to others, an odor of death unto death” (2 Cor. 2:16). These archers slew vices and evil spirits, driving them from those dwelling-places with arrows kindled by the fire of the Holy Spirit. This is what he says: “He made his arrows for the burning.” These arrows are the sayings which the holy apostles and teachers uttered in their sermons. The Lord both made and gave these arrows to those who are [Col. 0719B] burning, so that, kindled with such fire, they might set others ablaze and kindle to God’s love all whom they touched. It follows:

“Behold, he travailed with injustice, conceived pain, and gave birth to iniquity.” This verse is connected with the place where it says: “Lest at any time he seize my soul like a lion.” What other fruit could the devil conceive or bring forth except injustice, pain, and iniquity? For he works this in human beings: that they may be unjust and wicked, and thereby bring them with himself to pain and to the miseries of every punishment. Such is his activity, such his teaching, and such the fruit of his teaching. Hence it continues:

[Col. 0719C] “He opened a pit and dug it, and fell into the hole which he made.” This pit is hell, which the devil himself both made and covered. Such is the work of that evil craftsman, who delights only in the construction of torments and places of torment. Nor does he cease daily to dig a pit—larger for some, smaller for others—preparing it according to what they deserve. But he too will fall into the pit he made, because eternal fire has been prepared for him and his angels. Then what follows will happen to him:

“His pain shall return upon his own head, and his iniquity shall come down upon his crown.” The more wicked he is than every creature, the greater is the punishment prepared for him. “But I,” says the Prophet, “will give thanks to the Lord and praise the Lord according to [Col. 0719D] his righteousness,” because he is so righteous that he is never separated from righteousness. “And I will sing praise to the name of the Lord Most High.”

313. PSALM VIII. UNTO THE END, FOR THE WINEPRESSES: A PSALM OF DAVID.

What “unto the end” signifies, and that it is called “a Psalm of David.” There are as many winepresses as there are churches, wherever they may be. In these winepresses that wine is made and offered for drinking by which all the saints, [Col. 0720A] made drunk, forget every earthly thing. Hence another psalm says: “They shall be made drunk with the abundance of your house, and you shall give them drink from the torrent of your delight” (Ps. 35:9). Those were drunk with this wine who, when speaking in all tongues, were thought to be mad. [Note: [Col. 0720D] St. Augustine holds the same view concerning the meaning of this title.]

“Lord, our Lord, how admirable is your name in all the earth.” Thus the intoxicated speak; thus speak those who have been found worthy to drink Christ’s blood. They rejoice that the name of the highest and eternal God is now praised and proclaimed not merely in Judea, as formerly, but among all nations everywhere; and that those who formerly worshipped many names of false gods now praise and proclaim the name [Col. 0720B] of the one and only true God.

“For your magnificence is raised above the heavens: out of the mouth of infants and sucklings you have perfected praise.” From the time when God’s magnificence was raised above the heavens, this name began to be admirable throughout all the earth. God’s magnificence is Christ: either because the Father has been magnified through the Son, or because the Son himself was made so great by the Father that every creature, both in heaven and on earth, is subjected to him. Hence it says below:

“You have subjected all things under his feet.” These statements—that he was raised above the heavens and made great—must be referred to his humanity. For how can the divinity, which is everywhere, either ascend or descend? The infants and [Col. 0720C] sucklings are those of whom the blessed Apostle Peter says: “Like newborn infants without guile, desire the rational milk, that by it you may grow unto salvation” (1 Pet. 2:2). By them, of course, the whole body of Christians is to be understood. For of such the Lord says: “Unless you are converted and become like little children, you shall not enter into the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. 18:3). And the Apostle says: “Do not become children in understanding; but be little children in malice” (1 Cor. 14:20).

“For your enemies, that you may destroy the enemy and defender.” From persons so pure, innocent, and devout, he says, you willed your praises to be proclaimed, so that, as formerly you overcame Pharaoh by the most contemptible animals, so now you might overcome all your [Col. 0720D] enemies through the simple and childlike. Enemies and defenders are those who defend error and falsehood by whatever arguments they can. Although this can apply to others as well, it must be understood especially of heretics.

“For I shall behold your heavens, the works of your fingers, the moon and stars which you have founded.” “For your magnificence,” he says, “is raised above the heavens.” [Col. 0721A] It remains, then, for us also to ascend there and behold the works of your fingers, the moon and stars which you have founded. For the Lord himself said: “Father, I will that where I am, they also may be with me” (John 17:24). By the moon and stars we understand, universally, the whole Church and, individually, each believer. These are the stars of which the Apostle says: “For star differs from star in glory; so also shall the resurrection of the dead be, because one is the glory of the moon and another the glory of the stars” (1 Cor. 15:42). The works of God’s fingers are called saints, formed by the grace of the Holy Spirit in such fullness that they shine like the sun in God’s kingdom. That the Holy Spirit is meant by God’s finger the Lord himself shows when he says: [Col. 0721B] “If I cast out demons by the finger of God, by what do your sons cast them out?” (Luke 11:20). We read that the magicians in Egypt also said of this finger: “This is the finger of God.” The Lord founded them, and founded them in his faith and in his Church in such a manner that they can by no means be torn away from it.

“What is man, that you are mindful of him, or the son of man [Note: [Col. 0721D] Augustine teaches that “man” and “son of man” do not express the same thing: in the first, the old and earthly human being is designated; in the second, the new and heavenly human being. Our commentator speaks only of the latter, taking the former as understood.], that you visit him? You made him a little lower than the angels; you crowned him with glory and honor, and established him over the works of your hands.” The Apostle teaches us in the Epistle to the Hebrews of what man we should understand this, saying: “We see Jesus, who was made a little lower than the angels because of the endurance of suffering” (Heb. 2:9). In wonder, therefore, he says, [Col. 0721C] “What is man, or the son of man?” who [Note: [Col. 0721D] The same Ghisian manuscript: “because.”] is so great and such that human speech cannot explain him. He shows that he is crowned because he fought and contended lawfully. “And you established him over the works of your hands”; and he explains this when he says:

314. “You have subjected all things beneath his feet: all sheep and oxen, and moreover the beasts of the field; the birds of heaven and the fish of the sea, which pass through the paths of the sea.” Of the sheep the Lord says in the Gospel: “My sheep hear my voice.” [Note: [Col. 0721D] The same Ghisian manuscript: “By whom, of course, the whole multitude of believers is understood.”] The oxen are bishops and teachers, by whom God’s field, which is the Church, is cultivated and ploughed. The beasts of the field may be understood as all those outside [Col. 0721D] the Church, of whom the historian says: “Who are like cattle, whom nature made bent forward [Note: [Col. 0721D] The same Ghisian manuscript: “Whom nature made bent forward.”] and obedient to the belly?” He therefore aptly says, “and moreover the beasts of the field,” because not only believers but also unbelievers, though unwillingly, are subject to Christ the Lord. But what should we understand by the birds [Col. 0722A] of heaven if not all angels, both good and evil? The fish of the sea seem to me to be the more powerful persons of this age, ever ready for prey, who traverse, surround, afflict, and possess this great and wide sea. All things worthy of remembrance are enumerated in these few words. It is plain, therefore, that all things are subject to him. [Note: [Col. 0722D] Bruno’s interpretation agrees perfectly with Augustine.] This psalm does not end, because it begins when it seems to end; and perhaps for this reason: God’s praises ought always to be sung and never ended. [Note: [Col. 0722D] In the Psalter of the Vatican Basilica, however, the first verse is repeated: “Lord, our Lord, how admirable is your name in all the earth!”]

PSALM IX. UNTO THE END, FOR THE HIDDEN THINGS OF THE SON: A PSALM OF DAVID.

The hidden things of the Son of God are those which he was unwilling to reveal in this life even to his own disciples. When the apostles once asked him, [Col. 0722B] saying, “Lord, will you at this time restore the kingdom to Israel?” (Acts 1:6), he answered: “It is not for you to know the times or seasons which the Father has placed in his own power” (ibid.). Hence he says elsewhere: “But of that day and hour no one knows, except the Father alone” (Matt. 24:36). This psalm is fittingly entitled “unto the end,” because what is said here must be referred to the consummation of the age and the times of Antichrist.

“I will give thanks to you, O Lord, with my whole heart; I will recount all your wonders.” The Church speaks and promises to praise God not merely with her lips but with her whole heart and all the affection of her mind, and to recount all his wonders, so that we too may learn how we ought to praise God. When she says, “I will recount all your wonders,” this must be qualified: all that can come to my knowledge.

“I will be glad and rejoice in you, and sing praise to your name, O Most High.” Let others, he says, rejoice and exult in worldly honors and dignities; for me it is enough to be able to please you alone and to praise and proclaim your name.

“When my enemy is turned backward.” What he says, “when he is turned,” is as though he said: While I turn my enemy backward, I shall be glad and rejoice in you. The devil could not be turned backward or put to flight by human strength [Col. 0722D] unless divine help were present in immediate aid. Hence it follows: “They shall be weakened and perish from your face.” [Note: [Col. 0722D] Both the Vulgate and the text in St. Augustine read: “They shall be weakened and perish from your face.” Cassiodorus reads in the same way, as does Bruno.] It is not human strength, but the face of God—which he cannot endure—that terrifies him so that he turns backward. He first said “enemy” in the singular; but to show that there are many thousands in his army, he added the plural, saying: “They shall be weakened and perish.”

“For you have maintained my judgment and my cause; you sit upon the throne, judging equity.” My enemy is conquered, he says; he is put to flight, weakened, and perishes because I have a just cause and you have judged a just judgment for me. This is what he means by saying: “You have made my judgment and cause just,” that is, you have judged them to be just. These words clearly show that our Lord is a righteous judge, who considers not persons but causes, and who does not repel even the devil from his action or accusation except by just judgment. This is what follows: “You sit upon the throne, judging equity.” It is unworthy, therefore, for someone to sit [Col. 0723B] in a judicial seat who neither judges nor understands equity.

“You rebuked the nations, and the wicked man perished.” For in the Gospel the Lord says that, when the Holy Spirit comes, “he will rebuke the world concerning sin” (John 16:8). The Lord therefore rebuked the nations through apostolic preaching, in which it was not the apostles themselves but the Holy Spirit who spoke, as the Lord himself had said: “For it is not you who speak, but the Holy Spirit who speaks in you” (Matt. 10:20).—“And the wicked man perished,” because then the devil first lost both kingdom and power; until that time he had held and possessed all nations in his power. “You have blotted out their name for ever and ever.” All 315 the names of false gods, which are comprised under this single name—for all the gods of the nations are demons—have now been erased, because there is no nation that now venerates and worships them.

“The swords of the enemy have failed unto the end.” Utterly and completely, he says, have the swords of this enemy of ours failed; by them we may understand tyrants and heretics. He says they have already failed because he knows without doubt that they will fail. It is a customary mode of speech to say that something has already happened when we confidently hope that it will certainly happen.

“And you have destroyed their cities.” Rome herself, which is the head of other cities, was once a city of gods; but that city which belonged to them has now been destroyed and is now together with them in torments. [Col. 0723D] But the city which now exists is not theirs but the city of the holy apostles and of God himself.

“Their memory perished with a sound.” Jericho thus perished: we read that its walls fell not by engines, battering-rams, or any assault, but by the sound of trumpets alone. Thus the memory of false gods perished with a sound, because, as the apostles preached, idols were broken and temples destroyed. “But the Lord remains for ever, and of his kingdom there shall be no end.”

[Col. 0724A] “He has prepared his seat in judgment.” God’s seats are the apostles; God’s seats are bishops and priests, in whom God sits and judges. For the judgment is not theirs but God’s, because the law by which they judge is not theirs but God’s. “And he himself shall judge the world in equity”: now indeed through these persons, but afterward in that universal judgment, both through himself and through them. “He shall judge the peoples with righteousness.”

“And the Lord has become a refuge for the poor”—namely, those poor of whom the Apostle says: “As having nothing, and possessing all things” (2 Cor. 6:10).

“A helper in due seasons, in tribulation.” By adding “in tribulation,” he explained what he meant by “in due seasons”; for we have the greatest need of God’s [Col. 0724B] help when we are in some tribulation.

“And let all who know your name hope in you,” because, he says, you are a helper and do not abandon your saints in tribulations. “Let all who seek your name hope in you”—“because you do not abandon those who seek you, O Lord.”

“Sing praise to the Lord who dwells in Zion.” Zion is interpreted “watchtower,” by which the Church is understood; its watchmen are bishops and teachers. Thus Ezekiel is told: “Son of man, I have appointed you a watchman over the house of Israel” (Ezek. 3:13).

“Declare his wonders among the nations.” This has already been said: “Their sound has gone out into all the earth,” the apostles’ sound, “and their words unto the ends of the world” (Ps. 18:5).

“For, seeking their blood, he remembered them, and did not forget [Note: [Col. 0723D] When it says “he remembered,” let no one suppose that forgetfulness befalls God; rather, the judgment will come after a long time. St. Augustine, *Exposition on Psalm 9*.] the prayer of the poor.” [Note: [Col. 0723D] Cassiodorus followed the same reading.] Declare it, he says, and do not fear, because they can kill the body but cannot kill the soul. The Lord does not forget those who die for his name: in requiring their blood, he punishes their adversaries and brings them into eternal blessedness.

“Have mercy upon me, O Lord, and see my humiliation from my enemies.” The Lord, he says, has not forgotten the prayers of the poor—understand, of those crying out and saying: “Have mercy upon me, O Lord, [Col. 0724D] and see my humiliation from my enemies,” from whom, by your command, I endure so many and such great things.

“You who lift me up from the gates of death, that I may declare your praises in the gates of the daughter of Zion.” The gates of death are heretics and all who draw human souls to death and destruction. [Note: [Col. 0724D] “The gate of death is the devil, or every worldly enticement, since through these one unhappily enters into eternal destruction.” Cassiodorus.] Such a gate was Simon Magus; such were Arius and Sabellius; such also were many others, through whose teaching and persuasion many souls perished. Tyrants too were gates of death, who by the terror of tortures caused many to deny the faith. [Col. 0725A] Delivered and raised up from these gates, the saints do not cease to declare God’s praises “in the gates of the daughter of Zion,” that is, in the hearing and ears of faithful souls. For ears too are gates through which the words of holy preaching enter the hearts of the faithful. [Note: [Col. 0725D] The same manuscript: “of hearers.”]

“And I will rejoice in your salvation.” I shall rejoice, he says, in my own salvation, which is temporal, only as much as in your salvation, which is eternal. He says this of the salvation of the soul, which, [Note: [Col. 0725D] The same manuscript: “because.”] delivered from the gates of death, is now secure and no longer fears death.

“The nations have been fixed fast in the destruction which they made; in this snare which they hid for me, their foot has been caught.” This is what is said elsewhere: “He who prepares a pit for his brother will himself fall into it first” (Eccles. 10:8). Those [Note: [Col. 0725D] The same manuscript: “For those who.”] who strive to deceive others are themselves without doubt deceived.

“The Lord shall be known, making judgments; the sinner has been caught in the works of his own hands.” At present, he says, the Lord is not known by the impious and sinners, nor does he yet display to them the power and severity of his strength; rather, he makes his sun rise upon them and waits for them with great patience. Yet he will be known when he comes to judgment and displays the glory of his majesty. Then the righteous person will rejoice when he sees vengeance, “because the sinner has been caught in the works of his own hands.” Then too this sentence will be pronounced against them, as the following verse declares:

“Let sinners be turned into hell, all [Col. 0725C] nations that forget the Lord.” If sinners were not now in hell, it would certainly say, “Let sinners be turned into hell.” But now they are indeed there, where, after the sentence has been heard, they will be cast down together with their bodies.

“For the poor shall not be forgotten unto the end; the patience of the poor shall not perish unto the end.” For what does not happen unto the end never happens. Therefore the patience of the righteous shall never perish, since it does not perish unto the end. It is plain, then, that sinners are condemned especially because they afflicted Christ’s poor, [Note: [Col. 0725D] From the same Ghisian manuscript.] whose memory will never perish. As the Prophet said these things and described the afflictions of martyrs and the persecutions of tyrants and heretics, it was divinely granted to him to see greater things: he saw Antichrist himself, the son of perdition, of whom it is written: “For he shall exalt himself and be lifted above all that is called God or is worshipped” (2 Thess. 2:4). Then there will be such tribulation as, the Lord himself says, “has never been nor shall be” (Matt. 24:20). Beholding this in the Spirit, terrified by the great affliction of the saints who will then be living, the Prophet cries out:

[Col. 0726A] “Arise, O Lord; let not man prevail; let the nations be judged in your sight.” Arise, O Lord, he says, to help your saints, because this man is so wicked [Note: [Col. 0725D] The same manuscript: “and such a great army of all the wicked follows him, that…”] that no one can resist him. [Note: [Col. 0726D] A prophecy concerning the coming of Antichrist and the great devastation he will inflict upon the Church. Augustine understood it likewise, and Cassiodorus with him.] For it is written of this son of perdition that he will draw many people after him and countless persons before him. What he says, “Let the nations be judged in your sight,” is as though he said: Come quickly to judgment, and let his days be shortened; for if this wicked man reigns long, all your saints will perish. This is what the Lord says: “Unless those days had been shortened, no flesh would be saved” (Matt. 24:22). For he will reign, as it is written, “for a time, times, and half a time” (Dan. 7:26), that is, no more than three and a half years.

[Col. 0726B] “Set, O Lord, a lawgiver over them, that the nations may know that they are human beings.” Arise, he says—as though he meant—to help your faithful, lest he perhaps prevail against them. Set that lawgiver over the nations who follow, worship, and adore him, so that at last they may know and understand that they are human beings who, abandoning you, worship this monster. For he too will be a lawgiver, because, just as Moses and our Savior did, he too will give his own law. When he says, “that they are human beings,” it is as though he had said that they are foolish and senseless. In this sense too the Apostle says: “When one says, ‘I am of Paul,’ another, ‘I am of Apollo,’ another, ‘I am of Cephas,’ are you not human beings?” (1 Cor. 1:12).

[Col. 0726C] “Why, O Lord, have you withdrawn far away? Do you disregard us in due seasons, in tribulation?” Arise, he says: why do you delay? Why have you withdrawn far from your servants? Why do you not help them in due seasons—that is, amid such great tribulations? For your help will never be more timely for them than now, when they suffer the persecution of so great an enemy. [Note: [Col. 0726D] The same Ghisian manuscript: “at any time.”]

“While the wicked man is proud, the poor man is burned.” He is proud and rages, he says; but the poor man—that is, the holy Church—destitute of all human help, is burned and tormented. It may also be understood thus: the more he is proud and rages, the more she is kindled and inflamed in the love of God.

“They are caught in the thoughts which they devise.” His malice, he says, will not remain hidden long; the wickedness [Col. 0726D] of his heart will not long be concealed. Rather, he himself and all his disciples who are with him, conscious of the same iniquity and malice, will soon be caught and confounded. Of them the Lord says in the Gospel: “For many false Christs and false prophets shall arise and give many signs and wonders, so that, if it were possible, even the elect would be led into error” (Matt. 24:24). From here to the end of the psalm he writes the life and history of Antichrist himself.

[Col. 0727A] “For the sinner is praised in the desires of his soul, and he who commits iniquity is blessed.” Nothing moves and incites impious and wicked people more strongly to practice iniquity than flatterers who praise and extol their deeds. [Note: [Col. 0727D] The same manuscript: “wicked.”] [Note: [Col. 0727D] “When an evil person is praised, he is exalted and does not think of correction when he finds a flattering admirer.” Cassiodorus.] Hence it happens that they never return to repentance or cease from their perversity.

“The sinner provoked the Lord.” What does “provoked” mean except that he stirred and incited him against himself to immense wrath and indignation, so that God might destroy him by a harsh death and require and avenge the blood of the saints which he had cruelly shed? Hence it continues: “According to the multitude of his wrath, will he not inquire?” This 317 must be read as a question, as though he said: Shall the Lord, [Col. 0727B] thus provoked and stirred to such anger, not inquire according to the multitude of his wrath—namely, as we have just said, into that man’s destruction and the vengeance of his poor? Hence he says below: “Why has the wicked man provoked God? For he said in his heart, ‘There is no God.’”

“God is not before his eyes; his ways are defiled at all times. Your judgments are taken away from before him.” All God’s judgments are true and just. They are said to be removed from before his face because he will neither judge justly nor fear God’s just judgments. Had he feared them, he would not have raised himself to such great cruelty and pride.

“He shall rule over all his enemies.” Whom else should we understand as his enemies but the saints? Antichrist will rule over them in one sense, and in another sense he will not rule over them. He will rule because he will hold them in his power so as to torture and afflict them according to his will. But he will not rule because he will not be able to draw them into consenting to his perverse will.

“For he said in his heart: ‘I shall not be moved from generation to generation, without evil.’” Anyone can readily recognize how wicked and impious he is from the fact that he always delights in evil with such desire. From generation to generation, from place to place, he threatens that he will not pass without evil and without the destruction of souls.

“His mouth is full of cursing and bitterness [Col. 0727D] and deceit.” This Antichrist is rightly so called, because he is in every respect contrary to Christ. Of Christ the same Prophet says elsewhere: “How sweet are your words to my palate, O Lord, above honey and the honeycomb” (Ps. 118:103). But of this one, by contrast, he says that his foul mouth is full of cursing and blasphemies, bitterness and deceit.

“Under his tongue are labor and pain; he sits in ambush with the rich in hidden places, that he may kill the innocent.” The words beneath his tongue, he says, will bring the souls of his hearers to [Col. 0728A] labor, pain, and utmost misery. He is said to sit in ambush together with the rich of this world, who love only earthly and transitory things, whom he has deceived and enriched with his gifts, “that he may kill the innocent”—that is, overthrow and destroy the devout and holy soul by his wicked persuasions. [Note: [Col. 0728D] To kill the innocent is to make a sacrilegious person out of a devout one and condemn that person’s soul to everlasting death. Cassiodorus, whose interpretation Bruno generally followed.] He aptly adds “in hidden places,” because he will be more deceitful and cunning than all other people.

“His eyes look upon the poor,” not, of course, to show mercy, but to destroy and deceive. Hence it continues: “He lies in ambush in secret, like a lion in his den.” But for what does he lie in ambush? “He lies in ambush,” it says, “to seize the poor.” And what is it to seize the poor? It is to draw him and associate him with the error of his own [Col. 0728B] perversity. When he has done this, “he shall humble him in his snare,” because he will hold him thus captured and subjugated as his own slave. Wretched and altogether unhappy is the man who does not see the evils soon to come upon him, of which it now says: “He shall bend down and fall when he rules over the poor.” For he is the one whom, as the Apostle says, “the Lord Jesus shall kill with the spirit of his mouth and destroy by the brightness of his coming” (2 Thess. 2:8). And because he has exalted himself beyond measure, he will be humbled below the rest and cast down into punishments. “For everyone who exalts himself,” says the Lord, “shall be humbled, and whoever humbles himself shall be exalted” (Luke 14:11).

“For he said in his heart: ‘God has forgotten; he has turned away [Col. 0728C] his face, so that he may not see unto the end.’” While this wicked man, this most cruel son of perdition, slew God’s saints with refined tortures, he most foolishly thought in his heart that the Lord had wholly and permanently forgotten them because he did not immediately avenge them.

“Arise, O Lord my God, and let your hand be lifted up; do not forget the poor unto the end.” Arise, he says, to help your saints; let your hand—your strength and power—be raised over them, and do not forget the poor unto the end, as they maliciously suppose. For what does not happen unto the end never happens; and the saints’ end will never come.

“Why has the wicked provoked God?” This is an insult directed against him whom the Prophet already beholds, through the Holy Spirit, as having fallen so miserably into that deepest pit of torments. And he adds why this happened to him, saying: “For he said in his heart, God will not require it.” It is therefore a great sin not only to say, but even to think, something perverse concerning God’s justice.

“You see that you consider toil and pain, that you may deliver them into your hands.” You do not, he says, ever forget, but always see and, with fatherly compassion, consider the toil and pain which your saints suffer for your name, so that you may deliver and present them to the Father in your own hands. For the Apostle speaks of this handing-over when he says that then all things will be subject to him, when he has handed over the kingdom to God and the Father (1 Cor. 15:24).

“To you the poor man has been left; you will be a helper to the orphan.” From the time, he says, when the poor man left behind his former father, the devil, and, regenerated through water and the Holy Spirit, became your son, he has always clung to you alone; left to you alone, he has had no other guardian or defender. That the devil is the father of all wicked persons and of those not yet baptized, the Lord himself shows when he says: “You are of your father the devil, and you do the works of your father” [Col. 0729B] (John 8:44). To such persons the Apostle says: “You were once darkness, but now you are light in the Lord; walk as children of light” (Eph. 5:10). And the Apostle John says: “But as many as received him, he gave them power to become children of God, to those who believe in his name” (John 1:12). Therefore those who were formerly children of the devil are now children of God. They are called *pupilli*, that is, orphans—as another translation has it—either because their first father died to them, or because, while still pilgrims in this life, they have not yet been joined to God the Father in that blessedness. Hence the Lord said to his disciples: “I will not leave you orphans; I will come to you” (John 14:18). They would indeed have been orphans solely through his absence, if the Lord had not come to them.

[Col. 0729C] “You will break the arm of the sinner and of the malicious man.” Just as the Son is called the arm of the Father, of whom it is said through the prophet: “And to whom has the arm of the Lord been revealed?” (Isa. 53:1), so Antichrist is called the arm of the devil, because the devil works and fights in him and through him. His breaking and destruction have already been sufficiently discussed above.

“His sin will be sought out, and it will not be found.” The devil’s sin is pride; for he is recorded to have said in his heart: “I will ascend above heaven, and I will be like the Most High” (Isa. 14:13). For by pride Antichrist too is raised and exalted above everything called God or worshipped. But if this be sought after Antichrist’s death, in Christ’s kingdom, which is the Church, it will not be found. From this [Col. 0729D] we are given to understand that those who will then be living will serve the Lord in fear and trembling, and especially in humility. Hence it is written that “in his days Judah will be saved” (Jer. 33:16), and that “when the fullness of the Gentiles has entered, then Israel will be saved” (Rom. 11:25). For who would then dare to be proud, when he knows that Antichrist has been condemned for his pride and that the day of judgment is at hand?

“The Lord has reigned for ever and ever [Col. 0730A]; and, as it is written, there will be no end of his kingdom” (Luke 1:34). But you, nations, who have been condemned together with Antichrist, will perish from his land—that is, from the land of the living—because you will not enter it. “The Lord has heard the desire of the poor; your ear has heard the desires of their heart.” It is characteristic of prophets to put past tenses for future events, because they behold things still to come as though already past. The desire of the poor—that is, of the saints who will live in Antichrist’s time—will be that he may be condemned and judged as he deserves, and that God’s saints, delivered from his snares, may be brought into eternal blessedness. It should be understood that desire is not in the mouth but in the heart. God therefore looks to the heart and hears the heart’s desires rather than [Col. 0730B] the mouth’s prayers. The following words make clear when this desire of the saints is heard:

“To judge for the orphan and the humble.” When he comes, he says, to judge for the orphan and the humble, then the saints will receive according to their desires. To judge for the orphan is to show forth and proclaim the justice of the orphan’s cause. These things that have been said concerning Antichrist’s most righteous condemnation and destruction have been spoken and written so “that man may no longer set himself to magnify himself upon the earth,” lest things like those which he heard had happened to the one whom he did not fear to imitate should also happen to him.

## PSALM X. FOR THE END. A PSALM OF DAVID

> [Note: “[The] end always tends toward Christ; but at one time it signifies his Passion, at another his Resurrection. Here, however, it declares the holy faith, in which heretics contend against the most faithful Christians. It should therefore be understood that this psalm was set forth for the destruction of heretics.” Bede.]

This title has already been sufficiently explained above. It is repeated so often in order that all the psalms may be believed to be by the same author.

“In the Lord I trust; how do you say to my soul, ‘Migrate to the mountain like a sparrow’?”

> [Note: [Col. 0730D] “For this speech is directed to the persuading heretics, who desire to speak what is impious, so as to lead innocent souls astray by perverse disputes.” Cassiodorus.]

The Church speaks against the heretics, already wearied by their persuasions and arguments: “I trust in the Lord,” she says, “and therefore I make little of your counsels, which are received only by those who do not trust in the Lord. How then do you say to my soul: ‘Migrate to the mountain like a sparrow’?” Neither are you mountains, nor are we sparrows according to your understanding: you call yourselves mountains in exalting yourselves, and us sparrows in humbling us. Yet you too are mountains, swollen with the puffing-up of pride—

> [Note: [Col. 0730D] The same manuscript: “swollen.”]

—namely the mountains of Gilboa, which David once cursed. We too are sparrows, delivered from the hunters’ snare, by which snare your ambushes are signified. Hence elsewhere it is said: “The sparrow has found herself a house” (Ps. 13:4). Thus heretics reckon Catholic men to be sparrows by comparison with themselves; and our Savior himself showed them to be of little value when he said: “Are not two sparrows sold for an *as*?” (Matt. 10:29).

[Col. 0731A] “For behold, sinners have bent the bow; they have prepared their arrows in the quiver, to shoot in the dark at the upright in heart.” Holy Church directs the words of her address to the Lord himself and complains of the considerable persecution by heretics, saying: “You see, Lord, and know that these heretics against whom we speak, these sinners, have bent the bow.” Every false and heretical composition of the heretics, whether written or unwritten, is their bow, by which they kill the souls of the saints. Their quiver, however, is to be understood as their hearts, in which they keep the propositions of their deception gathered and ready like arrows, so that, when an occasion arises, they may deceitfully shoot at and wound the upright in heart in the dark.

[Col. 0731B] “For they have destroyed what you perfected.” This too, he says, is not hidden from you; rather, it is quite manifest to you that the holy and Catholic understanding which you taught us and perfected within us has now almost been destroyed. Thus their perverse doctrine signifies that very many have been deceived.

> [Note: [Col. 0731D] This is said hyperbolically, to signify the overthrow of many.]

We know that this happened in the time of Arius, who overturned almost the whole world and compelled it to pass over into his error. “But what has the righteous man done?” What follows is:

“He rains snares upon sinners.” For this is the order of the text. But let us first explain the passages inserted between; afterward we shall consider both this and what follows.

“The Lord is in his holy temple; the Lord’s throne is in heaven [Col. 0731C].” When the saints said these words, “The Lord is in his holy temple”—by which, indeed, we understand the saints themselves—“the Lord is in heaven, where his throne is,” this itself signifies that he considered and pondered these same matters in their hearts. Hence the Apostle says: “For we do not know what we should pray for; but the Holy Spirit prays for us with unutterable groanings” (Rom. 8:26). It is quite certain that the saints are called both God’s temple and God’s throne.

“His eyes look upon the poor.” For he would not look upon him if he did not love him. Thus it is written: “Because the Lord looked upon Peter” (Luke 22:61). His eyes therefore look upon the poor, that he may always have mercy on him, always guard him, and direct and order all his [Col. 0731D] thoughts and deeds.

“His eyelids examine the children of men.” By a glance alone, therefore, he knows all things; opening his eyes, he sees all things; and there is nothing that can be hidden from his examination—that is, from his penetrating inquiry.

“The Lord examines the righteous and the wicked.” The Lord, he says, examines both the righteous and the wicked; and it becomes known because the conscience of each answers him, and whatever lies hidden within them is disclosed to him as he examines and searches.

“But he who loves iniquity hates his own soul [Col. 0732A].” This is the definition of the wicked person. He is, as though the text said, wicked who loves iniquity and hates his own soul. Both seem very wicked: both loving iniquity and hating one’s own soul. Indeed, it is worse to love iniquity than to commit iniquity, just as it is a lesser evil to sin sometimes than to persist in sin.

“He rains snares upon sinners.” As we said above, this verse is joined to the place where it says: “But what has the righteous man done?” For in saying it beautifully, it shows a great abundance of snares. As many as sins are, so many are the snares by which sinners are caught and entangled. For the wicked man will be held fast by the cords of his own sins. He who has committed more and greater sins will therefore be held and bound by more [Col. 0732B] snares. “Fire, sulphur, and the spirit of storms are the portion of their cup” (Ps. 10:6). This is the cup of God’s wrath and fury, by which sinners will be made drunk and by which death itself and the torments of every punishment are signified. But if the things enumerated here are not the whole cup but only a part of the cup, many other and perhaps harsher torments still await them. Concerning fire, moreover, it is written in the Gospel that it is eternal and unquenchable. We may understand that those who have languished in luxury and fleshly pleasures will be punished in sulphur. But in the spirit of storms those will perish who, disturbing the holy Church, never wished to rest or to have peace. And because they themselves were like a stormy tempest in this [Col. 0732C] life, it is fitting that they too should always be driven and overwhelmed by the spirit of storms.

“For the Lord is righteous; he has loved justice; his face has seen equity.” The Lord has examined both the righteous and the wicked; and because he is righteous and loves justice, he grants to each according to his works, in accordance with what equity requires.

## PSALM XI. FOR THE END, FOR THE EIGHTH. A PSALM OF DAVID

This whole title has already been explained above; there is no need to explain it again.

“Save me, O Lord, for the holy man has failed; for truths have been diminished from among the children of men.” This is the voice of the righteous, before Christ’s incarnation, longing for [Col. 0732D] his coming. There was a time when not only Gentiles but also Jews, who were called the people of God, worshipped idols, adored demons, sought vanity, and all alike departed from the truth. Thus, when holiness and truth had failed everywhere and there was nowhere from which he could hope for help from God, the righteous man rightly cries out: “Save me, O Lord, for the holy man has failed.”

“They have spoken vain things, each one to his neighbour.” Each one, he says—Jew or Gentile—has spoken vain things to his neighbour. We must understand “neighbour” not so much by kinship as [Col. 0733A] by wickedness. For those who are neighbours in this way continually exhort one another in turn toward vanity and folly, having “deceitful lips in heart, and with a double heart they have spoken evil.” And what is said of the saints? “In all of them there was one heart and one soul” (Acts 4:32). But these, by contrast, are said all to have not one heart, but double hearts: double, indeed, because changeable and established by no constancy of truth.

“The Lord will destroy all deceitful lips, and the tongue that speaks great things”—that is, of those who said: “We will magnify our tongue; our lips are our own; who is lord over us?” At every time there have been such people, who, magnifying their tongue and knowledge, did not fear to sow errors. This is what the Gentile philosophers did, who were regarded as wiser within the people. Since they erred in everything relating to the worship of God, they did not all give one and the same teaching, but individually offered separate and diverse opinions of their own error. These, therefore, could say: “We will magnify our tongue” and our knowledge; our opinions are from ourselves, and we have received them from no other source. For who is our teacher and lord, to whom we ought to ascribe the things that we speak and know? The Apostle therefore rightly says that “the Lord has made foolish the wisdom of this world” (1 Cor. 1:20). For we also read that there were many heretics among the Jews, such as the Sadducees, who denied the resurrection; our Savior himself deigned to destroy their impious heresy with most certain [Col. 0733C] arguments. There is no doubt that this heresy descended from the philosophers.

“Because of the misery of the needy and the groaning of the poor, now I will arise, says the Lord.” This is the Lord’s reply to those who say at the beginning of this psalm: “Save me, O Lord.” “Now,” he says, “I will arise to help, and I will deliver the needy and poor from the devil’s power and from such great errors.” He makes known below how and through whom he will perform this aid of his goodness:

“I will set him upon my salvation; I will act confidently in him.”

> [Note: [Col. 0733D] “The Father calls his Word his salvation; it was made flesh, through which life came to mortals, while every believer attains it by abundant bounty.” Cassiodorus.]

God’s salvation is Christ, through whom the Lord worked this great salvation. Of this salvation [Col. 0733D] it is surely said in another psalm: “The Lord has made known his salvation” (Ps. 97:2). And the patriarch Jacob says of it: “I will await your salvation, O Lord” (Gen. 49:18). He says well, “I will act confidently in him,” because when such a great and such a leader fights before us, there is no danger; for it is written of him: “The Lord is strong and mighty, the Lord mighty in battle” (Ps. 23:8).

“The words of the Lord are chaste words.” Behold, the Prophet says, you have heard the words and promise of God. Therefore believe most firmly and do not doubt at all that what he has promised he will undoubtedly fulfil. Why so? Because his words are chaste and true, and he can in no way lie.

“Silver tried in the fire, purified from earth sevenfold.” The Lord’s words, he says, are of such a kind: so pure, so chaste, so true, and uncorrupted by any falsehood, like silver tried by fire. “Purified from earth sevenfold” is understood to mean that it is smelted so thoroughly until it is cleansed of every earthly impurity. Hence the number of perfection is used, in which all numbers are contained. What is therefore purified seven times needs no purification.

“You, O Lord, will preserve us and guard us from this generation for ever.” This is the voice of those who were granted to see Christ in the flesh. It is as though he said: “Behold, you have come; the Father’s promise and the words of the prophets have been fulfilled. We now fear nothing, because you will preserve and guard us from this present time unto eternity.” But what will happen to the wicked? It follows:

“The wicked walk in a circle.” They do not proceed, he says, on the straight path, but wander in a circle and cannot find the end and boundary of truth.

“According to your height you have multiplied the children of men.” It is as though he said: “If these always walk in a circle and do not know the way of truth, why have they multiplied so greatly? Why do they abound in all the good things of this life?” To this he replies: “This mystery is high, unsearchable, and calls for deeper inquiry.” This question concerning the misfortune of the good and the prosperity of the wicked is found in many places in Holy Scripture.

> [Note: [Col. 0734D] On this, St Augustine treats in *The City of God*, book 5, chapters 15 and 16.]

It can also be understood in this way: the number of the saints is to be multiplied according to the number of those who inhabit the height of heaven. Hence it is written: “He established the boundaries of the nations according to the number of the angels” (Deut. 32:8).

> [Note: [Col. 0734D] The Vulgate reads: “*Co*[lacuna]*lorum* (‘of the heavens’), according to the number of *filio*[lacuna] (‘children …’).”]

## PSALM XII. FOR THE END. A PSALM OF DAVID

This title has already been explained above.

“How long, O Lord, will you forget me unto the end? How long will you turn your face away from me?” This is the voice of the Prophet and of others awaiting Christ’s birth and the day of their redemption with great longing. [Col. 0734D] Of them the Lord himself says: “Many kings and prophets desired to see what you see, and did not see it; and to hear what you hear, and did not hear it” (Luke 10:24). These therefore complain that for so long a time the Lord had forgotten them, had been angry with them, and had turned his face from them, and that at last he had not visited them through the incarnation of his Son.

“How long shall I lay up counsels in my soul, pain in my heart by day?” My own counsel, he says, does not suffice for me; the counsel of [Col. 0735A] my soul does not suffice for me. Let that angel of great counsel come now; let him come, I pray, “that wonderful counsellor, father of the age to come, prince of peace” (Isa. 9:7), and take away this pain from my heart, which I bear by day—that is, on every day, or rather through longing for that day and light, by the brightness of whose coming I trust that I shall be enlightened.

“How long will my enemy be exalted over me? Look upon me and hear me, O Lord my God.” Do not, he says, turn your face further from me; but look upon me now and hear me, so that my enemy may no longer be exalted over me.

“Enlighten my eyes, lest I ever sleep in death.” Enlighten, he says, my eyes; enlighten the eyes of my mind. Send us your most bright [Col. 0735B] light, which enlightens every human being coming into this world; send us your Son, by whose blood death itself may die and original sin may be blotted out. For this is what the saints especially feared: that they might perish by the death of that sin.

“Lest at any time my enemy say, ‘I have prevailed against him.’” The enemy prevails over, and glories in the destruction of, those who either have not yet been delivered from original sin or die without repentance in more grievous sins.

“Those who trouble me will rejoice if I am shaken.” For this is the joy and exultation of malicious spirits: that righteous men may be shaken, separated from God, from faith, from truth, from justice, and from every good thing.

[Col. 0735C] “But I will hope in your mercy.” For there is nothing other than God’s mercy alone that can deliver us from their snares.

“My heart will rejoice in your salvation.” Behold, he says, I have what I desired, sought, and awaited for so long: namely, your salvation, Jesus Christ your Son. Henceforth my heart will be glad, rejoice, and exult in your salvation.

“I will sing to the Lord, who has bestowed good things upon me, and I will sing psalms to the name of the Most High Lord.” Whom should we understand by “the Most High” except God the Father? This speaker rightly promises to sing and make psalmody to him, because in the coming of his Son he has bestowed every good thing that can be desired or hoped for.

## PSALM XIII. FOR THE END. A PSALM OF DAVID

[Col. 0735D]

We have often said already what “for the end” signifies and what “a Psalm of David” signifies.

> [Note: [Col. 0735D] “The Church of Christ condemns the madness of the Jews; the face of the Lord that was sought in Psalm VII is here said already to have come. Thus, in the first manner, the Church rebukes the Jews, who by no means believed when they saw Christ: ‘The fool said.’ In the second manner, it says that those who refused to know the fruitful fear of the Lord are confounded by empty dread: [Col. 0736D] ‘Will not all who work iniquity know?’ Finally, their conversion at the end is foretold: ‘when the Lord has turned back.’” Bede.]

“The fool said in his heart, ‘There is no God’; they have become corrupt and abominable in their desires.” The Church speaks and rebukes the Jewish people, who, concerning our Lord and Savior, because he appeared humble and in the form of God, like a foolish and senseless person who did not understand the divine Scriptures, [Col. 0736A] “said, ‘There is no God.’” Hence they became corrupt, not holding to the faith and truth of the patriarchs and prophets; and they became abominable to God and to human beings in their perverse desires.

“There is none who does good; there is not even one.” There is none, he says, among that people; indeed, neither among another people nor among all others is there one who does good. Because they do not have faith, none of their works is reckoned good to them.

> [Note: [Col. 0736D] It should be observed that St Bruno does not teach that unbelievers perform no good at all, but that nothing is reckoned to them for merit, since they lack faith, which is the beginning of merit.]

For “without faith it is impossible to please God” (Heb. 11:6). But when he says, “not even one,” this is understood of those for whom there is one God, one faith, one baptism, and, as the Apostle says, one heart and one soul.

“The Lord looked down from heaven upon the children of men [Col. 0736B] to see whether there is one who understands or seeks God.” And what sort did he find them? It follows: “All have turned aside; together they have become useless.” It has therefore been established by divine authority that there is none who does good, not even one. They all turned aside together because, departing from truth, they all alike passed over to error. Thus they became useless, because they do what is useful neither to God nor to themselves.

“Their throat is an open tomb; with their tongues they acted deceitfully; the poison of asps is under their lips.” It does not suffice for them, he says, that they do not do good; rather, to add to their condemnation, they perform evil in every way they can. Their mouth is an open tomb because, for their hearers, they are a stench of death unto death, just as the Apostles are an odor of life unto life. Hence he rightly adds: “With their tongues they acted deceitfully; the poison of asps is under their lips.” The poison of asps is incurable. Therefore those who believe and hold their teaching are wounded in such a way that they cannot be healed.

“Their mouth is full of cursing and bitterness; their feet are swift to shed blood. Destruction and misery are in their ways, and they have not known the way of peace.” In saying, “they have not known the way of peace,” he shows that all these things are to be understood not of Jews alone but of all who are outside the Church and do not have Christ’s faith. For what is the way of peace except our Savior, [Col. 0736D] who is called both peace and way? “For he himself is our peace, who made both one” (Eph. 2:14); he himself is “the way, the truth, and the life” (John 14:6).

“There is no fear of the Lord before their eyes.” Because all these people of whom we spoke above have not known the way of peace, there is no fear of God before their eyes; and for this reason they are not ashamed to do evil and take no care to do good. It follows: “Will not all those [Col. 0737A] who work iniquity know, and who devour my people like food for bread,” and those who “did not call upon God, there trembled with fear where there was no fear”?

“For God is in the righteous generation,” which they strive so greatly to afflict and destroy. By those who work iniquity we may understand all wicked people, whether Jews or Gentiles. But by those who devour God’s people like food for bread, tyrants and heretics are particularly signified. Of such it is written: “For they ate Jacob and laid waste his place” (Ps. 78:7). How greedily they destroy God’s saints both in soul and body is clearly shown by his saying that they devour God’s people as food for bread. But by those who “there [Col. 0737B] trembled with fear where there was no fear,” we understand properly the Jews, who, conspiring against our Savior, said: “If we let him go on thus, the Romans will come and take away our place and nation” (John 11:48). Of them he rightly adds: “You have confounded the counsel of the poor man, because the Lord is his hope.” This is the poor man of whom the Apostle says: “Though he was rich in all things, for our sake he became poor” (2 Cor. 8:9). Miserable Jews despised, condemned, and refused to receive his counsel; rather, mocking him, they said: “He trusted in God; let him now deliver him if he wishes” (Matt. 27:43). This is what is meant by: “Because the Lord is his hope.”

[Col. 0737C] “Who will give salvation to Israel from Zion, when the Lord turns back the captivity of his people?” Who, he says, unhappy Jews, will give salvation to Israel, coming from Zion as your helper and defender, as your prophets testify? For thus it is written in the books of the prophets: “From Zion will come the one who removes Jacob’s captivity” (Rom. 11:26); and by him we understand none other than Christ. The Jews, therefore, are deceived in expecting Antichrist, whom they call Messiah.

“Let Jacob rejoice, and Israel exult.” If this is understood literally, it appears to have been said ironically, because not joy and exultation but great disaster and sorrow await them. But if it is understood of that part of the people which believed in Christ, or if Jacob and Israel are taken in a particular sense, the interpretation is clear.

> [Note: [Col. 0737D] “Jacob will rejoice, who received a medicine not set apart [from others]. Israel—that is, he will be consoled with inexpressible joy—will exult when he sees in reality what he most ardently desired in hope.” Cassiodorus.]

## PSALM XIV. A PSALM OF DAVID

Because “for the end” is not placed in this title, these words are referred to David himself, who writes them. And [Col. 0738A] in this psalm he questions God and is granted to receive God’s answer.

“Lord, who will dwell in your tabernacle?

> [Note: [Col. 0737D] Cassiodorus, teaching the etymology of *tabernaculum*, says that the ancients called the houses of the poor *tabernae*, because they were covered only with beams and not with tiles, and were therefore called *tabernae*. Since people dwelt and dined there, and it was ancient custom to take food once, one word is said to have been formed from two names. Hence we understand *tabernacula* correspondingly as temporary and improvised dwellings for an expedition. Therefore the Lord commanded a tabernacle to be made for himself, as a divine house within the camps of the Hebrews, moving with them.]

—or who will rest upon your holy mountain?” The Prophet speaks; indeed, the Lord himself speaks in the Prophet, as he says elsewhere: “I will hear what the Lord God speaks in me” (Ps. 84:9). He says these things for our instruction, so that, as the Lord answers, we may understand what we ought to do and hold fast, and what we ought to flee and heed.

“He who walks without stain and works righteousness.” For who is without stain except that one alone “who committed no sin, nor was deceit found in his mouth” (1 Pet. 2:22)? But how shall we understand also the saying, “At whatever hour the sinner is converted [Col. 0738B], I will not remember any of his iniquities” (Ezek. 33:16)? We should understand that such people enter without stain because, whatever they may formerly have been, once turned to repentance they do not persist in sins. He rightly adds, “and works righteousness,” because it is not enough to abstain from evil unless we do good. Hence: “Turn away from evil and do good” (Ps. 36:27).

“He who speaks truth in his heart and has not dealt deceitfully with his tongue.” This means that we should not speak one thing in the heart and another with the tongue, but should hold in the heart what the tongue utters.

“He has done no evil to his neighbour.” This is [Col. 0738C] what the Lord says in the Gospel: “What you do not wish for yourself, do not do to another” (Matt. 7:12). But what if he did it and afterward made satisfaction and did penance?
