Yet we must always keep in mind what the Apostle says to those persisting in evil: “According to your hardness and unrepentant heart you store up wrath for yourself on the day of the revelation of God’s righteous judgment” (Rom. 2:5). By this sentence many matters that seem very difficult may be determined.

“And he has not accepted reproach against his neighbour.” What does “has not accepted” mean? He did not find it pleasing, agreeable, or acceptable; but if he did it, he repented of having done it. For there are some, as it is written, “who rejoice when they have done evil and exult in the worst deeds” (Prov. 2:14).

[Col. 0738D] “The malicious man has been brought to nothing in his sight.” In accordance with customary usage, he has used the past tense for the future. The wicked man—that is, the devil, head of all the wicked, with all his army—will, at God’s command and under his gaze, be led to nothingness, to death and destruction, on the day of judgment. Then what follows will occur: “But he magnifies those who fear the Lord.” [Col. 0739A] Then the Lord will magnify and glorify his saints and exalt them above the heavens. Having inserted this verse, he returns to the matter of which he had begun to speak.

“He who swears to his neighbour and does not deceive him.” Every promise of the saints, if it is good, ought to be firm and stable like an oath; and although every oath is evil, that which is made for the sake of deception is the worst.

“He has not given his money at interest.” Even according to the letter this is a great sin, because in such conduct charity perishes and the poor are stripped of their possessions. Yet it can also be understood of those who do not freely give what they have freely received, and of those who do all their works in order to be seen by human beings. “And he has not accepted gifts against the innocent.” Let judges hear this; let the powerful of this world hear it, who often, after accepting gifts, afflict innocent persons.

“He who does these things will not be shaken for ever.” He who does these things enumerated above will dwell in God’s tabernacle and, resting upon his holy mountain, will not be shaken for ever.

## PSALM XV. AN INSCRIPTION OF A TITLE, FOR DAVID HIMSELF

It speaks of that title-inscription made in Hebrew, Greek, and Latin letters and placed above the head of our Savior as he hung upon the cross. That inscription contained: “Jesus [Col. 0739C] of Nazareth, King of the Jews.” When it says “for David himself,” it shows that all the things said in this psalm are to be referred to Christ the Lord himself, truly strong of hand.

“324 Preserve me, O Lord, for I have hoped in you.” — “Just as the rational soul and flesh are one human being, so God and man are one Christ” (*Athanasian Creed*). Whenever, therefore, our Savior asks something, whenever he asks to be preserved, aided, or delivered, whenever he says that he hopes or trusts in God, or says anything similar, nothing is to be referred to his divinity, but everything to his humanity. For Christ’s divinity, by which he is in all things equal and like to the Father, lacks nothing. Let Christ the Lord therefore say, not according to his divinity but according to his humanity: [Col. 0739D] “Preserve me, O Lord, for I have hoped in you.” He to whom he spoke was near; he in whom he hoped was present. His humanity asks his divinity, not terrified by fear, since it was upheld by so great a help, but speaking thus in order to show himself truly human: “I said, You are my Lord.” How do you prove this? “Because you have no need of my goods.” What, then, are your goods? “All that the Father has is mine” (John 15:16). And what does the Father have? All good things that belong to him are also his and mine. [Col. 0740A] The Father lacks nothing; the Son lacks nothing; and the Holy Spirit is God and one God, because he alone is content with his own goods and has nothing from the goods of another.

“To the saints who are in his land, I have made wonderful my wills among them.”

> [Note: [Col. 0739D] The Maurists note that some printed psalters have *mirificavi* (“I have made wonderful”), but they follow Augustine’s reading, which some manuscripts also prefer. The Vulgate reads *mirificavit* (“he has made wonderful”), a reading followed by Cassiodorus.]

For the Lord has made his wills wonderful, and exceedingly wonderful, in all the saints who are in his land. For whatever is in this world is in the land of him who, though rich in all things, chose to become needy and poor and to endure for us so many and such great things. But all others besides the saints, and those who are among them, do not marvel at these purposes of our Savior, because they believe none of these things to be true.

“**Their infirmities were multiplied; afterward they hastened**” [Col. 0740B]. These infirmities, however, which the saints and the others among them—those converted to faith in Christ through their teaching and preaching—had at first multiplied, afterward, when Christ the Lord preached and called them to faith, hastened: they ran, believed, and were healed. He healed many according to the flesh, but more according to the soul. Therefore, when he says that these infirmities had multiplied, we must understand infirmities not of bodies but of souls.

“**I will not gather their assemblies from blood**.” [Note: [Col. 0740D] It is evident that this expression, “from bloods,” is contrary to grammatical usage, since in grammar this word has no plural; therefore it must be reckoned among the idioms—that is, the distinctive usages—of Holy Scripture. Cassiodorus.] Here “assemblies” is taken in a favourable sense. These are those assemblies of which the Lord says: “In my Father’s house are many dwelling-places” (John 14:2). Into these assemblies [Col. 0740C], therefore, and into these houses, the saints shall be gathered. Though they had previously been weak and sinful—which is denoted by “bloods”—nevertheless all who shall assemble there will be pure and holy, cleansed from every stain of vice. “**Nor will I remember their names upon my lips.**” Such as they were, such names they formerly bore. For they were called fornicators, adulterers, murderers, sacrilegious persons, and by the other names by which evil people are usually called. But now they are called both gods and sons of God: “I said,” he says, “You are gods, and all of you are sons of the Most High” (Psalm 81:6).

“**The Lord is the portion of my inheritance and of my cup.**” These, he says, are my inheritance—an inheritance which I acquired by drinking the cup of suffering. [Col. 0740D] Of them the Apostle says: “For you were bought at a great price; glorify and bear God in your heart” (1 Corinthians 6:20). The Lord was the portion of Christ’s cup, because he shared in suffering at Christ’s passion. Thus it has been shown what Christ’s inheritance is and what the inheritance of the saints is. For the Lord alone is the inheritance of the saints, because, despising all things that are in the world, they chose the Lord alone as their portion. A good exchange: that they themselves should be the Lord’s inheritance, and should have the Lord as their inheritance.

[Col. 0741A] “**You are he who restored my inheritance to me.**” His humanity speaks and gives thanks to the divinity, when he conquered the strength of the devil, by whose gift he received the inheritance.

“**Measuring-lines fell to me in splendid places.**” People divide their inheritances with cords and measuring-rods; and those cords must sometimes fall upon good land, sometimes upon barren and stony ground, sometimes even among briars and thorns. But the Lord, commending his inheritance, shows it to be wholly splendid and fruitful when he says that the lines fell to him in splendid places. [Note: [Col. 0741D] “Christ’s inheritance is the predestined multitude of the saints. The word *to me* is added because, according to his humanity, he glories not in himself but in the Father.” Cassiodorus.] And even if, as often happens, it should perhaps seem splendid to others, it nevertheless seems altogether splendid to him. Hence it follows: “Indeed, my inheritance is splendid to me.”

[Col. 0741B] “**I will bless the Lord, who has given me understanding. Moreover, this too: I will bless the Lord, because even until night my reins rebuked me.**” The Lord and our Saviour, rejoicing in so splendid an inheritance won by his labour, blesses God the Father and gives thanks for all that he did and suffered from the Jews. Good understanding is Christ’s good teaching and preaching, through which the devil was conquered and the world delivered from death. This is that understanding and teaching of which he himself elsewhere says: “My teaching is not mine” (John 7:16). It was his according to divinity, but not his according to humanity. Therefore he says that his understanding is not his own but was bestowed upon him by God. His reins are the Jews [Col. 0741C], from whom he drew his origin according to the flesh. They did not cease, until death—which we understand by “night”—to rebuke him, blaspheme him, curse him, and cruelly persecute him. Yet he did not heed their persecutions, fortified by the great and mighty protection of his own divinity which was in him; and this is what he says.

“**I kept the Lord always before my sight, because he is at my right hand, that I may not be moved.**” In that most harsh passion, our Saviour was not moved—that is, angered—as often happens with others. On the contrary, wearied with compassion and mercy, he prayed for his very crucifiers, saying: “Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing” (Luke 23:34). Thus the divinity was at his right hand, urging him not to anger and vengeance but to compassion and mercy [Col. 0741D].

“**Therefore my heart rejoiced.**” Therefore, he says, my heart rejoiced because divinity is always at my right hand, directing and guarding me in all things. “**And my tongue exulted.**” That is, the tongue of the inner person, by which the understanding of which we have just spoken is signified. “**Moreover [Col. 0742A] my flesh too shall rest in hope.**” Namely, in hope that swiftly and promptly comes to meet it; hence it follows:

“**For you will not abandon my soul in hell, nor will you give your Holy One to see corruption.**” [Note: [Col. 0741D] Cassiodorus aptly observes here: “Where are the Apollinarians, who falsely suppose and say [Col. 0742D] that the Lord Christ did not possess a rational soul? Behold, he himself cries out; he himself gives thanks to the Father, because his soul was not abandoned in hell according to the common condition, but, glorified by a swift resurrection, attained the kingdoms of heaven.”] For the divinity descended into hell together with the soul, yet did not abandon the body in the tomb. The soul could be separated from the body, but the divinity could not, because God is everywhere and contains all things. It would have been utterly unworthy for that most holy flesh to see any corruption: flesh born from the Virgin without any corruption and living in this world without any sin.

“**You have made known to me the ways of life.**”—“I came forth,” he says, “from the Father and came into the world; again I leave the world and go to the Father” (John 16:28). All [Col. 0742B] ways are known to me; I have known the paths both of going and of returning.

“**You will fill me with joy by your countenance.**” To see God always and to be always with him is the highest joy. “**Delights**”—joy and exultation—will be mine as I sit “**at your right hand unto the end.**”

## Psalm XVI. A Prayer of David

Let us understand this prayer to be David’s, who composed it. Had he wished it to be understood as belonging to our Saviour, he would have added, as he customarily does, “unto the end.”

“**Hear, O Lord, my righteousness.**” This is the voice of the prophet, of the whole Church, and of all the faithful of both Testaments. “Hear,” he says, “O Lord, my prayer” [Col. 0742C]. One who knows that he possesses righteousness can pray to God with confidence. “**Attend to my supplication.**” This repeats the same petition, as does what is written in the following verse:

“**Receive my prayer with your ears, not from deceitful lips.**” The saints do not have deceitful lips, and therefore they offer prayers that are clean and pure.

“**Let my judgment come forth from your countenance; let your eyes behold equity.**” A person’s will is readily perceived in the face and eyes. Thus, even before a judge pronounces sentence against defendants, it is often recognized in his face and eyes. This is therefore as though he said: Show yourself angry; turn your face from my enemies; and let them recognize from your face that your judgment and my cause are just.

[Col. 0742D] “**You have tested my heart, visited it by night; you have examined me by fire, and no iniquity has been found in me.**” God tested Abraham, Job, and Tobias; he tested many others too, and visited them in the night of distress and tribulation. Hence it follows: “You have examined me by fire, and no iniquity has been found in me.” Indeed, how many even now are tested, yet do not know that they are being tested, and do not understand that the evils they suffer are for their testing [Col. 0743A]. Let them therefore remember these saints and, amid their own tribulations, give thanks, so that in them also no iniquity may be found.

“**That my mouth may not speak the works of men; because of the words of your lips I have kept hard ways.**” What I say, he says, I do not say for empty praise and commendation; for if I did so, then my mouth would speak the works of men. By the words of God’s lips we understand the precepts of both Testaments. Whoever wishes to keep and observe them must walk and remain upon hard and rough paths.

“**Perfect my steps in your paths, that my footprints may not be moved.**” No one can attain perfection by his own strength without God’s help. Therefore God’s mercy must always be sought, that he may establish our feet in the way of his commandments, so that no diabolical persuasion may move our steps away from what pleases him.

“**I have cried out, because you have heard me, O God; incline your ear to me and hear my words.**” Many times, he says, I have cried out, and I still cry out; many times you have heard me, and you still hear me. For, as though he said, by always hearing me you have given me this confidence to cry out, so that I may never cease to cry and pray to you.

“**Make wonderful your mercies, you who save those hoping in you.**” Every day God makes his mercies wonderful [Col. 0743C], because he both converts sinners to himself and, saving those who hope in him, frees them from the snares of wicked people and evil spirits. For these are those who resist God’s right hand; these are those who do not cease to fight against God’s Church.

“**Guard me, O Lord, from those resisting your right hand; protect me as the apple of the eye; beneath the shadow of your wings shelter me from the face of the ungodly, who have afflicted me.**” Nothing needs greater protection than the apple of the eye: if it is injured, sight is lost. The righteous person therefore compares himself to it, showing that without God’s protection he is frail and easily perishes. By God’s wings, what else should we understand than virtues, without which we cannot fly to heavenly things? If we possess them, we shall not fear the assaults [Col. 0743D] and snares of the ungodly. For the Apostle says of faith: “Through faith the saints conquered kingdoms, practised righteousness, obtained promises, stopped the mouths of lions, quenched the violence of fire, escaped the edge of the sword, were strengthened from weakness, became mighty in war, and so forth” (Hebrews 11:33). Faith, then, and the other virtues protect and defend us; without their fortification we cannot escape the snares of enemies.

“**My enemies have surrounded my soul.**” For what purpose? To capture and deceive it and entangle it in their errors. But as is said elsewhere: “Our soul has been rescued like a sparrow from the snare of the hunters” (Psalm 123:7).

“**They have shut up their fat.**” What should we understand by “fat” [Col. 0744A], if not the grossness and superabundance of every iniquity and deception? Elsewhere it is likewise said of this fat: “Their iniquity came forth as though from fat” (Psalm 72:7). Hence those who have been fattened with such fat are called fat bulls. But now the ungodly and sinful—namely tyrants, Jews, and heretics—have conceived this fat in their minds, shut it up in their hearts, and committed it to memory, so that in due time they might pour it out deceitfully and violently against God’s saints. Hence it follows: “**Their mouth has spoken pride.**” They did this when they blasphemed Christ and mocked the saints, saying in their curses that they worshipped a dead man, who could not deliver them from their hands, just as he could not deliver himself from the hands of the Jews [Col. 0744B].

“**Casting me out, they have now surrounded me.**” From where did they cast us out? Do you wish to hear? From our houses, our honours, our possessions, our dwellings, our offices, and our dignities. But why did they surround them? To capture, seize, bind, scourge, and, after many torments, condemn them to death. They did this because they did not know God and did not believe that another life existed after this one. Hence it follows: “**They fixed their eyes to bow down to the earth.**” Because they were ignorant of another life, they thought only of earthly and transitory things.

“**They received me like a lion ready for prey, and like a lion’s whelp dwelling in hiding-places.**” With how great a cruelty they killed God’s saints is shown in these few words.

“**Arise, O Lord; go before them.**” Arise, he says, O Lord, to help your saints; go before those who seek to forestall and deceive them, so that they may quickly perish and lose the riches they love. This seems to be said particularly against the Jews, who first stirred persecution against the Church and did not fear to lay impious hands upon Jesus Christ our Lord. When they sought to kill the holy apostles and utterly remove Christ’s name and memory from the earth, they were forestalled by the Romans, captured, overthrown, and led into slavery [Col. 0744C].

“**Deliver my soul from the ungodly.**” Deliver, he says, my soul from that ungodly people of the Jews, who, by misinterpreting the Law and the Prophets, deceived many and caused them to fall into error. “**The sword of enemies from your hand.**” By the enemies’ sword we should understand every instrument, material and spiritual alike, by which they can defend themselves and attack Christians. For Jews and heretics have killed more Christians by their reasonings, syllogisms, and arguments than by material weapons. The saints therefore ask the Lord to take this sword from them, lest they be able to kill and deceive the simple people by it. When he says “from your hand,” this is as though he said, “by your power and strength.” For we must attend not so much to the words as to the speaker’s intention [Col. 0744D].

[Col. 0745A] “**O Lord, divide them from the few of the earth.**” By “the few” we understand those of whom the Lord says in the Gospel: “For many are called, but few are chosen” (Matthew 21:14). In the judgment the wicked will be separated from these, when the lambs are placed on the right hand and the goats on the left. “**And supplant them in their life.**” Before the Jews depart from this life, they shall understand that they have been supplanted. This will occur after the death of Antichrist, when the truth becomes known and those then alive are converted to faith; of these it is also written: “They shall return at evening” (Psalm 58:7), and elsewhere: “In those days Judah shall be saved” (Jeremiah 33:16). It may also be understood thus when he says, “And supplant them,” as though he had said: Permit them to be supplanted. He said this not so much in imprecation as in prophecy, because he foresaw that it would happen.

“**Their belly has been filled from your hidden things.**” Their belly, he says—that is, the belly of the few from whom these others are separated—has been filled from your hidden things, that is, your mysteries. By these we understand the treasures of wisdom and knowledge, possessed by none but those who have merited to receive faith in Christ and the teaching of evangelical preaching. “**But these, on the contrary [Note: [Col. 0745D] Here the Maurists note that some manuscripts read *υἱῶν*, “with sons”; others *ὑῶν*, “with swine,” or *ὑείων*, “with pork” or “with swine’s flesh.” Since these words resemble one another, the Vulgate rendered it, “They are filled with sons”; while the most ancient Old Latin, as it is read in the Psalter of the Vatican Church, has, “They are filled with pork.” St Bruno followed this translation, as do St Augustine and Cassiodorus, who have the same interpretation and reading. [Col. 0746D]] are filled with swine’s flesh.**” Whatever the Lord has forbidden in the Law, the Prophets, and the books of the Gospels is signified by swine’s flesh. Thus, when he says, “They are filled with swine’s flesh,” it is as though he said: They are full of every vice and sin. Whatever the Lord forbade them to do in the holy Scriptures, they did not fear to do [Col. 0745C]. “**And they left what remained to their little ones.**” The same teaching and error which the Jews who lived after Christ’s passion taught and held, those now living hold; and those who shall come after them will hold it, down to those who are to be saved at the end of the age.

“**But I shall appear in your sight with righteousness; I shall be satisfied when your glory is revealed.**” I, says the prophet—the Church and the multitude of all the saints—shall appear in your sight with the righteousness which, at your command, I have kept and maintained. I shall be satisfied, not with swine’s flesh as they are, but with your ineffable delights, by which angels are nourished and refreshed [Col. 0745D], when your glory is revealed.

## Psalm XVII

### Unto the End. For David, the Servant of the Lord, Who Spoke to the Lord the Words of This Song on the Day When He Delivered Him from the Hand of All His Enemies and from the Hand of Saul; and He Said:

“Unto the end,” he says: these words must be referred to that end of which the Apostle says, “Christ is the end of the Law” (Romans 10:4), who also speaks of himself, saying: “I am Alpha and Omega, the first and the last, the beginning and the end” (Revelation 1:17). Therefore let these words be transferred unto the end and ascribed to David, the servant of the Lord—that is, to our Saviour. For David is interpreted “strong of hand.” But who is as strong as he of whom it is said: “The Lord is strong and mighty, the Lord mighty in battle” (Psalm 23:8)? Thus the Son spoke these things to the Father on the day of his passion, when he was delivered from all the snares of his enemies, the devil was overcome—signified by Saul—and ceased thereafter to pursue him.

“**I will love you, O Lord, my strength; O Lord, my firm support and my refuge.**” The Son speaks to the Father; humanity speaks to divinity, and shows both the affection and the cause of its love when it says that he is its strength, firm support [Col. 0746B], refuge, deliverer, helper, and protector. I think that he said this when he was being led to the cross, on which he did not doubt that he would conquer all his enemies and triumph over the enemy of the human race himself. Rightly, he says, I love you and shall always love you—a fact readily proved by this very demonstration of such great obedience. “O Lord, my strength; O Lord, my firm support, my refuge, and my deliverer; my God, my helper: I will hope in him.” It is characteristic of prophets suddenly to change persons.

“**My protector and the horn of my salvation.**” In Holy Scripture, “horn” is used for strength, as in the passage: “A vineyard was made for the beloved on a horn, son of oil [Col. 0746C] [Note: [Col. 0746D] Ghislerian manuscript: “for the son”; so also the Vulgate.]” (Isaiah 5:1). It follows:

“**My helper: praising, I will call upon the Lord, and I shall be saved from my enemies.**” He did this at that hour when he said: “Father, into your hands I commend my spirit” (Luke 23:46). Now, however, he briefly recounts the history of his passion itself.

“**The groanings of death surrounded me.**” This happened when the crowd—as the Gospel relates—and the one called Judas came with swords and clubs to seize him; when they laid hands on Jesus, held him, and led him bound to the chief priests. In saying that the groanings of death and the feelings of human suffering came upon him, he shows himself to be truly human, not phantom-like, as certain heretics preached; but in truth he himself was seized, bound, crucified, and died [Col. 0746D]. “**And torrents of iniquity troubled me.**” He calls the Jews torrents of iniquity because, like a flooding torrent, they came upon him that night with great violence and fury; hence the terrified disciples left him and fled.

“**The pains of hell surrounded me.**” This makes clear that he endured great and intolerable pains on that night and day. Although it was in his power, according to his will, to endure and mitigate those pains [Col. 0747A], it is nevertheless fitting that he says they were such as other human beings commonly endure. Thus his faithful may know and understand how greatly he loved us, since he freely chose to suffer such great things for us.

“**The snares of death went before me.**” The snares of death are those which catch and hold what they seize and draw it to death. Such snares were the Jews, who, forestalling him and rushing upon him together with Judas the traitor, did not leave him until his death.

“**And in my tribulation I called upon the Lord, and cried out to my God.**” And what did he do? It follows: “**And he heard my voice from his holy temple, and my cry before him entered [Col. 0747B] into his ears.**” We have heard in the Gospel what he cried and how he called upon God. We have also heard, now from his own statement, that he was heard; this we most firmly believe and do not doubt in any way. When he says, “from his holy temple,” what could more suitably be understood than himself? For he himself is God’s temple, in whom, as the Apostle says, “all the fullness of divinity dwells bodily” (Colossians 2:9). Hence he himself said: “Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up” (John 2:19). The Evangelist immediately explains this, saying that he said it “of the temple of his body.” Thus he who prayed and he who heard were in himself; nor did those whose will and consciousness were one need conversation [Col. 0747C]. Hence he says, “And my cry was before him,” because divinity is never separated from humanity, nor humanity from divinity. Thus far the Lord has woven the history of his passion; the Church speaks in what follows concerning the things done within it after Christ’s passion.

“**And the earth was moved and trembled.**” After the Lord, he says, ascended into heaven and sent his disciples to preach among all nations, the whole earth was moved: some defending, others attacking the truth. Then was fulfilled what the Lord said: “Do not think that I came to bring peace upon the earth; I came not to bring peace but a sword. From this time,” he says, “there shall be five in one house: two against three, and three divided against two. Son shall fight against father, daughter against mother, and daughter-in-law against her mother-in-law” (Matthew 10:34). Thus the earth was moved and thus it trembled. For each person feared for his own side, lest it should be defeated in so great a conflict [Col. 0747D].

“**And the foundations of the mountains were troubled and moved, because God was angry with them.**” Not only, he says, was the earth moved, but the mountains themselves and the foundations of the mountains were troubled and moved. For by the mountains what should we understand but the more powerful, prudent, and wise people of this world? For they stand in relation to lesser people as mountains stand in relation to lower plains. The foundations of the mountains, however, seem to me to be the Roman rulers, who at that time bore, governed, and sustained the whole world [Col. 0748A]. All these were moved and troubled against God’s saints and the Christian faith. Why? “Because God was angry with them.” For unless he had been angry with them, he would have drawn them to himself as he drew others. For the Lord says: “No one comes to me unless the Father who sent me draws him” (John 6:44). Hence he says: “I know whom I have chosen” (John 13:18). And the Apostle: “Consider your calling, brothers: not many noble among you, not many powerful; but God chose the ignoble things of the world” (1 Corinthians 1:26). Therefore let all wicked people who do not cease to assail truth and afflict the Church know that God is angry with them [Col. 0748B].

“**Smoke ascended in his anger, and fire blazes from before his face.**” This is what he says elsewhere: “The Lord troubled them in his anger, and fire shall devour them” (Psalm 20:10). And again: “A fire has been kindled in my fury, and it shall burn unto the lowest parts of hell” (Deuteronomy 32:22). This is that fire of which the Lord will say at judgment: “Go, accursed ones, into the eternal fire prepared for the devil and his angels” (Matthew 25:41). Therefore, if the fire is eternal, the smoke too is undoubtedly eternal. Both fire and smoke are great torments.

“**Coals were kindled by him.**” And who are these coals, if not wicked people, such as those whom he has just called mountains and foundations of mountains? Once kindled, they shall never afterward be extinguished, but shall burn always and without end [Col. 0748C].

“**And he bowed the heavens and came down, and darkness was beneath his feet.**” These are the heavens of which it is said: “The heavens declare the glory of God” (Psalm 18:1); by them we understand the apostles, whom the Lord bowed when he sent them into all the world to preach, saying: “Go, teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit” (Matthew 28:19). It is indeed a great bowing when heavens are sent down to earth, righteous people to sinners, and sons of God to idolaters and servants of demons. Such were those to whom the apostles were sent, to call, heal, wash, enlighten, and raise them [Col. 0748D]. He not only bowed and sent them, but also went and descended with them. For he promised them this, saying: “Behold, I am with you all days, even unto the consummation of the age” (Matthew 28:20). But what does he mean when he says, “And darkness was beneath his feet”? The Apostle says concerning sinners: “For once you were darkness, but now you are light in the Lord” (Ephesians 5:10). If darkness, then gloom. Such gloom and darkness, illuminated by the teaching of the apostles, rejoice to humble themselves and lie beneath Christ’s feet.

“**And he ascended upon the Cherubim, and flew upon the wings of the winds.**” Those whom above he called heavens, he now calls winds. [Note: [Col. 0747D] The same Ghislerian manuscript: “He now calls them Cherubim, and those whom he had called mountains he now calls winds,” etc.] For *Cherubim* is interpreted “fullness of knowledge.” And where is there such fullness of knowledge as among the holy apostles, whom first the Son of God and then the Holy Spirit instructed and taught? Observe the elegance of the expression: he is said to descend in the heavens and ascend upon the Cherubim. Heavens cannot otherwise be joined to the earth unless they bow themselves and descend. But he ascends upon the Cherubim so that, as they fly, he may pass beyond the wings of the winds. There are different reasons why the holy apostles are now called heavens, now Cherubim, now clouds, now oxen, now horses, and by other names appropriate to them for different causes. Therefore he ascended upon the Cherubim—that is, upon his apostles—to whom, as he himself said, he had given a mouth and wisdom which none of their adversaries could resist. “He ascended,” [Col. 0749B] he says, “and flew.” Where? “Above the wings of the winds.” The Apostle rightly says that he flew, to show the swiftness of those who in a very short time filled the whole world with their preaching. For elsewhere it is said: “Their sound went forth into all the earth, and their words unto the ends of the world” (Psalm 18:4). [Note: [Col. 0749D] The same manuscript: “But what does he mean when he says, ‘above the wings of the winds’?”] By winds, as we have said, are signified kings, rulers, and the other powerful persons of this age, who agitate and trouble this great and spacious sea—that is, this world—and scarcely ever allow it to be at rest. For winds alone rule the sea and display their power there most fully. Thus the Lord is said to have flown above such persons because his virtue and power surpass all the powers of this world [Col. 0749C], and nothing is not subject to his command. Or he flew above them because he did not take up a dwelling-place in them, but flew over them and hastened to others.

“**And he made darkness his hiding-place.**” [Note: [Col. 0749D] Augustine is briefer: “And he made the obscurity of the sacraments and hidden hope in the hearts of believers [Col. 0750D] his hiding-place, where he might hide, without abandoning them.”] Someone might ask: “If he thus flew, and flew above the wings of the winds, where shall we seek him? Where shall we find him?” The answer is: “He made darkness his hiding-place.” I say, then: if “God is light and there is no darkness in him” (John 1:5), how does he shine in darkness? Perhaps because, as it is written, “No one has ever seen God” (John 1:18). What cannot be seen is sufficiently in darkness. Yet the Lord hides in darkness in another manner: there he is readily found by those who seek him with devout desire. The Scriptures of both Testaments are called darkness because they are obscure and cannot be penetrated by anyone except the faithful. Whoever therefore seeks God and desires to know and see him should enter this darkness; there he will find that light which enlightens every person coming into this world. This was signified by Moses, who, in order to speak with the Lord upon Mount Sinai, is said to have entered cloud and darkness. It follows:

“**His tabernacle was round about him; dark water in clouds of air.**” Around, he says, [Col. 0750A] this hiding-place, God’s tabernacle—that is, religious persons and those of greater knowledge—continually remain. There they exercise their understanding; there they seek God’s will and knowledge, and by seeking find it. For when the Gospel or any other divine Scripture is read in church, and the entire people, called God’s tabernacle, stand around with attentive ears, then we see God’s tabernacle standing about this aforementioned hiding-place. Concerning this hiding-place he further says:

“**Dark water in clouds of air.**” For *tenebrosus* and *tenebrosa* (“dark”) derive their name from *tenebrae* (“darkness”). Since the hiding-place is in darkness, the water that is in the hiding-place is rightly called dark. [Note: [Col. 0750D] The same manuscript: “These clouds are understood as the apostles and prophets, and their Scriptures; since these are obscure, they are called dark.”] Let us hear what is said in the following words concerning these clouds:

[Col. 0750B] “**Before the brightness in his presence the clouds passed.**” Here “before the brightness” forms one phrase, as though he said: “The pre-eminent and shining clouds”—by which, as we said, the apostles are signified—passed. In their passage hail and burning coals came to be wherever they passed. In saying that they passed, he very plainly shows how great was their diligence in preaching. They did not remain long in one place, but continually went from place to place. What are the hail and burning coals but their words and discourses, by which they threatened sinners, unless they converted and repented, with the hail of every torment and with flames and conflagration of eternal fire [Col. 0750C]? Blessed John the Baptist scattered this hail and these burning coals when he said: “Repent, for the kingdom of heaven has drawn near. Already the axe has been laid to the root of the tree. Every tree that does not bear good fruit shall be cut down and cast into the fire” (Luke 10:9). He rightly says “in his presence,” because God always beholds them and never forgets them.

“**And the Lord thundered from heaven, and the Most High uttered his voice.**” This verse seems to explain the preceding one. Whether the apostles are called heavens, clouds, or Cherubim, the meaning is the same. “Therefore the Lord thundered from heaven, and the Most High uttered his voice,” when through the mouths of the apostles—whom above he called clouds—he made known what fire, what hail, what kind of punishment, and how great torments await sinners [Col. 0750D]. Hence he further says:

“**He sent forth his arrows and scattered them; he multiplied lightnings and troubled them.**” Behold, what he had called hail and burning coals, he now calls arrows and lightnings. The two brothers customarily sent and shot such arrows and lightnings, those called in the Gospel *Boanerges*, that is, “sons of thunder”: James [Note: [Col. 0751D] The same manuscript: namely.] and John. “But he scattered and troubled” those against whom he sent these arrows and lightnings, not in substance but in wickedness. For the Lord wished to scatter and trouble in this way those to whom he said: “Whoever wishes to come after me, let him deny himself” (Luke 9:13). The Apostle likewise shows that he himself was scattered and troubled when he says: “I live—yet no longer I; rather Christ lives in me” (Galatians 2:20). Would that we too might deserve to be scattered and troubled in this way! At first the archers and lightning-casters were few, but good; afterward, as the number of the elect grew, they multiplied beyond number. Then came to pass what follows:

“And the springs of waters appeared, and the foundations of the earth were laid bare. [Col. 0751B; Note: Col. 0751D, the same codex reads ‘of the world.’] At your rebuke, O Lord, at the blast of the breath of your anger.” There are as many springs of waters as there are prophets and apostles, all holy preachers, and the volumes of their books. They are also quite fittingly called the foundations of the world, because the whole Church has been founded upon them. Hence the Apostle says: “Built upon the foundation of the apostles and prophets” (Eph. I, 20). These springs and foundations then appeared and were revealed when the teachers of the Church, now exceedingly multiplied, began to preach throughout all nations, rebuke sinners, expound the Scriptures, and show from the Scriptures themselves that the wrath and indignation of God, and a flood of every punishment, await those who persevere in their sins and refuse to repent. Up to this point Holy Church has spoken of the apostles’ preaching and the conversion of the nations. From here it begins to relate the persecutions by tyrants which it suffered, and the great mercies of God which it experienced amid those persecutions and torments.

“He sent from on high and took me; he received me out of many waters. He delivered me from my strongest enemies, and from those who hated me, because they had become stronger than I.” It says that he sent from on high to deliver her; but what he sent is not stated here. Elsewhere, however, it is stated: “God sent forth his mercy and his truth; he delivered my soul from the midst of lion cubs” (Ps. LVI, 5). Thus those whom it there calls lion cubs, it here calls many waters and most powerful enemies. Holy Church has often been delivered from such people, aided only by the mercy and truth of God which it proclaimed. He sent from on high—from himself, who is the highest good, from the loftiest secret of his divinity, whence all good things come, as it is written: “Every best gift and every perfect gift is from above, coming down from the Father of lights” (Jas. I, 17). Thus it is read concerning such persons: she was delivered by God as though she were being drawn from the great depth of waters or from the jaws of lions.

[Col. 0752A] “They came upon me in the day of my affliction.” “They came upon me,” it says, and as though taking me unawares, they rushed upon me with great wrath and fury, dragged me before kings and governors, scourged me, and assailed me in many ways. But what did the Lord do? “And the Lord,” it says, “became my protector; he brought me into a broad place; he saved me because he willed it.” Because, it says, he loved me, willed it, and did not wish to lose me, he drew me out of great tribulations and straits and brought me into spaciousness. By spaciousness it signifies joy, exultation, and security.

“And the Lord will repay me according to my righteousness, and according to the innocence of my hands he will repay me.” And, it says, he delivered me from tribulations, [Col. 0752B] and I still await recompense and reward for my service, because he is just and will render to each according to his works. Hence it follows:

“Because I have kept the ways of the Lord and have not acted wickedly against my God.” This, therefore, is why she still awaits recompense. What is keeping the ways of the Lord except observing his commandments? One acts wickedly against God when one is separated from him by any event.

“Because all his judgments are always before my sight, and I have not rejected his righteousness from myself.” These are indeed great [Note: Col. 0752D, the same codex reads “and worthy.”] grounds for awaiting recompense. For one who keeps the ways of the Lord, does not depart from him under any circumstance, observes and maintains his judgments, and never casts his righteousness away from oneself—what more can one do? And as though someone said: “See, today [Col. 0752C; Note: Col. 0752D, the same codex reads “up to this day.”] you have done all this well, but you have not yet promised that you will do so in the future.” To this she herself replies:

“And I shall be spotless before him, and I shall guard myself from my iniquity.” “I have done it,” she says, “and I shall do it; I shall never return to the perversity and iniquity of my former conduct.” Therefore I am certain, says the Church—or any faithful soul—“that the Lord will repay me according to my righteousness and according to the innocence of my hands in the sight of his eyes.” Since deeds are done with the hands, all works, however performed, can be signified by hands; this is the cause put for the effect. And when it says, “in the sight of his eyes,” it shows that her works are such as please God and deserve his gaze.

[Col. 0752D] Now it changes person and directs the speech of its discourse to the Lord himself.

“With the holy you will be holy; with the innocent man you will be innocent; with the chosen you will be chosen; and with the perverse you will be subverted.” It seems to say this in these words: because the Lord is holy, he will not abandon the holy; because he is innocent, he will not harm the innocent; and because he is chosen for his people, he will not forsake his chosen one. But what follows—“and with the perverse you will be subverted”—must be understood like many other things which, though he himself does not do them, he is nevertheless said to do because he seems in some way to imitate those who do them. For although he is never repentant or angry, he is nevertheless said to repent and grow angry when he displays the disposition of one repenting or angry. So, although he remains always the same and unchangeable, he seems nevertheless to be overturned and changed from his own will when he rejects from himself, because of his perversity, one whom he formerly loved. Hence it follows:

“Because you will save the humble people, and humble the eyes of the proud.” For in the humble people whom the Lord will save are included all those whom he has just named: the holy, the innocent, and the chosen. By the proud, however, who are to be humbled, the perverse alone are signified.

“Because you, O Lord God, light my lamp; light my darkness.” The lamps of the Church [Col. 0753B] are bishops, priests, and all others by whose words and examples the remaining multitude is enlightened. Concerning darkness the Apostle says: “You were once darkness, but now light in the Lord” (Eph. V, 10). In the ecclesiastical body are included good and evil, righteous and sinful, perfect and imperfect, wise and foolish persons. Among these, many are called darkness. For if the good are called lamps because they enlighten others, why should the wicked not be called darkness, since by words and examples they blind others? Therefore the Church prays for such people, that they may be enlightened, lest, following the prince of darkness, they be submerged in greater darkness. For he himself is called the prince of darkness because he is the prince of wicked men, who are called darkness.

[Col. 0753C] “Because through you I shall be delivered from temptation, and in my God I shall pass over a wall.” Therefore, it says, I asked you to enlighten my darkness, because I suffer great temptation among them, from which I cannot be delivered except by you and through you. You, therefore, both through my prayers and through your goodness, will enlighten them and deliver them from their temptations; and I, in you—my God and protector—shall pass over the wall. A great wall is set between us and God, which we cannot cross without divine help. By this wall we understand the incitements of evil spirits and the impediments of every vice. Now it again changes person and, as though heard, proclaims and extols the praises of the Lord to whom it was speaking.

[Col. 0753D] “My God, his way is undefiled.” What sort of God, it says, is this my God—how merciful, how kind, how true! He deceives no one and never abandons those who hope in him. “His way is undefiled.” All his works are pure and holy, and all his ways are mercy and truth: “The words of the Lord are tested by fire; he is a protector of all who hope in him” (Ps. XVII, 31). The words of the Lord, it says, are tested by fire and proved by believers in tribulations, straits, and the burning of every torment, because he faithfully fulfilled whatever he promised them. And this is what it means when it says: “He is the protector of all who hope in him.”

“Who is God besides the Lord? Or who is God besides [Col. 0754A] our God?” Hence elsewhere it is said: “All the gods of the nations are demons, but the Lord made the heavens” (Ps. XCV, 3).

“God who girded me with strength and made my way undefiled.” The Church is girded with such strength that it conquers even when it is thought to be bound. It has no greater victory and no greater triumph than not to yield to torments and, [Note: Col. 0753D, the same codex reads “by dying.”] while suffering, not to lose patience. Hence it says that its way is undefiled because amid the very torments it preserved the faith and went to God by a straight and unviolated path.

“Who made my feet like those of a deer and set me upon high places.” The feet of the soul are good works, virtues, and honorable habits, by which it runs in the way [Col. 0754B] of the commandments, is sustained and carried, and is set and raised upon the heights of heaven. These feet are compared with the feet of deer because they bring it swiftly and easily to its appointed place.

“Who teaches my hands for battle and made my arms like a bronze bow.” By hands and arms are signified good understanding and good intention, which, wisely taught by the Lord, fight courageously against every snare of the wicked.

“And you gave [Note: Col. 0754D, the same codex reads “to me.”] me the protection of your salvation, and your right hand supported me, and your discipline itself will teach me.” One goes confidently into battle who is saved by such protection, supported by such a right hand, and taught by such discipline.

[Col. 0754C] “You enlarged my steps beneath me, and my footprints were not weakened.” Whether, it says, I wished to flee or to pursue enemies, I had strong and swift steps and footprints. Both fleeing and fighting are useful where necessary. Those flee who hide themselves wherever possible through fear of sinning, or who repel from themselves the instruments of sinning. But those pursue who overcome vices by severe repentance and repel evil spirits from themselves through prayers and fasts. Whoever does not understand this should read the struggles of the martyrs and the histories of the blessed Benedict, Antony, and Hilarion.

“I shall pursue my enemies and overtake them, and I shall not turn back until they fail. I shall afflict them, [Col. 0754D] and they shall not be able to stand.” One who speaks thus does not fear enemies and does not desire flight, but battle. Blessed are those who fight in this way, who kill within themselves every vice, every pleasure, and the lusts of the flesh. For this is what the Lord signified through Moses, when he commanded that all the nations possessing the land of promise be slain utterly.

“They shall fall beneath my feet.” We said just above that feet signify virtues and good works, by which the entire host of vices is conquered and trampled down. Behold, the Church again changes person and turns the words of its discourse toward the Lord himself.

[Col. 0755A] “And you girded me with strength for battle.” [Note: From the Vallicellian codex, supplying the edition.] In this battle, of which the Church now begins to speak, it shows that it fought not only against vices and evil spirits, but also against tyrants, Jews, and heretics. “And you girded me with strength for battle.” The Lord girded and fortified his saints with such strength that they could not be conquered by any kind of torment or by any philosophical disputation.

“You tripped up all those who rose against me beneath me.” What does “you tripped up” mean except “you made them fall”? Hence it has just said: “They shall fall beneath my feet.” This appears to be said particularly of the Jews, who everywhere are subject to Christians and can resist them neither by arms nor by arguments. Hence it follows: “And you gave me the back [Col. 0755B] of my enemies.” [Note: Col. 0755D, the same codex reads: “and you destroyed those who hated me.” Augustine interprets it otherwise: “And you converted my enemies and made them be a back to me, that is, so that they might follow me.”] For they too have been scattered and destroyed among all nations [Note: Supplement of the same Vallicellian codex.] and have no face for resistance, but only a back ready for lashes. Concerning them it further says:

“They cried out, but there was none to save them; to the Lord, but he did not hear them.” It is a great argument that they have been rejected by God: at the time of their siege, when they were captured by the Romans, they have now for more than a thousand years [Note: The age of St Bruno, when he wrote these commentaries, is indicated.] and beyond continued to cry to the Lord without being heard. Yet formerly, in all their afflictions, though chastised only briefly, they were always heard and delivered by God.

“And I shall crush them like dust before the face of the wind; I shall wipe them away like the mud of the streets.” At this point [Col. 0755C] the person of the Lord is fittingly introduced as answering the words of the Church. For the Church had just said that the Jews cried to the Lord and he did not hear them. To this he replies: “I neither heard them, nor shall hear them; but I shall crush them like dust before the face of the wind, and wipe them away like the mud of the streets.” This has already happened in great part and will still happen at the judgment. But because it had begun to speak of the Jews, turning to the Father it complains of their unbelief. This is what it says:

“You will deliver me from the contradictions of the people; you will set me as head of the nations. A people whom I did not know served me; at the hearing of the ear they obeyed me. Foreign sons lied to me; foreign sons grew old and limped from your paths.” [Col. 0755D] “You will deliver me,” it says, “O Father, from the contradictions of this people, who have always contradicted me and still contradict me, and refused to receive my teaching. And you will set me as head of the nations,” whom I have received as my inheritance in place of the Jews. For it says, as though: the people of the nations, whom I did not formerly know and whom I had made alien and foreign to my grace and goodwill, immediately, on hearing my name, served and obeyed me. [Col. 0756A] On the contrary [Note: “The Israelites, or foreign and spurious sons, lied to me, denying me their promised faith; and these foreign and spurious sons remained grown old in the old condition of the ancient law and, limping, departed from the paths prescribed to them by the law and the prophets, by which they ought to have come to me.” Cardinal Thomasius.], “foreign sons lied to me,” though I had always kept them as my own and dearest children until the time of my passion. “Foreign sons grew old” in the sin of their disobedience, or because, following the antiquity of the letter alone, they refused to receive the new teaching. And when it says, “they limped from your paths,” it signifies that they departed and went astray from the understanding of the law and prophets by which they ought to have walked. Thus far the Lord. From here the Church continues the prayer it began.

“The Lord lives, and my God is blessed; and may the God of my salvation be exalted.” The Lord lives, it says—the Lord whose resurrection the Jews dispute; and may he be blessed [Col. 0756B] in all things, may he be exalted above all his enemies, he who saved me by his death and delivered me from every danger. It follows:

“God, who gives vengeance to me and has subjected peoples beneath me; my deliverer, O Lord, from angry nations; and you will exalt me above those who rise against me; you will deliver me from the unjust man.” God, it says, who gives vengeance to me, partly in this age and wholly in the age to come, and has subjected peoples beneath me—some willingly to obedience, while the rest are unable to resist—you, I say, who are my deliverer from angry nations, by which we understand Jews, heretics, and tyrants: I hope, trust, and am certain, says the Church, that as you have always done, so you will always do for me. What?

[Col. 0756C] “You will exalt me above those who rise against me, and you will deliver me from the unjust man.” This unjust man and those who rise against her may fittingly be understood as Antichrist with all his host. It therefore says that as it was delivered from its first persecutors, so it will be delivered with God’s help from its last.

“Therefore I shall confess you among the peoples, O Lord, and sing a psalm to your name.” It promises that it will at all times praise God among the peoples scattered throughout all nations and exult in his name, since he is always and everywhere ready to hear and deliver it.

“Magnifying the salvation of his king, and showing mercy to his Christ David and to his seed for ever.” “I shall confess you,” it says, “who have greatly magnified the salvation of his king.” Why “his”? That is, of the people of whom the Lord had just said above: “A people whom I did not know served me.” God magnified this king’s salvation so greatly that he saved not only the king himself but also all those who believe in him. Hence it follows: “And, in showing, you have shown mercy to his Christ David and to his seed for ever.” This [Col. 0757A] manner of expression frequently occurs in Holy Scripture: “I have waited with waiting”; “going, they went”; “coming, they will come”; “rejoicing, I shall rejoice”; “doing, you will do”; and similar expressions.

## PSALM XVIII. TO THE END. A PSALM OF DAVID.

Let this psalm of David be referred to the end—to Christ, to the Church, and to those who say: “We are those upon whom the ends have come” (I Cor. X, 11).

“The heavens declare the glory of God, and the firmament proclaims the works of his hands.” The most holy apostles can be called heavens for many reasons: either because they are more eminent and greater in the whole Church; or because within the compass of their authority they encompass all things; or because they conceal and contain divine mysteries; or because they are the temple [Col. 0757B] of God and the Spirit of God, visibly given to them, dwells most fully in them; or because, in likeness to heaven, they are adorned and varied with every virtue as with certain most brilliant stars. These declare the glory of God; these proclaim the works of his hands. They are not undeservedly called the firmament, because the whole Church is both strengthened and founded in their faith. Hence the Apostle says: “Built upon the foundation of the apostles and prophets” (Eph. I, 20). Such persons were worthy to be sent throughout the whole world to preach God’s glory. Nor could the prophet speaking in this psalm call them by a more fitting name than heaven and firmament.

“Day utters speech to day, and night declares [Col. 0757C] knowledge to night.” “Day utters speech to day” has the same meaning as “the heavens declare the glory of God.” Those whom it had just called heavens it now calls day; the Son of God himself calls them light in the Gospel, saying: “You are the light of the world” (Matt. V, 14). This too is a name of honor and dignity. Day therefore utters speech to day when the holy apostles announce the word of evangelical preaching to the Christian people, who themselves are day, enlightened by the true light. But, O crime and intolerable evil! As day utters the word of God, so night also declares knowledge to night. For if the apostles and all believers are called day, why should all heretics and unbelievers not be called night? When these people preach their error and their blindness [Col. 0757D] to their hearers, then unquestionably night declares its knowledge to night.

“There are no tongues or speeches whose voices are not heard.” This is what is elsewhere said: “The apostles spoke in various tongues the mighty works of God” (Acts II, 11). They spoke in every language, and, filled with the Holy Spirit, caused discourses of all wisdom and knowledge to resound. Where?

“Their sound went out into all the earth, and their words to [Col. 0758A] the ends of the world.” And what did they say? It follows:

“He set his tabernacle in the sun, and he himself, like a bridegroom coming forth from his chamber, rejoiced as a giant to run his course. His going forth is from the highest heaven, and his course to its summit; and there is none who can hide from his heat.” This is the apostles’ first preaching, in which Christ’s birth, ascension, and final judgment are very briefly contained. Christ’s tabernacle is his humanity itself, in which, as the Apostle says, all the fullness of divinity dwells bodily (Col. II, 9). The Lord set this in the sun because he revealed it to all nations. For what is not in the sun is in darkness and cannot be seen. Thus only those things are in the sun which can be seen and are not in darkness. Hence elsewhere he says: “The Lord has made known his salvation; before the sight of the nations he has revealed his righteousness” (Ps. XCVII, 2). Therefore according to his humanity our Savior is in the sun; according to his divinity he is above the sun. For according to his humanity he could be seen; according to his divinity he could not be seen. He came forth like a bridegroom from his chamber—that is, from the virginal womb, where that ineffable union occurred, where divinity was ineffably joined to humanity. “He rejoiced as a giant to run his course.” This is that course of which he elsewhere says: “He drank from the torrent in the way; therefore he lifted up his head” [Col. 0758B; Note: St Bruno used these words in the past tense, “he drank … he lifted up,” although the Vulgate states them in the future, “he will drink … he will lift up,” following the reading of very ancient codices, in which *i* was written for *e* and *v* for *b*. But perhaps he understood it thus because prophets frequently use a past verb for the future.] (Ps. CIX, 8). By this it is plainly shown that he willingly endured all the sufferings written of him. His course, then, was to be born of a virgin, perform miracles, die, rise again, and finally, after all these things, ascend into heaven. But why is he called “a giant”? The Lord became like a giant because he is strong and unconquerable. Moreover, giants were thought to possess a double nature. Thus it is written in Genesis: “When the sons of God saw that the daughters of men were beautiful, they took wives for themselves from all whom they chose” (Gen. VI, 2), and giants are subsequently said to have been born from them. This is said according to human opinion [Note: This was the opinion of certain authors from very remote antiquity, derived from the apocryphal Book of Enoch: they wrongly supposed that transgressing angels entered into marriage with daughters of men and that giants were born from this. Gen. ch. VI.]. But “his going forth was from the highest heaven, and his course to its summit,” because, as he himself says: “I came forth from the Father and came into the world; again I leave the world and go to the Father” (John XVI, 28). [Col. 0758D] By the highest heaven, therefore, let us understand God the Father, who is above all things and above whom there is nothing. Thus to say “from the highest to the highest” means nothing other than: he is equal to the Father in all things. What it says—“There is none who can hide from his heat”—can be understood in two ways: either of the heat of the Holy Spirit or of the heat of eternal fire. For no human being can fail to feel one of these. Whoever, therefore, is inflamed in this life by the heat of the Holy Spirit will not endure the burning of that heat. This first preaching of the apostles having ended, let us see the second, in which it speaks most fully about the law and righteousness of the Lord, about his fear and judgments.

“The law of the Lord is blameless, converting souls; the testimony of the Lord is faithful, bestowing wisdom upon the little ones.” Hear, say the apostles; understand; receive the law of the Lord, because the law of the Lord is holy and blameless: it does not overthrow, deceive, or kill souls, but rather converts, saves, and leads them to blessedness. Hence it follows: “the testimony of the Lord is faithful.” It is faithful because it deceives no one, lies to no one, [Col. 0759B] but speaks truth to all and bestows wisdom even upon “the little ones.” The law and the testimony signify one and the same thing. By the little ones we may understand those of whom the Lord says: “Unless you are converted and become like little children, you will not enter the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. XVIII, 3). But the Apostle teaches how we ought to be little ones: “Do not,” he says, “become little children in understanding, but be little children in malice” (I Cor. XIV, 20).

“The righteous ordinances of the Lord are right, rejoicing hearts; the commandment of the Lord is bright, enlightening the eyes.” Behold, once again it calls the same law of the Lord by different names. Every Scripture that forbids evil and commands the doing of good is the law of the Lord. Whoever obeys and believes this law is, according to [Col. 0759C] the inner person, made joyful and glad. By contrast, one who acts otherwise is blind and walks in darkness, and great sorrow and sadness await him.

“The holy fear of the Lord endures for age upon age.” Of this fear it is elsewhere said: “The fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom” (Ecclus. I, 16). No one, therefore, can attain knowledge of this law and possess the wisdom contained in it unless one first believes in God, fears him, and worships him. The fear of the Lord is holy and eternal, because it makes those in whom it dwells holy and eternal. “The judgments of God are true, justified in themselves.” Whether you call it law, commandment, testimony, righteous ordinances, or judgments, there is no difference. God’s judgments are true and naturally true, justified in themselves and from no other source; they need no proof because they are established by natural truth.

“More desirable than gold and much precious stone, and sweeter than honey and the honeycomb.” What is as desirable as wisdom, righteousness, truth, and the knowledge of one’s Creator himself? All these things, and whatever else a just man who fears God can desire, are contained in the law of the Lord. Hence the first psalm says of the just man that “he will meditate upon the law of the Lord day and night.” From this it is evident that it is sweeter to him than honey and honeycomb, since, captivated by love for it, he is never separated from it.

[Col. 0760A] “For your servant also keeps them; in keeping them there is great recompense.” Therefore, it says, your servant loves and keeps your law and judgments, and considers them sweeter and more desirable than all things whatsoever, because he does not doubt that he will receive great recompense in keeping them.

“Who understands transgressions? Cleanse me, O Lord, from my hidden sins, and spare your servant from those of others.” Whoever understands his transgressions, whoever recognizes his sins, should say with me: “Cleanse me, O Lord, from my hidden sins.” David himself did this when he sinned with Bathsheba and killed Uriah. For, as it is written, the continual prayer of a just person is very powerful. Concerning the sins of others the Apostle says: “Do not lay hands hastily on anyone, nor share in [Col. 0760B] the sins of others” (I Tim. V, 22). It is foolish to foster another’s sins when one cannot sufficiently mourn one’s own.

“If they do not rule over me, then I shall be spotless and cleansed from the greatest sin.” This is what the Apostle says: “Let not sin reign in your mortal body” (Rom. VI, 12). Sin reigns and rules in those who not only think and do it, but also persevere in it. If they are converted and return to repentance, then they will be spotless, as it is written: “At whatever hour the sinner is converted and groans, he shall live and not die” (Ezek. XXXIII, 11). Then indeed he will be cleansed from the greatest sin, by which nothing else is more suitably understood than perseverance in sin. For this is the sin which will not be forgiven people either in this age or in the future; concerning it the Apostle also says: “According to your hardness and impenitent heart, you store up wrath for yourself on the day of wrath and revelation of the righteous judgment of God” (Rom. II, 5). This sin is rightly called greatest, since it is never forgiven by the Lord. But if it is read, as some codices have it, “if they do not rule over me,” it will be understood of evil spirits, who rule people only so long, and no longer, as they persevere in sin. It follows:

“And the words of my mouth and the meditation of my heart will be such as please you always in your sight.” If I am cleansed from this greatest sin, then both my words and my thoughts will please you, [Col. 0760D] and will always be worthy of your vision in your sight. Such is the mercy of our Creator that repentance and forgiveness occur in one and the same hour.

“O Lord, my helper and my redeemer.” He who redeemed also helps, lest we return again into slavery. Unless he had done this, that redemption at so great a price would have profited nothing.

## PSALM XIX. TO THE END. A PSALM OF DAVID.

These words are indeed referred to the end—that is, to Christ and to the times of Christ. Yet they are the voice of the prophet himself, who wrote them. Hence it is rightly called a psalm of David. [Note: “In this psalm the Prophet sings, in the person of the Church, concerning Christ.” St Jerome.]

[Col. 0761A] “May the Lord hear you in the day of tribulation; may the name of the God of Jacob protect you.” The Prophet speaks to Christ our Lord and entreats his very divinity on behalf of that same humanity. “May the Lord who is in you hear you,” he says—the one who, according to your humanity, is Lord to you. When? “In the day of tribulation,” that is, at the time of the Passion. “May the name of the God of Jacob protect you,” you who now suffer so unworthily such great persecution from the sons of Jacob. They do not know your name; they do not believe that you are he who, when Moses once asked what your name was, answered: “I am the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob: this is my name” (Exod. III, 6). May he protect you whose name this is. This says nothing other than: you yourself protect yourself, [Col. 0761B] because you who according to divinity are the God of Jacob are now, according to humanity, slain by the sons of Jacob.

“May he send you help from the Holy One.” From what Holy One? From yourself; for you are the Holy of Holies, at whose coming anointing ceased. Therefore seek help from nowhere else, because in you is he who provides help both to you and to all of us.

“And may he defend you from Zion.” By Zion our Savior himself may be understood. For he too is a mountain, and not merely any mountain, but one higher than all others: “The mountain of God, a mountain of curds; a rich mountain, in which God is pleased to dwell” (Ps. LXVII, 16). “May he defend you from Zion” has the same meaning as [Col. 0761C] “may he send you help from the holy place.” But if it is also said thus, “May he defend you from Zion”—that is, may he protect and defend you from those dwelling in this Zion that is to be destroyed—this will not be unfitting, since they are the ones who killed him.

“May the Lord remember all your sacrifice, and may your burnt offering become rich.” For he is the great priest according to the order of Melchizedek, who by wondrous power changed bread and wine into the substance of his body and blood and gave them to his disciples, saying: “Take and eat: this is my body; and this is the cup of the new testament in my blood” (Matt. XXVI, 26). On the following day, after doing this, he offered himself for us upon the altar of the cross. Then he made that rich, sweet, and God-pleasing [Col. 0761D] burnt offering, by which first and original sin was removed, and the human race reconciled to the grace of God. Heaven and earth were filled with the most sweet fragrance of this burnt offering, so that it is fittingly said of it: “The Lord smelled the odor of sweetness” (Gen. VIII, 21). All those burnt offerings offered by patriarchs and prophets from the beginning of the world signified this burnt offering.

“May the Lord grant you according to your heart and confirm all your counsel.” For the desire of his heart and his counsel were that he should die for our salvation, rise again, ascend into heaven, and send the Paraclete Spirit to his disciples, so that he might enlighten the world and turn it to himself. This [Col. 0762A] counsel and desire, as the Prophet had prayed long before, has now been fulfilled by the Lord’s own willing and ordering.

“We shall rejoice in your salvation, and in the name of our God we shall be magnified.” Therefore, it says, we ask and pray these things because we shall rejoice in your salvation—whether granted to you by the Lord or bestowed upon us by you. And in the name of the Lord our God—that is, in your holy name, by which we shall be called Christians—will be our magnification, exaltation, and glorying. Hence, still asking and praying for this very thing, we all say:

“May the Lord fulfill all your petitions.” When the Prophet had said this and recognized through the Holy Spirit that his prayers had been heard, he said reflectively: “Now I know that [Col. 0762B] the Lord will save his Christ.” What could be plainer? What more manifest? Wretched Jews, even now recognize that these things were foretold concerning Christ. “And he will hear him from his holy heaven.” As we explained above, let us understand this of himself: “In mighty deeds is the salvation of his right hand.” Truly it is in mighty deeds, because no one else ever overcame enemies with such glory, such honor, and such triumph.

“Some [trust] in chariots and some in horses, but we shall glory in the name of the Lord our God.” Let others, he says, glory, fight, and vaunt themselves in chariots and horses; for us it is enough to invoke the Lord’s name in our necessities, since “everyone who calls upon the name of the Lord shall be saved” (2 Tim. 2:19).

[Col. 0762C] “They are bound and have fallen, but we have risen and stand upright.” The Prophet teaches us that those who, abandoning divine help, place their hope in worldly supports, are more quickly ensnared and brought down by the very means from which they expect victory. But the saints, having hope in God alone, will never be deprived of his help and consolation.

“O Lord, save the king, and hear us on the day when we call upon you.” How greatly King and Prophet David always loved this descendant—or rather, his son (for the Lord is so called in many places)—he shows most clearly in that, even after having been heard on his behalf, he does not cease praying for him. “And hear us,” he says, “on the day when we call upon you” in his name, [Col. 0762D] so that what he promised his disciples may be fulfilled: “If you ask the Father for anything in my name, he will give it to you” (John 16:23).

337  
## Psalm 20. Unto the End. A Psalm of David.

This title and the preceding one have the same interpretation; and, as in that psalm, so in this the Prophet speaks of Christ.

“O Lord, the king shall rejoice in your strength, and he shall exult exceedingly in your salvation.” Behold again the love and concern which the Prophet bore in his heart concerning the humanity of our Savior. He seems to begin from the end of the preceding psalm. For he had said, “O Lord, save the king”; but now he says of the same king: “O Lord, in your strength [Col. 0763A] the king shall rejoice, and in your salvation he shall exult exceedingly.” In these words he shows most plainly both that his prayer has been heard, and Christ’s salvation and victory. For he could not otherwise have rejoiced and exulted unless his will and desire had been fulfilled. Therefore it follows:

“You have granted him the desire of his soul, and have not defrauded him of the will of his lips.” Although the will lies not in the lips but in the heart, it is nevertheless called the will of the lips because the will that is in the heart is shown in the lips.

“For you have gone before him with the blessing of sweetness.” Before our Savior was born of the Virgin, all the patriarchs and prophets blessed him with the blessing of sweetness.

[Col. 0763B] “You have placed upon his head a crown of precious stone.” — “No one is crowned,” says the Apostle, “unless he has striven lawfully” (2 Tim. 2:5). It was therefore fitting that our Savior should be crowned, whose contest and victory are related as so exceedingly renowned. Christ’s crown is the Church, wholly constructed and built from precious stones. Thus the Apostle also says to those whom he had converted to the faith: “My brethren, my joy and my crown, so stand fast in the Lord, most beloved” (Phil. 4:1). Thus, by this manner of expression, those who are the cause of the crown are taken for the crown itself. We may also understand the crown itself as victory, which is the cause of that crown; and if it is just and reasonable, it is then made of precious stone. Hence, conversely, it is said: [Col. 0763C] “Woe to the crown of pride of the drunken Ephraimites” (Isa. 28:1).

“He asked life of you.” He did indeed ask it when he said: “Father, if it be possible, let this cup pass from me” (Matt. 26:39). And what did you do? “And you gave him length of days for ever and ever.” You did more, he says, than he himself asked; for he sought a life of few days, but you “gave him length of days for ever and ever.”

“Great is his glory in your salvation; glory and great splendor you shall place upon him.” How?

“For you shall make him a blessing for ever and ever.” And beyond all this, “you shall make [Col. 0763D] him glad with joy in your presence.” All these things are far superior to this present life, because they are all eternal; whereas this present life, with all its goods, is perishable and swiftly passing.

“For the king hoped in the Lord, and through the mercy of the Most High he shall not be moved.” Rightly, he says, Lord, have you done all these things for him; and, if need be, you will do greater things, because he always hoped in you and not in himself, but trusts in your mercy. Therefore he is greatly commended to you, because there is nothing that is, or will be, able to move or separate him from you forever. We have often already said that whenever such things are written concerning Christ, all must be referred to his humanity, which the Prophet now so diligently and carefully [Col. 0764A] commends to his divinity. Thus far concerning the commendation of Christ’s humanity; now he inveighs against those who persecuted our Savior unto death.

“Let your hand be found by all your enemies.” He explains this: “And let your right hand find all who hate you.” Whether they find it or are found by it, woe will be theirs, because they will be able neither to escape nor endure this right hand of such great strength; once shattered, like potters’ vessels, they will no longer be capable of restoration.

“Make them like a fiery furnace.” When? “At the time of your countenance.” And what will the Lord do? “The Lord shall trouble them in his wrath.” And what will the fire do? “And fire shall devour them.” O harsh comparison! [Col. 0764B] If they are a furnace, they will burn continually within themselves, inwardly kindled, and will be unable to be extinguished. Such great evils, then, will come upon them at the very time when, coming before the presence of their Lord, they ought to have hoped for good things.

“You shall destroy their fruit from the earth, and their seed from among the children of men.” By this he signifies that they themselves, their goods, their works, and their children—by whom their imitators are meant—will all alike perish. And this deservedly.

“For they have turned evils against you; they devised a plan which they were unable to establish.” The plan of the Jews, by which they attempted utterly to erase Christ’s name, was destroyed.

[Col. 0764C] “For you shall make them turn their back.” In the divine page the Lord is often said to do what he is able to prevent and nevertheless permits to happen; as in the statement: “For the Lord hardened Pharaoh’s heart” (Exod. 9:11). Likewise here: “For you shall make them turn their back.” The Jews show their back, 338 and not their face, because even to this day they continually flee Christ and do not seek his mercy. And since they are such, not these men but those who will be at the end of the age are to be saved; and he fittingly calls them the remnant of the Lord. Of them it is written: “Though the number of the children of Israel be as the sand of the sea, the remnant shall return” (Rom. 9:27).
