They, therefore, are those whose countenance God has prepared, whose face he has illumined and enlightened to behold him.

[Col. 0764D] “Be exalted, O Lord, in your strength; we shall sing and chant your powers.” Be exalted, he says, O Lord; you have dwelt long enough among the ungodly; your enemies have been conquered, you have been crowned with a crown of precious stone; therefore be exalted, and so [Note: [Col. 0763D] The same manuscript: “crowned, ascend into the heavens.”] ascend into heaven. But we shall sing, and throughout all nations proclaim your powers. For this is why it is said in the Song of Songs: “Flee, my beloved; be like a gazelle or a young stag upon the mountains of spices” (Song 8:14).

## Psalm 21. Unto the End, for the Receiving in the Morning. A Psalm of David Himself.

What “unto the end” signifies has been sufficiently explained. The receiving [Col. 0765A] in the morning is Christ’s resurrection: on the third day, early in the morning, he was received from mortality into eternal immortality. He fittingly put the resurrection first in this psalm, though he was about to speak only of the Passion, so that those who are saddened throughout the psalm by Christ’s Passion may be consoled by the very inscription of the title, and, when they learn that he died, may not doubt that he will rise again.

“My God, my God, look upon me: why have you forsaken me, far from my salvation?” We have often said that our Savior is God and man: one part in him cries out, while the other hears the cry. Moreover, when his humanity cries out, it cries not so much for itself as for us; for, being ineffably joined to the divinity, it has nothing [Col. 0765B] to fear for itself. [Note: [Col. 0765D] In this exposition St. Bruno appears to have followed St. Maximus of Turin; for the latter says in Homily 45, Roman edition, 1784, p. 138: “He says these things in order to show that he was forsaken for our sake, whose sins he bore, and so that, seeing this, we too might learn to die for him, the Holy and Just One, since he too died for sinners.”] Thus the tongue also speaks for all the members; and, though it suffers nothing in itself, it nevertheless declares itself to suffer in each individual member. The eye, hand, or foot is struck, and the tongue says, “Why do you strike me?”—speaking, of course, not for itself but for the others, and showing their sufferings to be its own. In this manner of speech, then, our Savior according to his humanity says: “My God, my God, look upon me: why have you forsaken me?” And as though the divinity itself asked the reason for this cry, though in its presence he ought neither to cry out nor fear, he added: “Far from my salvation.” I do not cry, he says, for myself; I am the head, I am the tongue; I cry for my members, whom I see throughout the whole world already enduring such harsh torments for my name’s sake. [Col. 0765C] For my Passion will be the cause of their suffering all these things. Moreover, I cry also for those who, redeemed at so great a price by my blood, do not cease to sin and persevere in their iniquities; for them, indeed, it will be necessary for me to cry out to you now and always. And this is what he says:

“The words of my offenses.” These words are not mine; they do not pertain to me. They are the words of the offenses, infirmities, and sufferings of my faithful people. “My God, I shall cry by day, and you will not hear; and by night, and not unto folly for me.” By day and night let us understand all time, since, as the Apostle says, “He makes intercession for us daily” (Rom. 8:34). Yet by day and [Col. 0765D] night we may understand prosperity and adversity as well. Let our Savior say, let the humanity say to the divinity: At every time I shall cry out; I shall never cease praying to you; and let it not be imputed to me as folly, because, though this cry is not necessary for me, it is always necessary for those for whom I cry.

“But you dwell in the holy place, the praise of Israel.” I have no need, he says, to cry for myself, because you dwell in me and are with me; without crying [Col. 0766A] I am heard by you, whom Israel praises and proclaims. Yet the Lord sometimes cries even for himself, not because it is necessary for him to cry, but so that in his cry we may know his purpose and will. What follows will make this clear.

“In you our fathers hoped; they hoped, and you delivered them. They cried to you and were saved; they hoped in you and were not confounded.” One must always cry out, he says, and never cease crying; and, even if we are not heard at once, we must nevertheless not cease crying. This cry is not of the mouth but of the heart, although the cry of the mouth is also very useful, if hearts and mouths agree together. This our fathers did; this the patriarchs and prophets did. This also was done by the one who [Col. 0766B] writes this psalm. And because they believed firmly, 339 and hoped, they were heard and were not confounded. From this point he narrates in order the whole of his Passion and makes known to all nations, as though they had already happened, those things that were to occur after so long a time; so that those who refuse to believe the apostles may at least read and hear this psalm, believe, and know that these things are true.

“But I am a worm and not a man, a reproach of men and an outcast of the people. [Note: [Col. 0766D] “But now I speak no longer in Adam’s person: I, Jesus Christ himself, was born in the flesh without seed, so that I might be in humanity beyond other human beings, and so that human pride might at least deign to imitate my humility.” St. Augustine, Exposition on this passage.] All who saw me despised me; they spoke with their lips and shook their heads: ‘He hoped in the Lord; let him rescue him; let him save him, since he delights in him.’ Our fathers, he says, hoped in you and were delivered. They hoped and were not confounded.” Yet this very thing is cast in my teeth, [Col. 0766C] that I hope in you, as though my hope were vain and would do me no good. Thus we have it written both here and in the Gospel. Here it is said: “He hoped in the Lord; let him rescue him; let him save him, since he delights in him.” But there: “He is the Son of God; let him now come down from the cross, and we will believe him. He trusts in God; let him deliver him, if he desires him” (Matt. 27:42). What is said here, “He hoped in the Lord,” is there, “He trusts in God”; and what is said here, “Let him save him, since he delights in him,” is there, “Let him deliver him, if he desires him.” See, therefore, how well the words of the Prophet and the words of the Gospel agree.

Now let us consider the meaning. “I,” he says, “am a worm and not a man”; as though he said: As a worm is the vilest among [Col. 0766D] animals, so they reckon me an outcast and a sinner among men. Hence the Prophet speaks in their person, saying: “But we reckoned him as a leper, rejected by God, and humbled” (Isa. 51:1). Our Savior is in some manner a worm, because he was born of the Virgin alone, without any male union. For worms are thus born: either from wood alone or earth alone, without union of different sexes. [Note: [Col. 0766D] These statements follow the obsolete Peripatetic opinion admitting spontaneous generation from decay.] [Col. 0767A] I, he says, whom they reckon among the impious and sinners, was not begotten or born as other human beings are, conceived in iniquities and born in sins. Yet I was made a reproach and an outcast of the people; they despised me and chose the robber, saying: “Not this man, but Barabbas” (John 20:40).

“For you are he who drew me from the womb; my hope from my mother’s breasts. Upon you I was cast from the womb; from my mother’s belly, you are my God.” In saying, “You drew me from the womb,” he seems to answer what he had just said, “I am a worm and not a man,” so that we may understand that he was born contrary to the law of nature [Note: [Col. 0767D] St. Bruno takes *contra* in the sense of “beyond.” Whatever is beyond nature seems to us to be contrary to its laws; but, properly speaking, since God does nothing and cannot do anything contrary to nature’s laws, he would contradict himself. Whatever he does must accord with nature, lest it oppose the supreme Author, even though, as extraordinary, it appears to us contrary to nature’s laws.], and not like other men. But what follows—[Col. 0767B] “My hope from my mother’s breasts; upon you I was cast from the womb; and from my mother’s belly, you are my God”—must be understood in such a way that, before he assumed flesh and was born of the Virgin, because he was in all things equal to the Father, we firmly believe that he neither hoped in anyone nor had God, Lord, or superior over him. All these things, therefore, as we have often said, and those which follow, must be referred to his humanity.

“Do not depart from me, for tribulation is near and there is none to help.” Christ’s divinity is so joined to his humanity that it can never depart from it, and can so help it in all things that it needs the assistance of no other. But he says such things for our sake, so that we may know that our nature is in Christ, believe him to be true man, and understand how all these things took place.

“Many calves have surrounded me; fat bulls have besieged me.” By the fat bulls are meant the chief priests, scribes, and Pharisees, made fat and filled with every malice and wickedness. The calves are the remaining multitude of the people, who followed them as leaders and teachers.

“They opened their mouth against me like a ravening and roaring lion.” They opened their mouth against me, he says, all together crying in one voice: “Crucify him!” and, “According to the Law he ought to die, because he made himself the Son of God” (John 19:7). Because of their excessive cruelty, their voices are compared with a roaring lion.

“Like water I am poured out, and all my bones are scattered.” The Lord was poured out like water: for salvation and cleansing to some, but for ruin and perdition to others. For it is written of him: “Behold, this one is set for the ruin and resurrection of many in Israel” (Luke 2:34). For where water is poured out, people readily slip and fall. But by the words, “All my bones are scattered,” he seems to signify the flight of the disciples. They are not improperly called bones, because among all the members [Col. 0768A] of the ecclesiastical body they were firmer and stronger. Concerning them he adds:

“And my heart became like melting wax in the midst of my belly.” Christ’s heart is the apostles, in whom the Lord’s will, 340 counsels, and greater secrets are contained. By his belly we may understand those who are softer and more imperfect in the Church, such as those who at that time did not yet believe perfectly. For a great multitude had assembled for the feast day, believing indeed, but not perfectly. Because of fear of this crowd the chief priests said: “Not on the feast day, lest perhaps a disturbance arise among the people” (Matt. 26:3). Thus in the midst of such people the holy apostles became like melting wax, because, terrified by overwhelming fear, they offered consolation neither [Col. 0768B] to themselves nor to them.

“My strength has dried up like a potsherd.” We know that a potsherd is fragile and of slight strength. Our Savior therefore compares his strength to it, because at the time of his Passion he chose to show himself fragile and without strength. Thus he said to Peter, when Peter wished to fight: “Do you think that I cannot ask my Father, and he will presently furnish me with more than twelve legions of angels? How then will the Scriptures be fulfilled, that it must happen thus?” (Matt. 26:53). This, then, is why his strength dried up like a potsherd. “And my tongue clung to my throat.” This is what the Prophet says: “Like a lamb led to the sacrifice, he did not open his mouth” (Isa. [Col. 0768C] 53:7). — “And they brought me down into the dust of death”: namely, by their intention and desire, not because his flesh, as another psalm says, was to see corruption.

“For many dogs have surrounded me; the council of evildoers has besieged me.” He calls the Jews dogs and a council of evildoers, barking against him without cause or reason.

“They pierced my hands and my feet.” This is so plain that it needs no explanation. It is an especially powerful proof for refuting the Jews, because they can understand it of no one other than Christ, whose hands and feet they fastened with most cruel nails.

[Col. 0768D] “They counted all my bones.” There is no one whose bones can be counted and seen separately as can those of one stretched upon a cross. Therefore, when he says “they counted,” it is as though he had said: they made them countable. We may also understand by the bones, as we said above, the apostles themselves, who were perhaps counted so that none of them might escape.

“But they looked upon me and gazed at me; they divided my garments among themselves, and cast lots for my clothing.” The Prophet, beholding this in the Spirit, and the Evangelists, beholding it with their own eyes, spoke in one and the same manner. Let the person who refuses to believe the Evangelists, then, believe the Prophets. The one garment that was not divided is that of which the soldiers said: “Let us not tear it, but let us cast lots to see whose it shall be” (John 19:24), so that this Scripture might be fulfilled, as the Apostle John says.

“But you, O Lord, do not set your help far from me; look to my defense. Rescue my soul from the sword, my only one from the dog’s hand.” What do we understand by the sword but diabolical deception, by which the souls of all who perish and are condemned are beheaded? The dog is the devil himself, who, with all his army, never ceases to bark against the saints and speak irrationally. [Col. 0769B] Concerning him it follows:

“Deliver me from the lion’s mouth, and my humility from the horns of unicorns.” This lion is the devil, of whom it is said elsewhere: “For our enemy the devil, like a roaring lion, goes about seeking whom he may devour” (1 Pet. 5:8). By the unicorns, however, he signifies the Jews, who alone among all the Gentiles were defended by one horn: namely, the Law divinely given to them through Moses, in which they gloried uniquely. Having finished the history of his Passion, he now begins to speak of the Church.

“I shall declare your name to my brethren; in the midst of the Church I shall praise you.” He calls the apostles his brethren. Both through himself after his Passion and through the Holy Spirit [Col. 0769C] whom he sent them, he revealed to them the name and glory of the Father’s majesty, so that through their ministry he might govern and teach the Church and proclaim God’s mighty deeds among all nations. “You who fear the Lord, praise him; magnify him, all the seed of Jacob. Let all the seed of Israel fear him, for he has neither spurned nor despised the prayers of the poor, nor turned his face away from me; and when I cried to him, he heard me.” Every day the Lord preaches in the Church, because his words are preached daily in the Church; for whatever is written in both Testaments is his word. He, therefore, is the one who teaches; he is the one who preaches. Hence he says to the disciples: “For it is not you who speak, but the Spirit [Col. 0769D] of your Father who speaks in you” (Matt. 10:20). The seed of Jacob and Israel is ourselves, who have the Lord and Savior as our Father, signified through Jacob and Israel. He himself is Jacob, because he conquered and supplanted the devil. He himself is Israel, to whom all the glory of the Father’s majesty is revealed. Hence it is written: “No one has ever seen God; the only-begotten Son, who is in the bosom of the Father, has declared him” (John 1:18).

“With you is my praise in the great Church.” By saying “with you,” he speaks, as it were, concerning himself, because all praise of the Son is referred to the Father. The great Church is the catholic and universal Church, spread not in one part of the world but throughout the whole world. “I shall render my vows to the Lord before those who fear him.” [Col. 0770A] By his vows he seems to mean the sacraments of his body and blood, because of what follows:

“The poor shall eat and be satisfied.” These are rightly called vows, because before the ages he determined to offer them 341 to God the Father for our salvation. For his very determining was his vowing. These vows are rendered and offered daily before his faithful people and those who fear him. “The poor shall eat and be satisfied; they who seek the Lord shall praise him.” Those poor, he says, who seek not the world’s honors, riches, and dignities, but the Lord—those to whom poverty itself is pleasing for the Lord’s sake—shall eat that ineffable food and be satisfied according to the inward person, and shall praise the Lord for so great a benefit bestowed upon them. For “whoever [Col. 0770B] eats this bread,” the Lord says, “shall live forever” (John 6:59). Therefore it follows:

“Their heart shall live for ever and ever; all the ends of the earth shall remember and turn to the Lord.” In saying “shall remember,” he shows that they had been forgetful. And indeed, before the apostles preached, people had come to such forgetfulness both of God and of themselves that very few were found who knew the truth. When the apostles preached, therefore, they remembered that blessedness which they had lost in the first man, and all the ends of the earth turned to the Lord. This is what follows:

“And all the kindreds of the nations shall worship before him.” And rightly so, “for the kingdom is the Lord’s, [Col. 0770C] and he himself shall rule the nations.” Formerly the devil reigned and exercised dominion throughout the nations; but in Christ’s Passion he lost both kingdom and power.

“All the rich of the earth have eaten and worshipped.” He admirably now calls rich those whom he had shortly before called poor, because, though poor in passing and transitory riches, they are rich in eternal and spiritual goods. “All who descend into the earth shall fall down before him.” The phrase “who descend into the earth” seems to me to be used like the Gospel saying: “Who enlightens every person coming into this world” (John 1:8), so that descending into the earth and coming into the world [Col. 0770D] signify the same thing. All, therefore, who come into the world, all who descend into the earth, shall fall before God, as it is written: “As I live, says the Lord, every knee shall bend to me and every tongue shall confess” (Isa. 43:23).

“And my soul shall live to him, and my seed shall serve him.” That soul, therefore, is not Christ’s which does not live to God; nor is that seed Christ’s which does not serve God.

“A generation to come shall be proclaimed to the Lord; and the heavens shall proclaim his righteousness to the people that shall be born, whom the Lord has made.” The generation to come and the people that shall be born seem to me to signify one and the same thing. This generation is the people of the Gentiles, who, after the rejection of the Synagogue, were in those days to be preached to and called [Col. 0771A]. Hence the Apostle says to the Jews who would not hear the word of God: “It was necessary that the word of God should first be preached to you; but because you have rejected it and made yourselves unworthy of eternal life, behold, we turn to the Gentiles” (Acts 13:46). It is fittingly said, therefore: “The people that shall be born, whom the Lord has made,” because that people was then made by the Lord when it was regenerated through the water of baptism.

## Psalm 22. A Psalm of David.

See above.

“The Lord guides me, and I shall lack nothing; in a place of pasture he has set me.” The people of the Gentiles, newly regenerated and called to faith, speaks in this psalm. This is the people of whom it was just said at the [Col. 0771B] end of the preceding psalm: “The people that shall be born, whom the Lord has made.” It is said to have been made by the Lord because it was remade through the water of baptism from its former oldness into a new creation. Let this people therefore say: The Lord guides me; I now fear nothing. I have a good ruler and shepherd, who has set me in a place of pasture and joined me to the Church of his saints. Wherever the books of the New and Old Testaments are, there is the place of pasture; there are the foods by which the soul is refreshed and healed. Concerning these things it follows:

“He led me beside the water of refreshment; he converted my soul.” All divine Scripture and evangelical preaching are water of refreshment. This is the water of which it is said: “You who thirst, come to [Col. 0771C] the waters” (Isa. 55:1). It is called water of refreshment because whoever has been satisfied from it, as the Lord says, “shall not thirst again” (John 6:15). This is the water of all wisdom, by which the souls of believers are led, washed, and healed.

“He led me on the path of righteousness for his name’s sake.” What a beautiful order of expression! First he relates that he was led to a place of pasture, then to waters of refreshment, and finally to the path of righteousness. He walks on the path of righteousness who does not turn aside into error or depart from the truth. Jews, heretics, and pagans do not know this path. It belongs only to Christians, because they alone follow and hold the truth; they alone deserved to receive the Lord’s name [Col. 0771D] and, worthy of so great a patronymic from Christ, are called Christians.

“For even if I should walk in the midst of the shadow of death, I shall fear no evils, because you are with me.” Why should one fear whom the Lord guides and who walks upon such a path? Heretics and all other deceivers are the shadow of death. For in a shadow the form 342 and likeness of that whose shadow it is are naturally represented. Such people, therefore, are the shadow of death, because, as death kills bodies, so they kill souls. Holy men do not fear to walk through their midst because they have God himself as their protector, who does not allow them to be overcome or deceived.

“Your rod and your staff, they have comforted me.” I know, he says, that you have a rod and a staff. [Col. 0772A] Against those who sin less grievously, indeed, you carry the staff. Or again, because in this life you strike with the rod, whereas in the life to come you strike not with the rod but with the staff. This, therefore, is my consolation: I know you to be an avenger, who will not allow my enemies to pass without punishment.

“You have prepared before me a table against those who trouble me.” Behold another consolation, that you need not fear your enemies. He says that a table has been prepared before him, whose food and drink confer immortality, and by using it they defend themselves from every heretical perversity. This table is understood as divine Scripture and knowledge of both Testaments, by which ecclesiastical men, refreshed, do not fear the wiles of heretics.

“You have anointed my head with oil.” As though someone said to him: What will this table do for you if understanding is lacking? In reply, he shows that he has both the table and understanding, saying that his head [Col. 0772B] has been made rich with oil. What is meant by the head but the mind? What by oil but the graces of the Holy Spirit? Anointed with such oil, our Savior said: “The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because he has anointed me” (Isa. 61:1). Hence elsewhere it is said: “God, your God, has anointed you with the oil of gladness above your companions” (Ps. 44:8).

“And how excellent is your inebriating cup!” This cup is received from this table; intoxicated by it, the saints forget earthly things and do not recognize even their own injuries. This cup is excellent because it contains nothing clouded, nothing except sweetness and pleasantness, illumined with the radiance of truth.

[Col. 0772C] “And your mercy shall follow me all the days of my life.” This is as though he said: Behold, you have done many good things for me: you have set me in a place of pasture; you have led me beside water of refreshment; you have guided me on the path of righteousness; you have set a table before me; you have made me drunk with your cup. One thing alone remains to me: if I have it, it is enough for me; if I do not have it, I am nothing. This, then, is what I ask: that your mercy, like a pedagogue and teacher, may follow me and not allow me to depart from the right way all the days of my life; so that, when this life is ended, I may dwell in the house of the Lord—in that heavenly Jerusalem—for length of days. [Col. 0772D] Therefore let no one trust that he can be saved by his own works without God’s mercy.

## Psalm 23. A Psalm of David, on the First Day of the Sabbath.

The first day of the Sabbath is understood as Sunday. On that day God made heaven and earth; on that day he rose from the dead; on that day he gave the Holy Spirit to the apostles; and on that day the final resurrection will occur, when the Lord comes to judge the living and the dead.

“The earth is the Lord’s, and its fullness; the world and all who dwell in it.” Seeing through the Holy Spirit that, on that final and first day—for it is one and the same day, first and last—all, both good and evil, whoever have been, are, and [Col. 0773A] will be, will stand alike before Christ’s tribunal, with no one then disputing, no one then claiming anything for himself, but each awaiting judgment, the Prophet says: “The earth is the Lord’s and its fullness.” Where then will be kings? Where rulers? Where the powerful of this age? Where those who now deceitfully divide the earth and take away from their own brothers their portions? Each will hide himself, yet no one will be able to hide himself: “Then they shall say to the mountains, ‘Fall upon us,’ and to the hills, ‘Hide us’” (Luke 23:30). Then it will be manifest that the earth and its fullness, the world and all who dwell in it, belong to the Lord and to the Lord alone. For whose should it be except his who made it? And when did he make it? On the first day of the Sabbath. And when will he reclaim it? On the first day of the Sabbath.

[Col. 0773B] “He himself founded it upon the seas and established it upon the rivers.” Let philosophers dispute and inquire among themselves how the earth can stand upon a liquid element. Yet it does not seem to me more remarkable that it should be supported by waters than by air—if, indeed, it is supported either by waters or by air. I turn rather to an easier interpretation: we often use “upon” in the sense of “beside,” as when we say that a city is situated upon the sea or upon the Tiber, which we surely understand as beside, not above, the water. Thus the whole earth is situated either by seas or by rivers, so that its boundaries can nowhere be other than by seas or rivers.

“Who shall ascend the mountain of the Lord, or who [Col. 0773C] shall stand in his holy place?” I see, he says, all standing before the Judge; I see there rich and poor. Which of them will be called? Which of them will ascend the mountain of the Lord? Will the rich alone? Will the powerful alone? For these are the people who were accustomed to be called, 343 and honored. By the mountain of the Lord and his holy place is here signified the land of the living. Do you wish to hear who will ascend and who will stand there?

“Innocent in hands and pure in heart, who has not received his soul in vain, nor sworn deceitfully to his neighbour.” In these few words the Prophet teaches who shall ascend there and who shall stand there. He seems to me perfect who is innocent both in hands and in pure heart [Col. 0773D]. By this, of course, are signified those who harm others neither by deed nor by counsel; and such persons are indeed rarely found. In these straits and difficulties I always have recourse to those words of the Prophet in which he says: “The sinner, at whatever hour he shall be converted and groan, shall live and shall not die” (Ezek. XXXIII, 11). And after such conversion I trust that the sinner, now among the innocent, is no longer a sinner. “Who has not received his soul in vain.” For he receives his soul, purified and renewed by the waters of baptism, in vain, who afterward, not fearing to sin and persevering in sins, compels it to return to the deformity it had before. “Nor sworn deceitfully to his neighbour.” The Prophet does not forbid swearing, but forbids swearing deceitfully. Therefore he swears deceitfully who does not of his own accord keep what he swears. It follows:

“This man shall receive blessing from the Lord, and mercy from God his Saviour.” This man, he says, who is such a one—this man shall be called, this man shall ascend, this man shall now receive blessing: namely, that blessing which the Lord promises that he will give to his faithful: “Come,” he says, “blessed of my Father; receive the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world” (Matt. XV, 34). And the saints shall have this not from their own merits, but through the mercy of their Saviour.

“This is the generation of those who seek the Lord, who seek the face of the God of Jacob” [Col. 0774B]. All these, he says, who ascend to heaven, who are blessed and saved, have been gathered out of that generation of all humankind which seeks God and desires to behold his face.

“Lift up your gates, O princes; and be lifted up, O everlasting gates, and the King of glory shall enter.” Evil spirits have their own gates, by which we may understand the Jews, heretics, and tyrants, and every sort of deceiver; moreover, vices and sins, and all their teaching and seduction. Therefore the Prophet commands the evil spirits, whom he calls princes, to lift up these their gates and to have them with them in their own torments. For this is what the Lord will say at the judgment: “Depart, accursed ones, into the eternal fire which is prepared for the devil and his angels” [Col. 0774C] (Matt. XXV, 41). But the everlasting gates are the apostles and teachers, through whom, as through certain gates, entry will be made into the heavenly Jerusalem. Therefore the Prophet says that, when judgment has been accomplished, they shall be lifted up and opened, and that through them all the faithful shall be brought into their homeland. But when he says, “And the King of glory shall enter,” he shows that the humanity of our Saviour has come to judgment. For he himself shall judge, because “the Father judges no one, but has given all judgment to the Son” (John V, 22). For it is fitting that he who was judged should judge. Hence in another psalm it is said: “O God, give thy judgment to the king” (Ps. LXXI, 1). Therefore, since the humanity of the Saviour is local, after judgment has been completed it will return there [Col. 0774D] where it now is; therefore it is now said: “And the King of glory shall enter.”

“Who is this King of glory?” You yourself—of whose lineage he was born—say it, you who know him better. “The Lord strong and mighty, the Lord mighty in battle.”

> [Note: [Col. 0773D] “Therefore mighty because strong. And thus truly there is to be proclaimed that power which, supported not by another’s strength, but by its own power, subsists in every respect for itself.” [Col. 0774D] St Maximus of Turin, Sermon 46, Roman edition, 1784, p. 518.]

Concerning this battle the Lord himself says: “When a strong man armed guards his court, all that he possesses is in peace. But if one stronger than he comes upon him, he shall take away all his armour in which he trusted and distribute his spoils” (Luke XI, 21).

“Lift up your gates, O princes, and be lifted up, O everlasting gates, and the King of glory shall enter. Who is this King of glory? The Lord of hosts—he is the King of glory” [Col. 0775A]. It was not enough for him to say once what he greatly desired to see and in which he took the greatest delight. For he already saw the glory of all the saints, among whom he saw himself also standing. He saw likewise the condemnation and destruction of all the wicked. He saw the everlasting gates opened and lifted up, prepared to receive so great a multitude of believers. He saw also the gates of hell shut and destined for everlasting fires. He exhorts the good gates to rise upward to heavenly things; but to the evil princes he says that they should lift up and shut their gates, descend into hell, and then the gates of death shall be shut, because no one shall pass through them unto death.

## 344 PSALM XXIV. A PSALM OF DAVID, UNTO THE END.

[Col. 0775B]

In this psalm the Church speaks, and therefore it is entitled “unto the end,” because it is she, as the Apostle says, “upon whom the ends of the ages have come” (1 Cor. X, 11).

“To thee, O Lord, I have lifted up my soul: my God, I trust in thee; I shall not be ashamed.” To thee, he says, O Lord, I have lifted up my soul, which formerly lay crushed beneath a great weight of vices. Of this weight it is elsewhere said: “For my iniquities have been laid upon my head, and, like a heavy burden, have weighed me down” (Ps. XXXVII, 5). To those burdened with such a weight the Lord says: “Come unto me, all you who labour and are burdened, and I will refresh you” (Matt. XI, 8).—“My God, I trust in thee; I shall not [Col. 0775C] be ashamed.” This is as though he said: Because I trust in thee, let not my confidence be vain and useless; let not my enemies prevail, and “let not my enemy ever say: I have prevailed against him.” And this is what he says:

“Nor let my enemies mock me,” by whom we understand heretics, tyrants, and the evil spirits themselves.

“For all who wait for thee shall not be confounded.” In our great necessities we ought to hope and wait for divine, not human, aid. And if perhaps it does not come as quickly as we wish, we must wait and in no wise despair.

“Let the wicked who do evil be confounded.”

> [Note: [Col. 0775D] The Gis. manuscript: “vain things”; so also Augustine, *Exposition on this Psalm XXIV*. But the reading of the Vatican Basilica is: “Let those who do wicked things vainly be confounded.” In Cassiodorus one reads: “Let the wicked doing [Col. 0776D] vain things be confounded.” But in the Vulgate: “Let all those who act wickedly in every way be confounded.”]

Those, he says, who wait for thee are not worthy of confusion; rather, let the wicked be confounded, who do and work vain things. For although by the name of vanity every evil and every folly may be understood, nevertheless those seem to be called by this name who made and worshipped idols.

“Make known to me thy ways, O Lord, and teach me thy paths.” There is this difference between ways and paths: the difference between broad and narrow ways. The narrow way leads to life; the broad way to [Col. 0776A] destruction. Thus the Church asks the Lord to teach her his ways and paths, lest perhaps she turn aside into that broad way, which is called broad because a very great and countless multitude enters by it. Therefore it follows:

“Direct me in thy truth and teach me, because thou art God my Saviour, and I have waited for thee all the day.” “I,” says the Lord, “am the way, the truth, and the life” (John XIV, 6); “no one comes to the Father except through me” (ibid.). This, therefore, is that way to which she prays to be directed, since by no other can she attain the blessedness toward which she hastens. Whoever does not walk by the way of truth, therefore, errs and travels by a crooked path unto death.

“Remember thy compassions, O Lord, [Col. 0776B] and thy mercies, which are from of old.” It is not, he says, new or unfamiliar to thee to show mercies and hear thy faithful. For thou didst begin to do this from that age when thou didst will to show that greatest and ineffable mercy. For although the Lord had previously shown many mercies, yet from the time of his passion and our redemption he displayed a greater abundance of his mercy, because he redeemed not one people but all nations by his blood. Hence: “Praise the Lord, all nations; praise him, all peoples.” Why? “Because his mercy has been strengthened over us” (Ps. CXVI, 1). Of this mercy, indeed, what follows speaks:

“The offences of my youth and of my ignorance [Col. 0776C] do not remember; according to thy great mercy remember me, O God.”

> [Note: [Col. 0776D] The same reading occurs in Augustine and Cassiodorus.]

Thus the Church asks the Lord to remember his great mercy, which has been established over us by so strong an evidence. By the offences of youth and ignorance we may understand those which she committed before conversion, while she was still held in the darkness of ignorance.

“For thy goodness’ sake, O Lord.” This, he says, which I ask, I ask not because I am worthy of so great a benefit from thee, but because of thy goodness, O Lord, which thou art accustomed to show to those who hope in thee. “The Lord is sweet and upright; therefore he has established a law for those who transgress in the way.” This is the way of God’s commandments, of which it is said: “Blessed are the undefiled in the way, who walk in the law of the Lord” [Col. 0776D] (Ps. CXVIII, 1); and: “I have run in the way of thy commandments” (ibid., XVIII). Yet many transgress in this way and do not walk in it with the purity and diligence they ought to have. But because the Lord is sweet and readily merciful, “who wills not the death of the sinner, but rather that he be converted and live” (Ezek. XXXIII, 11), therefore “he has established a law for those who transgress in the way.” And what law? Since it is written: “You have sinned: cease; turn away from evil and do good” (Isa. I, 16); at whatever hour you are converted, I shall not remember any of your iniquities [Col. 0777A]. There is nowhere any room for despair, because the most sweet Lord has established for us a most sweet law. And surely few, or none, could have been saved unless the Lord had established this most sweet law. [p. 345] Appropriately he adds: “And upright,” because, though sweet, he never departs from uprightness. Of him it is written that “he will render to every one according to his works” (Matt. XVI, 27). He is sweet, therefore, to the penitent, but upright toward those who persevere in wickedness.

“He shall guide the meek in judgment; he shall teach the gentle his ways.” *Mites* (“meek”) and *mansueti* (“gentle”) signify the same thing. For serious and mature persons are called *mites*, of whom it is said: “I will praise thee among a weighty people” (Ps. XXXIV, 18). But *mansueti* are so called as though “accustomed to the hand” (*manu assueti*) [Col. 0777B]. Accordingly, by contrast, we call those animals unruly which shrink from hands and do not allow themselves to be touched. Therefore God guides in judgment and teaches his ways to the gentle, because he does not permit such people to stray from the way of justice and equity. For only those are good judges and judge well who reject evil and choose good. But what are the ways of the Lord? “All the ways of the Lord are mercy and truth.” And for whom are these ways prepared? “For those who seek his covenant and his testimonies.” By these ways he himself walks; by these let us walk also, that both he may reach us and we may be able to reach him. Those walk by these ways who love, seek, and keep the testimonies of both Testaments.

“For thy name’s sake, O Lord, thou wilt be propitious [Col. 0777C] to my sin, for it is abundant.” But what is the name of the Lord? The name of the Lord is Jesus. Now *Jesus* is interpreted “Saviour.” Thus the angel said to Blessed Mary: “Behold, thou shalt conceive and bear a son, and shalt call his name Jesus” (Luke I, 31). Why? Because “he himself shall save his people from their sins” (Matt. I, 21). Therefore the Lord saves, is propitious, and shows mercy to his faithful for his name’s sake—that is, in accordance with the meaning of his name—because for this reason he was called Saviour: that he might save and grant mercy to those who call upon him. He said improperly that his sin was “abundant,” in order to show that it was very great.

“Who is the man that fears the Lord? He has established for him a law in the way which he has chosen.” Who is the man, he says, [Col. 0777D] who fears the Lord? Let him fear nothing if he has sinned; let him repent, rejoice, and be glad, because the Lord has established for him a law in the way which he has chosen. He chose, he says, to walk in the way of truth; if perhaps he has turned aside from it, let him remember that a law has been set before him; let him only repent, and it shall be forgiven him.

“His soul shall abide in good things, and his seed shall possess the earth.” So great is the power of the law established by the Lord for sinners that whoever keeps it and repents of his sins shall not be deprived of eternal good things; rather, both they and their seed—by which their imitators are understood—shall possess the land of the living as an inheritance [Col. 0778A]. In this verse the great mercy of almighty God is proclaimed, and great hope is given to the penitent.

“The Lord is a support to those who fear him, and his covenant, that it may be made known to them.” Both the Lord, he says, and the Lord’s covenant are a support to all who fear him. This covenant, moreover, has been given to us for this purpose: that through it and in it he may be made known to us who is the author of the covenant itself. We have great support and consolation, so that our hope may be firm, when we possess the knowledge of God. For that house is firm and stable which has been founded upon such a rock.

“My eyes are always toward the Lord.” And as though someone should say: “While you always fix your eyes upon him, you must beware lest you carelessly put your foot into a snare”; to this he replies: “For he himself shall pluck my feet out of the snare.” We read that this often happened to holy martyrs: while they sought God alone and desired to see and possess him, they were recognized in their very words and actions as Christians, and were immediately seized, bound, and ensnared, and dragged to punishments [Col. 0778B]. But the Lord, who never abandons those who hope in him, gave them such constancy that, by dying, they conquered their own enemies and could not be overcome by any tortures.

“Look upon me and have mercy on me, for I am alone and poor.” The Church calls herself alone and poor, because she alone among all the nations of this world worships and serves the one true God. She is also poor in those riches by which other people become rich [Col. 0778C]. When Holy Church speaks, she sometimes assumes the person of the perfect and sometimes that of the imperfect, as in this passage, where her words seem applicable only to the perfect.

“The tribulations of my heart have been enlarged; deliver me from my necessities.”

> [Note: [Col. 0777D] The same Gis. manuscript: “of my heart.”]

The times must likewise be distinguished, because not everything that she says can be applied to all times: she speaks differently in prosperity and differently in adversity. For now she says that the tribulations of her heart have been enlarged, since she suffers persecution from tyrants and heretics. Therefore she adds:

“See my humiliation and my labour, and forgive all my sins. Look upon my enemies [Col. 0778D], for they have been multiplied, and they hate me with unrighteous hatred.” She shows how greatly she has been humbled by enemies and worn out by labours, and complains that her enemies have multiplied and burned with unrighteous hatred. Therefore she now asks not for the present life, but only for remission and pardon of her sins. Thus the Apostle also says: “We do not want you to be ignorant, [p. 346] brethren, concerning our tribulation which came upon us in Asia, that we were burdened beyond measure, beyond our strength, so that we were weary even of life” (1 Cor. I, 8).

“Guard my soul and deliver me, O Lord; let me not be confounded, for I have called upon thee.” This [Col. 0779A] is as though she said: I do not ask for my body, nor do I desire to have this life—which is nothing to me except toil [Note: [Col. 0779D] The same manuscript: “and sorrow.”]—for long; guard and deliver my soul alone, and that is sufficient for me. “O Lord, let me not be confounded, for I have called upon thee.” But let these persons at last understand that calling upon thee is not shameful. For it is written: “The righteous shall stand in great constancy against those who afflicted them” (Wisdom V, 1). And then they shall recognize as wise the saints of God whom they thought foolish and stupid.

“The innocent and upright have clung to me, because I have waited for thee, O Lord.” Behold the kind of people for whom I now pray: they are innocent, they are upright, they are such as are worthy of thy grace and mercy. They have clung to me not with carnal love or carnal [Col. 0779B] affection; they have not clung to me because of me, but because I have waited for thee.

“Redeem, O God, Israel from all my distresses.” Then Holy Church shall be redeemed and delivered from all her distresses, when, whole, complete, and full with all her members, she shall be exalted above the heavens.

## PSALM XXV. A PSALM OF DAVID.

In this psalm David himself speaks, and together with him all others who are of the same perfection.

“Judge me, O Lord, for I have walked in my innocence, and, trusting in the Lord, I shall not be weakened.” The Prophet asks to be judged because he knows that he has a just cause; which indeed he would not have done had he known that his cause was unjust [Col. 0779C]. He says that he has walked in innocence because, even if he sinned, he nevertheless did not persevere in wickedness. For we know that he neither approached Bathsheba innocently nor killed Uriah innocently. But because he repented worthily and deserved to hear from the Lord through the Prophet: “Thy sin is forgiven thee” (2 Kings XII, 14), he shows himself innocent and just as though he had not sinned. For in an important matter consolation is given to sinners, that after repentance they may understand themselves to have been so saved from sins as though they had never committed them. And it seems to me that the Prophet said and wrote these things for this reason: that by his own example he might call others to so great a hope.

“And, trusting in the Lord, I shall not be weakened” [Col. 0779D]. What is “I shall not be weakened,” except that I shall not lose this innocence and health of soul which I now have? Yet he trusts that he can accomplish this not by his own powers, but by God’s mercy alone. In this saying he also gives others an example: that after repentance they should not return to sins.

“Test me, O Lord, and try me; burn my reins and my heart.” Even if the Prophet had not said this, it belongs to God, and to him alone, to search the reins and hearts. Thus he seems to have said these words not so much by petition as by declaration. For he [Col. 0780A] is the one who by his glance alone tests and tries, questions and knows what we have in our reins and in our heart; he sees whether our intention is good and our repentance fruitful; but if any rust and residue still remains there, he burns and heals it. Hence he himself says: “If thine eye be single, thy whole body shall be full of light” (Luke XI, 36).

“For thy mercy is before my eyes, and I have been pleasing in thy truth.” This is as though he said: If I had not kept thy mercy before my eyes and had not known that, through thy mercy, I who repent have been absolved from sins, I would never have asked thee to judge and test me. And appropriately he says: “I have been pleasing in thy truth,” because even in this life thy truth is magnified, since thou showest mercy to the penitent, as thou hast promised that thou wouldst do [Col. 0780B].

“I have not sat in the council of vanity, and I will not enter with those who work iniquity. I have hated the assemblies of the wicked, and I will not sit with the ungodly.” These two verses appear to say one and the same thing. Those are perfect who, whether before repentance or after repentance, can truly say these things. For what is more perfect than not to have yielded to vanity and to promise that one will do the same in the future? Of such persons the Apostle says that “where sin abounded, grace did more abound” (Rom. V, 20). Hence another psalm says: “Blessed are they whose iniquities have been forgiven and whose sins have been covered. Blessed is the man to whom the Lord has not imputed sin” [Col. 0780C] (Ps. XXXI, 1–2).

“I will wash my hands among the innocent and will compass thine altar, O Lord.” We cannot understand this literally as though King and Prophet David could have associated only with the just and innocent, unless perhaps we understand it thus: that in mind and will he associated with such persons, while he dwelt with others only in body. [p. 347] For in this way we can be together both with those absent and with those present: absent, of course, from those with whom we are, and present with those with whom we are not. For if the counsel of him who is with me does not please me, I am absent from him; but if the counsel of him who is not with me pleases me, wherever he is, I am present with him. Thus the Apostle says: “Our citizenship is in heaven” (Phil. III, [Col. 0780D] 20). Thus he also told the Corinthians that he was both absent and present. Therefore he washes his hands among the innocent, because, after the likeness of those with whom and among whom he converses in mind and soul, he purifies and sanctifies all his works, signified by hands. “And I will compass thine altar, O Lord.” Why?

“That I may hear the voice of thy praise and recount all thy wonders.” The Temple had not yet been built; but there was the tabernacle which Moses had made, the ark of the covenant, and the golden altar. He therefore promises that he will go around this altar and hear the things that were read. For only the Heptateuch [Col. 0781A] was then read there, because the books of the prophets had not yet been composed.

> [Note: [Col. 0781] That is, the volume containing the first seven books of the Old Testament.]

Therefore he heard there the praises of the Lord and all his wonders, which are most fully contained in those books. As he now promises to do, he afterward recounted and proclaimed them in all these psalms.

“O Lord, I have loved the beauty of thy house.” He explains this by adding: “And the place of the tabernacle of thy glory.” By these words he shows that he frequented greatly that house and place in which the aforesaid tabernacle and the things contained in it were kept. And he did this, as he has just said, that he might hear the voice of the Lord’s praise and recount all his wonders. How greatly he loved the beauty of the Lord’s house and the place of his tabernacle can sufficiently [Col. 0781B] be understood from the fact that he desired with great longing to build his Temple and prepared every expense necessary for it, by which afterward his son Solomon built the Temple of the Lord in his stead.

“Do not destroy my soul with the ungodly, nor my life with men of blood, in whose hands are iniquities.” Do not destroy my soul, he says, with the ungodly, nor join me in those punishments with those whose wicked counsels and assemblies I have always hated; instead, place me with the innocent, among whom I have conversed in mind and soul.

“Their right hand is full of gifts.” This is what he just said: “In whose hands are iniquities.” For he says that their hands are full of gifts [Col. 0781C] and iniquities, because they give or accept gifts in order to destroy and afflict innocent and simple people.

“But I have walked in my innocence; redeem me and have mercy on me.” I, he says, have walked in my innocence, and therefore I trust that I shall be with the innocent in that blessedness of thine. The man’s own words make most plainly evident how great was his purity and perfection. The Lord himself also demonstrates this, commending him highly in many places.

“For my foot has stood in the straight way; in the churches I will bless the Lord.” This seems to be an exposition of what he just said: “But I have walked in my innocence.” For there can be no doubt that the feet of those who walk innocently stand in the straight way [Col. 0781D]. And when he says, “In the churches I will bless the Lord,” this is a commendation of all these psalms, in which God is daily praised and blessed throughout all the Churches spread everywhere.

## PSALM XXVI. A PSALM OF DAVID BEFORE HE WAS ANOINTED.

He speaks of that anointing which was performed for him at Hebron after Saul’s death, when he was made king. Hence it is evident that this psalm was composed in the days when Saul, who pursued him with unrighteous hatred, was killed.

[Col. 0782A]

“The Lord is my illumination and my salvation. Whom shall I fear?” It seems to me that when the Prophet wrote these words he foresaw through the Holy Spirit both Saul’s death and that he himself would soon be made king. Therefore it is rightly said in the title: “A psalm of David before he was anointed.” The Lord, he says, is my illumination: he deigns so to enlighten me and reveal to me his secrets and future mysteries; through his Spirit speaking within me he promises to give me both salvation and defence. And whom shall I fear? No one, as though he said, shall I fear, protected by so great a helper and defender. Hence he adds:

“The Lord is the defender of my life: of whom shall I be afraid? When evildoers draw near against me, that they may devour [Col. 0782B] my flesh?” Of whom, he says, shall I be afraid, when evildoers draw near and plan to rush upon me, that they may devour my flesh? In saying “that they may devour my flesh,” he clearly shows the intensity of their hatred in persecuting him.

“My enemies who trouble me have themselves been weakened and fallen.” By these words he seems to signify the death of Saul and of the others who fell [p. 348] in battle.

“Though camps should stand against me, my heart shall not fear; though battle should rise up against me, in this I shall hope.” I have, he says, such a helper and defender that I fear no camps of adversaries, no armies of enemies, and no battles that rise up.

[Col. 0782C]

“One thing I have asked of the Lord; this I shall seek.” One thing, he says, I have asked of the Lord; I shall always seek it and prefer it to all else. If he gives it to me, I am rich; but if he does not give it to me, I count all other things as nothing. And what is it? “That I may dwell in the house of the Lord all the days of my life.” The powerful of this world do not say this. If they have honours, dignities, and riches, and their enemies cannot resist them—David possessed all this—they do not care to make such a request, because they love not eternal but transitory things. By the house of the Lord he means the heavenly Jerusalem, whose dwelling he preferred to all riches. And as though someone should say: Why do you so greatly desire to dwell in that house? He says:

“That I may behold the will of the Lord and be protected by his holy temple” [Col. 0782D]. No one in this life can fully know God’s purposes and counsels; consequently they often displease us when we see prosperity befall the wicked and adversity the good. Therefore the Prophet desires to be there, where he may know all truth and fear none of the enemies’ snares.

“For he hid me in his tabernacle; in the day of evils he protected me in the secret place of his tabernacle; he exalted me upon a rock. But now he has exalted my head above my enemies; I will go round about and sacrifice in his tabernacle a sacrifice of rejoicing; I will sing and chant a psalm to the Lord.”

[Col. 0783A]

For this reason, he says, I will go round about, sacrifice, and chant a psalm to the Lord: because he hid me in his tabernacle, and the rest that follows. Let us now consider the meaning. Saul and all my other enemies, as though he said, were able to drive me and my people from my house and my tabernacle; but they could not put me to flight and drive me out from the most spacious tabernacle of God. He understands this world as the tabernacle of God, covered like a tabernacle with the canopy of heaven. In this tabernacle the Lord hid and guarded him so that none of his enemies could either seize or find him. The days of evils are those in which evil people rule and do their own wills. When he says, “But now he has exalted my head above [Col. 0783B] my enemies,” this is as though he had said: But now, when Saul and my other enemies are dead, and the Lord has willed to establish me as king over his people, now, I say, the Lord has exalted my head—that is, my strength and might—above all my enemies. For, as is read in the books of Kings, at that time no one in those regions could resist his power and strength. And in return for so great a benefit bestowed on him by God, he now rightly says: “I will go round about and sacrifice in his tabernacle a sacrifice of rejoicing.” He has spoken sufficiently of this tabernacle in the preceding psalm. For this is that tabernacle which Moses made, concerning which the Apostle also says: “The first tabernacle was made, in which were the lampstand, the ark of the covenant, [Col. 0783C] and the table of the loaves of presentation, which is called the holy place” (Heb. IX, 2). This, indeed, was in that land in those days, and David could not approach it during the whole time of his persecution. But now, peace having been granted him, he promises that he will go there, pay his vows, offer sacrifices of praise and rejoicing, and sing to God in psalms. It follows:

“Hear, O Lord, my voice with which I cried to thee; have mercy on me and hear me.

“My heart said to thee: I have sought thy face; thy face, O Lord, I will seek.

“Do not turn thy face away from me, and do not turn aside in anger from thy servant.”

The Prophet speaks thus as though he had already come to the tabernacle of the Lord, where he had promised to sing and offer sacrifices of rejoicing [Col. 0783D]. It is as though he said: Behold, O Lord, I have come to thy tabernacle, which I always desired, and I stand before thy presence. Therefore now hear my prayer with which I cried to thee; now have mercy on me and hear me. Concerning what? Concerning that which he said above: “One thing I have asked of the Lord, this I shall seek: that I may dwell in the house of the Lord all the days of my life” (Ps. XXII, 6). This is what he says: “My heart said to thee: I have sought [Col. 0784A] thy face; thy face, O Lord, I will seek.” For what does “Thy face, O Lord, I will seek” mean except “One thing I have asked of the Lord, this I shall seek”? And who can see the face of the Lord except one who dwells in the house of the Lord?

> [Note: [Col. 0783D] Add from St Maximus of Turin: “For the whole most holy dispensation of Christ’s humanity intends and requires nothing other than that it direct us upward, so that, when the time of our mortality has been completed, it may bring us to the manifest vision of itself and satisfy us with the eternal glory of its face.” Sermon 48, Roman edition, [Col. 0784D] p. 520.]

O most wise king and most devout of all others, who desired with his whole heart to leave behind the kingdom which he had received in those days and to possess heavenly joys! “Do not turn thy face away from me; do not turn aside in anger from thy servant. Be my helper; do not forsake me or despise me, O God my Saviour.” The Prophet speaks thus as though the Lord had turned his face away from him, shown himself angry, and said to him: “You ask what is impossible; and what you request you cannot obtain now. It shall be given you in its own time; and do not fear, because I shall not abandon [Col. 0784B; p. 349] or forsake you.” This seems to be signified by what follows.

“For my father and my mother have forsaken me, but the Lord has received me.” Who is this father except the world, concerning which the Lord says: “The children of this world are wiser in their generation than the children of light” (Luke XVI, 8); and of which Jeremiah says: “Cursed be the man who brought news to my father, saying: A male child has been born to thee” (Jer. XX, 15). But the mother is iniquity, as the same Prophet testifies when he says: “For I was conceived in iniquities” (Ps. L, 7). It is also said of the devil that he beholds everything lofty and that he himself is king over all the children of pride. In this respect the pride of all the wicked is shown to be their mother. Therefore only those are received by the Lord whom this father and this mother forsake.

“Establish for me a law, O Lord, in thy way, and direct me into the straight path [Col. 0784C] because of my enemies.”

> [Note: [Col. 0784D] Vallicellian manuscript: “because of thy name.” Gis. manuscript: “because of my enemies.”]

Because, he says, my request cannot now be heard and thou commandest me still to dwell in this world amid the snares of my enemies, establish for me in thy way the same law that thou hast established for others. Of this law another psalm says: “Who is the man that fears the Lord? He has established for him a law in the way which he has chosen” (Ps. XXIV, 12).

> [Note: [Col. 0784D] The same Vallicellian manuscript: “fearing the Lord.” Gis. manuscript: “fears God.”]

And why does he say that the law should be established for him which he knows to have been established for all people, except because he fears more than others that he may sin if perhaps, on some occasion, he turns aside from the way of justice? Hence the Lord says: “The servant who knows his master’s will and does not do it shall be beaten with many stripes; but he who does not know and does not do it shall be beaten with few” [Col. 0784D] (Luke XII, 47).

“Do not deliver me into the souls of those who persecute me.” [Note: According to the historical sense, this may be understood of Saul, who pursued him with the bitterest hatred. But because he was king and could not alone do what he commanded, the plural number is suitably used here.] By these, however, we understand evil spirits, whose chief desire is to make righteous men turn aside from the straight path and fall into sins. For, as it is written, “his food is choice”; concerning them it follows: “For unjust witnesses have risen up against me, and iniquity has lied to itself.” For these are they who accused blessed Job, bore false witness against him, and do not cease day and night to accuse God’s saints before God’s presence. But iniquity has lied to itself. Hence we read in another psalm: “His pain shall return upon his own head, and his iniquity shall descend upon his own crown” (Ps. 7:17).

“I believe that I shall see the good things of the Lord in the land of the living.” Although, he says, false witnesses rise against me, yet I believe and do not in any way doubt that my petition has been heard and that I see the good things of the Lord in the land of the living. For I hear the Lord himself speaking within me; I hear the Holy Spirit consoling me and saying: “Wait for the Lord; act manfully, let your heart be strengthened, and wait for the Lord.” Hence he says elsewhere: “I will hear what the Lord God speaks within me” (Ps. 84:9).

## Psalm XXVII. A Psalm of David Himself.

This title seems to say that David himself speaks the things contained in this psalm: “of David himself,” that is, of Christ our Lord and Saviour.

“To you, O Lord, I cried; my God, do not be silent toward me, lest I become like those who go down into the pit.” This is not the voice of David alone, but of all others who possess the same faith as David. “To you,” he says, “O Lord, I cried; do not be silent toward me.” What does “do not be silent toward me” mean but “answer me”? And what is “answer me” but “hear my prayer”? For if you do not do this, “I shall become like those who go down into the pit.” Of this pit he says elsewhere: “He opened a pit and dug it, and he fell into the hole which he made” (Ps. 7:6).

“Hear the voice of my supplication, while I pray to you and lift up my hands toward your holy temple.” Hence he says elsewhere: “In the nights lift up your hands unto the holy place” (Ps. 133:1). For “unto the holy place” has the same meaning as “toward your holy temple.” Therefore, whenever we lift our hands in our prayers, we lift them toward God’s holy temple, because—even though we do not see that temple itself—they are directed there by the intention of the heart.

“Do not draw me away together with sinners, and do not destroy me with those who work iniquity.” This is a plain prayer and needs no exposition, since it is easy to understand.

“With those who speak peace to their neighbour, but evil things are in their hearts.” This was done by Judas the traitor, who betrayed our Saviour with peaceful words and deceit [Note: Codex Ghislerianus: “and with a kiss.”]; and whoever imitates him in such a deed need not doubt that he shares his lot. This is what the Prophet invokes against them in what follows.

“Give them, O Lord, according to their works, and repay them according to the wickedness of their pursuits. Render their recompense to them.” Namely, the recompense of which they are worthy.

“For they have not understood the works of the Lord, nor considered the works of his hands.” All the works of the Lord are good, for “God saw all things that he had made, and they were very good” (Gen. 1:31). Therefore we ought to direct all our works according to the example of so great a worker, so that in our works also nothing but good may be found. But these men did the opposite and wished that nothing but evil should exist in their works. Therefore let that happen to them which follows:

“Destroy them, and do not build them up.” A destruction is beneficial when good building follows it. Thus the Apostle, destroyed and rebuilt, said: “I live; yet no longer I, but Christ lives in me” (Gal. 2:20). But these will be destroyed as those of whom it is said: “You shall break them as a potter’s vessel.” “Blessed be the Lord, because he has heard the voice of my supplication” (Ps. 2:9). He gives thanks to God because he sees fulfilled all that he had invoked against the wicked and traitors. For the Spirit who spoke in him suddenly, in a moment, showed him what was to come as though it had already happened.

“The Lord is my helper and my protector; in him my heart hoped, and I was helped.” He now disdains to speak further against those whom he sees so miserably destroyed and condemned. Instead, he rejoices and, as he had begun, perseveres in giving thanks for the help and protection divinely granted him.

“And my flesh flourished again, and with my will I shall confess him.” This may also be understood of repentance and baptism, by which the whole person is made young and renewed. When he says, “with my will I shall confess him,” he shows that the confession which is praiseworthy is not compelled but voluntary, produced by charity, love, and affection.

“The Lord is the strength of his people.” This is what he says elsewhere: “Some trust in chariots and some in horses, but we shall be magnified in the name of the Lord our God” (Ps. 19:8). He is our strength, who said to his disciples: “Without me you can do nothing” (John 15:5).

“And he is the protector of the salvations of his Christ.” This is as though he said: Those whom the Son has saved and redeemed by his blood, the Father protects and defends; thus, by “salvations” we understand those who have been saved. Now the Prophet turns to God, asking him to save, bless, guide, and exalt his people and inheritance: “Save your people, O Lord, and bless your inheritance, and exalt them for ever.”

## Psalm XXVIII. A Psalm of David at the Completion of the Tabernacle.

This tabernacle is the holy Church. It was made both perfect and complete when our Saviour, hanging upon the cross, gave up his spirit. When they had given him vinegar mixed with gall, and he had tasted it and would not drink, he said: “It is completed”; and, bowing his head, he gave up his spirit (John 19:30). “Completed,” he says: the tabernacle in which, throughout the time of my incarnation until this hour, I have not ceased to labour, is complete and perfect.

“Bring to the Lord, sons of God; bring to the Lord the sons of rams.” The sons of God are those of whom the Evangelist says: “As many as received him, he gave them power to become sons of God—to those who believe in his name” (John 1:12). And elsewhere: “Beloved, we are sons of God, and it has not yet appeared what we shall be” (1 John 3:2). The rams, however, are the apostles and teachers, who are greater in the whole ecclesiastical flock and hold the first place; and who, by water and the Holy Spirit, beget for the Lord not kids but lambs. Therefore let the Prophet say, and with him every believer: Behold, the tabernacle is complete, and it is most fitting that at its completion we should offer gifts to our God. But what gifts? “The sons of rams.” And what do we understand by the sons of rams but lambs—that is, the innocent, simple, and meek? Such gifts the sons of God, that is, bishops and priests, offer to God daily. Hence the Lord says: “Render to Caesar the things that are Caesar’s, and to God the things that are God’s” (Luke 20:25).

“Bring to the Lord glory and honour; bring to the Lord glory for his name.” Those offer him glory and honour who proclaim and praise him in word and deed. Those also offer glory for his name who give him thanks for the salvation he has worked in us, magnify him, and bless him. For his name is Jesus, which is interpreted “Saviour.”

“Worship the Lord in his holy court.” Behold, he says, the tabernacle has been built and God’s court—by which the Church is understood—has been completed. Worship him there; proclaim and magnify him there. When the Prophet said these things, he saw in the Spirit the apostles and preachers throughout all nations praising and proclaiming God, and an innumerable multitude hastening to the faith of Christ and to the Church. Moved by exceeding joy, he said: “The voice of the Lord is upon the waters; the God of majesty” — understood: “thundered” — “upon the waters, and the Lord thundered upon many waters.” The many waters are, as it is written, many peoples. [Note: Codex Ghislerianus: “Therefore upon these waters.”] Therefore the voice of the Lord sounds and thunders upon the waters when holy preachers proclaim the word of God in the Church. And because it is not they who speak, but the Holy Spirit speaks in them, it is rightly said here that “the God of majesty thundered upon many waters.” We may also understand the many waters as the waters of baptism, over which the voice of God blessing is heard daily through the mouths of priests. And as though someone should ask, “How do you prove that this is the voice of the Lord which thundered upon many waters?” he adds:

“The voice of the Lord is in power; the voice of the Lord is in magnificence.” Unless, he says, it were the voice of the Lord, it would not possess such great power and efficacy. For what could be more wonderful or glorious than to give sight to the blind, cleanse lepers, raise the dead, and so suddenly sanctify the ungodly and sinners in the waters of baptism? This voice destroyed temples of gods, shattered idols, drove away demons, humbled the greater powers of this world from the height of their pride, and converted them to faith in Christ. Hence it is said in what follows that it shattered cedars, divided flames, shook wildernesses, prepared stags, and revealed thickets. It is thus proved that this is the voice of the Lord, displayed with such power and magnificence. But whose Lord?

“The voice of the Lord shattering cedars; and the Lord shall shatter the cedars of Lebanon, and crush them like a calf of Lebanon, and the Beloved One like a son of unicorns.” By cedars we ought to understand the rich and powerful of this age. Some of these are shattered of their own accord and humbled under Christ’s yoke, but such shattering is good. Others, raised to an excessive height of pride, shall be cut down, shattered, and cast into the fire, as it is written: “Every tree which does not bear good fruit shall be cut down and cast into the fire. And the Lord shall shatter the cedars of Lebanon” (Matt. 3:10). By Lebanon and the cedars of Lebanon Jerusalem and its inhabitants are signified, since that city was once the noblest among cities, and its inhabitants were rich, powerful, and wise. We see that these have now for the most part been shattered and crushed; nevertheless, we think that still greater punishment awaits them in the judgment. Thus the prophet Zechariah says: “Open your gates, O Lebanon, and let fire devour your cedars” (Zech. 11:1). This was fulfilled in the time of Titus and Vespasian, when the city was captured and, together with that most noble temple, was wholly burned. Its inhabitants perished miserably by fire, famine, and other punishments, apart from those who were led away by their enemies into captivity and slavery. Of them it is further said:

“And he shall crush them like a calf of Lebanon.” He speaks of that calf of which it is written in Exodus and Leviticus: before it was offered, it was entirely cut into pieces and laid upon a pile of wood; then, after fire had been set beneath it, it was wholly burnt. By comparison with it he threatens that these most proud cedars shall be crushed.

“And the Beloved One like a son of unicorns.” Of this Beloved One the Lord says: “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased” (Matt. 12:18). Of him the Church says in the Song of Songs: “My beloved is white and ruddy, chosen from among thousands” (Song 5:10); and again: “Flee, my beloved; be like a roe or a young stag upon the mountains of spices” (ibid. 8:14). Therefore this Beloved One shall crush, shatter, and scatter that impious and ungrateful people, like a son of unicorns which, when enraged, throws down and crushes everything that meets it. This animal is called *rhinoceros* in Greek; it has a single horn above its nose, of such strength that no animal can resist it. Therefore our Saviour is excellently compared with the rhinoceros, of whom it is written: “The Lord shall judge the ends of the earth, and shall give dominion to his king, and shall exalt the horn of his Christ” (1 Sam. 2:10).

“The voice of the Lord cutting apart the flame of fire; the voice of the Lord shaking the wilderness, and the Lord shall move the desert of Kadesh.” There was a great flame between Jews and Gentiles, because each people, inflamed by the fire of its own law and religion, was unwilling to have any fellowship with the other. Thus blessed Peter was reproved by the Jews because he had entered the house of an uncircumcised man. But when he gave his account, he extinguished all that flame and indignation which was stirring in their hearts. In this example it plainly appears how the voice of the Lord cuts apart the flame of fire. Hence it follows that “the voice of the Lord shook the wilderness”—that is, the Gentiles—“and shall move the desert of Kadesh,” that is, the Jews. For both these and those, having heard the word of preaching, were shaken and moved by fear of the future judgment, converted to faith in Christ, and began to do repentance. When they asked him, blessed John, the forerunner of the Lord, is recorded to have answered: “I am the voice of one crying in the wilderness: prepare the way of the Lord” (Luke 3:4); and again: “Do repentance, for the kingdom of heaven has drawn near” (ibid.). To the Jews he said, “He who has two tunics, let him give to him who has none” (ibid., v. 11); but to the soldiers, who were from among the Gentiles: “Do violence to no one; accuse no one falsely; be content with your wages” (ibid., v. 14). Thus the voice of the Lord both shook the wilderness and moved the desert. But what desert? The desert of Kadesh. For *Kadesh* is interpreted “holy,” and by it that people is quite suitably represented which had been chosen and sanctified by God from among all nations.

“The voice of the Lord preparing stags; and he shall reveal the thickets, and in his temple all shall speak glory.” What do we understand by stags but the apostles: swift in running, quick in preaching, killing serpents, fearing no poison, and longing for springs of water? The Lord prepared them to preach the Gospel and to unveil and expound the Scriptures. Hence it follows: “And he revealed the thickets.” Through them the Lord shall reveal the thickets and the very obscure mysteries of both Testaments. Thus when the Apostle John saw these thickets and beheld a book sealed with seven seals, he wept greatly because no one worthy to open the book could be found. But he was told not to weep, because “the Lion of the tribe of Judah, the root of David, has conquered, to open the book and loose its seven seals” (Rev. 5:5). Thus the Lord first deigned to reveal these thickets to the apostles, and through the apostles to us. “And in his temple all shall speak glory”: which they certainly would not have done unless the book had been opened and the thickets unveiled.

[Note: The Vulgate reads: “The Lord makes the flood to dwell.” This is excellently explained by St Maximus of Turin: “Let us consider the whole world, look upon the barbarian nations, and survey also the Roman empire: everywhere they are baptized into our Lord; and so it comes about that there is not one body of water, but, as it were, a flood of those being baptized.” Sermon 10, Roman edition, p. 403.]

“The Lord shall inhabit the flood, and the Lord shall sit as king for ever.” Above he spoke of many waters; now he speaks not of many waters but of the flood itself, in which no water was lacking. By this we understand that the whole world shall be converted to faith in Christ before the consummation of the age. Hence it follows: “The Lord shall sit as king for ever.” For when all things have been made subject to him and all the nations of this world have received his faith, then it will be manifest to all that he alone, king and Lord, reigns for ever.

“The Lord shall give strength to his people.” He has already given it, but he will yet give greater strength, because the whole world shall be judged through him and by him. Thus the Apostle says: “Do you not know that you shall judge the world? If then the world shall be judged by you, are you unworthy to judge the smallest matters?” (1 Cor. 6:1). And then indeed “he shall bless his people in peace.” What is “in peace”? In himself. “For he himself is your peace, who made both one” (Eph. 2:14). Therefore those who receive that blessing shall receive eternal life together with him.

## Psalm XXIX. A Psalm of Song at the Dedication of the House of David.

The house of David is the Church, which is daily built and sanctified. Therefore this psalm is to be sung daily, since it is commanded to be sung at the dedication of the house of David. Its completion indeed took place in a short time; but its dedication continues for a long time. For although a person is baptized and made a Christian in a short time, yet throughout the whole time that he lives he must be dedicated, purified, and sanctified. [Note: Codex Ghislerianus: “washed.”] Hence God commands through Moses concerning priests that, after their consecration, their hands should still be anointed for seven days. For whatever is done for seven days is done throughout all time, because there are only seven days.
