“I will exalt you, O Lord, because you have received me, and have not made my enemies rejoice over me.” The Church herself speaks these words at her dedication and at the dedication of her children. “I will exalt you,” she says, “O Lord; I will praise and magnify your name.” Certainly God cannot be exalted, for he is exalted above all things, and “there is no end of his greatness” (Ps. 144:3). Yet he is said to be exalted by us when we proclaim his greatness, power, and glory and announce him to those who do not know him. When she says, “Because you have received me,” it is as though she said: I offended you greatly; I withdrew far from you, for “salvation is far from sinners” (Ps. 118:155). I went where I ought not to have gone, into a far country; I fed swine; I began to be in want; and finally, returning to myself and remembering your sweetness, I returned to you through repentance. But what did you do? You received me, adorned and beautified me, called me to your banquet, satisfied me with the delights of your body and blood; and therefore, mindful of these great benefits, I shall exalt you. “And you have not made my enemies rejoice over me.” Our enemies, evil spirits, rejoice when we sin; they delight and exult when we persist in sins. Therefore that soul may say and sing this which repents quickly and does not remain long in sin. Hence it follows:

“O Lord my God, I cried to you, and you healed me. O Lord, you drew my soul up from hell; you healed me from among those going down into the pit.” My soul, he says, was already greatly weakened and already counted among the dead; it was being drawn by evil spirits toward hell with those going down into the pit. But when, remembering both myself and you, I cried to you, you heard me, though I was unworthy; you healed me, drew me up from hell, and by your compassion and mercy alone saved me from among those going down into the pit. Do you not see how well all this accords with the dedication of the Church?

“Sing psalms to the Lord, you his saints, and confess to the remembrance of his holiness.” “Sing psalms,” says the Church, “to the Lord, all you his saints. Praise, proclaim, and magnify him in this dedication of mine and yours: he who so loves us, cleanses us, heals us, washes us, and purifies and sanctifies us from every stain of our sins. And confess to the remembrance of his holiness,” just as he always remembers us and never forgets his faithful ones. Above all, it is very necessary to do this. Why?

“For wrath is in his indignation, and life is in his favour.” Strive, he says, to appease him and obtain his favourable will; do not provoke him to indignation and anger, since wrath in his indignation is unbearable, while eternal life is in his good will. And as though someone should say, “You command us to sing psalms and preach, yet you do not consider the snares of enemies, who are ready to seize, hold, and kill us,” the Church replies:

“Weeping shall linger until evening, and joy shall come in the morning.” This persecution, she says, will soon pass; this sadness will soon be turned into joy. He who has sorrow until evening shall have joy in the morning. “Therefore do not fear those who kill the body, because they cannot kill the soul” (Matt. 10:8). By evening, therefore, which is the end of the day, let us understand this temporal death, which is itself the end of our life. At that end all weeping and sorrow of the saints cease, and immediately they come to morning—that is, to the beginning of that day of which it is written: “One day in your courts is better than thousands” (Ps. 83:11). We may also understand by evening the end of this world, and by morning the beginning of the other life, when the saints, going out from the darkness of this life, shall enter into the blessedness of eternal light. How excellently the holy mother Church consoles her members and children in the time of her dedication!

“But I said in my abundance, I shall not be moved for ever.” “I am rich,” she says, “I abound in every good thing: ‘The Lord shepherds me, and I lack nothing’” (Ps. 22:1). In this my abundance I said, and say, “I shall not be moved for ever: neither death nor life, neither height nor depth, neither things present nor things to come, nor any creature, shall be able to separate me from the love of God which is in Christ Jesus” (Rom. 8:39). Let enemies rage as much as they wish; let them threaten flames, crosses, and every kind of torture: I am established upon the firm rock, and I shall not be moved for ever.

“O Lord, in your good will you gave strength to my beauty.” You gave me beauty, she says, and upon that beauty added this strength which I possess. This came not through any preceding merits, but from your good will. Hence the Apostle says: “It is not of him who wills, nor of him who runs, but of God who shows mercy. For what have you that you did not receive?” (Rom. 9:16). Therefore all virtue, steadfastness, and strength of the saints belong not to themselves but to God. Hence it follows:

“You turned your face away from me, and I became troubled.” The Lord does not indeed turn his face away from his saints; but, so that they may be tested and made manifest, he sometimes permits them to be afflicted, and then he seems to have turned his face away. Yet if they are troubled and cannot endure the tortures themselves, he is immediately at hand to protect and console them, so that they may easily understand that they cannot fight by their own strength. Hence they say elsewhere: “In God we shall do valiantly, and he shall bring our enemies to nothing” (Ps. 59:14). But what should the saints do when they recognize that they are troubled amid the very tortures? It follows:

“To you, O Lord, I will cry, and to my God I will make supplication.” See how, and with what weapons, the devout mother equips her children for battle. For we read that our Saviour warned his disciples at the time of his passion: “Pray,” he said, “that you may not enter into temptation; for the spirit is willing, but the flesh is weak” (Matt. 26:39). Therefore the saints pray not that they may escape death, but that in their torments they may not do anything against God. Hence it follows: “What profit is there in my blood, while I go down into corruption?” This is as though he said: What benefit is it to me to have shed my blood and endured so many and such great tortures, if now my enemies can corrupt and deceive me? This may also be understood of Christ’s blood, which the Church calls her own because it was shed for her alone.

“Will dust confess you, or declare your truth?” This is that dust of which it is said elsewhere: “Which the wind casts away from the face of the earth” (Ps. 1:4). Therefore, if the saints perish and are corrupted from the sincerity of their faith by fear of torments, who will confess the Lord? Who will further preach and declare his truth? It follows:

“The Lord heard and had mercy on me; the Lord became my helper.” The Lord, the consoler of all the afflicted, heard these words which the Church, or the holy martyrs, spoke—or rather pondered in their minds—at the time of their affliction, and gave them fitting and necessary consolation. Hence it follows:

“You turned my mourning into joy for me.” The Lord did this when he either delivered his saints from their torments or granted them the strength and steadfastness to endure them.

“You tore my sackcloth and girded me with joy.” What do we understand by sackcloth but the mortal and corruptible body, in which the soul is shut up and contained as in the meanest sack? Unless this is torn and the soul flies freely from it, God’s saints cannot possess full joy. “So that my glory may sing to you, and I may not be pierced with grief.” “These things,” she says, “O Lord, who are my glory, you granted me: you turned my mourning into joy; you tore my sackcloth; you girded me with joy, so that henceforth, secure and free from every care, I may sing to you a song of joy and exultation and not be pierced with grief.” There is no compunction there where there is neither sin nor any fear of sin. “O Lord my God, I will confess you.” This confession, as in many places, is used for praise: by it, together with the angels in the heavenly Jerusalem, all the saints acclaim the Lord with ineffable joy and gladness.

## Psalm XXX. For the End, a Psalm of David.

We have often already said what “for the end” signifies and what “a psalm of David” signifies. “For we are they,” says the Apostle, “upon whom the ends of the ages have come” (1 Cor. 10:11). Therefore the Church speaks in this psalm; and because all are contained in her, she assumes the persons of all: now of the apostles and other teachers of the Church; now of martyrs; now of confessors; now of the perfect; now of the imperfect; now of some; now of all. Even if she should sometimes speak for the Head himself, this would not be unfitting, because the head too is part of the body, indeed its greatest and principal part. Thus in the preceding psalm she says: “What profit is there in my blood?”—that is, in the blood which you shed for me.

“In you, O Lord, I have hoped; I shall not be confounded for ever. In your righteousness deliver me and rescue me. Incline your ear to me; hasten to rescue me. Be to me a protecting God and a place of refuge, that you may save me.” Our mother, Holy Church, teaches us how earnestly we ought to apply and persist in prayer, because she repeats this very thing so often. For the Apostle also says: “Pray without ceasing” (1 Thess. 5:17). And the Lord in the Gospel: “Ask,” he says, “and you shall receive; seek, and you shall find; knock, and it shall be opened” (Matt. 7:7). He also gives the example of the man who asked his friend for three loaves (Luke 11:5). Although the friend refused to rise throughout the whole night, the other continued throughout the whole night in his request; at last, wearied by his persistence, he rose and gave him as many as he needed. “In you, O Lord, I have hoped,” and so forth: because I have hoped in you, I shall not be confounded for ever. Hence also the Apostle: “Hope,” he says, “does not confound” (Rom. 5:5). For it would confound if one always hoped and never received the things hoped for. As nothing is worse than despair, so nothing is better than firm hope. When he says, “In your righteousness deliver me and rescue me,” it is as though he said: [Note: Codex Ghislerianus: “because you are just.”] Do as your righteousness requires. The remaining words which follow have the same meaning.

“For you are my strength and my refuge.” Therefore, he says, I said: “Be to me a protecting God and a place of refuge,” because I have no protector, strength, or refuge other than you. For I know that everyone is cursed who hopes in man, places his hope in his own arm, and whose heart withdraws from God. “And for your name’s sake you will be my guide and nourish me.” The Lord’s name is Jesus, and Jesus is interpreted “Saviour.” There is therefore great reason why, for his own name’s sake, he should save, protect, lead, and nourish his faithful people: he was called so in order to do these things, and if he were not going to do them, he would not have been called so.

“And you will bring me out of this snare which they have hidden for me, because you are my protector, O Lord.” [Note: Codex Vallicellianus: “You will bring me out of the snare which they have concealed,” etc. Codex Ghislerianus: “You will bring me out of this snare which they have hidden.”] Who can enumerate all the snares which tyrants, heretics, and evil spirits have concealed for Christ’s saints and faithful? Why, then, is “this snare” spoken of here in the singular, except because, though deception is one in kind, there are many forms of deception? Thus it is said elsewhere: “My soul has been delivered like a sparrow from the snare of hunters” (Ps. 123:7); and: “For he has delivered me from the snare of hunters and from the harsh word” (Ps. 90:3).—“Because you are my protector, O Lord, into your hands I commend my spirit.” “I fear,” he says, “the snare of enemies; I fear their hidden and cunning deceits. Let them do whatever they wish to my body, but I commend my spirit to you.” This too is written of blessed Job: when the Lord had given Satan power over him, he commanded that his soul be preserved (Job 2:6). Our Saviour himself, hanging on the cross, commended his spirit to the Lord [Note: “Let us consider why the very words which the Gospel text relates are set down here. For there it likewise says: ‘Into your hands I commend my spirit’; and, bowing his head, he gave up his spirit—so that here also you might know that the one who spoke was he who, after so many ages, was to utter the same words while hanging on the cross.” Cassiodorus.], in order to teach us what we ought to do in such an event.

“You have redeemed me, O Lord God of truth.” “I commend my spirit to you,” he says, “who have guided me beyond measure, when you redeemed me at the price of your blood. You did this lest my spirit should perish.” By calling him the God of truth, he shows that he has greater confidence from this fact, because God cannot fail to do what he has promised. For he said: “I will not leave you or forsake you” (John 14:18); and: “Behold, I am with you all days, even unto the consummation of the age” (Matt. 28:20); and again: “Do not fear those who kill the body, but cannot kill the soul” (Matt. 10:8).—“You have hated those who observe vanity in vain.” Solomon says concerning vanity: “Vanity of vanities, and all is vanity” (Eccl. 1:1). And the Apostle: “For the creation was subjected to vanity, not willingly” (Rom. 8:20). And this same Prophet: “Yet every living human being is altogether vanity” (Ps. 38:6). Since, therefore, no one is without vanity, “in vain” is rightly added here, so that we understand him to hate only those who perform and observe vanity in vain—not those who, even unwillingly, are subjected to vanity, as the Apostle teaches (Rom. 8:20). Thus those are subjected to vanity in vain for whom vanity itself is so pleasing that they never cease from vanity. By these we understand those who persist in their wickedness to the end.

“But I will hope in the Lord, and rejoice and be glad in your mercy.” Whoever speaks in this way plainly shows that he is not among those who observe vanity in vain.

“Because you have regarded my humility, you have kept my soul safe from distresses; and you have not shut me up in the hands of the enemy. You have set my feet in a spacious place.” Therefore, he says, I shall rejoice and be glad in your mercy, because I know that your mercy toward me is greatest and beyond estimation. This is shown by the fact that, in the time of persecution, you regarded my humility, kept my soul safe from many distresses, and—when my enemy thought that I had been captured, deceived, and wholly overcome—you liberated me and did not shut me up in the enemy’s hands, but set my feet in a spacious place. For I was enlarged all the more precisely where they believed me narrowed and reduced to nothing. At no time did the Church grow so greatly or expand so widely as in the time of persecution. One person was killed, and by that person’s faith and constancy many others were converted to the faith.

“Miserere mihi, Domine, quoniam tribulor.” “Have mercy on me, O Lord, for I am troubled.” From where? “My eye, my soul, and my belly are disturbed in anger.” When the Church now says that she is joyful and heard, and delivered from all her straits and necessities, yet at another time complains that she is disturbed, afflicted, saddened, and surrounded by many injuries, this must be referred to different times. For [Note: [Col. 0796D] The same manuscript: “at times.”] at times the saints rejoiced in the peace divinely granted to them; but at other times they were afflicted by such great [Col. 0796B] straits that they were weary even of living (2 Cor. 1:8), as the Apostle says. Therefore she now says: “Have mercy on me, O Lord, for I am troubled.” And immediately, showing the cause of this very trouble, she adds: “My eye, my soul, and my belly are disturbed in anger.” But what are we to understand by the eye of the Church, if not the apostles and teachers? For these are they who enlighten the rest, show the way of truth, direct them into the way of God’s commandments, and do not permit them to go astray. By the soul, moreover, the same persons are signified, since they also bestow life upon others. And they are in the Church as the soul is in the body. The belly, however, denotes those who are softer and more imperfect than all the others. Yet the whole Church consists in these persons. In the anger and fury of wicked men [Col. 0796C] the Church shows herself wholly disturbed, when she says that her eye, soul, and belly are disturbed.

“For my life has failed in sorrow, and my years in groanings.” This, therefore, is the reason why the Church is thus disturbed: all the days of her life are spent and end in sorrow and groaning. “My strength has been weakened in poverty, and my bones are disturbed.” The poverty of persons is greater than the poverty of riches. Thus the Church calls herself poor when, for some reason, she loses her children. She is weakened by such poverty, because, when they fail, there is no one able to defend the truth. Hence she also says that her bones are disturbed; by these we understand the stronger persons [Col. 0796D] who were accustomed to bear and sustain the other members.

“Above all my enemies I have become a reproach, exceedingly so to my neighbours, and a terror to those known to me.” For it sometimes happened that neighbours and relatives afflicted and mocked the saints more than did their other enemies. We know that the friends of blessed Job once did this as well. They were also a terror to those known to them—that is, to those of the same religion, though not of the same 356 perfection—because they were often afraid to approach them, lest perhaps they too should be seized and [Col. 0797A] held with them. Nicodemus did this as well, for he came to Jesus not by day but by night (John 3:1). Hence it follows:

“Those who saw me fled from me outside; I was cut off from the heart as though dead.” [Note: [Col. 0797D] The Vulgate reads: “I was given over to forgetfulness, as one dead from the heart.”] Those, he says, who saw me—that is, those who desired to see me—immediately upon seeing me fled because of my case, described above. Consequently, they forgot me altogether. And this is what he says: “I was cut off from their heart and memory as though dead. And I became like a lost vessel,” because they regarded me as impious and liable to destruction. Hence the Lord says in the Gospel: “The hour will come when everyone who kills you will think that he is offering service to God” (John 16:2). It is very customary [Col. 0797B] in divine speech for a human being to be signified by vessels; hence the apostle Paul is called a vessel of election. Mother Church can also say this in the person of our Savior, who became like a lost vessel because “he was numbered among the wicked” (Luke 22:37). He himself heard the reproach of many dwelling round about, when they mocked him as he knelt, saying: “Ha! You who destroy the temple of God and rebuild it in three days” (Matt. 27:40), and much else besides.

“While they were all gathering together against me, they took counsel to take my life.” For this was the counsel of the wicked, and for this reason they assembled: that by an evil death they might destroy and kill the saints, and by harsh torments wrench out their [Col. 0797C] souls. But what did they do? Let the Church speak:

“But I,” she says, “have hoped in you, O Lord; I said: You are my God; my times are in your hands. Deliver me and rescue me from the hands of my enemies and from those who persecute me. Make your face shine upon your servant, and save me in your mercy. O Lord, let me not be confounded, for I have called upon you.” These are the weapons of the saints: thus let them defend themselves; let them fight not with swords but with prayers. Our times are in God’s hands, because according to his judgment we must both live and die. He makes his face shine upon us when he shows himself gracious to us and hears our prayers.

“Let the ungodly be ashamed and be brought down into hell; [Col. 0797D] let deceitful lips be made mute, which speak iniquity against the righteous in pride and contempt.” This will occur at the judgment, when the ungodly and sinners recognize that they have erred; recognizing it, they will be ashamed, and thus, confounded, they will sink into hell. Then at last deceitful lips will be made mute—the lips which now speak against the righteous and catholic man in pride and contempt.

“How great is the multitude of your sweetness, O Lord, [Col. 0798A] which you have hidden for those who fear you, and have perfected for those who hope in you in the sight of the children of men.” At the same time, he says, when the ungodly are ashamed and brought down into hell, the saints will know, and by experience itself will understand, how great is the multitude of God’s sweetness, which is still hidden from them. But when he says, “And have perfected it for those who hope in you in the sight of the children of men,” this is what the Lord says in the Gospel: “Whoever confesses me before men, I too will confess him before my Father who is in heaven” (Matt. 10:32). But after the Lord has revealed this multitude of his sweetness to his saints, let us hear what he will do for them next.

“You will hide them,” he says, “in the secrecy of your countenance from the disturbance of men; you will protect them in your tabernacle [Col. 0798B] from the contradiction of tongues.” The tabernacle of God and that secret place in which the visage and face of God may be seen signify the same thing. By this, what else are we to understand than the palace of the heavenly kingdom? There the saints of God, who are thus disturbed and wearied in this world, will rejoice without end together with God their Creator, free from any disturbance and contradiction. Hence the Church blesses the Lord, who has so magnificently made wonderful his mercy to his saints in that most fortified city. And this is what she says:

“Blessed be the Lord, who has made his mercy wonderful in the city of enclosure.” What is here called “in the city of enclosure” is called “in the fortified city” in another translation. And rightly is that city called a city of enclosure, since it is fortified by so many saints and defenders.

“I, however, said in my fear [Note: [Col. 0797D] The Vulgate reading is: “But I said in the excess of my mind,” etc., which Cardinal Thomasius explains thus: “But when formerly I had been struck by the greatest evils, and was in great fear and stupefaction, and had almost already lost my mind, I said this: Clearly I have been cast forth, O Lord, from the gracious sight of your eyes.”]. I have been cast away from before your eyes.” I, says the Church, in my fear, in the time of my pain and unbearable affliction, said what I ought to have said. What? “I have been cast away from before your eyes.”

“Therefore you heard the voice of my supplication when I cried to you.” Therefore, she says, in order to show—and to make me understand with complete certainty—that I had not been cast away from before your eyes, as soon as I cried to you, you heard the voice of my supplication. From this the Church exhorts her own people to love God, act manfully, and be strengthened in the Lord. For this is what she says:

[Col. 0798D] “Love the Lord, all his saints, because the Lord will require truth, and will repay those who practice pride abundantly. Act manfully, and let your heart be strengthened, all you who hope in the Lord.”

## PSALM XXXI. A PSALM OF UNDERSTANDING FOR DAVID

The Prophet speaks of himself and says that the understanding of this psalm was divinely given to him. For it concerns [Col. 0799A] the praise of repentance and confession of sins. Thus he understands that by repentance and confession he has been reconciled to God, from whom he departed through his sin concerning Uriah and Bathsheba.

“Blessed are those whose iniquities have been forgiven and whose sins have been covered.” This is the voice of the Prophet and of others who recognize that they have sinned, and who trust and rejoice that through confession and repentance they have forgiveness of sins. For what profit is there in doing penance unless, after repentance, one trusts that one’s sin has been forgiven? Who would not believe the prophet saying: “At whatever hour the sinner is converted and groans, he shall live and shall not die?” (Ezek. 33:11). Therefore the Prophet calls blessed those whose iniquities and sins [Col. 0799B] have been forgiven and covered through confession and repentance. “For charity, as it is written, covers a multitude of sins” (1 Pet. 4:8).

“Blessed is the man to whom the Lord has not imputed sin, and in whose spirit there is no deceit.” For this is what the Lord says through the prophet: “At whatever hour the sinner does penance, I will remember none of all his iniquities” (Ezek. 18:22). It is certain that he will not impute them if he does not remember them. But the phrase, “There is no deceit in his mouth,” seems to pertain to pure repentance and unreserved confession; hence it is also said elsewhere: “Pour out your hearts before him” (Ps. 61:9); and: “Return to me with your whole heart” (Joel 2:12); likewise: “Rend your hearts and not your garments [Col. 0799C]” (ibid.).

“Because I kept silent, all my bones grew old while I cried all day.” This silence is more in the heart than in the mouth; for if the heart is silent while the mouth speaks, it profits nothing. God looks not to the mouth but to the heart. Therefore repentance is in the heart, and true confession is in the heart, according to the words: “God does not despise a contrite and humbled heart” (Ps. 50:19). Thus that person cries with the heart who is inwardly afflicted over committing sin, and with his whole heart casts away from himself the sin in which he previously delighted. “Because,” he says, “I kept silent, all my bones grew old.” But that which grows old and ages, the Apostle says, is near to destruction. Therefore every power, every vigor and strength of soul—which are signified by the bones [Col. 0799D]—fails and perishes when a person delights in sins and the heart keeps silence: it neither cries, nor repents, nor confesses that it has sinned. But what does he mean when he says, “While I cried all day”? For if he was silent, how did he cry? This, then, is what we have just said: if the heart is silent, the cry of the mouth is worthless. Let the one who desires to be heard cry with the mouth and cry with the heart, and more with the heart than with the mouth.

“Because day and night your hand was heavy upon me, I was turned in my misery while the thorn is driven in.” Blessed is he upon whom the hand [Col. 0800A] of the Lord is made heavy, and whom the Lord deigns to afflict and visit for his sins. [Note: [Col. 0799D] “The Godhead does nothing with hands, but by the power of its will orders and accomplishes all things.” Cassiodorus.] “For, as it is written, he scourges every son whom he receives” (Heb. 12:6). Conversely, he says to the sinning people: “I will be angry with you no more. I was turned in my misery while the thorn is driven in” (Isa. 54:9). See how greatly it profited him that the Lord’s hand was heavy upon him and that he was pricked and wounded by the thorn of correction: for in this misery and affliction he was turned to repentance. Hence it follows:

“I have made my offense known to you, and I have not covered my injustices.” Nothing is hidden from God: he sees all things; he is the one who searches the reins and hearts. Yet we then disclose to him our offenses and injustices [Col. 0800B] when by harsh repentance, tears, and contrition of heart we show that we have sinned.

“I said: I will declare against myself all my injustices to the Lord; and you forgave the impiety of my heart.” Every person ought to say this and determine in his heart not to hide or cherish his sins, but to declare and reveal them against himself—and this to the Lord. [Note: [Col. 0800D] The same manuscript: “But what will he himself do? It follows.”] “And you forgave the impiety of my heart.” For this is what is said elsewhere: “First declare your sins, that you may be justified.” And: “The righteous man is at the beginning the accuser of himself” (Prov. 18:17). And the Apostle says: “If we judged ourselves, we would certainly not be judged” (1 Cor. 11:31). For one who judges himself declares his injustices against himself.

[Col. 0800C] “For this every saint will pray to you at the fitting time.” For this cause, namely, that you may forgive him the impiety of his heart, every saint will pray to you. For there is none among the saints who does not daily say to the Lord: “Forgive us our debts, as we forgive our debtors” (Matt. 6:12). But by “at the fitting time” he means this present life, which is indeed 358 suitable for repentance, prayer, and satisfaction, as the Apostle says: “Behold, now is the acceptable time; behold, now is the day of salvation” (2 Cor. 6:2). These things will have no place after this life.

“Yet in a flood of many waters they will not come near him.” The holy man prays daily for his sins, although sins cannot [Col. 0800D] approach him, as one placed and established amid a flood of many waters. For how, one might say, can the stains of sins pass through to one who is fortified on every side by a flood of so many waters? Here is the New Testament; here the Old Testament; here the books of the prophets; here the writings of the apostles and of all teachers; here an abundance of tears; here confession and repentance. Finally, whatever washes and wipes away sins may be counted among the waters. [Note: [Col. 0800D] The same manuscript: “pass through.”]

“You are my refuge from the pressure that has surrounded [Col. 0801A] me; you are my exultation; redeem me from those surrounding me.” The saint prays, he says, as stated above. But what does he pray? What we have just said: You are my refuge; you are my exultation; redeem me from those surrounding me. How excellently it is said, “from those surrounding me.” The holy man stands amid the waters mentioned above; he sees vices and sins, and all his enemies standing around, desiring [Note: [Col. 0801D] The same Ghislerian manuscript: “desiring to come to him.”] to come to him; and he prays, and by praying drives them away from himself. If, therefore, the holy man prays lest he be attacked and captured, how much more ought one already held captive to pray that he may be delivered?

“I will give you understanding and instruct you in this way in which you shall walk; I will fix my eyes upon you.” This is that understanding which, as the title says, [Col. 0801B] was given to David. It is now promised to the holy man, provided only that he foresee and guard himself lest he lose the understanding given him and become like the horse and mule, in which there is no understanding. By the horse and mule, what are we to understand except proud, powerful, and lustful persons? If they had possessed this understanding, by which this psalm is entitled and which is given to penitents, they would not have rushed at such an easy pace into such great crimes. But let us hear what the holy and religious man ought to do against such persons.

“With bit,” he says, “and bridle you shall break the jaws of those who do not come near you.” If, he says, these horses and mules flee from you and refuse to draw near to you and return to repentance, you shall break their jaws with bridle and bit. By bridle and bit [Col. 0801C] we can understand nothing more fittingly than curses, prohibitions, excommunications, and every form of separation from the faithful. For these are the restraints by which such horses and mules, restrained though unwilling and resistant, are customarily brought back to understanding and repentance.

“Many are the scourges of sinners, but mercy will surround those who hope in the Lord.” Let sinners know, says the Lord, whose words these are, that unless they come to their senses and repent, many scourges, many torments, and many great sufferings await them. But if they are converted and hope in God’s mercy, let them believe and in no way doubt that mercy will surround those who hope in the Lord. See how great is the power of repentance and true confession [Col. 0801D] of sins. [Note: [Col. 0801D] “O repentance,” says Cassiodorus, “an inestimable [Col. 0802D] medicine, which not only absolves from sins but also grants the blessed rewards of the saints.”] Now the Lord turns to those who have been justified by confession and repentance, and exhorts them to rejoice, exult, and glory. But let this be in the Lord, in whom and through whom they have conquered all their enemies. And this is what he says: “Rejoice in the Lord and exult, you righteous; and glory, all you upright in heart.”

## PSALM XXXII. A PSALM OF DAVID

David himself, who composed this psalm, speaks in it, and it is said to be his. Therefore that which is confirmed by the testimony of so great a man has no slight [Col. 0802A] authority.

“Rejoice in the Lord, you righteous; praise befits the upright.” Let others, he says, rejoice in the honors and dignities of this world, in deceptive riches and pleasures, whose joy will indeed soon end; but you righteous, rejoice in the Lord, because the Lord is eternal and your joy will be eternal. Thus the Lord says to his disciples in the Gospel: “I will see you again, and your heart will rejoice, and no one shall take your joy from you” (John 16:22). “But praise befits the upright,” because praise is not precious in the mouth of a sinner. “For God said to the sinner: Why do you recount my justices?” (Ps. 49:16). Therefore let those praise him who love him and [Col. 0802B] who are upright, who have their hearts and eyes directed upward. But how shall they praise? With the lyre, he says, and the psaltery. This is what he says:

“Confess to the Lord with the lyre; sing to him on the ten-stringed psaltery.” David played on the lyre and soothed Saul’s frenzy, 359 and drove away from him the demon by which he was afflicted. Such a lyre-player was the Apostle, in whose words the philosophers themselves delighted. But on the ten-stringed psaltery those sing who keep the ten commandments of the Law. Yet this belongs to the Old Testament; now let us hear concerning the New.

“Sing to him,” he says, “a new song; sing well to him with jubilation.” The New Testament has no need of wooden instruments; it seeks the human voice [Col. 0802C] and the rational tongue. The new song is the song of Christ’s birth, passion, resurrection, and ascension. But those sing well and sing with jubilation who praise God with heart and mouth, and fulfill in deeds the good things they say. Hence it follows:

“For the word of the Lord is upright, and all his works are in faith.” An upright word requires an upright preacher; and because all his works are faithful, they ought to be proclaimed well and faithfully.

“He loves mercy and judgment; the earth is full of the mercy of the Lord.” This, then, is what we ought to sing; this must be proclaimed to all. Let us love what the Lord loves, practice mercy [Col. 0802D] and justice, and devote ourselves especially to mercy, because he himself exalts mercy over judgment; indeed, the earth is full of the Lord’s mercy. It is mercy, assuredly, that God has compassion on both good and evil persons. And as if to say, “Consider, if you can, what kind of and how great is this Lord whose mercy fills the earth,” he adds:

“By the word of the Lord the heavens were established, and by the spirit of his mouth all their power.” Hence he immediately says in what follows:

“For he spoke, and they were made; he commanded, and they were created.” For if he spoke, he spoke by the Word. But to speak was to will. And the Word of God and the will of God are the Son himself. In brief, the mystery of the Trinity is declared in this verse. For what are the Lord, his Word, and his Spirit, except Father, Son, and Holy Spirit? Therefore there is one God, by whose will the heavens were made. [Note: [Col. 0803D] The same Ghislerian manuscript: “and by whose inspiration they were established.” — The same exposition occurs in Cassiodorus: “If we search carefully, he here signifies the holy Trinity. For in saying ‘by the Word’ he declares the Son; by adding ‘of the Lord’ he names the Father; and by ‘the Spirit of his mouth’ he plainly intends the Holy Spirit, who proceeded from the Father before time. And so that you might understand manifest unity in the three persons, ‘his’ is said, not ‘their.’”] Hence it is also said elsewhere: “In your will all things have been established, and there is none who can resist your will; for you made all things, heaven and earth, and all things contained within the compass of heaven.” But if by the heavens we understand the apostles, it is evident that by the word of the Lord—through which we understand our Savior—they were made, established, and redeemed, and that, according to his own promise, they received the power and strength of the Holy Spirit.

“Gathering the waters of the sea as into a wineskin, placing the depths in treasuries.” We have already spoken of this manner of expression in another psalm, where it is said: “Magnifying the salvation of his king” (Ps. 17:51). For just as there “magnifying” means “he magnifies,” so here, “gathering” means “he gathers,” and “placing” means “he places”: the Lord gathers the waters of the sea as into a wineskin. By the waters of the sea, what are we to understand except all the nations of this world? God gathered them, as into a wineskin, into one catholic and universal Church. This wineskin is great and contains many waters within itself. The holy apostles filled it and were brought into God’s treasuries. Hence it follows: “Placing the depths in treasuries.” For the same thing is signified both by the sea and by the depths. From where else but from the abyss is such an abundance of waters [Col. 0803C] poured forth? But concerning treasuries the Lord says in the Gospel: “Lay up for yourselves treasures in heaven” (Matt. 6:20); and: “Where your treasure is, there also is your heart” (ibid., 21); and: “The kingdom of heaven is like a treasure hidden in a field” (Matt. 13:44); and: “Sell all that you have and give to the poor, and you will have treasure in heaven” (Matt. 19:21). Therefore among these treasures the Lord places both the depths and the waters of the sea. Concerning them the Lord also says to blessed Job: “Have you entered the treasuries of snow, or seen the treasuries of hail?” (Job 38:24).

“Let all the earth fear the Lord; let all who inhabit [Col. 0804A] the world be moved by him.” For, as the Apostle says, God is not a respecter of persons (Acts 10:34); but in every nation whoever fears him and works righteousness is acceptable to him; and he places sea, depths, hail, and snow in his treasuries. Therefore let all the earth fear him, and fear no other, because no other is to be feared and worshiped. Let all inhabitants of the earth be moved by him and flee to him; for who is to be feared except the one who made all things? This is what he says:

“For he spoke, and they were made; he commanded, and they were created. The Lord scatters the counsels of the nations, but reproves the thoughts of peoples and reproves the counsels of princes.” Fear no one, says the Prophet, because the Lord is with you, who [Col. 0804B] reproves and scatters all counsels and thoughts of those who rise against you. But the counsel of the Lord remains forever, the thoughts of his heart unto age upon age. As he has ordained and predetermined before time, so—and not otherwise—it must come to pass. The punishment of the wicked and your glory have been so ordained that they cannot at all be changed. Blessed, therefore, are those who believe in him and who have been pre-elected and predestined by him, because they will in no way be deprived of the blessedness predestined for them. This is what he says:

“Blessed is the nation whose God is the Lord: the people whom the Lord chose for his inheritance.” Here he adds and sets forth the order of this election itself.

“From heaven the Lord looked down and saw all [Col. 0804C] the children of men.” From heaven, he says—from the most profound secret place of his majesty—he looked down and saw and knew all the children of men; some indeed he predestined to glory, but others to punishment. Hence the Apostle says: “Does not the potter have power over the clay, to make one vessel unto honor and another unto dishonor?” (Rom. 9:21). Thus the Lord will say at judgment to the good that they should receive the kingdom prepared for them from the origin of the world, but to the wicked that they should go into the eternal fire prepared for the devil and his angels. Notice that he says both that a kingdom was prepared for the former and punishment prepared for the latter. [Note: [Col. 0803D] What St. Bruno says here—that God, knowing all the children of men, “predestined some indeed to glory, but others to punishment”—must be understood only of the will to save those who deserve it and condemn those who do not deserve it. For since, as the Psalmist says in Psalm 118, “the Lord is just, and his judgment upright,” he did not decree reward and glory except for those who deserve them, just as he did not appoint damnation and punishment except for those who by their own faults had provoked his indignation against themselves. Thus divine [Col. 0804D] providence, just as from eternity it destined the good to become heirs and sharers in its kingdom, so from eternity it established that the wicked should be afflicted with the perpetual fire of hell. This is also the teaching of St. Fulgentius, who says near the end of Book I addressed to Monimus: “He predestined such persons to destruction because he prepared for such persons the punishment of just retribution. The Lord himself clearly taught this when he showed that there was prepared not only a kingdom in which the good might rejoice, but also eternal fire in which the wicked might be tortured. For he will say to the good: Come, blessed of my Father, receive the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world. But to the wicked he will say: Go, accursed, into the eternal fire prepared for the devil and his angels. See to what the Lord predestined the unjust and impious: namely, to just punishment, not to any unjust work; to penalty, not to fault.” Thus in those being saved predestination shines forth, while in those condemned reprobation appears; but both relate to merits [Col. 0805C] and demerits: the former predestination, namely, entails effective goodness, while the latter—that is, reprobation—presupposes wickedness completed in act. St. Thomas teaches this in Question 23, Article 3: “Just as predestination,” he says, “is a part of providence with respect to those who are divinely ordered to eternal salvation, so reprobation [Col. 0805D] is a part of providence with respect to those who fall away from this end. Hence reprobation does not denote foreknowledge alone, but adds something in conception, as does providence, as was said above. For just as predestination includes the will to confer grace and glory, so reprobation includes the will to permit someone to fall into fault and to inflict the penalty of damnation for fault.” That this, and no other, was St. Bruno’s meaning is also more clearly evident from what follows.] Hence it is clear that no one is predestined to do evil or sin, [Col. 0805A] but all are predestined either to glory or to punishment. It follows:

“From his prepared dwelling-place he looked upon all who inhabit the world.” This appears to repeat what has been said.

“He who fashioned their hearts individually, who understands all their works.” God made the hearts of all individually, because he gave neither all wisdom to everyone nor equal wisdom and understanding to all. “Who understands all their works”; and because he understands the works of all, he repays each according to his merits. From the place where it says, “From heaven the Lord looked down,” to this place, the course of the sentence hangs suspended; and here at last one must supply what we said above.

[Col. 0805B] “The king shall not be saved through his great strength, nor shall the giant be saved through the multitude of his might.” Only those, he says, will be saved who fear God, keep his commandments, and are predestined to eternal life. But the rest should not trust in the multitude of their strength, because neither a king can be saved by his own power nor a giant by his strength.

“A horse is false for salvation, and in the abundance of his strength he shall not be saved.” By these words he seems to mean nothing other than that God’s mercy alone can save a person and rescue him from punishments. Let no one trust in the speed of a horse, for it often deceives and, falling suddenly, can save neither itself nor its rider. What is said of king, giant, and horse should also be understood of all other things.

“Behold, the eyes of the Lord are upon those who fear him and hope in his mercy, that he may rescue their souls from death and feed them in famine.” This is as though he said: Those who trust in themselves, in their own strength and power, will not be saved; but those who fear God and hope and trust in his mercy alone are secure, [Col. 0806A] because the Lord always watches over them and does not allow them to stray or perish. For he feeds them with spiritual food in the famine which wicked people suffer in this world, concerning which it is said through the prophet: “I will send upon them not a famine of bread nor a thirst for water, but of hearing the word of God” (Amos 8:11). Yet this can also be understood of that famine by which the wicked are tortured in hell. Hence the rich man said to Abraham: “Father Abraham, send Lazarus to dip the tip of his finger in water and cool my tongue, for I am tormented in this flame” (Luke 16:24).

“But our soul waits for the Lord, because he is our helper and protector. And our heart shall rejoice in him, and we have hoped in his holy name.” [Col. 0806B] He exhorts himself and his own soul, and in himself all others, to be secure and wait patiently, because they have both a good teacher and shall receive, without any doubt, the things for which they hope and wait. This is what he says:

“Let your mercy, O Lord, be upon us, as we have hoped in you.” Great is the power of hope, which is so highly commended throughout all the psalms. Malignant spirits have lost it, and labor with utmost zeal to bring those whom they deceive to despair. This is the sin which will not be forgiven to human beings either in this age or in the age to come. He rightly used the plural, “our soul,” because, as is read in the Acts of the Apostles, “They all had one heart and one soul” (Acts 4: [Col. 0806C] 32); hence it is also said elsewhere: “Our soul has been rescued like a sparrow from the snare of hunters.”

## 361 PSALM XXXIII. A PSALM OF DAVID, WHEN HE CHANGED HIS COUNTENANCE BEFORE ABIMELECH, AND HE DISMISSED HIM, AND HE DEPARTED

[Note: [Col. 0805D] The title prefixed to this psalm by Bruno is the same in St. Augustine. In the Vulgate, however, David is said to have changed his countenance before Achimelech. But in 1 Kings, chapter 21, verse 13, we read that this happened before Achish, king of Gath, and his servants. St. Augustine reconciles this great discrepancy in a lengthy dissertation. But we prefer Bede’s shorter account, which Cardinal Thomasius also gives: “When Saul persecuted David, he fled to King Achish. While there, having become suspect through envy, he cleverly changed his countenance, filling his mouth with saliva, so that, considered demon-possessed, he might be released unharmed through pity. David, therefore, is Christ; Achish is the Jewish people. Christ was incarnate among that people, but appeared unrecognizable because of those who envied him. Hence Achish is said to mean ‘How is it!’—the expression of one marveling and not recognizing—because the Jews, while marveling at Christ’s miracles, did not at all recognize him as God. And fittingly David, having changed his countenance, let saliva fall upon his beard: saliva signifies weakness, but the beard strength, because Christ, though he was in the form of God, emptied himself, taking the form of a servant (Phil. 2). Nor is there error in the king’s name: since one born of a kingly father could also be called Abimelech, which means ‘my father is king’ or ‘the kingdom of my father.’ The mystical sense is also pleasing, because the Jews had the Father as king, concerning whom it is said: ‘But the children of the kingdom shall be cast into outer darkness.’ “He dismissed him, and he departed”: he left the Jews and departed to be believed by the Gentiles. It may also be said that he changed his countenance before Abimelech the priest when, in order to obtain weapons and bread for himself and his companions, he pretended that Saul had sent him.” The same interpretation is found in almost the same words in Cassiodorus.]

David is not said to have changed his appearance before Abimelech, but rather before Achish, king of Gath, when he pretended to be mad, fearing that Achish might kill him, since he had slain many from Achish’s kingdom. [Col. 0807A] Thus he calls Achish Abimelech, because in David’s preservation Abimelech was such as Achish was, since each allowed him to depart unharmed. And just as Achish did, so Abimelech at that time did not recognize David’s appearance—that is, his disposition and intention. For afterward Abimelech, together with all his household, was slain by Saul because he had not detained David but allowed him to depart. Thus it is true that David changed his appearance both before Achish and before Abimelech: before Achish, indeed, when he pretended to be mad; before Abimelech, because, when asked by him why he had come alone, he replied, “The king commanded me concerning a matter, and does not wish anyone to know.” By this he plainly indicated that he had not been safe in Abimelech’s house. Therefore in this psalm [Col. 0807B] he praises and blesses God, who guarded him both in Abimelech’s house and in Achish’s house.

> “I will bless the Lord at every time; his praise shall always be in my mouth.”

The Prophet teaches us how we ought to bless and praise God: not merely for an hour, but at every time, both in prosperity and adversity.

> “My soul shall be praised in the Lord; let the meek hear and rejoice.”

“For this reason,” he says, “I shall praise the Lord at every time: because whatever I am, I am from him; nothing praiseworthy is found in me that belongs to myself. Therefore let my strength and power, my humility, wisdom, and patience, and whatever good may be found in my soul, be referred to him. Let the humble and meek hear this and rejoice with me; nor let them regret [Col. 0807C] having always been humble and meek.” Thus elsewhere he says: “Remember, O Lord, David and all his meekness” (Ps. 131:1).

> “Magnify the Lord with me, and let us exalt his name together.”

The Prophet is kindly disposed: he seeks companions and exhorts others to praise God, so that whoever joins him in praise and magnification may also share in the reward.

> “I sought the Lord, and he heard me, and delivered me from all my tribulations.”

Here too he shows us very plainly the affection of his goodwill, when by his own example he teaches us what we ought to do in our tribulations. He says that in his tribulations he sought the Lord and was heard [Col. 0807D], in order that we too may do likewise and likewise be heard. For this is what he says:

> “Draw near to him and be enlightened, and your faces shall not be ashamed.”

Whence comes this? “Because this poor man cried, and the Lord heard him and delivered him from all his tribulations.” He calls himself poor because, although he was rich, he did not place his hope in riches and regarded this world’s wealth as nothing. “Draw near,” he says, “through repentance—you who withdrew from him through disobedience—and be enlightened.” For he “is the true light, which enlightens every person coming into this world” (John 1:9). Moses also says of him: “Those who draw near at his feet shall receive of his teaching” (Deut. 33:3). And surely his teaching is the illumination of the inner person. But those enlightened in this way will not be put to shame at judgment; hence it is said here: “And your faces shall not be ashamed.” [Col. 0808A]

> “The angel of the Lord will encamp around those who fear him and will deliver them.”

Hence the Apostle says that angels “are ministering spirits, sent forth for those who are to receive the inheritance of salvation” (Heb. 1:14).

> “Taste and see that the Lord is sweet; blessed is the man who hopes in him.”

The one who says this had already tasted his sweetness—perhaps in the place where he says: “How sweet are your words to my palate, O Lord, sweeter than honey and the honeycomb to my mouth” (Ps. 118[119]:103). [Col. 0808B] But what are those words that bestow such sweetness upon the saints? Read in the Gospel, and you will find them: “When I am lifted up from the earth, I shall draw all things to myself” (John 12:32).—“He who believes in me has eternal life” (ibid. 6:47).—“Where I am, there also my servant shall be” (ibid. 12:26).—“He who believes and is baptized shall be saved. Whoever comes to me I shall not cast out” (Mark 16:16).—“Rejoice, because your names are written in heaven” (Matt. 5:12). These and similar sayings are what he urges us to taste, so that in them we may see and know how sweet and pleasant the Lord is.

> “Blessed is the man who hopes in him.”

Thus elsewhere he says: “Hope in him, all the congregation of the people, and pour out your hearts before him, because God is a helper for ever” (Ps. 61[62]:9). For blessed is the one whose helper is God for ever. [Col. 0808C]

> “Fear the Lord, all you his saints, for nothing is lacking to those who fear him.”

This is why Solomon says: “Fear God and keep his commandments” (Eccl. 12:13). Every human being was made for this purpose: to fear God and keep his commandments. Whoever fears God neglects nothing. This, then, is what he says: “Fear the Lord, all you his saints.” He embraces all the commandments of the Law and the Prophets, and there was nothing further that he could have said. For whoever fears out of love for God desires to do all that God commands and to flee all that he forbids; and nothing is lacking for perfection in one who has attained [Col. 0808D] this love. Hence it follows: “For nothing is lacking to those who fear him.”—“The fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom” (Sir. 1:16).

> “The rich have been in need and hungry, but those who seek the Lord shall not lack any good thing.”

How many things do the rich lack, and in how many ways do they suffer want? Yet the saints possess everything that they desire to possess. Even if they do not yet possess all things in actuality, they possess all things in hope. They could not be blessed if anything were lacking to them. Hence the Apostle says: “As having nothing, and yet possessing all things” (2 Cor. 6:10). How could those who possess all things together in God lack anything?

[Col. 0809A]

> “Come, children, listen to me; I shall teach you the fear of the Lord.”

Above he told them to fear God; now he shows how they ought to fear him. “Come,” he says, “and return to me, because by sinning you withdrew from me.” Then, when they have been gathered and assembled into one, he says:

> “Who is the man who desires life and longs to see good days?”

And as though someone answered, “I do,” he adds:

> “Restrain your tongue from evil, and let not your lips speak deceit. Turn away from evil and do good; seek peace and pursue it.”

In these few words is a complete instruction in the fear of the Lord and a perfect teaching of the Christian religion. [Note: [Col. 0809D] See St Maximus of Turin, Homily 106, Roman edition, p. 351, for his copious and elegant teaching on guarding the tongue.] Here is stated in full both what we ought to avoid and what we ought to do. For “the one who does not stumble in word is a perfect man” [Col. 0809B] (Jas. 3:1); and: “He who guards his tongue guards his soul” (Prov. 13:3). The person who seeks and pursues peace loves everyone and hates no one. Hence the Apostle says: “If it is possible, as far as it depends on you, live at peace with all people” (Rom. 12:18). And elsewhere: “With those who hated peace I was peaceable; when I spoke to them, they attacked me without cause” (Ps. 119[120]:7).

> “The eyes of the Lord are upon the righteous, and his ears toward their prayers. But the face of the Lord is upon those who do evil, to destroy their memory from the earth.”

He has stated what we ought to do and what we ought not to do; now he says that God is the watcher above, who considers the deeds of each person. He looks upon the righteous [Col. 0809C] in order to hear them; but upon the unrighteous, in order to destroy them from the land of the living. Hence it follows:

> “The righteous cried, and the Lord heard them, and delivered them from all their tribulations.”

But why be surprised that he heard them and delivered them from tribulations, when he is always with them and is never separated from them? This is what he said:

> “The Lord is near to those who are troubled in heart, and he will save the humble in spirit.”

God does not despise a contrite and humbled heart (Ps. 50[51]). By “humble in spirit,” however, he seems to me to distinguish them from those who are humble in body—that is, who display outward humility but do not possess it inwardly. Hypocrisy makes such persons; but the grace of the Holy Spirit alone makes persons humble in spirit. Such humble persons [Col. 0809D] the Lord will save; but of others he says: “Salvation is far from sinners” (Ps. 118[119]:155).

> “Many are the tribulations of the righteous, and the Lord has delivered them from all of them.”

He says that they have already been delivered, because he knows with complete certainty that they will be delivered.

> “The Lord guards all their bones; not one of them shall be broken.”

We read that the bones of saints have often been broken—not merely broken, but burned and reduced to dust. But just as elsewhere [Col. 0810A] it is said, “The Lord guards you from every evil” (Ps. 120[121]:7), and immediately explains how this should be understood by saying, “The Lord will guard your soul,” so here we ought to understand not the bones of the body but the bones of the soul. By the bones of the soul are meant faith, hope, charity, humility, mercy, and the other virtues, without which the soul is weak and cannot run in the way of God’s commandments. These are the bones which the Lord guards, and of which he permits not one to be broken: “For whoever stumbles in one point has become guilty of all” (Jas. 2:10).

> “The death of sinners is most evil, and those who hate the righteous shall offend.”

That death is indeed most evil which destroys both body and soul. “And those who hate the righteous shall offend.” Even if the wicked sinned in nothing else [Col. 0810B] except in hating the righteous without cause, that would suffice for their destruction. By “the righteous” we may also understand our Savior, who says of himself and his adversaries in the Gospel: “They hated me without cause” (John 15:25). It is rightly said of them that they shall offend, because to this day they do not cease to sin against Christ, nor will they cease until the consummation of the age.

> “The Lord shall redeem the souls of his servants, and shall not forsake all who hope in him.”

We may quite suitably understand this redemption as that which the Lord accomplished by the shedding of his blood; nor is it credible that he should forsake those whom he redeemed at so great a price.

## Psalm 34. Of David himself

[Col. 0810C]

King and prophet David indicates that this psalm is to be ascribed to David himself—that is, to our Savior, who is truly called “strong in hand.” In this psalm our Savior speaks, but, as we have often said, according to his humanity. [Note: [Col. 0809D] As our author frequently does, St Augustine [Col. 0810D] says that David—that is, Christ—is interpreted “strong in hand” or “desirable.” He explains this as follows: “He is strong in hand in that he conquered our death; desirable in that he promised eternal life.”]

> “Judge, O Lord, those who injure me; overcome those who attack me.”

“Judge,” he says, “O Lord, those who injure me, and repay them as they deserve; and overcome those who attack me, so that they may not be able to resist their own enemies.” We must understand this to have been spoken against those who were incorrigible and persisted in their malice until the end. For while hanging upon the cross the Lord prayed for others and said: “Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they do” (Luke 23:14). [Col. 0810D] It is therefore not inconsistent that he appears now to pray for them and now against them, because some are those for whom he prays and others those against whom he prays.

> “Take hold of weapons and shield, and arise to help me.”

The Lord does not need such weapons, since by his mere will he can destroy all his enemies. Yet he asks that that nation be destroyed by arms, since it had been so ordained. He calls this his help because he chose to employ these weapons in overcoming the Jews. Hence it follows:

[Col. 0811A]

> “Draw out the sword and shut in those who persecute me; say to my soul: I am your salvation.”

By the sword we understand Titus, Vespasian, and the Roman army, by whom the Jewish people were killed and destroyed in many ways. “Draw out,” he says, “the sword against those who persecute me, and shut them in” within the city of Jerusalem. [Note: [Col. 0811D] Jerusalem was utterly overthrown by Titus and Vespasian, and the whole Hebrew people was either slaughtered by Roman swords or led into captivity, as Josephus likewise recounts in *The Jewish War*, books 6 and 7.] For it is written that, during the Paschal festival, when according to custom all the people had gathered in one place, the army suddenly arrived and enclosed them, so that none could escape. By God’s just judgment they were besieged in the very days on which they had not feared to lay hands upon Christ our Lord. Yet God’s power was wondrous: for forty-two years he had waited, in order to spare them, if they should wish to repent. [Col. 0811B] [Note: [Col. 0811D] Since it is established that Jerusalem was captured and destroyed in A.D. 70, counting back forty-two years brings us to A.D. 28, which, according to the most widely accepted opinion of chronologists, preceded the year of Christ’s death. We may readily conclude that the Lord uttered these predictions then; thus our author’s accuracy in calculating the years is remarkable. The distinguished Lazzeri took the same view in his notes on St Bruno’s Commentary on Matthew, p. 386, and in his Commentary on Luke, p. 265. St Paulinus of Nola held the same opinion, as the celebrated Muratori notes in Dissertation 21 on the poems of that holy Father, along with very many others.] But because they persisted in their malice, many were slain by famine, thirst, swords, and fires, while the rest were handed over to all nations for reproach and slavery. “Say to my soul: I am your salvation”—he of whom they falsely said: “There is no salvation for him in his God” (Ps. 3:3).

> “Let my enemies, who seek my life, be confounded and ashamed. Let those who devise evils against me be turned back and put to shame.”

If these words are understood literally, they are plain; indeed, reason itself compels their literal understanding, since they appear to have been fulfilled literally. If the Jews had repented at the time of Christ’s passion, had been ashamed of what they intended to do, had turned back from [Col. 0811C] their wicked purpose, and had not crucified our Savior, these two verses could have been expounded favorably. But some of the things said in this Psalm appear to have been said before the Passion, some in the Passion itself, and others after the Passion. This should seem inconsistent to no one, since he who spoke and he to whom they spoke have past and future things present to them, and see what is in no different way from what will be.

> “Let them become as dust before the wind, with the angel of the Lord afflicting them.”

For just as dust cannot resist the wind but is scattered, swept away, and blown about everywhere, so that people, unable to withstand the assault of their enemies, was dispersed throughout the nations. [Col. 0811D] By the angel of the Lord who afflicts them, we may understand either all their enemies, who serve the Lord in this matter, or some angel appointed for their affliction. For of such angels it is elsewhere said: “He sent upon them the fury of his indignation, indignation and wrath, an onslaught through evil angels” (Ps. 77[78]:49). [Col. 0812A]

> “Let their way be darkness and slipperiness, with the angel of the Lord pursuing them.”

The Lord indicated such paths to them when he said: “See that your flight does not occur in winter or on the Sabbath” (Matt. 24:10). But if we inquire allegorically, what are the Jews but dust, trampled under everyone’s feet and cast by the wind from the face of the earth? All their paths are dark and slippery: blinded by their malice, they are always in error and hasten toward darkness and destruction; continually falling and sinning in all things, they cannot rise to do any good. But what wonder is it when the evil angel [Col. 0812B] of the Lord pursues them, who never urges them except toward evil?

> “For without cause they hid for me the destruction of their snare; in vain they reproached my soul.”

“Without cause,” he says, “they hid for me the destruction of their snare and deceit.” By this snare we may understand Judas the traitor, who ensnared and held him with the kiss of feigned peace. They vainly reproached that most holy soul, [Note: [Col. 0812D] “They vainly reproached my soul” means: “They falsely accused me,” when the Jewish people charged the Lord Savior’s truthful sayings against him as though they were some crime. In their mad falsehood they cried: “This is he who said, ‘I shall destroy the temple of God,’” etc. Cassiodorus.] reckoning it among the impious and sinners, as it is written of him: “He was numbered among the wicked” (Luke 22:37). Hence, reproaching him, they said: “He is deserving of death; and unless he were an evildoer, we would not have handed him over to you. And according to the Law [Col. 0812C] he ought to die, because he made himself the Son of God” (John 18:30).

> “Let the snare which they do not know come upon them; let the trap which they hid seize them; and let them fall into their own snare together.”

As it is written: “He who prepares a pit for his brother shall himself first fall into it” (Sir. 27:29); and, “With the same measure with which you have measured, it shall be measured back to you” (Matt. 4:24). Thus it happened to the Jews: the snare which they did not know came upon them. For in the Gospel it is written: “When the Lord drew near to Jerusalem, seeing the city, he wept over it, saying: ‘For if you had known’”—that is understood to mean, “you would have wept”—“but now they are hidden from your eyes” (Luke 21:1). [Col. 0812D] They were hidden indeed because, as is said here, “the snare which they did not know came upon them, and the trap which they hid seized them. And they fell into their own snare together”—that is, all at once and all together. These words show quite plainly [Col. 0813A] that the Passion of Christ alone was the cause of their downfall and destruction.

> “But my soul shall rejoice in the Lord, and shall delight in his salvation.”

He foretells the joy of his resurrection, which took place immediately on the third day, when hell was despoiled by the Savior’s own soul and his body was raised from the tomb.

> “All my bones shall say: O Lord, who is like you? You will deliver the needy from the hand of one stronger than he, the destitute and poor from those who plunder him.”

By Christ’s bones we understand the apostles and all others who are stronger in the Church, and by whom the whole ecclesiastical body is borne and supported. All these praise and magnify God, who delivered our Savior with such great triumph from the hands of [Col. 0813B] his enemies, who appeared to be stronger and more powerful than he. He is called needy, destitute, and poor because, at the time of his Passion, when friends and helpers seemed most necessary, there was no one to help him.

> “Rising up, unjust witnesses asked me things that I did not know; they repaid evil for good, and barrenness to my soul.”

[Note: [Col. 0813D] The Vulgate has: “They sought false testimony against Jesus in order to hand him over to death, and they did not find it, though many false witnesses had come forward. But at last two false witnesses came and said: ‘This man said: I can destroy the temple of God and rebuild it after three days’” (Matt. 26:60). Our Lord Christ indeed said in John, chapter 2, verse 19: “Destroy this temple, and in three days I shall raise it up.” But Jesus spoke this not of the material Jerusalem temple [Col. 0814D] but of his human body, as St John himself explains in the same second chapter, verse 21: “But he was speaking of the temple of his body.”]

For, as we read in the Gospel, many false witnesses came before him, whose testimonies did not agree. Finally some came, questioning him and saying: “Did you not say that you would destroy this temple made with hands and rebuild it in three days?” The Evangelist relates this in the third person; but we need not doubt that it was also said of him in both the third and second person. Yet because these men lied, and God does not acknowledge falsehood, it is rightly said: “They asked me things that I did not know.” [Col. 0813C] They repaid evil for good, as the Lord himself says: “I have done many good works among you; for which of these do you wish to kill me?” (John 10:25). Likewise: “If I have spoken evil, bear witness concerning the evil; but if I have spoken well, why do you strike me?” (John 18:23). They rendered barrenness, because, like bad and fruitless trees, they produced no good fruit. This is that chosen vineyard which gave vinegar instead of wine and, when it ought to have produced grapes, produced wild grapes (Isa. 5).

> “But while they troubled me, I clothed myself in sackcloth and humbled my soul with fasting; [Col. 0813D] and my prayer returned into my bosom.”

The Apostle speaks of this sackcloth when he says that Christ “appeared in the likeness of sinful flesh, so that he might condemn sin in the flesh” (Rom. 8:3). We should therefore understand Christ’s flesh as sackcloth, [Note: [Col. 0814D] “While the Jews troubled him with insults and plots, he concealed his divinity from their darkened minds beneath the covering of flesh, because they did not deserve to recognize him whom they treated with such impiety.” Cassiodorus.] by which he was clothed and was judged a sinner [Col. 0814A] and worthy of sackcloth. In the time of his Passion he chose to show only the sackcloth, because he did not reveal the power of divinity hidden beneath that sackcloth. He humbled his soul with fasting because, although he prayed for them and desired to incorporate them into his own body, he nonetheless united and incorporated few to himself in those days. [Note: [Col. 0814D] “Therefore the Lord fasted because the unbelieving crowd had withdrawn itself from him.” Cassiodorus.] Blessed Peter suffered such a fast when the Lord said to him: “Slay and eat” (Acts 10:18). What we eat is transferred into our substance in such a way that it becomes one and the same with us. Hence the Lord says: “He who eats my flesh and drinks my blood remains in me, and I in him” (John 6:56). Let us therefore pray that he himself may eat us and transform us into the substance of his body, [Col. 0814B] so that we may never be able to be separated from him. When he says, “And my prayer returned into my bosom,” he clearly implies that he prayed in his heart for these very enemies, that they might not perish. And certainly this prayer saved all from that people who were saved. I think, however, that the prayer which returned within Christ’s breast was framed in this manner: that his death should not be imputed to any of that people who should be converted; but those who persisted in their malice would be punished both in this life and in the next.

> “As for a neighbor and as for our brother, so I pleased; as mourning and sorrowful, so I was humbled.”

“I pleased myself,” he says, “and delighted in that people as in a neighbor and [Col. 0814C] brother.” For grammatically the phrase may be construed in this way, and no other construction works. Conversely, “as mourning and sorrowful, I was humbled by him.” This is what is said elsewhere: “Those who repaid me evil for good slandered me” (Ps. 37[38]:21).

> “They rejoiced against me and gathered together; they gathered scourges against me, and they did not know.”

All this was fulfilled literally. But when he says, “and they did not know,” the Apostle explains it: “For if they had known, they would never have crucified the Lord of glory” (1 Cor. 2:2). Moreover, they did not know the cause and reason why they ought to do this.

> “They were dissolved and were not pierced with remorse; they tempted me and mocked me; they gnashed their teeth [Col. 0814D] at me.”

“They were dissolved,” he says: they are held by no bond of the Law; they do what they wish and follow the desires of their own hearts. Nor were they pierced with remorse for the great crime they committed in my death, tempting me, mocking me, gnashing their teeth over me. [Col. 0815A] It is beyond doubt that the Jews did all these things and other evils against Christ.

> “Lord, when will you look? Restore my soul from their evildoings, my only one from the lions.”

“Lord,” he says, “when will you look? When will you come to avenge me? When will you restore my soul from their evildoings, and my only one from these lions, raging so cruelly?” “They have not yet ceased,” he seems to say, “from persecuting me; they still persecute me with blasphemies and injuries; as far as lies in them, they still kill my soul, because they deny that I have risen.” For the Jews do not yet believe that Christ our Lord has had his soul restored to him.

> “I will confess you, O Lord, in the great Church; in a weighty people I will praise you.”

“Behold,” he says, “I have left the Synagogue; I have left the folly and frivolity of the Jews. Henceforth I shall confess and praise you through my faithful in the great Church—the Catholic Church, spread throughout the whole world. [Col. 0815B] And I shall praise you in a weighty people,” one not lifted up by the wind of pride and vanity.

> “Let not those who oppose me unjustly rejoice over me, those who hate me without cause and wink with their eyes.”

Because the whole world now believes in Christ, the Jews can neither insult Christ nor dare to do so. But they wink with their eyes: they conceal malice in their hearts, while displaying goodwill in face and eyes. This is what the Jews did, repeatedly praising our Savior’s teaching and assenting with their eyes and whole expression to his words, while thinking how [Col. 0815C] they might ensnare him in his speech. And it follows:

> “For they indeed spoke peacefully to me, but deceitfully devised against wrath.”

They devised against the wrath which they had in their hearts but feared to display. Yet wrath was not enough for them; besides their wrath they also devised deceits by which to kill him. [Note: [Col. 0815D] “The impious deceitfulness of the Jews is foretold, described not in our words but in the words of the Gospel. They seemed to speak peacefully when they said: ‘Teacher, we know that you are truthful and teach the way of God in truth. Is it lawful to pay tribute to Caesar or not?’” (Matt. 22:16). Cassiodorus.]

> “They opened their mouth wide against me; they said: ‘Aha, aha, our eyes have seen it.’ You have seen, O Lord; do not be silent. O Lord, do not depart from me.”

The Jews opened their mouths wide and spoke too proudly against the Lord after they learned that he had given up his spirit. Going to Pilate, they said: “Lord, we know that this deceiver said while still alive: ‘After three days I shall rise.’ Therefore command that [Col. 0815D] the tomb be guarded, lest perhaps his disciples come and steal him and say to the people that he has risen, and the last error shall be worse than the former” (Matt. 27:63). Thus the Jews opened their mouths wide, calling him a deceiver and proclaiming that he would never rise. And then they said “Aha, aha,” which every people is accustomed to say after victory according to the idiom of its own language. When he says, [Col. 0816A] “our eyes have seen,” it was as though they said: “At last we have seen and learned what sort of person he was, who deceived his people by his impostures and said that he was the Son of God. Behold, he is dead and could not free himself from death.” [Note: [Col. 0815D] “Could he not, while alive, have descended from the cross’s gibbet to confound them, when after death he was able to rise from the tomb on the third day? But it did not suit divine power to be moved by the words of those insulting him, so that they might be still more ashamed when all that had been foretold came to pass.” Cassiodorus.] They said these things. But you, O Lord, who heard and saw their pride, do not be silent, but answer fools according to their folly. “O Lord, do not depart from me,” but be my help; scatter them in your power and destroy them, O Lord my protector.

> “Arise, O Lord, and attend to my judgment, my God and my Lord, to my cause.”

“Attend,” he says, “now at last, and enter into my judgment and cause, and begin to judge [Note: [Col. 0816D] Ghislerian manuscript: “and reveal it to all nations.”] how [Col. 0816B] unjustly I was judged and condemned, especially by my own people, whom I loved so greatly, to whom I gave such great benefits: whom I delivered from Egyptian slavery, for whom I opened the Red Sea, whom I fed with manna for forty years, whom I brought into the land of promise, and finally for whom I came into the world and assumed flesh. For he himself said: “I was not sent except to the lost sheep of the house of Israel” (Matt. 15:24).

> “Judge me according to your great mercy, O Lord my God, lest my enemies insult me; lest they say in their hearts, ‘Aha, aha, to our souls’; lest they say, ‘We have swallowed him up.’”

“Judge me,” he says, “according to your great mercy, which has been so widely extended as to fill the whole world and leave no one worthy of mercy for whom it would not exact justice from his adversary. Judge me,” he says; “let the judgment be reviewed, and in their very destruction and ruin let it be known that they were deservedly condemned. [Col. 0816C] Let them not insult me or say what they are accustomed to say, ‘Aha, aha, blessed be our souls,’ when they see the swords of your vengeance hanging over their necks.”
