> “Let those who rejoice at my evils be ashamed and confounded together; let those who speak evil against me be clothed with shame and reverence.”

This has indeed already been wholly fulfilled, and it will be wholly fulfilled at the judgment.

> “Let those who desire my righteousness exult and rejoice, and let them always say: ‘Let the Lord be magnified, who desire the peace of his servant.’”

Most excellently, after the destruction and confusion of the wicked, he commands those whom he knows to rejoice in his righteousness to exult and be glad. And let those who desire to possess and maintain Christ’s peace always magnify the Lord, because without peace it is impossible to please God. [Col. 0816D]

> “But my tongue”—the humanity of our Savior speaks—“shall meditate upon your righteousness, upon your praise all day long.”

He says that his tongue meditates upon God’s righteousness and praise because it always holds them in memory and never forgets them. [Col. 0817A]

## Psalm 35. To the end: a Psalm of David, servant of the Lord

[Note: [Col. 0817D] St Augustine says nothing on this title. The Vulgate reads: “To the end: to the servant of the Lord, to David himself.” In Isidore Clarius the title reads: “To the conqueror, David, servant of the Lord.” St Bruno gives no reason why he rendered *servus* (“servant”) as *puer* (“boy” or “servant”), although the terms are sometimes used with the same meaning. Cassiodorus gives the title according to the Vulgate. [Col. 0818D]]

This is that child of whom it is written: “A child is born to us, and a son is given to us” (Isa. 9:6). Therefore, in this psalm King and Prophet David says to this servant of the Lord, David: “You will save men and beasts, O Lord.” We have often already explained what “to the end” signifies and what “A Psalm of David” signifies.

> “The unjust man said, that he might sin within himself: There is no fear of God before his eyes.”

The unjust man, he says, said this within himself, thought it in his heart, and determined it in his mind in order to sin. [Col. 0817B] What does “in order to sin” mean? To steal, kill, and commit fornication; to commit perjury and bring about destruction; to deceive his brother and perform other works of iniquity. And this is because “there is no fear of God before his eyes.” Had he feared God, he would not have desired to do such things.

> “For he acted deceitfully in his sight, so that he might find his iniquity and hatred.”

From this, he says, it will be known that there is no fear of God before his eyes: he acted deceitfully in God’s sight, not merely speaking in his heart but acting in deed. Therefore it is fitting that he should find his own iniquity and hatred. For the same measure with which he measured shall be measured back to him.

> “The words of his mouth are iniquity and deceit; he refused to understand, [Col. 0817C] that he might do good. He devised iniquity upon his bed; he stood in every way that was not good, and did not hate evil.”

He is rightly called unjust who does such things. These matters are plain and need no exposition.

“Lord, your mercy is in heaven, and your truth reaches to the clouds.” The prophet marvels at the many various and differing wills of human beings: while some pursue vices with such desire, others imitate virtues with such zeal. He shows that no one perishes except through pride, and no one is saved except through mercy. “Lord,” he says, “your mercy is known not fully on earth, but perfectly and wholly in heaven.” For all who are there have been saved solely by God’s mercy: “For,” as the Apostle says, “while we were all sinners, Christ died for us” (Rom. 5:3). And this was done by mercy alone. Hence it is rightly said: “The Lord is gracious to all, and his mercies are over all his works” (Ps. 114:9). For if each of the saints, because he is now in heaven or will be there after judgment, were asked individually, “How did you come here?” or “How did you enter here?” what else could he answer except, “Mercy brought me here”? Thus it is rightly said here: “Lord, your mercy is in heaven.” It follows: “and your truth reaches to the clouds.” If, he says, mercy is in heaven—found and known in heaven—where is truth? Do you wish to hear where? In the clouds. For by “clouds” are signified the prophets and apostles, bishops and priests, and all teachers of the Church. These are they who rain upon the Church and water the whole earth with the showers of spiritual teaching. God’s truth has therefore reached this point: they have deserved to receive an understanding of the holy Scriptures.

“Your righteousness is like the mountains of God [Note: [Col. 0818D] ‘Although usage has: “Your righteousness is like the mountains of God,” a translation on Jerome’s authority is far more exact, since it reads “of the Lord” rather than “of God.” Cassiodorus], and your judgments are a great abyss.” If he had said, “Your righteousness is like your mountains,” it would have been clearer. But this manner of expression occurs frequently in the divine page [Col. 0818B], while in other writings it occurs rarely or never. Such also is the statement: “God, give your judgment to the king, and your righteousness to the king’s son” (Ps. 71:2). For he ought to have said, “to your son,” because he himself was the king to whom he was speaking. Above he said that “the truth of God reaches to the clouds”; now he gives the reason why it reaches to the clouds and goes no further. It is as though he said: God’s truth does not descend to lower things, because God’s righteousness and God’s judgments, which are established and sustained by truth, are exceedingly high [Note: [Col. 0818D] The same, Codex Ghis., “and exceedingly deep.”], difficult to approach; high indeed like the mountains of God, and deep like a great abyss. Yet the same thing is signified by both the mountains of God and the abyss. These are the mountains of which it is said: “I lifted up [Col. 0818C] my eyes to the mountains, from which help will come to me” (Ps. 120:1).

“One abyss calls upon another in the sound of your cataracts.” By the mountains, therefore, and by the abyss we understand the volumes of both Testaments. They are so lofty and profound that very few can attain knowledge of them. Since righteousness and God’s judgments are contained in these volumes, they are said to possess the same height and depth. It is clear, therefore, that the truth, righteousness, and judgments of God, and the volumes of both Testaments, are unsearchable and cannot be investigated by human ability. Hence the Apostle says: “O the depth of the riches of the wisdom and knowledge of God! How incomprehensible are his judgments, and untraceable [Col. 0818D] his ways!” (Rom. 1:33). Let us rejoice that God’s truth descends to the clouds, because something from those things which are in the clouds will also distil down to us. Wretched are the Jews, over whom these clouds have been forbidden to rain: “I will command my clouds,” says the Lord, “that they rain no rain upon them” (Isa. 5:6).

“You will save human beings and beasts, Lord, according to the abundance with which you have multiplied your mercies, [Col. 0819A] O God.” What are meant by human beings except the wise, rational, and just? And what by beasts except the foolish, senseless, lustful, and those given over to pleasures of the flesh? As far as human beings differ from beasts, so far do these seem to differ from one another. Yet the Lord saves both the one and the other, for he came not to call the righteous but sinners to repentance (Luke 5:12). We have seen many leading a holy and religious life in monasteries who were formerly like horse and mule, which have no understanding. The prophet marvels at such great mercy of God and says: In what manner, to what measure, with what great overflowing abundance, have you multiplied your mercies, O God?

“But the children of men will hope in the protection of the wings [Col. 0819B] of yours.” The wings of God are mercy and truth, faith, hope, and charity, and the other virtues, without which neither can he himself come to us nor can we fly to him. For what brought him to us except charity and mercy? Christians should therefore hope in their protection, since they have nothing else by which they can defend themselves from vices and evil spirits. He calls them “children of men,” perhaps to distinguish them from those whom he had called beasts. “They will be made drunk from the abundance of your house, and you will give them drink from the torrent of your delight.” Both here in the Church and afterwards in that heavenly Jerusalem, the saints will be made drunk from the abundance of such delights as abound both here and there. Thus the holy apostles were drunk: because they spoke in all tongues, [Col. 0819C] the Jews thought them drunk not with the Holy Spirit but rather with wine.

“For with you is the fountain of life, and in your light we shall see light.” Not only, he says, will they be made drunk, but they will also be enlightened, because with you is the fountain of life and the light of life. Christ is the light of life and the fountain of life: he enlightens and refreshes his faithful. Whoever drinks from this fountain will thirst no more. And this is the light that enlightens every person coming into this world (John 1). The Father too is light—not two lights, however, but one light. Thus it is said here: “And in your light we shall see light,” because unless through you, we cannot come to that light. For the Lord himself says: [Col. 0819D] “I am the way, the truth, and the life; no one comes to the Father except through me” (John 14:6).

“Extend your mercy to those who know you, and your righteousness to those who are upright of heart.” This is as though he said: So that we may be able to come to that light, send your mercy to those who know you, that it may govern and guide us and bring us into the brightness of that light. Send also your righteousness to those who are upright of heart, because it is just that those who have kept the commandments of righteousness should be guided by righteousness.

“Let not the foot of pride come upon me, nor let the hand of sinners [Col. 0820A] move me.” Let your mercy and your righteousness themselves guide me, he says; let not the foot of pride carry me, nor the hand of sinners draw me away. Let pride not be my foot, because by this foot all workers of iniquity fell. The devil was carried by this foot when he said: “I will ascend into heaven above the stars of God; I will build my throne; I will sit on the mountain of the covenant; and I will be like the Most High” (Isa. 14:13). They were therefore rightly expelled from that heavenly blessedness and could not stand, because they had such wicked hands and were borne upon such a foot.

## PSALM XXXVI. A PSALM FOR DAVID HIMSELF.

Let this psalm be ascribed to David himself, who wrote it, [Col. 0820B] and let him himself speak in it. [Note: [Col. 0819D] “The whole psalm concerns the correction of morals. For the Church, now introduced as speaking, instructs humankind through salutary precepts lest it be joined to deadly errors, deterring the wicked by punishment and promising rewards to the good.” Cassiodorus.]

“Do not emulate those who act maliciously, nor be envious of those who do iniquity.” Do not emulate, he says, do not imitate, do not take pleasure in dwelling among those who act maliciously; nor be envious of those who commit iniquities, so as to teach like things [Note: [Col. 0820D] Codex Ghis.: “do like things.”] and desire like things.

“For like grass they will quickly wither, and like the vegetables of herbs they will soon fall.” Such persons, as though he said, seem for a time to flourish and prosper in their iniquities. But like grass that exists today and tomorrow is cast into the oven, they will quickly wither; and like vegetables and the green growth of herbs, they will soon fall—and fall so as to be unable thereafter to rise, because after this there will be no place for repentance [Col. 0820C] for them.

“Hope in God, and do goodness; dwell in the land, and you shall feed on its riches.” “Hope,” he says, “in the Lord,” not in your own strength or in the uncertainty of riches; and “do goodness”: give alms, practise mercy and piety, so that you yourself may find mercy; “and dwell in the land”: rule your flesh, do not abandon the Church of God; remain there, learn there, form your character there, and shape your whole life there according to its example. “And you shall feed on its riches,” by which we understand the Law of both Testaments, and also Christ’s body and blood. These riches are to be preferred to all the riches of this world.

[Col. 0820D] “Delight in the Lord, and he will grant you the petitions of your heart.” Do not, he says, delight in the world or in the vanities and desires of the world, for the world passes away and its desire; rather delight in the Lord. Let him be all your good and all your delight, and he will give you whatever your soul desires. Whoever delights in the Lord desires always to be and dwell with the Lord. This will be given to the saints, because they will remain with him without end.

“Reveal your way to the Lord, and hope in him, and [Col. 0821A] he will act.” How shall I reveal what he knows and understands better than I? For he knows human thoughts and searches hearts and reins. We reveal our ways to him if we do not conceal our sins; and we do not conceal them when we blot them out with tears and repentance. Or again, “Reveal your way to the Lord”: if there is some good desire in your heart, do not delay; begin to do the good you desire. Only hope in him, and he will act [Note: [Col. 0821D] Although Saint Bruno has explained what precedes, Cassiodorus has said it more fully; these words may be added from him: “He added, ‘and he will act’: he who is omnipotent, he who is strong in hand, he indeed at whose commands all things obey.”]; he will bring to a good result what you fear and hesitate to begin.

“And he will bring forth your righteousness as light, and your judgment like midday.” Hope in him, he says; follow him. He will direct your way and illumine it with his most brilliant light, nor will he permit you to go astray. [Col. 0821B] The righteousness you desire to practise, and your judgment by which you propose to judge yourself, he will reveal to angels and to human beings, and will make them shine like light and like midday.

“Be subject to the Lord, and entreat him.” This alone, as though he said, is necessary for you: be subject to the Lord alone, and if anything adverse happens to you, do not forget to pray to him. How excellently and persuasively he exhorts us to the service of God and to the conduct of a better life. “Do not be envious of him who prospers in his way”: this he explains as “the person doing iniquity.” Be envious, he says, of one who prospers in God’s way, who is diligent in God’s service—not of one who prospers in his own way, that is, in his iniquity. For the way of the wicked is itself iniquity. Certainly we see many such persons who, by acting wickedly in this life, prosper greatly for a time; yet we do not doubt that they will perish.

“Cease from anger and abandon fury; do not be envious, so as to act wickedly.” Anger is a brief disturbance of the mind; fury is anger grown old. Both must be avoided, because frequently becoming angry is a sin, since it cannot occur without scandal to brethren. What shall I say of fury, when it differs little or not at all from hatred? “Do not be envious, so as to act wickedly.” Emulate others in good, he says; but emulate no one in evil.

“For those who act wickedly will be cut off.” To be cut off is nothing other than to be put outside the boundaries. Those who are outside the boundaries will not enter the inheritance promised to the saints, [Col. 0821D] concerning which inheritance he adds:

“But those who wait for the Lord, they shall possess the land as an inheritance.” That land, namely, of which it is elsewhere said: “I believe that I shall see the good things of the Lord in the land of the living” (Ps. 37:20). He himself teaches us how we ought to wait for the Lord: “Watch,” he says, “for you do not know at what hour your Lord will come” (Matt. 25:13). Therefore the one who waits for the Lord must watch; and the one who perseveres in good works watches.

[Col. 0822A] “A little while longer, and the sinner will not be; you will seek his place, and you will not find it.” Human life is brief, and even those who love this life pass quickly out of it; in passing, they lose all things along with it. Afterwards, if their place is sought, it will not be found, because they have their place in this age.

“But the meek shall possess the land, and shall delight in an abundance of peace.” For the Lord says this in the Gospel: “Blessed are the meek, for they shall possess the land” (Matt. 5:5). Then they will indeed delight in an abundance of peace, although scarcely anyone can possess peace fully and perfectly in this world, while the spirit desires against the flesh and the flesh against the spirit (Gal. 5).

“The sinner will watch the righteous man, and will gnash [Col. 0822B] his teeth against him; but the Lord will mock him, because he foresees that his day will come.” This is understood of the martyrs, whom wicked men watched with treachery, seized and dragged to punishments, and killed while gnashing their teeth against them, through cruel and elaborate torments. But the Lord mocked them—that is, he judged them worthy of derision—for he foresaw the time and day of the saints and of those men’s destruction.

“Sinners have drawn the sword and bent their bow, to deceive the poor and slay the upright in heart.” This is a most evident prophecy concerning tyrants and martyrs, although it can also be understood of heretics. For both the former, with material weapons, and the latter, with the swords of their deceptions, have slain many saints. By swords we may understand open persecution, and by bows hidden deceit. Hence he adds:

“Let their sword enter into their own heart, and let their bow be broken.” The swords of tyrants enter into their hearts because their very swords, by which they killed the saints, are the cause of their death and destruction. But the bow of the heretics has already [Col. 0822C] been broken, because all their heresy and deception have been condemned in many councils.

“A little is better for the righteous than the great riches of sinners.” This is as though he said: The saints are poor and have been stripped of their riches and honours for Christ’s name; but the little they have is better than the many riches possessed by sinners. The former have little, and it suffices them. The latter have much, yet are tormented by the desire to possess and by avarice.

“For the arms of sinners shall be broken, but the Lord strengthens the righteous.” By the arms of sinners we understand the strength of all such persons, which we see consists chiefly in riches. If they lose these through some misfortune, we see immediately that they have lost all their strength with them. But the Lord strengthens the righteous, because through the loss of temporal [Col. 0823A] things they become richer and stronger; for on this account they receive a hundredfold and obtain eternal life.

“The Lord knows the ways of the blameless, and their inheritance shall be for ever.” Therefore, he says, the Lord strengthens the righteous because he knows their ways. They are those of whom it is said: “Blessed are the blameless in the way, who walk in the law of the Lord” (Ps. 118:1). Those who walk thus are worthy to receive the Lord’s help. “And their inheritance shall be for ever.” It is as though he said: They were poor and lost their inheritances for Christ’s name, but their inheritance will be both greater and better for ever.

“They shall not be put to shame in an evil time.” What is “an evil time”? A time prepared for evils: that is, the day of judgment, [Col. 0823B] when the wicked will receive eternal evils.

“And in days of famine they shall be satisfied.” What are “days of famine”? The same time of which we have just spoken. For the saints will neither hunger nor thirst any more, as it is written (Rev. 7:16); but the wicked will suffer every hunger and every want. Hence it adds: “For sinners shall perish.” They will perish not only through the affliction of hunger, but also through every kind of torment. And he proves this:

“But the enemies of the Lord, as soon as they have been honoured and exalted, will fail away; they will fail away like smoke.” When he says “as soon as,” he does not mean that it will happen immediately, but that it will happen shortly and afterwards. They will fail away like smoke [Col. 0823C] because, in raising and exalting themselves in pride, they fail away. Such is the nature of smoke: it fails away by lifting itself from the earth.

“The sinner borrows and does not repay, but the righteous shows mercy and lends.” This too is a just reason why the wicked perish: they are unwilling to repay what they borrow. For what do we possess except what we have received on loan? So the Apostle says: “What do you have that you did not receive? Why do you boast as though you had not received it?” (1 Cor. 4:7). A loan (*mutuum*) is so called as if it were “mine-yours” (*meum tuum*). For what is given on loan is not given entirely, because something is expected from it. But what does the Lord expect from us from the things he has given us? Hear him say: “What you did to one of my least ones, you did to me” (Matt. 25:40). Therefore what [Col. 0823D] we give to his least ones, we give to him—or rather, we do not give it, but repay it. “But the righteous shows mercy and lends.” The sinner, he says, will not repay what he has received on loan; the righteous, by contrast, repays even what belongs to others, gives generously from his own possessions, and lends.

“For those who bless him shall possess the land, but those who curse him shall utterly perish.” From all that has been said above, he says, anyone can easily understand that those who bless him shall possess the land. Yet not only human beings, but every creature blesses the Lord. For unless every creature blessed the Lord, those three boys placed in the furnace would not say: “Bless the Lord, all works of the Lord” (Dan. 3:1). But if every creature blesses the Lord, who are those of whom it is said here: “Those who curse him shall utterly perish”? The Apostle says to certain evil-doers: “You are those because of whom the name of God is blasphemed among the Gentiles” (Rom. 2:24). These, therefore, are those who curse the Lord. This may nevertheless be understood especially of the Jews, of whom it is said: “They will curse, and you will bless; let those who rise up against me be put to shame” (Ps. 118:26).

“From the Lord the steps of a man are directed, and he greatly desires his way.” Whoever is directed by the Lord can proceed securely. Those are directed by the Lord who do not depart from the way of his commandments. The Lord loves this way. Elsewhere he says that he has run along this way: “I ran in the way of your commandments, when you enlarged my heart” (Ps. 118:32) [Col. 0824B].

“When the righteous falls, he shall not be troubled, because the Lord strengthens his hand.” It cannot happen that a person on a long journey does not stumble, and no one can live without sin in this life. For the righteous person falls seven times (Prov. 24) and rises again; therefore “he shall not be troubled, because the Lord strengthens his hand.” What does “strengthens his hand” mean, except that he supports him while falling and prepares and equips him again for good work?

“I was young, and I have grown old, and I have not seen the righteous forsaken, nor his seed begging bread.” The Prophet seems to me to say this in these words: From the time of my youth, when God deigned to reveal these things to me, until the consummation of the age—through each succeeding age, while the Holy Spirit taught me—I have considered all things [Col. 0824C], and have not seen the righteous forsaken, nor his seed, that is, his children and imitators, perish by hunger. For those perish through hunger who are not nourished with spiritual food.

“All day he shows mercy and lends, and his seed shall be in blessing.” If he were in need, he could not assist others. But he is shown to abound in this: he shows mercy and lends to others, and shares with others the spiritual and temporal goods he possesses. Therefore his seed shall be in blessing, because it will always grow and advance toward what is better.

“Turn away from evil and do good, and dwell for ever and ever.” This counsel is sufficient for everyone’s salvation. This is the rule of perfection: to flee evils, do good things, and not depart from the fellowship of the Church and the faithful [Col. 0824D].

“For the Lord loves judgment and will not forsake his saints; they shall be preserved for ever.” Turn away from evil and do good, he says. Why? Because the Lord loves judgment and will render to each according to his works. He will not forsake those who turn away from evil and do good, but will preserve them for ever. What, then, will happen to the wicked? It follows:

“But the unrighteous shall be punished, and the seed of the ungodly shall perish. But the righteous shall possess the land as an inheritance, and shall dwell upon it for ever and ever.” This may be understood of the present Church and of the land of the living. But because it says “for ever and ever,” [Col. 0825A] it is more suitably understood of that land which can never be taken away and which they will possess eternally.

“The mouth of the righteous shall meditate wisdom, and his tongue shall speak judgment.” It is just that the one who, placed in this age, has devoted himself to wisdom alone and has not departed from truth should possess an eternal inheritance. For what is it to speak judgment except to speak and maintain the truth? Hence it adds:

“The law of his God is in his heart.” How can one who judges according to God’s law and knows no other law depart from truth? “And therefore his steps shall not be tripped up.” Those are tripped up who are led into error and separated from truth. But those who have the law of the Lord in [Col. 0825B] memory and heart, and meditate upon it constantly, do not fear this.

“The sinner watches the righteous and seeks to destroy him.” He watches, he says, observes and lies in wait for him, seeking how he may destroy and deceive him. But the Lord, who never abandons those hoping in him, will not leave him in his hands. This sinner is the devil, the greatest of all sinners, who always lies in wait for the saints and never ceases to accuse them. It follows: “Nor will he condemn him when judgment is given for him.” He did not say, “when he judges him,” but “when judgment is given for him,” because he made that strict judgment for the condemnation of the wicked and for the vindication and glory of the good.

“Wait for the Lord and keep his ways, and he will exalt [Col. 0825C] you so that you may dwell in the land.” Wait for the Lord, he says; be secure and fear nothing. He will come to judge not you, but for you. Keep his ways, from which the enemy strives to draw you and to lead you into his own ways. He will exalt you to that heavenly blessedness, so that you may dwell in that land where you fear neither death nor the snares of enemies. “When sinners perish, you will see it.” It is a great consolation to behold the punishments and destruction of enemies.

“I saw the ungodly highly exalted and raised above the cedars of Lebanon. I passed by, and behold, he was not there; I sought him, and his place was not found.” Lebanon, interpreted “whiteness,” signifies the holy Church, cleansed and washed by the water of baptism and made whiter than snow. By cedars we understand [Col. 0825D] those in the Church who are loftier and stronger in wisdom, holiness, and virtues. Yet we often see the ungodly exalted and raised above these, trampling and despising them as though they were the lowest shrubs. When he says, “I passed by, and behold, he was not there,” it is as though he said: After seeing the ungodly so exalted and raised, I passed in mind and thought to the things that would happen to him shortly; and behold, he was not there—namely, where he had formerly been accustomed to be. I sought him among the pretentious pinnacles of his houses, and his place [Col. 0826A] was not found, because others occupied everything, though they will give him no thanks for it.

“Keep truth and behold equity, for there are remnants for the peaceful person [Note: [Col. 0825D] How there are remnants for the peaceful person. “Let us consider how we ought to understand this phrase: ‘Remnants for the peaceful person,’ when his hope is fulfilled by the Lord’s recompense. For it remains that after this life he should receive the rewards of eternal blessedness.” Cassiodorus].” Observe the elegance of the expression: how alternately he describes the rewards of the righteous and the destruction of the wicked, so that in one respect he may urge hearers toward good and in the other draw them away from evil. Keep truth and behold equity, he says; do not emulate those who act maliciously, nor imitate those who, though so exalted and raised, so quickly fall and fail away, for there are remnants for the peaceful person. The wicked, as though he said, suddenly lose both themselves and whatever they have; but saints departing from this world become richer. Nothing that they seemed to possess in this life is anything in comparison with the remnants [Col. 0826B] reserved for them in the other life.

“But the unrighteous shall utterly perish; together the remnants of the ungodly shall perish.” As is his manner, he sets contrary things against their opposites: the things which the good will have, the wicked will not be able to have.

“But the salvation of the righteous is from the Lord,” because they have presumed nothing upon their own strength; he is their protector in time of tribulation, and therefore they could not be overcome by enemies.

“And the Lord will help them and deliver [them], and rescue them from sinners, and save them, because they hoped in him.” Such repetition and insistence upon the same point should make the promise firmer. We should always note how great is the power of hope, which is commended everywhere in this way.

## PSALM XXXVII. [Col. 0826C] A PSALM OF DAVID, FOR REMEMBRANCE OF THE SABBATH.

The Sabbath is interpreted as “rest,” by which rest we understand the repose of eternal blessedness. Hence the Apostle says: “There remains a sabbath-rest for the people of God” (Heb. 4:9). Mindful of this rest, therefore, the children of the Church perform severe repentance for their sins in this psalm.

“Lord, do not rebuke me in your fury, nor correct me in your anger.” These emotions, as we have already said in another psalm, are not in God. Yet they seem to be in him when he does the things which angry people are accustomed to do. This is the voice of a penitent person, fearing God’s judgment and imploring God’s mercy. It is as though he said: I have sinned greatly; and when I read and consider the day of judgment and the torments prepared for the wicked, I am overcome by excessive terror and fear. But, Lord, on that day of dreadful judgment, show mercy to your servant; do not rebuke me in fury or correct me in anger. For “if you observe iniquities, Lord, who shall endure?” (Ps. 129). “Do not,” therefore, “enter into judgment with your servant” (Ps. 142:2).

“For your arrows are fixed in me, and you have strengthened your hand over me.” God’s arrows are those judgments sent against sinners in both Testaments. We have just heard many such judgments in the preceding [Col. 0827A] psalm, and we find many in the Gospels and other divine Scriptures. Such is this: “Now the axe has been laid to the root of the trees. Every tree which does not bear good fruit will be cut down and cast into the fire” (Matt. 3:10). And the Apostle says: “According to your hardness and impenitent heart, you store up wrath for yourself on the day of wrath and revelation of the righteous judgment of God, who will render to each according to his works” (Rom. 2:5). He says that these arrows are fixed in him because his mind is wounded and shaken with great terror by these and similar words. This is what he means when he says: “You have strengthened your hand over me.” Blessed are those who feel this hand and know themselves wounded by these arrows. Those who do not grieve over their sins do not recognize God’s hand hanging over them and prepared to strike. Hence he adds:

“For my iniquities have set themselves above my head; like a heavy burden they have weighed upon me.” Here the cause of the whole affliction is revealed in this verse. I have become so weak, he says, because my iniquities have set themselves over my head and, as it were, established their seat there—by “head” meaning the mind. Once this head has been subdued, there will be nothing able to resist them. “And like a heavy burden they have weighed upon me”: I can no longer bear their weight. No one except those alone who perform worthy repentance can say this, for all others regard their sins not as burdensome but as very light and delightful. To this end [Col. 0827C] the Prophet sets forth this one penitent person, so that all others may learn from his words how they ought to repent.

“My scars have become putrid and worsened [Note: [Col. 0827D] This means the same as “they became worse.” The Vulgate reads: “My scars have become putrid and corrupt.” From the Hebrew, Mazochius translates: “My bruises reddened and wasted away.” *Spicilegium* on Psalm 37. The same reading occurs in Augustine’s exposition of this Psalm 37.] because of my folly.” Wherever there are scars, there is no doubt that wounds or sores once existed. Since he says that through his own negligence and folly he has worsened and made his scars putrid, he shows that he had long since been healed from infirmity and has again become infirm. This happens to those who, after completing repentance, return again to sins. Such persons too are healed by mercy, but scars of this kind reach salvation with greater difficulty. [Note: [Col. 0827D] See Ambrose, exposition of Psalm 37, no. 30.]

“I have been afflicted with miseries unto the end; all day I went about sorrowing.” For such and so great sins, he says, I have been afflicted, distressed, and sorrowful unto the end—that is, thoroughly and wholly.

“For my soul is filled with delusions, and there is no health in my flesh.” The soul [Note: [Col. 0827D] Augustine’s remarks on this passage must not be omitted: “By reason of these very delusions, we are sometimes scarcely permitted to pray. We do not know how to think of bodies except as images; and often images we do not seek rush in. We wish to pass from this one to that, and from that to another; sometimes you wish to return to what you were thinking and leave what you are thinking; something else occurs, you wish to recall what you had forgotten, and it does not come to mind; instead something else comes which you did not wish.”] suffers many delusions when sins rule it, because after many wicked thoughts it is sometimes brought to despair. When he says, [Col. 0828A] “And there is no health in my flesh,” he shows it to have been weakened either by fasting or afflictions, or violated by luxury, pleasures, and other corruptions.

“I am bowed down and humbled utterly.” Many penitents are bowed down and humbled, but not utterly, because although they practise severe repentance, they nevertheless do not cease to sin in certain respects. “I roared from the groaning of my heart.” Nothing is more fruitful for a penitent person than such groaning and roaring of compunction. Hence elsewhere it is said: “A contrite and humbled heart, O God, you will not despise” (Ps. 50:50). “And before you is all my desire, and my groaning is not hidden from you.” Whatever I may formerly [Col. 0828B] have been, and whatever things my desire may have occupied itself with, you nevertheless see what my desire is now. This repentance of mine, these tears, and this groaning of mine cannot be hidden from you.

“My heart has been troubled within me, and my strength has forsaken me.” There can be no doubt that one who outwardly makes satisfaction by such severe repentance is greatly troubled inwardly. Such disturbance, however, is good, because through it all evil humours are expelled and the infirm soul is healed. “And my strength has forsaken me.” If the strength properly and naturally belonging to a human being had not forsaken him, he would by no means have been overcome by vices. One must therefore persist in tears and prayers until the lost strength returns and the mind rests from the disturbance of its fervour. “And the light of my eyes is not with me.” He says that God himself is the light of his eyes, and rightly laments and grieves that, because of the sins he committed, God has withdrawn from him. Thus far we have heard the cry of the penitent; now let us hear our Saviour speaking of his passion. Certainly our Saviour suffered for sinners, and therefore he seems in this place to recount his passion so that consolation may be given to this penitent person who has repented so worthily.

“My friends and my neighbors drew near against me and stood [there].” There is nothing, he says, O man, of which you may complain; nothing for which you should lament your miseries. See me afflicted, see me crucified, [Col. 0828D] see me bearing your sins, see me enduring and taking away the miseries of the world. Therefore be comforted, have hope, do not be broken by adversity. Do you not know how “my friends,” the Jews (this is irony—for he likewise called Judas friend: “Friend, for what have you come?” [Matt. XXVI. 50], although he was certainly not a friend), “and my neighbors” (according to the flesh) [Col. 0829A] “drew near against me and stood”? For they did not draw near in order to believe, but rather in order to kill. “And my neighbors stood afar off.” This, however, is understood of the disciples, who, “leaving him,” as the Gospel relates, “all fled” (Matt. XXVI. 36).

“And those who sought my life used violence.” They did indeed use violence, because they both dragged him forcibly after them and, as we have just said, compelled the disciples to flee. “And those who sought evils for me spoke vanity.” And what else did the Jews speak but vanity—raging and raving against him, crying “Crucify him,” producing false witnesses, and mocking him with many reproaches and blasphemies? “And they devised deceits all day long.” Because, [Col. 0829B] as it is written, they found no cause of death in him, they therefore devised all day long the deceits by which they might accuse and kill him.

“But I, as one deaf, did not hear.” He says that he did not hear because he did not wish to answer their blasphemies and questions. It is a customary manner of speaking for us to say that we do not hear things to which we do not trouble ourselves to reply. Thus some of them said: “Do you not hear how many things these men testify against you?” (Matt. XXVI. 62.) “And like one dumb, not opening his mouth.” For he is the one of whom it is written: “Like a sheep he was led to the slaughter, and like one dumb he did not open his mouth” (Isa. LIII. 7). Hence it follows:

“And I became as a man who does not hear and [Col. 0829C] has no rebukes in his mouth.” For with such patience did he bear their words, as though he had nothing to answer them, or nothing by which he might rebuke them—he who saw all secrets and could reproach each one for everything that he had done wickedly.

“For in you, O Lord, I hoped; I said: You will hear me, O Lord my God.” Therefore, he says, I wished neither to rebuke them nor to defend myself in any respect, because I hoped not in myself but in the Lord, whose strength and power over them and over all things I knew, and who could adequately defend me. “I said: You will hear me, O Lord my God.” This is as though he said: He was sufficient for me, whom I knew would hear me according to my will. For why should he weary himself by speaking, answering, or in any [Col. 0829D] other manner, when his will alone and the prayer of his heart sufficed?

“Because I said: Let not my enemies ever exult over me.” Thus this was his will, this prayer was in his heart: that his enemies might not be able to exult over him. But when he says, “ever,” this must be understood after the Passion and Resurrection, since during those three days power was given them to do to him whatever they wished. Thus he himself said: “This is your hour and the power of darkness” (Luke XXII. 33). And elsewhere: “As Jonah was in the belly of the whale three days and three nights, so shall the Son of Man be in the heart of the earth” (Matt. XII. 40). [Col. 0830A] That is, in the affection and will of the Jews, that they might do to him whatever they wished. But after the Passion and Resurrection the Jews could by no means exult over him, since they themselves were scattered everywhere on account of this sin, while Christ’s name and glory are preached everywhere. “And while my feet were shaken, they spoke great things against me.” The feet of God are the apostles, 374 who carried his Gospel into all the earth. Of them it is said: “How beautiful are the feet of those who proclaim peace, who proclaim good things” (Rom. X. 15). These feet were shaken when the Lord said: “If you seek me, let these go” (John XVIII. 8). Thereafter the ungodly Jews spoke against the Lord great, evil, foolish, and impious things, as is recorded in his Passion.

[Col. 0830B] “For I am ready for scourges, and my sorrow is always before me.” I did not, he says, prepare myself to resist, but to receive scourges. For he could have resisted and easily destroyed all his enemies, had he wished; as he said to blessed Peter, when he was fighting and wished to defend him with the sword: “Put your sword back into its place. Do you think that I cannot ask my Father, and that he will immediately furnish me with more than twelve legions of angels? How then shall the Scriptures be fulfilled, that thus it must happen?” (Matt. XXVI. 52.) And this is as though he said: Unless this happens, I cannot be freed from the sorrow I have over the devil’s power and the destruction of humankind. And this is what he says: “And my sorrow is always before me”—always, indeed, until, by dying, I conquer [Col. 0830C] and rescue those held captive.

“For I will declare my iniquity, and I will consider my sin.” This is as though he said: They condemn and judge me as unjust and sinful, and as one blaspheming God [Note: [Col. 0829D] Codex Ghis.: “and acting against the law” (*et contra legem agentem*; the printed *argentem* is apparently an OCR error).]; but I myself declare and make known what my iniquity is and what my sin is. I willed that the world should be saved and that humankind should be rescued from the devil’s power: this is my sin; for this, if need be, I myself will take thought.

“But my enemies live and have prevailed over me, and those who hate me unjustly have multiplied.” These words should be read as questions, with a certain indignation. “My enemies,” he says, “live?” They shall not live, but shall die by death—by temporal death, certainly, and eternal death. [Col. 0830D] “And have they prevailed over me?” They have not prevailed, but have been humbled and scattered. “And have those who hate me unjustly multiplied?” They have not multiplied, but, as they deserve, have been diminished in every way. And certainly, as we see, that people does not now increase, although before Christ’s Passion it grew and sprouted like grass [Note: [Col. 0830D] The same codex: “of the earth” (*terrae*).].

“Those who repaid me evil for good slandered me.” The Lord himself showed that the Jews repaid him evil for good when he said: “I have done many good works among you; for which of these do you wish to kill me?” (John X. 32.) Since their slanders are sufficiently well known, [Col. 0831A] there is no need for us to explain them, because they pursued righteousness.

“Do not forsake me, O Lord my God; do not depart from me; attend to my help, O Lord, God of my salvation.” Our Savior teaches us that those who possess righteousness may confidently seek God’s help, in that he sets himself before us as an example and, because he pursued righteousness, is not forsaken by the Lord.

## PSALM XXXVIII. FOR IDITHUN: A CANTICLE OF DAVID.

Idithun [Note: [Col. 0831D] Concerning the translation into Latin of this Hebrew name, namely Idithum or Idithun, St. Augustine, expounding this psalm, says: “As far as we have been able to discover by inquiry from those names which have been translated for us from Hebrew speech into Latin by students of the divine writings, Idithum is interpreted ‘leaping over them.’ But others now interpret this word differently, namely, ‘his law’ or ‘giving praise.’” This may be seen in the literal version of Hebrew names, etc., at the end of the Biblical Dictionary compiled by the most learned Calmet. But St. Ambrose should also be heard, writing on this psalm as follows: [Col. 0832D] “The psalm which David wrote he gave to Idithum, a man trained in Levitical and priestly disciplines, to be sung; Idithum was most skillful in leading the series of psalms before the ark of the Lord. Therefore, because Idithum did not write this psalm, but the prophet David wrote it and gave it to Idithum, skilled in singing, to be sung with psalmody, the title is thus inscribed.” AMBROSE, *Exposition on Psalm* XXXVIII. See Calmet, *Dictionary*, s.v. “Idithum.”] is interpreted “leaping over them.” David therefore sings this psalm in praise of those who leap over and pass by, as though not hearing, those who speak vanities against them and strive by every kind of folly to provoke them to indignation. By these [Col. 0831B] we may understand all who are more perfect, who have chosen silence lest they sin even through the frivolity of speech. For Jeremiah says of such persons: “It is good for a man when he has borne the yoke from his youth; he shall sit alone and be silent” (Lam. III. 27).

“I said: I will guard my ways, that I may not sin with my tongue.” “I said,” he declares—that is, I resolved in my mind, established in my heart, and firmly confirmed my purpose to guard my ways and my actions so carefully that I might not sin with my tongue. For it is very difficult for a person not to sin with the tongue. “For,” Scripture says, “he who does not stumble in word is a perfect man” (Jas. III. 2). And: “He who guards his tongue guards his soul” (Prov. XIII. 3). And: “Death and life are in the hand of the tongue” (Prov. XVIII. 21).—“For whoever thinks himself [Col. 0831C] religious, while not restraining his tongue but deceiving his heart, that man’s religion is vain” (Jas. I. 26).

“I set a guard upon my mouth when the sinner stood against me.” This is what is said elsewhere: “Fence your ears about with thorns [Note: [Col. 0832D] The Vulgate, Ecclesiasticus, chapter XXVIII, 28, reads: “Fence your ears about with thorns; do not hear an evil tongue; and make doors and bars for your mouth.”], and make for your mouth a door and thorns.” Holy men ought indeed to do this when their words produce more scandal than benefit. Thus the Lord says: “Do not give what is holy to dogs, nor cast pearls before swine” (Matt. VII. 6). Therefore let us avoid conversing with those who are not edified by our words, but are instead stirred up to blasphemies and reproaches. Hence it follows:

“I became dumb, and was humbled, and kept silence even from good things, and [Col. 0831D] my sorrow was renewed.” Because, he says, the sinner stood against me, ready to resist and assault the truth, and I understood that my words could then profit neither him nor others, I became dumb and was thus humbled, as though I could not answer his foolishness [Col. 0832A]. And I kept silence from good things, because I ceased to sow and scatter holy and catholic words among swine. This too was done by the Apostle, who, when the Jews would not assent, said to them: “It was necessary for the word of God to be preached first to you; but because you have rejected it and made yourselves unworthy of eternal life, your blood be upon your own head: behold, we turn to the Gentiles” (Acts XIII. 46).—“And my sorrow was renewed”: namely, over the destruction of those who resisted the truth so obstinately and refused to receive the remedy of their salvation.

“My heart grew hot within me, and in my meditation a fire shall blaze.” My heart, he says, grew hot within me through the kindling of the Holy Spirit; and in that meditation of mine the fire of charity and love [Col. 0832B] began to burn, while I still prayed for them, that God might soften their hearts and recall them to the knowledge of himself and to the way of truth.

“I spoke with my tongue: Make known to me, O Lord, my end, and what is the number of my days, that I may know what is lacking to me.” Holy and perfect men, who speak in this psalm, desire to remain in this life not for themselves but for others. Since they cannot benefit others, they pray for themselves, that at last they may be received into that blessedness. “I spoke,” he says, “with my tongue”: with the tongue of the inward person I asked you to make known my end to me. As long as we are in this life, we are not certain to what end we shall come. Whoever, [Col. 0832C] therefore, says with the Apostle, “I desire to be dissolved and to be with Christ” (Phil. I. 23), undoubtedly desires to see his own end. Moreover, he desires to see the number of his days: that number, namely, which is, and always is, and has no end. For these days have no number, because when one is present, another has already passed and another is not yet. But when it is not, how can it be numbered? One can say that it was or will be, but one cannot say that it is. “That I may know what is lacking to me.” Whoever comes to that blessedness will certainly know how much was lacking to him in this life. For God will be all in all, and no one will lack anything.

“Behold, you have made my days old, and my substance [Col. 0832D] is as nothing before you.”—“For,” says the Apostle, “what grows old and becomes aged is near to destruction” (Heb. VIII. 13). Thus he shows that his days have already come to their end by calling them aged. But this temporal substance of ours [Col. 0833A] is as nothing before God, because not only this, but, as the prophet says, “all nations before him are as though they were not” (Isa. XL. 17). Since God is eternal and all things before him are eternal, temporal and passing things are reckoned before him as nothing.

“Nevertheless, every living human being is altogether vanity. Although man walks in the image of God, nevertheless he is vainly troubled.” Although, he says, this substance of ours is nothing, foolish and vain man nevertheless labors and is troubled over it. For a human being is altogether vanity as long as he lives, because unless he first dies to the world and the desires of the flesh, he does not withdraw from vanities. It is good for a person to die thus, because one who dies thus lives better. And [Col. 0833B] it is indeed altogether unfitting that a man made in the image of God should be occupied and troubled over things so vain and useless. He ought [Note: [Col. 0833D] Codex Ghis.: “He ought” (*deberet*).] to look to him in whose image he was made. If he could retain and preserve that image, nothing would ever be lacking to him.

“He stores up treasure and does not know for whom he will gather it.” He labors, he says, and wearies himself [Note: [Col. 0833D] The same codex adds: “and is troubled.”], that he may gather riches soon to perish with him; and he does not know for whom he gathers them, because the possessions which he hopes to leave to his sons and grandsons he leaves instead to his adversaries and enemies.

“And now what is my expectation? Is it not the Lord? And my substance is as nothing before you.” Let others, he says, do what they wish; let them possess these [Col. 0833C] riches which please them. They do not please me, for all my substance, all my riches, and my expectation are the Lord. If I possess him, he is enough for me; and I count all 376 my substance as nothing, because, as we have just said, my substance is as nothing before you. What is as nothing before you is likewise as nothing before me.

“Rescue me from all my iniquities; you have made me a reproach to the fool.” Grant others, he says, such riches as seem good to you; but grant me this alone: rescue me from all my iniquities, and send me no longer among fools and senseless persons. This is what he says: “You have made me a reproach to the fool.” Therefore I also became dumb and did not open [Col. 0833D] my mouth. Why should I speak to those who would not hear me, who blasphemed you, beat me, mocked me, and cursed you?

“I became dumb and did not open my mouth, because you made me; remove your blows from me, for by the strength of your hand I have failed under rebukes.” He aptly said, “because you made me,” so that he might the more readily be moved to help when he is reminded that he is Maker and Creator. For if human beings and all animals love their children so greatly because they begot them, how much more ought we to believe that he who created and [Col. 0834A] made all things loves all his creation? And if he loves all, he especially loves that which seems better than the rest. “Remove your blows from me,” he says. These, as though he said, are your blows; you inflict them upon me—you, I say, who make assaults through evil angels; who handed Job over to Satan to be scourged and sent evil spirits into the swine; to whom we not without reason daily say: “Do not lead us into temptation, but deliver us from evil” (Luke XI. 4). By the strength of your hand, which permits me to be so grievously afflicted, I have failed under your rebukes and chastisements. For I know that you correct and chastise every son whom you receive, and that you do nothing without cause. And this is what he says:

“For iniquity you rebuked man and made [Col. 0834B] my soul waste away like a spider.” Human nature was so wounded in the first man that there is no person who, so far as he himself is concerned, is not worthy of scourges. Therefore one who is not scourged ought to attribute this not to his own merits but to God’s mercy alone. The spider, however, seems here to have a favorable meaning. Thus that soul wastes away like a spider which never ceases daily to afflict itself in the diligence of the work divinely enjoined upon it. We may fittingly understand this of those who, devoted to vigils, fasts, and prayers, meditate upon the law of the Lord day and night.

“Nevertheless, every living human being is altogether vanity.” This is not found in another translation; and it seems to mean: Although the good, laboring daily in God’s [Col. 0834C] service, mortify and afflict themselves, the wicked, taking no good example from this, nevertheless persist in their vanity.

“Hear, O God, my prayer, and receive my supplication with your ears; attend to my tears; do not be silent toward me.” Four prayers are contained in this one utterance, by which nearly one and the same thing is signified; in them we are surely taught with what earnestness we ought to pray to God.

“For I am a sojourner in the land and a stranger, like all my fathers.” He is worthy to be heard who is a sojourner on earth while in mind and spirit he is with God. A sojourner is one who tills not his own but another’s land. Such were those who said: [Col. 0834D] “We do not have here a lasting city, but we seek the city to come” (Heb. XIII. 14). He is also a stranger because he is far from his homeland and hastens to return to it. For this reason the patriarchs and prophets called themselves strangers: they were hastening toward the inheritance promised to them, by which our inheritance also was signified.

“Forgive me, that I may be refreshed before I go away and am no more [Note: [Col. 0833D] “David rightly asks that forgiveness be granted him, [Col. 0834D] knowing that it had not been granted to the priests who were according to Aaron, but had been reserved for the Gospel.” St. AMBROSE, on this passage.].” Into that inheritance or city, as it is written (Rev. XXI), no [Col. 0835A] defiled or unclean person shall enter. Therefore, before going there, he entreats the Lord to forgive him all the vices and sins by which the soul is burned. That soul experiences refreshment which knows itself to have been freed from the heat of vices and the desires of the flesh. When he says, “and I shall be no more,” this is to be understood thus: Unless, before I go—that is, depart from the body—he has forgiven my sins, I shall no longer be able to be there with your elect. In this life, therefore, every sin is forgiven to those who are to be saved; but the punishment of sin is not forgiven to all.

## PSALM XXXIX. TO THE END: A PSALM OF DAVID.

This title has been explained above.

“Waiting, I waited for the Lord, and he looked upon me, [Col. 0835B] and heard my supplication, and drew me out of the pit of misery and the mire of dregs.” The Church speaks in this Psalm, whose members are all those predestined to life, from the first man 377 until the end of the age. “Waiting,” it says, “I waited for the Lord.” For all the patriarchs and prophets, and all others whom the Holy Spirit enlightened, awaited Christ’s coming with great desire. Thus the Lord himself says: “Many prophets and kings wished to see what you see and did not see it, and to hear what you hear and did not hear it” (Matt. XIII. 17). For they knew that unless he came, they could not be freed from the sin of the first man. Among them was that righteous man Simeon, “who had received an answer from the Holy Spirit that he would not [Col. 0835C] see death before he had seen the Christ of the Lord” (Luke II. 26). They awaited him, and the Lord looked upon them and heard their supplication, sending them, at the appointed time, him for whom they had waited so long. Thus the Apostle says: “But when the fullness of time had come, God sent his Son, born of a woman, made under the law, in order that he might redeem those who were under the law” (Gal. IV. 4). And he drew them out of the pit of misery, by which we understand hell, in which all the souls of the saints were held captive until that time; and out of the mire of dregs, by which he signifies the corrupt and erroneous teaching of the Jews. For what is the mire of dregs but the sediment of wine? This [Col. 0835D] teaching held by the Jews, then, is not wine, but rather the dregs of wine and the refuse of wine—namely, of the Law and the Prophets. This wine is drunk only by those who understand the Scriptures not according to the letter but spiritually. Therefore those who do not follow their interpretation and error were drawn out of this mire.

“And he set my feet upon a rock, directed my steps, and put a new song in my mouth, a hymn to our God.” The feet, eyes, hands, and tongue of the Church are the holy apostles and their successors. The Lord set these upon that rock of which the Apostle says: “And the rock was Christ” (I Cor. X. 4). Thus it is said elsewhere: [Col. 0836A] “No one can lay another foundation besides that which has been laid, which is Christ Jesus” (I Cor. III. 11). Behold, he set your feet upon the rock; and what did he then do? “And he directed my steps.” Did he do something else for you? “And he put a new song in my mouth.” For what purpose? “A hymn to our God.” A fine sequence of expression: he established the feet, directed the steps, taught the song, and commanded that song be sung to God alone. The new song, a song previously unheard, is evangelical preaching, in which Christ’s birth, Passion, Resurrection, and Ascension are declared. Of it it is also said elsewhere: “The Lord commanded a new song to be sung”; yet the unhappy Jews are unwilling to sing anything but the old song. To sing the old song is to walk in the oldness of the letter and not in the newness of the Spirit. [Col. 0836B] Therefore those who understand the Law according to the letter sing the old song.

“Many shall see and fear and hope in the Lord.” For many were blind and sat in the darkness of error; when they heard the preaching and were baptized in the Lord’s name, they were enlightened. And they began to fear God and hope in him alone; formerly they feared offending false gods and placed their hope in the uncertainty of riches. Of such people the Apostle says to Timothy: “Command the rich of this age not to think proudly, nor to hope in the uncertainty of riches” (I Tim. VI. 17).

“Blessed is the man whose hope is the name of the Lord, and who has not looked to vanity and false madness.” Let the name of the Lord therefore be our hope, and in all [Col. 0836C] our necessities let us invoke him [Note: [Col. 0835D] “Among other things, the name of the Lord is eternal Savior; and he places his hope in that name [Col. 0836D] who believes that he is to be saved not by his own merits but by the Lord through his grace.” CASSIODORUS.], because, as the Apostle says: “Whoever calls upon the name of the Lord shall be saved” (Acts II. 21). But those looked to vanity and false madness who worshiped vain, mute, and deaf idols and adored false gods. By “false madness” we may also understand possessed persons, from whom wretched people sought responses. “You, O Lord my God, have done many of your wonders, and none is like you in your thoughts.” Who can number God’s wonders? God has made nothing that is not wonderful. Yet more wonderful is this: that he so humbled himself, took our flesh, and was willing to endure our miseries. It is also very wonderful that he converted the world in such a manner and through such persons, and [Col. 0836D] separated it from its ancient superstition. Who could ever have conceived such things? Who imagined such mercy? Who, not merely for evil servants but even for most beloved children, thus humbled himself? Therefore let the Church speak, let the apostles say: “You, O Lord my God, have done many of your wonders,” you who gave us such efficacy and power for proclaiming the Gospel, who subdued all things to yourself through so frail a ministry. And this is what it says:

“I declared and spoke; they were multiplied beyond number.” When the apostles proclaimed and preached Christ’s faith, the faithful multiplied, [Col. 0837A] and the multitude of believers was so great that, like the stars, it could not be counted. They also multiplied beyond number in this respect: the number of those baptized is far greater than the number of the elect. Thus the Lord says in the Gospel: “Many are called, but few are chosen” (Matt. XX. 16).—“Sacrifice and offering you did not desire, but you prepared a body for me.”—“For,” as the Apostle says, “Christ is the end of the Law for righteousness to everyone who believes” (Rom. X. 4). The Gospel also says: 378 “The Law and the Prophets were until John” (Luke XVI. 16). Sacrifices and offerings, therefore, had their time until Christ, because they signified Christ’s Passion. Thereafter they were not necessary, because the shadow had to cease when the truth arrived. [Col. 0837B] Thus it is rightly said here: “Sacrifice and offering you did not desire,” because that which had previously existed in signification began to be enacted in reality. And this is what it says: “But you prepared a body for me.” This is as though it said: In place of all those sacrifices that had been offered until that time, you gave me your body and your blood.

“Burnt offerings also for sin you did not require.” Why should he thereafter require burnt offerings for sin, when by his own blood he blotted out every sin? A burnt offering is called “wholly burned” (*holocaustum*), because such a victim was entirely burned for the Lord. “Then I said: Behold, I come.” Thus far the Church has spoken; now our Savior speaks, responding to the first verse of this psalm, as though he says: You waited, waiting for me, and desired my coming; and then I said: Behold, I come, I take flesh and hasten to set you free.

“In the beginning of the book it is written of me, that I should do your will, O my God; I have willed it, and your law is in the midst of my heart.” Our Savior has just said according to his divinity, “Behold, I come” [Note: [Col. 0837D] “It is certainly written of Christ at the beginning of the Old Testament that he would come in order [Col. 0838D] to do the will of God the Father in the redemption of humankind.” St. Ambrose, on this passage.]; now humanity, united to divinity, promises him submission and obedience, saying: “At the beginning of this book it is written of me that I should do your will. But I, O my God,” as though with the highest desire, say: “I have willed this,” and I will it; and I am ready to do in every respect and in all things whatever you command me. But what is said at the beginning of this book, [Col. 0837D] “His will was in the law of the Lord,” is what is said here: “that I should do your will.” And what is said, “He shall meditate upon his law day and night,” is what is said here: “your law is in the midst of my heart.” These correspond quite fittingly. In these few words the divinity and humanity of our Savior spoke to one another for our consolation; the former, by coming, fulfilled what it had promised, while the latter, by obeying and doing his will, redeemed us by dying. Now let us return to the words of the apostles and hear what they next mean.

“I have proclaimed your righteousness well in the great Church. [Col. 0838A] Behold, I will not restrain my lips.” The Church, or congregation of apostles, had said above: “I declared and spoke; they were multiplied beyond number.” Now it says not merely that it proclaimed, but that it proclaimed well. “I proclaimed well,” it says, because I fulfilled in deed what I said in word; “I proclaimed well,” because I did not show partiality to any person. This was in the great Church, the catholic Church spread throughout the whole world. “Behold, I will not restrain my lips.” I, as though it said, have nothing in preaching except lips alone; all else is yours. You said to me: “Open your mouth and I will fill it” (Ps. LXXX. 11). You commanded me not to consider what I should say; for it is not we who speak, but your Spirit who speaks in us [Col. 0838B] (Matt. X. 20). Therefore speak, for I will not restrain my lips from speaking, and I shall not fear to say whatever you inspire in me.

“Lord, you have known; I have not hidden your righteousness in my heart; I have spoken your truth and your salvation. I have not concealed your mercy and your truth from the great Synagogue.” Behold, it has been sufficiently demonstrated that he proclaimed God’s righteousness well in the great Church; and he calls God as witness that he did not conceal righteousness, that he spoke words of truth and salvation, and did not hide mercy and truth. Whoever proclaims in this manner proclaims well, and cannot proclaim better.

“But you, O Lord, do not make your mercies far from me.” Rather, as you are accustomed, always help me [Col. 0838C] in speaking and protect me from adversaries who rise against me. For he had promised that he would not restrain his lips from speaking, and since he does not doubt that stripes are ready for him after words, he prays that mercy may be at hand and not withdraw farther away. When he says, “Your mercy and your truth have always upheld me,” he shows that he had this boldness—or rather confidence—in speaking because God’s mercy and truth had never forsaken him. For the Lord himself promised them: “I will not leave you or forsake you” (John XIV. 18);—“And behold, I am with you until the consummation of the age” (Matt. XVIII. 20).—“For evils without number have surrounded me.” This is what the Apostle says: “I do not want you to be ignorant, brothers, concerning our tribulation which befell us in Asia: for we were burdened beyond measure, beyond our strength, so that we were weary even of life” (II Cor. I. 8).

“My iniquities have overtaken me.” The righteous person is the first accuser of himself. It is characteristic of the saints to attribute the evils that happen to them to themselves and not to others, and to say that they happened to them because of their sins. “And I was not able to see.” I was not able, he says, to look around and see anyone present except an adversary and enemy. Hence he continues:

“They have multiplied beyond the hairs of my head, and [Col. 0839A] my heart has forsaken me.” Grammarians call this manner of expression hyperbole; it is found frequently not only in pagan books, 379 but also in the divine page. “And my heart has forsaken me.” We say that our heart has forsaken us when, through the immensity of fear, we are beside ourselves and suffer a diminution of our accustomed strength. Yet by our heart we may understand our friends and relatives. For of such people it is said: “They were all of one heart and one soul” (Acts IV. 32). When persons of this kind are separated from one another, each may say: “My heart has forsaken me.”

“May it please you, O Lord, to rescue me; O Lord, look to my help.” Let it please you, he says, because now it has pleased me also, to rescue me, [Col. 0839B] because without your help I cannot be delivered.

“Let my enemies be confounded and ashamed, who seek my life in order to take it away.” Malignant spirits do this; heretics and tyrants do this, for they desire to kill and destroy [Note: [Col. 0839D] Codex Ghis.: “and lose” (*et perdere*).] the soul more than the body. Yet this can also be understood favorably: that they may be ashamed of their sins and turn to the Lord. Hence it follows:

“Let those who devise evils against me be turned backward and put to shame.” Let them turn from their evil intention, by which they hasten to run toward evil, as the Apostle says: “What fruit, then, did you have in those things of which you are now ashamed?” (Rom. VI. 21). To be ashamed in this manner is praiseworthy. “Let those who say to me, ‘Well done, well done,’ immediately bear [Col. 0839C] their own confusion.” This is the voice of those who mock and boast of victory. Yet this too, like the foregoing, can be understood in both a favorable and an unfavorable sense.

“Let those who seek you, O Lord, exult and rejoice, and let those who love your salvation always say: ‘Let the Lord be magnified.’” For as grief and sadness await the wicked, so joy and eternal gladness await the good, who love Christ our Lord and, as far as they can, exalt and magnify him.

“But I am needy and poor; the Lord has care for me.” The saints were needy and poor because they lacked not only necessary things but every human assistance and strength [Col. 0839D]. This was for Christ’s sake, because though he was rich in all things, “for our sake he became poor” (II Cor. VIII. 9). But the Lord cares for them, he who “is rich toward all who call upon him.”

“Be my helper and my deliverer, O Lord; do not delay.” He prays to the Lord not to delay his coming or make postponements, but to come swiftly for judgment and help and deliver his saints, lest they suffer any longer such great calamities of this world.

## Psalm XL. To the End. A Psalm of David.

[Col. 0840A]

This psalm must be referred to the End, for it speaks of Christ, who is the beginning and the end.

“Blessed is he who understands concerning the needy and poor man.” “I,” says the Prophet, “compose psalms, yet they are not to be understood as concerning myself. Blessed, however, is he who understands the needy and poor man in the psalms and in the other Scriptures.” For the Lord himself says: “Everything written concerning me in the Law, the Prophets, and the Psalms must be fulfilled” (Luke 24:44). At least the Jews ought to have noticed that the psalms are entitled “to the End.” [Note: [Col. 0839D] This entire psalm is a prophecy concerning Christ’s Passion, as the testimonies reported by the Evangelists show. Hence Ambrose said: “Open your ears, you who begin to know the mysteries of the Lord’s Passion. Therefore it is said to you: ‘He who has ears to hear, let him hear.’”] For if the Prophet had wished it to be understood of himself, he would by no means have said “to the End.” He calls our Savior needy and poor, who [Col. 0840B] became poor in order to make his faithful rich. Indeed, he wished his disciples to be poor after his own example; to them he said: “Whoever does not leave all that he possesses cannot be my disciple” (Luke 12:44). Therefore, “having left everything, they followed him” (Matthew 4:24). It follows: “The Lord will deliver him in the evil day.” The day of judgment is called an evil day, because on it the wicked are to be punished. On that day those will be secure who have received Christ’s faith, believed the prophets and apostles, and understood the holy Scriptures as concerning Christ. [Note: [Col. 0840D] The same manuscript: “concerning Christ.”] Of him it is further said:

“May the Lord preserve him, give him life, make him blessed, cleanse his soul upon the earth, and not hand him over into the power of his enemy.” [Col. 0840C] Seeing through the Holy Spirit that our Savior was approaching his Passion and that the Jews were gathering against him from every side, the Prophet offers for him this prayer which we now hear: “May the Lord,” he says, “preserve him” from every danger and the snares of his enemies, “and give him life” on the third day. He would not have said this unless he had foreseen that he would die; for nothing is restored to life unless it first dies. “And make him blessed,” by placing him upon his throne at the right hand, as the Apostle says: “Being the radiance of his glory and the exact representation of his substance, he sits at the right hand of Majesty on high” (Hebrews 1:3).—“And cleanse his soul upon the earth.” This is not found in another translation. But [Col. 0840D] from what could Christ’s soul be cleansed, unless perhaps from the Jews’ false suspicion, since they called him a deceiver? “And do not hand him over into the power of his enemy.” This enemy is understood to be the devil, of whom the Lord himself says: “For the prince of this world is coming, and he has nothing in me” (Matthew 14:30). Had the Lord been handed over into his power, he could never have bound him.

“May the Lord bring him help upon his bed of pain; you have turned all his couch in his weakness.” [Col. 0841A] This bed and couch of our Savior signify his flesh, in which, as upon a most noble bed, his most holy soul rested together with his divinity. He now calls it a bed of pain because he suffered for us and endured all those sufferings in his flesh alone. By saying that his whole couch was turned in weakness, he shows that his entire body, from the sole of the foot to the crown of the head, was afflicted and distressed. Hence the Passion of the Cross is shown to have been the harshest among sufferings.

“I said: Lord, have mercy on me; heal my soul, for I have sinned against you.” “To you,” he says, “thus afflicted, thus condemned to a most shameful death, I said—and I say—‘Lord, have mercy on me; heal my soul,’ which could be healed by no other remedy than this Passion which you are now [Col. 0841B] suffering. Heal it, I say, ‘for I have sinned against you’; for this is what he says elsewhere: ‘Against you alone have I sinned’ (Psalm 50:6).” This was the sin he committed concerning Uriah and Bathsheba, for which he plainly wrote that psalm whose beginning is [Note: [Col. 0841D] Codex Ghis.: “when he published that psalm whose beginning is ‘Have mercy on me.’”]: “Have mercy on me, O God” (ibid., 1). Thus here also he says: “I said: Lord, have mercy on me.” “I,” he says, “said it, and said it then: ‘Lord, have mercy on me.’” Thus far speaks the Prophet; now the Lord speaks. “My enemies spoke evil of me: ‘When will he die and his name perish?’” The same is said in another psalm, where the person of our Savior is introduced: “My friends and my neighbors came near against me” (Psalm 37:12). Those who are called enemies here are called friends there, but in the contrary sense. “My enemies,” he says, “spoke evil of me,” consulting together on how to kill me. For it is written: “The chief priests and Pharisees gathered a council, to seize Jesus by deceit and kill him” (John 11:47). Hence one of them, named Caiaphas, said: “You know nothing, nor do you consider that it is expedient for you that one man die for the people, and that the whole nation not perish” (ibid., 50). This is what is said here: “When will he die and his name perish?”—“From that day,” says the Evangelist, “they planned to kill him” (ibid., 53). For their planning to kill him was their saying: “When will he die and his name perish?”

[Col. 0841D] “And they entered in to see; their heart spoke vanity; they gathered iniquity to themselves.” Our Savior describes how his betrayal was carried out. There is no doubt that it occurred in the order here narrated. “They entered,” he says, some of them to see what the chief priests and other leaders had arranged and decided, by what death [Col. 0842A] they wished to kill him, and what did they find? “Their heart spoke vanity”—vanity indeed, because they planned both to kill him and utterly blot out his name. Hence “they gathered iniquity to themselves,” because their iniquity was turned back upon their own heads. “And they went out and spoke.” Thus instructed, and having learned the entire wicked plan, they went outside and spoke with the others who were partners in the same betrayal and iniquity about what they had learned within. And what were those others doing? “Together they whispered as one.” Here he makes sufficiently clear how unanimous they all were in the killing of the Savior. Hence it follows: “All my enemies thought evil against me.” No one opposed it; it pleased them all; all had one will: that the salvation of the world should be killed. Thus, in this order, our Savior was seized, bound, scourged, judged, condemned, crowned with thorns, and led to the gibbet of the Cross. “They decreed an iniquitous word against me.” That iniquitous word was the cry “Crucify!” which all shouted with one harmonious voice.

“But will not he who sleeps add that he may rise again?” For this is what he says elsewhere [Note: [Col. 0841D] “The flesh received an addition, as though taken from man and assumed from the Virgin; but, as God, he himself effected that addition, who rose by his own power, so that he might be the agent of his own resurrection.” AMBROSE.]: “I slept and took my rest, and I rose again” (Psalm 3:6). Christ’s death was sleep: he slept as long as he wished; he rose when he wished. Had he not wished, he would never have fallen asleep. [Note: [Col. 0841D] St Augustine also admirably illuminates this passage: [Col. 0842D] “Why,” he says, “did he sleep? Because Adam was a figure of the one to come; and Adam slept when Eve was made from his side. Adam was a figure of Christ, Eve a figure of the Church; hence she was called the mother of the living. When was Eve fashioned? While Adam slept. When did the sacraments of the Church flow from Christ’s side?
