When he slept on the Cross.”] “For the man of my peace, in whom I trusted, who ate my bread, has greatly increased treachery against me.” Woe to you, Judas, against whom these words are spoken: you who betrayed the Lord and Master [Col. 0842C] of peace with a kiss; who had previously had good hope of you and loved you like the others; who nourished you with his bread, both spiritual and bodily; and through you also baptized and worked miracles. Wretched man, you greatly increased treachery against him; of your own accord you offered yourself for the betrayal; you said: “What will you give me, and I will hand him over to you?” (Matthew 26:15), though no one urged you to betray him but the devil and your avarice.

“But you, Lord, have mercy on me, raise me up, and I shall repay them.” This prayer of Christ’s humanity was inward, in his heart, in his will alone; he needed no words for prayer, since he possessed all things according to his own will. [Col. 0842D] These things, then, were written for our sake; had they not been written, they would not have come to our knowledge. It was very necessary that these things, and many others like them, should be foretold by the prophets, so that, when they had occurred and been fulfilled, they might be believed more readily, and so that Jews and heretics might thereby be refuted. Let the Jews believe, even from this, in Christ’s resurrection: they see that they have already received their recompense.

“By this I knew that you willed me, because my enemy shall not rejoice over me.” What does “by this I knew” mean, except: “By this I made those who are to read and hear these things know”? It is like what was said to Abraham: “Now I know that you fear God” (Genesis 22:12). This enemy is understood as either the devil or the Jewish people, who could not rejoice in Christ’s death, because both lost the strength and power they possessed.

“Because of my innocence you received me and established me before you forever.” Great is the power of innocence, which the Lord himself so highly commends that he shows that his own [Col. 0843B] humanity pleased God through innocence. For that humanity was made such that the stain of sin could have no place in it. If it had not been such, why would it have pleased God above all others? By these words, then, the Lord also calls us to innocence, and by those other words in which he says to the disciples in the Gospel: “Unless you are converted and become as little children, you shall not enter the kingdom of heaven” (Matthew 18:3).

“Blessed be the Lord God of Israel, from age unto age. Let it be, let it be.” It was fitting that our Savior should bless God because of the resurrection of his humanity, his reception into heaven, and his establishment at the Father’s right hand. Israel, moreover, is interpreted “a man seeing.” [Note: [Col. 0843D] “Israel” means “a man seeing” according to the Hebrews and according to the literal sense, as St Jerome testifies in his commentary on Isaiah 44; he himself, in his commentary on Malachi 2, prefers the interpretation “upright of God” to that according to which, in the view of some, Israel means “a man seeing God.” Moreover, others interpret it as “ruling over,” or “prevailing over, God”—that is, the angel wrestling with the patriarch Jacob. This interpretation cannot easily be rejected, since it rests upon divine Scripture (Genesis 32:28).] It signifies not the Jews [Col. 0843C] but Christians, because the former have been blinded, while the latter have been enlightened to see and know. Hence the Lord says: “For judgment I came into this world, that those who do not see may see, and those who see may become blind” (John 9:39).

## Psalm XLI. To the End. An Instruction for the Sons of Korah.

[Note: [Col. 0844D] St Augustine discusses admirably the exposition of this title, with which St Bruno agrees, though he is much briefer than the holy Doctor.]

Korah is interpreted “Calvary.” Our Lord was crucified at the place of Calvary, and there he begot and redeemed the Church for himself. Therefore the understanding of this psalm is attributed to the sons of Korah [Note: [Col. 0844D] Namely, the Levitical singers descended from Korah, mentioned repeatedly in the First Book of Chronicles and elsewhere.], that is, to the Christian people, who say in this psalm: “For I shall enter into the place of the wondrous tabernacle, even to the house of God.”

[Col. 0843D] “As the deer longs for springs of waters, so my soul longs for you, O God.” Deer long for springs of waters, though not always. When, according to their custom, they devour serpents and suffer the excessive burning of the poison thickening within them, then they desire to come to springs of waters so that, by the refreshment of water, [Col. 0844A] they may extinguish thirst and heat. Every vice and sin is the soul’s poison. We cannot be free from these unless we approach God, flee to him, and drink his waters, of which the Lord says: “He who drinks from the water that I shall give him shall never thirst” (John 9:14).

“My soul thirsted for the living God.” He suffered this thirst who said: “I desire to be dissolved and to be with Christ” (Philippians 1:23). So also Isaiah said: “Would that you might rend the heavens and come down” (Isaiah 64:1). Many others suffered it, to whom this life was a burden and who longed with all their strength for that other life. “My soul thirsted for the living God”; and while thirsting it said: “When shall I come and appear before the face of God?” The Lord is rightly called the living God, [Col. 0844B] because all life is in him, all things live in him, and nothing can live without him.

“My tears became my bread day and night, while it is said to me daily: ‘Where is your God?’” The pagans were accustomed to say in mockery to Christians: “Where is your God? Let him now arise, if he can, and help you; and if he is God, let him deliver you from our hands.” Thus Nebuchadnezzar said to those three youths: “And who is the God who will deliver you from my hands?” (Daniel 3:15). They most wisely answered him: “God is able, if he wills, to deliver us from your hands; but if he does not will it, know [Note: [Col. 0844D] The Vulgate reads: “let it be known to you, O king.”] that we do not worship your gods, nor adore the golden statue that you have set up” (ibid., 18). But what did the saints do when such things were said to them? They wept and [Col. 0844C] prayed, feeding upon their own tears. Such refreshment is not known to everyone; it belongs to the perfect, to whom the contemplation of God alone is pleasing.

“I remembered these things and poured out my soul within me.” “When such things were said to me by unbelievers,” he says, “I remembered: ‘For I shall enter into the place of the wondrous tabernacle and arrive at the house of God’; and then I shall see my God, my Savior, of whom these people now say to me: ‘Where is your God?’” For when they attain that blessedness, the saints will see Christ’s humanity with bodily eyes and his divinity with spiritual eyes, so that each form of sight may be useful and neither remain idle. Hence the Apostle John says concerning the Lord: “We know that, when he appears, we shall be like him, because we shall see him as he is” (John 3:2). “These things,” he says, “I remembered, and I poured out my soul within me”; that is, I restrained it as though fleeing, and recalled it to the strength of its former vigor.

[Col. 0845A] “With the voice of rejoicing and confession: the sound of one feasting.” “I shall enter,” he says, “into the place of the wondrous tabernacle. But how shall I enter? ‘With the voice of rejoicing and confession.’” The Prophet teaches us with how great a joy and gladness the souls of saints are received into that blessedness. Hence it follows: “the sound of one feasting.” That voice of rejoicing and confession, he says, will be like the sound of one who feasts, lacks nothing, applauds and rejoices, and is refreshed by ineffable delights. He could find no more fitting comparison to show the sweetness and delight of that reception.

“Why are you sad, my soul, and why do you trouble me? Hope in God, for I shall confess him.” In exhorting and consoling himself, he gives his hearers a great example of how they ought to conduct themselves when wearied by grave reproaches and injuries from the wicked. “Why are you sad, my soul? Endure patiently and do not be troubled, because all these things will quickly pass. Rather, hope in God, who never forsakes those who hope in him. Let adversaries rage as much as they wish, threaten and inflict death and whatever punishments they wish: for I shall confess him and shall never deny my God through fear of death.” They say: “Where is your God?” I say that he is present and will immediately receive my departing soul [Note: [Col. 0845D] Codex Ghis.: “from the body.”] to himself. But now he turns to the Lord himself and speaks to him, confessing the disturbances which he suffers within himself: “O [you who are] the salvation of my countenance and my God: [Col. 0845C] my soul is troubled within me; therefore, that you may console it, I shall remember you, Lord, from the land of the Jordan and Hermon, from the little mountain.” He calls him the salvation of his countenance because no one can preserve the countenance and image of God, according to which we were made, unless he himself guards and saves it. Hence he confesses that his own soul, in which God’s likeness and image are especially expressed, is troubled and deformed from its beauty. For a person loses God’s countenance and image when separated from God by some sin, and receives the countenance and image of the one to whom he joins himself by sinning. It is therefore as though he said: “Preserve in me, Lord, your image, which my enemies and yours seek to take away.” [Col. 0845D] He himself explains what the land of the Jordan and Hermon signifies when he says: “from the little mountain.” The land of the Jordan is a plain, and Hermon also, as is said here, is a small mountain. Therefore, by the land of the Jordan and Hermon we understand the humble and meek. The one who speaks here is seated in such a land and on such a mountain, promising to serve God in humility and meekness. God loves such people, of whom it is written that he casts down the mighty from their thrones and exalts the humble (Luke 1:52).

“Deep calls to deep in the sound of your cataracts; [Col. 0846A] all your heights and your waves have passed over me.” The Church speaks in the person of the martyrs, as though saying: “All the heights of your wisdom and knowledge have passed over me, because deep calls to deep in the sound of your cataracts.” This, then, is why it cannot be separated from God’s love either by tortures or by death itself: the teaching of both Testaments, proclaimed to it through the Apostles, strengthens and confirms it. It calls each Testament a “deep” because of the depth of wisdom and knowledge. God’s cataracts, or windows, are the Apostles, by whom the entire house and whole Church is enlightened. Thus, in the sound of God’s cataracts, deep calls to deep, because by the voice and preaching of the Apostles [Col. 0846B] the two Testaments correspond with and agree with one another.

“By day the Lord commanded his mercy, and by night he will make it manifest.” [Note: [Col. 0845D] Thus the Vatican manuscript, as Cardinal Thomassius noted, and likewise St Augustine. The Vulgate has: “And by night his song.”] What happens by day is not hidden, nor what is made manifest in the night without light. Therefore the Lord commanded his mercy by day because he revealed it to all nations, when “he did not spare his own Son, but handed him over for us all” (Romans 8:32). He also made the same mercy plain and manifest by night, and daily makes it plain and manifest, when he frees and rescues his faithful from great dangers and tribulations. Mindful of so great a benefit, therefore, the holy man says to his soul: “Hope in God, for I shall confess him.”

[Col. 0846C] “Within me is a prayer [Note: [Col. 0846D] The same manuscript reads “to God,” and so do other manuscripts preferring the Psalter according to the Old Latin, together with the Vulgate translation.] of my life; I shall say to God: ‘You are my protector.’” “With me,” he says, “and in my heart is the prayer that I wish to speak to the God of my life.” The God of my life is he who gave us life and preserves the life given; who breathed into the face of the first human being and gave him the breath of life. But what is that prayer? It follows: “I shall say to God: You are my protector. Why have you forgotten me, and why have you cast me away, and why do I go in sadness while my enemy afflicts me? While my bones are being broken, those who trouble me reproach me, while it is said to me every day: ‘Where is your God?’” Thus far extends the prayer which he promised that he had within himself and would speak to God. At the beginning of this prayer [Col. 0846D] he seeks goodwill and says that God is his protector. God is rightly called our protector: he receives us at birth; receives us when we come to the Church and to faith; receives us when we return to him through repentance; receives us when we depart from this life; and finally receives us when we return to the promised homeland. “Why have you forgotten me, and why have you cast me away?” He seems to say things contrary to what he has just said. For if God has received him, how has he forgotten him, or how cast him away? Let us hear the Church herself: “And why,” she says, “if you have not cast me away, do I go in sadness while my enemy afflicts me?” “If,” she says, “you had not cast me away, I would have rejoiced in my afflictions and endured all things patiently.” We read of many saints who rejoiced amid their very torments and desired greater sufferings to be inflicted upon them. Mother Church, therefore, grieves for those who have not deserved to reach such great perfection. The same prayer continues: “And why do I go in sadness while all my bones are being broken?” She does not grieve because her bones are broken, but rather because she was sad while they were being broken. By this breaking of the bones—which is surely a most grievous affliction—we should understand all the other sufferings of the saints. Although the saints endured them with pain, nevertheless they rejoiced that they endured them for Christ’s name. It continues still further: “And why do I go in sadness because those who afflict me reproached me, [Col. 0847B] while they say to me every day: ‘Where is your God?’” He teaches us not to keep injuries inflicted upon us in our heart, but to rejoice that we have endured whatever we endured for faith in Christ. Hence it follows:

“Why are you sad, my soul, and why do you trouble me?” “Let all sadness cease,” he says; “let us bear all things with joy, because ‘the sufferings of this present life are not worthy to be compared with the future glory that shall be revealed in us’” (Romans 8:18).—“Hope in God, for I shall confess him: the salvation of my countenance and my God.” “Hope in God,” he says to himself and to his soul; and though we should grieve because we have performed the things we did less perfectly, nonetheless let us have good hope in this: that we shall always confess him, and “neither [Col. 0847C] death nor life shall be able to separate us from the love of God which is in Christ Jesus” (ibid., 39), who is the salvation of our countenance and our God.

## Psalm XLII. To the End. A Psalm of David.

We have already often explained what “to the End” and “a psalm of David” signify.

“Judge me, O God, and distinguish my cause.” This is the voice of a believer imploring God’s help. “Judge me, O God,” he says; and he explains this by adding, “and distinguish my cause.” He seems to seek no other judgment here than that his case might be distinguished from that of his adversaries. For he knows that he has done nothing against them to deserve such affliction. Thus, because he trusts that he has justice on his side, he prays that his cause may be distinguished. We see this happening very often even now: men who are Catholic suffer such great injuries from people thought to be Christians that they implore God’s help against them; though they ought to pray for such people, they are compelled to pray against them. For the Lord himself says: “Pray for those who persecute and slander you” (Matthew 3:44). It follows: “Deliver me from an unholy nation, from an unjust and deceitful man.” This person seems to pray not against others but only for himself; he shows that this alone is enough for him—that he himself alone be delivered—even if vengeance is not taken upon them. “For you are my God and my strength.” “You,” he says, “deliver me, you who alone [Col. 0848A] are my God and my strength; for I have no other weapons and no other helper. Therefore, if you leave me, there will be no one to assist me. But why have you cast me away?” As though he had said, “I have not cast you away,” he adds: “Why, then, do I go in sadness while my enemy afflicts me?” For in this the saints fear that they have been cast away and have lost God’s grace: that they did not possess complete patience in their injuries and, saddened, wished to avenge themselves. Hence it follows:

“Send forth your light and your truth; they have guided me and brought me to your holy mountain and to your tabernacles.” So that something of this sort may not happen again, as though he said, and so that I may not desire to avenge myself on my enemies or go sadly because of the injuries [Col. 0848B] done to me, send forth your light [Note: [Col. 0847D] Codex Ghis.: “and your truth.”] to me. Because he did not have the patience he ought to have had, he fears that he has lost light and truth. Light and truth are so joined to one another that neither can exist without the other. For one who sees does not err, while one who errs does not see. “Send me your light and your truth,” he says, “and thus enlighten the eyes of my mind and confirm my whole self in your truth, that I may be unable to do anything displeasing to you. They have guided me and brought me to your holy mountain and to your tabernacles.” What should we understand by God’s holy mountain and God’s tabernacles except God’s Church: one, indeed, by faith, but many according to diversity of places? Into this one Church, or into all these churches, we have been brought by light and truth; and those who have not yet entered the holy Church are still in darkness and error and have not yet come to light and truth.

“I shall enter unto God’s altar, unto God who makes my youth glad.” “By this light and truth by which I was brought into the Church, and with it guiding and leading me, I shall enter unto God’s altar, unto God who makes my youth glad.” This altar is in heaven; this altar is our Savior’s humanity. For *altare* (“altar”) is derived from *altitudo* (“height”); Christ’s humanity is loftier and higher than every creature, and therefore is rightly called an altar. He rightly says: “unto God who makes my youth glad,” because all human beings are to rise again at this age. Hence the Apostle says: “We shall all meet God in a perfect man, in the measure of the age of Christ’s fullness” (Ephesians 4:13). For it was at this age that Christ the Lord rose from the dead.

“I shall confess you upon the harp, O God, my God.” Meanwhile, he says, and before I arrive at that altar, I shall confess you and praise you in this your Church and on your holy mountain. How? Upon the harp and in sweet melody: in evangelical preaching, by which both the frenzied are calmed and demons are put to flight. For the harp calmed Saul’s mind from frenzies. Then he turns to himself and to his own ear and sharply reproves his soul because, at some adversity in this world, [Col. 0849A] it became sad, afflicted, and troubled. This is what he says: “Why are you sad, my soul, and why do you trouble me?” One who awaits such great goods in heaven has no reason to be sad. “Hope in God, for I shall confess him,” who is “the salvation of my countenance and my God.”

## Psalm XLIII. To the End. For the Sons of Korah, for Understanding.

Korah, as we have already said, is interpreted “Calvary.” Calvary is a small hill outside the gates of Jerusalem, where the Jews crucified Jesus. Other Jews, indeed, are called sons of Zion and sons of Jerusalem; but these chose to be called sons of Calvary, and the hill of Calvary seemed to them of greater honor and dignity [Col. 0849B] than all the height and strength of Mount Zion and Jerusalem. It is rightly said “for understanding,” because, as regards practical use, it is of no great consequence for someone to be called a son of that hill.

“O God, we have heard with our ears, and our fathers have told us the work which you performed in their days, in days of old.” In this psalm the sons of Korah speak, by whom we understand the holy martyrs. They tell us not their own deeds but what they heard from their fathers, and what the Lord did in ancient days. [Note: [Col. 0849D] Cassiodorus likewise applies this entire psalm to the holy martyrs who endured glorious struggles for Christ’s faith.] Moses relates in his books how the Lord scourged Pharaoh and Egypt; how he freed the Hebrews from Pharaoh’s impious slavery; how he opened the Red Sea for them and made them pass through its midst on dry feet; how for forty years he fed them manna in the wilderness; and how on Mount Sinai he gave them the Law and commanded the tabernacle of testimony to be made. Then Joshua and those after him recount marvelous and astonishing acts which the Lord performed for that people. “O God,” say the sons of Korah, “we have heard with our ears” what “our fathers have told us.” What did they tell us? “The work which you performed in their days, in days of old.” And what was it?

“Your hand destroyed the nations, and you planted them; you afflicted peoples and drove them out.” For the Hivites, Jebusites, Hittites, Girgashites, and other nations described as very strong possessed that land [Col. 0849D] when the children of Israel entered it at the Lord’s command. But because the Lord’s hand fought for the Israelites against them, they could not resist; all were scattered and destroyed. These nations are vices and evil spirits, whom we cannot overcome by our own strength without God’s help. Yet we must overcome them if we wish to keep and possess our land and flesh in peace. Therefore we must always fight, and never make peace with them until they are conquered and expelled.

“For they did not possess the land by their own sword, and their arm did not save them.” “Your hand,” he says, [Col. 0850A] “and your strength destroyed the nations, and you planted and caused our fathers to dwell in the inheritance promised them. You afflicted peoples and drove out those who had previously possessed it.” You certainly did this, because they could not have done it; for they did not possess the land by their own sword, and their arm and strength did not save them. Who, then, did?

“But your right hand, your arm, and the illumination of your countenance, because you were pleased with them.” Concerning this right hand it is written: “The right hand of the Lord has wrought might” (Psalm 117:16). Of this arm it is said: “And to whom has the arm of the Lord been revealed?” (John 12:38). Concerning this illumination of the Father, the Apostle says: “Being the radiance of his glory and the exact representation of his substance” (Hebrews 1:12). [Col. 0850B] Therefore Christ our Lord saved them and delivered them from their enemies. Had they continued to worship and believe in him, they would have lost neither land nor nation. What does “because you were pleased with them” mean except that they pleased you?

“You are yourself my king and my God, who commands salvation for Jacob.” “You,” he says, “who saved them, delivered them from enemies, and subjected all their enemies to them—you yourself are my king and my God, who commands salvation for Jacob,” by whom we understand the Christian people, who, in repenting of their sins, daily overthrow evil spirits; for Jacob is interpreted “supplanter.”

“In you we shall winnow our enemies with a horn, [Note: [Col. 0850D] The word *horn* is indeed read in the Vulgate version, but is absent from the Old Latin manuscripts.] [Col. 0850C] and in your name we shall despise those rising up against us.” Since, he says, we have you as helper, whose strength no one can resist, we are secure: for in you and in your strength we shall winnow our enemies and, as by a great whirlwind, drive and put them to flight; in your name, which we shall invoke, we shall despise all those rising against us. “For everyone who calls upon the name of the Lord shall be saved” (Acts 2:21).

“For I shall not hope in my bow, and my sword shall not save me.” “You,” he says, “are all my hope and all my strength. I trust neither in bow nor sword, because neither bow nor sword can save me without your help.” By bow and sword we understand every kind of human strength and defense.

[Col. 0850D] “For you delivered us from those who afflicted us, and put to shame those who hated us.” “We,” he says, “have already experienced your help; we have no doubt about your power, because you have often already ‘delivered us from those who afflicted us, and put to shame those who hated us,’ so that, with you helping us, they could not resist us.”

“In God we shall boast all day long, and in your name we shall give praise for ever.” Our praise, he says, is God’s, not our own; for it is God who accomplishes our victories and our triumphs over enemies, fighting and conquering through us and within us. And in your name, by which we are called and are Christians [Col. 0851A], we shall confess and praise you throughout all ages.  
[Note: [Col. 0851D] Codex Ghisleri: “Moreover, *confitebimur* is used passively here, a usage indeed found only rarely.”]

What praise or glory could be as great for us as to be called and to be Christians? Thus far those children of the Church have spoken who lived in prosperity; and they gave thanks to God because, like the ancient fathers, they had always been protected by God and feared no snares of their enemies. Now, however, the holy martyrs speak, especially those who endured greater torments and severer sufferings, such as we read occurred in the time of Decius, Diocletian, and Maximian.

“But now you have rejected and put us to shame, and, O God, you do not go forth with our forces.” This answers what was said above: “For you delivered us from those afflicting us, and put to shame those who hated us.” [Col. 0851B] But now “you have rejected and put us to shame.” The Church is one; according to the differing times, she now speaks on behalf of those who were prosperous, and now on behalf of those who were in adversity. “Now,” she says, “in this time of such great persecution, you have rejected and put us to shame.” God never rejects his saints and never puts them to shame. He merely appears to reject and put them to shame when he does not hear them as they pray and does not assist them in great afflictions. But lest anyone suppose that these things happen through impotence, let him read what precedes, and he will be able to recognize God’s omnipotence. Perhaps those earlier words were placed first so that no one who hears these things might be troubled.

But when it says, “And you will not go forth, O God, with our forces,” it must be read not affirmatively but as a question. [Col. 0851C] God goes forth with the forces of his saints when he helps them and makes them conquer their enemies. For they conquer if, even by dying, they do not yield to their enemies’ wishes.

“You turned us back before our enemies, and those who hated us plundered for themselves.” In another translation this is read thus: “You turned us back before our enemies, and those who hate us plundered for themselves.” This is easy enough to understand: “You turned us back before our enemies”—that is, further back than our enemies—showing that they themselves fled while their enemies held the field. Let us understand these enemies as evil spirits, because of what follows: “And those who [Col. 0851D] hated us plundered for themselves.” These, however, are the Jews, heretics, and pagans. It is therefore as though he said: When our enemies, the evil spirits, could not hold us and utterly subjugate us to themselves, they began to plunder for themselves those who hated us—namely Jews, heretics, and pagans—so that, since they could not possess us, they might at least not lose those others.

“You gave us like sheep for food, and scattered us among the nations.” The martyrs were once like sheep for food, destined only for death; for they were not kept in prison in order to be released, [Col. 0852A] but in order to be punished by a greater and more exquisite penalty. They were scattered among the nations because they were sent far from their homeland into exile.

“You sold your people without a price, and there was no abundance in exchange for them.” “You sold” is said improperly, since buying and selling cannot occur without a price. Thus “you sold” means the same as “you handed over.” The saints were often given up without a price, and there was no great price in exchange for them.  
[Note: [Col. 0851D] “But God seems to sell without a price when he hands over the Christian people to foreigners to be afflicted. [Col. 0852D] This often happens by a hidden judgment, either for the merit of testing or for the effect of correction.” CASSIODORUS.]

At other times, however, they were not given without a price, because many, seeing their constancy and the miracles performed through them, were converted to faith in Christ.

“You made us a reproach to our neighbors, an object of derision and contempt to those who are around us.” [Col. 0852B] No one who has heard the passions and lives of the saints can doubt that this occurred, as it is said.

“You made us a byword among the nations, a shaking of the head among the peoples.” At one time, anyone wishing to curse his enemy would take an example from Christians and say: “May I see you as I saw this or that Christian!” They were also a shaking of the head among the peoples, because, when they were dragged to punishments naked, chained, and surrounded on every side by blows, whoever saw them shook their heads over them and said that they were vain and foolish. We read the same thing of the Jews: shaking their heads over our Savior and mocking him, they said, “Ha! You who destroy the temple of God” (Matt. XXVII, 40).

“All day long my shame is before me, and confusion of face has covered me.” Whence? “From the voice of one reproaching and reviling, from the face of the enemy and persecutor.” [Col. 0852C] These matters are plain and need no exposition; each person can readily consider another’s shame in himself.

“All these things came upon us, yet we have not forgotten you, nor have we acted unjustly in your covenant; and our heart has not turned back.” This manner of speech seems not to be boasting but rather thanksgiving. Although, he says, all the things mentioned above came upon us, nevertheless we have not forgotten you; rather, we have forgotten ourselves for your sake. “Nor have we acted unjustly in your covenant,” because we have faithfully kept all your commandments. “And our heart has not turned back”; rather, we have always stretched forward toward what lies before us, hastening toward the promised prize.

“And you turned our paths aside from your way.” This is as though he said: Because our paths had previously not been good, you separated them from your way and taught us to walk only in your way. Therefore we cannot go astray, because we have walked and do walk not on our own paths but on your way. [Col. 0853A] “For you humbled us in a place of affliction, and the shadow of death covered us.”

“If we have forgotten the name of our God, and if we have stretched out our hands to a foreign god, will not God inquire into these things?” We have not, he says, forgotten the name of our God, nor stretched out our hands to a foreign god, knowing that God himself investigates such matters. Nor would it benefit us that we were humbled in a place of affliction and covered by the shadow of death; “For no one who puts his hand to the plough and looks back is fit for the kingdom of God” (Luke IX, 62). By “the shadow of death” may be understood both impious people and the torments themselves. For just as we know a body is present from its shadow, so, where these things are present, we understand death to be present.

It follows: “For he knows the hidden things [Col. 0853B] of the heart.” Therefore, he says, he will inquire into these things, because nothing is hidden from him and he sees all things: whatever is in the heart, whatever is anywhere, cannot be concealed from his eyes.

“For for your sake we are afflicted with death all day long; we are accounted as sheep for slaughter.”  
[Note: [Col. 0853D] Saint Paul used this passage of the Psalm at Romans VII, 36, to express the greatness of the tribulations in which he found himself for Christ’s sake.]

The person who is afflicted with death is not yet dead; being affected by death is suffering itself, and one is so afflicted as long as one is harassed by torments. Sheep for slaughter are those kept for no purpose except death. Likewise, the saints were held in prison for a long time, not for release but rather for destruction.

“Arise, why do you sleep, O Lord? Arise, and do not reject us utterly. For he who guards Israel shall neither slumber nor sleep.” God [Col. 0853C] is said to sleep when, as if not perceiving it, he permits his saints to be afflicted. That person is rejected utterly who is wholly separated from God.

“Why do you turn away your face?” He who turns away his face does not wish to see the one from whom he turns it. Thus for the Lord to turn away his face is not to see his faithful ones in their afflictions. Hence follows: “Do you forget our poverty and our tribulation?” Neither sleep nor forgetfulness nor anger nor indignation, nor anything of that kind, can exist in God; yet they are said to exist in him, and why they are so said we have often already explained.

“For our soul has been humbled into the dust; our belly clings to the earth. Arise, [Col. 0853D] O Lord, help us, and deliver us for your name’s sake.” Arise, he says, O Lord, to help us, and deliver us from these great tribulations for the sake of your name, which we invoke and by which we are called Christians, since “our soul has been humbled into the dust.” For “the corruptible body weighs down the soul, and the earthly dwelling depresses the mind that thinks many things” (Wisdom IX, 16). Or it has been humbled in the dust because it has become worse through association with wicked people. This is that dust [Col. 0854A] which the wind casts from the face of the earth.

The soul is also humbled in the dust when the belly clings to the earth in prayer, and such humility is good. By the belly we may understand those in the Church who are weaker and imperfect, and who cling more to earthly than heavenly things. Prayer must be made for such people, because in a time of persecution they are easily deceived, fearing to lose earthly and passing things. “Arise, therefore, O Lord, to help us, because our soul has been humbled into the dust.”

## PSALM XLIV. TO THE END: FOR THOSE WHO SHALL BE CHANGED. A SONG OF THE SONS OF KORAH FOR UNDERSTANDING, FOR THE BELOVED.

This Psalm, he says, was composed for the sons of Korah, [Col. 0854B] though not for all of them, but only for those who shall be changed unto understanding. In this it plainly shows that even among the sons of Korah there were some changed to spiritual understanding. They sing this song for the beloved, namely for that beloved of whom the Lord said, “This is my beloved Son” (Matt. III, 17), and to whom this Psalm also says: “Fair in beauty above the children of men; grace has been poured out upon your lips; therefore God has blessed you for ever.”

“My heart has uttered a good word; I speak my works to the king.” The Prophet speaks; one of the sons of Korah speaks: “My heart has uttered a good word.” By “good word” he means this person of whom the Psalm speaks; he confesses that he did not sing it with his mouth, but uttered it from the secret chamber [Col. 0854C] of his heart. By this we may understand how firm, stable, and authoritative is all that this Psalm contains. “I speak my works to the king.” This is the king who says elsewhere: “But I have been appointed king by him” (Ps. II, 6). To this king the Prophet speaks his works, which he has just uttered from the hidden place of his heart.

“My tongue is the pen of a scribe writing swiftly.” My tongue, he says, is like a writing pen that writes swiftly; by this he shows that he saw and prophesied many things suddenly and in a very short time.

“Fair in beauty above the children of men; grace has been poured out upon your lips.” Behold, he now begins to speak [Col. 0854D] his works to the king, whom he calls fair in beauty above all the children of men.  
[Note: [Col. 0853D] “Not because his appearance shone with the beauty of milky complexion, flashed with yellow hair, or towered conspicuously in remarkable stature; but he was truly more beautiful than the human race because he had no sins. For that is rightly called beautiful which is adorned by the grace of most pure purity; although Father Augustine says that the appearance of his body was praiseworthy.” CASSIODORUS.]

For who is so fair as he “who committed no sin, nor was deceit found in his mouth?” (1 Pet. II, 22). He alone was born without sin, and in him alone human nature did not lose its form and beauty. Such grace was upon his lips that he could easily and without any hindrance say whatever he wished. Hence the Gospel says that “all marveled at the things proceeding from his mouth” [Col. 0855A] (Luke IV, 22); and elsewhere it says that “all marveled at his teaching” (Matt. XXII, 33). These speaking lips had instructed Moses when he said that his tongue was impeded and slow.

“Therefore God has blessed you for ever.” Therefore, he says, because you are fairer and more eloquent than all, God has blessed you for ever. All people are blessed when they are baptized; nevertheless, many afterward lose their blessings by sinning, and their blessing does not remain for ever.

“Gird your sword upon your thigh, O most mighty one.” You, he says, most mighty one, being such as you are, gird your sword around your thigh and prepare for battle, because you are to undertake many and very harsh conflicts and to triumph over the devil and all his army. [Col. 0855B] We too must always be girded about the thigh with the sword of chastity, by which we may both fight against enemies and overcome the fleshly impulses that rule in the loins and thigh. Hence the Lord says, “Let your loins be girded” (Luke XII, 35).

“Direct your attention, in your splendor and your beauty; proceed prosperously and reign.” Because, he says, you are most beautiful, direct your attention in your splendor and beauty, and refashion your faithful and your Church according to this pattern, so that she too may be beautiful, without spot or wrinkle. Thus the Apostle says: “My little children, with whom I am again in labor until Christ be formed in you” (Gal. IV, 19). For Christ is formed in those who are refashioned according to his beauty. The Lord proceeds prosperously and [Col. 0855C] reigns everywhere, because, as is said elsewhere of him: “Whatever he shall do shall prosper” (Ps. I, 3); and, “His power is an eternal power, which shall not be taken away, and his kingdom shall not be destroyed” (Dan. VII, 14).

“Because of truth and gentleness and justice; and your right hand shall lead you wonderfully.” Proceed, he says, and your right hand—your power and strength—will lead you wonderfully, because you need no other help and no one can resist your strength. He rightly says “wonderfully,” because he converted the world by miracles, conquered by patience, and through simple and unlettered people destroyed all worldly and philosophical wisdom. And this was “because of [Col. 0855D] truth and gentleness and justice.” For it is fitting and altogether appropriate that a king should be truthful, gentle, and just; one who lacks these should be called not a king but a tyrant.

[Col. 0856A] “Your arrows are sharp, O most mighty one; peoples shall fall beneath you in the hearts of the king’s enemies.” Since *populus* (“people”) is a collective noun, one may say “most mighty of a people” just as “most mighty of peoples.” The Lord’s arrows are sharp because, as the Apostle says, “The word of God is living, effectual, and more piercing than any two-edged sword” (Heb. IV, 12). Christ’s arrows, therefore, are all those utterances drawn from the quiver of either Testament to convict enemies.

Thus let it be said: “Your arrows are sharp, O most mighty one; peoples shall fall beneath you.” Where? “In the heart of the king’s enemies.”  
[Note: [Col. 0855D] In the archive of the Vatican basilica there survives a manuscript work of the most distinguished Lucas Holstenius, bearing this title: “Certain Collations of the Roman Psalter used by the most holy Vatican basilica, with two manuscripts of the same basilica and two others, one Florentine and the other Cassinese; likewise with the Greek version of the Seventy, in the Sixtine and Complutensian editions; and also with the Ambrosian and Cajetan Breviaries.” In this work Holstenius, discussing what, according to the Roman Breviary, ought to be recited in the weekday office of Matins at Psalm XLIV, 6, observes as follows: “*In corde* (‘in the heart’) is in our better manuscript, that is, that of the Vatican basilica; but Cajetan has *in corde*, as do the Vulgate and St Bruno. But the Septuagint has ἐν καρδίᾳ, ‘in the heart,’ which Faber also recognizes, as does the Vatican [manuscript], namely the celebrated Vatican Library codex containing the Greek version of the Seventy interpreters and published at Rome in print in 1587.” [Col. 0856D]]

Had he said “in the heart of your enemies,” it would have been clearer. But this manner of expression, as we have already said elsewhere, is frequently found in the Old Testament; whether it occurs in other writings, I do not know. [Col. 0856B] He excellently says, “they shall fall beneath you,” because nothing can fall upon him: since all things are beneath him, he can strike no one except beneath himself. Wherever these arrows fall, they can now fall beneficially, because enemies are driven away by fear of them and the whole army of vices is scattered. But at the judgment, wretched will be all those upon whom they fall, because once wounded they will never afterward be able to be healed. From these considerations we sufficiently understand what those arrows will be which shall shoot the wicked at the judgment.

“Your throne, O God, is for ever and ever; a straight rod is the rod of your kingdom.” He whom he called the beloved in the title, and now called king in this Psalm, he now more plainly and manifestly calls God, so that the Jews, corrupters of the Scriptures, cannot interpret the passage of Solomon or of anyone other than Christ. Christ’s throne is for ever and ever because his kingdom shall have no end. “A straight rod is the rod of your kingdom.”  
[Note: [Col. 0856D] “The Vulgate and Augustine’s text have ‘a rod of direction’; concerning this reading he says: ‘The rod of direction is that which directs people.’”]

Your rod and sceptre of kingship, he says, are straight and do not depart from justice and equity. You strike no one with the rod without cause, and permit no one worthy of scourging to depart unpunished. Hence follows:

“You have loved justice and hated iniquity.” The straightness of that rod of correction is proved by the fact that he loves justice and hates iniquity. “Therefore God, your God, has anointed you with the oil of gladness above your companions.”  
[Note: [Col. 0856D] “‘He anointed me.’ Observe that, speaking to God, he said to him: ‘God, your God, has anointed you’; that is, your Father has anointed you, the Son, with that ointment of eternal gladness, eternal sacrament, heavenly mystery,” etc. ST MAXIMUS OF TURIN, *Treatise against the Jews*, p. 737.]

This is what the Lord himself says through the Prophet: “The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because he has anointed me; he sent me to preach good news to the poor” (Luke IV, 18). The Spirit is given to others by measure (Eph. IV), but in him all [Col. 0857A] the fullness of divinity dwells bodily (Col. II). His companions are the apostles and all others chosen, not by their own merits but by his adoption, to share in the inheritance. This oil is rightly called the oil of gladness, because it grants joy and gladness to all who are anointed, provided they do not lose the anointing. Of this anointing it is written: “And his anointing will teach you concerning all things” (1 John II, 27).

“Myrrh and *gutta* and cassia from his garments.” By these three kinds all the others are understood. Myrrh is indeed the bitterest among them; cassia, which is also called *fistula*, is the sweetest. But *gutta*, called *amomacum*, cures many serious diseases. These and all other remedies for infirmities, therefore, flowed from Christ’s garments, [Col. 0857B] because, as the Gospel reads, all who touched him were healed of whatever infirmity held them (Matt. XIV, 36). Christ’s garment is his humanity itself, the precious clothing in which divinity was clothed and could not be seen by human beings. For we read that even the fringes of his garment healed many sick persons. Those able to approach Christ’s garments had no need to receive medicines, since not merely substances suited to healing, but healing itself, flowed from his garments.

It follows: “From ivory steps.” Likewise, he says, myrrh, *gutta*, and cassia flowed from ivory steps, by which steps we understand those of whom the Lord said: “He who believes in me shall also do the works that I do, and shall do greater than these, because I go to the Father” [Col. 0857C] (John XIV, 2). For we read that the apostles healed many people not only by the touch of garments but by the shadow of their bodies themselves. Hence it is written that “the sick were placed in the streets, so that, when Peter came, at least his shadow might overshadow one of them” (Acts V, 15).

But why are these called ivory, except because they were white, strong, and most chaste? Ivory is the bone of the elephant; elephants are most chaste animals and mate only once. The apostles are rightly called steps, because through them one ascends to the throne of God. Hence follows: “From which the daughters of kings delighted you in your honor.” “From which,” he says—that is, through whom—the daughters of kings ascending delighted you, singing and, implicitly, chanting psalms in [Col. 0857D] your honor. The daughters of kings are the individual Churches wherever they are, whom the holy apostles begot for the Lord. These are the kings of whom it is said: “Kings shall offer gifts to you from your temple in Jerusalem” (Ps. LXVII, 30).

“The queen stood at your right hand in a garment of gold, clothed round with variety.” There are many daughters of kings, but one queen, by whom we understand either the catholic Church or the Blessed Virgin Mary, who is also queen and lady of that Church. She stood at God’s right hand because she is honored by God more than every created thing.  
[Note: [Col. 0857] Codex Vallicellianus: “because she is the one honored by God more than every creature.” Likewise Codex Ghisleri.]

But how does she stand? “In a garment of gold, clothed round with variety.” [Col. 0858A] The first man lost this garment when he sinned—namely the immortality of the flesh. Thus, knowing himself naked, he said: “I heard your voice, Lord, and hid myself, because I was naked” (Gen. III, 10). This garment is called varied because it is interwoven with every virtue. It is also golden because it is wisely composed; for gold signifies wisdom, since wisdom is among the other virtues as gold is among other metals. Every virtue not gilded with the gold of wisdom is foolish. Other people also possess virtues, but only the virtues of Christians are gilded. What does chastity profit the Jew? What does humility profit the pagan? For the one perishes with his chastity and the other perishes with his humility.

[Col. 0858B] “Listen, daughter, and see, and incline your ear.” Although this can suitably be understood of the whole catholic and universal Church, I shall nevertheless expound it particularly of the Blessed Virgin Mary, who, as I have already said, is lady of the whole Church. Thus the Prophet, seeing through the Holy Spirit the archangel Gabriel speaking with her and announcing Christ’s incarnation to her, addresses her and says: “Listen, daughter, and see. Listen, my daughter, of my race, of my offspring, the nobility and glory of my lineage; listen to what the angel says, what the heavenly messenger promises you. Be chaste, be attentive, listen carefully, because what is announced to you is exceedingly great. See, therefore, and understand; incline your ear and receive the word in your heart and womb: a virgin, you shall conceive, [Col. 0858C] and a virgin, you shall give birth. Incline your ear, because he who will be born from you shall enter into you through the ear. For he is the Word, and the ear is the pathway of the Word. The Blessed Mary conceived in no other way than by hearing and believing: had she not heard, she would not have believed; she heard and believed, and by believing conceived.

“And forget your people and your father’s house.” Mary needed to forget that people who killed her Son and hates that same Son deeply and above all things.

“Because the king desired your beauty.” For she was exceedingly beautiful, she who alone of all women was chosen and could draw the Lord himself to love of her. We have already heard above what must be understood by this beauty, and shall still speak of it in what follows. “For he is the Lord your God,” [Col. 0858D] who promises that he will be born to you from you.

“And the daughters of Tyre shall worship him with gifts.” See, he says, how great this son of yours shall be: the daughters of Tyre, most noble among other women, shall worship him with gifts. But because Tyre is interpreted “narrowness,” by the daughters of Tyre we understand souls that recognize themselves to be in this world as in a prison and in narrow confines, and desire with all their longing to pass into the spaciousness of heaven. The gifts offered by saints to God are understood as virtues and good works.

“All the rich of the people shall entreat your face.” Not only, he says, shall the daughters of Tyre worship your Son, [Col. 0859A] but they shall also entreat you and pay vows to you. And even if we understand her face and image, it would not be inappropriate, since we see it venerated by all wherever it is painted.  
[Note: [Col. 0859D] Painted images of the Blessed Virgin Mary ought to be held in veneration, and their cult is very ancient in the Church.]

In another way, all the rich of the people entreat the face and beauty of the Blessed Virgin Mary, because there is no one who does not desire to possess her beauty and holiness. The rich of the people are those souls that abound not in temporal but spiritual riches. “All the glory of the king’s daughter is within.” Do not, he says, attend to outward beauty; consider that which is inward, because all her glory is within. For even if bodily virginity shines outwardly, that which is inward is more commendable along with all the other virtues. [Col. 0859B] But do you wish to hear the Blessed Virgin herself glorying more in humility than in virginity? “My spirit,” she says, “has exulted in God my Savior, because he has looked upon the humility of his handmaid” (Luke I, 48).

“In golden fringes, clothed round with variety.” This variety is not of colors but of virtues, signifying that she possessed in herself an abundance of all virtues. The fringes, which touch the ground, show her splendid, holy, and wisdom-filled manner of life in this world. They are rightly called golden, because gold in divine discourse signifies wisdom, according to the saying: “A desirable treasure rests in the mouth of the wise” (Prov. XXI, 27).

“Virgins shall be brought to the king after her.” She, he says, as queen and lady, will go first and lead the way; all the others [Col. 0859C] will follow her and be brought after her to Christ the Lord, the king. “Her companions shall be brought to you in gladness and exultation.” Those are called her companions who imitate her in mind and spirit and resemble her by living well. All these together with her shall be offered to the Lord in gladness and exultation and brought into the king’s temple.

“In place of your fathers sons were born to you.” Jacob had twelve sons, whom we call patriarchs; from them the whole multitude of the Jews derived its origin. They are called the fathers of our Savior because, according to the flesh, he was born from their stock.  
[Note: [Col. 0859D] The Lord Christ, according to the flesh, is reported in Matthew, chapter I, verse 2, and Luke, chapter III, verse 33, to have descended in direct line from Judah, Jacob’s son. [Col. 0860D]]

Likewise Christ had twelve disciples, from whom the whole ecclesiastical multitude [Col. 0859D] was begotten. Therefore, instead of fathers, the Lord had sons whom, according to the number of the aforementioned fathers, he chose as sons for himself—that is, as holy apostles. Of them it follows: “You shall appoint them princes over all the earth” (Ps. XLIV, 17). These are those of whom the Lord said: “When the Son of Man shall sit on the throne of his majesty, you also shall sit upon twelve thrones, judging the twelve tribes of Israel” (Matt. XIX, 28).

“They shall remember your name, O Lord, in every [Col. 0860A] generation and generation.” For they themselves remember it in their writings; and through all who have believed by their teaching and preaching, they perpetuate the everlasting remembrance of Christ’s name. Hence follows:

“Therefore peoples shall praise you for ever, and unto age upon age.” This, therefore, is what apostolic preaching accomplished: that all peoples might praise the Lord at every time.

## PSALM XLV. TO THE END, FOR THE SONS OF KORAH: FOR THE HIDDEN THINGS. A PSALM.

This Psalm, which the sons of Korah sing, is entitled “for the hidden things” because it contains Christ’s incarnation, which the Jews refused to believe and which remains hidden and concealed from them to this day. For Christ’s incarnation is here expressed in the words: “The Lord of hosts is with us”; for he is Emmanuel, which is interpreted “God with us.”

“Our God is a refuge and strength, a helper in tribulations which found us exceedingly.” This is the voice of the Prophet and of others of the same faith before Christ’s incarnation. “Our God,” they say, “is our refuge, strength, and help in the many tribulations which we have suffered. He never abandoned us, although our enemies were much more numerous and stronger than we.” Why, then, should we fear, fortified by the protection of so great a helper? And this is what follows:

“Therefore we shall not fear, though the earth be troubled and the mountains be moved into the heart of the sea.” Therefore, he says, neither we nor those who will live in that [Col. 0860C] time shall fear when the whole earth is troubled against the Church and all wicked people conspire for the death of the saints. But what does he mean by saying, “and the mountains shall be moved into the heart of the sea”? The mountains are the apostles and doctors; the heart of the sea is the Roman rulers and the other powerful people of this world, whose counsel and will all others followed. Thus the mountains were moved into the heart of the sea when the apostles and doctors were brought before kings and rulers. But what happened afterward?

“Its waters sounded and were troubled.” The waters of the sea sounded and were troubled because all peoples and nations, signified by the waters, were stirred by excessive anger and began to cry out against the saints for their death. [Col. 0860D] But what did the saints do? “The mountains were troubled by his strength.” They were troubled when they were confined in prison, dragged away bound with chains, struck with scourges and scorpions, and burned with fire set beneath them.  
[Note: [Col. 0860D] Codex Ghisleri: “when they were scraped with claws, when they burned upon the rack.”]

But who can enumerate every kind of torment by which the saints of God were afflicted by the impious? Our Savior indicated this disturbance when, at the time of his passion, he said that he was troubled unto death. The drops of blood sweating from his whole body signified these diverse sufferings of the holy martyrs. [Col. 0861A]

“The rush of the river makes glad the city of God.” Outwardly, he says, in body and for a time, the Church is troubled by the affliction of the saints; inwardly, however, she is consoled and made glad by the flooding of the Holy Spirit.  
[Note: [Col. 0861D] “For the city of Christ is made glad when the people within it are purified and carried along by the course of evangelical teaching, and its hall is filled, as it were, by the rush of preaching through the commerce of holiness.” [Col. 0862D] ST MAXIMUS OF TURIN, Sermon 14, Roman edition, p. 434.]

For the Holy Spirit is like a great river, from which seven gifts flow forth as seven streams and irrigate, satisfy, gladden, and make fruitful the whole city of God, which is the Church. “The Most High sanctified his tabernacle.” By the waters of this river, he says, the Most High sanctified, cleansed, and purified his tabernacle, so that, since he himself is holy, his tabernacle also might be holy. [Col. 0861B] For he says: “Be holy, because I, the Lord your God, am holy” (Lev. XI, 44).

“God is in her midst; she shall not be moved.” Secure is the house that has such an inhabitant; because he is never moved or separated from it, it is never utterly overcome by enemies. Of it indeed it was said: “The gates of hell shall not prevail against it” (Matt. XVI, 18). Hence follows:

“God shall help her with his countenance.” What does “he shall help her with his countenance” mean except by the illumination and gladness of his face? Thus it is said elsewhere: “May the Lord cause his face to shine upon us and have mercy on us” (Ps. LXVI, 1). For when the Lord helps us, he is described as having a joyful face; and when he does not [Col. 0861C] help, an angry face.

“**The nations were troubled, and the kingdoms were bowed down; the Most High uttered his voice, and the earth was moved.**” This disturbance is good. Behold, the nations that above were troubled against the saints and against the Church are now said to be troubled against themselves. They begin likewise to abhor what they loved and to love what they hated. “And the kingdoms were bowed down,” because the emperors themselves humbled themselves beneath Christ’s yoke and joyfully received the faith which they had persecuted. This may fittingly be understood of the time of the Emperor Constantine, when all the saints had been released from their chains, the churches were opened, and no one dared to rise up against the Christian faith [Col. 0861D]. And now, while all preach freely, almost the whole world has been converted to the faith. Hence it follows: “The Most High uttered his voice, and the earth was moved.” For the Most High gave his voice through the mouths of bishops and teachers, and the earth was moved from unbelief to faith, from darkness to light, from the devil to God. But what did the earth say in that great movement of its own? It follows:

“**The Lord of hosts is with us; the God of Jacob is our protector.**” This is as though it said: Our gods have been defeated, because they were false, wretched, and powerless [Col. 0862A]. But now “the Lord of hosts is with us”: the Lord strong and mighty, mighty in battle, whom no creature can resist, who so suddenly and wonderfully turned the whole world to himself. “The God of Jacob is our protector,” because, after the Jews were cast out, he received us Gentiles into his inheritance.

“**Come and see the works of the Lord, the wonders which he has wrought upon the earth, removing wars to the ends of the earth.**” The saints rejoice and marvel at so great a peace, granted to them by God so suddenly. “Come,” they say, “and see the works of the Lord.” These are truly and especially works of the Lord, such as no one but he alone could have done; and therefore what has now taken place is called wonders and great miracles. But what are these? “Removing wars to the ends of the earth” [Col. 0862B]. For although, a little before, the Church had nowhere enjoyed peace, suddenly, through God’s mercy, it came to pass that no one dared speak against her even to the ends of the earth. Concerning this peace it further says: “He shall break the bow, shatter the weapons, and burn the shields with fire.” This seems to be said against the Arians, whose impious heresy was condemned at the Council of Nicaea at the same time as its leader. And although all their armour has been dispersed, nevertheless everlasting fire still awaits both their weapons and their warriors.

“**Be still, and see that I am God; I shall be exalted among the nations, and I shall be exalted in the earth.**” “Come,” he says, “and see the works of the Lord; and let us give him thanks, who, peace having been granted, exhorts us, saying: ‘Be still, and see.’” Be still, he says, for reading, prayer, and every spiritual work [Col. 0862C]. And see: know and understand that I am God, whose strength and power you now so greatly admire. “And I shall be exalted,” as though he said, among all nations and throughout all the earth, which until these times seemed to oppose me.

“**The Lord of hosts is with us; the God of Jacob is our protector.**” They repeat what he said above and, rejoicing, affirm that it is altogether true: the Lord of hosts is with us, since, unless he were strong and mighty, he could in no way have done the things stated above.

## 392. Psalm XLVI. For the end; for the sons of Korah. A psalm.

[Col. 0862D]

This psalm was made for the sons of Korah—that is, for the apostles, who glory only in Christ’s Passion and cross. Hence the Apostle says: “Far be it from me to glory except in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ!” (Gal. 6:14). Of them it is said in this psalm: “The princes of the peoples have assembled with the God of Abraham, because the mighty gods of the earth have been exceedingly exalted.”

“**All nations, clap your hands; shout to God with a voice of exultation.**” The ancients had the custom of clapping their hands for joy. Hence the saying: “Clap your hands, Romans; I, Calliopius, have revised [this text].” [Col. 0863A] The Church therefore exhorts all nations to rejoice and exult beyond expression because our Saviour has ascended into heaven. For to clap one’s hands signifies a joy greater than can be expressed in words. And those rightly clap their hands who show by good works the joy that they have in the Lord, since works are done by the hands. Shouting with a voice of exultation is an inexpressible joy, which is sounded more in the heart than in the mouth.

“**For God is most high, terrible, and a great king over all gods; he has subjected peoples to us and nations beneath our feet; he has chosen us as his inheritance, the beauty of Jacob whom he loved.**” He gives a twofold reason why we ought to clap our hands and shout: one concerning ourselves, the other concerning our Saviour [Col. 0863B]. The reason concerning ourselves is this great benefit: he has subjected peoples to us and chosen us as his inheritance. Clap, he says. Why? Because the Lord, who lately appeared poor and humble, is now shown to be most high and terrible, a great king over all gods. He is most high because all things whatsoever are in heaven or on earth are subject to him. He is terrible because he will render to each according to his works. And he is indeed the great king over all gods, “for all the gods of the nations are demons, but the Lord made the heavens” (Ps. 95:5). “He has subjected peoples to us and nations beneath our feet.” For there is no nation or people among whom some saints have not humbled themselves at their feet. And when he says, “He has chosen us as his inheritance,” [Col. 0863C] this is what the Lord says elsewhere: “The lines have fallen to me in pleasant places; indeed, my inheritance is splendid to me” (Ps. 15:6). He calls this same inheritance—that is, the holy Church—the beauty of Jacob, because it is she of whom the Apostle says: “He chose for himself a glorious Church, without spot or wrinkle” (Eph. 5:17). And what follows, “whom he loved,” is what the Lord says elsewhere: “Jacob I loved, but Esau I hated” (Rom. 9:13).

“**God ascended amid shouts of joy, and the Lord with the sound of a trumpet.**” Again, he says, clap your hands—and clap them yet more—because “God ascended amid shouts of joy, and the Lord with the sound of a trumpet.” The Lord ascended amid shouts of joy—that is, amid the greatest joy and gladness of the apostles, who saw him ascend in such glory and power [Col. 0863D]. Or he ascended amid the shouts of the angels, all of whom, we ought not doubt, came to meet him with supreme exultation. Though we do not know what their voices and praises, so surpassingly excellent, were like, we may understand them through the sound of the trumpet. And who could ever say or conceive how great was the joy in heaven when Christ the Lord ascended there? I seem to see all angels and archangels humbly worshipping that most glorious humanity of our Saviour and giving thanks for so great a victory over the most proud enemy, thus overcome. And I think all this is signified by the words here spoken: “Amid shouts of joy and with the sound of a trumpet” [Col. 0864A].

“**Sing praises to our God, sing praises; sing praises to our king, sing praises.**” How full of joy must the heart of this man have been, who so often and so insistently commands us to sing praises. He seems to me to say in these words: Sing praises, sing praises, and sing praises without ceasing, lest the angels surpass you in singing; but do on earth what they do in heaven. And lest anyone, thus admonished and exhorted, might suppose that in excessive joy he ought, as once before, to rise into bodily movements and salutations, he added: “Sing praises wisely.” Why? “For God is king of all the earth.” He to whom you sing is no ordinary king; he is great and mighty, king and lord of all the earth [Col. 0864B]. And would you hear how he proves this?

“**The Lord shall reign over all nations.**” The enemies, he says, have been defeated, and the devil has lost both kingdom and power—not only over the Jews, but also over the Gentiles. Let sin reign no longer in your mortal body, because Christ alone is king and reigns everywhere. And where is he? “God sits upon his holy seat,” as it is written: “The Lord said to my Lord, ‘Sit at my right hand’” (Ps. 109:1). And elsewhere: “The Lord—his seat is in heaven” (Ps. 10:4). But lest we seem far away, hear the Apostle saying: “Do you not know that you are God’s temple and that the Holy Spirit dwells in you?” (1 Cor. 3:16). For the soul of the righteous person is the seat of wisdom; indeed, the Lord did not disdain to sit upon an ass [Col. 0864C].

“**The princes of the peoples have assembled with the 393 God of Abraham, because the mighty gods of the earth have been exceedingly exalted.**” Moses asked the Lord what his name was; and the Lord answered: “I am the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob” (Exod. 3:6). This, therefore, is that God and Lord with whom, on the day of the Ascension, the princes of the people—namely, the holy apostles—assembled. On that very day they received the command to go into the whole world and preach the Gospel to every creature (Mark 16:16). Then indeed so many mighty gods of the earth were appointed by the Lord, just as, when Moses was sent to Pharaoh, the Lord said to him: “Behold, I have made you God to Pharaoh” (Exod. 7:7) [Col. 0864D]. These were mighty gods, and stronger than all others, because they received power not only on earth but also in heaven, to shut and open for whomsoever they wished. Hence the Lord said to blessed Peter: “Whatever you bind on earth shall be bound in heaven; and whatever you loose on earth shall be loosed in heaven” (Matt. 16:19). Therefore it is said here: “They have been exceedingly exalted.” “Exceedingly,” indeed, as regards human opinion. But another translation does not say “exceedingly,” but “very greatly exalted,” which seems a much more fitting expression.

> [Note: [Col. 0863D] St Augustine and the Psalter mentioned above, edited by Giuseppe Bianchini, have “very greatly” [Col. 0864D]; but many copies of the Old Latin version read “exceedingly.”]

## Psalm XLVII. [Col. 0865A] A psalm of a canticle; for the sons of Korah. The second day of the Sabbath.

The sons of Korah are those who do not doubt that at the place of Calvary Christ was crucified, the devil defeated, original sin erased, and the human race redeemed by Christ’s blood. The phrase “the second day of the Sabbath” is to be understood thus. On the first day of the Sabbath the Lord rose and manifested himself to his disciples. On the second, made utterly certain of his resurrection, they began to confer among themselves how they might make his resurrection known and proclaim his glory. But what else is the preaching of the apostles than the building up of the Church? This whole psalm concerns the building of the Church.

“**Great is the Lord and exceedingly worthy of praise in the city of our God, on his holy mountain.**” He is great because he contains all things and is everywhere. He is also exceedingly worthy of praise because he cannot be praised as much as he deserves. But where is he worthy of praise except in his city and on his holy mountain? His city and holy mountain are the Church, signified by Zion and Jerusalem. The Lord does not deign to be praised elsewhere than in his city and on his holy mountain—that is, Mount Zion, concerning which it follows:

“**Mount Zion, extending the rejoicings of the whole earth, the sides of the north, the city of the great king.**”

> [Note: [Col. 0865D] The Vulgate reads: “Mount Zion is founded for the rejoicing of the whole earth,” etc. Augustine’s text reads: “Extending the rejoicings of the whole earth, the mountains of Zion,” etc. Bruno’s reading agrees with Augustine’s through the words “of the whole earth,” but afterward agrees with the Vulgate: “Mount Zion, the sides of the north,” etc. St Augustine explains why “mountains,” rather than “mountain,” is read; we omit that explanation here as unnecessary, especially since our commentator agrees with it. The translation used by Cassiodorus conforms to Bruno’s text throughout.]

Because the Church has been made from Jews and Gentiles, we understand the Jews through Zion and the Gentiles through the sides of the north. Hence the Lord is called [Col. 0865C] the cornerstone, joining two walls: one from the uncircumcision, the other from the circumcision. The whole Church consists of these two walls. Therefore the Lord says in the Gospel: “I have other sheep which are not of this fold; them also I must bring, and there shall be one fold and one shepherd” (John 10:16). By “the sides of the north” are understood all those whom the devil blows upon and tosses about; for there was his seat, as he himself says: “I shall set my seat in the north, and I shall be like the Most High” (Isa. 14:14). Hence it is said elsewhere: “From the north evil shall be opened upon all who dwell in the land” (Jer. 1:14). Holy Church was therefore built from such persons, because the Lord came not to call the righteous but sinners to repentance (Matt. 9:13). And when it says, “extending the rejoicings of the whole earth,” [Col. 0865D] it is as if it said: Mount Zion is the city of the great king, extending the rejoicings of the whole earth. For, as it is written, “the law shall go forth from Zion, and the word of the Lord from Jerusalem” [Col. 0866A] (Isa. 2:3). From there came the apostles; from there came Christ’s faith and teaching; from there came these psalms; from there came every joy and exultation in which the Church rejoices and which has spread throughout the whole world.

“**God shall be known in her steps, when he receives her.**” The Lord, he says, came to this city of his, though not yet his because it had not yet been redeemed by his blood; and he was neither known nor received: “He came to his own, and his own did not receive him” (John 1:11). But when he receives her, he shall be known in her steps. This will be at the judgment, when both good and evil shall stand before Christ’s tribunal.

> [Note: [Col. 0865D] “For then God shall be known—that is, his power and strength shall be made manifest—when the Church, by his own gift, is shown to offer him blessed men; while the holy people, according to the degrees of their merits, are placed at his right hand.” Cassiodorus, [Col. 0866D].]

These are the steps of which it was said above: “from ivory steps.” The steps of the Church are the apostles, because they bear and sustain us, and [Col. 0866B] through them we all ascend. In them the Lord is known, for in and through them he will judge all things. And rightly the master will be known in his disciples, because if they are wise, there can no longer be doubt about the master.

“**For behold, the kings of the earth were assembled and gathered together as one.**” This is what is meant in the title by “the second day of the Sabbath.” On the second day of the Sabbath, after the Lord rose from the dead, the disciples assembled and gathered together. As the Gospel relates, they remained shut in together for fear of the Jews; among them Christ appeared once and again and said: “Peace be with you; it is I; do not be afraid. Therefore the disciples rejoiced when they saw the Lord” (John 20:21). This is what it says [Col. 0866C]:

“**They, seeing, then marvelled.**” He rightly says “then,” because at the very beginning it is no wonder that they marvelled at the novelty of so great a miracle. Yet they should not have marvelled that he rose from the dead, since in their presence and before their eyes he raised others and still has the power to raise all.

> [Note: [Col. 0866D] St Bruno, who attempted to refer all deeds, figures, and prophecies of the Old Testament to the signification of the New, diverted the words of this verse and the preceding one—which plainly speak of kings of the earth—from their obvious sense, applying them to Christ’s disciples in order to expound their astonishment and amazement upon hearing of Christ’s resurrection. This does no injury to the truth of Scripture and should not be regarded as discordant with mystical interpretation.]

But the Prophet now turns his attention to what the apostles suffered after they separated from one another and began to preach among all nations. For he could say nothing other than what was inwardly shown to him. Hence he himself says elsewhere: “I will hear what the Lord God speaks in me” (Ps. 84:8). Thus it happens that prophets do not maintain continuity and order of subject matter, but suddenly pass now to one thing and now to another, and very often say first what happened later [Col. 0866D].

“**The mountains were troubled and shaken; trembling seized them; there were pains as of a woman in labour: with a violent spirit you shall shatter the ships of Tarshish.**” After the apostles began to preach and demonstrated with complete certainty that the worship of the gods was false, announced the terror of the judgment to come, and confirmed their teaching by many signs and miracles, all who heard them were troubled and shaken; trembling seized them [Col. 0867A]. They were troubled: some well, others not well. But now we wish to speak of those who were well troubled and shaken. A person is rightly troubled when, having lived badly, he believes against himself and is disturbed against his former way of life. They were moved from unbelief to faith, passing from darkness to light and from falsehood to truth. This was because the terror of the coming judgment and of the punishments awaiting unbelievers seized them. “There were pains as of a woman in labour.” These are good pains because they are quickly changed into joy. Thus the Lord says: “When a woman gives birth, she has sorrow because her hour has come; but when she has borne the child, she no longer remembers the anguish because of her joy that a human being has been born into the world” (John 16:21). Such pains, therefore, were experienced by those coming to faith, who grieved and wept for their sins [Col. 0867B].

“**With a violent spirit you shall shatter the ships of Tarshish.**” Do you not see how suddenly the person changes here? Search from the beginning of the psalm to this point, and you will not find the prophet addressing the second person except here. I say this so that we may not look for everything in the prophets that we are accustomed to look for in other Scriptures. “With a violent spirit,” he says, “O Lord, you shall shatter the ships of Tarshish” [Col. 0867C]. This is the spirit of which we read in the Acts of the Apostles: “Suddenly there came from heaven a sound as of a violent rushing spirit, and it filled the whole house where they were sitting” (Acts 2:2). This spirit shattered the ships of Tarshish because it shattered, according to their former condition, and changed for the better innumerable cities, towns, castles, and villages of this world, which are signified by ships. Tarshish fittingly signifies the world, since it was situated by the sea and devoted only to shipping, commerce, and deceit.

“**As we have heard, so have we seen in the city of the Lord of hosts, in the city of our God; God has founded her for ever.**” The Prophet places himself with all others who marvel at the conversion of all nations so suddenly accomplished. “As we have heard,” he says, “from the patriarchs and prophets, so have we seen in the city of the Lord of hosts,” by which the Church is signified [Col. 0867D]. Our Saviour is called the Lord of hosts because he is the one who works such mighty acts everywhere through himself and through his own. He rightly says: “God has founded her for ever,” because her foundation cannot be moved. Hence the Lord says: “The gates of hell shall not prevail against her” (Matt. 16:18).

[Col. 0868A] “**We have received your mercy in the midst of your temple.**”

> [Note: [Col. 0867D] “This is the Word that became flesh and dwelt among us. For just as Christ is redemption, so also he is mercy.” St Ambrose.]

Whoever desires to find mercy and be freed from sins, let him come to God’s temple; let him come to God’s Church, because nowhere else is there remission of sins.
