“**According to your name, O God, so also is your praise unto the ends of the earth.**” As, he says, your name is heard everywhere, and there is no nation that does not know your name, so cause your praise also to spread and extend everywhere, 395 so that there may be no nation, even to the ends of the earth, which does not praise and magnify you. Blessed are those who praise you; wretched are those who do not praise you. Why so? Because “your right hand is full of justice,” which “will render to each according to his works” (Matt. 16:27).

[Col. 0868B] “**Therefore let Mount Zion rejoice, and let the daughters of Judah exult**”—that is, the souls of confessors, who likewise persevere in your praises. For Judah is interpreted as “confessor” or “one praising the Lord.” “**Because of your judgments, O Lord.**” For your judgments are such as will make blessed and gladden all your faithful. But now he turns directly to the apostles, exhorting them to be concerned for this mountain and to fortify and guard it with every diligence. This is what he says:

“**Surround Zion and embrace her; proclaim [this] in her towers; set your hearts upon her strength, and distribute her steps, that you may recount [them] to another generation.**” Surround Zion, he says—you who are her guards and watchmen—and fortify her on every side with your defences [Col. 0868C]. Embrace her with the arms of love and charity, lest she perhaps be plundered by other lovers. “Proclaim” and preach “in her towers,” by which we understand the individual churches, separated from one another not in mind but by place. “Set your hearts upon her strength”: that is, direct your whole heart and attention to her power and strength. “And distribute her steps”: appoint bishops, presbyters, and other ecclesiastical ranks in individual cities, “that you may recount [them] to another generation.” This is what the Apostle says: “More priests were made according to the law, because death prevented them from continuing” (Heb. 7:23).

> [Note: [Col. 0868D] The Greek text does not contain the words “according to the law,” though the Latin Vulgate had them before it was revised.]

For if they always lived, they alone would suffice and there would be no need to appoint others; but now, as some die, others must succeed them, through whom apostolic teaching may be recounted to another generation [Col. 0868D]. But what shall be recounted to another generation?

“**For this is our God for ever and ever, and he himself shall rule us for ages.**” It is sufficient, therefore, for us to preach this in the Church: that Christ is our God and king for ever; and because he rules and loves us, let us never depart from his government, nor ever pass over to another teaching. Let us humbly do whatever he commands, receive no other ruler [Col. 0869A], and let this suffice us.

## Psalm XLVIII. For the end; for the sons of Korah. A psalm.

This title has already been sufficiently explained.

“**Hear these things, all nations; give ear, all who inhabit the world, both earthborn and children of men, rich and poor alike together.**” The Prophet shows that he is about to speak great things in this psalm, since he summons all nations. He leaves no one out: he calls all and commands both rich and poor to listen.

“**My mouth shall speak wisdom, and the meditation of my heart understanding.**” He makes us at once attentive and well-disposed by promising to speak wisdom and understanding [Col. 0869B]. And truly this is supreme wisdom: that a person should not trust in his own strength or glory in his riches; that he should love mercy, know himself, and not subject his flesh to luxury and pleasures.

“**I shall incline my ear to a parable.**” In saying that he will incline his ear to a parable and speak by a parable, he shows that he is not speaking his own words but another’s. This is what he says elsewhere: “I will hear what the Lord God speaks in me” (Ps. 84:9).—“**I shall open my proposition upon the psaltery.**” The psaltery is a musical instrument having ten strings and no more. There are ten words of the law, in which all commandments are contained. Therefore he sings upon the psaltery who keeps and fulfils the commandments of the law [Col. 0869C].

“**Why should I fear in the evil day?**” He now begins to speak in a parable and sets himself as a likeness for others, so that each person may understand in himself what he says concerning himself. The evil day is the day of judgment, prepared for wicked people to receive evils alone. Why, he says, should I fear on the evil day? “**The iniquity of my heel shall surround me.**” That heel is wicked which does not stand firm and causes the whole person to fall. We have many heels, more within us than without. All our works are heels to us: good heels if they are good works, evil heels if they are evil works; for by them we either fall or stand. Therefore he will not fear on the evil day [Col. 0869D] who, while he lived, had a good heel:

“**Those who trust in their own strength and glory in the abundance of their riches.**” Let those, he says, fear on the evil day who trust in their own strength and glory in their many riches. They ought therefore to fear, because they have wicked heels; for such wicked heels soon fail and cannot support those whom they carry. And how does he prove this?

“**A brother does not redeem; shall a man redeem?**” Who is this brother whose redemption is so necessary?

> [Note: [Col. 0869D] “Let us understand by ‘man’ the Lord Jesus, who took on the human condition in order to crucify in his flesh the sin of all and erase, by his blood, the bond written against all.” St Ambrose.]

This is he who says elsewhere: “I shall proclaim your name to my brothers” (Ps. 21:23). He, therefore, is our Saviour, who certainly does not redeem those “who trust in their own strength and glory in their riches.” And if he does not redeem them—he who is both God and man—will any mere man redeem them? Can a priest or Levite heal those whom the Samaritan did not heal? “**He shall not give to God his petition**”

> [Note: [Col. 0869D] Both in the Vulgate edition published and annotated by Isidore Clarius according to the Venetian edition of 1542, and in the Psalter published at Rome in 1741 by the Venerable Cardinal Thomasius with notes, the reading is: “He shall not give God his propitiation.” Cardinal Thomasius notes: [Col. 0870D] “Nor shall any of those, whether strong or rich, give anything for himself by which he may himself make God favourable to him.” Clarius says similar things. Cassiodorus likewise has, “He shall not give God his propitiation,” and explains it thus: “‘He shall not give’ is negative, because no offering, no propitiation, can compensate for that by which the Divinity deigned to redeem us.”]

“**nor the price of the redemption of his soul.**” Therefore, he says, he will not be redeemed, because God does not hear his petitions and because he does not pay the price for his soul’s redemption [Col. 0870B]. God receives the petitions and prayers of those who have a good intention and beseech him with a pure heart. But those redeem their souls who make satisfaction for their sins by alms and other works of piety and mercy. “**He shall labour for ever and live unto the end.**” Because, he says, the wicked are such as these, they shall labour for ever and never attain rest. They shall live unto the end, but never arrive at an end; for they would wish to die and reach an end if they could.

“**For he shall not see destruction, when he sees the wise dying.**” Therefore, he says, wicked people shall live amid torments and pains unto the end, because they do not understand or consider how justly and holily wise people die: “Precious in the sight of the Lord is the death of his saints” (Ps. 115:5) [Col. 0870C]. But they think and say in their hearts: The condition of all is one—good and bad, righteous and sinners, wise and foolish; all alike die and are dissolved into dust; there is no difference. Let us enjoy this life, because we do not know what shall happen in the other. Such a thought is wicked and full of despair. Therefore “the senseless and the fool shall perish together.” This is the senseless person “who said in his heart, ‘There is no God’” (Ps. 13:1), by whom unbelieving people are understood. But the fool is one who loves only earthly and transitory things, which are lost so quickly and easily [Col. 0870D]. These therefore perish in one and the same manner, because such a believer differs little or not at all from an unbeliever. Such was the fool to whom the Lord said: “Fool, this night they shall demand your soul from you; and the things you have prepared, whose shall they be?” (Luke 12:10).

> [Note: [Col. 0870D] Codex Ghisleri: “your soul shall be snatched away.”]

Hence it follows:

“**And they shall leave their riches to strangers.**” This is what is said in another psalm: “They heap up treasure and do not know for whom they gather it” (Ps. 38:7).—“**Their tombs are their houses for ever.**” Once they begin to dwell in tombs, they will never afterward have other houses; for hell too is a tomb, and their bodies themselves are tombs, foul and full of decay [Col. 0871A].

“**Their tabernacles endure through every generation and age; they shall call upon their names in their own lands.**”

> [Note: [Col. 0871D] “Because their works are corruptible and earthly, their names are therefore written where they preferred to live. But because they exalted their works, it is said to them: ‘Do not rejoice that the demons are subject to you; rather rejoice that your names are written in heaven’ (Luke 10:20).” St Ambrose.]

For just as there are many dwelling places in the heavenly Jerusalem, so in hell there are many tabernacles and receptacles of punishments. And as there some differ from others in glory, so here some differ from others in torments. Their “tabernacles,” therefore—that is, those of the evil spirits, who shall dwell with them in those very tabernacles—endure “through every generation and age,” by which endless time is denoted [Col. 0871B]. Among the torments by which they shall torture them, they shall call them by the most shameful names, so that this itself will be a greater punishment and sorrow to them: that they are called by such names. We must understand, therefore, that amid the very scourges evil spirits, who remember such things better, shall call them adulterers, fornicators, sacrilegious persons, thieves, robbers, perjurers, murderers, sodomites, plunderers, and by other names, for ever. That people of the earth shall indeed be their earth, in which they shall dwell eternally.

“**And man, when he was in honour, did not understand; he was compared with senseless beasts and became like them.**” This is the reason why wicked people suffer the things stated above: although they were in honour and made in God’s image and likeness, they did not understand in whose image they had been made. Instead, living luxuriously and shamefully, they chose to become like senseless beasts [Col. 0871C]. Thus they became brutish, though, if they had wished, they could have been gods. For it is written: “I said, ‘You are gods, all of you sons of the Most High’” (Ps. 81:6). “**This way of theirs is a stumbling-block to them.**” Who can say how many stumbling-blocks and dangers this way of the wicked produces for them, both in this life and in the next? This way causes them never to have peace, to kill one another in turn, and to pursue one another with wicked hatred. “**And afterward they shall bless with their mouth.**” [Col. 0871D] This may be understood to mean that after stumbling-blocks and disputes, such persons bless one another—not in their hearts but with their mouths—which seems to concern a feigned peace. But if we understand it of after this life, what else would “afterward they shall bless with their mouth” mean except that afterward they will desire that they had blessed? [Col. 0872A] And this “with their mouth,” by which we may more fittingly understand thought than spoken words.

“**They are set in hell like sheep.**” They are now compared to sheep for no other reason than that they shall defend themselves by no reasoning; deprived of all power and strength, they shall be led to death like the vilest animals. And what shall death do? “**And death shall feed upon them.**” He did not say “devour,” but “feed upon,” so that after this we may understand death itself to be inexhaustible and ever returning to life.

“And the righteous shall have dominion over them in the morning.” [Note: [Col. 0871D] The Vulgate reads: “And the righteous shall have dominion over them in the morning, and their help shall grow old in hell, away from their glory.” On this St Ambrose says: “Those who refused to let Christ feed them, death shall feed upon. … Although in this life they pursued power and riches, so as to rule others, at the resurrection there shall be servitude, when the morning splendour shines upon the righteous. Jacob’s precedence over his brother is a figure of this. Miserable indeed is that servitude: at the very time when others are called into the glory of splendour and light, their glory grows old and is consumed in the darkness of hell.” CASSIODORUS also follows the Vulgate reading here; St Ambrose agrees with his interpretation.] Therefore the righteous shall have dominion over them, because the wicked will lie powerless and be unable to do anything against them. This will be in the morning, when the longest night has passed and the sun of righteousness rises for the righteous. “And their help shall grow old in hell;” [Col. 0872B] where they themselves are, there also will be their help—by which we should understand all their friends and relatives who were accustomed to assist them. These shall grow old in hell, because they will dwell there for no short time, “and they have been driven out from their glory.” If this had been said at the beginning, it would seem more suitable, for when they died, then indeed they were driven out from their glory. But such matters are not to be sought in the prophets, because wherever the spirit goes, there the wheels follow.

“But God shall deliver my soul from the hand of hell, when he receives me.” As though someone said to him: Do you speak thus about others, as though you too ought not to descend into hell and dwell there? [Col. 0872C] To this he replies: I know that I shall descend; nevertheless, God shall deliver my soul from the hand of hell. When? When he receives me. Happy was that day, and exceedingly happy, on which our Saviour descended there and rescued the souls of the saints who were held captive there. Hence he himself says elsewhere: “You shall give joy and gladness to my hearing, and humbled bones shall rejoice” (Ps. 50:10).

“Do not fear when a man has become rich, and when the glory of his house has been multiplied.” Do not fear, he says, either the rich or the poor; for the rich quickly become poor, and the poverty of the saints is quickly changed into riches. Religious men often fear when they see impious and proud men, [Col. 0872D] who hate them, increasing in power and riches. The Prophet now consoles and urges them not to fear, because such men quickly fail.

“For when he dies, he shall not take everything, nor shall the glory of his house descend with him.” Such men should indeed be mourned because they perish; but [Col. 0873A] there should also be rejoicing, because their iniquities receive their due reward.

“For his soul shall be blessed during his lifetime.” The wicked man shall be blessed only during his life, and by flatterers and those like himself. But after he has died, he awaits an eternal curse. “And he shall praise you when you have done well to him.” We see such people, when prosperity according to their own desire comes upon them, often blessing and praising; yet they do not depart from iniquity, but become worse through their very prosperity.

“And he shall enter even into the generation of his fathers.” [Note: [Col. 0873D] Thus the Ghislerian and Vallicellian codices: “He shall enter into generations.” Many manuscripts have “into generations,” and this is also the reading in the text used by Clarius and Thommasius, cited above. But “into the generation,” as St Bruno reports, is read by CASSIODORUS and by the Casinensian and Florentine manuscripts, as Lucas Holstenius also notes on this passage.] For they themselves commonly say, almost in jest, that they wish to be and dwell where their fathers are. But their fathers are those [Col. 0873B] whose works they imitate. They will therefore be in punishment with those from whom they do not differ in works. Hence it follows: “And for ever he shall not see light,” because from the darkness of blindness and error they will go into the outer darkness; there shall be weeping and gnashing of teeth.

“And man, when he was in honour, did not understand; he was compared to senseless beasts and became like them.” He had already said this above; but by repeating it he shows that they persevered in their wickedness.

398. PSALM XLIX. A PSALM OF ASAPH. [Note: [Col. 0873D] “Asaph was the son of Berechiah, of the family of Gershon son of Levi. In 1 Chronicles, chapter 6, he is said to have been chosen among the four masters of singers, to make psalms resound to the Lord upon musical instruments. He was not the author of this psalm, as has been said of others, but, being an outstanding musician, he nevertheless deserved to be placed in this title because of the significance of his name; for it means ‘Synagogue.’ Yet here we must understand that faithful Synagogue which both believed in the Christ who was to come and most willingly received him when he came. It should certainly be known that this psalm prophesies both advents of the Lord.” BEDE.]

Asaph means Synagogue, that is, congregation. Therefore in this psalm she says that she received this command from the Lord: that she should cease from the sacrifices which she had been accustomed to offer, and should offer God a sacrifice of praise and rejoicing.

“The God of gods, the Lord, has spoken, and summoned the earth, from the rising of the sun to its setting. From Zion is the splendour of his beauty.” The Evangelist says of those who received Christ that “he gave them power to become children of God, to those who believe in his name” (John 1:12). Therefore all the faithful are both gods and children of God, of whom the Lord also says: “I said: You are gods [Note: [Col. 0874D] “Men are called gods when by good conduct they receive the grace of the heavenly majesty; as he says in another psalm, Psalm 81:6, ‘I said,’ etc. Thus they are called sons just as they are called gods, because grace, not nature, bestows both. But the God of gods is the Lord Christ; for he, together with the Father and the Holy Spirit, is truly called God of gods. This name is not altogether proper to divinity; yet, as we have already said, human language cannot indicate his supreme excellence beyond this.” CASSIODORUS.], and all are children of the Most High” (Ps. 81:6). Therefore God, who is especially Lord of gods—that is, of all saints, for they are those who serve and obey him—has spoken, both through himself and through [Col. 0873D] his apostles. “And he summoned the earth.” What earth? “From the rising of the sun to its setting”—“for he is not the God of the Jews only, but also of the Gentiles; since one is God, who justifies circumcision by faith and uncircumcision through faith” (Rom. 3:29). Hence elsewhere it is said: “Their sound has gone out into all the earth, and their words to the ends of the world” (Ps. 18:4). “From Zion is the splendour of his beauty.” All, he says, have been called from east to west; but Zion and Jerusalem lie in the middle, according to the saying: “But God, our king before the ages, has worked salvation in the midst of the earth” (Ps. 73:12). It was therefore excellently said that the city is situated in the midst, from which all around it were to receive faith and doctrine, comeliness and beauty. For in Zion that blood was shed by which the whole world, purified, recovered its ancient [Col. 0874B] beauty and splendour. These things have been said concerning Christ’s first advent; now let us hear of the second.

“God shall come openly, our God, and shall not keep silence.” In his first advent he came hidden, in the form of a servant, and therefore was not known. “For if,” as the Apostle says, “they had known, they would never have crucified the Lord of glory” (1 Cor. 2:8). But he shall come openly, not to be judged, but to judge. Hence he himself says: “When the Son of Man comes in his majesty, then all nations shall be gathered before him” (Matt. 25:32). Therefore it is said: “Gather to him his saints.” And he certainly shall not keep silence—he who formerly “was led as a sheep to the slaughter and did not open his mouth” (Isa. 53:7). [Col. 0874C] He kept silence, as it is written, but he shall not be silent always; keeping silence and judging are incompatible.

“A fire shall burn before him, and a mighty tempest round about him.” Prophecies are difficult because in many places they preserve neither time nor order. This verse should have been spoken later, because the things which follow will happen before those narrated in this verse. First heaven and earth above will be summoned, the people will be separated from the people, all the saints will be gathered before the judge, and first the heavens will render judgment and announce righteousness; and only then shall fire burn before him, “and a mighty tempest round about him.” Such is the order, and this is what he says:

[Col. 0874D] “He summoned heaven [Note: [Col. 0874D] *He summoned heaven.* What St Bruno says here—that prophets often use the past tense for future events—is indeed true. But this explanation does not seem applicable here, since the Vulgate reads *he shall summon* and agrees with the Hebrew text and with the Greek text of the Seventy translators. St Gregory, like St Bruno, cites this passage five times, namely as “he summoned heaven,” and Clarius adds this note to these words: “He made both heavenly minds and mortals serve in this world for the removal of Satan’s tyranny.”] above, that he might distinguish his people from the earth.” It belongs to prophets to use past tenses for future events, because they see future things as though they had already happened. By heaven and earth the whole multitude of good and evil people is signified. The good are rightly called heaven, because they are going there and because they have always loved heavenly things. The evil are no less rightly called earth, because they love only earthly and transitory things and must be drawn down to the lower parts of the earth. Therefore the Lord shall summon heaven and earth above, because both good and evil people, as the Apostle says, “must all stand before the judgment-seat of Christ, that each may give an account of his sins” (2 Cor. 5:19). The word “above” plainly shows that judgment will occur not on earth but above, in the air. But why did he summon them? “That he might distinguish his people.” Thus it is written in the Gospel [Col. 0875B] that “he shall separate the good from the evil, as a shepherd separates lambs from goats, and shall set the lambs on his right hand and the goats on his left” (Matt. 24:33). 399. From their very position they will sufficiently understand for whom glory and for whom punishment has been prepared.

“Gather to him his saints, who established his Testament above sacrifices.” You angels, he says, whose office it is, gather to him his saints—by whom he means bishops, priests, and all of the ecclesiastical order. It is fitting that they are gathered not together with the others but separately by themselves. After them come the apostles, of whom it follows: “The heavens shall declare his righteousness.” Then the Lord and our Saviour himself is set forth, of whom it is said here [Col. 0875C]: “For God is judge.” Bishops and priests established God’s Testament above sacrifices because in the very sacrifices of the Jews they expounded and showed the New Testament to be signified. Although both Testaments are God’s, only that is called his which is understood spiritually. For what is understood literally in both Testaments is Old; and what is understood spiritually is New. Therefore the letter alone makes the difference between us and the Jews. If they did not follow it, all of them would today be Christians with us; but the letter kills, just as spiritual understanding gives life to the Church. Thus the New Testament is an exposition of the Old Testament. A Jew sacrifices a lamb, a goat, and a bull; and I say that Christ is signified in these. What else is this than to establish the Testament above sacrifices?

“The heavens declared his righteousness, for God is judge.” They shall declare, he says, not their own righteousness but God’s judgment, “for God is judge,” whose righteousness and judgment the others shall announce. For not apostles only, but also the queen of the South and the Ninevites shall judge in that judgment; yet all these will judge as disciples, whereas Christ will judge as Lord and master. When sentence has been given and [Col. 0876A] the judgment completed in this order, then what he said above shall follow: “A fire shall burn before him, and a mighty tempest round about him.” These things should be feared rather than explained, and contemplated with fear rather than uttered by the tongue. Thus far Asaph—by whom we understand all the patriarchs and prophets—has spoken of both advents of Christ. Now he begins to reply to what has been said.

“Hear, my people, and I shall speak, Israel; and I shall testify to you, for I am God, your God.” You have spoken enough, as though he said; now hear, and I shall speak, and I shall speak to you under testimony, so that you may hold most firmly what I say and presume in no way to change it: “For I am God, your God,” who shall not allow you to escape unpunished if you do not obey [Col. 0876B] me. Whom should we so hear and so obey, if not our God and Lord? What is stated much further below—where he commands that we listen most attentively and promises that he will speak—namely, “Offer to God a sacrifice of praise, and pay your vows to the Most High,” and at the end of the Psalm, “A sacrifice of praise shall honour me, and there is the way in which I shall show him God’s salvation,” has this sense: You yourself above praised and called those companions who established God’s Testament above sacrifices; see therefore that you understand the Scriptures not according to the letter but according to the spiritual sense. If you do so, then your sacrifices shall please me; understood otherwise, they are wholly vain. This is what he says:

“I shall not rebuke you concerning sacrifices; but your burnt offerings are always before me.” I shall not rebuke you, he says, concerning your sacrifices, because sacrifices made and understood in this manner ought not to be rebuked but praised. Such burnt offerings please God and are always before his eyes. Thus we read of Abel’s sacrifice: “The Lord looked upon Abel and his gifts, but upon Cain and his gifts he did not look” (Gen. 4:4). Hence it is evident that the holy patriarchs and prophets, and all others in whom the Holy Spirit was present, understood spiritually the sacrifices which they performed. This is proved most clearly in this Psalm, in which David the prophet speaks so [Col. 0876D] and such things concerning sacrifices:

“I shall not take calves from your house, nor goats from your flocks.” These words seem contrary to those above, but they are not. There are goats and calves which the Lord receives, and there are goats and calves which the Lord does not receive. The goat is a lustful person; the calf, a proud man. If they return to repentance and begin to sacrifice and afflict their flesh, such a goat and such a calf are received by the Lord. Hence the Apostle says: “I beseech you, by the mercy of God, to present your bodies as a living sacrifice, holy, pleasing to God—your rational service” (Rom. 12:1). [Col. 0877A] But God does not care for other calves and goats. Yet he once received them for their signification, not because of the shedding of their own blood.

“For all the wild beasts of the forests are mine, the cattle on the mountains, and the oxen.” Why does he reject calves and goats when he receives oxen and cattle? He rejects not the animals but the sacrifices, for these too are good, just as the others are. Indeed, those sacrifices also once pleased the Lord because of their signification; if they were performed now, they would be judged sacrilegious. But what do we understand by the wild beasts of the forests except fierce men devoted to plunder? They too belong to the Lord, because they are often changed for the better and serve the Lord. [Col. 0877B] Cattle, however, 400, and oxen, because they are on the mountains, seem to have a good signification. Thus there are cattle, but good cattle, because they bear the burdens of others’ labours. Of them the Apostle says: “Bear one another’s burdens, and thus fulfil the law of Christ” (Gal. 6:2). The oxen are bishops and priests, who continually cultivate God’s field with the ploughshare of the tongue; and they are on the mountains, by which we understand the Churches.

“I have known all the birds of heaven, and the beauty of the field is with me.” By the birds of heaven he signifies all those in the Church who are wiser and fly more highly. Such was blessed John, who is described as having the form of an eagle. Such also was blessed Paul, who says that he was caught up to the third heaven. Such are [Col. 0877C] all others who meditate day and night upon understanding and expounding the Scriptures. By the beauty of the field we understand choirs of virgins of both sexes, whom the Lord says that he has with himself because he delights in such persons. Thus he himself says in the Song of Songs: “I am the flower of the field and the lily of the valleys” (Song 2:1).

“If I were hungry, I would not tell you.” This is as though he said: If you wish henceforth to offer me such a sacrifice, and suppose that I delight in such food, I do not want you as my cook, I do not want you as my servant, I do not want you as adviser and provider of my food. Why? “For the world is mine, and its fullness.” These are sufficient for me if the Jews refuse to hear me and insist on holding to the letter which kills them.

“Shall I eat the flesh of bulls, or drink the blood of goats?” He says this mockingly, showing that he utterly abominates Jewish sacrifices. For in Christ’s Passion all those sacrifices were fulfilled. We have one sacrifice, and it is eternal, according to the order of Melchizedek. “Christ is the end of the law for righteousness to everyone who believes” (Rom. 10:4). We also have other sacrifices, namely those of praise and rejoicing; hence it follows:

“Offer to God a sacrifice of praise, and pay your vows to the Most High.” This is that sacrifice of which it is said: “Through him, therefore, let us always offer to God a sacrifice of praise, that is, the calves of lips confessing [Col. 0878A] his name” (Rom. 13:15). The Church makes such sacrifices day and night, spending all its time in singing, chanting psalms, and preaching. We ought therefore to pay our vows to the Most High, so that we do not delay in rendering the good desires which we have in our hearts.

“Call upon me in the day of tribulation; I shall deliver you, and you shall glorify me.” He has told us what we ought to do, and he promises the reward of recompense if we do it. But as we are sluggish in acting, so we are also sluggish in asking.

“But to the sinner God said: Why do you recount my righteous ordinances?” Praise is not precious in the mouth of a sinner. But who is without sin? “For if we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, [Col. 0878B] and the truth is not in us” (1 John 1:8). Of what sinner, then, do we understand this, except one who perseveres in sin and despises returning to repentance? What business has one who is opposed to righteousness itself in preaching God’s righteous ordinances? Of such people the Apostle says: “You who preach that one must not steal, do you steal? You who teach that one must not commit adultery, do you commit adultery? You who abhor idols, do you commit sacrilege?” (Rom. 2:21). “And you take my Testament in your mouth.” This repeats what was said, because the Testament, which is holy, ought not to be preached with so polluted a mouth. We may also understand Christ’s body and blood by the Testament; hence the Lord says: “This is the cup of the New Testament, which [Col. 0878C] shall be shed for you and for many unto remission” (Mark 14:24).

“But you hated discipline.” And do you preach it? “And you cast my words behind you”—and do you proclaim them? He casts God’s words behind him who of his own will acts against them and disdains to look toward them.

“If you saw a thief, you ran with him.” He runs with a thief who commits such things or consents to them. “And you placed your portion with adulterers.” For this is what the Apostle says: “He who is joined to a harlot becomes one body” (1 Cor. 6:16).

“Your mouth abounded in wickedness, and your tongue devised deceit.” In this verse heretics, deceitful and fraudulent preachers, all deceivers, and [Col. 0878D] flatterers are denoted.

“Sitting, you spoke against your brother, and against the son of your mother you set a stumbling-block.” Every Christian is our brother and the son of our mother. To sit means to persevere: he speaks of one who perseveres in his wickedness to the end. How are such people not ashamed to preach? Hence Moses commands that a leprous man should always have his mouth closed and covered.

“You did these things, and I kept silence; you wickedly supposed that I would be like you.” You have done, he says, all the things stated above: I saw, I knew, and I kept silence. But I shall not always keep silence; rather, I shall answer you with fitting corrections, otherwise I would be like you. For those who act and those who consent differ little in guilt. [Col. 0879A] If you supposed this, you committed a great iniquity and added a great sin to the former ones.

“I shall rebuke you, and set them before your face.” I shall not, he says, keep silence; but as you deserve, I shall rebuke you, and I shall set before your face all those evils which you committed and which you think that I have forgotten, so that you may answer for each one and receive a fitting recompense for every one. “Understand these things, all you who forget the Lord, lest at some time he snatch you away and there be none to deliver.” This is not a threat directed at one person, but a common and universal threat: what seems to be said to one sinner, all and each should understand to be said to himself. Why? “Lest at some time he snatch you away”—he, namely, who is accustomed to snatch away. “And there be none to deliver.” Who could deliver one against whom [Col. 0879D] God himself is known to be angry?

“A sacrifice of praise shall honour me.” This verse, as we have already said, is connected with those above and therefore does not seem to belong to what is now said. “And there is the way in which I shall show him God’s salvation.” There, he says—that is, in the sacrifice of praise—is the way in which I shall show God’s salvation to the one who walks in it and perseveres in it. Salvation, or the saving help which God shall give, will be not temporal but eternal; whoever receives it shall fear neither weakness nor death any longer.

PSALM L. TO THE END: A PSALM OF DAVID. WHEN NATHAN THE PROPHET CAME TO HIM, AFTER HE HAD GONE IN TO BATHSHEBA.

David wrote this psalm for the sin which [Col. 0879C] he committed against Uriah and Bathsheba, giving other sinners an example of how they ought to repent and of how they ought not to be ashamed to reveal their sins. His repentance was sufficiently worthy, since it moved the Lord so quickly to mercy. For it is written: “Nathan the prophet came to him and said to him: Your sin is forgiven you” (2 Sam. 12:13). But why does it say “to the end,” though this Psalm concerns David himself, unless because he speaks to our Saviour, through whom he hopes to be delivered from sin?

“Have mercy upon me, O God, according to your great mercy.” God has always shown, and will show, many mercies; but that mercy by which he redeemed the world and blotted out original sin with his own [Col. 0879D] blood was greater than all others. This is the mercy of which he says elsewhere: “For his mercy has been strengthened over me” (Ps. 116:2). It was indeed strengthened, because there it was proved how great his mercy was. He therefore first asks for this mercy to be shown to himself, because he had recognized that his sin was greater than all sins. And he has great hope that God will forgive lesser sins, since he is so ready to cancel so great a sin.

“And according to the multitude of your compassions, blot out my iniquity.” Having called mercy singularly great, he now speaks in the plural of a multitude of compassions, so that it may also be understood that that mercy is not only great but [Col. 0880A] immeasurable and beyond estimation. He calls that sin his iniquity because it was common to all and therefore alike killed and afflicted all. But now he speaks of his own sin, and beyond the common remission of all he asks that this be granted to him more abundantly and specially. This is what he says:

“Wash me yet more from my injustice, and cleanse me from my offence.” For many have been delivered from original sin, but unless they are washed more fully, that does not suffice for them. That sin could not be forgiven except through that great mercy of which we have just spoken, by which we mean Christ’s Passion. But all other sins, before and after, could not be forgiven without Christ’s blood. It is therefore as though he said: I know and am certain that:

“You shall sprinkle me with hyssop, and I shall be cleansed; you shall wash me, and I shall become whiter than snow. But now wash me yet more from this injustice of mine and cleanse me from this offence.” That washing and remission shall indeed be common to all; but grant this additional washing specially to me, who repent wholly from the heart. This is what he says:

“For I know my iniquity, and my offence is ever before me.” He shows that he is performing worthy repentance when he says that he knows his iniquity and always has his offence before his eyes. In many places the Lord promises forgiveness to those who repent in this manner. He therefore gives us an example of how we too [Col. 0880C] ought to repent.

“Against you alone have I sinned, and done evil before you.” David was king, and most powerful in his time; he feared no one except God, and therefore says: “Against you alone have I sinned”—to you alone must I render account, because there is no one else who now dares rebuke me for my sin. Nor can I hide myself from you, because I did what I did before you, who see all things and from whom no secret is hidden. “That you may be justified in your words, and prevail when you are judged.” Behold, he considers that the Lord will forgive his sin if he wishes to uphold his own words as righteous. David knew the Lord’s words, since, as he himself says, he was one in whom the Lord spoke; and he had recognized such constancy and firmness in God and in [Col. 0880D] his words that God could not utterly deny what he had promised. Therefore, considering both the repentance of his heart and the Lord’s words, by which forgiveness is promised to those who worthily repent, he could in no way doubt that mercy and forgiveness would be granted to him. Thus he judged both himself in his repentance and God in his words, and saw that the two agreed. For he said in his heart: Forgive me my sin, “that you may be justified in your words,” that is, that your words may be found righteous and without reproach, “and that you may prevail when you are judged.” For if God’s words were not true, God would not prevail but rather be overcome. For he is overcome in judgment whose words are found blameworthy. Therefore God prevailed by forgiving [Col. 0881A] the sin, because it happened as he had promised, and his words were proved true. By these words all who perform worthy repentance are instructed never to distrust God’s mercy, because what he has promised is firm and stable. It follows:

“For behold, I was conceived in iniquities, and in offences my mother bore me.” He gives another reason why the Lord should incline himself to show him mercy: because he was conceived and born in iniquities, and from his very root was disposed to be subject to the pleasures of the flesh.

“For behold, you have loved truth.” You, he says, love truth and know that what I say is true; therefore I speak confidently, because I know that I speak truth. Hence it follows:

[Col. 0881B] “You have made known to me the uncertain and hidden things of your wisdom.” Through the Holy Spirit the Prophet had learned many things, both present and future, which were uncertain and hidden to other people and which could not be known except through the Holy Spirit. Such also is what follows.

“You shall sprinkle me with hyssop, and I shall be cleansed; you shall wash me, and I shall become whiter than snow.” Hyssop here stands for blood, because the blood of the slaughtered lamb was sprinkled with hyssop. What then is, “You shall sprinkle me with hyssop,” except, You shall sprinkle me with the blood of your Son? Since he says, “You shall sprinkle me,” and mentions hyssop, with which sprinkling is made, yet does not say what it is that is sprinkled, what else can we understand except what was formerly sprinkled with hyssop by the Lord’s command? This was the blood of that lamb which signified the Lamb who takes away the sins of the world. Sprinkled with his blood, we have been cleansed from original sin. “He loved us,” as the Apostle says, “and washed us from our sins in his own blood” (Rev. 1:5). Nothing is found whiter than snow, yet he says that he shall become whiter than snow, thereby signifying the inestimable glorification of the saints.

“You shall give joy and gladness to my hearing.” This joy was fulfilled when our Saviour descended into hell and rescued this man, together with all the other saints, from those dark places. Hence it is written: “O death, I shall be your death; I shall be [Col. 0881D] your bite, O hell” (Hos. 13:14). “And humbled bones shall rejoice.” For David is believed to have been one of those who rose together with the Lord; hence he not unreasonably says that his bones rejoice, since for so long they had lain humbled in the dust.

“Turn your face from my sins, and blot out all my iniquities.” Turn your face now, he says, from my sins, forget them, look upon them no longer, and have mercy on me, whom you are to receive into such glory and call before others. For it is not fitting that you should allow one to remain stained here for whom you prepare so great a glory in the other life.

“Create a clean heart in me, O God,” and drive every vanity, every folly, and every evil thought from my heart; for there is the source and origin [Col. 0882A] of good and evil. There vices arise, there they put down roots; unless these are quickly pulled up, they grow immeasurably beyond measure. “For from the heart proceed evil thoughts, thefts, adulteries, perjuries, murders, false testimonies, and similar things, which defile a man” (Matt. 15:19). Hence it is written: “Keep your heart with all diligence, for life proceeds from it” (Prov. 4:23).

“And renew a right spirit in my inward parts.” The Holy Spirit, who is right and makes people right, cannot be renewed; yet he is said to be renewed when he begins anew to dwell in the house which he had left because of its offences.

“Do not cast me away from your face, and do not take your Holy Spirit from me.” By these words he shows that before he had repented God had been angry with him and the Holy Spirit had departed from him. He therefore prays that the Holy Spirit may be restored to him, by whose illumination he was formerly consoled.

“Restore to me the joy of your salvation, and strengthen me with a ruling spirit.” The right Spirit, the Holy Spirit, and the ruling Spirit are one and the same, and there is no difference in him. Yet the Holy Spirit is called by other names according to the diversity of graces. Thus, when he makes people right, he may be called the right Spirit; when he makes them holy, the Holy Spirit; and when he restores someone to authority or to his honour, the ruling Spirit. So he is called the Spirit of wisdom, the Spirit of understanding, the Spirit of counsel, and the Spirit of might. [Col. 0882C] As for the words:

“Restore to me the joy of your salvation,” it seems to me that he had then lost the great joy which he had customarily possessed concerning the incarnation of our Saviour, and could no longer see it as before.

“I shall teach the wicked your ways, and the ungodly shall be converted to you.” Grant, he says, what I ask you to grant, so that I may teach the wicked your ways, 403, so that they may be instructed by that example; and by those ways through which they know that I have come to you and been reconciled to your grace, they too may come to you by the same ways and be reconciled to your grace. And not only the wicked, but also the ungodly, may be converted to you by my example.

“Deliver me from blood-guilt, O God, God of [Col. 0882D] my salvation, and my tongue shall rejoice in your righteousness.” “Flesh and blood shall not possess the kingdom of God” (Matt. 16:17). Although every sin may be understood by “blood-guilt,” he seems to be speaking particularly of the pleasures and desires of the flesh. Of these the Apostle also says: “Not in chambers and impurities, but put on the Lord Jesus Christ” (Rom. 13:13)—that is, the lover of all chastity—“and make no provision for the flesh in its desires” (ibid., 14). “And my tongue shall rejoice in your righteousness.” The tongue of the inner man, the tongue which speaks to you in my heart concerning your righteousness: that you are very righteous in vindicating your creature and not permitting your enemy to rule over it.

[Col. 0883A] “Lord, you shall open my lips, and my mouth shall declare your praise.” Lord, he says, you shall open my lips, which until now have been closed, because in my consciousness of sin I feared to open them in your praises. But because my sin has been forgiven me through your grace and mercy, from now on I shall not keep silence; rather, my mouth shall declare your praise.

“If you had desired sacrifice, I would certainly have given it.” Nor would I have been ashamed to offer a goat for sin, as your servant Moses commanded that I, and those like me, should offer. Certainly, “you will not delight in burnt offerings.” “I know well enough,” he says, “that sacrifices of this kind do not please you, unless you receive them solely for their symbolic meaning.” And as though someone were to say: If God does not accept this sacrifice, what other sacrifice is he to accept? To this he himself replies:

“Sacrifice to God is a troubled spirit; a contrite and humbled heart God does not despise.” This sacrifice indeed belongs to those who repent of their sins. It was signified by all those sacrifices which Moses commanded to be offered for sin. For it is far more fitting that a person should sacrifice, afflict, and offer himself to God than that, in his place, he should slaughter a goat, a she-goat, or other animals; for that slaughter signified this contrition, affliction, and humiliation.

“Deal graciously, O Lord, in your good will with Zion, that the walls of Jerusalem may be built.” Zion is interpreted “watchtower,” by whose strength Jerusalem was guarded and defended; and by it we understand the guardians and watchmen of the Church, that is, the apostles, bishops, and priests. Therefore the Prophet, who until now has prayed, now, having been heard, begins according to his custom to speak of the Church and to pray for her. He prays, then, for those who construct and build her walls, through whom, as we have said, bishops and priests are signified, without whom neither walls can be built nor stones hewn. As many Christians as there are, so many are the stones of this city; joined by the mortar of charity, they remain firm and steadfast.

“Then you will accept the sacrifice of righteousness, offerings and burnt offerings; then they will place calves upon your altar.” Then, he says, when Jerusalem—that is, the holy Church—shall be built and her walls constructed, you will accept, that is, you will regard as pleasing and acceptable, the sacrifice of righteousness: not bulls or goats, as formerly, but offerings and burnt offerings—namely, offerings and burnt offerings of that same righteousness. Hence all saints are called righteous, because they practise, preach, and preserve righteousness. For this reason the saints suffer persecutions even to this day: because they preach and defend righteousness. And what else is their affliction and persecution than a sacrifice pleasing and acceptable to God? Of such a sacrifice it is truly said that “the Lord smelled the odour of sweetness” (Gen. VIII.21). “Then they will place calves upon your altar”—surely, the calves of lips confessing his name. But what are the calves of lips except a sacrifice of praise and rejoicing? Bishops and priests offer such calves when they proclaim God’s praises in the Church, when they expound the doctrines of both Testaments, and offer and place them upon the altar of our hearts. For our hearts too are altars, upon which true daily sacrifices of praise and rejoicing are made.

## Psalm LI. 404. To the end. The understanding of David, when Doeg the Edomite came and told Saul, and said to him: David has come into the house of Abimelech.

[Note: Col. 0883D. According to the Septuagint translators this name is used thus; many Latin Psalters agree with them, as do Cassiodorus and the Roman edition. But the Hebrew text reads *Achimelech*, which the Vulgate follows both in the title of this psalm and in 1 Kings, chapters XXI and XXII, where the story of the killing of Abimelech is narrated. The same priest who showed kindness to David is called Abiathar, not Achimelech or Abimelech, in St Mark, chapter II, verse 26; perhaps because both Achimelech the father and Abiathar his son bore two names, or because David, while a fugitive, received the holy loaves from each of them. St Augustine has the same title for this psalm, and thinks that the titles were varied because of the similarity of the names and the difference of one syllable; hence some manuscripts read *Achimelech*, others *Abimelech*.]

“To the end,” he says: this psalm is to be referred to the end of this age, according to the understanding of David, who in it laments what occurred at that time, when Doeg the Edomite came to Saul and reported to him that David had come into the house of Abimelech. Then, as it is written, that same Doeg, at Saul’s command, killed Abimelech the priest and all the other priests of his household. Appropriately, moreover, Doeg the Edomite is interpreted “stirred by blood,” since he could be so easily stirred to kill the Lord’s priests and shed so much blood. He signifies Antichrist,

[Note: Col. 0884D. Cardinal Thomasius developed this interpretation, and Cassiodorus before him.]

who likewise will be most ready to shed the blood of the saints. Abimelech, however, is interpreted “the kingdom of my father,” by which we understand the Church, called a holy nation and a rule of priests; Antichrist will kill her priests because they have received Christ our Lord.

“Why do you glory in malice, you who are mighty in iniquity?” Such will be the malice and power of Antichrist that, unless, as is read in the Gospel (Matt. XXIV.22), the Lord had shortened his days, no flesh would be saved; but for the elect’s sake those days will be shortened. “For he will reign,” as it is written, “for a time, times, and half a time” (Apoc. XII.13), that is, for three and a half years and no more. During them he will convert almost the entire world to himself, both personally and through his disciples. Hence it is written that he will draw all men to himself, with innumerable multitudes before him. This man, therefore, will glory in malice alone, he who said in his heart: “I shall not be moved from generation to generation, without evil” (Ps. X.6)—“whose mouth is full of cursing, bitterness, and deceit” (Ps. XIII.3). To him the Prophet now says, not without indignation: “Why do you glory in malice?” What is this glory of yours, O vilest and wickedest of all human beings? What is this power of yours, which works nothing but malice and iniquity? It is not enough for you to act wickedly; beyond this, you glory in crime, rejoicing when you have done evil and exulting in the worst deeds (Prov. II.14).

“Your tongue devised injustice all day long.” “All day long,” he says—that is, throughout the whole course of his life—he will devise and ponder how to work injustice and iniquity, how to kill and deceive the saints, and how to convert miserable people to himself and draw them with him to destruction.

“Like a sharp razor you have wrought deceit.” For a sharp razor often wounds the flesh while it ought to shave the hair. Thus that most wicked man, while pretending to defend righteousness and destroy evil people, will turn weapons against the saints and proclaim that they deserve to be killed. “And then there will indeed be such tribulation as has not been from the beginning of the world until now, nor ever will be” (Matt. XXIV.21). Few indeed will remain who are not seduced by his deceits and frauds, when they see him most powerful, most wise, and resplendent with miracles.

“[Col. 0885C] You loved malice more than kindness, iniquity more than speaking equity.” The Apostle speaks of his malice and iniquity, saying: “Unless the departure comes first and the man of iniquity, the son of perdition, is revealed—he who will be lifted up and exalt himself above everything called God or worshipped, so that he sits in the temple of God and shows himself as though he were God” (2 Thess. II.3). Hence it continues:

“You loved all words of ruin, O deceitful tongue.”

[Note: Col. 0885D. In St Augustine one reads: “You loved all words of submersion, a deceitful tongue.” On this he says: “What is a deceitful tongue? A deceitful tongue is the servant of fraud, belonging to those who hold one thing in their heart and utter another with their mouth. But in these there is overthrow; in these, submersion.” Col. 0886D.]

And to whom would these words just spoken not appear ruinous and deceitful? Who was ever worthy of such a headlong fall and such a sinking into the abyss as he whose deceitful tongue does not fear to utter such blasphemies? For the Apostle says of him that “the Lord Jesus will kill him by the spirit of his mouth and abolish him by the brightness of his coming” (ibid., 8). Yet there is no doubt that an even greater downfall still awaits him at judgment; hence it follows:

“Therefore God will destroy you utterly; he will pluck you out and remove you from your tabernacle, and your root from the land of the living.” 405. Therefore, he says, because you are so wicked, so proud, so iniquitous and deceitful, God will destroy you utterly. What means “utterly”? Completely and wholly: not merely so that you cease to exist, but so that you have no honour whatever and are in every misery and distress. He will pluck you from this world’s dwelling-place, in which you deceived and destroyed so great a multitude of people. And he will cause you to depart from your tabernacle, that is, from that most abominable body in which the entire fullness of iniquity dwelt more than in any other human being. “And your root from the land of the living,” so that all your life may forever be in the land of the dying and of those who never fail in evil.

“The righteous will see, and fear, and laugh at him, and say.” The righteous, he says, will see. But what will they see? The ruin, destruction, and terrible downfall of this most abominable man. And what will they fear? Their Lord and Creator, whose omnipotence they will see to be greater both than this man—most powerful in this age—and than all others. And they will laugh at him. For to laugh is to rejoice, since laughter is joy.

“Behold the man who did not make God his helper, but hoped in the abundance of his riches and prevailed in his vanity.” It is evident how wicked that man will be, at whose ruin all the righteous will look, rejoice, and bear such witness against him. “Behold,” he says, “the most utterly lost of all human beings, who never sought God’s help, who gave himself wholly to the service of the devil, and received his name from his iniquity; so that, because he was to be contrary in every respect to Christ the Lord, he would be called Antichrist. He hoped in the abundance of his riches,” because, overflowing with all the riches of this world and enjoying in fullest abundance everything belonging to delight and pleasure, he called himself God and commanded himself to be worshipped as God. “And he prevailed in his vanity,” because everything happened as he wished. This is the beast of whom it is read in the Apocalypse: “Power was given to it over every tribe, people, language, and nation; and all who dwell on the earth worshipped it, whose names are not written in the book of life of the Lamb” (Apoc. XIII.8). Thus this man prevailed in his vanity, doing everything according to the wicked desires of his heart.

“But I, like a fruitful olive tree in the house of the Lord, have hoped in the mercy of my God for ever and unto age upon age.” That man, he says, of whom we have spoken until now, hoped in the abundance of his riches; but I have hoped in the mercy of my God alone, and I shall hope for ever and unto age upon age. David was like a fruitful olive tree in the house of the Lord because, anointed and filled with the oil of the Holy Spirit, he enlightened, healed, and gladdened many others with the richness of mercy. This is that olive tree from the root of Jesse, from which came forth the rod, upon whose flower “rests the Spirit of wisdom and understanding, the Spirit of counsel and might, the Spirit of knowledge and piety, and the Spirit of the fear of the Lord” (Isa. XI.2); and of whom it is elsewhere said: “God, your God, has anointed you with the oil of gladness above your companions” (Ps. XLIV.8).

“I will confess to you, O Lord, for ever, because you have done.” He said, “because you have done,” and did not say what he had done, so that by this we may understand that he has done all things. And who else ought to be praised except him who made all things? “And I shall await your name, because it is good, before the sight of your saints.” This is the name of which the prophet says: “Behold, the name of the Lord comes from afar, his anger burning and grievous to bear” (Isa. XXX.27). The name of the Lord, the Word of the Lord, the utterance of the Lord, and the wisdom of the Lord is Christ, who at his coming will appear both delightful to the good and angry toward the evil. Hence it is rightly said:

“Before the sight of your saints.” Your name, he says, is good, sweet, and delightful to behold. But where? Before the sight of your saints. To them it will appear such as it is; but to the rest, such as was said above: his anger burning and grievous to bear.

## Psalm LII. To the end, for Amelech, the understanding of David.

[Note: Col. 0887D. In Cardinal Thomasius’s edition of the Psalter, the title of this psalm is written thus: “To the end, for Maeleth, the understanding of David.” In the Roman edition: “For Amalech, the understanding of David.” Isidore, Clarius, and Vincent have differently: “For Machalach, the understanding of David.” The history of Amalech is related in 1 Kings, chapter XXX, concerning which Bede writes in this title. The interpretation of the name Amalech also varies. Amalech is interpreted “a licking people,” because those who desire earthly things too greatly seem already, by embracing them, as it were to lick them; therefore this psalm is composed for their conversion or punishment. So Bede. But where *Maelech* is found in place of *Amelech*, as in St Augustine and the Vulgate, that name is interpreted “giving birth” or “sorrowing.” According to St Jerome, this psalm contains the voice of the Prophet reproving sinners and ungodly persons; St Bruno followed him in his exposition, portraying the perfidy of the Jews.]

Amelech is interpreted “a brutish people,” concerning whom it is said at the beginning of this psalm: “The fool said in his heart: There is no God.” And indeed he who says this is foolish, brutish, and senseless. This, moreover, is the understanding of David and of all others who believe that God exists.

“406. The fool said in his heart: There is no God.” Although this may generally be understood of all nations that do not know God, it is especially understood of the Jews, who, seeing our Saviour clothed in human flesh, believed him to be merely human and not God. Hence they also said: “According to the law he ought to die, because he made himself the Son of God” (John XIX.7). But the Apostle says, on the contrary: “He did not consider equality with God a thing to be seized” (Phil. II.6). Likewise the Lord himself says: “If you do not believe me, believe the works” (John X.38). And elsewhere: “If I had not done among them works which no one else did, they would not have sin; but now they have no excuse for their sin” (John XV.22).

“They are corrupted and have become abominable in their desires.” They are corrupted, he says, from the faith of the patriarchs and prophets, because the one whom they deny to be God was adored and worshipped by the patriarchs and prophets. Thus they rightly became abominable both to God and to human beings in their perverse desires. “There is none who does good, not even one.” Because, he says, they are such and have departed from the faith of the holy Fathers, there is no one among them who does good, because whatever is not from faith is evil. Indeed, their prayers too, as it is written (Ps. CVIII.7), become sin for them. Therefore there is none among them who does good; yet there is none among all others either, down to the one. Thus there is one people, and that alone, which does good: by it the Christian people is signified. For there is no other faith able to save except the faith of Christians alone. The following words make this clear.

“The Lord looked down from heaven upon the children of men, to see whether there is one who understands or seeks God.” Behold what he found them to be. It follows:

“All have turned aside; together they have become useless. There is none who does good, not even one.” It has therefore been proved by divine authority that there is none who does good, not even one—except that one through whom, as we have just said, the Christian people is signified. For it alone has the understanding mentioned in this psalm’s title, “the understanding of David”; it alone seeks God, because it alone possesses the faith that leads to God. But all the rest have turned aside. From where, and to where? From truth to error, from light to darkness, from good to evil. They all did this together and equally, and therefore they all became useless and vain: useless, indeed, because they can benefit neither themselves nor others.

“Will not all who work iniquity know, who devour my people as the eating of bread? They did not call upon God; there they trembled with fear where there was no fear. For God scatters the bones of those who please themselves. They were confounded, because God despised them.” Will not all who do these and such things someday know and understand that God scatters the bones of those who strive to please themselves rather than God? For what should we understand by bones except all their strength and power? This has in large part already been scattered, and in the end will be scattered altogether. By this we should understand not Jews alone, but tyrants and heretics as well. For all these alike work iniquity and devour God’s people as the eating of bread. Of such people it is said: “For they have devoured Jacob and laid waste his place” (Ps. LXXVIII.7). By this it is most clearly signified with what avidity these wicked people killed God’s holy people. These are those of whom the Apostle says: “Although they knew God, they did not worship him as God, but became vain in their reasonings; and, claiming to be wise, they became fools. They changed the glory of the incorruptible God into the likeness of corruptible man, birds, and serpents” (Rom. I.21). Hence it continues: “There they trembled where there was no fear.” For such things ought not to have been feared—things which, blinded by their own malice, they feared and worshipped as God. They would not have killed Christ unless they had feared losing both place and nation, saying: “If we let him go on thus, the Romans will come and take away both our place and our nation. They were confounded, because God despised them” (John XI.48). And God rightly despised them and chose the nations in their place, because they themselves despised God, saying: “We have no king but Caesar, and we will not have this man reign over us” (John XIX.15); and they preferred a robber to Christ the Lord.

“Who will give salvation to Israel out of Zion, when the Lord turns away the captivity of his people?” It is read in the books of the Prophets that “from Zion will come he who will take away and turn away captivity from Jacob” (Zeph. II.7). He is our Saviour, who worked salvation in the midst of the earth—that is, in the city of Jerusalem—and liberated all his faithful from the captivity of the devil. The Jews therefore wait in vain for another who will rescue them from captivity. “Jacob will exult and Israel will rejoice.” In this, he says, and not in another, Jacob will exult: namely, he who supplants evil spirits and vices. And Israel will rejoice when he sees God face to face. For although Jacob and Israel are the same person, he is called Jacob in one respect and Israel in another: Jacob in this life, Israel in the other life. In this life he is a supplanter; in the other he will see God, as John the Apostle says: “Now we are children of God, and what we shall be has not yet appeared; but we know that, when he appears, we shall be like him, because we shall see him as he is” (1 John III.2).

## Psalm LIII. To the end, in hymns, the understanding of David, when the Ziphites came and said to Saul: Is not David hidden among us?

[Note: Col. 0889D. The title of this psalm is given in the same manner by all expositors of the Psalter. It comprises the story of David’s betrayal by the Ziphites, as found in 1 Kings, chapter XXVI. Throughout the psalm, therefore, the Prophet sings of his deliverance and gives God thanks for it. In Bede, Ziphites is interpreted “flourishing”; in our Bruno, “sprouting.” He himself draws out and explains the mystical sense from the literal sense.]

Wherever David sets forth his “understanding,” he shows that what he says is to be understood not literally but spiritually. For who could not understand literally the matters related in this title? But he understood them one way, and others another. Nor is a simple history related here: the Ziphites, interpreted “sprouting,” are said to have come to Saul in order to deliver David to him. By the Ziphites, therefore, let the Jews be understood, who abounded in the offspring of riches and children. These are the people who handed our Saviour over to the rulers of the earth for death.

“O God, save me in your name, and deliver me in your power.” “O God,” he says, “save me in your name,” that is, through the invocation of your name. For the Son invoked the Father by name when he said: “Father, into your hands I commend my spirit” (Luke XXIII.46). For this is the proper name of him who is Father of all things; yet he is Father of the Son by nature, while he is Father of others by adoption or creation. “And deliver me in your power,” which is so great that no one can resist it.

[Note: Col. 0890D. Ghislain manuscript: “nothing.”]

This power alone restrains evil spirits, so that they cannot carry out their will everywhere; if it had not opposed them, nothing else could have resisted them. Hence it is written of their prince: “There is no power upon earth”

[Note: Col. 0890D. The same Ghislain manuscript: “under heaven.”]

“that can be compared with him, who was made to fear no one.” Nevertheless, they are so bound by God’s power that they do not even have power over swine.

“O God, hear my prayer; receive with your ears the words of my mouth.” Prayer was not necessary for him whose will alone was sufficient. Therefore he prays not for himself but for us, so that by his example and instruction we may learn what we ought to do in such an event.

“For strangers have risen up against me, and the strong have sought my soul; and they have not set God before their sight.” Above the Jews were called Ziphites; now they are called strangers, because, though they were close in flesh, they made themselves strangers in mind and evil will by rising against him with such hatred. These are they of whom it is elsewhere said: “Alien sons have lied to me” (Ps. XVII.46). They were strong, not in bodily strength but in an abundance of iniquity and malice. Such is the strength they possess. “And they have not set God before their sight.” For if they had kept God before the eyes of their mind, they could never have acted so impiously and cruelly; but their malice blinded them, and they did not consider what they were doing.

“For behold, God helps me, and the Lord is the receiver of my soul.” The Father helped the Son as much as the Son himself willed, for he had come for the purpose of dying; had he not wished to die, he could by no means have been killed. But what benefit would there have been in his being born if he had not died? Thus the Father helped him in that he fulfilled his whole desire: destroying death, conquering the devil, and liberating humanity. Hence it is also said: “You have granted him the desire of his soul. And the Lord is the receiver of his soul.”

[Note: Col. 0890D. Ghislain manuscript: “my soul.”]

For who else ought to receive it except the divinity itself, which was ineffably united to it? As soon as our Saviour gave up his spirit, that most holy soul, together with the divinity, penetrated the barriers of hell; and, after despoiling hell, brought out with itself the souls of the saints who were held captive there. Therefore he who received Christ’s soul was stronger than those who maliciously sought Christ’s soul. Of them it continues:

“Turn back evil upon my enemies.” Turn back, he says, upon my enemies those evils which they wished to do to me. For, if they could, they wished to remove his memory from the earth; their own names, deservedly, have been erased from the book of life.

“And in your truth destroy them.” What is said now, “in your truth destroy them,” is like what he says elsewhere: “that you may be justified in your words” (Ps. L.6). For in many places the Lord threatens death and destruction to the Jewish people if it should depart from faith in and worship of him. It is therefore necessary that they be destroyed and confounded, so that God may be true and his words fulfilled.

“I will sacrifice to you willingly, and confess your name, O Lord, because it is good.” They, he says, rise against me and seek to destroy my soul, and what I am going to do of my own accord, they wish to compel me to do as though unwilling. Yet I shall willingly sacrifice to you and offer myself, so that by this death of mine I may rescue from eternal death those who will believe in me. “And I shall confess your name”: through my disciples and faithful ones I shall praise your name among every nation. For this is good, holy, and just: that your name should everywhere be praised and proclaimed.

“For from every tribulation you have delivered me.” It lay in his power both to restrain his enemies and to lessen tribulations; whatever was in his will was wholly in his power. Hence he himself says: “I have power to lay down my soul and power to take it up again” (John X.18). “And your eye has looked upon my enemies.” It looked, indeed: it saw and knew; it mercifully received those who repented, but destroyed those persevering in malice and will never again have mercy on them.

## Psalm LIV. To the end, in hymns, the understanding of David.

Where “understanding” is set down, the letter is excluded and a deeper understanding is sought.

“Hear, O God, my prayer, and do not despise my supplication; attend to me and hear me.” Our Saviour teaches us with what persistence we ought to pray, by repeating one and the same thing so often. We have often said already that such prayers were not necessary for him, in whose will and power all things are placed. But if Christ’s humanity spoke this in its heart, the divinity that heard was at hand.

“I was grieved in my exercise and troubled by the voice of the enemy and by the tribulation of the sinner.” These afflictions are common and natural to all human beings; unless our Saviour had had them, he would not have been believed to be a true human being. It was therefore necessary that he show that he had them and refute heretics who believed and preached otherwise. Thus the Lord had these affections, but he had them as he willed: he was grieved as much as he willed and troubled as much as he willed. Thus it is read in the Gospel (John XI.33) that at Lazarus’s death he groaned in spirit and troubled himself. But what does he mean when he says, “in my exercise”? What was Christ’s exercise? Our Saviour was not idle: every day he devoted himself to preaching and, through miracles and words, summoned his hearers to the way of truth. Yet in this activity he was sometimes grieved, more by their unbelief than by the injuries inflicted upon him through their perversity.

“For iniquities have turned aside against me.” “Therefore,” he says, “I was troubled by the voice of the enemy and by the tribulation of the sinner, because iniquities have turned aside against me”: that is, the iniquities which the wicked and ungodly displayed in my Passion and made manifest by turning and directing them against me.

[Note: Col. 0891D. Ghislain manuscript: “all their iniquities.”]

By calling them “the enemy” and “the sinner,” he uses the singular for the plural, a practice very common in both sacred and secular writings. “And in anger they afflicted me.” It is difficult to say how many torments those most wicked people inflicted on our Saviour by scourging, spitting upon him, striking him with blows, and doing similar things.

[Note: Col. 0891D. The same Ghislain manuscript reads: “It shames one to say.”]

“My heart was troubled within me, and fear of death fell upon me.” That disturbance quickly passed; that fear could indeed fall upon him, but could not remain. For if in so great a storm he had in no way been troubled, he would not have been thought to share our nature.

[Note: Col. 0892D. The edition is corrected from the Ghislain manuscript.]

Hence it follows:

“Fear and trembling came upon me, and darkness covered me.” Fear and trembling indeed came upon him, but could do nothing against him. When he went out to meet the Jews coming to seize him and cast them all to the ground with one word, he showed clearly enough both that he did not fear and that whatever he willed was in his power. Where there is such power, fear can have no place. By the darkness that covered him, however, we understand the raging multitude of wicked people, of whom John the Apostle says: “The light shines in darkness, and the darkness did not comprehend it” (John I.5). That sinners are called darkness, hear the Apostle saying: “You were once darkness, but now you are light in the Lord” (Eph. V.10).

“And I said: Who will give me wings like a dove, that I may fly and be at rest?” This means as though he said: “I am now weary of association with these people; I am weary of dwelling in this place. I must pass elsewhere and seek another people who will obey me.” This is what he says elsewhere: “Your house will be left to you desolate” (Matt. XXIII.38). And, as Josephus reports, voices of angels were heard in the Temple: “Let us leave these dwellings.” Therefore the Lord took wings like those of a dove, left the land of the Jews, flew to the nations, and rested there—he who found no rest in Judaea. Hence he says: “Upon whom will my Spirit rest, except upon one humble, quiet, and trembling at my words?” (Isa. LXVI.2). The Lord rightly took a dove’s wings: those, namely, of the dove that is read to have descended upon him when the Father’s voice was heard: “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased” (Matt. XVII.5).

“Behold, I fled far away and remained in solitude.” He sought wings and found them, for he himself possessed them; he flew and rested in solitude. A solitude is called a place where there is no human habitation. Such, however, was formerly the people of the nations, because, like brute animals, it was given over to pleasure and had no knowledge of God. And as though someone said: “Would that he had done this from the beginning, rather than remain so long with that impious and ungrateful nation!” he says: “I waited for him who would save me from faintheartedness and the storm.” Thus, he says, he taught in such a way that everything happened in its proper order and I awaited the ordering of the divinity, which

[Note: Col. 0893D. Ghislain manuscript: “which [governed] me everywhere, etc.”]

governed all things and saved me from faintheartedness and storm. Anyone who reads their histories can readily understand that the Jews are naturally fainthearted. Hence they are often called rebellious and unbelieving.

“Cast them down, O Lord, and divide their tongues, for I have seen iniquity and contradiction in the city by day and night.” The Jews were cast down because throughout all nations they were forcibly dragged away and subjected to servitude. Their tongues were divided because they do not speak one language as before, but some speak Greek, others Latin, and others barbarian languages, according to the provinces and places in which they dwell. By this he already signified that they were to be divided and scattered into all parts of the world. They are rightly divided and separated from one another, so that they may fail and cease even through their small number, since they are ready day and night to quarrel and contradict. For even to this day, wherever they are, the Jews do not cease to speak and fight against the truth. In this passage the Lord testifies that he saw their iniquity and contradiction through individual cities, and especially in the city of Jerusalem, saying: “For I have seen iniquity and contradiction in the city by day and night.”

“Iniquity will surround her upon her walls, and toil and injustice in her midst.” Iniquity, he says, and toil and injustice, rooted and established in her midst, will surround her upon her walls. For this is the sense: wretched is that city which is fortified, all around and in its centre, by such defences.
