What should we understand by her walls except the scribes, priests, and all others who appeared to be the people’s protection? The wiser they were, the more they abounded in every iniquity and malice.

“And usury and deceit did not depart from her streets.” If usury and deceit were in the streets, what do we suppose was in hidden and secret places? If such things were done openly, we do not doubt that far worse things were done in concealment.

“If my enemy had cursed me, I should surely have endured it; and if one who hated me had spoken great things against me, I should surely have hidden myself from him. But you, a man of one mind with me, my leader and my acquaintance, who together with me took sweet food, in the house of God we walked in agreement” [Col. 0894B]—it is understood: acquiescing in their evil counsels, you delivered me to death. “Let death come upon them,” upon those who led you into this crime. But let us now consider the meaning.

It is commonplace for an enemy to curse, persecute, and speak evil of an enemy. But for a friend to betray, persecute, and curse his lord and master is altogether absurd, unfitting, alien, and unbearable. For who could hide himself from such a man, or escape the snares of such a man? Judas, until that time, had been of one mind with the Lord, familiar with him, and a participant in his secrets and counsel. The Lord loved him as he loved the others, although he knew that he would someday become such a man [Col. 0894C]. The Lord judges only the present: he looks neither to the past nor to the future. Whatever you may have been, if you are good now, be secure: “In whatever hour the sinner is converted, says the Lord, I shall not remember any of his iniquities” (Ezek. XXXIII, 13). Yet one must always keep watch, because we do not know the day or the hour. “But you,” he says, “a man of one mind with me, my leader”—that is, a leader and apostle, appointed by me like all the other apostles. “And my acquaintance,” whom I counted among my foremost and most intimate disciples.

“You who together with me took sweet food”: both spiritual and bodily food, according to the saying, “He who dips his hand with me in the dish, he shall betray me” (Matt. XXVI, 23). For he himself was one of those [Col. 0894D] to whom the Lord said: “To you it is given to know the mystery of the kingdom of God, but to the rest in parables” (Mark IV, 11). These indeed were the most sweet foods which he took together with the Lord: “in the house of God we walked in agreement.” For he often followed the Lord into Solomon’s Temple, with agreement and reverence, and showed before all the people that he was both his friend and disciple. Therefore, if he did not fear God, he ought at least to have been ashamed before men.

“Let death come upon them.” Upon those who shared in your counsel, who gave you money, and who were privy to so great a crime. “And let them descend alive into hell.” Behold, they have already been judged [Col. 0895A] and condemned; the sentence of death has already come upon them. Nothing remains except that, when the resurrection has taken place, they may descend alive into hell—those who are now there in soul, suffering torments.

“For wickedness is in their dwellings, in their midst.” For unless wickedness were in their hearts, which we understand by “dwellings,” they could never have committed so great a crime.

“But I cried out to God, and the Lord heard me.” This cry was not of the mouth, but of the will alone. Great is the cry of his will; it resounds most clearly in the ears of divinity, and there is no delay between prayer and being heard. For Moses too, though far inferior to Christ, cried out in his heart; and nevertheless the Lord said [Note: [Col. 0895D] The same manuscript: “and his lips were not moving.”]: “Why [Col. 0895B] do you cry to me?” (Exod. XIV, 15).

“In the evening, and in the morning, and at noon, I shall recount and proclaim, and he will hear my voice.” It should be noted that, with the order changed, he first placed evening, then morning, and afterward noon. Our Savior therefore promises that through his disciples and faithful people he will recount and proclaim what happened to him in the evening, in the morning, and at noon, because these events are most worthy of remembrance and occurred in the order in which they are set down. For in the evening, placed upon the cross, he gave up his spirit. Hence the saying: “The lifting up of my hands is an evening sacrifice” (Ps. CXL, 2). In the morning, on the third day, he rose again; at noon he ascended to heaven. The Church therefore recounts what occurred in the evening, morning, [Col. 0895C] and noon, because it never ceases daily to sing and preach Christ’s passion, resurrection, and ascension. God hears this voice, because there is no praise or jubilation in which he takes greater delight.

“He will deliver my soul in peace from those who draw near [Note: [Col. 0895D] The Vulgate reads *appropinquant*, ‘draw near’; so too Cassiodorus.] to me, because among many they were with me.” Who are these who draw near to the Lord, whom he says were with him among many others, and from whom he nevertheless asked that his soul might be delivered so that it might have peace? For how were they with him if he desired his soul to be delivered from them? I think that some were assigned to guard him at the very time of his passion, lest he should escape. Hence elsewhere he says: “Flight has perished from me, and there is none who seeks my soul [Col. 0895D]” (Ps. CXLI, 6). That we may understand this more readily from an easy example, I know that the same happened to me: when I was once captured, certain persons were assigned to guard me. They hated me more than the others; they were always with me, sat beside me, and I could do nothing without them. Thus they were with me, but not for good, nor were they with me by my will. I think it is easily understood from this example how those were with the Lord whom he says were with him among many. Thus far our Savior has spoken; the Prophet speaks the remainder [Note: [Col. 0896D] (589) The Ghislerius manuscript: the edition supplies this reading.].

[Col. 0896A]

“God will hear and humble them—he who is before the ages and remains for eternity.” God, he says, will hear, and without doubt will hear the evil and improper things which the Jews speak against him; and he will humble them, so that, just as they were once more exalted than all nations, so conversely, for their iniquities, they may be subjected to all nations.

“He who is before the ages and remains for eternity.” Him they mocked, saying (John VIII, 57): “Now we know that you have a demon: you are not yet fifty years old, and have you seen Abraham?” To them he said: “Before Abraham came to be, I am.”

“There is no change in them, and they have not feared God.” There is no change in them, he says—that is, in those who do not fear God—by which they might be changed from their wickedness through repentance and healed. Hence the Lord also says through the prophet: “Blind the heart of this people, lest perhaps they be converted and I heal them” (Isa. VI, 10). And therefore not without reason “the Lord stretched out his hand in repaying them.”

“They have defiled his covenant.” The Jews defile God’s covenant because they expound it perversely and contrary to faith, and proclaim that the things said concerning Christ were said concerning Antichrist. Therefore they have quite deservedly been divided and scattered throughout the whole world. “By the anger of his countenance.” He aptly said, “by the anger of his countenance,” because anger is recognized most swiftly in the face. “And his heart drew near.” Formerly the heart and will [Col. 0896C] of God were far from the Jews, because they could not know his will; but now, expelled from their homeland and exiled for so long, they can know [Note: [Col. 0896D] The Ghislerius manuscript: “and oppressed by other calamities, they can easily know God’s will.”] and understand that God is angry with them. God’s heart and wisdom also drew near to the Jews in another way, when our Savior began to preach among them.

“They softened their words beyond oil, and they themselves are darts.” The Jews did this when they said: “Teacher, we know that you are truthful, and teach the way of God in truth; and you care for no one, for you do not regard the person of a man” (Mark XII, 14). Do not these words seem sufficiently soft and sweet to you? Yet they are darts by which they strove to strike and wound him. For they said this, as is read in the Gospel, in order to catch him in his words. But Jesus, knowing their wickedness, said: “Why do you test me, hypocrites?” (Matt. XXIV, 18).

“Cast your thought upon God, and he himself will nourish you.” You, he says, Christian and faithful man, flee the fellowship of the Jews, because, as the Apostle says, “Their speech spreads like cancer” (II Tim. XI, 17), and they easily deceive their hearers. “Cast your thought upon the Lord,” and he will teach you. He will nourish you with Catholic and spiritual teaching. This is what the Apostle James says: “If anyone lacks [Col. 0897A] wisdom, let him ask God, who gives abundantly to all, and it shall be given him” (James I, 5).

“He will not give the righteous man eternal wavering.” He gives wavering when he places a person amid things contrary to temptation; “but God tempts no one” (ibid., 12). Therefore, when a person is tempted by things that appear contrary to faith, let him quickly return to himself and recognize that such a thought—or rather, temptation—is not from God. “But you, O God, will lead them down into the pit of destruction.” They strive, he says, to cast your faithful into the pit of error; but, more unhappily for them, he will lead them into the pit of ruin and perdition.

“Men of blood and deceit shall not halve their days.” This is a universal threat against murderers, [Col. 0897B] Jews, heretics, and all deceitful persons, deceivers, and murderers of souls. These will not halve their days, because they will not live as long as they hope to live. Hence it fittingly follows:

“But I will hope in you, O Lord, and shall not set for myself long days of this life; but at whatever hour it pleases you, and you wish to call me, I shall be ready.” He fittingly said “their days,” because God orders and disposes their days differently from the way they themselves do, and they do not attend to what is said elsewhere: “You have appointed his bounds, which cannot be passed” (Job XIV, 5).

## PSALM LV. TO THE END: FOR THE PEOPLE WHO HAVE BEEN MADE FAR FROM THE SAINTS; DAVID, FOR THE INSCRIPTION OF THE TITLE, WHEN THE FOREIGNERS HELD HIM IN GATH.

[Col. 0897C]

That people which was made far from David’s saints and faithful ones is the Jews. But when did this happen? In the inscription of the title, when they denied that Christ was their king, saying to Pilate: “Do not write, ‘King of the Jews,’ but, ‘He said, I am King of the Jews’” (John XIX, 21). Then the foreigners held him in Gath [Note: [Col. 0897D] *Allophyli* is a Greek word, from ἀλλόφυλος, meaning a man of another tribe, race, or nation; therefore by this name we understand strangers. Accordingly, St Bruno’s interpretation can be sustained, as will become clear to anyone who gives it a little attention.]. *Allophyli* is interpreted “without a head”; by them we understand these same Jews, who have been beheaded and are without a head, having neither king nor priest from their own nation. Gath means “winepress.” It signifies the city of Jerusalem, in which, as grapes in a winepress, that whole people was pressed, and drenched and bloodied all that land with its own [Col. 0897D] blood. Thus Jerusalem became a winepress not only for the saints killed in it, but also for its own nation.

“Have mercy on me, O Lord, for man has trampled me down; all day long, waging war, he has afflicted me.” The Church speaks against those who have been made far from the saints. In many ways evil men—namely, Jews, heretics, and tyrants—formerly trampled down and afflicted the holy Church, and false Christians still do not cease to afflict and trample it down. Therefore he very fittingly said, “all day,” because this affliction and trampling will not cease except when the day ends.

[Col. 0898A]

“My enemies have trampled me down all day.” Not only, he says, has man trampled me down—not only that people which, though near, was made far from the saints in the inscription of the title—but all my other enemies too have trampled me down, and indeed still do not cease to trample me down, because the day of trampling is not yet ended. But tell me: when did this trampling of you begin? “From the height of the day.” This day is Christ, who says of himself: “I am the light of the world; he who follows me does not walk in darkness” (John VIII, 12). From the time when this day was exalted and lifted above the heavens, the holy Church began both to be afflicted and to be trampled down. For the Lord himself foretold this to his disciples: “The hour will come,” he said, “when everyone who kills you will think that he offers service to God” (John XVI, [Col. 0898B] 2).

“Because many who fight against me will fear; but I will hope in you, O Lord.” The Church consoles herself, considering what punishment is prepared for her adversaries and what glory is prepared for her afflictions. Those who fight against me, she says, will fear at the judgment; but I, because I shall hope in you, shall fear nothing. Therefore my sorrow will be turned into joy, while their joy will be turned into sorrow.

“In God I shall praise my words; all day I shall hope in God; I shall not fear what man may do to me.” Let each person therefore praise his own words, not because they are his own, but rather because they speak of God [412] and are from God. Our words are praiseworthy if they do not depart from truth and if they suit the time and place [Col. 0898C]. Such words our conscience can praise; otherwise it cannot praise them. “All day,” throughout the whole time of my life, whatever happens to me, whether prosperous or adverse, “I shall hope in the Lord,” and therefore “I shall not fear what man may do to me.”

“All day they cursed my words against me.” I, he says, praised my words in God and declared them faithful and Catholic; they, conversely, were busily disputing against me, blaspheming all my words and striving to weaken and destroy them by their arguments. Hence it follows: “All their counsels are for evil.” For all the counsels of Jews and heretics are for evil [Col. 0898D]: they both kill souls and cause simple people to depart from the way of truth.

“They will dwell and hide themselves; they themselves will watch my heel.” Such were those of whom the Gospel says that, “when Jesus entered the house of a certain ruler of the Pharisees on the Sabbath to eat bread, they watched him” (Luke XIV, 1). Hence the Apostle complains of certain false brothers who slipped in to spy out their consciences; concerning them the Lord himself also says: “Beware of false prophets, who come to you in sheep’s clothing, but inwardly [Col. 0899A] are ravening wolves” (Matt. VII, 15). Dwelling deceitfully among the saints and concealing the malice of their hearts, these men pretended to be Christians. Whomever they could, they either accused or deceived. They watched their heels: if they had learned that they had offended in anything, fallen, or acted contrary to the law, they committed it to memory and, at a suitable time, raised it against them in accusation. A heel signifies a fall, because one who falls falls upon the heel. It follows:

“My soul waited; for nothing you will save them.” It is the desire and expectation of the saints that the ungodly should be punished as they deserve, unless they turn from their ungodliness to God. What he says, “for nothing you will save them,” is as though he said [Col. 0899B]: There is nothing in them for which they ought to be saved. Hence it follows: “In anger you will crush peoples.” This will occur at the judgment, when, understanding that God is angry with them, they will be cast into eternal fire.

“O God, I have declared my life to you; I have placed my tears before you.” Blessed is the conscience of that man who so entrusts his life to God and places his tears before him. God sees all things; our very hearts speak to him and declare to him whatever is in them.

“As in your promise, my enemies will turn backward in whatever day I call upon you.” As you promised, he says, whenever I call upon you, let my enemies turn backward, so that they may not be able to withstand me [Col. 0899C]. For his promise is this: “I will not leave you or forsake you” (John XIV, 18); and, “Behold, I am with you all days, even to the consummation of the age” (Matt. XXIV, 20). Likewise: “I will give you a mouth and wisdom, which all your adversaries will not be able to resist or contradict” (Luke XXI, 15).—“Behold, I have known that you are my God.” Behold, he says, I have known that you are my God, who never forsake those hoping in you; and behold, you deign suddenly to reveal inwardly to me what is to happen to me. For while the saints were speaking, they were often suddenly instructed by the spirit of prophecy concerning what was to happen to them.

“In God I shall praise the Word, and in the Lord I shall praise the saying; in God I shall hope; I shall not fear what [Col. 0899D] man may do to me [Note: [Col. 0899D] Cassiodorus understands these words as spoken by the orthodox Church: “For in the Father she promises to praise the Son, so that whatever is said of the one may equally be thought of the other. For when we preach the eternal and omnipotent Father, we undoubtedly confess the eternal and omnipotent [Col. 0900D] Son. The proclamation is one for both, because the power of both is one, their glory undivided, since their nature is indivisible,” etc.].” Because you are my God, he says, I shall praise the Word in you and praise the saying in you: the faith which I have preached and the teaching which I have proclaimed. I shall never deny it, but shall uphold it even unto death. And because I shall hope in you, I shall not fear what man may do to me. For human strength can do nothing against God’s power and will.

“In me, O God, are vows which I shall render: praises to you.” No one, whether rich or [Col. 0900A] poor, can excuse himself. Each has within himself and in his heart something which he can vow and render to God. You do not have gold; you do not have silver; you do not have money to offer God. Nor does he require this of you. Hear him himself saying: “Render to Caesar the things that are Caesar’s, and to God the things that are God’s” (Matt. XXII, 21). Let this always be your vow and desire: that you may always praise and bless him and cease from every iniquity; and that is enough for you. Hence it is so often said in these psalms: Praise the Lord; bless the Lord; give thanks to the Lord; sing psalms to the Lord; and so forth. You can fulfill these even in silence, if you have a pure heart and delight and rejoice in him who made you. Hence it is said elsewhere: “Delight yourself in the Lord, and he will give you the petitions of your heart” (Ps. XXXVI, [Col. 0900B] 4). And the Apostle says: “Rejoice in the Lord always; again I say, rejoice” (Phil. IV, 4). This indeed is the sacrifice of praise which we ought daily to offer to God.

“Because you have delivered my soul from death”—not at any ordinary price, but by your own blood. Hence the Apostle says: “For you were bought at a great price; glorify and bear God in your body” (I Cor. VI, 20).—“My eyes from tears,” which smoke, deceit, or some affliction commonly causes to flow. For those who are in fire cannot be without smoke and [413] affliction. But those of whom it is said will not feel this affliction: “God will wipe away every tear from the eyes of the saints, and death shall be no more, nor mourning, nor crying, nor any pain; for the former things have passed away, and all things have become new” (Apoc. XXI, 4).—“My feet from slipping.” What advantage, then, was it to those of whom it is said above: “They will watch the shoe” (Ps. LV, 7)? “Woe to one alone, because when he falls, there is no one to lift him up” (Eccles. IV, 10). But the saints are not alone, because they are always with the Lord, and say: “You have held my right hand, that I may please the Lord in the light of the living.” Therefore, he says, “You have delivered my soul from death, my eyes from tears, my feet from slipping, that I may please the Lord in the light of the living,” because otherwise I could neither have been there nor pleased the Lord. He fittingly said “in the light of the living,” because they alone will be in the light; they alone will have life [Col. 0900D]. For that life which is always in torments ought rather to be called death than life.

## PSALM LVI. TO THE END: DO NOT DESTROY DAVID, IN THE INSCRIPTION OF THE TITLE, WHEN HE FLED FROM THE FACE OF SAUL INTO THE CAVE.

When was it said, “Do not destroy”? In the inscription of the title. When was that inscription? When David fled from the face of Saul into the cave. This, however, never occurred according to the letter, and therefore must be referred to the end. For in the inscription of the title, concerning [Col. 0901A] which we have already spoken above, when the Jews said to Pilate, “Do not write, ‘King of the Jews,’” he answered them: “What I have written” (John XIX, 22). This was as much as if he had said, “Do not destroy.” The inscription was therefore preserved; and, whether the Jews wish it or not, Christ is King of the Jews. Then David—that is, our Savior—fled into the cave of the tomb from the face of Saul, by whom we understand the Jewish rulers. He fittingly said “fled,” because his body was entrusted to burial almost secretly and in haste [Note: [Col. 0901D] Cassiodorus explains the title’s words, “When he fled from the face of Saul into the cave,” otherwise: “This action appears very similar both in David and in the Lord. For as David, fleeing Saul, hid himself in a cave, so the divinity of the Lord Savior is shown to have been hidden from faithless Jews within the temple of his body. Thus the individual events which happened in the histories of David and Christ are common to them under this allusion,” etc.].

“Have mercy on me, God, have mercy on me, because my soul trusts in you.” The Church can say this confidently, because he is still dead, that he may have mercy upon her. “My soul trusts in you,” she says, who loved me so greatly that you laid down your soul for mine. “For no one has greater love than this, that a man lay down his soul for his friends” (John XV, 13).

“And I shall hope in the shadow of your wings, until iniquity passes away.” I see you, he says, as though saying, now hanging upon the cross and stretching out your hands and arms like wings. Protect me beneath the shadow of these wings, because I hope in the shadow of your wings. For the whole hope of Christians is the cross and passion of the Lord. The Church has this hope until the world passes away with its iniquities; afterward hope will no longer exist, once all that can be hoped for has been received. Hence the Apostle says: “But now faith, hope, and charity remain; but the greater of these is charity [Col. 0901C]” (I Cor. XIII, 13), because it will remain forever.

“I shall cry to God Most High, and to the Lord who has done me good.” I shall cry, he says, until iniquity passes away; afterward there will be no need to cry. But to whom shall I cry? To the Lord Most High and to the highest good; I shall cry to him from whom all good things proceed, to the Lord who has done me good. Count now, if you can, how many good things God has done for you. When you did not exist, he created and made you; and he not only made you, but made you in his own image and likeness. He gave you life and mercy: “He did not spare his own Son, but delivered him up for us all” (Rom. VIII, 32). But let us hear further how the Lord has done good to us.

“He sent from heaven and delivered me; he gave those who trampled me down over to reproach.” He sent, he says, from heaven—from himself, from his bosom and from his heart—and delivered me. “He gave those who trampled me down over to reproach”: namely, evil spirits, Jews, heretics, and tyrants. All these were given over to reproach because, as soon as they depart this life, they are plunged into darkness. He sent from heaven—but what did he send?

“God sent his mercy and his truth”: that is, Jesus Christ, his Son. He spoke excellently when he called him, not “merciful” and “true,” but rather, because of the greatness of his excellence, mercy and truth [Col. 0902A].

“He delivered my soul from the midst of young lions,” by whom we understand hostile people and evil spirits, because they were already prepared to devour it. Among them I slept for a long time, but I slept troubled; it was not sleep of quiet and peace, but of trouble and forgetfulness. Thus the frenzied commonly sleep, as do those who see terrible things in dreams. For those often frightened and troubled by dreams are afraid to sleep again, lest they happen to see similar things.

[414] “The sons of men: their teeth are weapons and arrows, and their tongue is a sharp sword.” It is no wonder, he says, that I slept troubled among such people and, forgetting myself, could not have peace and rest among those whose teeth are weapons and arrows, whose tongues are sharp swords, always ready to dispute, litigate, blaspheme, curse, deceive, and contradict [Col. 0902B].

“Be exalted above the heavens, O God, and let your glory be over all the earth.” He said above, “God sent his mercy and his truth,” that is, our Savior, concerning whom the title says that he lay hidden in the cave of the tomb. Now, however, he asks him to ascend above the heavens and reveal his glory to all nations. Having done this, he returns to the narrative and recounts in order the things he began.

“They prepared a snare for my feet and bent down [Col. 0902C] my soul.” Many are the snares and deceptions which wicked people set before the saints, by which they catch them and cause them to fall. The soul that stands upright contemplates heavenly things; but the bent soul looks only upon earthly and transitory things. Therefore, whoever seeks only earthly and transitory things ought not to doubt that his soul is bent down.

“They dug a pit before my face, and they themselves fell into it. For thus it is written elsewhere: He who prepares a pit for his brother himself falls into it first” (Eccles. X, 8). The pit, therefore, is deceit and deception; whoever makes it prepares a pit for himself, not only of deception but also of death and perdition. Concerning this pit the Lord says: “If the blind lead the blind, both fall into the pit” (Matt. XV, 14).

“My heart is ready, O God, my heart is ready; I shall sing and make psalm to the Lord [Note: [Col. 0902D] The Ghislerius manuscript: “and I shall say a psalm to the Lord.”].” Let them do whatever they wish, say whatever they wish, praise their doctrines, and disparage ours; yet my heart is always ready to sing, rejoice, praise, and proclaim the word of life and salvation, which must be announced to all nations. This is what he says: “I shall sing and say a psalm to the Lord.” But [Col. 0903A] where? On the psaltery and harp. For this is what follows:

“Awake, my glory; awake, psaltery and harp; I shall arise at dawn.” What do we understand by the psaltery and harp except the Old and New Testaments? The psaltery has ten strings, because there are ten words of the law. Three or four suffice on the harp. The three signify the mystery of the Trinity, while the four signify the corresponding number of Gospel books. The saints sing, therefore, either on the psaltery or on the harp, because they have no other song and harp than the Old and New Testaments. If the psaltery and harp are removed from the Church, it will have nothing to say, sing, or preach. Therefore all its glory is in the psaltery and harp, because without song, teaching, and knowledge it can have no glory. Although every melody of psaltery and harp is sweet and pleasant to hear, yet the sweetest is that which is played on the harp with three strings. Such is that song which, as the prophet Isaiah and the evangelist John say, the Seraphim and the four living creatures do not cease to sing: “Holy, holy, holy, Lord God almighty; the whole earth is full of his glory” (Apoc. IV, 8). The Church therefore rightly says: “Awake, my glory; awake, psaltery and harp”; and I shall indeed rise very early. You, she says, psaltery and harp, always be perfect [Note: [Col. 0903D] The Ghislerius manuscript: “ready.”], so that you may cause me no hindrance or delay, because I shall rise very early to sing. By saying that she will rise at dawn, she promises that throughout the whole day, from morning to evening—that is, throughout all the time of her life [Col. 0903C]—she will sing and rejoice.

“I shall give thanks to you among the peoples, O Lord, and sing a psalm to you among the nations.” I am ready, she says; I have a psaltery, I have a harp; and upon psaltery and harp I shall give thanks to you and praise you among the peoples, O Lord, and sing a psalm to you among the nations. Because the Jews are unwilling, she promises that she will sing psalms among the nations. To sing psalms is to fulfill the commands of the law in word and deed.

“Because your mercy has been magnified unto the heavens, and your truth unto the clouds.” God’s mercy and God’s truth are our Savior, because he is full of all mercy and truth, and in him and through him the Father’s mercy and truth have been revealed to all nations. This, she says, I shall give thanks for; this I shall preach; this I shall proclaim among all nations: that your mercy and truth have been magnified and exalted unto the heavens and unto the clouds—indeed, above all heavens and all clouds [Col. 0903D]. But, that this proclamation of mine may be true, come now out of the cave; come forth from the tomb. Be exalted, O God, above the heavens, and let your glory be manifest over all the earth. “Be exalted above the heavens, O God, and let your glory be over all the earth.”

## PSALM LVII. [415] TO THE END: DO NOT DESTROY DAVID, IN THE INSCRIPTION OF THE TITLE.

[Col. 0904A]

David commands that neither Pilate nor the Jews should dare to destroy what was placed in the inscription of the title. For it was written there in Hebrew, Greek, and Latin: “This is Jesus of Nazareth, King of the Jews” [Note: [Col. 0903D] Matthew, ch. XXVII, v. 37, has: “This is Jesus, [Col. 0904D] king of the Jews.” John, however, ch. XIX, 19: “Now there was written: Jesus of Nazareth, king of the Jews.”]. Therefore Hebrews, Greeks, and Latins alike are witnesses that the unhappy Jews crucified their king and their Lord.

“If indeed you speak justice truly, judge rightly, sons of men.” The Prophet himself speaks and rebukes the Jews for their iniquity. If indeed, he says, what you do is to speak justice, why do you not judge justly—unless it is because you are sons of men? “For every man is a liar, but God is true” (Rom. III, 4). As it is written that the sons of men are liars, so the sons of God are truthful: “But to as many as received him, he gave power to become sons of God, to those who believe in his name” (John I, 12). Christians alone, therefore, are truthful, since Christians alone are sons of God. You call Christ a good teacher; you say that he teaches the way of God in truth; you say that he cares for no one and does not regard the person of a man. You speak truly; you speak justice, because what you say is so. Why then do you not judge justly? Why do you condemn him to death? Why do you cry, “Crucify him,” against him, and accuse him as though he were an evildoer?

[Col. 0904C]

“For indeed you work iniquities in your heart upon the earth; your hands fashion iniquities.”—“From the heart,” says the Lord, “come forth evil thoughts, thefts, murders, perjuries, false testimonies, and the like” (Matt. VII, 21). These, then, are the things which evil and wicked men work in their heart—that is, upon earth—because such a heart is earth: foolish, heavy, and drawing downward. The hands of those persons fashion iniquities whose deeds agree in malice and iniquity.

“Sinners have been estranged from the womb; they have gone astray from the belly; they have spoken falsehood.” These are the sinners of whom it is said elsewhere: “Alien sons have lied to me” (Ps. XVII, 46); and again: “For aliens have risen up against me” (Ps. LIII, 5). Those who were near have become alien, and conversely those who were alien have become near. Hence it is written: “I will call ‘my people’ those who were not my people, and ‘having obtained mercy’ her who had not obtained mercy” (Rom. IX, 25). But to the former it is said: You are not my people. These men went astray from the womb, because from the time they were born they refused to receive the truth, and thus from the belly they spoke falsehood. For what can one who goes astray speak except falsehood?

“Their wrath is according to the likeness of a serpent.” But of what serpent? “Like that of a deaf asp which stops [Col. 0905A] its ears, which will not hear the voice of charmers or enchantments charmed by a wise man [Note: [Col. 0905D] The Vulgate reads: “and of the enchanter charming wisely.”].” The asp is a most cruel kind of serpent, of which it is written that “the venom of asps is incurable” (Deut. XXXII, 33). No charm can prevail against it unless it hears its own incantations; for when it is charmed, it blocks its ears with its tail and thus counts all incantations as nothing. Such are the Jews, who, with hardened hearts, always oppose the Christian religion and refuse either to hear or to receive evangelical preaching. The charmers are holy preachers, who, though they charm them wisely, are nevertheless despised by them; the Jews refuse to hear their words and charms and make themselves readier to contradict and curse than to hear [Col. 0905B] and believe. But their disputations and arguments are easily conquered and scattered. Hence it follows:

“God will break their teeth in their own mouth; the Lord will shatter the molars of lions.” What are we to understand by their teeth and molars, if not their arguments, syllogisms, and difficulties drawn from the Scriptures, by which they attempt to wound and deceive us? For often, when we speak with them, we see all their reasonings so suddenly crushed and broken that they have absolutely nothing they can answer. Hence it is added:

“They shall come to nothing, like water running down.” For it often happens that one who, shortly before, seemed like a flooding torrent to abound in examples and arguments, is soon dried up and deprived of arguments, utterly unable to find what to say. Whoever does not understand this should read the disputation which blessed Sylvester is said to have held with the Jews.

> [Note: Col. 0905D: Saint Bruno drew this from the Acts of Saint Sylvester, commonly circulated; Natalis Alexander, *Ecclesiastical History*, fourth century, dissertation 23, *On the Baptism of the Emperor Constantine*, demonstrates that they are apocryphal. Col. 0906D.]

This happens because the Lord “bends his bow until they are weakened.” God’s bow is the apostles and doctors, through whom the Lord sends his arrows and the most certain arguments of the Scriptures against them, until, weakened and conquered, they cease. Hence the Lord says to his disciples: “I will give you a mouth and wisdom which none of your adversaries will be able to resist or contradict” (Luke 21:15).

“They shall be taken away like melted wax.” This will occur at the judgment, and after the judgment, when they are cast with their prince into the fire. Hence it is added: “Fire fell upon them, and they did not see the sun.” In his customary manner he uses the past for the future. At the judgment, he says, as soon as that terrible sentence has been pronounced, they shall be taken away like melted wax, because they will be unable to resist so great a force. Then that fire by which the whole world will be set ablaze shall fall upon them, and thus they will pass from fire into fire. “And they shall not see the sun,” because, as it is written: “Let the wicked be taken away, lest they see the glory of God” (Isa. 26:10). For even if for a moment they see him, because it is written that “every eye shall see him” (Rev. 1), they shall immediately be removed from him; and this itself will be torment to them: they will desire to see him and will be unable to do so.

“Before your thorn-bush produces thorns, as living men, so in wrath he swallows them up.”

> [Note: Col. 0906D: Another Vulgate reading: “Before your thorns understood the thorn-bush.”]

The *rhamnus* is a kind of thorn-bush which has both a very pleasing flower and exceedingly sharp thorns. It signifies our Savior, the most beautiful flower from the root of Jesse, who speaks of himself, saying: “I am the flower of the field and the lily of the valleys” (Song 2:1). This thorn-bush now gives flowers, whose fragrance and sweetness refresh and delight our minds. By these flowers, of course, we understand his fragrant and most sweet words [Col. 0906B]. But he does not yet display the thorns; rather, with great patience he waits for sinners: “For he does not will the death of the sinner, but that he should turn and live” (Ezek. 33:11). He will appear thorny and terrible in judgment—but to sinners, who will be unable to endure his wounds and stings.

But before this your thorn-bush, O holy and faithful people of God, produces thorns and displays the stings of his severity, fire will swallow them up in wrath, as living men. For the Lord has not yet come to judgment, yet already the souls of all the wicked and condemned are swallowed up and tortured by fire. Before the judgment, therefore, souls alone will be tormented; after the judgment, both bodies and souls together will be tormented. Then indeed “the righteous man shall rejoice when he sees the vengeance of the wicked.” Meanwhile [Col. 0906C], “he shall wash his hands in the blood of sinners.” Sins indeed have no blood; but by blood we understand death, since we know death to be present in the shedding of blood. Never can God’s saints better wash their hands and their works—signified by hands—than by slaying the sins by whose contagion they had been defiled.

“And man shall say: If indeed there is fruit for the righteous, then indeed there is a God judging them upon the earth.” Opposites correspond to opposites, and it is as though he said: Let every person say, know, and understand that if the good receive fruit and recompense for their goodness, the evil likewise will endure judgment and punishment for their wickedness. But where is God? Everywhere. Therefore he is upon the earth; he sees and judges all things that are on the earth.

## PSALM LVIII. TO THE END: “DO NOT DESTROY”; OF DAVID, FOR THE INSCRIPTION OF THE TITLE, WHEN SAUL SENT AND GUARDED HIS HOUSE IN ORDER TO KILL HIM

No one will be able to destroy what the Holy Spirit has forbidden to be destroyed. Yet the chief priests and the other Jews, signified by Saul, wished to do this [Col. 0907A]. But because they could not do so, they sent guards to watch his tomb and to kill him. But how could those who was still lying dead in the tomb kill him again? They wished to kill him in that they tried to prevent his resurrection. For even to this day there are those who, as far as lies in them, kill him by contradicting his resurrection.

“Deliver me from my enemies, my God, and free me from those who rise up against me.” We have often said that whenever Christ asks something, prays for something, and shows himself to need something, all this pertains not to his divinity but solely to his humanity. Yet even his humanity had no need of speech or supplication, since it had and possessed all things in will alone [Col. 0907B]. All that was in Christ’s will was fulfilled; and the Prophet writes these things so that we too may know them—things which, unless they had been written, would not have come to our knowledge.

Thus Christ’s humanity obtained by will alone what other human beings commonly obtain by prayers and petitions. Our Savior also prays aloud, not for himself but for us, that by praying he may teach and instruct us, and make us know both his will and our benefit.

> [Note: Col. 0907D: The same manuscript: “sometimes.”]

Therefore what is said here—“Deliver me,” “free me,” and “save me”—is as though he said: I will that you deliver me; save me “from workers of iniquity and from men of blood.” Thus Christ’s will speaks and prays: it speaks not by asking, but by willing. We too are accustomed to speak this way concerning all matters which we know to rest with complete certainty in our will and power.

“For behold, they have seized my soul; strong men have rushed upon me; neither my iniquity nor my sin, O Lord.” Our Savior had no need to say these things, but we had need to hear them. Yet if he said them, he said them inwardly, in his heart; the Prophet, taught by the Holy Spirit, heard and wrote this. The Jews seized Christ’s soul not merely in deed, but in desire and hope. It is a very common manner of speaking for us to say that we possess what we most certainly hope to possess.

“Strong men have rushed upon me.” They are called strong because they brought their desire concerning Christ’s death to fulfillment [Col. 0907D]. For each person is strong in that matter in which he is able to accomplish his intention. “Neither my iniquity nor my sin, O Lord.”

“Without iniquity I ran, and I was directed.”

> [Note: Col. 0907D: The Vulgate has *direxi*, “I directed.”]

And who does not know it? What is this excuse? What is this defense? Did the divinity not know it—the divinity that was ineffably joined to the humanity and knew it to be wholly pure and blameless? Nevertheless, it is not unfitting that Christ’s prophet wished to write this concerning Christ’s conscience in order to convict wicked people. For our conscience says many things inwardly to God which our tongue does not say outwardly.

“Arise to meet me, and see.” I will, he says, that you come to meet and assist me and resist their purposes, so that, contrary to the permission of my will, they may have no power over me. This is what the Lord said to Pilate: “You would have no power over me unless it had been given you from above” (John 19:11).—“And see.” What? Their impious purpose and perverse intention: that they desire not merely to kill me [Col. 0908B]—which also pleases both me and you—but even to remove my name and the remembrance of my name entirely from the earth.

“And you, Lord God of hosts, God of Israel, attend to visit all the nations.” He is the God of hosts, in whose hand and power are all powers, who gives them to whom he wills and draws to himself whomever he wills.

> [Note: Col. 0907D: The same Ghisian manuscript: “he distributes as he wills and repels from himself whom he wills.” Saint Bruno says this in accordance with the Apostle’s teaching concerning God’s free and absolute election to glory, and concerning those whose hardening in sin he permits: “It is not of him who wills, nor of him who runs, but of God who shows mercy. Therefore he has mercy on whom he wills, and whom he wills he hardens” (Rom. 9:15). Col. 0908D.]

He is the God of Israel, by whom we understand all who believe in him, love him, and know him. “You, Lord God of hosts, God of Israel, attend to visit all the nations,” because those to whom I was sent refused to receive me. This has now been fulfilled, because through his disciples the Lord visited all nations and called them to faith, saying: “Go into all the world; preach the Gospel to every creature” (Mark 15:11).—“Do not have mercy on all who work iniquity.” All indeed were called, but not all were chosen. For those who work iniquity and persevere with hardened heart in wickedness until the end—even if they have been baptized and received Christ’s faith—God will nevertheless not have mercy upon them.

“They shall return at evening, suffer hunger like dogs, and go around the city.” These Jews who now exist, he says, are unconvertible; but those who are to come will at last be converted to you.

> [Note: Col. 0908D: The same manuscript: “But when? At evening. These vices will be ended. Then this world will come to evening, and now indeed the Jews will be converted.”]

Thus it is written: “In those days Judah shall be saved, and Israel shall dwell confidently” (Jer. 23:6) [Col. 0908D]. And elsewhere: “Though the number of the children of Israel be like the sand of the sea, they shall return” (Isa. 10:21).—“And they shall suffer hunger like dogs.” “Now,” he says, “full of indignation and of their own error and wickedness, they disdain to believe the word of life. But then, like very hungry dogs, they will importunately press themselves forward to receive ecclesiastical and spiritual food, and will show that they have endured a long hunger.”

> [Note: Col. 0908D: Cassiodorus gives the same interpretation of this passage. After citing Romans 11:25—“I do no[lacuna], brethren, [concerning] this mystery, that you may not be [lacuna]pient [reading incomplete]: because blindness has happened in part to Israel, until the fullness of the Gentiles should enter in, and so all Israel should be saved,” etc.—he says: “You see that there also is a promise that, although by a late conversion, yet by one bringing salvation, they will someday be saved; and therefore the evening, the end of the world, is fittingly described by comparison with the day,” etc. The remainder likewise agrees with Cassiodorus’s commentary. Col. 0909D.]

Hence it is added [Col. 0909A]: “And they shall go around the city,” namely, the holy Church, so that they may be nourished by its spiritual foods, which they previously refused to touch, and may faithfully guard it with a dog’s vigilance.

“Behold, they speak with their mouth, and a sword is in their lips.” Behold, he says, those Jews who now exist and refuse to receive the faith will speak against the apostles and doctors of the Church: “with their mouth,” with a perverse mouth, ready for disputing and contradiction. This is what he means when he says: “And a sword is in their lips.” For as the word of God is the sword of the Spirit, so the Jews’ words are the sword of death and destruction.

“For who has heard?” The Jews said this against the apostles, and to this day say it against the Church’s doctors [Col. 0909B]. “For who has heard?” Which of the prophets announced this new doctrine that you preach? They say this because the letter kills them and they cannot attain spiritual understanding, since their wickedness has blinded them. Nor did they alone think thus; other nations also held similar views. Hence it is added: “But you, Lord, will deride them, and the Lord will mock them.” The Lord indeed regards all nations as nothing, because, as the prophet says: “All nations are before him as though they were not; they are counted by him as nothing and emptiness” (Isa. 40:17).

“I will preserve my strength for you, because you, O God, are my protector.” You, he says, regard as nothing all nations, whom I too would likewise regard as nothing if I wished. But I do not wish to display my strength; rather, I shall refer all that strength to you and reserve it for you, and, as though deprived of my own powers, shall always await defense and help from you. “For you, O God, are my protector,” who supply all things to me according to the judgment of my will.

“My God, his mercy will go before me.” He speaks according to his humanity, and therefore says that he has God and awaits mercy from elsewhere—a mercy so ready at hand that, if it needs to be invoked, it always goes before him.

“My God, show me good things among my enemies.” What good things? “Do not kill them.” Why? “Lest they should ever forget your law.” This he says not concerning Jews but concerning Christians, lest they forget his law. Hence another translation has not “your law,” but “my people.” This mercy, therefore, was shown to the Jews so that they might not be utterly slain, lest perhaps the law itself should perish and be delivered to oblivion together with them, when there was no one to teach it [Col. 0910A].

> [Note: Col. 0909D: “The Jews were therefore scattered, either that they might be stirred to a zeal for conversion, or—as some maintain—that amid the disputes of heretics the Church might have, from its enemies, the prepared testimony of the old law; for what is confirmed by the support of an adversary is believed without hesitation.” Cassiodorus. Col. 0910D.]

“Scatter them in your power, and cast them down, my protector.” Lord, he says, do not kill them in this very close siege in which they are shut up together; rather, scatter them among all peoples, tribes, and nations, in your power, which no one can resist. And cast them down, not that they may be killed, but rather that they may be stripped of their former rank, honor, and glory.

> [Note: Col. 0910D: The following portion of this psalm is absent from the edition of Marchesi and is supplied from the Vallicellian manuscript noted above. It is also absent from the Ghisian manuscript.]

Behold, the judges have been scattered; we have the law, and they are not dead. Yet everywhere they are without law, priesthood, and honor.

“The sin of their mouth is the word of their lips; and let them be caught in their pride.” The sin of their mouth, he says, is the word of their lips [Col. 0910B], with which they spoke too proudly against God. They committed all those evils set forth above, and therefore it is fitting that they should be caught in their pride, so that at last they may know and understand their folly. These things are understood of those Jews who exist even now; what follows is understood of those who are to come at the end of the age. Of them he now adds: “And because of cursing and lying, let them be constrained in the wrath of consummation, and they shall not be.”

Those, he says, have been scattered and cast down and remain in their pride and frenzy. But those who are to be present in the wrath of consummation shall be compelled and forced by the saints to answer for their cursing and lies, and to repent. “And they shall not be”—understand: they shall not be in the wrath of consummation [Col. 0910C], but shall be with the saints in the house of the heavenly dwelling. The wrath of consummation begins with the death of Antichrist, because the most certain signs of the coming judgment will appear, and the Jews, having recognized the truth, will flee to the Church and repent of their blasphemies and lies.

“And they shall know that God shall rule Jacob and the ends of the earth.” These, he says, do not know this; but those will know and understand that the God and Lord whom their parents crucified will rule Jacob—that is, the Jewish people, which derives its origin from him—“and the ends of the earth,” that is, all nations.

“They shall return at evening and suffer hunger like dogs.” This verse has already been explained above.

[Col. 0910D] “Behold, they shall be scattered in search of food, and if they are not satisfied, they shall murmur.” They shall be scattered among individual churches; and wherever they learn that there is someone receptive to the Christian religion, so great will be their desire to learn and receive divine and spiritual food that, “if they are not satisfied, they shall murmur” [Col. 0911A]. It is characteristic of that people to murmur, and they have scarcely ever been without murmuring. They will therefore murmur if they are not satisfied, and if the bishops, priests, and other preachers of the Christian law who will then be present do not satisfy them in everything about which they are questioned. Would that these writings of ours might be found, so that they may be ashamed, as it were, and cease from their murmuring! For who can fully explain everything contained in the sacred books?

“But I will sing your power and exalt your mercy in the morning.” Therefore, while they ask questions, wish to know everything, and raise questions about everything, I will through my faithful ones—through my bishops and priests—sing and preach [Col. 0911B] your power, and exalt your mercy in the morning. What will be evening for them will be morning for those coming to faith, because then they will leave the night and, renewed by the waters of baptism, attain the true day of light and brightness. Then at last they will recognize God’s power and mercy.

“For you have become my protector and my refuge in the day of my tribulation. My helper, I will sing to you, because you, O God, are my protector: my God, my mercy.” With what affection Christ’s humanity humbles itself to his divinity and promises to sing to it and obey it, because it was so ready at hand for him and so effectually fulfilled all his wills! And deservedly he now calls it both his protector and, again, his refuge and his mercy [Col. 0911C], because together with his members he is received by it and raised to the glory of eternal blessedness. Therefore all that this psalm contains will be fulfilled when, after the judgment has been completed, our Savior ascends to heaven with all the saints.

## PSALM LIX

> [Note: Col. 0911D: This psalm and the following five are absent in Marchesi and in the Ghisian manuscript; we have supplied them from the Vallicellian manuscript.]

**To the end, for those who shall be changed, for an inscription of the title, of David himself, for instruction, when he set Mesopotamia of Syria and Sobal on fire, and Joab returned and struck Edom in the Valley of Salt, twelve thousand.**

> [Note: Col. 0911D: This title is the same in the Roman edition; in the Psalter published by Cardinal Thommasi certain details differ. It reads: “He set Mesopotamia of Syria and Sobal on fire, and Joab returned and struck Idumea in the Valley of Salt, twelve thousand.” Col. 0912D. In Clarius, the psalm-title reads: “For the victor; for those who shall be changed; the insignia of David, for instruction, when he set Syria of Mesopotamia and Syria of Soba on fire, and Joab returned and struck Idumea in the Valley of Salt, twelve thousand.” 2 Samuel 8 and 10; 1 Chronicles 18. The Venerable Bede likewise teaches that Christ is here to be recognized in the person of David, and that the whole psalm speaks of him.]

“To the end,” he says: these things must be referred to the end and not understood according to the letter, but should rather be understood of those who, upon hearing the inscription of the title, will be changed into the new man and will recognize Christ as their king and Lord [Col. 0911D]. David—that is, our Savior—effected this change when he came, mighty in hand, in his teaching; for through his soldiers, or disciples, he set on fire and destroyed every pride, loftiness, and vain oldness of this age. For he himself says: “I came to cast fire upon the earth; and what do I desire but that it be kindled?” (Luke 12:49).

For Mesopotamia is interpreted “elevation,” Syria “loftiness,” and Sobal “vain oldness.” That is, Joab the commander and chief of David’s army turned himself against those who opposed him; and he struck twelve thousand of Edom in the Valley of Salt. Joab is interpreted “enemy.” He is the one of whom the Lord says in the Gospel: “Be in agreement with your adversary quickly, while you are on the way with him” (Matt. 5:23). Our adversary is the divine word; and it is indeed the greatest commander and the greater conqueror of enemies in David’s whole army. Whoever does not agree with it will perish.

This one therefore struck twelve thousand of Edom, which is interpreted “vigorous.” All people are earth because they were made from earth; but only those are blessed who are slain by Joab’s sword. It is a good sword and a good death which gives life by slaying [Col. 0912B]. But what do we understand by the Valley of Salt except the holy Church? There is the salt of which the Lord says to his disciples: “You are the salt of the earth” (Matt. 5:13). In this valley Joab’s sword holds dominion, because there is no one who dares to contradict it. Thus in David’s battles and victories the battles and victories of David our Savior are signified.

“God, you have rejected us and destroyed us, and have had mercy on us.” The Lord rejected and separated from himself the entire human race when he drove our first parents from Paradise. You destroyed us, moreover, because from such glory, loftiness, strength, security, and even the immortality with which they had been endowed, he subjected them to the laws of death. He was angry with us when he said: “Cursed is the earth in your work; when you have worked it, it shall not yield its fruit, but shall bring forth thorns and thistles for you” (Gen. 3:17) [Col. 0912C]. But he had mercy on us because he did not utterly cast us away and kill us. Thus their judges are accustomed to show mercy to those whom, after condemning them to death, they reserve alive and permit to depart after severely beating them or depriving them of some limb.

“You have shaken the earth and troubled it; heal its breaches, for it has been shaken.” For our earth had been established and could not be troubled, because it feared no discomforts, weaknesses, or hardships, and inhabited that land which was better and more pleasant than all others. But now, shaken, troubled, weakened, and scattered in every way, it needs much consolation because it suffers innumerable afflictions. And this is what he says: “Heal its breaches, for it has been shaken.”

“You have shown hard things to your people; you have given us wine of compunction to drink.” This is the people of whom it is said elsewhere: “But we are his people and the sheep of his pasture” (Ps. 94:7). For although all peoples are his, yet that people is specially called his own [Col. 0913A] which in both Testaments believed and believes in him, and did and does his will. This is the people to whom the Lord always shows harder things and permits greater afflictions. Perhaps, then, lest they be deceived by the world’s flatteries and pleasures and seek and love earthly rather than heavenly things, the wine of compunction may be understood as the cup and drink of every pain and affliction.

There is also another good compunction, by which the saints are refreshed with their tears, of which it is written: “My tears have been my bread day and night” (Ps. 41:4). And elsewhere: “You shall feed them with the bread of tears, and give us bread of tears in measure” (Ps. 55:9).

“You have given those who fear you a sign, that they may flee from the face of the bow and your chosen ones may be delivered.” This is the bow of which it is said elsewhere: “For behold, sinners have bent the bow; they have prepared their arrows in the quiver” (Ps. 20:2), etc. But how has the Lord given those who fear him a sign by which they may flee and escape this bow and these archers? By these archers we must understand all adversaries of the Church, especially Jews and heretics. We have a sign against these, namely, the authorities of all the saints. But do you wish to hear a clear sign? Hear the Lord himself saying: “Beware of false prophets, for they come to you in sheep’s clothing, but inwardly they are ravening wolves; by their fruits you shall know them” (Matt. 7:17).

“Save me by your right hand and hear me,” says the Church, “that your chosen ones may be delivered” [Col. 0913C]. Save me by your right hand and your power, and hear me. The salvation of this most loving mother is the deliverance of all her children.

“God has spoken in his holy one; I shall rejoice, divide the spoils, and measure out the valley of tabernacles.”

> [Note: Col. 0913D: The Vatican reading has “I shall divide Sichem.”]

The Prophet now speaks and consoles the Church, which had lamented the calamities of humankind from the very beginning, but which nevertheless rejoiced in the sign because it could flee from the face of the bow. “God has spoken in his holy one,” that is, in his beloved Son, and has spoken those things which will give you joy and exultation.

> [Note: Col. 0913D: “God the Father spoke in his holy one, that is, in Christ, when the Word was made flesh and the Savior of the world appeared. By ‘he spoke’ is signified evangelical truth, through which came the redemption of believers and the blessedness of saints.” Cassiodorus. Col. 0914D.]

For he will extend you to the ends of the earth and give you the whole earth, which he has measured and divided into its parts. “I shall rejoice,” he says, “and divide the spoils.” The Lord excellently begins with joy, because his joy brings gladness to all his faithful. Thus, announcing joy to the shepherds at his birth, the angel said: “Behold, I announce to you great joy, which shall be for all the people, because today a Savior has been born to you, who is Christ Jesus, in Bethlehem, the city of David” (Luke 2:10).

Sichem is interpreted “shoulder,” and signifies the shoulder-piece which the high priest is commanded to wear in Exodus. These are the holy apostles, bishops, and priests, who have their shoulders adorned with it in order wisely and bravely to carry all others [Col. 0914A]. They are those to whom the Lord says: “Take my yoke upon you and learn from me, for I am meek and humble of heart” (Matt. 11:29). The Lord therefore sent these, and divided the whole valley of tabernacles among them. The valley of tabernacles means this whole world, in which God’s tabernacles are set, by which all churches are signified. Of these it is added:

“Gilead is mine, and Manasseh is mine; Ephraim is the strength of my head. Judah is my king; Moab is the pot of my hope; into Idumea I shall stretch out my sandal; foreigners have become subject to me.” Behold, all things are his. All these belong to the Church, and thus the holy mother Church has been magnified and enlarged among all nations [Col. 0914B].

But what do we understand by Gilead, interpreted “heap of testimony,” except the teachers and masters of the Church? For they are those in whom the testimonies of both Testaments are heaped together, and by which they ought to defend both themselves and all others. They are deservedly placed first, since among all others they hold the chief rank. Manasseh, however, is interpreted “forgetfulness,” by which are signified those who, intoxicated by the cup of the Holy Spirit, forget all earthly things and desire heavenly things alone. Such were those of whom it is said in the Acts of the Apostles that “they all had one heart and one soul, and no one said anything was his own, but all things were common to them” (Acts 4:32). Monks and hermits also belong among these.

By Ephraim, however, who is called fruitful, we must understand all those who render the fruit of good work to the Lord. Among them are understood clergy and laity, men and women, rich and poor, free persons and slaves, and all others who are not idle but labor faithfully in God’s vineyard [Col. 0914C]. When he says, “the strength of my head,” it is as though he said, “my strength.” In this sense we are accustomed to call our oxen and laborers our strength.

“Judah is my king.” Judah is interpreted “confession.” These are those who fight for others, constantly praise and bless God, and, amid their very torments, confess the Lord and their Creator to be Christ. Such persons are worthy to be acknowledged by the Lord as kings.

“Moab is the pot of my hope.” He rightly places the pot after confession, because the confession of the saints alone filled the pot with bodies and led them to fire and other torments. For in this place the pot signifies every kind of torment. Moab is interpreted “from the father,” by whom are understood those to whom the Lord says in the Gospel: “You are of your father the devil” (John 8:44) [Col. 0914D]. Finally, the Lord hoped to have the pot for his faithful ones. He hoped, indeed, because he willingly and of his own accord endured the Passion.

“Into Idumea I shall stretch out my sandal,” that is, “my shod ones” [the Latin is OCR-corrupt], by which he signifies the apostles, who, as Scripture says, were shod in the preparation of the Gospel of peace (Eph. 6:18) [Col. 0915A]. The Lord stretched these out and sent them into Idumea, which is interpreted “bloody”; this signifies that it is altogether manifest. “The Allophyli are subject to me.” By the Allophyli, interpreted “without a head,” we must understand all unbelievers universally, those who have no understanding. For how did those have a head who were blind and deaf and had neither ears nor eyes? Had they possessed eyes, they would never have called wood and stones gods. These have been made subject to our Savior by apostolic preaching, because the walls of the Church were built from such people. These are the unpolished and uncircumcised stones which iron did not touch, because from such persons the Lord established an altar for himself.

Thus far the Lord has spoken; now the Church continues the order of its discourse.

“Who will lead me into the fortified city? Who will lead me as far as Idumea?” Who, therefore, will lead me into the fortified city—that is, the heavenly Jerusalem—where I need fear neither the pots of Moab, of which he has just spoken, nor the swords of the Idumeans stained with the blood of the saints? Or if you wish to stretch me out into Idumea, who will lead me, show me the road, and guard me as I go and return?

“Surely you, O God, who rejected and destroyed us, were angry with us and had mercy on us—will you not go forth, O God, with our powers?” You will indeed go forth [Col. 0915C], because you promised us this, and we hope that you will do it. This is what the Lord says in the Gospel: “He who believes in me shall also do the works that I do, and shall do greater works than these, because I go to the Father” (John 14:12). And again: “These signs shall follow those who believe: in my name they shall cast out demons; they shall speak with new tongues; they shall take up serpents; they shall lay their hands upon the sick, and they shall be well” (Mark 16:17).

Give us help in tribulation, because we hope from no other source; and man’s salvation is vain, since “every man altogether is vanity” (Ps. 38:6).

“In God we shall do valiantly, and he himself shall bring to nothing those who afflict us.” “In God,” he says, “we shall do valiantly, and he himself will enter into our powers” [Col. 0915D], because, as he himself said, we can do nothing without him. “And he himself shall bring to nothing those who afflict us.” This is like what is said elsewhere: “He shall come to nothing, like water running down” (Ps. 57:8). He whose intention is not fulfilled is brought to nothing. For it is a very common manner of speaking for us to say that someone has done nothing when he could not do what he began to do. Thus those who could not bring your purposes to effect came to nothing.

> [Note: Col. 0915D: Cassiodorus concludes his exposition, from which our Bruno does not greatly differ, thus: “What need have you, most faithful one, of weapons, since you are proved to possess such aids? For he himself fights for you, and none can resist him; he himself pursues, and none can evade him. Indeed, he brings the enemies of his faithful to nothing, because he blots them out from the book of the living, where they seemed to have been written in pride.” Col. 0916D.]

## PSALM LX. TO THE END, IN DAVID’S HYMNS

[Col. 0916A]

David commands these things to be sung in hymns and praises, where joyful and prosperous matters are announced.

“Hear, O God, my supplication; attend to my prayer. From the ends of the earth I have cried to you.” This is the voice of the Catholic and universal Church, which says that it cries out to him from the ends of the earth, that is, from all parts of the world. He too cries from the ends of the earth who, having brought to an end and overcome within himself the pleasures and desires of the flesh, joyfully cries to the Lord and gives thanks.

“While my heart was distressed, you lifted me up upon the rock.” The heart of the Church is the apostles, bishops, and teachers, because in them are contained the wisdom, will, and counsel of the Church. When these were distressed, afflicted, tortured by harsh punishments, and killed, yet could not be separated from faith in Christ, then the whole Church and the entire multitude of believers were lifted up upon the rock and made firm by the deep roots of faith. “And the rock,” as the Apostle says, “was Christ” (1 Cor. 10:4); those firmly founded in his faith overcome the assaults of the winds. And holy Church was indeed greatly strengthened in faith in Christ, since it beheld such constancy in its preachers.

“You have led me, because you have become my hope: a tower of strength against the face of the enemy.” Daily the Church is led onward; for daily the righteous who depart this life are transferred to heavenly things. Thus peoples are in the Church as though in a river: some go before, others follow; and none can remain in it for long, but they find a better place of dwelling, because the Lord himself is the fountain from which they proceed. There they have a fortified and strong tower, to which no enemies can approach.

[Note: [Col. 0916D] “For Christ himself is the tower,” Augustine says; “he himself became for us a tower against the face of the enemy; he is from the rock upon which the Church has been built.” St Augustine, *Expositions on Psalm 60*, verse 5.]

“I shall dwell in your tabernacle for ages; I shall be sheltered under the covering of your wings.” Here he speaks as if saying: I cannot remain for a long time here; and, moreover, because I am not secure here, there I shall dwell through all ages, and under the protection of your wings there will be nothing that I need fear. God does not have wings; but by his wings all his protection is metaphorically signified.

“For you, my God, have heard my prayer: you have given an inheritance to those who fear your name.” This, he says, was what I prayed for; this was what I desired to be heard concerning: that I might attain those tabernacles and receive that inheritance. Behold, thanks be to God, I have been heard, because you have given an inheritance to those who fear your name. Therefore the same thing is signified both by the tabernacles and by the inheritance.

“You will add days upon days to the king; his years unto the day of generation and generation.” Our king is Christ, who according to divinity is eternal, [Col. 0917A] but according to humanity temporal and of few years. But because humanity has its own days and years, days have been added to him upon days, and years upon years—that is, temporal days have been added upon eternal ones—so that he is at once temporal and eternal: temporal in one respect, eternal in another. The eternal have neither beginning nor end; the temporal indeed have a beginning, but no end. I think that the Prophet intended to say this in refutation of heretics who know how wrongly to distinguish Christ’s divinity and humanity, such as Nestorius and Eutyches are said to have been. Thus you will add days upon days to the king, and years upon years, unto the day of the age and unto eternal ages.

[Col. 0917B] “And he himself shall remain in his presence, and shall sit at his right hand.” Not God only, nor man only, but at once God and man, eternal and temporal, through all ages.

“Who shall seek out their mercy and truth?”

[Note: [Col. 0917D] Augustine has another reading in the passage cited: “His mercy and truth—who shall seek them out for him?” There he writes: “What does ‘for him’ mean? Who shall seek out enough for him? Why did he add ‘for him,’ unless because many seek to learn his mercy and truth in his books, and, once they have learned them, live for themselves and not for him, seeking their own interests and not those of Jesus Christ?” In the Vulgate the word *eorum* (“their”) is lacking, as is *ei* (“for him”).]

He has just said above that he gave an inheritance to those who fear his name. Now he shows that together with the inheritance he gave them blessedness. And this is what is meant by, “Who shall seek out their mercy and truth?” There is no one in this life who does not need these two things and continually seek them. For to whom is mercy not necessary, so that one may be able to know the truth concerning all things? For the Apostle says: “Now we see through a mirror in an enigma, but then face to face” (1 Cor. 13:12).

[Col. 0917C] “Thus I shall sing psalms to your name, that I may pay my vows day by day.” This psalm is entitled “in hymns,” and ends in hymns. Thus, he says, I shall sing psalms to your name, O God, at every time; thus I shall sing and thus praise you, that each day I may pay my vows and daily fulfil the desires of my heart in hymns, psalms, and spiritual songs.

## PSALM 61. UNTO THE END, FOR IDITHUN: A PSALM OF DAVID

What should we understand by Idithun, which is interpreted “one who leaps over,” except the more perfect members of the Church, who surpass others in wisdom, constancy, strength, and devotion? These are they who profess themselves subject to God; they are not leaning walls [Col. 0917D], but like a most strong tower against every adversity.

“Shall not my soul be subject to God? For from him is my salvation.” The Church speaks against Jews, heretics, and tyrants in the person of the perfect, whom they strive to separate from God by flatteries and persuasions, syllogisms and arguments, threats and terrors. But she comforts herself and speaks in the secrecy of her heart, saying: “Shall not my soul be subject to God?” For these malicious people desire to subject it to their errors. For from him is all [Col. 0918A] my salvation: he saved me by his blood and freed me from everlasting death. I ought to obey him alone, who daily tells us in the Gospel: “Do not fear those who kill the body but cannot kill the soul; but rather fear him who can destroy both body and soul in Gehenna” (Matt. 10:28). Therefore I shall fear him; in all things I shall be subject to him; and I shall no longer be moved away from him, to whom I am bound without ceasing by the bonds of faith and love. And this is what he says:

“For he himself is my God and my saviour, my helper; I shall be moved no more.” Once, he says, I was moved—and moved well—because I passed from darkness to light and from errors to truth. I abandoned the devil and came to Christ; for he [Col. 0918B] is my God, who saved me by his blood. “My helper” in the time of tribulation: “I shall be moved no more.” Cease, therefore, since you labour in vain, you who think that you can tear me away and separate me from him.

“How long do you rush upon men?” They are men, he says, upon whom you rush: they possess reason and acknowledge truth. But you are blind, who worship wood and stones as God. How long do you rush upon them “as upon a leaning wall and a driven-down fence”? They are not such as you think them to be; they are firm and steadfast. They can indeed be killed, but they cannot be moved; and therefore you kill them all, because you cannot separate any of them from faith in Christ and love for him. Of these was the man who said: “For I am convinced [Col. 0918C] that neither death nor life, neither height nor depth, nor any creature can separate me from the love of God which is in Christ Jesus” (Rom. 8:39).

“Yet they planned to cast down my honour; I ran in thirst.” Although, he says, they were such, their enemies nevertheless did not cease to tempt them and most foolishly imagined that they could deceive them. The honour of the holy martyrs was victory itself, because, had they been conquered, they would have lost all honour. Yet they ran to death with as great a desire as a man exceedingly thirsty runs to a spring of water. This is what is meant by “I ran in thirst.” They thirsted to die because they knew that through death they would come to eternal life. “With their mouth they blessed, and in their heart they cursed.” It is characteristic of flattering and deceitful people to have one thing in outward deed and another in their heart. Hence someone also says: they held one thing ready in their heart, another on their tongue.

“Yet my soul shall be subject to God, because from him is my patience.” Let them say whatever they wish, think and do whatever they wish; let them curse and bless. I count their curses and blessings as nothing, because by no ingenuity or cunning will they be able to separate my soul from God. [Col. 0919A] And this is so because “from him is my patience.” For the saints could not otherwise have endured so many and such great torments unless God had given them strength and patience to bear them.

“For he himself is my God and my saviour, my helper; I shall not depart.” This has already been explained above; it is repeated also so that it may be believed most firmly.

“In God are my salvation and my glory; the God of my help, and my hope, are in God.” My salvation is in him, he says, because he frees and saves me from all my distresses. Hence he says elsewhere: “In God we shall do valiantly, and he shall reduce our enemies to nothing” (Ps. 59:13). “The God of my help, and my hope, are in God.” He himself, he says, is both the Lord [Col. 0919B] and author of my help, because I expect help from nowhere else. “My help is from the Lord, who made heaven and earth” (Ps. 120:2), and all my hope is in God. “And hope does not disappoint” (Rom. 5:5). “Blessed are all who hope in him” (Ps. 33:9). “Therefore hope in him, all assembly of the people; pour out your hearts before him: God is our helper for ever.” All the multitude of believers, and all of you who do not place hope in the uncertainty of riches, pour out your hearts before him—that is, reveal and make known to him whatever you have in your heart. And as it is written: “Confess your sins to one another, and pray for one another, that you may be saved” (Jas. 5:16). For you confess to God what you confess to his vicars, that is, bishops and priests. But the person who shows no sign of repentance conceals his sin from God. The greatest signs of repentance are sorrow, tears, and compunction of heart, because God does not despise a contrite and humbled heart. Therefore let us pour out our hearts before him, because God is our helper. For he raises those who lie fallen; he binds and heals wounds; and he himself sets the lost sheep, once found, upon his shoulders and brings it back to pasture.

“Yet vain are the sons of men; lying are the sons of men in the balances, that they may deceive, they themselves, from their vanity, into one and the same thing.” Although God, in his mercy and goodness, is the helper of all who hope in him, the sons of men do not consider this; they distrust [Col. 0919D] the mercy of so great a helper, who never abandons those who hope in him. They persist in their vanity and, by lies, deceptions, theft, and robbery, seek only earthly and passing things. This is what he says: “Lying are the sons of men in the balances.” Their measure, weight, and balance are called deceitful by Scripture. Deceit is abominable. Those also are lying in the balances who, judging unjustly, show partiality. Or likewise those who are alike in deceits, and who differ not in the art of deception. [Col. 0920A] Hence follows: “from their vanity, into one and the same thing.”
