“Do not hope in iniquity, and do not desire robberies.” He explains this by saying: “If riches abound, do not set your heart upon them.” For the Apostle also says: “Command the rich of this age not to be high-minded, nor to hope in the uncertainty of riches” (1 Tim. 6:17). Hence the Lord says: “Make friends for yourselves from the mammon of iniquity” (Luke 16:9); showing such riches to be iniquitous, especially if they are defiled by robberies [424] and deceptions.

“God has spoken once. These two things I have heard: that power belongs to God, and to you, O Lord, mercy, because you will render to each according to his works.”

[Note: [Col. 0919D] The Vatican reading is: “Because you will render to each according to their works.” St Augustine interprets this passage concerning the generation of the Word: “And he saw that God spoke once; he saw the Word through whom [Col. 0920D] all things were made, and in whom all things are together,” etc. Cassiodorus is more extensive here in discussing the eternal generation of the Word.]

God has spoken once and does not repeat the same thing a second time. He speaks once whose word is firm, stable, and unchangeable—plainly in contrast with deceitful people, who continually alter their words, so that one can scarcely interpret what any one of them has chiefly said. Therefore God has spoken once because, as he himself says: “Heaven and earth shall pass away, but my words shall not pass away” (Luke 21:33). Thus, while he speaks, the Prophet—or the Church—says: I have heard these two things: that power and mercy belong to God. What power? Let him say it himself: “I have power,” he says, “to lay down my life and to take it up again” (John 10:18). No one else had this power, to lay down his life when he wished and take it up when he wished. What is there to say concerning mercy? Surely, if he had not had mercy, he would not have died for us. For when he had once told his disciples that he had to be delivered up and crucified, and blessed Peter replied, “Far be it from you, Lord; this shall not happen to you,” he answered, showing that he possessed this mercy: “Get behind me, Satan, because you do not savour the things of God but those of men” (Matt. 16:23). These are the two most excellent things which the Prophet says he heard while the Lord was speaking. What follows—“because you will render to each according to his works”—is referred to power, so that one who rightly had such mercy cannot be doubted also to have had that power. For no one except God alone—Father, Son, and Holy Spirit—can render to each according to his works. [Col. 0920D] Therefore he who has power to render to each according to his works had power, as he wished, both to lay down and to take up his life.

## PSALM 62. A PSALM OF DAVID, WHEN HE WAS IN THE DESERT OF IDUMAEA (1 Sam. 22:25)

Idumaea is interpreted “earthly and bloody.” It signifies this world, which for the most part is inhabited by earthly and bloody people. From the time, therefore, [Col. 0921A] when our Saviour began to be in the desert of Idumaea—that is, in this world, or in Judaea—this psalm is sung and resounds clearly in the Church. John the Baptist says of this desert: “I am the voice of one crying in the wilderness” (John 1:23).

“O God, my God, from the light I keep watch for you.”

[Note: [Col. 0921D] “Sleep is good for the body,” Augustine says, “by which bodily health is restored. But the sleep of the soul is to forget its God. Whatever soul has forgotten its God sleeps,” etc. *Expositions on Psalm 62.*]

“The night,” he says, “has passed, but the day has drawn near” (Rom. 8:12). “The true light has come, which enlightens every person coming into this world” (John 1:8). “Arise therefore, be enlightened, O Jerusalem, for your light has come and the glory of the Lord has risen upon you” (Isa. 60:1). “For the people that sat in darkness saw a great light” (Isa. 9:2). From the time of this light and this day, therefore, the Church keeps watch, according to the Apostle’s command to keep watch: [Col. 0921B] “Watch,” he says, “and pray; stand firm in faith; act manfully; be strengthened in the Lord; let all your things be done in love” (1 Cor. 16:13). This is the manner of watchfulness. Thus the Lord also commands us to watch, because we know neither the day nor the hour.

“My soul has thirsted for you; how greatly my flesh has thirsted for you.” “Blessed are those who hunger and thirst for righteousness, for they shall be filled” (Matt. 5:6). My soul has thirsted for you—that is, longing in love and desire to see you, come to you, and be with you. My soul suffers this thirst, but my flesh a far greater one, since it is oppressed by greater anxieties and tribulations. This is what he says: “How greatly my flesh has thirsted for you.” Hence the Apostle says: “For the creation was subjected [Col. 0921C] to vanity, not willingly, but because of him who subjected it in hope; because creation itself shall be freed from the bondage of corruption into the freedom of the glory of the children of God” (Rom. 8:10).

“In a desert, trackless, and waterless land, thus I appeared to you in the sanctuary, that I might see your power and your glory.” This, therefore, is the cause of such great thirst and desire. For, as the Apostle says: “While we were still sinners, Christ died for the ungodly” (Rom. 5:8). If he died for the ungodly, we think that through him we have likewise been justified. Thus I appeared to you in the desert and manifested myself to you in this manner among the ungodly and sinners, that I might be worthy to see your power and glory. Only Christians, still placed in this [Col. 0921D] world, can as yet see and know this power and glory in a mirror—that is, through a mirror. Others cannot. This mirror—or rather, the mirror of mirrors—is our Saviour, who made us such and illuminated and purified the eyes of our mind so that we can understand his power and glory. Peter, James, and John deserved beyond the others to see this power and glory when they saw him transfigured on the mountain (Matt. 17). Before the Lord came, this world [Col. 0922A] was a desert, utterly abandoned, without a way leading to the fatherland and without the water of wisdom that would wash and heal us. But to show that he possessed all these things not by his own merits but solely by God’s mercy, he added:

“Because your mercy is better than lives, my lips shall praise you.” God’s mercy is better than life, because it gives life and many other things above life itself, without which all human life is wretched. Hence he deserves always to be praised and glorified by all his faithful.

“Thus I shall bless you in my life, and in your name I shall lift my hands; as with fat and richness may my soul be filled.” Good fat and good richness, by which the soul is made fat, signify faith, hope, love, and the other virtues; without them every soul is miserably thin and weak and cannot defend itself against its adversaries. Therefore, that our soul may be filled with such fat and richness, let us bless and glorify God throughout our whole life, lift our hands to do good work, and do whatever we do in the name of the Lord. “And lips of exultation shall praise your name.” Only the lips of the saints are lips of exultation, because whatever they say, sing, or preach produces joy and exultation both for themselves and for those who believe and obey. Other lips are not lips of exultation but rather of sadness and sorrow, teaching nothing but vanity, impurity, and iniquity.

[Col. 0922C] “Thus I remembered you upon my bed; in the mornings I shall meditate on you.” Thus I have remembered you until now upon my bed; in the mornings, at every time, I shall meditate on you, so that my soul may be filled with fat and richness. Ungodly people and sinners are in night and darkness; but the saints are in the mornings, because they see the light of truth and draw near to the sun of righteousness. “Because you have become my helper.”

[Note: [Col. 0922D] “Unless God assists our good works, they cannot be fulfilled by us; and we ought worthily to work—that is, as though in the light—when we work with Christ showing us the way.” Augustine, *Expositions*, same passage.]

Therefore I have deservedly always remembered you, and shall remember you, because everywhere and in all my necessities you have always become my helper.

“And under the covering of your wings I shall rejoice; my soul has clung after you; your right hand has upheld me.” What should we understand by God’s wings except perfections? There are as many wings as there are angels and virtues, and testimonies of the holy Scriptures, by which he protects and defends his faithful. Among these wings, however, love, devotion, and mercy seem to me especially prominent. “My soul has clung after you; your right hand has upheld me.” You did not despise what my soul says, which clung to you by faith and love and ran after you, captivated by longing for your love; but you stretched forth your right hand, received me, and drew me out of the mire of the deep.

[Col. 0923A] “But they sought my soul in vain; they shall enter into the lower parts of the earth; they shall be delivered into the hands of the sword; they shall be portions for foxes.” In vain indeed, because you held it by your right hand, defended it, and protected it under the covering of your wings. They, he says—those whom you know better—my enemies, “sought my soul in vain; they shall enter into the lower parts of the earth; they shall be delivered into the hands of the sword; they shall be portions for foxes.” The lower parts of the earth are places of punishment where the ungodly are tormented. By the hands of the sword, however, all kinds of torments are signified. Foxes are evil spirits, ever fraudulent and deceitful; they shall receive these people as their portions, because the lambs shall be divided from the goats and the righteous from sinners.

“But the king shall rejoice in God; all who swear by him shall be praised, because the mouth of those speaking iniquity has been stopped.” Christ was judged, condemned, and crucified—but according to his humanity. Therefore Christ shall judge, and shall judge according to his humanity. “For the Father judges no one, but has given all judgment to the Son” (John 5:22). He shall judge, he to whom all are subject, because “at the name of Jesus every knee shall bend, of things in heaven, on earth, and under the earth” (Phil. 2:10). He shall judge, of whom it is said: “Every eye shall see him, even those who pierced him” (Zech. 12:10; John 19:37). For the ungodly will not be able to see divinity itself; they will scarcely see even his humanity glorified beyond the sun’s ray. To them it shall also be said: “Let the ungodly be taken away, lest they see the glory of God” (Isa. 26:10). Therefore [Col. 0923C] Christ shall sit in judgment with the senators of the earth and with the princes of his people; and then he shall rejoice in the Lord over such glory of divinity granted to him, because, as is said elsewhere, “Great is his glory for ever and ever.” With you also all who swear by him shall be praised. How shall they be praised? “I was hungry,” the Lord says, “and you gave me food; I was thirsty, and you gave me drink; I was a stranger, and you received me; I was sick, and you visited me” (Matt. 25:35). These praises of the saints are written in the Gospel, but we do not doubt that others are to come. All Christians swear in the Lord, and no one is admitted to the faith without an oath. How they swear and what they swear is very well known and needs no exposition. “Because the mouth of those speaking iniquity has been stopped.” The good, [Col. 0923D] he says, shall be praised by the Lord; but the evil shall be praised by no one, because no one will dare to open his mouth to praise, excuse, or defend them.

## PSALM 63. UNTO THE END, A PSALM OF DAVID

This psalm, he says, is to be referred unto the end, that is, to Christ, in whom the mystery of his passion is contained.

“Hear, O God, my prayer when I am afflicted; deliver my soul from fear of the enemy.” We have often said already that whenever our Saviour prays, asks something, or seems to stand in need of anything, it must all be referred to his humanity. Yet this humanity does not pray for itself, but for us, because whatever [Col. 0924A] is in his will is also in his power. Thus, for him to pray was to will. But we cannot know his will except through prayer, just as we in turn cannot know one another’s wills except through speech. It was therefore necessary for his will to be stated to us, because we could not otherwise understand it. The Prophet is therefore a messenger between us and Christ’s will: what he sees there, he announces to us, and he introduces that will as praying. Let Christ’s will therefore cry out, and cry out again; and let the Prophet announce to us what he saw and heard in Christ’s will. “Hear,” he says, “O God, my prayer”; and hear it now, because I am now afflicted; and deliver my soul from fear of the enemy. This enemy is understood as the devil and the Jewish people, [Col. 0924B] who were attempting to take Christ’s life.

“You have protected me from the assembly of the malignant and from the multitude of those working iniquity.” He whose will was heard so immediately had no need to pray long. For in him will and the effect of will were alike; nor could he will anything before possessing what he willed. For what lies between petition and being heard, except that the two cannot be spoken at the same time? For as soon as he said, “Deliver my soul from fear of the enemy,” immediately showing that he had been heard, he added: “You have protected me from the assembly of the malignant.” Christ’s will, therefore, could precede prayer, but could not precede being heard. What need then had he who was heard before asking to ask or pray? “You have protected me,” he says, “from the assembly of the malignant and from the multitude of those working iniquity,” because unless I had willed it, they could have had no power over me. And I suffered nothing except what I willed, although they did many things to me which they ought not to have done. Let us hear from the Prophet’s narrative what those things were.

“Because they have sharpened their tongues like a sword; they have bent the bow, a bitter thing, that they may shoot the blameless in secret.” The Prophet speaks and narrates Christ’s passion in order. “The Jews have sharpened their tongues like a sword,” he says, because, after taking counsel together, they jointly prepared themselves to accuse our Saviour. They bent the bow in order to shoot the blameless in secret, because [Col. 0924D] they resolved among themselves that all should cry out together with one voice. From a deceitful bow, deceitful and wicked arrows are shot. From an ungodly and wicked heart proceeds an ungodly and bitter judgment. Accursed tongues, accursed hand, accursed arrows, which did not fear to commit so great a crime! He was indeed taken because that wicked counsel of destruction and perversion was devised in secret. But the arrows were shot openly, because publicly, in the hearing of all, “Crucify!” was shouted once and again. As many as were the voices of those crying out, so many were the archers shooting those deadly arrows. But what follows will make it clearer.

“They shall shoot him suddenly, and shall not fear; they have strengthened for themselves an evil word.” They shall shoot him suddenly—and indeed suddenly. For when Pilate said, “Which of the two do you wish me to release to you, Barabbas or Jesus who is called Christ?” the Jews answered, “Barabbas.” And when he said, “What then shall I do with Jesus who is called Christ?” they suddenly, without deliberation, reason, accusation, judgment, legal sentence, or will, like madmen and lunatics cried out, saying: “Let him be crucified” (Matt. 27). This is what he means by “They shall shoot him suddenly”: not only did they shoot him, but, as we have just said, they shot him suddenly and before a hearing. “And they shall not fear.” The Prophet marvels not only that they did this, but also that they did not fear to do it. [Col. 0925B] And it is indeed worse to sin boldly than fearfully. It is very strange that these men did not fear when they condemned to death such a great man, whom they did not doubt to be blameless, holy, and just; whom in those very days they had seen raise Lazarus, already four days dead, from death; who, before their eyes, gave sight to the blind, cleansed lepers, healed paralytics, drove out demons, and did many other astonishing things among them which no one else had ever done. How, then, did they not fear? “Because they strengthened for themselves an evil word.” The Prophet saw many things concerning Christ’s passion and the Jews’ impious plot which the evangelists themselves do not recount. For by these words he shows that the Jews had confirmed [Col. 0925C] and sworn among themselves that they would kill our Lord and Saviour without any reconsideration. Perhaps, therefore, they did not fear because they encouraged one another mutually to accomplish this, which they had jointly resolved.

“They discussed how to hide snares; they said: Who shall see them?” They discussed, he says, and deliberated among themselves for a long time how they could convict him by deceit and false assertions. Having conspired, they strove by every means to prevail against one whom they knew they had an unjust case against. For what were all those deceptions which they plotted in secret against our Saviour except snares? They thought that they had contrived them so wisely, cunningly, and shrewdly that no one besides themselves could know or understand them. This is what follows: “They said: Who shall see them?” But I say in reply: who was so foolish there that he did not know them and see that everything they did was done deceitfully and fraudulently?

“They searched out iniquity and failed in searching the search.” They searched, he says, and worked hard at this, that they might find some iniquity which would seem suitable for deception and accusation. And they failed while searching because they could find nothing of the kind in that investigation of theirs. [Col. 0926A] Thus the Evangelist says that, although many false witnesses came forward against him, finally two false witnesses came, saying: “This man said, I can destroy this temple made with hands, and in three days raise another not made with hands” (Matt. 26:61). “And their testimony,” he says, “was not consistent”; and thus all failed in searching the search. Yet they prevailed, and by cheating, lying, deceiving, condemning, and crying “Crucify!” finally dragged him to death and the cross. This is what is meant when it says: “Man shall come to the lofty heart, and God shall be exalted.” Man, he says, comes to the cross; and we have rightly said “man shall come,” because although he was at once God and man, only man was crucified. Therefore [Col. 0926B] man came—but not just any man: a lofty, sublime, and profound heart, full of all wisdom and knowledge, of whom the Apostle says that in him all the fullness of divinity rests bodily (Col. 2:9). This is the flower of whom Isaiah says: “Upon him shall rest the Spirit of the Lord: the spirit of wisdom and understanding, the spirit of counsel and strength, the spirit of knowledge and piety; and the spirit of the fear of the Lord shall fill him” (Isa. 11:2). “And God shall be exalted.” For this is what the Lord himself says: “As Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness, so the Son of Man must be lifted up” (John 3:14). Understanding this, the Jews said: “Who is this Son of Man? We have heard from the Law that Christ remains for ever. How then do you say that the Son of Man must be lifted up?” (John 12:34). Therefore the Lord was lifted up on the cross so that, as he himself says, he might draw all things to himself.

Some manuscripts read: “Man came to the lofty heart,” by which we understand that after Christ’s passion the book sealed with seven seals was opened (Rev. 5:3). Man came to the lofty heart—that is, to a greater and spiritual understanding. And God was exalted in the hearts of those who deserved to attain the heart. God is exalted in the heart of those who, rightly and catholicly understanding his loftiness and magnificence, magnify and exalt him as is worthy. God is also exalted in another way: the more subtly we think of him and desire to see him with the inward eyes, the more sublimely he eludes the gaze [Col. 0926D] of our mind. Hence in the Song of Songs it is said to the Church: “Turn away your eyes, because they have made me fly away” (Song 6:4). And Solomon says: “I tried wisdom, and it withdraws farther from me” (Eccl. 7:24).

[Note: [Col. 0925D] The Vulgate passage reads: “I tested all things in wisdom. I said, ‘I shall become wise’; and wisdom itself withdrew farther from me.”]

And when Moses desired to see God’s face and majesty, it was said: “No man shall see me and live” (Exod. 33:20).

“The arrows of little children became their wounds, and they counted them as nothing.” The arrows of little children, because they strike with a weak force, can inflict either no wounds or very small ones.

[Note: [Col. 0926D] Cassiodorus, who throughout this psalm discusses Christ the Lord’s passion as foretold by the Prophet, as does St Bruno, says this concerning the Jews’ futile attempts [Col. 0927C] to destroy Christ: “The arrows of little children are empty missiles. In play, they are accustomed to throw frail reeds in imitation of arrows. Thus the Jews’ designs, with their ineffectual and most savage malice, inflicted not a lamentable death, but rather a most glorious passion; and they gave such wounds that death itself might die, and the promised salvation of the world might swiftly be fulfilled.”]

All those words and snares of the Jews are reckoned [Col. 0927A] as such by the Lord, because they could do against him only so much, and no more, as he himself willed and permitted. Therefore the Jews had such arrows to no purpose, uselessly and without cause: by them they could do nothing against God’s will, but rather wounded themselves with their own arrows. This is what he says: “Their own tongues are against them.”

“All who saw them were troubled, and every human being was afraid.” These are among the 428 of whom the Gospel says: “And all the crowd who had gathered together for this spectacle, seeing the things that were done, returned striking their breasts” (Luke 23:48). Among them also the centurion glorified God, saying: “Certainly this man was righteous” [Col. 0927B] (ibid., 47).—“But the righteous and those known to him stood at a distance, and the women who had followed him from Galilee, seeing these things” (ibid., 49).—“Therefore all were troubled,” seeing them act so cruelly and impiously. “And every human being was afraid”; and whoever was not afraid and did not grieve at such great cruelty was a devil, not a human being. Let these things, then, be said concerning the passion of our Savior. But now let us hear what the apostles subsequently did.

“They proclaimed the works of God, and understood his deeds.” For this is what the Gospel says: “And they went forth and preached everywhere, the Lord working with them and confirming the word by the signs that followed” (Mark 16:20). They, he says, proclaimed the works of God and his wonders, which he performed through himself and through his faithful ones [Col. 0927C]. And all peoples, tribes, and languages, hearing these things, understood his deeds; converted from their unbelief to faith, they believed in Christ the Lord.

“The righteous man shall rejoice in the Lord and hope in him, and all the upright in heart shall glory.” Henceforth, therefore, the righteous man shall rejoice in the Lord, who formerly rejoiced in the vanities and pleasures of this world. And he shall hope in him who previously hoped in the uncertainty of riches. “And all the upright in heart shall be praised.” As all who are upright in heart are worthy of praise, so the crafty and deceitful are to be condemned. He has an upright heart who does not depart from truth and rectitude; whereas, on the contrary [Col. 0928A], those have a perverse heart who follow him of whom it is written: “For he was a liar from the beginning and did not stand in the truth” (John 8:44).

## PSALM LXIV

[Note: [Col. 0927D] This title differs in a few particulars, as it is read in the Psalter expounded by Cardinal Thomasius. It reads: “Unto the end, a psalm of David: a song of Jeremiah and Ezekiel, for the people of the migration, when they began to go out.” I shall append the Venerable Bede’s elucidation of this title:

“Since the opening elements of the title are already known, we shall explain the following words briefly. When the people of Israel had been carried away into Chaldaea, the prophets named foretold that after seventy years they would return to their homeland and restore Jerusalem, which the enemy had destroyed, to a better condition. Jeremiah and Ezekiel, therefore, did not compose the psalm; rather, it bears the names of those whose period accords with its history. Many authors assert that this was done by Ezra [Col. 0928C], saying that he assigned titles to all the Psalms, gathered into a single volume those which until then had not been arranged and had been scattered according to the authority and diversity of their times [Col. 0928D]. Spiritually, however, the people who, leaving Babylon after captivity, hastened toward Jerusalem refers to those who, after their former sins have been condemned amid the confusion of this world, strive to come to Christ’s Church. By the authority of the Fathers, this entire psalm must be applied to them.”

Cassiodorus long ago arranged this title differently, observing that Jeremiah and Ezekiel had died before the Jews’ return to Jerusalem. He accordingly sets it out thus: “Unto the end, a psalm of David, a song concerning the people of the migration, through the prophecy of Jeremiah and Ezekiel, when they began to depart.” Thus it is correctly understood, so that the words seem to refer more to the people than to Jeremiah and Ezekiel.]

**UNTO THE END, A PSALM OF DAVID. A SONG OF JEREMIAH AND EZEKIEL CONCERNING THE WORD OF THE EXILE, WHEN THEY BEGAN TO DEPART** (4 Kings 24:14).

David wrote this psalm concerning the Babylonian captivity, and calls it a song of Jeremiah and Ezekiel because they too wrote about the same captivity and were in it. What David prophesied and wrote, Jeremiah together with Ezekiel endured and saw. For these two prophets were carried into captivity together with others; they comforted them [Col. 0928B], urged them to be of good courage, and said that after seventy-two years they would return to their homeland. Meanwhile, they preached that the city would be restored, the Temple rebuilt, and hymns and psalms sung there.

This is what bishops and priests do daily in the Church. They are signified by those two prophets, and they affirm that after seventy years all the saints held in this sort of captivity will return to the homeland of the heavenly Jerusalem. For what are the seventy years but this whole present life? For seven times ten, or ten times seven, makes seventy. Yet each number signifies totality, since all numbers are contained in ten and all days in seven.

[Col. 0928C] “A hymn is fitting for you, O God, in Zion, and a vow shall be rendered to you in Jerusalem.” Each people, liberated from captivity, speaks: one from that of the Babylonians, the other from that of demons. “For as long as I was in captivity,” that people seems to say, “I could not praise you, because I was oppressed by harsh captivity, nor did it seem fitting to me to sing the Lord’s song in a foreign land. But now, because we have been set free, it is very fitting that we sing your praises and hymns, resound most clearly to you in Zion, and, having returned, render to you in Jerusalem the vows which we made to you in captivity.” Those also who have been liberated [Col. 0929A] through repentance and reconciled by the Church’s sacraments can say this.

“Hear my prayer; all flesh shall come to you.” Hear, he says, my prayer, so that the whole world, purified, may come to you—though I confess and recognize that I have been stained in many ways, having lived for so long among wicked people, vices, and sins. For I know and am certain that all flesh shall come to you. This is what the Lord says through the prophet: “As I live, says the Lord, every knee shall bow to me, and every tongue shall confess” (Isa. 45:23). Hence the Apostle also says: “For all of us, whether good or evil, shall stand before the judgment-seat of Christ” (Rom. 14:10).

“The words of the wicked have prevailed against us, and you shall be propitious to our impieties.” He needs much purification and much mercy because the words of the wicked have prevailed over him and stained him. But have good hope, for the Lord will have mercy on him.

“Blessed is he whom you have chosen and taken up [Note: [Col. 0929D] Saint Augustine interprets this passage of the psalm as concerning the humanity assumed by the Word of God; *Enarrationes in Psalmos*.], he shall dwell in your courts.”—“Many are called, but few are chosen” (John 14:2). But blessed is he whom the Lord in his mercy has chosen and taken to himself from so great a multitude of human beings. Such a one cannot perish; without any doubt, he will receive the blessings predestined for him. He indeed shall dwell in his tabernacles, concerning which the Lord himself says: “In my Father’s house are many dwelling places” (John 14:2).

“We shall be filled with the good things of your house; your temple is holy [Col. 0929C], wonderful in righteousness.” Before, he says, we come to those tabernacles of yours—may we someday be able to reach them!—we shall here be filled with the good things of your house, by which the holy Church is signified. But who can enumerate what and how great are the blessings in God’s Church, by which the faithful are daily fed and filled? Here we have all the books of both Testaments; here we have many others which the holy Fathers produced for us; here we have the indescribable riches and delights of Christ’s body and blood.

These, then, are the good things of which he says here: “We shall be filled with the good things of your house”; and concerning this house he adds: “Your temple is holy, wonderful in righteousness.” Not only, he says, are those heavenly tabernacles holy [Col. 0929D], with which surely no other tabernacles can be compared; this temple of God on earth also is holy and venerable. “And wonderful in righteousness.” You see that the Church is praised for righteousness; yet few are those to whom this praise seems applicable. For it is said of her that she “has neither spot nor wrinkle” (Eph. 5:27), which cannot stand if it is referred to the whole body without qualification.

“Hear us, O God our Savior, the hope of all the ends of the earth and of those far away in the sea.” Hear us, he says, [Col. 0930A] O God our Savior, by whose blood we have been saved and redeemed, in whom all the ends of the earth hope and through whom they trust to be delivered from every evil. By these ends, the whole universal and catholic Church is signified. By those who are far away in the sea we may understand the Scots, Britons, and the other islands of the sea.

“Preparing the mountains in your strength, girded with power, you who trouble the bed of the sea—who can endure the sound of its waves?” Hear us, he says, you who prepare the mountains in your strength. By these we understand the apostles and teachers, who are higher than all others in the word of wisdom and in religion. [Note: [Col. 0929D] “We fittingly understand the prepared mountains allegorically as the apostles [Col. 0930D], chosen for the word of preaching: possessing the strength of faith and height of holiness, humble in conduct but loftier in merit.” Cassiodorus.] The Lord prepared them for warfare and preaching, for refuting heretics [Col. 0930B], and for governing and directing the whole people.

The Lord is girded with power—such and so great a power that no one can resist him. Hence elsewhere it is said: “Gird your sword upon your thigh” (Ps. 44:4). Of such swords it is written: “And two-edged swords in their hands” (Ps. 149:6). Hence the Apostle says: “The word of God is living and effective, and sharper than every two-edged sword” (Heb. 4:12). He, therefore, is girded with power who is armed with such a sword.

The Lord also troubles the bed of the sea, as he himself says through Isaiah: “I am the Lord who troubles the sea, and its waves swell” (Isa. 51:15). What is signified by the sea except this world? Elsewhere it is said of it: “This great and wide sea; there are creeping things [Col. 0930C] without number” (Ps. 103:25). Let us therefore hear how this sea is troubled by the Lord: “I came,” he says, “to cast fire upon the earth; and what do I will but that it be kindled?” (Luke 12:49). “I came not to bring peace, but a sword” (Matt. 10:34).—“Henceforth there shall be five in one house, two divided against three, and three against two” (Luke 12:52).

Thus the Lord troubles the bed of the sea when he separates the good from the evil and causes some to rise against others: while some attack righteousness and others fight for righteousness even to death. “Who can endure the sound of its waves?” This sea has both good and evil waves. Good waves are good people; evil waves are evil people. These and those cry out [Col. 0930D], and often make so great a sound that neither party can endure the other. The good do not wish to hear the foolishness of the wicked, nor do the wicked wish to endure or receive the life-giving voices of the good. Yet it often happens that those who disdain to hear the voices of the saints are converted upon seeing signs and miracles. Hence he adds:

“The nations shall be troubled, and all who inhabit the ends of the earth shall fear because of your signs.” Seeing the signs performed by the holy apostles, those very people who had formerly mocked their preaching were immediately troubled [Col. 0931A] and changed to astonishment; they began to fear Christ, in whose name they saw such marvelous and stupendous things done.

“You shall delight the goings out of the morning and the evening.” A good going forth is one in which the Lord delights. One going forth was that of Israel from Egypt and of the house of Jacob from a barbarous people. Therefore the Lord delights in the departure of those who leave and flee the company of the wicked. The morning departure is one made quickly or in early life; the evening departure is made late or in old age. Yet God receives all, and gives the denarius to the first and the last. Recall that Gospel in which the householder hires laborers for his vineyard (Matt. 20:1).

“You have visited the earth and made it drunk; you have multiplied to enrich it.” The Prophet marvels at the sudden conversion of all nations and at the great multitude flowing from every side into the Church. Thus he rightly says that the earth has been visited by God. Hence also: “Blessed be the Lord God of Israel, because he has visited and wrought redemption for his people” (Luke 1:68).

God made the earth drunk from the abundance of his house and gave it drink from the torrent of his delight. By this, clearly, we understand the graces of the Holy Spirit, by which the Church, made drunk, speaks in every tongue and expounds all the Scriptures; having forgotten all earthly things, she is thought by foolish people not merely to be drunk but even mad. This is a good intoxication, which can so convert people. But what is meant by “You have multiplied to enrich it,” except, “You have enriched it in many ways”? In many ways indeed: with wisdom and knowledge, strength and piety, virtues and honorableness, glory and honor, and every good thing that may be desired from a righteous person [Col. 0931C].

“The river of God is filled with water; you have prepared their food, for such is its preparation.” What wonder, he says, if the earth has been made drunk when it is watered by so great a river? This is the river of which it is elsewhere said: “The rush of the river makes glad the city of God” (Ps. 45:4). This river is filled with water because the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit proceed from this one river, and by them all who dwell on the earth are refreshed and satisfied. Hence he adds: “You have prepared their food, for such is its preparation [Col. 0931D].” This water is food, refreshment, and the whole means of sustenance. The Lord prepared this food for his saints, because without it they could not be prepared to endure so great a labor.

“Making its streams drunk, multiplying its generations, it shall rejoice in its drops as it springs up.” [Note: [Col. 0931D] The Vulgate text: “Make its streams drunk; multiply its produce; in its drops it shall rejoice, springing up.” Clarius has differently: “You make its furrows drunk, press down its clods [Col. 0932D], soften it with falling drops, and bless its growth.”]

This water also has its streams through which it continually runs and flows. These are the bishops and priests who supply necessities to all others, and to whom others bring their little vessels as if to streams, receiving from them more or less according to the capacity of their understanding. Therefore let it be said: You, O Lord [Col. 0932A], prepared this water as their food, making its streams drunk and multiplying its generations. Certainly you would not have done this unless you had made its streams drunk and multiplied its generations. For if it were not found in the streams, where would this water be sought? But because the streams are drunk, all who seek it find it ready.

The Lord multiplies the generations of this water because many and innumerable people are daily born again from it; for no one in the Church is not counted among its generations. Rich and poor, and whoever is in the Church, are all its children. “Unless one is born again of water and the Holy Spirit, he shall not enter the kingdom of God” (John 3:5). There is, then, water which washes people outwardly, and water which washes inwardly; the one can be seen [Col. 0932B], but the other cannot.

“It shall rejoice in its drops as it springs up.” As soon, he says, as this water rises from the river and is derived from it, it rejoices in its drops. Those whom above he called streams he now calls drops. Yet by drops may fittingly be understood those who are lower than streams and of lesser merit. Whoever, then, receives the flowing water of the Holy Spirit is gladdened by spiritual joy at the very beginning of his rising.

“Blessing the crown of the year of your goodness, and your fields shall be filled with abundance.” This is connected with the preceding passage, as though it said: You, by making its streams drunk, multiplying its generations, and blessing its crown, accomplish the things spoken above.

The year of God’s goodness began from the time when our Savior came into this world. Of that year the Lord himself says: “The Spirit of the Lord is upon me; therefore he anointed me, sent me to preach the Gospel to the poor, to proclaim release to captives, sight to the blind, and a year acceptable to the Lord” (Luke 4:18). Of it the Apostle says: “Behold, now is the acceptable time; behold, now is the day of salvation” (1 Cor. 6:2). This whole year has been crowned because the faithful daily battle against vices and wicked spirits, conquer, and are crowned. “For no one,” says the Apostle, “shall be crowned unless he has contended lawfully” (2 Tim. 2:5).

All years before this year were under a curse; but this year and the crown of this year deserved to receive Christ’s blessing. It should be noted [Col. 0932D], however, that the Lord is said here to bless not the year, but the crown of the year, so that we understand that this blessing belongs to combatants and victors alone. “And your fields shall be filled with abundance.” God’s fields are the individual Churches, filled with the fruitfulness of both Testaments, the abundance of the Holy Spirit, and every virtue. All the earth, cursed in the first man, was barren; but in our Savior it received both blessing and fruitfulness.

“The borders of the wilderness shall grow fat, and the hills [Col. 0933A] shall be girded with exultation.” By the borders of the wilderness we understand those who, although close to the wilderness, are not in the wilderness: for although they live among others, they do not imitate the wicked. These shall grow fat with the fatness of which another psalm says: “Let my soul be filled as with marrow and fatness” (Ps. 62:6). Those borders that are thus fat are fertile in the fruitfulness of every good work.

“And the hills shall be girded with exultation.” By these we must understand all those whom we see to be more eminent in the Church in religion, virtue, and holiness. They are girded with exultation because they possess the best swords with which they slay their enemies. Blessed are those who are girded with such swords and so prepared for battle.

[Col. 0933B] “The rams of the sheep have been clothed [Note: [Col. 0933D] “One must supply: ‘with exultation.’ For with the exultation with which the hills shall be girded, the rams of the sheep are clothed.” Augustine.], and the valleys shall abound with grain; indeed, they shall cry out a hymn.” This seems in this place to exclude those rams who are barren and not useful to the sheep for the begetting of offspring. Therefore those rams—the teachers and leaders of the whole flock—are clothed with glory and honor, with the wedding garment and the robe of immortality, who devote themselves to the word of preaching and beget many children for the Lord.

“And the valleys shall abound with grain.” What are the valleys but the humble, gentle, simple, meek, and the whole multitude of the faithful? Receiving the seed of God’s word from elsewhere—that is, from the Church’s cultivators, namely bishops and priests—they abundantly render to the Lord the grain of good work, praise, and jubilation. Hence he adds [Col. 0933C]: “Indeed, they shall cry out and sing a hymn.” This is therefore the grain which the valleys render to the Lord, and this is the fruit of lips confessing his name. For there is nothing in which God delights more than the sacrifice of praise and jubilation.

## PSALM LXV

**UNTO THE END: A PSALM OF DAVID. A SONG OF THE RESURRECTION.**

He speaks of that resurrection of which the Apostle says: “If you have risen with Christ, seek the things above, where Christ is seated at the right hand of God” (Col. 3:1). Whoever wishes to rise again must first die. Hence the Apostle says: “I have died to the world” (Rom. 7:10). But he says that he himself has risen again: “I live—yet not I; Christ truly lives in me” (Gal. 2:20). And elsewhere: “Foolish one,” he says, “what you sow is not made alive unless it first dies” (1 Cor. 15:36). He therefore rises well who dies while living and lives to God, such as those who rejoice and sing psalms in this psalm.

“Make jubilation to God, all the earth; sing a psalm to his name; give glory to his praise.” The Church speaks and exhorts the whole earth to the praise of God and jubilation. Jubilation is ineffable joy held in the mind from the love of God. To sing a psalm is to sing [Col. 0934A] upon the psaltery. He sings on the psaltery who sounds and touches its ten strings, that is, who keeps the ten commandments of the Law. “Make jubilation,” he says, “to God, all the earth”: let him himself be your joy and your life. “Sing a psalm to his name,” so that whatever you do, you do in his name. Give glory to his name, so that your jubilation and singing may become glorious and praiseworthy.

Anyone can praise God, but to give glory to praise belongs to the perfect, who fulfill by their works what they sing. Such persons sing psalms well, sing well upon the psaltery, and render the sweet and harmonious sound of all the strings.

“Say to God: How terrible are your works; in the multitude of your power your enemies shall lie to you [Col. 0934B].” This is what the Apostle says: “Does the thing formed say to him who formed it, ‘Why have you made me thus?’ Or does not the potter have power over the clay, to make one vessel unto honor and another unto dishonor?” (Rom. 9:20). “O the depth of the riches of the wisdom 432 and knowledge of God! How incomprehensible are his judgments and unsearchable his ways!” (Rom. 11:33). Let this suffice us: let us admire God’s works and judgments; let us not scrutinize what is above us and exceeds our knowledge.

“In the multitude of your power your enemies shall lie to you.” This is as though he said: Because of the multitude of your might and strength, your enemies will not refrain from lying to you.

“Let all the earth adore you and sing psalms to you; let it sing a psalm [Col. 0934C] to your name, O Most High.” It is fitting that every creature should worship him by whom it was made. “For it is written: You shall worship the Lord your God, and him alone shall you serve” (Matt. 4:9). What it is to sing psalms and to sing a psalm has been said above.

“Come and see the works of the Lord, how terrible he is in his counsels above the children of men.” Come, he says, and see the works of the Lord contained below in this psalm; consider how terrible and fearsome he is in his counsels and purposes concerning all that he does above the children of men. Since we cannot comprehend them, let them merely be for us an object of admiration and thanksgiving.

“He turned the sea into dry land, and they shall pass through the rivers on foot; there we shall rejoice in the same thing.” [Note: [Col. 0933D] “Here he hastens already to show the mysteries of those works, because the Christian people truly afterward rejoiced in their prefiguration. For the fact [Col. 0934D] that the Jewish people passed through seas foretold Christ’s baptism that was to follow; and the fact that it crossed rivers on dry feet without danger from their depth signified that the currents of this world can be safely crossed and that one can arrive at the most secure place of repentance,” etc. Cassiodorus.]

[Col. 0934D] By the sea let us understand the world, and by dry land the Church. The former is raised by storms and tempests; the latter always remains firm and stable. He turns the sea into dry land when Gentiles and idolaters enter the Church and embrace the faith of Christians. By the rivers, because many waters are many peoples, are signified the diverse peoples and nations of this world. We do not fear to enter rivers through which we can pass on foot. Therefore, when holy preachers [Col. 0935A], bishops, and priests preach safely and without fear among peoples, we may say that they pass through rivers on foot.

“There we shall rejoice in the same thing.” Where fear once was, joy is now announced. There, therefore—that is, among the peoples signified by the rivers—the saints now rejoice *in idipsum*, “in the same thing,” that is, all together and in common. Their joy is shared by all because all have one faith; no one contradicts another, but all alike praise and bless Christ. Of him he adds:

“Because he rules in his power forever; his eyes look upon the nations; let not those who provoke him in anger exalt themselves.” God alone rules by his own power, because he is almighty and needs no one’s assistance. Hence elsewhere it is said: “I said to the Lord: You are my God, because you have no need of my goods” [Col. 0935B] (Ps. 25:2). He rules forever because “of his kingdom there shall be no end” (Luke 1:34). “His eyes look upon the nations,” in order to protect them and defend them from the snares of every enemy.

But what do you say concerning the Jews? “Let not those who provoke him in anger exalt themselves.” This is that provoking house for which the Prophet is forbidden to pray. Let these enraged provokers and transgressors therefore see to it that they do not exalt themselves, that is, in their own power and strength; for all their strength and glory have been taken away. We see, then, that the Jews are rejected and the Gentiles chosen, so that what is written may be fulfilled: “I shall call ‘my people’ that which was not my people, and ‘beloved’ her who was not beloved, and ‘having obtained mercy’ her who had not obtained mercy” [Col. 0935C] (Rom. 9:25); and those to whom it was said, “You are not my people,” are called children of the living God. This is what he said above: “Come and see the works of the Lord, how terrible he is in his counsels above the children of men.”

“Bless our God, O nations, and give ear to the voice of his praise.” You nations, he says, whom the Lord has chosen and called into his inheritance, “bless the Lord our God, and make the voice of his praise heard.” For so another translation reads. But what does “make heard the voice of his praise” mean except to preach and proclaim those things that pertain to his glory? What is said here—“give ear to the voice of his praise” (*obaudite vocem laudis eius*)—seems to mean: When his praise is proclaimed, be ready, in turn, to hear and obey. Thus *obedire*, “to obey,” is said as though *obaudire*, “to hear in response.”

“He has set my soul unto life, and has not allowed my feet to be moved.” [Note: [Col. 0935D] “He himself—the Lord—has set the soul unto life; he himself directs the feet, lest they be changed, moved, and given over to motion; he himself makes us live, he himself makes us persevere [Col. 0936D] to the end, so that we may live forever.” Augustine, *Enarration on this Psalm*.] The Church is one, and she herself speaks for all. Therefore the souls of all believers live if the soul of the Church has life. Likewise, the feet of all believers stand firm if the Church’s feet are not moved. Her feet are faith, steadfastness, and good intention.

“For you have tested us, O God; you have examined us by fire [Col. 0936A], as silver is examined by fire.” In this testing it was sufficiently proved what these feet were like; for unless they had been firm, they could not have stood in such a crisis. The saints, then, were tested like silver in fire, by which fire every kind of torment is signified.

“You brought us into a snare; you placed tribulations 433 upon our back; you set men over our heads.” God is said to do what, although he can prevent it, he permits to be done. Hence we daily say: “And lead us not into temptation” (Matt. 6:13)—not because he himself leads us into it, but because he does not prevent us from being led into it. The snare of the wicked is all their deceitful fraud and violence by which they capture righteous people, hold them, and subject them to their power [Col. 0936B]. He laid tribulations upon their backs because he permits them to be afflicted by beatings and in many ways. Hence the Apostle says of himself: “Three times I was beaten with rods, and five times I received from the Jews forty lashes less one” (2 Cor. 2:25). He set men over their heads, either executioners to behead them, or those who had authority over their heads in any other way.

“We passed through fire and water, and you brought us into refreshment.” As we have said, every kind of torment is signified by fire and water. But they were brought into refreshment because, as soon as their souls departed from the body, they were introduced into the glory of heavenly blessedness.

[Col. 0936C] “I shall enter your house with burnt offerings; I shall render to you the vows which my lips have uttered.” I shall offer burnt offerings, he says, and through them enter into your house. A burnt offering is interpreted as “wholly burned.” He therefore offers a burnt offering who wholly sacrifices himself to the Lord, ready in all things to do his will.

“I shall render to you my vows, which my lips have uttered.” Whatever, he says, I resolved in my heart to do in your service, I shall render in full and omit nothing.

“My mouth spoke these things in my tribulation. I shall offer you fat burnt offerings with incense and rams; I shall offer you bulls with goats.” People placed in straits and tribulations are accustomed to make both more and greater vows [Col. 0936D]. These vows, he says, which my mouth spoke, I shall pay to you. The mouth of the inner person is that mouth which speaks to you alone and is heard by you alone in silence.

“I shall offer you fat burnt offerings”: that is, burnt offerings which are full, whole, joyous, rich, and diminished in nothing. Such is the sacrifice of which the Apostle says: “I beseech you through the mercy of God to present your bodies as a living sacrifice, holy, pleasing to God—your rational service” (Rom. 12:1). The burnt offering is offered with incense as a sweet fragrance, that it may please the Lord [Col. 0937A], like those of which it is written: “And the Lord smelled a sweet fragrance” (Gen. 8:21). Zechariah, the father of John the Baptist, offered this incense, concerning whom it is written: “He was chosen by lot to offer incense according to the order of his course” (Luke 1:9). Hence it is said in the Apocalypse: “An angel stood beside the altar of the Temple, and much incense was given to him, that he might burn it before the golden altar, which is before the presence of the Lord” (Rev. 8:3).

Rams also are offered in this burnt offering; by them we understand the apostles, the fathers, guides, and leaders of the entire ecclesiastical flock. [Note: [Col. 0937D] Saint Bruno adopted this exposition from Augustine, as he did very many others. For the holy Doctor says: “The rams are the leaders of the Church; the whole body of Christ speaks: this is what it offers to God. What is incense? Prayer. For the rams especially pray for the flocks. I shall offer you bulls with goats. We find bulls threshing, and they too are offered to God. He said that the Apostles who proclaim the Gospel are to be understood in the words written: ‘You shall not muzzle an ox while it is threshing’” [Col. 0938D], etc.]

Bulls are also offered, namely bishops and priests, by whom God’s field is cultivated, ploughed, and prepared to receive the word of life. Goats also are offered to the Lord in this burnt offering [Col. 0937B], by which sinners, cleansed and sanctified through harsh repentance, are signified. Very rich is the burnt offering in which such and so great offerings are made. With such a burnt offering, therefore, our mother holy Church promises that she will enter into God’s house, because she will present all these to the Lord in joy and exultation. This was signified by Noah’s sacrifice, in which one animal from every kind of clean animal was offered.

“Come and hear me, and I shall tell you, all who fear God, how great things he has done for my soul.” [Note: [Col. 0938D] Augustine understands this passage as concerning our conversion from Gentilism to the knowledge of the true God and of our Lord Jesus Christ, and concerning the great gifts bestowed upon us.] He invites all to hear, so that by his own example he may urge and inflame them to the love of God, who has done such great good things for those who love him.

“With my mouth I cried to him, and I exulted beneath [Col. 0937C] my tongue.” “With my mouth,” he says—with the mouth of the heart, the mouth of the inner person—I cried to the Lord; “and I exulted beneath my tongue,” that is, in the silence of my heart, whose exultation is inward and not expressed in speech. For exultation beneath the tongue is hidden in the heart, whereas exultation upon the tongue is heard outwardly.

“If I regarded iniquity in my heart, God would not hear me.” This is as though he said: If you wish to be heard, let your prayer be clean and pure; pray about and for those things which concern the salvation of your soul. For this is what the Lord says in the Gospel: “If you ask the Father anything in my name, he will give it to you” (John 14:13). But those who ask otherwise, even if they often receive what they ask, are nevertheless not heard [Col. 0937D] by the Lord, because the Lord knows how to give only good gifts to the children of men.

“Therefore God heard me and attended to the voice of my supplication.” Therefore, he says, because I did not regard iniquity in my heart so as to ask and desire that things pertaining to iniquity be granted to me [Col. 0938A], God heard me and acted 434 for me according to the desires of my heart.

“Blessed be the Lord, who has not removed my prayer (and hears it) nor his mercy from me.” Had he removed it, he would not have heard it. [Note: Col. 0938D. Augustine adds: “When you see that your prayer has not been removed from you, be confident that his mercy has not been removed from you.”]

## PSALM LXVI. TO THE END; IN HYMNS; A PSALM OF DAVID’S SONG.

Let this psalm be referred to the end and sung in hymns and praises. A psalm with a song signifies action together with praise. Many possess song who do not possess psalm, because they have praise without action.

“May God have mercy upon us and bless us; may he make his face shine upon us, and have mercy on us.” Behold, he says, as is read in what follows, “our land gave its fruit.” [Col. 0938B] And the Virgin Mother bore the Saviour. Therefore, “May God, our God, bless us; may God bless us.” God is named three times in this place, because God is Father, God is Son, God is Holy Spirit; and therefore it is said not in the plural but in the singular, “May God bless us.” The whole world lay under a curse; but at Christ’s coming it deserved to receive blessing. For he is the one concerning whom the Lord said to Abraham: “In your seed all nations shall be blessed” (Acts 3:25). And the Apostle says: “Christ Jesus redeemed us from the curse of the law, having become a curse for us” (Gal. 3:13). Hence the Church now says: “May God, our God, bless us; may God bless us.” He rightly says “our God,” because he is not [Col. 0938C] the God of the Jews alone, but God, Lord, and Saviour of all nations. Hence it is suitably added: “And may all the ends of the earth fear him.” Therefore may this our God have mercy upon us and bless us, who came for this purpose: to show mercy—and such great mercy as we can neither express nor conceive. Hence elsewhere it is said: “The earth is full of the mercy of the Lord” (Ps. 32:5).—“May he make his face shine upon us, and have mercy upon us.” May he make his face shine upon us, he says; may he show us a cheerful and joyful countenance, so that by this we may understand that all wrath and indignation have been driven away, and may know that we possess his grace and good will. Or again, “May he make his face shine upon us,” so that we may be refashioned according to his image and likeness. [Col. 0938D] Thus far he has spoken in the third person; now he addresses the Father himself, and speaks the following words in the second person.

“That we may know thy way upon earth, thy salvation among all nations.” He, he says, whom our land [Col. 0939A] gave forth and whom the Virgin Mary bore—may he have mercy upon us and bless us, so that we may be able to know this same one, who is our life and our salvation. Christians alone know him, and Christians alone understand how great his goodness and mercy are. Christ is the way to the Father, because through him one comes to the Father. Hence he himself says: “I am the way, the truth, and the life. No one comes to the Father except through me” (John 14:6). He is also salvation, because through him salvation is wrought among nations everywhere. This is the salvation of which it is elsewhere said: “The Lord has made known his salvation” (Ps. 97:2). And the patriarch Jacob says: “I shall await thy salvation, O Lord” (Gen. 49:18). Concerning him it is now said here: “May thy name be known and made manifest [Col. 0939B] among all nations.” [Note: Col. 0939D. Codex Ghislerianus: “Thy salvation.”] But why is it said “upon earth,” unless because he was known upon earth and in the flesh, though he could not be seen in the power of his divinity? The Jews, indeed, saw him but did not know him, because they saw only the earth.

“Let the peoples confess thee, O God; let all the peoples confess thee.” Because, he says, thy salvation, O Lord, has been revealed among all peoples and nations through apostolic preaching and the wonder of miracles, henceforth let the peoples confess thee, O God; let all peoples confess thee—whereas the Jews alone had hitherto been accustomed to confess and praise thee. For “God is known in Judah; his name is great in Israel” (Ps. 75:2). But now, while they alone have ceased from praise and confession, all nations and [Col. 0939C] all peoples confess thee.

“Let the nations rejoice and exult, because thou judgest peoples in equity and guidest nations upon earth.” Let the nations rejoice and exult, he says, because they have a good judge, who does not seek occasions to condemn and destroy them—for this the enemy of the human race was accustomed to do—but rather seeks to have mercy upon them and guide them in the way of truth.

“Let the peoples confess thee, O God; let all the peoples confess thee.” Few, he says, are those whom thou hast lost; innumerable are those whom thou hast acquired and redeemed by the blood of thy Son. The Jews are few in comparison with all the nations; many are those everywhere preparing themselves for thy praises and thanksgiving. [Col. 0939D] Therefore let the Jews be silent, since they are both few and unworthy to offer thee praise; and “let the peoples confess thee, O God; let all the peoples confess thee.” [Note: Col. 0939D. See how much St Augustine brings forth in his exposition of this psalm.]

(The remainder of this psalm is lacking both in the edition and in the manuscripts.)

## PSALM LXVII. TO THE END; A PSALM OF DAVID’S SONG.

In this psalm the prophet David himself sings; but because he speaks of Christ and the Church, he therefore prefixed “to the end.”

[Col. 0940A] “Let God arise, and let his enemies be scattered; and let those who hate him flee before his face.” Let God arise, he says, to aid his faithful; let Christ arise from the dead—he whom foolish and vain Jews guard, shut up in the tomb, as though they could keep him there. [Note: Col. 0939D. “It has already happened: Christ has arisen, who is God above all, blessed for ever; and [Col. 0940D] his enemies—the Jews—have been scattered among all nations, in the very place where they practiced their enmity, and thence dispersed everywhere,” etc. Augustine, *Exposition on This Psalm*.] And let his enemies be scattered, by whom we understand the Jews and evil spirits. These are those concerning whom it is elsewhere said: “They were scattered and were not pierced with compunction” (Ps. 34:16).—“And let those who hate him flee before his face.” Who doubts that evil spirits fled then—if indeed they were able to flee—when Christ the Lord descended into hell and rescued the souls of the saints who were held captive there? The Jews flee before his face even to this day, because blinded by their own malice they are unwilling either to see him [Col. 0940B] or to know him. But these things will be fulfilled more completely at the judgment, when, driven from before his face in disgrace, they will be sent into eternal fire.

“As smoke vanishes, let them vanish; as wax melts before fire, so let sinners perish before God.” Smoke vanishes as it rises from the earth and is lifted higher; so the Jews and all the proud vanish and perish in their exaltation. “As wax melts before fire,” and so forth. Thus may they perish: that they may burn forever and furnish fuel for that eternal and unquenchable fire with their very selves.

“And let the righteous feast, and exult in the presence of God, and delight in joy.” Let the righteous feast now, indeed, on the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth; but afterward on the delights of ineffable fullness and blessedness. [Col. 0940C] The very contemplation of the divine majesty is for them an inestimable refreshment and an inexpressible joy.

“Sing to God; sing a psalm to his name; make a way for him who ascends above the west; the Lord is his name.” Singing pertains to the voice, but singing a psalm pertains to action. Therefore we must both sing and sing psalms, so that we may fulfill in deed the things we sing. This is what it means to sing a psalm to his name, because the Lord is his name. Whoever understands him to be Lord and himself to be servant, and serves him with the diligence and reverence with which a good servant ought to serve his master, that person sings well, psalms well, and sings a psalm well to his name; for he speaks to him as a good servant ought to speak to his master. Those make a way for him who prepare within themselves the path by which he may come to them, according to what is written: “Prepare the way of the Lord; make straight the paths of our God” (Mark 2:3). If you have humility, you have prepared a way by which he may come to you. If you have patience and charity, these too are paths on which he delights to walk. As many virtues as you possess and as many good works as you have done, so many paths have you prepared by which the Lord may come to you. And he is the one who ascends above the west, because by dying he trampled down, cast down, and overcame death itself. He also ascended above the west in this respect: [Col. 0941A] from the very place whence he was thought to have fallen, he appeared lofty and a most mighty conqueror.

“Rejoice in his presence.” You, he says, who both sing and stand in his presence, rejoice and exult, because a worthy recompense for your service awaits you. “For his eyes are upon the righteous, and his ears are open to their prayers.” But what do you say of the others? “They will be troubled before his face.” For those who do not now sing to him, sing psalms to him, obey him, or know his name, will be troubled before his face, because at the judgment they will be taken away and cast into the fire, so that they may not see his glory. But do you wish to hear whose glory it is? It is that of “the father of orphans and judge of widows.” These are those orphans whose father was once the devil; these are those widows who [Col. 0941B] were once joined in a shameful marriage, but now, because their husband is dead and has been unwillingly separated from them, rejoice that they have the protection and defense of our Saviour. For just as the good will rejoice in his presence, so the evil will be troubled before the face of him who is father of orphans and judge of widows.

“God in his holy place; God who makes those of one mind dwell in a house.” [Note: Col. 0941D. According to another reading, “Thou who makest those of one disposition dwell in a house,” Augustine says: “What is this place? God makes it for himself. For God makes those of one disposition dwell in a house: this is his holy place.” Cassiodorus also reads, “who makes those of one mind dwell in a house.”] This, he says, is the God who makes those of one mind dwell in one house, that is, in a holy place. By this holy place the Church is signified. These are those of whom it is written in the Acts of the Apostles: “The multitude of believers had one heart and one soul; and no one said that anything [436] was his own, but they had all things in common” (Acts 4:32). Such still are those who dwell [Col. 0941C] in religious and regular communities, of whom it is rightly said: “Behold, how good and how pleasant it is for brothers to dwell together in unity!” (Ps. 131:1).

“He brings out those bound in strength; likewise those who provoke to wrath, who dwell in tombs.” By these we may understand the patriarchs, prophets, and all the souls of the saints, who were held captive in hell. [Note: Col. 0941D. The Apostle Paul expressed the same thing more clearly concerning Christ’s triumph through his death, in Colossians 2:15: “Stripping the principalities and powers,” he says, “he led them openly in triumph, triumphing over them in himself.”] Of them it is elsewhere said: “He brought them out of darkness and the shadow of death, and broke their bonds asunder” (Ps. 106:14). What need is there to say with how great power the Lord brought them out, when he undertook so great a labor in order to bring them forth and liberate them? [Col. 0941D] For what other reason was there that he came into the world, assumed flesh, and was willing to endure the passion of the cross, except to free the entire human race from the devil’s snares and chains? “Likewise those who provoke to wrath, who dwell in tombs.” It was no more difficult to snatch those souls from hell than to raise from the tombs in which they lie dead those who are in this world. [Col. 0942A] Those souls, indeed, were liberated suddenly and in one hour; these, however, are liberated and raised daily. Sinners are called tombs: whitewashed outside, but within full of stench and decay. But who are those who provoke to wrath, except those who sin daily and scorn to return to repentance? Such persons, “according to the hardness of their heart,” as the Apostle says, “store up wrath for themselves on the day of wrath” (Rom. 2:5). If they depart this life in that condition, God will never again be appeased toward them.

“O God, when thou didst go forth before thy people, when thou didst pass through the wilderness, the earth was moved.” These words are not to be understood literally of Mount Sinai, but [Col. 0942B] spiritually of the holy Church. For when the holy Apostles were sent forth to preach throughout the whole world, then the Lord went forth before his people and passed through trackless and desert lands. And then the earth was indeed moved, because an innumerable multitude from all nations was converted to the faith. In this wilderness blessed John the Baptist cried out when he said: “I am the voice of one crying in the wilderness” (John 1:23).

“For the heavens dropped before God, before the God of Israel.” The heavens are the Apostles, of whom it is said: “The heavens declare the glory of God” (Ps. 18:1). They dropped before God because the rain and doctrine which they preached and poured forth were not theirs but God’s. Hence the Lord says: “For it is not [Col. 0942C] you who speak, but the Spirit of your Father who speaks in you” (Matt. 10:20). Therefore they dropped before God. But before which God? “Before the God of Israel.” Thus there is one God of both Testaments, and one doctrine which both Moses and the Apostles preached. In this the Manichaeans are refuted, who maintained that the God of the Old Testament was one and the God of the New another. Mount Sinai likewise dropped before God; for not only the heavens—that is, the Apostles—but also the whole Church, signified by Mount Sinai, pours forth this same rain and proclaims this same doctrine. On Mount Sinai the Law was given, and on Mount Zion the Gospel was given. “I,” says the Lord, “have been established king by him [Col. 0942D] over Zion, his holy mountain, proclaiming the commandment of the Lord” (Ps. 2:6).

“Thou wilt set apart a voluntary rain for thine inheritance, O God; for it was weakened, but thou hast perfected it.” [Note: Col. 0941D. Let it not weary you to hear Augustine: “God, setting apart a voluntary rain for his inheritance, because he did not do so for every nation and did not make his judgments known to them. Therefore God set apart this voluntary rain for his inheritance in that he gave the Law. And either the Law itself or the inheritance itself was weakened. The Law can be understood as weakened because it was not fulfilled—not because it is itself weak, but because it makes people weak, threatening punishment but not assisting through grace, etc. But thou hast perfected it, because the fullness of the Law is charity; and the charity of God has been poured out in our hearts, not through ourselves but through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us.”] It was not the heavens or the Church, he says, but [Col. 0943A] thou, O God, who hast done all these things, setting apart a voluntary rain for thine inheritance. This rain is not compulsory but voluntary, because it is freely given and freely received. Since the Jews were unwilling to receive it, the Lord set it apart for his inheritance. Thus the Lord says concerning that vineyard which had turned to bitterness: “I shall command my clouds not to rain rain upon it” (Isa. 5:6). And elsewhere: “I shall rain upon one city, and upon another I shall not rain” (Amos 4:7).—[Note: Col. 0943D. Addition from Codex Ghislerianus.] “This rain was set apart for God’s inheritance, that it might restore, make fruitful, and heal it. For it was weakened; but as soon as it received this rain, it was healed. And this is what he says: ‘But thou hast perfected it.’ Therefore one who is weak is not perfect. Once healed, accordingly, [Col. 0943B] one immediately becomes perfect.”

“Thy living creatures shall dwell therein; in thy sweetness thou hast prepared for the poor, O God.” By God’s living creatures are understood all the faithful, of whatever sex, age, rank, or condition. These living creatures, which are nourished and remain in this inheritance of the Lord, are many and diverse. They were signified in Noah’s ark, which received every kind of clean and unclean animal. But who are these poor persons whom the Lord has prepared in his sweetness? They are those of whom he says in the Gospel: “Blessed are the poor [437] in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. 5:4). Of them the Apostle also says: “As needy, yet enriching many; as having nothing, and possessing all things” (2 Cor. 6:10). The Lord prepared them [Col. 0943C] in his sweetness when he said: “Be merciful, as your Father is merciful” (Luke 6:36);—“Do not judge, and you shall not be judged; do not condemn, and you shall not be condemned” (Matt. 7:1). He formed them according to his own sweetness, that they might love and heal all people and invite them to blessedness. The poor Lord chose poor disciples, because “although he was rich in all things, he became poor for our sakes” (2 Cor. 8:7).

“The Lord will give the word to those who proclaim the gospel with great power.” The Lord, he says, will give the word to his poor ones who proclaim the gospel with great power. For he himself says in the Gospel: “Lay it up in your hearts not to prepare beforehand how you shall answer; for I [Col. 0943D] will give you a mouth and wisdom which none of your adversaries will be able to resist or contradict” (Luke 21:15). Thus what is called “the word” here is called “a mouth and wisdom” there. The Apostles proclaimed the gospel with great power, as it is written: “The Lord working with them and confirming the word by the signs that followed” (Mark 16:20). And in the Acts of the Apostles it is said: “With great power the Apostles gave testimony to the resurrection of our Lord Jesus Christ, and great grace was upon them all” (Acts 4:33). But if we read “great power,” as some manuscripts [Col. 0944A] have it, this means those who preached Christ, the power of God and wisdom of God. It can also be understood by transposition: the Lord will give great power to those proclaiming the gospel and preaching the word.

“The king of the powers of the Beloved [Note: Col. 0943D. “The Father, therefore, is king of the powers of the Son. For when someone is not specifically identified as beloved, ‘the Beloved’ by antonomasia is understood to be the only Son.” Augustine.] and of the beauty of the house, to divide the spoils.” The Scriptures must be supplied where something necessary to the sense is lacking. The king of the powers is God the Father, who, wishing the Apostles to divide the spoils of his beloved Son and of the house of beauty, secretly commanded them by inspiration to sleep and rest between the two lots. This is what these words signify according to the letter. But now let us consider their meaning. By “powers” in this place we must understand not only powers, but also angels, archangels, principalities, [Col. 0944B] authorities, and the remaining orders, because no order can exist without power. “The spoils of the Beloved” and “the house of beauty” signify the same thing: namely, all the churches established throughout the world, though they are members of one universal and catholic Church. These are the spoils of the Beloved, that is, of him concerning whom the Lord said: “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased; hear him” (Matt. 17:5). These are the spoils of which it is said through the prophet: “As victors rejoice when they have taken prey, when they divide the spoils” (Isa. 9:3). Of these spoils our Saviour himself also says: “When a strong man armed guards his court, what he possesses is in peace; but if one stronger than he comes upon him [Note: Col. 0944D. Codex Ghislerianus: “coming upon him, conquers him.”], [Col. 0944C] he conquers him, takes away all his weapons in which he trusted, and distributes his spoils” (Luke 11:21). The Lord divided these spoils and these houses of splendor and beauty when he determined that the Apostles should go to preach through each province, each people, and each nation. Of them it is said: “Their sound has gone forth into all the earth, and their words unto the ends of the world” (Ps. 18:4).

“If you sleep between the two lots, you will be the wings of a silvered dove.” [Note: Col. 0944D. See Augustine, who is very full in this interpretation, from which Bruno certainly seems to have drawn his exposition.] This sentence is incomplete unless something is added to it: “If you sleep between the two lots,” he says, “you will be the wings of a silvered dove; and the hind parts of her back will follow you in the appearance of gold.” With these words understood in this way, the sense is easy. By the two lots are signified the two Testaments, or the active and contemplative life. *Clerus* means “lot” or “inheritance.” Therefore let the holy Apostles sleep between the two lots; there let all teachers of the Church sleep; there let bishops and priests sleep, rest, delight themselves, and meditate day and night, as is said of the righteous man in the first psalm: “He will meditate in his law day and night” (Ps. 1:2). Such sleep is delightful: one who rests in this manner is not idle. Let them sleep, therefore, between the two lots; let them have the New Testament on this side and the Old [Col. 0945A] Testament on that; from them let them receive what they may preach to others; from them let them take food by which they may nourish others. Let their preaching not be novel or foreign, but firm and full of authority. Let them hear the Apostle saying: “Do not be led away by diverse and strange teachings” (Heb. 13:9). But if they do this, they will be the wings of a silvered dove, by which, lifted up, they will fly over to heavenly things with light, swift, and easy course. This is the dove of which the Lord says in the Song of Songs: “My dove is one, my perfect one, my spotless one” (Song 6:8). The whole holy Church is called a dove because it is simple and innocent. Hence the Lord says in the Gospel: “Be prudent as serpents and simple as doves” (Matt. 10:10). But why is it called silvered? [Col. 0945B] Is it not because its utterances are true and pure, as though silver tested by fire, and corrupted by no falsity of error?
