Its utterances are such because the Lord’s utterances are such, as it is written: “The utterances of the Lord are chaste utterances, silver tested by fire, tried in the earth, purified sevenfold” (Ps. 11:7).—“And the hind parts of her back are in the paleness of gold.” If this dove had no front parts, it would have no hind parts. But because it has front parts, it must also have hind parts. Christ is the head of the Church; immediately after the head come the Apostles, bishops, and priests. They go before; they have been appointed by the Lord as leaders in the whole Church. All others follow and imitate them. These, indeed, are the hind parts who follow them in the appearance [Col. 0945C] of gold. But why in the appearance of gold? Is it not because all are splendid, all clean and pure, all baptized and made whiter than snow, all shining with the light of spiritual wisdom, and pleasing the Lord in gilded raiment? It follows:

“While the heavenly one distinguishes kings over her, they shall be whitened as snow in Selmon.” [Note: Col. 0945D. Bruno’s reading follows the Vulgate; Cassiodorus differs, reading “over the earth,” though he agrees in exposition.] Then, he says, the king of powers, the heavenly king, commanded the Apostles and teachers of the Church to sleep between the two lots when he established and ordained them kings over the Church. “They shall be whitened as snow in Selmon”: all these kings, and whoever has imitated them, shall be whitened as snow in Selmon. Selmon is interpreted “shade,” and signifies that heavenly Jerusalem, into [Col. 0945D] whose shade and refreshment whoever arrives will enter. The one who said, “Protect me under the shadow of thy wings from the face of the ungodly who have afflicted me” (Ps. 16:8), desired this shade. The saints will indeed be made white as snow in Selmon, because there they will receive white, splendid, bridal garments; and all there will have such garments as the Lord displayed to his three disciples when he was transfigured before them on the mountain. For it is written: “His face appeared radiant as [Col. 0946A] the sun, and his garments became white as snow” (Matt. 17:2). And as though someone asked the Prophet what he meant Selmon to be, he answered:

“Mountains of God, fruitful mountains.” [Note: Col. 0945D. Vatican reading: “mountain of God, fruitful mountain”; thus Cassiodorus. The Vulgate has: “mountain of God, fat mountain.”] This Selmon about which you inquire is “a curdled mountain, a fat mountain.” Truly it is mountains of God and fruitful mountains, because God alone reigns there, and there is such abundance of every good that no tongue can suffice either to think or to express it, as the Apostle says: “What eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has entered into the heart of man, what God has prepared for those who love him” (1 Cor. 2:6). That mountain is curdled because no one there needs milk; no one there has the imperfect knowledge signified by milk. Hence the Apostle says to some: “You have become such as need milk, not solid food” (Heb. 5:12). [Col. 0946B] For everyone who partakes of milk is unskilled in the word of righteousness, for he is a little child. But there all are perfect, and all use not milk but solid food, because all see everything not through a mirror and in an enigma, but face to face. That mountain is also fat—indeed, most fat—because it is wholly steeped in the oil of the Holy Spirit, and there is no one there who does not possess every grace of the Holy Spirit.

“Why do you look with suspicion on fruitful mountains? The mountain in which it has pleased God to dwell—for there the Lord will dwell unto the end.” [Note: Col. 0946D. The same codex reads *suspicitis*, as does the Vatican reading, which also has “fruitful mountain.” Here St Bruno’s text agrees with the Vulgate; Cassiodorus has, “Why have you received fruitful mountains?”] Thus far he has spoken of that heavenly mountain. Now he begins to speak of other mountains, namely Christ and John the Baptist. For as we read in the Gospel, [Col. 0946C] “All thought John to be the Christ; for he was a burning and shining lamp, but he was not the light, but was to bear witness to the light” (John 5:33). When priests and Levites came to him and asked whether he was the Christ, he answered: “I am not the Christ” (John 1:21);—“He is stronger than I, whose sandal strap I am not worthy to untie” (Mark 1:7). Blessed John, therefore, was a great mountain, very fruitful and full; but greater and higher was he to whom John bore witness. “Why,” he says, “do you look with suspicion on fruitful mountains? Why do you admire John? Why do you think him to be Christ?” He speaks against and rebukes those who came to John and thought him Christ. Hence it is added: Do you suppose that John is that mountain in which God is pleased to dwell? John is indeed a great mountain, to whom the Lord himself bears witness, saying: “Among those born of women no greater than John the Baptist has arisen” (Matt. 11:11). But he in whom God is pleased to dwell is of higher dignity. Ask John himself, and he will tell you how great the difference is between himself and that one. But let Christ himself say how God is pleased [Col. 0947A] to dwell in him: “I am,” he says, “in the Father, and the Father is in me. He who sees me sees also the Father. I and the Father are one” (John 14:9). Neither John nor anyone else can say this. God dwells in John, but as in another; the Father dwells in the Son as the same in the same. Although the Father is one person and the Son another, the Father is not one thing and the Son another thing. “For the Lord will dwell in him unto the end.” What is “unto the end,” if not utterly and wholly? Thus it is also said: “The patience of the poor shall not perish unto the end” (Ps. 9:19). Therefore the Father will dwell in the Son unto the end; and because neither Father nor Son will have an end, neither will this indwelling have an end. Therefore the Father is always in the Son, and the Son always in the Father, [Col. 0947B] and the Holy Spirit in both.

“The chariots of God are many tens of thousands, thousands of those who rejoice.” Someone may say: Behold, we have heard who Christ is and how the Father dwells in him; but what does he say about the others? What are they, and how is God in them? They are, he says, God’s chariots; and as he sits in his chariot, so he sits in them. When he wills, he ascends; when he wills, he descends; when he wills, he causes them to run; and when he wills, he causes them to rest. But do not inquire into their number, because it is infinite: they are many tens of thousands, and there are innumerable thousands of those who rejoice in this chariot. “Tens of thousands” signifies just as much as if he had said “innumerable thousands,” since every number is contained in that number. Thus the Apocalypse says that the saints will have tribulation for ten [Col. 0947C] days (Rev. 2:10), which is as though it said, “for all days.” It is also evident here that he set a finite number for an infinite one, because, after first saying “tens of thousands,” he afterward simply and without limitation put “thousands.” Therefore these chariots are infinite, and all rejoice and glory in the Lord.

“The Lord is among them, in Sinai, in the holy place.” This also pertains to his glory: although these chariots are innumerable and each distinct in itself, nevertheless the Lord is simultaneously in each and in all. This is because he is everywhere, which seems to be peculiar to him. The Lord, he says, is in them, but in Sinai—that is, through Sinai in them. But what is “in Sinai” except “in the holy,” that is, through what is holy? For Sinai is interpreted “commandment.” And concerning the commandment the Apostle says: “We know that the law is holy, and the commandment holy, just, and good” (Rom. 7:12). Therefore God dwells in no others except [Col. 0948A] those who receive and keep his commandment. Thus the Lord is in them, in holy Sinai—that is, through the holy commandment. [Note: Col. 0947D. Augustine aptly illuminates this passage: “But what would the commandment avail,” he says, “unless the Lord were there, concerning whom it is said: ‘For it is God who works in us both to will and to work according to his good pleasure’? For the commandment without God’s help is the letter that kills.”]

“Ascending on high, he led captivity captive; he gave gifts to men.” [Note: Col. 0947D. Another reading in the Psalter illuminated by Cardinal Thomasio: “Thou hast ascended on high; thou hast taken captivity; thou hast received gifts in men,” explained thus: “Thou, Lord, hast ascended on high; thou hast led captivity captive to thyself, subduing and making captive thine enemies; thou hast received thy gifts in order to give them to men.”] This God and our Lord, he says, ascending on high—first indeed to the cross and then to heaven—led captivity captive, as it is written: “When I am lifted up from the earth, I shall draw all things to myself” (John 12:32). All were captives of the devil, but more became captives of Christ—not all; for many are still held in captivity who, had they wished, would not be captive. He gave gifts to men, and very great gifts, when he sent the Holy Spirit to the Apostles and gave them such grace that they spoke in the languages [Col. 0948B] of all and healed every sickness and infirmity.

“For those who do not believe to dwell—the Lord God is blessed; blessed be the Lord from day to day.” [Note: Col. 0948D. Cassiodorus explains this passage thus: “For those who do not believe to dwell, the Lord God. Here ‘he converted them’ must be supplied, so that the sentence may stand complete for us. For those who do not believe to dwell—that is, those who neglect to come into the Lord’s inner dwelling, so that they may be able to dwell in his house with the faithful—the Lord God converts; for in mercy he grants his faith to the human race.” And for fuller understanding we may add Augustine: “For faith freed them from this condition, so that now, believing, they may dwell in the house of God, having themselves become the house of God and chariots of God, thousands of those who rejoice.”] But another translation has: “For those not believing the Lord God to have dwelt: blessed be the Lord from day to day.” This is as though it said: Those who formerly did not believe that the Lord God had assumed flesh, dwelt among human beings, and lived among them, now converted to faith through the Holy Spirit cry out and say: “Blessed be the Lord on each successive day.” In this translation the grammar itself seems so confused that we can scarcely understand it. Nevertheless, because both translations ought to signify the same thing, we must explain the more obscure by the clearer. Let us therefore punctuate it thus: “For those who formerly did not believe to dwell,” afterward enlightened by the Holy Spirit, say: “Blessed be the Lord God; blessed be the Lord God”; and this from day to day, that is, through every single day.

“May God our Savior, our God, make our journey prosperous; God is a God of saving, and to the Lord belong the issues from death.” The apostles said this after receiving the Holy Spirit, when they began to go throughout the whole world to preach. And indeed they had a prosperous journey, because they converted all nations completely and deserved to receive crowns of victory. “God our Savior,” he says, “will make our journey prosperous” [Col. 0948D]: by this we may understand especially the Son of God, who saved us by his death. And he himself is our God, because, although he is God of all, he is nevertheless properly the God of Christians. He too is “the God of saving” [Col. 0949A], because he came for this purpose, to redeem and save the world. And he is “the God of the Lord’s issues from death.” By this it is understood that he is God even of himself. For since he is both God and man, according to his humanity he is indeed a servant and a creature—his own creature and servant. Yet this servant is our Lord. And he himself is the issue from death, because, as all died in Adam, so all were made alive in Christ. He is the entrance into life and also the issue from death, because through him death withdrew and through him life approached.

> [Note: [Col. 0949D] Cassiodorus’s exposition must not be passed over: “The Lord’s issue from death is the wished-for resurrection of the faithful. Truly that issue was singular and wonderful, because he himself came forth from the lower world, and by his gift enabled us also to come forth from it.” In this exposition shine forth both the profundity of sacred doctrine and the discernment of the interpreting mind.]

“But God will crush the heads of his enemies, the hairy crown of those who walk about in their sins.” Although, he says, he is the issue from death [Col. 0949B], he will nevertheless kill many who are worthy of death. His enemies, those walking about in their sins, are the Jews, who persevere in their malice and do not depart from the path of iniquity. The Lord will crush their heads and their hairy crown—their pride, height, and exaltation—when he casts them into eternal fire. Of this crushing it is said in another psalm: “He shall judge among the nations; he shall fill up ruins; he shall crush many heads in a land abounding” (Ps. 109:6).

“The Lord said: I will turn back from Bashan; I will turn back from the depth of the sea.”

> [Note: [Col. 0949D] Clarius explains the literal sense thus: “I will turn back from Bashan, etc. That is, I will deliver my people, just as formerly I delivered them from the hand of Og king of Bashan and from the hand of the king of Egypt in the Red Sea; I so crushed them together with their peoples that the feet of Israel might be dipped in their blood and the tongue of dogs might lap the blood of enemies slain by the Lord [Col. 0950D]. According to another translation, *I will turn back* is read as *I will be turned into the depth of the sea*, or *from the depths*, where Augustine says that our Lord said this because, in his mercy, he would turn even into the depth of the sea, to deliver also those who were the most utterly desperate sinners.” Same exposition on Psalm 67.]

The Prophet knew when the Lord said this, because he heard him speaking within himself, as he himself says: “I will hear what the Lord God speaks in me” [Col. 0949C] (Ps. 84:8). Bashan is interpreted “confusion,” and signifies the land of the Jews, which came into confusion and dispersion because of their sins. The sea, however, is this world; by its depth are understood the greater powers and more wicked people. Therefore the Lord was turned from Bashan into the depth of the sea, because he passed from Judaea to the nations; and where the depth of the sea was, there the head and exaltation of the Church was established. Hence he says elsewhere: “Behold, I fled far away and remained in solitude” (Ps. 54:8). And the Apostle says: “It was necessary that the word of God should first be preached to you; but since you rejected it and made yourselves unworthy of eternal life, behold, we turn to the nations” (Acts 13:46).

“Until your foot is dipped [Col. 0949D] in blood.” As though he said: The Lord said that he would turn himself from Bashan into the depth of the sea [Col. 0950A], and I answered: wait a little, until your foot is dipped in blood. For it was not fitting that he should leave Judaea before his passion, since he was to be crucified by the Jews. Christ’s feet were dipped in blood because, nailed to the cross, they were stained with his own blood.

“The tongue of your dogs, from among the enemies.” These dogs, said to belong to God, are good dogs: they were made friends out of enemies. Namely, from those enemies of whom he had just said above: “Yet he will crush the heads of his enemies” (Ps. 109:6). Of these dogs only the tongue was necessary to us: it taught us, preached to us, and healed our wounds by licking them. Good dogs guard God’s sheep and protect them from the snares and rapacity of wolves.

“From that very foot your steps, O God, were seen; the goings of my God, who is in his sanctuary” [Col. 0950B]. From that foot, he says—the foot dipped in blood—your steps, O God, were seen and known, because that foot taught us to walk in your ways and not to depart from the way of piety and mercy. “The goings of my God and my King, who is in his sanctuary”: that is, who dwells in the humanity which he himself assumed and made, were seen in that most holy foot.

“The princes went before, joined with those singing psalms, in the midst of young women playing tambourines.”

> [Note: [Col. 0950D] “Young women playing tambourines: that is, maidens flourishing in the first bloom of youth, who directed their tambourines—that is, the tension of their bodies—to the Lord’s praises and glory, mortifying themselves with fasts and rejoicing still more in the mortification of the flesh; and divine power works this even today in many virgins.” —Cassiodorus.]

Those whom he had called dogs he now calls princes. Joined with those singing psalms—that is, with the whole multitude of the Church—these went before all others as leaders and teachers in psalmody, singing, preaching, and working miracles [Col. 0950C]. They sang and preached among young women playing tambourines. These young tambourine-players were the primitive Church, which the holy apostles themselves taught and preached to. They are rightly called tambourine-players, because all the saints of that time bore tambourines and were prepared to receive blows. Tambourines are made from dry, stretched skin; when struck with blows, they resound farther. The apostles bore tambourines when, as is read in the Acts of the Apostles, after being most severely beaten, “they went away rejoicing from the presence of the council, because they had been judged worthy to suffer insult for the name of Jesus” (Acts 5:41).

“In the churches bless the Lord, God from the fountains of Israel. There Benjamin, the younger, is in fear [Col. 0950D]; the princes of Judah are their leaders, the princes of Zebulun, the princes of Naphtali.” The Prophet commands the aforesaid princes [Col. 0951A], who came from the fountains of Israel, to bless our Savior, who himself according to the flesh derives his origin from those same fountains. There, he says, among those princes Benjamin the younger—that is, the blessed Apostle Paul—sings most excellently and wisely. Of himself he says: “For I too am an Israelite, of the seed of Abraham and of the tribe of Benjamin” (Rom. 11:1). And in the Acts of the Apostles it is said of him that “the witnesses laid their garments at the feet of a young man called Saul” (Acts 7:38).

> [Note: [Col. 0951C] Cassiodorus gives the same interpretation. On the words *the younger in fear*, he says: “He was the younger in fear when, at the Lord’s voice, he fell down—the Lord thundered to him in mercy: ‘Saul, Saul, why do you persecute me?’” (Acts 9:5).]

But where this text says “in fear,” another version says “in ecstasy”; and both signify the same thing, for ecstasy of mind rarely occurs without fear. Thus Daniel too says that, after his ecstasy, he was ill for many days [Col. 0951B] (Dan. 8:27). Yet this was no slight ecstasy, which had been prophesied long before: for he heard words which it is not lawful for a man to utter. By “the princes of Judah, Zebulun, and Naphtali,” said to be leaders of others, Peter and Andrew, James and John are especially understood. Hence it is written: “At the first time the land of Zebulun and the land of Naphtali was lightened” (Isa. 9:1); for the apostles were called from there, and are also called men of Galilee.

“Command, O God, your strength.” The Prophet asks the Lord to command his strength for his princes, so that, strengthened by it, they may fear no one and faithfully and wisely accomplish the work laid upon them. Hence it follows: “Confirm, O God, what you have worked in us” [Col. 0951C]. He rightly counts himself among them, for he was instructed and filled with the same Spirit along with them. He prays that this may be confirmed in them, without which he does not doubt that they can do nothing.

“From your holy temple, which is in Jerusalem, kings shall offer gifts to you.” He does not say that they will offer gifts in the temple; rather, he seems to say that they will receive from the temple the gifts which they will offer. Jerusalem, therefore, is the Church. The holy temple [Col. 0952A] within it is understood to be the Savior’s humanity, in which temple the whole fullness of divinity rests bodily. The kings are the apostles and all others who wisely govern themselves and others. These kings receive from this temple all the gifts which they offer to the Lord; and gifts not received from this temple cannot be offered to the Lord. That this temple is the Church, the Lord himself shows when he says: “Behold, I am with you all days, even to the consummation of the age” (Matt. 28:20).

“Rebuke the beasts of the woods, the assembly of bulls among the cows of the peoples, that those proved by silver may be excluded.” The beasts of the woods are heretics: beasts, indeed, because they are cruel and savage and desire to kill and devour human souls [Col. 0952B]; of the woods because they flee ecclesiastical fellowship and delight in solitary, alien food. Let the Lord rebuke such people and restrain them from their savagery, lest they deceive and destroy simple souls.

“The assembly of bulls among the cows of the peoples.” Evil bulls, evil cows, make an evil assembly: they gather in order that the saints may be excluded from the Church.

> [Note: [Col. 0951C] The history of the Council of Rimini is lengthy. There everything was done by the fraud and violence of the Arians, so that many Catholic bishops appeared to have defected from the Nicene faith [Col. 0951D]. Three formulas of faith were presented at that council. The first and third contained no error, and sinned only in this: the word *consubstantial* (*homoousios*, ὁμοούσιος), established by the Nicene Fathers concerning the Son of God in order to declare identity of nature with the Father, was absent; in its place the Son was said to be like the Father in all things—namely, *homoiousios* (ὁμοιούσιος). Catholic bishops subscribed to these formulas out of love of peace, but were deceived by the Arians, who used the same expressions while intending another sense: they admitted every kind of likeness between Father and Son, yet denied consubstantiality.
>
> The testimony of St Jerome in *Dialogue against the Luciferians*, no. 18, Vallarsi edition, is beyond all exception: “The bishops were not concerned about the word, since the meaning was secure . . . But at this the bishops all together, and the entire Church, received the statement of Valens with a certain applause and stamping of feet. If anyone thinks this was said by us [Col. 0952C], let him search the public records. Certainly the chests of the churches are full of them, and the memory of the affair is still recent. Men survive who were present at that synod; and, to confirm the truth, the Arians themselves do not deny that these things happened as we have said.”
>
> This is the same Jerome who, speaking hyperbolically of the Arian deception at that synod, said that the whole world groaned and wondered to find itself Arian [Col. 0952D]. What St Bruno said about the Council of Rimini must be understood with this clarification. Yet he rightly and deservedly called the other council of the Arians—the one gathered at Seleucia in 359—a council of Arians; according to St Athanasius, almost all its bishops were Arians.
>
> The Council of Ephesus, or rather the Robber Council, fell into still greater perversity: there the Nestorian heresy was asserted and defended by Dioscorus, patriarch of Alexandria, and the bishops who followed him, and St Flavian, archbishop of Constantinople and a most vigorous champion of Catholic truth, was condemned. On the Council of Rimini see Theodoret, book II, chapter 17, who reports the letter of the Roman synod held under Damasus, bishop of Rome. The same matter was treated very fully by the most learned Giovanni Vincenzo Bolgeni in his dissertation *On Dogmatic Facts*, Brescia, p. 109, edition of the past year, 1788. See also vol. I, observations on Fleury’s *History*, pp. 229 ff.]

Such was the Council of Rimini; such an assembly of Arians; such also the Council of Ephesus, in which all Catholic bishops were condemned and assigned to exile. Wretched those cows, wretched those souls, which are impregnated by such bulls and bear children from them. By the words “those proved by silver,” he means those tested, as silver is, by the fire of many afflictions [Col. 0952C].

“Scatter the nations that desire wars. Envoys shall come from Egypt; Ethiopia shall hasten her hand to God.” Although this may be understood of all nations which fight against the holy Church, it must be understood especially of the aforesaid heretics, whom he called bulls. Egypt is interpreted “darkness,” while Ethiopians are naturally black. By these, therefore [Col. 0953A], we may understand all who, separating themselves from the faith and unity of the Catholic Church, have plunged into the darkness and gloom of error; but afterward, having recognized the truth, they sent envoys concerning faith and unity, sought pardon, and promised obedience. Read the councils, and you will find Arians, Nestorians, and Donatists reconciled in this way: their bishops and presbyters—apart from the founders of heresies—were mercifully received by the Church with their own ranks preserved. For even literally, there is no doubt that many came from Egypt and Ethiopia. Spiritually, however, wherever they came from, the Prophet signifies that they came from Egypt and Ethiopia. Thus, when we see someone reconciled to the Church, we may quite fittingly say: “This man came from Egypt [Col. 0953B] or Ethiopia.” Envoys therefore come from Egypt when sinners seek peace and promise obedience. The statement “Ethiopia shall hasten” shows the swiftness and desire for reconciliation. “Her hand to God”—understood as prepared to obey, to subscribe, to swear, and to serve.

“Kingdoms of the earth, sing to God; sing psalms to the Lord.” Since, he says, the whole Church is united and all, from so many, so great, and such diverse opinions, have come together into the one Catholic and apostolic faith: sing, rejoice, and make music for so great a joy granted. “Sing psalms to God, who ascends above the heavens of heavens toward the east.” This is said of our Savior, who, while the disciples watched and marvelled, ascended above all heavens, transcended every order of angels, and reached the east, by which the Father is signified, from whom all things arise [Col. 0953C].

“Behold, he will give his voice, the voice of his power; give honor to God.” The Lord daily gives his voice, the voice of his power, through the Gospels, the law, the prophets, clergy, laity, and the entire Church together, who do not cease day and night to praise, honor, and bless him. And I do not doubt that the Prophet foresaw, when he wrote these things and commanded them to be sung, this jubilation and praise now occurring among all nations throughout the whole Church.

“His magnificence is over Israel, and his power is in the clouds.” What are we to understand by Israel except the Church and the Christian people [Col. 0953D]? For this alone among all nations deserved to see and know God. Israel is interpreted “the man seeing God.” His magnificence is therefore over this people, because it alone is magnified, glorified, and honored by him. “And his power is in the clouds.” The clouds are the apostles and teachers of the Church; unless the power of God were in them, they could never have done what they did. Of these clouds [Col. 0954A] it is written: “Who are these that fly like clouds?” (Isa. 60:8). By these clouds the whole earth, formerly dry and barren, was watered and made fruitful.

“God is wonderful in his saints, the God of Israel; he himself shall give power and strength to his people. Blessed be God.” “God,” he says, “is wonderful in his saints,” through whom the God of Israel works such great and magnificent things—the Israel of whom I spoke just above: “His magnificence is over Israel.” He himself will give the power which he now says is in the clouds, and strength to his people, by which they may overcome all their enemies.

> [Note: [Col. 0953D] “Lest anyone despair because of human frailty or think that he cannot attain such rewards, he is strengthened by a true promise: the Lord will give his faithful the power of patience and strength of faith, so that they may be able to attain eternal rewards.” —Cassiodorus.]

Therefore let us all give thanks and say: Blessed be God.

## PSALM 68. TO THE END: FOR THOSE WHO SHALL BE CHANGED: A PSALM OF DAVID.

[Col. 0954B]

For those who shall be changed and pass from unbelief to faith, the Lord prays in this psalm, saying: “Let not those who wait for you be ashamed in me, O Lord God of hosts.”

> [Note: [Col. 0953D] St Augustine aptly says: “And from what did this change come about, except from the passion of Christ?” [Col. 0954D]]

“Save me, O God, for waters have entered even to my soul.” We have often said, and it must often be said, that whenever our Savior asks for something or appears to stand in need of something, nothing is to be referred to his divinity, but everything to his humanity. Yet not even that humanity needed prayer, since everything it wished was in its power. Whatever Christ’s humanity either willed or did not will, the Prophet writes it [Col. 0954C] as though it had spoken these things, and introduces that same humanity as speaking. During his passion the Lord said very few things, which the Evangelists carefully report to us. Yet in this psalm and in others the Prophet says that the Lord said many things not found in the Gospels.

> [Note: [Col. 0954D] St Bruno aptly observes that Christ the Lord, in his passion, spoke few things with his mouth, carefully transmitted in writing by the Evangelists; but he placed many things in David’s heart, through whom we must receive the words of the Lord himself.]

It is therefore clear that the Prophet writes in like manner what the Lord spoke in his heart as what he spoke with his mouth. For he heard and saw both alike: both what the Lord spoke and what he willed or thought. But someone may say: If the Lord willed the things contained in this psalm and some others, and which he appears to request, why was it not done according to his will, when all things lay within his will? Read the Gospel and you will find that he both willed and did not will the same thing. For when he said, “Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass from me” (Matt. 26:39), he immediately added, “Nevertheless, not my will but yours be done” (ibid.). He undoubtedly willed what he asked for, but he so willed it if the Father also willed the same. Therefore, if he asks something and does not receive what he asks, let no one dare say on that account that his will was not fulfilled [Col. 0954D]. Nor is it unfitting that a changeable nature should have a changeable will. For we must not doubt that he assumed everything belonging to us except sin.

But when he says, “Save me, O God, for waters have entered even to my soul,” and many other things that follow, the Lord spoke not with his mouth but with the intention of his heart. Scripture says, “Many waters are many peoples” (Rev. 17:15). These waters, flooding in from every side and rushing violently upon him, are the Jews, said to have entered even to his soul because they did not cease persecuting him unto death.

“I am stuck fast in the mud of the deep, and there is no standing.” Falling into the aforesaid most profound waters [Col. 0955B], he reached even to the mud; by this mud we understand the most wicked will of the Jews. For he gave them power, during those three days, to fulfill their will against him. Hence he himself says in the Gospel: “As Jonah was in the belly of the whale for three days and three nights, so shall the Son of Man be in the heart of the earth” (Matt. 12:40). There was no firm ground to draw him out of that mud, because it was his own will that he should be held thus. Accordingly, he said to Pilate: “You would have no power over me unless it had been given you from above” (John 19:11).

“I came into the height of the sea, and the storm submerged me.” What is signified by the height of the sea is the same as what is signified by the mud of the deep. The storm [Col. 0955C] which submerged him was the raging multitude of the Jews, which seized, bound, and held him.

“I have labored crying out; my throat has become hoarse; my eyes have failed while I hope in my God.” This is as though he said: Nothing profited from my laboring so much among them, from crying out so much in preaching; thus my throat became hoarse, so that, like one mute and unable to speak, I did not answer them. Hence it is said: “Like a lamb led to the slaughter, he did not open his mouth” (Isa. 53:7). His eyes which failed seem to me to be the apostles, who did indeed fail at that time when they left him and fled. And this was because they placed their hope not in their own aid but in God’s alone. Therefore he said to Peter, who wished to fight: “Put your sword back in its place. Do you think that I cannot ask my Father, and he will immediately furnish me with more than twelve legions of angels? How then shall the Scriptures be fulfilled, that thus it must happen?” [Col. 0955D] (Matt. 26:52). They are called his eyes because through them he enlightens others and through them leads all others by a straight path to their homeland.

“Those who hate me without cause are multiplied beyond the hairs of my head.” The Jews hate the Lord gratuitously and without cause, as he himself also says in the Gospel: “They hated me without cause” (John 15:25). By saying that they are multiplied beyond the hairs of his head, he shows that they are infinite and innumerable. Not only those who existed at that time [Col. 0956A], but also those now alive and those still to come, remain in the same hatred. Perhaps this resulted from that curse which they called down upon themselves and their children, saying: “His blood be upon us and upon our children” (Matt. 27:25).

“Those who persecute me unjustly, my enemies, have been strengthened against me.” They were strengthened in the sense that they appeared powerful enough to do to him what they desired to do. “What I did not seize, then I repaid.” As they themselves represented it, this was the chief cause of his killing: that he called himself the Son of God. Thus they cried out: “According to the law he ought to die, because he made himself the Son of God” (John 19:7). This indeed would have been great robbery had the Savior not spoken the truth. But hear what the Apostle says: “He did not consider equality with God a robbery” (Phil. 2:6). Therefore he repaid what he had not seized, because he paid the penalty for declaring himself to be what he was. He also repaid in another way what he had not seized, because the robbery of the first man caused him to die for us [Col. 0956B].

“O God, you know my foolishness, and my offenses are not hidden from you.” To foolish and unbelieving people it seems a great foolishness that God should humble himself so greatly and die for human beings. The Jews also charged him with a great sin: that he healed on the Sabbath and testified that he was the Son of God. But he knew this sin and this foolishness—the one to whose obedience our Savior endured all these things [Col. 0956C].

“Let not those who wait for you be ashamed in me, O Lord God of hosts; let not those who seek you be confounded because of me, O God of Israel.” For they would have been ashamed if he had not risen again and had not done what he promised to do. The saints wait for and seek the Lord because they do not doubt that they will be blessed at his coming.

“For on your account I endured reproach.” It was a great reproach which the Son endured in obedience to the Father. Hence it follows: “Shame covered my face.”

“I have become a stranger to my brothers and an alien to the sons of my mother.” By these are understood the Jews [Col. 0956D], who were sons of the same Synagogue as he. But the Lord became a stranger and foreigner to them because, rejecting him, they said: “We do not want this man to reign over us. We do not want this man, but Barabbas. And we have no king but Caesar” (Luke 19:14).

“For zeal for your house has consumed me, and the reproaches of those who reproached you fell upon me.” The house of God is the Church, whose love consumed Christ and joined it inseparably to himself. For what we eat is so transferred, in some part of itself, into our substance that it cannot be separated from it. The reproaches of those reproaching the Father fell upon the Son because the Father endured reproaches only [Col. 0957A], while the Son endured both reproaches and passion.

“And I covered my soul with fasting, and it became a reproach to me.” “I wished,” he says, “to unite the Jews to myself and incarnate and associate them with my body, which is the Church; but I am fasting and was unable to receive this food.” Such was the food shown to blessed Peter in the sheet, when the Lord said to him: “Kill and eat” (Acts 10:13). In this fasting the Lord covered his soul, because he concealed both his desire for them and the power within him. This became a reproach to him because they took greater boldness precisely from seeing him humbled and apparently without strength.

“And I made my garment sackcloth, and I became a byword to them” [Col. 0957B]. The Lord covered and concealed his soul—that is, the power and strength in his soul. But he set sackcloth before their eyes, by which the flesh is signified; he showed himself to them as they thought him to be. Therefore the Prophet says in their person: “And we considered him as though a leper, struck by God and humbled” (Isa. 51:4). They saw sackcloth: namely, a humbled man in the likeness of sinful flesh, displaying no power or strength. Hence they said to Pilate: “If this man were not an evildoer, we would not have delivered him to you” (John 18:30). Had the Lord displayed the likeness of his soul and divinity, who could have resisted him [Col. 0957C]? Therefore, because he put on and displayed his garment of sackcloth, he became a byword to them, so that they spoke of him mockingly and proverbially.

“Those who sat in the gate spoke against me, and those who drank wine sang about me.” That entire night when our Savior was taken was an exercise of sport, dancing, and drunkenness. They sat in the gate of the temple—or rather, in the gate of death, where such gatherings are accustomed to occur.

“But I direct my prayer to you, O Lord.” “They,” he says, “did this; but I prayed in my heart and directed my prayer to you, O Lord.” But what did the Lord pray? Hear what follows: “The time of good pleasure, O God”—understood: “behold, it has come.” And who is this good pleasure? Let the Father himself say: “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased” [Col. 0957D] (Matt. 12:18). Although all the time of his incarnation may be understood as Christ’s time, it especially means that in which he worked the greater mercy: namely, the time of his passion. Hence it follows:

“In the multitude of your mercy hear me in the truth of my salvation.” “Let this mercy of yours be great,” he says, “and let this salvation, which you now work through me, be true, so that many may be saved and be saved by a true salvation.” For true salvation is that to which neither infirmity nor death can succeed; it is the greatest remedy, by which the sting of death was broken.

“Deliver me from the mud, that I may not stick fast; free me [Col. 0958A] from those who hate me and from the depth of the waters; let not the storm of water submerge me.” It was said above what we should understand by mud or mire, by the depth of the sea, and by the storm of waters. Above, indeed, he says that he is fixed in the mud of the deep and submerged by the storm. Here he prays to be delivered, because, as we have said, they had power over him until the third day; afterward, delivered from their power, they could do nothing further against him. But why does he here say, “Let not the storm of water submerge me,” when above he says, “the storm submerged me”? Unless we understand that he prays for his soul alone, that they may have no power over it. Thus, when Satan slandered blessed Job, the Lord is recorded as saying: “Behold [Col. 0958B], he is in your hand; only spare his soul” (Job 2:6).

“Let not the deep swallow me, nor let the pit press its mouth over me.” Here it is clearly shown that this prayer concerns not his body but his soul: for only the soul of our Savior descended into hell, which is signified by this deep pit. He could not be held there; but after binding the devil and despoiling hell, he ascended thence in great victory.

“Hear me, O Lord, for your mercy is gracious; according to the multitude of your mercies look upon me. Do not turn your face away from your servant, for I am troubled; hear me quickly.” He was heard very quickly, because in the very hour in which he willed, and as he himself had arranged with the Father, he rose from the dead [Col. 0958C].

“Attend to help my soul, and deliver it because of my enemies; rescue me, lest my enemies rejoice over me.” These things are plain and need no exposition. We have said above how these prayers of our Savior are to be understood.

“For you know my reproach, my confusion, and my shame.” All these mean the same thing. He says that the Father knows them because he does not doubt that he will receive great vengeance for them. “Those who trouble me are always before you.” You see them, you know them; they cannot flee from you. They must render account to you for all these things [Col. 0958D]. Wretched and altogether unhappy are those over whom such a severe accusation and so dreadful a judgment hangs!

“My heart expected reproach and misery.” When our Savior preached to the Jews, healed their sick, and raised their dead, he knew that all these things would befall him; and he ought not to have expected another vintage from such a vineyard.

“I waited for someone to grieve with me, and there was none; I sought one to comfort me, and I did not find one.” It is indeed remarkable that, although there were so many thousands there who knew him, had heard him preaching, and had seen so many of his miracles, no one came to him to share his suffering or comfort him. Such terror had seized all the good, and the devil had so stirred up [Col. 0959A] and inflamed all the wicked against him that they too were beside themselves and did not know what they were doing. For all the disciples left him and fled; and he who was greatest among them, and who, as commanded, ought to have strengthened the others, terrified by fear denied him three times. Hence the Lord said: “This is your hour and the power of darkness” (Luke 22:33).

“And they gave me gall for my food, and in my thirst they gave me vinegar to drink.” The Evangelist similarly relates this: “They gave him vinegar mixed with gall” (Matt. 27:34).

“Let their table before them become a snare, a recompense, and a stumbling block.” As Jews read this curse and all those that follow every day without understanding them [Col. 0959B], they excommunicate and curse themselves; they certainly would not have done this had the Prophet not written them. The Jews have the same spiritual food as we have—the law, the prophets, and the other Scriptures by which souls are nourished—but among them there is no one to break bread and explain the Scriptures to them. As it is written: “The little children asked for bread, and there was none to break it for them” (Lam. 4:4). Therefore they follow the letter, and, as the Apostle says, that very letter kills them; in this way it becomes a snare by which they are deceived and killed. They will have this recompense and stumbling block because they follow the letter alone and do not seek spiritual understanding. Hence it follows:

“Let their eyes be darkened so that they may not see” [Col. 0959C]. This is what is said through the prophet: “Blind the heart of this people, so that seeing they may not see, and hearing they may not understand” (Isa. 6:10).

“And bend their back for ever.” The back of the Jews is bent, and they do not look toward the things above, but toward those that lie hidden below; they seek temporal things, not eternal; they have become beasts rather than human beings.

“Pour out thy wrath upon them, and let the indignation of thy wrath overtake them.” This has already happened in part; but more fully it is awaited at the judgment.

“Let their habitation be made desolate, and let there be none to dwell in their tents.” Judaea is indeed inhabited to this day, but not by Jews, since it has been abandoned and laid waste by them; and there is none of them who dwells in it as though in his own inheritance. But why is this so?

“Because they persecuted him whom thou hast smitten, and they added to the pain of my wounds.” This is what is written elsewhere: “I will strike the shepherd, and the sheep of the flock shall be scattered” (Zech. 13:7). They also added another pain to his wounds, because it was not enough for them to kill the Lord unless they also slew his servants. These things were still future; yet he speaks of them as though they had already occurred.

“Add iniquity upon their iniquity.” The Lord cannot commit iniquity; but by “iniquity,” in place of [Col. 0960A] iniquity, we must understand the desert of iniquity—that which iniquity deserves. Thus the Lord adds iniquity upon iniquity because he enumerates all their iniquities, so that none may be passed over for which they do not receive punishment.

“And let them not enter into thy righteousness.” What is “into thy righteousness,” except into the place where the righteous and righteousness dwell? By this, surely, that dwelling-place of heavenly blessedness is signified.

“Let them be blotted out of the book of the living.” This he explains: “and let them not be written with the righteous.” The wicked are not written in that book; yet they are said to be blotted from it because they are not permitted to be written in it. What else is that book but the memory of almighty God, in which all things alike, both first and last, are contained?

[Col. 0960B] “But I am poor and sorrowful, and the salvation of thy countenance, O God, hath taken me up.” These, as though he said, are the graces which I receive from that people: though I was rich above all, I became poor and sorrowful for its sake. Hence it is said elsewhere: “Surely he himself bore our infirmities and carried our sorrows” (Isa. 53:4).—“And the salvation of thy good will, O God, hath taken me up”: he who, in order to heal others, willed to become weak. “Countenance” is used for “will,” because the will is recognized in the countenance.

“I will praise the name of my God with a song, and I will magnify him with praise.” This is that name of which the Lord himself says through the Prophet: “I am the Lord; this is my name; my glory I will not give to another” (Isa. 42:8). He praises that name, and praises it with song, who, recognizing both himself to be a servant [Col. 0960C] and him to be Lord, serves and obeys him as a good servant ought to serve a good master.

“And it shall please God more than a young calf bringing forth horns and hoofs.” This is the fatted calf of which it is said in the Gospel: “Kill for me the fatted calf, that we may feast and be satisfied” (Luke 15:23). The calf is young because never again has such a calf been sacrificed. Accordingly, it pleased God more than this calf, nor was he ever delighted in anything else in such a manner, so that it may rightly be said of him: “The Lord smelled an odour of sweetness” (Gen. 8:21). This calf brought forth horns and hoofs both for himself and for us, by which we are able to overcome enemies and tread them beneath our feet. Hence [Col. 0960D] the Apostle says: “The Lord will crush Satan under your feet swiftly” (Rom. 16:20). All the commandments of both Testaments are for us both weapons and horns for overcoming enemies.

“Let the poor see and rejoice; seek the Lord, and your soul shall live.” These are those poor who, following the example of their master, became poor willingly. Of the Jews it is said above, “Let their eyes be darkened, that they may not see”; but of these it is said, “Let the poor see and rejoice.” Thus may be fulfilled what the Lord says in the Gospel: “For judgment I came into this world, that those who do not see may see, and that those who see may become blind” (Matt. 13:13). Let the poor therefore rejoice, whose eyes [Col. 0961A] have been opened and illumined for seeing and understanding all divine mysteries. “Seek the Lord,” because you have been enlightened for this purpose: that you may seek and find him. The Jews cannot find him because they are blind and walk in darkness. Those who seek the Lord live, because in him they have found life.

“For the Lord hath heard the poor, and hath not despised his bound ones.” It is fitting, he says, that the poor should seek the Lord, who always hears their righteous desires. The Lord’s bound ones are those who restrain themselves as though bound with chains, so that they may not approach unlawful things. All divine commandments are certain bonds by which we ought to be restrained.

“Let heaven and earth praise him, the sea and all things that are in them.” If all these praise the Lord, nothing remains [Col. 0961B] that is not fit for his praises. For, as it is written: “But who shall confess thee in hell?” (Ps. 6:6.)—“For God will save Sion, and the cities of Judah shall be built.” Sion is the holy Church, whose watchmen are the aforesaid poor; for this reason they were told to see, because they have been set upon the watchtower in order to guard the city and see from afar. So great is the joy over Sion’s salvation that on this account every creature ought to praise and bless God. The cities of Judah are the individual churches, built by the Apostles throughout the whole world, which have Christians, not Jews, as inhabitants.

“And they shall acquire it by inheritance, and the seed of his servants shall possess it, and they that love his name [Col. 0961C] shall dwell therein.” This inheritance, he says, the seed and children of the Apostles shall possess. And all who love his name, and conduct themselves as his servants, shall dwell therein.

## PSALM LXIX. A PSALM OF DAVID, UNTO THE END: FOR REMEMBRANCE; BECAUSE THE LORD SAVED HIM.

“Unto the end,” he says: let these things be referred and directed to Christ, and let help be sought and expected from him; things which I have written, as though he said, for remembrance, because the Lord saved me. Let us say these words in all our necessities and place them before all our actions, words which the Prophet willed us to say after his own example.

“O Lord God, attend to help me; O Lord, make haste to help me.” This prayer suffices us in everything we ask, especially if we are afflicted by enemies and adversaries. God’s help must be sought everywhere and in all things, because it is necessary everywhere and in all things; for without his help we can do nothing. If we wish to do good, we pray well and profitably; and if we wish wrongly to do what we ought not, we still pray well and profitably. It is a great help from God if he resists evil desires and does not permit them to be fulfilled. Whoever therefore wishes to do some evil should first say: “O God, attend to [Col. 0962A] help me,” and he will be unable to do what he desires. Therefore let the Lord hasten to help the good, that they may do what they will; and hasten also to help the evil, that they may not do what they will.

“Let my enemies be confounded and ashamed that seek my soul.” This prayer is made both against enemies and for enemies: for enemies, if they repent; against them, if they persist in wickedness. He is rightly confounded and ashamed who, acknowledging his sins, ceases from iniquity and begins to love him whom he had wished to kill. Therefore it follows:

“Let them be turned backward and blush that devise evil against me.” Let them, he says, be turned backward from their wicked purpose and return in repentance [Col. 0962B] with satisfaction. Let them be ashamed with that shame of which the Apostle speaks, saying: “What fruit therefore had you then in those things of which you are now ashamed?” (Rom. 6:21).

“Let them be turned away immediately and blush that say unto me, Aha, aha.” Let them, he says, turn quickly and not delay in turning to the Lord, nor put it off from day to day; and let them turn in shame, lest they too hear what is said through the Prophet: “The face of a harlot hath become yours; you know not how to be ashamed” (Jer. 3:3). The phrase “aha, aha” is an insult which wicked people were accustomed to direct against the saints, as though they had already overcome them.

“Let all that seek thee, O Lord, exult and rejoice.” Whatever kind of people they may have been, say the martyrs, and however [Col. 0962C] they may have afflicted us: if they seek thee and turn to thee, we ask that they may share with us the same joy and exultation. They are good disciples who, following their master’s example, pray for persecutors and slanderers. Thus the Lord himself prayed for those who crucified him, saying: “Father, forgive them, for they know not what they do” (Luke 23:34).—“And let them that love thy salvation always say: Let the Lord be magnified.” Those who love the Son also love the Father, and together with the Son glorify the Father.

“But I am needy and poor; O God, help me.” The saints were needy and poor, and deprived of human assistance, because apart from God there was no one who dared give them help. Therefore each one [Col. 0962D] says to the Lord: “O God, help me,” and what follows: “Thou art my helper and my deliverer.” They signify that they are in great affliction by seeking help with such urgency. Hence it follows: “Do not delay”: come quickly to our aid, they say; our strength now fails, and we cannot resist.

## PSALM LXX. A PSALM OF DAVID, OF THE SONS OF JONADAB, AND OF THOSE FIRST TAKEN CAPTIVE (Jer. 35:6)

> [Note: [Col. 0961D] “The prophet Jeremiah relates that Jonadab was a priest of God, who commanded his sons not to drink wine and to dwell not in houses but in tents, [Col. 0962D] and that they obtained great favour with the Lord because of this obedience. They are now set forth as figures of the faithful and devout; hence Jonadab is interpreted [Col. 0963D] ‘the Lord’s willing one,’ who can say, ‘I will sacrifice to thee willingly.’ With them the earlier captives likewise pour forth tears: that is, those who first deserved to be taken captive and afterwards redeemed; captive through sinning, but redeemed through repenting, they say: ‘And thou hast brought me up again from the depths of the earth.’” —BEDE.]

This is that Jonadab who commanded his sons not to drink wine [Col. 0963A] and not to have an inheritance in this world. Jeremiah set wine before them and commanded them to drink. But they refused, saying that their father had forbidden it to them. Therefore the Lord says through the same prophet: “The word of Jonadab has prevailed over my words, and the sons of Jonadab obey their father more than the sons of Israel obey me” (Jer. 35:18). These, then, and all others who were greater and better in that captivity, together with all the rest signified by them, now speak in this Psalm and implore God’s help. This Psalm therefore concerns not the whole captivity, but only those who are better both in this captivity and in that one.

“O God, in thee have I hoped; O Lord, let me never be confounded; deliver me and rescue me in thy righteousness.” They say that they have hoped in the Lord. The Apostle says that “hope does not confound” (Rom. 5:5). God is righteous; and therefore they are delivered and rescued from all their distresses.

“Incline thine ear unto me, and deliver me.” For the Lord to incline his ear to someone means nothing other than to hear him; just as, conversely, to turn one’s ear away from someone’s voice means nothing other than to refuse to hear.

“Be thou unto me a protecting God and a fortified place, that thou mayest save me.” God is both protector and most strongly fortified place for his faithful people, because no snares of enemies can prevail against one whom he wills to defend. Therefore it follows:

[Col. 0963C] “For thou art my strength and my refuge.” He is strength, because without thee there is no power; he is refuge, because for those who flee to thee thou art protection and blessedness.

“O my God, deliver me from the hand of the sinner, and from the hand of the transgressor of the law and the unjust.” Sinners, unjust persons, and transgressors of the law are Jews, heretics, and tyrants; from these all saints pray to the Lord to be delivered.

“For thou art my patience, O Lord, my hope from my youth.” Thou knowest, he says, that I bear such great injuries from them that, unless thou hadst given me patience, I should already have utterly succumbed. But thou art my patience and my hope from my youth—that age, namely, at which I took up arms against the devil. This age includes children, youths, old men, and all who are fit [Col. 0963D] to fight. For youth is the flower of life, the age at which assuredly all the dead shall rise, and at which our Saviour rose. Whoever therefore bears himself manfully and fights manfully, whatever his age, ought to be counted among the young.

[Col. 0964A] “Upon thee have I been strengthened from the womb; from my mother’s belly thou art my protector; in thee is my song always.” “I said,” he says, “that thou art my patience and my hope from my youth”; yet I could not have reached youth itself unless thou hadst strengthened, brought up, taught, and advanced me. Therefore all that I am, I am by thy grace. And my song shall always be in thee, because at every time I shall sing and rejoice in thee.

“I am become as a wonder unto many; but thou art a strong helper.” A wonder is something new and unusual. It is called *prodigium*, as it were *pro digito* (“for the finger”), because it is pointed out from afar with the finger.

> [Note: [Col. 0963D] Vossius, in his *Etymologies*, says that *prodigere* derives from *pro* or *porro agere*, “to drive forth”; for, he adds, *prodigere* means to expend beyond measure. Hence *prodigere* may also be said to mean acting beyond the common measure, in which the nature of a miracle is indicated.]

Thus the saints were a wonder to many: seeing the most severe torments which they suffered for Christ’s faith, people [Col. 0964B] pointed at them and stood amazed and astonished. And then the Lord was present as a strong helper in timely moments, in tribulation.

“Let my mouth be filled with thy praise, that I may sing thy praise, thy magnificence all the day.” Because, he says, thou hast become a strong helper to me, it is fitting that my mouth should be filled with thy praise, and filled abundantly, so that throughout the day, at every time, I may sing thy glory and magnificence—thou who art so wonderful in thy saints and makest them so strong and powerful to fight against thine enemies.

“Cast me not off in the time of old age.” What is “in the time of old age”? “When my strength fails, O God, forsake me not.” Whatever a person’s age may be, when strength and constancy fail in him, he is reckoned among the old; just as, conversely, we have said above concerning youth that it is determined more by vigour for fighting than by one’s time of life. He therefore asks that, if strength should at any time fail in him, God may be present according to his custom and never forsake him.

> [Note: [Col. 0964D] Augustine speaks admirably on this passage: “God answers you here: indeed, let your strength fail, so that mine may remain in you; so that you may say with the Apostle: ‘When I am weak, then I am powerful.’”]

“For my enemies have spoken evil against me, and they that watched my soul took counsel together, saying: God hath forsaken him; pursue and seize him, for there is none to deliver him.” It is no wonder that he seeks assistance, when his enemies have formed against him such a wicked and unjust plan. These and certain other words in this Psalm may also fittingly be understood of [Col. 0964D] our Saviour. For wicked people often afflicted God’s saints more severely for this very reason: they believed them forsaken by God and judged them impious and sacrilegious because God delayed his help and did not come to their aid so quickly. Therefore it follows:

“O God, be not far from me; O my God, look to my help,” so that their counsel may be found empty and [Col. 0965A] useless, when they recognize that thou art both present in person and a helper.

“Let them be confounded and fail that slander my soul; let them be covered with confusion and shame that seek evils for me.” For it is certain that, if they were confounded and ashamed and ceased and rested from their iniquity, they might still obtain forgiveness through the prayers of the saints whom they kill. But if they persist in wickedness, they shall be confounded with everlasting confusion, fail, and perish. The judge is more readily moved to mercy if the person who suffered injury begins to pray for the accused.

“But I will always hope in thee, O Lord, and will add to all thy praise.” Let them do, he says, what they will, and what wicked people [Col. 0965B] are accustomed to do; they will never be able to take away my hope. In prosperity and adversity alike I shall always hope in thee, O Lord, and I shall add thy praise to every praise. What is it to add praise to every praise except always to praise and never to cease from praises? Therefore it follows:

“My mouth shall proclaim thy righteousness, thy salvation all the day.” Certainly, proclaiming God’s righteousness belongs to the highest praise of God. God’s salvation is Christ, whom we ought to praise and preach throughout the day and at every time.

“Because I have not known dealings of trade, I will enter into the powers of the Lord.”

> [Note: [Col. 0965D] The Vulgate has: “Because I have not known learning,” which Augustine explains: “Let us then seek the learning which this man did not know, in whose mouth is the praise of God all day. There is a certain learning of the Jews—for we must refer this also to them—and there we shall find what has been said. Just as we sought him in relation to traders because of deeds and works, we find that the detestable dealing of trade is so called, which the Apostle notes in Rom. 10:3, saying: ‘For being ignorant of God’s righteousness and seeking to establish their own, they have not submitted to God’s righteousness.’ Against this the Apostle says: ‘Not of works, lest perhaps anyone should exalt himself.’ How then? Shall we not work? We shall work, but with him working in us. For we are his workmanship, created in good works,” etc. Eph. 2:9.]

It is not fitting for traders to proclaim the Lord’s righteousness and the Lord’s salvation, nor is it fitting that they should enter [Col. 0965C] into the powers of the Lord. This must be understood particularly of Simoniacs, who, because they were cast out of the temple by the Lord himself, were surely forbidden both to preach and to enter into the powers of the Lord.

> [Note: [Col. 0966D] See what he said above on Psalm LXVII concerning heretical bishops returning to the Church, etc.]

What else should we understand by “the powers of the Lord” but ecclesiastical dignities? Let those enter into the powers of the Lord, let those receive the dignities of the Church, who have not known such dealings of trade. All dealings are evil that are carried out through fraud and deception.

“O Lord, I will remember thy righteousness alone.” I shall proclaim, he says, no other righteousness; I shall preach no other righteousness but thine—namely, that righteousness which thou, O God, hast taught me from my youth. This is that household righteousness which is found in both Testaments, by which persons are justified and judged mercifully. The righteousness of the young and perfect is to judge according to the law and not depart from the commandments of the Lord. “And unto [Col. 0966A] this present I will proclaim thy wonders.” “Unto this present” does not seem sufficient if “present” is understood simply; but because it signifies the present time, he appears to proclaim God’s righteousness unto the present who proclaims it at every time. “And unto old age and grey hairs, O God, forsake me not.”

> [Note: [Col. 0966D] Since Cassiodorus applies these words to the Church, it will not be unpleasant to hear him: “The Church’s youth was found when the Lord Christ was crucified, when the multitude of martyrs fought, and when the Church’s power appeared in the deaths of believers. By old age we mean the age now occurring, near its end, when faith advances and the people increase throughout the churches, while the fleeting times of this world decline. By grey old age, however, I think that final time is to be understood, when that cruel tyrant will come, and the multitude of martyrs will bring this life to its desired end.”]

What do we understand by old age and grey hairs but extreme old age and life’s end? It is therefore as though he said: I shall indeed proclaim thy wonders at every time; and do thou be present with me at every time against those who refuse to hear thy wonders.

“Until I proclaim thy arm to every generation that shall come; thy power and thy righteousness, O God, even unto the highest works of greatness which thou hast done.” This is that arm of which it is said: [Col. 0966B] “And to whom hath the arm of the Lord been revealed?” (Isa. 53:1). By it our Saviour is understood, through whom all things were made, and without whom nothing was made. The saints proclaim this arm when they say that the Father accomplished all things through the Son. This preaching of theirs extends to every generation yet to come. They also proclaim God’s power and righteousness, proclaiming him all-powerful and most just. Moreover, they proclaim the highest mighty works which the Lord has done. By these we do not understand the creation of the world, the flood, the divisions of the Red Sea, Pharaoh’s destruction, or many other things that appear exceedingly great; but those works that are highest above all things: namely, Christ’s incarnation, passion, resurrection, [Col. 0966C] and ascension. Thus, moved by excessive wonder, he exclaims: “O God, who is like unto thee?”

“How great tribulations hast thou shown me?” Do you wish to hear how great? “Many”; and of what sort? “Evil.” Who could count how many and how grievous were the tribulations that the saints endured for Christ’s name? We can scarcely suffice even to enumerate the tribulations of blessed Paul.

“And thou, being turned, hast quickened me, and hast brought me up again from the depths of the earth.” Unless he had first been turned away, it would not be said, “being turned, thou hast quickened me.” He was turned away from us and angry, and we were dead because the prince of death ruled us. He turned to us, and he who is life gave us life and brought us up again from the depths of the earth. He brought us back when [Col. 0966D] he despoiled hell; he brought us back when he delivered us from the manner of life and vain superstition of this world. He will bring us back at the judgment, when he calls all his faithful to himself; and because this will undoubtedly happen, he appropriately speaks of it as already done.

[Col. 0967A] “Thou hast multiplied thy righteousness.” The Lord indeed multiplied his righteousness, since he showed many and evil tribulations to those whom he also gave life and brought back again and again from the depths of the earth. “And, being turned, thou hast comforted me.” The Lord has comforted his faithful through laws, prophets, evangelists, and Apostles; and daily he exhorts and teaches us what we ought to do. “And I will confess unto thee upon instruments of psalms.” Instruments of psalms are musical instruments having ten strings and no more. He sings well and sweetly to the Lord upon them who keeps the Ten Commandments of the law.

“I will sing thy truth unto thee on the harp, O God, the Holy One of Israel.” As we have said elsewhere, the harp belongs [Col. 0967B] to the New Testament; three or four strings suffice it, because the New Testament is contained in the four Gospels, in which the mystery of the Trinity resounds most clearly and sweetly. Above all, God’s truth is sung upon the harp, by which Christ is understood, who says of himself: “I am the way, the truth, and the life” (John 14:6).

“My lips shall rejoice when I sing unto thee, and my soul which thou hast redeemed.” My lips, he says—the lips of the inward person, lips which speak to thee in silence and are heard by thee alone—shall rejoice when I sing to thee, because they expect no small reward for their song. And my soul, which thou hast redeemed, shall do likewise.

[Col. 0967C] “Yea, and my tongue shall meditate upon thy righteousness.” The same thing is signified by tongue and lips, because meditation is not of the mouth but of the heart; thus that entire song is shown to be not merely of the mouth, but rather of the heart.

“While they are confounded and ashamed that seek evils for me.” The saints meditate upon God’s righteousness, and especially meditate and praise when they see their enemies confounded: whether with a good confusion, so that they may be ashamed of sins; or, persisting in wickedness, so that they may be eternally confounded and perish. Then they rejoice that great justice has been done to them when they understand that their enemies are ashamed and repent of the things they have done against righteousness.

## PSALM LXXI. A PSALM: CONCERNING SOLOMON.

[Col. 0967D]

Solomon is interpreted “peaceful.” He signifies our Saviour, of whom the Apostle says: “He [Col. 0968A] is our peace, who made both one” (Eph. 2:14). He is that peaceful king whose face the whole earth desires (1 Kings 10:24). He indeed rules from sea to sea; all kings of the earth shall worship him, and all nations shall serve him. If this is understood of the first Solomon, it is not true.

> [Note: [Col. 0967D] “The title of this Psalm is indeed prefixed, ‘Concerning Solomon’; but things are said in it which cannot be applicable to Solomon, king of Israel according to the flesh, in accordance with what holy Scripture says about him. Yet they can most fittingly be attributed to the Lord Christ. Thus it is understood that even the name Solomon itself is employed in a figurative sense, so that Christ is understood in him.” —St Augustine, on this title.]

“O God, give thy judgment to the king, and thy righteousness to the king’s son.” The Prophet says this of our Saviour, who speaks of himself: “The Father judges no one, but has given all judgment to the Son” (John 5:22). He is both king and king’s son; he shall judge the world in equity and peoples in righteousness. Therefore let him hold judgment and administer righteousness, for he does not respect the person of anyone [Col. 0968B] and is able to render to each according to his works.

“To judge thy people in righteousness, and thy poor in judgment.” Give, he says, O Lord, thy judgment to the king’s son—that is, to thy Son. This form of expression is very frequent in the books of the Old Testament. “To judge” means: for judging thy people in thy righteousness, and thy poor in thy judgment. He, as though he said, shall never depart from thy righteousness and thy judgment, because he who does not differ from thee in substance does not differ from thee in righteousness. God’s poor are those who are voluntarily poor and seek not earthly but heavenly things.

“Let the mountains receive peace for the people, and the hills righteousness.” Let mountains and hills, he says, receive [Col. 0968C] this peace and righteousness which thou now givest thy people. To say or understand this means nothing other than that they receive thy Son: “For he is our peace” (Eph. 2:14), as the Apostle says; he is righteousness, without whom no one is justified. But what are mountains and hills except Apostles and teachers, or churches and cities?

> [Note: [Col. 0968D] “By mountains, we have often said, the Apostles and Prophets are signified, who are firmly raised to heavenly things and drawn near to heavenly grace.” —CASSIODORUS.]

For these are higher than others and, as mountains, rise above them.

“In his righteousness he shall judge the poor of this people, and shall save the children of the poor.” This king’s son, he says, shall judge the peoples of this age in his own righteousness, which he possesses naturally and substantially, and has not received from elsewhere.

> [Note: [Col. 0968D] Ghislain manuscript: “the poor of this people.”]

He has just said, “to judge thy people.” He himself shall judge the poor, since the rich are judged by the devil. “And he shall save the children of the poor.” The poor and the children of the poor are the Apostles and their imitators. These are the poor who, “leaving all things, [Col. 0969A] followed the Lord” (Luke 5:11). The Lord shall save them and judge them in his righteousness.

“And he shall humble the slanderer.” By this the devil is signified, who never ceases to slander and accuse God’s people. Because he exalted himself beyond measure, he shall be pressed down and humbled by every punishment. “And he shall endure with the sun, and before the moon, from age unto age.” He shall endure for ever with the sun, he who existed before the moon and before the sun, since he himself made sun and moon. To have existed before the moon is one thing; but what is it to remain with the sun? Elsewhere it is said of him: “And his throne shall be as the sun before me, and as the perfect moon for ever” (Ps. 88:18). We may therefore understand brightness by the sun, so that, as “light from light” is said, “sun from sun” and “brightness from brightness” may also be said. Thus he remains with the sun for ever because he never departs from the Father, but always remains with the Father in the same glory and brightness. He remains before the moon because, as the entire Church serves its Lord, so it serves him.

> [Note: [Col. 0969D] St Augustine explains this passage concerning the Church’s duration: “What great thing is it for him through whom all things were made, and without whom nothing was made, to remain with the sun, unless this prophecy was set forth for those who think that the religion of the Christian name will endure in this world only for a fixed period and thereafter will not exist? He shall therefore remain with the sun as long as the sun rises and sets—that is, as long as these times roll on. The Church of God, that is, Christ’s body on earth, shall not be lacking.”]

In his remaining before her, however, an affection of love is indicated.

“And he shall descend like rain upon the fleece, and like drops distilling upon the earth.” The story of Gideon is well known. When he was once about to go to battle and fight with enemies, he received from the Lord this sign of victory: he was to place a fleece on the threshing-floor. He placed it both once and again: first the fleece appeared wet while the ground was dry; then the fleece appeared dry [Col. 0969C] while the ground was wet (Judg. 6:36). This likeness is fulfilled in Christ’s incarnation. The fleece in the midst of the threshing-floor is Judaea in the midst of the earth. As rain first fell upon the fleece, so Christ first descended into Judaea. But afterward, when the fleece had been dried, drops distilled upon the earth: for, Judaea having been left behind, the Lord and the Lord’s teaching passed into all lands and all nations. This occurred when “the sound of the Apostles went forth into all the earth, and their words unto the ends of the world” (Ps. 18:4). They were the clouds by which the whole world was watered.

“Righteousness shall arise in his days, and abundance of peace, until the moon be lifted up.”

> [Note: [Col. 0969D] In some copies the reading is *tollatur* (“be removed”); in others, *auferatur* (“be taken away”). Augustine’s exposition suits either word. But Bruno preferred that exposition which speaks of the Church: “Until the moon be lifted up,” that is, says the holy Doctor, “until the Church is raised through the glory of resurrection, to reign with him who preceded her in this glory as the firstborn from the dead, that he might sit at the Father’s right hand; thus remaining with the sun before the moon, which afterward would be lifted up like the moon.”]

This peace and righteousness arose among the saints and in the Church from the days of our Saviour [Col. 0969D] because they are those who preserve righteousness [Col. 0970A] and peace. For even according to the letter, when the Lord was born, the greatest peace prevailed everywhere, since the whole world was under Roman rule. Therefore at his birth the voices of angels were most fittingly heard crying and saying: “Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace to people of good will” (Luke 2:14). This peace and righteousness shall not be taken away from the saints and Christ’s Church until the Church itself is raised and exalted above the heavens; here it is signified by the moon. The moon receives the light of its brightness from the sun, and the Church receives it from Christ.

“And he shall rule from sea to sea, and from the river even unto the ends of the earth.” Christ rules everywhere; no nation is not subject to his [Col. 0970B] power. For he “makes his sun rise upon the good and the evil, and rains upon the just and the unjust” (Matt. 5:45). What is signified by “from sea to sea” is also signified by “from the great river Euphrates unto the ends of the earth.”

“Before him the Ethiopians shall fall down, and his enemies shall lick the earth.” By Ethiopians, who are naturally black, all sinners are signified. Ethiopians therefore fall down before him because sinful persons who long ago lost their beauty, having turned to the faith, worship, adore, and venerate him. His enemies, however, are the Jews, who persecuted him with wicked hatred even unto death.

> [Note: [Col. 0970D] Cassiodorus gives the same exposition.]

Those lick the earth who seek only earthly and transitory things. The love with which they love the earth is shown [Col. 0970C] by their being said to lick it. Yet by these enemies we may also understand the aforesaid Ethiopians: although formerly enemies, they now, having known the truth, worship and venerate him suppliantly, and with great humility kiss the very earth for love of him.

“Kings of Tarshish and the islands shall offer gifts; kings of Arabia and Saba shall bring presents.” Tarshish means “the exploration of joy”; Arabia, “ambushes”; and Saba, indeed, “captivity.” Therefore those who, seeking only pleasure, were devoted to sensuality; those who lay snares for others and tried to destroy and deceive them; and those who, like captive slaves, were held by the devil—afterward, once baptized and accepting Christ’s faith, offer both their gifts and themselves to the Lord.
