[Note: [Col. 0970D] Saint Augustine’s exposition on the words, “they shall bring presents,” seems not to be omitted: “Could this have been said of victims to be sacrificed? Far be it that such righteousness should arise in his days. Rather, these gifts which were foretold as to be brought seem to me to signify people whom the authority of kings brings into the fellowship of the Church; although persecuting kings too have brought gifts, not knowing what they were doing, by offering up the holy martyrs.”] The islands do likewise; being situated in the sea, they signify the individual Churches contained amid the stormy expanse of this world.

“And all kings of the earth shall worship him; all nations shall serve him.” This is what the Apostle says: “At the name of Jesus every knee should bend, of those in heaven, on earth, and under the earth” (Phil. 2:10). Hence elsewhere: “As I live, says the Lord, every knee shall bow to me, and every tongue shall confess” (Isa. 45:23).

“For he shall deliver the poor from the mighty, and the needy man who had no helper.” Every day the Lord delivers the poor from the mighty; every day he casts down the mighty from their throne and exalts the humble. Yet the devil may be understood by “the mighty,” while by “the poor” and “the needy” is meant any sinner converted to repentance. For he is indeed very poor who serves the devil; whereas, conversely, those alone are rich who serve the Lord.

“He will spare the poor and needy, and save the souls of the poor.” This is what is said elsewhere: “At whatever hour the sinner is converted and groans, he shall live and shall not die” (Ezek. 33:11). For we have said that the sinner is signified by “the poor,” who was poor precisely because he did not possess true riches.

“He shall redeem their souls from usury and iniquity.” They could not be rich when they paid usury every day; but to whom, if not to the devil, did they pay usury?—to that cruel and most avaricious moneylender. For he too puts his money out at interest, so that when he comes he may receive it back with usury. The devil’s money is every evil; his money is sin, whose interest is the soul itself. Whoever receives and keeps this money must render back his soul as interest. Let his money therefore be returned to him, so that the soul may be able to be freed from his usury. But because this cannot be done without God’s help, it is said here: “He shall redeem their souls from usury and iniquity. And a glorious name shall be before him.” The glorious name is that of which the Lord says: “I shall no longer call you servants, but friends; and you are the light of the world; you are the salt of the earth” (John 15:14). They are also called by other names, very glorious and fitting to them.

“And he shall live, and to him shall be given of the gold of Arabia.” He shall live, he says, not temporarily like other kings, but for eternity and unto ages of ages. “And to him shall be given of the gold [Col. 0971D] of Arabia.” This was fulfilled in the Magi, who came from there and brought gold, frankincense, and myrrh to the Lord. Arabian gold is of the finest kind; it seems to be given by those who serve God purely and wisely, since gold is used as a figure for wisdom. “And they shall pray concerning him always.” [Note: [Col. 0971D] Saint Augustine reads here both “and they shall worship concerning him always,” as the Vulgate has it, and “they shall pray concerning him always.” What the Greek has, πρὸ αὐτοῦ, some have translated “concerning him,” others “for him,” or “for his sake.” But what is “concerning him,” unless perhaps what we pray when we say, “May your kingdom come,” etc.?] He himself taught us to pray; from him we have that most excellent and most complete prayer which we offer daily: “Our Father, who art in heaven” (Matt. 6:9), etc. When our Savior taught this prayer to his disciples, I believe that already then the Prophet was there in spirit and delighted in this prayer, so beautiful and concise. “All day long they shall bless him.” For just as we pray all day long, so also all day long we bless the Lord. For the Apostle says: “Pray without ceasing” (1 Thess. 5:17). If we cannot do this with the mouth, we can nevertheless do it by desire and good intention. For unless desire prayed, it would never be said: “Your ear has heard the desires of their heart” (Ps. 20:3).

“And there shall be a firmament upon the earth.” What does “there shall be a firmament upon the earth” mean except that heaven shall be upon earth? Moses says precisely this: “The Lord called the firmament heaven” (Gen. 1:8). The Lord is aptly called the firmament because in him are the sun, [Col. 0972B] the moon, and the beauty of all the stars. He himself is the firmament upon earth, because the Church is established and founded in him, as the Apostle says: “No one can lay another foundation besides that which has been laid, which is Christ Jesus” (1 Cor. 3:11).—“It shall be raised high upon the tops of the mountains.” No mountain is so lofty, no power so exalted, that it is not subject to him and beneath him. Hence in another psalm he says: “Why do you look with envy upon fertile mountains? The mountain in which it has pleased God to dwell” (Ps. 67:17).—“Its waves shall be above Lebanon.” By Lebanon, which means “whitening,” Jerusalem is understood, a city more beautiful and noble than the others. Of it the prophet Zechariah says: “Open your gates, O Lebanon, and let fire devour [Col. 0972C] your cedars” (Zech. 11:1). Since, therefore, this mountain stood in its pride and, like the other mountains, refused to humble itself before our Savior, waves, storms, floods, the wrath and indignation of God descended—and shall descend—upon Lebanon. “And they shall flourish from the city like the grass of the earth.” The Prophet himself explains his words: what he had called a mountain he calls a city. “And they shall flourish,” he says, having been shamefully expelled and violently driven out from the city, like the grass of the earth, which is here today and tomorrow is cast into the oven.

“And his name shall be blessed for ever.” Let us read in the Gospel and hear the blessing of Mother and Son: “Blessed are you,” he says, “among women, and blessed is the fruit of your womb” (Luke 1:42). This blessing will have no end, but will remain [Col. 0972D] through eternal ages. “His name shall endure before the sun, and his throne before the moon.” [Note: [Col. 0972D] Vatican reading: “His name shall endure before the sun, and his throne before the moon.”] If “before” signifies time in this passage, what is said is no great thing, since we read that trees and herbs existed before the sun. It should therefore be understood as stated above: “And he shall endure with the sun, and before the moon, unto ages of ages.” Where Christ is, there too is Christ’s name. Therefore his name is with the sun and before the sun—that is, with the Father and before the Father, namely in the Father’s presence—for Father and Son are correlatives and cannot exist without [Col. 0973A] one another. His throne is also before the moon, by which Christ’s humanity is signified; all the saints always desire to see it and to hold it before their eyes. Of this throne it is said: “Heaven is my throne, but the earth is the footstool of my feet” (Isa. 66:1).

“And all tribes of the earth shall be blessed in him.” For he is the one of whom the Lord said to Abraham: “In your seed all nations shall be blessed” (Gen. 26:4). The Apostle explains this: “He did not say, ‘in seeds,’ as though of many, but as of one: ‘and in your seed,’ who is Christ” (Gal. 3:16).—“All nations shall magnify him,” according to that saying: “Praise the Lord, all nations; praise him, all peoples” (Ps. 116:1). But how shall they magnify him?

[Col. 0973B] “Blessed be the Lord God, who alone does great wonders.” Therefore Christ is magnified by all by whom this psalm is sung; he alone performs wonders, because the Father, he himself, and the Holy Spirit are one sole God, who accomplishes all things. “And blessed be the name of his majesty for ever, and unto ages of ages.” What is the name of his majesty except his praise and renown, his glory and power? By this praise the preaching of the Gospel may, indeed, be understood. “And all the earth shall be filled with his majesty.” This is the stone cut from the mountain without hands, which Daniel says grew so greatly (Dan. 2:35) that it filled the whole earth. But because the Prophet saw that this was still to come, he prays that it may come quickly and, out of excessive joy, says twice, “Let it be, let it be.”

## PSALM LXXII. THE PRAISES OF DAVID, SON OF JESSE, HAVE CEASED. A PSALM OF ASAPH

[Note: [Col. 0973D] He was a Levite, one of the three chief singers appointed by David in the house of the Lord.]

The words, “The praises of David, son of Jesse, have ceased,” belong to the preceding psalm. What follows, “A Psalm of Asaph,” is the title of the next psalm. “It is enough for you,” as though he said, “to have praised David son of Jesse until now; from now on, praise David Son of God. Behold, he has been born. In the preceding psalm we prophesied and proclaimed his birth according to the flesh, and his great and glorious praises. It remains now for us to say at all times: [Col. 0973D] ‘Blessed be the Lord God of Israel, who alone does great wonders; and blessed be the name of his majesty for ever and unto ages of ages. A Psalm of Asaph.’” Asaph means “assembly,” by whom the Church is understood, gathered from all the nations of this world. [Note: [Col. 0973D] Cassiodorus interpreted this title in no other way; Bruno also followed his view in his exposition [Col. 0974D] of the psalm.] Of this Church the present psalm says: “Lord, in your city you will reduce their images to nothing.”

“How good the God of Israel is to those who are upright of heart.” This is the voice of the Prophet, or of the Church, marveling at God’s goodness and power. “How good,” he says, [Col. 0974A] “is the God of Israel—but especially to those who think rightly and catholically, and do not turn aside to false thoughts and dangerous disputations.” For human hearts are tormented when they think otherwise than they ought, whether concerning God himself, his ordering of things, or the truth of realities. Hence it follows:

“But my feet were almost moved; my steps had almost slipped, because I was envious of sinners when I saw the peace of sinners.” He speaks of the feet and steps of the heart and soul, which are moved and fall when a person murmurs or is scandalized against God over some matter. This speaker saw wicked and sinful people enjoying peace and prosperity, abounding in the glory and riches of this world; while he himself and others serving the Lord [Col. 0974B] suffered want and were tormented by many adversities. He began to envy them and desire similar things. Nor did it seem just to him that evil persons should receive prosperity and good persons adversity; and from this he fell into the temptation which he here recounts. [Note: [Col. 0974D] He reports the complaints of those who lament God’s providence.] But coming back to himself, considering what rewards are prepared for the good and what punishment for the wicked, he consoled himself and made firm and stable his feet, which had already been moved and were falling. Hence it follows:

“For there is no escape from their death, nor any support in their scourging.” He therefore came to abhor their peace and prosperity, as though saying, and became content with his own privation, because there is no path by which they can turn aside from and escape eternal death; and they are so stricken and wounded that no remedy can help them. He used “support” for medicine, because it is by medicine that the infirm are strengthened and healed.

“They are not in the labors of men, nor shall they be scourged with men.” Therefore, he says, there is no escape from their death because they are not in the labors of men. Good are the labors that make people immortal, and good are those people who labor so as to become immortal. Let us understand the same concerning scourges, by which the apostles “went away rejoicing from the presence of the council, because they had been counted worthy to suffer disgrace for the name of Jesus” (Acts 5:41). For those scourges are good by which the Lord scourges every son whom he receives.

[Col. 0974D] “Therefore their pride has taken hold of them.” For pride grows together with riches, peace, and prosperity. “They are clothed in their iniquity and impiety.” Wretched are those who have such garments and such ornaments. They cannot be at God’s banquet; and as they are, so shall they appear in judgment, and their very garments will make them abominable.

“Their iniquity came forth as if from fatness.”—“Out of the abundance of the heart the mouth speaks” (Luke 6:45). The heart from which such great iniquity proceeds is not empty: the devil dwells there, the fountain and origin of all iniquity. [Col. 0975A] Hence it follows: “They have passed into the disposition of the heart.” That is: they proceeded to do those things which had been arranged in their hearts by the devil. And he explains this:

“They devised and spoke wickedness.” The sin done with deliberation and counsel is greater. “They spoke iniquity on high.” These are those of whom it is said: “They proclaimed their sin like Sodom” (Isa. 3:9). Those especially speak on high who blaspheme God and do not fear to malign him—such as that fool “who said in his heart, ‘There is no God’” (Ps. 13:1), and all those who worshiped idols and adored false gods, concerning whom it further says:

“They set their mouth against heaven.” To set one’s mouth [Col. 0975B] against heaven is to speak against divinity itself. The pagans did this when they sought divinity not in heaven but in statues of gold and silver. Heretics and Arians too set their mouth against heaven when, arguing falsely concerning the Godhead itself, they attempted to divide the Son from the Father. “And their tongue passed over the earth.” If it passed over the earth, where did it go except that it ascended into heaven? Thus one and the same thing is signified: “They set their mouth against heaven, and their tongue passed over the earth.” [Note: [Col. 0975D] Augustine’s interpretation should be consulted; it soundly rebukes people who boast of themselves and make proud threats: “He does not consider,” he says, “that a man can suddenly die when he speaks; as if he were going to live forever, he threatens. His thought passes beyond earthly frailty; he does not know with what vessel he is covered,” etc.]

“Therefore my people shall return here.” They had gone where they ought not to have gone and thought thoughts that ought not to have been thought when, envying sinners, their feet were moved. But because there is no escape from their death, “therefore my people shall return here.” What is “here”? To the sound understanding of which we are now speaking. We shall choose for ourselves the labors and privation of the good rather than the peace and abundance of the wicked. “And full days shall be found in them.” Full days are those that abound in every good thing. The saints will have such days after this life, when in that blessedness they shall overflow with every good.

“And they said: How does God know, and is there knowledge in the Most High? Behold, these sinners, abounding in the world, have obtained riches.” This is what he was saying just now: “Therefore my people shall return here.” For they had wandered far when they thought and said these things. Do you not hear that they were saying: “Behold, these sinners, abounding in the world—how have they obtained such great riches? Did God know this, and is knowledge of this matter with God?” This was as if they said: God does not know what occurs in this world, because if he knew, he would not permit so great an evil to occur. But such [Col. 0976A] reasoning and thought is evil and greatly contrary to the Christian religion. Hence it follows:

“And I said: Therefore in vain I have justified my heart, and washed my hands among the innocent; in vain I have been scourged all day, and my judge has been in the morning.” Mother Church grieves for those who held this thought and argument. “If,” she says, “that argument were true, and if there were no knowledge on high, what would it profit me to have endured so many and such great things for the Lord? Then in vain I justified my heart, fearing to offend not only in deed but even in thought; in vain I fled the company of sinners and strove to purify my hands and works among the innocent; in vain I endured so many and such great scourges from ungodly people; and in vain my judge—and my most harsh and wicked teacher—beginning in the morning, beat me all day like a bad pupil and tried to draw me into his error.”

“If I said, ‘I shall relate it thus.’” The construction is: I said, “If I shall relate it thus, as those mentioned above do—behold,” with the implied sense, “the generation of your children, to whom I intended to say these things, has perished.”

“I thought in order to understand this; it is labor before me.” Behold, his people who had gone astray has returned to the Church, of whom he had said just above: “Therefore my people shall turn back here.” Now he speaks against those from whom they return and by whose persuasions that people had been induced into that argument. Certainly this sort of debate troubled even philosophers not a little. Hence [Col. 0976C] one wise man among them said: “If there is no God, whence are good things? But if there is, whence are evils?” [Note: [Col. 0975D] All creatures proclaim that God exists, because they are good according to the ordering of the universe. Yet none is evil by its own nature; for God, Moses says, saw all that he had made, and they were very good. Nor does it hinder that some created things suffer defect, that is, deprivation of good; for this arises from their nature, which is not supremely good, unlike the divine essence, which is of itself incapable of defect and immutable. But God’s infinite wisdom, through his omnipotence, turns evil into good. “For,” Augustine says, “God almighty, whom even unbelievers confess to possess supreme power over things, since he is supremely good, would in no way allow any evil to exist in his works, unless he were so almighty and good that he made good even out of evil.” *Enchiridion*, ch. 4. See also *The City of God*, bk. 12, chs. 3–4.] “I thought,” he says, “in order to understand.” What? “That there is no escape from their death, nor any support in their scourging.” Yet to understand this itself is labor before me; and unless I directed the eye of my mind to their last things, I could not understand it at all. This is what he says: “Until I enter into the sanctuary of God and understand their last things.” Of this sanctuary the Lord says: “Enter into your chamber and, having shut the door, pray to your Father” (Matt. 6); by which we understand the inward secrecy of the heart. For who sees the powerful of this age abounding in every good thing and does not judge them happy? People are accustomed [Col. 0976D] to say that such persons are loved by the Lord and could not otherwise possess and enjoy such great goods. Therefore only their last things are to be considered. Hence it follows:

“Yet because of deceit you have appointed evils for them.” [Col. 0977A] What evils? “You cast them down while they were being lifted up.” For suddenly, when such persons seem to be in greater prosperity, they fall and die, and are dragged to punishment without any regard for mercy. “The rich man died and was buried in hell” (Luke 16:22). No one, therefore, can know such matters before the end. But the end itself makes all things manifest.

“How they were made desolate; suddenly they failed; they perished because of their iniquities, like the dream of one who rises.” All things that are in this age pass quickly, even if they seem long-lasting. They are like the dream of one who rises: before awakening from sleep, he saw in his dream that he possessed great riches; but rising, he finds nothing. So too the rich, asleep in the sleep of death, when they awaken and rise again, will find nothing of all their great riches.

“Lord, in your city you will reduce their images to nothing.” The city of God is the Church, in which these imaginary riches are counted as nothing because it hastens toward true riches. “For my heart was delighted.” Delighted, indeed, not in the aforesaid riches but in you, in your love, in spiritual riches. “And my reins were dissolved.” My reins, he says, were melted by your fire as wax; and the enemy has no strength or power in them. Of him it is said elsewhere: “His strength is in his loins, and his might in the navel of his belly” (Job 40:11).

“And I was reduced to nothing,” according to the opinion of evil people, who judge me to be as though dead [Col. 0977C] and wholly useless to this world. “And I did not know.” What does “I did not know” mean? I showed myself foolish and ignorant, according to the Apostle’s saying: “If anyone among you seems wise, let him become foolish that he may be wise” (1 Cor. 3:18). He who despises worldly honors and riches and does not obey fleshly pleasures is regarded as foolish by the unwise.

“I became like a beast of burden before you.” You appointed me to this service, to serve others and bear others’ burdens. Hence the Apostle says: “Bear one another’s burdens, and so you shall fulfill the law of Christ” (Gal. 6:2). Our Savior too deigned to become like a beast of burden: he placed the lost sheep upon his shoulders and carried it back to pasture. “And [Col. 0977D] I am always with you.” Whoever does not depart from God’s faith and love is always with God, even though he is in this world.

“You held my right hand, and in your will you led me, and with glory you received me.” What is this right hand by which the Church is held, led, and received with glory? Our right hand is good intention; our left hand, evil intention. Hence in the Gospel the Lord says: “Let not your left hand know what your right hand does” (Matt. 6:3). Someone who gives alms can do so—or give—with either right or left hand: he gives with the right who gives with a good intention and in secret, that God may see; he gives with the left who gives with an evil intention and for vain glory, that people may see. Of such persons the Lord says that “they have received their reward” (ibid., 16). Therefore the Church acts with the right hand, not the left; and so it is deservedly held, led, and received with glory by the Lord through the right hand. It is characteristic of prophets to speak of future things as though already done, because they know without doubt that whatever they see will come to pass.

“For what remains to me in heaven, and what have I desired from you upon earth?” He reproves himself because he wished to possess something on earth, though such great glory was prepared for him in heaven. Things possessed on earth are nothing in comparison with those possessed in heaven.

[Col. 0978B] “My heart and my flesh have failed.” They have failed, as though he said, from longing for those things prepared for me in heaven. My heart and flesh have now failed in their former condition and seek not earthly things but heavenly. Hence it follows: “God of my heart, and God is my portion for ever.” “I desire no other portion,” he says; “I seek no other share from among all things whatsoever. Let God be my portion, the portion of my heart and of my entire desire through all ages.”

“For behold, those who remove themselves from you shall perish.” Those alone, he says, shall live who have you as their portion and cling to you; but those who flee you shall undoubtedly perish.

“You shall destroy all those who fornicate away from you.” Who are those who fornicate away from you except those who remove themselves [Col. 0978C] from you? For they seek other lovers, to whom they unlawfully join themselves. Hence it is written: “Israel committed fornication after the gods of the nations” (Judg. 8:27). It is great fornication to consent to the devil and have children by him. All vices and all sins are the devil’s offspring and seed.

“But for me it is good to cling to God, to place my hope in my God.” “I,” he says, “will not remove myself from God; I will not flee him; I will not receive another lover. I shall cling to him alone, serve him, and place all my hope and love in the Lord.”

“That I may proclaim all your praises in the gates of the daughter of Zion.” It is the Church that speaks, [Note: [Col. 0977D] Augustine speaks wonderfully, and his reflection is pertinent to our own days: “In the courts of the daughter of Zion,” he says, “because preaching God outside the Church is empty. It is too little to praise God and proclaim all his praises. Proclaim them in the courts of the daughter of Zion. Strive for unity; do not divide the people, but draw them into one and make them one.”] and thus speaks of [Col. 0978D] the Church itself as of another. For it is the daughter of Zion, of whom it is said elsewhere: “Rejoice greatly, daughter Zion; cry out, daughter Jerusalem” (Zech. 9:9). Had it said, “that I may proclaim all your praises in my gates,” the sense would have been clearer. But, as we have often said, this manner of speech was very frequent among the ancients. So too is the saying: “O God, give your judgment to the king” (Ps. 71:1), where, although it ought to have said, “and your righteousness to your son,” it did not say “your son” but “the king’s son.” But what should we understand by “gates” except ears? For they are [Col. 0979A] what receive and hear God’s praises, and to which God’s praises are proclaimed.

## PSALM LXXIII. A PSALM OF UNDERSTANDING BY ASAPH

Asaph, [Note: [Col. 0979D] “Asaph in Latin is called *congregatio* (‘assembly’); in Greek, *Synagoga*.” Augustine, on this title.] as said above, means “Synagogue.” It is the Synagogue itself that speaks in this psalm, complains, and laments the destruction of Jerusalem that occurred in the time of King Nebuchadnezzar. [Note: [Col. 0979D] As the Venerable Bede observes concerning this psalm, commentators differ in opinion: “Jerome thinks it was sung against the Chaldeans; Cassiodorus, against the Romans; Arnobius, against the Philistines, when the priests Hophni and Phinehas had been slain and the ark of God captured.” Others think the psalm is a prophecy of Jerusalem’s overthrow as punishment for the killing of Christ the Lord.]

“Why, O God, have you cast us off unto the end?” “Many times,” they say as though speaking, “you have cast us off and afflicted us because of our sins; but never have you cast us off as you have now.” For what is casting off unto the end except casting off entirely and to the very end? “The fury of your anger has been enraged against the sheep of your pasture.” Against whom are you angry? Against whom do you show [Col. 0979B] such wrath and indignation? We are sheep from your flock: simple, unarmed, without strength; and without your help we are unable to resist such power.

“Remember your congregation, which you created from the beginning.” For from the beginning the Lord created these people together with other human beings. Yet “from the beginning” may suitably be understood as from the times of Abraham. For from him the Jewish people received both faith and circumcision, so that they might be called God’s people in a special sense.

“You redeemed the rod of your inheritance.” What should be understood by “rod” except scepter and correction? And by “inheritance” except the same Jewish people? Thus it is said through the prophet: [Col. 0979C] “Do not rejoice, all Philistia, because the rod of your striker is broken” (Isa. 14:29). And elsewhere: “Woe to Assyria, the rod of my fury” (Isa. 10:5). That people was once like a rod in God’s hand, because through it he scourged and chastised all the surrounding nations. But the Lord delivered this people many times: first from Egyptian slavery, then from many distresses. “Mount Zion, in which you dwell.” “This,” they say, “is your inheritance: Mount Zion, in which you promised to dwell,” according to the words: “His place was made in peace, and his dwelling in Zion” (Ps. 75:3). The phrase “in one and the same place” may be understood to mean that he dwells there together and in common with all who are with him, so that by this he is in some way obliged to defend both [Col. 0979D] the place and the nation.

“Lift up your hand against their pride unto the end.” Here “unto the end” is to be understood as above in “Why, O God, have you cast us off unto the end?”

“How greatly the enemy has acted wickedly in your holy places, [Note: [Col. 0980D] Saint Augustine’s text likewise reads “in your holy places.” The Vulgate, however, has “in the holy place.” But the following accords in both: “And those who hated you gloried in the midst of your solemnity.”] and those who hate you have gloried in the midst [Col. 0980A] of your court.” Many holy and good people were then carried into captivity, though they were very few in comparison with the wicked. The following words show how the enemy acted wickedly against the saints and how they gloried in the midst of the courts.

“They set up their signs as signs, and they did not know as on the way above.” The fact that they say twice, “their signs as signs,” indicates great grief. “They set up,” they say, “their signs as signs.” But where did they set them? “Above, at the summit.” Victors still do this today: once cities are taken, we see them set up their standards above, that is, upon towers and in higher places. In this, both their glory and the misery of the place are displayed most clearly.

“And they did not know, as on the way.” [Note: [Col. 0980D] Ghis. codex: “This way is perpetual and memorable.”] This is that way which the Lord made in the Red Sea, in which Pharaoh and all his army perished as he most foolishly pursued God’s people along such a way. They, indeed, came to know. What did they come to know? God’s omnipotence and their own folly. But the Chaldeans learned nothing of the kind and saw no sign; rather, boldly and confidently, they did whatever they wished.

“Like men in a forest of trees, they cut down its doors with axes; with a two-edged axe and hatchet they cast them down.” This shows that they behaved securely and without reverence toward the sanctuary, since they cut down the very doors of the temple with axes and other tools as though they were ordinary wood. The phrase “in one and the same place” shows that they had one and the same will in this most wicked undertaking. [Col. 0980C]

“They burned your sanctuary with fire; they defiled upon the ground the tabernacle of your name.” All these things happened according to the letter, though they can also be understood spiritually.

“Their kindred said in their heart, together: Come, let us suppress all the feast days of the Lord from the earth.” This was the one thought and will of all: that everything should be destroyed [Note: [Col. 0980D] The codex adds: “And reduced to nothing.”] so that solemnities might never again be held there, nor feast days observed.

“We have not seen our signs,” as we were accustomed to see them from ancient times in such an event. “There is now no prophet” among us who dares to speak the truth. Jeremiah was there, but for that reason he was thrown into a pit, because he announced the truth to them. “And he will know us no longer.” Thus wretched people are accustomed to speak when they fall into great calamities and, almost despairing, say that they have been utterly abandoned by the Lord.

“How long, O God, will the enemy reproach? Will the adversary provoke [Col. 0981A] your name unto the end?” When they say “unto the end,” they indicate that the enemies spoke great and numerous blasphemies against the Lord. Nor should it be believed that those who committed such acts with their hands spared their words.

“Why do you turn away your face,” and not look upon such great afflictions of your people? “And your right hand from the midst of your bosom unto the end?” God’s bosom was that city in which, before it offended God, the treasures of all wisdom and knowledge lay hidden in the Law and the Prophets. There too were God’s right hand and such great power and strength that it conquered all surrounding enemies.

“But God, our king before the ages, has worked salvation in the midst of the earth.” Up to this point the Synagogue and the Jewish people have spoken, lamenting their miseries and calamities. From here the Church speaks and rejoices in its own blessedness. “God,” it says, “is now our king—ours in a special sense—but before the ages he is the God of all and has worked salvation in our days in the midst of the earth.” What is “in the midst of the earth”? In the city of Jerusalem, situated in the midst of the nations; or in the midst of the earth, in the womb of the Virgin; or in the midst of the earth, in assumed humanity; or he worked salvation in the midst of the earth because he willed this salvation to be common not to one nation but to all nations. Now it turns to the Savior himself and addresses to him the remaining words that follow.

“You strengthened the sea in your power.” This is [Col. 0981C] that sea of which it is said: “This sea, great and broad” (Ps. 103:25), by which this world is signified. The Lord strengthened it in his power so that it might no longer surge as before, but remain calm and offer itself to the Lord who rejoices and walks upon it as something tangible and treadable. The sea is named from bitterness; but, strengthened and anointed by the grace of the Holy Spirit, it has turned all bitterness into sweetness.

“You crushed the heads of the dragons upon the waters.” The heads of the dragons are vices and sins. If these are cut off, the evil spirits, signified by dragons, are as though dead and beheaded and can do nothing. The Lord crushed these heads upon the waters [Col. 0981D] because he wiped away all vices and sins in baptism.

“You shattered the heads of the great dragon.” This is that great dragon who spoke with the woman in Paradise, deceived her, and made her eat from the forbidden tree; and through this sin, sin entered into the world, and through sin, death, because “through the envy of the devil death entered into the world” (Wis. 2:24). But the head of this great dragon, by which original sin is signified, was shattered by Christ’s death and blotted out by his blood. The great dragon had a great [Col. 0982A] head, which had to be crushed with a great hammer. “You gave him as food to the people of the Ethiopians,” so that, conversely, he may be devoured by those whom he formerly used to devour. To devour, moreover, means to overcome. By Ethiopians, naturally black, sinners are signified, who, regenerated by the waters of baptism, have been made whiter than snow. [Note: [Col. 0981D] After this exposition, which is the same as that found in Saint Augustine, the Holy Doctor aptly adds this exhortation: “Brothers, I beg you, pay attention: these things are heard with great delight, things which, once heard, are also known throughout the world. When they were spoken, they had not [Col. 0982D] yet come to pass, because they were then promised, not fulfilled; but now with what delight are we moved when we see in the world fulfilled what we read was foretold in the book?”]

“You burst open springs and torrents.” By springs and torrents are meant the books of the Law and the Prophets, and the volumes of both Testaments—springs which had formerly been shut and stopped up. But the Lord opened their veins and burst the very tight bonds by which they were closed, and commanded a flow of waters to issue from them. Hence, when the apostle John saw the book sealed with seven seals [Col. 0982B] and wept greatly because no one worthy to open the book could be found, it was said to him: “Do not weep; behold, the Lion of the tribe of Judah, the root of David, has come to open the book and loose its seven seals” (Rev. 5:5). Therefore, what else was it to open the book than what is said here: “You burst open springs and torrents. You dried up the rivers of Ethan.” Ethan means “strong,” by whom the devil is understood, of whom the Lord says in the Gospel: “When a strong man, armed, guards his courtyard, the things he possesses are in peace” (Luke 11:21). But what are his rivers except all the books of heretics and every doctrine of impiety? The Lord dried them up when, in many councils, through the doctors of the Church, he destroyed every heresy. And it was indeed fitting [Col. 0982C] that he should dry up the rivers of Ethan who opened the springs and torrents of the Church.

“Yours is the day, and yours is the night.” It is read in Genesis that “God divided the light from the darkness, and called the light day and the darkness night” (Gen. 1:5). — “And then he made two great lights, namely the sun and the moon: the greater light to rule the day, and the lesser light to rule the night” (ibid., 16). Therefore, day signifies Christians and night Jews. The greater light rules the day, the lesser the night. The greater light is the New Testament, whose brightness and teaching, like the sun, illuminated the whole world. The lesser light is the Old Testament, which, as though in night, [Col. 0982D] grows pale and dark over the Jews. Hence the Apostle says: “For that which was made glorious was not glorified in this respect, because of the surpassing glory” (2 Cor. 3:10). So great is the brightness of the New Testament that the brightness of the Old Testament is regarded as darkness. Yet both Testaments are one, and both are bright and splendid if spiritually understood. Therefore, when he says, “yours is the day, and yours is the night,” it is as though he said: Christians and Jews alike, enlightened and blind, good and [Col. 0983A] evil, are yours, because you made them all; and you shall judge them all by one righteous judgment.

“You made the sun and the moon.” It has just been said what is signified by the sun and by the moon. Wretched Manichaeans, who said that one God belonged to the New Testament and another to the Old! For behold, our Savior is said in this passage to have made both Testaments.

“You made all the boundaries of the earth; summer and spring, you made them.” For there is nothing that Christ did not make, because he is he through whom all things were made, and without whom nothing was made. Yet it pleased the Church, or the Prophet, to enumerate these things individually, so that, by expounding them in this way, he might exalt Christ’s omnipotence. By summer and spring, however, we may understand the perfect [Col. 0983B] and the imperfect: the former are kindled by the most fervent fire of the Holy Spirit; the latter approach that same fire and are already near it.

“Remember this creature of yours.” He seems to speak to the divinity and to commend to it the humanity which it assumed. He calls it a creature in order that our Savior may be believed to be true God and true man. It was very fitting that he who had thus far spoken so much of the power of Christ’s divinity should also say something about his humanity, and remove an occasion from those heretics who believed him to be not a man, but God only. [Note: [Col. 0983D] The heretics who maintained that the divine Word assumed human nature only in appearance were the Marcionites, Manichaeans, Priscillianists, and before them Simon Magus and his disciples. Saint John strikes at them in 1 John, chapter 4, and calls them antichrists because they “dissolve Christ,” that is, separate the human nature from the divine.]

“The enemy reproached the Lord, and a foolish people provoked your name.” Therefore, he says, remember this [Col. 0983C] creature of yours, because the enemy of the human race, the devil, and with him the foolish people of the Jews, will greatly oppose him. It is characteristic of the prophets to put past tenses for future events; for they set forth many insults that those people brought against the Lord in the Gospel. The devil himself even went so far in temptation as to invite him to worship himself.

“Do not hand over to beasts the souls confessing you; and do not forget forever the souls of your poor.” He now prays for all those against whom, after Christ’s Passion, he sees every kind of beast rising up. By beasts we must understand evil spirits, heretics, and tyrants. Of these the Apostle says: “What does it profit me that I fought with [Col. 0983D] beasts at Ephesus, if the dead do not rise?” (1 Cor. 15:32). And truly all these are most cruel beasts, who strive to destroy not only bodies but souls as well. We have often already said what “forever” (*in finem*) signifies.

“Look upon your covenant, for those darkened upon earth have been filled with houses of iniquities.” Look, he says, upon your covenant, by which we understand the Church, [Col. 0984A] which deserved to receive that covenant and suffers many tribulations on its account. It is indeed very necessary that you should look upon her. Why? “For those darkened upon earth have been filled with houses of iniquities.” It was not enough for them to be full of iniquities unless they also received into themselves the very houses of iniquities. The houses of iniquities are evil spirits, because they are full of every malice and iniquity. Therefore, those darkened by the murk of earth have been filled with houses of iniquities. By them are signified the Jews and heretics, all unrighteous human beings, darkened and blinded by the murk of earthly error so that they cannot see the light of truth. Look, therefore, upon your covenant, because all these aim to efface and [Col. 0984B] destroy it.

“Let not the humbled man turn back ashamed.” This humbled man is every faithful person, who would indeed be driven back and turned away if he could not defend the covenant given to him; and this, God forbid, would bring him great shame. “The poor and needy shall praise your name.” By the poor and needy he signifies this same humble person. The poor person is one who has nothing; the needy person, although without wealth, nevertheless has something required by nature.

“Arise, O God; judge your cause.” Arise, he says, O God, to help your servants; defend and judge your own cause, which these malicious persons attempt to destroy by their arguments. “Remember [Col. 0984C] your reproaches—I mean those which come from the foolish man all day long.” What great evils and what abominable things Jews and heretics say against Christ, if indeed there is any place where they dare to speak.

“Do not forget the voice of those seeking you.” Do not forget, he says, the voices of those who seek you, but hear and deliver them from all their distresses, as they deserve. Likewise, may their pride continually rise up to you, so that you may always see it, always exact vengeance from them, and never forget such evil.

## Psalm LXXIV. Unto the End: Do Not Destroy. A Psalm-Song of Asaph

[Note: [Col. 0983D] “Asaph, as we have often said, means Synagogue: that Synagogue which truly believed, not that which remained obstinate. For after the Lord’s resurrection we read that many thousands of Jews confessed him; this Asaph now admonishes them not to corrupt their faith unto the end, that is, unto the Lord Savior.” Bede. Cassiodorus understood the interpretation of this title in no different way; Bede also adopted his words.]

This psalm is to be referred to the end, that is, to Christ. [Col. 0984D] The phrase “do not destroy” can be understood in many ways: for example, do not corrupt the inscription of the title; or do not corrupt any Scripture, as the Jews are accustomed to do; or do not corrupt yourself, that is, do not commit any unlawful corruption. Asaph means Synagogue. This is the good Synagogue which praises God and recounts his wonders.

“We shall confess to you, O God, we shall confess to you, and [Col. 0985A] invoke your name.” The Synagogue promises to praise our Savior both universally, in all persons, and individually, in each one; to invoke his name and recount all his wonders. Thus the people are recorded as once having said to Moses: “All that the Lord has commanded us, we shall do” (Exod. 19:8); and yet they did not do it. But those who make these promises do not seem to offend, since, according to their own intention, they judge others also, and it is their wish that all others should do likewise. For those who said, “Hosanna to the Son of David; blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord, the King of Israel; hosanna in the highest” (Matt. 21:9), had a good will. It was their desire that others also should praise and bless him. Now [Col. 0985B] let us consider what follows.

“When I receive the appointed time, I shall judge with justice.” Our Savior speaks these words and responds to what precedes. When I receive the appointed time, he says, I shall judge justly and give to each according to merit; and I shall reward with worthy gifts those who confess me, invoke my name, and proclaim my wonders. This will occur at the judgment, when all, good and evil alike, shall stand before Christ’s tribunal. There will Asaph be; there will be the whole Synagogue; and there they shall be separated from one another—those who confessed and praised Christ, and those who denied him.

“The earth and all who dwell in it melted away.” When the earth and its inhabitants are said to have melted, they are shown to be without strength, fortitude, proper form, or beauty. “I established its pillars.” The pillars of the whole earth are the apostles and teachers. The Lord was strengthening these pillars when he said: “Do not fear those who kill the body but cannot kill the soul” (Matt. 10:28); [Col. 0985C] and, “Be strong in battle, and fight against the ancient serpent” (2 Kings 10:12); and, “I shall give you a mouth and wisdom which none of your adversaries will be able to resist or contradict” (Luke 21:15). These pillars have been well strengthened: they can bear and sustain the whole earth. Yet many refuse to climb upon them.

“I said to the unjust: Do not act unjustly; and to those who transgress: Do not raise up the horn.” The Lord said this through the Law, through the prophets—namely Isaiah, Jeremiah, and Ezekiel—through the Psalms themselves, and through the Scriptures of both Testaments. He said this through the apostles, and he says it daily through bishops and priests. Yet the ungodly do not cease to act unjustly, and transgressors exalt the horns of their own power and iniquity. By the horns of the wicked all their power and strength are represented.

“Do not lift your horn on high.” He explains this by adding: “And do not speak iniquity against God.” Those speak iniquity against God who, disputing concerning the divinity itself, introduce perverse doctrines. Arius did this, as did the Manichaeans and many other sons of perdition. For the Jews too [Col. 0986A] spoke iniquity against God when they cried “Crucify him” against the Savior.

“For neither from the east nor from the west nor from the desert mountains”—there is for you, understood, any way of escape. He has named all the boundaries of the world, because by desert and uninhabitable mountains the southern and northern regions are indicated; for no one can escape God’s judgment. Of this he adds: “For God is judge.” But how does he judge? “He humbles this one and exalts that one.” He casts the mighty down from their seat and exalts the humble: he humbles those who ought justly to be humbled; he exalts those who deserve to be exalted. It lies in his power to humble and exalt whom he wills; no other possesses this power. And this is so because:

[Col. 0986B] “A cup of pure wine, full of mixture, is in the Lord’s hand; and he tilted it from this to that, yet its dregs have not been emptied.” This cup in the Lord’s hand is the measure of recompense. It is rightly said to be in the Lord’s hand because it is in his hand and power to render to each according to his works. In this cup are contained both pure, unmixed wine and wine mixed with dregs. Some drink pure wine from this cup, others mixed wine, and others its dregs. We must therefore say who drink pure wine, who mixed wine, and who dregs. Those drink pure wine who depart this life with nothing in themselves requiring punishment. Mixed wine is drunk by those sinners who receive repentance from the heart. Hence it is written: “At whatever hour the sinner turns and groans, [Col. 0986C] he shall live and not die” (Ezek. 33:11). For these, as the Apostle says, shall indeed be saved, but “as through fire.” But to be saved through fire—what else is that but to drink mixed wine? Those sinners drink dregs who persevere in their wickedness to the end. Of them the Apostle says: “By your hardness and unrepentant heart you store up wrath for yourself on the day of wrath and revelation of the righteous judgment of God, who will render to each according to his works” (Rom. 2:5). The words “and he tilted it from this to that” concern God’s great mercy: from pure wine he tilts only so much into mixed wine that those drinking may not perish, but may be able to endure both the remedy of repentance and punishment. [Col. 0986D] But the dregs are not diminished, because those who drink dregs are far more numerous than all those who drink either pure wine or mixed wine. Hence it follows:

“All sinners of the earth shall drink.” Namely, the dregs, which always abound in such a way that they are not diminished. By this is understood that the punishment of the wicked will have no end. For thus it is read in another translation. But the phrase in this version, “from it,” is understood of the cup. From the cup, moreover, sinners who persevere in their wickedness drink, as we said above, nothing other than dregs.

“But I shall rejoice forever; I shall sing to the God of Jacob.” They, as though he said, will be able neither to rejoice nor to sing, who without ceasing, daily and endlessly, drink the dregs of every torment. But I [Col. 0987A] and my faithful ones shall rejoice forever and sing to the God of Jacob, and I shall intoxicate them with the sweetness of ineffable delight. Hence it is said elsewhere: “They shall be intoxicated from the abundance of your house, and you shall give them drink from the torrent of your delight” (Ps. 35:7).

“And I shall break all the horns of sinners, and the horns of the righteous shall be exalted.” We say that horns signify power and strength, because the good will then be strong and powerful, whereas the wicked will be wretched and unhappy in every respect.

## Psalm LXXV. Unto the End, in Praises: A Psalm of Asaph; a Song against the Assyrians (4 Kings 19)

It is read concerning Sennacherib, king of the Assyrians, when he came to besiege Jerusalem, that the angel of the Lord struck down one hundred and eighty-five thousand Assyrians in one night. Therefore, in praise of so great a victory, Asaph sings this song “against the Assyrians,” that is, against the Assyrians. But because it says “unto the end,” it shows that the events which occurred according to the letter are to be referred spiritually to the Church.

“God is known in Judah; his name is great in Israel.” For the whole world was in error and served idols when Judah alone had knowledge of the true God. Hence it is rightly said here: “God is known in Judah; his name is great in Israel.” But because Judah means “confession,” while Israel means “a man seeing God,” Judah signifies the Church, which alone among all nations confesses and praises God. Israel signifies the Christian people, who [Col. 0987C] know and worship the one true God alone.

“And his place was made in peace, and his dwelling in Zion.” Jerusalem means “vision of peace,” and it is the place of which it is now said: “His place was made in peace,” because Solomon built the Temple there. Zion and Jerusalem differ in that Jerusalem was the whole city, while Zion was the name of the citadel and fortress alone. Of it it is said: “David captured the citadel of Zion” (1 Chron. 11:5). Both signify the holy Church, in which our Savior, King and High Priest appointed by the Lord, says: “But I have been appointed King by him over Zion, his holy mountain, proclaiming the commandment of the Lord” (Ps. 2:6).

[Col. 0987D] “There he shattered the horn, bow [Note: [Col. 0987D] The Vulgate reads “the powers of bows”; Augustine has “the strengths of bows.”], shield, sword, and war.” According to the letter, this is what we have just said: the angel of the Lord struck down one hundred and eighty-five thousand of Sennacherib’s men. Then their whole army was shattered and scattered. This also occurs daily in the Church: all the weapons of the devil’s art and all his warfare are broken and scattered daily by many people. The devil’s horns are those who call others and incite them to battle. The bow signifies heretics and deceivers, who secretly shoot and wound the good. Shields signify all their arguments, or [Col. 0988A] whatever other means they use to defend themselves against truth. By the sword we understand those who rage against the Church through open persecution.

“You enlighten wonderfully.” You, he says, wonderfully enlightening your Church, shattered within her all the things mentioned above. The illumination which the Holy Spirit works is marvelous. The apostles proved this: they were so suddenly made such persons that even philosophers could not resist them. Hence the Lord himself says: “I shall give you a mouth and wisdom which none of your adversaries will be able to resist or contradict” (Luke 21:15). — “All the foolish of heart were troubled by the eternal mountains.” The eternal mountains are apostles and teachers. By them philosophers, heretics, [Col. 0988B] and all others wise in speech and verbosity but foolish in heart were disturbed, when they could not answer their wisdom and arguments.

“They slept their sleep, and all men of riches found nothing in their hands.” But whence came this very powerful sleep? “At your rebuke, O God of Jacob, those who mounted horses slumbered.” If this is understood of the Assyrians, it is clear that they suddenly lost both themselves and everything they possessed, sleeping the most grievous sleep and never afterwards awakening. Those also who are signified by them, who likewise persecute the people of God and the holy Church, daily fall asleep and die, losing themselves and all they have; they will find nothing of their riches. This happens by God’s rebuke, [Col. 0988C] who continually says to each of them in the Gospel: “Fool, this night your soul shall be taken from you; and whose shall be the things you have prepared?” (Luke 12:10). By horses are signified all those things by which people become more powerful and stronger. Thus we are accustomed to say that someone sits upon a good horse when we see that person endowed with riches, honor, or some great advantage. “You are terrible, and who shall resist you, from then on because of your wrath?” Therefore, he says, those who mounted horses slept at your rebuke because you are terrible and no one can resist your will from then on because of your wrath. What he said, “from then on,” he explained by saying, “because of your wrath.” For as soon as he becomes angry, all those against whom he is angry must be overcome and fall. Hence it follows:

“From heaven judgment was hurled, and immediately the earth trembled and was still.” [Note: [Col. 0987D] The Vulgate reading is: “You caused judgment to be heard [Col. 0988D] from heaven; the earth trembled and was still.” Augustine has another reading: “From heaven he hurled judgment; the earth trembled,” etc.] As soon, he says, as judgment was hurled from heaven and the sentence issued from your throne, immediately what you commanded was done. The Assyrians, he says, were secure and feared nothing; suddenly sentence was given in heaven, and immediately they were all slain by the angel. This is what he says: “The earth trembled and was still.” He calls them earth, because in one hour they both trembled and became still. In this he shows that their destruction was so sudden that they scarcely had time to fear or grieve. Thus also happened [Col. 0989A] to Pharaoh: as he securely pursued God’s people through the midst of the Red Sea, judgment was hurled from heaven and he was immediately plunged into the depths with his whole army. Whoever wishes to seek them can find many other such instances in the divine Scriptures. “When God arose in judgment, to save all the quiet of the earth.” [Note: [Col. 0989D] Another Vulgate reading: “all the meek of the earth”; Augustine has another: “all the meek in heart.”] Then, he says, God did the things just mentioned against the Assyrians, when he arose in judgment against those whose pride he had endured for a long time. At last he arose in order to save all the quiet of the earth, by whom we understand all those shut up in Jerusalem. At that time the prophet Isaiah, King Hezekiah, and many other religious men were there. Let us therefore hear the Apostle saying: “All these things happened to them in [Col. 0989B] figure; but they were written for our correction” (1 Cor. 10:11). Let sinners return to repentance and not delay to turn to the Lord, lest judgment be hurled from heaven, for already the axe has been placed at the roots of the trees. Let the quiet of the earth rejoice, because the Lord rises daily in judgment for this purpose: to save all the quiet of the earth. Of these it follows: “For the thought of man shall confess you.” Therefore, he says, the Lord saves the quiet of the earth because the thought of a quiet person praises and confesses him. Hence he himself says: “Upon whom shall my Spirit rest, unless upon the humble, quiet person who trembles at my words?” (Isa. 66:2). — “And the remnants of thoughts shall keep feast for you.” By remnants of thoughts [Col. 0989C] may be understood good thoughts, which without interruption succeed other good thoughts. These keep a feast for the Lord, because without them no feast is acceptable to God. For good works spring from good thoughts, just as evil works, conversely, arise from evil thoughts.

“Vow and render to the Lord your God, all you who around him bring gifts.” You, he says, who are shut up in the city and dwell around the Temple, in which you do not doubt he is present, and who daily offer him sacrifices and gifts to make him favorable and gracious toward you—make your vows and fulfill them to the Lord your God. Whoever is engaged in some sin, let that person abandon it and vow to act rightly. [Col. 0989D] Isaiah, the greatest of prophets, is with you; hear him saying: “Cease to do perversely, learn to do good, seek judgment, assist the oppressed, judge for the orphan, and defend the widow” (Isa. 1:17).

“To the terrible one, and to him who takes away the spirit of princes—to him who is terrible among the kings of the earth.” Vow, he says, to the Lord your God, the strong and terrible Lord, who so suddenly takes away the spirit of princes and is so terrible among the kings of the earth. There is no doubt that many kings and princes were in that army and perished together with the others. All these things are true according to [Col. 0990A] the letter and can very easily and suitably be applied to a spiritual understanding. But we have followed the title, which is written against the Assyrians.

## Psalm LXXVI. Unto the End: For Idithun. A Psalm of Asaph

[Note: [Col. 0989D] “Asaph means congregation. Therefore the congregation speaks here, leaping over in order to reach the end, which is Christ Jesus. What, then, must be leapt over so that we may reach that end, the text of the psalm itself shows.” St Augustine.]

Those psalms whose title bears Idithun belong to the perfect; Idithun means “leaping over others.” This has already been explained in other psalms.

“With my voice I cried to the Lord; with my voice to God, and he attended to me.” With my voice, he says—that is, personally, with the voice of the inner person—I cried to the Lord with the whole intentness of my mind. My voice went to the Lord and entered his ears, as it says elsewhere: “And my cry entered before him into his ears” [Col. 0990B] (Ps. 17:7). And the Lord attended to me. What does “he attended to me” mean except that he heard me? Thus should one pray who desires to be heard.

“In the day of my tribulation I sought God with my hands.” In the day, he says, of my tribulation, I sought the Lord, who is a helper in seasons of need, in tribulation. But how did I seek him? “With my hands.” It is greater to seek the Lord with one’s hands than with one’s mouth. Those seek the Lord with their hands who strive to come to him through doing good.

“At night before him, and I was not deceived.” Those who seek the Lord by night and in tribulations are not deceived, “for the Lord is near to those who are troubled in heart” (Ps. 33:19). — “Many are the tribulations of the righteous, and from them all the Lord will deliver [Col. 0990C] them” (Ps. 7:20). The Prophet likewise shows that he sought God by night: “At midnight I rose to confess you” (Ps. 118:62). And again: “In the nights lift up your hands in the sanctuary, and bless the Lord” (Ps. 133:1).

“My soul refused to be comforted.” When I was in tribulations, he says, I had many comforters, whose consolations my soul refused to receive. Thus blessed Job said to his comforters: “You are all burdensome comforters” (Job 12:2). So too “Rachel, weeping for her children, refused to be comforted, because they are not” (Matt. 2:18). Therefore this was carnal consolation, which this holy man refused to receive: “I remembered God and was delighted” (Ps. 76:1). [Col. 0990D] I remembered God, he says, who “emptied himself, taking the form of a servant” (Phil. 2:7), and endured such great tribulations for us all; and I was delighted in my tribulations, for “the sufferings of this present time are not worthy to be compared with the future glory which shall be revealed in us” (Rom. 8:18).

“I was exercised, and my spirit failed for a little while.” The Apostle underwent such an exercise when he said: “We do not wish you to be ignorant, brothers, concerning our tribulation which befell us in Asia: we were burdened beyond measure, beyond our strength, so that we were weary even [Col. 0991A] of living” (1 Cor. 1:8). His spirit indeed failed for a little while, since he was weary even of living. Thus holy martyrs in their contest were often exercised so that, as their spirit failed briefly, they desired to depart from this life.

“My eyes anticipated the watches.” It was not surprising that he could not sleep when he was in such an exercise, especially since the Lord says: “Watch, for you know neither the day nor the hour” (Matt. 25:13). He watched and preferred death to life, because the torments he endured were harsher even than death itself. Hence it follows: “I was troubled, and I did not speak.” How indeed could he fail to be troubled, surrounded on all sides by so many and such great distresses? But his perfection is proved by this: [Col. 0991B] he did not speak and patiently endured everything, following the example of our Savior, who “like a lamb led to slaughter did not open his mouth” (Isa. 53:7).

“I considered ancient days, and I had eternal years in mind.” — “I considered ancient days,” he says, and found that all who wish to live godly in Christ must suffer persecution (2 Tim. 3:12) from the ungodly and from such persons. Thus Abel, Abraham, Moses, David, and other saints endured. “And I had eternal years in mind.” [Note: [Col. 0991D] “What are eternal years?” Augustine asks. “A great thought. See whether this thought does not require great silence! Let the person who wishes to consider these eternal years rest inwardly from every outward noise, from every tumult of human affairs.”] And I knew and saw that the glory of the saints will be eternal and the torments of the wicked will have no end. All good people ought to maintain this consideration and receive this consolation in their distresses. Hence he further adds:

[Col. 0991C] “And I meditated by night with my heart; I was exercised, and I winnowed my spirit within me.” I thought upon these things at night, he says; I considered them in my heart. This was my exercise and occupation, and in this so noble meditation I winnowed my spirit. “I winnowed” is excellently said, so that his spirit, inflamed with indignation, might receive refreshment from this most delightful meditation.

And I said: “Will God cast off forever? Or will he not yet add that he may be well pleased? Will he cut off his mercy unto the end, from age to generation? Will God forget to show mercy, or will he contain his mercy in wrath?” Behold, he who refused to be comforted by others now comforts himself, and under the form of questions affirms what he seems to state negatively. It is as if he said: The foolish think that the Lord has cast us off and that, being angry, he will thereafter have no mercy on us. But it is not so. He who now seems unappeasable will quickly show himself gracious; nor, as they think, will he cut off his mercy to the end, from this age [Col. 0991D] unto the age to come. Hence it follows:

“And I said: Now I have begun.” What means “Now I have begun”? Now I have known and understood that God will never forsake [Col. 0992A] his saints. From past events, as though he said, it is known what the Lord will do in things to come. This is what he says: “This is the change of the right hand of the Most High.” What change? “Because I remembered the works of the Lord, and because I shall remember from the beginning your wonders, and because I meditated upon all your works, and because I shall exercise myself in your observances.” All this, he says, is the change wrought by the right hand of the Most High; and all this the Lord’s right hand accomplishes, so that a person may thus be changed from first things into last, and from last things into first, and thus remember and call to mind the Lord’s works and wonders. In such a transformation and meditation the saints come to know both the rewards of the good and the punishments of the wicked; and this gives them no small consolation. Observe here how [Col. 0992B] he alternates past and future: “I remembered,” he says, “and I shall remember”; “I meditated,” and “I shall meditate.” God’s wonders must always be kept in memory, his works always meditated upon, and we must always exercise ourselves in his commandments and observances.

“O God, your way is in the Holy One; what god is great like our God? You are the God who alone works wonders.” He now begins to recount God’s wonders, as he promised above that he would do when he said: “Because I shall remember from the beginning your wonders.” God’s way is in the Holy One, because he never departs from holiness and justice. By “the Holy One,” however, we may understand the Son of God himself, who said of himself: “I am the way, the truth, and the life” (John 14:6). And indeed God’s way is in him, because “all things were made through him, and without him nothing was made” [Col. 0992C] (John 1:3).

“What god is great like our God? All the gods of the nations are demons, but the Lord made the heavens.” And he alone works wonders, because whatever all others do—if indeed what they do is good—they do not do it from themselves, but from him.

“Thou hast made known thy power among the peoples.” What power? “Thou hast redeemed thy people, the children of Israel and of Joseph, by thy arm.” This is the power by which the Lord delivered his people from Egyptian slavery; it was made known to all peoples and nations, since it is exceedingly glorious and memorable without end. Yet no less praiseworthy [Col. 0992D] is that power by which the Lord, by his arm—that is, through his Son—delivered the whole human race from the slavery of the devil. For this was signified in that earlier event, and both this and that were accomplished by one and the same arm. When he says, “the children of Israel and the children of Joseph,” this seems to be said as in the Gospel: “Go, tell his disciples, and Peter” (Mark 16:7). For Peter too was one of the disciples, just as Joseph was one of the children of Israel. The reason why Peter was named is clear. But what else ought we to understand concerning Joseph, except that all the others were delivered by the Father’s grace, whereas Joseph was delivered through his own [Col. 0993A] merit? By these, moreover, we should understand all Christians, who see and know the one God, and grow in faith and goodness 464 of heart. For Israel is interpreted “a man seeing God”; Joseph, however, “increase” or “one who increases.”

“Waters saw thee, O God; waters saw thee and feared; the depths were troubled.” This may be understood literally, when the children of Israel crossed the Red Sea dry-shod, with the waters withdrawing on either side—an event which must certainly be reckoned among God’s greatest and most splendid miracles. According to the spiritual interpretation, “many waters” are many peoples; after the Lord had delivered his people by his arm, they were converted from unbelief to faith, [Col. 0993B] believed in him, saw him, and feared. The depths, however, were troubled; by them we understand the more powerful persons of this age, who are in this world as the depths are in the midst of the sea. Hence the Apostle says: “Consider your calling, brethren: not many powerful, not many noble, not many wise are among you; but God chose the foolish things of the world to destroy wisdom, and chose the weak things to confound the strong, and the things which are not, that he might destroy the things which are” (1 Cor. 1:26). These men, however, were disturbed and rose against the saints with great fury. An infinite and stormy multitude of wicked people followed them. Of this it is further said: “A multitude, the sound of waters.” What wonder if, from the disturbance of the depths, the sound of many [Col. 0993C] waters went forth? What wonder if, from the savagery of the rich and powerful, the cry of a foolish and undisciplined people broke out against the saints? For who stirred up all that multitude against our Saviour, so that all should cry with one voice, “Crucify him,” except the rulers and priests? Thus, then, from the disturbance of the depths came the sound of many waters. But for this reason the apostles and teachers did not fall silent or cease from preaching Christ. Hence it is further said:

“The clouds gave forth their voice; for thy arrows passed through; the voice of thy thunder was in the wheel.” Far greater and more terrible are the voices of the clouds than the voices of the waters; and those arrows which go forth from the clouds produce very great fear and terror, [Col. 0993D] especially when the voice of so great a thunder is in the wheel, and apostolic preaching does not occupy one region only but fills the whole world [Note: [Col. 0993D] Codex Ghislerianus: “fills it round about.”]. For the clouds are the apostles and teachers, by whose doctrine the whole Church is watered and made fruitful. The arrows, however, are understood as their pronouncements, by which the army of vices and evil spirits is put to flight.

“Thy lightnings shone upon the world; and the earth was moved.” These lightnings, which go forth from clouds and thunderings, are the signs and miracles [Col. 0994A] which were performed everywhere through the apostles. The earth saw these and was moved, because chiefly on account of the signs and miracles that were performed, all unbelievers and the faithless were converted to the faith. Hence the Gospel says of the apostles that they “went forth and preached everywhere, the Lord working with them and confirming the word by the signs which followed” (Mark 16:20).

“Thy way is in the sea, and thy paths in many waters, and thy footprints shall not be known.” This may literally be understood of our Saviour, who walked dry-shod upon the waters of the sea, where human footprints cannot be found. Spiritually, however, the sea signifies the world, as has already often been said in other psalms. “Many waters” are many peoples, as we have likewise often said. [Col. 0994B] The Lord therefore made a way for himself in the sea and paths in many waters, because, since this world was converted to his faith, he has not ceased invisibly to walk through it and to visit his churches everywhere. As he himself says to his disciples: “Behold, I am with you all days, even to the consummation of the age” (Matt. 28:20). His footprints are not known, either because he does this invisibly, or because, in comparison with the wicked, few imitate his footsteps. Thus the Lord himself says of the Holy Spirit, who is likewise invisible: “The Spirit breathes where he wills, and thou hearest his voice, but knowest not whence he comes or whither he goes” (John 3:8). Hence its footprints also are shown to be invisible. But if these words are understood literally of the children of Israel [Col. 0994C] as well, this will not be inappropriate: they had ways and paths in both the Red Sea and the Jordan, as sacred history relates. Hence it follows:

“Thou hast led thy people like sheep by the hand of Moses and Aaron.” By Moses and Aaron we may understand bishops and priests, who govern and lead the Christian people—for it is the people of God—and guide them by the straight path into the land of the living, signified by the promised land.

## 465. PSALM LXXVII. THE UNDERSTANDING OF ASAPH

Asaph intends that this psalm should be expounded according to his understanding; and therefore he says, “I will open my mouth in parables,” so that it may be understood not literally [Col. 0994D] but parabolically [Note: [Col. 0993D] “These words are ‘understanding,’ that is, they belong to the understanding given to Asaph himself; yet we understand it better as given not to one man, but to the congregation [Col. 0994D] of God’s people, from which we must by no means separate ourselves,” etc. St Augustine. These words show that our Bruno, as in his other interpretations, followed the thought of the holy doctor.].

“Give ear, my people, to my law; incline your ear to the words of my mouth.” In this psalm the Prophet, the apostles, and the teachers of the Church speak, to whom the whole people has been entrusted by the Lord. Let the apostolic assembly therefore say: Give ear, my people, entrusted to me to govern, to my law—the law which I preach and keep, the law by which I live and for which, should necessity require, I do not fear to die. “Incline your ear,” namely the ear of your heart, so that whoever has ears to hear may hear, “to [Col. 0995A] the words of my mouth,” because the things I am about to say possess a deeper meaning than they appear to have. Hence it follows:

“I will open my mouth in parables; I will utter propositions from the beginning of the world.” A parable is a likeness of some thing, when one thing is said and another understood. Such are the things called Solomon’s parables, and such also are those by which the Lord speaks most frequently in the Gospels. In this place, however, “parables” and “propositions” mean the same thing.

“How great are the things that we have heard and known, and that our fathers have told us.” There are many things, he says, which we have heard and come to know by hearing, and which our fathers told us, and which we now likewise proclaim to you in parables.

[Col. 0995B] “They have not been hidden from their children in another generation.” We, he says, their children, do not hide what we have heard from our fathers, but proclaim it in another generation, by which we understand the Gentile people; for “he who hides grain shall be cursed among the peoples” (Prov. 11:26).

“Relating the praises of the Lord, and the powers of the Lord, and his wonders which he wrought.” Our fathers, he says, told us everything: the praises of the Lord, his powers, and his wonders. Read the books of Moses and the other books of the Old Testament, and you will be able to find all these things.

“And he raised up a testimony in Jacob and set a law in Israel.” Israel, Jacob, and testimony signify the same thing. This is that law given by the Lord through Moses to the children of Israel [Col. 0995C] on Mount Sinai. Of it the text further says:

“How many things did he command our fathers?” For what purpose? That they might make them known to their children. And why? “That the next generation might know.” Therefore neither the law nor any knowledge ought to be hidden, when it was given for this purpose: that it might pass from some to others and, by passing on, benefit more people. Thus the law which had been given to the Jews reached even to the Gentiles, and has worked, and works daily, more in this people than in that one.

“The children who shall be born shall arise and tell it to their children.” The children who shall be born, he says, and be born anew into a new generation through water and Spirit, shall not [Col. 0995D] be idle, sluggish, or weary, but shall arise, manfully prepare themselves for preaching, and tell it to their children. This was fulfilled in the apostles and the successors of the apostles.

“That they may place their hope in God, and may not forget the works of their God, and may seek his commandments.” These children who shall be born, he says, will exhort their children to place their hope in God—not in uncertain riches, not in the worship or responses of false gods, nor in any other superstition—“and not forget the works of their God,” who delivered them so wonderfully from such great dangers, “and seek his commandments,” meditating upon them day and night.

“Lest they become like their fathers.” And what sort were [Col. 0996A] their fathers? Hear what follows: a crooked and exceedingly bitter generation, of whom the Lord himself says, “A crooked and perverse generation seeks a sign” (Matt. 12:39).—“A generation which did not set its heart aright.” It did not set it toward good, justice, or sound understanding, but rather twisted and bent it toward every iniquity. “And its spirit was not faithful with God.” If it did not entrust itself to God and refused to be with God, to whom did it entrust itself, and with whom was it? Certainly with those to whom it sacrificed its sons and daughters, as it is written: “They sacrificed their sons and their daughters to demons” (Ps. 105:31). This he proves by the children of Ephraim, because their spirit and will were not with God.

“The children of Ephraim, bending the bow and shooting [Col. 0996B] their arrows, turned back in the day of battle.” As is read in Isaiah, this occurred in the days of Ahaz king of Judah, when Ephraim, who ought to have aided his brothers, joined the nations in attacking Jerusalem (Isa. 9:9). 466 But because these things are spoken in parables, they must be referred to the times of Christians. For we often see this happen in the Church: those from whom the greatest hope is expected, and who appear readier for battle, lay down their weapons at the time of need and shamefully surrender themselves to their enemies. Of them it fittingly follows:

“They did not keep the covenant of their God, and they refused to walk in his law.” This is evident of the children of Ephraim: in the days of Jeroboam [Col. 0996C] they rejected the law of the Lord, worshipped golden calves, and wholly gave themselves over to idolatry. Likewise Christians often become heretics and do not fear to violate God’s law.
