“And they forgot his benefits and his wonders which he showed them.” Ungrateful children, deserving to be disinherited, are those who, forgetting their father’s benefactions, do not fear to ally themselves with his enemies in order to attack their own father—especially such a father, whose faith and doctrine they know to have been proved by signs and miracles. But someone will say: We have not seen miracles. To this he himself replies: “Before their fathers he wrought wonders in the land of Egypt, in the field of Tanis.” If you have not seen them, he says, your fathers saw them, and you ought to believe them no less than yourself. [Col. 0996D] He gave you witnesses who saw the miracles, the kingdom where they were performed, and the very place where they occurred, so that you should in no way doubt them. Nor indeed were the miracles later performed through the apostles and other saints throughout the world lesser than those which are recorded as having been done then through Moses in Egypt. Those miracles, indeed, benefited the Egyptians in no way; these, however, converted almost the entire world to the faith. These things are said against those who did not keep God’s covenant and refused to walk in his law.

“He divided the sea and led them through; and he set up the waters as in a wineskin.” This also is a parable and calls for an allegorical exposition. We have often already said that [Col. 0997A] the sea signifies the world, while many waters are many peoples. Waters enclosed in a wineskin cannot burst forth except by permission. Thus now all waters are shut up in a wineskin, and Christians go safely wherever they wish, fearing neither any flood of the sea nor the persecutions of tyrants.

“And he led them out in a cloud by day, and all the night in the illumination of fire.” This is what the Apostle says: “For all crossed the sea, and all were baptized in Moses in the cloud and in the sea” (1 Cor. 10:2). The cloud which went before them conferred a double benefit: shading them by day and giving light by night. This cloud, therefore, is the Holy Spirit; it overshadows God’s people, lest they feel the desires of the flesh and the heat of vices. Hence the angel says to Blessed [Col. 0997B] Mary: “The Holy Spirit shall come upon thee, and the power of the Most High shall overshadow thee” (Luke 1:35). It enlightens them and does not allow them to stray from the way of God’s commandments.

“He split the rock in the wilderness and gave them drink as from a great deep.” This is that rock of which the Apostle says: “And the rock was Christ” (1 Cor. 10:4). This rock was first struck and wounded by a reed, then by a lance, “and immediately blood and water came out” (John 19:34). Of that other rock it is also said that it was struck twice. So great a flood of waters flowed from this rock that it washed, satisfied, and cleansed the whole world from the contagion of sins. Hence it follows:

“And he brought water out of the rock, and brought forth waters like [Col. 0997C] rivers.” Four great rivers went forth from this rock, by which the holy Church is watered.

“And they continued to sin against him; in the dry land they provoked the Most High to anger.” It was not enough for them to sin in the matter of water, unless they likewise transgressed over food. They added sin upon sin, since they were dry of every goodness and at that time dwelt in a dry land.

“And they tempted God in their hearts, that they might demand food for their souls.” They sinned much more grievously by distrusting in their hearts than by crying aloud and asking for food. For their leaders Moses and Aaron are also recorded to have sinned similarly at the waters of contradiction. Therefore they were forbidden to enter the [Col. 0997D] promised land. Distrust, then, and having no hope in those things which are asked from the Lord, is a great sin.

“And they spoke evil of God and said: Can God prepare a table in the wilderness?” These are the words which they spoke inwardly and by which they tempted God in their hearts. With their mouths they asked for food, but in their hearts said: Can he give us food in the wilderness? This is what he says:

“For he struck the rock, and waters flowed, and torrents overflowed. Can he also give bread or prepare a table for his people?” Most foolish and senseless men! Would it not have been more fitting to say: Since he struck the rock, waters flowed, [Col. 0998A] and torrents overflowed, we are certain and do not in the least doubt that he who gave waters in such abundance will also supply us bread most abundantly? For it is no more difficult for God to give bread from heaven than to bring water from a rock. In these and similar matters we must be warned not to do likewise. Let this exposition suffice us.

“Therefore the Lord heard and delayed, and deferred.” 467 What did the Lord delay, and what did he defer to do? Namely that which is read in what follows: “While their food was still in their mouths, the wrath of God rose against them.” He delayed his wrath and fulfilled their request, so that they might first acknowledge God’s omnipotence, then their own unbelief and wickedness. Hence it follows: “And fire was kindled in Jacob, [Col. 0998B] and wrath rose in Israel.”

“Because they did not believe in their God, nor hope in his salvation.” Therefore, he says, the fire of God’s wrath and indignation was kindled against Jacob and rose over the children of Israel: because they neither believed nor hoped as they ought to have believed and hoped. Since they had seen so many and such great signs and wonders, they ought never to have doubted God’s omnipotence. These things are stated by anticipation, because the matters that follow occurred before these things.

“And he commanded the clouds above, opened the doors of heaven, and rained manna upon them to eat.” They had their clouds, their heavens, and their manna; we too have our clouds, our heavens, and [Col. 0998C] our manna, indeed of a much greater and worthier nature. Our clouds and heavens are the apostles and teachers; our manna is the doctrine and spiritual understanding of both Testaments. Such food descends from our clouds, and such bread is rained upon us by our heavens. We may also understand by this bread Christ’s body, concerning which we surely say daily: “Give us this day our daily bread” (Matt. 6:11). Concerning this bread it is further said:

“He gave them bread of heaven; man ate the bread of angels; he sent them provision in abundance.” The heavenly bread is Christ’s body; the heavenly bread is spiritual understanding and knowledge. By such food angels are refreshed, and by such bread all things above heaven live. Men too now eat such bread and receive such provision in the Church. This provision is made from that grain of which the Lord says in the Gospel: “Unless a grain of wheat, falling into the earth, dies, it bears no fruit; but if it dies, it bears much fruit” (John 12:24).

“And he stirred up the south wind from heaven and, in his power, brought in the southwest wind.” The south wind (*Auster*) and southwest wind (*Africus*) are the same. Of this south wind it is said elsewhere: “God shall come from the south” (Hab. 3:3). The Lord moved it and stirred it up according to the might of his power. And what did it do?

“And he rained flesh upon them like dust, and [Col. 0999A] winged birds like the sand of the sea.” First they demanded water, then bread, and afterwards flesh. Nothing was refused them, but everything was abundantly granted to them, by him “who is rich unto all that call upon him” (Rom. 10:12). The south wind is likewise stirred up over us, so that it may drive away the cold and sloth of the north wind, warm our hearts, and restore to life those almost dead through the vast intensity of excessive cold. But what is signified by flesh except carnal understanding? And what by winged birds except spiritual understanding? The Lord has given us both abundantly, because we understand and expound the Scriptures in both ways. Hence it follows:

“And they fell in the midst of [Col. 0999B] their camp, round about their tents.” These things fall both in the midst of and around the camps of Christians, because wise and foolish alike are daily satisfied here. This is what the text says:

“And they ate and were exceedingly filled; he gave them their desire, and they were not cheated of their desire.” At that time they did not seek those carnal foods with a greater appetite than Christians now seek spiritual food; but they sought in one way, while Christians now seek in another. Therefore they do not receive the same or equal merits. And concerning those people, because of their unbelief, the following is said:

“While their food was still in their mouths, the wrath of God rose against them, slew many of them, and hindered the chosen of Israel.” By saying that the chosen of Israel were hindered, he shows that not just any persons, [Col. 0999C] but the greater and stronger, had murmured.

“In all these things they still sinned and did not believe in his wonders.” How foolish, unbelieving, and wicked they were is shown in this: neither miracles nor punishments could correct and direct them. Hence it follows:

“And their days failed in vanity, and their years in haste.” What it means to fail in haste is made clear by what follows.

“When he slew them, then they sought him; they turned back before dawn and came to him.” Those who are killed in this manner certainly fail and die in haste. But because they stood before dawn and could not conceal the wickedness of their hearts, [Col. 0999D] they turned back, though not from the heart. They came to him, yet not in heart: they came in outward appearance and pretence.

“And they remembered that God is their helper, and that God Most High is their deliverer.” Had they not forgotten, it would not be said, “they remembered.” Such is what is said elsewhere: “He will confess thee when thou hast done him good” (Ps. 49:19).

“And they loved him with their mouth, and with their tongue they lied to him; but their heart was not right with him, nor was faith kept with them in his covenant.” This is what the Lord says in the Gospel and [Col. 1000A] through the Prophet: “This people honours me with their lips, but their heart is far from me” (Mark 7:6). And what does “nor was faith kept with them in his covenant” mean, except that they neither believed nor had faith in his covenant? All these things are spoken in parables, 468 so that no one may imitate those who fear to suffer like things. For those who do similar things deserve to suffer similar things. Yet in these matters God’s mercy must also be considered: as he is severe toward those who persevere in sins, so he is ready and merciful toward those who turn back and repent. Hence it follows:

“But he is merciful and will be propitious to their sins, and will not destroy them.” For whatever hour the sinner turns back and groans, he shall live [Col. 1000B] and shall not die.

“And he multiplied, that he might turn away his wrath from them.” What did the Lord multiply except mercy, pardon, and compassion? Because he abounded in these and was full of them, “he did not kindle all his wrath,” so as immediately to kill them for such great offences and their necessities.

“And he remembered that they are flesh,” which always resists the spirit and, as the Apostle says, lusts against the spirit: “A spirit going and not returning” (Ps. 77:34). Someone might say: And if the flesh were killed, what would the spirit do? He answers: It would go, he says, and would not return. For after the soul is separated from the body, unless by a divine oracle, it shall never return to it again until the time appointed for all [Col. 1000C] things.

“How often they provoked him in the wilderness and stirred him to anger in the waterless land!” Even to this day, those who are in the wilderness, far from the Church and not watered by spiritual waters, do not cease to provoke and anger him.

“And they turned back.” From where, and to where? From good to evil. “And they tempted God and provoked the Holy One of Israel.” The Jews are recorded to have tempted the Lord ten times then. The first temptation was at the Red Sea, concerning which it is written: “They provoked him as they went up to the sea, the Red Sea” (Ps. 105:7). The second concerned the making of the calf. The third was when they murmured: “Why hast thou brought us out of the land [Col. 1000D] of Egypt? Our soul loathes this very light food” (Num. 21:5); and he sent fiery serpents among them. The fourth and fifth were at the waters of contradiction: one before the death of Mary, the other after her death. The sixth was when the manna became putrid. The seventh and eighth concerned the quails. The ninth concerned Korah. The tenth concerned the spies. [Note: [Col. 0999] What is lacking from this psalm in Marchesius’s edition is supplied from Vallicellian codex C. XII; it is also lacking in Codex Ghislerianus.]

“They did not remember his hand, the day on which he delivered them from the hand of tribulation.” All these things are spoken in parables to us, who often forget such great divine omnipotence and do not have the faith which we ought to have.

[Col. 1001A] “As he set his signs in Egypt and his wonders in the field of Tanis.” Here he begins to recount them: “He turned their rivers into blood, and their rain-waters, that they might not drink.” The plagues by which the Egyptians were then struck signified those plagues by which, among all nations, all who imitate the Egyptians are scourged. The Egyptians drank not water but blood, though they thought it to be water and not blood. But Moses opened their eyes and caused them to understand what they drank. Egypt, interpreted “darkness,” signifies the world, which before the coming of our Saviour—prefigured by Moses—sat in darkness and the shadow of death. Hence it is written: “The people that sat in darkness saw a great light” (Isa. 9:2). [Col. 1001B] The waters of Egypt signify all the knowledge and doctrine of philosophers, poets, and heretics. These waters were changed into blood because “God made foolish the wisdom of this world” (1 Cor. 1:10), and what was formerly considered sound and useful is now abhorred by Christ’s faithful as blood and sin.

“He sent among them the dog-fly, and it devoured them.” By the dog-fly which devours the Egyptians, we understand luxury and pleasures of the flesh, which pursue adults and fornicators, signified by the Egyptians. “The frog, and it destroyed them [Note: [Col. 1001D] Clearly St Bruno speaks here according to the Hebrew idiom by which God is said to do what he himself permits under the laws of Providence. Thus in the Lord’s Prayer Christ taught us to pray: “And lead us not into temptation.”].” What does the frog signify except heretics, strong only in voice and chattering? [Note: [Col. 1001D] Thus St Vincent of Lérins, in the *Commonitorium*, §14, calls heretics frogs, gnats, and dying flies.] These are they who destroy and separate from the unity of the Church [Col. 1001C] all who delight in their song and teaching.

“And he gave their fruits to rust, and their labours to the locust.” The Lord says of rust in the Gospel: “Lay up for yourselves treasures in heaven, where neither rust nor moth destroys” (Matt. 6:20). By rust, therefore, which corrupts and destroys whatever it clings to, we understand hatred, envy, and vainglory, which destroy and ruin all the fruits of the soul. Let the one who loves the fruits of the soul and fears to lose good works therefore shake off such rusts. By the locust, however, pride is signified; because it is the mother and mistress of vices, it always proceeds with an army and multitude, [Col. 1001D] as appears characteristic of locusts. Yet the locust cannot rise very high, because the Lord is above, humbles the proud, and does not allow them to reign long. Let us therefore drive this locust away from ourselves, lest we lose our labours.

“And he killed their vines with hail, and their mulberry trees with frost.”—“Those who fear frost,” as it is written, “snow shall come upon them” (Job 6:[Col. 1002A] 16). By hail and frost, therefore, 469 are signified all kinds of torments by which those who resist God’s will and afflict his people must be killed and punished. Hence it follows:

“And he gave their cattle to the hail, and their possessions to the fire.” By cattle and possessions we may understand their bodies, which they had as beasts and in whose dung they rotted, because they had wicked owners. These shall be delivered to hail and fire because they shall be tortured by everlasting punishments. Hence it fittingly follows:

“He sent upon them the wrath of his indignation—indignation, wrath, and tribulation—dispatches through evil angels.” [Note: [Col. 1002D] “God therefore uses evil angels not only to punish the wicked, as in all these instances of which the psalm speaks, and as in the case of King Ahab, whom a spirit of deceit, by God’s will, led astray so that he might fall in battle; but also to test and reveal the good, as he did in Job.” Augustine.] This whole verse seems to concern the Day of Judgment rather than the times of the Egyptians, [Col. 1002B] because then there will be greater indignations, greater wraths and tribulations, and more dispatches through evil angels.

“He made a way for his path.” He explains this as follows: “And he spared not their souls from death.” As broad is this way and open this path, so final is it. The gate of God, which was previously narrow and as though proceeded along a path, later grew immensely and began to run along the broad way. Hence it follows:

“And he spared not their souls from death, and shut up their cattle in death. And he struck every firstborn in the land of Egypt, the firstfruits of all their labour in the tents of Ham.” [Col. 1002C] Our firstborn were original sins. In his Passion the Lord struck these not only in Egypt but throughout the entire world, wherever there were tents of Ham, by whom we understand the devil; for Ham is interpreted “cunningness” [Note: [Col. 1002D] For *διάβολος* means “slanderer,” “accuser.”].

“And he took away his people like sheep and led them like a flock in the wilderness.” Once the firstborn had died and original sin had been destroyed, the Lord took his people away from the devil’s power, removed them from Pharaoh’s cities, and placed them in a pastureland. For in the land which had previously been a desert, God’s sheep are now especially nourished.

“He led them in hope, and they did not fear.” They would not have entered the sea unless they had possessed the greatest hope in God, when they saw the waters of the sea standing like a wall on both [Col. 1002D] sides. “And the sea covered their enemies.” These, however, were led not by hope but by the devil, who had blinded their eyes so that they did not know what they were doing. Likewise Pharaoh, by whom the devil is signified, now pursues God’s people with all his army as far as the waters of baptism; there he plunges them into the abyss and destroys them.

“And he brought them into the mountain of his sanctification, [Col. 1003A] this mountain which his right hand acquired.” This is Mount Zion and the city of Jerusalem, by which the holy Church is understood. Hence it is said elsewhere: “Come, let us go up to the mountain of the Lord and to the house of the God of Israel” (Isa. 2:3). The king and Lord of this mountain says: “But I have been appointed king by him over Zion, his holy mountain, proclaiming the precept of the Lord” (Ps. 2:6).

“And he cast out the nations before them and divided the land among them by lot with a measuring-cord of distribution.” Likewise the Lord casts out before the face of heretics, schismatics, and vices the nations, and divides the whole land into portions.

“And the tribe of Israel dwelt in their tents.” The children of Israel now dwell everywhere—not only carnal Israel, [Col. 1003B] but spiritual Israel—because the whole earth has become its possession.

“And they tempted and provoked God Most High, and did not keep his testimonies.” They should by then have ceased from temptation after entering the land of promise. But these things are recounted to us so that we too may not do likewise, but may keep the Lord’s law.

“And they turned away and did not keep the covenant.” They turned away, he says, from God and did not keep his commandments and testimonies. But, “like their fathers”—those fathers, namely, whose imitators they were—“they were turned into a perverse bow.” A perverse bow is one which directs its arrows against friends and attacks what it ought to have defended.

[Col. 1003C] “They provoked him to anger on their hills,” namely on the hills where they sacrificed to demons. Hence it is said elsewhere: “They sacrificed to demons and not to God, while they sought him” (Ps. 103:37). This is what he says: “And they provoked him to jealousy by their graven images.” What does “they provoked him to jealousy” mean except that they provoked him to indignation?

“The Lord heard and rejected them, and brought Israel greatly to nothing.” They could hide nothing from God, since thoughts themselves speak; and he reduces them greatly to nothing because, to his injury, they serve his enemy.

“And he rejected the tabernacle of Shiloh, his tabernacle [Col. 1003D] in which he dwelt among men.” Read the books of Kings and you will find that the ark of God was captured because of the insolence of Eli’s sons, who abused their priesthood, and because Eli himself neglected to correct them as he ought (1 Sam. 4). The sin for which the Lord is said to have rejected his own tabernacle was no small one. 470 Let the Lord’s priests hear this and conduct themselves manfully; nor let them neglect to correct the people entrusted to them.

“And he delivered them into captivity, their strength and their beauty into the hands of the enemy.” Likewise, when the ark of God was captured, those who seemed stronger, more handsome, and more noble among that people were captured. For the sons of Eli, Hophni and Phinehas, priests, are also recorded to have fallen in that battle. Yet by “their strengths and their beauties” we may fittingly understand the ark itself, in which all their strength and beauty were contained.

“And he shut up his people to the sword, and despised his inheritance.” The Lord is indeed patient and merciful, and waits long for sinners to repent. But once he is angered, as the Apostle says, “It is a fearful thing to fall into the hands of the living God” (Heb. 10:31). Therefore it is further added:

“The fire consumed their young men, and their maidens were not lamented.” So great was the enemies’ cruelty, [Col. 1004B] and so great the wretches’ fear, that they did not dare to weep and mourn the most grievous death of their young men.

“Their priests fell by the sword, and their widows were not mourned.” This may be understood not only of the sons of Eli, who fell in battle, but also of the other priests of that same people. Hence the Apostle says by way of comparison that he will not spare the wild olive if he did not spare the olive tree (Rom. 11).

“And the Lord awoke as one sleeping, like a mighty man made drunk with wine.” The Lord appears to sleep when he does not help his own and permits them to be afflicted. Thus it is also said elsewhere: “Arise, why do you sleep, O Lord? Do not cast us off utterly” (Ps. 43:23). Read the book of Judges, and you will see the Jews: at one time, because of their sins, miserably delivered to their enemies; at another, converted to repentance, marvelously freed by the Lord. Thus, when the ark was captured, he who had seemed to sleep, because he was giving them no help at all, immediately began, as though roused from sleep like one drunk and overcome with wine, to rage against the Philistines and afflict them most severely. Hence it follows:

“And he struck his enemies in their hind parts; he gave them everlasting reproach.” The history is well known which says that the Lord struck them in the more private part of their buttocks, and their protruding intestines rotted away. [Note: [Col. 1003D] “They carried the ark of the God of Israel about. But while they were carrying it about, the hand of the Lord came upon each city with an exceedingly great slaughter; and [Col. 1004D] he struck the men of each city, from the least to the greatest, and their protruding intestines rotted away.” 1 Reg. 9.] These things may also signify spiritual realities, [Col. 1004D] because at the time when our Savior rejected his tabernacle and repudiated the Synagogue, rising from the sleep of death like a mighty man overcome with wine, he struck his Jewish enemies and delivered them to everlasting reproach. For they too were struck in their hind parts—not in body, however, but in age. For in the final age he struck them so forcefully that throughout all the time which follows, until the end, they cannot be healed.

“And he rejected the tabernacle of Joseph, and did not choose the tribe of Ephraim.” The eleven tribes followed Jeroboam, [Col. 1005A] who was of the tribe of Joseph and Ephraim; all of them, devoted to idolatry, worshiped golden calves. Therefore the Lord rejected them and separated them from his faithful people.

“But he chose the tribe of Judah, Mount Zion, which he loved.” Judah is interpreted “confession,” and signifies those who, confessing God amid torments themselves, can rather be killed than conquered. Of them the Lord says in the Gospel: “Whoever confesses me before men, I too will confess before my Father” (Matt. 10:32). Mount Zion signifies the same thing; it is interpreted “watchtower.” Good watchmen are those who keep continual watch, lest, caught unawares, they be seized by enemies.

“And he built his sanctuary like that of unicorns; [Col. 1005B] in the earth he founded it for ever.” [Note: [Col. 1005D] In St Augustine one reads: “And he built his sanctuary like that of unicorns”; or, as some translators coined a new word, “his sanctificium.” Cardinal Thommasius explains this aptly: “And upon that mountain he built his sanctuary, lofty, strong, and unique, after the likeness of the single horn of unicorns.”] God’s sanctuary is the Church, built out of unicorns alone. But where was it built, except upon the earth, which remains always firm and immovable? The Church has a firm foundation; therefore it fears neither rains, nor floods, nor wind. All Christians are unicorns, because they have one mouth and one faith, which none of their adversaries can resist or contradict. Hence it follows: “He founded it for ever.” The Church is founded for all ages, because Christ is its foundation; of him the Apostle says: “No one can lay another foundation than that which has been laid, which is Christ Jesus” (1 Cor. 3:11).

[Col. 1005C] “And he chose David his servant, and took him from the sheepfolds; from following the ewes with young he took him, to feed Jacob his servant and Israel his inheritance.” He built, he says, the sanctuary, and to rule and govern it he chose not just any man, but David himself, his servant. He took him not from royal palaces, not from a school of philosophers, but from sheepfolds; he took him from following ewes with young. David had good sheep—not barren and empty ones, but fruitful ones. Such are those of whom it is said: “Your teeth are like flocks of shorn sheep which have come up from the washing; all bear twins, and none among them is barren” (Song 4:2). Such also are those of whom the Lord says: [Col. 1006A] “My sheep hear my voice and follow me, and I, the Lord, know them” (John 10:27).

“And he fed them in the innocence of his heart.” Whose heart? That of the people mentioned above, of whom he has just said, “to feed Jacob his people.” He fed the people and nourished them with spiritual food, but he did not nourish the wickedness of its heart; rather, he uprooted it manfully and wisely. Hence the Apostle says to Timothy: “I charge you before God and Christ Jesus, who is to judge the living and the dead: preach the word; be urgent in season and out of season; rebuke in all patience and teaching” (2 Tim. 4:1).—“And with the understanding of his hands he guided them.” [Note: [Col. 1005D] The Vulgate has “in understandings.” But the version used here by St Augustine reads “in the understanding of his hands.” The exposition, however, is the same.] The best understanding of hands is that which they accomplish not by thinking or speaking, but by doing. Nor is there any understanding by which people are more easily [Col. 1006B] led and drawn to that heavenly blessedness than the understanding of hands, which is one of the five senses.

[Note: [Col. 1005D] St Augustine teaches that this psalm can admit a threefold interpretation. First, if the prophecy is referred to the Assyrians, who led the Hebrews, God’s people, captive to Babylon and desecrated and destroyed the holy Temple. Secondly, it is fully seen in the Romans’ final siege, [Col. 1006D] when Titus took by force the city and Temple of Jerusalem, with the entire people partly slaughtered by the sword and partly taken captive, and with the sacred buildings utterly demolished and leveled to the ground. A third interpretation may be found in the Church, devastated and afflicted under so many and such great enemies from its earliest times onward. St Bruno chiefly follows this interpretation, transferring to the Church’s labors and persecutions what had been foretold concerning Jerusalem and the destruction of the Synagogue.]  

## PSALM 78. A PSALM OF ASAPH.

What the psalm of Asaph signifies has already often been said. In this Psalm, however, the faithful Synagogue, signified by Asaph, mourns its calamities; in these, the Church’s many and countless persecutions are also signified. [Note: [Col. 1006D] The Psalms which follow are from the same Vallicellian manuscript, ch. XII.]

“God, the nations have entered into your inheritance; they have defiled your holy temple.” [Note: [Col. 1006D] Concerning King Antiochus, 1 Maccabees 1 says: He commanded the holy things and the holy people Israel to be defiled; he commanded altars, temples, and idols to be built, and they sacrificed swine’s flesh.] The Synagogue endured many persecutions and was taken captive many times: first by the Assyrians and Chaldeans, [Col. 1006C] then by the Greeks and Romans. But those great persecutions signified the Church’s far greater afflictions. For God’s inheritance, God’s temple, and God’s city are the holy Church; those who wish to know its persecutions should read the passions of the holy martyrs. We may also understand by the Greeks vices and malignant spirits, by whom God’s inheritance and people are in many ways defiled and violated.

“They have made Jerusalem like a watchman’s hut in an orchard,” [Note: [Col. 1006D] Both the Vulgate and the text in St Augustine have “a watch-post.”] in which those who guarded fruit were accustomed to remain. So too were the walls and ruins of Jerusalem, all its inhabitants having been led away captive. For it is also recorded that, in certain places, so great a slaughter of Christians occurred in the Church that scarcely anyone could be found.

[Col. 1007A] “They have given the corpses [Note: [Col. 1007D] The Vulgate has *morticina* (“carcasses”). Here St Augustine teaches: “Those who rendered it ‘carcasses’ translated better than those who, like some, rendered it ‘mortal things.’ For *morticina* is said only of the dead, whereas *mortalia* can also name the bodies of the living.”] of your servants as food to the beasts of the earth.” We know that this happened literally both in the Synagogue and in the Church: the bodies of the saints—which alone in them were mortal—were often given to the beasts and birds of heaven. By these may be understood malignant spirits, to be devoured by whom those were handed over who were compelled by harsh torments to deny Christ’s faith.

“They poured out their blood around Jerusalem, and there was none to bury them.” Nor is there any doubt that this happened literally around Jerusalem and around the Church. For even if there were people willing to bury them, they did not dare to do so.

“We have become a reproach to our neighbors, mockery [Col. 1007B] and derision to those around us.” Hence it is said in the Gospel: “Parents will rise up against children, and children against parents; and you will be hated by all on account of my name” (Matt. 10:22). Likewise: “The hour is coming when everyone who kills you will think that he is offering service to God” (John 16:2). Therefore in both Testaments the good were held in reproach and derision by the wicked.

“How long, O Lord, will you be angry unto the end?” This explains it: “Your zeal is kindled like fire.” For the Lord seemed wholly angry with his servants unto the end when he allowed them to be so afflicted and did not help them at all.

“Pour out your wrath upon the nations that have not known you, [Col. 1007C] and upon the kingdoms that have not called upon your name.” Do not, he says, pour out your wrath and indignation against your servants, but rather—as is fitting—against the nations that have not known you and have not called upon your name, but, foolish and senseless as they are, have worshiped false gods. “For they have devoured Jacob.” But how did they devour him? He explains immediately: “And they have laid waste his dwelling-place.” It is a customary expression to call ravagers “devourers.”

“Do not remember our former iniquities.” What are our former iniquities, except those committed by our fathers, or those which we ourselves committed from childhood? For the Lord visits, as it is written, [Col. 1007D] the sins of the fathers upon the children to the third and fourth generation—provided that the children are such as imitate their fathers and do not depart from their wickedness. Otherwise, “the son shall not bear the iniquity of the father, and the soul that sins shall itself die” (Ezek. 18:20).

“Let your mercy swiftly come before us, for we have become exceedingly poor.” These people were poor, not only through lack of possessions, but because they were deprived of human help and placed their hope in God’s mercy alone. [Col. 1008A] That mercy comes before them when it not only rescues them from dangers but does not even permit them to experience the dangers themselves.

“Help us, O God our Savior,” for we have no helper besides you. “And for the honor of your name, O Lord, deliver us.” Great honor comes to his name when it is said: These men are servants of that God who never forsakes those who hope in him, but powerfully and wonderfully hears them in all their necessities.

“And be merciful to our sins for your name’s sake,” so that all may understand that it is not without reason that you are called Jesus and Savior. For the Apostle also says that “everyone who calls upon the name of the Lord shall be saved” (Rom. 10:13).

[Col. 1008B] “Lest the nations should say, ‘Where is their God?’” For pagans were accustomed at times to say this both against Jews and against Christians when they saw them miserably perishing without God’s help, though the Lord had formerly been accustomed to defend them so marvelously from every adversity.

“And let it be made known among the nations before our eyes”—understand what we are about to say. It is some consolation to us if we see miserable those who made us miserable. [Note: [Col. 1008D] This indeed is evil if a person is consoled by it solely from self-love; but it is virtue if it arises from love of divine justice. Thus in the Apocalypse the souls of the slain cried out: “Avenge, O Lord, our blood,” ch. 16:10.]

“Avenge the blood of your servants which has been shed. Let the groaning of the fettered enter into your sight,” and the rest which follows. Avenge, he says, O Lord, while we see and are present, the blood of your servants which was shed for your name’s sake. All the saints will see this vengeance for their blood, if not now, then at the judgment. Let the groaning enter into your sight of those who, for your sake, are shackled and bound with most harsh chains and shut up in dark prisons.

“According to the greatness of your arm, take possession of the children of the slain.” This is as though he said: We pray that those who killed parents by a cruel and harsh death may not kill the children also. Or: take possession, in the greatness of your arm, of the children whose parents you permitted to be delivered into enemies’ hands. Let not those who possessed the parents and kept them captive for so long possess the children too.

“Repay our neighbors sevenfold.” Not only the Jews, but also their neighbors dwelling round about them were led into captivity; these deserved a greater punishment because they rejoiced over the Jews’ ruin, whereas they ought to have grieved for them as companions and friends. “Sevenfold” signifies a full and complete punishment, because this number is perfect and contains all numbers within itself. Hence also: “Sevenfold vengeance shall be taken for Cain, but for Lamech seventy-sevenfold” (Gen. 4:24).

“Their reproach, with which they reproached [Col. 1009A] you, O Lord.” These words plainly show that they not only rejoiced, but also blasphemed God, as though he had been unable to defend his people. Let this reproach be in their bosom and heart, so that they may either be afflicted or corrected by the memory of it, and may themselves also say: “My sin is always before me” (Ps. 50:5).

“But we, your people and the sheep of your pasture, will confess you, O God, for ever; from age to age we will recount your praise.” Asaph says this; the Synagogue says this: whatever may happen, whether adversity or prosperity befall them, they will nevertheless never depart from God. They will always be his people and the sheep of his pasture; they will always confess [Col. 1009B] and praise him; they will always recount his wonders and praises. But all these things must be understood not only of the Jews, but also of the martyrs, who suffered from their persecutors no lesser or lighter—indeed, greater and more grievous—torments than those endured by the Jews from the Assyrians.

## PSALM 79. 473. UNTO THE END: FOR THOSE WHO SHALL BE CHANGED, A TESTIMONY OF ASAPH. A PSALM.

When “unto the end” is placed in the title, what is said, although it may seem literally to concern the Synagogue, must nevertheless be understood spiritually concerning Christ and the Church. Asaph, in the faithful Synagogue, gives this testimony for those who will be changed [Col. 1009C] from unbelief to faith, and who will pass from the letter to spiritual understanding. For these are the vine which, in this psalm, is described as transferred and changed from Egypt into the land of promise.

“You who rule Israel, give heed, [Note: [Col. 1009D] In St Augustine one reads: “O you who feed Israel, give heed.” He immediately says: “What is this: ‘O you who feed Israel, give heed, who lead Joseph like sheep’? He is invoked that he may come, awaited that he may come, desired that he may come.”] you who lead Joseph like a sheep.” Our Lord and Savior himself is the one who governs Israel, by whom we understand all those who know him and believe in him. He also leads Joseph like a sheep, by whom are signified those who, endowed with humility and patience, bear fruit through the offspring of good works. For Joseph is interpreted “increase” or “growing.” The other brothers are indeed called Israel after their father’s name, but Joseph is designated by his own proper name, because they are governed and led by the Lord not by their own, [Col. 1009D] but by their father’s name. Joseph, however, is governed, led, and loved by his own particular goodness.

“You who sit upon the cherubim, appear before Ephraim, Benjamin, and Manasseh.” Because our Lord and Savior is the source and origin of all wisdom—for “all wisdom is from him, and has always been with him, and is before all time” (Ecclus. 1:1)—he is described as sitting upon the cherubim, a term interpreted “fullness of knowledge.” Therefore the Prophet speaks to him and asks Christ to descend from that most exalted seat [Col. 1010A] of his majesty and, having assumed humanity, to appear visibly in this world before Ephraim, Benjamin, and Manasseh. These three belong to Joseph, who is placed in the midst of the sons, since he was their brother. Jeroboam, who caused Israel to sin, was from the tribe of Ephraim; Saul, who fiercely persecuted the Church at its beginning, was from the tribe of Benjamin. Therefore let us understand by these any wicked persons whatsoever, and hear the Lord himself saying: “I have not come to call the righteous, but sinners to repentance” (Matt. 9:13).—“Those who are well have no need of a physician, but those who are ill” (Luke 5:31). I receive Saul the persecutor, nor do I reject Ephraim, who made golden calves to my dishonor, of whom it is said through Isaiah: “Woe to the crown of pride, to the drunkards of Ephraim” [Col. 1010B] (Isa. 28:1). This psalm shows that evil children arise from good parents. Jacob, or Israel, was very good; Joseph also was very good; but those descended from him were very wicked. It should be noted that, when about to speak of evil sons, the Prophet first set forth their good parents, so that by their favor the Lord might more readily be moved to mercy.

“Stir up your power, and come to save us.” In his first coming the Lord seems not to have stirred up his power but to have laid it aside, because he came humbly and in the form of a servant. But in the second he will stir up his power, because, coming in the majesty of divinity, he will appear as he is. He saved us in the first coming because he rescued us from the devil’s power. He will save us [Col. 1010C] in the second because he will free us from every misery and gladden us with eternal blessedness.

“O Lord God of hosts, turn us back.” The Prophet prays for the Jews, that because they proved unconverted at the first coming, they may at least be converted to faith at the second: “They shall return at evening” (Ps. 58:7); “In those days Judah shall be saved” (Jer. 23:6); and “Though the number of the children of Israel be as the sand of the sea, a remnant shall return” (Rom. 9:27). And: “Show your face, and we shall be saved.” He did indeed first show it, but not to all, because “he came unto his own, and his own did not receive him” (John 1:11). Hence he himself said: “Many prophets and kings desired to see what you see [Col. 1010D] and did not see it” (Matt. 13:17). Hence also the Apostle says that “if they had known, they would never have crucified the Lord of glory” (1 Cor. 2:8). But only those see the face and glory of God who believe in him catholically.

“O Lord God of hosts, how long will you be angry with the prayer of your servant?” [Note: [Col. 1010D] “You are indeed angry in the manner of a father correcting, not of a judge condemning.” Augustine.] The Lord appears to be angry with our prayers when, after many prayers and supplications, he does not hear us. This name suits him well, that he should be called Lord God of hosts, because he alone is strong and powerful over all earthly things, [Col. 1011A] and is illustrious and wonderful in every power.

“Will you feed us with the bread of tears, and give us tears to drink by measure?” By the bread and drink of tears is understood every bodily affliction and tribulation. With such food and drink all the faithful of both Testaments were long satisfied, in measure, according to the Apostle’s saying: “God is faithful, who will not permit you to be tempted beyond what you are able, but with the temptation will also provide the way out, so that you may be able to endure it” (1 Cor. 10:13). Hence elsewhere God is said to have made all things in weight, number, and measure. He himself is said to do this because he permits to happen what could not happen if he were unwilling.

[Col. 1011B] “You have made us an object of contradiction to our neighbors, and our enemies have mocked us.” What point is there in saying how greatly and in how many ways their enemies and neighbors contradicted them and made them objects of reproach and derision? Hence, as it is written, at the judgment they will say in grief and repentance: “These are they whom we once held in derision and as a likeness of reproach” (Wis. 5:3).

“O Lord God of hosts, turn us back.” He fittingly repeats what he saw to be very difficult, namely, the conversion of the Jews. For the Lord had come to convert them, if they had been willing to obey him. Therefore he himself said: “I was sent only to the lost sheep of the house of Israel” (Matt. 15:11). And elsewhere, to Jerusalem: “How often I wished to gather [Col. 1011C] your children as a hen gathers her chicks under her wings, and you were unwilling!” (Matt. 23:37). And the Apostle: The word and kingdom of the holy Lord ought first to have been preached to you; but because you rejected it, you have made yourselves unworthy of the grace of that word and knowledge (Acts 13:46). “Show your face, and we shall be saved.” This has already been explained above.

“You transferred a vine from Egypt.” This then is the vine which you transferred from Egypt, concerning which the prophet also speaks: “A vineyard was made for my beloved on a hill, the son of oil” (Isa. 5:1). For the house of the God of hosts is called a vineyard.

“You cast out the nations and cast them down.” For the Lord cast the nations out from the promised land which they had formerly inhabited, and caused the children of Israel to dwell in their cities. [Col. 1011D]

“You made a way before it,” because he opened for them the Red Sea and the waters of the Jordan and led them through the midst of them on dry feet. No one else could have made such a way; and thus it is deservedly always memorable.

“And you planted its roots, and the earth was filled.” He speaks of the people as though of a vine, because he follows the vineyard metaphor. But by this vine the holy Church was signified. It was then planted on the mountains of Israel, but later had a more noble planting. Hence it follows:

“Its shadow covered the mountains, and its branches the cedars of God.” What should we understand by the mountains and the cedars of God except [Col. 1012A] the apostles and prophets? The vine and its branches covered them, because the whole Church is founded upon them. As the Apostle says: “Built upon the foundation of the apostles and prophets, Christ Jesus himself being the cornerstone” (Eph. 2:20).—“Its foundations are in the holy mountains” (Ps. 86:1). The apostles are called cedars because of the excellence and purity of their lives. For cedar is a tall, incorruptible tree with a fragrant nature.

“You stretched out its shoots as far as the sea, and its branches as far as the river.” These are the shoots and branches of which the Lord says in the Gospel: “I am the vine and you are the branches. Whoever abides in me, and I in him, bears much fruit, because without me you can do nothing. As the branch cannot [Col. 1012B] bear fruit of itself unless it abides in the vine, so neither can you unless you abide in me” (John 15:1, 4–5). The Lord extended these as far as the sea, because “their sound has gone out into all the earth, and their words to the ends of the world” (Ps. 18:5). But of the Synagogue it is said that its boundaries will extend as far as the western sea and as far as the great river Euphrates.

“Why have you broken down its wall, so that all who pass along the way pluck it?” The wall of the Church is the apostles, doctors, and all bishops and priests. When these are cast down and killed, there is no one to defend it or drive away from it the snares of robbers and heretics. It is therefore plucked and trampled by those who pass along the way and do not walk in the way of righteousness. Hence it follows:

[Col. 1012C] “The boar from the forest has ravaged it, and the solitary wild beast has fed upon it.” This boar and solitary wild beast is any heretic, such as Arius and Simon Magus; by him we may likewise understand tyrants. They are rightly said to come from the forest, since they are wild and alien and do not bring domestic teaching. But those are members of the household of whom it is said: “You are no longer strangers and foreigners, but fellow citizens with the saints and members of God’s household” (Eph. 2:19). These devour God’s vine, since they never cease to scatter the Church of God both bodily and spiritually.

“O Lord God of hosts, return” now, because your vine is being plucked, ravaged, and trampled. Return now, because “behold, now is the acceptable time; behold, now is the day of salvation” [Col. 1012D] (2 Cor. 6:2). And because the Jews are unconverted, let the Gentiles at least be converted to faith.

“Look down from heaven,” from that most exalted and radiant secret place of your divinity, “and see” mercifully, “and visit” powerfully “this vine”; direct it toward yourself, and do not permit it to stray after heretical flocks. “Which your right hand has planted.” And where did it plant it? “Upon the son of man whom you strengthened for yourself.” This is our Savior, who says of himself: “You will see angels ascending and descending upon the Son of Man” (John 1:51). [Col. 1013A] The Church is planted upon him because, as the Apostle says, “No one can lay another foundation than that which is Christ Jesus” (1 Cor. 3:11). And by the words “whom you strengthened for yourself” is meant what is said elsewhere: “I will set him in safety; I will act confidently in him” (Ps. 11:6). For the Lord most worthily strengthened him, the commander of his host, for the praise and glory of his name.

“Burned with fire and dug up by hand, they shall perish at the rebuke of your countenance.” See, he says, and visit this vine, lest it perhaps be burned by the ungodly and dug up; for all things which have been burned with fire and dug up by hand will perish at the rebuke of your countenance. This rebuke will occur at the judgment, when it is said: “Let the ungodly be taken away, lest they see the glory of God,” and “Let sinners be turned into hell” (Isa. 26); and, “Go, accursed ones, into everlasting fire” (Matt. 25:41). Fire is every sin [Col. 1013B] by which the soul is burned, dug up, and torn away from the foundation of its stability.

“Let your hand be upon the man of your right hand, and upon the son of man whom you strengthened for yourself, and we shall not depart from you.” The Prophet prays in the person of all the faithful that the Lord may protect and defend by the hand of his power this man of his right hand, this Son of the Virgin, our Savior; that he may rule us and draw us after himself, and that, with him as leader and guide, we may not depart from him. He fittingly calls him the man of his right hand because, raised up in the Spirit, he sees him sitting at his right hand.

“You have given us life, and we shall call upon your name.” We are dead, he says, because in the first man [Col. 1013C] we lost immortality and life; but you, O Christ, gave us life by your death, and we shall always and everywhere call upon your name in all our necessities: “For,” says the Apostle, “everyone who calls upon the name of the Lord shall be saved” (Rom. 10:13).

“O Lord God of hosts, turn us back, show us your face, and we shall be saved.” The Prophet sees that no one can be saved except through Christ, and that no one can be saved unless he believes in Christ; therefore he repeats so often that he may come, show his face, turn the world to himself, and save us.

## PSALM 80. UNTO THE END, FOR THE WINEPRESSES, OF ASAPH; THE FIFTH DAY FROM THE SABBATH.

[Note: [Col. 1013D] For a clearer understanding of this title, I shall append the Venerable Bede’s words on its exposition: “The fifth day from the Sabbath is the fifth day after the Sabbath, called by the Gentiles the day of Jupiter, and by us the fifth feria. On it God said: ‘Let the waters bring forth creeping things with living souls, and flying things above the firmament of heaven,’ mystically signifying that persons of diverse virtue would be born from the waters of baptism. The intention of this title, therefore, is as follows: ‘unto the end’ designates the Lord Christ; ‘for the winepresses,’ the Church tested by persecutions; ‘Asaph,’ the congregation; ‘the fifth day from the Sabbath,’ baptism. Hence it follows that the Psalm will speak in the Lord’s Church concerning the regenerated congregation. For Asaph speaks historically indeed to the Jews, but is more properly understood by the Christian people.”]

[Col. 1013D] Let this psalm “for the winepresses” be referred unto the end. The end occurred on the fifth day from the Sabbath, when old things passed away and all things became new. For that day was the end of the Old and the beginning of the New Testament, the day on which Aaron’s sacrifice was rejected and sacrifice according to the order of Melchizedek was confirmed. There are as many winepresses as there are churches, [Col. 1014A] in which new wine is received and all the clusters of both Testaments are pressed and expounded; by these the master of the feast and the apostles are made drunk, and new and old things are marvelously interpreted.

“Rejoice in God our helper; shout for joy to the God of Jacob.” You, the Prophet says, who are in the winepresses and make and offer new and wonderful wine through new teaching, rejoice in God our helper, because this alone is a useful, praiseworthy, and eternal rejoicing. “Shout for joy to the God of Jacob.” It is as though he said: He who has now come to our aid and freed us from the devil’s power, he is the God of Jacob; he is the God of both Testaments. Therefore shout for joy and sing to him; worship and adore him alone. How?

“Take up a psalm, and give the timbrel, the pleasant psaltery [Col. 1014B] with the harp.” Who are those who take up the psalm except those who praise and bless God with heart and voice? In time of persecution such people gave timbrels, because immediately after preaching they endured blows. For timbrels do not sound unless they are struck. [Note: [Col. 1014D] Bruno seems to have drawn this interpretation from Cassiodorus, whom he also followed in the remainder.] Blessed Paul was a precious timbrel: from the Jews he received five times forty lashes less one (2 Cor. 11). The timbrel is given to those who afflict the flesh with its vices and desires. “The pleasant psaltery with the harp.” Take up the psalm, he says; sing and preach. Do this with the psaltery and harp. The psaltery belongs to the Old Testament, the harp to the New. Since the psaltery has ten strings, the Old Testament is contained in the Ten Commandments. Three or four strings [Col. 1014C] suffice for the harp, and the New Testament is contained in the four Gospels, in which the mystery of the Trinity is most clearly preached. The Jews do not know this mystery, and therefore do not know how to sing on the harp. Christians, however, sing both on the harp and on the psaltery, because they receive and preach both Testaments. The psaltery is pleasant with the harp because, in our discourses, one Testament confirms the other.

“Sound the trumpet at the beginning of the month, on the day of your solemn feast.” This beginning of the month and this day of solemn feast began on the fifth day from the Sabbath, of which we spoke in the title, and will endure until the first day from the Sabbath, when the Lord will come [Col. 1014D] to judge. The Jews did this every month, whenever the new moon appeared. Hence another translation has not “beginning of the month,” but *neomenia*, by which the new moon is signified. It was therefore necessary to sing and preach most diligently when the moon was still new. That the moon signifies the Church is very clear. [Col. 1015A] To sound the trumpet is to praise and preach God in a clear and loud voice.

“For it is a commandment in Israel, and an ordinance of the God of Jacob.” This, therefore, is the commandment in Israel, and this ordinance is given by the God of Jacob: that you ought to sing in this manner at the new moon and at this first feast, in which old things passed away and all things became new.

“Thou hast appointed it as a testimony in Joseph, when he went forth from the land of Egypt.” And the Lord established this testimony not only in Israel, but also in Joseph. Why Israel is mentioned separately and Joseph separately has already been explained in other psalms.

When he went forth from the land of Egypt, “he heard a language which he did not know.” But in this translation, where it says, “he appointed him,” there is nothing to which we can refer this pronoun [Col. 1015B], unless perhaps to the day of the distinguished festival. Therefore the Lord appointed that day as a testimony for Joseph, because that day bears witness to them with what diligence and care he serves the Lord and celebrates His feasts. For Joseph in this passage signifies all those who, in the likeness of the new moon, daily increase until they reach the fullness of perfection and advance to what is better. Indeed, Joseph is interpreted “increasing.” When these went forth from the land of Egypt and passed from the darkness of ignorance to faith, they heard a language which they had not previously known, learned the knowledge of both Testaments, and most steadfastly preached at the new moon—that is, at the beginning of the nascent Church. This is attested by the day itself; this is confirmed by the distinguished festival itself [Col. 1015C], since they were killed for Christ’s faith and for the name which they proclaimed. The first Joseph, however, heard the language he did not know not when he left, but when he entered the land of Egypt.

“He turned away his back from burdens; his hands served in baskets.” Since he had begun to speak of Joseph, he follows his metaphor. Joseph first bore burdens upon his own shoulders; afterward Pharaoh appointed him ruler of the people, and he served with baskets, by which grain is measured and carried. Likewise the Lord turns the backs of the saints away from burdens, when He says: “Come unto me, all you who labor and are burdened, and I will refresh you” (Matt. 11:28). They served in baskets after they began to minister and preach to the peoples the provision [Col. 1015D] of the word of God. These were signified by those baskets which the apostles filled with the remnants of the loaves (Matt. 14). Therefore they serve in a basket who minister to others the bread of Gospel teaching.

“In tribulation thou didst call upon me, and I delivered thee.” This is fittingly understood both of Joseph and of the saints signified by him, because both he and they, calling upon the Lord in their tribulations, were heard and delivered. Hence it follows:

“And I heard thee in the hidden place of the storm”: that is, in a sudden and unforeseen calamity that came upon them. Such a storm came upon blessed Job, who was entirely ignorant [Col. 1016A] why he was afflicted. The holy martyrs also endured such a storm, and in dying they were heard, because it was their desire to expire amid the very torments; hence they provoked the tyrants against themselves with harsh words and did not wish to find them merciful.

“I tested thee at the water of contradiction.” What are we to understand by the water of contradiction except evangelical preaching? For Jews, heretics, and all unbelievers most obstinately oppose these waters. Here, indeed, the saints are tested, because they may be killed, but they cannot be restrained from preaching.

“Hear, thou also, my people, and I will speak; O Israel, and I will testify to thee.” Now our Savior speaks especially [Col. 1016B] to the Jews, who chiefly persecuted Him because He said that He was the Son of God. He therefore teaches them and commands them under solemn testimony to hear Him, understand Him, and assent to His teaching. This is what He says:

“O Israel, if thou wilt hear me, there shall be no new god in thee, neither shalt thou worship a strange god. For I am the Lord thy God, who brought thee out of the land of Egypt.” I, therefore, am the Lord thy God. I am not one person, and He who brought thee out of Egypt another; rather, “I myself who spoke, behold, am present” (Isa. 52:6), and for thy sake I became man: I came to teach, deliver, and save thee. If thou wilt hear me, if thou wilt believe in me, there shall be no new god in thee, neither shalt thou worship a strange god: “I am [Col. 1016C] in the Father, and the Father is in me; and I and the Father are one” (John 10:30).

“Open thy mouth wide, and I will fill it.” The Lord wished to teach, cherish, [p. 477] and fill the Jews with spiritual food; but they would not have it. This is what He says:

“But my people did not hear my voice, and Israel did not give heed to me.” Thus the Lord Himself also says: “I spoke, and you did not believe” (John 10); and likewise: “He who is of God hears the words of God; therefore you do not hear, because you are not of God” (John 6:47). And elsewhere: “If I had not come and spoken to them, they would not have sin; but now they have no excuse for their sin” (John 15:22).

[Col. 1016D] “And I let them go according to the desires of their heart.” Wretched is the person whom the Lord lets go, so that he may do the desires of his own heart. Thus the Lord had let Pharaoh go, so that he followed the desires of his heart even unto death.

“And they shall walk in their own wills.”  
[Note: [Col. 1015D] The Vulgate reads: “in their own devices.”]

For why shall they walk in their own wills, except because they will never repent, but will persevere in their wickednesses to the end?

“If my people had heard me, if Israel had walked in my ways, I would have brought their enemies to nothing, and would have stretched out my hand over those who afflicted them.” These words give great consolation to all who hear and keep the words of God and walk in the ways [Col. 1017A] of His commandments; for they are assured, and can in no way doubt, that they will at some time receive vengeance upon their enemies.  
[Note: [Col. 1017D] Some material seems to be missing in the manuscript, and therefore the sense is incomplete.]

The Jews lost this vengeance because they would not hear the words of God. Of them it follows:

“The enemies of the Lord lied to him, and their time shall be forever.” Now the Prophet speaks and threatens the Jews with eternal punishment, saying that their time—that is, the time of death and perdition—will be forever. They are the enemies of the Lord; they are those of whom the Lord Himself says that “they hated me without cause” (John 15:25). And they lied to Him, because “he came unto his own, and his own did not receive him” (John 1:10), although they had formerly promised Moses: “Whatever the Lord commands us, [Col. 1017B] we will do” (Exod. 19:8).

“He fed them with the fat of wheat, and filled them with honey from the rock.” This is a reproach against those who were not ashamed to render evil for good. “The Lord fed them,” he says, “with the fat of wheat,” and satisfied them with both temporal and spiritual feasts. Elsewhere it is said of this fatness: “Let my soul be filled as with fat and richness” (Ps. 62:6). Holy Scripture is wheat: this wheat supplies bread rough to some and delicate to others. They received honey from the rock who deserved to hear words of life from the breast of the Savior. Of these it is said: “How sweet are thy words to my palate, more than honey and the honeycomb to my mouth!” (Ps. 118:103).

## PSALM LXXXI. A PSALM OF ASAPH.

[Col. 1017C]

We have often already said what a psalm of Asaph signifies. Behold Asaph, whose name is interpreted “synagogue,” and through whom the congregation of all good things is understood. He speaks of the synagogue of evildoers and rebukes it because it would not believe our Savior speaking to it in person.

“God stood in the synagogue of gods, and in the midst he distinguishes the gods.” Wherever there are strong men, wise men, and men preeminent above others by merit of life, there is the synagogue of gods. The Prophet thus speaks both of future and present things and presents as already accomplished that which was to occur much later [Col. 1017D]. For the Lord and our Savior stood in the synagogue of gods—or rather, of Jews and ungodly persons—and rebuked and judged them with fitting authority not only for their deeds but also for their perverse thoughts. Thus it is said in the Gospel that He did not speak as the Pharisees did, but as one having authority. They themselves also bear witness to this, saying: “Master, we know that thou art true, and teachest the way of God in truth, and carest for no one; for thou dost not regard the person of man” (Matt. 22:6). But how does He distinguish and judge them? It follows:

“How long will ye judge unjustly and accept the persons of sinners?” They said: “This man is not [Col. 1018A] from God, because he does not keep the Sabbath” (John 9:1, 6). But He said to them: “Which of you whose ass or ox falls into a pit will not immediately draw it out on the Sabbath day?” (Luke 14:5). “How long will ye judge unjustly?” “Why do ye transgress the commandment of God because of your tradition? For He said: Honor thy father and mother; but ye say: Whatever gift is from me shall profit thee” (Matt. 15:3–5). This, however, is injustice and contrary to God’s commandment. They accept the faces of sinners who show partiality in judgment, or who become like sinners by judging. For *facies* (“face”) is said to derive from *faciendo* (“doing”). Therefore he has the same face as sinners who does what sinners do.

“Judge for the orphan and the needy; justify the humble and the poor [Col. 1018B].” If, he says, an orphan and needy person, a humble and poor person, has a just cause, judge for them; grant them justice and victory. Look not at the person, but at the cause. Hence it follows:

[p. 478] “Rescue the poor and needy; deliver them from the hand of the sinner.” Do not be frightened by the power of the rich and sinful person, but steadfastly show the poor person’s cause to be just, if it is just.

“They did not know, nor did they understand.” “They did not know,” says the Prophet, and they would not understand the most saving words which the Lord spoke to them; therefore “they walk in darkness”: surely in the darkness of blindness and error, because they are blind and leaders of the blind. “All the foundations of the earth shall be moved.” Against [Col. 1018C] these unjust judges, he says, all the foundations of the earth will be moved; by these foundations we understand the apostles, who will justly judge and condemn those who did not fear to judge and condemn others unjustly. This will occur at the judgment, because, as it is written, the apostles “will sit upon twelve thrones, judging the twelve tribes of Israel” (Matt. 20:28). The Prophet inserted this verse; from this point our Savior resumes the sequence of His discourse.

I said: “Ye are gods, and all of you sons of the Most High.” This is what is said in the Gospel: “As many as received him, he gave them power to become sons of God, to those who believe in his name” (John 1:12). For they are gods; they are sons of God. The Lord said this; He established it. He gave this power to human beings—but to those who received Him, believed in Him, and kept His commandments. But what of the rest? “Yet ye shall die like men, and shall fall like one of the princes.” You would not, He says, be gods; you would not become immortal; you would not ascend again to the heavens. Therefore you shall die like men and fall like one of the princes. Those die as men who die in both body and soul; they will fall like one of the princes, by whom the devil is signified. These also will fall in the same way as he, and all together, at one time, will be cast into the fire. Thus far the Lord speaks; the Prophet speaks the rest.

[Col. 1019A]  
[Note: [Col. 1019D] All the preceding psalms are absent from the Chisian and Marchesian manuscripts; here, however, the edition and the Ghisian manuscript continue.]

“Arise, O God, judge the earth.” Arise, O God, he says, whom I behold seated at the right hand of the Father; come to judgment and judge the earth. Condemn the ungodly and sinners, and let those who do not look upward but seek only earthly and transitory things fall like one of the princes. Let thine own be enough for thee: honor and glorify them, “for thou shalt inherit among all nations.” For there is no nation in which the Lord has not inherited and chosen some as His own portion; because, as it is written, “all nations shall serve him” (Ps. 51:11).

## PSALM LXXXII. A PSALM-SONG OF ASAPH.

Asaph desires that this psalm be sung with song and praises, for in it God’s power and magnificence [Col. 1019B], and the destruction and perdition of the wicked, are proclaimed.

“O God, who shall be like thee? Do not keep silence, nor be restrained, O God.”  
[Note: [Col. 1019D] Augustine also explains that the Prophet speaks here of Christ the Lord: “For what great thing is said when it is said to God, ‘Who shall be like thee?’ unless it is said to Him who willed to become like men, taking the form of a servant, made in the likeness of men, and found in appearance as a man,” etc. Phil. 2:7.]

When thou comest, O God, to judge the earth, as is read at the end of the preceding psalm, who shall be like thee? Thou didst once come humble and in the form of a servant; we saw thee without comeliness or beauty. But thou shalt come most glorious and powerful upon the throne of thy majesty; and who shall be like thee? Who will not fear thee, O Lord? Who is like God among the sons of God? “Do not keep silence, nor be restrained, O God.” Thou wast silent; like a voiceless lamb led to sacrifice, thou didst not open thy mouth. Repay them, O Lord. They spoke, and in their time they spoke most proudly; do thou also speak in thy time. Let those who refused to recognize thee as humble recognize thee as exalted.

“For behold, thine enemies made a tumult.” They indeed made a tumult—foolishly, cruelly, and without provocation—crying, “Crucify him” (Luke 23). “And those who hate thee raised their head.” Thus the Gospel says that “they mocked him, shaking their heads” (Matt. 27:39). To raise one’s head against the Lord is to be proud.

“They devised a crafty plan against thy people, and devised against thy saints.”  
[Note: [Col. 1019D] This alternative reading is found in Augustine and Cassiodorus.]

Not only against thee, he says, but also against thy people and thy Church, both the Jews and all the others of whom we are now to speak devised an evil plan. And they did so cunningly, deceitfully, and fraudulently. “And they devised against thy saints”: and let us hear what [Col. 1019D] they devised:

“They said: Come, let us destroy them from being a nation, and let the name of Israel be remembered no more.” It should be noted that whenever Asaph speaks, he always draws parables from ancient history, so that we may transfer figuratively to the Church those events that happened to the ancient fathers [Col. 1020A]. Thus in this place Israel is taken for the persecutors of the Church. For the enemies of the Church not only [p. 479] devised and said this, but even attempted to do it: to remove the Christian name entirely from human memory. Hence it follows:

“For they devised a counsel together as one.” They devised, he says, and came together in one agreement—an evil and perverse agreement—to destroy the Church, kill God’s saints, and utterly erase the Catholic faith.

“They made a covenant against thee.” Who? “The tents of the Edomites and the Ishmaelites, Moab and the Hagarites, Gebal and Ammon and Amalek, and the Philistines with the inhabitants of Tyre,” and the remaining peoples that follow. [Col. 1020B] By those who once severely persecuted the Jewish people, we understand those who persecute the Church of God to this day. For Jews who interpret the Law wickedly, heretics, pagans, and all others who introduce a new teaching have made a covenant against their Lord; they intend to make another covenant against the Lord. But let us now see who these people are who persecute the holy Church.

First are “the tents of the Edomites,” interpreted as “earthly people.”  
[Note: [Col. 1019D] This interpretation [Col. 1020D] agrees perfectly with Augustine.]

By them we understand all who serve not the soul but the body, and love only earthly and transitory things. They do not differ from “the Ishmaelites,” interpreted as “obedient to themselves.” Those are obedient to themselves who follow the desires of their own hearts [Col. 1020C] and are not ashamed to go wherever their will leads them.

“Moab,” interpreted “from a father,” conceived in drunkenness through a furtive and unlawful union, signifies those who are generated from heretics by the sacraments of the Church. Such people seem to have good parents, but are proved to have the devil for their father.  
[Note: [Col. 1020D] Here St Bruno seems to indicate what he had said above in his exposition of Psalm 67, p. 442: namely, that persons ordained by Arian, Nestorian, and Donatist bishops who returned to the Catholic Church were mercifully received while retaining their own orders. In reporting this, he admits the validity of their ordinations, though not their lawfulness; the Church granted this concession kindly. But whenever they do not renounce their errors, although they have truly received the sacraments, they nevertheless have the devil as their father. What St Bruno thinks of Simoniacs will be stated in its proper place.]

But what do we understand by “the Hagarites,” called “strangers,” except those who are far from the Church and refuse to receive the faith and teaching of the saints? “Gebal” is called “the vain valley,” by which are signified those who are barren and fruitless and who feign false humility. “Ammon,” however, interpreted “a turbulent people,” denotes heretics, just as does its brother “Moab,” of whom we spoke above. They are children of drunkenness and fornication, being mad and begotten in error. By “Amalek,” called “a brutish people,” we understand foolish and undisciplined people, who regard pleasure as the highest good and suppose that the soul dies together with the body. “The Philistines” [Col. 1021A] are those who worship idols and have no knowledge of God.

The inhabitants of Tyre were devoted to ships and trade. The Prophet describes how rich they were, such that they might have been rulers of other cities. He also writes concerning the king of Tyre, whom he says was adorned with every precious stone; yet he fell because he raised himself into great pride. “Tyre,” therefore, signifies the world; its inhabitants signify the rich and powerful of this world. Thus, when he says that the peoples named above came against God’s covenant together “with the inhabitants of Tyre,” we are to understand that not only many provinces and nations, but the entire world generally, conspired against the Church. But what wonder is this, when the devil himself, their [Col. 1021B] prince, ruled and directed them according to his own will? This is what follows:

“For Assur also came with them.” Assur, indeed, is interpreted “directing.” The devil directs no others to himself except those whom he turns away from the way of truth and causes to wander. “They became a support to the children of Lot.” All these, he says, of whom we spoke above, became a support and aid to the children of Lot, by whom, we said, heretics are signified. Heretics are the greatest and chief enemies of the Church; therefore all who persecute the Church are helpers of heretics. Now, however, he excommunicates them and curses them with great imprecations.

“Do unto them as unto Midian and Sisera, and as unto Jabin at the torrent Kishon. All these perished at Endor; they became as dung for the earth.”—“Midian” is interpreted “from judgment”; “Sisera,” “the exclusion of joy”; “Jabin,” “wise,” but wise in a worldly sense; “Kishon,” “their hardness”; and “Endor,” “of generation.”  
[Note: [Col. 1021D] In these interpretations St Bruno followed Cassiodorus.]

“Midian,” therefore, signifies those who will depart wretched from judgment. “Sisera” signifies those from whom all joy will be excluded and who will always be in pains. “Jabin,” however, denotes the wise of this world, who are called foolish before God. All these will perish in “Kishon and Endor,” that is, in their own hardness and at the very source of their generation: by this is meant original sin. Whoever has not been delivered from it by Christ’s blood will beyond doubt perish eternally [Col. 1021D]. This battle was fought under Barak and his wife Deborah.

“Make their princes like Oreb and Zeeb and Zebee and Zalmunna: all their princes who said, ‘Let us take possession of the sanctuary of God as an inheritance.’” These four kings were defeated by Gideon in a marvelous battle. [p. 480] “Oreb” is interpreted “a hole”; “Zeeb,” “a wolf”; “Zebee,” “a victim”; “Zalmunna,” “the shadow of prohibition.” By “Oreb” we understand those who are pierced through on every side and offer no obstacle to the entry of vices and evil spirits. “Zeeb” signifies the rapacious and predatory. “Zebee” are the devil’s martyrs, who, slaughtering one another in turn, [Col. 1022A] are daily sacrificed to him everywhere. “Zalmunna,” however, denotes hypocrites, who are nothing but shadow and pretence and who often ardently desire to be done what they appear to forbid. Therefore there is no doubt that all who do not fear to attack the sanctuary of God, the inheritance of God, and do not shrink from claiming for themselves what belongs by divine right, will perish in the likeness of these. And rightly the leaders of such persons are cursed especially in this passage: either because by their evil example they impel others to this crime, or because they do not repel them by their authority.

“My God, make them like a wheel,” that they may suddenly roll down to the lower regions of the earth with swift and headlong course.

[Col. 1022B] “And like stubble before the face of the wind,” so that they may be dragged to ruin and death by the violent whirlwind of evil spirits. “And like fire that burns forests, as a flame sets mountains ablaze: so shalt thou pursue them in thy tempest, and in thy wrath shalt thou trouble them.” They are fittingly compared to forests because they are many, and to mountains because they are swollen with the spirit of pride; for them, as the Gospel says, eternal fire and unquenchable flame are prepared.

“Fill their faces with disgrace.” And indeed they deserve disgrace and such curses, they who so trample underfoot, subject to themselves, and heap such insults upon the sanctuary of God and its ministers. [Col. 1022C] Read all the divine Scriptures and you will find no others so excommunicated and cursed as those who afflict churches and who do not fear to think and say: “Let us take possession of the sanctuary of God as an inheritance.” For all such people are sacrilegious; and we know that all sacrilegious persons are excommunicated, cursed, and condemned.
