This is what is said here: “Fill their faces with disgrace.” And when they seek thy name, saying, “Lord, Lord,” then let them be confounded with everlasting confusion and troubled, not for an hour but for age upon age. “And let them reverence thee, and perish; and” then at last “let them know that thy name is the Lord,” whom they did not fear to offend despite so many interdicts, prohibitions, excommunications, and curses [Col. 1022D].

“Thou alone art the Most High over all the earth.” Then, he says, when thou comest, O Lord, to judgment, let all, friends and enemies alike, “know that thy name is the Lord,” and that “thou alone art the Most High over all the earth.” And then, O God: “Who shall be like thee? Do not keep silence, nor be restrained, O God, for behold thine enemies made a tumult, and those who hate thee raised their head.” Thou indeed art the Most High; yet to their own ruin they did not fear to lift up their head.

## PSALM LXXXIII. UNTO THE END, FOR THE WINEPRESSES, FOR THE SONS OF KORAH.

[Note: [Col. 1023D] “We have interpreted the sons of Korah as sons of the Bald One, or perhaps as something else unknown to us. Meanwhile, consider what occurs to us, because it is full of mystery. The sons of Korah are the sons of Christ. For the Bridegroom also calls them his sons when He says, Matt. 9:15: ‘Can the sons of the bridegroom fast while the bridegroom is with them?’ Therefore those winepresses belong to Christians.” St Augustine, on this title.]

[Col. 1023A]

This psalm is referred “unto the end,” namely to Christ, of whom it is said here: “Look upon the face of thy Christ.” It is “for the winepresses”: with whose sweet and new wine the saints are inebriated, forgetting all earthly things and desiring only to see and enter the tabernacles of God. It is given to be sung by the sons of Korah, that is, by the Christian people, who glory more in the place of Calvary than in all Jerusalem. For Korah is interpreted “Calvary.” Others are called sons of Zion; but we are called, and are, sons of Calvary.

“How lovely are thy tabernacles, O Lord of hosts: my soul longs for and faints in [Col. 1023B] the courts of the Lord.”  
[Note: [Col. 1023D] Augustine has another reading: “How dearly beloved are thy tabernacles, O Lord of hosts.” In the treatise [Col. 1024D] of St Maximus of Turin against the Jews, p. 745 of the Roman edition, the reading agrees with Bruno’s text: “How lovely are thy tabernacles,” etc.]

These are the tabernacles of which the Lord says: “In my Father’s house are many dwelling places” (John 14:2). Hence the Apostle says: “Christ, becoming the high priest of good things to come, through a greater and more perfect tabernacle, not made with hands,” etc. (Heb. 9:11). Therefore He has many tabernacles and one, because many dwellings are contained in one house. The saints of God who desire to come to these tabernacles and their courts faint with excessive longing. But from what do they faint? [p. 481] From all the pleasures of this world and from whatever can be possessed or desired in it.

“My heart and my flesh have rejoiced in the living God.” It is an excellent hope of resurrection that he says his soul [Col. 1023C], signified by the heart, and his flesh have rejoiced in the living God, because they trust that they will come to Him and His tabernacles. But what wonder if holy men, beloved by God, hasten to those tabernacles, when the sparrow and the turtle-dove, small creatures, seek and find houses and nests for themselves? This is what he says:

“For the sparrow has found herself a house, and the turtle-dove a nest where she may place her young. Thy altars, O Lord of hosts, my King and my God,” will they not find for themselves—understand, a house and tabernacle—where they may be placed and established?  
[Note: [Col. 1024D] A learned and copious exposition of this comparison is found in Augustine.]

The saints are called God’s altars because they are consecrated to God; God dwells in them, and in them the holocausts and sacrifices [Col. 1023D] of God are daily offered. Hence the Apostle says: “I beseech you by the mercy of God, that you present your bodies a living sacrifice, holy, pleasing to God, your reasonable service” (Rom. 12:1).

“Blessed are they who dwell in thy house, O Lord.” Therefore, he says, the saints long with such great desire to come [Col. 1024A] and dwell in thy house, because they know that those who dwell in thy house are blessed. This same Prophet says elsewhere: “One thing have I asked of the Lord; this will I seek: that I may dwell in the house of the Lord all the days of my life” (Ps. 26:6). But let us hear whence that blessedness comes: “They shall praise thee for ever and ever.” Free from every occupation and toil, they will be devoted solely to God’s praises and rejoicings. And this is what they desire: to be able to praise and bless God at every time and without interruption. Whoever possesses what he desires is blessed. Yet no human being can possess this in the present life.

“Blessed is the man whose help is from thee, O Lord”: blessed, he says, is the man whom thou so helpest in this life [Col. 1024B] that, by thine aid, he may be able to ascend to that house. For no one comes to thee unless thou drawest him. “He has set ascents in his heart.” Where? “In the valley of tears and in the place which thou hast appointed for him.”  
[Note: [Col. 1024D] Augustine used the same translation and says: “Whence do we weep? Is it not from that from which the Apostle cried himself wretched, Rom. 7:23, because he saw another law in his members resisting the law of his mind? And whence comes this to us? From the punishment of sin.”]

The valley of tears, and the place of labor and conflict appointed for us by God, is this world. Here we must weep for sins, because “blessed are they who mourn, for they shall be comforted” (Matt. 5:5). Here we must labor in God’s vineyard, because whoever labors will receive a reward. Here we must strive with all our strength against vices and evil spirits, because “no one shall be crowned unless he has striven lawfully” (2 Tim. 2:5). Let us arrange and order ascents in our heart and make for ourselves certain steps by which we may ascend from this valley to that mountain where that [Col. 1024C] house is. If you resolve to fast, you have made one step; if you resolve to give alms, you have made another; if you resolve to forgive your debtors their debts and pardon all who sin against you, that too is a step. Thus the ladder is made by which one ascends from this most deep valley into heaven. Whoever does this will be blessed. Why is this? It follows:

“For behold, he who gave the law will give a blessing; they shall go from strength to strength; the God of gods shall be seen in Zion.” He who gave this law, he says, and appointed this place in which we serve Him, will Himself give the blessing by which we are brought to blessedness. “Come,” He says, “ye blessed of my Father, receive the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation [Col. 1024D] of the world” (Matt. 25:34). Then “the God of gods shall be seen in Zion,” namely in that Zion which is quite fittingly interpreted “contemplation.” But by whom will He be seen? By those who go from strength to strength and ascend by the ladder of which we have spoken above. It is a beautiful path to go [Col. 1025A] from strength to strength: from faith to hope, from hope to charity, from charity to humility, from humility to patience, from patience to obedience, from obedience to continence, and thus pass from strength to strength until one comes to the highest strength—that is, to our Savior, who is the power of God and the wisdom of God.

“O Lord, God of hosts, hear my prayer; give ear, O God of Jacob.” This is as though he said: In whatever way I may be able to ascend to thee, hear my prayer, because otherwise I cannot come to thee. By Jacob are understood those who overcome vices, trip up evil spirits, and such persons are rightly reckoned in God’s army.

[Col. 1025B] “Look upon us, O God our protector,” and stretch forth thy hand to those who come to thee; for unless thou drawest us along this most arduous path, we shall without doubt fail. “And look upon the face of thy Christ,” who therefore became man and assumed the form of our humanity, so that where He is we also may be, and may always see our King and the sharer in our humanity, and rejoice in seeing Him.

“For one day in thy courts is better than thousands.” Therefore, he says, I hasten with such longing to enter that house, or the threshold of that house, because one [p. 482] day is better—a single day, indeed, which has no end: for, as it is written, “there shall be no night there” (Rev. 21:25). One day, he says, is better—not, I say, in thy house, but outside in the courts of thy house—than [Col. 1025C] thousands, wherever they may be. Therefore all things whatsoever and wherever they are amount to nothing in comparison with that blessedness.

“I chose to be cast down in the house of the Lord rather than to dwell in the tents of sinners.” Although one star differs from another in glory there, no one there will be cast down. Yet he would rather be the least there than most powerful in this world, where there are only tents of sinners; for the conversation of the saints is in heaven (Phil. 3).

“For the Lord loves mercy and truth; God will give grace and glory.” He will give grace to sinners because He is merciful, but glory to penitents and those who serve Him because He is true. The former are saved by mercy alone; the latter are crowned for victory. Otherwise He could be called neither merciful nor true.

“The Lord will not deprive of good things those who walk in innocence.” Those walk in innocence to whom the Apostle says: “Do not defend yourselves, beloved, but give place to wrath” (Rom. 12:19). The Lord Himself says: “If they persecute you in one city, flee into another” (Matt. 10:23); and: “Love your enemies, do good to those who hate you” (Matt. 5:44). For whom will he harm who loves even his own enemies? “He will not deprive of good things those who walk [Col. 1026A] in innocence. O Lord God of hosts, blessed is the man who hopes in thee.” Such persons will not be deprived of good things, but will enjoy eternal delights with the Lord. Therefore blessed is he who will dwell in thy house. He is the one to whom it is said: “Hope in the Lord, and he will grant thee the desires of thy heart” (Ps. 36:4).

## PSALM LXXXIV. UNTO THE END, FOR THE SONS OF KORAH, A PSALM.

Many good things are promised and given in this psalm to the sons of Korah, because they alone are those for whom Christ’s incarnation and passion were fruitful. David himself speaks in this psalm, and speaks of future things as though they were past; he says that, in the coming of His Son, the Lord blessed His land and delivered it from the power of the devil.

[Col. 1026B] “Thou hast blessed, O Lord, thy land.” In the coming of thy Son, he says, thou hast blessed, O Lord, thy land, which still lay under that curse pronounced upon the first man: “Cursed is the earth in thy work” (Gen. 3:17). Thou hast blessed thy land, he says: namely, that land which believes in thee and serves thee; the other land, however, still remains under the ancient curse.

“Averted the captivity of Jacob.” That is, of the Jacob who deserved to receive his father’s blessing, by whom the Christian people is signified, liberated from the devil’s power by Christ’s blood and the water of baptism.

“You forgave the iniquity of your people; you covered all their sins.” He speaks of the Christian people, whose sins, together with original sin, are all forgiven in baptism [Col. 1026C] [Note: [Col. 1025D] “To forgive is to remit a debt, not through the intervention of any cause, but out of regard for mercy. Thus the Lord forgave guilt when he brought the accused to pardon,” etc. Cassiodorus.]. Hence it is said elsewhere: “Blessed are those whose iniquities are forgiven and whose sins are covered” (Ps. 31:1).

“You softened all your wrath.” So great was God’s wrath and indignation until that time that even the patriarchs and prophets necessarily descended into hell.

“You turned away from the wrath of your indignation.” You turned yourself away, he says, from the wrath of your indignation; and those whom formerly you were unwilling to look upon, you now embrace as dearest sons.

“Convert us, O God our Savior.” Since, he says, you have turned toward us in your free goodness and deign to look upon those who greatly offended you, convert us also to yourself, because our ways [Col. 1026D] through which we were accustomed to walk are crooked. For you are God our Savior, and our whole salvation rests in you alone. “And turn away your wrath from us, so that you may not be angry with us forever.” Thus, he says, convert us to yourself, and so turn away your wrath from us that you may never again be angry with us. For that which is not done forever is never done. Hence he adds:

“Nor prolong your wrath from generation to generation.” You were angry, as it were, with the first generation; we ask that you not be angry with the last. Let it be enough that the preceding generation experienced your wrath; henceforth let the generation [Col. 1027A] which is to follow find your mercy [Note: [Col. 1027D] What Bruno stated concisely is explained by Cassiodorus’ fuller exposition: “It must be investigated why he set forth two generations. The first is, as some hold, from Adam to Christ; the second is that which, through the grace of baptism, is brought forward and concluded at the end of the age. He therefore asked that, since the Lord was justly angry with the former generation in proportion to its obstinacy, he might not wish to be angry with the second generation. Although it cannot be free from sin, it nevertheless desires to be cleansed from the stains of its faults through the grace of baptism and satisfaction for its sins.”].

483 “O God, when you turn, you will give us life,” for you would by no means give us life unless you turned us. For no one will be made alive unless he has been turned away from his former manner of life. “And your people will rejoice in you,” wholly turned to you from the evil way. And because so great a conversion and transformation cannot occur except through the coming of your Son, let him now come—the one long desired and awaited for so great a time. This is what he says:

“Show us, O Lord, your mercy, and give us your salvation” [Note: [Col. 1028D] “‘Give us,’ that is, grant us ‘your salvation,’ as something to be embraced, possessed, and enjoyed as the gift of eternal glory. He appeared only to the faithless; he was not also given to them.” Cassiodorus.]. For in this the Lord showed his mercy: that he gave us his salvation. This mercy surpassed all others, because “he did not spare his own Son, but delivered him up for [Col. 1027B] us all” (Rom. 8:32). He showed how merciful he was by exceeding the measure of mercy. When the Prophet was considering these things, he suddenly perceived the Lord speaking within him and answering his petition, and said:

“I will hear what the Lord God speaks in me.” Therefore it is the Lord who speaks in the prophets, and the things prophets say are not the prophets’ words but God’s [Note: [Col. 1028D] From the fact that the Holy Spirit himself, who speaks in the prophets, declares himself to be God, Cassiodorus argues his equality, identical nature, and substance with the Father and Son, from whom he proceeds.]. Hence the Lord also says to the disciples: “For it is not you who speak, but the Spirit of my Father who speaks in you” (Matt. 10:20).

“For he will speak peace to his people, and upon his saints, and upon those who turn to him.” What does “he will speak peace to his people” mean except that he will give peace to his people and [Col. 1027C] his saints? Thus, at Christ’s birth, the voices of angels were heard saying: “Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace to people of good will” (Luke 2:14). What is said as “people of good will” is what is said as “those who turn to him.” For this peace is not given to others, but only to those who have good will and turn to him—by whom, plainly, Christians alone are signified. What then will become of the Jews, who were unwilling to turn to him? Hear the Apostle say: “Blindness has happened in part to Israel” (Rom. 11:25).—“For God has not rejected his people whom he foreknew” (ibid., v. 2). That people was in part unconvertible; nevertheless many of them believed in Christ. For their sake the Lord wished both to be born among them, to come first to them, and [Col. 1027D] to preach first to them. Of these he adds:

“Yet his salvation is near to those who fear him.” Although, he says, the greater part of that [Col. 1028A] people was unwilling to receive God’s Son, “yet his salvation is near to those who fear him.” For it would not have been just for him to reject the good because of the evil, or for friends and those who fear him to perish because of enemies. Therefore, because of these few who feared him and believed in him, it came about “that glory might dwell in our land.” From there came the most blessed Virgin Mary, and from there the apostles, in whose supreme and principal glory the whole Church rejoices. Hence it is said through the prophet: “Unless the Lord of hosts had left us a seed, we would have been like Sodom, and made like Gomorrah” (Isa. 1:9).

“Mercy and truth have met each other; righteousness and peace have embraced one another.” These came to pass in Christ’s birth and in his most glorious humanity [Col. 1028B], mutually embracing one another, because there was no goodness, no virtue or moral excellence that was not in him. For, as the Apostle says, “in him all the fullness of divinity rested bodily” (Col. 2:9). Indeed, he himself is mercy; he himself is truth and righteousness; he himself is our peace, who made the two one (Eph. 2). And this indeed is:

“Truth has sprung up from the earth, and righteousness has looked down from heaven.” The blessed Virgin Mary is called both earth and heaven: earth by nature, heaven by grace; earth, because she was made from earth; heaven, because she is God’s dwelling-place. “Truth therefore sprang up from the earth,” because our Savior was born from the Virgin; for he is the way, the truth, and the life (John 14). “And righteousness looked down from heaven,” because the same Lord our Savior, who [Col. 1028C] was born from her who is called both heaven and earth, deigned mercifully to look upon this world and to justify the impious and sinners. He fittingly called her heaven whom he had called earth, lest he seem to have insulted so great a person by such a name.

“Indeed, the Lord will give goodness, and our land will yield its fruit.” Believe most certainly, he says, and be unwilling to doubt at all, that the Lord will truly give goodness and, as he promised through me and through the other prophets, will send us his Son at the appointed time; and our land, as I have just said, will yield its fruit. Blessed land that gave such fruit! Most blessed Virgin who bore such a Son!

“Righteousness will walk before him.” Righteousness, he says, [Col. 1028D] will walk before him, because in all things he will follow righteousness and in nothing depart from it. “And he will set his steps in the way.” For those set their steps in the way of righteousness who walk through the way of righteousness. Of them the Lord says: “Blessed are those who hunger and thirst for righteousness, for they shall be satisfied” (Matt. 5:6) [Col. 1029A].

484 PSALM LXXXV. A PRAYER OF DAVID [Note: [Col. 1029D] A prayer of David. “Because our Lord is David’s son according to the flesh, but according to divinity David’s Lord and David’s creator; and not only before David, but also before Abraham, from whom David came; and also before Adam, from whom all human beings came; and also before heaven and earth, in which is every creature.” St. Augustine.].

The prophet David speaks, in the person of the whole Church, to David himself, who is truly called David—that is, “strong of hand.” Of him it is said elsewhere: “The Lord strong and mighty, the Lord mighty in battle” (Ps. 23:8).

“Incline, O Lord, your ear to me, and hear me, for I am needy and poor.” This psalm is plain and wholly full of petitions, and does not require much exposition. But “blessed are the poor, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. 5:[Col. 1029B] 3). But what is said to the rich? “Woe to you rich, who have your consolation” (Luke 6:24). Behold, this speaker hopes especially to be heard because he is needy and poor. Hence the Apostle says: “Command the rich of this world not to be high-minded, nor to place their hope in the uncertainty of riches” (1 Tim. 6:17). For what hope can those have in God who place their hope in the uncertainty of riches? The poor are those who have nothing. Of them the Apostle says: “As having nothing, and yet possessing all things” (2 Cor. 6:10). But the needy are those who lack much and are content with little, even the least. Let us therefore understand these words of those who are voluntarily needy and poor.

[Col. 1029C] “Guard my soul, for I am holy.” Whoever is holy is worthy to be guarded by the Lord. But I understand as holy all those who, sanctified by the Church’s sacraments, hold to the faith and do not depart from the Church, even though they appear to be sinners. Thus the laws also state concerning places dedicated to the Lord: if they are destroyed, the place nevertheless remains sacred. “Save your servant, my God, who hopes in you.” Here likewise the reason is given why the Lord ought to save him, when he says, “who hopes in you.” For it is certain that “hope does not disappoint” (Rom. 5:5), and that the Lord never forsakes those who hope in him.

“Have mercy on me, O Lord, for I have cried to you all day.” He shows that he has cried for a long time by saying that he has cried all day [Col. 1029D]. Hence the Apostle says: “Pray without ceasing” (1 Thess. 5:17). And the Lord says in the Gospel: “Ask, and it shall be given you; seek, and you shall find; knock, and it shall be opened to you. For everyone who asks receives; and whoever seeks finds; and to him who knocks it shall be opened” (Matt. 7:7–8). Elsewhere it is said that “the kingdom of heaven suffers violence, and the violent seize it” (Matt. 11:12). These words therefore show how powerful violent and enduring prayer is.

[Col. 1030A] “Make glad the soul of your servant, because to you, O Lord, I have lifted up my soul.” That soul is worthy to be gladdened which is offered and presented to the Lord. By good deeds the soul is raised up to God, just as by evil deeds it is plunged into hell.

“For you, O Lord, are sweet and gentle, and abundant in mercy to all who call upon you. Give ear, O Lord, to my prayer, and attend to the voice of my supplication.” He no longer asks to be heard on account of his own deeds, but solely on account of God’s goodness. Hear, he says, my prayer and my supplication. Why? Because you are sweet, because you are gentle, and kind to sinners who turn to you; moreover, you are abundant in mercy to all who call upon you. Many call upon you and ask mercy, [Col. 1030B] but your mercy is more abundant than can be spoken or conceived.

“In the day of my tribulation I cried to you, because you heard me.” In my many tribulations, he says, I have experienced your kindness, because on the day of my tribulation I always cried to you, and cried confidently, because you always heard me. But the gods of the nations cannot do this, nor can they hear those who cry to them in their tribulations. This is what he says:

“There is none like you among the gods, O Lord, and none can do according to your works. For the gods of the nations are demons, but the Lord made the heavens.” Therefore “all the nations, whatever you have made,” leaving their gods that can neither help them nor deliver them from tribulations, [Col. 1030C] “shall come to you and worship before you, O Lord, and glorify your name.” This has already happened in great measure, and will still happen toward the end of the age, when the fullness of the Gentiles enters and Israel is saved (Rom. 11). And rightly so.

“For you are great and work wonders; you alone are God.” If those gods were gods, he says, they would deserve worship and honor. But because you alone are God, you alone deserve honor and worship.

“Lead me, O Lord, in your way, and I shall walk in your truth.” All believers are in God’s way, just as all unbelievers are in the devil’s way. Yet they need to be 485 led by the Lord and sustained by his aid, so that they may be able to walk in truth [Col. 1030D] and in no way be drawn into error.

“Let my heart rejoice, that it may fear your name.”—“The fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom” (Ps. 110:10). Hence it is said elsewhere: “Fear God and keep his commandments, for this is the whole of man” (Eccl. 12:13). Those hearts fear God which are suffused with spiritual joy; and those suffused with spiritual joy no longer love and hope for earthly things, but heavenly things. What then is “let my heart rejoice, that it may fear your name,” except: Give me a perfect heart [Col. 1031A], full of the joy of your love? But if you do this and give me such a heart, “I shall confess you, O Lord my God, with my whole heart, and glorify your name forever.” And rightly so. Why is this?

“Because your mercy is great over me, and you have delivered my soul from the lowest hell” [Note: [Col. 1031D] Augustine discusses at length in this exposition a twofold hell, higher and lower. He argues that there is a higher hell for the souls of the righteous, in which the impious rich man saw Abraham and Lazarus [Col. 1032D], and another in which that unhappy man was tormented. “David said that God delivered his soul from the lower hell because he freed him from such sins as could have led him down to the torments of the lower hell.”]. Great indeed is the mercy that delivers a soul from the lowest hell. As in that heavenly blessedness some differ from others in glory, so in hell some differ from others in torments. Thus those souls are delivered from the lowest hell which are delivered from greater and more grievous torments—not because they were ever there, but because they would have been there unless God’s grace had delivered them.

“O God, the unjust have risen against me, and the assembly [Col. 1031B] of the mighty have sought my soul, and they have not set you before their eyes.” Whether David or the Church speaks here, he complains of his adversaries. What they say is true: the unjust rose against them and, without regard for or fear of God, sought to destroy their souls. For David suffered many persecutions from Saul and the other wicked persons with him, and the Church from tyrants and heretics.

“But you, O Lord my God, are compassionate and merciful, patient and very merciful, and true. Look upon me and have mercy on me; give strength to your servant, and save the son of your handmaid.” This great repetition of words signifies profound submission and great love; and he earnestly desires to please him whom he addresses with such praiseworthy, so to speak, flattery [Col. 1031C]. The Lord gave strength to his servant David even in this life, for he made him a very powerful king and saved him from all his enemies. Likewise, he bestowed great power over serpents and scorpions, and over every power of the enemy, upon the children of the Church, who are here called his handmaid.

“Make with me, O Lord, a sign for good, that those who hate me may see and be ashamed.” The Lord performed many signs with his saints, all for good, because it was especially through the signs that were done that Gentiles were converted to the faith. When malicious spirits and their other enemies saw these, they were ashamed [Col. 1031D] and tormented by great grief and envy. The Lord makes a sign for good with sinners when he turns them to himself by divine inspiration and causes them to undertake severe repentance. Often the change of some impious and wicked person into good is so sudden that it is regarded as a sign and miracle. Hence it is fittingly said through the prophet: “Lebanon shall be turned into Carmel” (Isa. 29:17). Therefore let every sinner say: Make with me, O Lord, a sign for good, so that all good people may marvel and give you thanks for my conversion; and let those [Col. 1032A] who hate me see and be ashamed—ashamed because “you, O Lord, have helped me and comforted me.”

PSALM LXXXVI. A PSALM OF A SONG FOR THE SONS OF KORAH

The sons of Korah sing this psalm, rejoicing because the Church is first built upon the place of Calvary, concerning which it is said here: “Its foundations are on the holy mountains.” Because this is a Psalm of a Song, it is not to be read but sung, so that we may understand it to be filled with greater joy, because it is commanded to be sung rather than read.

“Its foundations are on the holy mountains.” Its foundations, he says, are on the holy mountains; “the Lord loves the gates of Zion above all the tabernacles [Col. 1032B] of Jacob.” The foundations have already been discussed above. “No one,” says the Apostle, “can lay any other foundation than that which has been laid, which is Christ Jesus” (1 Cor. 3:11). And of him the Lord said to blessed Peter: “You are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my Church” (Matt. 16:18). Christ, then, is the foundation of foundations, since the apostles and prophets too are foundations. Therefore, of the city founded upon such mountains it is rightly said, 486 “Its foundations are on the holy mountains. The Lord loves the gates of Zion above all the tabernacles of Jacob.” If he loves merely its gates, tell me, I pray, how greatly he loves the whole city! The tabernacles of Jacob mean those Jews who, having departed from the Lord, are scattered throughout the nations [Col. 1032C].

“Glorious things have been said of you, city of God.” But what glorious things have been said? Perhaps that it is said to be built wholly of gold, pearls, and precious stones? These are certainly glorious. Yet other things have been said of it. Do you want to hear which? “I will remember Rahab and Babylon, who know me.” These are truly glorious, indeed more than glorious. Consider what just persons may hope and presume concerning God’s mercy, if the Lord will remember even Rahab and Babylon. The one was a prostitute; the other held God’s people captive. The former hid the spies so that they would not be killed; the latter, by God’s command, held the transgressing people in servitude for some time [Col. 1032D]. The Lord, therefore, will remember such as these, since he remembers all who know him. He would not otherwise remember these women unless they knew him and, though after many crimes, at last deserved to believe in him. For it should be carefully noted that he says, “who know me.” Whatever a person may formerly have been—whether prostitute or persecutor of the saints—if at last converted and having come to know the Lord, that person shall be saved. Hence the Lord himself says: “This is eternal life: that they may know you, the true God, and Jesus Christ whom you sent” (John 17:[Col. 1033A] 3). Let us now hear the other glorious things said of the city of God.

“Behold,” he says, “foreigners, Tyre, and the people of Ethiopia: these were in her.” This is what the Apostle says: “Is God the God of Jews only? Is he not also of Gentiles?” (Rom. 2:19). Likewise the apostle Peter says: “In truth I have found that God is no respecter of persons; but in every nation, whoever fears him and works righteousness is acceptable to him” (Acts 10:34). Therefore whoever fears God and practices righteousness, wherever he may come from, is received by this most merciful city and regarded not as a foreigner but as a citizen and native. Thus the centurion Cornelius was received, becoming the first child of the Church from among the Gentiles. This was also signified by the vessel [Col. 1033B] full of unclean animals, when it was said to the Apostle, “Kill and eat” (Acts 10:13). This too is signified by the apes brought to Solomon together with peacocks. What is uglier than an ape? What more beautiful than a peacock? In the Lord’s tabernacle there were both haircloths and goat-hair; nor did the Lord reject a goat for a burnt offering, though bulls and lambs were offered to him. Gold, stones, wood, and the other things of which the Lord’s temple was built were not produced there, but brought from elsewhere. Thus the Church of God, built from every nation, receives every nation and rejects no one who comes to it. “And Tyre, and the people of Ethiopia: these were in her.” These glorious things can give great hope to both righteous persons and sinners and bring immeasurable joy [Col. 1033C]. Do you wish to be received into the Church? Imitate the Tyrians, by whose labor and assistance the Lord’s temple was built. Imitate also the centurion who built a synagogue for the Jews. Moses, as is read, took an Ethiopian woman as wife; because his sister Miriam murmured against her, she was struck with leprosy by the Lord and cast outside the camp. The Ethiopians of whom it is now said, “And the people of Ethiopia: these were in her,” are children of this Ethiopian woman. She is the Ethiopian woman who speaks in the Song of Songs, saying: “I am black, but beautiful, daughters of Jerusalem” (Song 1:4). But because the Synagogue hates her, it has therefore been struck with leprosy and will not be received within the Church’s camp until the consummation of the age. These, then, are glorious—indeed most glorious—things said of the city of God, in [Col. 1033D] which slaves become free and the ignoble glorious; and there, not elsewhere, is the water which can change the Ethiopians’ color. This city has such care and concern for all people that it is not undeservedly called the mother of all. Hence he adds:

“Man shall say, Mother Zion.” As if to say: This is a mother, and truly a mother, who opens the bosom of compassion to all, closes maternal affection against none, receives all, and cherishes and nourishes all with love. It follows: “And a man was born in her, and the Most High himself founded her.” Many glorious things have been said above concerning [Col. 1034A] this city; but what is now said is more glorious than every glory. No glory can be compared with this glory: the Most High himself, who founded and made her, himself became man and was born in her. How do you prove this? Do you want to hear how?

“The Lord has recounted it in the writings of his peoples and of their rulers, who were in her.” Ask your fathers and they will tell you; your elders and they will declare it to you (Deut. 32:7; Ps. 43:2). Read the Scriptures of all peoples—that is, of the prophets and apostles—which are common to all and written for our instruction and that of all people, and they will teach you. Read Moses, Isaiah, and Jeremiah, and you will find it. Read the Gospels, which are of no less authority than those. Read Paul, servant of Jesus [Col. 1034B] Christ, “who was called an apostle and set apart for the gospel of God, which he had promised beforehand through his prophets in the holy Scriptures concerning his Son, who was made from the seed of David according to the flesh” (Rom. 1:1). It has therefore been proved that a man was born in her, and the Most High himself founded her. One glorious thing still remains which was said of this city; let us hear it:

“As the dwelling-place of all of us who rejoice is in you.” For this too is very glorious: that the inhabitants of this city shall have perpetual joy and feel no misery. For where misery is, joy has no place. This joy is spiritual; this gladness is not a temporary festival, but belongs to eternal blessedness. Of it the Apostle says [Col. 1034C]: “The sufferings of this present time are not worthy to be compared with the glory to be revealed in us” (Rom. 8:18).—“Therefore rejoice in the Lord and exult, you righteous; glory, all you upright in heart” (Ps. 31:11).—“Rejoice in the Lord always; again I say, rejoice” (Phil. 4:4).

PSALM LXXXVII. A SONG OF A PSALM FOR THE SONS OF KORAH; TO THE END; FOR MAHALETH, FOR RESPONSIVE SINGING; AN INSTRUCTION OF HEMAN THE EZRAHITE [Note: [Col. 1033D] “Mahaleth, or Amalek, is interpreted as a choir chanting divine words; and the addition ‘for responsive singing’ signifies that the musical instruments preceded and the choir responded solemnly, mystically indicating the Lord’s passion, which is sung in this psalm.” Bede.].

If it is a song of a psalm, it must both be sung and read. For this psalm proclaims Christ’s passion, which produces in us both joy and sorrow. Who does not rejoice in his salvation? Who is not grieved by Christ’s passion? Let us therefore sing [Col. 1034D] this psalm, rejoicing in our redemption—for we are the sons of Korah, by whom it is commanded to be sung. Let us also read the same psalm, suffering with Christ in his passion. Let it be referred to the end, that is, to Christ, because “Christ is the end of the law” (Rom. 10:4).—“He is Alpha and Omega, the beginning and the end” (Rev. 1:17). This is an instruction of Heman the Ezrahite because Heman the Ezrahite understood this title in this manner. Heman means “their strength”; Ezrahite, “seed of God.” Let us therefore understand the apostles by him: they are a terror to the Jews, because they will judge and condemn them. They too are the seed of God, of whom it is said through the prophet: “All who see them shall say that these are the seed whom the Lord has blessed” (Isa. 61:9). From this small seed, sown by the Lord throughout the world, the whole multitude of the Church sprang up. To whom would twelve grains of wheat not seem a small seed?

“O Lord God of my salvation.” The Son, according to his humanity, speaks to the Father and complains of the faithlessness of the Jews, who treated him so dishonorably and cruelly. The Jews lie when they say: “There is no salvation for him in his God” (Ps. 3:3), though he himself calls him the God and Lord of his salvation. “By day I cried out and by night before you.” By day and [Col. 1035B] by night, in prosperity and adversity, the Lord cried out and publicly preached in the synagogues of the Jews, so as to turn them from error and bring them to know the truth. Hence he invokes his Father as witness by saying that he did this before him. For he himself says in the Gospel: “I have spoken openly to the world; I have spoken nothing in secret, and I always taught in the synagogues of the Jews, where all the Jews assembled” (John 18:20). “If I had not come and spoken to them, they would not have had sin; but now they have no excuse for their sin” (John 15:22).

“Let my prayer enter before you; incline your ear to my petition, O Lord.” Until now, as though he said, I have cried out and preached; but my crying out and preaching profited little [Col. 1035C], because those who ought to have believed and obeyed me became worse through my words. Therefore now I do not preach to them, but rather pray to you that you may defend me from their impiety. Why is this?

“Because my soul is filled with evils.” If the Lord suffered voluntarily, then his soul was also voluntarily filled with evils, and nothing evil could happen to his soul against his will. Hence it is said elsewhere: “He was offered because he himself willed it, and he did not open his mouth” (Isa. 53:7).—“And my life drew near to hell.” He fittingly says that his soul drew near to hell, because, although he was there, he suffered none of its harms [Col. 1035D] when he despoiled it. Thus he was both far from torments and drew near to torments. He speaks according to the Jews’ estimation, who thought that in enduring torments he differed in no way from other people. Hence he adds:

“I was reckoned among those who go down into the pit; [Col. 1036A] I became like a man without help [Note: [Col. 1035D] “I became like a man without help, free among the dead.” Thus the Vulgate, and this is also the reading in St. Augustine, who explains the passage thus: “In these words the person of the Lord is especially evident. For who else is free among the dead, except he who, in the likeness of sinful flesh among sinners, alone was without sin? He therefore is free among the dead who had power to lay down his soul and to take it again. No one took it from him, but he himself laid it down willingly.” Origen, Ambrose, Jerome, and other Fathers agree; thus it is remarkable that anyone should deny that they taught this view.].” But I was free among the dead, 488 and found no hindrance there. Therefore the Lord became a man without help, like other men who descended into hell—not according to the truth of the matter, but according to the foolish opinion of the Jews. The things said above can likewise be understood according to the same estimation.

“Like the wounded asleep, cast out in tombs, whom you remember no more; indeed, they have been driven away from your hand. They placed me in the lowest pit, in darkness and in the shadow of death.” Thus, he says, according to their estimation and judgment, the Jews placed me in darkness and the shadow of death, as wounded persons asleep and [Col. 1036B] cast out in tombs are placed there. By these persons are signified the wicked, wounded and slain by diabolical arrows, sunk and cast down into infernal tombs. They are far from God’s remembrance, sleeping in punishments and always, without end, dying. This is because, on account of their crimes, they were expelled from God’s hand into those penal places. Yet the foolish estimation and opinion of the Jews did not fear to place our Savior among them.

“Your wrath was made firm upon me, and you brought all your billows upon me.” Everywhere one must understand: according to their judgment and estimation. For they thought that God was angry with him and that all those evils which they inflicted upon him happened to him deservedly. These punishments are aptly called billows and compared to the storms of a raging sea [Col. 1036C] [Note: [Col. 1036D] “‘And you brought all your billows upon me.’ This is still said insofar as it belonged to the Jews’ wicked deliberation. God was believed to have brought billows—that is, the greatest indignations—upon Christ when he allowed him to be crucified; they considered that death penal because they did not perceive the glory of his dispensation.” Cassiodorus.].

“You have made my acquaintances far from me.” He calls the apostles his acquaintances; terrified by fear, they all fled after leaving him. Of them it is read in the Gospel that “his acquaintances stood afar off, to see the end” (Luke 23:49).—“They made me an abomination to themselves.” Those who placed him in the lowest pit, as we said above, also did not fear to regard him as abominable.

“I was delivered up, and I did not go out.” What need was there for him to be captured by betrayal, when he moved among them and did not go anywhere? The Lord did not flee; rather, when they came, he went of his own will to meet them. As they rushed upon him, he said: “Whom do you seek?” When they [Col. 1036D] answered, “Jesus of Nazareth,” he said: “If you seek me, let these go” (John 18:7–8), speaking of his disciples, concerning whom he adds:

“My eyes have grown weak through want.” He calls the apostles his eyes [Note: [Col. 1036D] Cassiodorus also understands the apostles by “eyes,” saying that they grew weak through want “because they had not yet received the Holy Spirit, by whom, strengthened afterward, they did not in any way fear human torments” [Col. 1037D].], because of the exceeding love with which he loved them. Hence he himself says: “As the Father has loved [Col. 1037A] me, so I have loved you” (John 15:9). In the same sense he says elsewhere: “If your eye causes you to stumble, pluck it out and cast it away from you” (Matt. 18:9), plainly signifying by “eye” those whom we hold dearest and love as our eyes. At the time of the passion, however, they were so weakened by fear of death that even he who was considered the stronger among them denied him three times. This indeed was through want; abundance and want are opposites. Christ was the apostles’ abundance, because in him they had and possessed strength, steadfastness, courage, and whatever else they needed. Since, therefore, they fled abundance, they had want of every good thing.

“I cried to you, O Lord; all day I stretched out my hands to you.” As is read in the Gospel, he cried [Col. 1037B] with a loud voice, saying: “Father, into your hands I commend my spirit”; and, bowing his head, he gave up the spirit (John 18:30). While set upon the cross, he stretched out his hands all day, as it is said through the prophet: “All day I stretched out my hands to a people who did not believe and contradicted me” (Rom. 10:21; Isa. 65:2). By this gracious stretching forth of his hands, the Lord embraced the whole world and drew all believers to himself.

“Will you work wonders for the dead, or will physicians raise them up, and will they give thanks to you?” The Lord cried out on the cross, and the Prophet makes known what he cried. Yet these words were heard by the Father alone, to whom alone the Son was speaking. The other things which he spoke not merely in his heart but also with his mouth could be heard by all who stood by [Col. 1037C]—as when he said: “Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing” (Luke 23:34). Therefore our Savior cried out both for those who at that time believed in him and for all others who would believe in him throughout the whole world. But he calls all the rest dead men and darkness, those whom he knew would believe neither words nor miracles. And this is what he says: “Will you work wonders for the dead?” The Lord worked many wonders through his saints before the ungodly and sinners, whom he calls dead; but they said that these had been done not by divine power but by magical arts: “Or will physicians raise them up, and will they give thanks to you”—and praise you? They are, he says, so dead and made insensible that they cannot be raised up either by words, [Col. 1037D] or by miracles, or by medicines. God’s physicians are the apostles and teachers, who both raised the dead and healed every sickness and infirmity.

“Will anyone declare your mercy in the grave, or your truth in destruction?” Such people, as though he said, are not merely dead, but are already foul-smelling and, handed over to destruction, rot in whitewashed tombs: who, then, could preach God’s mercy and truth to them?

> [Note: [Col. 1037D] “He means those who will not believe in the Lord, because no one appears to have declared the Lord’s mercy to them, which they refused to receive with a devout mind” [Col. 1038D]. Cassiodorus.]

“Will your wonders be known in darkness, [Col. 1038A] and your righteousness in the land of forgetfulness?” These people, he says, are darkness, a land of forgetfulness, in whose memory there is nothing good, since they are wholly enveloped in the darkness of error. It is therefore superfluous and useless to work God’s wonders for such persons and to preach his righteousness.

“But I have cried out to you, O Lord.” Yet I have not cried out to you for these people: “For I know whom I have chosen” (John 13:18). For whom, then, did the Lord cry out? Certainly for his disciples and for all others who were to believe in him through their words. Read the Gospel, and you will find that he did so. And for such persons he was immediately heard by the Father. For this is what he says: “And in the morning my prayer shall come before you.” Morning is said to occur when something happens suddenly and without any delay; just as, conversely, what happens late is said to occur in the evening [Col. 1038B].

“Why, O Lord, do you reject my prayer and turn your face away from me?” This statement seems contrary to the preceding one: for he says that he has been heard, and immediately says that his prayer has been rejected. For how was he heard, if his prayer was rejected? It must therefore be determined that this is understood according to different times or according to different persons. For the Father never rejected his prayer, never turned his face away from him; yet he is said to have rejected and turned away because he does not so immediately free and hear the saints when they are placed in great afflictions, but permits them to suffer for a time.

> [Note: [Col. 1038D] Saint Augustine gives the same exposition.]

Therefore Christ’s prayer is not rejected, although in some persons it is heard in the morning and in others in the evening; but he shows [Col. 1038C] how great is his compassion for his servants, since he does not allow them to suffer for too long.

“I am needy and in labors from my youth.” For these persons, he says—for whose unbearable sufferings I grieve—I, though rich in all things, became needy and poor; for them also I have been in labors and weariness from my youth. From the time when I began to preach in Judaea, for them I was lifted up on the cross, humbled in the tomb, and put to shame, condemned by the ungodly to the disgrace of the cross and to a most shameful death.

“Your wrath passed over me, and your terrors troubled me.” For this is what is said elsewhere: “Then I paid what I had not stolen” (Ps. [Col. 1038D] 68:5). All God’s wrath, which was due to sinners, passed over upon Christ, because, dying for all, he appeased all God’s wrath and indignation. God’s terrors also troubled him because, as he himself says, they would have had no power over him unless it had been given to them from above.

“They surrounded me like water all day long; together they encompassed me.” By these words he shows that he was surrounded and guarded by the Jews both by many persons and with great urgency and diligence, lest he should be able to escape.

[Col. 1039A] “You have removed friend and neighbor far from me, and my acquaintances from misery.” By these we understand the apostles, who, leaving him, all fled; and, though he willed and commanded it, they could not be held. For he himself said: “If you seek me, let these go” (John 18:8), so that the saying might be fulfilled: “Father, of those whom you gave me, I have lost none of them” (John 13:9).

## Psalm LXXXVIII. A Contemplation of Ethan the Ezrahite

> [Note: [Col. 1039D] This is the title according to the Vulgate. In Augustine one reads: “A Contemplation of Aethan the Israelite.” Aethan and Aeman were sons of Zara, as in 2 Chronicles 6; hence perhaps “Zarites” or “Ezrahites.”]

> [Note: [Col. 1039D] The interpretation of this title, handed down by St. Bruno, is taken from Bede, as are almost all the others, as readers will see from Cardinal Thommasius’s observations; and Bruno followed the same Bede in his exposition of the mystical sense.]

Ethan is interpreted “strong,” and Ezrahite “seed of God.” We must therefore pursue and hold to the understanding of the strong and of the sons of God, by whom the apostles and martyrs are signified in this psalm. This psalm is the Testament of the Church, so that she may most firmly [Col. 1039B] believe and in no way doubt concerning all that is promised to her by this little charter of donation.

“I will sing your mercies, O Lord, forever; from generation to generation I will proclaim your truth with my mouth.”

> [Note: [Col. 1040D] Thus it is also read in St. Augustine: “Your mercies, O Lord.” In the Vulgate, *your* is omitted.]

The Prophet promises that he will sing God’s mercies forever and proclaim his truth through all generations. And he gives the reason why he does this.

“For you said: Mercy shall be built up forever in heaven; because you said [490] that your truth shall be prepared forever in them.”

> [Note: [Col. 1040D] Vatican reading: “For you said: Mercy shall be built up forever; your truth shall be prepared in the heavens.”]

All the saints are called heavens, just as, conversely, all sinners are called earth. Hence it was said also to the first man: “You are earth, and into earth you shall go” (Gen. [Col. 1039C] 3:19). Since the saints are eternal, eternal is the mercy and truth by which they were saved.

> [Note: [Col. 1040D] On this St. Augustine excellently says: “For truth would not be displayed in the fulfillment of the promises, unless mercy had first gone before in the remission of sins.”]

But if it is eternal, they must praise God eternally, because every good work always praises its maker. Therefore all who have been saved through the Lord’s mercies will forever praise the Lord’s mercies.

“I have established a Testament with my chosen ones.” This is another reason why he sings the Lord’s mercies forever: “because, he says, you said, ‘I have established a Testament with my chosen ones,’” and you promised to give your faithful ones the remaining things that follow. Therefore, both through myself and through those who receive these words of mine, I shall sing your mercies forever.

[Col. 1039D] “I have sworn to David my servant: I will prepare your seed forever, and I will build your throne unto age upon age.” This, then, is that Testament which the Lord determined to give to his chosen ones. In saying that he swore, the Lord demonstrates the firmness of his word, because everything that he promises is like an oath, indeed more than an oath, since [Col. 1040A] it can in no way be changed. “I will prepare your seed forever,” he says, because your words shall never fail, nor shall your children ever fail. And your throne shall be built unto age upon age, because one shall be born from you whose throne and kingdom will remain forever. Therefore David sings, as we have already said, the Lord’s mercies forever, since his seed and his teaching remain forever.

“The heavens shall confess your wonders, O Lord, and your truth in the assembly of the saints.” Those heavens, he says, in which your mercy and truth have been prepared forever, will confess and praise your wonders and your truth in the assembly of the saints. These heavens are rational, for they have learned to praise God [Col. 1040B] and to preach. And all who preach the Gospel undoubtedly preach many wonders and the truth.

“For who among the clouds shall be equal to the Lord? Or who shall be like God among the sons of God?” The heavens preach this also, and what they preach is true, because no creature, however great its merit, can be compared with the Son of God. He alone is Son of God by nature; all others are so by grace and adoption. When people saw the wonders done through the apostles and wished to worship them as gods, then indeed the apostles were compelled to say: “For who among the clouds shall be equal to the Lord? Or who shall be like God among the sons of God?” We, as though they said, are human beings, [Col. 1040C] and servants of him whom you foolishly think not to exist. These are those clouds of which it is said: “Who are these that fly like clouds?” (Isa. 60:8). These clouds gave rain, yet not from themselves, but the rain which they received from that most bright fountain.

“God, who is glorified in the counsel of the saints.” This, he says, is that God who is glorified and magnified by all the saints. “Great and dreadful above all those who are around him.” Those are around him and approach his throne who are more intimate with him and more greatly loved by him. Hence John the apostle says in the Apocalypse that he saw one seated upon a throne, and around the throne twenty-four elders (Rev. 5:8). All these are both great [Col. 1040D] and dreadful, but he is greater and more dreadful. Therefore it follows:

“O Lord God of hosts, who is like you? You are mighty, O Lord, and your truth is around you.” Now the Prophet teaches us who those are who are around him, and above whom all he is stronger and more powerful, as the God of hosts, to whom no one [Col. 1041A] is like. “For your truth is around you.” Those, as though he said, are around you and cleave to you more intimately who preached and taught your truth—by whom we understand the patriarchs, apostles, and teachers. They are rightly called God’s truth, because in the words of these men it has been proved by many demonstrations how truthful God is.

“You rule over the power of the sea.” This is that sea of which it is said: “This sea, great and broad” (Ps. 103:25), by which this world is signified, whose prince and power is the devil. Of him the Lord says: “For the prince of this world comes, and has nothing in me” (John 16:11). Hence the Apostle also says: “Our struggle is not against flesh and blood, [Col. 1041B] but against principalities and powers, against the rulers of the world of this darkness, against spiritual forces of wickedness in heavenly places” (Eph. 6:12). Over this power—or rather these powers, for they are many—the Lord rules and restrains them according to his will, so that they cannot disturb this sea as much as they wish. This is what he says: “But you calm the movement of its waves.” For so great is the devil’s puffing-up and the breath of his malice that, unless the Lord had calmed the anger of men continually infected with his poison, all human beings would kill one another in turn.

“You humbled the proud one as one wounded.” For he is not only proud, but elsewhere is called king over all the children of pride. [491] Yet the Lord humbled him [Col. 1041C] as one wounded, because he powerfully bound him and plundered his house. He is the one who is said to be released after a thousand years. “And in the strength of your arm you scattered your enemies.” By these enemies we can understand the Jews, who, cast out from their homeland, were scattered throughout the whole world by the strength and power of our Savior.

“The heavens are yours, and the earth is yours; you founded the world and its fullness.” You, he says, whom the Jews crucified, are Lord of heaven and earth; you yourself founded the world and made all things in it. No human being can know what its foundation is like unless by your revelation.

“You created the north and the sea.” Great praise [Col. 1041D] and great glory belong to our Savior, since he is described as Creator of all things. By the north we may understand him of whom it is said: “From the north evils shall be opened upon all the inhabitants of the earth” (Jer. 1:14); and by the sea, his ministers and those obedient to him, since winds alone rule the sea. Therefore the devil is God’s creature, although, lifted up by excessive pride, he dared to say that he would become like the Most High. Hence the Lord says to blessed Job [Col. 1042A]: “Behold Behemoth, whom I made with you” (Job 40:10), showing that, just as he made Job, so he also made Behemoth.

“Tabor and Hermon shall rejoice in your name.” Tabor is interpreted “coming light,” but Hermon “his anathema.” These two mountains signify the apostles and the Church, who themselves are called mountains in many places. For the apostles are coming light: not given over to idleness but diligently running everywhere, they illuminated the whole world by their teaching. The Church, however, has continually in her mouth the anathema of him whom it is wearisome and shameful to name, because she never ceases to excommunicate, exsufflate, and curse him. You may prove this if you hear priests when they conduct the scrutinies.

> [Note: [Col. 1041D] From this passage we still have testimony that, in the eleventh century, when St. Bruno flourished, the Church preserved the most ancient custom of holding scrutinies for those who were solemnly to be baptized on Holy Saturday. These scrutinies—that is, examinations whether they knew the Creed, the Lord’s Prayer, and so forth by heart—were conducted by bishops or pastors on the fourth and fifth Sundays of Lent [Col. 1042D]. At that time exorcisms were also performed over those to be baptized, to expel demons, and the new faithful were prepared for the sacrament of Baptism. See Chardon, *On the Sacraments*, book I, chapter 7; Trombellius, *On the Sacrament of Baptism*, etc.]

And these persons [Col. 1042B] always rejoice in his name, because they rejoice exceedingly both to be called and to be Christians. “Your arm is with power.” The Son is the Father’s arm, and the apostles are the Son’s arm. So great was the power in the apostles that they drove out demons, overcame all their enemies, and healed every sickness and infirmity.

“Let your hand be strengthened, and your right hand exalted.” Arm, hand, and right hand signify the same thing. This hand and right hand were so strengthened and exalted when the apostles received the Holy Spirit, because then they became both priests and more excellent than all other human beings. Hence the Lord himself says to them: “I will give you a mouth and wisdom, which all your adversaries will not be able to resist or contradict” [Col. 1042C] (Luke 21:15). “Let your hand be strengthened,” he says, “and your right hand exalted.” For what purpose? To build and prepare your throne. By what instruments? “Righteousness and judgment are the preparation of your throne.” God’s throne is the Church, in which our Savior was ordained the supreme High Priest. Hence all bishops call the churches in which they are ordained their sees. God’s throne is prepared in righteousness and judgment, because there is no beauty where righteousness and judgment are absent. What then of mercy? Is it not also necessary for this preparation? To this he himself responds:

“Mercy and truth shall go before your face [Col. 1042D].” For this is what he says elsewhere: “Mercy and truth have embraced one another” (Ps. 84:11). Mercy and truth, which is also called righteousness, are joined together in Christ and are naturally conjoined: for in doing righteousness he is merciful, and in doing mercy he is just. Therefore these two virtues go before Christ’s face, because he follows them in all his actions and never departs from mercy and righteousness. Hence it is rightly said elsewhere [Col. 1043A]: “All the ways of the Lord are mercy and truth” (Ps. 24:10).—“Blessed is the people” of Christians, “who alone know jubilation.” Jubilation is ineffable joy, possessed inwardly concerning God in the secret place of the heart, which can be expressed neither in words nor in letters. The Prophet said this because the words he now speaks ought to awaken joy and jubilation in all the faithful.

> [Note: [Col. 1043D] Ghis. codex: “ought to produce [it] in all the faithful.”]

“O Lord, they shall walk in the light of your countenance.” O Lord, he says, your Christians shall walk in the light of your countenance, because you will be their eye and will illuminate their eyes after the likeness of your lights. Christians alone, therefore, are enlightened; all others are blind and walk in darkness. “And in your name [Col. 1043B] they shall rejoice all day long”: they glory in so great a patronymic, because they are called Christians from Christ. “And in your righteousness they shall be exalted.” If our Savior did not have such righteousness, those who die for him would not be exalted; rather, those who speak evil of him would be.

[492] “For you are the glory of their strength.” You, he says, are their glory, reward, and crown of strength. Hence they can rejoice and exult not merely all day, but at all times. Great glory accrues from one’s own strength to him who deserves to have God himself as the victory of his strength. “And in your good pleasure our horn shall be exalted.” If you are asked about the horn of Christians—that is, how their strength and power have been so greatly exalted [Col. 1043C]—answer that it so pleased God, and that in his good pleasure, with no preceding merits, they have been so exalted and lifted up.

“For the assumption belongs to the Lord, and to the Holy One of Israel our King.”

> [Note: [Col. 1043D] Since Augustine’s text reads, “For protection belongs to the Lord,” he appropriately adds: “He himself is your protection; he himself enlightens you. In his light you are safe; in his light you walk; by his righteousness you are exalted. He has taken you up; he guards your weakness; he makes you strong from himself, not from yourself.”]

He speaks of the assumption of our flesh, which not an angel nor an archangel, but the Son of God himself deigned to assume in person, in order to redeem and exalt us. In this assumption, therefore, is all our strength and might, glory and power, and all our blessedness. An apostrophe to the Father.

“Then you spoke in vision to your sons, and said—

> [Note: [Col. 1043D] The same reading occurs in Augustine: “Then you spoke in vision to your sons, and said.” The holy doctor adds: “You spoke in your vision; you revealed this to your prophets; therefore you spoke to them in vision, that is, in revelation, whence prophets were called seers” [Col. 1044D]. Cassiodorus likewise has *in vision*, whereas the Vulgate reads *in a vision*. I shall append Cassiodorus’s excellent exposition of this passage: “By this expression,” he says, “this is shown: that whatever the prophets said, they did not speak in ignorance, but, established in most certain contemplation, they saw what they proclaimed with their mouths.”]

—I have placed help upon the mighty one, and have exalted one chosen from my people.” He speaks of future things as though [Col. 1043D] of things past, according to the custom of prophets. Then, he says, when our Savior assumed flesh, the Lord spoke to his sons—by whom all the nations of the world are understood—and caused all his faithful to understand the things written concerning Christ’s passion, resurrection, and ascension [Col. 1044A], whether in these psalms, in the Law and Prophets, or in other Scriptures. Hence he says that he spoke in vision: that is, openly and manifestly, whereas formerly he had been accustomed to speak in secret and obscurely. Let us now hear, then, what the Lord spoke to his sons concerning his only-begotten Son, whether through prophets, apostles, or any other preachers whatsoever. “I have placed,” he says, “help upon the mighty one, and have exalted one chosen from my people.” When these things are said, we must look not to divinity but only to humanity. For the Lord placed the help of our redemption and salvation upon the mighty one—indeed, upon the almighty one—of whom he says elsewhere: “I shall set him in salvation; I shall act confidently in him” (Ps. 11:6).—“But I have been established [Col. 1044B] king by him upon Zion, his holy mountain, preaching the commandment of the Lord” (Ps. 2:6).

“I have found David my servant.” I have found, he says, David my servant: a strong and wise man, without sin, and born without the concupiscence of the flesh. Christ is called servant, however, with respect to his flesh.

“I have anointed him with my holy oil,” of whom it is said elsewhere: “Therefore God, your God, has anointed you with the oil of gladness above your companions” (Ps. 44:8).—“For in him, as it is written, all the fullness of divinity rests bodily” (Col. 2:9). He says elsewhere of himself: “The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because he anointed me; he sent me to proclaim good news to the poor” (Luke 4:18).

“For my hand shall help him, and my arm [Col. 1044C] shall strengthen him.” The Father’s hand and arm are power and strength, which helped as much as Christ willed.

“The enemy shall gain nothing against him, and the son of iniquity shall not harm him.” This is that enemy, the son of iniquity, of whom the Lord himself says in the Gospel: “For the prince of this world comes, and has nothing in me” (John 16:11). No other person in this world besides Christ has been born in whom the devil found nothing of his own, for he alone was born without sin. He is the one “who committed no sin, nor was deceit found in his mouth” (1 Pet. 2:22). Therefore the devil seeks in a human being only what is his own; and he can harm by his accusations no one in whom he finds nothing of his own [Col. 1044D]. How, then, could he harm our Savior, whom, had he willed, he could never have approached? Hence it follows:

“And I will cut down his enemies before his face, and turn those who hate him to flight.” This [Col. 1045A] can be understood of evil spirits and of all other enemies. Yet if it is referred to the judgment, it will not be inappropriate.

“And my truth and my mercy are with him.” By the Father’s truth and mercy, which were with and in him, we may understand his divinity itself, which always ruled and cherished him in all things. Hence it follows: “And in my name his horn shall be exalted.” There is one name of Father and Son, because both the Father and the Son are called God. Therefore the Savior was exalted in the Father’s name, because his humanity was exalted neither in its own name nor by its own power, but in the name of divinity.

“And I will place his hand upon the sea, and his right hand upon the rivers [Col. 1045B].” By sea and rivers this world is signified, for “many waters [are] many peoples.” Therefore the Lord’s hand is upon the sea and the rivers, because his strength and power are proclaimed among all nations.

> [Note: [Col. 1045D] Ghis. codex: “rules.”]

“He shall call upon me: You are my Father, my God, and the protector of my salvation.” “You are my Father” pertains to divinity, while the remaining words pertain to humanity. Read the Gospel, and you will find that in many places he called his Father his God. Hence the Jews said to Pilate: “According to the law he ought to die, because he made himself the Son of God” (John 19:7).

“And I will make him firstborn, exalted above the kings of the earth.” For according to divinity he is both the Father’s firstborn and only-begotten; and according to humanity he is both the firstborn and only-begotten of his mother. Yet the Father made him, according to humanity, firstborn over all, because he appointed him to possess the honor and dignity of the firstborn among all. Esau lost this honor when he sold his birthright for a meal of lentils. And he made him not only firstborn but also exalted above all kings.

“I will keep my mercy for him forever.” At one time, according to his humanity, he needed the Father’s mercy, since he too suffered want like other human beings. This is proved because, when weary and thirsty, he asked the Samaritan woman for a drink. But now it is not necessary for him; [Col. 1045D] it is always necessary for us. Therefore “forever” is said on our account, because we have been saved by God’s mercy alone. “And my Testament [shall be] faithful to him.” The Testament is certainly faithful because it is firm and stable, and nothing that it promises can be made void.

“And I will place his throne unto age upon age.” This is what the angel says to most blessed Mary: “The Lord will give him the throne of David his father, and he shall reign in the house of Jacob forever” (Luke 1:32). And elsewhere: “His power is an everlasting power, which shall not be taken away, and his kingdom, which shall not be destroyed” [Col. 1046A] (Dan. 7:14). Hence it follows: “And his throne [shall be] as the days of heaven.” Earthly days are bodily and will someday end; but the days of heaven are eternal and will never end. Therefore his throne will be as the days of heaven, because it will be eternal and have no end. What follows pertains to the Church and shows God’s ineffable mercy toward her.

“If,” he says, “my sons forsake my law and do not walk in my judgments; if they profane my ordinances and do not keep my commandments.” What shall I do to them? Do you wish to hear what?

“I will visit their iniquities with a rod, and their sins with scourges.” And what more? “But I will not scatter my mercy [Col. 1046B] from him; nor will I harm him in my truth; nor will I profane my Testament; and I will not make void the things that proceed from my lips.” What greater or equal thing could the Lord have promised his servants? No place is left for despair, because he grants mercy to all—indeed, to all who turn to repentance. This promise is not made to others; for, as the Lord himself says: “In whatever hour the sinner turns and groans, I shall not remember any of his iniquities” (Ezek. 33). What does “any of his iniquities” mean? Precisely what is said here:

“If my sons forsake my law, if they do not walk in my ways, if they profane my ordinances [Col. 1046C] and do not keep my commandments.” By God’s ordinances we must understand all ecclesiastical sacraments. “I will visit their iniquities with a rod, and their sins with scourges.”

> [Note: [Col. 1045D] This verse is absent in the edition.]

The Lord visits our iniquities with a rod and our sins with scourges when, on account of sins which would deserve punishment by the gravest penalties, or even by death itself, he chastises us with a light correction, whether in this life or in the next he deigns mercifully to afflict and correct us.

“But I will not scatter my mercy from him; nor will I harm him in my truth; nor will I profane my Testament; and I will not make void the things that proceed from my lips.”

> [Note: [Col. 1046D] These are again absent, and the text is found mutilated.]

And this the Lord promises in his truth, so that he may be believed most firmly—he in whom truth always is and who can never lie. But the Lord would profane his Testament and make his words void if he did not fulfill what he says and did anything contrary to it. In saying in the singular, “I will not scatter [my mercy] from him, nor will I harm him,” he means as much as if he had said it in the plural, to them; because he is our head and we are his members. Of them he himself says to the Father: “Father, I will that, as you and I are one, they too may be one in us” (John 17:24).

“Once I have sworn in my holy one, if I lie to David.” [Col. 1047A] For it is said elsewhere that the Lord speaks once and does not repeat the same thing a second time, because everything he says is firm and stable and needs no repetition.

> [Note: [Col. 1047D] “He had one oath for our life: he who sent his only Son to death for us.” Augustine.]

Therefore the Lord firmly swore in his Holy One, that is, in his beloved Son, that he would never lie to him. Through the Son he swore by himself, because he had nothing greater by which he could swear.

But what did he swear? “His seed shall remain forever, and his throne as the sun before me, and as the perfect moon [494] forever, and as a faithful witness in heaven.”

> [Note: [Col. 1047D] By this testimony St. Augustine incontrovertibly proves and confirms the Catholic doctrine of the resurrection of the flesh, which even those pagan philosophers who admitted the immortality of the soul openly contradicted, saying: “It cannot happen that this earthly flesh can ascend into heaven.”]

Therefore his seed, his teaching, and his sons will remain forever. His throne is the Church, or every faithful soul, because the soul of the righteous is the throne of wisdom. This [Col. 1047B] will be as the sun before him, because, as the Lord himself says: “The saints shall shine like the sun in the kingdom of God, and like the perfect moon forever” (Matt. 13:43); because it will never again diminish, but will remain forever in its perfection and fullness. And from all these things which I have sworn and promised, our Savior is for you the faithful witness in heaven: he speaks for us, pleads our cause, and intercedes for us daily. Thus far the Lord has spoken; now the Prophet speaks and complains that his Testament has been rejected by the Lord. This is what he says:

“But you have rejected and despised, and have delayed your Christ; you have turned away the testament of your servant; you have profaned his sanctuary upon the earth.”

> [Note: [Col. 1047D] Lest the things the Prophet here says seem contrary to the foregoing praises, according to St. Augustine and Cassiodorus the persons must be distinguished. “Before this, the kingdom of Christ is celebrated, whose glory and stability are promised to endure forever; but here the discourse concerns David, who is tried and afflicted by many calamities [Col. 1048D]. David himself is also called Christ because he was anointed; and David appears to have been rejected from royal dignity by God’s sentence through Nathan the prophet, on account of the sin committed with Bathsheba.”]

But you, he says [Col. 1047C], confirmed forever the Testament of your son David, and rejected, despised, and turned away the testament of your servant David. And this was because you delayed your Christ. For if you had sent him to us, it would not be said of us what was said of those to whom he was sent: “He came unto his own, and his own did not receive him” (John 1:11). In the period from David to Christ, the Synagogue suffered many great persecutions: first from the Assyrians in Isaiah’s time; then from the Chaldeans in Jeremiah’s time; afterward from the Greeks in the time of the Maccabees. For the temple was destroyed, the city laid waste, and many Jews were transferred from their ancestral laws to the Gentile rite. This, then, is what the Prophet laments and what he complains of: that the testament given to him had been profaned. In saying that holiness was profaned [Col. 1048A] upon the earth, he signifies that swine’s flesh was sacrificed upon the altar.

> [Note: [Col. 1048D] The Vulgate reads: “You destroyed all his hedges; you made his strongholds a terror.”]

“You destroyed all his walls; you made his fortifications a terror.” There was, as though he said, no strength that could have defended them: their very strong walls were destroyed as though they were mere boundary walls. Their neighbors also, who had formerly been accustomed to fear them, now joined with their enemies and held them in reproach.

“All who pass along the way plundered him; he became a reproach to his neighbors.” Whatever is done against that people, David says was done to himself. And those who plunder God’s people are those who pass along the way and do not know how to walk in the way of uprightness.

> [Note: [Col. 1048D] “That condition,” Cassiodorus says, “of the Jewish kingdom is known to have been stripped both of faith and of wealth. For passers-by, taking away its resources, most violently transferred to themselves the riches of that religion, believing rather those to whom the Lord had not come bodily in order to admonish them; as he himself said in Psalm 17:45: ‘A people whom I did not know served me; at the hearing of the ear they obeyed me.’”]

Their neighbors also, who had formerly been accustomed to fear them, now joined with their enemies and held them [Col. 1048B] in reproach.

“You exalted the right hand of his enemies; you made all his enemies glad. You turned away the help of his sword and did not aid him in battle.” These things are literally true if they are referred to the times of the Chaldeans. For the remaining things which follow must likewise be understood according to the letter.

“Thou hast stripped him of purification, and hast dashed his throne to the ground.” These things were fulfilled when they lost the sacrifices by which, according to the Law, they were accustomed to be purified. For Jews are not permitted to sacrifice outside their homeland.

“Thou hast shortened the days of his time; thou hast covered him with confusion.” Those days were shortened in which that people hoped to reign and to possess that land. [Col. 1048C] Hence they were accustomed to say, “The temple of the Lord, the temple of the Lord it is,” placing their hope, that is, in that temple, and believing that city to be impregnable. Thus far the Prophet speaks.
