From this point the Church speaks, whose immeasurable afflictions and tribulations were signified by those persecutions which, as the Prophet has related, the Jewish people had endured until then. It was therefore fitting that he should place these after those, because they are alike in many respects and, as we have said, were signified in them. Let the Church therefore speak, and amid the very torments she suffers, call to the Lord’s remembrance the mercies promised to her. For the Lord had promised that he would indeed visit her with the rod, but would not remove his mercy from her. [Col. 1048D] Yet perhaps, in God’s sight, what she herself considers torments is but a rod.

[Col. 1049A] “How long,” she says, “Lord, wilt thou be angry?” Will it be unto the end? Let thy indignation now cease, and have mercy on thy people. “How long shall thy wrath burn like fire?” She who speaks thus indicates that she feels not a rod but scorpions.

“Remember, O Lord, what my substance is.” “For my strength is not the strength of stones, nor is my flesh of bronze” (Job 6:12): I am earth, I am frail, and I cannot endure these harsh torments, 495 which thou countest as a rod. “For thou hast not created the children of men in vain”; for thou wouldst indeed have created them in vain if thou hadst allowed them to be tested beyond what they can bear and hadst not delivered them from such great afflictions.

“Who is the man that lives and shall not see death, [Col. 1049B] or deliver his hand from the hand of hell?” This is as though she said: unless the Lord had aided his saints while they were placed amid torments, all would deny him through fear of death; fleeing temporal death, they would encounter and endure eternal death, and would be unable to rescue their souls from the torments of hell.

“Where are thy former mercies, O Lord, as thou didst swear to David in thy truth?” Thou, she says, didst promise David—not David the prophet, but David thy Son—that thou wouldst not take thy mercies from him; and thou didst not merely promise, but didst swear in thy truth, since every promise of thine is an oath. Where, then, are those great mercies of thine now?

“Remember the reproach of thy servants, which [Col. 1049C] I have borne in my bosom, from many nations.” Remember, she says, that reproach with which thy servants were torn apart not only by Jews but also by many other nations; I, the Church, says that I have not forgotten it, but have firmly held it in my bosom and heart and committed it to memory. And what is it? It follows:

“Wherewith thine enemies have reproached thee, O Lord; wherewith they have reproached the exchange of thy Christ.” For this is what the Jews and other unbelievers habitually say against us, to our great injury: that we worship a man crucified and condemned to a most shameful death. Yet the Church rightly chose to call it an “exchange,” whereas they called it a most shameful death. And indeed it ought rather to be called an exchange than a death, by which one passes from darkness to light and from miseries to glory and supreme blessedness.

“Blessed be the Lord for ever: be it so, be it so.” I think that the Church suddenly felt God’s mercies to have come upon her when, amid her complaints, she inserted this blessing and thanksgiving so swiftly. For Job also, grievously afflicted, appears to have said something similar: “The Lord gave, the Lord has taken away; [Col. 1050A] as it pleased the Lord, so it has been done; blessed be the name of the Lord” (Job 1:21).

## PSALM LXXXIX. THE PRAYER OF MOSES, THE MAN OF GOD

> [Note: [Col. 1049D] For the elucidation of this psalm, the Venerable Bede teaches that this title was affixed to it because David either sang what Moses had written concerning the creation of the whole universe, or wished to imitate Moses as he entreated God for his people, and attributed this prayer to him. Was Moses not so much a minister of the Old Testament as a prophet of the New Testament? This is also maintained by St Augustine, citing the Apostle’s words: “All these things happened to them in a figure; but they were written for our correction, upon whom the end of the ages has come.” [Col. 1050D]]

This psalm is not found in the books of Moses; yet he of whom Moses says that he is the beginning in which God created heaven and earth is the same one of whom it is said here: “Before the mountains were made, or the earth and the world were formed, from age unto age thou art God.” The fall of humankind is also related in this psalm, whereas its creation is contained in those books. And it was fitting that the same man who wrote of creation should also write of humanity’s fall.

“Lord, thou hast become a refuge for us from generation to generation.” The Church speaks of the coming of [Col. 1050B] our Saviour, because she knows that she now possesses the best refuge, though before this time she had no helper. “Lord,” she says, “thou hast become a refuge for us from this generation and lineage of thy incarnation.” Fleeing to thee, we are secure, we who formerly had no refuge. Nor should the Jews say to thee, “Thou art not yet fifty years old” (John 8:57), since thou art not only before Abraham but also before heaven and earth. And this is what she says:

“Before the mountains were made and the earth and world were formed, from age unto age thou art God.” Thou art God, she says, and thou art eternal, having neither beginning nor end; yet now, for our sake and as our refuge, thou hast become man.

[Col. 1050C] “Turn not man away into humiliation.” What is meant by “into humiliation”? There is a good humility—which would that we all possessed—and an evil humility, by which a human being is subjected to vices and evil spirits. This humility, then, he fears and dreads should come upon him. “And thou hast said: Return, children of men.” Thou hast become our refuge, she says, and through thy prophets, apostles, and other preachers thou hast said to us, “Return, children of men.” This counsel of thine is good, and we must follow it with great desire. Why?

“For a thousand years before thine eyes are as yesterday’s day, which has passed away, and as a watch in the night, which is counted as nothing.” Thus—understand—[Col. 1050D] are their years: 496 “In the morning, like grass, let him pass away; in the morning let him flourish and pass away; in the evening let him fall, grow hard, and wither.” This whole present life, as it were, is nothing, even if a person should live a thousand years; for a thousand years before thine eyes are like a day that has passed, which was and is not. “And as a watch in the night,” which, because of its brevity, is counted as nothing, so are the years of all people, when unhappy man “passes away in the morning like grass.” Morning and evening are opposites: as evening signifies lateness, so morning signifies swiftness. Thus a person passes away in the morning like grass, because he quickly loses the flower of his beauty; and this is what he says: “In the morning let him flourish and pass away.” A person’s morning is when he is in youth; hence youth is called the flower of life. “In the evening let him fall.” What does “in the evening let him fall” mean, except that he dies and falls in old age? For old age is the setting of life. “Let him grow hard and wither”: that is, let dust return to dust, and let only dry, parched bones remain from that bloom and beauty. These words make it clear that Moses, in this prayer of his, described humanity’s fall no less carefully than its creation. It follows:

“For we have failed in thy wrath, and in thy fury we have been troubled [Col. 1051B].” And why? “Thou hast set our iniquities before thee, and our age in the light of thy countenance. And because all our days have failed, we too have failed in thy wrath.” Therefore “our years shall be reckoned like a spider’s.” Thus, he says, our years will be changeable, frail, brief, and vain, and will be pondered and reckoned like a spider’s, because, as was said above, we have failed in thy wrath and have been troubled in thy fury. This is indeed because of the sin of the first parent. The Lord set our iniquities before himself because he has not forgotten them and does not allow them to pass unpunished; and this is what he means by “our age in the light of thy countenance.” Our “age” signifies our life and our wicked manner of living. Behold, [Col. 1051C] we have heard the reason why our years are reckoned like a spider’s. It follows:

“The days of our years are few: in them there are sometimes seventy years” when health is good, and this happens to many; yet a few even sometimes reach eighty, but this belongs to the strong. A person is in good health when all his limbs retain their sound and unimpaired functions—like those called healthy, who are very seldom ill. Such persons are “strong,” because sound and unhurt, they are vigorous. Yet we see others who, at a lesser age, have for the most part lost sight, hearing, and the functions of their other limbs; and at this age, which is nearly the last, [Col. 1051D] some are vigorous, but for most it is labour and pain.

> [Note: [Col. 1051D] The errors of the edition are corrected from the Vallicellian manuscript.]

Some, he says, may reach this age in good health; but to pass beyond it is labour and pain—coughing, anxiety, distress, and miseries—especially since old age itself is an infirmity. What sweetness or pleasure of this life can there be for one who neither sees nor hears, who, having lost his teeth, cannot chew food, and who, like a stone fixed in almost one place all day, seems to differ little from the dead? We may also understand by seventy and eighty years the active and contemplative life: by seven, the active life, because this whole present life is contained in seven days; but by eight, the contemplative life, [Col. 1052A] because the eighth day begins another week, by which week the other life is signified. Those arrive at a good old age who devote themselves either to the active or contemplative life. Hence it is said elsewhere: “Give a portion to seven, and also to eight” (Eccles. 11:2)—that is, give a portion to the active life and a portion to the contemplative life, so that we may pass through temporal goods without losing eternal ones. But whatever lies beyond this and departs from both these lives is labour and pain.

“For gentleness has come upon us, and we shall be corrected.” Upon those old people, he says, who attain a good old age, gentleness comes, all pride and perversity having been driven away and overcome. And they are corrected because their entire life is changed for the better; [Col. 1052B] now, in the last hour, they begin to labour in God’s vineyard.

“Who knows the power of thy wrath?” Surely the one who fears to offend him. But one who does not fear to offend him has not yet learned how dreadful it is to fall into the hands of the living God (Heb. 10:31). “Or who can reckon thy wrath through fear?” Understand: who knows it? He reckons the wrath of God through fear who, converted by worthy repentance, considers within his heart how often and in what ways he has offended God.

“Make known to me, O Lord, thy right hand.” This may be understood as asking him to make us feel in this life the right hand of his correction, lest he afflict us more severely in the next life. But by God’s right hand we may understand our Saviour, because of what follows:

“And those instructed in heart in wisdom.” This is as if he said: that we may be able to know thy wrath, make known to us thy Son, thy prophets, and thy apostles, who are wisely instructed and whose words are very obscure and difficult. Whoever knows these lacks nothing for the fullness of true knowledge. Such a person knows the right-hand way which leads to life, and rejects the left-hand way which leads to death.

497 “Return, O Lord, a little.” Turn, he says, a little from thy indignation; “and be entreated and propitious toward thy servants,” whom thou hast loved so greatly that thou didst send them [Col. 1052D] thy Son.

“We have been filled in the morning with thy mercy, and we have exulted and delighted in all our days.” When the Lord was born, night preceded and ended, and morning came in this last age. From that morning, therefore, we have been filled with thy mercy, O Lord, and have exulted and delighted in all our days. What then do you say of those days in which you were afflicted and humbled by such great torments? It follows:

“We have delighted for the days in which thou hast humbled us, and for the years in which we saw evils.” Rather, as it were, we delighted and delight in those days because we await for them a greater honour and glory.

[Col. 1053A] “Look upon thy servants and upon thy works, O Lord, and direct their children.” His servants are his works, because he created and made them; and he then looks upon them when he does not permit them to wander or sin. Their children are those who imitate them in faith, works, and teaching. “And let the brightness of the Lord our God be upon us,” so that we who were made in his image may be re-formed after that same image. For the saints shall shine as the sun in the kingdom of God. Hence the Apostle John says: “Beloved, we are the children of God, and it has not yet appeared what we shall be. But we know that when he shall appear, we shall be like him, because we shall see him as he is” (John 3:2).—“And direct the works of our hands over us,” so that nothing crooked, perverse, or distorted [Col. 1053B] may be found in our works, as in the works of those of whom it is said: “For your thoughts are not my thoughts, nor your ways my ways, saith the Lord; for as the heavens are exalted above the earth, so are my ways exalted above your ways, and my thoughts above your thoughts” (Isa. 55:8).

## PSALM XC. A PRAISE-SONG OF DAVID

A praise-song of David is contained in this psalm—of that David, namely, of whom it is said: “A thousand shall fall at thy side and ten thousand at thy right hand; but they shall not come near thee. And thou shalt walk upon the asp and basilisk, and shalt trample the lion and dragon.”

“He who dwells in the aid of the Most High shall abide in the protection [Col. 1053C] of the God of heaven.” The Prophet speaks against the Jews and evil spirits, who laid snares against our Saviour and devised wicked things against him. He who dwells, he says, wherever he dwells—even if he dwells among his enemies and adversaries—dwells in the aid of the Most High; “he shall not fear the terror of the night, nor the arrow flying by day, nor the business that walks in darkness, nor ruin and the noonday demon.” And therefore he shall not fear, because he shall abide in the protection of the God of heaven. For what could he fear when the omnipotent Father and the very divinity which is in him always and everywhere protect and defend him?

“He shall say to the Lord: Thou art my protector and my refuge, [Col. 1053D] my God.” Our Saviour said this according to his humanity, because according to his divinity he possesses none of these things. He himself, the Prophet says, will say this whenever it is needful for him. And when he says it—or rather, when he thinks and wills it—his will is immediately fulfilled. What, then, will those do against him who foolishly rise up against him? “And I,” says the Prophet, “will hope in him.” If Christ the Lord had been unable to defend himself, it would have been vain and useless to hope in him. It has indeed been proved that he feared no one, he who is the sole hope and defence of all others.

“For he has delivered me from the snare of hunters, and from the harsh word.” Therefore, he says, I shall hope in him, because he will deliver me from all my distresses. [Col. 1054A] These hunters are evil spirits, in whose nets sinners are caught. As many as the vices are, so many are the snares by which they bind and hold wretched people. The harsh word is that which the Lord will utter at judgment: “Go, ye cursed, into everlasting fire” (Matt. 25:41). The Prophet now directs his words to Christ himself.

“With his shoulders he shall overshadow thee, and under his wings thou shalt hope.” For God has neither shoulders nor wings; but he speaks metaphorically, so that by shoulders and wings we may understand the whole of his protection and defence.

“His truth shall surround thee with a shield.” Truth is a great and invincible shield for convicting deceitful and unjust people. By this shield [Col. 1054B] the Jews were overcome, because they could find nothing in Christ’s words worthy of censure. “Thou shalt not fear the terror of the night.” He calls that the terror of the night when, on the very night in which he was betrayed, the Jews, together with Judas the traitor, rushed upon him with swords and clubs. Had he feared, he would have fled rather than met them. “The arrow flying by day.” The Lord was seized at night and shot with arrows by day. For the Jews shot him when they cried, “Crucify him.” But the arrows of children became their wounds. “The business that walks in darkness” (Ps. 63:9). 498 That business which walked in darkness is understood as the plot concerning the Saviour’s death that turned over in the hearts of the scribes and Pharisees. They are most fittingly called darkness here, since they are blind and guides of the blind.

“From ruin and the noonday demon.” After Pilate had been unable to defend him and, having washed his hands, handed him over to the power of the Jews to be crucified, that ruin occurred; then, rushing upon him with the savagery and cruelty of beasts, they dragged him to the cross. “It was the sixth hour, and they crucified him” (Mark 19:33 [sic]; John 19:18). Hence it is said here, “from the noonday demon”; for unless that most wicked people had been led and harassed by a demon, it could not have committed so great an evil. “A thousand shall fall at thy side, and ten thousand at thy right hand.” By the thousands and ten thousands we must understand all the multitudes of evil spirits, which [Col. 1054D] all fell in Christ’s Passion and lost every power and strength. For then the devil was bound, though he is said to be loosed after a thousand years. This might be understood of the future judgment, had he not said “at thy right hand”; for then none of them will be at the right hand, but they will be struck and fall on the left. “But they shall not come near thee.” They shall indeed fall and lose their power; and although all of them unite in one counsel and evil will to do harm, nevertheless they do not dare to approach our Saviour.

“Yet with thine eyes thou shalt behold, and thou shalt see the recompense of sinners.” Thou shalt endure all things patiently, as it were, and though thou canst immediately avenge thyself, thou wilt not at once take vengeance. Yet [Col. 1055A] thou wilt consider how they ought to be punished and behold the recompense of sinners, so that in its time thou mayest exact vengeance from them and carry out retribution.

“For thou, O Lord, art my hope; thou hast set the Most High as thy refuge. Evils shall not come near thee, and the scourge shall not approach thy tabernacle.” Each clause corresponds to another: what is said here, “For thou, O Lord, art my hope,” is what he said above, “I will hope in him.” And what is said here, “Thou hast set the Most High as thy refuge,” is what he said above, “He who dwells in the aid of the Most High.” Therefore let it be said: because thou, O Lord, art my hope, I am certain that the scourge will not approach thy tabernacle—that is, me—because I am thy tabernacle. Hence elsewhere it is said: “But thou [Col. 1055B] dwellest in the holy ones, O King of Israel” (Ps. 21:4). And because thou hast set the Most High as thy refuge, evils shall not come near thee; for evil cannot rise to such a height.

“For he has commanded his angels concerning thee, that they may keep thee in all thy ways. They shall bear thee in their hands, lest at any time thou dash thy foot against a stone.” Therefore, he says, thou shalt be borne by angels lest thou dash thy foot against a stone, because the Lord has so commanded them. There can be no doubt that angels were always ready to serve and obey him, since it is said even of others that “their angels always see the face of the Father” (Matt. 18:10). Hence it is also said elsewhere that “angels came and ministered to him” (Matt. 4:11). The angels therefore [Col. 1055C] guarded him lest perhaps stones should hurt him; by these stones we may understand the Jews and other wicked persons. But all these things are to be referred to his humanity.

“Thou shalt walk upon the asp and basilisk, and shalt trample the lion and dragon.” By the asp and basilisk, lion and dragon, we understand the devil. He is an asp because his venom is incurable; a basilisk because he is king of all wickedness; a lion because he always prowls about seeking someone to devour; and a dragon because he is crooked and never proceeds by a straight path. But the Lord walks upon and tramples him beneath his feet because he destroys and overcomes all his wiles. Thus far the Prophet speaks. Now the Father himself speaks of the Son, and this too is according to his humanity.

“Because he will hope in me, I will deliver him.” Hence he himself says: “Preserve me, O Lord, because I have hoped in thee” (Ps. 15:1).—“I will protect him, because he has known my name.” And this is what is said there: “I said to the Lord: Thou art my God” (ibid., 2). Everywhere the Son, according to his humanity, calls the Father his God, his Lord, and his King. “He shall call upon me, and I will hear him.” For the Lord himself says: “Father, I give thee thanks because thou hast heard me; for I knew that thou always hearest me” (John 11:41).—“I am with him in tribulation.” For the Father does not forsake the Son. Hence, when elsewhere he had said, “Why hast thou [Col. 1056A] forsaken me?” he immediately added, “Far from my salvation” (Ps. 21:2).

“I will deliver him and glorify him; I will fill him with length of days, and show him my salvation.” I, he says, will deliver him from all his distresses and necessities; “and I will glorify him” by placing him at my right hand. “I will fill him with length of days,” because he will reign for ever and ever, and his kingdom shall have no end. “And I will show him my salvation,” by which we understand eternal and unchangeable salvation.

## PSALM XCI. 499 A PSALM OF A SONG FOR THE SABBATH DAY

This psalm ought to be sung on the Sabbath day. The first feast is the Sabbath, which is observed by divine command. [Col. 1056B] Hence it is fittingly interpreted as “rest.” God blessed this day and forbade the performance of any servile work upon it. Servile work, however, is not what slaves do, but what makes even free persons slaves. Every sin, therefore, is servile work, because whoever commits sin is the slave of sin. Those rightly celebrate the Sabbath who flee evil and do good. Such persons should sing this psalm with song and harp upon the ten-stringed psaltery.

“It is good to confess to the Lord, and to sing to thy name, O Most High; to proclaim thy mercy in the morning, and thy truth in the night; upon the ten-stringed psaltery, with song and harp; because thou hast delighted me, O Lord, in thy work,” [Note: [Col. 1055D] These words are absent from the edition.] and therefore it is good for me to confess to the Lord. The Church speaks, delighted beyond measure in the work [Col. 1056C] of the Lord and in all his works which God performed during the six days up to the Sabbath. On the Sabbath itself, therefore, she desires to praise, bless, and proclaim the Lord, so that the Sabbath itself may not lack glory while all the other days are glorious for their actions. The praise is great and increases without measure if we wish to recount each thing that was made on those days. Nor can the Sabbath suffice us for such abundant praises unless we understand the Sabbath otherwise than the Jews do. “It is good,” she says, “to confess to the Lord,” to sing and praise thy name, O Most High, so that it may be heard by all. Hence elsewhere it is said: “Cry aloud, do not cease; raise thy voice like a trumpet” (Isa. 58:1). And again: “Raise [Col. 1056D] thy voice on high, thou who bringest good tidings to Jerusalem” (Isa. 40:9). And we ought at every time not only to praise and proclaim thee for these things, but also for thy mercy and truth. This is what he says: “To proclaim thy mercy in the morning, and thy truth in the night.” “Morning and night” here means “at every time,” so that by morning, which begins the day, we understand the whole day. For it was no greater thing to create the world than to redeem it, nor ought we to praise God more for creation than for redemption, which was accomplished for us solely by God’s mercy and truth. It is good, therefore, to praise, proclaim, and announce. But how?

“Upon the ten-stringed psaltery, with song and harp.” [Col. 1057A] The psaltery has ten strings, by which the ten commandments of the Law are signified. For the harp, however, either three or four strings suffice, as we have often already said. By the psaltery, therefore, let us understand the Old Testament, and by the harp the New. These two instruments suffice us for proclaiming God’s mighty works. But because this must be done with song, it signifies that joy is present in such speech. “Because thou hast delighted me, O Lord, in thy work.” This has already been explained above, and the sequence of the discourse extends thus far: “And in the works of thy hands I will exult.” And rightly so, for “not he who has begun, but he who has persevered unto the end, shall be saved” (Matt. 10:22).

“How magnificent are thy works, O Lord!” [Col. 1057B] A worthy exclamation and a noble expression of no slight wonder. Hence it is said elsewhere: “Thy knowledge has become wonderful to me; it has been strengthened, and I shall not attain to it” (Ps. 138:6).—“Thy thoughts are exceedingly deep.” Why one vessel is made for honour and another for dishonour; why Jacob is chosen and Esau rejected before they are born—let whoever can resolve this. Hence the Apostle rightly exclaims: “O the depth of the riches of the wisdom and knowledge of God! How incomprehensible are his judgments and unsearchable his ways!” (Rom. 11:33). They are unsearchable indeed because they are exceedingly deep.

“A foolish man does not know, and a fool does not understand [Col. 1057C] them.” A foolish man, he says, and a fool neither knows nor understands the works of God—the works, namely, which he has just called magnificent. But what are those works? That sinners perish for ever and ever. This is what he says:

“When sinners spring up like grass, and all who work iniquity appear, that they may perish for ever and ever.” Sinners spring up like grass, which, as the Lord says, exists today and tomorrow is cast into the furnace. They appear and walk more conspicuously among others, yet do not depart from wickedness, for no other purpose than that they may die and perish. Had the foolish man and the fool understood this, perhaps he would have ceased from his wickedness.

“But thou art Most High for ever, O Lord”; [Col. 1057D] understand: thou wilt punish them and make them know their own wickedness. Hence elsewhere it is said to the foolish man: “I will rebuke thee and set thee before thy face” (Ps. 49:21). And this is what he says:

“For behold, thine enemies, O Lord, shall perish, and all who work iniquity shall be scattered. And my horn shall be exalted like that of a unicorn.” 500 The horn of the Church—her strength, power, faith, and teaching—has been so exalted that no one can resist it. Hence the Lord himself says: “I will give you a mouth and wisdom which all your adversaries shall not be able to resist or gainsay” (Luke 21:15). For it is said of the unicorn that no animal can withstand its onset.

[Col. 1058A] “And my old age shall be in abundant mercy.” Hence it is said: “And thou shalt enter the grave in abundance” (Job 5:26). The old age of the Church is the consummation of this age, in which she will receive such abundant mercy that she will require no mercy thereafter. Great indeed is the mercy that excludes every other mercy: “And mine eye has looked upon my enemies, and mine ear has heard those who rise against me and malign me.” As if to say: I have no need to show or accuse my enemies before thee; thou hast seen and heard them, thou knowest best what vengeance thou oughtest to exact from them.

“The righteous shall flourish like a palm tree.” The righteous person is excellently compared to the palm, because in Holy Scripture the palm signifies victory. Hence Moses says: “If there be a cause between some persons and they appeal to judges, then those whom they discern to be righteous they shall give the palm of righteousness; but they shall condemn the ungodly to ungodliness” (Deut. 25:1). [Col. 1058B] Note that he compared the righteous person to victory itself, the more to exalt his praise. The righteous person therefore flourishes, shines, and glories like a palm, because he triumphs over all his enemies. “For no one is crowned unless he has contended lawfully” (2 Tim. 2:3).—“And he shall multiply like the cedar of Lebanon,” which is more beautiful, greater, and more excellent than other trees. As cedars are among other trees, so are righteous men among other people. But in what do such persons multiply, if not in knowledge, mercy, piety, and every spiritual wealth? Of these he adds further:

“Planted in the house of the Lord, they shall flourish in the courts of the house of our God.” The house of God is the Church, in whose courts righteous men are planted and founded so that they may always be seen by all. There teaching and righteousness flourish, and by the sweetness of their fragrance satisfy others. Hence the Apostle says: “We are the good fragrance of Christ in every place” (2 Cor. 2:15). For the cedar too is said to be fragrant by nature.

“They shall still multiply in fruitful old age.” So long as this world exists, he says, they shall yet multiply through the offspring of many children and an abundance of every virtue. In fruitful old age the saints are old, whatever their apparent age; their life is mature and free from every frivolity and vanity. [Col. 1058D] “And they shall be well enduring.” For thieves, adulterers, and many others are also often enduring, and are tortured with many and various torments because of their wickedness; but they do not endure well, because they receive no reward for their endurance. The saints will truly endure, in order that they may proclaim. What?

“That the Lord our God is righteous, and there is no iniquity in him.” This was the greatest and chief reason why the saints were put to death: because they said that all the gods of the nations were demons, and confessed that our Lord alone is the righteous and true God, who renders to each according to his works.

## PSALM XCII. A PRAISE-SONG OF DAVID HIMSELF, ON THE DAY BEFORE THE SABBATH, WHEN THE EARTH WAS FOUNDED

> [Note: [Col. 1059D] It will not be inappropriate here also to add Bede’s interpretation. “A song in praise of the divinity; ‘of David himself’ is fittingly applied to Christ. But it is asked how it says that the earth was founded on the day before the Sabbath—that is, Friday—when Genesis records that dry land appeared on the third day. Here, however, by earth we must understand man, to whom it is said, ‘Thou art earth and unto earth thou shalt go.’ As he was made by God the Creator on the sixth day, so in the sixth age of the world he was formed by the same Creator, from the seed of David: then the earth was founded, when the faith of the human race was established in him; and thus the praise of his holy incarnation is sung in the composition of this psalm.” [Col. 1060D]]

[Col. 1059A]

The praise of this song, he says, should be sung and jubilantly offered to David himself. To whom himself, if not to our Saviour, who truly is David himself—that is, “strong of hand”? It should be sung on the day before the Sabbath, because for the things which he accomplished on that day he must be praised and glorified by all nations. For on that day before the Sabbath our Saviour was crucified, the devil was overcome, the human race was delivered from his impious power, original sin was wiped away, and on that same day the earth was founded. Of this it is said: “For he has made firm the earth’s circle, which shall not be moved.” On that day the Church was founded, when he [Col. 1059B] washed us from our sins in his blood.

“The Lord has reigned; he has put on beauty.” The Prophet rejoices in the things done on the day before the Sabbath. For on that day the prince of this world was judged and condemned, our Saviour as victor and triumpher received the kingdom, and freed the human race from his violent dominion. But what beauty do we think he put on in his resurrection, when the disciples, because of the excessive splendour of his transfigured face, could not gaze upon it?

“The Lord has put on strength and girded himself with power.” After the resurrection the saints will possess such power and strength that no creature will be able to harm them in any respect. What need, then, is there to speak of the strength and power of our [Col. 1059C] Saviour?

“Indeed, he has established the world, which shall not be moved.” Here the thought continues from what is said in the title, concerning the time when the earth was founded. By “earth” the Church is signified, which was founded and made firm when our Savior deigned to undergo the cross and die for its redemption. It shall not be moved, and, mindful of so great a benefit, it shall never be separated from his faith and love. Of it there follows:

“Your throne, O God, is prepared from that time; you are from eternity.” This same Church is the throne of God, because God sits and judges in it; and, as it is written, the soul of the righteous is the seat of wisdom. This throne was prepared from that time and made worthy of so great a sitter, from the time when it was washed and cleansed by his blood [Col. 1059D]. His throne, indeed, was prepared from that time; but he himself is not from that time, but is from eternity. “He is from eternity” means the same as saying: he always is.

“The rivers have lifted up, O Lord, the rivers have lifted up their voice above the sound of many waters.” [Col. 1060A] After this throne had been prepared, and the preachers whom Christ appointed over it as his vicars and bishops began to preach, then the rivers lifted up their voices to the Lord, praising and blessing him, and giving thanks for their conversion and justification. For by rivers peoples are represented, because, as it is written, “many waters are many peoples.” And rivers fittingly signify peoples, because just as waves in rivers succeed one another as they flow downward, so among peoples one succeeds another as they hasten toward death.

“The liftings up of the sea are wonderful; wonderful is the Lord on high.” From the voices, he says, of many waters there arose the wonderful liftings up of the sea, because the whole world was disturbed and shaken against the voices of holy preachers and faithful peoples praising God [Col. 1060B]. Behold, the sea fights against the rivers: the rich against the poor, the proud against the humble, and the powerful of this world against those unwilling to defend themselves. No one, therefore, could have endured the swellings and assaults of so great a sea unless the power of God had been present to moderate the wrath of such fury. But let us hear what follows: “Wonderful is the Lord on high.” And certainly it was fitting that “wonderful” should be set against “wonderful”: he who fights against marvelous things is more wonderful than the swellings of the sea that assail the saints. And truly wonderful on high is he, performing miracles so astounding and admirable to all. Hence it follows:

“Your testimonies, O Lord, have become exceedingly trustworthy” [Col. 1060C]. In this place, “testimonies” means all his promises. For the Lord had promised his disciples that he would neither desert nor forsake them, and that they too would perform the works that he himself performed. Since, therefore, what he promised has come to pass, it is testified that his testimonies have become exceedingly trustworthy.

“Holiness becomes your house, O Lord, unto length of days.” This is what the Lord says: “Be holy, because I, the Lord your God, am holy” (Lev. 11:44). Therefore all holy things, and all good things distinguished by devotion and reverence, befit the Church of God, which is signified by the house. And this is so not merely for a time, but “unto length of days,” which means for eternity and for age upon age [Col. 1060D].

## PSALM XCIII. A PSALM OF DAVID HIMSELF, FOR THE FOURTH DAY FROM THE SABBATH

[Note: [Col. 1060D] “The fourth day from the Sabbath is the fourth weekday from the Sabbath: the day on which God created the lights of heaven. This is to be applied to holy men, shining on earth with a heavenly manner of life, of whom this psalm is about to speak.” Bede.]

It has been said what “of David himself” signifies. On the fourth day from the Sabbath the world was illumined; for on that day God made the sun, moon, and stars, by which the whole world is illumined. Those forget this day who dare to say that the God of heaven does not know and does not see all things [Col. 1061A], as do those in this psalm who say: “The Lord will not see, nor will the God of Jacob understand.” So too do those who endeavor to extinguish the brightest lights of this world, signified in those lights which the Lord made on the fourth day from the Sabbath, concerning whom the Lord himself says: “You are the light of the world” (Matt. 5:11). This psalm, therefore, is directed against the persecutors of the Church, who, because they are in darkness, cannot see the light. “For everyone who does evil flees the light” (John 3:20).

“God of vengeances, the Lord; God of vengeances has acted freely.” The Church speaks and rebukes tyrants, heretics, and other wicked persons, who so fiercely assail the truth and strive to defend error. It is as though she said: God, who is the Lord of vengeances [Col. 1061B], who leaves nothing unavenged but does justice to all who suffer injury, has acted freely—he has brought freedom, redeeming the world from the devil’s bondage; and do you, by contrast, endeavor to draw God’s people into error and the devil’s servitude? Cease now, cease, and turn your eyes toward the avenger and liberator. If you do not cease, he is an avenger; if you cease, he is a liberator.

“Rise up, you who judge the earth; render recompense to the proud.” She recognizes that they are incapable of conversion; therefore, turning to the Lord, she asks him to render recompense to those who persist in their pride, so that they may know him as avenger because they refused to have him as liberator. The Lord rises up and is lifted against the proud when he shows himself angry with them [Col. 1061C].

“How long shall sinners, O Lord, how long shall sinners glory?” The Lord waits for sinners and does not punish them immediately, in case they might be converted and healed. But they not only do not cease from sinning; worse still, they glory in their very iniquities.

“How long shall they utter and speak iniquity? Shall all who work iniquity speak?” It does not suffice for them to do evil unless they also teach others to do it. Such are those who sit in the chair of pestilence, since uttering and speaking belong to teaching.

“They have humbled your people, O Lord.” They humbled some by torments, others by flatteries and promises, and still others by the persuasions of false doctrine [Col. 1061D]. For what does “they have humbled” mean except “they have subjected to their own will”? “And they have afflicted your inheritance.” Such people are demons, and therefore those whom they attack are said to be afflicted. This is the great affliction of which we spoke above.

“They have slain the widow and the stranger, and killed the fatherless.” That this is literally true is beyond doubt. Allegorically, however, the widow signifies the soul divided from God and joined to their errors. For she is called a widow as though separated from her husband. The strangers are those who, leaving the Church, came to them and chose to be and dwell with them. By the fatherless are signified those who are simpler [Col. 1062A] and, like infants, are easily deceived. These, indeed, are those whom the persecutors of the Church are said to have killed.

“And they said: The Lord will not see, nor will the God of Jacob understand.” Only those who believed that the God of Jacob did not exist could utter such great blasphemy. For if he is God, he must necessarily both see and understand all things. Thus the Prophet, mocking the gods of the nations, says: “Tell me the things that were first, and the last things that shall be, and I shall say that you are gods.”

“Understand now, you who are senseless among the people, and you fools, be wise at last.” “Now,” as though he said, understand when you see so many signs and miracles performed in his name; believe that he is God, and recognize that he sees and understands all things. For who but God [Col. 1062B] made humanity? Who gave it ears and eyes? If he made all things, with what presumption do you dare to say these things? This is what he says:

“Will he who planted the ear not hear? Will he who formed the eye not see?” He who could do the greater can also do the lesser. For he who grants sight and hearing to all others cannot be without sight and hearing himself. Yet because he says “not see,” he seems rather to signify the inward senses.

“He who corrects the nations, will he not rebuke? He who teaches a human being knowledge.” He, he says, who corrects all nations and chastises them for their perversities—will he not rebuke you alone for your foolishness and stupidity? And has he who teaches every human being knowledge so lost his own knowledge [Col. 1062C] that he neither sees nor understands your iniquities?

“The Lord knows the thoughts of human beings, that they are vain.” Therefore he sees all things, he from whom even thoughts themselves cannot be hidden. Let the senseless among the people therefore be silent, and let fools at last be still; let them dare neither to think nor say such things any further.

“Blessed is the man whom you instruct, O Lord, and teach him from your law.” Those alone are blessed who are instructed by God and from God’s law. Conversely, those are miserable who have learned from philosophers, heretics, and other teachers of perverse doctrines the wisdom of this world, which is foolishness before God.

“That you may soothe him in evil days, until a pit is dug for the sinner.” God soothes in evil days those whom he preserves in his mercy, so that even among the wicked they may live faithfully and be preserved. Hence the Apostle says: “Redeeming the time, because the days are evil” (Eph. 5:16).—“Until a pit is dug for the sinner.” A pit is dug for the sinner daily, because the more he sins, the deeper a pit is prepared for him [Col. 1062D].

“For the Lord will not cast off his people, nor forsake his inheritance, until justice is turned into judgment; and all who are upright in heart hold to it.” The Lord will indeed soothe his saints in evil days, whether in this life or another, so that they may have evil days neither here nor there. And it is therefore clear that the Lord will not cast off his people [Col. 1063A] or forsake his inheritance, as he himself says: “I will not desert you or forsake you” (John 14:18); and: “Behold, I am with you all days, even to the consummation of the age” (Matt. 28:20). Then justice will be turned into judgment, because then each person and all people will be examined and judged as to whether they possess justice or injustice. And who are those who either hold it now or will possess it then? All who are upright in heart. This is what is said elsewhere: “How good God is to Israel, to those who are upright in heart!” (Ps. 72:1). Those have an upright heart who walk the straight way and do not turn aside toward falsehood and iniquity.

“Who will rise up for me against evildoers? Or who will stand with me against those who work iniquity?” From this it is proved that the Lord will not forsake his inheritance and his Church, because he is the one who rises to help it against evildoers and stands with it to fight against those who work iniquity [Col. 1063B].

“Unless the Lord had helped me, my soul would almost have dwelt in hell.” Unless this had been so—unless the Lord had helped me—I was so often crushed by such great calamities that I would almost have succumbed; and thus my soul would have dwelt in hell. But you, my excellent helper, were always near at hand. This is what he says:

“If I said, ‘My foot has been moved,’ your mercy, O Lord, helped me.” [Note: [Col. 1063] “It is remarkable how God tests people: our very dangers make the one who delivers us sweeter to us.” Augustine, *Exposition on this Psalm*.] The foot is moved when the mind is turned from its stability and, through fear, begins to doubt what it ought to do [Col. 1063C].

“According to the multitude of my sorrows in my heart, your consolations, O Lord, have gladdened my soul.” This is what the Apostle says: “As the sufferings of Christ abound in us, so through Christ our consolation also abounds” (2 Cor. 1:5). The Church of God could not otherwise endure the adversities of this world unless the Lord had so mercifully aided it in its great necessities. Yet it has been proved that when it is wholly deprived of human assistance, divine aid is then close at hand.

“Will the seat of iniquity cleave to you, you who fashion labor in the commandment?” This is what is said elsewhere [Col. 1063D]: “For the wicked will not dwell beside you, nor will the unjust remain before your eyes” (Ps. 5:6). It is well said here that the seat of iniquity will not cleave to him, of whom he said above: “he will not forsake his inheritance.” For it is fitting that one who associates the good with himself should also repel the evil from himself. Wicked persons are called the seat of iniquity because iniquity sits and dwells in them. The Lord fashions suffering in the commandment because his commandments cannot be kept without labor and pain. Hence he himself says: “Whoever wishes to come after me, let him deny himself, take up his cross, and follow me” (Matt. 16:24). Therefore iniquity does not please him who loves such great justice and equity.

“They will hunt for the soul of the righteous, and condemn innocent blood.” He teaches us that by the seat of iniquity we should understand wicked persons. For they are the ones who hunt for the soul of the righteous and condemn innocent blood to death. But what is it to hunt for the soul of the righteous except to thirst eagerly for his destruction [Col. 1064A]?

“And the Lord has become my refuge, and my God the help of my hope.” The one who firmly hopes to have the Lord himself as refuge and helper need not greatly fear the snares and persecutions of wicked people, as that man says: “Let your mercy, O Lord, be upon us, as we have hoped in you” [Col. 1064B]. He would not have said this unless he had had firm hope in God.

“And the Lord will repay them their iniquities, and in their malice the Lord our God will destroy them.” This will occur at the judgment, when, for their iniquities—and especially because they persecuted the Church of God with such hatred—they will be cast into eternal fire. To repay iniquities is nothing other than to render the recompense due for iniquities.

## PSALM XCIV. A PRAISE-SONG OF DAVID HIMSELF

Not every song is praiseworthy; but that song is worthy of praise which is sung to Christ not only with the voice but also with the attention of the mind. This is what “of David himself” means.

[Col. 1064C] “Come, let us exult in the Lord; let us sing for joy to God our Savior.” The Prophet invites us to come together, exult in the Lord, sing for joy, sing, weep, adore, bless him, and fall down before his face.

“For he is the Lord our God, and we are his people and the sheep of his pasture.” Therefore it is fitting that we serve him and obey him in every way and in all things. To exult and sing for joy to God is to resound with worthy praises for him in immeasurable love, inwardly and outwardly, in heart and mouth. What is said in the title, “A praise-song of David himself,” is what is said here: “Let us sing for joy to God our Savior,” because our Savior is Christ, who is signified by David.

[Col. 1064D] “Let us come before his face in confession.” The Lord will come for judgment, and every eye will see him, as it is written: “All flesh shall see the salvation of God” (Luke 3:6). Let us therefore come before his face in confession, so that when he comes he may not regard us as strangers and unknown persons, but may meet us with a joyful countenance, cause his face to shine upon us, and have mercy upon us. “And in psalms let us sing for joy to him.” From this, perhaps, the Church throughout all nations adopted the custom of never ceasing, day and night, to sing joyfully to God in psalms. To sing in psalms is to keep the ten commandments of the law, since psalms are named from the psaltery, whose ten strings signify the ten commandments of the law [Col. 1065A].

“For the Lord is a great God, and a great king over all gods.” Therefore, he says, we ought to sing and rejoice because he is a great God, a great Lord, and a great king over all gods. This is what he says elsewhere: “Great is the Lord and exceedingly praiseworthy, and there is no end to his greatness” (Ps. 95:4). Let the other gods, therefore, be abandoned, and let him alone be worshiped, who is greatest and most powerful throughout the whole earth.

“For the Lord will not cast off his people, because all the ends of the earth are in his hand, and he beholds the heights of the mountains.” We are his people, and therefore we ought to praise him, because he will not cast us off—neither from himself nor from his praises. “For all the ends of the earth are in his hand.” This answers what he said: “For the Lord is a great God.” Great indeed is he in whose hand all things are enclosed. The hand of God means his power and might. “And he beholds the heights of the mountains” [Col. 1065B]. In this likewise he is shown to be great and exalted above all. This passage seems to accord with the saying: “The Lord is exalted, yet he regards the lowly, and knows the high from afar” (Ps. 137:6). What, then, should we understand by mountains but the loftier and more powerful people of this world? Since their heights do not please God, he is said to know them from afar. There are, however, other mountains by which the apostles are signified; since their heights are good, the Lord delights to see them [Col. 1065C]. The heights of the saints are virtues and honorable morals. One person is elevated and surpasses others by humility, another by patience, another by self-restraint, another by some other virtue.

“For the sea is his, and he made it; and his hands formed the dry land.” In this likewise the Lord is shown to be great, since he is said to have made the sea and the dry land. By the sea we may understand this world, and by the dry land the Church, which has been founded by the Lord in the midst of this sea in such a way that it cannot be moved by its storms and tempests. He made both, because he made both good and evil persons, and there is nothing that he did not make.

[Col. 1065D] “Come, let us adore and fall down before God; let us weep before the Lord who made us, because he is the Lord our God, and we are his people and the sheep of his pasture.” Again he invites us to come, adore, and weep, and wholly humble ourselves before God, the maker and creator of all things, who made and remade us and reformed us to the ancient image. We ought most justly to do this, “because he is the Lord our God.” If we do not serve God and our Lord, we are altogether ungrateful and abominable. “And we are his people and the sheep of his pasture.” It is great glory and great honor for us to be called both his people and his sheep [Col. 1066A]. We are that people of whom it is said: “A people whom I did not know has served me; at the hearing of the ear it obeyed me” (Ps. 17:44). We are his sheep if we possess humility and patience, delight in his pastures—by which the books of both Testaments are signified—and hear his voice. As he himself says: “My sheep hear my voice, and I, the Lord, know them, and give them eternal life; and they follow me” (John 10:27). And he himself is the one who daily admonishes us, saying:

“Today, if you hear his voice, do not harden your hearts, as in the provocation, according to the day of temptation in the wilderness.” Today, he says, if you hear the voice of him whose sheep and people you are, do not do as your fathers did—whose children you are indeed if you imitate them in the same unbelief [Col. 1066B]. He says this of those who, whenever they tempted him in the wilderness, provoked him to anger, proved disobedient, and therefore did not enter into the land promised to them. Of them it is said elsewhere: “How often they provoked him in the wilderness and stirred him to anger in a waterless land” (Ps. 77:40). We are therefore told not to imitate them and not to harden our hearts against hearing and receiving God’s commandments, lest similar things happen to us as well. They tested and saw God’s works—in the divided sea, Pharaoh drowned, water from the rock, manna from heaven, and many other things too lengthy to enumerate—and yet they did not believe his words or hear the Lord’s voice [Col. 1066C].

“For forty years I was near to this generation, and said: These always err in heart.” The Lord was near them for forty years, to guide and preserve them, and sometimes also to punish them; yet neither benefits nor chastisements removed the hardness of their heart. Hence there follows: “And I said: These always err in heart.” God’s “saying” was his seeing and knowing; it is as though he said: I saw that they were always wandering and persevering in wickedness. This is what he says:

“But they did not know my ways.” What does “they did not know my ways” mean except that they refused to walk in my ways? “To whom I swore in my wrath: If they shall enter into my rest” [Col. 1066D]. In saying that he swore, he shows that this is firm and unchangeable. The words “if they shall enter into my rest” are a threat. This figure of speech is called ellipsis, where something is always lacking for the completion of the sentence; one may supply, “let me not be believed,” or “I shall no longer be able,” or something else that seems fitting.

## PSALM XCV. WHEN THE HOUSE WAS BEING BUILT AFTER THE CAPTIVITY. A SONG FOR DAVID

[Note: [Col. 1065D] Saint Augustine also explained this title and psalm in an allegorical sense, teaching that it is not to be understood of the material temple built by Solomon [Col. 1066D], but of the new spiritual temple—that is, the Church—whose stones, as the Apostle says, are the faithful, and whose builder is Christ the Lord [Col. 1067D].]

David the prophet saw when the house was being built after the captivity, and commanded that this song be sung [Col. 1067A] for this David, that is, our Savior, by whom that house was built. This house is the holy Church, which our Savior built on the wood of the cross after the long captivity in which the devil possessed and held the whole human race. Likewise, under Jesus the high priest, the temple of the Lord was rebuilt after the Babylonian captivity, by which the captivity of which we now speak was signified.

“Sing to the Lord a new song; sing to the Lord, all the earth.” What the Prophet commanded in the title—that this song be sung for this David—is what he now says: “Sing to the Lord a new song,” because by David the Lord himself and our Savior is signified. Not the Jews alone but all the earth are invited to sing, because “God is not the God of the Jews only, but also of the nations,” as the Apostle says [Col. 1067B; Note: [Col. 1067D] These words are absent in the edition.] (Rom. 3:29). They ought to sing a new song: the song of the nativity, passion, resurrection, and ascension. These are new and unheard of before. Moreover, those sing the new song who follow not the oldness of the letter but the newness of spiritual understanding.

“Sing to the Lord, and bless his name.” It is fitting that he should invite to singing once, twice, and many times those who ought to sing not as one nation but as all nations, peoples, and races. Sing, he says, and by singing bless his name; that is, live, act, and preach in such a way that his name may be blessed in you. Bless the Son in the Father, the Father in the Son [Col. 1067C], and the Holy Spirit in both; this is his name, because these three are one God. Who can hear the apostles of Christ recounting his powers and miracles and proclaiming his mercies without immediately saying: “Blessed be the name of the Lord”? “Proclaim well from day to day his salvation.” Proclaim well, he says, steadfastly and wisely, from day to day, at every time and on each day, that salvation which the Lord has wrought among all nations. Of this it is said elsewhere: “God, our king before the ages, has wrought salvation in the midst of the earth” (Ps. 73:12).

“Declare among the nations his works, among all peoples his wonders.” This is what the apostles did [Col. 1067D], because, as it is written: “They went forth and preached everywhere, the Lord working with them and confirming the word by the signs that followed” (Mark 16:20). And elsewhere: “Their sound went forth into all the earth, and their words to the ends of the world” (Ps. 18:5).

“For the Lord is great and exceedingly praiseworthy; he is terrible above all gods.” He is terrible above all gods because all the gods of the nations are demons. He is praiseworthy because he made the heavens [Col. 1068A]. For who is so great, so praiseworthy, and so terrible as he who made all things? By naming the heavens which he made, he shows him to be creator of all things by the prerogative of the greater part.

“Confession and beauty are before him.” Confession seems to signify martyrdom, and beauty baptism. Of confessors the Lord says: “Whoever confesses me before human beings, I too will confess him before my Father” (Matt. 10:32). Of baptism: “Whoever believes and is baptized shall be saved” (Mark 16:16). Hence it is said elsewhere: “You shall wash me, and I shall be made whiter than snow” (Ps. 50:9). Such, therefore, will be before God who have been sanctified either by martyrdom or by baptism. Those who are sanctified by either means become both holy and great. This is what he says: “Holiness and magnificence are in his sanctuary.” [Note: [Col. 1067D] Although “in his sanctuary” should properly be understood here as referring to the holy place, our author, following Saint Augustine’s mystical interpretation, took it to refer to the particular holiness of a human being [Col. 1068D]. For he says on this passage: “You were already seeking magnificence: first love holiness. When you have been sanctified, you will also be magnificent. For if, in the wrong order, you first wish to be magnificent, you fall before you rise; for you do not rise, but are lifted up,” etc.] “Confession” may also be understood as repentance, since it too sanctifies and frees from sins.

“Bring to the Lord, kindreds of the nations; bring to the Lord glory and honor; bring to the Lord glory for his name.” Bring, he says, to the Lord, kindreds of the nations; and hear what you ought to bring: “Bring to the Lord glory and honor.” And what glory? “Bring to the Lord glory for his name.” What does “for his name” mean? For the honor of his name, or such glory as is fitting for his name. Great is his name; great must be the glory. His name contains all things; let his glory fill all things.

[Col. 1068C] “Take offerings and enter into his courts; adore the Lord in his holy court.” His holy court is the Church and the multitude of believers. He therefore wishes us to offer our sacrifices there, where they may be seen by many, so that our faith may not be hidden but manifest. Whoever has nothing else to offer the Lord should offer himself, his service, and his faith, because there is nothing greater that he can offer. If you have promised chastity, humility, patience, obedience, and things like these, you have offered a good sacrifice to the Lord. Do not be ashamed to adore the Lord before many, so that many may see you and receive a good example from you, so that in you may be fulfilled what is written: “Let your light so shine before human beings that they may see your good works and glorify your Father who is in heaven” [Col. 1068D] (Matt. 5:16).

“Let the whole earth be moved before his face.” You, as though he said, are his face, his image and likeness, because you were made in his image and likeness. Let the whole earth therefore be moved by you; let nothing of earthly corruption remain in you, so that you may be wholly reformed to the face and beauty of him in whose image you were made. “Say among the nations [Col. 1069A] that the Lord has reigned from the wood.” [Note: [Col. 1069D] The Vulgate has only: “The Lord has reigned.” This addition, “from the wood,” is also found in Saint Augustine, where he says that Christ the Lord began his reign from the wood of the cross—namely, in his victory over the devil and destruction of sin [Col. 1070D].] Those who are such are worthy to say such things. The Lord began to reign from the wood because through the wood he redeemed his kingdom. People did not formerly recognize their king; but after dominion was made upon his shoulder, the Lord was recognized and took up the reins of the kingdom. “Indeed, he has corrected the world, which shall not be moved.” A king is so called because he rules and corrects; and he proves that he is king because he ruled and corrected the world. We should understand not the whole world, but the better part of the world, namely the Christian people, which has been so corrected and instructed by its king that it shall never be separated or moved away from him. “He will judge peoples in equity.” This will be at the judgment, when he renders to each according to his works [Col. 1069B]. “And the nations in his wrath,” because they did not do his will. Hence it is said elsewhere: “The Lord has troubled them in his wrath, and fire shall devour them” (Ps. 20:10).

“Let the heavens rejoice, and let the earth exult; let the sea be moved, and its fullness.” These words express as great a joy as can be had in this life. This joy, then, will belong to the saints when the Lord judges peoples in equity. By the heavens are understood the apostles; by the earth, the Church; and by the sea and its fullness, all those regenerated by the waters of baptism. The Lord promised such fish to the apostles when he said: “Come after me, and I will make you fishers of men” (Mark 2:17).

“The fields and all things in them shall rejoice.” [Col. 1069C] What is signified by the sea and its fullness may also be understood through the fields and what is in them. “Then all the trees of the forests shall exult.” These likewise signify the things spoken of above. For human beings may be called fish of the sea, animals of the earth, and trees of the forest for different reasons. But why will all these rejoice and exult then? It follows: “Before the face of the Lord, because he comes, because he will come to judge the earth.” There will be a twofold joy: one because he first came to redeem and teach; the other because he will come to judge the earth. For unless he had first come to redeem, there would be no joy in the second advent. Therefore those will rejoice at the second advent who know that they were redeemed and chosen at the first [Col. 1069D], whether they have been fish of the sea, brute animals of the fields, or hard and fruitless trees of the forests. The Lord therefore comes to judge the earth. But how will he judge?

“He will judge the world in equity, and peoples in his truth.” This verse produces joy for the good and sorrow for the evil.

## PSALM XCVI. A PSALM OF DAVID HIMSELF, WHEN HIS LAND WAS RESTORED

What this Psalm says took place when the land was restored to David himself. For our Savior’s land was restored to him when the devil was overcome and [Col. 1070A] the world began to serve and believe in him. We may also understand by “his land” his own flesh, which, after he had left it dead on the cross, was restored to him alive on the third day.

“The Lord has reigned; let the earth exult; let many islands rejoice.” Let the earth, he says, exult; let the Church rejoice; let many islands rejoice, by which individual churches are signified. Although they are divided by distances of place, they are one in faith and love and make one Church. But why should they rejoice? Because the Lord has reigned, because his land and kingdom have been restored to him. Let them rejoice because they have a good ruler, having grieved for so long while oppressed beneath the devil’s harshest bondage. He, as though the Psalm says, was not recognized at his coming because he appeared humble, in the form of a servant, and did not wish to reveal his majesty in his first advent [Col. 1070B]. This is what it says:

“Cloud and darkness are round about him.” By cloud and darkness he means the flesh with which divinity was clothed and enveloped and therefore could not be seen. “If they had known him,” as the Apostle says, “they would never have crucified the Lord of glory” (1 Cor. 2:8). Of this cloud it is written: “Behold, the Lord will ascend upon a light cloud and enter Egypt, and all its idols shall fall together” (Isa. 19:1). From this cloud issue those rains by which the whole Church is watered. But when the Lord comes upon the throne of his majesty, then this cloud will not be dark; rather, it will appear in such splendor that by its brightness the sun will be obscured and [Col. 1070C] the moon lose its light. The foundation of that throne will be correction, justice, and judgment; and this is what it says: “Justice and judgment are the correction of his throne.” The whole world will be judged and corrected from this judicial throne. But how? Not unjustly or rashly, but in justice and judgment.

“And then fire shall go before him and shall burn his enemies round about.” After, he says, that throne has delivered the sentence of its correction, fire will immediately go before him “and burn his enemies round about,” so that the ungodly may pass from the temporal fire in which the world will burn into eternal fire, which will have no end.

“His lightnings shone upon the world; the earth saw and was shaken” [Col. 1070D]. Now he returns to the first coming, of which he had begun to speak at the beginning of the psalm, and recounts in order what was then done. He, as it were, concealed the power of his divinity; but his lightnings—by which we understand the apostles and teachers—plainly shone and gleamed for all. These lightnings, terrible both through the greatness of their voice and through the splendour of their miracles, moved the whole earth. This is what he says: “The earth saw and was shaken.” Some were moved for good, others for evil. Concerning this disturbance the Lord says: “Do not think that I have come to bring peace upon the earth; I have not come to bring peace, but a sword. For I have come to set son against his father, daughter against her mother, and daughter-in-law against her mother-in-law; and a man’s enemies are those of his own household” (Matt. 10:34).

“The mountains melted like wax before the face of the Lord; at the face of the Lord all the earth trembled.” Those whom he just called lightnings he now calls mountains. And the apostles are rightly called mountains, because they are higher than all others both in holiness and in knowledge. They melted like wax because they enlightened many others. He rightly said, “before the face of the Lord,” because it is fitting that such lampstands and such candles should always stand before the Lord’s face. “At the face of the Lord all the earth trembled.” What is “at the face of the Lord” except through the knowledge of truth? Therefore that earth trembled which deserved to know the Lord [Col. 1071B]; for “the fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom” (Ecclus. 1:17). Hence it continues:

“The heavens declared his righteousness, and all peoples saw his glory.” Behold, the apostles are again called heavens, so that they may be believed to be higher even than mountains. These are the heavens which proclaim and recount the righteousness and glory of God: namely, the glory of the resurrection and ascension, which those—and only those—peoples see who believe in Christ and receive the Christian faith.

“Let all who worship carved images be put to shame, who boast in their idols.” Worthy of every shame are those who, after the preaching of the apostles and such power and manifestation of miracles, are still not ashamed to worship idols and to boast in their images [Col. 1071C]. “Worship him, all his angels.” By the angels commanded to worship our Saviour we may understand not only angelic powers but also the apostles 508 and teachers, since *angels* means “messengers.”

“Zion heard and rejoiced.” This is what he said above: “Let the earth exult, and let the many islands rejoice.” Thus the same thing is signified by Zion, the earth, and the islands. Of these he further says: “And the daughters of Judah exulted because of your judgments, O Lord.” By the daughters of Judah are understood the individual churches or cities, which rejoice because they know that the judgments are true, and do not doubt that they will be avenged upon their enemies.

[Col. 1071D] “For you are the Lord Most High over all the earth; you are exceedingly exalted above all gods.” All, he says, ought to worship you, because you alone are Most High over all the earth, and every creature is subject to you, according to the words: “You have subjected all things under his feet” (Ps. 8:8). The Lord is exceedingly exalted above all gods, because not only demons, but even all the angels themselves, are subject to him.

“You who love the Lord, hate evil.” Nothing but evil is to be hated, for our God loves all his creation and hates evil alone [Col. 1072A]. Therefore whoever loves God should love every creature of God, but not evil, because evil is not God’s creature. Hence even wicked people are to be loved; but the vices in them, because they are evil, are not to be loved. “The Lord keeps the souls of his servants, and he delivered them from the hand of the sinner.” Hate evil, he says, and do not fear the wicked person. “Do not fear those who kill the body, because they cannot kill the soul” (Matt. 10:28). This is what he says: “The Lord keeps the souls of his servants; he delivered them from the hand of the sinner.”

[Note: [Col. 1071D] Cassiodorus explains this passage as referring to deliverance from sin: “He delivers souls from the hand of sinners when he does not allow them to be overthrown by any depravity, but rescues them unharmed, insofar as he knows them to be pleasing to himself.”]

They have power not over the soul but over the body alone. Hence it is said elsewhere: “The Lord keeps you from every evil” (Ps. 120:7). And lest you perhaps understand this of bodily afflictions, he added, saying [Col. 1072B]: “May the Lord keep your soul.”

“Light has arisen for the righteous, and joy for the upright in heart.” This light of which we have spoken thus far, he says, is our God, who is Most High over all the earth. This joy, at which Zion rejoiced and the daughters of Judah exulted, has not arisen for all, because it has not been received by all. For this light “came into his own, and his own did not receive him” (John 1:11). For whom, then, has it arisen? For the righteous and upright in heart, by whom we understand the Christian peoples. Hence it rightly continues: “Rejoice, you righteous, in the Lord,” because the Lord has been born for you; “and give thanks at the remembrance of his holiness,” because he has not forgotten his promise, but, coming and taking flesh, fulfilled whatever he had promised through the Law and the Prophets.

## PSALM XCVII. A PSALM OF DAVID HIMSELF.

[Col. 1072C]

What *of David himself* signifies is sufficiently clear. In this psalm, *of David himself* signifies the same thing that *unto the end* signifies in the preceding psalms.

“Sing to the Lord a new song, for the Lord has done wonderful things.” The Jews do not understand this; and therefore, remaining in the oldness of the letter, they kill themselves. For the Apostle also says: “The letter kills, but the Spirit gives life; Christ is the end of the Law” (2 Cor. 3:6), because in him the letter has come to its end; and after him, to understand the Law according to the letter is a grave sin. Therefore let us sing to the Lord a new song: a song of his birth, passion, resurrection [Col. 1072D], and ascension. For these are the wonders which the Lord is here said to have done. What is more wonderful than Christ’s birth? What more wonderful than his resurrection and ascension? And what more wonderful than his passion, in which his own right hand saved him and, by dying, overcame all his enemies? This is what he says:

“His right hand saved him, and his holy arm.” He had no need to seek help elsewhere; his own right hand and the strength of his own arm were sufficient for him. Christ’s death was voluntary, not due to weakness. He died because he willed it—he who, had he not willed it, could never have been killed. He now begins to recount [Col. 1073A] how these wonders were accomplished; and he says that God the Father did this, who did not spare his own Son, but ordained that he should both become incarnate and die for us all. This is what he says:

“The Lord has made known his salvation; before the sight of the nations he has revealed his righteousness.” The salvation of God is Christ, who, born of the Virgin, has been made well known to us by many proofs. Hence the Apostle says: “I judged that I should know nothing among you except Jesus Christ, and him crucified” (1 Cor. 2:2). Likewise the blessed apostle Peter says: “You are Christ, the Son of the living God” (Matt. 16:17). As to the words, “Before the sight of the nations he has revealed his righteousness,” 509 we must understand either Christ himself or the evangelical preaching, which was made manifest among all nations both through him [Col. 1073B] and through his disciples. Hence the Apostle says: “I am not ashamed of the Gospel, for it is the power of God unto righteousness for everyone who believes” (Rom. 1:16).

“He was mindful of his mercy toward Jacob, and of his truth toward the house of Israel.” If it is said that Jacob was mindful of God’s mercy, and the house of Israel likewise, the meaning is plain; but it differs greatly from the other translation. For the other translation signifies this: that “God was mindful of his mercy which he promised to Jacob, and of his truth which he promised to the house of Israel.” Therefore, so that both translations may agree, let it be said thus: he was mindful of his mercy, which he promised to the sons of Jacob, and of his truth, as he promised to the sons of the house of Israel.

[Note: [Col. 1073D] Cassiodorus reconciles the two translations thus: “And lest the dissimilarity of the different names confuse our understanding, let us examine why it was added, ‘and of his truth toward the house of Israel’: so that we may understand this gift to have been given not only to the people called Christians after the Lord’s coming, but also to those who believed that he would be born of a Virgin.”]

Jacob and Israel signify the same thing, by whom we understand the Christian people, who both supplants vices and sees God by the inward sight of the mind [Col. 1073C]. Yet in this life it may rightly be called Jacob, and in the other Israel. This people has always been, and will be, mindful of God’s mercy and truth. Nor was God unmindful of it; rather, he faithfully fulfilled what he promised.

“All the ends of the earth have seen the salvation of our God.” This is what is said elsewhere: “Their sound has gone out into all the earth, and their words unto the ends of the world” (Ps. 18:4). To see, moreover, is to know. At the judgment, however, both good and evil will see him also with bodily eyes. Hence it is written: “All flesh shall see the salvation of God” (Luke 3:6).

“Make joyful noise to God, all the earth; sing, exult [Col. 1073D], and make melody.” These words indicate great joy, because making joyful noise, exulting, singing, and making melody appear to signify nothing other than joy and gladness. Yet jubilation is inward, while the rest are outward acts. Attend, then, to how you ought to make melody.

“Make melody to our God with the harp, and with the harp.” He has set down two harps, one of which I think belongs to the New Testament, the other to the Old [Col. 1074A]. He therefore wishes holy preachers to confirm and proclaim the mystery of the Trinity by the authority of both Testaments. For we have often already said that three or four strings suffice in the Church; and what that signifies has often been stated. As for the voice of the psalm, since the whole Church everywhere resounds day and night, why should we seek another explanation?

“With beaten-metal trumpets and the voice of a horn trumpet, make joyful noise before the King, the Lord.” The Jews had both horn trumpets and silver trumpets, by which they urged the people now to battle, now to return to camp and rest. By these we may understand the long and extended, bright and clear discourses of the saints, through which they teach and preach to God’s people [Col. 1074B], and make joyful noise to the Lord before the sight of their King. They ought to rejoice with great propriety, sweetness, and wisdom; for there is nothing that is not before his sight. He sees all things, and nothing can hide itself from him.

“Let the earth be moved, and its fullness; the world, and all who dwell in it.” There was nothing which was not moved by this clear and magnificent sound of trumpets and harps: some opposing it, others praising and blessing God.

“The rivers shall clap their hands together.” Rivers could not clap their hands unless they signified peoples. But, as it is written, “many waters, many peoples.” Therefore the rivers clap together, because many peoples persevere with one harmonious voice in the praises of God [Col. 1074C]. “The mountains exulted before the face of the Lord.” This has already been explained in other psalms, and it has often been said that mountains signify the apostles. They are said to exult because the Lord both came and will come: first to redeem, but second to judge the earth. The following words will make plain how he will judge.

“He will judge the world in righteousness, and peoples in equity.” This is what is said elsewhere: “He will render to each according to his works” (Matt. 16:27).

## 510 PSALM XCVIII. A PSALM OF DAVID.

Since it has often been said what *a psalm of David* signifies, it needs no exposition [Col. 1074D].
