“The Lord has reigned; let the peoples be angry; he who sits above the Cherubim—let the earth be moved.” I said it once, I said it again; now I say it a third time: “The Lord has reigned.” And I said it so that the peoples might be angry and confounded, because, whether they wish it or not, the Lord has reigned.

[Note: [Col. 1074D] Saint Augustine has very briefly embraced the contents of this psalm: “Let your charity, then, attend with us to this psalm,” he says, “and let us seek Christ here. Surely he will appear to those who seek him, he who first appeared to those who did not seek him; and he will not forsake those who desire him, he who redeemed those who neglected him.”]

Let good peoples be angry against those who until now afflicted and held them captive [Col. 1075A]. Let them hear the Apostle saying: “Let sin no longer reign in your mortal body” (Rom. 6:12). Nor is it fitting, when the Lord reigns, that they should allow another to reign over them. But which Lord has reigned? Certainly he who sits above the Cherubim. *Cherubim* is interpreted “fullness of knowledge”; by them we may understand the apostles, whom the Holy Spirit filled with the fullness of all knowledge. It belongs to the praise of our Saviour whether he is said to sit above these Cherubim or above those other Cherubim. For these and those, and every creature, are subject to him; he sits over every order of angels and human beings and holds dominion. What is now said—“let the earth be moved”—is what was said above: “let the peoples be angry.”

[Col. 1075B] “The Lord is great in Zion, and exalted above all peoples.” This Lord of ours, he says, who began to reign from the time of his passion, is greater and more exalted in heaven, on earth, above angels, and above all human beings. But if you wish to know how great the Lord is, go to Zion; proceed to the Church, and there you will be able to know how great the Lord is. For there his greatness, power and strength, honour and glory are proclaimed without ceasing by all. Hence it continues:

“Let them give thanks to your great and terrible name, for it is holy.” The name of Christ is indeed great, terrible, and holy; at its invocation the dead are raised, demons flee, lepers are cleansed, and all diseases and infirmities are healed [Col. 1075C]. We ought always to praise and proclaim it. And why is this? “Because the honour of the King loves judgment” (Ps. 98:4). The honour of the King is praise and proclamation. Therefore those who praise and proclaim the King—Christ is so interpreted—with sincere affection in this life will not fear at the judgment; for they would not love it if they feared it. But since it has been said that “the honour of the King loves judgment,” confession makes it possible for us not to fear judgment but rather to love it.

“You have prepared equity; you have accomplished judgment and righteousness in Jacob.”

[Note: [Col. 1075D] The Vulgate reads: “You have prepared directions.”]

You, he says, have prepared and accomplished such a judgment that it ought rightly to be called not merely equitable but equity itself. Who, then, does not love your judgment, provided that he has honoured your name? Let those fear who have opposed you and blasphemed your name. “And you have accomplished righteousness in Jacob.” If we understand this of carnal Jacob, who does not cease daily to blaspheme Christ’s holy and terrible name, righteousness has been accomplished in him in part [Col. 1076A], because he has been scattered among all nations.

“Exalt the Lord our God.” Exalt him, he says; proclaim and honour him, because, as we have just said, the honour of the King loves judgment, and whoever worthily proclaim and honour him will receive reward and honour at the judgment. “And worship his footstool, for it is holy.” Our Saviour is both God and man. Every human being, moreover, is earth; and earth is God’s footstool. Thus the Lord himself says: “Heaven is my throne, but earth is the footstool of my feet” (Acts 7:49). Therefore we ought to worship his footstool, that is, the humanity of our Saviour, because it is holy, as the angel said to the Virgin: “The Holy Spirit shall come upon you, and the power of the Most High [Col. 1076B] shall overshadow you; therefore the holy thing which shall be born from you shall be called the Son of God” (Luke 1:35). He is the one whom Abraham worshipped when, standing by the oak of Mamre, he saw three men coming to him and worshipped one (Gen. 18:1–3). He is the one whom Moses and Aaron served, and whose name they invoked. Hence it continues:

“Moses and Aaron were among his priests, and Samuel among those who invoke his name.” Moses and Aaron, according to the letter, were not priests.

[Note: [Col. 1075D] Moses, indeed, was not properly a priest, though Aaron certainly was, as is found in Exodus chapter 28, where we read that God commanded which garments he should use in the ministry of the priesthood: “And you shall speak,” God says to Moses, “to all who are wise in heart, whom I have filled with the spirit of wisdom; and they shall make the garments of Aaron, in which, having been sanctified, he may minister to me.” Augustine understood this passage in this way; yet, relying on the authority of the psalm, he called Moses a priest because he always presented the vows of the peoples before God, which is shown to be the office of a priest. Therefore, as Cassiodorus says, he too is here called a priest, since, when the Lord was angry, he pleaded for the people with great prayers.]

Yet they are called a royal priesthood, a holy nation, and a people for possession. Thus, although they do not perform a priest’s office, all who live a priestly and religious life are priests.

[Col. 1076C] “They invoked the Lord, and he heard them; and he spoke to them in a pillar of cloud.” These men, he says, and all the rest invoked this King and Saviour of ours, and no other; and he, and no other, heard them. “And he spoke to them in a pillar of cloud.” He who then spoke in a pillar of cloud would afterwards speak in a pillar of flesh: first veiled in cloud, afterwards in flesh.

[Note: [Col. 1076D] “In a pillar of cloud. Therefore the Lord spoke to them in this form, which announced the future structure of the Church. But because he then spoke words to them through a cloud, he has deigned to speak and appear more plainly to us through his holy footstool, that is, through the Incarnation.” Cassiodorus.]

He could indeed be heard, but could not be seen. Wretched Jews, these things alone could have sufficed for you, if the letter did not deceive and kill you. A cloud still stands before you, lest you should be able to see him through it. “For blindness has happened in part to Israel, so that seeing they may not see and hearing they may not understand” (Rom. 11:25).

“They kept his testimonies and his commandments, which he gave them.” Therefore he is the one who gave the Law; he is the one who wrote the tablets; and he is to be believed the one and same author, Lord, and lawgiver of both Testaments. Lord our God, who became man, who was born of the Virgin, who was crucified [Col. 1077A], rose from the dead, ascended into heaven, and willed to become a footstool—you, and no other, heard them. “O God, you were gracious to them.” Who can enumerate all the acts of propitiation which the Lord performed for that people? Yet the Lord punished their sins in this life, lest he destroy them in the other. This is what he says: “And avenging all their undertakings.” Thus he was most gracious to them precisely when he took vengeance for their transgressions.

“Exalt the Lord our God, and worship upon his holy mountain, for the Lord our God is holy.” You have heard, as though he said, who, what kind, and how great the Lord our God is. Exalt him; worship him—you who are upon his holy mountain, who know him and dwell in the Church. For the Lord our God is holy [Col. 1077B], who for your sake and for your sins was willing to be reckoned among the wicked.

## PSALM XCIX. A PSALM IN CONFESSION.

This entire psalm pertains to joy and seems to sound nothing but cheerful and pleasant things. Therefore it ought always to be sung in confession, in hymns, praises, and thanksgiving.

[Note: [Col. 1077D] Saint Jerome gives the title: “A song in thanksgiving.” Indeed, according to Cassiodorus, we make a twofold confession: “One is when, bewailing our sins, we confess ourselves guilty and liable, and implore through devout tears that the Lord’s mercy be granted to us. The other is when we praise benefits bestowed either upon ourselves or upon others, revering them with great exultation.”]

“Make joyful noise to God, all the earth.” We have often already said that jubilation is the ineffable joy which the mind possesses from contemplating heavenly blessedness. Therefore the Prophet wishes all the earth to make joyful noise to the Lord and, putting aside all things that are in the world, to be held by love and desire for God alone, serving God in gladness. Many serve God, but not in gladness, because they do so unwillingly rather than freely. The Apostle teaches us to serve in gladness when he says [Col. 1077C]: “Rejoice in the Lord always; again I say, rejoice. Let your gentleness be known to all people; for the Lord is near” (Phil. 4:4). Likewise the Prophet exhorts the Church, saying: “Rejoice, barren woman who does not bear; break forth and cry out, you who do not travail; because the children of the desolate are more numerous than those of her who has a husband” (Isa. 54:1; Gal. 4:27).

“Enter before his presence with exultation.” For if everything that exists is before his presence and nothing can hide itself from his eyes, where were these persons who are commanded to enter before his presence? In a certain sense they both are and are not before his presence [Col. 1077D]. Those are not before him of whom the Lord will say: “Amen I say to you, I do not know you” (Matt. 25:12). But those are before his presence who are worthy of that vision. To enter before his presence, therefore, is nothing other than for a person to prepare himself, so that the Lord may deign to look upon him. Everything ought to be done in exultation, joy, and spiritual gladness.

[Col. 1078A] “Know that the Lord himself is God.” And how do you prove this? “Because he made us, and not we ourselves.” Therefore he alone is God, who made all things, and not those whom humans made. Of them it is written: “The idols of the nations are silver and gold, the works of human hands.” You did not make your son, nor did your father make you; God alone made us, and we did not make ourselves. What, then, are we?

“But we are his people and the sheep of his pasture.” He, he says, is our God, Lord, and Creator; but we are his people, created and made by him, and delivered from the devil’s power. We are also the sheep of his pasture, all of us who hear his voice. For he himself says: “My sheep hear my voice, and I know them” (John 10:27). This is [Col. 1078B] that pasture of which he says elsewhere: “He placed me in a place of pasture” (Ps. 22:1), by which the books of both Testaments are signified.

“Enter his gates in confession, his courts in hymns of confession.” He seems to speak of the gates of the heavenly Jerusalem, because he invites those who are in the Church. And since we have already entered these gates, he exhorts us also to enter those. But we cannot enter them except in hymns and confessions. Therefore it is first necessary that we confess our sins.

[Note: [Col. 1077D] Let those who rarely confess hear Augustine: [Col. 1078D] “It is difficult in this life for a person to be so changed that nothing may be found in him deserving rebuke. You must rebuke yourself, lest he rebuke you who will condemn you.” *Exposition on this Psalm.*]

Then, in hymns of confession, we may reach his courts. Hence it is written: “Confess your sins to one another, and pray for one another, that you may be saved” (Jas. 5:16). Since praise is not precious in the mouth of a sinner [Col. 1078C], the confession of sins must precede that confession which pertains to praise and jubilation. One kind of confession will exist both here and there; the other will not exist there, for no one will confess sin where there will be no sin.

“Praise his name, for the Lord is gracious; his mercy is forever, and his truth unto age upon age.” This praise will have no end, because the Lord will be praised both in the Church for as long as it is here and afterwards in the heavenly Jerusalem—praised eternally and unto age upon age for his graciousness, mercy, and truth. To praise the Lord and to praise the Lord’s name are one and the same thing.

## PSALM C. A PSALM OF DAVID HIMSELF.

[Col. 1078D]

When it says *of David himself*, it must be understood of our Saviour, to whom the Church speaks in this psalm and whom it praises for mercy and truth.

[Note: [Col. 1078D] A psalm signifies holy activity. “Where *of David himself* is placed, everything is applied to Christ’s powers; so that you should understand nothing of that earthly king, but understand that everything was said of the heavenly one.” Cassiodorus.]

“I will sing of mercy and judgment to you, O Lord.” The fiftieth psalm is full of mercy throughout; but this hundredth psalm exalts judgment [Col. 1079A], and says that all sinners are to be slain in the morning. The Church therefore rightly praises him for mercy and proclaims his judgment, in which it knows sinners are to be punished. “I will make melody and understand in the blameless way, when you come to me.” — “Blessed are the blameless in the way, who walk in the law of the Lord” (Ps. 118:1). Such people indeed make melody well, both in voice and in deed; for they make melody by walking. And what is greater, they say that they make melody in such a way as to understand when the Lord will come to them. For those who sleep cannot know or understand when the Lord will come to them. But those who are watchful and attentive cannot be taken unawares. Hence the Lord says: “Watch, because you do not know at what hour your Lord [Col. 1079B] will come” (Mark 13:35). They must therefore watch so that they may see and recognize the coming Judge from afar. This is what the Church now says: I will make melody, and I will make melody in such a manner that I may understand and know when you come to me. I shall not doze or sleep, but shall watch and sing, and be attentive so that I may perceive and behold you while you are still coming from afar. The Church now recounts its life and conduct in this world, that we may be taught by its example how we too ought to live.

“I walked in the innocence of my heart, in the midst of my house.”

[Note: [Col. 1079] An edition lacking this verse is supplemented and corrected.]

“I walked,” he says, “the path of your commandments,” by running and keeping them. Of this path the Apostle says: “I have fought the good fight, I have finished the course [Col. 1079C], I have kept the faith” (2 Tim. 4:7). But how did I walk? “In the innocence of my heart.” If innocence is in the heart, wickedness will not be in one’s deeds. “For out of the heart,” the Lord says, “come evil thoughts, murders, perjuries, false testimonies, and the other things which defile a person” (Matt. 15:19). Let us hear where she walked: “In the midst of my house.” By the house of God may be understood either the whole people of Christians or this world; but by the Church which speaks here we ought to understand the more perfect persons. It walks in the innocence of its heart in the midst of God’s house because it provides to good and evil, believers and unbelievers alike, a good example through its holy and upright conduct. Hence the Lord says: “Let your light so shine [Col. 1079D] before people that they may see your good works and glorify your Father who is in heaven” (Matt. 5:16).

“I did not set an evil thing before my eyes.” She surely would have set it there if she herself did evil things or consented to those who did them. But she did not do this. What, then, did she do? “I hated,” she says, “those who commit transgression. And a perverse heart did not cling to me.” Transgressors are those who go beyond the law laid upon them. Now this law has been laid upon us: to turn away from evil and do good. But who is there who never stumbles in this command? Therefore, by “those who commit transgression” we understand those who never return to repentance, but persevere at all times in evil deeds. Such people are worthy of hatred because they are condemned before God. They have a perverse, unyielding heart, hardened in wickedness to such a degree that it cannot receive the words of life.

“I did not know the malicious who turn away from me.” For malicious people are all those who turn away from the Church and avoid receiving its saving words. The Church does not know them; rather, it regards them as unbelievers, wholly alien and estranged, and does not share the divine sacraments with them.

“The one who secretly slandered his neighbour, him I persecuted.” Slander is a great sin, on account of which the Church is so moved that [Col. 1080B] it inflicts persecution upon the slanderers themselves. The Church’s persecution is carried out through interdictions and excommunications. Those who slander secretly are not without hatred, and such persons are counted among murderers. Our neighbour means every Christian, because he is both our brother and the child of the same Father. To slander is to seek to diminish another’s own goodness.

“With proud eye and insatiable heart, I did not eat with him.” He rightly marked the proud by the eye, because nowhere can pride be detected so much as in uplifted eyes and brows. Pride is the beginning of every sin; elsewhere it is said of it: “Let not the foot of pride come against me” (Ps. 35:12). For it is pride that caused even the angels to fall. By the insatiable heart, moreover, the avaricious are signified; and he seems to have put the definition in place of the thing defined. For the avaricious person is one who has an insatiable heart [Col. 1080C]. The Apostle commanded that one should not even take food with such a person. Such persons, therefore, are most rightly separated from Christ’s body.

“My eyes were upon the faithful of the earth, that they might sit with me.” Those people, as though she said, I drove away and separated from myself; but I looked mercifully upon the faithful and joined them to myself. The faithful of the earth are all who hold the catholic faith in the Church and faithfully serve God. The Church therefore wishes such persons to sit and dwell with her, and to judge with her. “He who walks in a blameless way ministered to me.” The ministers of the Church are bishops and priests. The Lord himself, showing himself to be a minister, says: “I came not to be ministered to, but to minister” (Matt. 20:18). Therefore the Church chose for ministry those who are blameless and without fault. Hence the vessels of the altar are commanded to be of purest gold, and no vessel ministers at the altar except those that are of the purest gold [Col. 1080D].

“He who commits pride shall not dwell in the midst of my house.” Under the name of pride all vices and sins are contained. But this is to be understood of that pride which reaches such obstinacy that it utterly scorns to humble itself and return to repentance [Col. 1081A]. This is characteristic of malignant spirits. Hence the Apostle says: “Let no temptation seize you except what is human” (1 Cor. 10:13). — “He who speaks iniquitous things did not walk straight before my eyes.” This seems to be said particularly of heretics, who direct neither themselves nor others into the Church, but turn away from it whomever they can.

“In the morning I was slaying all the sinners of the earth.”

[Note: [Col. 1081D] Augustine’s exposition of this passage is quite long; we shall offer part of its conclusion. “What,” he says, “does ‘in the mornings’ mean? When the day comes—that is, the day of death—when the night of life has passed, ‘in the mornings I was slaying all the sinners of the earth.’ Why does he spare them until morning? Because it was night. What does ‘it was night’ mean? Because it was a time for sparing: he spared while human hearts were hidden. For it is night, and God endures all, because he is long-suffering. He endures them in order that sinners may turn to him; but those who do not correct themselves during this time of mercy will be slain.”

Cassiodorus explains the passage differently: “By ‘in the mornings,’ he means at the very beginnings: when diabolical suggestions begin to appear in us like doubtful dawn-light, then they ought to be cast out by prayer; then driven back by abhorrent execration, lest, gradually growing harmful, they seize us like a most clouded day.”]

Therefore, as was shown above, the Church drove away proud transgressors, the avaricious, malicious persons, slanderers, and deceivers, and avoided their company because it saw that all such persons stood condemned before God. Hence it says that it slew all sinners in the morning, because it judged that they were to be condemned and slain at the judgment [Col. 1081B]. Thus by its own sentence the Church has already condemned and slain all those whom it knows are to be condemned at the judgment. This manner of speaking is often found in the divine page. Thus Moses, writing concerning lepers, commands the priest to confine them for seven days and, if he sees that the leprosy has increased, “he shall declare them unclean” (Lev. 13:6). What does “he shall declare them unclean” mean except that he shall judge them to be unclean? That day is called morning because it will be the end of this age and the beginning of another. This, the Church says, I did, “that I might destroy from the city of the Lord”—that is, from the heavenly Jerusalem—“all who work iniquity,” by whom we understand those who persevere in wickedness. But what does “that I might destroy” mean except “that I might show them to be destined for destruction” [Col. 1081C]?

### Psalm 101. Prayer of a Poor Man When He Is Anxious and Pours Out His Petition Before the Lord

This title is plain and needs no exposition. Every person is poor in that in which he needs another’s assistance. This, then, is the prayer of all those who implore divine help in their necessities.

> “Lord, hear my prayer, and let my cry come to you. Do not turn your face away from me. On whatever day I am afflicted, incline your ear to me; on whatever day I call upon you, hear me swiftly.”

These poor persons who speak here are those who make themselves poor willingly, and who, leaving all things behind, followed the Lord. Of them the Apostle says: “As having nothing, and yet possessing all things” (2 Cor. 6:10). They themselves teach us with what urgency, with what disposition of mind, and with what devotion of heart we ought to pray to God, when, repeating and reiterating the same words, they say one and the same thing so many times. Such seems to be the case when we say again and again, many times, “Kyrie eleison”—“Lord, have mercy.” Prayers please the Lord not so much by their composition as by the disposition of the mind.

> “For my days have failed like smoke, and my bones have been scorched as in a frying-pan.”  
> [Note: Col. 1082D. The Vulgate reads: “And my bones have dried up like fuel”; Cardinal Thommasio explains this as follows: “And my bones and limbs have dried up as though scorched in a frying-pan, and, like dry wood, are easily burned.”]

We were made immortal; but because of the sin of our first parent, we have come to such brevity of days that our days are not undeservedly compared to smoke, since amid tears, darkness, and every bitterness they quickly fail. “And my bones have been scorched as in a frying-pan.” This indeed often happens even literally to the saints, since both by voluntary affliction and by calamity coming upon them from elsewhere, they are burned and tormented beyond measure. By the bones of the Church we may also understand the apostles themselves and the other stronger members, who endured no lesser torments than if they had been scorched in a frying-pan.

> “I have been struck down like grass, and my heart has withered.”

Truly the people are grass: “The grass has dried up, and the flower has fallen” (Isa. 40:8). All human beings are struck down like grass; when struck down, they die, and immediately, deprived of every greenness, every flower, and every joy, they fail and wither, and dust is turned into dust. For when he says that the very heart, in which all life resided, has withered, he sufficiently makes known the misery of the other members. But let us hear why this happens to him.

[Col. 1082C]

> “Because,” he says, “I have forgotten to eat my bread.”

All people still follow the example of the first parent, who, though abounding in every abundance, forgot the bread granted to him for eating, approached the forbidden tree, and ate food prohibited to him. So we too more willingly hear and do those things forbidden to us than those by which souls live and without which they cannot live. For then the soul eats its bread when it does those things by which it is led to eternal life.

> “At the sound of my groaning, my bones clung to my flesh.”

For what could a person so stricken and wounded do but suffer pain and groan? At the sound of so great a groaning, both bones and flesh were joined together, because both felt the common pain. What do the bones of the Church signify but its stronger members? The flesh, however, denotes the weaker and more imperfect. Therefore both the perfect and the imperfect are joined together in this: that in bodily sufferings, in groaning and pain, and in death itself, they do not differ. Thus some are like the pelican, some the night-raven, and others the sparrow, so that they can scarcely bring aid to such great weakness. And this is what he says:

> “I have become like a pelican in the wilderness, and I have become like a night-raven in its dwelling; I have kept watch, and have become like a solitary sparrow on the roof.”

Let Elijah and John the Baptist, Antony, Hilarion, and blessed Benedict be examples to us: fleeing human society, like the pelican, they chose the solitary life. The pelican is a bird as large as a stork; delighting exceedingly in solitude, it suffers such scarcity of food that it can scarcely cling to its bones.  
[Note: Col. 1083D. According to Jerome and Cassiodorus, the pelican is an Egyptian bird resembling storks in bodily size, always afflicted by natural leanness; they say there are two kinds, aquatic and winged. But St Augustine doubts whether this creature really exists, saying: “This bird, therefore, if indeed it is truly so, has a great likeness to the flesh of Christ, by whose blood we have been made alive.” Col. 1084D.]

Such, then, were those religious men of whom we have just spoken; so many thousands of people imitate them even to the present day that the walls of the heavenly Jerusalem seem to be built especially from them. Jeremiah speaks of such persons, saying: “It will be good for a man when he has borne the yoke from his youth; he shall sit alone and be silent” (Lam. 3:17).

A person may also be solitary in a city, if he does not entangle himself in worldly business, but devotes himself to vigils, fasts, reading, and prayer. The night-raven, also called the owl, is well known to us: it appears not by day but by night, and spends the whole night in some sort of song and in watchfulness. The righteous man is likened to it, when, having become like a night-raven in its dwelling—that is, in the elevation of his own body—he says that he kept watch. [Col. 1083C] It is as though he said: “I became like a night-raven in its dwelling,” namely because I kept watch. Watchfulness alone, then, produces this resemblance between them: its watchfulness is on the summit of houses; his watchfulness is on the summit of the eyes.

Of such watchfulness the Lord says: “Watch, because you know neither the day nor the hour” (Matt. 25:13). And again: “Watch and pray, lest you enter into temptation” (Matt. 26:41). And the Apostle says: “Watch and pray; stand firm in faith; act courageously; be strengthened in the Lord; let all that you do be done in charity” (1 Cor. 16:15). He watches well who perseveres in good work. Would that we all watched thus and were thus like owls, so that in the dark night of this life we might not sleep but persist in good works.

> “And I have become like a solitary sparrow on a building.”

It belongs to great humility that he wished to compare himself to a sparrow. For the sparrow is a small bird, both in body and in price, as the Lord says in the Gospel: “Are not two sparrows sold for an as?” (Matt. 10:75.) This man who humbles himself so greatly had read that “everyone who exalts himself shall be humbled, and whoever humbles himself shall be exalted” (Matt. 23:12). For the Lord casts down the mighty from their seat and exalts the humble. He says not only that he is a sparrow, but also solitary and alone: one with no household, no riches, and in need of daily food. He is “on a building” who is not separated from the Church.  
[Note: Col. 1084D. Another exposition of the Psalms made by St Bruno is mentioned; it is lacking along with his other writings.]

These matters have been explained differently in that exposition which I made upon another translation of the Psalms; whoever wishes to hear it may read it there and become acquainted with it.

> “All day long my enemies reproached me, and those who praised me swore against me.”

Holy persons always have enemies and adversaries; there are never lacking those who lie in wait for them and speak ill of them. It often happens that those who first praised them later, led by envy, conspire against and persecute them. We read that this happened to our Savior himself and to the apostles. Nor would examples be lacking to us, had we chosen to provide more.

> “For I ate ashes like bread, and mingled my drink with weeping.”

“My enemies reproached me and slandered me,” he says, “because I received everyone and joined even idolaters converted to repentance to myself.” For as great as is the difference between ashes and bread, so great is the difference between sinners and saints. Thus the blessed apostle Peter was commanded to eat ashes like bread when a sheet full of unclean animals was shown to him and he heard the Lord say from above: “Kill and eat” (Acts 10:13). They mingled their drink with weeping because they joined such people, mourning and weeping, to themselves at their table.

This is why the Jews, reviling our Savior, said: “Why does your master eat and drink with tax collectors and sinners?” (Mark 2:6.) This is why the Pharisees murmured concerning Zacchaeus, because he had gone in to lodge with a sinful man (Luke 19:7). Likewise, one said: “If this man were a prophet, he would surely know what kind of woman this is who touches him, because she is a sinner” (Luke 7:39).

> “From before your wrath and indignation, because, lifting me up, you dashed me down.”

Because of your wrath and indignation, as though he said, I do not doubt that all the things mentioned above happened to me. For at the very beginning of my creation, after greatly exalting and raising me up, and forming me in your image and likeness, you justly dashed me down because of my disobedience, and subjected me, once immortal, to the laws of death. I had been so created by you that, had I not sinned, I would never have experienced either death or the miseries and sufferings of the flesh.

> “My days declined like a shadow, and I withered like grass.”

From the time, he says, when, lifting me up, you dashed me down, my days declined like a shadow, passed with every swiftness, and I, like grass, having lost the greenness and beauty of the flower, withered; made from dust, I returned into dust. Moreover, our days pass like a shadow if our works imitate only the likeness of truth and do not possess truth itself.

> “But you, O Lord, remain forever, and your memorial endures unto age upon age.”

Our days, he says, quickly fail; but you, Lord, remain forever, in whom all things live and endure, even if they seem to have failed. Therefore our hope is firm in you, and let us not wholly fail even though we seem to fail. Your memorial thus remains unto age upon age, because remembrance of you will never fail among your saints.

[Col. 1085B]

> “You, rising up, will have mercy on Zion, because the time has come to show her mercy.”

Zion itself, speaking all these things, is the Church of God. Every day the Lord rises up to help, and every day he has mercy on his Church. “Because the time has come to show her mercy”: from the time when her Savior suffered for her. Thus the Apostle says: “Behold, now is the acceptable time; behold, now is the day of salvation” (2 Cor. 6:2).

> “For your servants have delighted in her stones, and they will have pity on her earth.”

These servants are the apostles and the rest who build the walls of that city. It is fitting, therefore, that the Lord should love and have mercy upon that city whose walls are made of such precious stones that not only the stones of its walls, but the entire land with its appurtenances, are shown to please its very builders. These are the stones of which it is said: “Living stones roll upon the earth,”  
[Note: Col. 1085D. The Vulgate has: “And the Lord their God shall save them in that day, as the flock of his people, because holy stones shall be raised up over his land” (Zech. 9:16).]  
by which holy and catholic men are signified.

> “For the Lord has built Zion, and he shall be seen in his majesty.”

From what did he build it, except from the stones gathered from among the nations? But where shall he be seen in his majesty except in this Zion, his city? For here the Lord is known and proclaimed exalted by all.

> “And he looked upon the prayers of the poor, and did not despise their petitions.”

It is well said here that the Lord looked upon the prayers of the poor, since this Psalm is entitled *Prayer of the Poor*. The poor are all the saints, because they place no hope in the uncertainty of riches; yet they are rich in spiritual riches, which no one can steal from them.

> “Let these things be written.” And why should they be written? “For another generation.” And why this? “And the people who shall be created will praise the Lord.”

For if they had not been written, they would not have come down to us, but would long ago have been forgotten. Therefore the things written have been useful, because in them and through them the Lord is praised and proclaimed in this other generation and among this other people, created and baptized afterward.

> “For he looked down from his holy height; the Lord looked down from heaven upon the earth.”

For what purpose? “That he might hear the groaning of those in bonds and set free the children of the slain.” It is a worthy reason why we ought to praise the Lord: “because he looked down from his holy height,” from that most exalted inner chamber of his majesty, in order to hear the groans of those held bound in prison for his name, and to set free those same persons—the children, that is, of those slain for him. And truly it was fitting that the children of such great parents should be set free through their parents’ favor; for if they had not been freed, how could his name and praise have been announced in Zion and Jerusalem? This is what he says:

> “That the name of the Lord may be proclaimed in Zion, and his praise in Jerusalem.”

Zion and Jerusalem are the holy Church, in which the name of the Lord and his praise are proclaimed daily by those who have been freed and delivered from the snares of the devil.

> “When the peoples are gathered together as one, and kingdoms, to serve the Lord.”  
> [Note: Cols. 1085D, 1086D. “By saying ‘as one,’ the power of catholic truth is shown; for although this people is gathered from different parts of the world, they nevertheless come together as one, since they are held by one rule of faith.” Cassiodorus.]

Then, as though he said, the Lord’s name and praise ought to be proclaimed more earnestly when a great multitude gathers as one to hear the word and serve the Lord. Therefore we too should be admonished that, on great feast days, when many people gather in church, we should praise God and proclaim his mighty deeds.

[Col. 1086C]

> “He answered him in the way of his strength: Make known to me the fewness of my days.”

We read in the Gospel that, going out from the temple, Jesus said to his disciples: “Do you see these buildings and these great stones? Amen, I say to you: not one stone shall be left upon another that shall not be thrown down” (Mark 13:1). And when he sat on the Mount of Olives, his disciples answered him: “Tell us, when shall these things be, and what shall be the sign of your coming?” (Matt. 24:3).

This, then, is what the Church which follows, now in the other generation, says concerning the primitive Church: when, he says, the Lord was in the way of his strength and revealed his power and might to the peoples by many signs and miracles, then the primitive Church—the apostolic assembly—answered him: “Lord, make known to me the fewness of my days”—“and whether at this time you will restore the kingdom to Israel” (Acts 1:6); do not conceal it from us. For they thought that the Lord’s words signified that the end of the world was very near. Hence the Lord says: “When you hear of wars and disturbances, do not be terrified; these things must first happen, but the end is not immediately yet” (Luke 21:9).

> “And do not call me back in the middle of my days; your years are unto age upon age.”

The apostles might also have said or thought this at that time, although it is not found in the Gospel. For the Prophet often writes down people’s thoughts no less than their utterances. They prayed, then, whether for themselves, for the city of Jerusalem, or for the whole world, that they might not be called back in the middle of their days, because they had not yet lived as long as they hoped to live. These are our days: days promised and assigned to us not by divine providence, but by ourselves. Thus it is said: “Men of blood and deceit shall not halve their days” (Ps. 54:14).

Let him therefore say: “And do not call me back in the middle of my days,” because it lies in your power to appoint whatever end you will for anyone, since all years are yours and all obey your will. He proves that all years are his, and that the earth and heavens are his, because he himself made all things. This is what he says:

> “In the beginning, O Lord, you founded the earth, and the heavens are the works of your hands.”

Whether one says, “In the beginning God made heaven and earth,” or “In the beginning God made earth and heaven,” there is no difference. For something is not earlier or later simply because it is named first, since, as it is written, “He who remains forever created all things together.”  
> [Note: Cols. 1087D, 1088D. It should not be thought that the Psalmist and Moses contradict one another because the former said that God created the earth in the beginning while the latter placed heaven first among created things; Solomon affirms that all things were created together by God—that is, that God established the matter of all things from nothing at the same time.]  
> (Ecclus. 18:1).

> “They shall perish, but you shall remain, and all shall grow old like a garment.”

For so the Lord says in the Gospel: “Heaven and earth shall pass away, but my words shall not pass away” (Matt. 23:35). They shall pass away because they will be changed from the form in which they now exist into another. For there shall be, as it is written, “a new heaven and a new earth” (Rev. 21:1); and those higher heavens too shall be changed for the better.

> “But you are the very same, and your years shall not fail.”

Every creature, as though he said, is in some way changeable; and insofar as it is changeable, what it was seems in some manner to have perished. But you are altogether unchangeable, always the very same, and can be nothing other than what you are. “And your years shall not fail.” Those years, therefore, will not be produced by the circuit of the sun, but in some other way not yet revealed to us.

[Col. 1087D]

> “The children of your servants shall dwell there.”

Where? In those heavens changed for the better.

> “And their seed shall be directed unto age upon age.”

Seed and children signify the same thing, by which we understand all who imitate the saints. These indeed will dwell there because, for as long as they are in this life, they are directed throughout all ages: always making progress toward what is better, never straying from the path of truth, and imitating in all things those whose children they are said to be.

### Psalm 102. Praise of David

[Col. 1088A]

What “A Psalm of David” signifies has often been said.

> “Bless the Lord, O my soul, and let all that is within me bless his holy name.”

In the preceding psalms David exhorts all other people to praise and bless God; now, however, he exhorts himself—his soul and all that is within him. By this he shows most plainly how greatly he loves the Lord and how greatly he desires to cling to him, serve him, and obey him. “Bless the Lord, O my soul,” he says, because you are that which was made in his image and likeness—an image and beauty that you cannot recover except through him. And let “all that is within me” bless “his holy name.”  
[Note: Col. 1088D. According to Augustine, we bless the Lord even by the virtues not so much while awake as while asleep: “Your innocence, even in one asleep, is the voice of your soul.”]

His name is the Son, because through him we know both the Father and the Son himself. Remove the name, and knowledge of the thing is lost. The Son is rightly called both the name and the knowledge of the Father, because the Father is known through him. “For no one knows the Father except the Son, and anyone to whom the Son wills to reveal him” (Luke 10:22). When you wish to know someone, you ask for his name; likewise, if you wish to know the Father, look upon the Son. Hear him himself saying: “Whoever sees me sees the Father also” (John 14:9).

We do this so that God may have a name, because otherwise we cannot know or invoke him. But if we cannot know him otherwise, he is himself his name, through whom we know him. Yet through what do we know him, except through the Word, speech, wisdom, and truth? Nothing is known except through these, and all these are the Son. Therefore through the Son we know the Father; and thus the Son is the name of the Father. Concerning this name the Prophet now says that all that is within him should bless his holy name.

> “Bless the Lord, O my soul, and do not forget all his recompenses.”

Let us hear what these recompenses are:

> “He who has been gracious to all your iniquities; who heals all your infirmities; who redeems your life from destruction; who satisfies your desire with good things; who crowns you with compassion and mercies; your youth shall be renewed like the eagle’s.”

These recompenses are great—so great that we ought never to forget them. For the Lord has been gracious to all our iniquities, because by his blood he has blotted out not only original sin but all other sins together with it. This is what he says: “Who heals all our infirmities”—all, indeed, because he leaves none unhealed. He speaks to the soul and speaks of its infirmities. He has redeemed its life from destruction, which could not happen unless he had first forgiven its sins. He has also satisfied its desire with good things, because he has granted it the most steadfast hope of eternal happiness. Thus the Apostle says: “For by hope we have been saved” (Rom. 9:24). He crowns it in compassion and mercy, because he who gives the crown is the same who gave the victory; nor could it have conquered unless his help had been present.  
[Note: Col. 1089D. “We who were conquered in ourselves conquered in him. Therefore he crowns you because he crowns his gifts, not his merits.” Augustine.]

> “Your youth shall be renewed like the eagle’s.”

This seems to refer to the resurrection, when the human being will be wholly renewed to his former dignity. It is said of the eagle that, when it reaches extreme old age, it becomes young and renewed again. This passage gives the assertion very great authority. Whether it happens once or many times may be doubted.

> “The Lord performs mercy and judgment for all those who suffer injury. He made his ways known to Moses, his wills to the children of Israel.”

Although the Lord performs both mercy and judgment for all who suffer injury for his name, this appeared most plainly in Moses and the children of Israel. The Lord spoke with them as a man with his friend and worked such wonderful and astonishing things among them that they seem unbelievable to those who do not believe that all things are possible to God.

> “The Lord is merciful and compassionate, patient and greatly merciful; he will not be angry to the end, nor be indignant forever.”

All sinners can draw great hope and great consolation from these words, in which the immeasurable mercy of almighty God is proclaimed. He will be angry, as though he said, but not to the end; he will be indignant, but not forever. At whatever hour a sinner is converted, he shall be saved.

> “He has not dealt with us according to our sins, nor repaid us according to our iniquities.”

From past things, as though he said, we know future things. Many times we have offended him, many times provoked him to anger; but he has not dealt with us according to our sins. Had he done so, he would long ago have utterly destroyed us.

> “For according to the height of heaven above the earth, the Lord has established his mercy upon those who fear him.”

But how far has he removed our iniquities?

> “As far as east is from west, he has removed our iniquities from us.”

We see, therefore, that his mercy is immeasurable and that our iniquities have been separated from us without measure. Let us take care, then, that mercy may not depart farther from us and that iniquities may not come nearer to us. So great is mercy that it draws a human being from earth to heaven; iniquities are so far removed that they are believed to be wholly dead and altogether nonexistent. Therefore we must be very careful lest perhaps others arise in their place.

> “As a father has compassion on his children, so the Lord is merciful to those who fear him.”  
> [Note: Col. 1089D. The Vulgate reads differently: “As a father has compassion on his children, the Lord has had compassion on those who fear him, because he himself has known our formation.”]

This is a noble comparison for declaring immeasurable mercy. But now let us hear the compassion of the one who feels pity, from which so great a mercy follows:

> “For he,” he says, “knows our formation.”

He knows from what fragile material we were made, because “he made us, and not we ourselves” (Ps. 99:3). Therefore, as the most loving Father, he spares such frailty in his children. Hence it follows:

> “Remember, Lord, that we are dust; man—his days are like grass, and like a flower of the field, so he shall bloom.”  
> [Note: Col. 1090D. The Vulgate also has another reading, both for this verse and the following: “He remembered that we are dust. As grass are the days of man; as a flower of the field, so he shall bloom. For the spirit shall pass through him, and he shall not endure.” In almost all the remaining verses of this Psalm the Vulgate differs.]

See from what material humanity was made; see how unstable and frail it is. What is more worthless than dust? What is more weak than a flower? Such is the human being, and such are his days: like grass, which within one hour both blooms and loses its greenness. And he proves this:

> “For the spirit passes away from him, and he shall not be; and he shall no longer know his place.”

For we see that in a single moment a man both is and is not, because as long as the spirit is in him, he is a man; but as soon as it departs from him, he is no longer a man. “And he shall no longer know his place”: indeed, it is no longer his place, because with his spirit he loses both his place and everything else. After a person dies, he has nothing in this world; in the other world, however—to speak of the wicked—only torments remain for them.

> “But the mercy of the Lord is from age to age upon those who fear him.”

This, then, is the mercy that does not abandon a person even after death; this is what a human being—yet a good human being—will always possess.

> “And his righteousness is upon the children of children, upon those who keep his covenant and retain his commandments in memory, in order to do them.”

Likewise, after death it remains with all those who keep God’s covenant and commandments. For what good is it to retain them in memory unless we also do them in deed? Thus some receive mercy alone, while others receive righteousness and mercy; without mercy no one is saved.

> “The Lord has prepared his throne in heaven, and his kingdom shall rule over all.”

After the many mercies which the Lord has shown to his servants, he also shows in what place he is to dwell with them. He prepared his throne there, where, glorious after his Passion, he ascended while his disciples watched. His kingdom shall rule over all, because there is no nation, power, or height that is not judged by the Church.

> “Bless the Lord, all his angels, mighty in strength, who perform his word, to hear the voice of his utterances.”

He first summoned his own soul; now he summons the angels themselves and all creation to praise and bless the Lord. By angels, whose name means “messengers,” we may understand all who have the office of proclaiming the Gospel, among whom the apostles hold first place. For these too are mighty in strength; they hear his word, proclaim it, and perform it.

> “Bless the Lord, all his powers, his ministers, who perform his will.”

This may fittingly apply to the saints through whom the Lord has performed such powers that they are not undeservedly called his powers.

> “Bless the Lord, all his works.”

All his works bless the Lord, since they have been made so wisely and wonderfully that the Lord is blessed in all of them.

> “In every place of his dominion, bless the Lord, O my soul.”

But there is no place that is not under his dominion. Therefore, in every place, bless the Lord, O my soul. And as this Psalm does not end, so may the blessing not end.

### Psalm 103. A Psalm of David Himself

David composes this Psalm for David himself—that is, for our Savior: for him who made all things, redeemed the world, rose from the dead, and ascended into heaven, “who makes the cloud his ascent and walks upon the wings of the winds.”  
[Note: Cols. 1091D, 1092D. In this Psalm David is employed only as the person speaking. “But it is agreed that everything is to be narrated concerning the Lord Savior, who in the beginning made heaven and earth. This Psalm is so perfectly arranged that here you may understand certain things which you know to have been left unspoken in the book of Genesis. Therefore we shall explain literally those things suited to a literal explanation; but those which appear to indicate knowledge of our faith—as we have received from our elders—we shall explain in a spiritual sense.” Cassiodorus.]

> “Bless the Lord, O my soul.”

He exhorts himself to bless, so that all others may follow him and do as he does. He is the best teacher who instructs his disciples not only by words but also by action itself.

> “O Lord my God, you have been greatly magnified.”

God, who is great by nature, has been greatly magnified through apostolic preaching, because in the Church he is proclaimed and believed to be as great as he is.

> “You have put on confession and beauty.”

The Lord has put on confession, because he is not only praised by all, but is so clothed and surrounded by praise that it cannot be separated from him. It is a beautiful and well-arranged garment, without which other ornaments do not please. For what would please except that which is praiseworthy? But who could say how great and what kind of beauty the Lord put on in his resurrection, when it is said of his saints that “they shall shine like the sun in the kingdom of God” (Wis. 3:7)? Hence it follows: “clothed with light as with a garment.” These, then, are the adornments of our Savior: confession, beauty, light, charity, loveliness. Add to these immortality, power, strength, and the other virtues. This is the garment of confession with which the Lord is now clothed in this Psalm.

> “Stretching out heaven like a skin, who covers its upper parts with waters.”

By this the Prophet teaches us that God made the heavens themselves easily and without any difficulty; and it belongs to his great praise and glory that this greatest and principal work is said to have been made without labor. Concerning the waters over heaven, we have this written elsewhere: “And let the waters that are above the heavens praise the name of the Lord” (Ps. 148:4). Likewise: “And he divided the waters which were above the firmament from those which were below the firmament” (Gen. 1:7).

By the heavens we may understand the apostles, whom the Lord stretched out like skins because he made them vessels for wine. These are the new vessels of which the Lord says in the Gospel: “No one puts new wine into old vessels, but puts new wine into new vessels” (Matt. 3:17). Drunk with this wine, many forget all earthly things. Their upper parts, however, are the prophets, who are covered not with wine but with waters. They are rightly said to be covered, so that these waters may be shown to be not inside but outside, because prophets are often not understood even by prophets themselves.

> “Who makes the cloud your ascent, who walks upon the wings of the winds.”

This is what is said of the Lord in the Gospel: “While the disciples watched, he was lifted up, and a cloud received him from their eyes” (Acts 1:9). He walked upon the wings of the winds because no winds can rise to that height. Here we ought to seek no other exposition, lest we seem perhaps to do injury to an interpretation so utterly true and clear.  
[Note: Col. 1092D. Nevertheless, St Augustine explained this passage allegorically: “He ascended upon the wings of the winds. We said that winds are rightly understood figuratively as souls. What are the wings of winds, the wings of souls, except those by which they are raised upward? Therefore the wings of souls are virtues, good works, upright deeds. All have wings upon two pinions; for all commandments are contained in two.”]

[Col. 1092C]

> “Who makes your angels spirits, and your ministers a burning fire.”

Since angels means “messengers,” those who are spirits by nature become angels when they are sent. Such, then, is Christ’s power that whenever he wills, he makes angels from spirits and sends the Seraphim themselves—whose name means “burning” or “kindling”—to minister whatever he wills. This is what he says: “and your ministers a burning fire.” For the prophet Isaiah says that “the Lord sent one of the Seraphim, who touched his lips with a coal” (Isa. 6:6).

But if we say, in terms of manner of life, that the Lord makes his angels and ministers spirits and burning fire, it will not be unsuitable. Angels, ministers, and rulers of the Church may fittingly be called both spirit and fire.

“Who founded the earth upon its stability.” If this is understood literally, it is clear enough. Yet what its stability is cannot be known, unless it is simply the power and might of God. “It shall not be moved for ever and ever.” These words are most true, because he who speaks [Col. 1093A] cannot lie. By “earth,” however, we understand the Church, whose foundation and stability is Christ; and because it is founded upon a firm rock, as the Lord says, it shall not be moved for ever and ever. Of this foundation the Apostle says: “No one can lay another foundation besides that which has been laid, which is Christ Jesus” (1 Cor. III, 11).

“The deep as a garment is his covering.” Now the deep is the immeasurable depth of waters; and many waters, as it is written, are many peoples. The earth signifies the Church. Thus at one time the deep—that is, the raging multitude of peoples—covered the whole Church, just as a garment covers completely that upon which it is laid. Hence it continues: “Upon the mountains the [Col. 1093B] waters shall stand.” What are meant by the mountains, if not the apostles and teachers of the Church? Upon them the waters stood, because they afflicted both prelates and subjects. For even to this day we see that not only the Church, but even the bishops themselves, endure this violence of the deep.

“At thy rebuke they shall flee; at the voice of thy thunder they shall be afraid.” These waters of which we speak often fled at God’s rebuke, because peoples, terrified by signs, miracles, and the preaching of the apostles, were converted to faith in Christ. For in the voice of thunder the preaching of the apostles is signified.

“The mountains rise, and the plains descend unto the place which thou hast founded for them.” These are those mountains [Col. 1093C] of which we have just spoken: “Upon the mountains the waters shall stand.” When the waters flee, these rise, because, persecution having ceased, the preachers of the Church are raised up, honoured, and revered by the peoples. The plains, however, descend because the whole ecclesiastical multitude humbles itself beneath their feet. For as plains lie beneath mountains, so all Christians ought to be subject to bishops and priests. Hence the former are called prelates and the latter subjects. The former rise to their own place and the latter descend to theirs, because the former hold the first place and the latter the second place in the Church. “Thou hast set them a boundary which they shall not pass, neither shall they return to cover the earth.” The Lord set a boundary to the aforesaid [Col. 1093D] waters, which had occupied both earth and mountains, a boundary which they may not cross; for the wicked can do no more against the Church than the Lord permits them to do. Hence elsewhere it is said: “Who shut up the sea with doors?” (Job XXXVIII, 8). “I surrounded it with my bounds, and set bar and doors, and said: Thus far shalt thou come and no farther; and here shalt thou break thy swelling waves” (ibid., 10–11).

“Who sendest forth springs in the valleys: the waters shall pass through the midst of the mountains.” These are the valleys of which it is said elsewhere: “And the valleys shall abound with corn” (Ps. LXIV, 14); by them we understand the individual churches, which in humility and simplicity render abundant fruit of good works to the Lord [Col. 1094A]. These are watered by the springs of the holy Scriptures, which the Lord sends among them and causes to flow abundantly. This is what he says: “The waters shall pass through the midst of the mountains.” For mountains, valleys, springs, and waters signify the same thing in this passage.

“All the beasts of the forest shall drink thereof.” By the beasts of the forest are understood those who have been converted from Gentile savagery to faith in Christ. These now drink these waters and delight in their most sweet draught. “The wild asses shall wait in their thirst.” Of these wild asses the Lord says elsewhere: “Who has let the wild ass go free, and who has loosed his bonds? To whom I gave a house in the wilderness and dwelling-places in the land of salt” (Job XXXIX, 5). By these, therefore, we understand those [Col. 1094B] who, free and released from all the hindrances of this world, serve the Lord either in monasteries or in solitary places. They likewise await these waters in their thirst, because they are refreshed by them daily in their great longing.

“Over them shall the birds of heaven dwell; from the midst of the rocks they shall give forth their voices.” By the 521 birds of heaven the preachers of the Church are signified; by the rocks, the churches themselves. Thus the birds of heaven give forth their voices from the midst of the rocks when bishops and priests preach the word of God in the midst of the churches. They are rightly said to dwell over the waters because they do not depart from the divine books, but meditate day and night upon the law of the Lord.

“Watering the mountains from thy heights.” Thou, O Lord, he says, [Col. 1094C] dost accomplish all these things, watering the mountains from thy heights. For these mountains have heights by which they are watered by the Lord. By the heights of the mountains we understand knowledge of both Testaments and the graces of the Holy Spirit, by which the teachers of the Church are watered and satisfied. Hence it continues: “The earth shall be filled with the fruit of thy works.” For the earth is the Church, daily satisfied by the fruit of God’s works, whether we understand spiritual or bodily satisfaction. For he is both creator and worker of spiritual and bodily food. “For all wisdom is from him, and has always been with him, and is before the age” (Ecclus. I, 1).

“Bringing forth grass for cattle and herb for the service [Col. 1094D] of men.” From thee, he says, thy earth is satisfied; yet it, not being ungrateful or forgetful of thy benefits, supplies hay to thy cattle and produces herbs for the service of men. God’s cattle are bishops and priests: cattle, indeed, because they bear the burdens of others. Hence the saying: “I became as a beast before thee, and I am always with thee” (Ps. LXXII, 23). The Church ought to supply bodily food to those from whom it nevertheless receives food for the heart. Hence the Apostle says: “If we have sown spiritual things for you, is it a great thing if we reap your carnal things?” (1 Cor. IX, 11). And the Lord says in the Gospel: “The labourer is worthy of his wage” (Luke X, 7). This is what he says:

“That thou mayest bring bread out of the earth, and that wine may gladden [Col. 1095A] the heart of man.” The Church is that earth, and they too are earth. It gives its fruit, and they likewise give theirs. It gives good fruit but receives better; it gives hay but receives bread. And what kind of bread? Surely the living bread which came down from heaven. It likewise receives wine, namely, the cup of the New Testament. This gladdens the heart of man because it bestows eternal life.

“That he may make the face cheerful with oil, and that bread may strengthen the heart of man.” The Church receives not only bread and wine but also oil from the apostles, by which the graces of the Holy Spirit are signified. Without this oil there is no spiritual gladness. He rightly mentioned the face, because both joy and sadness are recognized in the face; and he who had said, “wine gladdens the heart of man,” [Col. 1095B] suitably adds: “And bread strengthens the heart of man.” Hence the Lord says: “Unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man and drink his blood, you shall not have life in yourselves” (John VI, 54). Where life is absent, neither life nor strength can exist.

“All the trees of the forest shall be satisfied, and the cedars of Lebanon which thou hast planted.” Good trees and good cedars, which are satisfied with such bread. By these the people of the Gentiles are signified, from whom the house of God is built, the Jewish people having been rejected. The Lord planted these cedars, and therefore they can grow to such a height. Hence he says elsewhere: “Every plant which my heavenly Father has not planted shall be rooted up” (Matt. XV, 13).—“There [Col. 1095C] the sparrows shall build their nests.” Sparrows build their nests in these trees because, under their protection and authority, the servants of God build monasteries in which they serve the Lord night and day.

“The home of the coot; the leader is theirs.”  
[Note: [Col. 1095D] Ἐρωδιός in Greek; in Latin *fulica*, a water-bird.]

Water is the home of the coot, since this bird lives and remains in waters. He therefore calls the sparrows the household of the coot, because the saints of God cannot fly to heavenly things without the guidance of waters. Hence the Lord says: “Unless someone has been born again of water and the Holy Spirit, he cannot enter into the kingdom of God” (John III, 5). Christians alone, therefore, have this guide, because they alone are regenerated from water and Spirit. “The high mountains are for the stags; the rock is a refuge for hedgehogs.” We have two high mountains, namely the New and Old Testaments. Here the stags of the Church find refuge, by whom the apostles and teachers are signified. Of these is the one who says: “I have lifted up my eyes to the mountains, whence help shall come to me” (Ps. CXX, 1). To this, therefore, we must always have recourse, where we always find counsel and consolation. The rock is a refuge for hedgehogs, by whom sinners are understood, full and surrounded on every side by the spines of vices: “The rock,” says the Apostle, “was Christ” (II Cor. X, 4);—“who, as he himself says, did not come to call the righteous, [Col. 1096A] but sinners to repentance” (Mark II, 17).

“He made the moon for the seasons; the sun knew its setting.” At one and the same time the Church, signified by the moon, had its beginning, and Christ, the sun of righteousness, came to his setting. For as Eve was made from the side of sleeping Adam, so the Church was fashioned from the side of Christ hanging upon the cross.

“Thou hast appointed darkness, and night came to be; in it all the beasts of the forest shall pass through.” At the time, he says, when our Saviour set, darkness came to be, by which the wretched Jews were blinded both inwardly and outwardly; and night and the gloom of darkness came upon them. In that night all the beasts of the forest passed through, by which all malignant spirits are signified; they possessed excessive power to deceive them and draw them [Col. 1096B] to themselves. Of these it further says:

“The young lions roaring, that they may seize and seek food for themselves from God.” Hence it is said elsewhere: “For our enemy the devil, like a roaring lion, goes about seeking whom he may devour” (1 Pet. V, 8). Yet these can neither seize nor have food without God’s permission. The devil nevertheless has confidence that Jordan may flow into his mouth: “For,” as it is written, “his chosen ones are his food.” He wished to devour Job but could not; Judas, however, he devoured along with many others.

“The sun rose, and they were gathered together, and shall be placed in their dens.” The sun rose because our Saviour rose from the dead on the third day. Then [Col. 1096C] the young lions were gathered together and placed in their dens. Greatly terrified by our Saviour, they waited in grief for him whom they did not doubt would come there.

“Man shall go forth to his work, and to his labour until evening.” This was fulfilled when, after his resurrection, our Saviour said to the disciples: “Go into the whole world and preach the Gospel to every creature” (Mark XVI, 15). Then the apostles, who are signified by this man, went out to their work and began to proclaim Gospel preaching to all nations; and until evening, that is, until the end of their lives, they steadfastly and faithfully performed the task entrusted to them [Col. 1096D].

“How magnificent are thy works, O Lord! Thou hast made all things in wisdom; the earth is filled with thy creature.”  
[Note: [Col. 1095D] The Vulgate has: “the earth is filled with thy possession.”]

This is not wonder at the creation of heaven and earth, but at the sudden conversion of this world. Yesterday, as it were, the apostles began to preach, and today the earth is filled with a new creation and a new people. Hence he says that God made all things in wisdom, because these things could in no way have been done except through Christ. For he is the power and wisdom of the Father.

[Note: [Col. 1095D] “Thou hast made all things in wisdom.” This wisdom, therefore, is the Son, as the Apostle says: “Christ, the power of God and the wisdom of God,” through whom all things were made, and without him nothing was made. And, in order to show the cooperation of that power, he says that the Father acts through the Son: “Thou hast made.” The same Apostle says this also concerning the Holy Spirit: “One and the same Spirit works all things, distributing to each as he wills.” Cassiodorus. [Col. 1096D–1097D]]

[Col. 1097A] “This great and spacious sea: there are creeping things there without number.” He speaks of this world, which, like the sea, is always disturbed and has scarcely ever been able to be quiet. Now, however, filled with the new people of Christians, it receives the ships of the apostles, so that there is fishing and sailing everywhere. Christ’s fishermen now sail safely where even emperors themselves were formerly accustomed to perish and be drowned. By the creeping things without number are signified those who are joined to the earth with their whole body and seek only earthly and transitory things; their multitude, indeed, is so great that it cannot be numbered. There are also in this sea other animals, small and great, by which we may understand poor and powerful, good and evil, wise and foolish persons. Here also [Col. 1097B] is that ancient dragon, who is the devil and Satan, who according to Scripture deceives the whole world. This is what it says:

“This dragon, which thou hast formed to make sport of him.” After this dragon fell through his pride, the Lord made him such and reduced him to such a condition of abasement that not only men, but women themselves also, may mock and deceive him. “All wait upon thee, O Lord, and thou givest them food in due season.” All animals, he says—good and evil alike, those who offend thee and those who serve thee—do not possess food in abundance except from thee; for thou art he who makest thy sun rise upon the good and evil and rain upon the righteous and unrighteous.

“When thou givest to them, they shall gather; when thou openest [Col. 1097C] thy hand, all shall be filled with abundance.” Therefore he himself causes us to abound in all good things; he himself causes us to suffer want of all things. Hence it continues:

“But when thou turnest away thy face, they shall be troubled; thou wilt take away their spirit, and they shall fail and return to their dust.” The Lord is not angry with all who are troubled; but all with whom he is angry must necessarily perish and be troubled. Of them it is said elsewhere: “Let them be ashamed and troubled for ever and ever; let them be confounded and perish” (Ps. VI, 11). What he says, “Thou wilt take away their spirit, and they shall fail and return to their dust,” appears to be common to good and evil alike. But the spirit will be taken from the good in one way and from the evil in another. From the good it will be taken so that they may rest in peace; from the evil, so that, wasting away, they may fail, be tormented, and perish. These, indeed, shall be wholly changed back into their dust; for as they were corruptible before, so after the resurrection they shall be both corruptible and capable of suffering.

“Send forth thy Spirit, and they shall be created, and thou shalt renew the face of the earth.” No human being would fail to return to such dust, nor would anyone fail always to be wretched and corruptible, unless the Lord [Col. 1098A] sent forth his Spirit to recreate and renew human beings.

[Note: [Col. 1097D–1098D] “As often as the Lord deigns to restore us from the oldness of sin into the new man, so often he creates us, as is read in Psalm 50: ‘Create in me a clean heart, O God.’” Cassiodorus.]

The Prophet therefore prays that the Lord may deign to send his Spirit, by whom the face of the earth 523 may be recreated and renewed. He rightly said “face,” because the substance will remain the same, only its appearance and beauty being renewed.

“May the glory of the Lord be for ever; the Lord shall rejoice in his works.” Let the glory of the Lord, he says, be in his works, so that they may remain glorious for ever and ever, just as they were created beautiful and glorious by him. Otherwise the Lord will not rejoice in his works.

“He looks upon the earth and makes it tremble; he touches the mountains and they shall smoke.” The Lord looks upon the earth and makes it tremble when, by his inspiration, [Col. 1098B] he visits a sinner and converts him to repentance, so that he may serve him in fear and trembling. By the mountains the rich and powerful are signified. Though they enter the kingdom of God with difficulty, when touched by the Holy Spirit they begin to smoke outwardly and burn inwardly. To smoke outwardly is to show repentance daily through tears and contrition. For unless the fire burned within, smoke would not appear outwardly.

“I will sing to the Lord in my life; I will make melody to my God as long as I am.” It is as though someone said to him: “You have sung enough and rejoiced enough; now it would be time to rest, and singing should be ended.” To this he replies: “I have sung, and I shall sing—not for an hour, but through all the days of my life. And I shall make melody to my God, not only now [Col. 1098C], but as long as I am; and this alone I pray for: that my praise may please thee, because I shall always delight in him.” This is what he says:

“May my praise be pleasing to him; [Note: [Col. 1098D] The Vulgate has: “May my speech be pleasant to him.”] but I shall delight in the Lord. Let sinners fail from the earth, and the wicked, so that they may not be.” There are many in the Church who grow weary of hearing singing, readings, and preaching, and often murmur not only in their hearts but also with their mouths because the praises of God do not end sooner; for they delight more in tales and vanities than in God’s praises. To these the Prophet then speaks, saying: “Let sinners fail from the earth.” Let the wearisome depart from the Church, and let the wicked so fail that they “may not be” in it, since they profit neither themselves nor others, but hinder others. “But do thou bless, [Col. 1098D] O my soul, the Lord,” and never yield to their persuasions; rather, as thou hast begun, persevere at all times in the praises of God.

## PSALM CIV. ALLELUIA.

Alleluia means “Praise God”; and assuredly, unless praising the Lord were exceedingly acceptable to God and most useful to us, the Prophet would never so often command us to praise the Lord.

[Note: [Col. 1098D–1099D] “This psalm especially recounts the history of the Fathers, but it must be understood spiritually; for all things that happened of old happened figuratively, so that we might be instructed.” St Jerome.]

[Col. 1099A] “Give thanks to the Lord and call upon his name; proclaim his works among the nations.” The Prophet speaks to those who have been converted from the Gentiles to the faith, and recounts the history of the ancients: how the Lord struck the Egyptians with many plagues and most gloriously delivered his people from their most harsh slavery. In this, too, the deliverance of the Church and the destruction of persecutors are signified. You, as though he said, who were accustomed to praise false gods, now confess and praise the Lord, because he alone is both God and Lord. “And call upon his name,” because no other is to be invoked. Proclaim his works among the nations, so that you may teach and enable all others to understand the things you have learned.

“Sing to him and make melody to him; recount all his wonders.” Sing and make melody to him, he says; seek not your own glory but his; recount his mighty deeds and wonders. Hence the Apostle says: “We do not preach ourselves, but the Lord Jesus” (II Cor. IV, 5). Hence it continues:

“Glory in his holy name.” Let your praise not be your own; rather let all praise and glory be referred to him who is wonderful in his saints. The saints often grieved when, after miracles, great honour was shown them by the people. “Let the heart of those who seek the Lord rejoice.” Let the heart of those who seek the Lord rejoice, he says, not in working miracles, but in the Lord alone. Thus the Lord says to his disciples in the Gospel: “Do not rejoice because the demons are subject to you in my name. [Col. 1099C] Rather rejoice in this, because your names are written in heaven” (Luke X, 17).

“Seek the Lord and be strengthened; seek his face always.” Seek the Lord in the Scriptures; seek the Lord in miracles; and when you have known him, be strengthened in his love. “Seek his face always.”

[Note: [Col. 1100D] “Let discovery not put an end to this seeking, which signifies love; rather, as love increases, let the seeking of the One found increase.” Augustine.]

Moses sought this face when he said: “If I have found favour in thy eyes, show me thy face, that I may see thee” (Exod. XXXIII, 13). For we must always seek how we may come before his face secure and joyful.

524 “Remember his wonders which he has done, his prodigies and the judgments of his mouth.” In these the Lord is sufficiently [Col. 1099D] known, because unless he were God, he could in no way have done them. The Prophet therefore wishes that his signs and miracles, his words and judgments, should be preached everywhere among the nations, so that those unable otherwise to know him may at least know him through his mighty deeds. But who are those commanded to know and proclaim him?

“The seed of Abraham his servant, the children of Jacob his chosen.” The Jews say in the Gospel: “We are the seed of Abraham” (John VIII, 33). In reply, the Lord says: “If you were the seed of Abraham, you would do the works of Abraham.” Therefore they are not the seed of Abraham [Col. 1100A] or the children of Jacob unless they imitate Abraham and Jacob. Both believed in Christ; for, as it is written, Abraham worshipped him, and Jacob is recorded as saying: “I will await thy salvation, O Lord” (Gen. XLIX, 18).—“He is the Lord our God; his judgments are in all the earth.” We, he says, are his seed, and he is the Lord our God, whose judgments have been received not by the Jews but by the whole earth.

“He remembered for ever his covenant, the word which he commanded for a thousand generations.” Of this covenant it is read later that the Lord promised the land of Canaan to Abraham as an inheritance. He commanded this word for a thousand generations when he said: “Thus shall thy seed be as the stars [Col. 1100B] of heaven and as the sand which is on the shore of the sea” (Gen. XXII, 17). He used a finite number for an infinite one, because in comparison with the stars of heaven and the sand of the sea, a thousand generations are very few. But since it is written, “In Isaac shall thy seed be called” (Gen. XXI, 13), this covenant appears to have been made more for Christians than for Jews. Hence the Apostle says: “He did not say ‘and to seeds,’ as though of many, but as of one: ‘and to thy seed,’ which is Christ” (Gal. III, 16).
