“Which he ordained to Abraham, and his oath to Isaac; and he established it for Jacob as a commandment, and for Israel as an everlasting covenant, saying: To thee I will give the land of Canaan, the measuring-line of your inheritance.” [Col. 1100C] The Lord, he says, established and commanded Jacob, not Esau, to hasten toward that inheritance owed to him by the written instrument of an everlasting covenant, saying to them: “To thee I will give the land of Canaan,” and with it the whole measure and measuring-line of your inheritance. In this are signified the Perizzites, Jebusites, Hittites, and the other nations. The Lord said this to them while they were still very few and lived in that land as sojourners and strangers. But because they had firm hope and firmly believed the Lord’s words, everything which God had promised them was fulfilled. These things are recounted to us so that we too may have firm hope and faithfully believe that we shall not be deprived of the inheritance promised us, if we imitate our fathers [Col. 1100D] and hold their faith and teaching, knowing that through many tribulations we must enter the kingdom of heaven, which is far better than the land of the Canaanites. Hence it continues:

“When they were few in number, very few, and strangers in it, and passed from nation to nation, and from one kingdom to another people.” If, then, they attained with such labour that inheritance which is temporal, how much more earnestly must we hasten toward that which is eternal!

“He did not permit a man to harm them, and rebuked [Col. 1101A] kings for their sake.” For Scripture records that Pharaoh and Abimelech were rebuked because of them. To these the Lord gave command, saying: “Do not touch my anointed ones, and do no evil to my prophets.” He calls them his anointed, not because they were anointed with visible oil, but because they were divinely endowed with the grace of the Holy Spirit.

“And he called famine upon the land, and broke all the support of bread.” Why the Lord wished this famine to be upon the land is made clear by what follows.

[Note: [Col. 1101D] “‘He called famine’: this must be understood as, ‘He said that there should be famine’; so that ‘to call’ means ‘to name,’ ‘to name’ means ‘to say,’ and ‘to say’ means ‘to command.’ For he called famine who calls things which are not as though they were.” Augustine.]

This famine was the cause that Joseph, who had been sold into Egypt, was made lord of the land, and that the land was delivered from the danger of famine by his foresight. It was the cause that Jacob descended with his sons into Egypt and found unharmed the son whom he believed [Col. 1101B] to be dead. This is what it says:

“He sent a man before them; Joseph was sold into slavery.” Thus Joseph was sold by God’s ordering and the malice of his brothers, so that we may understand that many things occur in this world by God’s ordering which appear to have an evil beginning. For the passion, sale, and betrayal of our Saviour were likewise accomplished by God’s ordering for our salvation, though we do not doubt that they were unjust.

“They humbled his feet in fetters; iron passed through his soul, until his word came; his utterance inflamed him.” In saying that iron passed through his soul, it shows that he endured great pains and distresses. But [Col. 1101C] after his word came and the utterance of the Lord inflamed and enlightened him so that he could interpret the king’s dream, he was immediately delivered from these great 525 distresses. This is what it says:

“The king sent and released him, the ruler of peoples, and let him go; and he appointed him lord of his house and ruler of all his possessions, that he might instruct his princes as himself and teach wisdom to his elders.” Pharaoh is shown to have recognized great wisdom in Joseph, whom he appointed prince and lord of the whole land and ordained to teach the great and the elders. For they thought that he possessed that interpretation of dreams not through divine favour but through mastery of an art and exalted natural ability. Therefore they thought he could teach this doctrine to others just as [Col. 1101D] to himself. There are many features in this event applicable to our Saviour. For as Joseph was sold by his brother Judah, so he himself was sold by Judas his disciple. Appointed by the Father king and lord of all nations, he delivered not Egypt only but the entire world from perpetual famine. Of this famine the Prophet says: “I will send upon you not a famine of bread nor a thirst for water, but of hearing the word of God” (Amos VIII, 11). He is himself supremely skilled not only in interpreting dreams but also in revealing all the deepest mysteries of the Scriptures.

“And Israel entered Egypt, and Jacob dwelt in the land of Ham.” Canaan was born from the stock of Ham, from whom the Egyptians derive their origin. If Jacob did not fear to enter Egypt, why should our people fear to enter the world in order to preach, when they hear that “the Lord increased his people exceedingly and strengthened him above his enemies”? For both they and we have multiplied greatly and been strengthened above all our enemies.

[Col. 1102B] “He turned their heart so that they hated his people and dealt deceitfully with his servants.” Why should the Egyptians be reproved for what they did if God turned their hearts and they had wished to do it? This mode of expression is customary in the divine page: the Lord is said to do what, although he could prevent it, he permits to be done.

[Note: [Col. 1101D–1102D] For fuller understanding, let us bring forward Augustine: “Is God then the author of these very grievous sins—he who must be believed to be the author of no sin, however slight? Who is wise and shall understand these things? For he is that wonderful goodness of God by which he makes good use even of evils, whether of angels or of men. Though they are evil through their own fault, he makes good from their evil. For before they hated his people they were not good; rather, they were such malignant and impious persons as would readily envy their prosperous resident aliens,” etc.]

For the Lord gives the wicked occasion for their unjust desires to be manifested outwardly and for the evil which they have in their heart to be unable to remain hidden. When, therefore, the Egyptians were severely afflicting God’s people, he commanded Moses and Aaron to come for their consolation. This is what it says: “He sent Moses his servant, and Aaron whom he chose. He set among them the words of his signs and his wonders in the land of Ham.” Let us hear what those [Col. 1102C] wonders were.

“He sent darkness and darkened those who embittered his words.” That darkness which then darkened the Egyptians signified the darkness which Jews, heretics, and pagans were then and always will be destined to suffer. For these are those who embitter his words and oppose Catholic and apostolic doctrine.

“He turned their water into blood and killed their fish.” The waters of the Egyptians, changed into blood, signified the teaching of philosophers and heretics, which is nothing but poison, blood, and sin. Therefore those perish who drink this blood and do not fear to embrace this teaching.

“He sent frogs into their land, and into the chambers of their kings [Col. 1102D].” By these frogs are understood poets, philosophers, Jews, and heretics, who glory in mere talkativeness and never cease to speak against the truth. Such persons are indeed familiar to kings and powerful men, who delight in their vanities and errors.

“He spoke, and dog-flies came, and gnats in all [Col. 1103A] their borders.” *Coenomyia* is a most foul and troublesome kind of fly. *Ciniphes*, however, are called gnats, which, the smaller they are than other insects, are the more grievous in their stings. What, then, is signified by the dog-fly and gnats except lust, which is proved to be among vices the most foul and troublesome? Because this vice is of the flesh and naturally clings to the flesh, it cannot be overcome and driven away without labour and God’s help.

“He made their rains into hail, and burning fire in their land. And he struck their vines and fig trees and shattered every tree of their borders.” By hail and burning fire we may understand the immense wrath and fury of God, by which wicked people, along with all that they possess, are to be scourged and destroyed.

“He spoke, and locust and caterpillar came, without number, and consumed all the grass in their land.” The locust and caterpillar, which always advance as though with an army and multitude, signify every kind of vice. By these all the grass of that land is consumed and laid waste; by the grass we understand the people themselves, since the people are signified by grass.

526 “And he struck every firstborn in the land of Egypt, the first fruits of all their labour.” This plague frightened the Egyptians more than all the others, so that they begged the Hebrews to go and compelled them to depart; it alone among the others seems to have a good signification. [Col. 1103C] For it signifies that original sin in all human beings has been blotted out by Christ’s blood. Up to this point he has written of the plagues of the Egyptians; from this point he begins to write of the benefits divinely bestowed upon the Jews by God.

“And he led them forth with silver and gold, and there was none infirm among their tribes.” Not Christians alone, but other nations too possess gold and silver: virtues, upright customs, and skill in many arts; and it is not sinful to receive and borrow all these from them. It should be noted that those who follow God do not become infirm, provided that they walk the royal road and do not depart from it.

“Egypt rejoiced at their departure, because fear of them fell upon them; and he spread a cloud for their protection, and fire, that it might give them light [Col. 1103D] by night.” Of this cloud the Apostle says: “All were baptized into Moses in the cloud and in the sea” (1 Cor. X, 2); that is, from water and the Holy Spirit, so that by the sea we understand water and by the cloud the Holy Spirit. He therefore is the one who protects us from heat and all tribulations, illumines our darkness, and shows the way of truth.

“They asked for flesh, and the quail came.” By the quails spiritual understanding is signified, which has its origin from [Col. 1104A] above and from waters. That all these things are to be understood spiritually is taught us by the Apostle, who says: “They all ate the same spiritual food, and all drank the same spiritual drink; for they drank from the spiritual rock that followed them, and the rock was Christ” (1 Cor. 3, 4). Hence it continues: “And he satisfied them with bread from heaven.” For that bread which came down from heaven is either Christ’s flesh or spiritual understanding.

“[He] split the rock, and waters flowed out, and rivers ran through the dry land.” Likewise, from Christ’s breast four great rivers burst forth, by which the whole earth, formerly dry and parched, was abundantly watered and satisfied. And the Lord did all these things of which we have spoken above [Col. 1104B] for his people because “he remembered his holy word, which he spoke to Abraham his servant.” For the Lord had promised Abraham that in his seed all nations would be blessed, and that his seed would be as the stars of heaven and as the sand on the shore of the sea.

“And he brought forth his people in exultation, and his chosen ones in joy.” For how could those whom the Lord so cherished, defended, and enriched with such great benefits be without joy and exultation? “And he gave them the regions of the nations, and they possessed the labours of peoples.” For what purpose? “That they might keep his ordinances and seek his law.”

> [Note: Col. 1103D] “His ordinances are that we should love God with all our heart, regard our neighbours as ourselves, honour our father, hold our son dear, and the other acts of justice commanded in the various kinds of human affairs.” Cassiodorus.

For unless, after conquering their enemies, they had enjoyed peace and possessed the land in tranquillity, they could neither lawfully keep the ordinances [Col. 1104C] nor diligently seek the law.

## PSALM 105. ALLELUIA, ALLELUIA.

The first *Alleluia* belongs to the preceding psalm; the following one, to the psalm that follows.

The Prophet teaches us with what earnestness we ought always to praise God: he ends in praises and begins in praises. When the psalm ends, he commands praise; and when it begins, he commands praise, so that the praise of God may be continual and that no interruption may occur in God’s praises.

> [Note: Col. 1103D–1104D] “Behold, it is briefly commanded that the Lord be sung to with the jubilation of the whole psalm. But let us observe that he is not known to have changed either the title or the subject from what was said above. For the title is *alleluia*; the subject is confession, which is in a wonderful way altogether fruitful for the praises of the Lord.” Cassiodorus.

“Give thanks to the Lord, for he is good, for his mercy is for ever.” A noble reason [Col. 1104D] why we ought to praise God is that he is good and merciful. For if every good thing is praiseworthy, and nothing ought to be praised except what is good, how greatly must he be praised who alone is good and from whom all good things come! We read in the Gospel that when someone said to the Lord, “Good Master,” he answered: “Why do you call me good, when no one is good except God alone? If you believe me to be God, you speak rightly; but if you do not believe it, why do you say this?” [Col. 1105A] (Matt. 19:17.) For God is good from himself and substantially; other things, however, neither exist nor are good from themselves, but whatever they are, they are from God. [527]

Let us therefore praise the Lord, because he is good, substantially good, and can never be anything but good. “And because his mercy is for ever.” What he says, “for ever,” amounts to saying “unto eternity.” Thus elsewhere it is said: “I will sing the mercies of the Lord for ever” (Ps. 88:1).

“Who shall declare the powers of the Lord, make heard all his praises?” Behold, as though someone said: We are prepared to praise, but we are not sufficient to praise. For who shall fully declare the powers of the Lord? And who, by speaking and crying out without ceasing, shall make all [Col. 1105B] his praises heard? They are innumerable; they exceed measure: “Great is the Lord and exceedingly praiseworthy, and there is no end to his greatness” (Ps. 47:8).—“Blessed are those who keep judgment and do righteousness at every time.” If, as it were, you cannot do that, at least do this, and you shall be blessed. Blessed indeed are those who keep his judgment; but what is his judgment? “Turn away from evil and do good” (Ps. 36:27). It is true that you cannot utter all God’s praises; yet who cannot turn away from evil and do good? Those do righteousness at every time who keep the commandment according to their ability, because turning away from evil is righteousness and doing good is righteousness.

“Remember us, O Lord, in the good pleasure of your people [Col. 1105C], and visit us with your salvation.” He rightly said, “in the good pleasure of your people,” because the Lord remembers both the good and the evil: the good, indeed, in order to show mercy; the evil, in order to punish. But such remembrance pleases the good and does not please the evil. The Prophet prayed that the Lord might visit them with his salvation. If this is understood of Christ’s incarnation, it did indeed happen, but not in the Prophet’s own time; nevertheless, even before his incarnation, he visited, ruled, and governed them.

“To see the goodness of your chosen ones, to rejoice in the joy of your nation, that you may be praised with your inheritance.” Visit us thus, he says, with your salvation: so that we may see ourselves and share in that goodness which you will confer upon your chosen ones. And let us rejoice in [Col. 1105D] the joy of your nation, by which nation the Christian people is plainly signified. This is what the Lord said to the unbelieving Jews: “Many kings and prophets wished to see what you see and did not see it, and to hear what you hear and did not hear it” (Luke 10:24). For all desired Christ’s coming, and all desired to be numbered with and joined to Christ’s Church. “That you may be praised in your inheritance.” Make us, as it were, share in the joy of your nation, so that you too may be praised by us together with your inheritance, and there may be one fold and one shepherd.

> [Note: Col. 1105] From these things it is plainly known how great was the faith and hope of St David and the righteous of the Old Testament in the Redeemer to come.

Here he begins to recount [Col. 1106A] the transgressions of that people, who always proved unbelieving, tested God in many ways, and provoked him to anger. Daniel likewise does this: he confesses his own sins and the sins of his people, so that at last the Lord may be moved to mercy by his prayers and supplications. “We have sinned with our fathers; we have acted unjustly; we have done iniquity. Our fathers in Egypt did not understand your wonders, nor were they mindful of your mercy.” These are the fathers of whom the Apostle says: “Because they were unbelieving, their bodies were strewn in the wilderness” (1 Cor. 5 [citation as printed]). Of them too the Lord says: “They shall not enter into my rest” (Heb. 4:6). For if they had understood the wonders of God which they had seen in Egypt, and had remembered the great mercy [Col. 1106B] which the Lord had shown them, they would never have feared to go against their enemies. And those who had not previously feared to enter the Red Sea afterward dreaded to fight against the Canaanites. Perhaps they would not even then have entered the Red Sea, had they not feared the Egyptians rushing upon them.

“And they provoked him when they went up to the Red Sea.” Hence Moses said to them when they were afraid and despairing: “Do not fear the Egyptians, for the Lord will fight for you, and you shall be silent” (Exod. 14:14). This, therefore, was the first trial by which they provoked the Lord after they began to leave Egypt. “And he delivered them,” not because of their merits, but for the sake of his name; for unless he had delivered them, he would have caused great loss to his own name, since everyone would have said [Col. 1106C] that he had been unable to deliver them. He did this “to make his power known to them.” But what did it profit, since they themselves refused to know it?

“And he rebuked the Red Sea, and it was dried up; and he led them through many waters, as through a wilderness; and he delivered them from the hand of those who hated them, and redeemed them from the hand of their enemies; and water covered those who afflicted them; not one of them remained.” What are we to understand by the Red Sea except baptism? And what by Pharaoh and his army except the devil and the multitude of vices? These pursue the people of God as far as baptism; but there they perish and are destroyed.

“And they believed his words and sang his praises; they acted quickly, and forgot his works [Col. 1106D], and did not endure his counsel.” Seeing, he says, the wonders God had done, they believed his words and sang his praises; they did this quickly, but suddenly failed, forgot his works, and did not endure his counsel. For if they had endured [528] and carried out his counsel, they would not have perished.

“And they desired desires in the wilderness, and tested God in the dry land.” The Apostle teaches what these trials signify when he says: “Neither let us test God, as some of them tested him and perished by serpents” (1 Cor. 10:9).—“And these things,” [Col. 1107A] he says, “all happened to them as a figure; but they were written for our correction” (1 Cor. 10:11).

“And he gave them their requests, and sent fullness into their souls.” The Lord gave them what they asked, so that at least in this way they might cease from murmuring and not doubt his omnipotence.

“And they provoked Moses in the camp, and Aaron, the holy one of the Lord. The earth opened and swallowed Dathan, and covered the congregation of Abiram; and fire blazed up in their congregation, and flame consumed the sinners.” Those who speak against God’s priests and violently attempt to seize the priesthood for themselves deserve such a death.

“And they made a calf in Horeb and worshipped a graven image; and they changed their glory into the likeness [Col. 1107B] of a calf eating hay.” God is our glory. The Jews changed this glory into a calf when they worshipped a calf in place of God. This calf devoured them, because they are hay, as it is written: “Truly the people are hay” (Isa. 40:7); and a calf eats hay.

“And they forgot God who delivered them, who did great things in Egypt, wonders in the land of Ham, terrible things in the Red Sea. And he said that he would destroy them, unless Moses his chosen one had stood in the breach before him, to turn away his wrath lest he destroy them.” This happened when the land of promise had been surveyed and Joshua, Caleb, and the others who were with them returned. When they reported what they had seen, the people were terrified and refused to cross over there, forgetting so many and such great miracles which the Lord had already worked before them, both in Egypt and in the Red Sea. Therefore the Lord, angered, wished to kill them; but Moses broke and turned away his wrath, lest he kill and destroy them. Hence it follows:

“And they regarded the desirable land as nothing.” As nothing indeed, because they were unwilling to expose themselves to dangers for its sake; and thus they did not enter the land which they had desired with such immense longing both to see and to possess. “And they did not believe his words,” by which Moses, Joshua, and Caleb encouraged them and strengthened them not to fear.

“And they murmured in their tents, nor [Col. 1107D] heard the voice of the Lord; and he raised his hand over them in the wilderness, to cast down their seed among the nations and scatter them through the regions.” Saying to Moses: “Leave me, that I may destroy this people and make you into a great nation” (Deut. 9:14). This history is indeed related to us, but it deserves very careful reflection and remembrance, lest we too forget Christ’s miracles and his mighty acts which are read to us every day, or think lightly of the inheritance promised to us. Rather, let us fight bravely against all our adversaries, that we may be able to pass over into it.

“And they were consecrated to Baal-peor, and ate [Col. 1108A] sacrifices of the dead.” I do not know what more abominable act they could ever have done—those who consecrated themselves to the devil, sacrificed to him, and ate of the very wicked sacrifices. Therefore the Lord, angered, said to Moses: “Take all the leaders of the people and hang them on gibbets before the sun, that my anger may be turned away from Israel” (Num. 25:4).

“And they provoked him by their pursuits, and destruction was multiplied among them.” All this arose from Balaam’s counsel. He taught Balak to set his maidens before the Jews, so that the wretched men, conquered by love for them, might sacrifice to their gods and come to this immeasurable crime. Therefore, entering among them with great eagerness and in great numbers, they stirred up great wrath against themselves, until Phinehas came and [Col. 1108B] killed the fornicators with the sword. And already twenty-three thousand persons had fallen when Phinehas prayed for them and was heard. This is what he says:

“Phinehas stood and pleaded, and the shaking ceased; and it was reckoned to him as righteousness from generation to generation, for ever.” We too, therefore, must imitate him, so that wherever it may be found, we may pierce the spirit of fornication with the sword of God’s word.

“And they provoked him at the waters of contradiction, and Moses was afflicted because of them, because they embittered his spirit, and he made a distinction with his lips.” These are the waters of contradiction, where the children of Israel quarrelled against the Lord, when Moses said to them: [Col. 1108C] “Hear, you rebels and unbelievers: shall we be able to bring forth water for you from this rock?” (Num. 20:10). At that time Moses “made a distinction with his lips,” by which is signified that, with great supplication, he entreated the Lord for them in the secret place of his heart.

> [Note: Col. 1107D–1108D] “Yet Moses, while preserving his holiness, deserved this punishment only because he doubted: he was not to enter the land of promise, since he had not presumed to promise great things from the Lord.” Cassiodorus.

Those waters signified the four rivers of the Gospels, flowing from Christ’s body and abundantly sufficient for all to drink. They are rightly called waters of contradiction because very many contradict them. Here he begins to recount what happened after [Col. 1108D] they crossed the Jordan [529] and entered the land of promise. The Lord had commanded them to destroy all the nations whose land they were to possess; because they did not do so, they later suffered many evils from them. But because all these things happened to them as a figure and were written for our correction, let us strive to kill and destroy utterly the entire nation of vices which dwells and rules in our flesh, so that they may never again be able to rise against us, lest perhaps it be said of us also what follows:

“They did not destroy the nations which the Lord had commanded them; and they mingled among the nations, and learned their works, and served their graven images; and it became a stumbling-block to them. And they sacrificed [Col. 1109A] their sons and their daughters to demons, and poured out innocent blood, the blood of their sons and daughters, whom they sacrificed to the graven images of Canaan; and the land was defiled with blood and polluted by their works.” The history is related here plainly, and it shows most clearly how foolish and wicked they were, and how greatly they had degenerated from their first forefathers, to whom the land had been promised—so that all might understand that by God’s just judgment all the evils happened to them which are reported to have come upon them. For their whole land was so violated and polluted by their iniquities that God rightly ought to have abhorred it.

“And they committed fornication in their inventions, and [Col. 1109B] the Lord was angry with his people, and abhorred his inheritance, and gave them into the hands of the nations; and those who hated them ruled over them, and their enemies afflicted them, and they were humbled under their hands. Many times he delivered them.” In this, indeed, God’s great mercy is shown, because although they had offended God so grievously, whenever they humbled themselves and cried out to him, he heard them and delivered them from the hands of their enemies. Whoever reads will find that this occurred especially in the time of the Judges.

“But they embittered him in their counsel, and were humbled in their iniquities.” For if they had trusted his counsel, they would not have departed from his command; thus they would not have been humbled in their iniquities by their adversaries [Col. 1109C].

“And he looked upon them when they were afflicted”—provided that they prayed to and invoked him in repentance. For this is what is meant by the words, “when he heard their prayers.” How could he hear their prayers unless they had invoked and prayed to him?

“And he remembered his covenant and repented according to the multitude of his mercies.” God does not repent, but seems to repent when he imitates the disposition of one who repents; if someone were suddenly to begin embracing and honouring the person whom he had been afflicting, he would seem to repent.

“And he gave them over to compassion in the sight of all who had taken them captive.” For their captors did not kill them or compel them to depart from their ancestral laws; and they always had prophets with them, who consoled them and promised them God’s mercies [Col. 1109D].

“Save us, O Lord our God, and gather us from among the nations, that we may give thanks to your holy name and glory in your praise.” The Prophet now speaks especially of those who shall be at the end of the age, of whom it is said elsewhere: “In those days Judah shall be saved, and Israel shall dwell securely” (Jer. 33:16). Likewise: “Though the number of the children of Israel be as the sand of the sea, a remnant shall return” (Isa. 10:21). The Prophet prays for these, whom he sees scattered among all nations, that they may be gathered into one faith, confess Christ, and glory [Col. 1110A] in him, because they have been made worthy merely to praise him.

“Blessed be the Lord God of Israel from age unto age; let it be, let it be.” Now, he says, because Jews and Gentiles from every part of the world have been gathered into one and all have come together in one faith, they all bless him and, confirming his blessings, say: “Let it be, let it be.”

## 530 PSALM 106. ALLELUIA.

What *Alleluia* signifies has indeed been sufficiently said, but it has not been sufficiently done. Therefore the Prophet so often exhorts us to praise the Lord, because we can never praise him sufficiently.

“Give thanks to the Lord, for he is good, for [Col. 1110B] his mercy is for ever.” The Prophet now exhorts to the praises of the Lord those who have been redeemed by Christ’s blood and gathered from every part of the world into the one Catholic Church.

“Let those now say who have been redeemed by the Lord, whom he redeemed from the hand of the enemy and gathered from the regions.” Now, he says, in this time of their redemption, let all who have been redeemed by the Lord give thanks to him, speak his praises, and proclaim them: namely, those whom the Lord redeemed from the hand of the enemy, freed from the devil’s power, and gathered from all nations into one faith. This is what he says:

“From the rising and the setting of the sun, from the north and from the sea.” The sea, which surrounds the whole world, here stands only for [Col. 1110C] the southern quarter.

“They wandered in the wilderness, in a waterless place, and did not find a way to a city of habitation.” All these, he says, wandered; but they were enlightened by Christ’s grace. But where did they wander? In the wilderness—and not merely in the wilderness, but in a dry wilderness. This is the wilderness of which the Prophet says: “I am the voice of one crying in the wilderness” (John 1:25). The whole world was a wilderness when the Lord came; the whole earth was dry and barren. People had not yet found that way which leads to the city of habitation: “I,” the Lord says, “am the way, the truth, and the life; no one comes to the Father except through me” (John 14:6). This, therefore, is the way which leads to the Father and to the city of habitation—the one city of habitation [Col. 1110D] into which whoever enters has an eternal and blessed dwelling.

“Hungry and thirsty, their soul fainted within them.” All were still hungry and thirsty, he says, because they had not yet tasted the food and drink of truth and wisdom; thus their soul had fainted within them through hunger and thirst—not, as the Prophet says, “a hunger for bread nor a thirst for water, but for hearing the word of God” (Amos 8:11).

“And they cried to the Lord when they were afflicted, and he delivered them from their necessities.” This happened when, having heard the Gospel preaching, they recognized that they were in error and in the devil’s snares. But when they immediately cried out and did penance, [Col. 1111A] they were saved and delivered. Then “the Lord led them out upon the right way, that they might go to a city of habitation.”

“Let them give thanks to the Lord for his mercies and for his wonders to the children of men.” It is excellently said that they should praise the Lord for his mercies and wonders, because through the mercies he has done and the wonders he has shown to the children of men, the Lord is praised and magnified. It is fitting indeed that those who have deserved to receive the good things set forth above should praise him.

“For he satisfied the empty soul and filled the hungry soul with good things.” This is what he said above: that “he delivered them from their necessities,” since they were hungry and thirsty. Those souls were empty [Col. 1111B] which were void of faith in and knowledge of Christ. God filled them with every good thing, because he enabled them to understand the sweetness and truth of both Testaments.

“Those sitting in darkness and in the shadow of death, bound in poverty and iron chains.” It is understood: the Lord delivered them. For this is continued below, where it says, “he delivered them from their necessities.” This is the people of whom the Prophet says: “The people who sat in darkness saw a great light; for those walking in the region of the shadow of death, a light arose” (Isa. 9:2). They sat in the darkness of error and blindness, and beneath the shade of that tree which gave not refreshment but death. They were in iron chains, in poverty, because they were poor in spiritual [Col. 1111C] riches and were bound by the hard chain of the devil. The following words reveal why this befell them.

“Because they embittered the word of the Lord and provoked the counsel of the Most High.” Neither by themselves nor through their teachers could they know the truth; nor were they willing to believe those who proclaimed him by divine oracle. Instead, they strove in every way to defend their error against the preachers of the divine law. This was to embitter the word of the Lord and provoke his counsel. Hence it follows:

“And their heart was humbled in labours; they were weakened, and there was none to help.” It is a great labour to seek out truth, which no one can discover by his own intellect without divine help. Therefore all the wise people of the age became foolish, and could not attain knowledge of the truth. The heart is exalted when it conquers and humbled when it is conquered. What is said here—“their heart was humbled in labours”—therefore means this: [Col. 1111D] [531] although they had laboured greatly, thinking and meditating by day and night, their heart and intellect were nevertheless conquered and humbled, because they could not attain knowledge of truth by their own intellect. They were wholly weakened, and among them there was neither Scripture nor any wise person able to assist them in this labour. Thus, while they were troubled and afflicted by such meditation, they suddenly heard the Gospel preaching, [Col. 1112A] were enlightened, and by crying to the Lord were delivered from these great necessities. This is what he says:

“And they cried to the Lord when they were afflicted, and he delivered them from their necessities.” Let us hear what these necessities were:

“And he brought them out from darkness and the shadow of death, and broke their bonds.” We have already explained this above: they were suffering the darkness of error and blindness.

“Let them give thanks to the Lord for his mercies and for his wonders to the children of men.” This too has been explained simply. Yet it deserves to be repeated often, because God’s mercy is great, as are the wonders narrated to us in this psalm. But [Col. 1112B] what wonders?

“For he shattered the bronze gates and broke the iron bars.” He shows them to have been exceedingly hard and strong by calling them bronze and iron. All the devil’s devices are so strong that they may rightly be called bronze and iron. It is therefore not surprising that the words of life cannot penetrate the hearts of wicked people, since these are so firmly shut and barred. All vices and sins are devices of the devil, resisting the word of God so that it cannot penetrate the human heart. Yet the strength and power of God prevails: however shut in and bound the wretched human being may be on the path of iniquity, God nevertheless draws him from it and calls him back to the way of truth. This is what he says:

“He received them from the way of their iniquity.” And [Col. 1112C] as though someone asked, “What is the reason that human beings can thus be bound and humbled by the devil?” he says: “For they were humbled because of their injustices.” As though to say: This happens to those who love falsehood and injustice and hate the truth which they ought to love. This is what he says:

“Their soul abhorred every food, and therefore they drew near even to the gates of death.” Their soul, he says, abhorred every health-giving and life-giving food, by which the teaching of both Testaments is signified; and therefore they drew near to the gates of death, because they joined themselves to heretics, schismatics, and other deceivers. These are the gates of death, because through them one enters into death.

[Col. 1112D] “And they cried to the Lord when they were afflicted, and he delivered them from their necessities.” This has already been explained above. But how he delivered them from their necessities follows:

“He sent his word and healed them and rescued them from their destruction.” This is understood of our Saviour, who was sent by God to heal and deliver all nations.

“Let them give thanks to the Lord for his mercies and for his wonders to the children of men.” Now, as though he said: Mercies and wonders are necessary, because holy preachers are sent to preach and to offer the sacrifice of praise. This is what he says:

“That they may offer a sacrifice of praise and proclaim [Col. 1113A] his works in exultation.” The Apostle says concerning this sacrifice: “Through him, therefore, let us continually offer to God a sacrifice of praise, that is, the calves of lips confessing his name” (Heb. 13:15). The calves of the lips are the praises, discourses, and words which the apostles are sent to preach and proclaim. But that they may be able to do this in exultation, it is necessary that God’s mercies and wonders go with them.

“Those who go down to the sea in ships, doing work upon many waters, they have seen the works of the Lord and his wonders in the deep.” Those who go down to the sea in ships are the apostles and teachers. They did work upon many waters because they preached and performed many miracles among many peoples. This is what he says: “They have seen the works [Col. 1113B] of the Lord and his wonders in the deep.” For the apostles saw wonders in the depths of the sea when, among ungodly and sinful people, they raised the dead, gave light to the blind, and performed other miracles. Each one goes down in the little ship of his own body, which indeed is frail and destined for shipwreck; but the spirit presiding over it is strong and skilled in navigation. Hence the Lord says: “The spirit indeed is willing, but the flesh is weak” (Matt. 26:41).

“He spoke, and the spirit of the storm stood, and its waves were lifted up.” This is what the Lord says through the Prophet: “I am the Lord, who trouble the sea and make its waves swell” (Isa. 51:15). For the wicked could do against the good only so much, and no more, as the Lord allowed them. “Therefore the Lord spoke”—that is, to speak was to will—“and the spirit of the storm stood.” Because the Lord willed that the spirit of the storm should stand and that the sea should persist in its boiling and tempest, its waves were lifted up [Col. 1113C]. What then did those do of whom we have just spoken, who go down to the sea in ships?

“They ascend even to the heavens and descend even to the depths.” To ascend is evil, and to descend is worse; in both [532] there is danger. Hence it says that “their soul wasted away in evils”: that is, placed amid the violence of calamities and pains, they could scarcely avoid failing in courage. We may understand that they ascended when they were dragged before tyrants to the tribunal of judgment; but they descended [Col. 1113D] when they were thrust into the lowest part of the prison.

“They were troubled and moved like a drunken man, and all their wisdom was swallowed up.” What else do these words signify except the unbearable immensity of fear and disturbance? Thus the Apostle says: “I do not wish you to be ignorant, brothers, concerning our tribulation which happened to us in Asia: we were burdened beyond measure, beyond our strength, so that we even despaired of life” (2 Cor. 1:8).

“And they cried to the Lord when they were afflicted, and he delivered them from their necessities.” Let us hear how he delivered them. “He made its storm into a breeze, and its waves were silent; and they rejoiced because they were silent, and he brought them to the harbour of their desire.” Thus he delivered them from their necessities [Col. 1114A]. These things are plain and pleasant to understand.

“Let them give thanks to the Lord for his mercies and for his wonders to the children of men.” And why? “That they may exalt him in the assembly of the people and praise him in the seat of the elders.” It is clear, then, that they cannot otherwise exalt him unless God’s mercies and wonders are present. Hence it is said elsewhere: “Having gone forth, they preached everywhere, the Lord working with them and confirming the word by the signs that followed” (Mark 16:20). What is “in the assembly of the people” except among the people of the Gentiles? And what is “in the seat of the elders” except in the synagogue of the Jews? The Lord says of this seat: “The scribes and Pharisees have sat on the seat of Moses” (Matt. 23:2).

[Col. 1114B] “For he made rivers into a wilderness and springs of waters into thirst; a fruitful land into saltness, because of the wickedness of those who dwell in it.” Conversely, “he who made a wilderness into pools of water and placed the hungry there, and they established a city of habitation.” This, therefore, is why apostles and preachers ought to exalt and praise the Lord both in the assembly of the people and in the seat of the elders: because he puts down the proud and exalts the humble; because he turns Lebanon into Carmel, and Carmel is reckoned a forest; because he turns wilderness into fruitful land and fruitful land into wilderness. To state it more plainly: because he rejected the wickedness of the Jews and chose the simplicity of the Gentiles. For what else was Gentile life but wilderness, thirsty land, and a land without [Col. 1114C] water? There, indeed, the Lord placed rivers and springs of waters, because he gave them the apostles and the volumes of the holy Scriptures. But Judaea was once a fruitful land; through the wickedness of those dwelling in it, however, it was turned into saltness and barrenness. What follows—“He made a wilderness into a pool of water and waterless land into springs of waters”—is a repetition. There, that is, in the waterless land by which the Church is signified, the Lord placed the hungry: namely, those of whom it is said, “And the hungry were filled” (1 Sam. 2:5). These established, completed, built, and caused to abound in every good thing the city of habitation, by which either the Church or heavenly Jerusalem [Col. 1114D] may be understood.

“And they sowed fields and planted vineyards, and produced the fruit of increase.” Every day God’s field is sown and God’s vineyard planted; every day they yield new fruit, the fruit of birth and new birth. “For, as the Apostle says, many were made priests according to the law, because they were prevented by death from remaining” (Heb. 7:23), so that some continually succeed others and do not cease to labour in God’s field and vineyard.

“And he blessed them, and they were multiplied exceedingly, and he did not diminish their beasts of burden.” In this place the beasts of burden are bishops and priests. They have not been diminished because, as we have just said, others are ordained in the place of others. They are called *iumenta* (“beasts of burden”), as though *iuvamenta* (“helps”); and who does not understand how fitting this name is for this order? [Col. 1115A]

“They became few, and were afflicted by the tribulation of evils and sorrows.” Now, as though he said, the beasts of burden were not diminished, even though at times, during persecution, the preachers in the Church became very few and were greatly troubled and afflicted by wicked people.

“Contempt has been poured out upon their princes, and they led them astray in a trackless place, and not on the way.” [Note: “[Col. 1115D] Contempt was poured out upon the princes. And he led them astray in a trackless place, and not on the way.” Such is the reading in St Augustine. On this he adds: “What, then, does ‘he led them astray, left them in a trackless place and not on the way’ mean? God gave them over to the desires of their heart. For this is what ‘he led them astray’ means: he handed them over to themselves.”]

Thus, as though he said, the saints were afflicted by the tribulation caused by evil men because contempt was poured out upon their princes, who led them astray in a trackless place and not on the way. These princes are heretics, always ready to contend: they deceive their own followers and do not allow the saints to rest. They deceive them in a trackless place and not on the way, because there is no one who is deceived in every respect. Where a person is led astray, he is in a trackless place; where he is not led astray, he is on the way.

533 “And he helped the poor man out of poverty, and made families like sheep.” Those of whom he said above, “They became few,” he now calls poor on account of that very smallness. Fewness and poverty are akin, and seem almost to mean the same thing. He explains how he helped the poor man out of poverty—that is, out of the aforesaid smallness—when he says, “And he made families like sheep,” because, as flocks of sheep, so he multiplied them. We may understand this of the individual Churches.

“The upright shall see and rejoice, and all iniquity shall stop its mouth.” The upright, he says, shall see those things [Col. 1115C] written in this psalm and shall rejoice, because this entire psalm is full of mercy. But let the wicked be silent and speak no further against God. No one who does not turn away from wickedness after such an abundance of mercies will be able to offer any excuse.

“Who is wise and will keep these things, and then understand the mercies of the Lord?” He, he says, is wise who keeps these things. And whoever has kept them will undoubtedly understand the mercies of the Lord. Here, however, to understand means to receive; for no one will understand them as does the one who receives them.

## PSALM CVII. A SONG OF THE PSALM OF DAVID.

[Col. 1115D] What is a song of a psalm but the praise of good action? Thus good works, and those who perform them, are praised in this psalm. He speaks against philosophers and heretics, who, exalting their own knowledge, ridicule the teaching and simplicity of the saints. But the righteous man pays no attention to them, nor on that account does he cease to proclaim the knowledge and teaching of the divine law.

“My heart is ready, O God, my heart is ready: I will sing and make melody to the Lord.” Let them do whatever they wish, say whatever they wish, praise their own doctrines, and criticize ours; my heart is always ready to sing, to rejoice, to praise, [Col. 1116A] and to preach, and to announce to all nations the word of life and salvation. This is what he says: “I will sing and make melody to the Lord.” But where? On the psaltery and harp. For this is what follows:

“Awake, my glory; awake, psaltery and harp;” I will arise at dawn. What are we to understand by the psaltery and harp except the Old and New Testaments? The psaltery has ten strings, because there are ten words of the law. On the harp, however, either three or four strings suffice: three signify the mystery of the Trinity, while four signify the same number of books of the Gospels. Thus the saints sing either on the psaltery or on the harp, because they possess no other song or doctrine than that of the Old and New Testaments. If, then, psaltery and harp are taken away from the Church, [Col. 1116B] it will have nothing to say, sing, or preach. Therefore all its glory lies in psaltery and harp, because without song, teaching, and knowledge it can have no glory.

And although every melody of psaltery and harp is sweet and pleasant to hear, yet sweetest of all is that which is played upon the three strings of the harp. Such indeed is that song of which, as the prophet Isaiah and the apostle John say, “The Seraphim and the four living creatures do not cease to sing: Holy, holy, holy is the Lord God Almighty; the whole earth is full of his glory” (Rev. IV, 9). Rightly, therefore, does the Church say: “Awake, my glory; awake, psaltery and harp”; and I indeed will arise at dawn. You, he says, psaltery, and you, harp, always be ready, so that you may cause me no [Col. 1116C] hindrance or delay, because I shall rise very early to sing. In saying that it rises at dawn, it promises thereby to sing and rejoice throughout the whole day, from morning until evening—that is, throughout every time of its life.

“I will give thanks to you among the peoples, O Lord, and make melody to you among the nations.” I am ready, he says; I have psaltery and harp, and on psaltery and harp I will sing to you and praise you among the peoples, O Lord, and make melody among the nations. Since the Jews refuse to listen, it promises to sing psalms among the nations. To sing psalms, moreover, is to fulfill the commandments of the law in word and deed.

“For your mercy has been magnified above the heavens, and your truth unto the clouds.” The mercy of God and the truth of God are our Savior, who is full of all mercy and truth; and in him and through him the Father’s mercy and truth have been revealed to all nations. This, he says, I shall confess; this I shall preach; this I shall announce among all nations: that your mercy and your truth have been magnified and exalted unto the heavens and unto the clouds. But that my preaching may be true, now come forth from the cave, emerge from the tomb, and be exalted above the heavens, O God; let your glory be made manifest over all the earth. “Be exalted above the heavens, O God, and let your glory be over all [Col. 1117A] the earth, that your chosen ones may be delivered.”

534 “Save me with your right hand, and hear me.” The Church says: that your chosen ones may be delivered, save me by your right hand and power, and hear me. The salvation of this most loving mother is the deliverance of all her children.

“God has spoken in his Holy One: I will rejoice, and divide Shechem, and measure out the valley of the tents.” The Prophet now speaks and consoles the Church, which, beginning from the very origin of the human race, lamented its calamities, though it rejoiced in the one sign by which it could flee from the face of the bow. “God,” he says, “has spoken in his Holy One,” that is, in his beloved Son; and he has spoken things that will give you joy and exultation, because [Col. 1117B] he will enlarge you to the ends of the earth and give you the whole earth which he has measured and divided into its parts. “I will rejoice,” he says, “and divide Shechem.”

The Lord fittingly begins with joy, because his joy supplies gladness to all believers. Thus at his birth the angel, promising joy to the shepherds, said: “Behold, I announce to you great joy, which shall be for all the people, because today there has been born to you a Savior, who is Christ the Lord, in the city of David” (Luke II, 10). *Shechem* is interpreted “shoulders,” and signifies those shoulders that are commanded to bear the ephod in Exodus. These are the holy apostles, bishops, and priests, who have adorned shoulders so that they may bear all others wisely and strongly. For they are those to whom the Lord says: “Take my yoke upon [Col. 1117C] you, and learn from me, because I am meek and humble of heart” (Matt. XI, 29). Therefore the Lord divided this, and apportioned among them the entire valley of the tents.

By the valley of the tents the whole world is understood, in which the tents of God have been set, through which all the Churches are signified. Of these he continues:

“Gilead is mine, and Manasseh is mine, and Ephraim is the strength of my head. Judah is my king; Moab is the pot of my hope. Into Idumea I will stretch out my sandal; the foreigners [Note: “[Col. 1117D] Codex Ghisleri: *aliens*.”] are subject to me.” Behold, all things are his; all these things belong to the Church, and thus holy mother Church has been magnified and enlarged among all nations.

But what are we to understand by “Gilead,” which is interpreted “heap of testimony,” except the teachers and masters of the Church? For they are those in whom the testimonies of both Testaments have been heaped together, and by which they ought to defend both themselves and all others. Rightly they are placed first, since they hold precedence above all others. “Manasseh,” however, is interpreted “forgetfulness,” and by it are plainly signified those who, intoxicated with the cup of the Holy Spirit, forget all earthly things and desire heavenly things alone. Such were those of whom it is said in the Acts of the Apostles: “For they all had [Col. 1118A] one heart and one soul, and no one said that anything was his own, but all things were common to them” (Acts IV, 32). Monks and hermits are also numbered among these.

But by “Ephraim,” who is called fruitful, we ought to understand all those who render to the Lord the fruit of good work. Among these are understood clergy and laity, men and women, rich and poor, free persons and slaves, and all others who are not idle but labor faithfully in the vineyard of the Lord. When he says, “the strength of my head,” it is as though he said, “my strength.” In this sense we are accustomed to call both our oxen and our laborers “our strength.” “Judah is my king.” Judah is interpreted “confession.” These are those who fight for others, unceasingly praise and bless God, and amid tortures themselves confess that their God and Creator is Christ. Such persons are worthy indeed to be made kings by the Lord.

“Moab is the pot of my hope.” Well does he place the pot after confession, because the confession of the saints alone filled the pot with flesh and brought them to the fire and to other torments. By the pot here are signified all kinds of tortures. “Moab” is interpreted “from the father,” by which we understand those to whom the Lord says in the Gospel: “You are from your father the devil” (John VIII, 54). These, then, were those whom the Lord hoped first to have as his own pot, and then as the pot of his faithful. He hoped, indeed, because he willingly and of his own accord endured his Passion.

“Into Idumea I will stretch out my sandal,” that is, my shod ones, by whom he signifies the apostles, who, as it is written, “were shod in readiness for the Gospel of peace” (Eph. VI, 18). These the Lord stretched out and sent into Idumea, which is interpreted “bloody”; what this signifies is clear. “Foreigners are subject to me.” By foreigners—[Note: “[Col. 1117D] *Allophylus*, as we said elsewhere above, signifies a man of another tribe, or of another people and nation; and St Bruno’s interpretation is sustained in this sense also, if indeed we understand persons given over to idolatry, and thus belonging to a nation very different from the Jewish people and religion.”]—who are interpreted “without a head,” we must understand universally all unbelievers and all who have no knowledge of God. For how could those have had a head who, blind and deaf, had neither ears nor eyes? Had they possessed eyes, they would by no means have said that wood and stones were gods.

Yet these were made subject to our Savior by apostolic preaching, because the walls of the Church were built from such people. These are those unpolished and uncircumcised stones, 535 which iron did not touch, because from such the Lord commanded an altar to be made for himself. Thus far the Lord has spoken. From this point the Church maintains the sequence of its discourse.

“Who will lead me into the fortified city? Or who will lead me as far as Idumea?” Who, she says, will lead me into the fortified city, that is, into the heavenly Jerusalem, where I may fear neither the pots of Moab, of which you have just spoken, nor the swords of the Idumeans stained with the blood of the saints? Or, if you wish to stretch [Col. 1119A] my feet into Idumea, who will lead me, show me the path of the journey, and guard me both going and returning?

“Is it not you, O God, who rejected us and destroyed us? Were you angry and yet merciful toward us? And will you not go forth, O God, in our powers?” You certainly will go forth, because you have so promised us, and we hope that you will act thus. For this is what the Lord says in the Gospel: “He who believes in me shall also do the works that I do, and shall do greater works than these, because I go to the Father” (John XIV, 12). And again: “These signs shall follow those who believe: in my name they shall cast out demons, they shall speak with new tongues, they shall take up serpents, they shall lay hands upon the sick, and they shall be well” (Mark XVI, 17).

[Col. 1119B] “Give us help in tribulation,” because we expect help from no other source. “And the salvation of man is vain,” for man himself is altogether vanity.

“In God we shall do valiantly.” In God, he says, we shall do valiantly, and he himself will go forth in our powers, because, as he himself said, without him we can do nothing. “And he himself will bring to nothing those who afflict us.” This is like what is said elsewhere: “They shall come to nothing, like running water” (Ps. LVII, 8). He is brought to nothing whose intention is not fulfilled. This is a most common manner of speech: we say that someone has done nothing when he could not accomplish what he began to do. Thus those came to nothing who could not bring their desires to effect.

## PSALM CVIII. UNTO THE END: A PSALM OF DAVID.

[Col. 1119C] This title has already been explained many times. When the Prophet writes “unto the end,” he does not wish it to be understood of himself but of Christ. He himself speaks in this psalm and complains of the Jews, who were ungrateful for such great benefits and returned evil for good.

“O God, do not be silent concerning my praise.” Our Savior desires the whole world to know and proclaim his mercy, power, and patience. Although with a single word he could have destroyed all his enemies—which pertains to his power—he did not wish to do so; but, filled with exceeding mercy, [Col. 1119D] he prayed for them, saying: “Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing” (Luke XXIII, 34). And, led as a sheep to slaughter, while they mocked him, cursed him, bound him, scourged him, condemned him, crowned him with thorns, and—what I tremble to say—spat upon him, struck him with their fists, crucified him, and gave him vinegar to drink, he nevertheless endured everything patiently. But who could recount it all? Better that we hear him himself and let him tell us what that foolish and senseless, ungodly and ungrateful people did against him.

“For,” he says, “the mouth of the sinner and the deceitful man has been opened against me.” Truly the mouth of a sinner, who did not fear to commit that sin with which no sin can ever be compared. Truly that of a deceiver, who, while praising him, extolling him, calling him good master, setting snares in every way, accusing him with false witnesses, and alleging offenses against the law, lied that the very maker of the law had acted against the law: “We,” they say, “have a law, and according to the law he ought to die, because he made himself the Son of God” (John XIX, 7). When Pilate could find no cause of death in him and therefore wished to release him, they all, to the contrary, cried out with one voice, saying, “Crucify, crucify!” And when he said: “What evil, then, has he done?” (ibid.), having nothing they could answer him, they did not answer what was asked, but again cried, “Crucify!” Then indeed was fulfilled what the Lord has now said: “For the mouth of the deceitful man and the sinner has been opened against me.” You say, Jews, that you have the law; why then do you not judge according to the law? Why do you condemn the just and innocent man? Why do you cry, “Crucify, crucify!” against one who has neither been defeated nor confessed? But let us hear what the Lord says:

“They spoke against me with a deceitful tongue, and surrounded me with words of hatred, and attacked me without cause.” What will you say to this? Did not your Prophet foretell it? The Holy Spirit speaking in him could not lie. He revealed your wicked counsels, your deceits, and your words full of hatred and falsehood many years beforehand; he made known this immeasurable evil which you would commit to your own destruction. It is true, then, and you cannot deny it, that you [Col. 1120C] spoke against him with a deceitful tongue: a lying tongue, a tongue deservedly condemned and to be tormented in eternal flames. It is true, I say, and you cannot deny it, that you surrounded him with words; and, as he himself says, you hated him without cause and could find no just ground against him.

I know that you would defend your cause, though it is unjust, 536 and would contend and fight against the truth, as you have always been accustomed to do, had not your Prophet and King foretold these things—him whom you do not dare contradict. But let us again hear what the Lord says:

“Instead of loving me, they slandered me.” And you, Lord, what did you do? “But I was praying: they set evils against me in return for good, and hatred in return for my love.” For this is what the Lord says through the prophet: “My chosen vineyard, I planted you; how have you turned into the bitterness of a strange vine?” (Jer. II, 21). And elsewhere: “My people, what have I done to you, or in what have I grieved you? Answer me” (Mic. VI, 3). It would be long to recount what great and numerous benefits the Lord did for that wicked and ungrateful people. “I am not sent,” says the Lord, “except to the sheep that have perished from the house of Israel” (Matt. X, 6). This is a great ground for love: for this reason they ought to have loved him greatly, since he himself testifies that he came for them. He raised their dead, gave sight to the blind, healed paralytics, cleansed lepers, and cured those with dropsy. Yet what did they say in their slander? “This [Col. 1121A] man is not from God, because he does not keep the Sabbath” (John IX, 16). In these matters, then, and in many others they slandered him, when they ought rather to have loved and honored him exceedingly. Yet he prayed, both for those very enemies of his and for all others, so that his Passion might profit all unto eternal life.

“Set a sinner over him, and let the devil stand at his right hand.” It is fitting that sinners should receive a sinner, and that those who would not receive Christ the Savior should receive Antichrist the deceiver. The devil stands at the right hand of this people because he draws them after himself, drives them to the left, and tears them away from the straight path: he shows them the left-hand way, closes the right-hand way, and does not allow them to pass by it.

[Col. 1121B] “When he is judged, let him go forth condemned.” This will occur in the judgment, when he is sent into eternal fire together with the one whom he now follows. “And let his prayer become sin.” The Jews pray daily and read the psalms and prophets, but all their prayer turns into sin for them, because they offend the Lord in this very thing: they dare to speak his words with an ungodly and polluted mouth. [Note: “Because, namely, they refuse to understand, and violently interpret in an alien sense those things which are most illustriously written in the Scriptures concerning Christ the Messiah.”]

“Let their dwelling become desolate, and let there be no one to inhabit it.” This verse is superfluous in this place and is not found in another translation. But perhaps it was added so that the number of curses might correspond to the number of coins for which the Lord was sold. [Note: “Although this curse is omitted by other interpreters, it is nevertheless not useless to retain. [Col. 1122D] For it belongs to the character of Hebrew poetry that the same matter should be expressed by different phrasing for a more forceful significance.”]

“Let his days be few.” Their days indeed were few, [Col. 1121C] because after forty-two years, when the city was taken and the temple destroyed, they were all led into captivity. If it is understood of Judas, they were neither many nor few, because he immediately went away and hanged himself with a noose.

“And let another receive his bishopric.” Matthias received Judas’s bishopric; but the Church received the Synagogue.

“Let his children become orphans, and his wife a widow.” Who could say how many of that wretched people became orphans in that miserable captivity, and how many women became widows? Yet it is not written of Judas that he had either wife or children; but because the Prophet says this, it ought not to be doubted.

“Let his children be shaken and driven away, and let them beg, [Col. 1121D] and be cast out from their dwellings.” This too happened literally: they were shaken, driven away, made beggars and poor, and expelled from their own dwellings.

“Let the moneylender search out all his substance, and let strangers plunder all his labors.” This moneylender is the devil, who gave them his money at the table and will never receive it back without interest. The interest was souls; the money, vices and [Col. 1122A] sins. Strangers will plunder his labors because whatever they have done will belong to evil spirits.

“Let there be no helper for him, nor anyone to have mercy upon his fatherless children.” For more than a thousand years this people has been in captivity, and it has deserved no help from either God or man by which it might return to its own land; nor has there been anyone to show mercy either to them or to their children.

“Let his descendants be for destruction; in one generation let his name be blotted out.” This was fulfilled in the siege of which we have already spoken above. His name was blotted out in one generation because, after the passing of forty-two years—which complete one generation—no land was afterwards called [Col. 1122B] the kingdom of the Jews.

“Let the iniquity of his fathers return to remembrance before the Lord, and let not the sin of his mother be blotted out.” For this is what the Lord says in the Gospel: “And let all the righteous blood shed upon the earth come upon you” (Matt. XXIII, 35), so that whatever either they themselves or their parents committed may be avenged upon them.

“His mother’s sin,” whether the sin of Jerusalem or the original sin committed by Eve, mother of all living beings, seems to me to be intended. This sin is blotted out in no others except those redeemed by the blood of Christ.

537 “Let them be before the Lord always, and let their memory perish from the earth.” Why is it that, having spoken in the singular up to this point, he now speaks in the plural, except that we may understand the same thing to be signified whether these things are said in the singular or in the plural? He speaks of those who persevere in wickedness and never wish to return to repentance. He desires, therefore, that such persons should always act contrary to the Lord and become ever worse in themselves; and, as it is written (Rev. XXII, 11), that the filthy should become still more filthy, so that they may suffer greater torments. Let their memory, therefore, perish from the land of the living, and let them not be written in the book of life. And why is this?

“Because this people [Note: “In the Vatican Psalter the words ‘this people’ are lacking.”] did not remember to show mercy,” although it received so many and such great mercies from the Lord.

“And persecuted the poor and needy man”; [Col. 1122D] he speaks of himself, “who, though rich in all things, became poor for our sake” (II Cor. VIII, 9)—“and delivered to death the one pierced in heart.” It is great cruelty not to spare one who is needy and poor and pierced in heart. The Lord is shown to have been pierced in heart by the fact that he wept both for Lazarus and, as is written, for the city of Jerusalem, which was already conspiring against him.

“And he loved cursing, and it shall come upon him; and he did not desire blessing, and it shall be far from him.” He loved him whose mouth is full of cursing, bitterness, and deceit; and he did not wish to have him in whom all nations are blessed. Therefore, whoever did not wish to possess blessing with Christ will possess cursing with Antichrist.

“And he put on cursing as a garment, and it entered like water into his inward parts, and like oil into his bones.” These words show that the curse adheres to him and is joined to him both inwardly and outwardly in such a way that it cannot be separated from him. Hereby an unrepentant heart and hardness of mind are signified. Hence it follows:

“Let it be to him as the garment with which he is covered, and as the girdle with which he is always girded.” In saying [Col. 1123B] “always,” he shows an inseparable union.

“This is the work of those who slander me before the Lord, and who speak evil against my soul.” The Jews speak evil of Christ daily and never cease slandering him. Therefore it is clear that, as is said here, this work is prepared for them: that all the curses of this psalm may come upon them.

“But you, Lord, Lord, deal mercifully with me for your name’s sake, because your mercy is sweet.” We have often said already that whenever the Savior asks anything and seems to need something, nothing should be referred to his divinity, but everything to his humanity. Yet even his humanity lacked nothing except insofar as he willed to lack. He asks, therefore, for us who are his members; he asks in order to teach us to ask in our necessities, since we must fight not with weapons but with prayers. Thus the Father dealt mercifully for the sake of his name, which he invoked; and his mercy is sweet because it is present when it is needed.

“Deliver me, because I am needy and poor.” He is needy and poor who cannot defend himself against his enemies. Such, in respect of itself, was Christ’s humanity; but because divinity was joined to it, there was nothing it could not do. Thus at once he was poor and rich, needy and not needy.

“And my heart is troubled within me.” This [Col. 1123D] likewise pertains to his humanity. For who but a human being, as it is written of him, “began to be distressed and sorrowful”? (Mark XIV, 33). His humanity did what belonged to it, and his divinity what belonged to it; for unless he had done this, who would have believed that he was human? Had he displayed only the nature and power of divinity, no one would have believed that he was human. [Note: “His heart, namely Christ’s, could be troubled, whose flesh was known to be extinguished for us, as he himself declared when his Passion was near: ‘My soul is sorrowful even unto death,’ Matt. XXVI, 38. All these things are narrated by a saving dispensation, so that, against heretics, the perfect nature of man in Christ the Lord may be shown, and we may be taught how we ought to pray.” Cassiodorus.] It was therefore very necessary for us that our Savior should show these affections to be in himself.

“Like a shadow when it declines, I have been taken away.” [Col. 1124A] When the shadow declines, the brightness of the sun is suddenly taken from us. So, as the darkness of blindness and error increases, the Jews cannot see the sun of righteousness and the light of truth. “And I was shaken off like a locust.” They tried to drive him away from themselves as though he were a devastator and plunderer, because unless they did so they feared they would lose both place and nation.

“My knees have been weakened through fasting, and my flesh has been changed for want of oil.” Here knees and flesh mean the apostles, who elsewhere are called eyes, feet, bones, and every kind of strong member. This is because in Christ’s Passion they appeared weak and timid, easily slipping and ready to flee. Yet this is no wonder, because they were still fasting and had not yet received the full anointing of the Holy Spirit; [Col. 1124B] therefore they were weakened and, leaving him, fled. But after receiving the Holy Spirit, how strong they were their deeds bear witness.

“And I became a reproach to them”; the apostles, he says, were weakened, and I myself became a reproach to them. “They saw me and shook their heads.” 538 They saw me scourged, crucified, and crowned with thorns, saying: “Aha, you who destroy the temple of God and rebuild it in three days, save yourself” (Matt. XXVII, 40).

“Help me, O Lord my God, and save me according to your mercy, that they may know that this is your hand, and that you, O Lord, have done it.” For this is what he says elsewhere (John XIX, 11): they would have had no power over him unless it had been given them from above. The Jews did this, and the Lord did this; [Col. 1124C] but the Jews could not have done it unless the Lord had willed it. The Lord indeed did this for us and for our salvation; the Jews did it because of their hatred and envy. The Lord did this because, as it is written, “He did not spare his own Son, but delivered him up for us all” (Rom. VIII, 32).

“They will curse, and you will bless.” The Jews curse daily, but their curses return upon their own heads. They cannot conceal their malice, because the same Prophet exposes all their sacrileges. For this is what Isaac says when blessing his son: “Let him who curses you be cursed, and let him who blesses you be filled with blessings” (Gen. XXVII, 29). Hence elsewhere it is written: “I will curse your blessings and bless your curses. Let those who rise up against me be put to shame” (Mal. II, 2). For they were put to shame because God rejected them. But a greater shame awaits them, of which he continues:

“Let those who slander me be clothed with shame and reverence, and let them be covered with their confusion as with a double garment.” Who are those who slander our Savior except those who say that he is merely a man, or inferior to the Father? They are clothed not merely with confusion, [Col. 1125A] but with double confusion, namely temporal and eternal. Thus the prophet says elsewhere: “Bring upon them a day of affliction, and crush them with a double destruction, O Lord our God” (Jer. XVII, 18). This is signified by the *diplois*, by which a double kind of garment is understood.

“I will give abundant thanks to the Lord with my mouth, and in the midst of many I will praise him.” For the Lord is great and exceedingly worthy of praise. But the Son alone can praise him exceedingly; the rest cannot praise him sufficiently. Therefore he praises him exceedingly by comparison with others, because no one can attain this measure of praise. But where does he praise him? “In the midst of many.” What is “in the midst of many”? In the Catholic Church, spread throughout [Col. 1125B] the whole world.

“Who stood at the right hand of the poor man, to save my soul from its persecutors.” Christ’s divinity stood at the right hand of his humanity, because it stood to console, direct, support, and defend it in all things. Moreover, the Father stands at the right hand of the Son, and the Son sits at the right hand of the Father, so that we may believe that according to divinity they are alike in all things.

## PSALM CIX. A PSALM OF DAVID.

In this psalm the lesser David speaks of the greater David, whom he calls his Lord and shows to be equal to the Father. [Note: “Cassiodorus seems to call ‘this psalm a certain sun of our faith, a mirror of the heavenly mystery, an armory of the Holy Scriptures, where in summary is said everything that is narrated by the preaching of both Testaments.’”]

“The Lord says [Note: “In the Vatican Psalter, as in the Vulgate, the reading is *dixit* (‘said’), so also in St Augustine.”] to my Lord: Sit at my right hand [Col. 1125C] until I make your enemies the footstool of your feet.” Let us first set forth the sequence, and then proceed to the exposition. The Father speaks to the Son, as the Prophet testifies in these three expressions: “The Lord says to my Lord,” “Until I make,” and “With you is the beginning.” The Prophet speaks to Christ in these two verses: “The rod of your power,” and “The Lord has sworn and will not repent,” and so forth. Finally, the Prophet speaks to the Father, beginning “The Lord at your right hand,” to the end of the psalm. Let us therefore begin to explain them in the order in which they are set down.

We must remember what the Lord said to the doctors of the law in the Gospel: “What do you think of Christ? Whose son is he? They say to him: David’s. He says to them: How then does David in the Spirit call him Lord, saying: ‘The Lord says to my Lord, Sit at my right hand’? For how does he call him Lord if he is his son? And,” says the Evangelist, “they could not answer him a word” (Matt. XXII, 42–43). This question [Col. 1126A] remains insoluble among the Jews even to this day; for no one can understand it except one who believes Christ to be God and man. Thus the question is very easy for us, who do not doubt that our Savior is David’s Lord according to divinity and David’s son according to humanity.

This, then, is what he says: The Lord Father says to my Lord, his Son, “Sit at my right hand.” To sit with God on one seat, and to sit at the right hand, signifies equality. But the Jews believe neither that he is God, nor equal to God, nor that he ascended into heaven, nor that he sits together with him at his right hand on the same seat. They will not depart from this unbelief until they are made the footstool of his feet. This will occur at the judgment, when, seeing him in his majesty, they shall know with complete certainty that he is both God and man. The Prophet therefore proves, by the authority of the Father himself, that the Son is equal to the Father, and that he sits and will sit at the Father’s right hand until his enemies are made his footstool. After 539 this has occurred, the Prophet’s testimony will no longer be necessary, because all will see that it is so.

“With you is the beginning in the day of your power, amid the splendors of the saints.” And this, says the Prophet, the Lord says to my Lord: that he is together with him the beginning of all creatures. [Note: [Col. 1125D] St Augustine discusses this passage more profoundly: “Since both the Father, from whom is the only-begotten Son, and the Son, in whom ‘the Word was in the beginning,’ because ‘the Word was with God,’ are beginning: what then? If both Father and Son are beginning, are there two beginnings? Far from it. For just as the Father is God and the Son is God, yet Father and Son are not two gods but one God, so the Father is beginning and the Son is beginning, yet Father and Son are not two beginnings but one beginning.”] In this respect he is nevertheless shown to be equal to the Father.
