But that he himself is the beginning, and sits at the Father’s right hand, in the day of his power and amid the splendors of the saints, will be revealed to all nations. The day of his power will be that day when he reveals himself as about to judge the world together with his saints in the splendor of his majesty. For then the saints will receive that splendor of which it is said: “The righteous shall shine like the sun in the kingdom of God” (Wisdom 3:7).

“From the womb, before the day-star, I begot you.” Likewise, says the Prophet, the Lord says this to my Lord: “I begot you.” From where? “From the womb.” When? “Before the day-star.” No time is indicated when it is said “before the day-star,” because one ascends into infinity. But what is “before the day-star,” except before it can be spoken, understood, or conceived? For to me a day-star is whatever reveals something obscure to me and enables me to understand it. It is therefore called a day-star [Col. 1126D], because it bears light. Therefore the Lord was begotten before the day-star—that is, before we can receive him in the mind. For what is not bounded by time cannot be grasped by the human mind. [Note: [Col. 1126D] “To show something, I know not what, to be incomprehensible, he says that he was begotten before that thing existed which is accustomed to announce to the world the coming day. For the beginning of him by whom all things were created cannot be comprehended.” Cassiodorus.] But what does he mean by saying, “From the womb”? For God has neither heart nor womb, nor is there any division of parts in him who always and wholly is what he is. Therefore, when he says, “From the womb, before the day-star, I begot you,” it is as though he said: “From myself, before every creature, and before he can be spoken of or conceived, I begot you.” [Note: [Col. 1127D] “From the womb: from the secret place, from what is hidden, from myself, from my substance—this is ‘from the womb’; for ‘who shall declare his generation?’” St Augustine. Below, the same doctor teaches that this may prophetically be understood of the virginal womb of Mary. He says: “For if that Virgin, drawing her offspring from David’s flesh, bore Christ from that womb, he was, as it were, begotten from David’s womb. From a womb to which no male had come. Truly from a womb, properly from a womb, because he alone came from that womb alone. Therefore, ‘from the womb,’ says he who had called him his Lord. ‘From the womb, before the day-star, I begot you’; and this very phrase ‘before the day-star’ was spoken pointedly and properly, and so fulfilled. For the Lord was born by night from the womb of the Virgin Mary,” etc.]

Thus far the Father speaks to the Son; now the Prophet likewise speaks to the Son himself.

“The Lord will send forth from Zion the rod of your power.” — “For the Law shall go forth from Zion, and the word of the Lord from Jerusalem” (Isa. 2:3). Therefore the rod of the Lord’s power is his Law and word and the evangelical preaching by which all nations are ruled and corrected. This went forth from Jerusalem when the Lord said to his disciples: “Go into all the world; preach the Gospel to every creature” [Col. 1127B] (Mark 16:15). — “You shall rule in the midst of your enemies.” All Jews and Gentiles were his enemies until that time; among them the Lord now rules and holds rod, scepter, and dominion.

“The Lord has sworn, and he will not repent: You are a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek.” For what does “he has sworn” mean except that he has determined and established it firmly? Every word of God and every ordinance of his is a covenant. “He will not repent,” because he is the one in whom he is fully well pleased. “You are,” he says, “a priest forever,” according to what the Apostle says: “But this man, because he remains forever, has an everlasting priesthood” (Heb. 7:24): not according to the order of Aaron, [Col. 1127C] which has now been destroyed, but according to the order of Melchizedek, whose generation, as it is written, has neither beginning of days nor end. Melchizedek’s sacrifice was bread and wine, in which Christ’s body and blood were signified. [Note: [Col. 1127D] I shall not pass over St Augustine’s splendid elucidation: “For insofar as he was born God from the Father, coeternal with the begetter, he is not a priest; but he is priest because of the flesh assumed, because of the victim which he would offer for us, accepted for us.”] The great priest made the great sacrifice by which he reconciled the whole world to God the Father. Thus far the Prophet speaks to the Son; now he speaks to the Father, saying:

“The Lord at your right hand [Note: [Col. 1128D] “What is said to have been done by the Father is certainly also wrought by the Son and the Spirit. Yet this may trouble someone: at the beginning of this Psalm the Father said to the Son, ‘Sit at my right hand’; now again the Prophet says that the Father’s power works at the Son’s right hand. This is said so that, when this reciprocal equality is set forth, no greater or lesser thing may in any way be supposed here.” Cassiodorus.] shall crush kings in the day of his wrath.” Your Son, my Lord, he says, whom you said above sits at your right hand, shall crush kings in the day of his wrath. For he is that stone cut from the mountain without hands which, in Daniel, crushed the statue [Col. 1127D] by which all the kingdoms of the world were signified [Col. 1128A] (Dan. 2:34). This great crushing will occur at the judgment, when it shall be said to the hostile powers: “Go, you cursed, into the eternal fire prepared for the devil and his angels” (Matt. 25:41). Hence it follows:

“He shall judge among the nations; he shall fill up ruins; he shall shatter heads in the land of many.” [Note: [Col. 1128D] Cassiodorus reads, “he shall shatter heads in the abundant land,” on which he says: “He calls abundant land that which nourishes sinners in abundance, as though it were a harvest and growth of vices.”] 540 Then indeed the Lord shall judge all nations; then he shall complete the ruins, because after that ruin no ruin shall ever happen again. Then he shall shatter many heads: he shall humble many exalted, wealthy, and proud persons. And this shall be in an abundant land—indeed, a most abundant one. For there shall be all angels, both good and evil; there shall be all human beings, whoever have been, are, and shall be; there also shall be the Lord himself, judge of all and [Col. 1128B] our Savior, who shall judge peoples in equity and nations in his wrath. Because “he drinks from the torrent on the way, therefore he has lifted up his head.” For more than thirty years our Savior, like other human beings, was on the way: he hastened toward death, drank from the torrent, endured human miseries and sufferings, and therefore lifted up his head. For he could not otherwise be exalted, who according to his divinity is Most High, and beyond whom there is nothing to which he might be further exalted.

## PSALM 110. ALLELUIA.

“Praise the Lord,” he says. This alone is sufficient for us: to praise, proclaim, and bless the Lord.

“I will confess to you, O Lord, with my whole heart, in the counsel of the righteous and in the congregation. Great are the works [Col. 1128C] of the Lord, sought out according to all his wills. His work is confession and magnificence, and his righteousness endures for ever and ever.” The Prophet teaches us how we ought to praise and proclaim God when he says, “with my whole heart.” For the Lord himself says: “You shall love the Lord your God with your whole heart, with your whole mind, and with all your strength” (Matt. 22:37). Whoever thus loves him, praises him with his whole heart, even if he is silent and his tongue does not move. But where ought we to praise him? “In the counsel of the righteous and in the congregation.” Therefore the Lord is to be praised in the Church, because there alone is the counsel and congregation of the saints. [Note: [Col. 1128D] St Bruno is not to be understood here as saying that the Church consists only of the righteous, since elsewhere he acknowledges that sinners are in it; rather, he calls it a congregation [Col. 1129D] of saints either because it is holy in itself or because it makes people holy. Or, with Cassiodorus, the future Church may be called the counsel of the righteous, when the blessed shall judge with the Lord at the time of resurrection. But the former interpretation accords better with St Bruno’s context, for he immediately contrasts this congregation of the righteous with those outside the Church, namely heretics and unbelievers. The holy Bruno also knew that all Christians, simply because they are Christians, are called saints by New Testament writers, undoubtedly for the reasons indicated by us at the outset.] Do not praise together with those outside the [Col. 1128D] Church, because there is no fellowship of Christ with [Col. 1129A] Belial (2 Cor. 6:15), no share for the believer with the unbeliever. Thus the Prophet says: “Go out from their midst, and touch no unclean thing” (Isa. 52:11).

“Great are the works of the Lord, sought out.” He commanded us to praise; he said how; he said where. Now he provides the subject matter by which we ought to praise him. His works are the matter in which his praises are found, provided they are diligently sought out. Our Lord God is great and praiseworthy not only in his greater works, but also in his lesser ones. Let us not seek examples far away, but say with the same Prophet: “Your knowledge has become wonderful from me” (Ps. 138:6). And the Apostle says: “O the depth of the riches of the wisdom and knowledge of God! How incomprehensible are his judgments, and unsearchable his ways [Col. 1129B]!” (Rom. 11:33). Great, therefore, are the works of the Lord, but they must be sought out.

“According to all his wills are confession and magnificence.” If, as though he said, you ask concerning his will, and wish to know what the Lord requires from us, know that confession and magnificence jointly accord with all his wills. For this is what the title of this Psalm means: “Praise the Lord.”

“His work and his righteousness endure for ever and ever.” [Note: [Col. 1129D] In these expositions St Bruno connects the Prophet’s words differently from their presentation, and is illuminated by St Augustine. Thus the holy doctor says: “Great are the works of the Lord, sought out according to all his wills; by which mercy abandons no one who confesses, and no one’s iniquity goes unpunished, when he chastens every [Col. 1130D] son whom he receives. But if the righteous man is scarcely saved, where shall the sinner and ungodly appear? Confession and magnificence are his work. What is more magnificent than to justify the ungodly? But perhaps a human work precedes this magnificence of God, so that when a person has confessed sins, he may deserve to be justified . . . This is the Lord’s magnificence: the justification of the sinner.”] Therefore, even among evil things, God’s creature shall never wholly perish; and righteousness would not be eternal if either the elect lacked rewards or the condemned lacked punishments. Above he had said, “Great are the works of the Lord, sought out”; now he shows that they are great in that he shows that they shall endure for ever and ever. Nor is it without purpose that he first says “works” in the plural and afterwards “work” in the singular, because all things are one in this: that they are good.

“The merciful and compassionate Lord has made a memorial of his wonders; he has given food to those who fear him.” The works which he had called above, he now calls wonders. And this 541 rightly, because God made nothing that is not wonderful. Therefore God was pleased to make a memorial of these works or wonders, lest perhaps they be consigned to oblivion through age. By “memorial” he means letters and knowledge, contained in the New and Old Testament. Therefore God willed that Scriptures should be made and sacred volumes written, for remembrance of his works. This memorial [Col. 1129D] and this spiritual food he gave as food to those who [Col. 1130A] fear him. The Lord says: “Man does not live by bread alone, but by every word of God” (Matt. 4:4). Therefore the words of God are food, [Note: [Col. 1130D] “What he said, ‘he has given food to those who fear him,’ certainly signifies spiritual food. For who would suppose that ordinary food is given to the faithful as a reward, when it is plainly known to be allotted indiscriminately also to sinners?” Cassiodorus.] since human beings live by them.

“He will remember his covenant forever; he will declare to his people the power of his works, to give them the inheritance of the nations.” The Lord will remember his covenant forever because, as he promised and confirmed by covenant, so he has done for his people. To this people, of course, he declared the power of his works and caused it to understand how great a power is in his works. For God’s works have this power: they can bestow eternal life upon those who do them. Thus it follows: “That he may give them the inheritance of the nations.” [Note: [Col. 1130D] “For he revealed the reason why he would declare to his people the power of his works: namely, in order to give them the inheritance of the nations. For this was the very purpose of the miracles: that they might believe, and that by believing they might receive the promised rewards.” Cassiodorus.] By the inheritance of the nations we understand the heavenly [Col. 1130B] Jerusalem, from which that proud one was expelled together with his entire people.

“The works of his hands are truth and judgment.” Therefore we ought to imitate him, so that our own works too may be true and just—the works whose power, as we have just heard, he has deigned to declare and reveal. “All his commandments are faithful, established for ever and ever.” They are indeed faithful, and have been confirmed and strengthened by all who preceded us; and whoever keeps them shall be blessed. “Made in truth and equity,” because nothing false, unjust, or impossible is found in them. “For his yoke is sweet and his burden light” (Matt. 11:30).

“He sent redemption to his people.” And what redemption, [Col. 1130C] except the blood of his Son? Thus the Apostle says: “For you have been bought at a great price; glorify and bear God in your body” (1 Cor. 6:20). — “He commanded his covenant forever.” The Lord, he says, commanded and firmly ordained that his covenant, the covenant confirmed by his Son’s blood, should endure forever. Thus the preceding Psalm says: “The Lord has sworn, and he will not repent: You are a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek.” — “Holy and terrible is his name.” Holy to the good, terrible to the evil; indeed holy and terrible to both good and evil, because both the good and the evil ought to venerate and fear it. By this name all things are sanctified; by [Col. 1130D] this name demons are driven out. Whoever does not [Col. 1131A] fear this name is foolish and senseless; but whoever fears it is wise. Hence it follows:

“The fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom.” It is rightly said that God has made foolish the wisdom of this world (1 Cor. 1:20). “Good understanding.” But for whom is it good? “For all who do it.” He speaks well and understands well who says, “The fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom,” provided that he does what he understands, so as to fear the Lord. Hence elsewhere it is said: “Fear God, and keep his commandments: this is the whole of man” (Eccli. 12:14).

“His praise endures for ever and ever.” The praise, he says, of the person who thus understands and thus fears the Lord endures for ever and ever, because those alone are to be praised who understand well and act well.

542 ## PSALM 111. [Col. 1131B] ALLELUIA OF THE CONVERSION OF HAGGAI AND ZECHARIAH.

[Note: [Col. 1131D] The title prefixed to this Psalm agrees with that read in Augustine: “The conversion,” he says, “of Haggai and Zechariah”; but there is another exposition, as follows. These prophets did not yet exist when these things were sung. For between the time of David and the deportation of the people of Israel to Babylon, fourteen generations are counted, as divine Scripture, especially the Evangelist Matthew, testifies. The rebuilding of the destroyed temple, according to the prophecy of St Jeremiah, was hoped for seventy years after that deportation. When these were completed [Col. 1132D] under Darius, king of Babylon, the two prophets Haggai and Zechariah were filled with the Holy Spirit, and both began to prophesy successively within a single year, which seems to concern the restoration of the Temple, as had been predicted so long before.]

The Prophet commands that we praise the Lord for the conversion of Haggai and Zechariah, who returned to their homeland after a long captivity. Haggai is interpreted “festive,” Zechariah “memory of the Lord.” They signify those who, living festively and solemnly, avoid doing servile work, and, always keeping God in memory, do not cease to praise and bless him until they are transferred from this world’s captivity to their heavenly homeland. The Prophet speaks in this Psalm concerning such persons.

“Blessed is the man who fears the Lord, who delights greatly in his commandments.” It is true, therefore, that the fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom, since blessed is the person who fears the Lord. He speaks of the fear of love, because another fear does not avail for blessedness. For demons too fear him, but such fear has not blessedness but punishment. Yet the person who fears the Lord with chaste love delights greatly in his commandments. He rightly said “greatly,” because he cannot serve and obey in his commandments as much as he desires to serve and obey him.

“His seed shall be mighty in the land.” This too belongs to blessedness. His seed are those who imitate him. And what land is meant, if not the land of the living? Therefore those who are children through imitation of this man shall be mighty there. Hence it follows:

“The generation of the upright shall be blessed.” [Note: [Col. 1132D] “The generation of the upright which is blessed is not that of the flesh, but that which is known to have been propagated through likeness of works by imitation of the righteous.” Cassiodorus.] That is, with the blessing by which the Lord will say at judgment [Col. 1131D]: “Come, blessed of my Father; receive the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world” (Matt. 25:34).

“Glory and riches are in his house.” — “In my Father’s house,” says the Lord, “there are many dwelling places” [Col. 1132A] (John 14:2). — “There one star differs from another in glory” (1 Cor. 15:41). But in whichever of those dwelling places the blessed and righteous man shall be, he will possess glory and riches. “And his righteousness endures for ever and ever.” If the righteous person is eternal, his righteousness too will be eternal; and while the righteous person remains, righteousness cannot perish.

“A light has arisen in darkness for the upright in heart.” And what light? “The Lord is merciful, compassionate, and righteous.” From this light, therefore, the upright in heart possess all that has been said and the reason why it is to be said, because Christ’s birth benefited no one except those who follow him and believe in him with upright heart.

“Pleasant is the man who has compassion and lends.” [Col. 1132B] The person, he says, who has compassion and lends, who bestows either spiritual or temporal substance, ought to be festive, pleasant, and cheerful. For, as the Apostle says: “God loves a cheerful giver” (2 Cor. 9:7). And likewise: “He who has compassion, let him do so with cheerfulness” (Rom. 12:8). This verse seems especially to concern Haggai, whose name is interpreted “festive,” and all others whom he signifies.

“He shall order his words in judgment, because he shall not be moved forever.” This man, he says, shall order his words in judgment, because before speaking he will judge all his words; and he will speak with such gravity that you would think him delivering a judgment in court. And this is what he says: “Because he shall not be moved forever”; he will not be bent to either side [Col. 1132C] from truth. Such were the holy Apostles; such ought to be the rulers of the Church.

“The righteous shall be in everlasting remembrance.” Likewise this verse concerns Zechariah, whose name is interpreted “memory of the Lord,” and others whom he signifies. Since they were always mindful of the Lord, they too shall always be in the Lord’s memory. “And they shall not fear evil report”—the report which those will hear to whom it shall be said at judgment: “Go, you cursed, into eternal fire” (Matt. 25:33).

“His heart is prepared to hope in the Lord; 543 his heart is strengthened; he shall not be moved until he sees his enemies.” Therefore, he says, the righteous person will not fear, because his heart is prepared to hope in [Col. 1132D] the Lord. “For hope,” as the Apostle says, “does not disappoint” (Rom. 5:5). Hence elsewhere the righteous man says: “In you, O Lord, I have hoped; I shall not be confounded forever.” [Note: [Col. 1132D] Ambrosian Hymn, at the end.] But one has a heart prepared for hope who serves the Lord in such a way that he ought deservedly to hope. [Col. 1133A] Hence it follows: “His heart is strengthened,” namely in hope and love. And from this he shall not be moved until he sees his enemies. What is “until he sees his enemies”? Until he comes to judgment, where he sees his enemies fearing the evil report.

“He has scattered; he has given to the poor.” This is the summit of perfection, as the Lord says in the Gospel: “If you wish to be perfect, go, sell all that you have and give to the poor; and follow me, and you shall have treasure in heaven” (Matt. 19:21). Whoever does this is therefore secure. Hence it follows: “His righteousness endures for ever and ever; his horn shall be exalted in glory.” Both he himself and his righteousness, strength, and power—which are signified by the horn—shall be forever; and they shall not merely be forever, but shall forever be exalted in glory [Col. 1133B] above the heavens.

“The sinner shall see and be angry.” The sinner, by whom the devil is understood, shall see this exaltation of the righteous and be angry. “He shall gnash his teeth and waste away.” By the outward movement the inward malice is signified; and how much the devil grieves over the salvation of the saints is shown by his being described as angry and gnashing his teeth. Then “the desire of sinners shall perish”: either the desire malignant spirits have for the destruction of the good, or that which wicked human beings have concerning their deliverance. There will no longer be a place either for the good to fear evils or for the evil to hope for goods.

## PSALM 112. ALLELUIA.

[Col. 1133C] We have often already said what Alleluia means. Nor does the Prophet wish us to cease from the praises of God, since he so often commands us to praise God.

“Praise the Lord, children; praise the name of the Lord.” Children are so called from purity. These are the children of whom it is said: “As newborn infants, desire rational milk without deceit, that by it you may grow unto salvation” (2 Pet. 2:2). For praise is not precious in the mouth of a sinner. “For God said to the sinner: Why do you recount my righteous deeds?” (Ps. 49:16). Therefore, you pure ones and children, praise the Lord; praise the name of the Lord. What is it to praise the name of the Lord, or what is the name of the Lord? Hear what the Lord says through the Prophet: “I am the Lord; [Col. 1133D] this is my name! My glory I will not give to another” (Isa. 42:8). This is the name of the whole Trinity, because the Father is Lord, the Son is Lord, and the Holy Spirit is Lord; yet they are not three lords, but one Lord. This name is proper to [Col. 1134A] him who is Lord of all and has no lord. For there is no other who is Lord of all and has no lord. Those praise this name who know themselves to be servants. What, then, is “praise the name of the Lord,” except “know and confess that you are servants”? Whoever acts otherwise denies and condemns the name of the Lord. We ought to confess not so much with our voice as with our works, so that we may faithfully serve him as a gracious Lord.

“Blessed be the name of the Lord.” Praise, he says, and say: “Blessed be the name of the Lord.” From when and until when? “From this present time and forever.” What is “from this present time”? From the present time, because “now” signifies the present time. And what is “forever”? Until the beginning [Col. 1134B] and until the end; because before the beginning there is no age, and after the end none. Behold, it is as though he said: we have heard from when and until when; but from what place and as far as where ought we to praise?

“From the rising of the sun to its setting, praise the name of the Lord.” These too are fitting bounds, because we cannot go beyond them. Therefore go, preachers, and praise the Lord from sunrise to sunset; praise him for all things whatsoever have been made from the beginning of the world and whatsoever shall be made until the end. And praise him most highly, because he is Most High. This is what he says:

“The Lord is exalted above all nations, and his glory above the heavens.” The Lord is exalted above all nations, whether those in heaven or those on earth: angels in heaven, human beings on earth; but he is above all and Lord of all. “And his glory is above the heavens.” His glory in this world is great, as though he said, but in comparison with that glory which is above the heavens, this glory is nothing.

“Who is like the Lord our God, who dwells on high and looks upon the lowly, and knows lofty things from afar?” From how great an impulse of mind, and from how great a love and desire of heart, do these words proceed! As much 544 as he loves him, so much does he delight in his praises. But it should be noted that the Lord dwells on high, although he loves only the lowly: he regards the lowly in heaven and regards the lowly on earth. [Note: [Col. 1133D] Here St Bruno seems to have followed the Vulgate reading: “who dwells on high, and looks upon the lowly in heaven and on earth.” If this verse is explained according to the character of Hebrew syntax, it appears exceedingly beautiful. It should be observed that, according to Hebrew syntax, when qualities are stated of two things, they are customarily expounded crosswise, as they say. Thus where it is said, “I am dark but beautiful, like the tents of Kedar, like the curtains of Solomon” (Song 1:4), it should be understood thus: “I am dark like the tents of Kedar, but beautiful like the curtains of Solomon.” More learned interpreters should be consulted on this point. [Col. 1134D] Accordingly, the verse, “Who is like the Lord our God, who dwells on high and looks upon the lowly in heaven and on earth?” ought to be apportioned thus: “Who is like the Lord, who dwells on high in heaven? Who is like our God, who looks upon the lowly on earth?” From this we understand that God looks upon the lowly not in heaven but on earth. This certainly better accords with reason, especially since in Sacred Scripture “to look upon” is taken in a favorable sense, as meaning “to love.” This is wonderfully confirmed by the following verses of the Psalm, for it says: “raising up the needy from the earth,” etc.] For here and there he loves only the lowly. He cast down the proud from there, [Col. 1134D] and daily humbles the proud and exalts the humble. But what are “the heights”? The heavens, the angels, the Apostles, Christians. For Christians also are sufficiently high, because whoever are not Christians are beneath them.

[Col. 1135A] “Raising up the needy from the earth, and lifting the poor from the dungheap, that he may place him with the princes of his people.” Behold how the Lord regards the lowly in heaven and on earth: he regards only the humble in heaven, because no others are there; he draws only the humble into heaven, because no others can be there. Consider how great is the mercy of almighty God: these whom he receives from earth and raises and restores from dung and decay are needy and poor, yet he places them with the princes of his people in the heavenly places.

“Who makes the barren woman dwell in a house.” No longer barren, but a mother—a most fruitful mother rejoicing in many children. This is that barren woman of whom it is written: “Rejoice, barren woman who does not bear; break forth and cry aloud, you who do not labor, because [Col. 1135B] the children of the deserted woman are more numerous than of her who has a husband” (Gal. 4:27). The children of this barren woman are those children who praise the Lord in this Psalm. She dwells in that house—indeed, she is now mistress and queen of that house in which the Synagogue and Gentile world dwelt. We may also understand by this house the heavenly homeland, in which Mother Church shall dwell with all her offspring.

## PSALM 113. ALLELUIA, ALLELUIA.

What Alleluia means has both often been said and must often be said. For it means “Praise the Lord.” The Prophet would not have said this so many times unless he knew it to be greatly necessary. Let this, then, be the work of the Church; let her delight in this work and rejoice in it day and night [Col. 1135C].

“When Israel went out of Egypt, the house of Jacob from a barbarous people: Judah became his sanctification, Israel his power; Israel reigned in it.” [Note: [Col. 1135D] These words are absent from the Vulgate.] Under the figure of the Israelite people, the Prophet describes the Christian people delivered from the devil’s power and the darkness of this world. [Note: [Col. 1135D] “Here we must understand that exodus which occurs when we come out from the bonds of sins. For then we are freed from the Egyptian throng, that is, from demons, when we do not endure the laws of that barbarous severity; and we truly become Israelites when the pomp of this world begins to depart from our mind.” Cassiodorus.] Israel and Jacob signify the same thing. When, he says, Israel—that is, the Christian people who know and see God—went out from the land of Egypt, that is, from this world’s darkness and errors; and when the house of Jacob, by which this same people is signified, went out from the barbarous people, by which is understood the army of malignant spirits and vices, then his sanctification came to be. Whose sanctification? His whom we are commanded to praise in the title of the Psalm, where it says: “Praise the Lord.” Judah, which is interpreted “confession,” is the Church, which does not cease to confess and praise the Lord even amid torments themselves. This became his confession because he alone sanctified it and cleansed it from every contagion of vices. Likewise Israel became his power, because he holds kingdom, rule, and power in the Christian people. [Col. 1136A] But the following words, “Israel shall reign in it,” are not found in another translation. Yet by Israel we may understand our Savior, who says of himself: “No one knows the Father except the Son, and anyone to whom the Son wills to reveal him” (Luke 10:22). For Israel is interpreted “the man who sees God.” By those who are first said to have gone out from Egypt, we understand the Apostles and the others who were in the primitive Church; through them the whole world was afterwards converted to faith in Christ. Hence it follows:

545 “The sea saw and fled; the Jordan turned back.” Elsewhere it is said concerning this sea: “This great and wide sea,” by which this world is signified. Therefore the sea saw the Apostles and other preachers coming to it and fled. What does “fled” mean except that it yielded them place and opened a way for their passage? Such flight is good: it proceeds not from hatred but from service. Those who flee in this manner are prepared not to resist but to obey. By the Jordan, however, the baptized people are signified: formerly they rushed headlong down to lower things, but after receiving faith in Christ they began to return to higher things and ascend to heaven.

“The mountains leapt like rams, and the hills like lambs of sheep.” The mountains and hills signify the rich and powerful. When these saw the signs and wonders performed through the Apostles, they immediately turned to faith and leapt with such joy that you would not doubt that they were rams and lambs. By these are signified all the Church’s prelates and subjects; and thus they are shown to belong to Christ’s sheep, because together with the others they rejoice in the same spiritual gladness. He fittingly placed the sea first, then the mountains and hills, because the lesser began to believe first and the greater afterwards. Thus the Apostle says: “See your calling, brothers: not many powerful, not many noble among you; but God chose the foolish things of the world in order to confound the strong” [Col. 1136C] (1 Cor. 1:26).

“What is the matter with you, O sea, that you fled, and you, O Jordan, that you turned back? Mountains, why did you leap like rams, and hills like lambs of sheep?” This great wonder proceeds from great joy. For the Prophet rejoices because he sees the whole world being converted everywhere. “What is the matter with you,” he says, “O sea, that you fled; and you mountains, why did you leap?” This does not come from yourselves. This flight and this leaping come from God. For this is what he says:

“At the presence of the Lord the earth was moved, at the presence of the God of Jacob.” What is “at the presence of the Lord”? At the knowledge of the truth. For unless people had seen God and known the truth, they would not have made so great a movement. [Note: [Col. 1136D] “Listen, you converted ones; listen, most faithful Christians, to this movement—that is, this transformation—which happily befell the human earth, made not by the trembling custom of mountains but by the people’s prosperous conversion.” Cassiodorus.] Hence he is the God of Jacob [Col. 1137A], who so suddenly taught his people to put the devil to flight and overthrow vices.

“Who turns the solid rock into a pool of water, and the crags into springs of waters.” He, he says, is the true God, who brings water forth from a rock alone and causes springs to flow from dry crags. Of the rock the Apostle indeed says: “And the rock was Christ” (1 Cor. 10:4). The crags, however, signify the apostles and teachers, from whom he brings forth for a thirsting people springs leaping up into eternal life.

“Not to us, O Lord, not to us, but give glory to your name.” He counts himself among the other prophets, because he too is a crag from which no small springs burst forth. This, he says, is your glory; these springs of water are yours; what we do is not ours, [Col. 1137B] because we do not act from ourselves [Note: [Col. 1137D] “When he bestows good things on the undeserving, what he grants is shown to belong to his own glory.” Cassiodorus]. “Not to us, therefore, not to us, but give glory to your name.” Let our labor be your glory; let all know that without you we can do nothing. Yet we ask this, that you do it out of your mercy and truth alone, because you promised to act thus. And this is what he says:

“Upon your mercy and your truth, lest at any time the nations should say: Where is their God?” Let the nations never presume to say this; but if they do say it, let them know that our God is everywhere, in heaven and on earth, and everywhere does whatever he wills [Note: [Col. 1137D] “This is the very cry of tyrants, the very cry of the heathen: ‘Where is their God?’—as though he could not rescue those whom, in order to crown them, he permits to undergo torments.” Cassiodorus]. This is what follows:

“But our God is in heaven, above in heaven, and on earth he has done all things whatsoever he willed.” But what do the other gods do, or what are they? They do nothing, [Col. 1137C] and they are nothing. Yet if you wish to hear what they are, so that you may understand from this that those which are such are not gods, hear what follows:

“The idols of the nations are silver and gold, the works of human hands. They have a mouth, and shall not speak; they have eyes, and shall not see; they have ears, and shall not hear; they have nostrils, and shall not smell; they have hands, and shall not touch; they have feet, and shall not walk; they shall not cry out with their throat; for there is no breath in their mouth.” It is sufficiently proved that those which are such are not gods. “Let those who make them become like them, and all who trust in them.” He seems to pray not against them but for them, because gold is good, silver is good, and they do nothing, nor can they do anything.

[Col. 1137D] “The house of Israel hoped in the Lord; he is their helper and their protector.” By these let us understand the patriarchs, prophets, and apostles, who, filled with the Holy Spirit, deserved beyond others to see and understand God. These hoped in the Lord and received what they hoped for.

“The house of Aaron hoped in the Lord; he is their helper and their protector.” These are the bishops, priests, [Col. 1138A] and all the rest who serve the Lord in clerical rank.

“Let those who fear the Lord hope in the Lord; 546 he is their helper and protector.” The whole Church is contained in these three verses, and the Lord has become helper and protector to all who are in it. Hence it is added:

“The Lord has been mindful of us, and has blessed us.” Had he not been mindful of us, he would not have sent his Son to redeem and bless us. For he is the one of whom it is written: “In your seed all nations shall be blessed” (Gen. 22:18). Therefore the Lord has blessed us. But perhaps you ask: whom? The Lord has blessed the house of Israel; he has blessed the house of Aaron; he has blessed all who fear him, the little with the [Col. 1138B] great. No one has been left out; all have been blessed, provided they belong to the house of Israel or the house of Aaron, among those who fear God.

“May the Lord add to you and to your children.” May the Lord the Father, he says, add to you, and to your children and imitators, all the blessing and sanctification of good works that have been mentioned [Note: [Col. 1137D] “‘May he add’ seems to be understood in two ways: either that the Lord grants in part to his saints in this age the blessing [Col. 1138D] in question; or that he may add faithful peoples to your number. This he does in our times and does not cease to do until the end of the age, so that the Church predestined from among the nations, gathered into one flock, may rejoice together and enjoy the glorious rule of one shepherd.” Cassiodorus].

“Blessed are you by the Lord, who made heaven and earth.” The Lord made both heaven and earth; he himself made the good and the evil, the righteous and sinners, and there is nothing that he did not make.

“Heaven of heaven is for the Lord; but he gave the earth to the children of men.” He gave heaven to the Lord of heaven, because he gave it to our Savior for saving and governing the Church; [Col. 1138C] but he gave the earth to the children of men, because he permitted sinners to rule over other sinners.

“The dead shall not praise you, O Lord, nor all who go down into hell. But we who live bless the Lord, from this time forth and forever.” Upon us, he says, who live, who are now no longer on earth but in heaven—for the Church is called heaven—upon us, I say, pour out your blessing, “for the dead shall not praise you, O Lord.” For those separated from you are dead. “Nor all who go down into hell, but we who live and bless the Lord from this time forth,” that is, from the present time which now lies before us, “and forever.”

## PSALM 114. ALLELUIA.

[Col. 1138D]

You know well enough what Alleluia signifies. Praise the Lord, therefore, because that is what Alleluia means.

“I have loved, because the Lord heard the voice of my prayer.” I have loved, he says, the Lord of whom this title says, “Praise the Lord.” And deservedly have I loved, because the Lord heard the voice of my prayer. What more ought he to have done for me?

[Col. 1139A] “Because he inclined his ear to me.” He not only heard me, but also inclined his ear to me. He is exalted; I am lowly. But “he regards the lowly” (Ps. 112:6); and therefore “in my days I will call upon him.” I have experienced his goodness; I do not fear adversity. If it should come, I will call upon him all the days of my life.

“The sorrows of death surrounded me; the perils of hell found me.” And he himself, as is read in what follows, delivered me. He shows that the sorrows and perils were great, calling them sorrows of death and perils of hell. For great are those sorrows which are compared to the pains of death, and great are those perils which are likened to the perils of hell.

“I found tribulation and sorrow, and I called upon the name of the Lord, [Col. 1139B] saying: O Lord, deliver my soul. The Lord is merciful and just, and our God will have mercy.” It is not the one who is sought, but the one who seeks, who is said to find something. This man, therefore, was seeking tribulation and sorrow, which he shows that he found. In this is plainly shown how greatly the saints desired to die for Christ’s name. “And I called upon the name of the Lord, saying: O Lord, deliver my soul.” He does not pray for the body; he makes no mention of the body, but asks for the deliverance of the soul alone. “The Lord is merciful and just, and our God has mercy.” How?

“The Lord guards the little ones.” How do you know this? Because already often “I was humbled, and he delivered me.” Because he has often delivered him, he is certain from this that he will yet deliver [Col. 1139C] him. “Merciful and just.” These are the two things which can give the greatest hope to all good people: that the Lord is merciful and just, and never abandons those who hope in him. Humiliation here is used in the sense of affliction and tribulation.

“Return, my soul, to your rest, because the Lord has dealt kindly with me.” Because he understands that his soul has been delivered by God’s mercy, he now urges it to return to its rest, forget all earthly things, and henceforth delight in the contemplation of God alone. The Lord indeed dealt kindly—and very kindly—who delivered him from such great dangers.

547 “Because he delivered my soul from death, [Col. 1139D] my eyes from tears, my feet from stumbling; I shall please the Lord in the land of the living.” From this, he says, I believe and do not doubt at all that I shall please the Lord in the land of the living: because he has already delivered my soul from death and freed it from all the snares and deceptions of the devil. Moreover, he delivered my eyes from tears, with which I used to soak my bed every night, and my feet from stumbling, because he who lay in wait for my heel has been conquered.

## PSALM 115. ALLELUIA, ALLELUIA.

Praise the Lord, he says, praise him—especially in this psalm, in which everyone who believes is commanded to praise.

“I believed, therefore I spoke; but I [Col. 1140A] was greatly humbled. I said, in the ecstasy of my mind: Every man is a liar.” The Prophet speaks in the person of the martyrs and exhorts them to the cup of suffering. I, he says, raised in an ecstasy of mind, examined human nature most carefully from the first man to the last, and found it so corrupted and vitiated in all that my mind compelled me to say, “Every man is a liar.” Falsehood is not only in words but also in things. Thus we call coins counterfeit, and say that gold and silver are false; and whatever degenerates from the purity of its own nature, we do not hesitate to call deceitful. Therefore, when I saw all human beings thus corrupted, and knew that they could not be freed from this corruption except by Christ’s blood, I believed in [Col. 1140B] Christ; because I believed, I spoke; and because I spoke, I was greatly humbled. For the Lord himself says in the Gospel: “Unless you believe that I am he, you will die in your sin” (John 8:25). Unless, he says, you believe that I am Jesus, which means Savior, without whom no one can be saved, you will die in your sin. This, therefore, is the reason why each of the holy martyrs says: “I believed, and because I believed, I spoke”: I preached and openly proclaimed Christ’s faith to all who heard. And because I did this, I was humbled, afflicted, and tortured by many torments; and this indeed was excessive in regard to the weakness of the flesh, though not in regard to the goodness of divine recompense. Hence it is added:

“What shall I render to the Lord for all that he has rendered [Col. 1140C] to me?” Hence blessed Job says to the Lord: “Did you not milk me like milk and curdle me like cheese? You clothed me with skin and flesh, knit me together with bones and sinews, gave me life and mercy, and your visitation guarded my spirit” (Job 10:11). Hence too the Apostle says: “The sufferings of this present time are not worthy to be compared with the future glory that shall be revealed in us” (Rom. 8:18).

“I will take the cup of salvation, and call upon the name of the Lord.” Because, he says, I have nothing greater with which I can repay him, behold, I offer myself: I will take the cup of salvation; and in taking it I will call upon the name of the Lord, confessing and praising him in death itself. For I know that “precious in the sight of the Lord [Col. 1140D] is the death of his saints.” Truly precious: it merits eternal life and immediately introduces the soul departing from the body into eternal blessedness.

“O Lord, because I am your servant; I am your servant and the son of your handmaid.” It is just, he says, that I should die for you, because I am your servant—your servant, I say, and a servant by birth, as the son of your handmaid. Your handmaid is the Church, whose son is this man who glories that he is God’s servant.

“You have broken, O Lord, my bonds; I will sacrifice to you a sacrifice of praise.” I was bound, he says; the harsh chain of the devil held and dragged me. But you have broken my bonds; you have loosed original sin, [Col. 1141A] which could not be loosed except by your blood. To you I will sacrifice a sacrifice of praise; to you I will render the calves of my lips. If you command it, I will also take the cup of salvation.

“I will pay my vows to the Lord.” Where? “In the courts of the house of the Lord.” And where is this? “In the sight of all his people.” Show this more plainly. “In your midst, Jerusalem.” I have vowed, he says, and firmly promised that I would sacrifice to the Lord a sacrifice of praise and rejoicing. These things I shall indeed render to the Lord, not in secret nor in any ordinary place, but in a celebrated and public place: in the very courts of the house of the Lord, and in the sight of all his people, in your midst, Jerusalem, where all gathering from every side may see me, and on seeing me may praise and glorify the name of the Lord. For this is what the Lord says: “So let your light shine before men, that they may see your good works and glorify your Father who is in heaven” (Matt. 5:16).

[Col. 1141B] 548 ## PSALM 115. ALLELUIA, ALLELUIA.

What this title signifies is declared by the beginning of this psalm.

“Praise the Lord, all nations, and praise him together, all peoples; because his mercy has been established over us, and the truth of the Lord remains forever.” The Prophet invites not the Jews alone, but together with them all nations, to praise the Lord, because he is the Lord not only of the Jews but of all nations. For God was formerly known in Judah, [Col. 1141C] and his name was great in Israel; but now, because he suffered for all and redeemed all nations by his blood, all ought to praise and bless him. For now “his mercy has been established over us,” and now it has been proved by the surest reasoning how gracious and merciful he is: he “loved us and washed us from our sins in his blood” (Rev. 1:5).—“And the truth of the Lord remains forever,” because what he promised through his prophets in the holy Scriptures concerning our deliverance and the restoration of his people has been fulfilled, according to the saying: “And he delivered us from our enemies and from the hand of all who hate us” (2 Kings 19:9),—“as he spoke through the mouth of his holy [Col. 1141D] prophets, who have been from of old” (Luke 2:70).

## PSALM 117. ALLELUIA.

This title seems especially suited to this psalm, as though it belonged properly to it and not to others. Hence he says later: “Appoint a solemn day amid crowded assemblies, as far as the horn of the altar.”

“Give thanks to the Lord, because he is good, because his mercy is forever.” No more fitting reason can be found for praising him than that he is good and merciful. For if he were not good and merciful, what could there be in him for which he should be praised? Remove goodness, and nothing praiseworthy remains. But God is good in one way, and every creature of his is good in another. He is good from himself; [Col. 1142A] all other things are good not from themselves but from him. Let us therefore praise the goodness and mercy of the Lord, and especially praise them now, when his mercy has been established and his goodness has been made so manifest. Hence it is added:

“Let Israel now say that he is good, that his mercy is forever.” Let it say this now, he says, because now it should especially be said, when the right hand of the Lord has wrought power and the right hand of the Lord has exalted me.

“Let the house of Aaron now say that he is good, that his mercy is forever.” Let all who fear the Lord now say that he is good, that his mercy is forever. Let all say this, because all have experienced this mercy. [Col. 1142B] Whoever refuses to say it will not share in this goodness and mercy. But only those who fear the Lord should say it; those who do not fear him, even if they say it, gain nothing by having said it. But by Israel, interpreted “seeing God,” what else should we understand than the patriarchs, prophets, apostles, and others more familiar with God? And by the house of Aaron, what is signified except bishops, priests, and others of the same order? But by those who fear God is denoted the whole multitude of the Church.

“In tribulation I called upon the Lord, and he heard me into spaciousness.” This too concerns goodness and mercy: as often as the Church has been in tribulations, so often has she cried to the Lord and been heard; and she has not merely been heard, but heard abundantly, magnificently, and [Col. 1142C] into spaciousness.

“And the Lord is my helper; I shall not fear what man may do to me.” Human strength need not be feared where the Lord grants help. For even if a man does what human beings are accustomed to do, one is nevertheless not deprived of blessedness. “The Lord is my helper, and I shall look upon my enemies.” I, he says, shall look upon my enemies, but the Lord will fight for me, and no one can withstand him.

“It is better to trust in the Lord than to trust in man. It is better to hope in the Lord than to hope in princes.” Hence it is said elsewhere: “Cursed is the man who trusts in man, makes flesh his arm, and whose heart departs from God” [Col. 1142D] (Jer. 17:5). It is not, however, a sin to seek human help; but to seek it in such a way that one places all hope in that help and doubts that one can be delivered from one’s needs without human aid—that is a great sin. For the Lord is accustomed to grant his help to the faithful when they despair of human help.

“All nations surrounded me, and in 549 the name of the Lord I took vengeance on them.” In this place the preposition *in* must be understood, so that it is said, “upon them,” as another translation has it. In the Hebrew none of this occurs, but it says only: “In the name of the Lord I took vengeance.” There is no nation that has not surrounded the Church and persecuted her; but the Lord delivered her from them all, and not only delivered her, [Col. 1143A] but also took vengeance, because all her persecutors are immediately led away to torments when they depart this life.

“Surrounding, they surrounded me, and in the name of the Lord I took vengeance on them.” This signified nothing other than the great urgency of affliction and persecution. Hence it is added:

“They surrounded me like bees.” Like bees indeed, because they were many and, inflamed with excessive fury and indignation, did not cease to wound and afflict them. For the poet says of bees (Virgil, *Georgics*, IV.236):

> Their wrath exceeds all measure; when wounded they breathe venom  
> through their bites and leave hidden wounds.  
> They fasten upon the veins and lay down their lives in the wound.

[Col. 1143B] “And they burned like fire among thorns.” Truly, their fire and wrath burned among thorns, and in burning consumed the very thorns. For what are wicked men but thorns, full of prickles and stings? “And in the name of the Lord I shall be avenged upon them.” Although the Church is avenged daily upon such people, she nevertheless still awaits a greater vengeance from them.

“I was driven and overthrown, that I might fall, but the Lord upheld me.” In many ways the saints were driven, shaken, and tested, that they might fall from the state of their uprightness; yet those whom the Lord upheld could not fall completely, and when at times they were near to falling, he made them firm and steady. Hence it is further added:

[Col. 1143C] “The Lord is my strength and my praise, and he has become my salvation.” That I stood against them, he says, that I fought, that I conquered and was strong—this is not my strength nor my praise; rather, the Lord is all my strength and my praise, he who has become my salvation. Hence elsewhere holy men say: “In God we shall do valiantly, and he will bring to nothing those who afflict us” (Ps. 59:14).

“The voice of rejoicing and salvation is in the tents of the righteous.” Hence, he says, the voice of rejoicing and salvation is in the tents of the righteous: because the Lord defends them and has become their salvation. Unless the Lord had done this, there could be no rejoicing among them, since they could in no way have resisted their adversaries.

[Col. 1143D] “The right hand of the Lord has wrought power; the right hand of the Lord has exalted me” [Note: [Col. 1143D] “The right hand of the Lord exalts when it grants the kingdoms of heaven to earthly human beings. For what is more powerful than for mortals to put on immortality, for the corruptible to put on incorruption, for sinners to receive blessedness, and for the weak to be given victory over the strongest enemy?” Cassiodorus]. The Son is the right hand of the Father, because through him he works all things. This right hand performed all this strength of the saints when our Savior overcame the devil by his death; for there all the saints were exalted in constancy and courage above all their enemies and freed from the danger of eternal death. Hence it is added:

“I shall not die, but live, and recount the works of the Lord. In chastening he chastened me, and did not [Col. 1144A] hand me over to death.” He does not speak of bodily death, which is unavoidable, but rather of the death of the soul, which alone dies when it is separated from God. Hence the Lord says: “Do not fear those who kill the body, because they cannot kill the soul” (Matt. 10:28). Thus the saints may indeed be chastened, but they cannot be killed.

“Open to me the gates of righteousness.” Why? “Having entered through them, I shall give thanks to the Lord.” Because, he says, I no longer fear death, open to me the gates of righteousness; teach me what I ought to do. He addresses this to the teachers of the Church, who, possessing the key of knowledge, show others the way of righteousness. See with what confidence he speaks: “Having entered through them,” he says, “I shall give thanks to the Lord.” Nothing will be able to frighten me into failing to preach righteousness [Col. 1144B] and confess the Lord. But they, showing not many gates but one, said: “This is the gate of the Lord; the righteous shall enter through it.” Do not seek many gates, they say, because there is one through which the righteous enter. If anyone questions you about anything, say only, “I am a Christian,” and that is enough for you. This is the gate of the Lord; the righteous enter through it; and whoever climbs in by another way is a thief and a robber.

“I will give thanks to you, O Lord, because you heard me and became my salvation.” He found the gate he was seeking and understands that this very gate is Christ, to whom he also speaks, saying: “I will give thanks to you, O Lord.” I shall seek you; I shall praise you; “because you heard me,” and by delivering me from all dangers, [Col. 1144C] “became my salvation.”

“The stone which the builders rejected has become the head of the corner.” Come, the Church says, and see the stone which the builders rejected: this stone, unjustly cast aside and rejected, has become the head of the corner, joining in himself the two 550 walls, one coming from circumcision and the other from uncircumcision, so that there may be one flock and one shepherd [Note: [Col. 1144D] St. Peter used this passage in his address to the Jewish people at Jerusalem, Acts 4:11, and in 1 Peter 2, where he showed that Christ had been foretold as gathering Jews and Gentiles into the one body of the Church.]. Evil builders, who reject the better stone and strive to set the most worthless stones in the construction of God’s house. These are the builders who, badly establishing—or rather destroying—the Synagogue, said of our Savior: “We do not want this man to reign over us” (Luke 19:14), and: “Not this man, [Col. 1144D] but Barabbas” (Luke 23:18). With this stone rejected, the whole Synagogue fell; but this was done by the Lord, and it is marvelous in our eyes. Who would not wonder that the whole Church is built upon this stone which foolish Judea rejected? Hence it is said elsewhere: “A people whom I did not know served me” (Ps. 17:15), and: “Foreign children have lied to me” (ibid., 46). What wonder, then, if the obedient, the deceitful, and the impious are rejected?

[Col. 1145A] “This is the day which the Lord has made; let us exult and rejoice in it.” This, he says, is the day on which this stone was rejected and the Church was redeemed by Christ’s blood. This is the day which the Lord made for our gladness and exultation. Let us exult and rejoice in it, and let each of us say: “O Lord, save me; O Lord, grant prosperity.” No day is more fitting for asking salvation and prosperity than that which is the beginning of salvation and prosperity and has been dedicated to us for salvation and prosperity. Let us all likewise say: “Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord,” so that he by whom all things are blessed may himself be blessed by human beings. The Lord came in the name of the Lord, as he himself said while speaking to the Jews: “I came [Col. 1145B] in the name of my Father, and you did not receive me; but another will come in his own name, and you will receive him” (John 5:43). But what does it mean that he will come in his own name, except that he will come from himself and to glorify himself?

“We have blessed you from the house of the Lord; our God, and he has shone upon us.” Bless the Lord, he says, because we too have already blessed you in another psalm, saying: “Blessed are you by the Lord, who made heaven and earth” (Ps. 113:15). We did not receive this blessing from you, but from the house of the Lord and from the Lord himself, who truly is God and Lord and has shone upon us. He has indeed shone upon us, because when we were still in the darkness of ignorance and blindness, he enlightened us and opened the gates of righteousness [Col. 1145C] and truth. In remembrance of him we ought always to celebrate this day joyfully and solemnly. Hence it is added:

“Appoint a solemn day amid crowded assemblies, as far as the horn of the altar.” Gather all together, he says; let no one dare absent himself; and let the multitude and gathering of the people be so great that they press upon the horns of the altar itself. Let each person in this great solemnity confidently say: “You are my God, and I will give thanks to you; you are my God, and I will exalt you.”

“I will give thanks to you, O Lord, because you heard me and became my salvation. Give thanks to the Lord, because he is good, because his mercy is forever.” This final verse is not connected with those preceding, [Col. 1145D] because it is the beginning of this psalm; it is placed at the end so that praise may not end, but may revolve endlessly in a circle like a wheel.

## PSALM 118. [Col. 1146A] 551 ALLELUIA

[Note: [Col. 1145D] In the edition of Marchesius the Alleluia title of this psalm is omitted, though it is found in the Vulgate and in Cassiodorus. The same commentator prefaces the psalm as follows: “A desirable Alleluia is prefixed to this festive psalm, exceedingly full of the power of divine things, so that the worthiness of the divine song may be recognized by the honor of its title. For it is most lofty in the depth of its senses, and its composition consists, as it were, in a repetition of similar words: now confessing what it has received, now again hoping for the same things that it has obtained.”]

“Blessed are the undefiled in the way, who walk in the law of the Lord.” This psalm is written according to the order of the Hebrew letters; eight verses begin with each letter. The first is Aleph, which is interpreted “doctrine”; the last is Tau, which is called “sign” or “completion.” Therefore, whoever desires to attain completion, perfection, and the highest good should follow and hold fast to the doctrine of this psalm. Let him be marked with the sign of the cross, so that he may be recognized as belonging to Christ’s militia. The letters are few indeed—twenty-two—yet they contain all divine and human knowledge. By this the great perfection of this psalm is most clearly declared. [Col. 1146B] The fact that each letter extends through eight verses signifies nothing other than that all divine and spiritual teaching instructs us to leave temporal things and seek eternal ones. For the eighth day is both the end of this life, which is lived in seven days, and the beginning of the other life, which will have no end. Hence certain psalms are entitled “for the eighth.” Therefore these letters and verses teach us to hasten toward the eighth day, so that, setting this life aside, we may hasten toward the other [Note: [Col. 1145D] I think Dallaeus’s criticism, in *On the Use of the Fathers*, p. 244, of St. Ambrose is well known: namely, that he did not successfully attain the interpretation of the Hebrew letters. The Maurist Fathers excuse the holy teacher on the ground that there were few interpreters in that period and that he relied too much upon Philo’s etymologies, which abound in errors. Some severe critic may perhaps accuse our Bruno of the same error; but he will find that Bede fell into it as well, and Bruno followed him as his guide in these interpretations, as in others. Yet St. Jerome, older in his interpretation of these same Hebrew terms and most skilled in that language, first of all gave, in his letter to Paula, formerly 155 and now 30, the interpretations used by St. Bruno.].

### ALEPH.

“Blessed are the undefiled in the way, who walk in the law of the Lord.” Blessed, he says, are those who walk in the law of the Lord, provided that they are undefiled in this life and lead an undefiled life. For this is what it means to walk in the law of the Lord, because the law of the Lord commands [Col. 1146C] that we be undefiled and walk the way undefiled. Hence it is added:

“Blessed are those who search his testimonies,” provided that “they seek him with their whole heart.” Those indeed seek him with their whole heart who keep themselves from stain. To walk in the law of the Lord and to search his testimonies mean the same thing. There is no verse in this psalm in which one does not find either “word,” “utterance,” “saying,” “justification,” “testimony,” “judgment,” or some other expression that seems to signify the law. It follows:

“For those who work iniquity have not walked in his ways.” He called blessed those who search his testimonies; yet from them all who work iniquity must be separated, [Col. 1146D] since such people neither walk in his ways nor seek him with their whole heart.

“You commanded your commandments to be kept exceedingly.” [Col. 1147A] Exceedingly, indeed, in view of human frailty and negligence, because scarcely anyone is found who keeps them as he ought. And because his commandments must be kept exceedingly: “O that my ways and works might be directed to keeping your justifications,” which are signified by the commandments. For then I shall not be confounded, when I look to all your commandments, which, as we have just said, you commanded to be kept exceedingly. To look to them is to keep them. And therefore, that I may not be confounded and that my service may be acceptable to you, “I will give thanks to you, O Lord, in uprightness of heart.” What is “in uprightness of heart” except with a right and pure heart? In that I have learned the judgments of your righteousness. Thus, he says, I shall praise you with an upright heart, having learned and [Col. 1147B] recognized that the judgments of your righteousness are right.

“I will keep your justifications,” which you commanded to be kept exceedingly; and therefore “do not utterly forsake me,” that is, do not ever abandon me completely.

552 ### BETH.

This is interpreted “house.” The house of God is the Church, whose inhabitants hold and keep this doctrine; through it, when this sevenfold period is ended, they hope to come to the eighth day, and thereafter trust to ascend to the highest good, signified by the last letter.

“By what means does a younger man correct his way? By keeping your words.” By the first letter, interpreted “doctrine,” are signified the words, commandments, utterances, justifications, and the other things already mentioned above. Therefore those young men correct their ways who keep this doctrine and these words contained in this psalm. Adolescents and young men need to correct their ways because they are those who sin more easily and more often.

“With my whole heart I have sought you; do not drive me away from your commandments.” The Lord seems to drive away from his commandments the person to whom he does not grant help, so that the person may be willing and able to keep his commandments. Therefore this man asks for help so that he may keep them, because he has a great desire to keep them. This is what he signifies in saying: “With my whole heart I have sought you.” For one who seeks God with the whole heart greatly desires to do his will.

[Col. 1147D] “In my heart I have hidden your utterances, that I may not sin against you.” Those who store God’s words in their heart and entrust them to memory sin with difficulty. But the utterances of God must be hidden in another way as well, and not revealed to everyone, as the Lord himself says: “Do not give what is holy to dogs, nor cast pearls before swine” (Matt. 7:6). Therefore I refused to make your utterances known to such people, lest perhaps, as they are accustomed to do, on hearing them they should blaspheme and curse you, and I should thereby sin against you. But you are blessed and do not heed such curses; I, however, cannot bear to hear them. “Teach me your justifications.” This is what he said above: “Do not drive me away from your commandments.”

“With my lips I have declared all the judgments of [Col. 1148A] your mouth.” Teach me, he says, your justifications, because although I concealed them from some, I nevertheless revealed them to others, and preached to those to whom I ought to preach.

“In the way of your testimonies I delighted as in all riches.” Not only, he says, did I declare the judgments of your mouth, but in declaring them I delighted as in all riches. Some preach yet do not walk in the way of the commandments; instead they proceed by another path, far from God’s testimonies. Hence the Apostle says: “Do not be led away by diverse and strange teachings” (Heb. 13:9).

“I will exercise myself in your commandments.” This man does not wish to depart from the doctrine contained in this psalm and commanded to be preached, nor does he forget how the first letter is interpreted. He further remembers [Col. 1148B] that verse in which it was said above: “Blessed are those who search his testimonies; they seek him with their whole heart.” Hence, continuing, he says:

“In your ordinances I will meditate; I will not forget your words.” Blessed indeed is the one who meditates on the law of the Lord day and night. This psalm commands nothing else than to meditate upon the Lord’s law, upon his commandments, and to search out his testimonies.

GHIMEL. This is interpreted “recompense” or “fulness.” What is signified by this letter is that those who have faithfully held and kept the teaching contained in this psalm will receive a full recompense from the Lord. For the first letter, which is interpreted “teaching,” runs through all the others until it is joined to the last. For to what other end than teaching alone were all the letters devised? Everything pertains to teaching: both what is spoken in proclaiming and what is spoken in commanding or doing.

“Reward your servant, and I will keep your words.” It is no small teaching when we are taught by others how we ought to pray to God. “Reward,” he says, “your servant with what you promised to reward those who keep your commandments.” For the Lord says in the Gospel: “If anyone keeps my word, he shall never taste death” (John 8:52). Therefore, as though he said: Grant me this reward, that I may live for ever and keep your words.

“Unveil my eyes, and I shall contemplate the wonders of your law.” Do you not see how he seeks recompense from those things which he promises that he himself will do? “If,” he says, “you open the eyes of my mind, I shall contemplate the wonders of your law, and I shall teach and keep your law.” For what good is it otherwise to contemplate?

“I am a sojourner on the earth; do not hide your commandments from me.” This is what the Apostle says: “We have here no abiding city, but we seek the one to come” (Heb. 13:14). “Open my eyes,” he says, “because I desire to see and possess not earthly but heavenly things; therefore do not hide your commandments from me.” Teach me, as though he said, your doctrine, which carnal eyes cannot see or understand. Thus the Lord says to his disciples: “To you it has been given to know the mystery of the kingdom of God, but to the rest it is in parables” (Mark 4:11).

[Col. 1149A] “My soul longed to desire your ordinances at every time.” Not only, as though he said, did I desire to perform your commandments, by which your faithful are justified; but I also desired this: always to desire to perform them, and that my mind might never depart from so noble a desire. “You rebuked the proud; cursed are those who turn aside from your commandments.” For what is prouder than to despise the commandments of one’s Lord? The Lord rebukes the proud when he says: “He who is of God hears the words of God; therefore you do not hear, because you are not of God” (John 6:47). But if they are not of God, they are certainly cursed. He speaks of those who persist and disdain to return to repentance. In every verse the teaching of this psalm makes clear how useful and necessary it is for all.

“Remove from me reproach and contempt, because I have sought out your testimonies.” To seek God’s commandments, it is not enough merely to read and understand them; one must also keep them. Those who do this are delivered from every reproach and contempt of wicked people, and are at the same time honoured by the Lord with the saints. What these reproaches were is made clear by what follows.

“For princes sat and spoke against me.” They spoke, plainly, things tending to the unbearable reproach and contempt of the righteous man. But what did he do? “Yet your servant was exercised in your ordinances.” He was exercised by meditating, reading, keeping them, and enduring harsh torments for their observance. Hence it is added:

“For your testimonies are my meditation, and your ordinances are my consolation.” Since commandments, ordinances, sayings, words, and the other terms mentioned above have the same meaning, one is almost everywhere used for another. “I was exercised,” he says, “and meditated upon your commandments, and this alone was my consolation.” Hence the Apostle says: “Whatever things were written were written for our instruction, that through the patience and consolation of the Scriptures we might have hope” (Rom. 15:4).

DALETH. This is interpreted “tablets” or “door.” Not merely all the letters together, but each one separately, possesses such beauty of doctrine as seems sufficient in itself. This letter teaches us to open the doors of our heart to this holy teaching, so that it may be inscribed and impressed upon the tablets of our mind. Of these tablets the Apostle says: “You are our letter, written not with ink on tablets of stone, but by the Spirit of the living God on tablets of flesh” (2 Cor. 3:3).

“My soul has clung to the pavement; give me life according to your word. I have declared my ways, and you heard me; teach me your ordinances.” This is the word which the Lord spoke through the prophet: “In whatever hour the sinner turns and groans, he shall live and shall not die” (Ezek. 33:12).—“Give me life,” he says, “according to your word,” because I have turned back and have declared to you my ways and [Col. 1150A] my sins, saying: “My soul has clung to the pavement.” My soul was defiled by the dust of the pavement, to which it had adhered excessively and whose pleasures it had followed. This pavement is the flesh, to which the soul is joined and by whose dust of sins it is excessively stained. This is what he says: “And you heard me.” But henceforth teach me your ordinances, so that I may obey not the pleasures of pavement and flesh, but your commandments. Hence it is added:

“Make known to me the way of your ordinances, and I shall be exercised in your wonders.” This, then, is what a person ought to do after conversion and repentance: persevere always in good works and remember his sins. For this is what follows:

[Col. 1150B] “My soul has slumbered through weariness.” Of weariness it is said elsewhere: “My soul is weary of my life” (Job 10:11). Therefore the soul slumbers through weariness, because at times, through recollection of sins, it ceases from a good work and in some manner loses confidence that it can correct everything. For this reason it rightly accuses itself and asks to be delivered from this excessive temptation. This is what it says: “Strengthen me in your words,” so that I may most firmly believe your aforesaid promise, in which you promise pardon to the sinner who turns back.

“Remove the way of iniquity from me.” For to slumber in this way is to follow the ways of iniquity, since it is close to despair.

“And have mercy on me through your law.” For this is [Col. 1150C] the most gracious law which the Lord established for sinners: “If,” he says, “you forgive people their sins, your Father also will forgive you your sins” (Matt. 6:15). You have sinned against God; another person has sinned against you. Forgive that person, so that you too may be forgiven, and so that for a hundred denarii you may not be compelled to repay ten thousand talents and be cast into prison.

“I have chosen the way of truth; I have not forgotten your judgments.” Having heard, as though he said, such great mercy from God, I have removed from myself every temptation of diabolical deceit and have chosen the way of truth alone, by which one who walks cannot go astray. Thus I have not forgotten your judgments, but have committed them most firmly to memory. For one who forgets them does not know how to walk in the way of truth.

[Col. 1150D] “I have clung to your testimonies, Lord; do not put me to shame.” What does “I have clung to your testimonies, Lord” mean, except what he just said: “I have not forgotten your judgments”? Such a person has no reason to be put to shame or blush.

“I ran in the way of your commandments when you enlarged my heart.” This verse explains the preceding one. For one can take great delight in the way of God’s commandments when, after finishing the race, one expects so great a reward.

HET. It is interpreted “itself”: this doctrine itself, he says, which is signified by the first letter of this psalm, gives us understanding and leads us into the path of God’s commandments; it itself inclines our heart toward his testimonies and turns away our eyes lest they see [Col. 1151A] vanity, and so forth; and finally it leads us to Thau, that is, consummation and eternal happiness.

“Set before me, Lord, the law, the way of your ordinances, and I will seek it always.” “Set before me,” he says, “this teaching and this law—the way that leads me to your ordinances—and I will seek it always.” For what ought to be sought, loved, and kept as much as that by which we hope to be justified and sanctified?

“Give me understanding.” For what purpose? “And I will search out your law and keep it with all my heart.” The one who does this has good understanding; but one who does not do it and does not keep the Lord’s law has no good understanding, because [Col. 1151B] “good understanding belongs to all who do it.”

“Lead me in the path of your commandments, because I have desired it.” He no longer seeks the way, which is broader, but asks for the path, because “narrow is the way that leads to life” (Matt. 7:14). For he knows that through many tribulations we must enter the kingdoms of heaven. Many walk on the way who are unable to walk in the narrower path of the commandments of the greater saints. But, as the Apostle says: “Each has his own gift from God” (1 Cor. 7:7).

“Incline my heart, O God, toward your testimonies and not toward greed.” Greed is not only greed for money, but also for honour and rank. Thus he desires his heart to bend toward the testimonies of the law, so that he may do nothing contrary to the law and repel from himself every worldly desire. The following words make this clear.

“Turn away my eyes lest they see vanity; give me life in your way.” There are many worldly vanities which we ought not to see either with inward or outward eyes. But the one who is given life in God’s way is constant in good works and does what he does not negligently but diligently.

“Establish your word for your servant in your fear.” What benefit is it to know and understand God’s sayings if we do not fear to offend God and to fail to do those sayings? [Note: [Col. 1151D] Codex Ghisianus: “and to act against the sayings,” etc.] Certainly, not a few suffer from this fault.

“Cut off my reproach, which I have suspected; for your judgments are delightful.” “Cut off,” he says, “this reproach and fault of mine which people suspect to be in me, whether it is true or not. If what they say is true, cut it off so that it may cease to be. If it is untrue, cut off this also, so that it may no longer exist in their opinion; for such an opinion both afflicts me and destroys them.
