For your judgments are delightful.” Those who call good evil and evil good depart from justice.

“Behold, I have desired your commandments.” “Behold,” he says, [Col. 1152A] “in the things said above I have sufficiently shown that I have not only done your commandments, but desired to do them.” Anyone can indeed act; but to act with desire is the gift of heavenly grace. [Note: [Col. 1151D] The power of doing good—for example, of keeping God’s commandments—through sufficient grace is possessed by everyone; but that one should will and accomplish them comes through the efficacy of heavenly grace, according to the Apostle’s words in Phil. 2:13: “God is the one working in us both to will and to accomplish according to his good pleasure.” This is the meaning of St Bruno, who cites this same statement of St Paul on p. 633, from which he concludes that we can do no good without God’s help.] “Give me life in your righteousness.” What does “give me life in your righteousness” mean, except: since you are fair and just, render my reward to me?

556 VAU is interpreted “and he himself.” He himself, he says, gave us this teaching: he from whom is all wisdom, who was always with him and is before the ages—Christ our Lord, who is Aleph and Thau, Alpha and Omega, that is, the beginning and the end.

“And may your mercy come upon us, Lord—your salvation—according to your word.” Read the Gospel, and in many places you will find that our Saviour promised his faithful mercy, salvation, the kingdom [Col. 1152B] of heaven, and eternal life. This, then, he asks: that according to his word he may grant him mercy and salvation.

“And I will answer with a word those who reproach me, because I have hoped in your words.” “This word,” he says, “I will answer to those reproaching and cursing me: that I have hoped in your words; and thus I shall not fear what man may do to me. For you said to us: ‘I will not abandon you or forsake you’ (John 14:18),” and many similar things; and in these your words we have great hope.

“And do not take the word of truth altogether out of my mouth, because I have hoped in your judgments.” What does “I have hoped in your judgments” mean except what he just said: “because I have hoped in your words”? He asks [Col. 1152C] that God never allow him to depart from the word of truth through fear of death.

“And I will keep your law always.” What is “always”? “For ever and unto age of age.” One keeps God’s law well enough if one never departs from the word of truth. By this he shows how he had previously conducted himself and how faithful he had been to the Lord.

“And I walked in spaciousness, because I have sought out your commandments.” One walks in spaciousness who keeps charity and loves God and neighbour. For this is the greatest and first commandment, of which it is said elsewhere: “Your commandment is exceedingly broad.” Hence also the Apostle says: “The fullness of the law is love” (Rom. 13:14). Since all the commandments are contained in this [Col. 1152D] one commandment, it is rightly said here: “because I have sought out your commandments.”

“And I spoke of your testimonies before kings, and I was not ashamed.” In brief, this verse declares the wisdom and patience of the martyrs. For they were wise, since they spoke of the Lord’s testimonies; they were strong, since they did not fear to speak before kings themselves; and their patience is shown in that they were not ashamed because of the very wrongs done to them.

“And I meditated on your commandments, which I loved exceedingly. [Col. 1153A] I will never,” as though he said, “forget your commandments; but day and night I shall meditate upon those which I have always loved greatly, so that I would not hesitate to hand myself over to death for their observance.” For someone seems to love exceedingly what he loves more than himself. Yet this is said according to human judgment, because not even life itself ought to be preferred to the love of God.

“And I lifted up my hands to your commandments, which I loved, and I was vehemently exercised in your ordinances.” How greatly he loved them he also shows by saying that he lifted up his hands to them. One lifts and directs one’s hands toward God’s commandments who strives not only to hear and understand, but also, as far as possible, to perform them. Hence he promises to exercise himself in them vehemently. For what is “vehemently” except to act with every [Col. 1153B] faculty of understanding and action?

ZAIN. Zain is interpreted “olive” or “fornication.” This letter therefore teaches us to be peaceable and fruitful, so that with the righteous man we may say: “But I am like a fruitful olive tree in the house of the Lord” (Ps. 51:10), and so that we may always love mercy, signified by the name “olive.” Let us also hear the Apostle say: “Flee fornication” (1 Cor. 6:18), and why we should flee fornication of mind and body.

“Remember your word to your servant, in which you gave me hope.” For the Lord says in the Gospel: “Blessed are the merciful, and blessed are the peacemakers” (Matt. 5:7), who are here signified by the letter Zain. “Remember,” he says, [Col. 1153C] “your word and promise, in which you gave great hope to me your servant and to all others who love peace and mercy.”

“This has consoled me in my humiliation, because your word has given me life.” “This hope,” he says, “has consoled me in my humility and affliction, because your word and promise will give me life.” Hence he says elsewhere: “I have been humbled exceedingly; Lord, give me life according to your word.” He shows from what he was humbled:

“The proud acted wickedly beyond measure.” How impiously and wickedly the proud acted against him is shown by his saying that they acted wickedly beyond measure: “But I did not turn aside from your law.” I did not turn aside because I always held it 556 in [Col. 1153D] memory. This is what he says:

“I remembered your judgments from of old, Lord.” What is “from of old” except “always”? “And I was consoled.” “I was consoled,” he says, “by your judgments, by which you promise many good things to your faithful.”

“Faintness of spirit seized me because of sinners who forsake your law.” How great was his zeal in keeping God’s law is shown by the fact that he grieved so much for sinners and transgressors that he fell into faintness of spirit.

[Col. 1154A] “Your ordinances were songs to me in the place of my sojourning.” Here too no small zeal is shown when he says that God’s ordinances were songs to him. They would not have been songs to him unless he performed them with great love and joy. Hence it is added:

“I remembered your name, Lord.” He kept God’s commandments very well, for even at night and amid the torments themselves he did not fear to confess God’s name. “And I kept your law”—namely, that law in which it is said: “Do not fear those who kill the body but cannot kill the soul” (Matt. 10:28).

“This came to me because I sought out your ordinances.” Keeping God’s commandments alone was the cause of that [Col. 1154B] night and tribulation; for if he had been willing to depart from God’s commandments, he would not have suffered that night and those torments. [Note: [Col. 1153D] Cassiodorus explains it differently: “This became to me”—understand, “consolation.” This should be understood more of the night than of the law: what is blindness to sinners seems to be illumination itself to holy men. Thus believers do not suffer darkness, although they dwell amid this world’s blindness. The reason follows [Col. 1154D] why night became consolation to him: “Because I sought out your ordinances.” For if he had said “my ordinances,” he would still have endured the densest darkness; but because he said “your ordinances,” he could not be blinded by the darkness of the world.]

HETH. This eighth letter—rightly interpreted “life,” since the resurrection of the dead will take place on the eighth day—teaches us that, of all things in the world, God alone and eternal life are to be sought.

“The Lord is my portion; I have said that I will keep your law.” Let others, as though he said, choose for themselves from worldly things whatever pleases them; for me it is enough that the Lord is my portion, my possession, and all my riches. And in order that I may obtain this, I promise to keep the law of the Lord.

“I entreated your face with my whole heart; [Col. 1154C] have mercy on me according to your word.” One entreats God’s face with the whole heart who strives with utmost zeal to be refashioned in his image; or who desires to come before his face, like the one who says: “Show us your face, and we shall be saved” (Ps. 79:8).

“Because I considered my ways and turned my feet toward your testimonies.” You, he says, promised pardon to the sinner who turns back and repents. Therefore have mercy on me according to your word, because I have indeed turned back, considered and corrected my ways, and directed my feet and steps toward your testimonies. And I did this willingly and with good intention [Note: [Col. 1154D] Codex Ghisianus: “I do.”], because you do not love compulsory service. This is what he says:

“I am ready and have not been troubled, to keep [Col. 1154D] your commandments. The cords of sinners have encircled me, but I have not forgotten your law.” The cords of sinners are tyrants and heretics, who strive to draw Catholic men into sins. But those who do not forget God’s law cannot be dragged by such cords.

“At midnight I arose to confess to you because of the judgments of your righteousness.” For if he had forgotten God’s law, he would never have risen at midnight to make confession. By midnight we may understand the time of most savage persecution; but the righteous man, not even then terrified, did not cease from confessing God, but amid the torments themselves cried aloud that he was a Christian. He confesses because of the judgments of God’s righteousness who maintains that God’s law is righteousness. No exposition of the law is clearer than such a confession.

“I am a companion of all who fear you and keep your commandments.” The joy alone which he has in everyone’s good work and in the service of God performed by all makes him a companion of all.

“Your mercy, Lord, fills the earth; teach me your ordinances.” “You who show mercy to all,” as though he said, “show this mercy to me too, by teaching me your law and ordinances.” The whole earth is full of the Lord’s mercy, [Col. 1155B] for he sends rain upon the just and unjust and makes his sun rise upon all. [Note: [Col. 1155D] “When he says, ‘Your mercy, Lord, fills the earth,’ he clearly shows the spread of the Christian faith, which he filled so mercifully that the name of utterly vain superstition is shown to have been emptied out on every side.” Cassiodorus, [Col. 1156D].]

557 TETH is interpreted “good,” and it exhorts us to seek God’s goodness, knowledge, discipline, and ordinances. In these the whole doctrine of the Church is contained.

“You have done goodness to your servant, Lord, according to your word.” All the good things which the Lord promised he would do for his faithful were fulfilled in Christ’s Passion. Yet individually, as he promised, he bestows a particular good upon each person: one upon the humble, another upon those enduring persecution [Note: [Col. 1156D] Codex Ghisianus: “another upon those showing mercy.”], and similarly.

“Teach me goodness, discipline, and knowledge, because I have believed your commandments.” Teach me, he says, [Col. 1155C] to do goodness, preserve ecclesiastical discipline, and defend Catholic knowledge. For I have obeyed and believed not the persuasions of heretics, the fables of poets, or the superstitions of philosophers, but your commandments alone.

“Before I was humbled, I sinned.” Before, he says, I was humbled under your yoke, which is sweet, and cast away from myself the pride and swelling of the devil, I sinned in many ways and offended you in many things. “Therefore I kept your word,” so that I might fulfil in myself what is written: “Where sin abounded, grace abounded beyond measure” (Rom. 5:20).

“You are good, Lord”—good by nature and the one without whom nothing is good. “And in your goodness teach me your ordinances,” so that my understanding may be good and pleasing to you. For this reason the doctrine of heretics is wicked: it is not in God’s goodness but in their malice.

“The iniquity of the proud has been multiplied against me.” They were sufficiently wicked, since by afflicting me they became yet more wicked. “But I will search out your commandments with my whole heart.” Let them do whatever they can and become still [Note: [Col. 1156D] Codex Ghisianus: “and still, if they wish.”] more wicked, for neither death nor life [Col. 1156A] will be able to separate me from your love and from the keeping of your commandments.

“Their heart has curdled like milk,” because, as though he said, they could not deceive us by soft words and flatteries; now their heart is hardened against us so that they spare us in nothing further. But I have meditated upon your law and have not forgotten what your law commanded me to do.

“It is good for me that you have thus humbled me” and permitted me to be afflicted with such scourges, so that I might learn your ordinances. What I could not learn by hearing or reading, I understood most fully by suffering.

“The law of your mouth is good to me beyond thousands of gold and silver.” Things lasting and eternal cannot be compared with fleeting and temporal things without injustice.

[Col. 1156B] JOD is interpreted “knowledge” or “beginning.” This letter invites us to true knowledge: to understand the law and prophets spiritually rather than according to the letter, as the Jews do; and to know that he whose hands made and formed us is the beginning of all things.

“Your hands made me and formed me.” What is signified by hands except his own strength and power? Let nothing bodily be understood in these words, for God works not with hands but by will. “For he spoke, and they were made; he commanded, and they were created” (Ps. 32:9). Look back to the first letter, interpreted “knowledge,” lest the letter deceive you into wishing to understand these words literally. Hence follows: “Give me understanding, that [Col. 1156C] I may learn your commandments.” Do you not hear that he too seeks spiritual understanding? For, as the Apostle says: “The letter kills, but the spirit gives life” (2 Cor. 3:6).

“Those who fear you will see me and rejoice, because I have hoped in your word.” This will happen at the judgment, when all who fear God, whether angels or human beings, see the holy Church glorious and shining as though with rays of the sun, and rejoice in her glory and honour. But she will possess this because she placed most firm hope in the word of God, in his promises, and could not be separated from him for any reason.

“I have known, Lord, that your judgments are righteousness.” All God’s judgments are true and just, whether prosperity happens to the wicked [Col. 1156D] or adversity to the good, although even righteous men are sometimes scandalized by this. But the Church says that she has recognized this, and therefore rejoices in her calamities and afflictions. Hence it is added: “And in your truth you humbled me.” The Lord is truthful both when he exalts and when he humbles his saints, because he assists them no less by humbling than by exalting them. He seems to say this because the Lord 558 says: “I will not abandon you or forsake you” (John 14:18). This is not [Col. 1157A] abandonment, but testing and preparation for greater glory.

“Let your mercy now come to console me.” “I rejoice,” as though he said, “in the things I have endured; but now I ask that consoling mercy be granted to me, according to your word to your servant.”

“May your mercies come to me, and I shall live.” “May your mercies now come to me, your servant,” he says, “and I shall live according to your word and your promises.” Such is the order. He rightly says, “according to your word,” because in many places of both Testaments the Lord promises mercy and help to his faithful. “For your law is my meditation.” This is a good reason why the Lord should have mercy on him. On whom will the Lord have mercy [Col. 1157B] if he does not heed those who keep his commandments?

“Let the proud be put to shame, because they have unjustly committed iniquity against me.” “Let the proud,” he says, “be put to shame and blush because they committed iniquity against me—unjustly, because I invited them to the way of truth.” This is a good shame, because he prays not against them but for them. “But I was exercised in your commandments.” This is the study and exercise of the saints: always to keep God’s commandments.

“Let those who fear you and know your testimonies turn to me.” For all who fear God and understand his testimonies, wherever they go, always turn to the Church and follow her precepts. Many separate themselves from her daily by sinning, but return to her by repenting.

“Let my heart be unstained in your ordinances, that I may not be put to shame.” Let those, then, be put to shame who presume to handle God’s ordinances with a foul and stained heart. This is characteristic of heretics, who interpret the divine Scriptures with a perverse heart.

CAPH. This element, interpreted “hand,” invites us to fight and labour. Such hands has the one who says: “Blessed be the Lord my God, who teaches my hands for battle and my fingers for war” (Ps. 143:1). And the Apostle: “Let each work with his own hands, doing [Col. 1157D] what is good” (Eph. 4:28). Elsewhere: “You shall eat the labours of your hands” (Ps. 127:2). The Church shows herself to be in a great battle in this passage [Note: [Col. 1157D] Thus Codex Ghisianus.], when she says: “For I have become like a wineskin in frost” (Ps. 118:83), and (232): “They have almost consumed me on earth” (ibid., 87).

“My soul has failed for your salvation, and I have hoped in your words.” So great, as though he said, was my desire for your salvation, which is eternal, that the desire for my own salvation, which is temporal, wholly failed within my soul. Therefore I have hoped in your word and promise, which grants me eternal salvation. [Col. 1158A] This is a good failing, which brings the soul to so great a restoration.

“My eyes have failed for your word.” These eyes are not of flesh but of the mind; they fail to see and despise the world’s vanities, so that they may contemplate divine sayings alone, “saying: When will you console me?” Such eyes speak, as is said elsewhere: “Let not the pupil of your eye be silent” (Lam. 2:18). All our members speak to God, and he hears the eyes no less than the tongue. God sees through every member of our body and understands the intention of our heart.

“For I have become like a wineskin in frost.” This, then, is why he seeks consolation. Nothing could have shown more fittingly the calamity of the saints than a wineskin constricted and frozen in frost.

“I have not forgotten your ordinances.” “I have not,” he says, “forgotten your ordinances because, surrounded by such miseries, I have become like a wineskin in frost.”

“How many are the days of your servant?”—that is, how many days must I endure amid these calamities? “When will you execute judgment upon my persecutors?” “My hands,” as though he said, “now fail, and I cannot fight against them.”

“The wicked have told fables” by which they endeavour to deceive my mind. “But they are not” like “your law, Lord.” Why is this? “All your commandments are truth”; but their fables [Col. 1158C] are full of every falsehood and error.

“The wicked have persecuted me; help and assist me.” These words show the persecution to be exceedingly harsh and intolerable. Hence it is added:

“They almost consumed me on earth.” This is an evil consummation, by which human life on earth is ended. One who ends in this way does not attain eternal blessedness. “But I did not abandon your commandments.” Had I done so, I would have been wholly consumed on earth [Note: [Col. 1157D] Codex Ghisianus.].

“According to your mercy, give me life,” so that, as I have begun, I may always “keep the testimonies of your mouth.” Not without reason does one who says that he is like a wineskin in frost ask to be given life.

[Col. 1158D] 559 LAMED. Lamed is interpreted “discipline.” All Christians are disciples of this discipline: they hold and preach it, defend it, and hope to be saved through it.

“For ever, Lord, your word remains in heaven.” All divine Scriptures, and especially the Gospels, teach us that the Church is called heaven. Therefore in the Church the word of God and the doctrine of both Testaments remain for ever. Hence the Lord says: “Heaven and earth shall pass away, but my words shall not pass away” (Mark 13:31). [Note: [Col. 1158D] The Vulgate reads: “Your truth is from generation to generation.”]

“And your truth unto age of age.” The same thing is signified both by the word of God and by the truth of God. For all God’s teaching is truth, and there is nothing blameworthy in it.

“You founded the earth, and it remains.” This earth is the Church, which he has just called heaven; its foundation is Christ, as the Apostle says: “No one can lay another foundation than that which is laid, which is Christ Jesus” (1 Cor. 3:11). This likewise remains for ever, though it does not remain in this world for ever.

“By your ordinance the day endures, because all things serve you.” Apart from angel and human being, all other things keep the order appointed to them by the Lord. But these are good days that persevere in the Lord’s ordinance, by which we may understand the apostles and their successors. The earth preserves its stability, and the days also preserve their order. “All things,” however, [Col. 1159B] “serve you.” Rightly, he says, did you establish the earth and order the days, because through these and in these all other things serve you.

“Unless your law were my meditation, perhaps I would then have perished in my humiliation.” “Then,” he says, “when I was humbled, when the ungodly scourged and tormented me, perhaps I would have perished in that very humiliation and affliction, unless your law were my meditation,” for it strengthens and consoles me. Hence the Apostle says: “That through patience and the consolation of the Scriptures we may have hope” (Rom. 15:4).—“For ever I shall not forget your ordinances.” And this is because “in them [Col. 1159C] you have given me life”; for, as I have just said, perhaps without them I would have perished in my humiliation.

“I am yours; save me.” He speaks of the salvation of the soul, because the Lord saves no others in respect of the soul except those who are his. Although all things are his, only those are said to be his who serve him and believe in him. “Because I have sought out your ordinances.” For many reasons he gives this account of his salvation: because he keeps the Lord’s commandments.

“Sinners waited for me, to destroy me.” And what did you do? “I understood your testimonies,” and therefore they could not destroy me. Nor did I fear those who kill the body, because they cannot kill the soul; and this too is your testimony.

“Of every perfection I have seen the end; your commandment is exceedingly broad.” “I have seen,” he says, “tested, and most certainly recognized that your commandment is exceedingly broad, being the end of every completion and perfection; and whoever keeps it is secure and cannot be overcome by enemies. For whoever loves God and neighbor fears offending God and neighbor. This commandment is broad—indeed, exceedingly broad—because all the others are contained within it.”

MEM. *Mem* is interpreted “from which,” or “from these.” It is connected with what precedes and still speaks of the same first and greatest commandment. It is rightly said here, “from which,” or “from these,” because it speaks of that commandment [Col. 1160A] which is both one and many. Let us therefore hear what the following words say, both from it and from them.

“How I have loved your law, O Lord! It is my meditation all the day.” And indeed he would not have done this unless he had loved it greatly. “But the greatest and first commandment is: You shall love your God with your whole heart and with all your strength” (Matt. 22:37), etc.

“You have made me wiser than all my enemies through your commandment, because it is mine for ever.” This commandment, he says, has made me more prudent and wiser than all my enemies, because it grants me eternal life. And this is what he says: “Because it is mine for ever.” Whoever offends against it becomes guilty of all. But the remaining commandments [Col. 1160B] are five hundred and sixty in number. Accordingly, we may understand what “from which,” or “from these,” signifies.

“I have understood more than all who teach me, because your testimonies are my meditation.” Disciples readily understand better than their own teachers if they keep the law; for the person who observes it meditates well upon the law. Hence the Apostle says: “For not the hearers of the law are righteous before God, but the doers of the law shall be justified” (Rom. 2:13).

“I have understood more than the elders, because I have sought your commandments.” I have sought them, however, more by doing than by reading. Neither teachers nor elders understand the law unless they do what they understand.

“I have restrained my feet from every evil way, that I may keep your word.” For he could not otherwise have kept the word [Col. 1160C] of God unless he had turned away from evil, since the Lord commands one to turn away from evil.

“I have not turned aside from your judgments, because you have laid down the law for me,” so that I should not turn aside from your judgments. “If you wish,” says the Lord, “to be perfect, keep the commandments” (Matt. 19:21). Likewise: “Whoever loves me keeps my commandments” (John 14:15).

“How sweet are your words to my palate, more than honey and the honeycomb to my mouth.” Only those can say this who desire both to hear and to do the words of God. For there are many—including myself among them—to whom hearing is sweet, but doing seems exceedingly bitter.

“From your commandments I have gained understanding.” He does not merely say, as it were, “I have understood your commandments,” but that from them I received the manner of understanding and understanding itself, which I did not previously possess. “Therefore I have hated every way of iniquity”—that way, namely, which those who do not understand your commandments greatly love. The words which follow, “because you have laid down the law for me,” are not found in another translation. Yet there is great reason for us to hate iniquity, because a law of righteousness and equity has been laid down for us.

NUN. This letter, which is interpreted “everlasting,” or “fish,” signifies that this teaching is everlasting and promises eternal life to all who keep it. But those who desire through it to come to blessedness must become fish and swim in the waters of baptism. Hence the Lord says: [Col. 1161A] “Unless one is born again of water and the Holy Spirit, he cannot enter the kingdom of God” (John 3:5).

“Your word, O Lord, is a lamp to my feet and a light to my paths.” This word of yours, he says, and this teaching of yours, are a lamp and a light to me, so that I may be able to walk along the right road; for those not led by this light are blind and walk in darkness. Therefore, “I have sworn and resolved to keep the judgments of your righteousness.” All who receive the faith of Christ make this oath. For this reason also, “I have been utterly humbled, O Lord.” Those are truly humbled, and humbled wholly, who are illuminated by so great a light and such a lamp. “Give me life according to your word.” For this is the word of which the Lord says: “Everyone [Col. 1161B] who exalts himself shall be humbled, and whoever humbles himself shall be exalted” (Luke 18:14).

“Make acceptable to yourself, O Lord, the freewill offerings of my mouth.” What are these freewill offerings, which he asks may so please the Lord, except those oaths which he said just above that he had vowed and resolved: “And teach me your judgments,” because otherwise I cannot keep them, even with an oath.

“My soul is always in my hands [Note: Augustine observes: ‘Some manuscripts read “in my hands,” but more read “in your hands,” and that is plainly correct. For the souls of the righteous are in God’s hand. In his hand are both we and our words’ (Col. 1161D)].” Blessed Job similarly says: “Why do I tear my flesh with my teeth, and carry my soul in my hands?” (Job 13:14). He carries his soul in his hands who presents it to the Lord by good works. May our soul always be in our hands, so that we never forget it and never [Col. 1161C] allow it to fall; “and I have not forgotten your law.” Those who forget God’s law do not have their soul with them. But those who keep it before their hands cannot forget God’s law.

“Sinners have laid snares for me, and I have not strayed from your commandments.” Had he forgotten the law of God, he could not have kept God’s commandments amid the snares of sinners.

“I have gained your testimonies as an inheritance for ever.” If he had held God’s testimonies as something alien and merely lent to him, he could never have possessed them eternally; but because they were gained by right of inheritance, he does not fear losing them. This is why the letter from which these verses begin [Col. 1161D] is interpreted “everlasting.” “For they are the exultation of my heart.” God’s testimonies are therefore hereditary to those who keep them with exultation; from others, however, they readily slip away.

“I have inclined my heart to perform your statutes for ever.” And why is this? Because of the reward which I do not doubt that I shall receive for doing this. He promises to perform God’s statutes for ever [Col. 1162A] because he has gained them as an everlasting inheritance.

SAMECH is interpreted “help”; hence it is said here: “You are my helper and protector. Help me, and I shall be saved.” Those indeed shall have this help who keep this teaching and this law.

“I have hated the unrighteous, and I have loved your law.” He loves the law who observes the law’s commandments. The law commands, as the Lord says: “You shall love your friend and hate your enemy” (Matt. 5:43). But another law, on the contrary, says: “Love your enemies” (ibid.). Let us therefore love unrighteous people according to their nature, but not love them according to the vice which they practise; thus we may do both things: love the law and hate the unrighteous.

[Col. 1162B] “You are my helper and protector, and I have hoped in your word.” Thus the letter *Samech* signifies that the Lord is the helper of those who hope in his word and await his promises with the fullest confidence.

“Depart from me, you wicked.” Why? “And I will search out the commandments of my God.” Because I love those, but hate you. These are the unrighteous of whom he has just said, “I have hated the unrighteous”; unless they withdraw and depart from him, he cannot search out God’s law, “for evil communications corrupt good manners” (1 Cor. 15:33).

“Uphold me according to your word, and I shall live.”—“Everyone who comes to me,” says the Lord, “I will not cast out” (John 6:37). Only those received by the Lord live. “And do not confound [Col. 1162C] me in my expectation.” Those shall be confounded in their expectation to whom the door will be shut at judgment, and to whom the Lord will say: “Truly I say to you, I do not know you” (Matt. 25:12).

“Help me, and I shall be saved; and I shall meditate continually on your statutes.” God is the one who works in us both the willing and the ability (Phil. 2:13), and without his help we can do nothing good [Note: The necessity of God’s grace even for the beginning of any good action is taught against the Semi-Pelagians, in accordance with the mind of St Augustine (Cols. 1161D, 1162D).].

“You have despised all who depart from your statutes, because their thought is unjust.” Unjust and wholly wicked is the thought of those who so depart from the Lord’s commandments, by which people are made righteous, that they do not afterwards return to them by repentance.

[Col. 1162D] “I have considered all the sinners of the earth transgressors.” All human beings were made transgressors in Adam [Note: Codex Vallicellianus: “they transgressed.”], who, violating the law imposed upon him, approached the tree forbidden to him. In that transgression all perish who have not been redeemed by Christ’s blood [Note: Infants without baptism perish; for they too are transgressors of the law given by God to Adam in paradise, and therefore need God’s grace—namely baptismal regeneration—in order to be saved. This is Augustine’s opinion.]. But those who have been redeemed become transgressors unless they keep the law given to them. Therefore there can be no doubt that all sinners are [Col. 1163A] transgressors. “Therefore I have loved your testimonies.” For they are the very things in relation to which people become transgressors, and through which they are freed from the sin of transgression.

“Pierce my flesh with your fear.” Let the desires of the flesh, wounded by the sword of your fear, not be stirred.

“For I have feared your commandments.” Your commandments have taught me and made me understand how great a sin it is to be driven by pleasures of the flesh.

AIN is interpreted “spring,” or “eye.” Thus this teaching is a living spring by which souls are satisfied, and a most bright eye by which they are enlightened. Those who do not drink from this spring always thirst, and those not illuminated by this eye are never freed from the darkness of error.

[Col. 1163B] “I have done judgment and justice; do not hand me over to those who persecute me.”—“With the same measure with which you have measured,” says the Lord, “it shall be measured back to you” (Matt. 7:2). Therefore one who has done right judgment and justice need not fear being handed over at judgment to persecutors. These persecutors are evil spirits; whoever is handed over to them shall not be released until the last farthing.

“Choose your servant for good, that the proud may not falsely accuse me [Note: The Vulgate reads: ‘Uphold your servant for good.’ In Augustine one reads: ‘Receive your servant for good; let not the proud falsely accuse me’; to which the holy Doctor adds: ‘They drive me that I may fall into evil; do you receive me for good’ (Cols. 1163D, 1164D).].” He speaks of that choosing which will take place at the judgment, when the sheep are placed on the right and the goats on the left. “Choose,” he says, “your servant, and place me on the good side, so that those proud persons may not falsely accuse me—those who never wished to humble themselves even before you.”

[Col. 1163C] “My eyes have failed for your salvation; and teach me your statutes.” These words are signs of inexpressible desire. But our eyes fail in both kinds of contemplation, because in this life we can perfectly comprehend neither our Savior nor his words.

“Deal with your servant according to your mercy, and teach me your statutes.” Grant me, he says, this mercy: deem me worthy to be refreshed and enlightened by that spring and that eye of which I spoke just above.

“I am your servant; give me understanding, that I may know your testimonies.” Understanding ought to be given only to the one who knows himself to be a servant and fears offending the commandments of his Lord. If he does not keep them, he shall be liable to condemnation—commandments which he cannot keep without understanding.

“Time to act, O Lord: they have destroyed your law.” Now, he says, is the time to do what I ask, because understanding is especially necessary now, when heretics fight against truth. This is what he means by: “They have destroyed your law.”

“Therefore I have loved your commandments above gold and topaz.” Among metals gold is most precious, and among gems topaz. Therefore, he says, I have loved your commandments above everything that can be desired in this world, because I am your servant and desire in every way to please you and [Col. 1164A] do your will. “Therefore I was directed likewise toward performing all your commandments,” and therefore “I hated every way of iniquity.” A good servant, agreeing with his Lord’s will, loves what the Lord loves and hates what he knows the Lord hates.

PHE is interpreted “mouth,” of which the following words speak: “I opened my mouth and drew in breath.” This letter teaches us to open our mouths, receive this most holy and perfect teaching, commit it to memory, and store it in the dwelling-place of the heart.

“Your testimonies are wonderful, O Lord; therefore my soul has searched them out.” The person who speaks thus has a great and perfect mouth. God’s testimonies are wonderful because they are so lofty that they cannot be understood by human capacity; so true that none can resist them; and of such power that they free the soul from death and lead it to eternal life. “Therefore my soul has searched them out.” For what knowledge is so perfect that it should be searched out with great desire?

“The unfolding of your words enlightens me and gives understanding to little ones.” The Church says: The unfolding and exposition of your words enlightens me, and grants understanding to the little ones who are in me. Such, therefore, is this teaching that, according to the capacity of those who use it, it is suited both to the greater and the lesser.

“I opened my mouth and drew in breath.” He opened the mouth of the inner person and, the Lord granting it, received the spirit of wisdom and understanding. “Because [Col. 1164C] I desired your commandments.” Wisdom is therefore given to those who desire it with a pure heart. Hence the Apostle James says: “If anyone lacks wisdom, let him ask of the Lord, who gives abundantly to all and does not reproach them, and it shall be given to him” (Jas. 1:5).

“Look upon me and have mercy on me, according to the judgment of those who love your name.” According to the judgment, he says, and testimony of the apostles and prophets who love you. Look upon me, have mercy on me, and grant me that mercy which you promised through them to grant me.

“Direct my steps according to your word, and let no injustice have dominion over me.” This is what is said elsewhere: “The steps of a person are directed by the Lord, and he greatly desires that person’s way” (Ps. 36:23). And elsewhere: “To give light to those who sit in darkness, to direct our feet into the way of peace” (Luke 1:79). Where the steps of the mind are directed, injustice cannot rule.

“Redeem me from the false accusations of people, that I may keep your commandments.” There are many false accusations by which people unjustly slander the saints and do not allow them rest; consequently, they cannot keep God’s commandments with the diligence they ought.

“Make your face shine upon your servant.” Then the Lord makes his face shine upon us [Col. 1165A] when he shows us a joyful countenance, driving away adversities and granting prosperity. “And teach me your statutes.” He never forgets the law and the commandments, but in almost every verse desires that knowledge of the law be given to him.

“Streams of waters have passed through my eyes, because they have not kept your law.” What great perfection in a man who says that he has passed beyond streams of waters in a flood of tears because he could not keep the Lord’s law as he wished!

SADE is interpreted “righteousness,” of which it is said: “Your righteousness is righteousness for ever, and your law is truth.” This letter therefore summons us to righteousness, a virtue of no small importance contained in the teaching of this psalm.

[Col. 1165B] “You are righteous, O Lord, and your judgment is right.” The Lord therefore loves righteousness, and this letter therefore summons us to righteousness: because he is righteous and all his judgment is right. We ought to imitate him, as Lord and teacher, in every respect and in all things.

“You have commanded righteousness—your testimonies—and your truth exceedingly.” Because the Lord is righteous, he has commanded that righteousness, his testimonies, and his truth be kept most strictly. “Exceedingly,” indeed, because life itself must be set aside in keeping them. The word “exceedingly” is said not with reference to the contemplation of righteousness, but to human opinion.

“My zeal for your house has made me waste away [Note: The Vulgate reads: ‘My zeal has made me waste away.’ St Augustine comments: ‘My zeal makes me waste away, or, as other manuscripts read, your zeal. Some also have “for your house,” and not “makes me waste away,” but “has consumed me.” This seems to me to have been corrected from another psalm, where it is written, “Zeal for your house has consumed me.”’ He shows that each reading contains an excellent sense, as anyone may see (Cols. 1165D, 1166D).], because [Col. 1165C] your enemies have forgotten your words.” This is like the saying elsewhere: “Zeal for your house has consumed me” (Ps. 68:10). He shows that he had wasted away with excessive grief because he saw God’s house being destroyed and scattered by heretics. For they are his enemies who have forgotten God’s words and sound understanding, and expound the Scriptures otherwise than they learned from the ancient Fathers [Note: It is characteristic of innovators to twist the sacred Scriptures into a perverse meaning and to depart far from the interpretations of the holy Fathers, which oppose their errors (Col. 1166D).].

“Your word is exceedingly refined by fire, and your servant has loved it.” God’s word is intensely fiery: by it the eyes of the mind are enlightened, sins are burned away, and the hearts of the faithful are kindled with love of God. “And your servant has loved it.” For unless he had loved it, he would not have fought for its defense even unto death.

[Col. 1165D] “I am younger and despised.” My enemies, he says, regard me as younger; they say that I possess childish understanding, and despise me as foolish and unintelligent. “But I have not forgotten your statutes,” unlike those whose forgetfulness caused me to waste away.

“Your righteousness is righteousness for ever.” Your righteousness, he says, is not of such a kind that it ought to be handed over to oblivion; it must be everlasting and cannot be overcome. Hence it follows: “And [Col. 1166A] your law is truth.” Truth cannot be overcome by falsehood. But for the sake of this righteousness of yours, which I have labored with such earnestness to retain and defend, “tribulation and anguish have found me.” And what did you do? “But your commandments are my meditation.” For if they had been willing to cease from the righteousness alone which God’s saints proclaimed, they would not have suffered such great tribulations and anguish.

“Your testimonies are equity for ever.” He excellently says that God’s testimonies are not merely equitable but are equity itself, thereby showing that he fought for them most justly and not without cause.

“Give me understanding, and I shall live.” He asks only for understanding, and affirms that his life is in it: understanding by which he may both defend God’s testimonies against enemies [Col. 1166B] and overcome the enemies themselves.

COPH is interpreted “calling.” This letter admonishes us always to call and cry to the Lord without ceasing, as the following words show, that he may assist us in all our needs and rescue us from our persecutors.

“I cried with my whole heart; hear me, O Lord.” Let the person who desires to be heard cry out in this way: not with the voice but with the heart, because God looks not at the voice but at the heart. The voice is raised in vain unless prayer proceeds from the heart. “I will seek your statutes.” And this is no small reason why the prayer should be heard.

“I cried to you; save me, that I may keep [Col. 1166C] your commandments.” We cannot otherwise keep his commandments unless he himself protects and saves us, defending us from the assaults of vices and demons.

“I anticipated at the fitting time and cried, and I hoped in your word.” *Maturitas* here means what is fitting and timely. “All things have their time” (Eccl. 3:1). And it is said of that most noble tree that “it shall yield its fruit in its season” (Ps. 1:3). He cries, therefore, at the proper time because he cries when one ought to cry, and cries as one ought. Whoever thus cries can hope with the fullest confidence in God’s word and promise. Hence it follows: “And I hoped in your word.”

[Col. 1166D] “My eyes came before you at daybreak, that I might meditate on your words.” At daybreak, he says, very early in the morning, after night had passed and the darkness of error and shadows had been driven away, I came to meditate upon your words, so that I might thus reach you and knowledge of you. Whoever wishes to see the light must leave the darkness.

“Hear my voice, O Lord, according to your mercy, and according to your judgment [Col. 1167A] give me life.” He asks to be heard not according to merits but according to mercy, and seeks to be justified according to God’s judgment, who grants mercy only to the penitent.

“Those who persecute me have drawn near to iniquity, but they have become far from your law.” The wicked, he says, have drawn near to me in order to destroy and deceive me; but they are far from your law, which they contradict in every way.

“You are near, O Lord.” They, he says, are far from your law because they are in error and falsehood; but you, Lord, are near, because you are where truth is. Hence it follows: “And all your commandments are truth.” All God’s commandments are true because they are established by Truth itself.

[Col. 1167B] “From the beginning I knew concerning your testimonies that you founded them for ever.” The beginning is Christ, who says of himself: “I am the beginning, the one speaking to you” (John 8:25). But Christ says this concerning his testimonies and his words: “Heaven and earth shall pass away, but my words shall not pass away” (Luke 21:33). From that very beginning, therefore, we have known and been taught that his testimonies are founded for ever. Foolish, then, are those who try to scatter and destroy them.

RES is interpreted “head.” This is that head or beginning of which it is said elsewhere: “At the head of the book it is written of me” (Ps. 39:9). This is also spoken of in what follows: “The beginning of your words is truth.” This beginning, therefore, is Christ, from whom [Col. 1167C] we have received all these commandments. This letter accordingly commands us always to look to the head and, out of reverence for the head, faithfully keep all these commandments.

“See my humiliation and rescue me, because I have not forgotten my law.” See, he says, this humiliation and affliction of mine, and rescue me, because many persecute and trouble me. Yet I have not forgotten your law, for the sake of which I endure all these sufferings and humiliations.

“Judge my cause and redeem me.” He asks that his cause—in which he was unjustly judged and condemned by the wicked—may be judged and vindicated; and he asks to be redeemed and liberated from their impious servitude. “Give me life for the sake of your word.” This is the word of which the Lord says: “If anyone keeps [Col. 1167D] my word, he shall never see death” (John 8:51).

“Salvation is far from sinners, because they have not sought your statutes.” The good, he says, are saved and given life because they seek and keep the Lord’s words. Since the wicked neglect to do this, salvation is far from sinners.

“Your mercies are exceedingly many, O Lord; give me life according to your judgment.” This is that judgment full of mercy, by which the Lord says: “If you forgive people their sins, your Father also will forgive you your sins” (Matt. 6:14). [Col. 1168A] Likewise: “Forgive, and you shall be forgiven” (Luke 6:37).

“Many are those who persecute and trouble me.” But I, as you yourself know, “have not turned aside from your testimonies,” nor amid the very torments have I ceased to confess and praise you.

“I saw those who did not keep the covenant, and I wasted away, because they did not keep your words.” He says this concerning Jews, or Christians who deny the Lord through fear of death, because he greatly grieved and wasted away over their not observing the covenant and not keeping the Lord’s words. To them the Lord says: “Do not fear those who kill the body” (Matt. 10:28), because “after this they have nothing further that they can do” (Luke 12:5).

“See that I have loved your commandments, O Lord; in your [Col. 1168B] mercy give me life.” It should be noted that a man of such great perfection, as though fearful about the future, always asks for mercy.

“The beginning of your words is truth.” I have loved, he says, all your commandments, whose beginning is truth, the source from which all things of the same purity flow. Therefore “all the judgments of your righteousness remain for ever.” If they were not true, they could not remain for ever, since everything false quickly fails and perishes, and nothing which departs from truth is enduring for long.

SIN is interpreted “teeth.” Tyrants and heretics are the teeth of the devil, striving to deceive and devour the saints; of them it is said elsewhere: “For they have devoured Jacob and laid waste his dwelling-place” (Ps. [Col. 1168C] 78:7). The Church likewise says of them here:

“Princes have persecuted me without cause, and my heart has feared at your words [Note: See Augustine on what he brings forward concerning this passage (Col. 1167D).].” They indeed did this without cause, for there was no just reason why they should have done it. Hence the Lord says to the Jews in the Gospel: “They hated me without cause” (John 15:25).—“And my heart has feared at your words.” I feared, he says, not so much them as that I might offend you and, terrified by fear, sin against your words.

“I shall rejoice over your words as one who finds abundant spoils.” He counts God’s words as spoils, which, once his enemies had been overcome, he was able to retain and defend.

“I have hated and abhorred iniquity, but I have loved your law.” I hated and abhorred not the unrighteous persons who cruelly persecuted me, but their iniquity, so that it may be understood that they did this gratuitously and without cause. “But I have loved your law,” for which I did not hesitate to give myself up.

“Seven times a day I have spoken praise to you.” He uses a finite number for an infinite one, as though he said: As often as they tempted me in the day, so often they found me ready to proclaim and confess your praises. This is what he means by: “For the judgments [Col. 1169A] of your righteousness.” To what else did these praises belong but to the judgments of God’s righteousness? From this arose the custom that the Church sings praises to the Lord seven times a day.

“Great peace is for those who love your name, O Lord.” Great peace belongs to the one who loves even his own enemies. Hence the Apostle says: “If it is possible, so far as it depends on you, live peaceably with all people” (Rom. 12:18).—“And there is no stumbling-block for them.”—The Lord says: “Blessed is the one who shall not be offended in me” (Luke 7:23). It would have been a stumbling-block to them if they had murmured and had not endured everything patiently [Note: According to St Augustine, no one ought to be scandalized if he sees persons of any holy profession fall away from the law; rather, let him love the law, so as to obtain peace from it (Col. 1169D).].

“I awaited your salvation, O Lord.” Therefore, he says, I was not scandalized amid the very torments, because I awaited your salvation, which I did not doubt would be mine. And for this reason “I loved your commandments,” [Col. 1169B] which have never deceived me and which I have found true in all things. Hence he further adds:

“My soul has kept your testimonies and loved them exceedingly.” He repeats the same point again: I have kept your commandments and your testimonies—which you yourself know better. Why is this so? “Because all my ways are before your sight.”

TAU is interpreted “sign” or “completion,” as was said at the beginning of this psalm. Since it has been explained there, it does not seem necessary to explain it again. “Let my prayer draw near before you, O Lord; according to your word give me understanding.” This is the word of which he says elsewhere: “I will give you understanding and instruct you” (Ps. 31:8). He asks, therefore, that God give him understanding, as he promised that he would.

“Let my petition enter before you, O Lord; according to your word rescue me.” Likewise, this is what the Lord says: “I will not leave you or forsake you” (John 14:18). And: “Behold, I am with you always, even to the completion of the age” (Matt. 28:20). Likewise: “Call upon me,” he says, “in the day of your tribulation; I shall rescue you, and you shall glorify me” (Ps. 49:15).

“My lips shall pour forth a hymn when you have taught me your statutes.” He therefore asked that understanding be given to him because he desires to pour forth and proclaim God’s statutes most fully.

“My tongue shall pronounce your words.” And I shall proclaim this [Col. 1169D] to all: that all your words and all your commandments are righteous, holy, and equitable, and that nothing shall be able to frighten me away from their praises.

[Col. 1170A] “Let your hand be present to save me, because I have chosen your commandments.” I, he says, have chosen to announce and proclaim your commandments to everyone; only grant me your help, lest my enemies prevail against me. For there is no one able to resist your right hand.

“I have desired your salvation, O Lord, and your law is my meditation.” He seeks not salvation of the body but salvation of the soul, which the Lord has especially promised to grant his faithful, saying to them: “Do not fear [566] those who kill the body but cannot kill the soul” (Matt. 10:28). Hence it is said elsewhere: “The Lord guards you from every evil” (Ps. 120:7). And the psalm specifies how he guards: “The Lord shall guard your soul” (ibid., v. 8). This is what he says: “My soul shall live and praise [Col. 1170B] you, and your judgments shall help me.” Your judgments, he says, which I proclaim, and your law, which is my meditation, shall themselves help me and free me from every danger.

“I have gone astray like a sheep that was lost; seek your servant, O Lord, because I have not forgotten your commandments.” The Lord speaks in the Gospel (Luke 15) of a man who had a hundred sheep and, leaving ninety-nine, came to seek one which had been lost. When he found it, he placed it upon his shoulders and carried it back to pasture; he relates that great joy was made over finding it. This sheep is human nature, for whose sake the Lord came into the world: he sought it, found it, and still seeks it daily, carrying it when found to heavenly things [Note: St Augustine explains why he omitted the interpretation of the Hebrew letters: “As for the Hebrew alphabet, in which eight verses stand under each letter and thus the whole psalm is composed, it is no wonder that I said nothing, since I found nothing belonging specifically to this matter,” etc. (Col. 1169D).].

## PSALM 119. A SONG OF ASCENTS.

[Col. 1170C]

Fifteen psalms are entitled “Song of Ascents.” [Note: [Col. 1169D] Theodoret sheds much light on the understanding of these psalms: “Theodotion,” he says, “renders it ‘Song of Ascents,’ but Symmachus and Aquila, ‘for ascents.’ The ascents or steps indicate the return of the captive people from Babylon, since the grace of the Holy Spirit foresaw both the servitude and the future freedom, foretold both, providing for their benefit and bringing us profit thereby. Yet not every one of the Psalms of Ascents prophesies the same thing: one foretells the calamities that befell them in Babylon and the glad tidings of this return; another, joy on the journey; another, the wars waged after the return; another, the rebuilding of the Temple; and the song’s variety of prophecy calls for an abundance of hymns. Moreover, each psalm is framed as spoken by the choir of saints who existed at that time, since the prophetic word introduces them as saying the things here set forth. But the first of the Ascents recounts both calamities and divine good will.”]

We must first, therefore, discuss the number itself: why there are only fifteen. There are five books of Moses which, when understood in threefold fashion, rise to fifteen. The first understanding is literal, the second spiritual, and the third practical. The first kills; the second gives life; the third leads a human being to blessedness. For of the third it is written: “Good understanding belongs to all who practise it” (Ps. 110:10). Likewise: “It is not the hearers of the law who are righteous, but its doers” (Rom. 2:13). Thus, to read and to hear is good; to understand spiritually is better; but to do what is understood is best. Yet who can do what he does not understand? Who understands what he has neither heard nor read? Thus spiritual understanding arises from the letter, and action proceeds from spiritual understanding. For in those five books, if they are understood in this manner, every divine and spiritual understanding is most fully contained. The fifteen psalms, therefore, display knowledge threefold and perfect.

But it should be noted that they are not called the first ascent, the second ascent, or the third ascent; rather, each is called a “Song of Ascents,” as though each were sufficient in itself to bring one who ascends to the goal toward which he is tending. [Note: [Col. 1171D] St Hilary, in the Prologue to the Songs, says the following concerning the fifteen ascents under which the following psalms are inscribed: “We must remember that these same psalms are not all to be understood bodily merely because the meaning of bodily events is set before us in them; rather, beneath this general commemoration of events we ought to pursue the spiritual understanding.”]

Of these fifteen psalms, [Note: [Col. 1171D] “When we hear of ascents in the Psalms, let us not suppose that something earthly, to be undertaken with bodily steps, is meant; rather, let us understand an ascent of the mind. For this reason ‘Song’ is prefixed, so that we should apply it instead to the soul’s progress.” Cassiodorus.] the penultimate contains the Church of the saints singing and saying: “Behold, how good and pleasant it is for brothers to dwell together in unity!” (Ps. 132:1). Such were those of whom it is said: [Col. 1171B] “The multitude of believers had one heart and one soul; and no one said that anything was his own, but all things were common to them” (Acts 4:32). Then, ascending one step to the last psalm, they exhort themselves, saying: “Behold, now bless the Lord, all servants of the Lord, who stand in the house of the Lord” (Ps. 133:1). The Prophet recounts, moreover, and introduces these same persons as speaking throughout the individual psalms: how they abandoned the manner of life of the world, what hindrances they encountered, and what befell them as they came.

“Unto the Lord, when I was afflicted, I cried, and he heard me.”

One from that holy assembly says this: while he endured many tribulations in the secular life of this world, and, desiring to cleave more closely to God, could not fulfil the vows of his desire, he at last cried to the Lord from his inmost heart and was heard. Let us hear how he cried.

“Lord, deliver my soul from unjust lips and from a deceitful tongue.”

Not only heretics, who tried to deceive him and draw him to themselves, but even his own relatives and friends created a great impediment for him. Drawing him toward the pleasures and vanities of the age, they wished to entangle him in worldly affairs. Therefore he rightly calls their lips unjust and their tongue deceitful, since they strove to change so holy and beneficial a purpose of his mind and draw him to the precipice of death. But while he endured these scandals, [Col. 1171D] he spoke thus to himself and to his own soul:

“What shall be given to you, or what shall be added for a deceitful tongue?”

What counsel can you find for avoiding and repelling their deceits and seductions?

“The sharp arrows of the Mighty One, with desolating coals.”

“The arrows of the Mighty One,” he says, “will be given to you: defend yourself with them; set them against those people. Say to them what the Lord [Col. 1172A] says: ‘He who loves father or mother more than me is not worthy of me’ (Matt. 10:37); and, ‘He who does not take up his cross and follow me is not worthy of me’ (Luke 14:27); and, ‘Unless anyone leaves all that he possesses, he cannot be my disciple’ (ibid., 33); and, ‘If you wish to be perfect, go, sell all that you have, follow me, and you will have treasure in heaven’ (Matt. 19:21).” These are the arrows of the Mighty One—indeed, of the Almighty—sharp with the coals of the Holy Spirit, by which all the devil’s snares and devices are laid waste.

“Woe is me [Note: [Col. 1172D] Thus also in St Augustine.] that my sojourning has been prolonged: I have dwelt with the inhabitants of Kedar; my soul has been a sojourner for a long time [Note: [Col. 1172D] In St Augustine: “My pilgrimage has become prolonged.”].”

“Thus,” he says, “I have been delivered from them; yet I grieve deeply because [Col. 1172B] I acted too late, and because I lived among them for so long. For truly I dwelt with the inhabitants of Kedar, and my soul was for a long time a sojourner among them and in agreement with them.” Kedar means “darkness.” Therefore, one dwells with the inhabitants of Kedar who lives among such persons; for such people are darkness and imitate the prince of darkness.

“With those who hate peace, I was peaceable.”

Not that I consented to their vices and iniquities, or did not, as far as I could, often oppose them. But while I spoke to them and proclaimed words of salvation, “they attacked me without cause.”

## PSALM 120. SONG OF ASCENTS.

[Col. 1172C]

“I lifted up my eyes to the mountains, whence help shall come to me.”

The same person who spoke above continues to speak. “Since,” he says, “I could not otherwise defend myself against unjust lips and a deceitful tongue, I lifted up my eyes to the mountains: I looked to the apostles and their imitators, that I might experience the help of those whose example I desired to imitate.” And immediately he deserved to receive the help both of them and of the Lord. This is what he says:

“My help is from the Lord, who made heaven and earth. May he not let your foot be moved, nor shall he who keeps you slumber.”

He speaks to himself, as above when he said: “What shall be given to you, or what shall be added for a deceitful tongue?” For he recounts what had happened to him before he joined the congregation of the saints. Thus he first [Col. 1172D] comforted and strengthened himself, and prayed that the foot of his mind might stand firm, so that it could not be moved from that vow and holy purpose.

“Behold, he who keeps Israel shall neither doze nor sleep.”

“Be secure,” he says, “for your guardian is always awake and never forgets his own. He who keeps Israel will never sleep.” By Israel, let us understand those who delight in the contemplation of him and always desire to see him.

“The Lord keeps you; the Lord is your protection at your right hand.” [Note: [Col. 1173D] St Augustine’s reading: “The Lord is your covering at your right hand.”]

This sufficiently shows that he was strengthening himself in every way possible, so that he need not fear to fulfil his vow and desire, having so great a guardian, protector, and defender.

“By day the sun shall not burn you, nor the moon by night.”

Even according to the letter, this is often true of saints who choose for themselves a secluded and solitary place suited solely to contemplation, where they suffer injury neither from sun, moon, nor any other thing. But by the sun we understand Christ, who is the sun of righteousness, from whom all things are illumined. By the moon [Col. 1173B] are signified those who, throughout the whole Church, are more illustrious after the sun in virtue and miracles. They indeed will judge; at their command all who are condemned in judgment will be sent into the fire. By day and night every time is signified. Therefore neither sun nor moon will ever scorch those who do the Lord’s will, because there is no time that is not day or night.

“The Lord keeps you from every evil.”

But lest you suppose that this refers only to bodily afflictions, hear what follows: “The Lord shall keep your soul.”

“May the Lord guard your entrance,” into the congregation of the saints, “and your departure,” as you hasten from this world to heavenly things, “from this time forth and forever.” What is “from this time forth”? From this present time, in which you resolve to do these things, if you persevere in this good will.

## PSALM 121. SONG OF ASCENTS.

This psalm also belongs to those ascents by which one climbs to the summit of perfection.

“I rejoiced at the things that were said to me: ‘We shall go into the house of the Lord.’”

“I had read,” as though he said, “in the Scriptures of both Testaments, and had seen there the sharp arrows of the Mighty One with desolating coals, by which the sayings and testimonies of the divine law are signified. And I greatly rejoiced at the things said to me, and said: ‘From now on I have no doubt; I am certain that we shall go into the house of the Lord and, as we desired, [Col. 1173D] shall dwell in the congregation of the saints.’”

“Our feet stood in your courts, Jerusalem.”

“I had not yet,” he says, “come to Jerusalem—that is, to that congregation of saints—yet already my feet, in certain hope and desire, stood and were established there.” Such is what the Apostle says while still [Col. 1174A] placed upon earth: “Our commonwealth is in heaven” (Phil. 3:20).

“Jerusalem, which is built as a city whose fellowship is in the same thing.”

“I do not speak,” he says, “of that Jerusalem which killed the prophets, but of that which ‘is so built as a city whose fellowship is in the same thing’ [Note: [Col. 1173D] Let Augustine be heard as interpreter: “What is ‘the same thing’? That which always exists in the same manner; that which is not now one thing and now another. What, then, is ‘the same thing’ but that which is? And what is that which is? That which is eternal.” Cassiodorus’ interpretation accords with this: “Its fellowship is in the same thing—that is, the fellowship of this city is in the Lord the Saviour, who is properly ‘the same thing.’ For ‘the same thing’ signifies eternity, [Col. 1174D] which never ceases to be what it is, but always remains in one and the same manner: unfailing power, unchangeable might, a substance abiding through itself, able effectively to accomplish all that it wills.”]”: its inhabitants both will and do not will the same thing, namely that very same thing; all have one heart and one soul. Of them it is rightly said: “Behold, how good and pleasant it is for brothers to dwell together in unity.”

“For there the tribes went up, the tribes of the Lord, the testimony of Israel, to confess your name, O Lord.”

As though someone were to ask: “Who are those who dwell in this Jerusalem, in which you say there is such great concord?” He answers: “All the tribes of the Lord, all Catholic and devout men, all martyrs and confessors, and all who faithfully serve God, are inhabitants of this city. There also ascends the testimony of Israel.” For what purpose? “To confess your name, O Lord.” This is the testimony given by the Lord to the children of Israel on Mount Sinai. Therefore it is not the Jews but Christians who possess this testimony: those who understand it not according to the letter but spiritually, and in it confess and praise the Lord.

“For there sat seats for judgment, over the house of David.”

Rightly, he says, did the tribes of the Lord and the testimony of the Lord ascend there, because there sat and sit seats prepared for judgment—those [Col. 1174C] seats apportioned over the house of David. The Lord himself speaks of these seats to his disciples: “You who have left all things and followed me shall sit upon twelve seats, judging the twelve tribes of Israel” (Matt. 19:27). Thus these seats are apportioned, and the whole house of David—that is, the whole Church—is divided among them, so that each apostle has his own seat there. Even to this day every bishop calls his see the church in which he was ordained.

“Pray for the things that belong to the peace of Jerusalem.” [Note: [Col. 1174D] St Augustine reads, “Inquire concerning the things that belong to the peace of Jerusalem,” and refers this to the judges seated upon the twelve seats, who will question those to be judged: “and those whom they find to have performed mercy they will call to Jerusalem, because these are the things that belong to Jerusalem’s peace.”]

“All of you,” he says, “who dwell in Jerusalem, and whoever hears these words, pray for the things that pertain to the peace of Jerusalem; for without peace it is impossible [Col. 1174D] to please God. And say: ‘May there be abundance for those who love you’—an abundance of all blessedness, so that those who rejoice in your peace may themselves enjoy everlasting peace.” Hence he adds:

“Let peace be in your strength, and abundance in your towers.”

“Let there be,” he says, “peace in your strength, so that what [Col. 1175A] we cannot possess from ourselves we may obtain through your merits. And let abundance be in your towers,” by which the shepherds and rulers of the Church are signified, through whom the whole city is defended and guarded. They need an abundance sufficient for all others as well.

“For the sake of my brothers and my neighbours, I spoke peace concerning you.”

These are the brothers who say: “Behold, how good and pleasant it is for brothers to dwell together in unity!” We must always pray for them, that they may persevere forever in that peace and concord.

“And for the sake of the house of the Lord my God,” which is built from your stones, “I sought good things for you.” Hence elsewhere it is said: “Deal graciously, O Lord, in your good [Col. 1175B] will with Zion, that the walls of Jerusalem may be built” (Ps. 50:20).

## PSALM 122. SONG OF ASCENTS.

“To you I lifted up my eyes, you who dwell in the heavens.”

God’s dwelling is both in the assembly of angels and in the Church, which is signified by heaven. Hence elsewhere it is said: “But you dwell in the holy place, the praise of Israel” (Ps. 21:4). “To you,” he says, “I lifted up the eyes of my mind, desiring to come to you and see you: you who dwell in heaven, who flee what is base and dishonourable, and in whom fair and pure things find pleasure.”

“Behold, as the eyes of servants are upon the hands of their masters, and as the eyes of a maidservant are upon the hands of her mistress, so are our eyes upon the Lord our God [Col. 1175C] until he has mercy on us.”

Servants and maidservants look to the hands of their masters and mistresses either to receive necessities from them or to be freed by them if they are scourged. So too we must always look to the Lord, that he may supply what we need and deliver us from every danger and adversity.

“Have mercy on us, O Lord, have mercy on us, for we are greatly filled with contempt.”

Not only by others, but even by perverse and proud Christians themselves, God’s servants are often held in contempt, because their life differs from the life of such people and because they flee worldly wisdom, which is foolishness before God.

[Col. 1175D] “And our soul has been greatly filled.” With what? “With the reproaches of the rich and the scorn of the proud.” [Note: [Col. 1175D] Vatican Psalter: “reproach from the prosperous, and scorn from the proud.”] For these are especially the ones who despise and ridicule them, because they flee riches and subject themselves to all in excessive humility. But this scorn and reproach will be turned back upon them, for the time is near when the rich will become poor and the humble will tread upon the necks of the proud, because, as it is written: “The Lord puts down the mighty from their seat and exalts the humble” (Luke 1:52).

## PSALM 123. SONG OF ASCENTS.

[Col. 1176A]

“Had it not been that God [Note: [Col. 1175D] Ghislerius manuscript: “Had it not been that God.”] was with us—let Israel now say—had it not been that the Lord was with us, when men rose up against us, perhaps they would have swallowed us alive.”

“Now,” he says, “let the saints gathered into one, whose heart is one and whose soul is one, recall their former way of life, how many dangers the Lord delivered them from, and say: ‘Had the Lord not delivered us, we were near death and destruction.’” These are rightly called Israel, since they delight with such affection and desire in the vision and contemplation of God. Those are swallowed alive who, unless they die temporally, will die eternally, separated from God. Hence he continues:

[Col. 1176B] “When their anger was enraged against us, perhaps they would have swallowed us up like water.”

Those swallowed in this manner perish not in soul but in body. Thus all the martyrs were swallowed up, who certainly would not have been swallowed up if they had wished to deny the truth. But because the Lord was present, they were so delivered that they suffered loss neither of body nor soul.

“Our soul passed through the torrent; perhaps our soul would have passed through intolerable water.” [Note: [Col. 1175D] St Augustine reads differently: “Our soul passed through the torrent; perhaps our soul passed through [Col. 1176D] water without substance.” There he says: “What is water without substance but the insubstantial water of sinners? For sins have no substance; they have poverty,” etc.]

Note that he says “our soul,” as though many possessed one soul, because they are among those whose heart is one and whose soul is one. He says that they passed through a torrent, by which he indicates a harsh and sudden but endurable suffering. Even if it had been intolerable, [Col. 1176C] nevertheless, with God’s help, they would have passed through it courageously.

“Blessed be the Lord, who did not give us as prey to their teeth.”

And this shows it: “Our soul has been rescued like a sparrow from the snare of hunters.” And how? “The snare has been broken, and we have been delivered.” By whose help? “Our help is in the name of the Lord, who made heaven and earth.” By these words he clearly demonstrates both that nets of deception had been spread around them and that they had fallen into those very nets; that by signs or arguments they broke the nets; and thus, with God’s help, escaped. But it should be noted that the apostles lay their nets in the sea, whereas evil spirits lay them in the air. For they are those of whom [Col. 1176D] the Apostle says: “Our struggle is not against flesh and blood, but against principalities and powers, against the rulers of the world of this darkness, against spiritual forces of wickedness in the heavenly places” (Eph. 6:12).

## PSALM 124. SONG OF ASCENTS.

“Those who trust in the Lord are like Mount Zion: he who dwells in Jerusalem shall not be moved forever.”

Mount Zion was a very strongly fortified place in Jerusalem, [Col. 1177A] built for the protection of the whole city; by it the apostles and the other guardians and defenders of the Church are signified. “As Mount Zion,” he says—namely, that Mount Zion which dwells in Jerusalem, by which we have just said some assembly of saints is signified—“shall not be moved or separated from it forever, so all who trust in the Lord shall not be moved forever, nor divided from that congregation of saints, where there is one heart and one soul.” Whether they are on earth or in heaven, they will all be together, citizens and inhabitants of the same city, and will all rejoice without end. [Note: [Col. 1177D] “Here too we must recognize Jerusalem as the heavenly fatherland, signifying the vision [Col. 1178D] of peace. No one who has deserved to be established in its firmness can in any way be moved from it.” Cassiodorus.]

“Mountains are round about it.”

“Let Jerusalem not fear,” he says; “let the congregation [Col. 1177B] of saints and peaceable persons not fear, for mountains surround it, protecting and defending it. And not mountains only, but the Lord himself ‘watches around his people from this time forth and forever,’ according to his promise to his disciples: ‘Behold, I am with you all days, until the consummation of the age’ (Matt. 28:20). Therefore let those remain secure who are fortified not only by the guardianship of angels and apostles, but also by that of the Lord himself.” And how do you prove this?

“For the Lord will not leave the rod of sinners upon the lot of the righteous.”

And this is so “that the righteous may not stretch out their hands to iniquity.” Thus the Lord defends his saints and confirms them by this protection, so that although sinners often rage against the body, [Col. 1177C] they cannot overcome the soul. The Lord also turns aside that rod itself and does not permit sinners to scourge his saints as much as they wish. The Church is called the lot of the righteous because it is that which he chose as his own portion.

“Do good, O Lord, to the good and the upright in heart.”

What does “do good” mean except: deliver, protect, guard, turn aside the rod of sinners, and restrain their hands lest they stretch them out toward iniquity?

“But those who turn aside into entanglements the Lord will lead away with the workers of iniquity.”—“No one serving as a soldier of God,” says the Apostle, “entangles himself in worldly affairs, so that he may please him to whom he has proved himself” (2 Tim. 2:4). There are many entanglements of the devil by which he binds and draws people. What is said here is greatly to be feared: those who turn aside into such entanglements will be led with the workers of iniquity to eternal punishments. And they will then indeed be led away when eternal and unfailing peace comes upon Israel. Let monks and those who have abandoned the world hear this; having learned how good and pleasant it is for brothers to dwell together in unity, let them not wish to turn again toward worldly affairs.

## PSALM 125. SONG OF ASCENTS.

“When the Lord turned again the captivity of Zion, [Col. 1178A] we became like those who are comforted.”

In this psalm the Prophet foretells what the Jews said when they returned from their captivity, and likewise what Christians said when they too returned from their captivity. The Jews say: “When the Lord turned again the captivity of Zion and recalled us from Babylonian captivity to our homeland, we became like those who are comforted.” Then indeed “our mouth was filled with joy, and our tongue with exultation.” They were not completely comforted but became as though comforted, because, although they lived in their homeland, they had not yet been restored to freedom but were still held under Babylon’s power. Nevertheless, they were filled with great joy and exultation as they saw the Temple rebuilt, the city restored, and each person remaining—as he had greatly desired—under his own vine and fig tree. But now let us hear what the Prophet says also about the captivity of Christians.
