“Then,” he says, “they shall say among the nations: ‘The Lord has done great things for them; the Lord has done great things for us; we became joyful. Turn again, O Lord, our captivity, like a torrent in the south.’”

Until the time of the Emperor Constantine, wherever Christians were among the nations, they were oppressed beneath the harsh bondage of pagans. Then indeed they said what the Prophet had foretold they would say. This is what follows: “The Lord has done great things for them”—that is, for the Jews, whom he preserved among enemies and finally delivered from captivity. “The Lord has likewise [Col. 1178C] done great things for us”; therefore “we too became joyful” and were filled with no less joy and exultation than they. Only one thing remains that we ask, and may it happen quickly. What is it? That our captivity too may be turned again. The Lord indeed did greater things for Christians in their captivity than for Jews in theirs, for at that time he worked many signs and miracles through Christians which we do not read that he performed through the Jews.

The south wind is rainy; it fills dried-up torrents with waters and sets them flowing. Thus it came about in the captivity, when all the captives returned to their own homes in a great host, like a full river. We read that in the time of the aforesaid ruler all the saints returned from exile with great honour.

“Those who sow in tears shall reap in joy; going they went and wept, casting their seed.”—“Blessed are those who mourn, for they shall be comforted” (Matt. 5:5). They sowed and wept; they preached and mourned; and they wept and prayed not only for the good, but also for their persecutors themselves. Therefore they shall reap with joy, because all those whom they converted by weeping and suffering they shall present to the Lord with joy at the judgment. Hence he adds:

“But coming they shall come with exultation, carrying their sheaves.”

He fittingly says “they shall come,” [Col. 1179A] because they are in heaven and will come from there; and however many souls each person has converted, so many sheaves he offers to the Lord.

## PSALM 126. SONG OF ASCENTS.

“Unless the Lord builds the house, those who build it labour in vain. Unless the Lord guards the city, those who guard it watch in vain.”

For this is why the Lord says to his disciples: “Without me you can do nothing” (John 15:5). Hence the Apostle also says: “Neither he who plants nor he who waters is anything, but God who gives the growth” (1 Cor. 3:7). Preaching profits nothing unless the Holy Spirit works inwardly. [Note: [Col. 1179D] Augustine aptly adds: “No one has anything good unless he has received it from him who alone is good.”]

[Col. 1179B] “It is vain for you to rise before light; rise after you have sat down, you who eat the bread of sorrow.”

He speaks against heretics and all false preachers, of whom the Lord says in the Gospel: “Beware of false prophets, who come to you in sheep’s clothing but inwardly are ravening wolves” (Matt. 7:15). And the Apostle says: “Many,” he says, “walk, of whom I used to tell you, but now tell you even weeping, that they are enemies of Christ’s cross, whose end is destruction, whose god is their belly” (Phil. 3:18). These are the people who rise before light and eat the bread of sorrow. But it is vain for them to rise before light, since they are blind and guides of the blind. Those rise before light who begin to preach and teach before they have been enlightened and taught. Hence he adds:

[Col. 1179C] “Rise after you have sat down.”

First, he says, sit down; first be disciples; first listen to the teachers of the divine law; and receive from them not the bread of sorrow and error, but spiritual and Catholic food.

“When he gives sleep to his beloved, this is the inheritance of the Lord: sons, the reward, the fruit of the womb.”

Now, as though he says, it is difficult to distinguish the good from the bad, because both preach, both receive the sacraments of the altar, and both praise and bless God. But then the Lord’s inheritance, the Son’s reward, and the fruit of the womb will be recognized, when the Lord gives sleep to his beloved. Sleep in this place signifies rest. This, therefore, will be at the judgment, when the Lord calls his servants from the vigils and labours [Col. 1179D] in which he commanded them to watch, to sleep and rest and everlasting blessedness. These indeed are the Son’s reward, because Christ received this reward for his labour. They are the fruit of the womb, whom the most blessed Virgin Mary bore to the Lord all together in her one only-begotten and firstborn Son. [Note: [Col. 1179D] Cassiodorus reads and explains: “Behold the inheritance of the Lord: sons; the reward, the fruit of the womb.” “Behold the Lord’s inheritance—namely, children of the Church, born of water and the Holy Spirit, who are known to be the Lord’s inheritance. And who these children are is explained in what follows: ‘the reward, the fruit of the womb.’ The reward of this fruit of the womb—that is, of the birth from the virginal womb—is his entire inheritance, which, rising again, is sent into the possession of heaven and shall rejoice in everlasting blessedness with the Lord.”]

“Like arrows in the hand of a mighty man, so are the children of those driven out.”

[Col. 1180A] These “driven out”—the chosen and expelled—are the apostles. The Lord himself says to them: “If they persecute you in one city, flee to another” (Matt. 10:23). Their children are all who imitate them; and those who imitate them are like arrows in the hand of a mighty man. With these arrows the army of vices is put to flight; with them the multitude of demons is overcome; with them every host of heretics is conquered.

“Blessed is the man who has filled his desire from them.”

And who are those who fill their desire from them, except those who gladly hear them and keep their teaching and commandments? Such persons “shall not be put to shame when they speak with their enemies at the gate.” Our enemies are evil spirits, who will be prepared to accuse at the judgment, when the gate of life is opened to the good and the gate of death to the evil. Then those will be put to shame who are unable to resist them; by these we understand those who, persevering in sins, did not return to repentance.

## PSALM 127. SONG OF ASCENTS.

“Blessed are all who fear the Lord, who walk in his ways.”

“Blessed,” he says, “are those who fear not death, not the loss of temporal goods, not the miseries of the world, but the Lord.” Hence the Lord says: “Do not fear those who kill the body, but rather fear him who can destroy both body and soul in hell” (Luke 10:28).—“Blessed are those who walk in his ways” and keep [Col. 1180C] his commandments, because his commandments are the ways by which we must come to him.

“You shall eat the labours of your fruits; you are blessed, and it shall be well with you.”

In another translation, not “of your fruits” but “of your hands” is found. Hence the Apostle says: “Let each person labour with his hands at what is good” (Eph. 4:28). But a human being is not blessed because he lives from such labour. It must therefore be understood of the soul’s labour, which, for the good work it performs in this life, will enjoy heavenly delights in the life to come. This figure is called in Greek *hypallage*, when something is said by reversal. For people do not eat the labours of their fruits, but the fruits of their labours. It would be like saying, “Let this man be given to that horse,” when one should say, “Let that horse be given to this man.” Such is the passage in Virgil:

> . . . . . *dare classibus Austrum*  
> “to give the south wind to the fleets,”

when one should say: “to give the fleets to the south wind.”

“Your wife shall be like a fruitful vine at the sides of your house.”

What are those who have no wives to do here, if this is understood literally? Every virtue that you love greatly and in which you delight greatly is your wife—whether wisdom, humility, mercy, obedience, or any other. She will be to you like a fruitful vine, always fruitful, sweet, and pleasant wherever you may be in this vast house which the Lord has prepared for you and all living beings. A good wife does not leave her husband and, wherever she is, always affords him joy and honour. A man who brings such a wife with him is honourable everywhere.

“Your children shall be like young olive plants around your table.”

Your children are those who imitate you and hold and keep your teaching. If you fear God and walk in his ways, they will be around your table and around the teaching [Col. 1181B] of your breast like young olive trees, full of the fruit of peace and mercy. “Behold, thus shall every man be blessed who fears the Lord.” “Behold,” he says, “you have heard what blessing all who fear God receive: how well they live and what kind of wives and children they have. Moreover, may this further blessing come upon you and remain always.”

“May the Lord bless you out of Zion, and may you see the good things of Jerusalem all the days of your life, and may you see your children’s children.”

And may eternal and unfailing peace be upon Israel—namely, that Israel which knows and loves God. This is that Zion of which elsewhere the Lord says: “But I have been established by him as king upon Zion, his holy mountain, [Col. 1181C] to proclaim and teach his commandment” (Ps. 2:6), by which the Church is signified. Yet preaching seems more the office of bishops than of kings. From there, therefore—from Zion—Jesus, supreme king and high priest, blesses his faithful, that they may see the good things that are in the heavenly Jerusalem all the days of their life, which will never end; and that they may see their children who imitate them, and their children’s children, not merely to the third and fourth generation, but forever and ever.

## PSALM 128. SONG OF ASCENTS.

“Many times have they assailed me from my youth,” let Israel now say. “Many times have they assailed me from my youth, yet they could not prevail against me.” [Note: [Col. 1181D] Augustine understands the Church here to speak through the Prophet: “And from the beginning—that is, from its youth—its assault began. Even now the Church’s old age is being assailed; but let her not be afraid. Let her say: Many times have they assailed me from my youth. Has she therefore not reached old age because they have not ceased assailing her? Have they been able to destroy her? Let Israel now say; and let Israel—the Church—console you by examples from the past, and say: Many times have they assailed me from my youth.”] [Col. 1181D] As in the preceding psalm all good people are blessed with an eternal blessing, so in this one all wicked persons and sinners are cursed with an eternal curse. But when it says, “let Israel now say,” this is a taunt against those who boasted that they had conquered the people of God. Now, he says, after victory, secure and happy, let Israel say—let the people who know and see God say: My enemies have often assailed me from my youth, as they themselves claim; they have often assailed me. Yet they have not in fact conquered me, nor have they been able to prevail against me.

“Upon my back sinners built; they prolonged their iniquities.” Sinners, as though he were saying, did indeed fight fiercely against me; but they lie if they say that they conquered me. They made me into an anvil and a forge, and with hard and mighty hammers they wrought upon my back; and indeed they turned me into a most beautiful and precious vessel, while for themselves they prolonged their iniquities. Hence John the Apostle says in the Apocalypse: “For the time is near: let the one who does harm continue to do harm; and let the one who is filthy continue to be filthy; and let the righteous continue to be made righteous” (Rev. 22:11).

“The righteous Lord will cut down the necks of sinners.” [Col. 1182B] Rightly will those necks be cut down which, lifted up into excessive pride, did not fear to hurl blasphemies against God himself. Here he begins to curse them, because he knows that they are incapable of conversion and subject to death. “Let all who hate Zion,” he says, “be put to shame and recoil.”

“Let them become like the grass of rooftops, which withers before it is pulled up.” Wicked people are like grass on buildings: since they possess no moisture of faith and goodness, they easily dry up and are prepared for eternal and unquenchable fire.

“Of which the reaper will not fill his hand, nor the gatherer of sheaves his bosom.” These reapers are angels, who will gather that foul grass neither into hand nor bosom; but, as is read in the [Col. 1182C] Gospel, they will bind it into bundles and cast it into the furnace of fire: there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth (Matt. 13:42).

“And those who passed by did not say: ‘The blessing of the Lord be upon you; we bless you in the name of the Lord.’” I do not curse these without cause, he says, because they saw and heard the holy apostles and preachers passing among them and preaching, yet did not deserve to receive their blessings, since they refused to believe their words. Therefore there is no doubt that all those who did not receive evangelical and apostolic preaching are destined for eternal death.

## PSALM 129. A SONG OF ASCENTS.

[Col. 1182D]

“Out of the depths I have cried to you, O Lord; Lord, hear my prayer.” In saying that he cried out of the depths, he shows that he had been in great straits, both spiritual and bodily. That person too cries out of the depths who entreats God from the inmost heart.

“Let your ears be attentive to the prayer of your servant.” It might have sufficed for him to say, “Hear my prayer”; [Col. 1183A] but he asks that God’s ears be attentive to his prayer, by which we may understand the swiftest hearing of God’s kindness. He also calls himself a servant, so that he may more easily obtain the Lord’s mercy.

“If you should mark iniquities, O Lord, Lord, who could endure it?” For if the Lord had looked—not, I say, at other sins, but merely at the iniquities of the first man—no human being could have been saved.

“For with the Lord there is propitiation, and because of your law I have waited for you, O Lord.” The Lord will not mark our iniquities, as though he were saying, because great propitiation and mercy naturally reside with him; he does not desire the death of the sinner, but rather that he should turn and live. Hence it follows: [Col. 1183B] “And because of your law I have waited for you, O Lord.” This is that law given by the Lord: “In whatever hour the sinner turns, he shall live and shall not die” (Ezek. 33:11). Of this he further says:

“My soul has waited for your word; my soul has hoped in the Lord.” And indeed this most gracious law, full of loving-kindness and mercy, gives great hope to sinners.

“From the morning watch until night, let Israel hope in the Lord.” Let Israel hope in the Lord, he says—not carnal but spiritual Israel; not that Israel which killed him, but that which believes in him and hopes most firmly in him. “From the morning watch,” at which the Lord himself rose from the dead, “until night,” [Col. 1183C] at which this day and this final age will end. For who can possess such great hope as the people for whom the Lord died and rose again?

“For with the Lord there is mercy, and with him abundant redemption.” This is the greatest and most convincing reason why Israel should hope in the Lord [Note: [Col. 1183D] “A wonderful reason has been given why Israel ought to hope in the Lord: because mercy is in his hand, which can make the righteous out of the perverse, the immortal out of the weak, and one like the angels out of the fleshly. For this is what he customarily shows in us, a result to which human nature cannot attain by itself.” Cassiodorus], because, although it has sinned greatly, mercy and redemption nevertheless prevail. Great redemption, and exceedingly abundant: that Christ’s most precious blood should be shed for a single sin. Hence the Apostle says: “For you were bought at a great price; glorify and bear God in your body” (1 Cor. 6:20).

“And he himself will redeem Israel from all its iniquities.” Let us give thanks to our Savior, because this redemption has already been accomplished, though the Prophet foretold that it would be future. [Col. 1183D]

## PSALM 130. A SONG OF ASCENTS.

“O Lord, my heart has not been exalted, nor have my eyes been lifted up.” This is the voice of the perfect; nor do they say these things in self-display, but so that [Col. 1184A] others may imitate them and fear to do such things. “O Lord,” he says, “my heart has not been exalted,” so that I might be lifted up and grow proud because of knowledge or other virtues which you have granted me. “Nor have my eyes been lifted up,” in which pride is most commonly observed and detected. [Note: [Col. 1183D] Cassiodorus briefly explains the contents of this psalm: “This psalm,” he says, “proclaims humility, teaches moderation, and enjoins patience.” [Col. 1184D]]

“Nor have I walked in great things,” so as to delight in things that seem great and precious to everyone. “Nor in wonders above me.” For many have gone astray because they attempted to reach into matters above us and beyond human understanding. Such wonders, therefore, are to be admired, revered, and believed—not handled through dialectical arguments. [Note: [Col. 1184D] It should be borne in mind that St Bruno, a most learned man, did not absolutely reject the use of dialectic in relation to sacred mysteries, but its excess and abuse—just as the Apostle condemns not knowledge but vain knowledge. Indeed, in expounding this psalm, St Bruno reproves in heretics the twists and turns of dialectic, the mazes of deception and sophistries, but not the proper method of reasoning. Thus below in the exposition of Psalm 139.] For this reason unhappy Arius fell: he did not fear to dispute dialectically concerning the inseparable Trinity. Hence it follows:

“If I did not think humbly, but exalted my soul—as a weaned child [understand: if he sins] upon his mother—so will you repay my soul.” For this is what the Apostle says: “Do not set your minds on high things, but associate with the lowly” (Rom. 12:16), because, as it is written, “God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble” (1 Pet. 5:5). The Catholic faith was taught not by the proud but by the humble. How great a sin it is not to think humbly, to exalt oneself above others, and to preach another faith and teaching—and thereby scandalize the holy Church, mother of all Christians—is shown by this Catholic man’s statement: “As a weaned child,” if he sins, [Col. 1184C] “upon his mother”—not upon his own mother, but by preaching another doctrine—he is rightly to be condemned and excommunicated; “so will you repay my soul.” This is that weaned child of whom the Prophet says: “Whom will he teach knowledge? Whom will he make to understand what is heard?” (Isa. 28:9)—“Those weaned [575] from milk, torn away from the breasts”—by whom are understood those who have learned ecclesiastical doctrine and have reached such knowledge that they no longer need milk, as the Apostle says, but solid food. Such persons, therefore, are not to be spared if they should wish to preach an alien doctrine.

“Let Israel hope in the Lord from this time forth and forever.” For after Israel humbled itself, received the Catholic faith, and feared to offend mother Church, it was able most firmly to hope in the Lord. Had it done otherwise, it could have had no hope.

## PSALM 131. A SONG OF ASCENTS.

“Remember, O Lord, David and all his meekness.” He speaks of our Savior, who, [Col. 1185A] like a meek lamb led to the sacrifice, did not open his mouth. He therefore asks the Father never to forget the humility, meekness, patience, and obedience of his Son. [Note: [Col. 1185D] Cassiodorus gives a fuller commentary on this passage, showing that the prophetic utterance must be understood wholly of Christ the Lord.]

“As he swore to the Lord, he vowed a vow to the God of Jacob.” Likewise he prays that God may remember the oath and vow which he swore and made to the Lord. [Note: [Col. 1185D] “Let no one presume to fulfill by his own strength what he has vowed. He who exhorts you to vow also helps you fulfill it.” St Augustine, Expositions on the Psalms.] Christ’s unchangeable will to build the Church is regarded as an oath and vow. This is what he says:

“If I enter into the tabernacle of my house, if I climb upon the bed of my couch, if I give sleep to my eyes, or slumber to my eyelids, or rest to my temples, until I find a place for the Lord, a tabernacle for the God of Jacob.” [Col. 1185B] This entire repetition of phrases signifies the same thing, and is repeated so that it may be believed more firmly. It is as if he said: I shall not first enter the tabernacle of my house—namely, the heavenly Jerusalem—nor climb upon the bed of my couch, by which that dwelling-place of ineffable rest is signified, until I find a place for the Lord and a tabernacle worthy of his habitation. And just as he prepared a house for me in heaven, so I too shall prepare a house for him on earth. By sleep, slumber, and rest is signified the same thing as we said was signified by house and bed. It is as though the humanity of our Savior said: I shall not first enter that house of eternal rest and blessedness until I have built the Catholic Church on earth.

[Col. 1185C] “Behold, we heard of it in Ephrathah; we found it in the fields of the forest.” [Note: [Col. 1185D] Bruno is singular in this reading. All the holy Fathers and expositors whom I have seen read with the Vulgate: “We heard that it”—that is, the ark of the Lord—“was in Ephrathah; we found it in the fields of the forest.” But Bruno’s interpretation agrees with St Hilary. For he says that Ephrathah signifies rest. Therefore it is heard in Ephrathah. “Ephrathah is the same as Bethlehem, [Col. 1186D] where the Lord was born of Mary. The Prophet is our witness, saying: ‘And you, Bethlehem, house of Ephrathah, are not least among the thousands of Judah; from you shall come forth one who will be king of Israel.’ For there God’s rest is first heard, where the first-begotten, the only-begotten God, inhabited a body of human flesh; and what is heard in Ephrathah is found in the fields of the forest. The beginning of the Church, therefore, is heard in Bethlehem; it did not begin to exist from Christ, but is found among the Gentiles, who are in the fields of the forest: shining from being dreadful, fruitful from being barren, a region of living food from being fodder for fire, and from dens of wild beasts, God’s rest, house, temple, and possession.”]

In Ephrathah, which is also called Bethlehem, the Lord was born; there he was first seen and heard, there he uttered the first cries of his infancy, to which the angels sang in harmony: “Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace to people of good will” (Luke 2:14). The fields of the forest are Judaea, which the Lord himself cultivated, sowed, and preached in; he uprooted the evil trees of vices and rooted out the thickets of malignant spirits. Perhaps that land is also called the fields of the forest because the forests of the Gentiles who lived in it were cut down and uprooted there by the children of Israel. There, therefore, the Church began; later spread throughout the whole world, it is in this place called the tabernacle of God. [Col. 1185D] Of it he continues:

“We entered into his tabernacle; we worshiped in the place where his feet stood.” He shows that the tabernacle [Col. 1186A] has already been built, which the Lord had promised under oath to build; and he shows that he himself entered it with others and worshiped there. His feet are the apostles, who carried his faith and teaching among all nations. Of them it is said: “Blessed are the feet of those who proclaim peace, who proclaim good things!” (Rom. 10:15). This can also be understood literally, since Christians worship in the place where our Savior walked with his feet.

“Arise, O Lord, into your rest, you and the ark of your sanctification.” Behold, as though he were saying, the vow has been fulfilled; you have done what you promised. Arise into your rest, and take with you that ark which you have now made the ark of your sanctification. The Church is rightly called an ark, because all its mysteries and better things are stored in it. This ark cannot now ascend all at once in its entirety; [Col. 1186B] yet it ascends daily, and at the Judgment it will ascend altogether.

“Let your priests be clothed with righteousness, and let your saints rejoice.” You, he says, arise; but let your priests—your apostles and their successors—be clothed with righteousness, so that they may govern your ark and Church justly and wisely, and that all your saints may rejoice under their rule and protection.

“For the sake of David your servant, do not turn away the face of your Christ.” This verse is joined to the first verse of this psalm, where it says, “Remember, O Lord, David.” He therefore asks the Lord not to turn away the face of Christ his Son, but everywhere and in all things to hear him [Col. 1186C] and fulfill all his wishes. Since he has no one greater or dearer through whom he can entreat God, he beseeches him through that same person, saying: “For the sake of David your servant, I entreat you, do not turn away the face of your Christ.” Hence the Lord says: “Whatever you ask the Father in my name, he will give you” (John 16:23). Now, however, he suddenly shows that it has been revealed to him how greatly the Father loves him and fulfills his will, when he says:

“The Lord swore truth to David, and he will not fail in it: ‘Of the fruit of your womb I will place one upon my throne.’” As the Son swore to the Father, so the Father swore to the Son, so that we may understand from this their equal power and equality. [Note: [Col. 1186D] Ghis. MS: “and equals.”] The sons of our Savior and the fruit of [Col. 1186D] his womb are the apostles, who were created and begotten from the seed and teaching of his breast. His throne is the Church, upon which these were appointed kings and high priests. “If your sons keep [Col. 1187A] my covenant and these testimonies of mine, which I will teach them, then their sons also shall sit upon my throne for ever and ever.” Not only, he says, will I place his sons upon my throne, but they and their sons—by whom their imitators are signified—will sit upon my throne for ever and ever, “provided that your sons keep [Note: [Col. 1187D] Ghis. MS: “Thus, provided that they keep.”] my covenant and these testimonies of mine, which I will teach them.” By these are signified the testimonies of both Testaments, spiritually understood.

“For the Lord has chosen Zion; he has chosen it beforehand as his dwelling.” Therefore, understood here, he said of it: “This is my rest for ever and ever; here I shall dwell, because I have chosen it.” There was no other reason why he should dwell in it except that he himself chose it as his dwelling. [Col. 1187B] “For he has mercy on whom he wills, and hardens whom he wills” (Rom. 9:18)—“It is not of the one who wills, nor of the one who runs, but of God who shows mercy” (ibid., 9:16), who according to his will “loved Jacob, but hated Esau” (Mal. 1:3).

“I will surely bless her widow; I will satisfy her poor with bread.” Christ’s widow is the Church, which he has just called Zion. But why a widow, except because she longs to see her husband and cannot see him? She is called a widow as though separated from her husband. Thus she has a husband and is a widow, because she is not yet joined to her husband in immortality. “I will satisfy her poor with bread.” Christ’s poor are those of whom it is said: “Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. 5:3). [Col. 1187C] They are satisfied with bread because they abound in spiritual riches.

“I will clothe her priests with salvation.” By them bishops and priests are signified. They are clothed with salvation because they are arrayed in the adornment of truth and wisdom. Hence the Apostle says to them: “Put off the old human being with his deeds, and put on the new, who is created according to God in righteousness and holiness of truth” (Eph. 4:22). “And her saints shall rejoice exceedingly.” Now indeed they rejoice in hope; later they will rejoice in reality.

“There I will bring forth a horn for David; I have prepared a lamp for my Christ.” For there—that is, in Zion and in the Church—the Lord brought forth and sent ahead, before the other preachers, David’s horn: John the Baptist, the forerunner of his Son. Showing himself to be the horn, he said: “I am the voice crying in the wilderness: Prepare the way of the Lord” (John 1:23). He is the one whom the Lord prepared as a lamp for his Christ, as it is written: “For John was a burning and shining lamp; but he was not the light, but bore witness to the light” (John 5:35).

“I will clothe his enemies with confusion, but upon him my sanctification shall flourish.” Let the enemies of both Christ and John be clothed in eternal confusion. But upon them sanctification has already flourished, because all the faithful believe them to be what they are.

## PSALM 132. A SONG OF ASCENTS.

[Col. 1188A]

“Behold, how good and how pleasant it is for brothers to dwell together in unity! For there the Lord commanded blessing and life forever. Like ointment upon the head, which descended upon the beard, the beard of Aaron, which descended to the edge of his garment; like the dew of Hermon, which descends upon Mount Zion.” Such is the order of the words; now let us consider their meaning. Blessed are these brothers upon whom God’s blessing and so great an abundance of graces descends. These are those brothers of whom the Lord says: “I will declare my name to my brothers” (Heb. 2:12). And elsewhere: “You are all brothers”; and, “Call no one on earth your father, for one is your Father, who [Col. 1188B] is in heaven” (Matt. 23:8–9). He is the one to whom we daily say: “Our Father, who are in heaven” (Matt. 6:9). Rich and poor, noble and low-born, master and servant, emperor and beggar—all say with one voice: “Our Father, who are in heaven,” thus showing that they are children of one Father and are brothers to one another. The better person is the nobler. Many who are servants here will be lords in the other life, and conversely, many who are lords here will there be oppressed by harsh servitude.

Good brothers were Sergius and Bacchus, who suffered such great torments for Christ; good were Cosmas and Damian; good John and Paul; good Maurice and his companions; good Dionysius with his companions; good too were many others who gave themselves over to death for Christ’s faith. “Of these indeed is the kingdom of heaven: they despised [Col. 1188C] the life of the world, attained the rewards of the kingdom, and washed their robes in the blood of the Lamb” (Rev. 7:14). Such brothers dwell in unity; such persons have one heart and one soul; no one calls anything his own, but all things are held in common among them. Evil brothers are those who are bodily together, yet are far from one another through hatred. “It is good,” he says, “and pleasant for brothers to dwell in unity.” Why is this so? Because there—that is, among such brothers—the Lord commanded his blessing and life without end. How does he command it? “Like ointment upon the head,” which descends from the head “upon the beard,” and from the beard even “to the edge of his garment”; and like the dew of Hermon, which descends upon Mount Zion.

Christ is the head of the Church, [Col. 1188D] whose members we all are. Of this body the Apostle says: “For just as we have many members in one body, yet all members do not have the same function, so we, though many, are one body in Christ, and individually members of one another” (Rom. 12:4–5). Christ therefore has a beard in his body; he has eyes and ears, hands and feet, and other members. Christ’s beard is the apostles: a beard because they are first in the body and joined to the head itself; a beard because they have nothing soft or womanish in themselves, but are manly, strong, and masculine. They are therefore rightly called not bearded men, but rather the beard itself. [Note: [Col. 1187] This kind of exposition by Bruno is taken from Augustine.] The Lord commands priests [Col. 1189A] not to shave their beard or grow their hair long. To grow one’s hair and have no beard belongs to women. Priests, however, ought to have faces not womanish but manly. Thus not only apostles, but also Christ’s holy martyrs, may be called the beard, because they too fought manfully and conquered most powerful enemies.

The ointment, therefore, descends from the head to the beard because the grace of the Holy Spirit first came from the divinity of our Savior to the apostles and martyrs. Of this ointment the Lord himself says: “The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because he anointed me; he sent me to preach the Gospel to the poor” (Luke 4:18). Of this the Psalmist also says: “You have loved righteousness and hated iniquity; therefore God, your God, has anointed you with the oil of gladness above your companions” (Ps. 44:8). The Church, experiencing this, says: “Draw me after you, and we shall run in the fragrance of your ointments” (Song 8:4). By this ointment the sick are healed; with it Jesus healed every disease and infirmity; with it priests and churches are consecrated; by this chrism both Christ himself and all Christians are named. This ointment, then, descends from the head to the beard—from Christ to the apostles—for the apostles possessed no virtue or grace which they had not received from him. Hence the Apostle says: “What have you that you did not receive? But if you received it, why do you boast as though you had not received it?” (1 Cor. 4:7). “To one is given through the Spirit a word of wisdom, to another a word of knowledge, to another prophecy, to another discernment of spirits, to another faith in the same Spirit, to another [Col. 1189C] gifts of healing, to another kinds of tongues, to another interpretation of utterances. But one and the same Spirit works all these things, distributing to each one as he wills” (1 Cor. 12:8–12).

From the apostles this great abundance of graces flows through the whole ecclesiastical body into the other members, reaching even to the edge of the garment. By the edge of the garment are understood those last ones who will exist at the end of the age. Consider, then, how great is the abundance of this ointment, which flows on through so long a course and anoints and heals so vast a people. Simon Magus wished to buy this ointment from the apostles; consequently, he was rightly condemned together with all his money. Our Savior is called Aaron—the first and greatest of all priests; priests are his sons, and those who are not his sons cannot be priests. Aaron is interpreted “mountain of strength,” an interpretation which seems especially fitting for him who is called “the Lord strong and mighty, the Lord mighty in battle.”

It follows: “Like the dew of Hermon, which descends upon Mount Zion.” “Hermon” means anathema (a curse), that is, division; [Note: [Col. 1189D] Augustine gives another meaning for this name, saying: “Hermon is a Hebrew name, and we have the interpretation from those who know that language: Hermon is said to mean ‘exalted light.’ [Col. 1190D] For the dew is from Christ. Now there is no exalted light except Christ. How was he exalted? First on the cross, afterward in heaven,” etc.] that is, division; “Zion” means contemplation. Hermon signifies the apostles, Zion the Church. The apostles are rightly called Hermon because they were the first of all to be divided and separated from the Synagogue [Col. 1190A] and to follow Christ the Lord. Hence the Apostle says: “But when it pleased him who separated me from my mother’s womb and called me through his grace” (Gal. 1:15), etc.

Not only the apostles, however, but all Christians may be called by this name. All receive this name in baptism, because there, renouncing the devil and all his pomps, they are separated from all sins and vices; passing from the left to the right, separated from the goats, they are joined to the lambs and sheep. Hence another psalm says: “My soul was troubled within me; therefore I will remember you, O Lord, from the land of Jordan and Hermon [Note: [Col. 1190D] Ghis. MS: “Hermonis.”] from the little mountain” (Ps. 41:7). The land of Jordan and Hermon consists of those who have been separated from vices through baptism, because Jordan signifies baptism and Hermon division and separation. Thus only the souls of the baptized praise the Lord from the land of Jordan and Hermon. Of them it is also said elsewhere: “Tabor and Hermon shall rejoice in your name” (Ps. 88:13).

Dew descends from Mount Hermon to Mount Zion, by which are understood the faith, teaching, and evangelical preaching that came from the apostles to the Church. With this dew and rain the whole Church is watered, made fruitful, washed, and cleansed. But the evil mountains are Gilboa, against which David pronounced a curse: “Mountains of Gilboa, let neither dew nor rain fall upon you, where Saul and Jonathan, the mighty ones of Israel, fell” (2 Sam. 1:21). These signify heretics, who are drenched not with apostolic dew but with a diabolical whirlwind. [Col. 1190C] Blessed are those brothers who, drenched with such dew, such rain, such ointment, and such grace, deserved to hear: “Behold, how good and how pleasant it is for brothers to dwell together in unity! For there the Lord commanded blessing and life forever.”

## PSALM 133. A SONG OF ASCENTS.

“Behold, now bless the Lord, all you servants of the Lord.” Now, he says, when you have gathered into unity, when you know and understand how good and pleasant it is for brothers to dwell in unity, now bless the Lord, because your blessings are praiseworthy and pleasing to the Lord. Therefore now bless the Lord, all you servants of the Lord, because the Lord receives the blessings of no others except those who are servants of the Lord. For whoever are not servants of the Lord are undoubtedly servants of the devil.

“You who stand in the house of the Lord, in the courts of the house of our God.” You who stand, he says, to obey, serve, pray, and fight in the house of the Lord—bless the Lord. Those who are outside are under a curse and can neither bless nor curse. But who are those in the courts, except those who guard the house and bring others in?

[Col. 1191A] “In the nights lift up your hands to the holy place, and bless the Lord.” Blessed are those who both do this literally and understand it, and who rise at midnight to confess the Lord, because this time is especially suitable for prayer. Those also lift their hands to the holy place who raise them to give alms. They do this at night if they do it secretly, so that the left hand does not know what the right does (Matt. 6:3). Such people bless the Lord, because all who receive these alms bless the Lord and give thanks.

“May the Lord bless you from Zion, he who made heaven and earth.” The entire congregation together pronounces this blessing upon the one who has newly come and joined himself to the others.

## PSALM 134. ALLELUIA.

[Note: [Col. 1191D] “After the most beautiful structure of the gradual psalms, which has reached that summit which makes people secure and happy forever, Alleluia is most fittingly placed, so that the holy Church, for which such a gift is known to be prepared, may enjoy the praises of the Lord.” Cassiodorus.]

[Col. 1191B]

“Praise the name of the Lord; praise him, servants of the Lord.” For what else does alleluia mean except “Praise the Lord”? A servant praises the Lord’s name when he shows himself a servant in both speech and obedience.

“You who stand in the house of the Lord, in the courts of the house of our God.” Those who depart from the house of the Lord and by their evil manner of life become strangers are unworthy to praise the Lord.

“Praise the Lord, for the Lord is gracious; sing praise to his name, for he is sweet.” You ought to praise him, he says, not only because you are servants, but also because he is so gracious and sweet that, because of his graciousness and sweetness, every creature ought to praise and bless him.

“For the Lord chose Jacob for himself, Israel as his own possession.” It has been proved by an excellent argument that the Lord is gracious and sweet: before Jacob was born, and before he had done anything good or evil, without any preceding merits, God chose him by his goodness alone. And he chose not only Jacob himself, but the whole of Israel—that is, all his offspring, which afterward was called Israel after him—as his own possession and inheritance.

“For I have known that the Lord is great, and that our God is above all gods.” This is why, he says, I say these things and proclaim him gracious and worthy of praise: because I know with complete certainty that the Lord and our God is great, great above all gods. And how do you prove this?

“For the Lord has done all that he willed in heaven and on earth, in the sea and in all the deeps.” He is therefore greater than all the angels in heaven and all the gods of the Gentiles whom foolish people believe to exist on earth, in the sea, and in hell; for whatever he willed, he did, wherever he willed to do anything.

“Bringing clouds from the end of the earth, he made lightnings into rain.” These clouds are the apostles and teachers, [Col. 1192A] whom the Lord sent from the ends of the earth into every part of the world to preach. By the rains of their teaching the whole earth was satisfied, watered, and purified. The lightnings became rain when, as the apostles preached, the Lord performed many miracles through them, and with the fiery arrows of Scripture killed vices and malignant spirits in human beings.

“He brings forth winds from his treasuries.” What are the winds, by which clouds are driven and scattered, except tyrants and powerful people who everywhere persecuted the holy preachers? God’s treasury is his own will, in which all things are contained, as it is written: “In your will, O Lord, all things are established” (Isa. 46:10). The winds thus come forth from God’s treasuries because it is by God’s [Col. 1192B] judgment that the wicked rise up and rage against the good. Hence the Lord says to his disciples: “If they persecuted me, they will persecute you also” (John 15:20). Yet they would have no power over them unless it had been given them from above.

“He struck the firstborn of Egypt, from human being to beast.” By the Lord’s striking all the firstborn of Egypt, it was signified that all universal sins throughout the world were to be destroyed in those who believe in him.

“He sent signs and wonders in your midst, O Egypt, against Pharaoh and all his servants.” Likewise, through his saints, before all people’s eyes, the Lord performed many signs and miracles throughout the world.

[Col. 1192C] “He struck many nations and killed mighty kings.” By the many nations and mighty kings are signified vices and malignant spirits, which were to be struck down and destroyed among all nations.

“Seon, king of the Amorites, and Og, king of Bashan, and all the kingdoms of Canaan he slew.” Now *Seon* is interpreted “temptation of the eyes,” *Amorites* “bitter,” *Og* “enclosure,” *Bashan* “confusion,” and *Canaan* “disturbance.” What, then, is denoted by “Seon,” if not lust? For it is lust that tempts the eye and makes it think upon and behold shameful and dishonourable things; it is also because of it that we daily say: “Turn away my eyes, lest they see vanity” (Ps. CXVIII [119]:36). And Seon is rightly called king of the Amorites, because lust, though sweet to the flesh, is nevertheless poisonous and exceedingly bitter to the soul. Og, whose name is interpreted “roof” or “enclosure,” signifies the greedy, who cover, conceal, and shut up everything. They are rightly said to reign in “Bashan,” that is, in confusion, since the greedy, through their greed, throw all things into confusion, seize them, and dissipate them. But Canaan, which is called “disturbance,” is the devil himself, king and prince of all vices, who unsettles and agitates the whole world and never permits it to be at rest. And because, unlike the others, he holds sovereignty not over one kingdom only, it is rightly said here: “and all the kingdoms [Col. 1193A] of Canaan.” Therefore the Lord struck many nations and slew mighty kings, because he put the devil himself to flight and overcame him together with his whole army. But what further?

“And he gave their land as an inheritance, an inheritance to Israel his people.” The whole world passed into the inheritance of the Church, over which the devil had formerly ruled.

“Lord, thy name is for ever; Lord, thy memorial unto age after age.” The enemies have been conquered, he says; all the kings of the earth have been overcome; “their memory has perished with a sound” (Ps. IX [9]:8); your name and your memorial alone remain for ever.

“For the Lord shall judge his people, and in [Col. 1193B] his servants he shall be comforted.” We know, as though he said, and are certain that henceforth not the kings mentioned above, but the Lord alone, who is a just judge, shall judge his people. And he shall take comfort in his saints, delivered by his grace from such great dangers. The remainder, down to the end of the psalm, has been explained above.

“The idols of the nations are silver and gold, the works of human hands. They have a mouth, and shall not speak; they have eyes, and shall not see; they have ears, and shall not hear; they have nostrils, and shall not smell; they have hands, and shall not touch; they have feet, and shall not walk; they shall not cry out with their throat, for there is no breath in their mouth. Let those who make them become like them, and all who trust [Col. 1193C] in them. House of Israel, bless the Lord; house of Aaron, bless the Lord; house of Levi, bless the Lord. You who fear the Lord, bless the Lord. Blessed is the Lord from Zion, who dwells in Jerusalem.”

## PSALM CXXXV. ALLELUIA.

This entire psalm is full of the Lord’s praises, which are signified by *alleluia*.

“Give thanks to the Lord, because he is good; because his mercy is for ever.” Praise the Lord, he says, because he is good and merciful by nature; this belongs properly to him alone, and no other possesses it naturally. “Give thanks to the God of gods; [Col. 1193D] give thanks to the Lord of lords.” Praise him, he says, and praise him always and without end: he is God and Lord of all gods and lords, by whom both you and every creature are ruled and governed, and without whom nothing exists.

“Who alone does great wonders.” And what great wonders did he alone perform?

[Col. 1194A] “Who made the heavens in understanding; who founded the earth upon the waters; who alone made the great lights: the sun to rule the day, the moon and stars to rule the night.” These truly are great things, and things which he alone, and no other, made. The intellectual heavens are those which are higher than the visible heavens: we can indeed think of and understand them, but cannot see them with our eyes. By them, moreover, prophets and apostles are signified, who are higher and possess greater understanding in the kingdom of heaven, which is the Church. That the earth is said to be founded upon the waters surpasses our knowledge. Yet it does not seem to me more wonderful that the earth should be founded upon the waters than that waters of the same weight should float through the air above the lands.

> [Note: [Col. 1193D] Cassiodorus interpreted this passage in two ways: “He could say that the earth is above the waters even though it seemed to be separated from them by much space; for in the same way we say that heaven is above us, although great expanses of air are known to intervene. Or, as some think, ‘above the water’ should be understood as ‘beside the water’ . . . Or certainly it should be understood spiritually: for upon the water of sacred baptism our earth, that is, the body, is renewed while it is made firm by the stability of religion.”]

We may also understand by the earth the Church [Col. 1194B], founded upon many peoples, who are signified by the waters; for “many waters [are] many peoples.” In Genesis it is read that “God made two great lights: the greater light, to rule the day, and the lesser light, to rule the night” (Gen. I:16). This is what is said here: “the sun to rule the day, the moon and stars to rule the night.” By these two great lights the two Testaments are signified. One of them, which is clearer, rules the day, that is, Christians; the other rules the Jews, who are always in night and walk in darkness.

“Who struck Egypt with their firstborn.” It has already been said above that Egypt signifies the world, whose first things were original sins [Col. 1194C]. But these were struck down and destroyed.

“And brought Israel out from the midst of it, with a mighty hand and an outstretched arm.” So too the Christian people have been delivered from the darkness of this world by the most mighty right hand of Christ, stretched out and raised upon the cross.

“Who divided the Red Sea into divisions, [and] brought Israel through the midst of it.”

> [Note: [Col. 1194D] “Men of ancient authority said that the Red Sea was divided into twelve divisions, corresponding to the number of Jewish tribes. For this reason the plural, ‘into divisions,’ was used, lest it be thought that the Red Sea was crossed by one route alone. But this may also fittingly be understood spiritually. The Red Sea is the mingled depth of this present age, which we cross by many divisions when, having been converted, we hasten by the Lord’s gift toward the land of the living.” Cassiodorus.]

We see this occur in baptism: each person being baptized opens a passage through it and comes forth cleansed and sanctified. There the devil perishes with his whole army, as the following verse makes clear.

“And he cast Pharaoh and his army into the Red Sea, [and] led his people through the wilderness.” The saints also, hastening through this wilderness, in [Col. 1194D] which John the Baptist cries out, toward their homeland, are filled with the delights of heavenly bread.

“Who brought water from the rock of the cliff.” — “And the rock,” says the Apostle, “was Christ” (I Cor. X:4), who cries to his faithful in the Gospel: “If anyone thirsts, let him come to me and drink; from his belly shall flow living waters” (John VII:37).

[Col. 1195A] “Who struck great kings and slew wonderful kings: Seon, king of the Amorites, and Og, king of Bashan, and gave their land as an inheritance to Israel his servant.” We have explained these matters above.

“Because in our humiliation the Lord remembered us, and redeemed us from the hand of our enemies.” For this reason, he says, the Lord struck the aforementioned kings and our enemies, who had greatly afflicted and humiliated us: because in that very humiliation and affliction he remembered us kindly and mercifully.

“Who gives food to all flesh.” In this his very great and ineffable mercy is commended. “Give thanks to the God of heaven,” because no other, but he alone, [Col. 1195B] is to be praised. “Give thanks to the Lord of lords, because he is good, because his mercy is for ever.”

## PSALM CXXXVI. A PSALM OF DAVID, OF JEREMIAH.

In this psalm David introduces Jeremiah speaking, who was led with the others into the Babylonian captivity.

“Upon the rivers of Babylon, there we sat and wept, when we remembered thee, Zion.” This psalm is understood literally of the Jews led captive into Babylonia, and spiritually of Christians who have suffered much in the captivity of this world at the hands of tyrants and heretics. Babylon is interpreted “confusion”; its rivers signify all the peoples and nations [Col. 1195C] of this world, since “many waters [are] many peoples.” Therefore the saints, mindful of the heavenly Jerusalem—into whose blessedness they desired to lead all others with them—preached and wept as though seated upon a high riverbank and fearing a precipice; yet often they made no progress at all. They wept, therefore, not from fear, but from excessive longing for that blessedness which they hastened to attain.

“Upon the willows in its midst we hung up our instruments.” By the willow, a very tough tree and quite suitable for binding something, memory is signified: for by memory we keep all that we know as though bound together in one bundle. Therefore, seeing that unbelievers despised their words and that they made no progress by preaching, many preachers at times ceased from preaching itself and entrusted the instruments of their preaching to memory.

“For there those who led us captive asked us for words of song.” They questioned them not in order to learn, but to rebuke and mock them. Thus the saints were silent and unwilling to answer, because they treated them as though they were entertainers. Hence it continues: “And those who led us,” mockingly [Col. 1196A] said, “Sing us a hymn from the songs of Zion.” To them we answered in our hearts:

“How shall we sing the Lord’s song in a foreign land?” This is what the Lord says: “Do not give what is holy to dogs, nor cast pearls before swine” (Matt. VII:6). Thus elsewhere it is said: “I have hidden thy words in my heart, that I may not sin against thee” (Ps. CXVIII [119]:11). This is why holy martyrs, when questioned by tyrants, as is read in their passions, were often unwilling to answer.

“If I forget thee, Jerusalem, let my right hand forget me.” Whoever loves this life alone and gives his entire self over to carnal pleasures and desires surely forgets the heavenly Jerusalem. His own right hand forgets him, because he does nothing [Col. 1196B] directed toward the benefit of his soul.

“Let my tongue cleave to my jaws, if I do not remember thee.” He wishes to become mute and tongueless in other matters if, whenever it is fitting, he has not proclaimed Jerusalem’s praises.

“If I do not set thee, Jerusalem, at the 582 beginning of my joy.” For he would not have set it there if he loved anything else more than it. What indeed ought to be desired and loved as much as the highest good and eternal life?

“Remember, Lord, the children of Edom in the day of Jerusalem, who say, ‘Lay it bare, lay it bare, even to its foundation.’” Edom, which is interpreted “bloody” or “earthly,” denotes all persecutors of the Church, and especially tyrants and heretics. These [Col. 1196C] are they who never cease to say in heart and voice that the Lord’s house should be destroyed down to its foundations. But on the day when Jerusalem is glorified, they shall come into the Lord’s remembrance, that they may be utterly confounded.

“O daughter of Babylon, wretched one: blessed is he who repays thee the recompense which thou hast repaid us.” The daughter of Babylon—the daughter of death and confusion—is our flesh: truly wretched and undeserving of mercy. It has afflicted us; it has subjected us to the laws of death and to such great sufferings and calamities. We ourselves too ought to do this to it: render it in kind, and, besides the sufferings it endures in life, afflict it with voluntary sufferings and tribulations.

“Blessed is he who shall seize and dash thy little ones against [Col. 1196D] the rock.” Blessed, he says, shall be the one who seizes, binds, restrains, and does not allow Babylon’s little ones to grow. By them are signified carnal impulses, pleasures, and desires, which must be put to death while they are small and can be restrained. Once grown, they cannot be restrained and overcome without great labour and great mercy from God. To dash them against the rock is to overcome them by the remembrance, strength, and help of Christ.

> [Note: [Col. 1195D] Cassiodorus commented similarly, understanding these little ones as vices of the flesh which must be restrained early in us before they grow up. On the words “shall dash [them] against the rock,” he says: “He shall dash [them] against the rock, so that, having seized them, he may not delay, lest a seductive will steal in. He shall dash [them], he says, against the rock—that is, against the Lord the Saviour, of whom it is written, ‘And the rock was Christ’ (I Cor. X:4)—so that, immediately broken, they may perish, these things which incited us to most foul impulses.” Cassiodorus.]

## PSALM CXXXVII. OF DAVID HIMSELF.

[Col. 1197A]

The Church speaks in this psalm of David himself—that is, of him who made all things, redeemed the world, is served by angels, looks upon the lowly, and knows the high things from afar—and praises and blesses him with its whole heart.

“I will give thanks to thee, Lord, with my whole heart.” I shall not praise you with lips only, as some are accustomed to do, but with my whole heart, because I know and understand that you look not to lips but to the heart. “Because thou hast heard all the words of my mouth.” You did this because his lips agreed with his heart and his heart with his lips. Hence the Lord also says: “If two of you agree concerning any matter, whatever you ask shall be done for you” (Matt. XVIII:19). He heard all the words of his mouth because he fulfilled the whole desire [Col. 1197B] of his heart. “And in the sight of angels I will sing psalms to thee.” Whoever sings psalms in the sight of angels ought to sing wisely. He sings wisely who praises God with the pure intention of the heart. By angels, moreover, we must understand not only the heavenly powers given to guard us, but also the rulers and guardians of the Churches.

“I will worship toward thy holy temple, and give thanks to thy name, Lord.” To worship toward the temple and in the temple signify the same thing here. Each of us worships God in his holy temple when he worships him in the secret place of his breast. Hence the Apostle says: “Do you not know that you are the temple of God, and that the Holy Spirit dwells in you? For the temple of God is holy, which you are” (I Cor. III:16). Hence the Lord also says: “But when you pray, enter into your chamber and, having shut the door, pray to your Father” (Matt. VI:6). Therefore we ought to pray in the heart and praise God in the heart.

“Because of thy mercy and truth.” I shall praise you, he says, and give thanks to your name for your great mercy and truth. Mercy and truth are joined in you, because mercy has done as it promised, and in doing so has shown itself to be truth.

“Because thou hast magnified thy holy name above us.” The Lord magnified his holy name above us because, according to the meaning of his name, he saved us; for *Jesus* is interpreted “Saviour.” In this his name has been fulfilled [Col. 1197D], because what it signifies has been magnificently accomplished.

“In whatever day I call upon thee, hear me.” And if you do this, “thou shalt multiply thy strength in my soul.” The Church is always heard, although it does not always appear to be heard, because it desires to be heard by God in nothing except those things which please God. Even if its petition is sometimes delayed, it is nevertheless heard when it is fulfilled in its own time. The Lord multiplies his strength in the Church, because he strengthens it with wisdom, [Col. 1198A] patience, and other virtues, 583 according to time and need.

“Let all the kings of the earth give thanks to thee, Lord, because they have heard all the words of thy mouth, and let them sing in the songs of the Lord.” Those kings of the earth who are said to have heard all God’s words and who are fit to give thanks and sing his songs are understood to be bishops, priests, and all rulers of the Church. Such persons ought, by reason of their office, strength, wisdom, and constancy, to praise and proclaim him. Let them therefore sing in the Lord’s songs, “because great is the glory of the Lord; because the Lord is high, and looks upon the lowly, and knows the high from afar.” In these few words almost the whole preaching of the Gospel is contained. First we must know [Col. 1198B] and believe that the Lord is glorious everywhere and in all things, exalted above all things, and that all things are subject to him as their Creator and Lord. Then we must know what he wills and does not will, because otherwise we cannot do his will. For, as is said here, he loves the humble; he rejects the proud, puts down the mighty from their seat, and exalts the humble: “he looks upon the lowly, and knows the high from afar.” He looks upon the former in mercy; he knows the latter in order to punish them.

“If I walk in the midst of tribulation, thou shalt give me life; and thou hast stretched out thy hand against the wrath of my enemies, and thy right hand has saved me.” Because, as though he said, you always look upon me and preserve me by looking upon me, I am therefore secure everywhere and do not fear even the tribulations inflicted upon me. For you will raise me up and give me life when dead, and you will avenge me upon all my enemies. “Lord, repay for me.” Repay, Lord, he says, to my enemies a fitting recompense for me—yet only if they persist in this wickedness of theirs. But if they are converted and recognize that they sin, show them mercy, “and do not despise the works of thy hands”; rather, let your mercy remain also upon them for ever.

## PSALM CXXXVIII. UNTO THE END, A PSALM OF DAVID.

The Prophet teaches us that this psalm must be referred to the End, by whom we understand Christ and the Church. “For Christ is the end of the law” (Rom. X:4). [Col. 1198D] He is “Alpha and Omega, the beginning and the end” (Apoc. I:8). The Apostle says also concerning the Church: “We are those upon whom the ends of the ages have come” (I Cor. X:11).

“Lord, thou hast proved me and known me.” In this psalm the Prophet speaks, together with others of the same perfection. Lord, he says, “thou hast proved me,” and by proving me “thou hast known me.”

> [Note: [Col. 1197D] According to Cardinal Thomasius’s interpretation, this psalm is composed in the person of the faithful people, understanding the Lord’s power and that not even secrets can escape his majesty. Accordingly, it introduces the Prophet as speaking thus: “Lord, you have fully searched and known me,” etc. St Bruno’s exposition makes it clear that he interpreted it in this way.]

Not that he who knows all things before they happen needs testing; therefore he tested for our sake, and by testing made them clearer, since otherwise we could not have known. “Thou hast known [Col. 1199A] my sitting down and my rising up.” You saw and knew how I sat, how I taught, how I persevered in good, and with what seriousness I conducted myself. And if at any time I fell through the frailty of the flesh, you know very well how, how quickly, and how courageously I rose again. How is this so? For “thou hast understood my thoughts from afar”: from afar indeed, since the Lord knew our actions and thoughts from eternity and before the foundation of the world. Hence he continues: “Thou hast searched out my path and my direction, and hast foreseen all my ways. And thou knowest that there is no deceit upon my tongue”: what I say is true, pure, clean, and without falsehood. For the Lord sees all things: both the narrow and broad ways through which we walk, [Col. 1199B] and the directions and corrections by which we guide and discipline our works and paths. Hence it continues:

“Behold, Lord, thou hast known all things, the last and the ancient.” For there has been, is, and shall be nothing that he does not know. “Thou hast formed me, and laid thy hand upon me.” Therefore, if there is anything praiseworthy in him, it belongs not to himself but to God. Such also is what the Lord says elsewhere: “Before I formed thee in the womb, I knew thee; and before thou camest forth from the belly, I sanctified thee” (Jer. I:3). The saints do not therefore praise themselves because they are such, but rather praise him by whom they were so formed.

“Thy knowledge has become wonderful from me.” And it is so wonderful, strengthened, and exalted that I am unable [Col. 1199C] to attain it. If, therefore, he cannot understand and know himself, how can he understand things outside himself? With what face does wretched man presume to dispute concerning God, when he does not know how to give an account even of himself? “Wonderful,” he says, “has thy knowledge become,” not only from you, not only from the creation of the world, 584 but from myself, who cannot see myself. Wretched is he who offends you, because he can nowhere escape your wrath. This is what he says:

“Whither shall I go from thy spirit? And whither shall I flee from thy face?” He puts himself in place of others, so that what he says of himself may be understood of all. Whither, he says, shall I go from the spirit of your wrath, and whither shall I flee from the face of your indignation—you who are everywhere and see all things?

[Col. 1199D] “If I ascend into heaven, thou art there; if I descend into hell, thou art present.” We ascend into heaven not with our feet but with prayers, when we invoke for our aid those who are in heaven. But we descend from there into hell when we similarly entreat those who are in this world. In comparison with heaven, this world is called hell, because *infernum* is so called from its being lower. Therefore, one with whom God is angry can have the help neither of those in heaven nor of those on earth. There is one sole and singular means by which a person can escape God’s wrath: namely, by fleeing from oneself and taking refuge in God. For a person cannot be swifter in repenting than God is in pardoning. For he himself says: “In whatever hour the sinner is converted, I will not remember any of his iniquities” (Ezek. XXXIII:11). Let a person therefore repent, and in this way he can escape God’s wrath.

“If I take my wings before the light, and dwell in the uttermost part of the sea,” then, understood, I shall be able to escape your wrath. Let us therefore take our wings, by which remedies of repentance are signified, without which we cannot fly to the farthest parts of this sea. We take up wings before the light if we reveal our sins from our whole heart before God, who is the true light. Thus “before the light” means as though it were said, “in the sight of the light” or “in the presence [Col. 1200B] of the light.” They dwell in the uttermost part of the sea who have escaped the shipwrecks and crimes of this world. The following words show how they escape.

“For even there thy hand shall lead me, and thy right hand shall hold me.” This right hand held Peter, to whom, while he was sinking, the Lord said: “O thou of little faith, why didst thou doubt?” (Matt. XIV:31).

“And I said, ‘Perhaps darkness shall trample me.’” If, he says, I wish to leave the world and fly to you, “perhaps darkness shall trample me.” We read that this happened to many in the time of the martyrs: fleeing to the faith of Christ, they were trampled by darkness, by which wicked people are signified. Of them the Apostle says: “You were once darkness, but now [are] light in the Lord” (Eph. V:10). And the Gospel says concerning them: “The light shines in darkness, and the darkness did not comprehend it” (John I:5). Such darkness trampled and killed those whom it saw passing over to Christ’s faith. It continues: “And night is my illumination in my delights.” Darkness, he says, will trample me and lead me to death, which is signified by night; but that very night and that very death shall be my illumination. Where? “In my delights.” For unless death had intervened first, he could not have reached those great delights.

“Because darkness shall not be darkened from thee, and night shall be enlightened as day.” Therefore, he says, I said that night would be my illumination, because I know and am certain [Col. 1200D] that “darkness shall not be darkened from thee.” Rather, as soon as I have been killed for your name, darkness driven away, I shall come to you by a straight and clear road. And that night shall be enlightened for me like day, in which it happens that I come from the darkness of this world to the glory of your brightness.

“As its darkness, so also is its light.” For just as the darkness of that night is great, so its light will be great and ineffable.

> [Note: [Col. 1199] This passage is mutilated in Marchesi’s edition; it is restored from the manuscript of Santa Croce Minor in the Laurentian Library. The Ghisian manuscript agrees with it.]

Nor shall the flesh receive more of night and darkness than the soul shall receive of light and brightness in that life.

“For thou, Lord, hast possessed my reins; thou hast received me from my mother’s womb. I will give thanks [Col. 1201A] to thee, Lord, because thou hast been magnificently terrible.” Therefore, he says, I shall give thanks to you, Lord, and praise you, because you possessed my reins and did not permit the sin of lust—the filthiest among all sins—to rule over me; and because you received me from my mother’s womb, preserved me under the guardianship of your protection, and delivered me from such great dangers. Moreover, I shall also give thanks to you, Lord, and praise you for this: “because thou hast been magnificently terrible.” The Lord has often shown himself magnificently terrible, crushing his enemies with many and very great plagues, as in the Flood, the Red Sea, Sodom, and many other places. “Wonderful are thy works, and my soul knows [them] exceedingly.” He is exceedingly wonderful whose works are so wonderful; and this man knows them well because he exercises himself in them, not only by reading but also by acting.

“My mouth was not hidden from thee, which thou madest in secret.” He speaks of the mouth of the heart, whose words God alone knows.

> [Note: [Col. 1201D] Here St Bruno indulged too greatly in the pursuit of a mystical sense, explaining *os ossis* (“bone”) in place of *os oris* (“mouth”). St Augustine, in order to remove the equivocation completely, used the unusual form *ossum*: “Behold,” he says, “my substance is in the flesh; my substance is in the lower parts of the earth; yet I have within me a bone which thou hast formed.” I shall not omit Cardinal Thomasius’s neat exposition: “Not even one of my bones, which thou madest for me in the hidden place of my mother’s womb, is hidden from thee.”]

585 How much humbler than others this man was appears in his statement that his substance was in the lower parts of the earth:

“My imperfection thy eyes saw.” You saw, he says, my imperfection and knew how much I lacked of full and perfect righteousness. Nevertheless, all your faithful and friends shall be written in your book—not imperfect, but perfect. This is what he says: “And in thy book all shall be written.” Of what sort? “The days shall be formed, and no one in them.” The book of God is his memory itself, in which [Col. 1201C] the names of all the saints are contained. All days shall be formed, because they shall be bright and shining; and, as it is written, “the righteous shall shine as the sun in the kingdom of God,” and no one shall lack its brightness and perfection.

“But thy friends, O God, have been exceedingly honoured by me; their dominion has been exceedingly strengthened.” They have indeed been greatly honoured both in heaven and on earth, since they have such great authority in heaven and on earth that whom they bind here and there are bound, and whom they loose are loosed. There they are written in the book of life; here their memory remains most bright and perpetual. Truly their dominion has been exceedingly strengthened: the world is not enough for them, but they possess dominion above the heavens.

“I shall number them, and they shall be multiplied above the sand.” [Col. 1201D] They are innumerable, he says, and cannot be counted, like the sand of the sea. They are multiplied even beyond the sand of the sea, because Christians are far more numerous than Jews, who are signified by the sand. Thus the Lord says to Abraham: “So shall thy seed be as the stars of heaven and as the sand which is on the seashore” (Gen. XXII:17), signifying Christians by the stars and Jews by the sand, which is trodden under foot.

[Col. 1202A] “I arose, and am still with thee.” Above he has just said, “Thy eyes saw my imperfection”; but now he says that he has risen from that imperfection and remained faithfully and steadfastly in the Lord, so that he too may be written with the others in the book of life, and be formed and glorified among the other days.

“If thou shalt slay sinners, O God: men of blood, depart from me.” All those are slain and die who are separated and divided from God. If, he says, you repel sinners from yourself and separate them from your presence, then I shall say to them, “Men of blood, depart from me”; nor will I have fellowship with those whom I know do not possess your grace. Sinners are then slain by the Lord when they are excommunicated and struck by the Church’s sentence.

[Col. 1202B] “Because ye say in your thoughts: ‘They shall receive their cities in vain.’” With good reason, he says, O men of blood, we flee you and separate ourselves from your fellowship, because you judge and think wrongly and wickedly both about God himself and about his Church. Men of blood are understood especially as heretics, who destroy body and soul and kill the whole person. They indeed say in their thoughts concerning holy and catholic men: “Let them receive their cities in vain,” for their wickedness has so blinded them that they believe whatever is done in the Church to be wholly vain and useless.

“Did I not hate them, O God, that hate thee, and did I not pine away because of thy enemies?” God rightly slays such sinners and repels them from his whole body, [Col. 1202C] which is the Church, because they are those who hate him and are especially his enemies. These words teach us how greatly we ought to flee and avoid such persons.

“With perfect hatred I hated them, and they became enemies to me.” It is a good and perfect hatred when we love nature but hate vice. “Avoid,” says the Apostle, “a heretical man after a first and second correction” (Tit. III:10). He surely would not have said this unless he knew that such a person’s fellowship is dangerous.

“Prove me, O God, and know my heart; question me, and know my paths.” Blessed is he whom his conscience so defends. He still desires to be tested, [Col. 1202D] although at the beginning of the psalm he said that he had been tested, because he understands himself to be clean and pure both in thought and in action. “And see whether there is a way of iniquity in me, and lead me in the eternal way.” After you have tested and questioned me, he says, and, if you wish, as though by fire examined and known me, and found no way of iniquity in me, lead me in the eternal way. Those are in the eternal way who no longer fear turning aside to the way of sin and death. But this way is not found in the present life.

## 586 PSALM CXXXIX. UNTO THE END, A PSALM OF DAVID.

We have often already said what “unto the end” signifies, and what “a psalm of David” signifies.

> [Note: [Col. 1203D] Throughout this whole psalm the Church speaks. So Cassiodorus.]

“Deliver me, Lord, from the evil man; free me from the unjust man.” The Church speaks and asks the Lord to deliver her from the evil man, by whom the devil and heretics are signified. For they are evil and unjust, and persecute the Church more than all others.

> [Note: [Col. 1203D] “Knowing how great an assault of the devil she suffered in her members, Mother Church anxiously cries [Col. 1204D] to the Lord, who alone can overcome his wickedness, that she may be delivered from his manifold temptation.” Cassiodorus.]

“Who have devised wickednesses in their heart.” They devise wickednesses in their heart because they labour especially to discover how they may deceive Catholic men and draw them into heresy [Col. 1203B]. “All day they prepared battles.” All day they desire to dispute and contend; they are ready with many arguments to assail the truth and defend their errors.

“They sharpened their tongues like serpents; the venom of asps is under their lips.” Heretics are rightly compared with serpents, because they are slippery, twisting, and full of venom. Their teaching is like the venom of asps, said to be incurable, because heretical doctrine too is deadly and incurable.

“Keep me, Lord, from the hand of the sinner, and deliver me from unjust men.” The sinner is the devil; the unjust are heretics: an evil teacher has evil disciples. He asks to be guarded and delivered from all of them because he fears the snares of all.

[Col. 1203C] “Who have devised to trip up my steps.” How? “The proud have hidden a snare for me.” Pride and arrogance alone make heretics, because, while they wish to think lofty thoughts and refuse to agree with the humble, they fall into heresy. Thereupon they devise how they may trip others up and draw them to their own opinion. They hide snares: they interpret the Scriptures deceptively and argumentatively, and attempt by syllogisms what they cannot accomplish by authority. Hence it continues:

“And they stretched cords into a snare for my feet; beside the way they set a stumbling-block for me.” He calls the disputation itself a snare; the cords, by which the snare is drawn from a distance, are the winding turns of dialectic and sophisms. By these simple people are ensnared, deceived, and drawn into the pit of error [Col. 1203D]. He sets a stumbling-block beside the way who takes something from Scripture itself—which is our way—and, by interpreting it badly, leads a person into error. Thus the Arians did when they said: “Does not the Son say, ‘The Father is greater than I’?” (John 14:28). How do you call equal one who confesses himself to be lesser? And this was a stumbling-block to simple people, because they did not know how to resolve it.

“I said to the Lord: You are my God; hear, O Lord, [Col. 1204A] the voice of my prayer.” The Church says that in that great battle with the heretics she cried out to the Lord, because she feared that she would lose all the simple, the unlearned, and those less trained in the divine Scriptures. “You,” she says, “are my God; I have no other. These men are striving to take you away from me. Hear me now in this battle and in this great necessity.” Let us hear, then, why he ought to hear her.

“O Lord, Lord, strength of my salvation, you have overshadowed my head in the day of war.” These words signify great terror. It is more dangerous to fight heretics than tyrants, because the latter kill the body, but the former kill souls. “O Lord,” she says, “Lord, strength of my salvation, without whose help and power I cannot be saved, you have overshadowed my head [Col. 1204B],” the head of my mind, “in the day of war,” so that their blasphemies may be unable to penetrate to my ears.

“Do not deliver me over, from my desire, to the sinner.” What is meant by “to the sinner”? To the devil and his members. Hence it is added in the plural: “They have devised against me,” because in the one name “sinner” many sinners are signified. For then—God forbid—the Church would be delivered over to sinners, disappointed of her desire, if they had been able to carry out their wicked designs against her.
