“Do not forsake me, lest they ever be exalted.” Consider now how greatly heretics would exalt themselves and prevail, since even when defeated they are not ashamed to defend their altar and their error.

“The head of their surrounding circuit—the toil of their lips—shall cover them.” The head of their circuit is the devil [Col. 1204C], because their master, the devil himself, taught them those circumlocutions of speech and those windings of so many deceptions. The toil of their lips is likewise called that same circuit, because, just as those who speak truth do not labor, so, on the contrary, those who lie must labor greatly. This circuit indeed, this deceitful discourse of theirs, so often covers them that their heresy cannot be comprehended. Let us hear what punishment awaits them for so great a deception.

“Coals shall fall upon them; you shall cast them into fire; they shall not endure in miseries.” This is what he says elsewhere: “He shall rain snares upon sinners; fire and sulphur and the spirit of storms are the portion of their cup” (Ps. 10:7). How, then, will they be able to endure in miseries [Col. 1204D], when they will burn with fire thus placed around them on every side?

“A man of much speech shall not be guided upon the earth.” The one who is not guided upon earth, once placed beneath the earth, awaits torments alone. Therefore the Apostle commands us to avoid a heretical person after a first and second correction, because such people are incorrigible; it is very difficult for them to be directed toward what is good. The heretic is rightly called a man of much speech, because he trusts in tongue and chatter alone. Of him it is further added [Col. 1205A]: “Evils shall seize the unjust man unto destruction.” “Evils,” he says, “shall seize him,” not for correction, that they may be saved, but unto destruction, that they may be tormented without end.

“I have known that the Lord will execute judgment for the needy, and vengeance for the poor.” Moreover, those are poor who seek not temporal but eternal riches. There is no need to doubt concerning their judgment and vengeance; for just as glory is prepared for the good, so punishment is prepared for the evil.

“Nevertheless, the righteous shall confess your name.” Let unjust men, as though he said, wage battles all day long; let them devise how they may trip up the steps of the saints. Nevertheless, the righteous do not cease to praise God and preach the truth. “And the upright shall dwell with your countenance.” What is “with your countenance,” except [Col. 1205B] in the presence of your glory? There the saints will praise; there they will rejoice eternally with the Lord.

## PSALM 140. A PSALM OF DAVID

This title has already been expounded many times above.

“O Lord, I have cried to you; hear me.” “Lord,” says the Church, “I have often cried to you, and now indeed I shall cry, that you may hear me—not only now, but at every time: when ‘I shall cry to you, attend to the voice of my prayer.’” She says this because she knows that it is to come about that, as the thickness of earth is cast up upon the ground, so his bones will be scattered beside hell. In this is signified a most grievous and utterly intolerable persecution. This is expounded in what follows.

[Col. 1205C] “Let my prayer be directed as incense in your sight.” Mother Church prays that, in the time of persecution, her prayers may thus be directed to her Lord and may please him, just as the good fragrance of incense rises to our nostrils and is pleasant to us.

“The lifting up of my hands is an evening sacrifice.” The evening sacrifice was Christ’s Passion, for at about that hour he gave up his spirit. The lifting up of hands is that of which it is elsewhere said: “In the nights lift up your hands in the holy place, and bless the Lord” (Ps. 133:2). Therefore let us pray to the Lord that the lifting up of our hands may be clean and pure, pleasing and acceptable to God, like an evening sacrifice.

[Col. 1205D] “Set, O Lord, a guard upon my mouth, and a door of restraint around my lips.” And why is this? “That my heart may not turn aside to an evil word, to make excuses in sins.” We have this vice from our first parents, who, after their sin and when questioned by the Lord, first found excuses. Adam indeed said: “The woman gave to me, and I ate” (Gen. 3:12); but the woman: “The serpent deceived me” (ibid., 13). Such excuses are evil and ought not to be made; by them sins are not diminished but rather increased. Indeed, all excuses are evil [Col. 1206A] by which repentance is hindered and vices are nourished. Thus it is said here: “That my heart may not turn aside to an evil word,” as elsewhere it is said: “Lead us not into temptation” (Matt. 6:13).

“With men who work iniquity, and I will not share with their chosen ones.” “I will not share,” he says, “nor associate with people who work iniquity and persist in wickedness—neither with them nor with their chosen ones.” By these chosen ones we understand their leaders and teachers, and all heresiarchs. For they have been chosen by them so that they may follow them, defend, and maintain their errors.

“The righteous man shall correct me in mercy, and shall rebuke me.” This is what the teachers of the Church do; this is what bishops and priests do, who daily [Col. 1206B] rebuke and correct sinners, and promise great mercy to those who turn and repent. “But let not the oil of the sinner anoint my head.” What is signified by the oil of the sinner except flatteries, adulations, persuasions, and deceptions? The head is put for the mind, which, once anointed and smeared with such oil, is easily drawn into sins.

“For still my prayer. But they have been swallowed up in their pleasures. Yet their judges, joined to the rock, shall hear my words. But because they were strong, as the thickness of earth is cast up upon the ground, so our bones have been scattered beside hell.” For this is the order of the text. Now let us consider its meaning. “Hear me,” he says, “because still—still remaining and not yet ended [Col. 1206C]—is my prayer, which I also requested at the beginning of this psalm, saying: ‘Attend to the voice of my prayer when I cry to you.’ But those of whom I spoke above—‘with men who work iniquity, and I will not share with their chosen ones’—have been swallowed up in the things that pleased them. They are good indeed, as they themselves think, since they delight in their own error and folly. Thus they have been swallowed up and devoured by the devil, so that they will no longer escape from that abyss. But those who are joined and united to the rock, by which Christ is signified, shall hear my words.” This is the rock of which the Apostle says: “The rock

> [Note: “[Col. 1205D] By ‘rock’ here, as in many places, Christ the Lord is signified. Standing beside this rock, heretical teachers, as though judges of their people, are submerged by sudden voracity; and they fall into the deep because [Col. 1206D] they do not choose to stand upon the rock [lacuna]. For only those stand firm in this solidity who do not lay fragile foundations upon sand.” CASSIODORUS, whom St Bruno also followed in the remainder.]

was Christ” (1 Cor. 10:4). To this rock all the good are indissolubly joined and united [Col. 1206D]. These hear and believe the words of the Church, which heretics disdain to hear. Thus they are proved most foolish, because they despise to hear what their judges admire and in which they take the greatest delight. Hence in the Song of Songs the Lord says: “You who dwell in the gardens, the friends listen: make me hear your voice” (Song 8:13). These judges are understood to be not only the apostles, but all the saints, among whom the queen of the South and the Ninevites are counted. It follows:

“Because they were strong, as the thickness of earth is cast up [Col. 1207A] upon the ground, so our bones have been scattered beside hell.” “Because,” he says, “those who were swallowed up were once strong, and because in this life they were strong and powerful, therefore our bones—our stronger members, by which the apostles and martyrs are represented—were scattered by their violence and strength beside hell. By hell tyrants and other wicked people are signified, by whom and among whom the saints of God, afflicted, tortured, and scattered as though in hell, suffered. Hence the Lord says concerning himself and all those who are his members: ‘I am a worm and not a man, a reproach of men and an outcast of the people. All who saw me despised me’” (Ps. 21:7). It is therefore not surprising if righteous men are compared to worms, when the Son of God himself [Col. 1207B] is called a worm.

“For to you, O Lord, Lord, are my eyes; in you I have hoped; do not take away my soul.” “Do not take away,” he says, “O Lord”—that is, do not permit my soul to be taken away and deceived by the aforesaid impious and wicked men, since I have raised my eyes to you, have hoped in you, and have no other helper.

“Keep me from the snare which they have set for me, and from the stumbling-blocks of those who work iniquity.” Much has been said in the preceding psalm concerning this snare and these stumbling-blocks, by which nothing other than the cunning and deception of tyrants and heretics is signified.

“Sinners shall fall into his net.” Sinners fall into the net of this snare, because they are the ones deceived by heretics and other wicked people [Col. 1207C].

“I am alone until I pass over.” The Church is alone in this life, because the good are very few in comparison with the evil; but after they have passed over, she will be many. For even if not greater in number, she will nevertheless be greater and more powerful than all others in virtue and strength.

## PSALM 141. AN UNDERSTANDING OF DAVID, WHEN HE WAS IN THE CAVE

> [Note: “[Col. 1207D] David, fleeing because of Saul’s snares, when he was hiding in a cave, signified what Christ the Lord would do in the body before his Passion. For when ‘understanding’ is prefixed to this prayer, it signifies that David understood, amid his distresses and the hiding-places of his flight, what the Lord would suffer from the Jews and how he would pray to the Father.” BEDE.]

“With my voice I cried to the Lord; with my voice I made supplication to God.” Not only with the inward voice by which he always spoke with the Lord, but also with the outward voice heard by human beings, the Son often cried to the Father; and in all things he was heard as he wished [Col. 1207D].

“I will pour out my prayer before him, and declare my tribulation before him, when my spirit fails within me.” “Now,” he says, “at the point of death and at the time of the Passion, when spirit and life fail and my soul is separated from my flesh, I desire to pour out my prayer before him, and that he may be present to hear and receive it. [Col. 1208A] Likewise I desire and wish to declare my tribulation before him, so that he may not forget to avenge me upon those who persist in their wickedness. ‘And you knew my paths.’” He now speaks to the Father, by whose counsel and will he came into the world, took flesh, lived among people, preached, and called the Jews to faith. These are his paths, which, he says, the Father does not fail to know:

“In this way in which I walked, they hid snares for me.” Read the Gospel, and you will find that the Jews prepared many snares and ambushes for the Lord, such as concerning the payment of tribute and the observance of the Sabbath.

“I looked on my right hand and saw, and there was no one who knew me.” The Lord considered nothing else [Col. 1208B], entertained nothing else in his mind, except what was on the right hand and what was done for everyone’s salvation and prosperity. Yet they did not recognize this, and returned evil for good.

“Escape perished from me.” “I could,” he says, “have fled had I wished; it was easy for me to avoid their anger and indignation. But if I had done this, what benefit would I have given the human race? I placed their salvation first and mine second. Yet there is no one who seeks my soul except to take it away. I cried to you, O Lord; I said: You are my hope, my portion in the land of the living.” The Lord cried, but inwardly, because his will was a great cry in the ears of the Father. He said, resolved, and established that he would not defend himself, but would hope in the divinity alone, [Col. 1208C] whose portion was not in the land of the dying but rather in the land of the living.

> [Note: “[Col. 1208D] My portion in the land of the living. This is proved especially by that passage when, placed upon the cross, he said to the thief: ‘Truly I say to you, today you shall be with me in paradise’—Luke 23:43. For paradise is the land of the living, into which only the blessed shall happily enter, since they shall live in eternity and security.” Cassiodorus.]

“You chose not the dead, O Lord, but the living; not the Synagogue, but the Church, because ‘the dead shall not praise you, O Lord, nor all who descend into hell. But we who live bless the Lord from this time forth and forever’” (Ps. 113:17–18).

“Attend to my prayer, because I have been exceedingly humbled.” Since the Lord speaks according to his humanity, he displays human affections. He did not need to pray, for all things were in his will and power; yet if he had chosen to use his power, who could have resisted him? And in that case, who would have believed that he was a human being? Truly, he humbled himself exceedingly [Col. 1208D], bending himself from his omnipotence to such impotence.

“Deliver me from those who persecute me, because they have been strengthened against me.” The Lord “was offered because he himself willed it” (Isa. 53:7). His enemies were strengthened against him because he willed it; he was delivered from their hands as he wished and when he wished.

[Col. 1209A] “Bring my soul out of prison, that it may confess your name, O Lord.” This prison is hell, from which the Lord brought out not only his own soul, but the souls of all the saints held imprisoned there. Therefore his whole Church confesses his name, and all the saints praise and bless him.

“The righteous await me, until you repay me.” All the righteous awaited this: that Christ should rise from the dead,

> [Note: “[Col. 1209] This passage, lacking in the edition, is completed from the cited manuscript of Santa Croce Minor in the Laurentian Library, with which the Ghisian manuscript agrees.”]

because they knew that they could not otherwise rise unless he first rose, “who is the firstborn of the dead and the ruler of the kings of the earth” (Rev. 1:5). But the risen Lord received a recompense worthy of so great a labor, because, as he himself says: “All power in heaven and on earth has been given to him” (Matt. 28:18).

## PSALM 142. WHEN HIS SON ABSALOM PERSECUTED HIM (2 KINGS 15:14)

[Col. 1209B]

David composed this psalm at the dictation of the Holy Spirit when his son Absalom persecuted him; and we too ought to sing it in all our distresses and necessities.

“O Lord, hear my prayer; give ear to my supplication in your truth; hear me in your righteousness.” This is like the passage in the Gospel where our one and the same Savior repeats the same thing so often: “Ask, and you shall receive; seek, and you shall find; knock, and it shall be opened to you” (Matt. 7:7). Hence elsewhere he says: “The kingdom of heaven suffers violence, and the violent seize it” (Matt. 11:12). Therefore the Apostle [Col. 1209C] also teaches us to pray without ceasing. “Hear me,” he says, “in your truth,” because you have thus promised me, and you are truthful and cannot lie, so that your righteousness may be manifested—a righteousness which everywhere follows truth and cannot exist of itself without it.

“And do not enter into judgment with your servant.” For if you do so, “every living person shall not be justified in your sight.” Human nature has been so violated that no one can defend himself if he comes to judgment together with God. “For every human being is a liar” (Ps. 115:11). And: “The stars are not clean in his sight” (Job 25:5). And, as the Apostle John says: “If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us” (1 John 1:8). Thus every day [Col. 1209D] we say: “Forgive us our debts, as we forgive our debtors” (Matt. 6:12). And this is because “the enemy has persecuted my soul; he has humbled my life to the ground.” This is the enemy of whom it is said: “Our enemy the devil goes about like a roaring lion, seeking whom he may devour” (1 Pet. 5:8). He persecutes our souls, humbles them to the earth, and does not permit them to think heavenly thoughts; he tramples them down to earth and entangles them in the pleasures of the flesh. Hence it is added:

“He has placed me in darkness like those dead from of old; and my spirit has been distressed within me, and my heart [Col. 1210A] has been troubled within me.” The dead of the age are those separated by sin from true life, which is Christ. Such people lie in darkness as long as they persist in sin. In them the spirit is distressed, because the soul wastes away through excessive weakness. The heart is troubled when it meditates upon vain and shameful things.

“I remembered the days of old, and meditated on all your works.” We must seek this remedy for recovering health whenever we feel that we have been placed in darkness and lie in the shadows of sins. Let us remember the days of old and reform ourselves according to the examples of the saints. Let us meditate on God’s works and strive to imitate so great a master, in whose works no evil is found, who saw all that he had made, and they were very good [Col. 1210B]. “And I shall meditate on the works of your hands.” Vices and sins are not among the works of his hands; therefore we ought neither to think nor to do them. Evil thought does great harm, for it is itself the cause and origin of sin.

“I stretched out my hands to you.” This is what is said elsewhere: “In the nights lift up your hands in the holy place” (Ps. 133:2). “My soul is to you as land without water.” He accuses himself because his soul was at one time before God barren and unfruitful, like dry land, barren and unfruitful. Therefore he entreats to be heard quickly, because it displeases him that he was once such a person. “For, as it is written, the righteous man is at the beginning his own accuser” (Prov. 18:17).

“O Lord, my spirit has failed.” My soul was once such [Col. 1210C], but when your Spirit came, by whom all things are made fruitful, my spirit, which dried it up, failed. This is that spirit of which it is said: “Blessed are the poor in spirit” (Matt. 5:3). “Do not turn your face away from me.” Why? “And I shall be like those who go down into the pit.” For if God did not hear his faithful ones, they too would descend into hell together with sinners.

“Make me hear your mercy in the morning, because I have hoped in you, O Lord.” A person comes out of night and into morning as often as he abandons sin and begins to do penance. “I am not in the night,” he says; “I am in the day. ‘The night has passed, but the day has drawn near’” (Rom. 13:12). Make me hear and know your mercy—namely, that mercy [Col. 1210D] which only those have who believe and hope in you.

“Make known to me the way in which I should walk, because to you, O Lord, I have lifted up my soul.” That way is known to us along which we walk frequently. Therefore let us not depart from God’s commandments, and the way by which we ought to walk will be known to us. The one who lifts up his soul to the Lord is one who separates it from vices and, rejoicing, offers it to the Lord by the steps of virtues.

“Rescue me from my enemies, O Lord; I have fled to you.” For you are a tower of strength against the face of the enemy. “Teach me to do your will, because you are my God [Col. 1211A],” whose will and service alone I ought to perform.

“Your good Spirit will lead me into the right way,” because my evil spirit, which led me into a perverse way, has failed. The right way is that which leads to the homeland and separates the soul from the hindrances of the world. “For your name’s sake, O Lord,” which I do not cease continually to invoke, “you will make me live in your righteousness.” “For everyone who calls upon the name of the Lord shall be saved” (Rom. 10:13). A person is made alive in righteousness when, fleeing iniquity, he begins to live justly and equitably.

“And you will bring my soul out of tribulation.” That soul is in tribulation which, although unwilling, is compelled to serve the pleasures of the flesh.

> [Note: “[Col. 1211D] Nevertheless, divine help does not fail it, so that it may restrain them, if it asks humbly.”]

“And in [Col. 1211B] your mercy you will destroy my enemies,” by whom vices and sins are signified, from which the soul is afflicted and troubled. Hence it is added:

“And you will destroy all who trouble my soul.” And this is because “I am your servant,” to whom I must wholly serve and obey.

## PSALM 143. DAVID AGAINST GOLIATH (1 KINGS 17:4)

David’s battle against Goliath signifies the Church’s battle against the devil. Although he may seem most powerful, he is nevertheless daily overthrown, trampled, and slain by the Christian people.

“Blessed be the Lord my God, who teaches my hands for battle and my fingers for war.” In this psalm the prophet and the Christian people give thanks to almighty God [Col. 1211C], who by his help overcame their most proud enemy.

“My mercy and my refuge, my defender and my deliverer, my protector, who subdues peoples beneath me, and in him I have hoped.” For this is the order of the text. He attributes nothing to himself, but refers everything to God: even that he is strong and wise, that he conquered his enemies, and that he could resist their many and great snares. He obtained all this because he hoped not in himself, not in his own powers, but only in God. By the peoples subjected to him we understand tyrants and heretics, vices and malignant spirits.

“O Lord, what is man, that you have made yourself known to him? Or the son of man, that you regard him?” [Col. 1211D] The prophet marvels that God should so honor, love, regard, and deign to reveal himself to a person so frail, proud, disobedient, and wretched. It is a great honor for a human being to possess knowledge of God, since those who do not possess it are to be counted not among human beings but among brute animals.

“Man has been made like vanity; his days pass away like a shadow.” Man was made in the image and likeness of God, but by his pride and disobedience he has become like such vanity that it is not without reason said of him: “When he was in honor, he did not understand; he has been compared with senseless beasts [Col. 1212A] and made like them.” Therefore “his days pass away like a shadow,” which fades as it grows and, when it seems greatest, suddenly vanishes into darkness.

“O Lord, bend your heavens and come down.” “So that man may be delivered from this vanity,” he says, “bend your heavens, O Lord, and come down; for unless you come down, he cannot ascend.” The heavens are the apostles, whom the Lord then bent and descended with them into the pit, that he might rescue those held throughout the world under the devil’s power, when he said to them: “Go into all the world; preach the Gospel to every creature” (Mark 16:15). It is a great bending when the heavens descend to earth and apostolic exaltation descends to preach to impious and sinful people [Col. 1212B]. Concerning these it is added:

“Touch the mountains, and they shall smoke.” For all the saints must be touched and softened by the anointing of the Spirit,

> [Note: “[Col. 1212D] Ghisian manuscript: ‘But especially those who seem stronger and harder.’”]

by whom we ought to understand the greater and more powerful people. He rightly says that they smoke, in order to show that, converted to faith, they burn in the love of God. Where there is smoke, fire too is shown to be present. Concerning this fire the Lord says: “I came to cast fire upon the earth; and what do I desire except that it be kindled?” (Luke 12:49).

“Flash forth your lightnings, and you shall scatter them; send forth your arrows, and you shall trouble them.” What is signified by lightnings except the disclosure of both Testaments, or signs, or miracles? By these the Gentiles, according to their former state, were scattered [Col. 1212C] and wholly changed for the better. Likewise the arrows are understood as the sayings of the holy Scriptures, of which it is elsewhere said: “The sharp arrows of the mighty, with desolating coals” (Ps. 119:4). Those wounded by such arrows are most rightly troubled against themselves. Of those thus troubled the Apostle says: “What fruit, then, did you have at that time in the things of which you are now ashamed?” (Rom. 6:21).

“Send forth your hand from on high; rescue me and deliver me from many waters and from the hand of foreign sons.” “Send forth your hand,” he says—your power and strength—from on high, from yourself, who are highest above all things. “And deliver me from many waters.” By waters many peoples are signified. “And from the hands of foreign sons,” concerning whom it is elsewhere said: “Foreign sons have lied to me” (Ps. 17:46). By them we understand all those who are said to be children not of God but of the devil. Such were those to whom the Lord said: “You are of your father the devil” (John 8:44).

“Whose mouth has spoken vanity, and whose right hand is a right hand of iniquity.” They are plainly proved to be children of foreigners because they speak vanity with their mouth and work iniquity with their hands. Heretics and tyrants are especially understood by them; all their speech is vanity and all their action iniquity.

[Col. 1213A] “O God, I will sing a new song to you.” Where? “Upon a psaltery of ten strings I will sing psalms to you.” A new song is sung and played upon the psaltery when the Old Testament is preached not according to the letter but spiritually. The Jews have the psaltery, but do not sing the new song upon it, because they interpret the Old Testament according to the letter alone.

“You who give salvation to kings, who deliver David your servant from the evil sword.” These kings are the apostles, of whom it is elsewhere said: “From your temple in Jerusalem kings shall offer gifts to you” (Ps. 67:30). This David is understood as our Savior; the evil sword signifies diabolical power. Therefore the prophet, and the Christian people also, pray [Col. 1213B] that he who gives salvation to kings and delivers David his servant and his Son from the evil sword may rescue and deliver him from many waters and from the hand of foreign sons.

“Whose mouth has spoken vanity, and whose right hand is a right hand of iniquity.” This has already been explained above. Yet by these kings we may understand not only the apostles but all Christians as well, who wisely and honorably govern themselves and their members.

“Whose sons are like young plants, established from their youth.” The sons of those who speak vanity and work iniquity, he says, are like young plants, established and strengthened from their youth—which is stronger than the other ages. By this it is signified that they abound in abundant, pleasing, and rhetorical speech [Col. 1213C]. But what should we understand by sons except their disciples and imitators?

“Their daughters are adorned, arrayed like the likeness of a temple.” By these their teachings are signified, decorated with much verbal elegance and variety. They are rightly compared to a likeness, because they do not possess the truth of the thing, although they make a display of possessing it.

“Their storehouses are full, pouring forth from one thing into another.” What is signified by storehouses except their hearts, overflowing with the abundance of many examples? They are said to pour forth from one thing into another because, passing from one book to another [Col. 1213D], they interpret Scriptures everywhere badly and perversely. Finally, they go from one thing into another because their doctrine has no foundation, but is always wandering and unstable.

“Their sheep are fruitful, abounding in their paths; their oxen are fat.” Of these sheep of the heretics the Lord says in the Gospel: “Beware of false prophets, who come to you in sheep’s clothing, but inwardly are ravening wolves” (Matt. 7:15). They are rightly called fruitful because such people beget many children for the devil. These same people are also fat oxen, whose god is their belly, who seek only earthly and transitory things, devoted not to labor but to pleasure and luxury.

[Col. 1214A] “There is no breach of the wall, nor passage, nor crying in their streets.” It would be good for them if they did not defend their wall. It would be good for them if they permitted holy preachers to pass through their streets and heard their voices and cries.

“They called blessed the people to whom these things belong.” Foolish and unlearned people, seeing this people abound in such riches and not understanding the punishments prepared for them, called it blessed. But it is not so. Blessed is that people whose God is the Lord of them, whose Lord is both God and Lord of all creatures. Such a God and Lord do not belong to those who make for themselves a god that is an image of error and falsehood.

## PSALM 144. THE PRAISE OF DAVID

[Col. 1214B]

In this psalm the prophet magnificently and splendidly praises and blesses God with many praises; rightly, therefore, this psalm is called “the praise of David,” because it is full of such great praises.

“I will exalt you, my God the King.” God is exalted by us when we worthily and praiseworthily proclaim his exaltation, glory, and honor. He is our king if sin does not reign in our mortal body; otherwise, that one is your king to whom you have handed yourself over to rule you.

“And I will bless your name for ever, and unto age upon age.” This is the name of which the Lord himself says: “I am the Lord; this is my name; I will not give my glory to another” (Isa. 68:11). [Col. 1214C] Only those bless this name who confess themselves, both in speech and action, to be his servants in every respect. Unless you are his servant, he will not be your lord. Concerning servants it is said: “Bless the Lord, servants of the Lord.”

“Every day I will bless you, and I will praise your name for ever, and unto age upon age.” Let us hear how he praises: “Great is the Lord and exceedingly praiseworthy, and there is no end to his greatness.” Let us also learn this manner of praise and thus bless him every day; thus let us not cease to praise him for ever and unto age upon age. “The Lord is great,” he says, and immediately explains to us how great he is: “and there is no end to his greatness.” Therefore no one knows how great he is, because no one can know the measure of what has no end [Col. 1214D]. Tell me, then, if you can, how exceedingly praiseworthy is one who is so great? “Exceedingly.” What does “exceedingly” mean? According to the abundance of his greatness. It is “exceedingly” for this reason: because no one can do this.

“Generation after generation shall praise your works, and shall declare your power.” The generation of the Jews first did this; now the generation of Christians does it.

“They shall speak of the magnificence of your majesty and your holiness, and shall recount your wonders.” For when we read and preach both Testaments, then we both speak and recount the magnificent works of the Lord which he has performed [Col. 1215A], and his holiness and wonders.

“They shall tell of the power of your terrible deeds and recount your greatness.” When we relate what happened in the flood, in the Red Sea, in the camp of Sennacherib, and many similar things, then without doubt we tell and recount God’s terrible powers and his greatness.

“Memory of the abundance of your sweetness they shall pour forth.” We pour forth the abundance of his sweetness when we proclaim those things that pertain to mercy, such as this: “He did not spare his own Son, but delivered him up for us all. And they shall exult in your righteousness” (Rom. 8:32). We exult, moreover, in his righteousness, who renders to each according to his [Col. 1215B] works, having appointed glory for the good and punishments for the evil.

“Merciful and compassionate is the Lord, patient and greatly merciful; the Lord is gracious to all, and his mercies are over all his works.” After so great a repetition of mercy, no place is left for despair. Only the person who does not believe these things, and who, having heard them, still persists in wickedness, can despair. Of such persons the Apostle says: “By your hardness and unrepentant heart you store up wrath for yourself on the day of wrath and revelation of the righteous judgment of God, who will render to each according to his works” (Rom. 11:5). His mercies, therefore, are over all his works, because there is nothing in his works [Col. 1215C] that can be compared with mercy. Mercy drew him down to earth and compelled him to undergo the death of the cross; mercy filled heaven and restored the fall of the angels.

“Let your works give thanks to you, O Lord, and let your saints bless you.” All the Lord’s works give thanks and praise the Lord, because there is nothing blameworthy in the Lord’s works: every craftsman is either blamed or praised in his works. Therefore no work of the Lord is evil, because there is nothing in it that is not praiseworthy. And although every creature blesses the Lord, it is nevertheless rightly said here, “And your saints shall bless you,” because their blessings are more acceptable to God. “They shall speak of the glory of your kingdom.” Your saints, he says, shall speak of the glory of your kingdom and shall declare [Col. 1215D] your power. For what purpose? “To make known to the children of men your power, and the glory of the magnificence of your kingdom.” Each point answers to its corresponding point. This was the effect of the saints’ preaching: that the whole world should acknowledge God’s power and understand how great is the glory of heavenly blessedness.

“Your kingdom, O Lord, is a kingdom of all ages, and your dominion in every generation and offspring.” This is what is elsewhere said [594]: “His dominion shall be multiplied, and there shall be no end of his kingdom” (Isa. 9:7). And elsewhere: “His power is an everlasting power, which shall not be taken away, and his kingdom one that shall not be destroyed” (Dan. 7:14).

[Col. 1216A] “The Lord is faithful in his words and holy in all his works.” The Lord lies to no one, does injustice to no one; nothing false is found in his words, nothing unjust in his works.

“The Lord lifts up all who fall, and raises up all who have been cast down.” This is understood of martyrs, or of those who, after the ruin of grave sins, turn to God with a pure heart. To the martyrs, indeed, the Lord himself says: “Do not fear those who kill the body but cannot kill the soul” (Matt. 10:8). But to penitents: “At whatever hour the sinner turns, I will remember none of all his iniquities” (Ezek. 33:11).

“The eyes of all hope in you, O Lord, and you give them food at the proper time.” This is [Col. 1216B] what is said in the Gospel: “He makes his sun rise upon the good and the evil, and sends rain upon the just and the unjust” (Matt. 5:45). We may also understand this of that food concerning which we daily say to the Lord: “Give us this day our daily bread” (ibid., 11).

“You open your hand, and fill every living creature with blessing.” According to his judgment and will, we abound in every good thing and endure scarcity of all things. When he grants something, the Lord is said to open his hand; and when he does not grant it, to close his hand.

“The Lord is just in his ways and holy in all his works.” Therefore we ought to imitate him, [Col. 1216C] so that we may walk in his way and do his works, and, with his help, may deserve to come where he is. Hence it is added:

“The Lord is near to all who call upon him in truth.” The way, he says, is not far off if you wish to come to him: he is near; call upon him and he will answer you—provided that you call upon him in truth. But let Truth itself say what it is to call upon him in truth: “If you ask the Father anything in my name,” he says, “he will give it to you” (John 14:13).—“He will fulfil the desire of those who fear him.” And how do you prove this? “He will hear the prayers of the righteous and save them.” For this is their desire, and if they obtain it, it suffices for them.

“The Lord preserves all who love him, and he will destroy all [Col. 1216D] sinners.” This will be fulfilled at the judgment, when the good will be called to glory and the evil drawn to punishment.

“My mouth shall speak the praise of the Lord.” This psalm, entitled “Praise of David,” begins with praises and ends in praises. The Prophet promises to persevere in God’s praises; and he commands that every human being should persevere with him in blessings and praises. This is what he says: “And let all flesh bless his holy name for ever and ever.”

## Psalm 145. Alleluia. Of Haggai and Zechariah.

> [Note: “Haggai means ‘festive,’ while Zechariah means ‘memory of the Lord.’ Such persons, therefore, are worthy to be sent to establish the walls of the heavenly Jerusalem: those who both love festivity, always keep God in memory, and are always held in God’s remembrance. They are festive because they are spiritually free from servile work and persevere in the praises of God.” —Bede.] [Col. 1217D–1218D]

[Col. 1217A]

“Praise the Lord, O my soul; I will praise the Lord in my life; I will sing to my God as long as I am.” The Prophet exhorts himself and his soul to praise the Lord, so that he who commands others to praise God may not himself be idle or found without praise. “Praise the Lord, O my soul,” he says. Do not cease: this life is brief; and I indeed “will praise the Lord in my life; I will sing to my God as long as I am.” Since, therefore, the saints will always exist, they will also praise God always and without end. Let us now learn to praise God in this life, since we shall praise him without end in the other life. Rightly, therefore, throughout this whole book the Prophet everywhere invites us to the praises of God, which we ought to sing both in heaven [Col. 1217B] and on earth.

“Do not put your trust in princes, nor in the sons of men, in whom there is no salvation.” Praise the Lord, he says; hope and trust in him, and do not trust in princes, who can deliver neither you nor themselves from eternal death. What can others do? Hence it is added: “Nor in the sons of men, in whom there is no salvation.” Therefore hope in him who gives salvation to kings and saves all who hope in him.

“His spirit shall go forth, and he shall return to his earth; on that day all their thoughts shall perish.” Now in the plural, now in the singular, the Prophet speaks and makes little account of grammatical rules. His spirit, namely the spirit of some prince, shall go forth, he says, and his flesh shall return [Col. 1217C] to its earth, as it is written: “You are earth, and to earth you shall go” (Gen. 3:19). Or again, his spirit shall return [595] to its earth, to the land of misery and darkness, to the place and land that he prepared for himself by living badly. “And on that day all their thoughts shall perish.” And what were those thoughts? To kill, commit adultery, steal, lie, and the like. These thoughts shall perish, because they will no longer be able to do these things.

“Blessed is he whose helper is the God of Jacob, whose hope is in the Lord his God, who made heaven and earth, the sea, and all things in them.” Miserable, he says, are those who trust in princes; but blessed are those whose helper is the God of Jacob—those who supplant and cast away vices, who worship and serve the true God [Col. 1217D], not those gods made by human beings, but him who made all things.

“He who keeps truth for ever, executes judgment for those suffering injustice, gives food to the hungry.” Other gods cannot do this, because they are all false, and will not judge but will be judged and condemned together with others. But God alone made and gave food, both bodily and spiritual, to the hungry.

“The Lord raises up the cast down”—namely those cast down [Col. 1218A] who seek forgiveness with their whole heart and recognize themselves as cast down. “The Lord loosens those in fetters,” so that they may run in a straight course along the way of God’s commandments. “The Lord enlightens the blind,” so that, freed from their darkness, they may be able to understand the truth. “The Lord directs the righteous,” because it is by his grace that they do not depart from the straight way. “The Lord preserves the stranger,” one coming from the Gentiles or from anywhere to the Church. “He will receive the orphan and the widow,” those whose wicked father and husband, the devil, has died. Let the orphans rejoice who have lost such a father; let those widows rejoice who have abandoned the shameful and unjust marriages of such a husband.

“And he will destroy the way of sinners.” The ways of sinners are destroyed because they are evil; but sinners are not destroyed [Col. 1218B] if they abandon those ways and wish to walk in the way of righteousness.

“The Lord shall reign for ever, your God, O Zion, from age to age.” The Lord your God, O Zion, shall reign for ever and ever; therefore rejoice and exult, and do not cease from his praises for ever and ever. He who has an eternal kingdom should have eternal praises.

## Psalm 146. Alleluia.

What Alleluia means is indicated by the beginning of this psalm.

“Praise the Lord, for a psalm is good.” That praise is called a psalm which is performed on the psaltery and is not performed without the psaltery. Yet we cannot sing on the psaltery unless the hand touches the strings and the tongue gives forth sound. A psalm, therefore, is good because that praise is good in which works harmonize with the voice. “Let praise be pleasing to our God.” Let us, he says, praise the Lord; let us do what is ours to do; but may he make our praise pleasing, and may he regard it as grateful and acceptable.

“The Lord builds Jerusalem and gathers the dispersion of Israel; the Lord receives the meek but humbles sinners.” The order is as follows: the Lord, he says, builds the heavenly Jerusalem out of living stones and gathers into it the dispersion of Israel—that is, the holy Church scattered among all nations. There he receives the meek and humble in heart, but humbles sinners to the earth, so that [Col. 1218D] what is written may be fulfilled: “He puts down the mighty from their throne and exalts the humble” (Luke 1:52).

“He heals those broken in heart, and binds up their wounds.” This is what is elsewhere said: “A contrite and humbled heart God does not despise” (Ps. 50:19). The Lord binds up their wounds because he changes all the saints’ sorrow and contrition of heart into joy. Hence it is elsewhere said: “Those who sow in tears shall reap in exultation” (Ps. 125:5).

[Col. 1219A] “He counts the multitude of the stars and calls them all by name.” These are those stars of which the Apostle says: “Star differs from star in glory” (1 Cor. 13:41). They are counted, and none of them can perish or be diminished from the number appointed by the Lord. For if all the hairs of our head are numbered, who can doubt concerning the number of the saints, whose number and names are known by him who knows all things? Hence it is fittingly added:

“Our Lord is great, and great is his power, and there is no number to his wisdom.” In the things just said above, the Lord is shown by sound reasoning to be great, strong, and most wise.

“Begin unto the Lord with confession; sing to [Col. 1219B] our God on the harp.” Above he said, “Praise the Lord”; now he admonishes them to begin praising with confession of praise and rejoicing. And because above he spoke of the psaltery, he now also commands praise on the harp, so that the psaltery may be joyful with the harp. The harp pertains to the New Testament, as we have already said many times above: to sing on the harp is either to preach the New Testament or to expound the mystery of the Trinity, because three or four strings suffice.

596 “He covers heaven with clouds and prepares rain for the earth.” The heavens are the apostles, covered with the clouds of spiritual doctrine; everywhere they bear that water by which the whole Church is watered, washed, and satisfied. [Col. 1219C] For the earth is the Church, for which this water has been prepared.

“He brings forth hay on the mountains and grass for the service of men.” These mountains are understood as the teachers of the Church, who, through the Lord’s generosity, abound in that hay and grass by which God’s animals are nourished; by these is signified the knowledge of both Testaments.

“He gives their food to the beasts of burden, and to the young ravens that call upon him.” These are the beasts of burden that carry the burdens of the whole Church, by which the apostles and teachers are signified. Recognizing himself to be such a beast of burden, the righteous man says: “I became as a beast of burden before you, and I am always with you” (Ps. 72:23). They are nourished with spiritual foods prepared for them by the Lord. Concerning the young ravens, however, the Apostle says: “You were once darkness, but now light in the Lord” [Col. 1219D] (Eph. 5:10). Hence elsewhere it is said: “Ethiopia shall hasten her hands unto God” (Ps. 67:32). Such are all sinners converted to repentance with their whole heart. When they call upon the Lord, that food is ministered to them which gives life to the world: namely, the living bread that came down from heaven.

“He will not take pleasure in the strength of a horse, nor is there good pleasure in the tents of a man.” This is an evil horse, whose strength does not please God; by it, plainly, tyrants and heretics are represented, upon whom the devil sits and spurs them with bloody spurs, making them rush violently into every crime. But the tents of a man are the conventicles of heretics [Col. 1220A], who, because they trust in their own strength, are called, as it were, from the strength of a man.

“The Lord takes pleasure in those who fear him, and in those who hope in his mercy.” What displeases and pleases God is declared in these words. Those alone please him who fear God and hope in his mercy.

## Psalm 147. Alleluia.

This praiseworthy title always exhorts us to the praises of God.

“Praise the Lord, O Jerusalem; praise your God, O Zion.” The Prophet now invites the whole Church to praise God, the Church being signified by Jerusalem and Zion. Jerusalem is interpreted “vision of peace”; Zion, “watchtower” or “contemplation.” [Col. 1220B] Both names suit the Church, which alone has peace, since “there is no peace for the wicked, says the Lord” (Isa. 57:21), and which, full of eyes before and behind, watches all things useful to itself. And because “his place has been made in peace, and his dwelling in Zion” (Ps. 75:3), Zion and Jerusalem, which here is signified through peace, are rightly commanded to praise the Lord.

“For he has strengthened the bars of your gates; he has blessed your children within you.” The gates of Jerusalem are the apostles and teachers, bishops and priests, who fortify and close it and open the entrance for entering. No one enters except through them; their bars are so strong that they can be opened or closed by no one except themselves. Hence the Lord says to them: [Col. 1220C] “Whatever you bind upon earth shall be bound in heaven, and whatever you loose upon earth shall be loosed in heaven” (Matt. 18:18). The Lord has blessed her children within her; that blessing, namely, belongs only to those who remain in her, while those who separate themselves from her lose it. Therefore the children of the Church are blessed, but they are blessed within her; outside her they are not blessed.

“He has made your boundaries peace.” Where peace is not, there neither is the Church, because the whole Church is enclosed within the boundaries of peace and does not extend beyond them.

“And he satisfies you with the fat of wheat.” Of this wheat the Lord says: “Unless a grain of wheat, falling into the earth, dies, it remains alone; but if [Col. 1220D] it dies, it bears much fruit” (John 12:24). The Church, therefore, is refreshed with the fat of wheat, being satisfied with Christ’s blood.

“He sends his word to the earth,” by which we understand evangelical preaching, concerning which the Lord himself says: “Go into the whole world; preach the Gospel to every creature” (Mark 20:16). And of this it is added: “His word runs swiftly.” For swiftly, and within a few years, as it is written, “Their sound went out into all the earth, and their words to the ends of the world” (Ps. 18:18, 5).

“He gives snow like wool and scatters mist like ashes.” [Col. 1221A] This is as though he had said: He gives snow and wool; he scatters mist and ashes. The Lord gives snow to his faithful when they are baptized; he gives wool with which they may be clothed; he often scatters from their hearts the mist and ashes by which they are blinded. Of this snow it is elsewhere said: “You shall sprinkle me with hyssop and I shall be cleansed; you shall wash me and I shall be made whiter than snow” (Ps. 50:8). The Lord therefore gives snow, that is, snow’s whiteness and beauty. He gives wool from which we may make garments for ourselves, so that we may walk clothed and not naked. This garment is incorporeal, yet body and soul are clothed and adorned by it. If you have humility, it is a garment for you; if you have patience, it is a garment for you; and whoever has charity is well clothed. Such garments [597] are made from this wool, [Col. 1221B] which we cannot possess unless we receive it from the Lord: “For what do you have,” says the Apostle, “that you have not received?” (1 Cor. 4:7). At that time, indeed, the Lord scattered mist and ashes, when the people sitting in darkness saw a great light. Now, thanks be to God, we have been delivered from the darkness of error, and every obscurity of mist and ashes has been driven away from us.

“He sends his crystal like pieces of bread; who can stand before his cold?”

> [Note: [Col. 1221D] The Vulgate has: “He sends his crystal like a morsel; who can endure before his cold?” Yet this reading accords with the text of St Augustine, from whose explanation St Bruno did not depart and instead expounds another reading. “Snow,” Augustine says, “having endured for a period of many years and through a succession of ages, is called crystal.” He applied the properties of light and transparency to the spiritual understanding of the Old Testament, by which one is led from obscurity to the clearest meaning. A person content with the appearance of things can maintain this interpretation. But physicists nowadays by no means admit that this transformation of snow endures for several ages.] [Col. 1221D–1222D]

The Old Testament, formerly most obscure, but now spiritually understood, is quite rightly called crystal, because for those who understand spiritually it has become most clear and transparent. For, as it is written: “The Lion of the tribe of Judah, the root of David, has conquered, to open [Col. 1221C] the book and loose its seven seals” (Rev. 5:5). And what, because of its hardness, could formerly neither be eaten nor understood is now, like bread divided into pieces, easily received and understood. Of this bread Jeremiah says: “The little children asked for bread, and there was none to break it for them” (Lam. 4:4). “Who can stand before his cold?” This is as though he said: Unless the Lord had done this, no one could have stood before his cold. Hence it is added:

“He sends his word and melts them; his spirit shall blow and the waters shall flow.” The Law was cold, hard, and without mercy, because, understood according to the letter, the fire of charity did not shine in it; it commanded death. “If anyone does this or that,” it said, “let him die the death.” Therefore the Lord sent his Word, his Son, our Saviour, who, by expounding it spiritually, melted it and made it bearable and intelligible. The Holy Spirit breathed upon it—the spirit of wisdom and understanding—and spiritual waters that had been confined flowed forth. The Lord did this by his gratuitous mercy, declaring and expounding his word and his law to Jacob—not the carnal but the spiritual Jacob—“his righteousness and judgments to Israel” [Col. 1222A], not carnal but spiritual Israel. Hence the Apostle says: “Blindness has happened in part to Israel” (Rom. 11:15). This and what follows make it clear.

“He has not done thus to every nation, and he has not revealed his judgments to them.” He revealed God’s words and judgments only to those who deserved to understand them spiritually.

## Psalm 148. Alleluia, Alleluia.

This title, repeated so often, brings us joy and gladness.

“Praise the Lord from the heavens; praise him in the heights.” It does not suffice the Prophet to invite human beings alone to God’s praises: he invites the angels and all things contained in heaven. He also invites the earth and whatever [Col. 1222B] it contains. Nor does he leave aside what is beneath the earth, but commands even the depths themselves to praise the Lord. Every creature praises God, because none fails to serve him and observe his commands. Praise the Lord, he says, you who are in heaven and derive your origin from heaven; and because you dwell in the heights, praise God more highly than the rest. You have clearer and loftier voices, because you are clearer and more exalted than all others.

“Praise him, all his angels; praise him, all his powers.” Under the names angels and powers are included all orders of blessed spirits. Consider now how great and what kind of praises are there, where the voices of so many and such singers resound.

[Col. 1222C] “Praise him, sun and moon; praise him, all stars and light.” Since this world was made, none of these has ever ceased from praise, because they have never abandoned the order of their service. Who can see the sun, moon, and stars without praising and blessing the Creator of such great lights? In nothing more than these are God’s power and wisdom admired and praised. Therefore, not without reason, after the angels they hold the second place in God’s praises.

“Praise him, heavens of heavens, and let the waters above the heavens praise the name of the Lord.” The heavens of heavens are those higher than all others, where God’s divinity and majesty are revealed more clearly and manifestly. For the Apostle also recalls that he was caught up as far as the third heaven. Moses shows that waters are [Col. 1222D] above the heavens, when he says: “God divided the waters that were above the firmament from those that were beneath the firmament” (Gen. 1:7).

“For he spoke, and they were made; he 598 commanded, and they were created.” If he spoke, he spoke by the Word; and let us understand that all things were made through the Word. This is why he used the word “spoke.” Note also the swiftness and ease with which all things were made: there was no delay between making [Col. 1223A] and speaking; rather, as soon as he spoke, all things were made.

“He established them for ever and ever; he set a command and it shall not pass away.” It has been established that all the things previously mentioned should exist for ever; this command has been set and cannot pass away.

“Praise the Lord from the earth, dragons and all depths.” As those are above, so these are below; the remaining things that follow stand in the middle. By dragons and depths we understand those contained in hell. The Prophet, therefore, invites even them to God’s praises, that they may obey him and not dare to resist. No creature will be able to excuse itself on the ground that it was not invited to God’s praises.

[Col. 1223B] “Fire, hail, snow, ice, stormy winds, which perform his word.” These are praised because they perform his word: they come only at his command and will, and as soon as it pleases him they do not delay to obey, while miserable human beings are found almost everywhere disobedient.

“Mountains and all hills, fruitful trees and all cedars, beasts and all cattle, creeping things and winged birds.” All these praise God because they have been created so wisely that their formation and beauty please everyone. The praiseworthy arrangement of each work is praise of its craftsman.

“Kings of the earth and all peoples, princes and all judges of the earth, young men and virgins, old men with [Col. 1223C] the younger: let them praise the name of the Lord.” Let every rational creature hear that dragons, serpents, beasts, and all cattle praise the Lord’s name, and let it blush and be ashamed if, though invited so often, it does not praise the Lord. Other creatures indeed praise God through human beings; but human beings ought to praise him by themselves. Even wicked and unrighteous persons, though unwilling, praise the Lord whenever they praise and admire the Lord’s works. But such praise does not suffice for them. Those praise well who believe in him, serve and obey him, and do his will.

“For his name alone is exalted; his praise is above heaven and earth, and he has exalted the horn of his people.” Let him be praised in heaven, he says, [Col. 1223D] because his name alone is exalted above all heavens. Let him also be praised on earth, because his name is exalted and named above all lands. This comes from his people, because he has exalted and raised up the horn—that is, the power and strength—of his people.

“A hymn for all his saints, for the children of Israel, a people drawing near to him.” This hymn, he says, is given for all his saints to sing and rejoice in, that is, for the children of Israel: the people who draw near to him by likeness, imitation, and good will.

## Psalm 149. Alleluia.

Whoever reads this title, let him praise the Lord, [Col. 1224A] because what is called *Alleluia* in Hebrew is called “Praise the Lord” in Latin.

“Sing to the Lord a new song; his praise in the assembly of the saints.” The old things, he says, have passed away; all things have become new. Let the Jews, grown old in evil days, sing an old song; but you, renewed by the waters of baptism, sing to the Lord a new song: namely, the song of Christ’s birth, passion, and ascension. Let this praise be in the Church of the saints, among the Christian people, not in the synagogue of the Jews.

“Let Israel rejoice in him who made him, and let the children of Zion exult in their king.” Let that Israel, he says, which sings the new song rejoice in him who made it, and believe itself to have been made by him who was crucified [Col. 1224B] for it. And let the children of Zion, children of that Jerusalem which is above and is our mother, exult in their king, who, having overcome the devil, reigned from the wood.

“Let them praise his name in the choir; let them sing to him with timbrel and psaltery.” What it is to praise the Lord in choir, timbrel, and psaltery has been said above and will be stated more fully in the following psalm.

“For the Lord takes pleasure in his people, and he will exalt the meek unto salvation.” This is a most worthy reason why they should praise him: they are those who greatly please him and whom he will exalt to eternal salvation and glory. Hence it is added:

“The saints shall exult in glory; they shall rejoice in their beds” [Col. 1224C]—namely, in those resting places in which, having been exalted, they will find glory and salvation.

“The exaltations of God shall be in their throats, and two-edged swords in their hands.” This will be at the judgment, when in great joy and exultation they will judge the world and wound the hearts of the ungodly with the swords of eternal condemnation, saying to them: “Go, you accursed, into the eternal fire which 599 has been prepared for the devil and his angels” (Matt. 25). And this is what he says:

“To execute vengeance upon the nations and rebukes among the peoples.” Such will be those swords by which universal vengeance and rebuke shall be inflicted upon peoples and nations. Hence they are called two-edged, because no ingenuity will be able to escape them.

[Col. 1224D] “To bind their kings with fetters and their nobles with iron chains.” Those swords, he says, will wound, strike down, condemn, and rebuke; and they will bind even kings and princes with hard iron chains.

“To execute upon them the written judgment.” Two-edged swords, he says, prepared in their hands for such diverse purposes, “to execute upon them the written judgment”: a fixed and unchangeable judgment, such as is found written in the divine books. “This glory is for all his saints.” This glory, he says, will be shared by all; not only the apostles, but all the saints will judge in that judgment.

## Psalm 150. Alleluia.

[Col. 1225A]

May the praises of the Lord never have an end, because at the beginning and the end of this psalm, which is the last of all, the Prophet commands us to praise the Lord. For when he says at its very end, “Let every spirit praise the Lord,” he plainly shows that he does not wish the praises to end, but that perseverance in the Lord’s praises should be unceasing.

“Praise the Lord in his saints; praise him in the firmament of his power.” The Prophet had invited heaven and earth, and all creatures in them, to God’s praises; now he supplies them with the subject matter by which they should praise him. Let each take what pleases him and what appears fitting and useful to him. “Praise the Lord,” he says, “in his saints.” [Col. 1225B] Take up this subject of praise, because in no other thing is he shown to be more worthy of praise. Say, therefore: “God is wonderful in his saints, the God of Israel; he himself will give power and strength to his people. Blessed be God” (Ps. 67:36). For if anyone wishes to consider the faith, wisdom, constancy, patience, and other virtues of the saints, which they deserved to receive from God, he will readily be able to recognize that God is both praiseworthy and wonderful in his saints. Hence elsewhere this speaker, speaking in his own person and that of others, says: “Your knowledge has been made wonderful from me; it has prevailed, and I shall not be able to attain to it” (Ps. 138:6).

“Praise him in the firmament of his power.” Remember to praise the Lord because of the firmament:

> The earth is strong in faith—what the Creator of the world gives you.

For this firmament, called heaven, which the Lord made by his ineffable power and might, signifies the apostles and other saints, who are endowed with such strength and brightness that no creature under heaven can be compared with them.

“Praise him in his powers.”  

> The strength by which you fight is not your own, O man; Christ bestowed it on you on the cross, when by dying he conquered.

Be certain, therefore, that you fight by his powers.

> [Note: [Col. 1225D] Codex Ghisleri: *viribus*, “strengths.”]

Whether we understand the powers of heaven, the powers of miracles which the Lord worked through his saints, or wisdom, righteousness, courage, temperance, and the other virtues with which we read that the saints were adorned—and by which they overcame vices, evil spirits, and all their adversaries—it is most fitting that in all these things God should be praised and glorified.

“Praise him according to the multitude of his greatness.” Always praise him, because he is contained by no limit. Perhaps you do not know how greatly we ought to praise him: consider how great he is, and multiply praises according to his magnitude. Therefore never rest from praise, because he whom you praise is boundless. “Therefore let my mouth speak the praises of the Lord, and let all flesh bless his holy name” (Ps. 144:21), not merely for a time, but “for ever and ever.”

“Praise him with the sound of the trumpet.” [Col. 1226A] May the loud voice of our trumpets never be silent; and the trumpet is a loud voice, a holy sound, a sacred praise. After the material for praise, he consequently set forth the instruments by which we ought to praise God. Trumpet, psaltery, harp, timbrels, choir, strings, organs, and cymbals are instruments of musical art suitable for divine praises. It is not for everyone to sound the trumpet: this is the office of bishops and teachers. For to them it is said: “Blow the trumpet at the beginning of the month” (Ps. 80:4); and, “Cry out, do not cease; raise your voice like a trumpet” (Isa. 58:1). These are the seven angels sounding trumpets in the Apocalypse. At the sound of trumpets the walls of Jericho fell, opening on every side an entrance for God’s people. With trumpets the Israelites were called to battle; with trumpets the year of jubilee was announced; and the people were prepared for the solemnity of [Col. 1226B] the whole year. All this was performed through the ministry of priests, 600 because it signified the voices of bishops and priests, to whom it is said through the Prophet: “If you do not announce his iniquity to the wicked man, I will require his soul from your hand” (Ezek. 3:19).

“Praise him with the psaltery.” The psaltery is borne by the person whom new life reforms, so that he may be able to attend to the ten words of the Law. Let every well-twisted string give forth a melodious sound. To sing upon the psaltery belongs to the perfect. God himself established this instrument and stretched upon it ten strings with his own finger, by which are signified the ten words of the Law. The first string, then, is called “one God”: “You shall have no other god besides me” (Exod. 20:3). The second: “You shall not make for yourself an image” (ibid., 4). The third: “You shall not take the name of your God in vain” (ibid., 7). The fourth: “Keep the Sabbath day” (ibid., 8). The fifth: “Honor father and mother” (ibid., 12). The five which follow are these: “You shall not kill; you shall not commit adultery; you shall not steal; you shall not bear false witness; you shall not covet your neighbor’s possession” (ibid., 13–18). Among these commandments of God there is such harmony that whoever offends in one necessarily offends in all. Hence the apostle James says: “Whoever keeps the whole Law, yet offends in one point, has become guilty of all” (James 2:10).

David had at one time sinned against two strings, by committing both adultery and murder; but after it was said to him, “Your sin is forgiven,” he immediately, rejoicing and approaching the psaltery, said: “Arise, my glory; arise, psaltery and lyre” (Ps. 56:9). Truly great glory belongs there to one who can keep these ten words and touch and play these strings without offense. Hence the Apostle says: “This is our glory: the testimony of our conscience” (2 Cor. 1:12). For he does not sin against the psaltery whom conscience does not accuse.

“Praise him with psaltery and lyre.” He sings on the lyre who calms hearts swollen with pride. For the lyre freed Saul’s mind from frenzy. The psaltery has ten strings, as we have just said; but on the lyre three strings suffice, through which the mystery of the Trinity is signified. Hence the four living creatures, and the Seraphim themselves, singing day and night, say: “Holy, Holy, Holy, Lord God of Sabaoth; the whole earth is full of his majesty” (Isa. 6:1). Yet many sing on the lyre who cannot bear the psaltery. The psaltery belongs to action, but the lyre to speech. Whoever preaches well and lives badly has indeed a lyre, but has no psaltery. The psaltery is pleasing with the lyre when speech agrees with action and action with speech; otherwise the lyre-player benefits himself little, although through his singing he benefits many others.

“Praise him with the timbrel.” Timbrels plainly teach us that the members of mortal flesh are mortified, because they are made of animal hide. This instrument belongs properly to martyrs, though it also appears to belong to those who crucify their flesh with its vices and desires. For the timbrel gives sound under blows, and unless it is struck and beaten, it does not sound. It is dry, stretched hide, which resounds farther through frequent striking. But if it delights you to hear the voice of the timbrel sounding well and giving praise, hear the Apostle saying: “Five times I received from the Jews forty lashes less one; three times I was beaten with rods; once I was stoned” (2 Cor. 11:24). Blessed Stephen’s timbrel, when it was beaten and he was stoned by the Jews, gave forth so great a sound that it opened the heavens and was heard more loftily before God’s throne. Thus he said: “I see the heavens opened and Jesus standing at the right hand of God” (Acts 7). Such men, therefore, praised God with timbrels: those who first afflicted and dried out their flesh by fasts, and then gave it over to be scourged by the lashes and torments of tyrants.

“Praise him with timbrel and choir.” There will be no choir wherever the clergy lack a rule. For they sit in order; therefore they ought to live in order. Thus those praised God in choir of whom it is said: “The multitude of believers had one heart and one soul” (Acts 4:32). Those clerics and monks who love one another, honor one another, mutually obey and serve one another, rise for one another, bear one another’s burdens, and live under rule and discipline—these, I say, praise God in choir. For God attends not so much to the harmony of voices as to the concord of souls and minds.

“Praise him with strings.” The saints are stretched by hands whenever tyrants torture them; God is praised with strings, for a string is called the torture of the flesh, the harsh tribulation of the flesh. By these strings, therefore, we understand no instruments other than the very bodies of the holy martyrs, which were often stretched upon the rack, the scaffold, and the cross, like strings upon a psaltery. Those, therefore, who suffered such things undoubtedly praised God with strings.

“Praise him with strings and organ.” May our organs praise God without end of days. The voices of teachers are called organs: sounds which they send forth from wooden instruments, conceived in the depths of bellows. Organs and timbrels have one meaning, for both signify the mortification of the flesh, whether through abstinence or through the suffering of martyrdom. Those preachings of bishops are made upon the organ which proceed from a body cut down and mortified through abstinence. Hence the Apostle says: “I chastise my body, lest perhaps, after preaching to others, I myself should become reprobate” (1 Cor. 9:27). That preaching, therefore, is reprobate which proceeds not from a chastised and mortified body, but from flesh made fat and delicate. For organs are made from the skins of dead animals and dry hides. Thus they rightly signify those afflicted by many abstinences.

“Praise him with well-sounding cymbals; praise him with cymbals of jubilation.” God’s well-sounding cymbals, indeed, are the two clerical orders: this one new, that one old; this one Paul, and this one Peter, who sings well. Long ago he sang, when he called us and Judas. For he sings with well-sounding cymbals who confirms his words and teaching by the authority of both Testaments. The two Testaments are two cymbals, which then sound sweetly when one is struck and they answer one another in turn. Hence “deep calls to deep”; hence we are commanded not to lord it over one another among the two clerical orders; hence the two Cherubim look toward one another; and the disciples are sent by the Lord two by two.

“Let every spirit praise the Lord.” Let every spirit bless him now and forever. Let it praise, love, and worship him whom mother Rachel worships—now indeed the second, formerly barren and without offspring. May the Father, the Spirit, and the Son hear this. Amen.

[Col. 1229]

## The Explanation of the Valiant Woman by St Bruno of Asti, Bishop of Segni

[Col. 1229A]

No one doubts that Solomon possessed preeminence above all others in both human and divine wisdom. It was therefore most fitting that so great a man should manage the greater affairs of his Lord. He considers and examines when, or in what place, he may find a valiant woman worthy to be joined to her Lord. For he says (Prov. 21):

“Who shall find a valiant woman?” What woman will be found so wise, so noble, so elegant, so beautiful, so rich, so adorned, that so great a king, and the son of so great a king, may join her to himself in marriage? “Far off.” It is not found, he says, in this time; it is not found in our kingdom. It is far off, distant; it is not merely in Judaea. For it is from the rising and setting of the sun, from the north and the sea. “And her price is from the uttermost borders” [Col. 1229B]—not content, he says, with one province, but rather from all parts of the world they will bring gold, silver, precious stones, and everything else belonging to her price and adornment. For she will be “clothed in gold and surrounded with varieties.” Therefore her price will be from the uttermost borders, because after the end of this age she will receive her price: a crown and an inheritance.

“The heart of her husband trusts in her.” She will not be wanton, he says, nor lascivious, nor adulterous; rather, chaste, sober, and most faithful to her husband. Therefore her husband trusts in her. He will not be jealous; he will not fear her folly or her unfaithfulness. Let adulterers flee; let the Jews desist; let heretics not tempt her: for her marriage chamber cannot be corrupted. “And he shall have no need of spoils.” For the Church has no need of spoils, because she always prevails over the multitude of the wicked. She continually overthrows vices, continually drives away evil spirits, and takes their spoils—that is, souls cleansed in the font of baptism. For who but a victor is said to be laden with spoils?

“She will render him good and not evil all the days of her life.” This bridegroom, he says, will not be harsh or hard, but sweet and gentle; he will render not good at one time and evil at another, but good, and never evil: “For his gifts and calling are without repentance” (Rom. 11:29). He has never repented of giving what he gave, doing what he did, or calling those whom he called. For scarcely does anyone acquire even something small without labor and distress. But after the Church has attained the days of life, she will always receive good and never evil. Conversely, the wicked will always find evil and never good.

“[Col. 1230A] She sought wool and flax, and worked with the counsel of her hands.” By wool and flax, in which the whole of women’s craft is contained, we understand the whole work of the Church. The Church has wool and flax with which she clothes both souls and bodies. She gathers flax around the distaff; she gathers hope around faith. Thread is not drawn out without a distaff, nor is hope extended without faith: “For faith is the substance of things hoped for” (Heb. 11:1). She did not seize it but sought it; she received it and worked with it. This she did with the counsel of her hands. For the counsel of hands is excellent, because the hands themselves perform what they deliberate; but the tongue knows how to speak and does not know how to do what it says.

“She became like a merchant’s ship.” A ship, certainly, because she is placed amid the waves of this world and is shaken by the hostility of many waves. A merchant’s ship, because our Savior is ever urgent: he stands at the door and knocks. For there are many merchants in the Church, many buyers and sellers. Give faith; receive life. Thus purchase is made in the Church. “From afar she brings her bread.” From afar—from heaven, from Moses and Elijah, Jeremiah, and the other prophets. Finally, from all parts of the world the apostolic company brought her bread and spiritual nourishment. But heretics do not bring it from afar; they do not receive it from the Fathers, but conceive error in themselves.

“She rose while it was still night, and gave prey to her household and provisions to her maidservants.” She rose at night so that, with lamps lit, she might meet the approaching bridegroom. Prey is given to the household, because ecclesiastical offices are taken away from heretics, simoniacs, and adulterers—from clergy and people—and bestowed upon men who are not unknown or newly converted, but known and tested. Through these men provisions are given to the maidservants, because through them the souls of subjects are refreshed with spiritual food.

“She considered a field and bought it.” What do we understand by the field except the heavenly homeland? The Church understood its fruitfulness, multiplication, and beauty; she sold everything she had, gave it to the poor, and bought this field.

“From the fruit of her hands she planted a vineyard.” From the fruit of his hands, indeed, he plants himself a vineyard in this world who, with the Lord’s help, performs those works by which he may taste the sweetness of eternal blessedness. Hence the Psalmist says: “They shall be made drunk from the abundance of your house” (Ps. 35:9).

“[Col. 1231A] She girded her loins with strength.” The loins are girded with strength when, through the vigor of chastity, the assault of lust is restrained. Hence the Lord says in the Gospel: “Let your loins be girded” (Luke 12:35). “And she strengthened her arm.” What is it to strengthen the arm except to perform good work without ceasing? She strengthened her arm lest she should be overcome and grow weary in carrying shield and weapon.

“She tasted and saw that her trade was good.” She tasted, that is, tested, knew, saw, and understood how good and useful was her upright trade, labor, and exercise. It is truly good, because it will lead her to the supreme good, the good without end.

“Her lamp shall not be extinguished in the night.” For she will not be among those who, in the darkness and night of their distress, will say: “Give us some of your oil, because our lamps are going out” (Matt. 25:8). Her lamp will not be extinguished, because by the radiance of virtues and works she will shine upon all.

“She put her hand to strong things.” What do we understand by the hand except teachers? For just as the hand is the more important part of the body, so teachers are in the ecclesiastical body. These are sent to strong things; these undertake greater affairs.

“And her fingers grasped the distaff.” By the fingers we understand whatever faithful people are of lesser merit and office. They grasp the distaff who administer lighter affairs and are fortified by faith and hope alone. For any little woman can spin; but to believe and hope is no great labor. Fingers do not spin without hands; subjects do not believe without teachers. Hence the Apostle says: “How,” he says, “shall they hear without a preacher?” (Rom. 10:14).

“She opened her hand to the needy.” Explanation: “And she stretched out her palms to the poor.” She did not clench them, he says, nor close them; if she opened her hand and stretched out her palms, she distributed alms to the poor.

“She shall not fear for her household from the cold of snow.” It is an excellent house, and its inhabitants are well clothed; they fear neither cold, ice, snow, nor winter or spring frost. Why is this?
