It follows: “For all her household are clothed with double garments.” The servants and household members of the Church are clothed doubly, because they pursue purity both of soul and body. Conversely, the wicked, clothed in the double garment of their shame, will be crushed by a double affliction.

“She made herself a patterned garment.” A patterned garment is a kind of clothing made with much variety. Thus the Church’s garment is patterned because it is painted with manifold variety. There humility, peace, patience, piety, gentleness, and the other virtues shine forth.

“Fine linen and purple are her clothing.” It is most fitting that so great a queen should be clothed in fair and beautiful garments. Yet, according to the character of their colors, these suit different orders of saints: red for martyrs and white for confessors. “Her husband is noble in the gates.” For although Christ our Lord appeared humble and in the form of a servant at his first coming, at the second he will appear noble in the gates with the senators of the earth. He is noble because he shines in his own and his Father’s glory. He is in the gates because he himself, who is the door, will cast sinners into hell and introduce the righteous into the heavenly house. He will sit with the senators because, as he himself says, when he comes upon the seat of his majesty, the twelve disciples will sit upon twelve seats, to judge the twelve tribes of Israel.

“She made fine linen and sold it.” The Church, he says, made fine linen: a white garment, a pure garment, a wedding garment. She sold it; she gave it to no one without a price; she bestowed it on holy children in baptism. Do you want this garment? Pledge faith; renounce Satan and all his works. This is the garment. “And she gave a girdle to the Canaanite.” What do we understand by the Canaanite except the Gentiles? They were loose, ungirded, and dissolute; they lived without the Law. She girded them and prepared them for this work.

“Strength and beauty are her clothing.” Christ too is said to have this garment. Hence the Prophet says: “The Lord has reigned; he has put on beauty; the Lord has put on strength” (Ps. 91:4). “And John says: ‘We know that we shall be like him’” (John 3:2). Therefore we shall be clothed with strength and beauty, because the flesh which we shall receive can no longer be corrupted. And with beauty, because the saints will shine like the sun in the kingdom of God.

“And she shall laugh on the last day.” Now is the time for weeping; then will be the time for laughing. Laughter belongs to one who rejoices, since to laugh is to rejoice. Therefore the saints will laugh on the last day; indeed, they will rejoice. Hence also: “The righteous shall rejoice when he sees the vengeance of the wicked” (Ps. 57:11).

“She opened her mouth in wisdom.” There was darkness over the face of the abyss; wisdom was covered, obscure, and shut up. But the Church opened it, taught it, and preached it. “And the law of clemency is on her tongue.” For the Mosaic Law was hard and heavy, harsh because it was formed upon stones; for if anyone did this or that against it, it commanded that he be killed. But the Church’s law is one of gentleness, clemency, and mercy: it does not kill, but has mercy and grants pardon to all who turn back.

“She considered the paths of her household.” She considered and wisely examined the paths by which the servants, sons, and maidservants of her household ought to walk. She commanded some to ascend to the kingdom of heaven by kindness, others by patience, others by chastity. She allowed none of her holy household to stand in the way of sinners, because she knew this way to be evil and useless. “And she does not eat the bread of idleness.” Hence the Psalmist says: “You shall eat the labors of your hands” (Ps. 127:10). And the Apostle: “Let each one labor, working with his hands that which is good” (Eph. 4:28).

“Her sons rose up.” They did not lie down, he says, nor sleep; rather, they rose, stood, and proclaimed their mother’s blessedness. For which of the prophets or apostles did not proclaim this blessedness? “And her husband will praise her,” as it is written: “All who swear by him shall be praised” (Ps. 62:1). But how will they be praised? Do you wish to hear how? “I was hungry,” he says, “and you gave me food; I was a stranger, and you took me in; naked, and you covered me” (Matt. 25:35). This will be the Church’s praise. Thus her husband will praise her.

“Many daughters gathered riches.” In respect of creation, whether good or evil, all are said to be God’s children. Thus many daughters had riches. The Jews were wise, and philosophers also were wise. “But she has surpassed them all,” because she did not learn worldly wisdom, nor the wisdom that puffs up: “I have understood more than the elders, because I have sought your commandments” (Ps. 118:100).

“Grace is deceitful, and beauty is vain.” Deceitful grace, he says, vain wisdom, and useless riches belong to many. All these are called grace because they are given freely and without price to all. Hence the Apostle says: “For what do you have that you did not receive?” (1 Cor. 4:7). And the Psalmist: “There is none that hides himself from its heat” (Ps. 18:7). Therefore all possess some grace; yet deceitful graces are found in most people. Although “all wisdom is from the Lord God” (Ecclus. 1) and is freely given by the Lord to all, it is deceitful if it does not serve the Lord; if it comes not from virtues but from outward appearances; if it is not eternal but passing. “The woman who fears the Lord, she shall be praised.” That is, the Church, which serves the Lord in fear and trembling: she shall be saved. Therefore she shall be praised by God, by holy works, by people, and by angels.

“Give her of the fruit of her hands.” You, he says, were begotten by mother Church; she planted you, taught you, cultivated and watered you. Give her, therefore, of the fruit of your hands: serve her, obey her, and believe her in all things as your most holy mother. Although all the faithful belong to the Church, yet those are principally designated by this name who govern and teach the rest. These must be served, “because,” the Lord says, “the laborer is worthy of his wage” (1 Tim. 5:18).

“And let her works praise her in the gates.” Her works praise the Church in the gates when, seeing and hearing the good works which she does, we exalt her with praises. For when the deeds of the apostles are recounted, do they not praise the apostles in the hearing and ears of the faithful, which are like gates through which words enter the inner places of the heart?

Thus they praise her:

We have most certainly learned  
That Solomon’s discourse  
Signifies the most valiant woman—  
The Church.

The wisest King,  
And mightiest of kings,  
Coming in human form,  
Chose her as his bride.

Within her are many prophets,  
Apostles and bishops,  
Confessors and martyrs,  
Widows likewise and virgins.

Yet you, Felicity,  
Thus proclaim sons:  
What is common to the others  
Seems to you your own.

You are strong, and strongest,  
A most prudent woman,  
Constant, and most constant,  
Blessed, and most blessed.

Through you be praise to the Unbegotten,  
Glory to the Only-begotten,  
With the Paraclete Spirit,  
The renowned Comforter. Amen.

[Col. 1233]

## The Exposition of St Bruno of Asti, Bishop of Segni, on the Song of Songs Begins: the Book *Shir ha-Shirim*, or the Song of Songs, by the Same Author

[Col. 1233]

### Chapter One

[Col. 1233C]

“Let him kiss me with the kiss of his mouth.” The voice of the aforesaid woman.

[Col. 1234C]

“You, envoys of the heavenly King,” she says, “have often reported many things to me: many things concerning his nobility, riches, strength, beauty, and wisdom. I saw Moses; I saw Elijah; I saw Jeremiah; I saw David; and I saw others who announced his coming to me. I believe their words; I languish with love; I am ready. Let the envoys cease; let him himself now come, make himself manifest, press his kisses upon me, give embraces, and speak to me with his own mouth.”

> [Note: Thus Origen understood the oracle of Isaiah, chapter 35:22: “The Lord is our judge, the Lord is our lawgiver, the Lord is our king; he himself will save us”; and with him St Jerome, Letter 146 to Damasus; St John Chrysostom, Homily 8 on the Creed, which concerns the Turtledove, vol. V; and others.]

An apostrophe. “I love and desire you,” she says; “I long to hear you and see you. Why is this? ‘Because your breasts are better than wine.’ Moses gave me wine, and the other prophets gave me wine: bitter, strong, austere, and harsh to drink. For the prophets’ words are difficult not only to perform but even to speak. Indeed, leaving aside the matter of saying and pronouncing them, they can scarcely be understood in certain places. But Christ’s preaching changed wine into milk. The two breasts are the two Testaments, which Christ, by teaching and explaining them, drew forth into milky and sweet gentleness.”

> [Note: It is established that Philo of Carpasia gave the same interpretation; his words are found in Ghislerius.]

“For those whom the Law saw fit to kill, he mercifully healed. The Jews wished to stone the woman caught in adultery, but Christ said: ‘Neither do I condemn you’ (John 7:10). These words are better than wine. ‘Fragrant with the best ointments.’ What is understood by ointment except the sevenfold grace of the Holy Spirit?”

> [Note: “Certain persons,” says Ghislerius, “consider that by Christ’s ointments his spiritual grace is signified, which is preferred to the ointments which we read that Moses compounded at God’s command and which, as we know, were figures of these. Thus, they say, Christ himself—whom the Father anointed with the Holy Spirit—is preferred to the words of the Law and the prophets, whose use and knowledge the Church, which speaks here, possessed.” He names Origen, Theodoret, Bede, and others as authors of this interpretation.]

“Both the New and Old Testaments are fragrant, gleaming, and sweet-smelling with these. Christ’s preaching brought this fragrance, because it made some wise, others understanding, others strong, others devout. ‘And the scent of your ointments above all spices.’ By spices we understand whatever things are fragrant. But what has so great a scent and such sweetness that it may be the very Spirit of whom the Apostle, filled with it, said: ‘We are the good odor of Christ to God’ (2 Cor. 2:15)?”

The voice of the Church to Christ: “Your name is poured-out ointment.”

> [Note: The Vulgate has “poured-out oil,” but others used “ointment” from the Septuagint version—the Syriac, Vatablus, and others—as Cornelius à Lapide explains. To these we add Matthew Cantacuzenus, translated into Latin by the very learned Vincent Riccard, Regular Cleric, at Rome in 1624. The holy Fathers discussed at length the excellence of the name Jesus, as Ghislerius teaches on the cited passage.]

“Your name,” she says, “like poured-out ointment, bestowed healing upon all believers. For Christ is so called from *chrism*, and all who have been cleansed in the water of baptism are called Christians from this name. Therefore the grace of the Holy Spirit, poured out upon the elect, united them. ‘Therefore the young maidens loved you.’ By the young maidens are understood the primitive and new Churches, which were recently begotten for God and baptized; they were frail in womanly fashion and had borne not many children. But having abandoned their former oldness and received the Holy Spirit, they loved Christ with all their strength and with every affection of motherhood.”

The voice of the Church to Christ:

“Draw me after you.” For Christ draws after himself all who imitate him, so that at his command they may be exalted above the heavens: “No one has ascended into heaven except he who descended from heaven” (John 3:13). He ascended indeed by himself, because he is both perfect God and perfect man. But the rest cannot ascend by themselves; they must be drawn.

> [Note: “For no one is able to run in the way of God’s commandments unless he is drawn by grace itself.” Thus St Gregory, Pope; Bede; Cassiodorus; and others.]

“They are drawn, therefore, as the Lord himself says: ‘When I am lifted up from the earth, I shall draw all things to myself’ (John 12:32). ‘And we shall run after the fragrance of your ointments,’ that is, in the sweetness of virtues, preachings, and graces. Those run after their fragrance who, captivated by their sweetness and delight, perform good works without ceasing. But those who stink with vices do not find all these things fragrant.”

The voice of the bride to the young maidens: “The king has brought me into his storerooms.” A change of person. “Already,” she says, “the King of kings has brought me, by faith and hope, into his storerooms and into eternal tabernacles. We may also understand by the storerooms the individual books of the prophets, into which the Church has been brought and made drunk with spiritual wine.”

> [Note: This interpretation accords with Cassiodorus and Bede, as found in Ghislerius. Others understand the revelation of divine mysteries; thus Cantacuzenus.]

“Hence the Psalmist says: ‘They shall be made drunk from the abundance of your house’ (Ps. 35:9).”

An apostrophe: “We shall exult and rejoice in you.” When ecclesiastical men find God’s praises and mighty deeds in the sacred volumes, they exult and rejoice in so great and such a man. Finally, when they attain that supreme blessedness and receive the highest and eternal goods, they will exult in him alone. “Remembering your breasts above wine.” “In you,” she says, “we shall exult, remembering your breasts above the wine that came before. Milk came after wine; the New Testament came after the Old; the wine was tempered, and the Law became sweet, mild, and intelligible. Therefore the New Testament was completed over the house of Israel and over the house of Judah.”

> [Note: This is the reading of the Riccardian manuscript; but the Vulgate has: “The upright love you.” All commentators conform to this version. Among them St Gregory says: “Uprightness is the foundation of the love of God, just as the love of God is the perfection of uprightness”; Cassiodorus teaches the same. Riccard, however, reads from Cantacuzenus: “Uprightness loved you.”]

“Kings love you.” Whoever rules himself and others is rightly called a king. The apostles, bishops, and priests are kings. Had the apostles not loved Christ, they would not have died for him. Therefore kings and upright persons love him by whom they become kings and upright.

The voice of the synagogue: “I am black, but beautiful, daughters of Jerusalem.” She called herself black because of the lowliness of her origin, but beautiful because of repentance and faith.

> [Note: “I am dark,” explains St Ambrose, Sermon 2 on Psalm 118: “Dark through guilt, beautiful through grace; dark through vice, beautiful through washing. I am dark because I sinned; beautiful because Christ now loves me.” Augustine, Sermon 201 on the Seasons, agrees.]

This is said by the Church of the Gentiles, or by the apostolic assembly. “You,” she says, “daughters of Jerusalem, daughters of Lebanon, are daughters of whiteness. But I was a daughter of Kedar, a daughter of darkness, a daughter of stags. I was the people sitting in darkness. I am she of whom it was said: ‘You were once darkness’ (Eph. 5:8). I grant, therefore, that I am black because I was born in sins: black according to creation and my former life, but whitened beyond snow according to regeneration. ‘I am beautiful’—but where beautiful? In my eyes, ears, and all my members. Eyes are deformed because they desire to see ugly and shameful things; ears are deformed because they delight in hearing idle talk and buffoonery. But, conversely, ‘how beautiful are the feet of those who proclaim peace, who proclaim good things!’ (Rom. 10:15). I am black outwardly, but inwardly most beautiful and lovely. What a person sees appears black; what is hidden from a person is most beautiful. For a person considers the face, but God considers hearts.

“Like the tents of Kedar.” Kedar means “darkness.” The blackness of darkness is driven away by light alone. Thus the Church was black like the tents of Kedar, but was made white when illuminated by the sun of righteousness. Hence the Evangelist says: “The light shines in darkness, and the darkness did not comprehend it” (John 1:5). The tents of Kedar are indeed those in which the princes of darkness dwell. In the flesh, the righteous are no more beautiful than the unrighteous.

“Like the skins of Solomon.” “I am black,” she says, “like the tents of Kedar, but beautiful like the skins of Solomon. Let Solomon, then, not despise me, since my skin accords with his skin.” Thus the Church is lovely and beautiful among women, because the aforesaid Solomon “is beautiful in form above the children of men” (Ps. 44:3).

The voice of the Church: “Do not consider that I am dark.”

> [Note: Riccard translates from Cantacuzenus: “Do not look upon me because I am black; for the sun has not looked upon me.” He adds: “For even if that true light has not yet appeared in me, it will nevertheless appear, and I shall be suffused with splendid glory.”]

This is spoken in the person of the apostles. “I am dark,” she says, “and, as to outward appearance, ugly; not anointed, not fat, not delicate, but rather rough and hard to look upon. Yet let no one despise these things; rather, let him consider more carefully what is within. ‘Because the sun has discolored me.’”

> [Note: The Fathers adopted many interpretations of this passage, as may be seen in Calmet, Cornelius à Lapide, and Ghislerius. Bruno chose to follow Cassiodorus and Bede.]

“I did not rest in shade; I did not give myself to idleness in bed. What then? I labored in the vineyard, cultivated the field, kept watch, fasted, suffered many adversities under the sun, and became discolored and dark. What wonder?”

The voice of the Synagogue: “For the sons of my mother fought against me.” “I had,” she says, “the opportunity for quiet, because I had to procure necessities and fight against enemies. For not only barbarians but also the sons of my mother waged war against me. Thus, outwardly battles; inwardly fears: here the sword of tyrants; there the disputation of Jews and heretics.”

> [Note: According to Origen, these words are understood to be spoken by the primitive Church, recounting the battles she sustained from the Jews, sons of her mother the synagogue. Cantacuzenus holds the same view.]

Understand her mother as Judaea or the synagogue. Hence the Apostle says: “When it pleased him who separated me from my mother’s womb” (Gal. 1:15), etc. We may also understand by this mother iniquity. Hence the Psalmist says: “For I was conceived in iniquities, and in sins my mother conceived me” (Ps. 50:7):

“The sons of my mother fought against me.” That is, the passions of the body assailed me; the enticements of the flesh discolored me; therefore the sun of righteousness did not shine upon me.

> [Note: St Ambrose, *On Isaac and the Soul*, book 4.]

“Watchmen set me in the vineyards.” Who, then, sets watchmen in vineyards except to ward off thieves? God planted one vineyard; because it turned to bitterness, many other vineyards were planted. Hence also that saying: “They sowed fields and planted vineyards” (Ps. 106 [107]:37). In these the apostles were appointed as watchmen, lest all who pass along the road should harvest it. “My own vineyard I did not keep.” “I left,” she says, “the one vineyard, but kept many vineyards” [Col. 1238C] [Note: [Col. 1238D] “This evil befell the synagogue through its disobedience toward the prophets: it did not keep its own vineyard of the divine Law.” Ambrose, Sermon 2 on Psalm 123, v. 1.]. The many vineyards are the many Churches; the synagogue, however, is one. The apostles left it, as it is written: “It was necessary that the word of God should first be spoken to you; but since you have rejected it and judged yourselves unworthy of eternal life, behold, we turn to the Gentiles” (Acts 13:46).

This may also be read as a question: “Did I not keep my vineyard?” I certainly did keep it. But by first using “vineyards” in the plural and then “vineyard” in the singular, he signified the unity of the Church, which, although divided according to the conditions of places, is nevertheless one in faith and love. The apostles and teachers guarded it, lest Arius, Sabellius, and the other thieves should deceitfully steal away any grape, or separate any believer from the Church.

The voice of the Church to Christ [Col. 1238D]: “Tell me, you whom my soul loves, where you pasture, where you lie down at noon” [Note: [Col. 1238D] Cantacuzenus reports that by these words the soul asks the divine Bridegroom where he rests; and that he answers, “at noon,” that is, in the bosom of the Father and of everlasting light; and that the time had not yet come for him to descend and show mercy to humankind.].

“Tell me,” she says, “make me know and know firmly, O shepherd, O ruler, whom I have loved and do love with my whole mind and all my strength [Col. 1239A] [Note: [Col. 1239D] “Rightly,” he says, “does she call the one whose protection she seeks the beloved of her soul; for the graver the danger from which she longs to be delivered, the more she loves him through whom she knows she will be delivered.” Bede.]; tell me where you pasture your flock, in what place and with what food you nourish your sheep.” For God’s sheep are fed in the assembly of preaching and by the sacred books. This is also made known to those bishops who, like mute dogs unable to bark, allow God’s creatures to perish from hunger.

“Where you lie down at noon.” What is meant by noon but the exceedingly burning affliction of the saints [Note: [Col. 1239D] In this exposition too, Bruno appears to have followed Cassiodorus and Bede.]? “Tell me,” she says, “tell me, Shepherd, where you lie down at noon; where are you when the saints are afflicted? Where are you when your lambs are torn apart by wolves? Are you not he who, as the good shepherd, lays down your life for the sheep? The heat is severe; the sheep are thirsty; they are scorched by the burning. Lead them to harbor; lead them into shade.”

“I know,” you will say, “I am in you; in you I lie down and rest. ‘For upon whom does my spirit rest, except upon the humble, the quiet, and the one who trembles at my words?’” (Isa. 66:2). And again: “Do you not know that you are the temple of God and that the Holy Spirit dwells in you?” (1 Cor. 3:16). Why, then, am I troubled? “I know,” you will say, “that through many tribulations we must enter the kingdom of heaven.” The answer is true. Now I fear nothing, since so great a guest guards the city. I do not dread the heat, because the living fountain is with me.

It follows: “Lest I begin to wander among the flocks of your companions.” What are the companions but heretics and philosophers [Note: [Col. 1239D] Thus Augustine in several places, but especially in Sermon 50 on the Words of the Lord.]? But why are they called companions? Because they too are shepherds and feed a flock. Yet through their flocks and conventicles wander those who do not know the way to the true pasture [Col. 1239C] and the divine meadow. Let us therefore ask our Lord to show us also the sheepfold and, in his mercy, set us in a place of pasture.

Likewise, verses:

> Why do you send me so many prophets, O royal Bridegroom?  
> Let the envoys cease, ever ready only to bring words.  
> You I desire; in you I believe; you alone I seek to see.  
> Now have mercy on me; now permit yourself to be seen.  
> Let it now be your care to give kisses to your bride,  
> And let the sweet melodies of your voice resound in our ears.  
> Let them sound now, I pray you, if any love of yours is in me.

The voice of Christ to the Church: “If you do not know yourself, O most beautiful among women, go forth.” “If you do not know yourself,” he says, “most beautiful of women, lovely in appearance; if, forgetful of yourself and unmindful of your nobility, go forth, depart, and wander, as you said, along the tracks of the flocks.” [Col. 1239D] Follow the heretics; imitate the philosophers. For we fail to know ourselves when, forgetful of our dignity, baptism, and renewal, we submit to error and vanity, and follow the tracks of flocks [Col. 1240A] of she-goats and goats.

“And pasture your kids beside the tents of the shepherds” [Note: [Col. 1240D] To preserve brevity, I shall cite one interpreter of this passage among many: St. Augustine, Sermon 50 on the Words of the Lord, and Epistle 48 to Vincentius. He teaches that believers who do not know the excellence of the Catholic Church easily fall into the sects of heretics.]. “If you do not know yourself,” he says, “and depart from me, your lambs will soon become kids.” For just as, in baptism, she-goats are transformed into lambs, so when we sin and depart from God, we turn pure souls and gentlest lambs into wanton, foul-smelling goats. These kids, beside the tents of shepherds and the gatherings of heretics, having rejected the sweet food of Scripture, feed on poisonous grass—that is, they imbibe corrupt doctrines.

The voice of Christ: “I have compared you, my beloved, to my cavalry among Pharaoh’s chariots.” “You ought neither to leave me nor forget yourself. For I have compared you to my cavalry among Pharaoh’s chariots.” The Church is compared to it in this respect: Pharaoh’s chariots and horsemen pursued the people of Israel. But just as Pharaoh, pursuing that foretold people with chariots and horsemen, was drowned in the sea, so too the devil, lying in wait for human souls with his multitude of vices, perishes in baptism. Therefore, having received so great a benefit, let no one forget either himself or God.

The young women to the bride:

“Your cheeks are beautiful like those of a turtledove.” Having heard these words as though they were a rebuke for what she had said above, she drew a blush of shame upon herself. For she had said, “lest I begin to wander.” Wandering belongs to prostitutes. Remembering this word and this rashness, she blushed. But when the Bridegroom saw this [Col. 1240C], he praised her virginal modesty. For he says: “Your cheeks are beautiful”—your face is modest and chaste [Note: [Col. 1240D] Origen observes, Homily 2 on the Song of Songs, that the Septuagint reads: “How beautiful your cheeks have become,” indicating that formerly they were not so, but became so after she received the Bridegroom’s kisses, and after he who spoke through the prophets had first come and cleansed his Church for himself by the washing of water, making her wholly lovely and beautiful. See Ghislerius.].

You blush to say that you have done, or even thought, shameful things. For you are not one of those who draw strength from crime. But how are they beautiful? Like those of a turtledove; like those of a virgin; like one who observes great chastity and marital fidelity. For the Church serves but one husband.

“Your neck is like necklaces.” “As other virgins,” he says, “delight in necklaces, so you delight in the beauty of your neck alone.” What is the neck but teachers? Through the neck food is sent into the stomach, and from it words also issue. The Church is nourished and instructed by teachers. Thus the office of the neck is performed by teachers. Moreover, weakness of the neck is the ruin of the whole body.

The voice of the friends: “We shall make for you little golden necklaces” [Col. 1240D]. Little necklaces are indeed ornaments of a virgin’s neck, so called from the fish *muraena*, the moray eel. They signify the lengthy, distinct, and praiseworthy sayings of the prophets. Moses, Isaiah, Jeremiah, David, and this man who wrote these things, Ecclesiastes, have made little necklaces for us [Col. 1241A]. “Variegated with silver.” They are little necklaces because they are flexible; golden because they shine with the light of wisdom; and said to be variegated with silver because they are distinguished by purity of speech.

Verses:

> Blessed virgin,  
> Made wondrous,  
> Modest bride,  
> Sweet beloved;  
> Wisely,  
> And fittingly,  
> Ordered in beauty,  
> Raised in morals,  
> Dear to my  
> Disciples:  
> Know these pastures  
> And approach them.  
> Much peace be yours;  
> All things are safe.  
> What pleases one  
> Is burdensome to none.

[Col. 1241B] The voice of the bride: “While the king was at his table, my nard gave forth its fragrance.” “While my king, my bridegroom, my beloved was at table”—in the bed of flesh, in the humanity which he assumed from the virginal womb [Note: [Col. 1241D] This is Ambrose’s view, Sermon 3 on Psalm 118, section 1: by the king’s reclining at table is to be understood the incarnation of the Son of God in the most pure Virgin, whom he chose as his mother and bride, pouring forth in himself the fullness of grace like a most precious fragrance.]—“my nard gave forth its fragrance.”

According to the letter, this may be understood of Mary, who poured an alabaster jar of ointment over the head of him reclining at table. At once the whole house was filled with the fragrance of the ointment. Spiritually, however, it is understood of the Church. Before our Savior came in the flesh, nard gave fragrance in a few persons, since the virtues and prayers of few pleased the Lord. But after he came in the flesh and the Lord, like a bridegroom, came forth from his bridal chamber, [Col. 1241C] at once the virtues and prayers of the saints gave fragrance. Hence the Apostle says: “We are a sweet fragrance to God” (2 Cor. 2:15). And the Psalmist: “Let my prayer be directed as incense before you” (Ps. 140 [141]). Thus John saw golden bowls full of incense (Rev. 5:8). After Christ’s incarnation, both the virtue and the number of the saints increased. Therefore nard gave its fragrance to Christ the Lord incarnate.

“My beloved is a bundle of myrrh to me.” He used myrrh because of its bitterness. Christ was for the Church a bundle of myrrh, a gathering indeed of great pain and great bitterness. For how could she be otherwise than in pain and bitterness, bereft of so great and such a husband? It may also be said thus [Col. 1241D]: “My beloved is to me”—for me and for my benefit he became a bundle of myrrh, because for my sake he submitted himself to death and the bitterness of suffering [Note: [Col. 1241D] Although commentators have offered many interpretations of this passage, the common sense of the Latin Fathers, as Ghislerius teaches, is that through these words the Church, the devout soul, or even the Blessed Virgin signifies her desire to hold Christ’s Passion continually in her heart, not only through unceasing meditation but also through imitation.].

Did he not carry [Col. 1242A] a bundle of myrrh and bitterness when he said: “My soul is sorrowful even unto death” (Matt. 26:38)? It was indeed a bundle, because it drew many to itself and slew many with itself. For all the martyrs, on account of his death, are gathered as it were in one bundle.

“He shall abide between my breasts.” The noble Bridegroom abides between the bride’s breasts because he is not separated from her remembrance and embrace. The place of the heart lies between the breasts; and where the heart is, there also is memory. Therefore he who abides between the breasts, since he lies in the heart, cannot escape remembrance. Happy—and exceedingly happy—is the soul between whose breasts Christ abides, in whose heart he lies, and which never forgets him.

“My beloved is a cluster of Cyprus to me.” The wine of the island of Cyprus is excellent [Col. 1242B] [Note: [Col. 1241D] Besides Bruno, there were others, as Ghislerius notes [Col. 1242D], who here took Cyprus not as the island but as the *cyprus* shrub or small tree bearing a sweet-smelling flower. These included St. Gregory, Cassiodorus, Bede, Anselm, Bernard, and others. From this flower is made an ointment or oil called Cyprian or privet oil, which Theophrastus, *On the History of Plants*, book 9, chapter 7, counts among the most fragrant ointments. Pliny also speaks of this plant, book 12, chapter 24: “In Egypt *cyprus* is a tree with leaves of the jujube, coriander-like seed, and a fragrant white flower,” etc. Richard gives the same material in his notes on Cantacuzenus, p. 121.]. Wine gladdens the human heart. Christ is a cluster of Cyprus to his saints, because they are gladdened by drinking his blood. Finally, if wine signifies joy, then he who was a bundle of myrrh in dying is fittingly called a cluster of Cyprus in rising again. Hence the Psalmist says: “Weeping will linger at evening, and joy in the morning” (Ps. 29 [30]:6).

He is therefore a cluster of Cyprus. Where? It follows: “In the vineyards of Engaddi.” Engaddi means “fountain of the kid.” The fountain of the kid is in the Churches. The Churches are the vineyards of Engaddi. For the font of baptism is in the Church: one who enters it is a kid; one who comes forth is a lamb.

Verses of *Shir ha-Shirim* (Song of Songs):

> The Lord who made all things deigned to take flesh;  
> By death he willingly redeemed the fallen human race.  
> Hanging upon the cross, as he suffered,  
> Believe that he was a bundle of myrrh;  
> For he said that he was sorrowful unto death.  
> Moreover Peter wept bitterly; but afterward  
> Nard gave fragrance when, in bloodstained garment, he sought the heavens.

The voice of Christ: “Behold, you are beautiful, my beloved.” A confirmation: “Behold, you are beautiful.” “You are beautiful,” he says; “you are without blemish; you are chaste inwardly and outwardly.” Great indeed is the friendship between Christ and the Church, since Christ did not hesitate to die for the Church, nor the Church for Christ: “No one has greater love than this, that someone lay down his life for his friends” (John 15:13).

The voice [Col. 1242D] of the Church: “Your eyes are those of doves.” “Your eyes,” she says, “your memory, understanding, and reason, are those of doves—that is, chaste and simple. You are in no way proud because of understanding or wisdom. For you are not among those [Col. 1243A] who say: ‘Our lips are our own’” (Ps. 11 [12]:5).

The voice of the Church, or of Christ: “Behold, you are beautiful, my beloved, and lovely.” In this the greatest harmony of both is shown: each praises the other’s beauty. His loveliness and beauty can neither be spoken nor even conceived.

“Our little bed is flowering.” What is meant by the little bed but the heart? Hence the Lord himself says: “Enter into your chamber” (Matt. 6). This bed flowers with virtues and purity of conscience. We may also understand by this bed that blessedness of the saints in which, resting in perpetual quiet and leisure, they will flourish like the righteous palm.

“The beams of our houses are cedar, our ceilings cypress.” Understand these houses to be the Churches spread throughout the world. In them Christ is both summit and foundation, because they are sustained by him. The apostles and prophets are the columns and walls. The beams are the rulers and teachers by whom they are governed, sustained, and covered. The ceilings, which belong more to ornament than use, are virgins and widows together with the order of monks. For the more they are separated from the world, the more they shine in virtues and holiness. They benefit themselves and do no harm to others. But why are the former said to be cedar and the latter cypress? Cedar and cypress are by nature unfading and fragrant. The saints too are immortal and are a fragrance most pleasing to the Lord [Note: [Col. 1243D] This entire exposition agrees perfectly with the Holy Fathers so often cited, and it is more than sufficient for the brief commentary St. Bruno had proposed for himself.].

610

## CHAPTER II

The voice of Christ: “I am the flower of the field.” He certainly does not deny that he is beautiful and lovely [Col. 1243C]; rather, he affirms that he is the flower, beauty, and honor of the whole world. Moreover, he is the flower of the field—that is, the son of that virgin and untilled earth of which it is written: “And our earth shall give its fruit” (Ps. 65 [67]:7). Hence Isaiah says: “A rod shall go forth from the root of Jesse, and a flower shall rise from his root” (Isa. 11:1).

“And the lily of the valleys.” This lily is not of mountains but of valleys, because the Lord loves not the proud but the humble. As he himself says: “Learn from me, for I am meek and humble of heart” (Matt. 11:29). The lily grows in the valley; the Savior dwells in the heart of the humble.

“As a lily among thorns, so is my beloved among daughters.” The lily [Col. 1243D] is pricked and pressed among thorns; yet it grows and gives fragrance. So too the Church is often afflicted, oppressed, and pricked by daughters—that is, by heretics and schismatics whom she bore at the font of baptism. This is according to the letter. Spiritually [Col. 1244A], however, the lily among thorns is Christ among Jews, and the righteous person among sinners [Note: [Col. 1243D] St. Ambrose, *On the Instruction of a Virgin*, chapter 14, says: “Christ was a lily in the midst of thorns when he was in the midst of the Jews.” Rupert the abbot likewise understands the Jews by thorns, while by daughters he thinks heresies are signified, which strive to choke Catholic truth like a lily.].

The lily is oppressed by thorns, but Christ is afflicted, wounded, and crucified by the Jews. The lily grows among thorns because Christ reigns from the wood. This lily on the cross gave the sweetest fragrance to the Father. Hence the Psalmist says: “Let my prayer be directed as incense before you; the lifting up of my hands, an evening sacrifice” (Ps. 140 [141]:2). The primitive and apostolic Church fittingly bears this likeness among the innumerable daughters whom she bore. Let one city now assemble—or rather, two or four, and an entire province. Set Peter in their midst; let Paul be said to be present: would not a lily among thorns, would not a most welcome flower among briars, seem to be there [Col. 1244B] to you?

Verses:

> I am the flower of the field, the beauty and praise of the holy order;  
> The angelic host is subject to me.  
> I embrace all things, heaven and the expanse of the sea:  
> Lord of all, Father and God—  
> Who but I alone? No one, I tell you, no one.

The voice of the Church: “As an apple tree among the trees of the forest, so is my beloved among the sons” [Note: [Col. 1243D] Concerning the force of this encomium, by which Christ is celebrated through the likeness of an apple tree, all the Fathers agree that a threefold praise is bestowed upon him: of beauty, according to Psalm 44 [45], “You are more beautiful in form than the sons of men”; of the fragrance of graces, according to “Your name is ointment poured out”; and of refreshment. Theodoret, Ambrose, Cassiodorus, Bede, Bernard, and Origen in Homily 2 take this refreshment generally as coming through words, teaching, and examples.].

For as an apple tree is fruitful among unfruitful trees, so Christ was among the Jews and, at one time, even among the apostles. This is that tree of which it is said that it “will give its fruit in its season” (Ps. 1:3). At that time the apostles were fruitless, while Christ bore much fruit in Judaea. In comparison with him [Col. 1244C], they seemed not merely fruitless but even dry. Hence he himself says: “If they do this in the green tree, what shall be done in the dry?” (Luke 23:31). But those who had previously been dry and fruitless, once they had tasted the fruits of this tree and received the Holy Spirit, bore fruit with such abundance as may be understood from the Savior’s own words: “That you may go and bear fruit, and that your fruit may remain” (John 15:16).

“Under his shadow, whom I had desired, I sat”: that is, I at last rested in his protection [Note: [Col. 1244D] All the Holy Fathers and interpreters understand this in the same way, saying that by the metaphor of shade is designated the protection of God, or of Christ the bridegroom of the soul, toward which his lovers ought to aspire.]. For the Church was dark and made swarthy by the heat of vices when she fled to the shade of this tree, when she knew its shade and felt relief from her own heat.

“And his fruit was sweet to my throat.” “I sat,” she says, “under the shade; I came to know the fruits of this tree, and in contemplating it I was refreshed and satisfied with sweet utterances.” Of these fruits the Church says elsewhere: “How sweet are your words to my palate, more than honey to my mouth!” (Ps. 118 [119]:103).

“The king brought [Col. 1245A] me into the wine cellar.” What is the wine cellar but the teaching of the New and Old Testaments? Of this cellar it is said: “For a cup of unmixed wine, full of mixture, is in the hand of the Lord” (Ps. 74 [75]:9). Drunk with the wine of this cellar, the Apostle said: “We speak wisdom among the perfect” (1 Cor. 2:6). And the Psalmist: “Your cup which intoxicates me—how excellent it is!” (Ps. 22 [23]:5). Brought into this cellar, the Church is intoxicated with the sweetness of heavenly wine.

“He ordered love in me” [Note: [Col. 1245D] “He ordered love in me.” According to the more common opinion of the Fathers, this means that the Church or devout soul signifies that, after God admitted her into the wine cellar, he granted her to love God himself and her neighbor in due order. Thus Ghislerius, with whom Cornelius a Lapide, Calmet, and others agree.]. How is love ordered in this cellar? Do you wish to hear? “You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, with all your mind, and with all your strength” (Matt. 22:37). What further? “And your neighbor as yourself” (ibid., 39). This is the order and true rule [Col. 1245B] of love: that we love God above all things and our neighbor as ourselves.

He ordered it in the first cellar; he ordered it also in the second. How in the first? “You shall love your neighbor and hate your enemy” (Matt. 5:43). What is said in the second? “Love your enemies; do good to those who hate you” (ibid., 44). Does this order seem contrary to you? Certainly not contrary, indeed fitting; otherwise it would not be order. For in the first saying “enemy” is understood of vice, and in the second of nature: thus, “You shall hate your enemy”—the vice, not the nature. “You shall love your enemy”—the nature, not the vice.

“Strengthen me with flowers; surround me with apples, for I languish with love.” The bride desires to be supported with flowers and pomegranates, that she may rest upon them [Col. 1245C] [Note: [Col. 1245D] Symmachus translates: “Make me rest among flowers”; that is, “Spread flowers beneath me, that I may rest upon them.” Jerome did not dislike this interpretation.]. “The Bridegroom’s love,” she says, “is now ordered in me. I love; I languish with love. Therefore you, my servants—faithful dependents, confidants, household members—strengthen me with flowers and surround me with apples.”

The apostles and teachers strengthen the Church with flowers and surround it with apples. Gregory, Ambrose, Jerome, and Augustine brought many flowers to the Church. By flowers we understand teachings; by apples, believers. We may also understand by flowers the beginning of a work and by apples its perfection [Note: [Col. 1245D] “For what are flowers but souls already beginning a good work and breathing forth heavenly desire? And what are apples from flowers but the minds of the perfected, which attain the fruit of good work from the beginning of a holy purpose?” St. Gregory.]. For flowers become fruit when hearers believe the teachings, and fulfill in action what they believe.

“His left hand is under my head, and his right hand will embrace me.” When Christ died for the Church, did he not hold his left hand under [Col. 1245D] her head? The left hand [Col. 1246A] signifies adversity. By this left hand, this adversity, this most cruel death of our Savior, we were raised from the slime of the deep and utter misery. For when, with bowed head, he gave up his spirit, he surely lifted the head toward himself. His right hand embraced the Church, because, rising from the dead and made immortal, he recovered in right hand and strength all things which he drew to himself [Note: [Col. 1246D] “In the left hand the holy soul reckons the remembrance of that love than which none is greater: that he laid down his life for his friends; in the right hand, the blessed vision promised to his friends, and the joy arising from the excellence of majesty.” St. Bernard, *On Loving God*.].

We may also understand by the left hand those things necessary to this life; by the right hand, that highest blessedness [Note: [Col. 1246D] “The left hand of God—that is, the prosperity of the present life—she has placed under her head, pressing it down with the intention of highest love. But God’s right hand embraces her because she is held with entire devotion under his eternal blessedness.” St. Gregory.]. While we live in this world, the Lord holds his left hand, as it were, beneath our head, sustaining us in adversity and supplying necessities. But when we leave this life, embraced by God’s right hand and clothed in immortality and strength, nothing left-handed, [Col. 1246B] nothing adverse, will any longer be possible for us.

The voice of Christ:

“I adjure you, daughters of Jerusalem, by the gazelles and the stags of the field, that you do not awaken or rouse my beloved until she herself wishes” [Note: [Col. 1246D] Cantacuzenus understands these words as signifying the oracles of the prophets which proclaimed the divine maternity of the Most Blessed Virgin, and which were not to be revealed until she herself wished—that is, until she came and gave birth to Jesus the Savior.].

What are the daughters of Jerusalem but all souls regenerated by the font of baptism? What are the gazelles and stags but virtues and good works, by which we both run to heaven and overcome the poisons of serpents and demons? And what is meant by the beloved but the soul devoted solely to contemplation of God? To awaken her from so great a sleep, to separate her from so great repose and blessedness, unless she herself wishes it or necessity compels it, is sin. Therefore, let whoever loves stags and gazelles, whoever dreads to lose feet, wings, strength, and righteousness, not trouble God’s beloved.

[Col. 1246C] Verses:

> As the apple tree among trees, pleasing in fruit and fragrance,  
> So is my beloved alone among the assembly of sons.  
> Under his shadow I sat; in its refreshment I rested.  
> I received from him sweet fruits for my throat.  
> He brought me into the cellar and commanded me to drink wine.  
> He gave me love, the mother of every virtue.  
> The left hand raises my head; the right embraces my head.  
> Unless he loved me for this, who would adjure me for his sake?

The voice of the Church: “The voice of my beloved.” “This voice,” she says, “this adjuration which I hear, is that of my beloved. For unless he had loved me, he would never have spoken so for me.”

“Behold, he will come.” But how will he come? “Leaping [Col. 1246D] upon the mountains.” Coming from heaven, he first [Col. 1247A] made a leap into the Virgin’s womb [Note: [Col. 1247D] “For in coming to our redemption, he made, so to speak, certain leaps. From heaven he came into the womb; from the womb he came into the manger; from the manger he came to the cross; from the cross into the tomb; from the tomb he returned to heaven.” St. Gregory the Great.]. This is the stone said to have been cut from the mountain without hands. For Christ came forth from the Virgin without a man’s embrace. You see, then, that Mary is called a mountain. Therefore he made a leap into the mountain—that is, into Mary. He made another leap as well, namely onto the cross. When he ascended into heaven, he made a leap upon the highest mountains.

Moreover, the apostles are called mountains, and Christ dwelt in them by leaping. But if you, O human being, desire to become a mountain, raise your mind, so that your hope and heart may be exalted from earthly desires. Then he who is said to leap upon mountains will leap in you.

“Leaping over the hills.” Truly he leaps over the hills, because he surpasses both the saints in holiness and all the mighty in power: “For who among the clouds shall be equal to the Lord?” [Col. 1247B] (Ps. 88 [89]).

“My beloved is like a gazelle or a young stag.” As though he said: Since he leaps on mountains and over hills, he is like a gazelle and a young stag; for these run over mountains and leap over hills.

“Behold, he stands behind our wall, looking through the windows, gazing through the lattices.” What is meant by the wall but sin? With this set between us and God, we cannot be joined to him. It is called our wall because we ourselves built it. Of this wall the Psalmist also says: “In my God I shall leap over a wall” (Ps. 17 [18]:30).

We may also understand the wall as humanity. Behind this wall—that is, enclosed in humanity—he could be known by few [Note: [Col. 1247D] “Christ stood as though behind our wall when, having become incarnate, divinity lay hidden in assumed humanity. Since human weakness could not endure his immensity if he displayed it, he interposed the obstacle of flesh; and whatever great works he did among human beings, he did them as though hiding behind a wall,” etc. The same St. Gregory.]. Therefore he stood [Col. 1247C] behind our wall because, veiled in human flesh, he lived among human beings. He looked through the windows because he fully knew what our eyes desire to see, our ears to hear, our mouth to say, and our hearts to think. He also gazes through the lattices because there is no one singing in choir whose intention he does not see. He sees the monk; he sees the bishop; he sees who sings with the mouth and who with the heart. For he knows who sings from love and who from favor.

“My dove, my beautiful one, come. Behold, my beloved speaks to me, saying: Arise, hasten, my beloved” [Note: [Col. 1247D] Cantacuzenus refers these words, as spoken to the Most Blessed Virgin, to the divine Word: “It is time, O mother, that you be born upon earth, that you be a dwelling for me who am to be born mortal from you. For the winter, namely unbelief, has passed, and the rain—the flood of idolatry—has departed together with evil works.”].

Hence Isaiah says: “Command again, command again” (Isa. 28:10). Arise, apostles; preach, teachers; proclaim the Gospel. “My dove,” without gall, without [Col. 1247D] bitterness, innocent and simple. Hence he himself says: “Be prudent as serpents and simple as doves” (Matt. 10:16). “My beautiful one,” made whiter than [Col. 1248A] snow, without stain or wrinkle. “Arise,” he says, “do what you are to do, and after wickedness has been overcome and your task completed, at last come to me.”

“For now winter has passed; the rain has gone and departed.” “Winter and rain have passed,” he says; “the cloudy, harsh, and grievous time has passed. ‘Behold, now is the acceptable time; behold, now is the day of salvation’” (2 Cor. 6:2). “The night has gone before, but the day has drawn near” (Rom. 13:12); now all things are clear, all things exposed and manifest [Note: [Col. 1248D] These words may be referred to John 3:29: “He who has the bride is the bridegroom; but the friend of the bridegroom, who stands and hears him, rejoices greatly because of the bridegroom’s voice.”].

“Flowers have appeared upon the earth.” “Now,” he says, “flowers appear upon the earth; now the Church gleams with the beauty of virtues; now, with every thorn and briar uprooted, our earth puts forth the Savior.”

“The time of pruning has come.” This is what the Lord said to his disciples in the Gospel: “Lift up [Col. 1248B] your eyes and see the fields, for they are already white for harvest” (John 4:35). Now is the time for reaping; now is the time for gathering the nations into one faith; it is time to cut away vices. Prune the vines, that grapes may arise; cut away vices, that virtues may arise.

“The voice of the turtledove has been heard in our land.” “The voice of the turtledove,” he says—the chaste, apostolic voice—“has been heard in our land: ‘The earth is the Lord’s and its fullness’” (Ps. 23 [24]:1).

“The fig tree has put forth its unripe figs.” What is meant by the fig tree but the Synagogue? It has put forth its unripe figs; it has produced the first fruits of the fig tree—namely, the patriarchs and prophets.

“The flowering vines have given forth their fragrance.” The flowering vines are the Churches; but why flowering, except because cultivators of virtue arise in them? They gave forth fragrance because, through virtues and prayers, the vines delight the Lord [Col. 1248C] [Note: [Col. 1248D] According to the more common view of the Fathers, Ghislerius says, the universal Church, or particular Churches, are signified as having flourished in virtues after Christ’s coming and given forth the fragrance of good renown. Thus Origen, Gregory of Nyssa, Jerome, and others.]; because to some they are a fragrance of death unto death, but to others a fragrance of life unto life (2 Cor. 2:16).

Verses:

> Leaping on mountains, leaping over hills, behold, my own comes—  
> Both Bridegroom and God—whom the wall of flesh conceals  
> From human eyes, so that the Jew may say, “He is not God.”  
> Do you not hear the voice that has penetrated my inmost heart?  
> Arise, come, come: for winter has passed, every rain has gone, summer opens.  
> The turtledove too is heard; the fig has produced unripe figs; it will yield clusters;  
> And the vines flower and offer fragrance.

[Col. 1248D] “Arise, my friend.” Do not sleep, he says, but arise and, through faith and love, do what is good. “My bride,” to whom I am joined by so great a love [Col. 1249A] that I deigned to take flesh for your sake. “And come, my dove.” My dove, he says, free from gall and every bitterness, come after me; follow me; have no leader but me. “And in the clefts of the rock,” understand: remain; that is, delight in the wounds of my flesh, and acknowledge that these wounds were the cause of your salvation. [Note: [Col. 1249D] “The clefts of the rock are the wounds which Christ received on the cross for our salvation: namely, the marks of the nails and the thrust of the lance. In these clefts, therefore, the dove—that is, the Church—remains, because she has placed all hope of her salvation in the Passion of her Redeemer.” Author of the Commentary attributed to Cassiodorus.] For Thomas had delayed, and was unwilling to believe; but afterwards, delighting in the wounds of this rock, he said: “My Lord and my God” (John 20:28).

“In the hollow of the wall.” This is a confirmation. We may also understand by the hollow of the wall the guardianship of teachers and angels, so that, now placed as it were within walls, she may be protected by their defense—she who formerly was openly shaken by the assault of vices, without fortification. “Show me your face” (Exod. 33:15). Let the quality of your renewal and your beauty be proved; teach others to be like you; fear no one except me. “Let your voice sound in my ears.” Preach and confess me, he says, so that by you, and by others through you, due praise and honor may be rendered to me. “For your voice is sweet.” [Note: [Col. 1249D] “The voice is sweet because confession is made with the mouth unto salvation; and the face is comely because she does not blush at her Author and is not ashamed of her Redeemer. Thus she shows her face by bearing the seal of the cross, and makes known her voice by assuming the authority of preaching.” Ambrose, Sermon 6 on Psalm 118, verse c.] I wish to hear it; “and your face is comely,” which I desire to see. Let the bride prepare herself and adorn herself with garments, since she is to be beheld by so great and such a bridegroom. Let her speak not feigned or indecent, but rather sweet and pleasant words.

A voice against heresies: “Catch for us the little foxes that destroy the vineyards.” What do foxes signify but heretics, vices, and evil spirits? While these are small and at the very beginning of their origin, they must be caught, restrained, and destroyed. Hence the Psalmist says: “Blessed is he who shall seize and dash your little ones against the rock” (Ps. 137:9). These foxes destroy this vineyard because they destroy and scatter Christ’s Church. For “our vineyard has blossomed.” [Note: [Col. 1250D] “That is, the Church, which throughout the whole world has widely put forth the flowers of virtues. And it should be noted that, although above he spoke of vineyards in the plural, now he speaks in the singular: ‘Our vineyard has blossomed,’ because from many churches one Church has been chosen.” Author of the Commentary attributed to Cassiodorus.] It has blossomed, therefore, because, with vices cut away, it is adorned with the brightness and beauty of virtues. It must therefore be guarded, lest, ravaged by foxes, it be deprived of its flowers.

> Arise, my friend; come, my dove,  
> Delight, thus healed, in my wounds.  
> May you appear beautiful; may you speak wisely.  
> For your voice is melodious and your face comely.  
> Let the foxes now be caught; let vices be destroyed,  
> Lest the vineyards’ flowers and fragrances perish.

[Col. 1249D] Thus speaks the Church: “My beloved is mine, and I am his.” My beloved, she says, gives me help and strength; but I serve him and obey him in all things. “Who feeds among the lilies.” This is the same one who rejoices and dwells amid the many bright and flourishing choirs of saints and virgins. Virgins delight in flowers. Accordingly, as thorns spring up among sinners, so lilies spring up among saints. He feeds among lilies, since he dwells among the saints.

“Until the day breathes and the shadows decline.” Thus he himself says: “Behold, I am with you always, even unto the consummation of the age” (Matt. 28:20). For the day will breathe when the Sun of righteousness rises for the saints, and that day begins which shall never end. Of it it is said: “For one day in your courts is better than thousands” (Ps. 84:10). But the shadows shall decline, because, when the adversities of this life have ceased, the prince of darkness with his attendants [Col. 1250B] will be cast down into hell.

“Return.” You have ascended into heaven, he says, and, the battle completed, have returned to the Father. But return: look upon the earth and hear the prayers of your people. “Be like a roe, my beloved,” which seeks the heights of mountains, “or like a young stag,” which both desires shade, strives frequently to revisit its mother, and freely presents itself to the eyes of its pursuers. He is therefore like a roe in ascending into heaven; like a young stag in revisiting his mother among the saints, who are not scorched by the heat of vices; and in dwelling there, and again, at his second advent, presenting himself to the eyes of the Jews: “They shall look on him whom they pierced” (John 19:37). “Upon the mountains of Bether,” [Note: [Col. 1250D] In the Vulgate it is written *Bether*, and likewise in the Hebrew text; but in the Arabic version, *Bethel*, the mountain famous for the vision Jacob had upon it, and this name is often found repeated in Holy Scripture.] understand: upon which you dwell. For Bether is interpreted “house of God.” Therefore let the saints stand as Bether, since it is the house of God. The house is called Bether by some “the rising house,” or “the house of watchings.” But the saints always rise from virtue to virtue toward higher things, and, watching, await him who will come like a thief in the night.

## Chapter III

The voice of the Church: “Upon my bed in the nights I sought him whom my soul loves; I sought him, and did not find him.” Formerly, says the Church, upon my bed—in my heart and in the leisure of searching—I sought my Lord, my bridegroom, whom my soul loves more than all things. But I sought through nights: without faith, in darkness, in human wisdom, in the blindness of the mind. And therefore I did not find him. This is what heretics sought; this is what philosophers sought. But, seeking in the night and trusting in their own wisdom, they did not find him. [Note: [Col. 1250D] See the Commentary on the Song of Songs under the name of Cassiodorus.] Hence the Lord himself says: “I confess to you, Father, Lord of heaven and earth, because you have hidden these things from the wise and prudent [Col. 1251A] and revealed them to little ones” (Matt. 11:25).

“I will arise and go about the city.” I will arise, says the Church. But what Church? The Church of the Gentiles: the people who sat in darkness and were given over to sleep, who had not yet said: “O God, my God, I keep watch for you from the dawn” (Ps. 63:1). I will arise, she says; I will sleep no longer; I will go about the city—that is, the congregation of saints and apostles—so that they may teach me those things concerning God which I could not know by myself. “Through the streets and squares, and in all places, I shall seek him whom my soul loves; I sought him and did not find him.” But this was by night, this was upon my bed. Therefore I shall seek by day, so that I may find him.

“The watchmen who go about the city found me.” I arose, she says, and went about the city already mentioned. [Col. 1251B] While I was doing this, the watchmen who guard the city found me. The city is the Church, and the watchmen are the apostles. They find those who seek God through faith and baptism. For the concern of the guards is directed around them; it is said not only that the Church found them, but also that they found the Church. When I had found them, I said—this is the Church speaking of Christ—“Have you seen him whom my soul loves?” This is as though she said: You who possess knowledge of God, show me God himself and the way of truth. “When I had passed them by a little, I found him whom my soul loves.” When, she says, I had passed through them by hearing and understanding, and had run through their counsels and preaching—for in this manner of speaking we are accustomed to say, “I run through a book”—through their indication I found [Col. 1251C] him whom my soul loves.

“I held him and will not let him go.” [Note: [Col. 1251D] “Christ, of course, is to be loved above all things, because he first loved us, washed us from our sins in his blood, and gave his life for us.” The same author.] I found him, she says, and sweetly embraced him. “I held him.” How? By mind, by action, and by perfect faith. “And I will not let him go”: rather, I shall cling to him in most ardent love, “until I bring him into the house of my mother.” [Note: [Col. 1251D] “It must not be supposed that the Church will then leave him when she has brought him into the chamber of her mother—that is, when the Synagogue has come to knowledge of him and faith. Rather, ‘until’ is used in the sense of ‘for ever’: that is, she will always be faithful to him and burn with most ardent love.” The same author.] That is, into the dwelling of this earthen vessel, which he fashioned with his own hands, with earth as mother. For the saints are God’s dwelling-place. Hence he himself says: “I will dwell in them and walk among them” (2 Cor. 6:16).

“And into the chamber of her who bore me.” That is, into the inner chamber of my heart. We may also understand the Synagogue by this mother, from whose house Christ departed when he said: “Behold, your house shall be left to you desolate” (Matt. 23:38). [Col. 1251D] “When the fullness of the Gentiles has entered, then all Israel shall be saved” (Rom. 11:25); then he shall bring the Church into the house of his mother. “My beloved is mine, and I am his.” He does not remain either here or there, but dwells with the saints until the day breathes and the end of shadows comes.

> To whom I said: Be like a roe,  
> Or upon the mountains of Bether like a young stag.  
> [Col. 1252A] Upon my bed through the nights I sought him;  
> But because I did not find him through the nights,  
> I arose to go about the city.  
> As I went through streets and squares,  
> The watchmen of the gates found me.  
> They told me where my beloved was.  
> Therefore I found him, and shall not let him go  
> Until I bring him into my mother’s bed—  
> That is, into the hidden substance of this vessel,  
> Or into the latter-day people of the Jews.

The Bridegroom to faithful souls: “I adjure you, daughters of Jerusalem, by the roes and stags of the field,” and the rest. By the roes and stags, he says—by the apostles and teachers, by virtue, faith, and good works, through which you run both toward heaven and toward the promised prize [Col. 1252B] and overcome the poisons of serpents—I adjure and beseech you, daughters of Jerusalem, you who possess knowledge of God, not to awaken my beloved, my bride, nor separate her from the work in which she delights. One delights in fasting, another in vigils, another in giving alms, another in building churches. To separate these persons from so great a sleep, from this delight, from this purpose of their soul, is a great sin. For graces are diverse, wills are diverse, and the works by which we may serve the Lord are diverse. Let each, therefore, abound in his own conviction.

The Synagogue concerning the Church: “Who is this who comes up through the wilderness?” Who, she says, what sort of woman, how beautiful, how wonderful is this who hastens upward to me from virtue to virtue? Of what courage and boldness, I ask, is she who comes to me through the wilderness? For through the wilderness and the adversities of this world the Church passed on to the Lord, fearing neither robbers’ ambushes, nor tyrants’ swords, nor lions’ teeth, nor the sophistries of Jews and heretics. But how did she pass through? “Like a pillar of smoke made from spices, namely myrrh and frankincense and every powder of the perfumer.” As though she said: I delight in her coming as in the fragrance and sweetness of every spice. By the myrrh and frankincense named here we understand the mortification of the flesh and the prayers of the saints.

> Who is this through the wilderness,  
> [Col. 1252D] When heaven is open,  
> Who rises like smoke,  
> Whom earth has not weighed down?  
> Thus she passed through the wilderness,  
> Found the narrow way,  
> Yet passed through the wilderness  
> Bearing a pleasing spice.

The voice of the Church: “Behold, Solomon’s bed: sixty mighty men surround it, from among Israel’s mightiest.” [Col. 1253A] Solomon is interpreted “peaceful.” “For he is our peace, who has made both one” (Eph. 2:14). Therefore, by Solomon’s bed we understand the Church, [Note: [Col. 1253D] “Although Solomon’s bed may be understood as that rest of heavenly blessedness in which God rests with his saints, it is more probably understood as the present Church, in which God’s saints, their tumultuous vices lulled to sleep, delight in the embrace of Solomon—that is, of the true Peaceful One.” The same author. Cantacuzenus says that this bed of Solomon signifies the tomb in which Christ’s dead body was laid and to which the Jews set soldiers to guard it.] which Christ joined to himself in holy love, having neither spot nor wrinkle. Concerning it he says through the Prophet: “This is my resting-place for ever and ever; here I shall dwell, because I have chosen her” (Ps. 132:14).

Sixty mighty men surround her; the apostles and teachers guard her, lest Jews, heretics, and false apostles, adulterating the word of God, defile Solomon’s bed and the consciences of the saints. But why are they said to be sixty, unless because the number sixty is composed of six and ten? For six times ten, or ten times six, makes sixty. And because God completed his work in six days, we rightly understand perfection of works by six. By ten, however, we signify the ten legal commandments. Therefore those who guard Solomon’s bed—that is, the holy Church—ought to be perfect in works and wise in the teachings and ordinances of the law. These are said to be not merely mighty, but from among Israel’s mightiest, because the teachers of the Church ought to be stronger than others.

“All holding swords.” Hence the Psalmist says: “And two-edged swords in their hands” (Ps. 149:6); and the Apostle: “And the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God” (Eph. 6:17). Let bishops therefore hold swords by which they may both destroy vices and defend the Church. “Most skilled in war.” Hence: “Blessed be the Lord my God, who teaches my hands for battle and my fingers for war” (Ps. 144:1). They are most skilled in battle because, by suffering—not by defending themselves—they conquered in humility and patience. “Each man’s sword upon his thigh.” Those have swords upon their thighs who repel the assaults of lust with the bridle of chastity. Hence the Apostle says: “I chastise my body and bring it into servitude” (1 Cor. 9:27). “Because of fears in the night.” The teachers, he says, are armed and girded with swords lest heretics and evil spirits, by deceit and in secret during the night, invade Solomon’s bed—that is, the holy Church.

The Church: “King Solomon made himself a litter from the woods of Lebanon.” What does the litter signify but the Church? This litter, this banqueting hall, [Col. 1253D] this house of sacred feasting the Lord made from the woods of Lebanon, because no one dwells in the Church who has not been made white by the water of baptism. For Lebanon is interpreted “whitening.” [Note: [Col. 1254D] “Lebanon is interpreted ‘whitening’ or ‘making white.’ Therefore the woods of Lebanon are the saints, made white and cleansed in baptism and adorned with the beauty of every virtue.” The same author.] Concerning this litter it is said in the Psalms: “In a place of pasture he has set me” [Col. 1254A] (Ps. 23:2). Those who sit in this litter ought to have wedding garments. Here Christ set before us his flesh to be eaten. Here we eat the living bread, the prefigured lamb, and the fattened calf; here we drink the cup of the New Testament; here we are inebriated with divine and most sweet wine.

Of Christ it says: “He made its columns of silver.” What do the columns signify but the apostles and teachers? But why columns, unless because they are supports of the whole Church? Of them it is said in the Psalms: “I have established its columns” (Ps. 75:4). Why silver? Because they shine with devotion to simplicity, moderation, and sobriety. These are those feathered columns which are said to be silvered. “Its backrest of gold.” He made a table, he says, [Col. 1254B] and a golden backrest, because the New and Old Testaments shine brilliantly with the light of wisdom. Of this table it is said: “You have prepared a table before me” (Ps. 23:5). Let us therefore come to this golden table so that we may be refreshed with divine and spiritual fare.

“Its ascent purple.” No one eats the food of this table unless he ascends by the purple way. The Jews do not receive this food, because they have not known the purple ascent. Of them it is said: “Let their table before them become a snare” (Ps. 69:22). For the purple way is that which Christ stained with his own blood. We may also understand by the backrest that heavenly blessedness. It is called golden because it is more precious than all things; its rest is eternal and its ascent purple. No one ascends there unless, redeemed by Christ’s death, he is led by his blood. The martyrs also rejoice that they have ascended there by the purple way.

“He paved its midst with love for the daughters of Jerusalem.” How did he pave and cover us in the midst with love, unless because he redeemed all by a common love? This he did for simple souls, who were being plunged into infernal darkness. [Note: [Col. 1254D] This is for simple souls, conscious of no virtue in themselves; the more they are aware of their own frailty, the more earnestly they strive to love the Savior and Redeemer. The same author.] He paved the midst with love because, crucified for universal salvation, he worked salvation in the midst of the earth.

The voice of the Church says of Christ: “Go forth and see, daughters of Zion, King Solomon.” Go forth, she says, daughters of Zion, outside the gate; go out, [Col. 1254D] daughters of Jerusalem, and see your king, see Solomon, see Christ, the truly Peaceful One. “In the diadem with which his mother crowned him.” This mother is understood to be the Synagogue, because the Lord was born according to the flesh from the Jewish people. She crowned her son, her Lord, [Col. 1255A] her king, and placed a crown of thorns upon his head. [Note: [Col. 1255D] “Go forth, daughters of Zion, and see in King Solomon the crown with which his mother crowned him—namely, the crown of thorns which she placed upon his head. On the day of his betrothal: that is, on the day when he suffered. For then, as a bridegroom, he took a wife, namely the chaste Church from among the Gentiles.” Thus Cantacuzenus.] When? “On the day of his espousal.” That is, on the day when Christ celebrated his wedding and betrothed the Church to the Father, fashioning his bride from his own side as he slept. For as Eve was made from one rib taken from the sleeping Adam, so the Church was made from Christ sleeping, when his side was pierced by a lance.

“And on the day of the joy of his heart.” [Note: [Col. 1255D] “He rejoiced to redeem the world from the devil’s power by his Passion,” etc. The same author, attributed to Cassiodorus.] O wonderful mercy! Dying, he rejoiced; he exulted in death, because he knew that by this means he would redeem the world and deliver the patriarchs and prophets from death. Although the flesh was sorrowful, the heart and divinity rejoiced.

> Behold, Solomon’s bed is surrounded by the mightiest men,  
> [Col. 1255B] All holding swords, most skilled in war.  
> For fear of the night they are girded with swords,  
> By which they are protection to their own and terror to strangers.  
> King Solomon made a litter from the woods of Lebanon,  
> Whose columns, indeed, are you, O apostles.  
> There he fashioned a golden backrest;  
> With his own blood he made the ascent purple.  
> Daughters of Zion, why do you stand still? Go out!  
> Behold your king crowned with thorns.  
> Yet you, Virgin Mary, crowned your Son,  
> Because, taking flesh from you, he is set in the midst.  
> Whom Zion surrounds with a choir of apostles, confessors, and virgins,  
> Like a crown of prudent soldiers.

## Chapter IV

The voice of Christ: “How beautiful you are, my friend, how [Col. 1255C] beautiful you are!” [Note: [Col. 1255D] “He repeats twice, ‘How beautiful you are,’ namely in work and in preaching. In work, because she does nothing foul or unworthy of my eyes. In preaching, because she does not cease to invite even her companions, the daughters of Jerusalem, to contemplate the mystery of my incarnation.” The same author.] Why does he say twice, “How beautiful you are,” unless because she is beautiful in work and speech, inwardly and outwardly, in soul and body? “Your eyes are those of doves”: that is, your understanding, reason, and vision are simple and keen, not clouded by anger, disturbed by the blood of rage, or raised up in pride. “Apart from what lies hidden within.” Much may be said of you, he says. You are praiseworthy in virtue, constancy, and wisdom. Great is what is seen; greater still is what lies hidden. Great is the work that shines in you; great is the recompense kept for you in the heavenly treasury. Great is the labor, but greatest is the hope.

We may also understand the prophets by the eyes, who foresaw long beforehand those things that were to come. These are called doves [Col. 1255D] because they served the Lord in humility and simplicity of heart. “Your hair is like flocks of goats.” By the hair we understand those who kept the faith from Adam until Christ. For no part of the body is higher than the hair. They are rightly called hair, therefore, since in time they precede the whole Church. But why are they compared to a flock of goats, unless because they lived carnally and served the pleasures of lust and flesh? For to them it had been said: “Increase and multiply” (Gen. 9:7). David and Solomon, whose concubines were innumerable, are proved to have been such persons. They are saved by faith alone. These are they who through faith conquered kingdoms. “Which have gone up from Mount Gilead.” Gilead is interpreted “heap of testimony.” They went up from Mount Gilead because, observing the testimonies of the Law and Prophets, they deserved to climb to the kingdom of heaven.

“Your teeth are like flocks of shorn sheep.” The teeth are the apostles. But why teeth, unless because, chewing over and expounding the weightier sentences of the prophets [Col. 1256B] and the Law, they feed and nourish the Church? Why flocks of shorn sheep, unless because, having sold all worldly possessions and given them to the poor, naked, shorn, and stripped of vices, they served the Lord in innocence and simplicity? “Which have gone up from the washing.” They went up from the washing because, cleansed by the water of baptism and having expelled all vices, they were raised to the summit of faith and doctrine, and to heaven. “All with twin offspring.” They have twin offspring because, sleeping between the two lots, they preach the New and Old Testaments. We may also understand by the twin offspring doctrine and practice, or likewise chastity of body and soul, or love of God and neighbor. [Note: [Col. 1256D] Cantacuzenus agrees in the same interpretation and, speaking of these sheep, says: “For, shorn and washed in the divine washing, they rendered the font of holy baptism fruitful through an unbroken succession of their children, and are always twin-bearing, exercising excellent contemplation of the soul and excellent practice alike.”] “And none among them is barren,” [Col. 1256C] because they bear fruit from manifold seed.

“Your lips are like a scarlet ribbon.” What do the lips signify but bishops, priests, and the rest who constantly praise and bless God? These are said to be a scarlet ribbon. But why a ribbon? Because, as it binds many hairs, so it binds many faithful in one faith; or because it gathers many virtues and many sayings together; or again because they restrain the thoughts of their heart so that they are not swept away by the wind of vanity into empty things. Why scarlet? Because they are kindled with the fire of the Holy Spirit and preach Christ’s Passion. Scarlet has the appearance of fire or blood. “And your speech is sweet.” The sayings of the saints are indeed sweet and pleasant to hear. Hence also: “How sweet are your sayings to my palate, more than honey to my mouth!” (Ps. 119:103).

“Your cheeks are like a fragment of pomegranate.” The cheeks [Col. 1257A] signify the martyrs of God, who, confessing Christ before his face and in his presence, died for him. [Note: [Col. 1257D] This is also the interpretation of the supposed Cassiodorus.] They are said to be a fragment of pomegranate because they have been stained with their own blood. They are called cheeks because they blush for sins; a fragment because they are cut down and broken for Christ’s name; and pomegranate because of the shedding of blood. “Apart from what lies hidden within.” Beautiful, he says, are the cheeks; rosy is the face; virginal and chaste is the countenance. Yet far more praiseworthy are those things which do not yet appear, which lie hidden in the heart, which are reserved for you in the heavenly treasury.
