“Your neck is like the tower of David.” By the neck we understand the teachers of the Church. Food passes through the neck by which the stomach is refreshed and satisfied; through the neck [Col. 1257B] also come forth words and all the teachings of doctrine; finally, the neck supports the shield by which the whole body is covered. The teachers nourish, instruct, strengthen, and defend the Church. Moreover, they join the Church to Christ as the neck joins the body to the head. They defend the whole Church just as the tower of David once defended all Jerusalem.

“Which is built with its battlements.” Thus the teachers also have battlements: namely wisdom and virtue, which no engines can storm and no implements of enemies destroy. “A thousand shields hang from it.” [Note: [Col. 1257D] By the thousand shields are understood the innumerable protections of divine defense by which the holy Church is enclosed and defended, etc. The same author. Cantacuzenus also understands by this tower or fortress the prefigured Blessed Virgin, surrounded on every side by fortifications and strengthened by protection, so that no enemy can prevail against her.] A thousand shields hang from the teachers because, by innumerable statements and arguments flowing from them, they protect [Col. 1257C] the Church. “All the armor of the mighty.” Nothing in it can be conquered or broken.

“Your two breasts are like two twin fawns of a roe.” For one roe is one Church, whose sight is keen, whose feet are swift, whose will seeks higher things, whose course ascends to heaven. It has two breasts because there are two twins. The two breasts are the two Testaments. The two twins signify the two peoples: Jewish and Gentile. These are called twins because they are both twin and observe a twofold love. “Who feed among the lilies until the day breathes and the shadows decline.” Those feed among lilies who delight in the sweet and fragrant sayings of the Scriptures. “Until the day breathes”—namely that day of which it is said: “For one day in your courts is better than thousands” (Ps. 84:10)—“and the shadows decline,” and the darkness flees, and the prince of all darkness with all his host is cast down into hell.

The Bridegroom says of the bride: “I will go to the mountain of myrrh.” I will go, says the Lord, to the mountain of myrrh; I will visit the earth and take flesh. For the mountain of myrrh is the flesh which he assumed. This is that mountain which grew so great that it filled the whole earth. It is called myrrh because it did not see corruption, according to the words: “Nor will you give your Holy One to see corruption” (Ps. 16:10). We may also understand this mountain as the Church, which, mortifying her flesh with its vices and desires, dwells always in bitterness.

“And to the hill of frankincense”: that is, to those whose prayers delight me like the sweet fragrance of frankincense. “You are wholly beautiful, my friend, and there is no blemish in you.” [Note: [Col. 1257D] Cantacuzenus believes these words were prophetically spoken of the Mother of God: considering her wholly free from every stain and destined to be the cause of salvation for the whole world, the sacred writer, inflamed by the divine Spirit, cried out to her: “You are wholly beautiful, my beloved, and there is no blemish in you.”] She is wholly beautiful because [Col. 1258B] she has neither spot nor wrinkle.

The Bridegroom to the bride: “Come from Lebanon, my bride; come from Lebanon, come.” You are in Lebanon, he says; you have been made white in virtues; you shine with the holiness of flowers; nothing dark, black, or obscure is seen in you. Therefore come to me, and you who have always loved beauty, shine like the sun for ever in my kingdom. [Note: [Col. 1258D] “And he says ‘come’ a third time, because he wishes her to be perfect in thought, speech, and deed. Or he calls her first so that she may come to him through faith; he calls her a second time so that she may receive the worthy recompense of heavenly rewards when her body has been set free; and a third time so that, on the day of the general resurrection, having resumed her body and adorned with a double robe, she may rejoice eternally.” The same author, the supplementary Cassiodorus.] He says “come” three times because there are three things without which one does not come to him: faith, hope, and love; or because she serves the Lord in thought, speech, and action. Why she is called bride has been said above. “You shall be crowned from the summit of Amana.” Amanus is a mountain of Cilicia, also called Taurus.

“From the summit of Senir and Hermon.” These mountains [Col. 1258C] are in Judaea. Lions and leopards dwell in them, as what follows makes clear: “From the dens of lions, from the mountains of leopards.” By these mountains we understand those in whom the armies of vices—lions and leopards, that is, evil spirits themselves—dwell. When these have been conquered and expelled, the Church is crowned: “For no one shall be crowned unless he has competed lawfully” (2 Tim. 2:5). Therefore she is crowned from the summit of the aforesaid mountains because, having conquered the devil, who is their head and lord, she receives a reward and crown for so great a contest.

“You have wounded my heart, my sister, my bride.” She is sister because she is the daughter of the same Father. Hence the Apostle says: “And if children, then heirs: heirs indeed of God and co-heirs of Christ” (Rom. 8:17). She is bride because Christ, taking our flesh, came forth from the virgin’s womb. This sister and bride wounded the heart of her Bridegroom through love, namely, and fear of death. “With one of your eyes.” [Col. 1259A] The Church has many eyes: she is full of eyes before and behind; she sees in every direction and everywhere repels robbers’ ambushes. Yet she has one most splendid eye: she is enlightened by one faith in the Trinity, without which no one will please God. Those who do not have this eye are blind and walk in darkness. [Note: [Col. 1259D] “With one eye and one lock of hair: by this is expressed the unity of holy teachers, and also the unity of the heavenly doctrine that they impart to those subject to them. For, as the Apostle says, there is one Lord, one faith, one baptism, and also one devotion of the faithful subjects.” The same author. “In our hearts,” says Cantacuzenus, “you have sown the most pure splendor of the one threefold subsistence, by which we are taught to worship one God, three in persons, in one essence.”] Hence the Apostle says: “Blindness has happened in part to Israel” (Rom. 11:25).

“And with one lock of hair from your neck.” This is a confirmation. The many hairs are the many examples and sayings of teachers. But why hairs? Because they are subtle and long. One hair, however, is one doctrine, the same among all, from which no Christian dissents: the doctrine preached by the apostles, for which the martyrs shed their blood, and which the holy Fathers [Col. 1259B] confirmed. “How beautiful are your breasts, my sister, my bride!” Beautiful are the breasts, and beautiful also are the children. But the breasts of the Synagogue are not beautiful, because she nourished her children with black milk, most filthy dregs, and an understanding of error.

“Your breasts are fairer than wine.” This is a metonymy. Behold, milk is compared to wine, though it is certainly whiter and sweeter. The Church suckles her own children; the Synagogue intoxicates her illegitimate children. The former, being wisely brought up, quickly grow; the latter, like drunkards, lose their understanding. Of them the Lord himself says: “Those who drank wine sang psalms against me” (Ps. 68:13).—“And the fragrance of your ointments,” that is, of virtues, sayings, and graces. For all these are called ointment [Col. 1259C], because they are sweet and heal the ailments of every weakness. “Above all spices,” that is, beyond all the sacrifices of the Jews. “Your lips are a dripping honeycomb.” For a honeycomb is honey in wax, through which spiritual understanding is signified within the letter. The lips of the Church drip honeycomb, that is, sweet and pleasant words. “Honey and milk are beneath your tongue.” By these every class of humankind is delighted. We may also understand by honey, which is produced from the dew of heaven, spiritual and loftier teaching; of this the Apostle says: “We speak wisdom among the perfect” (1 Cor. 2:6). By milk, however, we understand moderate teaching; hence he himself says: “I gave you milk to drink, not solid food” (1 Cor. 3:2).—“And the fragrance of your garments is like the fragrance of incense.” For the Church has a garment [Col. 1259D] which she herself has drawn out and woven with her own hands: joining virtues to virtues and linking good works with good works, she has fashioned for herself a wonderful robe. In it the bridegroom delights no less than in the very sweet fragrance of abundant incense.

“A garden enclosed [Col. 1260A] is my sister, my bride.” [Note: [Col. 1259D] “The Virgin was called by the Prophet an enclosed garden. A garden indeed, because she brought forth Christ as the fruit [Col. 1260D] of life; enclosed, however, because after childbirth she remained a virgin.” Cantacuzenus.] She is called a garden because, just as it contains diverse kinds of flowers and trees, so it contains diverse orders of saints and faithful persons: the holy apostles, confessors and martyrs, virgins and widows. It is enclosed because it is fortified by the defences of virtues and angels. [Note: [Col. 1260D] “This garden is enclosed because Holy Church is fortified by the help of her Redeemer and Lord, and surrounded by the protection of angelic powers; it lies open to none of the snares of mighty spirits.” The same author, supplement to Cassiodorus.] No gate stands open to vices, through which thieves and enemies may enter, steal, and carry off its goods.

“An enclosed garden, and a sealed fountain.” The fountain is surely baptism in the Church, by which the stains of vices are removed and the blemishes of soul and body are cleansed. Yet in this garden there is a living fountain: whoever drinks its water shall thirst no more. Of this fountain it is said: “My soul thirsted for God, the living fountain” (Ps. 41:3). But why is it sealed, except because it is sanctified and blessed in the name of the Trinity [Col. 1260B]? The fountain is sealed; the water is recognized. To it the saints run; from it both vices and malignant spirits flee. For by this mark the fountain is distinguished from others, because what this one accomplishes, the others cannot accomplish.

“Your shoots are a paradise of 619 pomegranates, with the fruits of orchard-trees.” [Note: [Col. 1260D] “It is surely the grace sent by God to the Virgin through Gabriel the messenger; for she truly opened paradise to us and set before us, for eating, the delights of its fruits.” Cantacuzenus.] The garden which he called above, he here calls paradise, because paradise is a garden of delights. Therefore the Church is called paradise because it is filled with an abundance of every delight. Here is the tree of the knowledge of good and evil, namely the New and Old Testaments, which teach us both to avoid evils and to do good. We also have the forbidden tree, that is, Christ, who is the living bread that came down from heaven. The four rivers of paradise are the four [Col. 1260C] Gospels.

But what are its shoots, what are its gifts, what are its fruits, and who are the flowers which this garden sends to the Lord as fruits of pomegranates? “It sends pomegranates,” he says, “and commends many martyrs to the Lord.” For you apostles are pomegranates, who shed your blood for Christ’s name. “With the fruits of orchard-trees”: it sends not martyrs only, he says, but together with the fruits of other trees it presents pomegranates along with virgins and confessors.

“Cyprus with nard; nard and crocus, calamus and cinnamon, with all the trees of Lebanon; myrrh and aloes, with every finest ointment”—that is, these are in this garden. By these we understand that every kind of spice is found in the holy Church. For by cyprus, from which [Col. 1260D] royal ointment is made, and by nard, which possesses a very sweet and strong fragrance, we can understand all the graces of the Holy Spirit, which surpass all things in sweetness and fragrance. Cyprus is placed with nard because those anointed with the divine and royal ointment are [Col. 1261A] a great and most pleasing fragrance to God. Hence the Apostle says: “We are the good fragrance of Christ to God” (2 Cor. 2:15).

By crocus, calamus, and cinnamon, which are short and do not grow tall, we understand the simple and humble, who, although ordinary people do not honour them, nevertheless possess great virtue and holiness. In them the person is humble, but the virtue exalted. “With all the trees of Lebanon.” By these understand the apostles and prophets, who excel the rest in height, strength, and beauty; for the trees of Lebanon are of great height. Myrrh and aloes, however, which resist decay and worms, signify chastity and other virtues, which preserve both soul and body unharmed from contact with vices. “With every finest” and greatest [Col. 1261B] “ointment”: by these may be signified faith, hope, and charity, which retain primacy for ages of ages.

“A fountain of gardens, a well of living waters.” Here, he says, is the fountain of gardens; here are the apostles and teachers; here is that water by which the whole world is watered. For the many gardens are the many churches. Behold the well of living waters; behold the depth of the Scriptures. For the teaching of the apostles is one, while the error of heretics is dead. Those who drink this water do not die; those who drink that cannot live. Yet they drink from the fountain who merely taste the surface of the Scriptures with the very tips of their lips. They do not draw deeper waters from the well, that is, they do not draw out the more difficult meanings.

“Which flow with force from Lebanon.” With force, he says—that is, with great [Col. 1261C] constancy, power, and abundance—these waters flow. But whence do they flow? From force, from Lebanon, from the white mountain. For Lebanon, as has often been said, is interpreted “whitening.” Christ summons forth graces.

“Arise, north wind, and come, south wind; blow through my garden, and let its spices flow.” Above he spoke of a garden, trees and fruits, a fountain and a well by which it is watered; now he commands the winds to arise, to blow through the garden, and to stir its spices, so that a sweeter fragrance may be returned to him. Winds rose against Christ’s garden when the assaults and rage of tyrants, in persecuting the Church, slaughtered the saints. Then the spices flowed; then the constancy and virtues of the martyrs gave forth their fragrance; then the most sweet [Col. 1261D] odour of a rational burnt offering and a pure sacrifice was borne before the Lord’s presence. [Note: [Col. 1261D] “The Lord knows how to bring certain good things out of human evils, but he holds persecution itself in his power, so that persecutors do not rage as greatly as they wish. Thus it is written: ‘He who made a weight for the winds,’ because he imposes a limit upon the blasts of persecutions.” The same author under the name of Cassiodorus.]

Yet by the north wind, which is a harsh and cold wind, we may understand the cruelty of tyrants. By the south wind, which is serene, the blandishments of deceit are indicated; hence it is said: “His enemies shall lick the earth” (Ps. 71:9).

Verses:

We have called the Church  
the royal Bride of the King,

[Col. 1262A] whose eyes are you, prophets;

you, Peter and Paul, are her strongest teeth,  
who customarily restore her.

Her ever-reddened cheeks  
are indeed the martyrs.

All the imperfect are hairs,  
weak persons of lesser merit,  
because they are unstable like them.

By the neck bearing shields  
we mean the bishops,

who stoutly defend their sheep,  
pursuing vices, lions,  
serpentine furies, and dragons.

It is the safest garden,  
the holiest of saints,

[Col. 1262B] lacking neither lilies nor roses;  
nor are its trees deprived of their fruits.

There is there a fountain of sweetest savour;  
the blasts of winds,

620 the bands of tyrants,  
trouble and stir it violently.  
The martyrs seek heaven with honour;  
the Lord delights in the fragrance.

## CHAPTER V

The Church says of Christ: “Let my beloved come into his garden.” Let my beloved come, she says—my bridegroom, my friend—into his own garden, into his Church, into the assembly of saints. For what purpose? “That he may eat the fruit of his orchard-trees.” Let him eat, she says, the fruit of the orchard; let him receive the sheaf, [Col. 1262C] the service, and the good works of the saints. The fruits are sweet, the trees are shaken, the martyrs are killed. Let the Lord therefore command that their souls be gathered into the heavenly treasury and into Abraham’s bosom.

Christ says: “I have come into my garden, my sister, my bride.” You ask me, he says, to come; but I have already come. [Note: [Col. 1262D] “To the Church, desiring the Bridegroom to come to her, he answers that he has already done this: ‘I have already come.’ I come to her in order to correct those who wander, strengthen weaknesses, confirm those in doubt, and increase the perfect with heavenly gifts.” The same author, supplement to Cassiodorus.]

“I have gathered my myrrh with my spices.” By myrrh we understand martyrs, chaste and incorruptible persons; by spices, the fragrance of good works. Myrrh is with spices when, after carnal desires have been conquered, a person associates only with virtues. Then the flesh is incorrupt; then virtues give forth fragrance; then the Lord commands the saints to come to him [Col. 1262D]. For when the Apostle said, “I desire to be dissolved and to be with Christ” (Phil. 1:23), did he not desire that his myrrh should be gathered?

“I have eaten my honeycomb with my honey.” How great is the sweetness and delight with which God receives his saints is declared in these words. “I have eaten,” he says, “my honeycomb with my honey”: I have received my love; I have welcomed my sweetest and most dearly beloved friends. This is a confirmation. “I have drunk my wine with my milk.” You apostles are the wine, made drunk with the divine cup [Col. 1263A] and possessing every kind of knowledge. The milk, however, is those adorned with moderate and imperfect knowledge. Therefore Christ came into his garden and bore away with himself in surpassing love the myrrh which the wind had blown upon—that is, the saints whom the tyrant had afflicted.

Christ says to the apostles: “Eat, my friends, and drink.” An apostrophe to the apostles. You, he says, are my friends: eat the doctrine of faith and my flesh; drink my blood. “For unless you eat my flesh and drink my blood, you shall not have life in yourselves” (John 6:54). Therefore eat the living bread; drink the cup of the New Testament. “And be intoxicated, dearly beloved.” For whoever is intoxicated by this cup is intoxicated with true knowledge. He who despises riches, desires death [Col. 1263B], forgets himself, disregards what he sees, and believes what he does not see—does he not seem drunk?

“I sleep, and my heart watches.” He slept according to the flesh, because he died and was buried; yet his heart watches, because divinity cannot sleep. This may also be understood thus in the person of the Church: I sleep, with the flesh conquered and subdued; but my heart watches, namely, the soul that perseveres in good works. We may also understand Christ’s apostles by the heart. These watch; these guard the holy Church day and night.

The Church: “The voice of my beloved knocking.” I hear, she says, the voice of my Lord; for he knocks upon his saints lest they sleep, and exhorts them to watch. For he stands at the door and knocks. If anyone opens, he will enter and sup with him.

[Col. 1263C] “Open to me, my sister.” She is his sister because both bridegroom and bride are children of the same Father: he by nature, she by adoption. “My friend,” for whom I did not hesitate to die—than which there is no greater love. “My dove,” without gall or bitterness. “My spotless one,” cleansed of all vices, without spot or wrinkle. Open to me, he says, your heart; open to me the gate through which I may enter both your conscience and that of others, “because my head is full of dew.” This is a confirmation. “And my locks with drops of the night.” [Note: [Col. 1263D] “The head of Christ, as the Apostle says, is God. His locks are the inmost thoughts, which do not flow loosely and disorderedly, but are bound together by the bond of the fear and love of God.” The same author.]

All night, he says, I have run; for your love I have kept watch. “Behold, I stand at the door and knock” (Rev. 3). Open to me, my sister. Christ endured many adversities, in the night, and in death itself, for this love. Hence also that saying: “Moreover, even unto the night my reins reproved me” (Ps. 15:7). It is therefore unjust not to open to him and not to receive so great a bridegroom into the chamber of one’s heart. Spiritually, however, dew upon the head signifies heavenly blessing and the grace of the Holy Spirit in him. Of this it is said [Col. 1264A]: “Like ointment upon the head, which descended upon the beard, the beard of Aaron” (Ps. 132:2).

Voice of the faithful soul. The bride to herself: “I have put off my tunic; how shall I put it on again?” Rightly, she says, you called me spotless, since I have put off my tunic: I have fled my former life, put off the old man, and rejected the world’s desires, the cares of the age, and the vices in which I was wrapped and entangled. I am spotless, and, clothed in the new man, I shall walk in newness of life and shall not again put on that former tunic; I shall not return to worldly things, but shall diligently perform what I have begun.

“I have washed my feet; how shall I defile them?” I have washed my feet, she says, and have driven away those vices in which human frailty most frequently stumbles. For this part 621 of the body, being nearer to the earth [Col. 1264B], is more often defiled. There are certain sins from which scarcely anyone is free: pride of mind, vain glory, idle words, and vain thoughts.

The voice of the Church concerning Christ: “My beloved put his hand through the opening.” [Note: [Col. 1263D] “The beloved puts his hand through the opening and touches the belly when the Creator visits the heart by inward inspiration and kindles it for progress in virtues; or again, when he recalls us to the memory of his works, so that we may consider that, though he was God, he deigned to become man for us.” The same author, supplement to Cassiodorus. [Col. 1264D] Since Cantacuzenus refers these words to the Blessed Virgin, he explains them thus: “By the good pleasure of his will he sent through Gabriel into me his overshadowing power, which he calls a hand. But when the angel’s voice came, as I conceived the Word of the Most High God, my belly was troubled over him; for I said: ‘How shall this be, since I know not a man?’ But when she learned the reason, she said: ‘Behold the handmaid of the Lord; let it be done to me according to your word’ (Luke 2:38).”]

My beloved, she says, put his hand—his teaching, the spirit of his power, and the remembrance itself of his Passion—through the opening and gate of my heart, which is never closed to him.

“And my belly trembled at his touch.” For who is there whom the Lord has touched and inspired with the Holy Spirit, who, recalling his Passion, does not tremble? Hence the saying: “Touch the mountains, and they shall smoke” (Ps. 143:5). Thus the Lord puts his hand through the opening and touches our heart; recalling the Passion, it is gripped by amazement and fear when the Lord suffered such things for servants, the just for the unjust, the Creator for the creature.

“I rose to open to my beloved.” I heard the voice, she says; I rose from the bed of my pleasure and left behind the blandishments of the age. I opened to my beloved: I believed his words and cleansed my heart of vices and error, in which so great a guest was to dwell. Hence it is said through the Psalmist: “At the hearing of the ear he obeyed me” (Ps. 17:45).—“My hands dripped myrrh.” What do hands signify but works? What does myrrh signify but incorruption? Therefore the hands drip myrrh, because good works make both body and soul incorrupt. “And my fingers are full of most excellent myrrh” [Col. 1264D]. What do fingers signify but the distinct performance of particular works: keeping watch, praying, fasting, and the like? These are rightly said to be full of most excellent myrrh, because they mortify the flesh not without great reward and prepare eternal incorruption.

[Col. 1265A] “I opened the bolt of my door to my beloved.” My heart, she says, was greatly hardened, barred with many bolts and fastenings. But after I heard his voice and conceived in my mind the teachings of truth, I opened the whole understanding of my heart and removed every obstacle of error by which my heart had, as it were, been shut with a bolt. [Note: [Col. 1265D] “They open the bolt of the door when the Church, or any faithful soul, prepares its heart for the coming Creator.” The same author, supplement to Cassiodorus.] I opened, indeed, so that I might receive him and understand truly, perfectly, and rationally who he is, what he is, and how he is. But in vain. Why? What follows explains it: “But he had turned aside and passed on.” For when people presume to search out the things of God, he turns away from them and passes on, because there is no way in which he can be comprehended. Hence the saying: “Man shall approach the deep heart, and God shall be exalted” (Ps. [Col. 1265B] 63:7).

“My soul melted when he spoke.” My soul, she says, which was harder than iron and stone, melted at the sound of the bridegroom’s sweetest voice, and, softened like wax, received within itself the writing of evangelical preaching. Thus, when we hear our teachers proclaiming the divine commandments, if we are perhaps pierced by fear and love and dissolve our eyes in tears, then we have a melted soul. But the souls of the Jews are not melted, because their hearts are too hardened to be inscribed by the stylus of the Spirit. This their law, formed upon stones, signified.

“I sought him and did not find him.” Many seek the Lord because they desire both to leave the world, to be freed from necessities, and to be with him. Thus one says: “Would that you would tear open [Col. 1265C] the heavens and come down!” (Isa. 64:1). And the Apostle says: “I desire to be dissolved and to be with Christ” (Phil. 1:23). Yet some seek him and do not immediately find him. “I called, and he did not answer me.” For they call and cry out, asking to be freed from this flesh, and the Lord does not hear them.

“The watchmen who go about the city found me.” The city is the Church; the watchmen are the apostles—the apostles and teachers, I say—who go around the Church and defend it from enemies. “They found me. They struck me,” namely, with the sword of the Spirit. “For the word of God is living and effective, and sharper than every two-edged sword” (Heb. 4:12).—“And they wounded me,” namely, with the fear of compunction and love, and with the teachings [Col. 1265D] of Scripture, which, like very sharp arrows, put the army of enemies to flight.

“The watchmen of the walls took my cloak away from me.” The apostles and teachers took away from me, she says, my cloak—my perverse will and multitude of vices, in which I was wrapped and covered—and clothed me in the garment of faith, in a white and wedding garment.

Apostrophe. “I adjure you, daughters of Jerusalem, if you find my beloved, tell him that I languish with love.” The daughters of Jerusalem signify the souls of the apostles. These have now ascended into Jerusalem [Col. 1266A], dwell with the Lord, and have found the object of their desire. Therefore God’s beloved, namely the Church, which still lives in this world, adjures them to report her love and longing to God. For the faithful are witnesses in heaven.

Verses:

Who is this who knocks at the door,  
breaking the sleep of night?

He calls me: O most beautiful of virgins,  
sister, bride, most splendid jewel,  
rise quickly and open, sweetest one.

I am the Son of the highest King,  
the first and the last,  
who came from heaven into these darknesses,  
suffered death and many injuries,

[Col. 1266B] to free the souls of captives.

At once I left my little bed,  
ran to the bolt,

so that my house might lie open to my beloved  
and my mind might most fully see  
him whom it most desires to see.

But he had already passed from there,  
and had left the door.

What then, what was I, most wretched one, to do?  
Weeping, I followed the young man  
whose hands fashioned man.

The city-watchmen found me,  
stripped me,

took away and gave me a garment;  
they sang to me a new song,

[Col. 1266C] by which I might be led into the King’s palace.

Voice of the Synagogue: “What is your beloved more than another beloved? What is your beloved more than another beloved, O fairest of women?” [Note: [Col. 1265D] “Beloved from beloved is Son from Father, just as [Col. 1266D] God from God, light from light. Or Christ is beloved from beloved in that respect in which he is to be loved, not in that in which he is to be feared.” The same author, supplement to Cassiodorus.] Nobler than the noble, stronger than the strong, wiser than the wise—what is he, I say? Tell what he is, “that you have so adjured us” to report your love for him.

Voice of the Church: “My beloved is white and ruddy.” White indeed, because no stain of vice has discoloured him; ruddy, because he has been stained with his own blood. According to that saying: “Who is this who comes from Edom, with dyed garments from Bozrah?” (Isa. 63:1.) “Chosen from among thousands,” that is, from the whole multitude of angels and human beings. “For who among the clouds shall be compared [Col. 1266D] with the Lord?” (Ps. 88:7.)

“His head is finest gold.” What does the head signify but divinity? Hence the Apostle says: “The head of man is Christ; the head of the woman is the man; and the head of Christ is God” (1 Cor. 11:3). This head is called finest gold because divinity surpasses all things. For what is made cannot be equated with its maker, nor creature with Creator. There are two natures in Christ: one is gold, the other earth—namely, divinity and humanity.

“His locks are like elevated palm branches.” The elevated branches of palms [Col. 1267A] are longer; they always stretch toward higher things and do not lose their greenness. Therefore the multitudes of faithful are elevated palm branches, because they always hasten toward higher things; they do not lose their greenness, cannot wither and die, and, growing from virtue to virtue, ascend to heaven. Of them it is said: “The righteous shall flourish like a palm tree; he shall be multiplied like a cedar of Lebanon” (Ps. 91:13). These are called Christ’s locks because they firmly cling to his faith, which is the head of every man.

“Black as a raven.” Why black? Because they are worn down, troubled, and suffer heat and many adversities. Hence above she said: “I am black, but beautiful.”

“His eyes are like doves,” that is, chaste and simple, neither lifted up nor clouded by anger. By the eyes [Col. 1267B] we understand the graces of the Holy Spirit by which the saints are enlightened. Hence the saying: “I saw a Lamb, as though slain, having seven horns and seven eyes, which are the seven spirits of God sent into all the earth” (Rev. 5:6). We may also understand by the eyes the patriarchs and prophets, to whom the Lord himself says: “You are the light of the world” (Matt. 5:14).—“Above streams of water,” [Note: [Col. 1267D] “They are well compared to doves above streams of water, because the Holy Spirit delights in pure and sincere minds. Doves do not rest above pools and marshes but above streams of water, because the Holy Spirit makes chaste and clean minds his dwelling-place.” The same author.] that is, dwelling there. For the apostles and teachers are above streams of water when they exercise themselves in the volumes of the Scriptures.

“Which are washed with milk.” Otherwise simple people and little children cannot drink from them. Therefore, because they are washed with milk, both wise and unlearned use them, because they contain in themselves the primacy of every branch of knowledge [Col. 1267C].

“His cheeks are beds of spices, planted by perfumers.” His cheeks, he says, are fragrant and pleasant to see. But what do cheeks signify except the knowledge we have of Christ? Hence the Apostle says: “He manifests through us the fragrance of his knowledge in every place” (2 Cor. 2:14). For what fragrance is sweeter, and what delight greater, than to possess knowledge of Christ? Therefore Christ’s cheeks are the forms of knowledge—those, namely, which appear concerning him and can be seen and understood—like collections of spices arranged and ordered by perfumers. [Note: [Col. 1267D] “These beds were prepared by perfumers. The perfumers are prophets or apostles, because the former described all these things as future, the latter as already accomplished.” The same author.]

“His lips, lips dripping first myrrh.” Christ’s lips were lips when, preaching baptism, he said: “You must be born again” (John 3:7). [Col. 1267D] Likewise: “Unless one is born again of water and the Holy Spirit, he cannot see the kingdom of God” (ibid., 5). When he said these things, lilies gave forth fragrance and beauty. But his lips dripped myrrh—mortification of the flesh and the incorruption of the whole human being—[Col. 1268A] [Note: [Col. 1267D] The authors cited above agree in this interpretation.] when he exhorted his disciples to be strong and fear nothing, saying: “Do not fear those who kill the body but cannot kill the soul” (Matt. 10:8); “Blessed are those who suffer persecution for righteousness’ sake” (Matt. 5:10); “If they persecuted me, they will persecute you also” (John 15:20); and likewise, “Whoever wishes to come after me, let him deny himself, take up his cross, and follow me” (Matt. 16:24).

“His hands are rounded, full of hyacinths.” Why rounded, except because he arranges and works all things regularly, easily, and in right order? He is the best craftsman; his skilled hands know how to paint well, sculpt well, and turn vessels most excellently. Why, moreover, are they golden, except because his works excel all others? For as [Col. 1268B] gold surpasses other metals, so God’s work surpasses all things. But why are they said to be full of hyacinths? The hyacinth is a stone of sky-blue colour, or alternatively a flower of purple appearance. Therefore the Lord’s hands are full of hyacinths: either because his work arouses us toward heavenly kingdoms—“For his invisible things,” as the Apostle says, “are clearly seen from the creation of the world, being understood through the things that are made” (Rom. 1:20)—or because of the blood from the nails. For blood and purple are of the same colour. The Lord’s hands are also full of hyacinths because all his works come about with admirable distinction. Thus he himself says that “not even Solomon in all his glory was clothed like one of these” (Matt. 6:29), when he was speaking of lilies.

“His belly is ivory.” [Col. 1268C] His belly, he says—his humanity and flesh—the man Christ born of the Virgin, is ivory: white, strong, and chaste. Mary’s belly is ivory, and Christ’s is ivory: both white, both strong and chaste.

“Adorned with sapphires.” The sapphire is a stone having the colour of the clear sky. Therefore Christ’s belly was adorned with sapphires, because the Word made flesh did at one time heavenly things as God, and at another human things as true man. [Note: [Col. 1268D] “By the sapphires, therefore, are understood the works of divine majesty which he performed in the flesh. The bridegroom’s belly was adorned with sapphires, but so adorned that the whiteness of ivory appeared among the sapphires. Thus the Lord performed those things which belonged to divinity without failing to perform those which belonged to humanity; and again he performed those which belonged to humanity without setting aside those which belonged to divinity. For in Christ the operation of divinity and humanity is distinct.” The same author, supplement to Cassiodorus.] Thus, because he is called a belly, man and earth are understood; but because he is called a sapphire, which we have said has a heavenly colour, he who came down from heaven is indicated.

[Col. 1268D] “His legs are marble columns.” By legs we understand paths and journeys; this is the cause for the effect. His legs—that is, his paths and journeys—are not weak, he says. They are not a reed shaken by the wind, but columns. What sort of columns? Surely marble ones: they can indeed be broken [Col. 1269A], but cannot be bent. Christ could be killed, but there was no power capable of turning him from his intended will.

“Founded upon bases of gold”: namely, faith in those things which God has taught us, and firmness of wisdom. For Christ’s divinity both governed and sustained the humanity he had assumed. We may also signify by the journeys the incarnation, Passion, resurrection, and ascension. These are said to be founded upon golden bases because before the foundation of the world they rested in the providence and counsel of the Father—which is surely a golden foundation. Hence he himself said: “You would have no power over me unless it had been given you from above” (John 19:11). This is as though he said: My foundation is most firm, and it will not allow me to be killed unless I myself will it.

“His appearance is like Lebanon, chosen like cedars.” For that mountain surpasses all the mountains of that land in height, while the majesty of Christ’s mountain fills and contains all things. Indeed, Lebanon is called “whitening,” and Christ is more beautiful in form than the children of men. Therefore his appearance is like Lebanon: lofty, beautiful, and surpassing all things. “Chosen like cedars.” The cedar is said to be a tree lofty, fragrant, beautiful, and incorruptible in nature. All these things suit Christ.

“His throat is sweet,” that is, the words which proceed from his mouth are delightful and sweet, sweeter than all honey. But why linger over individual things? “And he is altogether desirable.” I shall leave particulars; I shall say all things briefly and summarily. What shall I say? My friend is altogether desirable; he is altogether lovable. Therefore let us love him not in word but in deed and truth, with the whole heart, the whole mind, and the entire intention of the heart. “Such is my beloved,” to whom I have been betrothed with a faithful ring and joined by surpassing love and affection; “and he,” and no other—not a Jew, not a heretic—“is my friend, daughters of Jerusalem.” Truly he is a friend, because he shed his blood for her; and no love can be greater.

Verses:

Why inquire what he is like,  
when there is none such as he,

whose equal are the Father  
and the sovereign Spirit,  
God and man?

His head is pure gold,  
the light and splendour of souls;  
his locks are elevated palms,  
wondrously adorned with flowers,  
typically, the saints.

His eyes are not lifted up,  
but resemble doves,  
who above streams of water  
and the currents of Scripture  
always remain.

His cheeks are pleasant, 624  
burdensome to none who look upon them;  
his lips are exceedingly beautiful;

[Col. 1270A] myrrh drips from them.  
What more should I add?

His hands are golden,  
his belly ivory;  
this is adorned with sapphires,  
those are full of hyacinths:  
he knows all things.

His legs are of marble  
in their stability,  
very solid and hard,  
in no way to be broken:  
believe me.

Exalted like a cedar,  
white as Lebanon,  
he fills all things with majesty,

[Col. 1270B] and gives fragrance to all,  
God of gods.

His words are sweet,  
ever true and plain;  
they are tested by fire  
and approved by the Fathers,  
like silver.

Such is my beloved,  
and this is my friend.  
Because we cannot expound  
all his praises,  
this shall be the end.

## CHAPTER VI

“Where has your beloved gone, O fairest of women? Where has your beloved turned aside, that we may seek him [Col. 1270C] with you?” For those who speak here are imperfect; therefore, as though ignorant, they ask where God is, where he has turned aside, and in what place he died.

“My beloved has gone down into his garden.” What is it, she says, that you seek? Do you not know that my beloved has gone down into his garden? He indeed came into his garden and visited me, his bride and friend. Indeed, he said: “I will not leave you, nor forsake you.” Therefore, since he came into the world, since he joined me to himself with the bond of love, he is with me and dwells with me. He went to the Father, but did not leave me; he ascended to heaven, but did not forsake me. Therefore do not say, O man, “Where has he gone?” Do not say, “Where has he turned aside?” Do you wish to seek him with me? Make yourself able to perceive with me: do what I do; keep watch as I do. Take oil with you if you wish to ascend with me. You say, “I have none”; then you will not go farther with me. Therefore keep watch with lamps lit, so that you may joyfully meet him when he comes.

Why the Church is called a garden has already been said above. “To a bed of spices.” To a bed of spices, she says. By a bed is understood any faithful soul which, cultivated by heavenly discipline, carefully ordered, and adorned by equality of sides—that is, by the four chief virtues—cultivates in holy actions many spices to be burned for God.

“To feed among the gardens.” Do you wish to become a garden? You say, “I do.” Cleanse your heart, then; remove thorns and briars. Make your soul bloom; make it flourish with lilies and roses—with chastity and simplicity and the other virtues. [Col. 1271A] Then he will feed in your garden; then he will come, he who said: “If anyone opens [the door], I shall enter and dine with him, and he with me” (Rev. III.20).—“And gather lilies [Note: [Col. 1271D] ‘For he feeds upon our good deeds, so much so that he himself is refreshed in the poor. And “gather lilies” means: that he may bring holy souls, through the maturity of virtue, to perfect whiteness; gather them to himself out of this world; and make them rejoice with him in eternal blessedness.’ Same author; Cassiodorus, supplement.].” For God continually gathers lilies, continually joins souls to himself. For we know that the people are grass; and grass is baptized, from which God gathers lilies. You have vowed to serve God; you have promised to serve God in chastity and humility, patience and sobriety. These are the lilies which you present to God; these are the lilies which the Lord gathers.

“I am for my beloved, and my beloved is for me.” “I,” she says, “serve my beloved and obey him in all things, and prepare a place for his dwelling within me. And my beloved assists me, grants the rewards of service, and brings himself as a guest into me.” “Who feeds among the lilies”: that is, [Col. 1271B] he delights in the fragrance of virtues and the beauty of souls.

The bridegroom’s voice: “You are beautiful, my friend, sweet and lovely as Jerusalem.” Beautiful indeed, because you have been baptized. “But sweet and lovely as Jerusalem.” For Jerusalem is interpreted “vision of peace.” Rightly, therefore, the Church is called sweet like Jerusalem, since it knows and beholds peace, pursues peace, and believes in peace. [Note: [Col. 1271D] “The Church still on earth, or every faithful soul [Col. 1272D], is sweet and lovely in the likeness of that Jerusalem, because it imitates that peace as far as it is able.” Same author.] Hence it is written: “And his place came to be in peace” (Ps. LXXV.3). But because the heavenly Jerusalem is a daughter, the Church is said to possess its beauty and loveliness; concerning it the Apostle says: “That Jerusalem which is above is free; it is our mother” (Gal. IV.26).—“Terrible [Col. 1271C] as an army arrayed in battle-order.” Terrible indeed, because armed with faith and hope and the other virtues, she drives away the snares of evil spirits. Peter was terrible, and Paul too was terrible. For Peter commanded Ananias and his wife to die; Paul handed the adulterer over to Satan. The other saints were likewise terrible, who compelled evil spirits to depart from possessed bodies.

But why is she called like an army arrayed in battle-order? The ranks of an army are so arranged that each person, stationed in his own place, defends the position entrusted to him. So it is also in the Church. The bishop stands before the gates, lest the wolf enter and carry off the sheep. 625 But why say more? Each fights in his own rank. Teachers fight; the continent fight; married people fight as well. They are skilled in battle; [Col. 1271D] they destroy vices and overthrow evil spirits.

“Turn your eyes away from me, because they have made me fly away from you.” Since the Church, opening the bolt of her door above, wished to receive Christ within herself and began too greatly to probe the secrets of his divinity, she is therefore told here: “Turn your eyes away from me.” Hence the Apostle commanded that one should “not think more highly than one ought to think” (Rom. XII.3). Let us, therefore, [Col. 1272A] turn our eyes away; and let him who is of the earth speak of the earth. Let no one attempt to comprehend what is incomprehensible. “Because they have made me fly away from you.” For the more deeply it is investigated, the more divine wisdom escapes human minds. God escaped Arius; he escaped Sabellius; he escaped many other heretics also, because they looked upon him with oblique eyes and disputed, with carnal perception and human reason, about matters which they cannot know except by divine inspiration.

“Your hair is like flocks of goats that come up from Mount Gilead.” “Your hair,” he says—your judgments and thoughts, the multitudes of believers—like flocks of goats, always seek higher things and desire to be filled with heavenly food. And because “every good gift and every perfect gift [Col. 1272B] is from above, coming down from the Father of lights” (Jas. I.17), they despise earthly food, await food coming to them from heaven, and indeed offer themselves to the Lord. “Which appeared from Mount Gilead.” Gilead is interpreted “heap of testimony.” Why, then, these two Testaments are called Gilead is plainly evident.

“Your teeth are like flocks of shorn sheep which came up from the washing; all bearing twins, and none barren among them. Like the rind of a pomegranate are your cheeks, apart from your eyes.” The Lord praises his bride, and praises her in the same words as above; and he finds nothing else to rebuke in her except that she gazes upon him and strives with her eyes to discern things which human sight cannot see. Therefore he cries out again:

[Col. 1272C] “Turn your eyes away from me.” Do not look upon me as though I were localized, measurable, or possessed of some bodily form. I am eternal, immeasurable, incomprehensible. “No human being shall see me and live” (Exod. XXXIII.20).—“There are sixty queens.” What do the queens signify but apostles and teachers, who govern and teach others? [Note: [Col. 1272D] “The queens are teachers of the holy Church, who, by the merit of faith and knowledge, draw near to the bed of the eternal King and bear spiritual children for God.” Pseudo-Cassiodorus.] But why sixty? The number sixty is made up of six and ten: six times ten, or ten times six, makes sixty. Since God completed his work in six days, we rightly understand six as the perfection of works; while ten signifies the ten legal commandments. Thus Christ’s queens are sixty, because in the Church rulers are found who are [Col. 1272D] perfect in works and wise in the ordinances of the Law.

“Eighty concubines.” Concubines are understood to be those who, under the appearance of friendship, ruin the house of a friend, scatter his goods, deceitfully enter the bridal chamber of his lawful wife, and most greedily violate it. But why eighty? This number is made from eight and ten: eight times ten, or ten times eight, makes eighty. [Col. 1273A] These also preach the ten commandments of the Law, but not out of charity, so that they do not do what they preach. These are those of whom it is said: “They bind heavy and unbearable burdens and lay them upon people’s shoulders, but they are unwilling to move them with their finger” (Matt. XXIII.4). These are those who adulterate the word of God. Yet they are not found in the six days, because, given over to idleness, they do not exercise themselves in good works. Nor indeed will they have sabbatical rest or repose, since they have passed beyond the seventh day. But they will come to the eighth, in which the resurrection will take place. “For all of us, whether good or evil, shall stand before the tribunal of Christ” (Rom. XIV.10). Of this eighth day it is said: “Why should I fear on the evil day? The iniquity of my heel will surround me” (Ps. XLVIII.6), that is, on [Col. 1273B] the day when the wicked enter into eternity. Therefore there are eighty concubines, because many preach the Law who will be condemned in judgment on the eighth day.

Many monks and bishops, then, will be condemned: though good things flow from their lips and mouths, they keep vices within; and in judgment they will hear: “Go, you cursed, into eternal fire” (Matt. XXV.41). This word is also spoken to monks who remain alone and do not rightly employ what they possess; without doubt they will perish eternally.

“And there is no number of maidens.” What do the maidens signify but all believers regenerated by the water of baptism? [Note: [Col. 1273D] “Having been joined only once to Christ through divine baptism, he rightly called them maidens beyond number, both because of their multitude and because they fill all the ends of the earth.” Cantacuzenus.] Of them it is said: “Your youth shall be renewed like the eagle’s” (Ps. CII.5). Their number is known only to him who numbers the stars. [Note: [Col. 1273D] “The number of souls believing in Christ is infinite and cannot be comprehended by any human being. Yet all the elect are numbered by God.” Same author; Cassiodorus, supplement.]

[Col. 1273C] “My dove is one.” “There are many queens,” he says, “and many concubines also. Yet my dove is one”: that is, the holy and universal Church, which has one God, 626 one faith, one baptism, one will—that is, one heart and the same soul. She is truly called a dove because she is simple, spiritual, humble, and meek. “My perfect one,” to whom the number six most certainly belongs, since she does not cease from my works. “She is the one of her mother”: that is, the sole and singular daughter of the heavenly Jerusalem. “Chosen by her who bore her.” For just as she loves that heavenly homeland, so the heavenly homeland loves her. We are therefore children of earth according to the flesh, but children of heaven according to the soul. This [Col. 1273D] is earthly; that, however, is heavenly. [Note: [Col. 1273D] “This Church, therefore, is the one of her mother, because in this pilgrimage she is instructed and formed after the example of that Church which already enjoys Christ, and strives to attain that blessedness in which she reigns with [Col. 1274D] Christ.” Same author under the name of Cassiodorus.] Let us therefore serve not our earthly mother, but rather the heavenly one.

“The daughters saw her,” that is, the aforesaid maidens, [Col. 1274A] “and proclaimed her most blessed” (Prov. XXXI.28). For which prophet, apostle, or teacher of the Church has not proclaimed her blessedness? Which saint has not related her felicity? The implied answer is: none. “The queens and concubines praised her.” For the apostles and teachers praised her. Indeed, heretics and pseudo-apostles too exalted her with praises. Even now many concubines, many false preachers, many priests of deities rather than of God, praise the Church. For she is the one who, consisting of many persons of the faithful, makes the Church catholic—that is, universal.

Verses:

> You are beautiful, my sweet beloved,  
> Clothed all about in beautiful garments.  
>
> You have armies well armed,  
> Well arrayed, so that they cannot be conquered.  
>
> I gave you twin eyes  
> By which you may behold me.  
>
> I cannot be seen  
> By the eyes of heretics and philosophers.  
>
> I have sixty queens,  
> And indeed eighty concubines;  
>
> Maidens may be loved, may be praised,  
> But cannot be numbered.  
>
> Yet my dove is one;  
> My love for her is one.  
>
> Very many daughters both saw her and knew her,  
> And praised her.

“Who is this who comes forth like the rising dawn?” [Col. 1274C] “Who,” he says, “what kind, how beautiful is this woman who comes forth? She does not linger in idleness, but ascends to me, passing from virtue to virtue; with her greatness she fills the world and spreads abroad throughout all lands.” “Like the rising dawn,” shining with virtues, radiant with serenity, announcing to all nations the true and supreme Day. “Beautiful as the moon,” because she is illumined by the light of her brother and bridegroom alone. [Note: [Col. 1274D] “Natural philosophers maintain that the moon is illumined by the sun. The Church is beautiful as the moon because she is illumined by the brightness of her bridegroom Christ, so that she may shine with his grace.” Same author.]

“Chosen as the sun.” What is chosen is preferred to other things. The Church, then, is chosen because she imitates the sun’s radiance. Indeed, since Christ is called the sun and the Church the moon, she is rightly called chosen as the sun. For just as the Church chose the sun, so Christ our Lord, the Sun of righteousness, chose the Church. [Col. 1274D] [Note: [Col. 1274D] Cantacuzenus interprets this as a prophecy concerning the Blessed Virgin: “Struck with amazement at the excellence of the undefiled Mother of the Word of God: ‘Who is this,’ he says, ‘who bends herself like the dawn?’ For just as, at the approach of sunlight, the darkness of night withdraws, so at the splendor of the pure Virgin the darkness of sin withdrew. ‘Chosen as the sun.’ It is not absurd for her to be called both moon [Col. 1275D] and sun: sun indeed because she received the Word of God and the Father; a perfect moon, overflowing beyond measure, as the sun is in its own body.”] Hence it is said: “With the chosen you shall be chosen” (Ps. XVII.17).

—“Terrible.” Why terrible? Because prudent, strong, wise, and “like [Col. 1275A] an army arrayed in battle-order.” She is always watchful, always armed, never unguarded. Therefore she says: “You have girded me with strength for battle, and have cast beneath me those who rose up against me” (Ps. XVII.40).

—“I went down into the garden of nuts.” What does the garden of nuts signify but the Church? Why the Church is called a garden has already been stated above; but why nuts? For the walnut gives off a pleasant scent. Its fruit is covered by a double shell. The outer covering is bitter; the second is tough and hard. But what lies hidden within is sweet and pleasant. So the Church has an outer garment—namely, flesh—bitter, wretched, tearful, rough, and hairy. Beneath it is covered that strong, white, and unique garment which she herself wove with her own hands: [Col. 1275B] joining virtues to virtues and linking good works to good works, she fashioned for herself a wonderful garment. Clothed in it, she despises the arrows of enemies. Beneath this is hidden the soul, of wondrous sweetness and delight, free from all gall and bitterness.

“To see the fruits of the valleys.” Christ descended into this garden. But why did he descend? To see the fruits of the valleys, that is, the humility and patience of the faithful. Of this valley it is said: “Every valley shall be filled” (Luke III.5). He descended into the garden, saw the valley, and recognized and chose the humble. “And to see whether the vine had blossomed.” God’s vine blossoms when the saints prepare themselves for good work. “And whether the pomegranates had budded.” [Col. 1275C] Pomegranates are martyrs; pomegranates are virgins; pomegranates are all who blush for their sins. These 627 always bud; they produce and nourish not thorns and briars, but flowers and virtues.

“I did not know.” The voice of the Synagogue: “You came,” she says, “into the garden. But I did not know; I was ignorant of your coming.” Why this? Because “my soul troubled me”—and this “because of the chariots of Amminadab.” “I saw Amminadab,” she says, “and saw and heard Christ.” For Amminadab is interpreted “the willing one of his people.” Christ, then, is Amminadab, since he did not hesitate to pour out his own blood for us. [Note: [Col. 1275D] “Amminadab was the great-great-grandson of Judah, through whom Christ’s genealogy is traced. Amminadab is interpreted ‘the willing one of my people’; therefore he signifies Christ, who was the willing one of his people, because, though he is God, he willingly became man; though he was Maker and Creator, by his goodness alone he became the portion of his people.” Same author; Cassiodorus, supplement.]

The Synagogue saw his chariots. She saw Mary, who bore him in her womb and in her arms. She also saw the very flesh in which the Lord lay hidden. She saw the apostles, [Col. 1275D] whom Christ governed and directed as a good charioteer. Hence it is said: “You shall ride upon your horses, and your chariots are salvation” (Hab. III.8). The Synagogue saw this and was troubled. She was troubled because of Mary, and troubled also because of [Col. 1276A] the flesh, since she said that God could neither be human nor have a mother. She heard the apostles preaching and was troubled because they seemed to speak against the Law. For they preached “Christ crucified: to Jews indeed a stumbling block, but to Gentiles foolishness” (1 Cor. I.23).

The Church’s consoling voice: “Return, return, Shulammite; return, return, that we may behold you.” [Note: [Col. 1275D] “This is the voice of the Church inviting the Synagogue to faith: [Col. 1276D] ‘Return, O Synagogue, from unbelief to faith; return from hatred to love.’ Shulammite is interpreted ‘captive’ or ‘despised.’ Such was the Synagogue before Christ’s coming: captive, namely, in the bond of the devil, and despised by God because she did not recognize Christ, sent for her salvation.” Same author.]

The voice of the chariots—that is, of the apostles: “You, O Synagogue, being foolish and heedless, did not recognize him who descended into the garden; nor did you lose your hardness because of the sound of his chariots. But you, Shulammite, you people of the Gentiles, you Church, return.” Where? To the Lord, to the homeland, to the promised inheritance. Shulammite, however, is interpreted “captive” or “despised.” [Col. 1276B] The Church, formerly despised, has now been chosen by her husband. Rachel signified this. She is captive because, captured in battle, she was carried away by evil spirits. “Return” is said four times because there are four Gospels, which never cease to say, “Return, return.” For they always admonish us to return, to do penance, and to return to the Lord. “That we may behold you”: that you may not be submerged in darkness, but that we may see you with us in the heavenly Jerusalem, and behold your beauty for ever.

## Chapter VII

“What will you see in the Shulammite but the choruses of the camps?” For, as is customary, the choruses of camps rejoice and sing; they adorn the camps, polish their weapons, fortify their defenses, and equip themselves for courage and boldness. [Col. 1276C] In the Church, however, the praise of exultation and confession resounds; the flesh is understood as the horse of the soul and is adorned with virtues; the weapons and meanings of the Scriptures are made clear; and one person encourages another to God’s service.

Christ’s voice to the Church: “How beautiful are your steps in sandals, daughter of a prince!” [Note: [Col. 1276D] “From this point the bridegroom begins to set forth the praises of his bride. Notice that he begins to weave her beauty from her steps and ends in her praises, just as above he had begun with her eyes.” Same author.] Beautiful are your steps; beautiful your gait; beautiful also your action. Hence the Apostle says: “Let us walk honorably, as in the day” (Rom. XIII.13).—“In sandals.” “You are shod,” he says; “you are prepared to make the journey. Above you said, ‘I have washed my feet’; now, however, you are shod, lest they be defiled.” For patience shoes our feet, because it did not hesitate to shed the blood of the innocent and does not merely suffer. We may also understand the sandals as the examples of prophets who have died. Thus this king’s daughter, this daughter of the eternal Prince, is shod.

“The joints of your thighs are like necklaces, which have been fashioned [Col. 1277A] by the hand of an artisan.” What do the thighs signify but the generation of children? For generation occurs in the thighs. Hence Abraham made his servant swear upon his thigh, because he knew that Christ would come forth from it; and those who fear God do not dare to swear vainly by his name. Let it therefore be said: “The joints of your thighs are to you like necklaces”: that is, the union, love, and concord of your children. For children are a mother’s glory, and she is adorned by no necklaces more than by children, if she has them well behaved. And the greater glory ought to be found in them, insofar as a work established by the hand of a higher Artisan is worthier and more beautiful.

“Your navel is a rounded bowl.” [Note: [Col. 1277D] Cantacuzenus also explains this passage differently and excellently: “From the time,” says our Savior, “when the Word became flesh and gave his blood to the faithful as drink, from that time, I say, the bowl has not been lacking in the Churches throughout the world; indeed, it is daily filled with sacred, unbloody sacrifices, with life-giving and divine blood.”] What does the navel signify but the apostles? But 628 why the navel? Just as the navel occupies [Col. 1277B] the middle of the belly, so the apostles hold a place in the middle of the Church, according to the text: “In the midst of the Church he shall open his mouth” (Ecclus. XV.5). The apostles, therefore, are the navel. But why a bowl? Because they are filled with living water, heavenly nectar, and the overflowing abundance of all the Scriptures. Why rounded? What is made on a lathe does not depart from rule and order. Therefore the apostles are rounded: they always preserve the rule of truth; they are well-rounded, they are sound; no roughness, no obstacle worthy of offense can be found in them. “Never lacking cups,” because it is always full, always overflows, and always offers the cup of salvation to the thirsty.

“Your belly is like a heap of wheat.” By the belly we understand the multitude of subjects and the imperfect. [Col. 1277C] All the body’s limbs serve the belly: the feet carry it, the teeth nourish it, and the eyes guide it. So too preachers support, nourish, and enlighten the Church. The imperfect are called the belly because they are softer and less perfected. They are compared to a heap of wheat because they are numerous and have proceeded from one. Hence the Lord himself says: “Unless a grain of wheat falls into the earth and dies, it remains alone; but if it dies, it bears much fruit” (John XII.24). Therefore this grain of wheat fell into the earth, came into Mary, and from it arose that multitude of believers which in this place is called a heap of wheat. “Surrounded by lilies”: surrounded by virtues and the prayers of teachers.

[Col. 1277D] “Your two breasts are two twin fawns of a doe.” The two breasts are the two Testaments. But the one doe is the one Church, which always seeks higher things and awaits heavenly food from above. The two fawns are the two peoples, namely Jewish and Gentile. Therefore, as many breasts, so many children.

Christ’s voice: [Col. 1278A] “Your neck is like an ivory tower.” The neck, eyes, and nose are called the apostles. The neck, because they bear the shield, nourish the Church, and utter the words of doctrine; the eyes, because they enlighten the blind; the nose, because they discern both the fragrance of the sacred Law and virtues and the stench of the perverse teaching of heretics and of vices. The Church’s neck—that is, every preacher—ought to be a tower, the refuge of others and a lofty defense. Hence the text: “A tower of strength from the face of the enemy” (Ps. LX.4). Let it be ivory—that is, chaste, white, and strong.

“Your eyes are like pools in Heshbon.” Heshbon is interpreted “girdle of sorrow” or “city of multitude.” The Church contains many within herself and girds and binds many; she prepares many effeminate persons, [Col. 1278B] their garments girded up, for manly strength; many who are unbridled and dissipated, lest they wander through vain things, she restrains with bit and bridle. [Note: [Col. 1277D] “Heshbon is called the daughter of multitude, in the literal sense, because of the multitude of peoples gathering there. So too the holy Church is rightly called [Col. 1278D] daughter of multitude, because daily it gathers a great number of nations. Heshbon is interpreted ‘girdle of sorrow,’” etc. Cassiodorus, supplement.] By the pools in the Church we understand the font of baptism. In them fishers raise and catch many fish. Thus the eyes of the Church—that is, holy preachers—are clear and bright like the pools in Heshbon, especially since their preaching is the purification of souls. For those who are cleansed once in baptism must be cleansed many times by teachers. “Which are at the gates of the daughter of multitude.” The Church is called daughter of multitude because she does not cease daily to bear a multitude of children. These pools are at her gates, because no one enters her unless first baptized. Do you wish [Col. 1278C] to enter the city? Go down into the pool. Do you wish to be joined to the Church? Be baptized and believe.

“Your nose is like the tower of Lebanon.” Lebanon, interpreted “whitening,” and surpassing all the mountains of that province, signifies Christ. On this mountain, on the firmness of this stone, that tower is situated, that congregation of apostles is founded, which looks down from above upon and protects the whole Church. Hence bishops are called *episcopi*, as it were “those who see from above.” The tower, then, is lofty, and lofty also is its foundation. It does not fear stench, nor dread disturbances of the air. It seeks heavenly things and does not lie in the mire of vices. “Which looks toward Damascus”: that is, toward the devil and his angels. Damascus [Col. 1278D] is interpreted “drinking of blood.” Therefore the tower of God should look toward Damascus: that is, toward those who thirst for the blood of saints. For on the side from which danger is more feared, more watchmen must be stationed.

“Your head is like Carmel.” [Note: [Col. 1278D] “By the Church’s head is understood the ruling faculty of the faithful’s mind. For as the members are governed by the head, so thoughts are ordered by the mind. The Church’s head is rightly compared to Carmel because it knows that circumcision, once observed bodily, must now be observed spiritually,” etc. Same author.] What does the head signify but heart and understanding? As the head holds primacy in [Col. 1279A] the body, so understanding holds primacy in the soul. Carmel is interpreted “thought of circumcision.” The Church’s head, then, is like Carmel: great and lofty; it knows not lowly or carnal things, but heavenly and spiritual things. It follows not the letter that kills, but the Spirit who gives life; it has learned circumcision not of the flesh but of the heart.

“And the locks of your head are like the king’s purple, bound to the channels.” If the head is understanding, what are the locks of the head but thoughts adhering to the understanding? They are compared to purple because they continually blush for sins and love the shedding of blood for Christ. Kings do not glory more in purple than saints do in the clothing of such thoughts. This is the garment and purple of the saints: with these they are covered, with these [Col. 1279B] they are adorned. These are bound to the channels; they continually await washing and purification. Let the saints, therefore, have lofty understanding; let them be clothed and adorned with good thoughts; let them continually desire the purification of souls.

“How beautiful you are, and how lovely, dearest one, in delights!” What delights? Those of spiritual grace—that is, divine wisdom and heavenly joys. “Your stature,” that is, your perfect and lofty steadfastness, “is likened to a palm tree,” because it stands firm and straight and is never bent aside by winds; its branches are tall, its fruit sweet, and its greenness eternal. The palm belongs to victors; victory does not depart from the Church. “And your breasts [are] clusters,” that is, teachers or the twin Testaments, which at one time offer us milk, at another pure wine. Those who are intoxicated by this wine forget earthly things.

Verses:

> Return to your God, O Shulammite;  
> Believe the faithful words of the apostles:  
> Come, return.  
>
> Your feet are beautiful in sandals,  
> And your words in the examples of the prophets,  
> O daughter of the prince.  
>
> What shall I say of the joining of your thighs,  
> By which you are adorned through the merits of your children,  
> As with necklaces?  
>
> By the navel are described all those  
> Who speak spiritual things  
> In the midst of the Churches.  
>
> Your belly is called a heap of wheat,  
> From the one grain which is always multiplied,  
> Surrounded by lilies.  
>
> Neck, nose, and eyes are teachers,  
> Who feed the belly, drive away darkness and stenches,  
> Weighty in knowledge.

Christ or the Church: “I said: I will climb the palm tree.” For Christ said this; he foreknew beforehand [Col. 1280A] that he was about to ascend the palm tree and the Virgin, and the cross. The palm is Mary, because she is ever green and a virgin. The palm is the cross, because it is the instrument of victory. It always grows, always remains green; its praise is eternal, its power never grows old. “And I shall grasp its fruits [Note: [Col. 1279D] ‘That is, I shall reward the fruit of good works and labours in which the Church toils. Or again, according to the sense in which the cross is understood by the palm tree: that is, when the triumph of the Passion has been accomplished, I shall come to the glory of the Resurrection.’ Same author.].” Mary’s womb bore fruit, namely the renewal of the world. Christ’s cross also bore fruit, because, crimsoned by his blood, it made the dead live. You are this fruit: apostles, martyrs, and confessors. O palm tree! O victorious and wonderful tree, adorned with such great fruits! Christ climbed the palm tree and grasped its fruits, because he drew all things to himself. “And your breasts shall be like clusters of the vine.” For the breasts of the Church contain both wine and milk: with milk they nourish the simple; with wine they intoxicate the wise. [Col. 1280B] With this milk the Church nourishes her children; with this wine she gladdens both minds and hearts. This wine gives wisdom; these fruitful cups made the tongues of children eloquent. “And your scents like those of apples,” that is, pleasing and sweet. The scent is pleasant; the fruits are delightful. The utterances are sweet and weighty. The Church speaks: “Your throat is like the finest wine; your words are sweet and pleasant.” They are wine, but the finest wine, because, even if they are profound, they nevertheless proclaim sweetness and joy: they preach not death but life. For you do not will the sinner’s death, but life. Moses indeed gave wine when he said, “Eye for eye, tooth for tooth” (Deut. 19:21). But this wine seems harsh and bitter to drink. “Worthy for my beloved to drink.” [Col. 1280C] It is worthy, she says, this life-giving wine, so sweet and so pleasant; let my beloved drink it. It is worthy that words so honeyed should distil from his mouth. For from this throat, from this precious vessel, came forth that wine by which the Church is intoxicated. She tasted the wine and praises both the cupbearer and the wine. And as though asked whether the wine were good, she replied that it was worthy of the king. “And for his lips and teeth to chew.” What are meant by lips and teeth but apostles and teachers? These are they who both drink and chew over the wine aforesaid. These are they who subtly investigate the divine mysteries. For to chew wine is continually to turn over God’s testimonies both on the lips and in the heart [Note: [Col. 1279D] “Holy teachers chew the spiritual wine when they carefully examine the evangelical precepts, [Col. 1280D] investigate them by frequent meditation, and compare them with one another.” Same author.]. Hence the Apostle says: “Pray without ceasing” (1 Thess. 5:17).

[Col. 1280D] The bride concerning the bridegroom: “I am for my beloved, and his turning is toward me.” “I,” she says, “speak to my beloved and confess my desires to him; but he turns toward me, answers me, and hears me.” “Come, my beloved.” 630 This is the voice of the prophets and of all those who awaited Christ’s coming [Note: [Col. 1280D] “This may also be the voice of the Synagogue, speaking in the person of the holy Fathers who longed for Christ’s advent, in accordance with the Psalmist, Psalm 79:3: ‘Stir up your power and come’; and Isaiah 6:1: ‘Would that you would rend the heavens and come down.’” Same author.]. “Come, my beloved;” look upon the lands, take flesh. “Let us go out into the field,” that we may root out thorns and thistles from it. Let us cultivate the field; let us preach to the nations; let him who sows go out to sow his seed. [Col. 1281A] “Let us stay in the villages [Note: [Col. 1281D] ‘That is, let us proclaim your faith also to pagans who do not know you—not merely in passing, but let us stay there until we make them Catholics from pagans, your own from strangers.’ Same author.],” that is, let us dwell among the nations. For we were country folk and unlearned. We knew neither law nor judges nor judicial proceedings. But when God’s Son came into the world, he left the cities, he left Jerusalem. Hence he himself says: “Behold, I fled far away and remained in the wilderness” (Ps. 54:8). Now we have the law; now we speak in a civilised manner, because the universal king stays in the villages with law and judges.

“Let us rise early for the vineyards.”—“The night has passed, but the day has drawn near” (Rom. 13:12). Let teachers rise, because it is day; let them not sleep, because the night has passed. Rise, Paul, you who exhort others to watch: prune God’s vineyard, prepare and cleanse your plantation. For you planted, Apollo watered. [Col. 1281B] “Let us see whether the vine has flowered,” that is, whether it has now received faith and the teachings of the doctors. For this was what he watched for; these were the flowers desired by him upon whom lay concern for all the Churches. “Whether the flowers are bringing forth fruits.” Flowers bring forth fruits when good things come to fulfilment, or when we carry the good things we have begun through to their end. “Whether the pomegranates have flowered,” that is, whether martyrs still do not hesitate to die for Christ. Pomegranates bloom when the humble and poor shine with virtues and holiness. For the pomegranate tree is small and misshapen. “And there I shall give you my breasts.” Where? In the vineyards. I shall give you my breasts; I shall preserve my chastity for you; I shall nurse children to your praise and honour. Let Jews flee; let heretics also flee, [Col. 1281C] for they are not permitted even to touch these breasts. “The mandrakes gave forth a scent at our gates [Note: [Col. 1281D] ‘The mandrake is an aromatic herb whose root resembles a human body. Its fruits have an excellent scent, resembling a Marcian apple, which our people call the ‘apple of the earth.’ This herb is most suitable for medical uses. For it is said that those suffering from the troublesome effects of wakefulness are relieved by drinking this fruit and are able to sleep.’ Same author.],” that is, the apostles and teachers, because to some they were “the scent of death unto death,” to others “the scent of life unto life” (2 Cor. 2:16). These at our gates—that is, in the hearing of the faithful—gave forth their fragrance and their knowledge. But why are these called mandrakes? For mandrake counteracts barrenness. Above, concerning apostles and teachers, it was said that none among them is barren. Moreover, mandrake provides sleep to those who cannot sleep. These likewise grant all the repose of eternal life, and very often make those troubled by the cares of the world forget all earthly things. They give sleep and rest; they grant forgetfulness of the former life. [Col. 1281D] “All new and old fruits, my beloved, I have kept for you.” Old indeed, because they are patriarchs and prophets; new, because they are apostles and confessors. This may also be understood of old and new [Col. 1282A] sayings. The Church keeps fruits, then, and returns them to her beloved, though malicious spirits desire to steal them.

## CHAPTER VIII

“Who will grant that you may be my brother, sucking the breasts of my mother?” Who, she says, will grant me this—who will confer upon me this honour, this dignity, this blessedness—that you, the Son of the highest King, taking flesh, should become human and be called my brother, and should yourself say with your own mouth: “I will declare your name to my brothers” (Ps. 21:23)? Christ drew the breasts of his mother, the Synagogue, because he himself fulfilled the commands of the Law and the Prophets; or also because according to the flesh, as it is written, he “advanced in age and wisdom before God and men” (Luke 2:52) [Note: [Col. 1281D] “That is, that I may visibly see him made man. For God was, as it were, within, while he lay hidden in the bosom [Col. 1282D] of the Father’s majesty; but he was found outside when, made man, he showed himself visible to human beings and willed the incomprehensible to be comprehended.” Same author.].

[Col. 1282B] “And find you outside.” She says that she will find him outside: she will see you in a human being; you will proceed from the Father, come into the world, and be revealed to the nations. “And kiss you.” This is what is written at the beginning of this book: “Let him kiss me with the kiss of his mouth.” “Let no one despise me.” You, she says, loved me and took flesh for me: let no one despise me, since I am betrothed to so great a man [Note: [Col. 1282D] “For the Synagogue was, as it were, despised before Christ came, because, devoted to legal observances, she foretold Christ’s coming under type and figure, rather than in truth. But after Christ appeared and, by the grace of his coming, illumined the world, no one any longer despised the Church.
