Indeed, she was like an army drawn up in battle array to her enemies, because she preached Christ throughout the world and subjected the worldly empire to herself.” Same author.]. “I shall take hold of you and bring you into my mother’s house.” This is confirmed: “And into the chamber of my mother who bore me.” For she took hold of him because she clings to him in pious love. She brought him into her mother’s house—that is, into flesh, which was made from the earth, the universal mother. For love of the Church, our Lord Christ willed to become human. 631 “There you will teach me.” In this, [Col. 1282C] she says, in this house, in this tent, in this place of sleeping and death, you will teach me by what way and teaching I may be able to come to you. Christ’s humanity is rightly called a chamber, since he appeared to sleep there, though according to his divinity he can neither sleep nor die. “And I shall give you a cup of spiced wine.” For the first vineyard was turned into bitterness: when it ought to have given grapes, it produced wild grapes. But the Church gives wine well spiced, pleasing to God and pleasant to drink. Why spiced, except because the spiritual understanding is mingled with the letter? Paul gave spiced wine, for as someone delights in flavoured wine, so Christ delighted in his sound doctrine and sweet preaching. [Col. 1282D] He gave spiced wine when, among the perfect, he preached wisdom for God’s praise and honour. “And the new wine of my pomegranates.” No one doubts that new wine is [Col. 1283A] wine still fermenting, which does not cease to bubble until it is wholly clarified. But the pomegranates are the apostles and other martyrs. The new wine of these—their new song—delayed its fermenting until both the error of heretics and the unbelief of pagans ceased. Thus the Church gave new wine of pomegranates when Christ’s martyrs preached the New Testament and poured it forth with their own blood.

Verses:

Christ climbed the palm tree  
and grasped its fruits,  
because he was fixed to the cross,  
that the enemy might perish.  

Great glory to God!

[Col. 1283B] For new wine, like wine  
spiced with abundant honey,  
the Apostle drank  
and served to the nations.  

Great glory to God!

His bride said to him:  
“I speak to you, and you to me:  
Come, come, my beloved;  
be willing to dwell with country folk.”  

Great glory to God!

Let us go out to the vineyards;  
let us see whether they already bloom,  
whether the flowers have borne pomegranates  
and burst forth into fruits.  

Great glory to God!

[Col. 1283C] Your mandrakes, O Christ,  
give off a mighty scent.  
Your bride lifts up to you  
old and new fruits.  

Great glory to God!

Would that you were my brother;  
may one mother be ours!  
Your Father is immeasurable;  
no other is his equal.  

Great glory to God!

“His left hand is under my head, and his right hand will embrace me.” The voice of Christ: “I adjure you, daughters of Jerusalem, that you do not stir up or awaken my beloved until she herself wishes.” By the gazelles, [Col. 1283D] he says, and the stags—by the apostles and teachers, by virtues, faith, and good works, through which you run toward the promised prize and overcome the poisons of serpents. But since these matters have been explained above, they need no further exposition.

The Synagogue concerning the Church: “Who is this who comes up from the wilderness, [Col. 1284A] abounding in delights and leaning upon her beloved [Note: [Col. 1283D] ‘The voice of the Synagogue, marvelling at the Church gathered from the nations. Who is this, she says? That is, of what sort and what merit is she who comes up from the wilderness? For she had been abandoned by God because of idolatry and ignorance of the truth. Therefore she ascended by the steps of virtues from the wilderness—that is, from the error of unbelief, in which she had for a time been abandoned.’ Same author.]?” Who, she says, of what sort, how beautiful, how strong is this woman, who always ascends, always hastens to higher things, never descends, but seeks heavenly things by the steps of virtues? Yet whence does she come? “From the wilderness,” from a trackless and waterless land, once abandoned by God. But how does she come? “Abounding in delights,” rich in virtues, with lamps full. Who carries her? It follows: “Leaning upon her beloved,” joined to him and clinging to him, whom she loved with her whole mind and all her strength, and who promised to draw her after himself.

The bridegroom’s voice to the bride: “Under the apple tree I raised you up [Note: [Col. 1283D] ‘We must understand the apple tree as the Lord’s cross, under which tree the Synagogue was raised up, because she was redeemed through the cross from the transgression of original sin [Col. 1284D] and from the devil’s power. There she was raised up, she who had been dead in sins.’ Same author.].” You were dead, he says; you lay in sins. But I, taking flesh, raised you under the apple tree. Concerning this [Col. 1284B] apple it is said above: “As an apple tree among the trees of the forest, so is my beloved among the sons.” This tree, this flesh of our Saviour, overshadows those whom he raised up. This may also be understood of the cross, which, because of Christ’s blood, had the colour and appearance of this fruit. “There your mother was corrupted,” namely the Synagogue which crucified Christ the Lord, according to the saying: “They have become corrupt and abominable” (Ps. 13:1). “There your mother who bore you was violated,” because she abandoned her lawful bridegroom.

The Church says to Christ: “Set me as a seal upon your heart, as a seal upon your arm.” For Christ is both seal and key, the firm seal of the heart of the saints. The bodies of the saints cannot be broken, 632 nor [Col. 1284C] can their secrets be violated, guarded by so great and well-fortified a seal. We have made a sign; let friends remember. Christ gave us faith, the sign and pledge of love. Those bear this sign upon their arm who do everything they do in the Lord’s name. The seal is in the heart; the seal is in the hand, because the saints are always mindful of Christ both in thoughts and in works. Therefore let Christ be the sign and teacher of our heart, so that we may readily believe his sign and admonition. “For love is strong as death [Note: [Col. 1284D] ‘Christ’s love is strong as death. For as death separates the soul from the body, and thereafter it is permitted to desire nothing and to seek nothing in this present life, so Christ’s love, once it has truly seized someone, puts that person wholly to death to this world and renders him, as it were, insensible: living only to Christ and dead to the world.’ Same author.].”—“For perfect love casts out fear” (John 4:17). Love does not fear death; it is not overcome by love. Death is strong; love is strong. Christ’s disciples do not fear death, because their love is strong as death. [Col. 1284D] They fight with death and meet death. For they remember and have the seal that the Lord’s love was most firm upon them. For the Father “did not spare his own Son, but delivered him to death for us all” (Rom. 8:32). The Son says through the Prophet: “Zeal for your house has consumed me” [Col. 1285A] (Ps. 66:10).

Confirmation: “Jealousy is hard as hell.” Of this jealousy the Apostle says: “For I am jealous of you with God’s jealousy” (2 Cor. 11:2). Hell subdues everything; love overcomes everything. Love does not fear hell, nor its princes and inhabitants. This is metonymy. “Its lamps are lamps of fire and flames.” For hell always burns with unquenchable fire. Love is always kindled with unconquerable fire. Of this fire the Lord says: “I came to cast fire upon the earth” (Luke 12:49). This fire burns up vices and illumines hearts. “Many waters could not quench love.” Love is rightly compared to hell, since its fire, like that of hell, is unquenchable. “Nor shall rivers overwhelm it.” For, as the Apostle says [Col. 1285B] (Rom. 8:35), neither tribulation nor distress nor death nor life nor any persecution will be able to separate the saints from the love which is in Christ Jesus. “If a man gives all the substance of his house for love, he will regard it as almost nothing.” What, she says, should I say concerning love? With what praises shall I exalt it? It is greater than can be thought, greater than can be spoken. What price is there for love, which is compared to divine love? Do not despise love; do not say that it can be compared with riches. For if you give all that you possess, if you distribute all the substance of your house for love, and suppose that you have purchased love by these things, you despise love, which cannot be sold. You set a price upon that which has no price. For it surpasses every price. Riches flee, [Col. 1285C] friends remain; fortune deceives you, friends die for you. Therefore let us seek that friend who never dies, never abandons friends, never lies, and abounds in all things; who, praising friendship, says: “No one has greater love than this, that someone lay down his life for his friends” (John 15:13). Thus, by dying for us, he fulfilled this love.

Verses:

Who is this that comes,  
abounding in delights?  
She does not walk on her own feet,  
but is drawn by her husband.  

I was with you on the cross.  
[Col. 1285D] There I raised you up;  
but your mother fell  
and, like one violated, collapsed,  
because she fled from her support.  

Set me as a seal  
upon heart and arm.  

Love conquers all.  
Jealousy fears nothing  
when it has no action.  
Who is not quenched?  
Love does not die.  
This power is ineffable,  
[Col. 1286A] sublime, beyond telling,  
strong and unconquerable.  

If a man should give  
all that he possessed  
for this virtue, love is despised  
because it is appraised;  
for it is not sold for a price.

Christ to the Synagogue concerning the Church: “Our sister is little and has no breasts.” This sister means the Church of the nations [Note: [Col. 1285D] “The Church gathered from the nations was little in the days of the Lord himself and the apostles, both because it was small in the number of believers and because [Col. 1286D] it did not yet have breasts; that is, it was not yet able to beget spiritual children for God by preaching.” Same author.]. Therefore the apostles say, the Lord’s messengers say: “We are ambassadors; we seek a wife for our Lord. What then shall we give him? Our sister is small, newly born, foolish and unlearned. She has no breasts: she does not see the Testaments; she cannot yet bear children or nourish [Col. 1286B] them; she does not know a husband. Therefore she must be addressed and instructed concerning marriage. But ‘what shall we do for our sister on the day when she is to be addressed?’ By what words or promises shall we shape her mind?” It follows: “If she is a wall, let us build silver battlements upon it.” If, he says, we find in her a wall—steadfastness, faith, and strength—let us build upon it silver battlements and divine words. For the sayings of the prophets and the words of the teachers are battlements for the wall and for our faith, because by them we are defended, by them we overcome vices, by them we resist heretics. These [633] are called silver because no lead or bronze, no falsity whatever, is found in them. “If she is a door, let us fasten it with cedar boards,” [Col. 1286C] etc. Let us paint the door, he says, mark the gates, and adorn them in varied colours, so that God’s army and the multitude of virtues may find an entrance, recognise the sign, and delight in the ornaments of beauty. Or again, let us fasten and close them, so that, the gates being secured on every side, vices may not enter from any quarter. Let these be fortified by cedar boards—that is, imperishable prophetic examples and other sayings.

The Church speaks: “And my breasts are like a tower.” “I,” she says, “am a wall; I am strong and steadfast; I resist vices and defeat enemies. And my breasts are like a tower.” My breasts—that is, my doctrine and wisdom—are a tower. Doctrine is lofty; wisdom is great, well fortified and well armed, fearing neither the sophistries of heretics [Col. 1286D] nor those of philosophers. For these breasts nourish and defend children; hence they are called both tower and breasts. But from what time is such strength hers? It follows: “Since I became before him as one finding peace”; that is, since Christ loved me and reconciled me to the Father; since the angelic trumpet sang: “Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace to people of good will” (Luke 2:14).

The Synagogue says to the Church: “The peaceful one had a vineyard which has peoples.” Understand the Church by the vineyard, and Christ by “the peaceful one.” “For the vineyard of the Lord of hosts is the house of Israel” (Isa. 5:7).—“And he [Col. 1287A] is our peace, who made both one” (Eph. 2:14). This vineyard has peoples because it gathers Jews and Gentiles, Greeks and barbarians, and every nation into one. “He entrusted it to keepers,” that is, to apostles and teachers, that they might cultivate and prune it and guard it from thieves [Note: [Col. 1287B] “The keepers of this vineyard—that is, the Church—are the prophets, apostles, and successors of the apostles. [Col. 1287C] Or the keepers are the angelic powers, which defend the Church against the assaults of temptations and dragons.” Same author.]. “A man brings a thousand silver pieces for its fruit.” The number one thousand is used to signify the highest perfection and fullness. It is as though he said: the holy and Catholic man gives all that he possesses in order to enjoy the merit and blessedness of this vineyard.

Christ says: “My vineyard is before me.” My vineyard, he says—my inheritance or my Church—is before me and serves me; and although I handed it over to keepers, I am nevertheless always present, [Col. 1287B] protecting, preparing, and keeping it. “Your thousand, O peaceful one,” is understood: they are kept for you. Those whom he called silver above, he here calls peaceful ones. But why peaceful ones? Because they reconcile us to God, appease his enmity, wrath, and indignation, prepare peace for us, and bring us into peace. These are reserved for the Church and will be returned to her multiplied. “And two hundred to those who keep its fruits.” Two hundred of the thousand peaceful ones are reserved for apostles and teachers. For these, as kings and masters, are to receive a double honour, since they guard others and watch and die for others.

Christ says to the Church: “You who dwell in the gardens, friends listen.” You, Church, dwell in gardens; you delight in lilies; you lie among roses and violets. Everywhere are flowers, everywhere virtues, everywhere the sayings of teachers. You said, “Strengthen me with flowers”; your request has been fulfilled. [Col. 1288A] My friends—that is, angels and apostles—listen to you; they desire to hear what you believe, what hope you have, and toward what end you tend. “Make me hear your voice”: namely praise, jubilation, a song of praise and confession.

The Church’s voice to Christ: “Flee, my beloved; be like a gazelle and a young stag upon the mountains of spices.” Flee, she says; leave the earth and fly to the Father, so that those who think you merely human may believe you to be true God [Note: [Col. 1287C] “Flee, my beloved: that is, once the mystery of your Incarnation and Passion has been fulfilled, return to heaven, [Col. 1288B] so that I may begin to think of you no longer as a human being but as God above all things. Then you will hear [Col. 1288C] my voice, because then I shall preach more freely to the whole world. This is what the Lord says in the Gospel: ‘I tell you the truth: it is expedient for you that I go away’ (John 16:7).” Same author.]. [Col. 1288B] For my sake you came, entered my house, and have now kissed me; I am united and betrothed to you. Therefore return: draw me after you, make return, and bring me into your house. “Be like a gazelle”: seek the mountains, seek heaven, seek the things above; “and a young stag,” that you may dwell in shadow, in Selmon, and in refreshment; may you remain forever upon the mountains of spices, where the scent is most sweet, the place delightful, the radiance ineffable, and abundance beyond telling. There the saints exult; there the angels rejoice; there, with the Father and the Holy Spirit, praise, honour, and glory are sung to you forever. Amen.

Volume back matter

[Col. 1287C]
